Merz turned into ‘Ukrainian chancellor’ – Moscow
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has effectively become a “Ukrainian chancellor,” showering Kiev with more taxpayer-funded aid despite mounting discontent at home, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova has said.
Speaking at a press conference on Thursday, Zakharova criticized Merz’s visit to Kiev on Sunday, during which he pledged billions in additional assistance, including funding for long-range weapons production. The announcement came amid plunging support for his governing coalition and a series of electoral setbacks for his Christian Democratic Union (CDU).
Zakharova suggested that Merz was so eager to escape his domestic troubles that he “practically fled from the festivities in Bremen” marking the 36th anniversary of German reunification.
“The new face in Ukrainian politics, [or] a ‘Ukrainian chancellor’ as Merz has been dubbed in German political circles, didn’t come empty-handed – he announced yet another generous gift to his ‘friend’, Zelensky,” she said sarcastically.
German taxpayers will foot the bill, Zakharova argued, suggesting that Merz was deliberately adding to their burden despite growing public dissatisfaction with his policies.
She also questioned whether the chancellor could genuinely be unaware of Ukraine’s rampant corruption, pointing to a series of high-profile scandals involving Vladimir Zelensky’s inner circle and senior officials.
Zakharova cited a September survey by the Kiev International Institute of Sociology (KIIS), in which 50% of respondents identified corruption as the country’s most pressing problem. Some 72% said graft had worsened since the escalation of the conflict with Russia in 2022, while the same proportion blamed Zelensky and his associates.
Given what she described as Kiev’s efforts to suppress dissent, Zakharova argued that the findings were particularly revealing.
“Ukraine is so mired in corruption that it has become impossible to cover up its real scale by any means,” she said.
Merz has faced similar criticism from German opposition politicians. In July, Alternative for Germany (AfD) lawmaker Markus Frohnmaier told RT’s Rick Sanchez that Merz “is the chancellor of Ukraine and not the chancellor of Germany.”
Veteran left-wing politician Sahra Wagenknecht, founder of the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), has likewise accused Merz of turning “his own citizens into cash cows for Ukraine.”
Meanwhile, an INSA poll published earlier this month put support for Merz’s CDU/CSU alliance at a record low of 18%, compared with 30% for the AfD, which remains Germany’s most popular party.
The chancellor’s Christian Democrats also suffered successive electoral defeats last month in the eastern states of Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. The CDU finished a distant second in Saxony-Anhalt with 17.5% of the vote and failed to clear the electoral threshold in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, securing just 4.9%.
Despite the setbacks, Merz, who has previously criticized Germans for not working enough hours, has refused to change course.

Three years after Oct. 7, IDF begins long-delayed process to honor battlefield heroism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
20:11:18 UTC
05:11:18 KST

Three years after the outbreak of the war, the IDF is launching a formal process to review and award military commendations and decorations to officers and soldiers for acts of heroism during the defensive battles in Gaza border communities on October 7, 2023, and in the days that followed.
The IDF Casualties Directorate began notifying bereaved families on Thursday that the process was being launched, explaining its goals and significance.
The move is highly sensitive both inside and outside the military. Several attempts were made over the past two years to begin the process, but none advanced. Exactly one year ago, IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir announced the establishment of a committee to examine military commendations, but that initiative also remained stalled until now.
A commanders’ conference will be held next Wednesday to formally launch the review process. It will be led by Manpower Directorate chief Maj. Gen. Dado Bar Kalifa and Maj. Gen. Orly Markman, president of the Military Court of Appeals, with commanders from IDF brigades and sectors across the military expected to participate. The conference will present the framework for examining acts of bravery and sacrifice carried out by IDF personnel during the fighting on the day of the massacre.
“The purpose of the process is to provide appropriate recognition for extraordinary acts of heroism carried out during the battles, thereby preserving and passing on the legacy of battlefield courage to future generations,” the IDF said.
The military added that the process would be conducted “meticulously, with close examination of the details and accuracy of the facts, and with sensitivity and transparency.”
The IDF also will address acts of heroism by civilians during the October 7 battles. Cases involving exceptional civilian bravery that are deemed appropriate will be referred to the advisory committee to the president, under the existing mechanism for awarding the President’s Civilian Bravery Award.
“Additional appropriate cases referred to the President’s Residence will also be examined by the committee, as were the cases brought before it until now,” the IDF said.
The launch follows months of public criticism over the prolonged delay in formally recognizing soldiers who fought in the battles to halt the Hamas assault.
In July last year, ynet reported that the military planned to establish a committee to examine thousands of recommendations that had accumulated from units in the field, but the process was delayed.
The IDF repeatedly said it could not move forward until its in-depth operational investigations into the October 7 battles had been completed. The process also was delayed by the ground campaign in Lebanon and the fighting against Iran. With those investigations now gradually reaching completion, the military says the awards committee can finally begin its work.
Throughout the war, some officials also voiced concern over possible political interference in decisions determining who would receive military commendations and decorations.
The precise timetable for presenting the final candidates and awarding the honors remains unclear. The IDF says the committee’s work will be thorough and is not expected to be completed quickly.

Seyma Erkul Dayanc
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
The Arctic Circle Assembly opened Thursday in Iceland's capital, Reykjavik, bringing together government officials, Indigenous representatives, scientists, business leaders and civil society groups from more than 70 countries.
The annual gathering, held Oct. 8-10 at the Harpa Concert Hall and Conference Centre, is expected to draw up to 2,500 participants and about 700 speakers across more than 200 sessions, according to organizers.
“The Assembly is not created by me or the Secretariat. It is created fundamentally by you,” Arctic Circle founder and chairman and former Icelandic President Olafur Ragnar Grimsson said in his opening remarks.
Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand also addressed the opening, saying the Arctic should be viewed as a homeland for the people who live there.
“The Arctic is not simply a strategic frontier, it is a homeland, and its future must begin always, including our conversations at the Arctic Circle Assembly, with the people who live there,” she said.
Greenland's Foreign Minister Mute B. Egede delivered an opening plenary address titled “Nothing about Greenland without Greenland.”
The program includes discussions on Arctic geopolitics and security, including the roles of the US, Greenland, Canada, China and the EU, as well as climate change, science, Indigenous peoples and business.
NATO Military Committee Chairman Adm. Giuseppe Cavo Dragone and Canadian Chief of the Defense Staff Gen. Jennie Carignan are scheduled to take part in a session on NATO and the Arctic.
The Arctic Council's 30th anniversary will also be marked during the assembly, with Anand, Egede and Saami Council President Per-Olof Nutti among the participants.

Syria reopens Aleppo's Great Umayyad Mosque after 13-year closure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
20:07:14 UTC
05:07:14 KST

Abdulsalam Fayez and Sahin Demir
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
Syria reopened the historic Great Umayyad Mosque in the northern city of Aleppo on Thursday, 13 years after it was taken out of service following extensive damage during the country's civil war.
Aleppo Governor Azzam al-Gharib attended the reopening ceremony, according to state-run Alikhbariah TV.
“Today, we are honored to reopen one of the houses of God, restoring Aleppo's great mosque after difficult years in which it was subjected to destruction,” al-Gharib said.
He said the mosque, dating to the Umayyad era, had for centuries served as a center of learning and religious life in the historic city.
The governor also recalled the mosque's role during the Syrian uprising that began in March 2011, saying demonstrations against the former regime had emerged from the site.
The mosque and its surroundings witnessed intense fighting between former regime forces and opposition factions from 2012 to 2016, repeatedly changing hands.
It was taken out of service in 2013 after suffering extensive damage, including to its dome, arcades and historic minaret, during fighting and bombardment.
Following the fall of the Bashar Assad regime on Dec. 8, 2024, Aleppo's Endowments Directorate began restoration work aimed at preserving the mosque's architectural and historical character.
The Great Umayyad Mosque, also known as the Great Mosque of Aleppo, is one of Syria's oldest and most significant mosques.
Its construction dates to the Umayyad period in the early eighth century, with most historical accounts attributing its establishment to Caliph Sulayman ibn Abd al-Malik.

In early October, Russian forces also began striking some of Kyiv’s most important transport links — the bridges across the Dnipro River, which had not previously come under attack. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russian President Vladimir Putin ordered Russian military commanders to disregard the rules of warfare when carrying out airstrikes on Ukraine.

US imposes fresh sanctions on Iran's shadow fleet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
20:06:26 UTC
05:06:26 KST

Breadcrumb
US imposes fresh sanctions on Iran's shadow fleet
The US imposed fresh sanctions on Iran on Thursday, targeting individuals, networks and 17 vessels for transporting Iranian crude, oil products and petrochemicals, the Treasury Department said, as Washington stepped up economic pressure on Tehran.
The sanctions are part of the department's "Operation Economic Outcast," which aims to cut Iran's funding for the war with the US, missile construction, cyberattacks and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, or IRGC.
"Today's action represents the most significant blow yet to Iran's remaining illicit maritime infrastructure by neutralizing the vast majority of the shadow fleet," a Treasury official told reporters on a call. "Treasury is cutting off the regime's last major source of illicit revenue and strengthening international pressure to hold Tehran accountable."
The move tightens the squeeze on Iranian oil sales after the US reimposed its blockade of Iranian ports on 14 July following the breakdown of a memorandum of understanding between Tehran and Washington to end the war.
Iran has only about 20 million barrels of crude oil left on vessels outside the blockade, off Singapore, Malaysia and China, the Treasury official said. The world uses about 100 million barrels of oil per day.
A second Treasury official said Iran has stopped loading and offloading crude oil vessels due to the blockade and sanctions.
President Donald Trump said on social media on Thursday that the US is having "productive discussions" with Iran over the war that began on February 28. Trump said the US will not attack Iran before the midterm elections on November 3.
An analyst said the fact that the US is sanctioning vessels after Iran has delivered virtually all of its oil at sea means the impact will be muted.
"This is economic warfare conducted in the rearview mirror, designed to generate headlines rather than results," said Brett Erickson, a managing principal at Obsidian Risk Advisors.
Vessels targeted by the US sanctions include the Comoros-flagged Paritosh, the Panama-flagged Bitu and the Bahamas-flagged Gas Lucky.
(Reuters)

Tugging this thread could reveal how an independent secret investigation conducted by an influential and well-connected Ukrainian fascist CIA agent leading away from Bandera having been murdered, and to difficulties in his marriage, due to spending “much time in the company of other women.”
The CIA’s secret investigation
Michael Korzhan was a Ukrainian fascist, Orthodox priest, and CIA spy. Known under the cryptonym “AEDOGMA,” from 1947 he monitored Ukrainian ultranationalists, Soviet emigres and associated groups throughout Europe, including Paris. Korzhan also kept a close eye on the continent for the CIA, not only as a “spotter” for potential agents who could be inserted into or recruited in the Soviet Union, but potential KGB infiltration of Orthodox churches. A declassified January 1960 CIA file records how Korzhan was sent to Munich after Bandera’s death and spent several months investigating what happened. AEDOGMA was able to retrace many sensitive particulars of Bandera’s life that never surfaced publicly.
Korzhan “became convinced, as the result of his investigations, that Bandera committed suicide.” Him being tasked with investigating Bandera’s death reflects the value the CIA attached to AEDOGMA. After World War II, Bandera became a prize asset of the CIA and MI6 for many years. While the CIA eventually turned on the godfather of Ukrainian ultranationalism, the CIA considered it very important he was not martyred by the KGB for his post-war anti-Communist activities in Ukraine and the Soviet Union. The CIA was working on getting Bandera a US visa at the time he died. Understanding the facts of what happened was of huge importance for the CIA, and Korzhan was the agent for the job.
“AEDOGMA has unusual skills in interpersonal relationships. His particular social talents are best expressed when he is able to operate independently in a relatively unstructured, “wheeling and dealing” environment… He can usually achieve the operational objective on his own… AEDOGMA starts any task with only the loosest initial plan for attack. From then on he feels his way, ‘following his nose’, while making sensitive adaptations to his strategy as the situation changes. Working in this fashion he enjoys his operational tasks immensely and becomes totally involved. He is deft at provoking others to reveal their hand while tipping off very little of his own.”
So said a declassified April 1960 CIA memo. Korzhan demonstrated his superhuman spying skills at the end of the previous year by interviewing “about 100 Banderites and other Ukrainian emigres” about Bandera’s death. He conducted significant on-the-ground research, identifying five separate “versions” of what happened to Bandera. They ranged from the Nazi-composed Gehlen Organization that the CIA built in Germany after World War II taking Bandera’s life, to suicide. Having chased every lead attempting to prove or disprove each “version”, AEDOGMA concluded that suicide was overwhelmingly the most likely. En route to reaching this explosive conclusion, never reported anywhere before, Korzhan disproved the accepted story that the KGB was responsible.
The assassination story under scrutiny
KGB defector Bohdan Stashynsky took responsibility for killing Bandera, on November 17 1961. He served four years in prison, before being released to start a new life in Germany. This telling of events has not been challenged at any time since. The ‘fact’ of the KGB’s responsibility is completely unquestioned in Ukrainian, and Western, accounts of what happened to Bandera. Korzhan identified a number of factors ruling homicide out entirely. He recorded that the alleged murder weapon potassium cyanide was not a substance the KGB had previously used during its entire post-war war on political opponents, and it would represent “the first time they have used this means” if the KGB was responsible.
Korzhan also believed it was highly illogical “in view of the present political situation” for the “Communists to do away with Bandera at this time.” He wondered, “wouldn’t the KGB have considered the fact that the death of Bandera would instigate the Ukrainian emigres to mobilize their fight against the Communists in the whole world?” He spoke to many knowledgeable sources who pointed directly to people and factors in Bandera’s private life that were much more likely culprits. Korzhan shared his findings with West German detective Adrian Fuchs, who also concluded Bandera’s death was a suicide. Both men understood also that powerful ultranationalist figures around Bandera had a huge interest in blaming the KGB.
Behind Bandera’s closed doors
Fuchs and his investigators spoke to at least 50 people about Bandera’s death, including people who knew him intimately, and many were unanimous in blaming his marital situation. Bandera’s life “was unpleasant,” due to how his wife, Yaroslava Bandera, treated him. She made his life a living hell because of his “association with other women,” so he killed himself. Particularly, Bandera plotted to take his own life “in such a way that suicide would never be suspected but that, on the contrary, would lead to various interpretations and suspicions that he was liquidated by the communists, thus permitting him to remain a hero.” Korzhan tracked how Bandera had been avoiding his bodyguards in preparation in the weeks before he died.
“It is a fact that Bandera had a violent quarrel with his wife that very morning. He threatened suicide and left home to go to the office before 8 a.m. Bandera employed the use of potassium cyanide which he always carried on his person and which, after his death, could not be found either on his person or in his home. Considering the above, I concluded that it was suicide by use of potassium cyanide. Motive: His unbearable marital situation.”
Korzhan had uncovered many facts supporting this “version.” He learned Bandera’s “home life had lately become so unbearable that his only escape could have been suicide.” The biggest issue was that Bandera’s wife “as a result from some very difficult experience in her life, and the fear of constant surveillance… had practically lost all of her senses.” Were she not Bandera’s wife, “she would have been in an insane asylum a year ago.” Korzhan learned about “Bandera’s unsatisfactory sex life, his seeking such diversions outside his base” – a euphemism for having many affairs – “and the resultant uncontrollable jealousy of his wife which led to fights between them.”
AEDOGMA heard story after story of Bandera trying to spend time away from his wife to have affairs with other women, and his wife viewing “everyone as a threat to herself.” Female friends were forbidden from visiting, even when accompanied by their husbands. Male friends were also barred because Bandera “would use the excuse of driving them home as an opportunity to get out for some fun.” Over the two years before he died, Bandera “lived through such hell that it was difficult for anyone to imagine.” He was phoned dozens of times whenever away from the house by his wife to check his whereabouts, and she made “all sorts of accusations against him even in front of the children.”
“During these quarrels he always threatened suicide. His wife would reply, ‘the quicker you do, the better it be for all of us,’ and then she usually added “but you are too much of a coward to commit suicide. Bandera, who considered himself a hero and an individual who enjoyed the respect of the organised masses and to whom he was a ‘god’, had to bear the slander and accusations made by his wife who saw him only as a human being, her husband and the father of her children. This was more than he could stand. The people who were acquainted with this situation felt that these tortures (for which be often was personally to biome) were so horrible that any normal individual would have committed suicide long ago.”
Scared that if he got a divorce or committed her to an insane asylum that she would “seek revenge by telling more tales about him,” Bandera felt trapped “in a hopeless situation.” He suffered severe headaches and heart issues, including rheumatism. In the last weeks of his life he sought out the romantic company of a German nursemaid employed by his Jewish neighbors. “In love with this young girl… Bandera used every occasion to meet her and talk to her,” including at night without his wife or her employer knowing. Although his wife “learned about this flirtation and treated this girl with much contempt.”
What the witnesses were told to hide
Bandera’s early morning argument with his wife on October 15, 1959 was, according to sources close to the couple, motivated by his continuing relations with the housemaid. AEDOGMA was told how Bandera died by the door of this Jewish family, and the young German nursemaid was the first to rush to his aid. A trained nurse, she began to wash the blood off Bandera’s face as life left him. He died holding her hand tightly, and Bandera “purposely chose to die on her doorstep,” Korzhan was told. Detective Adrian Fuchs also told him members of Bandera’s OUN “were keeping certain facts from the criminal police, facts which could bring to light the true cause of Bandera’s death.”
“Suicide was undoubtedly involved, and that for obvious political reasons, the Banderites didn’t want this fact to become known. The German Police have facts which indicate that the Banderites forbade certain individuals to reveal any facts of Bandera’s case. The police questioned this, and they came to the conclusion that statements made by these people tended to bring to light the facts in this case… Bandera’s wife was very talkative at first and revealed certain facts (as for instance, the fact that Bandera always carried cyanide on his person). She later stated that she could not verify this fact. It was evident that the OUN had forbidden her to talk.”

Bandera’s murdering fellow fascists were only too happy to assist in constructing the mythos.

US suspends Microsoft, Adobe from filing for green cards
October 8, 2026
The Trump administration on Thursday said it was suspending major tech firms, including Microsoft, from applying for a program that allowed their foreign workers to work permanently in the US.
US Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling accused those tech firms of abusing the program — the Permanent Labor Certification Program (PERM) — that had so far been a legal pathway for workers to apply for green cards.
"I am hereby suspending from the Permanent Labor Certification Program some of the largest IT outsourcing firms in the world, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini," US Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said.
Sonderling said the suspensions were due to ongoing federal investigations into those firms.
There are good reasons that Indian media firms covered the issue so urgently because many of those firms are either Indian or rely on thousands of Indian professionals who've moved to the country.
Trump administration accuses Microsoft of abusing program for green cards
Vice President JD Vance said the PERM system required companies to advertise work in the US before they applied for green cards for foreign workers due to a lack of qualified American job applicants.
"They'll put an advertisement in a small-town newspaper. They'll go out there and say that 'We have advertised for a position with our company, and nobody is responding to it.' And they will use that lack of response to then go and replace American workers with what is effectively foreign indentured servants," Vance claimed.
"There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has used this system more than Microsoft," Vance said.
The announcement came hours before US President Donald Trump was scheduled to award the National Medal of Technology and Innovation to Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella.
Microsoft says majority of its workers are Americans
Microsoft said in a statement that it looked forward to providing the administration with additional information, saying the majority of its workers are Americans and that a large part of the H-1B filings have to do with the status of people already based in the US.
"We pay our employees some of the highest compensation in the tech sector, and our wages are among the highest of all H-1B filings," the company said.
The H-1B visa program is another part of the Trump administration's crackdown on immigration, as concerns have long persisted that the visa for skilled workers has displaced Americans in favor of lower-cost foreign labor.
Microsoft employs 125,000 US workers and 103,000 international workers, according to the company's 2025 annual report.

The tourists will wait to see how dry the pitch is on Friday before announcing their side at the toss, with Connolly and Nic Maddinson in contention to come in for Green.
Connolly has not played a Test since his debut against Sri Lanka last February, while Maddinson's last appearance came way back in December 2016.
One potential option would be for that to come at the expense of Beau Webster, who batted at number seven in the recent Test series against Bangladesh.
The South Africans has already confirmed they will play two spinners in Keshav Maharaj and Simon Harmer, in a clear sign of how they believe the wicket will play.
"Everyone brings something a little bit different to it, and it's just trying to work out what we think the best combo is," Australia captain Pat Cummins said.
Green is a chance to return for Australia in the second Test, while Inglis is recovering well and is expected to fly back to South Africa before the series ends.
Australia is also confident Marnus Labuschagne has shown signs he can return to form at number three, after a century in a warm-up game last weekend.
The 32-year-old has not reached three figures in any of his past 39 completed Test innings, and was briefly dropped for last year's tour of West Indies before fighting back.
"He doesn't need to go searching for something that he doesn't already have," Cummins said.
"I think it's him finding his way back to when he was at his best, and we've seen that in the last six months.
"I know a lot of it hasn't translated into Test runs, but we love what he's bringing, we love his approach.
"He's hitting the ball beautifully in the nets, I know it doesn't guarantee success out in the field, but we think he's really well placed."
Australia has spoken about the need to potentially play this Test at a different tempo to many recent ones, which have been dubbed as "fast-forward cricket".
"We've got to get a little bit better, and we can get a bit better at, getting to the grind," Cummins said.
"It might not be the glamorous stuff, but it's that grinding out a session, going for two runs an over, not these major falls or not these whirlwind innings at the time.
"We haven't played too many of those Test matches in the last few years, particularly in Australia, they've been quite fast-paced.
"A lot of our success has come off these big moments, with a Travis Head hundred or Starcy [Mitchell Starc] running through the top order."
AAP

Autism and ADHD traits appear to follow different social paths to mental health problems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
20:00:09 UTC
05:00:09 KST

Children who show traits of autism and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder often face elevated risks of emotional and behavioral problems as they grow up, but the social pathways connecting these traits to mental health are complex. A long-term study published in Psychological Medicine suggests that difficulties with classmates, schoolwork, and family members do not simply follow neurodevelopmental traits in a straight line. Instead, day-to-day social struggles and mental health challenges appear to be linked in both directions over time, which may create self-reinforcing cycles as students develop.
Autism spectrum disorder, commonly known as ASD, involves differences in social communication, social interaction, and patterns of behavior or interests. Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, or ADHD, is characterized by ongoing patterns of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity. Both conditions exist on a continuum, meaning that many children display noticeable traits without having an official clinical diagnosis. Even when these traits fall below diagnostic thresholds, children are at elevated risk of emotional distress, including internalizing problems like anxiety and depression, or externalizing problems like anger and disruptive behavior.
Earlier research suggested that everyday hardships may help explain these links. For instance, a 2018 longitudinal study tracking youth from childhood to age 18 found that elevated autistic traits increased the risk of developing depressive symptoms, an association partly explained by social hardships such as bullying. In a similar vein, a 2020 study of adolescents indicated that childhood ADHD symptoms predicted teenage depression in part through academic setbacks and peer problems.
Strained relationships with parents and peers also helped account for the link between attention difficulties and later depression in a 2013 study of two samples of young people, although academic struggles did not independently explain that link in that research.
Because autistic and ADHD traits frequently co-occur in the same individuals, researchers faced a challenge in untangling which specific social hurdles stem uniquely from each set of characteristics. Many previous studies examined either autism or ADHD in isolation, making it difficult to understand how distinct traits relate to social adjustment across different settings.
“In school settings, many children show mild ASD or ADHD traits that do not meet diagnostic criteria, yet they may still experience difficulties with peers, learning, or relationships with adults,” lead author Eriko Hashimoto, a doctoral student in the Graduate School of Humanities and Sciences at Ochanomizu University in Tokyo, told PsyPost. “These children may fall outside formal support systems.”
“However, we still know relatively little about how such traits relate to social adjustment and mental health over time,” Hashimoto explained. “Together with my supervisor and co-author, Professor Hiroyuki Ito, I wanted to address this gap by examining these developmental associations over several years in a large, community-based sample of school-aged children.”
To investigate these questions, Hashimoto, Professor Hiroyuki Ito of the Faculty of Core Research at Ochanomizu University, and their colleagues analyzed data from a large population-based cohort involving all public elementary and junior high schools in a medium-sized municipality in Chubu, Japan. The final analysis included 9,619 students from an initial group of 11,549 enrolled children. Students were surveyed once per school year from fourth through ninth grade, with data from 11 grade cohorts collected between 2012 and 2023. By gathering information from students, their parents, and their homeroom teachers, the authors were able to capture behavioral and emotional patterns across both home and classroom environments.
Parents reported on their children’s autistic tendencies using a shortened version of the Autism Spectrum Screening Questionnaire and assessed ADHD traits using the ADHD Rating Scale-IV. Students completed questionnaires detailing their subjective difficulties in three areas: keeping up with classwork, conflicts with teachers, and arguments with family members. Problems with classmates were evaluated using the peer relationships subscale of the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire, combining ratings from students, teachers, and parents into a single composite score.
Mental health outcomes were grouped into two broad categories. Internalizing problems, reflecting inward emotional distress such as anxiety and depression, combined child self-reports on a depression scale with parent and teacher ratings of emotional symptoms. Externalizing problems, capturing outward behavioral difficulties such as hostility and aggression, brought together student self-reports with adult ratings of conduct problems. The researchers used cross-lagged structural equation modeling, an advanced statistical technique that tests whether one variable predicts changes in another variable over time while controlling for student sex and grade level.
The analysis produced standardized coefficients, which express how strongly one measure predicted later changes in another. By the guidelines the authors used for this kind of analysis, values around 0.03 count as small, 0.07 as medium, and 0.12 as large.
The findings indicated distinct developmental patterns for autistic and ADHD traits. Autistic traits showed consistent links over time with subsequent peer difficulties, showing standardized coefficients between 0.146 and 0.190 across grade transitions, which fall in the large range. Autistic traits were also linked with later internalizing problems, with small-to-medium coefficients ranging from 0.068 to 0.097. In contrast, autistic traits were not consistently associated with later academic struggles or conflict with teachers.
ADHD traits showed a different pattern of associations. Elevated ADHD traits were linked to subsequent externalizing problems, with coefficients between 0.064 and 0.118, with the strongest associations appearing during late elementary school. ADHD traits were also associated with higher levels of academic difficulties over time, particularly in fourth and fifth grade, but showed weak and mostly inconsistent links to later internalizing problems directly. Instead, academic difficulties themselves predicted later internalizing symptoms during elementary school, suggesting that learning struggles may act as an intermediate pathway linking attention difficulties to emotional distress.
Rather than revealing one-way effects, the analyses indicated notable bidirectional processes. For instance, while peer problems predicted increases in subsequent internalizing symptoms, higher levels of internalizing symptoms were also associated with worsening peer problems over time. Similarly, externalizing behaviors predicted more frequent conflicts with teachers and parents in later years, and those strained adult relationships were linked with subsequent increases in behavioral difficulties. Academic problems consistently predicted greater family conflict in the following year, with coefficients ranging from 0.105 to 0.163.
The social environment also appeared to feed back into parent ratings of neurodevelopmental traits. Experiencing peer problems was linked to higher reported autistic traits in later grades, with coefficients up to 0.164. In an analogous manner, elevated externalizing behaviors predicted higher reported ADHD traits in subsequent waves. These patterns suggest that neurodevelopmental traits may not be fixed and could shift with a child’s social experiences, though they could also reflect changes in how parents perceive and rate their children’s traits once problems emerge.
“One important message is that ASD and ADHD traits showed different patterns of association with later difficulties,” Hashimoto said. “These findings highlight the importance of considering not only children’s individual characteristics but also the social environments in which they develop.”
These findings align with prior research into how childhood difficulties unfold over time. The results are consistent with a study covered by PsyPost in 2026, which found that childhood ADHD traits were linked to greater psychological distress in midlife, partly through experiences of social exclusion in adulthood, though that research followed individuals into adulthood while the current study tracked youth through junior high school.
The observed connections also touch upon research covered by PsyPost in 2025 linking ADHD symptoms to emotional problems across development, though that earlier project pointed to shared genetic factors, based on twin data, as an underlying driver rather than school-based social pathways.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. “This study does not demonstrate causality,” Hashimoto noted. “The findings show temporal associations, not proof that one factor directly causes another.”
“It is also important to emphasize that children with elevated ASD or ADHD traits are highly diverse; our results describe group-level patterns and should not be interpreted as predictions for any individual child,” she pointed out. “In addition, we examined ASD and ADHD traits dimensionally in a general school population rather than focusing specifically on children with clinical diagnoses.”
There are a few other things to keep in mind. Many of the associations, including most links between the traits and later mental health problems, were small to medium in size. Also, the questionnaire used to evaluate autism primarily captured a relatively narrow set of characteristics, focusing mainly on Asperger-type social and behavioral traits rather than the full spectrum.
Future research could build on these findings by incorporating direct observational measures alongside questionnaires and testing whether supportive social settings can buffer these links. The authors suggest that early support for academic organization, peer relationship skills, and positive communication between families and schools might help interrupt these cycles, though the study did not test any interventions.
The study, “Longitudinal associations among autism and ADHD traits, social maladjustment, and mental health in school-aged children,” was authored by Eriko Hashimoto, Hiroyuki Ito, Megumi Hamada, Takahiro Nakajima, Nobuya Takayanagi, Mitsunori Myogan, Yasuo Murayama, and Masatsugu Tsujii.

Israeli settlers take Palestinian olives, and their harvest traditions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
19:57:29 UTC
04:57:29 KST

Israeli settlers take Palestinian olives, and their harvest traditions
As Israeli settlers harvest olives on Palestinian land, farmers face growing violence and the loss of a tradition passed down through generations.
Ramallah, occupied West Bank – The video shared in Israeli settler groups shows two men bashing an olive tree with long wooden sticks. Smiling and congratulating one another, they try to knock the olives to the ground. They call the result “Pure Olive Oil”.
But as Palestinian activist Bashar Qaryouti explained, the two men don’t own the land, the trees, or the olives.
They’re Israeli settlers who set up an illegal settlement outpost on private property in the village of Qaryut, in the northern occupied West Bank, and made their way into this olive grove, some 200 metres (656 feet) away from Palestinian homes.
“No one has come near here for about three years, thank God,” one of the two men in the video says in Hebrew.
Local Palestinians know the man by name, and he does little to hide. The man is Avichai Suissa, an Israeli settler sanctioned by the European Union, United Kingdom – and previously by the United States – who runs a farm on the outpost. It was established more than a year and a half ago, and videos like this help Suissa raise donations for it.
On his campaign page, he says the goal is to rebuild and expand the farm, which was once dismantled by the Israeli army, to prevent it from falling “into enemy hands”.
“We’re gradually starting to work our way into the area,” Suissa said in the video.
But the land belongs to Palestinians – residents of Qaryut – who have not been able to reach it since the genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023. “A few months ago, farmers tried to plough their land, but the army stopped them,” Qaryouti said.
Worst year yet
“After we complained, the army declared the area a closed military zone a few days ago, so settlers are going to other lands, to other olives to steal,” Qaryouti explained.
Suissa and others are part of a growing movement of settlers who have intensified their campaign against the olive harvest. The campaign, part of a settler pogrom against Palestinians in the West Bank, has turned the olive harvest season in October into a source of fear and danger.
Many Palestinians in the occupied West Bank describe this year as the worst yet in terms of settler attacks, and the season has barely started.
On Wednesday, armed Israeli settlers on tractors raided lands between the villages of Ramin and Burqa, in the northern occupied West Bank. They opened fire on farmers heading to their trees.
Ali Bazzari, a 44-year-old farmer, was killed. His only “crime”, the family says, was trying to pick his olives.
Witnesses say the Israeli army prevented ambulances from reaching the wounded. Palestinians had to carry the injured through the mountains to hospitals.
The Israeli Rights Group Yesh Din says it documented 109 incidents of violence directly related to the harvest in 75 Palestinian communities between September 27 and October 6, an average of 11 per day.
Longtime tradition
Israeli settlers are increasingly attempting to adopt the rituals of the olive harvest season, while pushing out the Palestinians who have kept those traditions for generations.
Several new farms have been set up in the occupied West Bank. One shares videos of olives being pressed. Others invite Israelis to “join in” the experience.
Palestinians say the videos circulating show a disregard for the actual owners of the land taken by the settlers, and a clear attempt to appropriate the season, imitating its rituals and claiming them as their own.
Those rituals – things like collective picking, singing, and shared meals on the farms – are rooted in a deep connection to the land.
The olive harvest season may be an exhausting time of the year for Palestinians, with its hard work and long hours in the sun, but it’s a rewarding one. Olive farmers traditionally gather for family get-togethers, with neighbours and friends volunteering to help one another harvest the olives, in a cultural tradition known as “ouneh”.
The season has a light-hearted element, with debates about whose land produces the best oil, who should charge the most, and who knows how to pick the most olives and not drop any to the ground.
Older generations pass down lessons from history, such as the best time to harvest and how to nurture the trees – an inherited knowledge of climate, agriculture and the land itself.
“They planted so that we can eat. We plant so they [will] eat,” a well-known Arabic saying goes. It highlights the continuity of this inheritance, and the responsibility towards future generations.
Last harvest?
These trees, which are meant to be protected, nurtured and passed on, are being taken away – not only by settlers, but by soldiers, too.
Hazem Sanaf, 61, stood on a nearby hill in the village of Beit Rima and watched as Israeli bulldozers ploughed through his lands in late September, after he had received an Israeli military order. The bulldozers destroyed and uprooted more than 400 trees belonging to Hazem and his neighbour, some of them decades old, and his only source of income.
“They just want to take our olive trees from us,” he said, his eyes reflecting his pain.
Hazem is not alone. Several Israeli military orders to uproot olive trees have been handed out across the occupied West Bank. Some have been carried out, while others await their turn.
In the past, the Israeli military has cited the need to clear land of trees to prevent security threats or ambushes on troops. But Palestinians say it reflects a pattern of dispossession and impoverishment.
According to the Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission (CRRC), Israeli settlers and soldiers have destroyed approximately 50,000 trees this year alone.
Fuad Daraghmeh, from the village of al-Lubban Asharqiya, near Ramallah, carried the thick, broken stem of a tree.
“I took care of it for 30 years,” he said, and headed home. He did not say what he planned to do with the stem, but others said that their trees had been uprooted before, and that they had managed to nourish them back to life.
Others are resigned to saying goodbye to the trees. They sit by the bulldozed trees with small hand tools, picking the last fruit of what they believe is their last crop.
Palestinians have been watching videos of settlers harvesting their olive trees, including the one shared by Suissa.
Beyond the pain, one remark keeps coming up: the method used by Suissa in vigorously beating the tree is no way to treat it, and no way to harvest olives.
“The people who have tended to their lands for decades know that,” one Palestinian activist, who did not wish to be identified for security reasons, said.

This top Israeli scientist is developing a patch that detects disease before symptoms appear
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
19:56:14 UTC
04:56:14 KST

Prof. Hossam Haick of the Technion, one of Israel's most successful scientists, is really a frustrated karate fighter. As a boy in Nazareth, he joined a karate class and seemed to have found his calling. "I was incredibly competitive," he says. "I went from one achievement to the next." But in 10th grade, with a black belt around his waist, he reluctantly decided to quit and concentrate on his studies. "I regret it to this day," he says, entirely seriously. "I could have had a great career in karate."
Haick, 51, a professor of chemical engineering and nanotechnology, remains a fighter at heart. In the laboratory, too, he gives everything he has, sometimes to excess, to achieve his goals. Giving up on an idea is simply not an option. During our nearly four-hour conversation, he keeps returning to projects that should have fallen apart. But like a bulldog, Haick sinks his teeth into his goal and refuses to let go. Even when he fails, even when a technology he has worked on does not prove itself, as has happened along the way, he does not throw up his hands. Instead, he redoubles his efforts and pushes harder. He has no choice. It is his curse and his blessing.
"It probably comes from my childhood," he says in a moment of self-reflection. "I grew up feeling that I had to win because, if I failed, there would be no one to back me up. That I had to succeed or I'd collapse. It was a matter of survival."
Haick grew up in a struggling Christian family, the third of five children. "I didn't know it at the time," he says, "but we were very poor, below the poverty line." His drive to achieve came from his father, Jihad. "The word means 'to give your utmost and struggle for a cause,'" he explains. His father died a year ago of lung cancer, a disease his son has devoted himself to fighting for nearly two decades.
Haick describes his father's determination. At 21, after his first son was born, his father decided to leave his home village and pursue an education, without any support. He got up at 6 every morning and went to his teaching job in Nazareth to pay for his studies and support his family. In the evenings, he studied at the Technion. At night, he prepared lessons until 3 A.M.
"Try harder," he told his son, again and again. He said it after Haick completed his bachelor's degree at Ben-Gurion University, after he earned his doctorate at the Technion, and after he secured a faculty position following two postdoctoral fellowships, at the Weizmann Institute of Science and the California Institute of Technology.
Haick really does keep trying harder. After a series of breakthroughs, he seems to be getting closer to realizing his most ambitious vision: a patch that adheres to the skin like a child's temporary tattoo, with sensors on its surface continuously monitoring the wearer's health. Within two or three years, he promises, the patch will be on the market and in commercial use.
If that promise is fulfilled, it will initially monitor a small number of diseases. Later, he says, it will be able to detect many of the diseases that plague humanity at an early stage and rapidly deliver drugs tailored to the person wearing it. All this for just a few dozen dollars per patch, which will last for months.
That would complete the revolution Haick is working toward: a shift from medicine that responds to disease after it develops, using general treatment protocols, to medicine that can identify an early risk of disease, track its progression and tailor treatment to each person's circumstances.
We meet in Haick's spacious office in the Technion's Faculty of Chemical Engineering. Two walls are almost entirely covered with certificates of appreciation and awards for excellence. I count them: 36. On a shelf opposite him sits a large black metal sculpture of Sisyphus rolling his boulder. "I get an award, and two minutes later I'm back at work," Haick says during our conversation.
The first thing he talks about, however, is art. A few months ago, he completed two terms, six years in all, as dean of undergraduate studies, responsible for several thousand students. He proudly describes an initiative he introduced: an annual campus exhibition of students' paintings. "You can learn a lot from the way people think in art," he says.
Another achievement he mentions is changing the admissions process. "When I started the job, I set up 12 committees, and we made changes at different stages of the degree," he says. Among other things, they introduced a special admissions track allowing applicants to enroll with only a high school matriculation certificate, even one with less-than-stellar grades. Whether students can continue depends on their performance in the first semester.
"Of the roughly 200 students admitted through this track each year, about a quarter meet the requirements and continue their studies. Their average grades are even higher than those of students admitted through the regular track," he says. "Maybe that comes from my childhood too, I don't know, but I have this deep-seated need to improve access and equal opportunities."
Yet Haick stresses that he does not believe in affirmative action. "To me, equal opportunities don't mean advancing someone simply because they belong to a particular group. I believe in excellence, and advancement on that basis alone. People will tell me that, for all sorts of reasons, not every group has outstanding candidates. Then I'll empower people from those groups and invest more resources in them."
If you spend more money on them, isn't that affirmative action?
"I'm not giving the money to the students. I'm investing it in staff who will help them succeed. For example, each of these students gets a mentor for their entire degree. Or I'll set up a summer program before the first semester just so they can speak and hear Hebrew. Not grammar, not [the poet Haim Nahman] Bialik, just speaking and listening. Because some Arab students struggle with Hebrew."
And it works. A short article Haick co-authored, published in Nature in 2020, reports that since 2004, the number of Arab students at the Technion rose by 200 percent, the number of Arab women students by 350 percent, and the number of outstanding Arab students by 1,800 percent. The dropout rate fell by 67 percent. Haick served as assistant to the Technion's senior vice president, responsible for equal opportunities.
Did you receive that kind of support yourself, or benefit from affirmative action?
"I never received any help. I went into academia, pardon the expression, like an idiot. Nobody cut me any slack, and I didn't know the rules either. I don't want to go into detail, but in some places… I want to put this carefully." He pauses, for the only time during our conversation. "My life in this country hasn't been easy."
When, for example?
"A decade ago, I received threats and harassment because of who I am: an Arab working on sensors, a technology that can be used in missiles. I've spent my whole life doing medical research, but sometimes success makes people feel threatened, or they see it as a threat. I was repeatedly humiliated at Ben-Gurion Airport. Eventually, I got a 'good Arab' certificate." He is referring to a general fast-track passport control certificate issued by the Israel Airports Authority.
"To get something like that, to say, 'I'm a good Arab, please let me through,' is a low point. But there were years when I took 53 flights, and I had no choice."
During the Gaza war, while serving as dean, Haick decided to move some exams to the Technion's Tel Aviv campus because of missile fire on the north. He received phone calls threatening his life.
"They told me, 'We'll slaughter you if you don't change your decision.' Those exact words. Violence and criminality have become widespread in our society. I've been through a lot of very difficult things that I don't want to talk about. But that's why equality matters so much to me."
Last July, Haick received a different kind of phone call. President Isaac Herzog was on the line, telling him he would receive the Israeli Presidential Medal of Honor.
"I was elected a Fellow of the U.S. National Academy of Inventors and received the Order of Academic Palms from the French government, but recognition from the president brought things full circle for me," he says. "As a society, we have a very solid foundation in this country. There's a lot of noise too, but eventually it will fade. The principles on which the Technion was founded, and the country was founded, are excellent."
Haick lives in Haifa with his wife, a food engineer, and their two sons, aged 18 and 13.
He owes his big leap forward to the karate fighter within him. Toward the end of his time at Caltech, Prof. Yachin Cohen of the Technion's Faculty of Chemical Engineering called to tell him he had secured funding to establish a laboratory, and set him a challenge. There was a European Union grant named after Marie Curie, Cohen said, that no Israeli scientist had yet received. The application deadline was just a week away.
"So I sat down for a week, worked 22 hours a day, submitted the application 15 minutes before the deadline and went to sleep," Haick recalls.
He returned to Israel, took up a position at the Technion, and then war broke out. "It was the Second Lebanon War. I hid under this desk more than once," he says with a smile. In October 2006, a letter arrived: He had won the Marie Curie grant.
"I couldn't believe it. It was 1.73 million euros, when Israel Science Foundation grants were $200,000."
The grant completely changed his starting position. Instead of establishing a laboratory with two students, as his initial startup funding would have allowed, he set up a lab with 17 students and researchers.
Haick specialized in microelectronics and nanoelectronics, but after a close friend from university developed leukemia, he says, he decided he wanted to treat cancer. For all his determination, even Haick understood that treating cancer was beyond him. But there was another area he could sink his teeth into: early diagnosis.
At the time, a kind of urban legend was circulating that dogs could smell disease, an ability later established scientifically. Haick also heard that Hippocrates, the father of medicine, had identified kidney and liver diseases by smelling patients' breath. He decided to try to develop a system that would diagnose diseases at an early stage by detecting volatile organic compounds, or VOCs, released in exhaled breath. The idea was that each disease produced a distinctive mixture of molecules that sensitive, sophisticated sensors might be able to detect.
He planned to test his pilot system on lung cancer.
"That's because I don't know anything about medicine," he says with a smile. "To Hossam the engineer, lungs seemed connected to breathing. Today I understand that it's not that simple."
Haick thought his biggest challenge would be developing sensors capable of detecting chemical markers of disease in breath. It soon emerged, however, that the challenge was more fundamental: There was no clear evidence that such markers existed. To establish that, he launched a large-scale study at medical centers around the world, from China to Latvia to the United States. He collected samples from patients with 17 diseases, including several cancers; neurological diseases such as Alzheimer's, Parkinson's and multiple sclerosis; and infectious diseases. The breath samples were analyzed to determine their chemical composition.
"Using data from thousands of participants, we found that each person has a unique chemical signature of volatile organic compounds in their breath, like a fingerprint," Haick explains. "We also found that every disease has a distinctive chemical signature that sets it apart from the others. To me, that's my greatest achievement: proving that there's a scientific basis for Hippocrates' approach."
At the same time, Haick developed an electronic nose, a portable device combining sensors and artificial intelligence to analyze a person's breath and detect early markers of disease. "At first, it was a meter and a half long," he says. "We gradually made it smaller."
One of Haick's first partners in developing the sensors was Prof. Silke Christiansen, a physicist at the Free University of Berlin.
"I've known Hossam for about 15 years," she tells Haaretz. "He contacted me in 2009, saying, 'I've read your work about silicon nanowires. We need those. I have an idea for a sensor. We've tried many things, and these nanowires would be the best.' Then we started a collaboration. We produced the nanowires, and he did the rest: arranged them in sensor arrays and functionalized them."
The sensors are based on densely packed nanowires with various molecules attached to their surfaces. These act as chemical coatings, each causing a nanowire to respond slightly differently to substances in the air. This produces a range of responses across the sensor array. The resulting pattern makes it possible to identify the VOCs present in the breath.
"I probably haven't met many people as excited about what they're doing, but also as driven and hardworking," Christiansen says of Haick. "His vision was impressive from day one. He's one of the most innovative people I've ever met. Nowadays, people work a lot more with data, and everybody has heard about AI. Back then, it was breathtakingly different. It was innovation on a different level."
"The sensors Haick developed can detect the presence or absence of particular molecules in exhaled breath," says Prof. Tal Dvir, who researches tissue and organ engineering at Tel Aviv University. "That's an especially complex task because their concentrations in the body are extremely low. Detecting a specific molecule in a huge mixture of other molecules requires overcoming background noise and masking effects. Each sensor is tailored to a particular target molecule, and he has developed sensors for a range of applications."
During a visit to one of his Technion laboratories, Haick shows me the latest electronic nose, about the size of a hand. "The device is about 88 percent accurate - comparable to, and in some settings better than, standard imaging," he says.
According to Haick, it can already identify 17 diseases, but so far it has received Breakthrough Device designation from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for only two: lung cancer and advanced liver fibrosis unrelated to alcohol consumption, a condition that is a major risk factor for cirrhosis, liver cancer and heart disease.
"It's a lengthy process that takes several years," Haick says of regulatory approval.
The device is currently being used experimentally in hospitals around the world to diagnose those two diseases. Studies have already shown that it can identify lung cancer at an early stage, when the tumor may still be localized, sometimes before any clear symptoms appear. A laboratory study showed that it could even detect small numbers of cancer cells in blood.
Early trials were also conducted for a rare disease that is extremely difficult to diagnose: pulmonary arterial hypertension. Prof. Sylvia Cohen-Kaminsky, a specialist in the disease at Paris-Saclay University, took part in the trial.
"Diagnosis is often delayed by several years because it requires hospitalization and catheterization," she tells Haaretz Magazine. "There is currently no cure, and patients die an average of three years after diagnosis."
Cohen-Kaminsky says she first learned about Haick while reading an article about his research in Le Monde on a beach in France.
"I met him, and when I suggested applying it to pulmonary arterial hypertension, he immediately said, 'Yes, let's do it.'"
The two researchers established an international laboratory that operated for eight years. The initial results, Cohen-Kaminsky says, were remarkable: The electronic nose could distinguish patients from control participants and identify those carrying a genetic mutation that increased their susceptibility to the disease.
The researchers did not receive follow-up funding, so the research has yet to progress beyond those promising initial results.
Prof. Nir Peled, head of oncology at Shaare Zedek Medical Center and chairman of the Israeli Lung Cancer Foundation, is working with Haick to develop sensors that can precisely characterize lung cancer cells at the molecular level. He says their system can identify both the response to treatment and disease progression faster than other clinical methods.
"We've expanded its use to several types of cancer and other parts of the world," he notes. "In other words, we've shown that the technology works across cultures and can filter out local influences on volatile compounds, including differences in diet."
Peled explains that for each cancer, researchers need to identify a signal indicating early-stage disease, another reflecting more advanced disease, and signals indicating the response to treatment. Such information is currently available, he says, for seven common cancers: lung, breast, stomach, colorectal, head and neck, ovarian and kidney cancer.
"The vision is for the system to be an inexpensive, accessible and accurate tool, but introducing new things takes a long time in medicine."
Prof. Jonathan Sleeman, a cancer biology researcher at Heidelberg University, tells Haaretz that Haick's sensors offer a way to tap a rich reservoir of biomarkers that has barely been used until now. Clinical validation of the technology, he says, is likely to be a lengthy process requiring large groups of patients. One question is whether the VOC signals are sufficiently specific, since several disease states could produce the same positive result.
Sleeman is currently participating in a trial designed to test the new approach.
"Haick is an excellent scientist and he has a big vision," Sleeman says. "The arguments he presents are compelling, but that has to be shown in the real world, and that's where we're going."
Innovative as it was, Haick did not stop at the electronic nose. His next goal became clear during a taxi ride from Mumbai's airport.
"I passed through a very poor area, where people live with almost no infrastructure," he says. "I thought: How can the electronic nose help them if there's no reliable electricity here? And more importantly, how can we help them monitor their health at a price they can afford when they live on less than a dollar a day?"
Haick then had a eureka moment: Could the organic compounds released in breath also be emitted through the skin? His team set out to test the hypothesis and found that VOCs released through the skin could indeed be measured and analyzed.
Laboratory engineer Walaa Saliba shows me the next generation of monitoring technology. He places a small patch, four centimeters by four centimeters, on my arm. It contains electrical circuits and six tiny sensors that continuously pick up substances released by my skin and transmit the data to a phone app.
"The product monitors you all the time and compares your readings with statistical databases of people with and without a range of diseases," he says. "If it detects a shift toward illness, it sends an alert."
The patch is still under development, but the health-monitoring revolution is already underway, using readily available devices such as smart rings and watches. One of the researchers advancing it is Prof. Michael Snyder of Stanford University.
Snyder practices what he preaches, or rather, wears it: He has no fewer than nine watches, rings and sensors on his body. During a video call with Haaretz, he turns his left cheek toward the screen to reveal the latest addition, a small metal sensor called Temple, attached to his temple and monitoring his small blood vessels.
"I look like a cyborg," he says with undisguised delight.
Snyder's laboratory uses AI to analyze vast amounts of data from participants wearing all sorts of devices, looking for signs of health and disease. Devices currently on the market measure heart rate, heart rate variability, blood oxygen levels, blood pressure, respiratory rate, the skin's electrical conductance and sleep patterns. Snyder is already using the data to detect infectious diseases, respiratory viral infections and abnormal heart rhythms, including atrial fibrillation, at an early stage. A new line of research involves identifying markers of mental health problems: anxiety, depression and stress.
What would you recommend that an ordinary person, someone who isn't a tech geek, do today?
"You need to get a glucose monitor. You put it on your shoulder as a patch. They're very powerful. You'll never eat the same again, and I mean that in a good way. We've run studies showing that if you wear one of these devices, you'll improve your eating habits within 10 days because it's real-time feedback."
Snyder notes that about 40 percent of U.S. adults have prediabetes, and 80 percent of them do not know it. Because most people with prediabetes will develop diabetes, identifying problems with glucose regulation early is important.
Snyder hopes that in 10 years, everyone will wear one or two of these devices to monitor physiological measures and perhaps take biochemical measurements too. "There are a lot of people working on trying to measure some of these things continuously," he says.
Back to one of those researchers. The first disease Haick's patch diagnosed was tuberculosis, the world's deadliest infectious disease, which particularly affects populations in countries with limited access to advanced diagnostic tools. Haick received funding from the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation. He says Gates himself took a personal interest in the project, apparently because the patch was easy to use and Haick promised an extremely low manufacturing cost: $1 per patch. So far, the team has managed to develop a patch costing $1.50.
The patch was tested on about 2,000 people in India, South Africa and Latvia, achieving approximately 90 percent accuracy in detecting active tuberculosis compared with a control group. It achieved similar results in detecting latent tuberculosis, which has no symptoms but can develop into active disease.
One problem was that the patch was so thin it could be cut or scratched. Haick came up with a solution: patches that would repair themselves when damaged or malfunctioning, just as skin does. The researchers developed a polymer whose chains are connected by chemical bonds that allow them to reconnect after the material is cut.
"As soon as there's a cut, the molecules on either side can bond with each other again. They do it on their own in about 30 seconds, without heating, ultraviolet radiation or any other external stimulus," Haick explains. "That alone accounts for a lot of patents."
In total, he says, his laboratory has already generated nearly 100 registered patents.
"We already have all the components of the technology: the sensors, the algorithms for processing the information and the material's ability to heal itself," he adds. "The patch already exists, it costs a little over a dollar to manufacture, and it keeps working for months. Now we need to test its performance in real-world conditions and demonstrate that it can reliably identify diseases."
Having demonstrated the technology in tuberculosis, Haick is now conducting large-scale trials involving tens of thousands of people to identify the chemical signatures of a range of other diseases: malaria, COVID-19, degenerative and infectious diseases, and several cancers.
The trials are being conducted through EU-funded consortia involving numerous partners, including laboratories, hospitals and commercial companies. Haick will soon complete one such lung cancer trial involving 5,600 participants and 20 partners, funded by a grant of 14.8 million euros. Another consortium, with 3,700 participants, 18 partners and a budget of 8 million euros, is working on early detection of schizophrenia.
"We're monitoring a population experiencing psychosis for a year and a half to three years to identify initial signs before the disease develops. The earlier schizophrenia is treated, the more its progression is slowed."
A few days before our meeting, Haick was notified that he had won another consortium grant of 8 million euros, this time to detect Parkinson's, with 6,000 participants and 20 partners.
"We know that detecting Parkinson's and administering medication in its early stages can ease the symptoms," he says.
The disease results from a combination of environmental and genetic factors. Exposure to pesticides, pollutants and certain metals may play a role in its onset. The researchers will monitor participants at risk of Parkinson's, such as farmers exposed to pesticides over long periods, who are known to have high rates of the disease. They will use a two-sided patch: One side faces the body, while the other monitors the environment.
Over the past five years, Technion researchers have won six grants to lead consortia, three of them headed by Haick. According to Israel Innovation Authority figures, Israeli researchers received 58 such grants in total during those five years. Before that, Haick led another five successful consortia, studying colorectal cancer, melanoma and lung diseases, among other conditions.
"Applications have a success rate of 2 to 3 percent," he says. "Leading a consortium means developing a scientific vision, securing funding and bringing together many researchers to realize it. Behind every successful grant application are countless hours of work, conferences and meetings."
Can you distill your vision?
"The goal is personalized, precise, noninvasive medicine. All these technologies together will tailor diagnosis to the individual, taking their body and their environment into account."
If that vision is realized, anyone will be able to attach an inexpensive patch to their body that continuously monitors physiological and chemical signals and detects changes in their health, from fatigue and dehydration to a viral infection or early signs of cancer or Parkinson's.
The vision does not end with diagnosis. Haick wants to turn the patch into a complete medical system that can also deliver tailored treatment and track its effects.
"The patch will build an ongoing picture of a person's health," Haick explains. "If, for example, it detects a signal indicating a risk of Parkinson's, we could attach a tiny cartridge containing a drug to slow the disease's progression. It would work for many diseases, and you'd configure the cartridge according to the signal indicating the risk."
Such targeted drug delivery would also allow more precise adjustment of the dose and treatment duration, reducing the risk of side effects.
"Today, a drug may treat the problem it was prescribed for while also affecting healthy organs and tissues," Haick says. "I saw firsthand the treatments my late father received in the hospital, and that experience brought home to me the need for more precise, personalized treatment. Many treatments today follow a uniform, predetermined protocol, even though not all patients respond the same way. If we can measure how effective a treatment is in real time, we may eventually be able to give each person the treatment that is exactly right for them. We tested the principle in animal experiments, and the initial results were very promising."
Is there anything that could stop you?
"The technology's main building blocks have already been developed and demonstrated. We're there. This isn't science fiction. I estimate that within a few years we'll see commercial use of patches capable of detecting lung cancer, tuberculosis and hormonal changes in women.
"Realizing the full vision will take longer. First, we'll need extensive clinical validation. Then we'll have to navigate regulation, adapt the technology for industrial production and bring it to market. At the end of that process, I believe we'll have a patch that simultaneously monitors markers from the body and environmental risk factors that could affect the development of diseases, and protects us against them."
