Exclusive: Senate Investigation Challenges Big Tech’s Case for AI Data Centers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
19:56:08 UTC
04:56:08 KST

As the world's biggest technology companies race to build data centers across the country to power an AI boom, a yearlong Senate investigation argues that some firms are misleading the public about the true costs and benefits around those projects.
The findings, first shared with TIME, are expected to be part of a broader effort in the coming year by members of Congress hoping to put more guardrails around the massive, power-intensive projects.
“Congress must hold Big Tech accountable so these companies pay their fair share,” says Senator Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat who has called for a national moratorium on new AI data centers until developers agree to cover the full costs.
Warren's office led the investigation with fellow Democratic Senators Chris Van Hollen of Maryland and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, which focused on seven major data center developers—Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, CoreWeave, Digital Realty, and Equinix. The senators’ staff requested information from each company and interviewed employees.
The findings, which largely match reporting from various news outlets over the past year, offer a detailed look at the increasingly contentious economics of the AI buildout. Data center companies routinely point to construction employment when making the case for incentives. But when the senators’ staff asked for comprehensive information about permanent employment, several of the companies refused to provide it, according to the report. Some companies told investigators that permanent staffing was roughly one worker for every megawatt of power demand. A 100-megawatt data center, by that measure, could consume roughly as much electricity as 100,000 homes while employing about 100 permanent workers after construction.
“This report lays bare what we have long known: working Americans and local communities are footing the bill for Big Tech’s massive expansion of data centers, while these companies continue to operate without transparency,” Van Hollen says.
Notably, the Senate investigators found that the most lucrative incentives for data center developers are not necessarily the attention-grabbing property-tax breaks, but sales-tax exemptions on computer equipment. AI facilities require vast quantities of specialized hardware, and GPUs account for an estimated 39% of the spending at an average 1-gigawatt AI data center, according to the report.
All four of the major technology companies in the investigation—Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft—have routinely sought nondisclosure agreements during data center development, according to the report. Some acknowledged requesting them from government officials. While data center negotiations often deal with commercially sensitive information, the Senate report argues that NDAs have also restricted public scrutiny of deals involving tax dollars, utility rates, and public infrastructure.
Microsoft told the investigators it would stop seeking NDAs with local governments, although it would continue using them with state agencies, public utility commissions and utilities. Amazon has announced a similar policy. Google and Meta declined to commit to ending the practice with local governments, according to the report.
The report comes as data centers have become a hot-button issue on the campaign trail. About half of Americans say that data center construction is bad for the country, according to a recent Economist/YouGov poll. Both parties have been harnessing the issue, even as President Trump warns that opposition to data centers could push the AI buildout overseas.
Who Pays for the AI Power Boom?
A significant portion of the report explores whether tech companies are paying their fair share for data centers that are driving up the costs for nearby homeowners and businesses. State regulators and lawmakers are increasingly being asked to decide how much of that expansion should be paid for by the companies driving the demand, and how much should be borne by other customers and taxpayers.
The Senate investigators found none of the seven companies would agree to a standard that would require them to pay for the building of new power infrastructure that would not have been needed if not for their data centers. The companies generally said they would pay the direct costs of serving their data centers, but argued that larger investments in the electric grid—like new power plants and transmission lines—can benefit other customers and should not automatically be assigned to the company that helped drive the need for them.
The report points to a power plant in Richland Parish, Louisiana, that the local utility provider, Entergy, has sought to buy. Analysts argue the purchase was driven primarily by Meta’s planned $50 billion data center, which is expected to draw 4,500 megawatts of electricity—about four times the peak electricity demand of the entire city of New Orleans. Estimates indicate that the purchase could drive up electric bills for the average Entergy customer by $8-13 per month. Meta has disputed that its project is responsible for the costs.
Congress Debates New Data Center Laws
When Congress reconvenes after the midterm elections, data centers will be among the issues waiting for them. In September, the House overwhelmingly passed the bipartisan Ratepayer Protection Act, 417-3, which would direct states to consider standards requiring large-load customers such as data centers to cover the incremental costs of the generation, transmission, and distribution infrastructure needed to serve them.
But the measure stalled in the Senate, as Democrats argued it was toothless because it didn’t require states to push any costs to the companies. The Senate ultimately voted 57-43 against advancing the bill.
Much of the authority over electricity rates remains with state regulators, which means the biggest fights will continue to play out in statehouses and public utility commissions. But the Senate investigation gives Congress a new set of findings to work with as lawmakers consider whether federal standards should govern large electricity users, transparency around data center deals and the public subsidies supporting the industry’s expansion.
Van Hollen said Congress needs to pass a bill “that ensures that the corporations building and running data centers cover the costs of the energy they need, instead of pushing those costs onto the backs of consumers.”

NASA's Crew-12 splashes down in the Pacific Ocean after eight-month mission
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
19:54:51 UTC
04:54:51 KST

An astronaut crew that carried out an eight-month mission aboard the International Space Station splashed down as planned on Thursday off the coast of California.
After a more than 27-hour return journey, the Dragon capsule carrying Crew-12 landed safely in the Pacific Ocean, according to NASA's live broadcast.
"We are so excited to be back on planet Earth after an incredible mission on the International Space Station," said American astronaut Jessica Meir, the mission commander.
The spacecraft was then hoisted onto a specialised ship, and the four occupants — Meir, American Jack Hathaway, French astronaut Sophie Adenot and Russian cosmonaut Andrei Fedyaev — were helped out one by one.
They will undergo initial medical checks on the ship before being transported by helicopter to land, and then fly to Houston, Texas, home to the NASA centre responsible for astronaut operations.
During the mission, Adenot became the first French female astronaut to venture outside the space station for a spacewalk. In all, she undertook three spacewalks on August 18 and 25, and September 1.
Four new crew members for the ISS docked at the orbiting laboratory last week and will stay for approximately six months.
Continuously inhabited for the last quarter-century, the ageing ISS is scheduled to be pushed out of orbit before crashing into one of Earth's oceans sometime around 2030.
Despite many international cooperation agreements falling apart after Moscow invaded Ukraine in 2022, the United States and other ISS partners have continued working with Russia on the space station.

New Brazil Congress poses risk to environmental legislation, campaign group says

New Brazil Congress poses risk to environmental legislation, campaign group says
BRASILIA, Oct 8 - Brazil's next Congress is likely to pose a greater obstacle to legislation to protect the environment after elections this month, according to a study by climate advocacy group Observatorio do Clima, which found that almost 70% of elected lawmakers have little or no commitment to environmental issues.
The study analyzed bills, legislative proposals, speeches and public statements by new and re-elected lawmakers and concluded that 64 of the Senate's 81 members have a track record of "very low" or "low" commitment to environmental issues. In the lower house, 345 of 511 lawmakers were placed in the same category.
The Liberal Party, home to right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, who will face President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in a runoff election for the presidency later this month, has the weakest environmental credentials among major parties, the study found.
Bolsonaro defied pollsters to beat Lula in the first round, though he did not secure enough votes to avoid a second vote.
All of the party's 28 senators elected on Sunday, as well as members elected to the lower house, were classified as having very low commitment to environmental issues.
Other right-leaning parties, including Novo, Republicanos, Progressistas and Uniao Brasil, also showed low support for environmental causes, the study said.
Environmental advocates could face a more challenging political landscape with Congress shifting further to the right and if Bolsonaro -- whose past comments on climate change have caused concern -- is elected president, Observatorio do Clima said.
Reuters contacted the named parties but did not receive responses.
Proposals that could weaken environmental protections, including measures to reduce protected areas, allow mining on Indigenous lands and ease environmental licensing requirements, may gain momentum under the new Congress, the group added.
"This picture points to four years of difficult work for those focused on climate and environmental issues," said Suely Araujo, the group's public policy coordinator. REUTERS

Moldova pulls its border officers off Ukrainian soil again as Russian drones keep hitting crossings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
19:54:13 UTC
04:54:13 KST

Moldova is creating protective zones at border crossing points along its border with Ukraine amid the threat of drone attacks. It is also relocating its personnel from joint border crossings on Ukrainian territory back to Moldova. Moldovan Interior Minister Daniella Misail-Nichitin said this on 7 October, according to NewsMaker.
In recent months, Russian attacks on Ukrainian border crossing points near the country's borders with neighboring states have become more frequent. Ukrainian-Moldovan border crossings are among those most frequently targeted by Russia. As a result, Moldova now plans to withdraw all of its border personnel from Ukrainian territory.
A Moldovan border guard was also recently injured when a projectile struck near a passenger bus at the Palanca border crossing, Moldova's Border Police reported.
Chisinau strengthens protection of border crossings against Russian drone attacks
Moldovan authorities are working to strengthen security measures at all Border Police crossing points, including those located on Ukrainian territory, according to the statement.
Authorities are already setting up protective zones so that Border Police officers, government officials and civilians at the crossings can evacuate to a safe location if necessary, the minister said.
Moldova is also discussing moving its personnel from joint border crossings located on Ukrainian territory to Moldova. Personnel have already been withdrawn from two crossings, with plans to do the same at other joint crossings, Missail-Nikitin said.
NewsMaker clarified with Moldova’s Interior Ministry that the measure involves withdrawing Moldovan personnel from two joint border crossing points with Ukraine — Criva and Palanca.
Ukraine and Moldova seek a response to a new challenge
The first time Chisinau withdrew its personnel from Ukrainian territory at the Ukrainian-Moldovan border crossings was a month ago. Moldova temporarily changed the operating arrangements at three joint border crossings with Ukraine because of security risks linked to Russian attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure near the border, Moldova's Border Police reported on 11 September.
The crossings in question are Giurgiulesti–Reni, Briceni–Rossoșani, and Criva–Mamalyga, where Moldovan border guards and customs officers had previously carried out controls on Ukrainian territory, according to the Border Police.
Starting 12 September, Moldovan personnel returned to Moldovan territory for 90 days and began working from existing infrastructure on the Moldovan side. The crossings themselves remained operational, and the cross-border movement of people and vehicles continued. Only the location where Moldovan services carried out their duties changed, the authorities said.
Ukraine is also strengthening the protection of its border infrastructure. The State Agency for Restoration and Infrastructure Development plans to install 135 basic mobile shelters at 28 border crossing points and on access roads leading to them. The shelters are intended to protect civilians crossing the border and border crossing personnel. Procurement is being carried out by the Restoration Services in Vinnytsia, Odesa, Chernivtsi, Zakarpattia, and Volyn Oblasts, according to the statement.
Ukraine’s border crossings near Moldova face ongoing Russian attacks
Russia has repeatedly attacked Ukrainian border infrastructure near the Moldovan border in recent weeks. On 25 August, a Russian drone struck the Vynohradivka–Vulcănești border crossing in Odesa Oblast.
On 5 October, Russian strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure caused an incident near the Palanka–Mayaky–Udobne border crossing. A projectile fell near the crossing, ricocheted off the ground and struck a passenger bus. The control booth was also damaged, and one Moldovan border guard sustained a minor injury.
On 9 September, Russia attacked the Starokozache–Tudora border crossing. One drone struck the crossing, while two others crashed nearby on Ukrainian territory. Two people were killed and three others were injured in the attack, and the crossing was temporarily closed. Russia claimed that this strike on a border crossing was prompted by Ukraine transporting weapons through the facility, a claim Moldova has denied.

Mathematicians marvel, and grumble, at OpenAI’s trove of new results
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
19:53:38 UTC
04:53:38 KST

It’s been two days since OpenAI’s “slop drop” of AI-generated results on 372 open math and computer science problems. Scientists are just beginning to parse through the heap and pick out the most exciting breakthroughs in their own fields.
It will be months, perhaps years, before we understand just how much novel mathematics was added to the literature this week, but everyone agrees it’s been a week without precedent. “Yesterday will be the day when a new era of math and mathematical physics began,” Harvard University mathematician Michael Douglas told Scientific American on Tuesday. It was an even bigger moment, he thinks, than last month’s solution of the Navier-Stokes problem, one of math’s million-dollar challenges, by the same new internal model at OpenAI.
READ MORE: The most exciting claims from OpenAI’s heap of new proofs
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Already certain aspects of this new era are becoming clear. Many of the results, experts say, are far better written than the Navier-Stokes proof, suggesting that OpenAI’s math team is working to overcome its model’s inability to explain its math clearly to humans. Hector Pasten, a mathematician at the Pontifical Catholic University of Chile, says the papers he’s looked at improve on the company’s notorious lack of citations. “I think they are doing a better job of giving credit,” he says.
But the quality remains extremely uneven—mathematicians are finding some papers readable and others utterly nonsensical. “Others are much, much harder to make sense of—they’re sort of this AI slop,” says Roland Bauerschmidt, a mathematician at New York University. “If I had received these by e-mail from a nobody, I probably would have deleted it, it’s so badly written.”
Even much of that seeming nonsense, though, is ostensibly correct. At this point, 42 percent of the results are coded in the programming language Lean, which means their logic is almost certainly sound, even if their English-language write-up is too hard to follow.
On the other hand, three of the papers have already been withdrawn after experts uncovered a significant error, causing some to question the more than half of the proofs that aren’t yet Lean-verified. “While I expect most of these will ultimately be found to be correct, or at least correctable, we should expect some of the proofs to contain mistakes, possibly serious ones,” says Andrew Sutherland, a mathematician at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
The community’s reaction to the way OpenAI chose to drop the results has been mixed, to say the least. Sutherland argues that OpenAI should also release the problems its model failed to solve, which the company has said number in the thousands. “I expect they will not want to do that,” he adds, “but that is how open science works. You need to report your negative results along with your positive results.”
The lack of transparency goes further. A number of mathematicians have told Scientific American that they doubt anyone on OpenAI’s team would have thought to ask some of the questions the model answered, either because they’re extremely niche or because they contradict a belief most experts previously held. Several independently suggested that it seems the model itself is coming up with problems to solve, perhaps in an extended conversation between a swarm of agents. This idea seems corroborated by the fact that a number of papers contain strikingly similar ideas and methods—as if their authors were communicating. OpenAI didn’t reply to a request for comment on this question.
Others in the community have been more outspoken in their criticism. A statement from the Association for Human Mathematics decries the company’s actions. “Releasing over 700 files at once is not a demonstration of scholarship, but a demonstration of power,” it reads. “We urge mathematicians to discontinue their work with OpenAI and to return to a vision of science that centers human understanding.”

====================================================================================================

The most exciting claims from OpenAI’s heap of new proofs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
19:53:07 UTC
04:53:07 KST

On Tuesday afternoon OpenAI dropped more than 700 manuscripts reporting proofs, solutions and progress on 372 open problems across theoretical research.
It will take time for mathematicians to trudge through all the artificial-intelligence-generated results. No one, not even OpenAI researchers themselves, has been able to even read through everything yet. And not all of the proofs were certified as correct by the automatic logic verification platform Lean—in fact, some have already been retracted after outside scientists found mistakes. OpenAI also did not include full prompts or run-time details for how their agents uncovered the proofs, and officials admitted in a blog post about the results that citations and written descriptions of findings could be improved in future releases.
READ MORE: Mathematicians marvel, and grumble, at OpenAI’s trove of new results
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Despite these issues, experts say the results are jaw-dropping. The papers span mathematics, theoretical computer science, physics, and more. Some of the discoveries could have easily netted a human author a top research award just a year ago
Here are just some of the most important problems OpenAI claims to have solved, according to the experts.
MATH
Toward the Riemann Hypothesis
The Riemann hypothesis is the scariest open problem in math—experts told Scientific American earlier this year that they barely think about it because they have no idea how to even start tackling it. That might have just changed.
The hypothesis centers on a special, complicated equation called the Riemann zeta function—specifically, which numbers you can put into this function to make it come out to zero. If you could magically know all of these special inputs, you would essentially know all of the prime numbers—mathematicians’ favorite objects and the building blocks of the entire number line.
OpenAI’s drop contains two major results about these “zeros.” One proves the “quasi-Riemann hypothesis,” which is a huge step toward the holy grail of proving the full thing. “Plenty of applications of the Riemann hypothesis did not need the full Riemann hypothesis,” says Hector Pasten, a mathematician at the Pontifical Catholic University of Chile. “The quasi-Riemann hypothesis is way more than enough for many applications.” For instance, mathematicians now have a better estimate of where the primes sit as you go up the number line than they ever had before.
As to whether this proof is a path toward solving the full hypothesis, it’s too early to say. “Some people claim it is progress toward Riemann; other people say it’s not,” Pasten says. “Usually the word progress makes sense after the fact, when you see how it eventually gets solved.”
The second result shows that neither the zeta function nor many of its generalizations, called “Dirichlet L-functions,” have a “Siegel zero,” a certain, especially problematic type of zero that would contradict the hypothesis. “This is not just progress on Siegel zeros—it settles the question,” Pasten says. “This is amazing.”
Hilbert’s 10th Problem
Hilbert’s 10th problem is about which mathematical truths are and are not knowable. It asks whether it’s possible to build an algorithm that sorts all simple algebra problems into two piles. One pile holds equations that have whole-number solutions, such as y2 = 2x (where x = 2 and y = 2 is a solution). The other pile consists of equations without a solution in which the variables are whole numbers, such as y2 + x2 = –1.
In 1970 mathematician Yuri Matiyasevich showed that such an algorithm is impossible. No computer can tell you whether or not any equation has a solution with whole numbers. But since then mathematicians have been struggling to extend this result, asking if a computer can sort equations when you allow their variables to have a wider range of values, such as fractions, square roots or imaginary numbers. OpenAI’s model proved that even when the variables are allowed to be any rational number—a whole number or a fraction—the mathematical world remains unsortable.
The new proof uses two of Pasten’s ideas from seemingly different areas of mathematics—even he hadn’t realized they could be put together in this way. “It’s extremely surprising to me that they connect,” Pasten says. “Their general strategy is original.”
The Kakeya Conjecture
The Kakeya conjecture can be thought of as sliding and twirling a piece of chalk around on a tablet so that it points in every direction but covers as small an area with chalk as possible. Mathematician Hong Wang won a Fields medal this summer for solving the three-dimensional version of this problem with mathematician Joshua Zahl. In that version, you twirl the stick around in midair—showing the minimum possible 3D space the twirl can occupy. Now OpenAI’s model has solved the problem for four dimensions.
Artin, Erdős, and More
Other important number theory results include Artin’s conjecture on primitive roots, which is about special number systems that stop at a certain, highest number, as well as a proof of perhaps the most famous conjecture of storied problem-poser Paul Erdős and progress that is relevant to the Langlands program, a sweeping set of conjectures sometimes called “a Grand Unified Theory of Mathematics.”
PHYSICS
Baby Yang-Mills
On its face, the “nonlinear sigma model” doesn’t sound like it has anything to do with particle physics. At every point on a grid, you place an arrow in a different direction to represent interacting, spinning atoms. The goal is to show that rotations of the arrows in one place cannot be detected far away. But that aim bears a striking, hidden resemblance to “the Yang-Mills existence and mass gap problem,” one of the five remaining Millennium Prize Problems, which aims to underpin the “Standard Model” of particle physics with rigorous mathematics. “This goes back 50 years, much like Yang-Mills, and is widely considered the ‘warm-up’ for Yang-Mills,” says Michael Douglas, a mathematical physicist at Harvard University.
OpenAI’s repository contains several papers claiming to completely resolve the equivalent of the Yang-Mills problem for this simpler model. New York University mathematician Roland Bauerschmidt says the first of these papers is both groundbreaking and comprehensible. “I haven’t digested it or understood all the details, but it seems very reasonable,” he says. The rest of the papers related to this problem are incomprehensible slop, he says, too hard for even a human expert to verify. “The second paper is horrible,” Bauerschmidt says. “If these results had been sent to me by a nobody, I would have deleted the e-mail.”
Einstein’s Baby
Physicists know a strange state of matter called the “Bose-Einstein condensate” is possible because researchers have made it in a lab—winning them the 2001 Nobel Prize in Physics. This material is where all the atoms in a gas occupy the exact same quantum state, producing weird quantum effects at unusually macroscopic scales. Albert Einstein originally predicted its existence in work that built upon a 1924 paper by physicist Satyendra Nath Bose, but he only proved that the state is mathematically possible for an unrealistic gas where no two atoms interact. OpenAI’s model extended the prediction to a case with interactions. It used similar techniques to prove a major conjecture about the math of ferromagnetism—one that the famous mathematical physicist Freeman Dyson erroneously claimed with two collaborators in 1976.
COMPUTER SCIENCE
Faster Matrix Multiplications
Anyone who's taken a linear algebra course can attest that matrices—ensembles of numbers in a two-dimensional array—underpin many different fields of computer science. Manipulating and performing operations on them quickly is important for computer graphics, complex simulations and machine learning itself. “Matrix multiplication is needed all over the place," says Virginia Vassilevska Williams, a computer science professor at MIT who researches the problem. "But also, its complexity is one of the great mysteries in computer science." Multiplying two matrices together requires a tedious amount of arithmetic.
The number of mathematical operations it takes to do these matrix multiplications scales with the cube of the length of the matrices. Scientists have sought a way to shrink the size of the exponent. If they had to do fewer than a cube of the length, it could mean exponential time savings. A few years ago, Vassilevska Williams and her colleagues had gotten that exponent down from 3 to around 2.37, the lowest ever achieved. Problem 107 claims a new lowest boundof 9⁄4, or 2.25. Paper 109 supposedly uses similar methods to find new, faster ways to multiply integers together, too. “In a maybe diabolical sense, the advance on matrix multiplication can be seen as an attempt by the LLMs to speed themselves up," Vassilevska Williams says.
L = RL = BPL
If algorithms research is about the best ways to solve problems, complexity theory asks the reverse: How hard is it to find the best solutions to problems—the ideal algorithms that can’t be beat? This challenge involves thinking about what kinds of resources a computer has at its disposal and asking which resources let one solve more problems. A classic quandary about problems computers can solve called P versus NP, likely one of the hardest of the Millenium Prize Problems, is perhaps the most famous complexity problem.
A key to both algorithms and complexity is asking how the solution or problem scales with the size of its input. For example, in the case of multiplication, researchers would want to know not just the best way to multiply two 100-digit numbers but how long it takes to multiply numbers of any size as a function of how many digits they have.
L, also known as LOGSPACE, is the complexity class of problems that can be answered with very little space—logarithmic in the size of the problem’s description. RL and BPL, meanwhile, are randomized versions of LOGSPACE in which the computer can harness randomness and only needs to be right most of the time. Proving that L = RL = BPL, as Problem 103 claims to do, shows that every problem of this type that can be done with randomness can also be done without it, known as derandomization.
In practice, computer programs use randomness all the time, but many researchers think it probably doesn’t speed up algorithms. “We have strong reasons to believe that, but we don’t know how to prove it,” says Ran Raz, a complexity theorist at Princeton University. While there was evidence that L = RL was likely to be true, proving it directly has been elusive until now. “I didn’t see any directions that were promising [before],” Raz says.
Unique Games
The unique games conjecture also falls under complexity theory. First pitched in 2002, it implicitly asks how hard it is, given a set of constraints, to satisfy some portion of them. Here the resource under the microscope is approximation—that is, instead of getting an exactly correct answer to a given problem, the computer only needs to get close to the answer. Although the unique games problem isn’t explicitly about approximation, showing that it’s difficult would imply that finding approximate answers to many problems is as hard as finding the answer directly.
Problem 102 claims to do just that, proving that the unique games problem is hard. This solution has been a bit controversial. Other researchers who had caught wind of OpenAI’s work on the problem rushed out their partial progress toward the answer in fear of being scooped by AI.
Unitary Synthesis
Over in the land of quantum computing, meanwhile, Problem 283 could give a better picture at how difficult truly quantum problems are. Scientists understand how bits in a classical computer work and can be manipulated, but they have less of a handle on quantum computing’s analogue to the classical bit, the qubit.
The unitary synthesis problem was first posed by researchers Scott Aaronson and Greg Kuperberg in 2006. It tries to relate working with qubits to working with bits. In this case, OpenAI showed that for any manipulation of a quantum state of qubits—called a unitary—they can build a quantum circuit and a problem dealing with only classical bits such that the circuit and problem can be used to calculate these manipulations, i.e., it can “synthesize” that unitary. Importantly, this solution gives some evidence that hard quantum problems may not be that much harder than hard classical problems, a surprising result that was not clear to researchers in the field before now.
Fast Fourier Transform
The Fast Fourier Transform, an algorithm whose discovery dates back to 1965, is crucial to the Internet and other forms of digital communications. In many applications, including the Web and medical scans, it converts information received from signals into actual machine-usable frequency data. The transform works by summing a bunch of signals and multiplying each by a special exponential factor. Although brute forcing these multiplications takes quadratic time (the time is proportional to the square of the number of signals), the “fast” protocol takes about n log n time(where n is the number of signals received), which is fast enough to use for things like the Internet.
Paper 130 claims to reduce this n log n time to ... n (log n)0.999....Specifically, the model got it down from a factor of log n to a factor of (log n)^1–10–13, a tiny improvement over the state of the art. On an objective level, this is so close to n log n that the distinction almost doesn’t matter. It does break a longstanding barrier to digital communications, however, and many researchers hope that by studying the proof techniques used, they could one day find a Faster Fourier Transform.

AI generated
WASHINGTON - The Trump administration froze on Oct 8 some green-card filings by Microsoft, Adobe and major IT outsourcers and opened probes into nine top universities, widening a visa crackdown it says targets fraud and protects American jobs.
The twin actions mark the broadest strike yet against skilled-worker immigration programmes – potentially cutting off a common path to permanent residency for foreign tech workers – while putting some of the country’s top research universities on notice.
“There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused the system more than Microsoft,” Vice-President J.D. Vance said.
He said the company laid off 6,000 American workers in 2025 while benefiting from 6,300 H-1B temporary worker visas and nearly 3,000 green cards.
The announcement about the permanent labour certification process – PERM – came hours before Trump was due to give Microsoft chief executive officer Satya Nadella the National Medal of Technology and Innovation.
Under PERM, required for most employment-based green cards, employers must show that hiring a foreign worker will not harm US workers’ wages or job opportunities.
Microsoft is the largest filer of PERM applications, according to data from the US labour department.
The company said in a statement that about 80% of the H-1B applications it filed in the last fiscal year were to extend or change the status of current employees, not to hire new workers. In July, the company said it would cut 4,800 jobs, or about 2.1% of its global workforce.
Labour Secretary Keith Sonderling said the suspension would also cover Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini.
“We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labour certification applications involving these companies,” Sonderling said.
He said these companies had since 2009 sought almost three million foreign workers, and had received over 230,000 H-1B visa approvals and over 100,000 permanent labour certifications.
Amazon.com was the largest employer of approved H-1B beneficiaries in fiscal 2026, followed by Tata Consultancy Services, Infosys, Apple and Microsoft, according to US immigration data.
Vance said the suspensions would last “as long as it needs to,” adding that the administration wants the companies to change how they hire. He said some companies post ineffective job ads, then cite a lack of applicants to justify hiring lower-paid foreign workers.
Microsoft said in its statement that it pays its H-1B employees the same as any other employees doing comparable work.
“The immediate financial impact on major technology companies may be relatively limited at this moment, but the longer-term implications for innovation and competitiveness could be much more significant,” said Ken Mahoney, CEO of Mahoney Asset Management.
Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, HCL Technologies, Wipro and Capgemini did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Tata Consultancy Services declined to comment.
Nasscom, India’s IT industry body, said Indian tech companies in the US had significantly reduced their reliance on H-1B visas, and relatively few of their workers sought green cards through the PERM process.
Crackdown widens
The suspensions are the latest in a series of steps against skilled-worker programmes. In September 2025, the Labour Department launched an enforcement drive called “Project Firewall” as a White House proclamation imposed a one-time US$100,000 (S$128,000) fee on new H-1B petitions for workers hired from abroad.
During President Donald Trump’s second term, companies have faced growing pressure to keep jobs and production in the United States rather than move them overseas.
The action comes despite closer ties between the administration and tech leaders, who are lobbying for lighter AI regulation.
Universities under scrutiny
Vance also said nine universities, including Harvard, Yale and Stanford, would be investigated for what the administration called the misuse of exchange-visitor visas to undercut American wages.
The nine schools also include Brown and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Labour Inspector-General Anthony D’Esposito said subpoenas had already been served.
D’Esposito said investigators would examine whether foreign influence, improper financial relationships or visa abuse were compromising federally funded research.
“It could have an enormous economic impact on the whole US economy,” said Sarah Spreitzer, a vice-president at the American Council on Education, which represents college and university presidents. International students historically spent US$40 billion a year while in the US, she said.
The probe deepens the administration’s long-running fight with Harvard over foreign students.
In 2025, the Department of Homeland Security subpoenaed the university over alleged misconduct by international students and its compliance with immigration law.
Harvard called that subpoena “unfounded retribution” but said it would comply as far as the law requires. REUTERS

At least 81 US aircraft worth up to $3.3bn lost or damaged in Iran war

At least 81 US aircraft worth up to $3.3bn lost or damaged in Iran war
The damage, documented in a Congressional Budget Office report, comes as Trump faces criticism over war’s cost.
At least 81 United States military aircraft, including fighter jets and drones, have been lost or damaged during Operation Epic Fury, the code name for Washington’s military campaign against Iran launched earlier this year.
The statistic comes as part of a report released on Monday by the Congressional Budget Office (CBO), a nonpartisan government agency that provides budget-related research to the legislature.
It estimated that, as of August 1, the cost of the American aircraft losses during the US-Israeli war against Iran was between $1.9bn and $3.3bn.
The report this week highlights the growing price tag for the war, which began on February 28. A lasting ceasefire has remained out of reach as the conflict continues into its eighth month.
“The asymmetries of warfare show that even small countries with small militaries can inflict damage on the world’s best militaries,” said Harlan Ullman, a former naval officer and chairman of the Killowen Group, a government advisory firm.
He told Al Jazeera that Iran has managed to achieve a degree of success in damaging US military hardware and bases in the Middle East.
“Iran has plenty of US targets available, and you can imagine what a small drone can do to a major military asset. We have seen examples of that in the Gulf countries during the conflict,” Ullman explained.
Monday’s report listed 12 F-15E Strike Eagle fighter jets, one F-35A Lightning II jet and seven KC-135 Stratotanker aerial refuelling aircraft among those affected. Forty-five of the 81 aircraft identified in the report were MQ-9 Reaper drones.
Evolving nature of warfare
Experts like Ullman trace some of the US vulnerabilities to the changing nature of modern warfare, which is increasingly reliant on low-cost drones that are widely available.
Many have pointed to Russia’s war against Ukraine as an example of how a smaller military like Kyiv’s can keep a larger adversary at bay through drone warfare.
Rumours of a potential drone attack on Royal Air Force (RAF) Fairford — a British base that has hosted US assets during the Iran war — also resulted in the sudden departure of a dozen US aircraft on Sunday.
Ullman pointed to those instances as examples of how the threat of drone attacks has been effective in putting larger militaries on the defensive.
“We have seen the US had to relocate its B-1 bombers from the UK fearing Iranian attacks, and we have seen how the Ukrainian Operation Spiderweb, where small drones were launched from inside Russia, targeted and destroyed Russian military assets,” Ullman said.
Cost of war?
The rising costs associated with the war against Iran have also placed political pressure on the administration of US President Donald Trump.
Earlier this year, his administration requested a record $1.5 trillion in defence spending for fiscal year 2027, citing the demands of the war.
But the soaring price tag has sparked scepticism in Congress, particularly from Democrats.
Last month, 45 Senate Democrats and one independent wrote an open letter to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth demanding transparent accounting of the war’s costs.
They argued that a “detailed breakdown” of the costs was necessary before Congress considers further supplemental funding.
“American taxpayers have already paid an extra $100 billion out of their pockets for higher gas and diesel prices alone and at least another $60 billion in higher costs for things like groceries, mortgages, and plane tickets as a result of the war,” the senators wrote.
“Now you are asking that they pay again to fund a war of choice that Congress never authorized and the President launched with no strategic plan.”
In a separate report issued in September, the Congressional Budget Office estimated that the war with Iran has cost roughly $38bn, as of August 1.
That amount reflects the costs of replacing expended munitions and equipment lost in battle, as well as increased fuel costs and other operations.
“An additional month of conflict would cost $2 billion,” the office said.
However, it added that, “if the intensity of the conflict increased to roughly the level experienced in July, the cost per month would increase to $3 billion”.
The Pentagon said it had “nothing further to provide” in a response to Al Jazeera’s query about whether the losses reported this week were expected and how they would impact the department’s budget.
Polls indicate the war is widely unpopular among US voters, and analysts have speculated about whether reports of rising costs may have an impact on the US midterm elections, which will decide whether Trump’s Republican Party will retain control of Congress.
But Ullman is sceptical that reports like Monday’s will be a determining factor in the outcome of the vote.
“I do not think that report will influence the course of the upcoming midterm elections, as many Americans, even those who oppose the war, would see it as expected damage in a military operation,” Ullman said.

Russia has spent a decade trying to stop people from bypassing internet censorship. Now it plans to spend nearly 60 billion rubles over three years on traffic filtering.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
19:42:18 UTC
04:42:18 KST

Russia has spent a decade trying to stop people from bypassing internet censorship. Now it plans to spend nearly 60 billion rubles over three years on traffic filtering.
Russia is preparing a new wave of restrictions on tools used to bypass internet blocks. The budget for the next three years includes a record 60 billion rubles for traffic filtering. The Digital Development Ministry wants to make mobile internet much more expensive for VPN users, and there are plans to put companies’ corporate networks under strict oversight by the Federal Security Service (FSB). Dozens of other restrictions have accumulated in recent years. We looked back at the main ones to show how the state has methodically cut Russians off from the free internet — and where we are on that timeline right now.
VPN services were banned from bypassing Russian internet blocks (2017)
On November 1, 2017, a new Article 15⁸ was added to the law “On Information, Information Technologies, and Information Protection” to address VPNs and other ways to bypass internet blocks:
Measures to prevent the use within the Russian Federation of information and telecommunications networks and online resources that provide access to online resources and information and telecommunications networks to which access is restricted within the Russian Federation.
The authorities did not ban VPNs outright. Instead, they required providers to filter their Russian users’ traffic and block access to resources on the banned list. If providers failed to comply, Russian telecommunications operators were required to block their VPN services on instructions from Roskomnadzor, Russia’s internet regulator. The only exemptions were for the authorities themselves and companies that needed unrestricted access “for technical purposes necessary to support their operations.”
Internet providers were banned from explaining how to bypass blocks (2018)
In February 2016, the Association for the Protection of Copyright on the Internet proposed administrative fines for promoting VPN use to access banned websites. Roskomnadzor supported the idea but proposed fining only internet providers. An agency spokesperson said in April that inspections had uncovered “several instances in which telecommunications operators posted information about ways to bypass blocks on their block notification pages.”
In the end, no separate fine was introduced. But starting November 1, 2017, telecommunications operators were required to comply with rules governing “posted information about restrictions on access to online resources.” Roskomnadzor published the corresponding order in March 2018. It prohibited the following on block notification pages:
- News content
- Information about ways to access online resources containing information to which access is restricted under Federal Law No. 149-FZ
A center was created to manage Russia’s internet, along with equipment to filter traffic and block access (2019)
After their failed attempt to block Telegram in 2018, the authorities learned from their mistakes and passed a law on the “sovereign internet.” It took effect on November 1, 2019.
Among other things, the law allowed centralized control over the Russian segment of the internet. To that end, the authorities established a Center for Monitoring and Management of the Public Communications Network within the Main Radio Frequency Center, which reports to Roskomnadzor. The new center was supposed to be able to take control “in the event of threats to the stability, security, and integrity” of internet operations in Russia.
To counter such threats, every telecommunications operator was required to install TSPU, or “technical means of countering threats.” These hardware and software systems allowed Roskomnadzor to filter traffic at its discretion and block sites and services it deemed objectionable. The agency later made extensive use of TSPU to target VPNs and other tools for bypassing blocks. If you want to understand exactly how TSPU works, watch this five-hour video.
In October 2023, Roskomnadzor head Andrey Lipov said that all communications nodes in Russia were “100% covered by TSPU.”
Mass blocking of VPN services began (2021)
In May 2021, Lipov threatened to block VPN services that continued to ignore Russian legal requirements. The agency began targeting individual providers the following month. Roskomnadzor made its plans public in advance so the blocks would not affect companies using those VPN services “to keep technical processes running at businesses and organizations.”
By the end of the year, the agency had said it was restricting VyprVPN, Opera VPN, Hola! VPN, ExpressVPN, KeepSolid VPN Unlimited, Nord VPN, Speedify VPN, IPVanish VPN, Betternet, Lantern, X-VPN, Cloudflare WARP, Tachyon VPN, and PrivateTunnel.
Hi, I’m Yulia.
I’m an editor at Meduza, and for almost five years now, I haven’t been sleeping well for one reason: I’m worried about my colleagues in Russia.
I’m often woken up by messages from our freelance reporters inside the country. They sometimes work late at night or early in the morning, and they message me at all hours. I never silence my phone at night in case of an emergency. Every notification jolts me awake. Half-asleep, my first thought is always the same: they’re texting me because the police have come to search their home. In Russia, you can go to prison for working with Meduza. Sometimes I have nightmares about my reporters being interrogated by the FSB. Some of those nightmares have come true.
Meduza’s reporters risk their freedom to tell the world what’s happening inside Russia. They believe their work can help make a better future possible, and they refuse to leave. Please donate so they can keep reporting.
All instructions for bypassing Russian internet blocks were banned (2023)
On July 31, 2023, a new provision allowed authorities to add online resources to the unified register of banned websites for another reason:
Article 15¹. Unified register of domain names, website page addresses, and network addresses identifying websites containing information whose distribution is prohibited in the Russian Federation
5. The grounds for adding the information specified in Part 2 of this article to the register are:
m) information about ways and methods of providing access to online resources and/or information and telecommunications networks to which access is restricted within the Russian Federation;
Fines were introduced for VPN service operators (2025)
On September 1, 2025, a new Article 13.52 was added to the Code of Administrative Offenses:
Violation of the rules governing the use within the Russian Federation of hardware and software tools for accessing online resources and information and telecommunications networks to which access is restricted
It provides for fines for refusing to cooperate with Roskomnadzor or to block Russian residents’ access to banned resources. The fines can reach 80,000 rubles for individuals and 500,000 rubles for companies. Repeat violations carry steeper penalties: up to 200,000 rubles and 1 million rubles, respectively.
Using a VPN became an aggravating factor in criminal offenses (2025)
On September 1, 2025, a new item was added to the Criminal Code’s list of aggravating factors:
committing a crime using hardware and software tools for accessing online resources and information and telecommunications networks to which access is restricted
Now, if a court finds that an offender used a VPN to commit any crime, it can impose a harsher punishment. It can even deny offenders certain forms of leniency under the Criminal Code, such as sentencing limits for those who voluntarily report their crimes to the authorities or enter into a pretrial cooperation agreement.
VPN advertising was banned, and fines were introduced for it (2025)
On September 1, 2026, a new provision was added to Article 5 of the law “On Advertising,” which sets out general requirements:
10⁸. It is prohibited to distribute advertisements for hardware and software tools that provide access to online resources and information and telecommunications networks to which access is restricted under the laws of the Russian Federation
At the same time, fines for such advertising were added to the Code of Administrative Offenses (Part 18 of Article 14.3). The maximum fine is 80,000 rubles for individuals and 500,000 rubles for companies.
Major Russian companies began detecting users with active VPNs (2026)
In April 2026, the Digital Development Ministry forced major Russian companies with the most heavily visited websites and services to detect active VPNs on users’ devices. The companies were required to block those users’ access and, according to RBC, share data about their VPN connections with Roskomnadzor. In theory, this was meant to help the agency gather information about VPNs that successfully bypass blocks or go entirely undetected, so it could block them more effectively.
Authorities tried to cut VPN services off from Russian hosting providers (2026)
On June 26, 2026, the law “On Information, Information Technologies, and Information Protection” was amended to prohibit Russian hosting providers from serving VPN services that bypass Russian internet blocks:
Article 10²⁻¹. Specific rules governing hosting providers’ activities
5¹. A hosting provider may not supply computing capacity for storing information in an information system permanently connected to the internet to owners of information and telecommunications networks or online resources (a website and/or website page, information system, or computer program) that provide access to online resources or information and telecommunications networks to which access is restricted within the Russian Federation under this Federal Law, if those owners have applied to the hosting provider and have not complied with the requirements set out in Paragraph 1 of Part 7 of Article 15⁸ of this Federal Law.
Okay, folks, this brings us to the present day…
Roskomnadzor would monitor corporate VPNs that bypass blocks
Since 2017, the authorities have officially allowed companies to use VPNs that can bypass Russian censorship “for technical purposes necessary to support their operations.” Companies must also determine in advance which employees will use such a VPN.
A new bill to combat phone and cyber fraud would require companies to notify Roskomnadzor that they use corporate VPNs, though it is unclear how. The government and the FSB would also jointly approve rules for using these services and set requirements for employees who have access to them.
Using Russian hosting providers would become even harder for VPN services
The same bill would create a new Roskomnadzor register of individuals and companies that use servers in Russia to host VPN services. If caught bypassing blocks, they would be barred from entering into contracts with any provider in Russia for a full year. The government would develop procedures for Roskomnadzor and hosting providers to exchange this information.
Charges for international mobile internet traffic would be introduced to combat VPNs
According to Forbes, the Digital Development Ministry’s plans to charge mobile subscribers for international internet traffic first became known in March 2026. At the time, the ministry proposed an additional charge for subscribers who used more than 15 gigabytes of international traffic. This would put VPN users in a bind: When they connect to foreign servers, all their traffic becomes international. Using a good VPN on a mobile phone without additional workarounds would become very expensive.
At the time, telecommunications operators asked for the measure to be postponed. But officials have now returned to the idea. According to Kommersant, the government is proposing to raise the free international internet traffic allowance to 50 gigabytes and, for now, introduce the additional charge only on 5G networks.
The authorities plan to allocate even more money to combat VPNs
The draft federal budget for 2027–2029 provides for a sharp increase in spending on traffic filtering and internet blocks using TSPU. The annual subsidy to the Main Radio Frequency Center had been set at 9,870,441,200 rubles for 2027 and 9,844,821,700 rubles for 2028. The new draft budget simply puts a 1 in front of each figure. The planned subsidy for 2029 is roughly the same: 19,870,474,200 rubles. That amounts to nearly 60 billion rubles over three years. By comparison, in 2024, the authorities planned to spend almost the same amount, 59 billion rubles, on upgrading TSPU — but over six years (through 2030).

Sweden counts its difficult waters as an advantage
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
20:41:19 BST
04:41:19 KST

The Baltic archipelago that makes sonar so unreliable also gives a navy that knows it cover, concealment and freedom of manoeuvre, the commander of the Royal Swedish Navy’s 4th Naval Warfare Flotilla told the Apex Europe conference in London on Wednesday.
Captain Anna Jonsson, whose flotilla operates in the waters around Stockholm, opened a panel on countering undersea threats by describing the conditions her crews work in.
She said: “Sweden and my unit operates in a complex underwater environment. Our archipelago consists of tens of thousands of islands, narrow passages, shallow waters, and highly variable seabed conditions. Below the surface, rocks, wrecks and seabed formations create a challenging environment for our sensors.”
The behaviour of the water itself compounds everything the seabed is already doing. “Add variations of depth, temperature and salinity to that, and the performance of the sonar and underwater systems can change significantly from one area to another,” she said.
Her argument was that none of this amounts to a handicap for the navy that has learned to live in it. “Complexity is not necessarily a disadvantage always. For the force that understands the environment, it can provide cover, concealment and freedom of manoeuvre,” she said. “This has shaped the Swedish naval platforms, sensors, weapons and tactics for generations.”
That inheritance shows in what the Swedish navy buys, since small shallow-water submarines, mine countermeasures vessels, and corvettes built for the archipelago are a different proposition from blue-water designs, and the tactics that go with them have been refined over decades of operating in exactly these conditions.
“Sweden is in some way a small state. I have limited resources within my flotilla, but we still need to achieve combat effectiveness,” she said. “It’s important for us to understand the underwater terrain better than our adversary.”
The chair observed that the Baltic condenses problems that navies meet in diluted form elsewhere, with the Black Sea the closest comparison, and that anti-submarine warfare there is a different business from where NATO navies usually operate.
Commodore David Burton, who leads the alliance work on an allied underwater battlespace network, said understanding the environment is built into how NATO is organising its experimentation, with Allied Command Transformation targeting demonstrations region by region. The Baltic has had its turn, the Mediterranean has had another, and the High North comes next.
Sweden brought all of this into NATO when it joined.

Why Morocco is deepening ties with Israel despite public anger
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
19:33:11 UTC
04:33:11 KST

Breadcrumb
Why Morocco is deepening ties with Israel despite public anger
Morocco’s recent elections took place amid widespread disillusionment with electoral politics. Even the historic appointment of Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri as the country’s first female Prime Minister was largely seen as just a minor reshuffling of ministers. Real political power remains in the hands of the ‘Commander Of The Faithful’, King Mohammed VI.
And, while general election ballots were still being counted, the Moroccan Front for Supporting Palestine and Against Normalisation was leading three days of action across 45 cities to demonstrate opposition to normalisation with Israel. The people clearly felt that the streets were a much better space to have their views heard, and possibly change their political reality.
Abraham Accords
To understand Moroccan politics, the most important thing to know is that the King is still very much in charge. Although reforms following the 2011 Arab Spring gave the elected parliament some extra powers, the King still maintains executive authority over religious affairs, defence, foreign policy and national security matters. Therefore, different election results don’t necessarily signal change in Moroccan government policy on anything beyond traffic safety reforms.
The clearest example is Morocco’s increasingly friendly relationship with Israel. Despite the latest Arab Opinion Index finding that 89% of Moroccans opposed recognition of Israel (with only 6% supporting it), the government has announced that Morocco and Israel will upgrade their diplomatic relations to full embassies with ambassadors.
To really rub salt into the wound, it was also announced that Israel’s office will be relocated to Mehdi Ben Barka Avenue. Ben Barka was a Moroccan revolutionary socialist leader whose kidnapping and murder in 1965 was recently revealed to have been a Mossad operation.
Naturally, normalisation with Israel has provoked massive opposition among the Moroccan public, especially after the Gaza genocide. Even before the recent protests against normalisation, Moroccans have spent the past three years of Israel’s genocide in Gaza showing their solidarity with the Palestinians despite the risks of government repression.
Already in October 2023, it was being reported that ‘hardly a day goes by’ without a rally for Palestine led by a coalition of left-wing parties, trade unions, civil associations and Islamist organisations. Emmanuel Macron couldn’t even visit Israel without a demonstration being held outside the French consulate in Casablanca denouncing “the criminal position of the French government, which supports genocide in Gaza.”
The Moroccan security forces would forcibly break up a similar demonstration a year later, denouncing Macron for calling Hamas ‘barbaric’, with some activists requiring hospital treatment.
Mobilisations for Palestine continued elsewhere across 2024. In September, a national day of action resulted in simultaneous rallies in 50 cities demanding that humanitarian aid be allowed into Gaza. Meanwhile, students and university alumni organised the UM6P campaign to oppose normalisation with Israel in Moroccan universities, with specific opposition to ties with the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, known for its co-operation with the Israeli military.
The mobilisations escalated further in 2025, when Israel’s violation of the first Trump ceasefire agreement brought tens of thousands onto the streets in some of the biggest protests Morocco had seen so far. The government was said to have ‘tolerated’ most protests; however, anyone who had “implicated the monarchy in their complaints” was liable to be arrested.
The contradiction remains, however: the same public that shows such strong opposition to Moroccan foreign policy never utters even the mildest criticism of the monarch behind it.
Morocco’s official line is to position itself as a ‘mediator’ between Israel and the Palestinians, making the defence that this alignment allows it to influence Israel in a positive direction rather than just being treated as an enemy state. However, since the recent Gaza genocide, almost nobody actually believes this.
Quid pro quo
The more logical place to look for an explanation for Morocco’s warming towards Israel is Western Sahara, most of which has been illegally occupied by Morocco since 1975, despite the Polisario Front being recognised by the UN as its legitimate representatives. The United States and Israel are two of only a handful of states that recognise Morocco’s de facto sovereignty over Western Sahara as ‘legitimate’. This took place in 2020 as part of Donald Trump’s Abraham Accords.
The quid pro quo seems obvious here: Israel/the US recognise Morocco’s illegal annexation, and in return Morocco recognises Israel.
It should be noted that, although illegal, Morocco’s occupation of Western Sahara is far less violent than Israel’s treatment of the Palestinians. The most crucial difference is that Western Saharans, including the indigenous Sahrawi people, are legally treated as Moroccan citizens by the government and are permitted to move across the territory and into Morocco proper should they wish. They are not reduced to stateless non-citizens with no rights like Palestinians are.
Israel is also becoming an important supplier for the Moroccan military. According to the Jerusalem Post, Israel was the 3rd largest source of Moroccan military imports in 2019-23. These ties became public enough that in 2022 the Israeli military’s Chief of Staff even made an official visit to Morocco, though since the Gaza genocide they haven’t dared to be so brazen.
In August 2025, Morocco also conducted training exercises using EXTRA guided rockets provided by Elbit Systems (Israel’s largest weapons manufacturer), giving them access to precision medium-range munitions. Morocco also agreed to a $500m deal with Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI) to provide its Barak MX air defence system. Although this has not been publicly acknowledged, Reuters reported that Morocco will also purchase a $1 billion Ofek spy satellite from IAI to replace its existing satellites.
Not only has Morocco become a close military ally of Israel, but it is also making itself increasingly dependent on Israeli systems and technological infrastructure in the long term, making it difficult for even an anti-normalisation government to reverse the trend.
So what next for Morocco? So long as opposition is restricted to just expressing opinions against the treatment of the Palestinians, it’s likely that the government will continue to cosy up to Israel with impunity. This may even become more apparent if the United States continues to cut down on its forces in the region, leaving Israel as the more direct Western military outpost offering to protect local authorities from their own populations.
A potential flashpoint for popular opposition will be the 2030 World Cup, which Morocco is co-hosting and is currently busy preparing infrastructure for. If it goes smoothly, it will likely boost Moroccan soft power. However, the recent storming of Ceuta, where 70,000 Moroccans were so desperate to get into Spain that 141 drowned themselves trying, is not a sign of a happy country.
Daniel Lindley is a writer and trade union activist in the UK.

She Designed Meta’s New AI Logo. Then Came the Hate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
19:30:00 UTC
04:30:00 KST

Bay Area lettering artist Jesscia Hische knew that when she took a freelance gig to design the M logo for Meta’s new AI assistant Muse, it was bound to make some people angry. “AI is such a third rail, and Meta is such a third rail,” she tells me.
Still, as a small business owner who relies on client work to keep her two brick-and-mortar art and stationary shops in Oakland afloat, she says she needed the money. “New Work! (Don’t be mad at me),” Hische wrote in her newsletter last month. “I worked with Meta on an icon and logotype for their latest release: Muse, which just launched! It’s Meta’s foray into the AI agent / personal assistant world. I know folks have big feelings about both AI and Meta, but this has been a really fun project for so many reasons.”
The news quickly went viral on Threads, where dozens of fellow designers criticized Hische for selling out. She responded to the haters by trying to explain the decision:
“For the past year, I pretty much have 2-4 payrolls in my account at any given time, which if you own a small business, you know is pretty precarious,” she wrote. She added that she had also invested $100,000 in Studioworks, an admin platform she runs for creatives, and $30,000 in Drawling, her art shop for kids in Oakland, where she hosts classes and workshops. “I have 4 people on payroll including myself, my mom, and two shop employees,” she added. Nothing she said seemed to help.
“Disgusted,” wrote one user. “It’s not about money, it’s about ethics.”
Another person responded saying, “Doing this job is like doing a hit for the mob, and being surprised later when the mob takes you out too.” Other users posted photos of Hische’s house and speculated about her wealth and finances.
Hische had expected some pushback from the artist community, but the level of vitriol caught her off guard. Even if people didn’t like Meta, she felt the company should be commended for hiring an independent artist rather than using generative AI. But the backlash made it clear just how unpopular generative AI has become in some circles, to the point that working for one in any capacity is seen as a betrayal.
We spoke on the phone last week about the backlash, her design process, and whether she was instructed to not make the Muse logo look like a butthole.
This interview has been edited for clarity and length.
Zoë Schiffer: In your newsletter, you acknowledge that people have complicated feelings about Meta and about AI. Did that make it hard for you to take this job?
Jesscia Hische: The last year or two, my client work has been really slow, and my client work is what supports the other things I do, because the brick-and-mortar businesses are not hugely profitable. My margins are razor thin. I think between the two shops, I had like $10,000 in profit last year. I can't sustain myself on $10,000 a year.
So when the Meta project came around, it was like, alright! Let's get some money in the account so I can pay my staff and I don't have to feel so stressed out every time I have to run a pay cycle.
What were you hired to do, specifically?
I specialize in logo refreshes. I did the redesign of Squier from Fender, I redesigned Jeni’s Ice Cream a few years ago and did Southern Living magazine. When I work on logos, I want them to look like they went to the spa for a weekend—not that they went and got a ton of plastic surgery, you know? Just fresh and new, where you're like, “Oh, something's different. I can't tell what, but I like it.”
The [Meta] team had done an exploration of the M internally. They knew it wasn't quite right. It’s just a bunch of product designers and engineers designing type. Some of them are very skilled at typography, but it's just such a super unique thing to be able to draw letterforms. They wanted to refine what they had already done in terms of the M.
It was a huge sprint for that M. I did the work in two days. There were 32 different versions. The logotype took another two weeks.
What did the team tell you they wanted to change?
They had drawn the M as a single stroke, a vector stroke. It was the same width all the way around. When something is just a mono-weight stroke with no adjustments, there's not a lot of subtlety around the shape. This is where the fun happens with type design. As strokes touch each other and join, it creates this heavier pocket, visually. You get these little inky moments. And what type designers often do is sort of play with subtracting and adding bits of weight.
Their big ask was, “We want this thing to feel inspiring and creative and to get people thinking that Muse is a fun thing you can play with, not that it's like this very rigid, engineered, cold thing.”
How much do you get paid for a project like this?
I charged what I thought was an amazing fee for a two-day sprint for a big company, which was like $12,500. That’s an amazing amount of money to make in two days, but it’s not life-changing.
Meta chief AI officer Alexandr Wang has been talking about the logo recently, noting he’s happy it doesn’t look like a butthole, unlike some of Meta’s competitors.
I do think the “don't make it a butthole logo” thing was probably something they had top of mind internally. But for me, the discussions were more about looking at the Meta infinity loop logo and wanting the Muse logo to look like it was part of the same universe.
How did you decide to start talking about the work publicly?
I wanted to share it because I like sharing about my work. Within my newsletter group, everybody knows that my husband worked for Meta for ages, so they know that I have an association with the company.
I also wanted to acknowledge that AI is a very sensitive topic for people, but acknowledge it to an audience that understands my relationship to both Meta and AI.
I noticed that you responded to a bunch of the people criticizing you. Why?
Generally, if something happens online where there's a misunderstanding, I've been able to just come at [whoever is posting about me] and say “Hey, I hear you,” in an open and conversational way. I’m not trying to persuade them, I’m trying to say, “I agree with this part, but have you considered this?” That's always kind of worked for me in the past to help de-escalate stuff.
But with this, I made a comment about how hopefully, because of this job, I won't have to carry $50,000 in credit card debt through the holidays for my shop, because I have to do a bunch of inventory purchasing. Then that got taken out of context by someone being like, “This rich girl spends $50,000 on Christmas.” And I was just like, OK, wait, someone will see that and not the original post, and then all of a sudden it spins into this story about me being like a kajillionaire sitting on like a pile of emeralds, yelling at poor suffering artists, which is the opposite of my whole vibe.
How did it feel to you, when all this was happening?
The first day when I was like replying to people, I was not torn up about it at all, because I was like, “Oh, these people just don't understand that I'm a small-business owner, that I want to pay my employees. This helps me offer a health plan to like one of my employees. This is good!” And also, this company isn’t hiring me to use AI, I didn’t use AI at all in the process. Isn't this ultimately the future that we want? Large companies hiring independent artists to do things?
But then, as it started to escalate, it just blew up way bigger than I could have ever anticipated. It wasn't just a handful of people talking about it online. It felt like the entirety of Threads, you know? One of the things I have the hardest time with is feeling really misunderstood. I love teaching, but I'm not a guru that's making a predatory $1,500 course or whatever. I tend to charge $35 for a five-hour workshop.
I’m very intentional about things, and I don't just flippantly say yes to things that I obviously feel conflicted about, but I'm also like, this didn't feel like one of those conflicts just because they were paying me as an artist, and I wasn't using AI at all, you know?
So I felt deeply sad. I felt like I had been hit by a truck. For the two days following it, I sat in my bed and sobbed. It just made me feel so awful, like everything I have done up to this point, all the good decisions I tried to make, the free resources I've put out, have been for nothing.
Did it make you regret taking the job?
Not exactly. There was one camp of people who were like, “Of course, do the work if you need to, but just don't talk about it.” But I felt like I was doing a good thing for artists by commending a company that is hiring artists instead of making generative work.
Where do you think the reaction comes from, for designers in particular? Is it fear?
I mean, the fear is real. There’s real fears about AI's impact on commercial art. My husband and I really got into it at one point, because he was working on AI and really excited about it, and I was vehemently anti-AI. Eventually I started seeing the infrastructure, low-level data-processing side of it and how useful it is for things outside of creativity. Then I was like, OK, well, there are silver linings to using this thing. I think that softened the edges for me. My husband also came around to AI’s impact on commercial art, which helped.
Most of the folks in AI are like, “AI helps creativity because it makes human-made things more valuable!” Maybe in fine art, but that's not how commercial art works. Of course, there’s anti-AI purists, and their whole thing is that AI is built on theft, which is true. I think I’m going to benefit from the Anthropic settlement, because they've definitely scraped my books.
I don't use AI for generative art or anything like that. I just use it for admin and for help with coding and web building. But anytime that AI takes the place of a person or does the heavy lifting on stuff that requires human creativity, that's when it becomes problematic.
This is an edition of the Model Behavior newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.
