Russian billionaire Mikhail Gutseriev spent years fighting EU sanctions over Belarus. He finally won (but remains sanctioned over Russia’s war in Ukraine).
EU ambassadors removed Russian billionaire Mikhail Gutseriev from the bloc’s Belarus sanctions list on October 7, Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty reported.
The EU imposed the sanctions on Gutseriev in June 2021. The Council of the EU cited his close ties to Alexander Lukashenko, alleging that he financially supported Lukashenko’s regime and benefited from it. The council pointed to his investments in the construction of the Nezhinsky mining and processing plant and his attendance at Lukashenko’s 2020 inauguration.
Gutseriev spent several years challenging the sanctions in European courts. In May 2026, he won a ruling annulling the Council of the EU’s latest decision to renew them. The court found that the council had not presented enough up-to-date evidence that he still had ties to Lukashenko’s regime.
Removal from the Belarus list does not mean all sanctions against Gutseriev have been lifted. He remains subject to EU sanctions over Russia’s aggression against Ukraine.
In 2024, the Czech publications Denik N and Respekt reported that Gutseriev had offered to share information about Vladimir Putin’s and Lukashenko’s plans with Western intelligence services in exchange for having sanctions lifted. To that end, he met twice with representatives of the FBI and Czech police in Prague in 2022.
In September, the EU lifted sanctions against two Russian billionaires: USM Holdings founder Alisher Usmanov and Alfa Group co-founder Mikhail Fridman. Both were placed on sanctions lists after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. EU authorities considered both billionaires part of Putin’s inner circle.
France and Slovakia pushed to lift sanctions against Usmanov, while Luxembourg advocated for Fridman. The effort to lift Usmanov’s sanctions was intended to advance talks with Azerbaijan on the release of prisoners. Luxembourg’s support for Fridman has been linked to his lawsuit over frozen assets — he is seeking $16 billion from the country’s authorities.

Mélenchon declares ‘Bastille retaken’ after major student rally in Paris
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
17:21:29 UTC
02:21:29 KST

The mass student-led movement emerged over a range of issues including long school days, overcrowded schools, teacher absences.
Jean-Luc Mélenchon, leader of the hard left France Unbowed party took to X on Thursday to declare the Bastille had been "retaken", after students staged demonstrations across the country — including a major rally at Paris' infamous Place de la Bastille.
Meanwhile, later in the day, France's Education Minister Édouard Geffray announced in an interview with broadcaster TF1 later that 3,000 substitute teacherswould be deployed to schools facing critical shortages.
Thursday's major protests were part of the student-led movement which began on 17 September in the suburbs of Paris, before gradually developing into a broader campaign addressing issues including long school days, overcrowded schools, teacher absences.
The mass gathering which took place at the place de la Bastille started off peacefully, before clashes with the police later erupted, with tear gas and a water cannon fired at protesters.
On social media, Mélenchon stated "powerful demonstration by the youth who carry their demands in the most beautiful way possible! Immense pride. See you on Tuesday, October 13, at the call of the youth unions and workers."
The storming of the Bastille in 1789 marked a major turning point in the French Revolution and became a symbol of the people’s resistance to royal authority.
The leader of France Unbowed and his allies have been accused by their opponents of stoking unrest and manipulating young people for political gain. Mélenchon has rejected these criticisms, underlining that despite the fact that his party supports the protests, they were independently launched by students.
The student and professional union coalition has called for another day of protests and strikes on 13 October, with a further major mobilisation planned for 17 October.
What did protestors say on the ground?
Cathy, a history teacher in a secondary school located in Paris told Euronews she had decided to accompany her students to the Bastille rally, because she backed their demands in favour of a change in France's education system.
"The students have demands that are very close to the ones teachers have been putting forward years. The system is degraded and it's because there has been no response for so long, that this is happening," she stated.
Meanwhile, one schoolboy warned that it was "normal" if violent outbursts occurred, if students' demands were "not be heard."
"All the revolutions in history have served a purpose. In 1789, there were a lot of deaths. We don't want to have deaths, but we could revert to violence as a means of expression. The goal is not to perpetrate violence to hurt people, but it's to use violence to change the system that harms us", he said.
Despite this, many other school pupils said they backed peaceful protests, instead condoning police violence.
Many students questioned by Euronews at the rally had not heard of the government's mass online consultation, which was launched earlier in the week in order to collate student opinions and drive possible policy proposals. France's Education Ministry said it surpassed 40,000 responses within days of its launch.
Breaking down the numbers
According to the Interior Ministry, 71,500 people took part in Thursday's protests, with 24,500 in Paris. Meanwhile, an estimated 55,000 people took part in protests outside schools, amid school blockades that were staged across the country.
The Education Ministry said 375 schools were fully or partially closed for the day.
Authorities also reported an increase in what they described as cases of "urban violence", saying they took place on the "margins' of peaceful student demonstration, acting as a 'stain on their legitimate expression.'
Police have made more than 6,600 arrests since late September, when students, most of them under 18, began protesting to demand more education funding, according to the Interior Ministry.

US judge orders return of Egyptian deported to Equatorial Guinea
A US judge has ordered the Trump administration to facilitate the release and return of an Egyptian man who was deported to Equatorial Guinea this year and has since been jailed there.
Ahmed Soliman is one of hundreds of migrants sent from the US to African countries under so-called third-country deportation deals that the US government has used to accelerate removals.
Human Rights Watch said in a report published on Thursday that 536 people had been deported to African countries "that are neither their country of citizenship nor habitual residence" between January 2025 and August 2026.
Last month, Soliman said he had faced rough treatment by Equatorial Guinean police officers. Video obtained by Reuters showed police pulling firearms on migrants including Soliman.
After Reuters published its story, Soliman was taken into custody and has been held incommunicado at a gendarmerie station that has also been used to detain human rights activists.
In a ruling seen by Reuters on Thursday, US judge John C. Hinderaker said the Department of Homeland Security must facilitate Soliman's release from custody and his return to the US. That includes arranging any travel documentation he would need to return.
The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Equatorial Guinea has also not responded to requests for comment about Soliman's case.
Soliman wrote in a declaration to an immigration judge last year that he feared being killed in Egypt because he is gay.
Reuters has documented 40 cases in which migrants granted US legal protection after being persecuted for their LGBT status were deported to third countries in Africa that either criminalize same-sex relations or have been described by the State Department as hostile to LGBT people.

A lake pilgrimage and a quiet car ride to beach: last hours of sisters who took own lives in Brighton
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
17:19:48 UTC
02:19:48 KST

Jane Adetoro and her younger sisters, Christina and Rebecca Walters, were “the closest sisters and the best friends”, according to their family. Devoted to their father, Joseph, whom they messaged every day, the adult siblings lived quiet lives in the flat they shared in west London and would do everything together.
When they died in May this year, it was no different. Early in the morning of 13 May, the sisters’ bodies were recovered from the sea in Brighton, hours after a taxi had dropped the three women at the beachfront.
On Thursday, an inquest in the city found that the women, who all drowned, died by suicide a day after making a pilgrimage together to the lake in Birmingham where their mother died by drowning 16 years earlier.
In a statement, Joseph Jacobson told the inquest that the scale of his loss was indescribable. “There are no words that can adequately express the pain of losing a child. To lose all three of my precious daughters, Jane, Christina and Rebecca, is a heartbreak beyond anything I could ever have imagined.”
Jacobson, who attended the inquest by video link, said he could not understand why their lives had ended so suddenly. “You were my daughters, you will always be my daughters and I will love you for the rest of my life. May your beautiful souls rest in perfect peace,” he said.
Precisely why Jane, 36, Christina, known as Tina, 32, and 31-year-old Rebecca, or Becky, decided to end their lives may never be known, the senior coroner Penelope Schofield told the hearing at Woodvale coroner’s court in Brighton.
“These three sisters lived very secluded lives. They were incredibly private. We don’t know why they took this course of action or indeed why they chose to do it in Brighton,” Schofield said.
What police were able to establish, after initial public bafflement over the circumstances of the tragedy, is how the women spent the day before they died. On the night of 11 May, the sisters travelled by Uber from their home in Greenford, west London, to Birmingham, where they were dropped off at 11.36pm in Linton Walk, in the north of the city.
This was the address where Jane and Rebecca, then 20 and 15, were living with their mother, Janice Adetoro, when she disappeared on 5 January 2010, prompting an anguished public appeal by family members. (Christina, then 16, was reportedly living with her father at the time.) Janice’s body was recovered a month later from Brookvale Park Lake, which runs to the end of Linton Walk. She was 43.
Described as a doting mother, Janice had been suffering from “paranoid delusions”, the inquest into her death heard. She was sectioned and admitted to a psychiatric unit, the Sunday Times reported, but was discharged from a home treatment team weeks before her death.
The tragedy of the sisters’ deaths “wasn’t a story that started in May”, their cousin Natalie Walters-Daniel told the newspaper last month. “It was a story that started long before.”
DCI Mark Cullimore, of Sussex police, told the inquest there was no CCTV to show what the three sisters did in the time they were in Birmingham, but less than two hours after arriving, at 1.28am on 12 May, they were picked up by taxi and driven back to their London flat.
The inquest heard that Christina, who had recently graduated from Brunel University of London and worked as an accountant, had experienced anxiety and depression since her mother’s death and made “extensive searches” about suicide in the days before her own death.
Jane, who was also an accountant, had paid off a loan in full on 11 May. Described as “extremely intelligent”, Jane was said by family members to have taken on a maternal role after the death of her own mother.
Rebecca, “the baby” to relatives, worked in HR. She was previously described as “mischievous” and “the lively one who was always cracking jokes”.
The two younger sisters had changed their names to their mother’s maiden name after her death. “Their mother’s death was a hard thing to carry and bear,” their cousin said. “They held a certain level of their feelings to themselves … I believe it was their own coping mechanism.”
On the evening on 12 May, the inquest heard, the three women caught a train to Brighton, arriving at 10.20pm, and then took a car to the beachfront near the marina. The Uber driver was struck by the lack of conversation between them, he later told police.
Sussex police reviewed hundreds of hours of CCTV to establish that for at least four hours the women paced the seafront in the darkness. They were picked up periodically in snatches of footage, last being seen at 2.42am. It was a windy night and the sea was particularly rough, Cullimore told the inquest.
Emergency services were called after a cyclist reported seeing a body on the beach shortly before 5.45am. Jane was brought to shore by an RNLI crew and declared dead at the scene. Christina’s body was also located by the lifeboat crew. Rebecca’s body was recovered from Brighton beach where it appeared to have been washed to shore. None of the women had been able to swim.
Cullimore told the inquest he had “remained open-minded throughout and always considered whether there was third-party involvement” but he was now satisfied there had not been. There was no evidence that any of the sisters had used drugs or alcohol, and no indication of any violence.
The coroner found that all three had intended to die. “I will record in respect for each of them that on 12 May they entered the sea at West Beach, Brighton, to end their lives,” she said. “They could not swim and the conditions were adverse.”

Colombia faces hurdles to meet IMF commitments under possible lending deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
17:19:28 UTC
02:19:28 KST

Colombia faces hurdles to meet IMF commitments under possible lending deal
BOGOTA, Oct 8 - Colombia would face major hurdles in meeting any commitments it makes under a prospective agreement with the International Monetary Fund, from which it is seeking billions of dollars amid a fiscal crisis, according to current and former officials and economists.
A team from the country's finance ministry traveled to Washington this week to meet with the multilateral lender, at the direction of recently inaugurated President Abelardo De La Espriella, who is seeking a way out of a crisis marked by soaring debt and lower tax revenue.
According to 10 economists and current and former officials consulted by Reuters, Colombia could seek between $8 billion and $20 billion in assistance.
Most of them agreed the IMF instrument best suited to Colombia's circumstances would be the Precautionary and Liquidity Line, a facility designed for countries with sound economic fundamentals and institutional frameworks but that face vulnerabilities.
Colombia's government has projected a fiscal deficit of 7.2% of its gross domestic product this year and a record 9.4% of GDP next year. It has Special Drawing Rights equivalent to roughly $2.78 billion, allowing it to access about $16.6 billion over the lifetime of the SDR agreement.
While the Andean nation meets most of the criteria for a PLL, including a sound financial system, strong monetary policy framework and central bank independence, it would need to demonstrate progress on the fiscal sustainability of its debt to qualify. Repeated budget overruns have eroded confidence in its policy framework.
In its 2025 review, before Colombia's fiscal outlook deteriorated further, the IMF said the country needed to cut its budget by at least the equivalent of 3.2% of GDP over three years.
A PLL could be less politically costly than a Stand-By Arrangement because it is intended for countries whose economic policies are already broadly sound, although it can still include fiscal targets and reform requirements.
The government should seek $20 billion in loans from the IMF with an average maturity of four years, former Finance Minister Mauricio Cardenas said.
"I think it is an amount that is proportionate to the size of our economy," said Cardenas, who took part in previous IMF credit-line renewals. "An additional benefit is that it would allow us to prepay expensive debt and replace it with this cheaper debt."
Several others said an IMF agreement would boost market confidence, lower Colombia's risk premiums and help unlock additional funding from institutions such as the World Bank, the Inter-American Development Bank and other multilateral lenders.
"An agreement with the IMF expands confidence in that debt, and creditors could reduce the cost of Colombia's existing loans. It would generate that positive effect, not immediately, but rather as commitments are met over time," said Juan Carlos Ramirez, head of the autonomous committee that oversees compliance with the so-called "fiscal rule" meant to prevent a deterioration in government finances.
"But as long as the deficit persists year after year, it can only provide some relief over the coming years. It is not the solution to the problem," he added.
DIVIDED CONGRESS
Colombia faces the challenge of setting achievable fiscal targets, several of those consulted said.
"The main risk is failing to comply with IMF requirements. The world will be watching Colombia, and if we fail to meet any of the targets the IMF sets, not only could a disbursement be withheld, but everyone would see that the country was unable to deliver," said Munir Jalil, chief economist for the Andean region at BTG Pactual.
Analysts said a key commitment would be the so-called "Rescue Law," a bill containing spending cuts equivalent to 2.2% of GDP, or about $14 billion, that De La Espriella's government plans to propose to lawmakers in mid-October. The president faces a deeply divided Congress.
"There has never been a fiscal adjustment reform of that size in a single year (in Colombia)," said Andres Pardo, a former deputy finance minister and former head of macro strategy for Latin America at XP Investments. "That doesn't mean it can't be done, but frankly it seems difficult."
"While the government has majorities, they are quite fragile and depend on coalition parties," he added.
Colombia drew $5.4 billion from an IMF Flexible Credit Line to help address the COVID-19 pandemic, closing out the credit last year after it was fully repaid. REUTERS

Profanity and physical force during a lesson: a scandal has erupted in Odesa region over a teacher’s conduct

In Odesa region, a teacher was dismissed after a video emerged online in which he allegedly uses physical force against a student and uses obscene language. This was reported by UNN, citing a statement by Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets.
Details
According to Lubinets, he saw a video on social media showing a teacher swearing at and shoving a child during a lesson. Lubinets also noted that legal and educational mechanisms exist for resolving conflict situations in schools. In particular, parents, school psychologists, social educators and the administration of the educational institution can be involved.

"If the facts recorded on the video are confirmed, the competent authorities must provide an assessment," he added.
The Ombudsman emphasized that a school must remain a safe environment for children, where they can receive knowledge and support without fearing aggression from adults.

Israel’s downgrading of UK consulate aims to tighten its hold on Jerusalem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
17:16:03 UTC
02:16:03 KST

Israel’s attempt to close the British consulate general in Jerusalem was primarily designed to deter London from imposing sanctions on settlements in occupied Palestine. But it also served the current government’s ambitions to fully annex Jerusalem as a national capital, diplomatic and legal experts said.
The UK mission to the city has an unusual diplomatic status, which dates back to before the founding of the state of Israel, rooted in a vision of Jerusalem as a neutral enclave under international control.
Unlike other consulates general around the world, it is not a satellite of the British embassy in Tel Aviv. Instead its diplomats are part of an independent team, who report directly to London.
That is anathema to those in Israel who claim all of Jerusalem as their territory. Israeli forces occupied East Jerusalem in 1967, and the Knesset passed a law annexing the city in 1980, but that status has not been recognised by most of the world.
Gideon Sa’ar, the Israeli foreign minister, threatened to close the consulate general a month ago in an attempt to deter the UK government from proceeding with plans to bar trade with West Bank settlements and put sanctions on companies that provide them with services including financing.
The UK threatened to respond with a mass expulsion of diplomats but the two countries appear to have backed away from a full-blown diplomatic spat as Israel prepares for national elections, due on 27 October.
Britain will rebrand its consulate general as a UK “mission” and reduce the number of diplomats, but it will remain independent of Tel Aviv in a compromise one source described as a temporary “ceasefire”. If Israel gets a new leader in three weeks, negotiations on the status of the consulate and its staff could resume.
Maintaining a foothold in Jerusalem and the independent status of UK diplomats was important, said Daniel Seidemann, an Israeli lawyer and expert in the geopolitics of Jerusalem who has advised western diplomats including a British foreign secretary.
“The arrangement that the UK arrived at with Israel was probably the optimal among a number of options that were even worse. So I’m not faulting anybody, but this is far from a victory,” he said.
“The British presence in Jerusalem after almost a century and a half has been downgraded from one of the diplomatic mission to another office. And that is a stark qualitative change.”
There are seven other consulates general in East Jerusalem, all opened before 1948, representing their nations’ interests in Jerusalem and occupied Palestine. Like the UK one, they are independent and report directly to their foreign ministries.
They have long been a particular thorn in Israel’s side because of their unusual status, which reflects the designation of Jerusalem as “corpus separatum”, an independent body, under the UN’s 1947 partition plan for historic Palestine.
Never implemented, it envisaged Jerusalem as a sort of Vatican-like independent enclave, under international administration. That clashes with Israel’s claim on the city, and Sa’ar’s attack on the consulate should be seen in that context, and not purely as a response to sanctions.
“This is part of the overall attempt to establish the primacy of a very specific Jewish-Israeli Jerusalem,” Seidemann said. “Any diplomatic presence in Jerusalem that does not pay fealty to the government of Israel and Israel’s sole sovereignty is targeted.”
Other countries have missions based in Ramallah to manage relations with Palestinians, but these are technically subsidiary to Tel Aviv embassies.
The US had a consulate general but closed it after Donald Trump recognised Jerusalem as the capital of Israel during his first presidency.
The UK sanctions plan represents the most consequential attempt by one of Israel’s allies to halt settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank. Israeli banks are rattled by a proposal they fear could affect their business, Haaretz reported on Thursday.
An assessment by Israel’s Association of Banks laid out concerns that they could be affected, and they are refusing to say whether they will provide financial guarantees needed to underpin construction contracts for the E1 settlement in the West Bank.
When Ed Miliband, the UK foreign secretary, announced his plans, he said the timing was driven partly by the Israeli government’s decision to put out tenders for this project. Israel’s finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, has boasted that it will “bury” the possibility of a Palestinian state by severing parts of the occupied West Bank.
Ilan Baruch, a former Israeli ambassador to South Africa, left diplomatic service to advocate for a two-state solution, including pushing foreign governments to move beyond condemnations of Israeli policy to imposing a “meaningful price”.
The threats to Britain’s Jerusalem consulate were a sign the UK had finally done that. “I was relieved [by Israel’s position], realising Miliband touched a nerve,” he said.
Renaming the consulate while preserving its independent status indicated Israel had stepped back from confrontation, helped by Britain making smaller “face-saving” concessions, he said.

UK: Burnham faces challenge from Greens in Starmer's old seat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08

Breadcrumb
UK: Burnham faces challenge from Greens in first election test after Starmer's resignation
Voters in London are heading to the polls to cast their ballots in a by-election in former Prime Minister Kier Starmer's constituency of Holborn and St Pancras.
The vote is essentially a two-horse race between Camden Council leader Sagal Abdi-Wali, who is standing for the Labour Party, and Green Party leader Zack Polanski.
The election is the first real test at the polls for Labour's Andy Burnham since he became Prime Minister in July.
"We're feeling happy with our campaign," a Labour Party campaign source told The New Arab, "there are certainly people who are willing to give us another look."
The seat is up for grabs after Kier Starmer resigned as an MP shortly after being ousted from the premiership, despite his promise to stay and represent the North London constituency.
Starmer, who won Labour's biggest general election victory since 1997, received criticism for his frequent U-turns, his appointment of Peter Mandelson, who was linked to Jeffrey Epstein, as US ambassador, and his stance on Israel and Palestine.
In October 2023, Starmer said Israel had the right to withhold water and power from Palestinians in Gaza.
By officially recognising the state of Palestine last year, the former Prime Minister tried to recover his reputation among voters sympathetic to Palestinians.
In a June 2026 YouGov poll, 32% of the British public expressed sympathy for Palestinians as compared to 16% who are sympathetic to Israelis.
However, by the end of his term Starmer had very low approval ratings and never managed to regain the trust of voters.
Many in the Green Party credit their victory in February's by-election in the previously Labour-held seat of Gorton and Denton, as well as their success in the May local elections, in which they picked up more than 400 council seats, as a major reason for Starmer's resignation.
"We've ensured Labour have moved to the left and made some more progressive policies," Ben Jameson, a Green Party councillor who is campaigning in Holborn and St Pancras told The New Arab, "we'll see how those are delivered."
The Holborn and St Pancras by-election will be a test of how well the Greens are doing with Labour under new leadership.
Polanski's campaign has largely focused on his claim that in Parliament, he could hold Burnham's government to account.
Burnham has marked himself as a stronger left-wing voice than his predecessor, criticising 'neoliberalism,' and 'trickle-down economics.'
His government is also taking a stronger stance against Israel. In September he announced limited sanctions against Israeli settlements in the West Bank.
That move created a diplomatic row between the UK and Israel, resulting in Israel's illegal closure of the British Consulate in Jerusalem on the day of the by-election.
On Sunday, the Green Party voted in favour of a motion declaring that Zionism is racism.
The motion has created fractures in the party, which Green MP Adrian Ramsay said he was "deeply upset" by. After it passed, the motion's author, Lubna Speitan told The New Arab, "This is hope for the future of our people, for the future of all oppressed." Polanski did not vote on the motion.
"It's one of those really frustrating things where the motion has almost put away who the victims are in this whole thing, which are the Palestinians," Jameson said.
The results of the Holborn and St Pancras by-election may give some clarity on where voters stand on both Burnham's Labour and Polanski's Greens. However, a constituency of 75,000 people in a country of 69 million is just one part of a broader picture.
The results of the vote are expected in the early hours of Friday morning.

Russian missile strike on Ukraine kills 30 on packed city buses, as Moscow says "no clear path" to peace
At least 30 people were killed Thursday when a Russian guided bomb slammed into a street near two packed city buses in Kramatorsk, eastern Ukraine, according to officials. At least 18 more people were wounded in the attack, the Donetsk region's governor said.
"There is no doubt that Russia is cynically targeting civilians," Oleksandr Honcharenko, head of the Kramatorsk military administration, said in a statement, adding that rescue efforts were hampered by Russia launching further attacks with small drones.
Video shared online by Ukraine's Ministry of Internal Affairs showed bodies on the debris-strewn road near the charred, twisted metal shells of destroyed vehicles.
According to the ministry, three more people were killed by Russian shelling in neighboring villages, where emergency services pulled one body from a collapsed house.
It was the second consecutive day of heavy attacks by Russia. On Wednesday morning, a missile hit a five-story apartment building in the northern city of Pryluky, killing at least 22 people. Rescue workers said at least 50 more people were wounded in the strike.
"Russia comes to the Ukrainian land with death. It hits our cities, kills our people and multiplies its crimes every day," Donetsk Gov. Vadym Filashkin said after the Thursday attack in Kramatorsk, accusing Russia of deliberately trying to "kill as many people as possible."
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Thursday in Moscow that he didn't see a "clear path" to any peaceful resolution to the war, which was sparked by Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Last week, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the Reuters news agency his country would double down on attacking Russian oil refineries in response to what he said were expanding Russian tactics aimed at forcing people to abandon Kyiv and other major cities by increasingly targeting civilian infrastructure. Zelenskyy stressed that Ukraine would not target Russian civilians.
"We saw documents and we know that they allow them [Russian forces] to attack infrastructure, logistics, and especially to attack in the cities, in the villages, everywhere, roads, schools, hospitals," said Zelenskyy, "to pressure people to leave the capital, leave different cities. This is the goal of the operation."
Russia has always denied targeting civilians, despite regular attacks on residential buildings throughout the war. But the foreign ministry in Moscow, in a recent statement, urged foreign nationals and diplomatic personnel to leave the Ukrainian capital, warning of "systematic and sustained strikes against military targets in Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities."
The Ukrainian military said later Thursday that it had hit Russia's largest oil refinery, 1,550 miles from the country's shared border in Siberia. The sprawling facility in Omsk, operated by state company Gazpromneft, was last attacked in July, according to Reuters.
Ukraine's military did not provide details about the strike but said the refinery was supplying fuel to Russia's forces.
Another Ukrainian strike hit a data center belonging to Russian technology and AI company Yandex on Thursday, which said it was working to restore equipment at the facility after a fire that forced it to suspend operations at the site. The impact brought some of the tech giant's cloud services down.
Visiting Pryluky in northern Ukraine on Thursday morning, Zelenskyy reiterated his request for the U.S. to increase pressure on Russia, adding that Ukrainian negotiators would visit the U.S. for discussions on Friday and Saturday.

AI and Corporate Training: A Focus on Opportunities and Risks in London
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
19:11:22 CEST
02:11:22 KST

The Italian Embassy in London hosted the launch of a collaborative project between Angelini Academy and University College London (UCL) aimed at understanding how to reshape corporate training in light of the growing use of Artificial Intelligence. The event opened with remarks by the diplomatic mission’s deputy head of mission, Riccardo Smimmo, and the CEO of Angelini Industries, Sergio Marullo di Condojanni.
                                    
The panel featured Joe Devlin, professor of Cognitive Neuroscience at UCL, and other faculty members from the same London university: Vivianna Fang He, associate professor of Strategy and Entrepreneurship at the School of Management, and Davide Ravasi, director of the School of Management. Also in attendance was Andrea Prencipe, president of the Angelini Academy. The discussion was moderated by Alessandra Rizzo, a journalist for Sky News UK.  During the discussion, the speakers examined the potential risks of AI, including, in particular, the fact that the unregulated use of this technology—by providing shortcuts that appear to ensure efficiency and timeliness—would eliminate the cognitive effort essential to learning and thus, in the long term, the capacity for critical analysis and decision-making. However, it was noted that there are methods for employing artificial intelligence in teaching and learning that would not only preserve but actually strengthen these abilities. 
      These are the methods that the collaborative project between Angelini Academy and UCL aims to promote for the training of executives and managers and for experimenting with the regulated and responsible use of AI. The research findings will be used to develop training systems that can support professional development throughout one’s career.

France: Police clash with protesters at Paris student rally
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
17:10:00 UTC
02:10:00 KST

France: Police clash with protesters at Paris student rally
October 8, 2026
Thousands of students demonstrated near Bastille Square in Paris on Thursday afternoon, as France's nationwide student protests continue.
Crowds of students climbed the famous Bastille Monument. Some waved the French flag and sang the national anthem.
Footage from Reuters TV showed riot police charging at protesters with batons as they moved in to clear the square.
Across France, some 71,500 people took part in Thursday's protests and police detained more than 500, the Interior Ministry said.
France will send 3,000 substitute teachers "within the next hours" to struggling high schools, the education minister said Thursday.
"Within the next hours, 3,000 teachers will be joining these institutions," Education Minister Edouard Geffray told the evening news on the TF1 television channel.
Geffray said they would be at schools between Friday to Tuesday.
Students barricade high school
Earlier on Thursday, students barricaded Helene Boucher High School in northeastern Paris with trash bins before police broke up the protest with tear gas.
As students gathered at the school, riot police assembled in the side streets. Many protesters wore surgical masks or hoodies, apparently to avoid identification.
The school has been a flashpoint for clashes in the French capital and was one of hundreds of schools disrupted by protests on Thursday.
Although the rallies have largely been peaceful, some demonstrators have set fires and vandalized bus shelters.
In response, the police have used tear gas, batons, and blast balls. Human rights groups and children accuse officers of using excessive force.
Following an incident in which a teenager's hand was blown off, the government suspended the use of stun grenades for crowd control on Wednesday.
Since late September, when students, most of whom are under 18, began protesting to demand more education funding, police have made more than 6,600 arrests, according to the Interior Ministry.
Government promises response
On Wednesday evening, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu promised that the government would present "concrete, quick, and fully funded responses" to the protests by the end of October.
Nevertheless, student protest leaders said this was not good enough and called for more marches.
In a televised address, Lecornu also lamented the "violence, students and staff being attacked, police officers and gendarmes injured, schools set on fire or vandalized, thousands of hours of classes lost, not to mention threats and insults."

“They will explain, persuade, recruit, motivate, and get people out to vote. With God’s help, we can bring victory to the national camp and continue all the wonderful processes in settlement, security, Torah, education, Jewish identity, and extensive social work,” he added.
Netanyahu: Right coming together is 'matter of national survival'
Netanyahu praised Smotrich for his work as finance minister throughout the government’s term, while speaking at the conference.
“I’m talking about all those crossroads over these past three years when we had to overcome, together, pressure from within and from abroad to surrender, give in, retreat, and bow our heads,” Netanyahu said.
“This is not only a matter of national honor – it is a matter of national survival,” he added.
RZP stated that the goal of the conference was to “create a broad network of thousands of activists with the aim of bringing tens of thousands of right-wing voters to the polls.”
Recent polls have shown that neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the opposition bloc seeking to replace him can secure a majority without support from Arab parties. A Wednesday Channel 13 poll projected 55 seats for Netanyahu’s bloc and 50 for the opposition bloc, excluding Arab parties.
On Tuesday, Otzma Yehudit had accused Likud of seeking to form a unity government with Gadi Eisenkot, chairman of the Yashar party and the leading candidate for prime minister in the opposition bloc in recent polling.
Ben-Gvir on Thursday posted a picture of Smotrich at the joint conference on social media, alongside the message, “I love every Jew.”
Unclear if Otzma Yehudit will sign surplus-vote agreement
It remains unclear whether Otzma Yehudit will sign a surplus-vote agreement before the approaching submission deadline.
The RZP party platform has focused on Jewish identity, settlement expansion, and Israeli sovereignty in the West Bank.
The party has recently faced criticism over its support for contentious legislation advanced by Netanyahu’s coalition in the Knesset and sponsored by the haredi (ultra-Orthodox) parties. Critics argued that the legislation encouraged draft evasion amid the IDF’s severe manpower crisis.
Smotrich has pushed to expand Israeli settlements in the West Bank, with over 100 initiated during his tenure, sparking international condemnation.
In the previous election, RZP ran on a joint ticket with Otzma Yehudit, allowing both parties to cross the electoral threshold.
In August, Netanyahu urged Ben-Gvir and Smotrich to join forces again in the upcoming election to strengthen the right-wing bloc, but Ben-Gvir refused.

Anti-drone electronic warfare systems by Ukraine's Phantom Defense tested in Pentagon programme
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

Anti-drone electronic warfare systems by Ukraine's Phantom Defense tested in Pentagon programme
Electronic warfare (EW) systems developed and manufactured by the Ukrainian defence tech company Phantom Defense have been tested in the United States as part of the second stage of the Pentagon's Drone Dominance programme.
Source: Phantom Defense press service in a comment to Ukrainska Pravda
Details: The EW systems were tested at the Fort Carson military base in Colorado. According to Phantom Defense, the company became one of three manufacturers engaged by the Pentagon to create a counter-UAV environment for testing drones.
Quote from Phantom Defense press service: "For Gauntlet II, Phantom Defense deployed a counter-UAV system that combined video interception tools, a C2 [command and control – ed.] system for detection, classification, engagement and confirmation of suppression results, as well as EW systems."
The Ukrainian company used its Specter PRO dome and directional EW system in the US. It is designed to protect strongpoints, brigade headquarters and critical infrastructure facilities. In addition, Phantom Defense deployed other in-house devices during the programme, including its Specter L, X and XL family of compact systems.
Quote from Phantom Defense press service: "Phantom Defense also demonstrated Streamhunter, a video interception tool that successfully intercepted video signals from UAVs during the trials. All deployed solutions are integrated with the C2 system, which provided situational awareness, transmitted data on detected targets and coordinated the operation of countermeasures, specifically the EW systems and Streamhunter."
According to the company, the Ukrainian-made EW systems successfully suppressed the drones being tested during the Gauntlet II stage of the Drone Dominance programme. In addition to operating in various weather conditions, the systems recreated the environment that UAV operators face on the front line.
Quote from Phantom Defense: "The successful performance of the team and its counter-UAV solutions caught the attention of the US side: following Gauntlet II, Phantom Defense received an invitation to take part in a number of upcoming events and trials under the Drone Dominance programme."
The Drone Dominance programme has a budget of US$1.1 billion and involves testing solutions from 25 manufacturers in the initial phase of the competition. Following the first phase, plans are in place to procure around 30,000 drones from 11 companies for a total of US$150 million.
Background: Earlier, Ukrainska Pravda reported that the US military had placed an additional order for 1,320 F10 FPV attack drones from the Ukrainian company F-Drones as part of the Pentagon's Drone Dominance programme.

Mamdani denounces Gaza war in October 7 statement

Breadcrumb
Mamdani denounces Gaza war in October 7 statement, amid pro-Israel backlash
New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani issued a statement on Wednesday marking the third anniversary of the Hamas-led attacks on 7 October 2023, describing the killing of around 1,200 Israelis during the incursion that triggered a three-year genocidal war in Gaza as a “horrific war crime”.
However, pro-Israel groups attacked him for acknowledging Gaza's suffering in his statement.
In his first 7 October commemoration as NYC mayor since taking office earlier this year, Mamdani released a lengthy statement mourning the Israelis killed in the attacks and commemorating the 251 people taken hostage, describing the anniversary as “profoundly painful for so many New Yorkers.”
He also condemned Israel’s military campaign in Gaza, accusing the US government of complicity in Israeli war crimes.
“The suffering did not begin nor end that day,” he said, referring to the 7 October attacks.
“That suffering has intensified with every Israeli bomb dropped on ambulances waiting outside hospitals, every drone strike targeting a residential building or journalist, and every shipment of food aid turned away at a border crossing.”
“It instead continued through the Israeli government’s devastating, ongoing genocide in Gaza in which it has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians — including more than 21,000 children.”
The statement had received more than 11 million views on X by Wednesday evening, as pro-Israel organisations accused Mamdani of "minimising" Jewish and Israeli suffering following his criticism of Israel’s genocide in Gaza.
The backlash came from supporters of Israel, including conservative US politicians and Israeli government officials.
Israel’s ambassador to the United Nations, Danny Danon, described Mamdani’s statement as “an attempt to hijack the anniversary of Oct. 7 and turn it into yet another propaganda attack against Israel.”
In the US, Arkansas Governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders, the daughter of Mike Huckabee, US President Donald Trump’s ambassador to Israel, wrote on X that Mamdani’s statement was a “disgusting rant”, comparing it to condemning the US military response following the 9/11 attacks.
Rabbi Ammiel Hirsch, president of the New York Board of Rabbis, called Mamdani’s statement “morally perverse” and “like sticking a knife into the pain of the Jewish community in New York and in America.”
Meanwhile, Jewish organisations across New York held ceremonies to commemorate those killed in the 2023 attacks, including a candlelit vigil in Union Square organised by Israelis for Peace New York.
Mamdani attended the vigil but did not speak, standing solemnly throughout the event, as the organisers also commemorated Palestinians killed in Gaza.
Nerdeen Kiswani, founder of Within Our Lifetime (WOL), told The New Arab that acknowledging Palestinian suffering on the anniversary does not diminish anyone else's suffering.
“We reject the premise that acknowledging Palestinian suffering somehow diminishes anyone else’s,” she said.
“Palestinians have endured decades of dispossession, occupation, imprisonment, and violence, long before October 7, 2023. Their lives and histories should not disappear from public discussion because the date is politically sensitive.”
Kiswani’s comments came after her organisation joined a broad coalition of pro-Palestine groups, including the Palestinian Youth Movement (PYM) and PAL-Awda, in holding a separate protest.
Activists called for greater recognition of the political demands of the pro-Palestine movement in New York, including calls for Mamdani’s administration to translate his advocacy for Palestinian rights into “meaningful policies”.
“The broader debate should not be reduced to whether Mamdani said the right words on October 7, or whether Palestinian protesters were sufficiently deferential to him. The question is whether his administration will translate its stated opposition to genocide and apartheid into meaningful policies,” Kiswani told TNA.
She continued: “These are not demands invented in response to one October 7 statement. They are issues Palestinian organizations have raised consistently, including before Mamdani took office. Our criticism is about the gap between the principles he articulated as an organizer and candidate and the decisions he is making now that he holds executive power.”
Among the demands, Kiswani said, are calls for the removal of NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch, whom activists accuse of “policing and repressing Palestine protests”, as well as investigations into Israeli settlement-related business activity and calls for divestment in New York.
Mamdani last month unveiled a plan to combat antisemitism, highlighting tens of millions of dollars already allocated to prevent hate crimes in New York City amid a reported rise in antisemitic incidents.
However, some pro-Israel and Jewish organisations criticised the plan for not addressing Israel.
Other Jewish organisations and leaders have supported the distinction between antisemitism and criticism of the Israeli government, arguing that opposition to a foreign government's policies should not be conflated with hostility towards Jews as a religious or ethnic group.

MoD has objected to four windfarms in past year over radar interference fears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
17:00:24 UTC
02:00:24 KST

The Ministry of Defence has objected to at least four planned windfarms in the past year over fears the spinning blades could cause “unacceptable interference” with radars used to detect military aircraft.
MoD officials raised concerns in late June over plans for an onshore windfarm in County Durham that could result in aircraft “not being detected” within an RAF Low Flying Area, according to a letter to Britain’s planning authority.
The objection to the planned Hope Moor project, which could see 23 turbines built to heights of 200m, is understood to be the latest of at least four objections made against a planned windfarm on national security grounds in the last year.
The complaint risks putting the MoD on a collision course with the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ), which ended a decade-long block on onshore wind developments in England when Labour came to power in 2024 after it was put in place by the Conservatives almost 10 years earlier.
The government aims to double the UK’s onshore wind power capacity by 2030, and has designated Hope Moor a nationally significant project whose fate will be decided upon by the energy secretary.
The MoD has also warned against plans to build an onshore windfarm of six turbines at Burton Agnes, near Driffield in the East Yorkshire Wolds, and of the “unmanageable” risk of building a 13-turbine windfarm near the Scottish borders.
Meanwhile, plans for a far larger offshore windfarm in the Irish Sea have also raised concern within the ministry on the grounds that the proposed 87-turbine array could interfere with aviation radar systems at the Warton Aerodrome base in Lancashire, on the west coast of the UK.
The MoD has a long history of objecting to windfarm developments, but industry sources note that the precautionary concerns do not usually rule out development. The “well-trodden path to the negotiating table” usually leads to minor adjustments to the size or height of the turbines, which means they can move ahead, they said.
However, the ministry’s “routine” interventions are often used by those opposed to windfarms to support their campaigns, the sources added.
Hope Moor is one of four windfarms under fire from the “Not One Moor” campaign, led by former England cricketer Lord Botham. Others include the Scout Moor windfarm in Lancashire, the Walshaw Moor windfarm in West Yorkshire and Ray Fell windfarm in Northumberland.
Angus Thompson, a Conservative councillor in North Yorkshire, said: “The MoD’s stark warning is the nail in the coffin for this scheme … This hopeless project should be abandoned without delay.”
Alexandre Davies, the head of aviation at trade group Renewable UK, said the industry “works closely” to find solutions to radar issues, “and has done so for many years” to “deliver projects faster”.
A DESNZ spokesperson said: “We work closely with the Ministry of Defence. All onshore wind projects are subject to a rigorous planning process in which defence and security, the views of the local community and impacts on the environment are considered.”
The MoD was approached for comment.

====================================================================================================

What Will a Growing MQ-9 Presence in Latin America Mean for SOUTHCOM?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:59:08 UTC
01:59:08 KST

A reported surge of MQ-9 Reaper drones to Latin America could widen the scope of intelligence gathering and free up more strike options against cartels in the region, experts tell Air & Space Forces Magazine.
According to numerous media reports, the Pentagon has supplied Colombia and Ecuador with several Reapers and transferred an undisclosed number of MQ-9s from U.S. Africa Command to U.S. Southern Command.
Officials from Colombia and Ecuador have confirmed they are receiving MQ-9s to local media outlets, and CNN, the New York Times, and the Wall Street Journal have all reported that Reapers are moving from Africa to Central and South America.
Spokespeople from AFRICOM and SOUTHCOM both declined to comment on the movement of any aircraft, but the reports indicate how Reapers, long known for their role in counterinsurgency operations in the Middle East and Africa, are becoming more and more important to the U.S. military’s counter-narcotics efforts.
“We’re helping our partners build up their capabilities, and then that allows us to kind of push more resources into countries with fewer capabilities,” Henry Ziemer, an associate fellow with the Center for Strategic and International Studies Americas Program, told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
Marine Corps Gen. Francis L. Donovan, head of SOUTHCOM, has made a point of emphasizing the use of unmanned, autonomous systems in the region since taking command in February.
“U.S. Southern Command is focusing on integrating autonomous warfare systems to enhance domain awareness across maritime, air, and border areas,” SOUTHCOM spokesperson Steven McCloud told Air & Space Forces Magazine in an email. “These unmanned systems allow our partners to monitor their territory better and facilitate informed interdiction decisions. Improved data flows and situational awareness benefit everyone.”
SOUTHCOM established an Autonomous Warfare Command in April to lead its efforts on that front.
Any increase in the number of long-endurance intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance platforms in SOUTHCOM—both piloted and remotely piloted—will give the combatant commander more options and allow them to share intelligence with their counterparts, retired Air Force Maj. Gen. Julian “Ghost” Cheater told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
And demand for intel is surging amid a growing effort to combat the cartels and the flow of drugs in the region, led by President Donald Trump and boosted by allies and partners in the region.
Beginning in March, a U.S.-led effort helped create the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition, which has grown from an initial dozen members to 19 nations, with Colombia being the most recent. In August, SOUTHCOM announced its new Joint Task Force-Western Hemisphere, the region’s “action arm” for missions like counter-narcotics.
At the time, former Air Forces Southern Commander Lt. Gen. Norm Seip told Air & Space Forces Magazine that the new task force could lead to more prioritization of assets for the SOUTHCOM commander.
Cheater, who retired in June and most recently served as the director of strategy, policy, and plans for SOUTHCOM, added that any new allocation of ISR assets would be based on the combatant commander’s priorities—which would suggest Donovan is putting an emphasis on intelligence gathering.
“Ultimately, AFSOUTH is responsible for providing that comprehensive command and control of airborne operations in theater,” said Cheater, who has more than 3,700 flight hours, a good chunk of that on drones, and commanded drone units such as the 432nd Wing out of Creech Air Force Base, Nev. “This component reports directly to the combatant commander, and if AFSOC or another entity provides those assets, those are generally commanded and controlled via AFSOUTH.”
In addition to the reported MQ-9 transfers, SOUTHCOM also announced in mid-September the sale of more than $6 million worth of K1000 ultra-long endurance drones to Panama to “monitor remote borders, safeguard strategic maritime corridors, and dismantle illicit drug trafficking and human smuggling networks,” according to a command release.
Built by Kraus Hamdani Aerospace, the K1000 is a 45-pound, 9.8-foot-long drone with a 16.4-foot wingspan that can reach speeds up to 75 miles per hour and has a ceiling of 20,000 feet. It can fly continuously for 24 hours in its solar-recharge configuration or 12 hours in its electronic vertical take-off and landing configuration. It has a range of about 1,000 miles and can be controlled via line of sight comms within 90 miles or beyond line of sight using satellite comms. A three-person crew can pack it into Pelican cases in under 15 minutes.
The Reaper’s airframe costs between $30 and $50 million each; sensors and weapons can add to that cost. It is a medium-to-high-altitude, long-endurance drone with a 66-foot wingspan and a 50,000-foot ceiling. The drone can fly for 27 continuous hours and up to 42 hours in extended-range variants with a range of 1,000 to 1,400 nautical miles. It has similar line of sight/beyond line of sight command and control capabilities to the K1000.
As of Sept. 30, 2025, the Air Force reported 182 Reapers in its inventory, though at least 45 have been lost during operations against Iran.
What’s Changing
As operations in SOUTHCOM have ramped up under the Trump administration, the MQ-9 has already played a role.
Since September 2025, SOUTHCOM has conducted at least 71 lethal, kinetic strikes targeting alleged drug boats. The strikes, some of which have reportedly been made with MQ-9s, have killed at least 215 people, with another 17 missing or presumed dead, according to government accounts and media reports.
The strikes have mostly targeted vessels near Venezuela’s shores, in the Pacific Ocean, and across the Caribbean. Early strikes began before the Pentagon formally announced Operation Southern Spear in November 2025, the wider effort to target cartel assets with kinetic strikes and other means. That temporary operation has become the more permanent JTF-WH.
Drug Boat Strikes
Those strikes have sparked intense debate among legal experts and lawmakers, and the Washington Post reported in July that a Drug Enforcement Administration assessment found that they have not been effective in stemming the flow of cocaine into the U.S.
Ben Friedman, policy director at Defense Priorities, a D.C.-based think tank that promotes a restrained U.S. foreign policy, told Air & Space Forces Magazine that he doubts the strikes will ever be effective.
“I don’t think it—using military forces to counter the flow of narcotics—works particularly well, and we have decades of experience at that. Even if we intensify it, I think we’ll get the same result at a higher price,” Friedman said.
During Congressional testimony in March, Donovan indicated that SOUTHCOM is shifting to take a more comprehensive approach to the counter-cartel fight.
“We’ve seen changes in the narco-traffickers’ patterns, and in a closed setting I’d like to provide some more details specifically on that, but … the boat strikes aren’t the answer,” Donovan told Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) on March 19.
“What we’re moving for right now [is] … really a counter-cartel campaign process that puts total systemic friction across this network,” Donovan added.
More MQ-9s in theater could aid this expanded effort.
Currently, Reapers are tasked out of various locations, including U.S. facilities in Puerto Rico. And while the platform has a long loiter time, its eye-in-the-sky is not infinite. Having Reapers actually located in Ecuador and Colombia extends the regional reach by freeing up assets for other operations with other partners.
“These drones to SOUTHCOM, they can also be operated out of Colombia. I think the drones of Panama [are] really going to help find the targets that they’re looking for, targets being drug traffickers,” Wilder Alejandro Sanchez, president of the D.C.-based consulting firm Second Floor Strategies and nonresident senior associate at the CSIS Americas program, told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
Potential MQ-9 Operating Locations
Ziemer said increased use of drones like the MQ-9 will widen the ISR and data and communications sharing between the United States and regional allies and partners.
“Long-endurance UASs are tremendously useful to patrol large swaths of the jungle, patrol large maritime borders, looking for illicit activity,” Ziemer said.
That can include illegal mining and fishing, human trafficking and a host of other nefarious cartel and criminal organization or foreign terrorist organization practices, Ziemer said.
Retired Air Force Lt. Gen. Mark “Chris” Nowland, former deputy chief of staff for operations and commander of Air Forces Southern, told Air & Space Forces Magazine that the airborne assets will prove vital for building “patterns of life” on cartel activities.
“The advantage of the Reaper being there is it gives you this incredible distance that you can cover now and put ISR on,” Nowland said. “Now you just have something that you can cue and go and get better vigilance on or discover new stuff that you couldn’t because of the sensor capabilities they have.”
Risks
While the experts and former military officials lauded the increased capabilities the new MQ-9s could bring, they also noted limitations and risks with the move.
Sanchez, a Peruvian native, and Ziemer agreed that MQ-9s are not the only drones needed. Long-endurance, high-altitude drones play a crucial role, Sanchez said, but under the canopy of dense jungles or on remote mountaintops, smaller, nimbler, backpack-portable drones already feature in counter-narcotics operations and will become even more necessary.
“It’s not just big, expensive Reapers or MQ-4 Tritons, but also small … [drones] that they can transport in a backpack, so the small squads can deploy them and find the objective much faster when they’re on the ground,” Sanchez said.
Sanchez also noted that regardless of the platform, communication and intel sharing must ramp up, which will require building that capacity within under-resourced partner nations.
“Imagine the Reaper drone has some information. It’s going to be sent to a base … and then how long does it take for that information to be sent to the troops, who need to go to that location?” Sanchez asked.
Presuming Reapers operate out of partner bases, they face their own dangers, Nowland added.
“If these U.S. assets are effective, [they] could become targets,” Nowland said. “So how do you protect them wherever you put them…? This is a dilemma that I’m sure SOUTHCOM is thinking about.”
Friedman also worries that with a change in government, assets sold or given to partner nations could be used for unintended measures.
“South American politics are not nearly as unstable as they used to be, but there are changes of government, changes of leadership, even the potential for coups,” he said. “They might be doing things that lack discretion and control… to see a South American government just doing the kind of drone strikes that we do against their own populations with capability that we gave them.”
More broadly, Friedman argued that the overall push of military assets in Latin America is an escalation in the region and threatens to make the decadeslong Drug War into a literal war.
“I don’t see a lot of virtue in having a more militarized approach to the Western Hemisphere,” said Friedman. “In practice, I think you wind up doing a bunch of things if you’re doing it with the Pentagon that probably don’t make sense.”
“If I had my druthers, they’d probably be using [them] more for training in the United States and not either of these missions,” he said. “You know, preparing for a war that actually involves some kind of core U.S. interest.”
SOUTHCOM Shifts
- On Jan. 20, 2025, President Donald Trump signed an executive order declaring cartels Foreign Terrorist Organizations (FTOs) and asserting that the U.S. is in a “non-international armed conflict” with drug-trafficking entities.
- On Sept. 2, 2025, Trump and SOUTHCOM confirmed the first lethal drug boat strike, saying it killed 11 individuals belonging to the Tren de Aragua gang.
- In December 2025, the Trump administration released a new National Defense Strategy and National Security Strategy prioritizing the Western Hemisphere and military actions against drug cartels, including “targeted deployments to secure the border and defeat cartels, including where necessary the use of lethal force to replace the failed law enforcement-only strategy of the last several decades.”
- On March 5, 2026, at a Americas Counter Cartel Coalition conference, Trump said the U.S. will work with Latin American countries “to do whatever we have to do. We’ll use missiles. … But we’ll do whatever you need. The only way to defeat these enemies is by unleashing the power of our militaries.”

Two Latvian men arrested at UK base housing US and NATO intelligence hubs

The arrests come days after a major incident at another UK base led the US military to withdraw B-1 bombers stationed there.
UK police said Thursday they had arrested two Latvians inside a military base in southeast England housing US and NATO intelligence hubs after the perimeter fence was breached.
The incident comes days after an incident near another military base in southwest England.
Counter-terrorism police said the two men, age 36 and 32, were arrested at the Royal Air Force (RAF) Molesworth base in Cambridgeshire, southeast England.
They are being held on suspicion of trespass and suspicion of entering a prohibited place "for a purpose prejudicial to the UK", said police.
Both are Latvian nationals residing in the UK.
The arrests come after a major incident at RAF Fairford on September 27 that led to the arrest of seven men, all in their 20s, who have since been released on bail. One is a dual UK-Iranian national.
Following that incident, the United States withdrew its B-1 bombers stationed at the Fairford base.

"At this stage there is nothing to suggest this incident is connected to the events at RAF Fairford last week," said counter-terrorism policing head Helen Flanagan
But the authorities were "keeping an open mind", she added in a statement.
RAF Molesworth, formerly a World War II airbase, is now a non-flying facility managed by the US Air Force.
It also hosts the NATO Intelligence Fusion Centre, whose website says it has a workforce of more than 200; and Washington's intelligence operations in Europe and Africa, according to the CIA website.
Police said a security patrol had spotted an abandoned vehicle near the base and police found a "small breach" before arresting the men in the early hours of Thursday.
The nature of the threat at RAF Fairford is still not clear but police were called to the site after three white vans were spotted acting "suspiciously" in its vicinity.
Last June, pro-Palestinian activists broke into another airbase, RAF Brize Norton in southern England, posting video showing them spraying a plane with red paint.

====================================================================================================

Not since 9/11 has the UK faced such a security crisis – and threat to our liberal principles | Gaby Hinsliff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:55:39 UTC
01:55:39 KST

The first time the window-rattling roar of a B-1 bomber woke me up this summer, I thought for one crazed second we were under attack. By the second time, I’d learned to recognise the sound of US planes taking off from their base at RAF Fairford for what it was: a reminder that although Britain wants no part in this war with Iran, we cannot quite escape the consequences.
We’ll feel them at the petrol pump, or in the supermarket this autumn, or in this winter’s heating bills. But living under the flight path adds an extra edge to it. The skies finally fell silent last week, but only because the bombers have been hastily summoned home after an alleged terrorist plot to attack Fairford, in which (according to the prime minister) there are “strong indications that Iran played a part”. If Fairford is now a target of war, did that threat disappear when the Americans did? Nobody knows.
Rural Oxfordshire is peppered with military bases, and after 15 years here I don’t bat an eyelid at helicopters practising low-flying drills, uniforms on the school run, or the stash of Day-Glo marshmallow cereal our local supermarket used to keep for homesick Americans. But the Fairford incident follows a serious security breach at RAF Brize Norton last year – and though this involved pro-Palestinian protesters rather than the Russians, it didn’t inspire confidence – and news this summer that the Manchester synagogue attacker had scoped out the security arrangements for the nearby Shrivenham defence academy. Bases nationwide are on high alert, with two Latvians arrested on Thursday on suspicion of trespass inside RAF Molesworth in Cambridgeshire, home to a Nato intelligence hub. At Fairford, it was a farmer who sounded the alarm, raising some difficult questions about how vigilant to be in small rural communities where strangers tend to stand out. I don’t want to become paranoid about every passing dog walker, or leap to ridiculous conclusions on hearing a Russian accent. But not since living in London in the aftermath of 9/11 have I felt more alert to anything seemingly out of the ordinary.
And that, of course, is how terrorism works. It’s not just the attacks themselves, but the fear and distrust they engender. For a while after the 7/7 bombings, people would change train carriages rather than stand next to some poor kid with a rucksack. At the height of the Troubles in Northern Ireland, Irish émigrés in Britain faced hostility. Sadly, it’s usually minorities who are singled out for suspicion or – in areas prone to far-right protests or antisemitic attacks – forced to wonder which of their neighbours might have joined the marches, or daubed graffiti on Jewish-owned shops. This time, there’s a particularly grim risk of a backlash against asylum seekers, with Reform pouncing on unproven reports that Tehran may be using small boat crossings to smuggle covert operatives into Britain. (For the record, those arrested and released on bail in connection with the alleged Fairford plot have British nationality. However, a Kuwaiti citizen recently convicted of a terror plot against the Israeli embassy and two Iranian nationals recently charged with allegedly plotting to target Jews in Manchester reportedly got here in dinghies.) Whatever the truth, Tehran must be delighted to see such destabilising ideas spread.
For the second time since 9/11, Britain faces a dilemma over how much of a securocracy – a country dominated by security concerns, whose citizens live at a pitch of constantly heightened anxiety – it should become in response to increasing threats. As Andy Burnham will remember, the “war on terror” forced the last Labour government, of which he was part, into a painful rolling back of civil liberties at home. Since the threat this time is less from an ideology than from three hostile nation states with domestic reach – namely Russia, Iran and China – the coming dilemmas may be more over the movement of technology, assets and people.
Historically, Britain’s economy has been a relatively open one, even after Brexit. We let Gulf states buy our football clubs, Russian oligarchs prop up the prime London real estate market, and Chinese money bail out our cash-strapped universities and build our power stations, despite concerns about espionage, censorship and interference in domestic politics. (Tom Tugendhat, the shadow foreign affairs minister and longstanding China hawk, revealed last week that he still gets letters from Beijing to the family home “that say, basically, ‘we know where you live’”.)
London’s tech startups, expanding faster than they could hire domestically, snapped up skilled young Russian coders understandably anxious to escape a country at war. We didn’t slap tariffs on cheap Chinese EVs when the EU did, despite concerns they could kill off domestic car manufacturing – or even that some of their software might still be controllable from China, because trade wars are generally bad for business. (Though the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, suggested recently that that debate is not entirely closed.)
We chose not to become a fortress because for a long time, the benefits of being open to the world felt worth the risks, but perhaps also as a statement of our values. But there is an increasingly live debate in Whitehall about whether, in retrospect, autocracies saw that openness as a weakness to exploit. If nothing else, they’re certainly weaponising it now: both Iran and Russia are throttling shipping routes in the strait of Hormuz and Black Sea respectively, with consequences for oil and food prices that are now ringing serious alarm bells within governments.
Though it’s not entirely clear yet what Burnham makes of all of this, there are early signs of attitudes hardening. The Cabinet Office recently summoned CEOs of critical infrastructure companies to brief them on the threat of Russian sabotage, while last week MI5 issued a rare public warning to academics against working with a Chinese organisation regarded as a front for espionage. The concrete barriers hurriedly going up around Fairford last week may be a harbinger of what is to come: a signal that as the world moves closer to a war footing, our relaxed way of life may have to change.
But there’s a difference between being vigilant and being paranoid, let alone xenophobic, and we are going to need to hold that line in months to come. No foreign national in the UK should ever be persecuted for the sins of their country of origin: there’s no going back to the dark days of 1939, when Jewish refugees fleeing Nazi Germany and Austria were shockingly interned in Britain as “enemy aliens”. New powers of surveillance should always come with new safeguards.
And this government should remember that if the “war on terror” taught us anything, it’s that security crises test liberal principles to breaking point. I just hope Burnham is ready for that.
- Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist

Ukrainian drones attacked the town of Sasovo in Russia’s Ryazan Region overnight into Oct. 8, striking the Sasta machine-tool plant. The facility houses a data center run by tech giant Yandex, often dubbed “Russia’s Google.” The company confirmed that a fire had broken out at the site after the attack.
Ukrainian monitoring channels were among the first to report the drone attack and its aftermath, while authorities have not yet commented on the incident. A Russian Defense Ministry summary listed attacks on the Ryazan Region, along with strikes in the Moscow, Tambov, Tula, and Oryol regions, but gave no details about damage.
NASA FIRMS fire-monitoring maps showed a blaze at the same location as the Sasta plant and Yandex data center. The fire appeared on maps shortly after 2 a.m.
Yandex itself confirmed that the facility had been hit by drones.
“A fire broke out at the Yandex data center in Sasovo as a result of a drone attack, affecting part of the infrastructure. There were no injuries, and emergency services are working at the site to deal with the aftermath,” Kremlin-aligned outlet RBC quoted the company as saying.
The center’s operations are currently suspended, rendering some services unavailable to users. For example, the social media autoposting service Postmypost experienced temporary disruptions before later returning online.
Downdetector also recorded complaints about Yandex Search, Yandex Disk, and other services.
Notably, Russian news agency Interfax quoted the same company statement almost word for word — but with one exception. The phrase “a fire broke out as a result of a drone attack” was replaced with simply “an incident occurred.” The agency did not specify what kind of incident. State-run RIA Novosti also omitted any mention of a drone attack, describing what happened as a fire.
Yandex said in 2021 that its Sasovo data center housed two of the company’s three supercomputers that were built with Nvidia A100 chips and used to train its YandexGPT large language model. The company declined to say whether the systems were damaged in the attack, according to Reuters.
The Yandex data center in Sasovo opened in 2014. Local authorities had previously described it as a “highly promising high-tech enterprise.”
