Working with Taiwan key to regional stability, Tsai says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:46:23 UTC
01:46:23 KST

Deeper international cooperation with Taiwan would not only strengthen its security, but also boost stability in the Indo-Pacific region and the resilience of other democracies, former president Tsai Ing-wen (蔡英文) said on Wednesday.
Technology and economic resilience are increasingly tied to national security, Tsai said in her keynote speech at the Stanford Conference on Technology and National Security, according to a statement from her office.
The conference was hosted by Stanford DEFCON, a student network under the Stanford Gordian Knot Center for National Security Innovation at Stanford University.
Photo courtesy of Tsai Ing-wen’s office
Maintaining peace in the Indo-Pacific region, where military power, technology and economic security intersect, is one of the major challenges facing the world, the former president said in a speech titled “Building Security Together: Taiwan’s Role in Global Stability.”
Chinese military aircraft and ships, as well as coast guard vessels, operate regularly around Taiwan, while cyberattacks, cognitive warfare, information manipulation and economic coercion have become almost daily occurrences, she said.
Amid sustained pressure, Taiwan has to do more than prepare for a major military contingency, while bolstering its defense and preserving its freedom, Tsai said.
“The Taiwan Strait is one of the world’s most important trade and energy routes, and Taiwan is deeply integrated into global technology and manufacturing networks,” she said. “A serious disruption would be felt throughout the Indo-Pacific and beyond.”
International coverage still often portrays Taiwan as a security challenge that requires support from other countries, but “that is only a part of the picture,” she said.
Taiwan is among a small number of democracies capable of adding manufacturing capacity to the challenge rather than simply consuming it, she said, citing the role of Taiwan’s semiconductor industry in global technology supply chains.
Noting that the US accounts for about three-quarters of the world’s artificial intelligence (AI) computing capacity, Tsai said Taiwanese companies manufacture nearly all of the advanced chips used in those systems and about 90 percent of the AI servers built around them.
“The AI economy, therefore, depends heavily on what Taiwan builds, and our contribution extends well beyond semiconductors,” she said.
Meanwhile, in the satellite industry, Taiwanese companies are major producers of radio-frequency chips and circuit boards used in communications and satellite systems, she said.
These capabilities are increasingly relevant to security, as the line between civilian and defense technologies becomes less distinct, Tsai added.
Taiwan’s position at the center of the First Island Chain, combined with its democratic system, technological capabilities and industrial strength, gives it a difficult-to-replace role, she said.
“A secure and resilient Taiwan contributes to a more stable Indo-Pacific, while its technological and industrial strengths reinforce trusted supply chains and reduce vulnerabilities far beyond the region,” Tsai said.
“Deeper cooperation with Taiwan, therefore, strengthens not only Taiwan’s own security, but also the stability of the Indo-Pacific and the resilience of the wider democratic community,” she added.
Following her speech, Tsai took part in a fireside chat moderated by Stanford DEFCON copresident Gordon Kim and attended by several Taiwanese students studying in the US.
Chang Chia-chi (張家綺), an MBA student, said Tsai’s discussion of Taiwan’s role in geopolitics and technology echoed the increasingly frequent discussions of Taiwan in her classes.
Chang said she hoped to draw on her experience in Taiwan and the US to help more people understand her homeland.
Another student Lin Hsin-yu (林芯?) said Tsai’s discussion of Taiwan’s key role in advanced chip supply resonated with her, particularly the facts about Taiwan’s indispensable link in defense-related supply chain.
Tsai arrived in San Francisco on Monday for a week-long visit, her first to the US since she completed two four-year terms as president in May 2024.

Chiang’s proposal to remove Songshan airport sparks controversy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:46:21 UTC
01:46:21 KST

Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) yesterday proposed relocating Taipei International Airport (Songshan airport) and turning the site into an artificial intelligence (AI) park, drawing opposition from politicians across party lines.
Chiang’s plan would turn the 300 hectares into an AI park featuring tech clusters, residential communities and green space.
The industrial cluster would host 200 domestic enterprises, generate NT$12 trillion (US$376.47 billion) in output, and accommodate 65,000 jobs and 35,000 residents, he said.
Photo: Lo Pei-de, Taipei Times
Cabinet spokeswoman Michelle Lee (李慧芝) said the Executive Yuan was surprised by the announcement, as the Taipei City Government did not discuss the proposal with the central government before making it public.
Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator Yang Yao (楊曜) from Penghu County said that Songshan airport is a key transportation hub for residents on the outlying islands.
Relocating it without a detailed plan would not only affect regular travelers, but also undermine national defense and emergency medical services, he said.
DPP Legislator and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) asked what Chiang had done to advance the goal during his time as mayor and a lawmaker representing the district.
Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) candidate for Penghu County commissioner Chen Cheng-chung (陳振中) said Songshan is important to Penghu residents who seek medical attention, study, work and visit relatives in Taipei.
KMT Lienchiang County commissioner candidate Wang Chung-ming (王忠銘) said he supports the development of the AI industry, but such policies should not come at the expense of the rights and interests of residents in outlying islands.
KMT Legislator and Kinmen County commissioner candidate Chen Yu-chen (陳玉珍) took a more positive view, saying Kinmen supports AI development and welcomes infrastructure projects in Taipei, but added that residents in outlying islands are concerned about access to flights.
If Songshan airport services are relocated to Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport, the government should ensure sufficient flight capacity and provide dedicated shuttle services, transportation subsidies and other transport arrangements, she said.
Lu Yen-liang (盧衍良), director of the Department of Flight Operations at Chaoyang University of Technology, said Songshan airport serves military and civilian purposes, and plays a key role in emergency medical evacuations, transportation to outlying islands and general aviation.
Moving all flights to the Taoyuan airport could create operational and safety challenges, as the former handles aircraft ranging from helicopters and turboprops to jets, while the latter primarily handles jet aircraft, Lu said.
Songshan airport’s central location, similar to Tokyo’s Haneda Airport and Seoul’s Gimpo Airport, provides significant economic and medical advantages that would be difficult to replace, Lu added.
National Taiwan Ocean University professor Yen Chin-ju (顏進儒) said he was not opposed to relocating the airport, but its functions would need to be preserved and suitable alternatives must be established.
Relocation would face major challenges, particularly as Taoyuan airport’s planned capacity expansion would not be able to absorb Songshan airport’s redirected passenger traffic, he said.
With Taoyuan airport’s annual passenger volume expected to exceed 50 million this year, shifting Songshan airport’s traffic to Taoyuan — or even distributing it among other airports — would be difficult, he added.

Photo courtesy of the Presidential Office

No plans to further reduce flights: Mandarin Airlines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:46:14 UTC
01:46:14 KST

Mandarin Airlines chairman Chen Ta-chun (陳大鈞) said that there are no further plans to reduce flights after the airline cut its Kaohsiung-Hualien route from seven to five weekly, while adding that a Kaohsiung-Taipei route “could be possible.”
Starting this month, flights on the Kaohsiung-Hualien route have been reduced due to low passenger loads, while the Taitung-Hualien route would maintain three flights a week, the airline said.
Speaking at a news conference at Taipei International Airport (Songshan airport) during which the company announced its collaborations with the National Taiwan Symphony Orchestra (NTSO), Chen thanked the Civil Aviation Administration for approving the airline’s application to reduce flights.
Photo: Wu Cheng-ting, Taipei Times
Starting tomorrow, Mandarin Airlines’ flights would be authorized to play NTSO performances of Taiwanese folk songs aboard their flights.
Chen said that passenger load factors for Hualien-bound flights remained at 20 to 30 percent and have not increased despite the airline’s reduction in total flights.
Although the airline’s operations are still in the red, the measures have effectively dulled losses from overhead, Chen said.
Planes relieved of the Kaohsiung-Hualien flights would be directed to transporting passengers to outlying islands, such as the Kaohsiung-Penghu route, Chen said.
Minister of Transportation and Communications Chen Shih-kai (陳世凱) said that rail would serve as the main mode of transportation in eastern Taiwan, adding that a well-developed rail network would weaken the competitiveness of air travel.
In eastern Taiwan, a Taiwan Railway EMU3000 train can carry 538 passengers, compared with about 70 on an aircraft, meaning one train could carry about the same number of passengers as eight flights, Chen said.
He cited western Taiwan as an example, saying the introduction of high-speed rail had reduced demand for the Taipei-Kaohsiung and Taipei-Taichung air routes.
Separately, commenting on calls to reinstate Taipei-Kaohsiung flights as a result of surging crowds over the Mid-Autumn Festival and Teachers’ Day holidays, Chen Ta-chun said airline companies are not hidebound and that if a route was lucrative: “No one would shy from it.”
Chen Ta-chun said that airlines planning to operate charter flights on the Taipei-Kaohsiung route would need time to formulate plans.
He also suggested a mechanism for canceling flights with low passenger occupancy, such as notifying passengers at least one month in advance if a flight is to be canceled because of insufficient bookings.
Chen Shih-kai said that the Ministry of Transportation and Communications respects the airline industry’s assessment of restarting the Taipei-Kaohsiung route.
If airlines believe that the route would be competitive during long holidays, the ministry would welcome its resumption, he said.

Largan reports gross margin slide to 42.21 percent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:46:14 UTC
01:46:14 KST

Largan Precision Co (大立光), a key iPhone lens supplier, yesterday reported that gross margin slid to 42.21 percent in the third quarter — the lowest in 13 years — from 49.41 percent in the previous quarter and 47.24 percent a year earlier.
The decline was mainly due to lower yields for new smartphone camera lens products and higher green energy costs, Largan chairman Adam Lin (林恩平) told an earnings conference.
As green energy costs are structural and unlikely to ease in the near term, this quarter’s margin outlook would depend largely on improving yields for new lens products, Lin said.
Photo: Chen Mei-ying, Taipei Times
During the July-to-September period, Largan’s revenue fell 11.47 percent year-on-year to NT$15.65 billion (US$490.98 million), while net profit declined 27.65 percent to NT$5.18 billion.
Earnings per share were NT$39.62, down from NT$53.05 a year earlier, company data showed.
This month’s revenue is expected to remain flat from last month’s NT$5.78 billion before declining next month after smartphone customers began cutting orders last month, he said.
Apple Inc last quarter launched the iPhone 18 series with variable aperture lenses, for which Largan has an exclusive supply share.
Yields for variable aperture lenses are currently “rather OK,” Lin said.
However, shipment momentum is weakening as the peak season has passed, he said.
Factory utilization for smartphone lenses is expected to remain at full capacity this quarter, Lin said.
Customers are testing samples of upgraded camera lens modules for next year’s models, he said, adding that new periscope lenses are entering trial production.
As the company pushes into the copackaged optics business to supply fiber arrays (FAs), Largan has completed a trial automated production line for FAs after gaining customer certification last month, Lin said.
The company also plans to complete its first fiber array unit (FAU) production line by the middle of next year and begin volume shipment in the second half of next year, he said.
Largan aims to begin mass production of FAU products for one customer in the second half of next year, with sample deliveries slated for this month, he said.
The company integrates FAs with prism microlens arrays it sources externally to make FAUs, Lin said.
The FAU solution next year is expected to use grating couplers, while Largan is also working with customers on edge-coupling technology, he said.
Largan is also discussing next-generation FAU products with other customers, with timelines broadly pointing to 2028, he said.
Capital expenditure totaled NT$8.18 billion last quarter, mainly for land and factory purchases in Taichung, he said.
The purchases are to support the expansion of its FAU-related business, Lin said.
Construction is expected to begin next year and be completed by 2030, he added.

What it is like living between two worlds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:46:14 UTC
01:46:14 KST

A few days ago, we left our breakfast midway to catch a glimpse of the fighter jets in formation. It was a spectacular sight. We knew it was part of practice drills for Double Ten National Day celebrations and reminded us of the Annual Republic day celebration in India.
While channel surfing, I came across a news debate about immigration laws, where an academic asked a fellow panelist: “Why should we be interested in your point of view when you don’t even belong here?” That got me thinking. Was our enthusiasm about the upcoming Double Ten celebrations unwarranted? Was this a case of the Indian proverb, “Begaani shadi mein abdullah diwaana,” or “someone getting overly excited or involved in something that has nothing to do with them”?
According to Psychology Today, “Over the last century, many seemingly different psychological theories have come to similar conclusions: that our identity and sense of self is not a singular thing but an amalgam of many, sometimes conflicting parts. Psychoanalyst Philip Bromberg called these self-states, coming from the perspective of dissociation. Carl Jung referred to these as archetypes.”
This theory becomes even more interesting when we consider multi-colonial cultures such as Taiwan and India, which have seen a lot of upheaval on the cultural, political and social front. Here, there can exist very different beliefs, ideologies and practices, but common lived experiences and events also become a factor to bond over, and promote empathy and understanding between cultures.
The world today, with its depleting resources, divided borders, feverish jingoism and resource power play, wants people to be neatly divided into those who belong and those who do not. Yet, there is something innately simple and innocent about the human spirit that is always fighting to break out of these confines, for the sake of joy, peace, discovery, empathy and curiosity.
It is the very thing that drives us to every corner of Taiwan any free weekend we can find: From the devilishly beautiful shores of Yehliu Geopark to the temples of Tainan; the endless verdant miles of Yangmingshan to the undulating ocean kissing the sands at Kenting. Whether it is the Lantern Festival or the Pudu feast during Ghost Month, the Dragon Boat Festival or the Mid-Autumn Festival, there is so much to absorb and experience if one can only shed the arrogance of geography and civilizations.
I might sound like a philosophical Indian guru, but sometimes, the most complicated things are childishly simple, if we allow ourselves to tune in to our basic nature.
Last weekend, we drove out to Dasi town. While walking off the beautifully lit up bridge, I walked into a Taiwanese flag by mistake, as it was hanging very low. I touched it to my forehead, bowed and smiled. It was my way of respecting another flag that stands for decades of strife and triumphs, and reminding myself that for now, I belong right here and that when I go back home, I will take a part of it with me. That does not deplete me in any way.
Richa S Mukherjee is a former journalist and an author based in Taiwan.

Its central tool at sea is the “cabbage strategy”: the Chinese People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) layers fishing boats, maritime militia, coast guard cutters and warships around Taiwan’s contested waters in overlapping rings. Each layer normalizes daily coercion, narrows Taiwan’s freedom of movement and chips away at its maritime sovereignty — all while staying below the threshold of armed conflict. This is “gray zone” warfare at its most cost-effective — one of Beijing’s most promising

Finding comfort in monsters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:46:13 UTC
01:46:13 KST

You would never have guessed that a comic book featuring a giant snake would make you feel warm and safe.
And yet, the art of Huang Wen-yu (黃文妤) speaks to the heart through imagery suffused with monsters and dark shadows.
And that is because Huang is not only a cartoonist and illustrator, she is also an art therapist.
Photo: Julien Oeuillet
Under the title “Motherly Love is a Snake,” the show exhibits works from Huang’s books, and is the inaugural exhibition of the newly opened Manshio cafe in Kaohsiung.
“During art creation,” she tells the Taipei Times, “artists have inner changes, their mindset changes while they draw.”
Huang’s art is inspired by her work as an art therapist, which enables her to use images to express trauma and mental health recovery.
Her first book tells the story of a cat with a dinosaur tail, illustrated in large paintings where the cute animal is confronted by monsters and dangerous landscapes.
“The tail symbolizes our inner fears and our suppressed desires,” she says, “this dinosaur will pop out and devour and eat everything.”
The juxtaposition of such an innocent and fragile animal, in realistic drawings, with such dark scenery, allows viewers to connect with the emotional journey towards recovery.
“Every page represents different stages. First it’s in the sea and all is unclear, then there is more awareness of the inner desires which are represented by monsters, I acknowledge and accept them. Then all is sunny and clear. Every page is a different state of mind.”
FLEDGLING DISCIPLINE
Huang says that Taiwanese have little understanding of art therapy, so demand remains low.
“It’s only acknowledged academically and there is no national licence. There are now two academic associations for art therapy, but just above 200 registered art therapists, which is not a lot,” she says.
Huang works with both children and the elderly, and says that art therapy is often the first time in their lives that old people get to express a personal taste, “things as simple as what their favorite color is.”
There is an element of inter-generational tension in Huang’s work.
Further stories focus on a woman using a sort of magic gun to get ghostly shadows out of people.
“In this work,” she says, “I try to get to know how culture affects women, mother-and-daughter relationships.”
Snake imagery also appears in her personal experience working in an institution for children that functions in a similar way to an orphanage.
“The children’s parents can’t take care of them because of domestic violence or drug addiction or incarceration,” she says. “Many of these children have trauma or emotional regulation issues, so I do art therapy for them.”
One little boy who suffered from abuse made a snake out of clay that he used to express anger, pretending to bite her and then putting it to sleep in a box. “This is how he learned to manage his feelings.”
The transmutation of such a frightening image as a snake or spectral shadows or monstrous dinosaurs into a touching and human story invites the audience to see them in a positive light, and thus accept their emotions in a healthy manner.
Huang says she has grown sensitive to the cultural aspect of art therapy.
“Art in Taiwan comes a lot from colonial history,” she says, “Taiwan’s modern art developed during Japanese colonization, when Japan introduced Western oil painting. Art therapy is also a Western idea. Our professors all come from abroad to bring this concept here. I think if we want people to enjoy art therapy more we have to find our art, that relates to our daily life and experience.”

An imperial and colonial act, caning thus functioned to define and display social class boundaries. So it is with the new legislation permitting caning proposed by Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) legislators last week. Chinese-language exam reports record numbers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:46:13 UTC
01:46:13 KST

More than 1.3 million people have taken Taiwan’s Test of Chinese as a Foreign Language (TOCFL), the test’s organizers said yesterday, as it celebrated its golden anniversary.
Seventy-seven countries have adopted the exam as a standard language proficiency certification test, with India leading the numbers of test-takers, the test’s steering committee and Ministry of Education officials said at an event at National Taiwan Normal University (NTNU) in Taipei.
Last year, 1,496 Indians, 2,404 Thais, 202 Dutch, 134 Canadians, and 17,616 Vietnamese took the TOCFL, increasing by of 1,600 percent, 817.6 percent, 494.1 percent, 415.5 percent and 212.3 percent over the certification test’s history from 2019, the officials said.
Photo courtesy of the Taipei Economic and Cultural Center in India
TOCFL has become an important metric for universities to recruit foreign students and teach the Chinese language, Deputy Minister of Education Luo Kuo-wei (劉國偉) said.
The ministry is introducing artificial intelligence (AI) in Chinese-language education platforms up to A2 proficiency this year and up to C1 level proficiency next year, he said.
The long-term goal is to use Internet-based, AI-assisted technology to conduct tests remotely so that foreign students would not need to travel to take the test at authorized testing centers, he said.
Committee chairman Sung Yao-ting (宋曜廷), who is also the NTNU president, said that he had advocated for the ministry to put its stamp on TOCFL certificates to ensure the test’s credibility.
Officials used to carry the tests in hardcopy — which must be destroyed after use — to foreign-based TOCFL centers before computerization of the exam, he said.
Sung emphasized TOCFL’s importance to Taiwan’s representation in the field of Chinese-language studies, saying that he hopes the test would continue to grow.
The government has opened 93 centers in the US, Canada, the EU, Japan and New Zealand to promote Chinese-language education programs run by Taiwan, a Community Affairs Council spokesperson said.

Hamlet embraces cricket
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:46:12 UTC
01:46:12 KST

Visitors to the chateau in the tiny village of Liettres in northern France heard some unfamiliar terminology this weekend at an international cricket tournament.
“Howzat,” cried the players from France and Belgium taking part in the 11th edition of the Liettres Challenge 1478.
The tournament, the brainchild of the Lille Cricket Club, was launched in 2015 to celebrate the hamlet’s unlikely place in cricket history.
Photo: AFP
According to organizers, Liettres was the site of the earliest recorded cricket match.
A letter written to France’s King Louis XI in 1478 mentions an argument that broke out between a “poor gunner” at the Liettres castle called Estievenet le Grant and a man called Cotaine le Brasseur, who was playing “criquet” with others.
Words led to blows, and Le Brasseur was stabbed in the arm with a javelin and later died from his wound.
This reference predates by about a century the first known mention of cricket in English sources, in court papers from 1589 mentioning that a pupil from Royal Grammar School in Guildford had been playing “creckett.”
To celebrate the fact, the village contacted Philippe Dethoor, who was Lille president at the time, to ask if they would come down to put on a cricket workshop.
The club had other ideas and decided to create a tournament.
They secured access to a farmer’s field, rolled it and laid out a portable plastic wicket.
Lille invited a team from Belgium, 12 Stars Brussels, and another one from Whitstable in Kent.
“The English team were bowled out for 13 runs,” said James Worstead, who was the Lille secretary at the time, but now runs the leisure section at Viperes de Valenciennes, one of the invitees to this year’s Liettres Challenge. “Lille beat them for the loss of one wicket.”
Since then, the local authorities agreed to move the annual tournament to “a bumpy field behind the castle” and have also created a medieval fair around it, including jugglers, fire-eaters, pony rides, axe throwing, a javelin tournament, Viking battles and, of course, a bouncy castle.
“Initially, there were all these entertainment activities to attract people, but since the tournament was launched, we’ve noticed ever more interest in the game and people actually come to watch the matches — and they are connoisseurs,” said Franck Pailleux, from the regional Bethune-Bruay tourism office.
When the tournament was launched in 2015, it was widely covered in the British press and even by one Indian media firm.
“Historians claim cricket was invented by the FRENCH,” the Daily Mail wrote in an article on Aug. 30, 2015.
However, Dethoor says that was not the case.
“We never said that cricket was invented in France,” he said. “We know that cricket was codified in England. As far as we know — and it wasn’t contradicted at the time — it’s the first written trace referring to a cricket match.”
Worstead, who is an English-language teacher in nearby Valenciennes, said that there was “a good-humored ambiguity” to the suggestion that cricket could have been invented in France.
“There’s something quite iconoclastic about that,” he said. “Serious cricket historians do trace cricket back to Flanders and shepherds playing it. So, it’s not quite as outrageous as it might seem, but of course, for a tabloid headline, it’s: ‘The frogs say they’ve invented cricket.’”
However, some experts in the field dispute the idea that the “criquet” in the letter to King Louis XI relates to the game.
Neil Robinson, head of heritage and collections at the Marylebone Cricket Club, the guardians of the laws of the game, pointed to an article in the April 1973 issue of the Journal of the Society of Archivists.
It includes a detailed analysis of the handwriting and concludes that the word “criquet” is in fact “etiquet” and refers to a stake being used in a game, which was probably not cricket.
“I think it’s a pretty solid rebuttal and I think most historians who looked at it closely would probably agree with that,” Robinson said.
“It’s obviously a great story from the French point of view, but like so many other things in cricket history, I don’t think it happens to be true,” he said.
Still, there is a certain charm to the idea that a tiny hamlet of little more than 300 people could have a claim to a piece of cricket history.
“I love to believe it because it gives them [the French] a certain belongingness to the game itself,” said Judson Daniel Raj Moses, the tour manager at 12 Stars Brussels, who this year lost to Lille in the final.

Laws inadequate to fight transnational repression: MAC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:46:12 UTC
01:46:12 KST

Taiwan’s laws lack comprehensive provisions to address transnational repression, Mainland Affairs Council (MAC) Deputy Minister Liang Wen-chieh (梁文傑) said yesterday.
The nation has seen a rise in cases of suspected transnational repression, including the assault on Taiwan-based Japanese political commentator Akio Yaita, a feces attack on the Comedy Club in Taipei, and the alleged surveillance of Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator Puma Shen (沈伯洋) and President William Lai’s (賴清德) son, who is in the US.
Asked whether the government plans to toughen sanctions against those involved in transnational repression, Liang said Taiwan has two laws that could be applied to such cases: the Anti-Infiltration Act (反滲透法) and the National Security Act (國家安全法).
Photo: CNA
The Anti-Infiltration Act covers acts conducted at the direction of overseas hostile forces that violate provisions of the Public Officials Election and Recall Act (公職人員選舉罷免法), the Referendum Act (公投法), and the Assembly and Parade Act (集會遊行法), Liang said.
The National Security Act addresses offenses involving the establishment of organizations in Taiwan and the leaking of national secrets, he said.
“The problem is that we are seeing an increase in forms of transnational repression that are not punishable under either laws, including illegal surveillance, stalking and unauthorized filming, physical attacks, splashing paint and throwing feces at the direction of overseas hostile forces,” Liang said.
In Yaita’s case, the perpetrator could be prosecuted for assault under the Organized Crime Prevention Act (組織犯罪條例), while the Comedy Club case could be prosecuted under the Criminal Code’s property damage provisions, Liang added.
The perpetrators in Shen’s case could be prosecuted under the Personal Data Protection Act (個人資料保護法), he said.
However, none of these punishments are designed to deter transnational repression, Liang said.
By contrast, US law states that surveillance conducted at the direction of a foreign government can constitute a crime, with perpetrators facing a maximum prison sentence of 10 years, he said.
“We hope that any proposed amendments to the two acts will be passed by the legislature. Last year, we proposed an amendment to the National Security Act aimed at deterring transnational repression, but it has yet to be deliberated,” Liang said.
The council also produced a short film about Hong Konger Tong Wai-hung (湯偉雄), who is on Hong Kong’s wanted list after allegedly inciting people not to vote in the legislative election last year by questioning the fairness of the vote, he said.
Tong and his wife subsequently moved to Taiwan.
His Muay Thai studio in Taipei has been vandalized with paint twice by Hong Kongers posing as prospective customers.
The council has also met with other victims of transnational repression: Guan Jianzhong (管建忠), head of Lion Film and TV Culture Co, which distributed the documentary State Organs (國有器官) in Taiwan, as well as comedian Huang Yi-hao (黃逸豪), Liang said.
The council wanted the public to know that transnational repression exists and remind the government not to allow victims of such acts to feel isolated, he said.
“Ridiculing victims or dismissing them as delusional or overly self-important would only embolden perpetrators and make victims more fearful about their situation,” Liang said, adding that victims have demonstrated considerable courage.

The last word on soccer legend Lionel Messi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:46:06 UTC
01:46:06 KST

Ten years ago, Lionel Messi was defeated, dejected and absolutely heartbroken.
“I did everything I could, and it didn’t work out for me,” the great man told reporters as he announced his retirement from Argentina’s national team after losing a fourth tournament final.
What came after is history: Messi would reverse that hot-headed decision two months later and lead Argentina through its most glorious period. He won a World Cup in 2022 and reached another final this year, being the tournament’s best player at 39, an age when most of his colleagues are growing their bellies as TV commentators.
When Messi walked out onto a soccer pitch with Argentina for the final time on Tuesday, wearing a sky blue-and-white striped jersey specially designed for the occasion, it was a night of emotion and remembrance.
For me, it means saying goodbye to my superhero, the guy who for the past two decades has given me hope that all my soccer dreams could become reality. The memories are endless: from walking out of Rio de Janeiro’s Maracana in tears after watching him lose the 2014 World Cup final, a game Argentina deserved to win, to marveling at his leadership as he carried an exhausted team through Miami’s extreme heat to beat Cabo Verde in July. Not to mention his glories in Qatar and that England match.
I could bore you with crazy stats and achievements that prove his uniqueness. In my eyes, he is not only the best soccer player in history, but also the greatest athlete ever. I know that is controversial, but the defining fact is this: Messi has dominated his field — the world’s most popular sport, remember — pretty much since his meteoric emergence in late 2004.
Back then, former US president George W. Bush was struggling to contain the debacle in Iraq, Facebook was an incipient idea confined to Harvard and Venezuelans still believed in Hugo Chavez. That is how much the world has changed in 22 years, and yet we still have Lionel Messi doing unbelievable stuff on a soccer pitch, like that insane free-kick goal he scored for Inter Miami a few days ago. Neither Michael Jordan, Serena Williams, Muhammad Ali, Michael Phelps nor Usain Bolt, the other all-time greats, could claim that. Sorry if you disagree.
And yet, for all his magic on the field, it is his perseverance, passion and down-to-earth personality that strikes me the most. At a time when global stars have armies of advisers choreographing each of their moves, this guy seems simply motivated by kicking a ball and scoring more goals than the rival, soccer at its most essential form. He seems happier attending a fourth-division match in his hometown than enjoying the spotlight of big galas in Europe.
Messi was already Messi in 2016, when he made that imprudent retirement announcement. Having just turned 29, an age when players are starting to run out of options, he could have chosen the quiet life, enjoying his family instead of spending most summers training with the national team after a long club season. He nevertheless went back to business and endured new defeats for another five years before he could finally say he had won something with Argentina. That is an example of determination, mental strength and loyalty for his colors worth admiring.
That is why for Argentines, who did not always share my idyllic view of the Rosario-born star, Messi is now something akin to Churchill: The captain who, after so many years of economic decay and frustrations, gives the country an aura of invincibility, as if reviving past glories, even if we all know it is ephemeral.
Such defining influence is even more remarkable considering the disastrous management of the Argentine Football Association (AFA) off the pitch. Case in point: Argentina’s match on Tuesday, Messi’s historic farewell, was against 93rd-ranked Benin. His retirement, now for real even if I think he is rushing it again, would expose the institutional shortcomings of the AFA, as the national association is known. It would also force a long and painful restructuring of the national team, knowing he would not be around anymore to rub the lamp and pull us out of trouble when things go south.
Leo Messi is, above all, an anomaly: An alien who came to Earth to remind us that everything is truly possible, that you can always turn things around. While he still has a few battles to play with Inter Miami in Major League Soccer, it is clear his future is increasingly linked to business and entrepreneurship rather than astounding us on a pitch. I will miss watching him, expecting the unexpected and yet nonetheless being stunned into asking, when the magic happens, “just how did he do that.”
JP Spinetto is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering Latin American business, economic affairs and politics. He was previously Bloomberg News’ managing editor for economics and government in the region. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

Each layer normalizes daily coercion, narrows Taiwan’s freedom of movement and chips away at its maritime sovereignty — all while staying below the threshold of armed conflict. This is “gray zone” warfare at its most cost-effective — one of Beijing’s most promising

A total of 53,304 foreign travelers had registered between Thursday last week and Wednesday to participate in a program for repeat visitors to Taiwan, with plans to bring 10,017 accompanying friends and family members, the Tourism Administration said yesterday.
The Return to Taiwan, Double Your Luck program offers people who register a chance to win NT$5,000 in travel credits, plus NT$3,000 for an accompanying friend or family member.
The program is open to travelers who entered Taiwan on a passport other than a Taiwanese passport between Jan. 1, 2023, and the day before registration.
Photo courtesy of the Tourism Administration
Accompanying friends and family members are eligible if they have not visited Taiwan during that period.
Travelers planning to visit Taiwan for three to 90 days between Saturday and March 31 next year can register on the designated Web site, 5000.taiwan.net.tw, between seven and 90 days before their planned arrival.
The Web site opened at 10am on Thursday last week.
Draws are to be held every Wednesday at noon, and winners would be notified to complete identity verification within 24 hours of arriving in Taiwan and obtain a QR code to claim their prizes, it said.
Winners can use the spending credit at more than 7,300 7-Eleven stores nationwide to add to an icash2.0, EasyCard or iPass card, it said.
The top nationalities among those who registered over the initial seven-day period were Japanese, Hong Kong and Macau residents, South Koreans, Singaporeans and Filipinos, it said.
From January to last month, tourist arrivals in Taiwan rose to 6.175 million, a 1.93 percent increase from the same period last year, Tourism Administration data showed.
Taiwan welcomed 8.57 million tourists last year, with repeat visitors accounting for 42 percent, agency Director-General Chen Yu-hsiu (陳玉秀) said, adding that the proportion had returned to pre-COVID-19 levels.

Woman who sparked Spain protests dies at 87

Maricarmen Abascal, the 87-year-old Spanish woman whose dramatic eviction last month sparked mass housing protests that led to an early election, has died, the Madrid tenants’ union said on Wednesday, as thousands demonstrated over her death.
Abascal had been hospitalized for severe anxiety and exhaustion since her eviction on Sept. 23 from her home of more than 70 years, when police and social workers removed her by stretcher.
Her case ignited protests over a mounting housing crisis including a shortage of homes and surging rents. Activists camped out in a major Madrid square.
Photo: AFP
Following news of Abascal’s death, thousands marched from Puerta del Sol toward parliament, chanting: “This is not a death. It’s a murder.”
A cause of death was not announced.
“This was a completely avoidable death that symbolizes the drama that is the housing crisis in Spain,” 36-year-old marcher Dario Gomez said.
Demonstrators also held protests in Barcelona.
Trade unions on Wednesday announced a nationwide general strike over housing issues on Nov. 11.
The protests, along with parliament’s rejection last week of decrees aimed at curbing evictions and limiting rent pressures, prompted Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez to call an early election for Nov. 29.
Sanchez is seeking to shift the political narrative from his government’s handling of a migrant crisis in Spain’s North African enclave of Ceuta and a series of corruption cases involving his Socialist Party and his family to the housing crisis, hoping to tap into growing resentment over rising rents.
“Now, following her passing, we are left with the example of the fight she waged and the legacy Maricarmen has left behind. And, above all, we will honor what she always asked of us: ‘Fight, keep fighting for what is yours,’” the tenants’ union said in a statement.
Sanchez lamented Abascal’s death on X.
“A hug as well to all of us who feel this loss as our own today,” he wrote.
The leader of Spain’s opposition People’s Party, Alberto Nunez Feijoo, wrote on X that Abascal’s death should not be politicized.
There should be “no campaigns, no political parties, no other interests here,” he wrote. “In the face of someone’s death, respect is all that matters.”
Abascal was evicted after an investment fund bought her house. Several days later, her lawyer said she reached an eight-year agreement with her landlord that would allow her to return home and pay rent at the same prior amount.
She had planned to sign the deal once she felt better, but never had the opportunity to leave hospital.
A neighbor of Abascal said she was shaped by living through Spain’s authoritarian Franco regime, which ended in 1975.
“She was a fighter, with very clear ideas, a somewhat broad sense of justice, and, above all, perhaps a social conscience and ideas about solidarity,” he said.
Guillermo Ruiz, 31, an audiovisual specialist at the march, said he felt pessimistic about change.
“The best homage we can pay to her is to continue the fight, continue to mobilize, fight for a dignified life and that what happened to her doesn’t happen to anyone else,” he said.

European ruling parties must give young protesters hope for future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:45:59 UTC
01:45:59 KST

In Spain, tens of thousands of people in 50 cities have taken to the streets amid mounting fury over the country’s housing crisis, their feelings made plain on a banner at the burgeoning protest camp in Madrid’s Puerta del Sol plaza: “You can speculate on watches, jewels, crypto-bros and Ferraris. But not on our fucking homes.”
In France, as high-school pupils clash with police in often violent protests over long hours, missing teachers, crumbling classrooms and an opaque university admissions system, the angry slogans include: “More hours in class than for sleep,” “Fund study, not repression” and “I’d like to be worrying about my maths exam, not my future.”
They might stem from different specific grievances, but the two waves of mainly youth-led protest exemplify a growing problem for western European governments: A generation of young people feeling increasingly denied the basic socioeconomic security that, by and large, their parents enjoyed.
The trigger in Spain, where rents have risen by 80 percent in a decade, was — perhaps ironically — the high-profile eviction of an 87-year-old woman in Madrid after an investment fund increased her rent by 230 percent. For those spending more than half their income on housing (the monthly rental on a one-bedroom flat can cost an entire median salary), enough was enough.
Rocketing rents, rampant property speculation, the boom in short-term tourist rentals and stagnant wages have combined to make an independent adult life increasingly unachievable for many young workers — and the state is seen not as a neutral mediator, but an active enabler of property speculation.
In France, the protests began in the northern Paris suburbs, but quickly spread nationwide, fueled by young people’s anger at an underfunded education system that, the data show, entrenches social inequality.
Pupils routinely miss months of teaching owing to unfilled staff absences. Timetables run from 8am to 6pm — among the longest in Europe — in buildings with leaking roofs, cockroaches and collapsing ceilings. In Paris last week, students on high-school barricades saw budget cuts as a straightforward assault on their future. In their eyes, a system meant to promote social mobility now prevents it.
However, parliamentary majorities and facing varying degrees of budgetary constraint, neither government has much room for maneuver. Spainish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on Monday called a snap general election after right-wing parties voted down his emergency housing legislation.
In France, as student protests — and more than 5,000 arrests — forced the closure of up to 500 secondary schools on Monday, the centrist Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has urged local authorities to prioritize filling long-term teacher absences and called urgent meetings to discuss repairing dilapidated school buildings.
Taken together, the two crises highlight some core problems facing mainstream governments. First, young people in particular have come to see incremental measures — targeted tax credits, minor administrative reforms — as sticking plasters on altogether deeper socioeconomic wounds.
Second, facing mounting street pressure and opposition parties eager to exploit it, ruling coalitions — especially those that lack majorities — would struggle. And in France, heavy-handed policing risks alienating young voters from the mainstream even further.
Meanwhile, radicalized opposition parties are actively weaponizing the discontent. On the radical left, France’s Jean-Luc Melenchon — backed by 47 percent of voters under 35 — has sided openly with the street, while in Spain, left-wing parties Podemos and Sumar have blamed the housing crisis squarely on out-of-control financial capitalism.
At the same time, the populist far right is playing a law-and-order card, with Marine Le Pen’s National Rally in France seizing on footage of burning barricades to accuse centrist leaders of tolerating “unbridled violence” and Spain’s far-right Vox siding with the main conservative Partido Popular opposition to torpedo Sanchez’s emergency package, framing it as government overreach punishing landlords.
Squeezed from both sides, mainstream governments face a spiraling challenge. When an entire generation concludes that society’s existing frameworks guarantee them neither affordable homes nor functioning schools, political consent starts to evaporate and Europe’s establishment parties risk losing their legitimacy.
As Nando de Anguulo, a 26-year-old protester in Madrid, put it: the protests prove that as things stand, “it is us, the people, who have to adapt to the political parties — and not the politicians who have to adapt to what the people want. It can’t go on like that.”
China prefers to win without firing a shot in its bid to strangle Taiwan’s strategic autonomy. Chinese military strategist Sun Tzu (孫子) would have approved. Its central tool at sea is the “cabbage strategy”: the Chinese People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) layers fishing boats, maritime militia, coast guard cutters and warships around Taiwan’s contested waters in overlapping rings. Each layer normalizes daily coercion, narrows Taiwan’s freedom of movement and chips away at its maritime sovereignty — all while staying below the threshold of armed conflict. This is “gray zone” warfare at its most cost-effective — one of Beijing’s most promising
During a tour of Taipei’s Wanhua District (萬華) on Sept. 22, Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) proposed a seemingly appealing urban-planning vision for the area: linking Xinfu Market (新富市場), East Sanshui Street Market (東三水街市場), Longshan Temple (龍山寺), Bopiliao Historical Block (剝皮寮歷史街區), Bangka Park (艋舺公園), the underground mall and surrounding commercial areas through neighborhood redevelopment and environmental improvements, while encouraging specialty and boutique business. It would create what Chiang called Taipei’s version of Omotesando — an upscale, tree-lined boulevard and shopping district in Tokyo — to attract young people and international tourists. The Executive Yuan submitted the central government budget proposal for the coming fiscal year to the legislature at the end of August.
Revenue and expenditure are budgeted at NT$3.9266 trillion, including NT$235.7 billion earmarked for the proposed universal cash handouts.
Photo: Taipei Times
Eligibility for the payout would follow the same rules as the previous cash distribution program, the ministry’s plan states.
Taiwanese with a household registration would be eligible, including those born in Taiwan before the end of next year, as well as nationals without household registration who have residence permits, foreign permanent residents and foreign spouses of Taiwanese citizens with residence permits.
Government personnel stationed overseas on official assignments and their family members who hold Taiwanese nationality would also be eligible.
Registration for bank deposits would open on Jan. 25, with the first batch of payments deposited the following day, the ministry said, adding that the initial batch would include preregistered deposits, direct deposits and payments distributed through government rosters.
Five collection methods would be available: direct deposit, registered bank deposit, ATM cash withdrawal, post office collection, and roster-based distribution for prison inmates and residents of some remote areas, it said.
The ATM withdrawal system is expected to add Shanghai Commercial and Savings Bank (上海銀行), bringing the total number of participating financial institutions to 17, including eight state-run banks, CTBC Bank (中國信託銀行), Cathay United Bank (國泰世華銀行), Taishin International Bank (台新銀行), Taipei Fubon Commercial Bank (台北富邦銀行), E.Sun Commercial Bank (玉山銀行), Bank SinoPac (永豐銀行), Yuanta Commercial Bank (元大銀行) and Chunghwa Post (中華郵政).
The expansion of ATM networks is expected to raise coverage to 86.18 percent, up from 84.34 percent during the previous cash handout program, the ministry said.
Cash withdrawals through ATMs would become available on Feb. 15, while over-the-counter cash collection at post offices would begin on Feb. 22, it said.
The deadline for most recipients to claim the payment would be Aug. 31, while eligible newborns would have until Jan. 31, 2028.

Straightforward tribute tells inside story of fashion world’s great eccentric Karl Lagerfeld
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:45:57 UTC
01:45:57 KST

Karl Lagerfeld had never set foot inside a supermarket before he had one built on a catwalk in 2014, featuring models browsing aisles with baskets shopping for Chanel-branded fromage. It was classic Lagerfeld: very silly but a stroke of genius. The fashion designer was easy to poke fun at, with his white bouffant-plus-ponytail hairstyle and black leather gloves. But behind the persona was a man who spoke four languages fluently, a workaholic still running Chanel, Fendi and his own label Karl Lagerfeld into his 80s.
This dutiful, uncontroversial documentary is based on William Middleton’s biography Paradise Now: The Extraordinary Life of Karl Lagerfeld. As well as archive footage of Lagerfeld, film-maker Nick Hooker gets access to the designer’s inner circle, but ultimately his documentary fails to chip away at the persona. (This is no criticism: I once interviewed Lagerfeld, a frustrating 30 minutes during which the dark glasses stayed on and he answered questions with bon mot witticisms but gave nothing away.) In a clip at the start of the film, Lagerfeld admits that he has spent so long performing a role that not even those closest to him really know who he is.
Growing up in Germany, his mother was cold and distant, which seems to have left him with a life-long aversion to intimacy. At 19, he left for Paris, and after a long stint at Chloe took over Chanel in 1983, at a time when the legendary fashion house was dusty and on its uppers. He lost the great love of his life, partner Jacques de Bascher, to an Aids-related illness in 1989. Later in life, his smash hit collaboration with H&M gave Lagerfeld celebrity status, which he clearly adored. But glance away and you’ll miss the very quick reference to his controversial fatphobic comments.
Photo: Reuters
Of the interviews here, Lagerfeld’s famous pals Tilda Swinton and Penelope Cruz are all blather and platitudes, but more insightful are his collaborators, including Amanda Harlech, his right-hand woman at Chanel. I found it telling how well liked Lagerfeld was by his staff; the seamstress who worked for him for 50 years turning his sketches into clothes describes him as “the creme de la creme of men.” His longtime bodyguard says he was like a father. (Though, if Lagerfeld had actually been his dad there were times he’d have told him to “go fuck yourself.”) Overall, this is a diligent, if not definitive, profile.

In China’s Taoist martial arts schools, fighting is only part of the lesson
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:45:56 UTC
01:45:56 KST

There was a time when Chinese master Yuan Shimao thought martial arts were all about punching and kicking. As a young practitioner, he focused on speed and strength.
“I trained that way for many years without becoming still enough to search within myself,” said Yuan, who founded a kung fu academy in central China in 2004.
“But as you gradually settle into stillness, you begin to understand what the scriptures mean by spirit,” he added. “You can begin to rediscover yourself.”
Photo: AP
That process is known as “entering the Dao” in martial arts. It is a guiding principle at Yuan’s academy in the sacred Wudang Mountains, where disciplines like kung fu and tai chi draw on Taoist thought.
Practitioners like Yuan start by strengthening the body. As they progress, the mind becomes more resilient and willpower develops.
“The body is a vehicle or vessel within which the spirit resides,” Yuan said. “You therefore need a healthy body capable of carrying your spirit.”
A DEEPER MARTIAL ARTS PRACTICE
Yuan began practicing martial arts in the 1980s. Boxing and the Chinese combat sport of sanda attracted him at first.
He heard of Wudang later that decade. As his body ached with rheumatism, Yuan read an article claiming Taoist practices could heal him. So he packed his bags and moved to the mountains. There he became acquainted with Taoist temples and embraced practices such as standing meditation.
He came to understand that movement and stillness are interconnected, rather than opposites. That physical activity can help practitioners quiet the body, allowing them to become calm and grounded.
“I slowly became interested and eventually I benefited from the practice myself,” Yuan said. “That process was very profound for me.”
Yuan now seeks to share that knowledge with local and foreign students enrolled in the three programs at his academy.
One is a five-year course offering in-depth martial arts training. The second is focused on health and well-being, helping adults exercise and cultivate their minds. The third is a summer camp for children seeking exercise during school breaks.
TAOISM AT WUDANG
Chinese philosopher Laozi is believed to have passed on teachings foundational to Taoism to his first student more than 2,500 years ago. That disciple settled on the mountain and helped spread his master’s ideas.
“It did not develop into a collective religious faith until after the Qin and Han dynasties,” said Shu Chenghai, director of social education at Wudang Museum.
Wudang lay between present-day Xian and Luoyang, two major political centers in ancient China. That made it easier for practitioners to seek seclusion while remaining within reach of major population centers.
“The Taoist tradition was therefore never entirely about withdrawing from the world,” Shu said.
Wudang’s importance as a Taoist religious center came later. During the Tang era, prayers for rain at the mountain were believed to have been answered. Its standing continued to grow under subsequent rulers, reaching its height under Ming emperors.
TAOIST PHILOSOPHY AND MARTIAL ARTS
Guo Xinyi is a Chinese student who began training at Yuan’s academy five years ago. She knew of his decades-long commitment to preserving and passing down traditional Taoist martial arts. That made her feel she could trust him.
Within Chinese martial arts, teachers like Yuan are known as shifu. The closest English translation is “master.” But the Chinese term includes the character for “father.” Guo, therefore, thinks of Yuan not merely as a mentor, but as a father figure.
When she first came to his academy, she struggled with conflict with her parents. Her tai chi lessons, though, taught her to approach confrontation calmly.
“I invited Master Yuan to have tea and talk with us,” Guo said. “During that conversation, the conflict somehow seemed to dissolve almost invisibly.”
Yuan eased her father’s anxiety, tension and excessive concern for her, she said, adding that the conversation resembled a tai chi lesson.
“When we encounter conflict, our physical instinct is to resist or attack, to move forward and meet what is coming at us,” Guo said. “But tai chi does something different. First, you release tension. Then you sink. Only afterwards do you rise.”
TODAY’S STUDENTS
The number of students from China and abroad studying at Yuan’s academy has increased in recent years.
“In the past, most learners were middle-aged or elderly, but the student population has gradually become younger,” he said.
Among that younger generation is Jake Pinnick, an American practitioner who arrived at age 20 and, 16 years later, calls Wudang home.
Pinnick grew up in the US watching kung fu movies and playing sports that relied on competition. What he found in China forever changed his life.
“I came here for martial arts, but I stayed because of this philosophy,” said Pinnick, who also became a martial arts master and recently opened his own academy in Wudang.
Yuan said teaching methods have evolved to adapt to younger generations.
Physical training is less demanding and corporal punishment has been eliminated. New ways of motivating students have been introduced instead. Among them is the chanting of slogans aimed at building physical and inner strength.
“Faith in your heart, light in your eyes, and a smile on your face,” is one his students’ daily chants.
Routines at his academy vary depending on the program, but training can begin as early as 6 a.m. After breakfast, students practice fundamentals before splitting into groups for specific martial arts training. Their schedules also include theory classes and meditation.
Yuan believes learning in Wudang means immersing oneself in the Taoist culture that has shaped its martial arts tradition. That environment, he said, can help students cultivate harmony with nature, with others and within themselves.
“Consider how deeply this nourishes the human heart, mind and spirit,” he added. “If practicing martial arts can nourish you to such an extent, what more could you ask for?”

EU lawmakers reject China’s pressure on Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:45:56 UTC
01:45:56 KST

The European Parliament on Wednesday adopted a recommendation on EU-China political relations that rejected China’s efforts to restrict Taiwan’s participation in international organizations and exchanges.
The recommendation, addressed to the European Council, the European Commission and EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas, includes several references to EU-Taiwan relations and expresses support for closer ties, saying they would bring positive benefits and have strategic importance.
Describing Taiwan as a valuable partner in trade and technology, the European Parliament said it “rejects China’s attempts to coerce international organizations, third countries and other actors into restricting Taiwan’s international participation and contacts.”
Photo: EPA
It mentions as an example Chinese pressure over Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim’s (蕭美琴) participation in the European Conference of Ventotene for Freedom and Democracy organized by the European Parliament last month.
It also expresses “the EU’s strong disapproval of China’s transnational repression activities,” such as its investigation into Legislator Puma Shen (沈伯洋) under a 2024 judiciary guideline accusing him of launching the “pro-independence separatist organization” Kuma Academy.
The Kuma Academy is a nonprofit dedicated to training civilians on the basics of civil defense.
The recommendation reaffirms that the EU’s “one China” policy guides its policy toward Taiwan and stresses that the EU has never endorsed China’s “one China” principle, the recommendation says.
It also opposes any unilateral attempt to change the “status quo” by force or coercion, or any provocation or any change against the will of Taiwanese.
The recommendation calls for the EU and its member states to work with other democratic partners in the region on closer security coordination, including a continuous naval presence and joint exercises, to reinforce regional stability.
It also calls on the European Commission to fulfill its pledge to parliament to work toward deterring China from provoking or escalating tensions with Taiwan.
At the same time, the commission should continue to develop EU-Taiwan relations in various areas under the EU’s longstanding “one China” policy and encourage dialogue and constructive engagement across the Taiwan Strait, it said.
The recommendation also calls on the UN to reject Chinese demands and grant Republic of China passport holders, including tourists, journalists, non-governmental organization workers and political activists, access to tours and events at the UN.
The European Parliament also opposes what it describes as China’s distortion of UN Resolution 2758 to support its claims over Taiwan’s territory and sovereignty.
UN Resolution 2758 does not mention Taiwan and addresses only the issue of China’s UN representation. Beijing interprets the resolution as giving it the right to represent Taiwan.
The recommendation also stresses the importance of deepening economic and technological cooperation with Taiwan in areas such as semiconductors and cybersecurity to strengthen Europe’s resilience and protect critical supply chains.
It calls for the EU to begin preparations without delay for negotiations on a bilateral investment agreement or another arrangement, such as a memorandum of understanding on critical supply chains, with Taiwan.
Additional reporting by Kayleigh Madjar

Diplomats stationed in the Saudi Arabian capital were yesterday sheltering in place and international schools took safety measures, diplomats and residents said, after explosions echoed across the city.
The explosions heard in Riyadh came hours after Houthis in Yemen, which borders Saudi Arabia, claimed their latest attack on the kingdom.
The Iran-backed fighters have launched a wave of attacks on Saudi Arabia since they began a major offensive in Yemen against the internationally recognized, Saudi-backed government there.
Photo: EPA
Saudi Arabia and Yemeni government forces have struggled to contain the Houthis’ advance, despite a counteroffensive aimed at recapturing territory including the area around a waterway that is crucial to global energy flows.
In Riyadh, home to a large number of non-Saudi Arabians, diplomats were instructed to shelter in place in their respective embassies, diplomats said.
Several residents said that international schools were taking precautions, with at least one facility sending children into a basement for safety.
The measures came after repeated blasts were heard in the city, one of the loudest disturbances in the capital since the start of the Middle East war that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February.
Two people working in Riyadh’s business hub, the King Abdullah Financial District, said that some companies were evacuating staff from the area.
The latest blasts came a day after the Houthis claimed attacks on two international airports, while repeating a warning to airlines to avoid Saudi airspace.
“On Tuesday and Wednesday ... Abha International Airport and King Khalid International Airport were subjected to attacks targeting their facilities,” the Saudi Arabian General Authority of Civil Aviation said.
An Egyptian and an Algerian national were killed at Abha airport, while a Sudanese national was killed at Riyadh airport, the agency said.
The attacks wounded 36 people, it added.
On Wednesday in Yemen, clashes left at least 62 combatants dead, including 37 Houthis, military sources from both camps said.
Meanwhile, Syria might deploy troops to help Saudi Arabia fight the Houthis, a US official and a Syrian defense official said.
The possible entry of Syrian forces into the battle shows how Yemen’s reignited civil war has added new chaos to a region already aflame, and risks drawing regional states into grueling mountain fighting.
Saudi Arabia has pushed for support from allied nations, including Turkey and Pakistan, even if only in a logistical or purely defensive capacity.
Syria was carefully considering military support, including the option of defensive aid to protect Saudi Arabia from attacks or deployment in an offensive capacity to help Saudi-backed Yemeni troops take the fight to the Houthis, the US and Syrian officials aid.
Yemen’s long-running civil war, which paused with a ceasefire in 2022, has erupted again in the past few weeks with the Houthis seizing stretches of the Red Sea coast last month, including along the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The Houthis have said they were responding to attacks from the Saudi-backed government, which the government denies.
In response to a request for comment to the Syrian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, a diplomat said the country stood firmly with Saudi Arabia in the face of Houthi attacks, but that the government’s primary focus was on domestic priorities such as recovery from the country’s civil war.
“Should Saudi Arabia request any military cooperation or exchange of expertise, this would take place exclusively through official channels and within the framework of the bilateral agreements governing relations between our two brotherly countries,” the diplomat said in a statement.

Seasonal northeasterly winds are expected to bring intermittent rain to northern and eastern Taiwan from Friday through Sunday, while other parts of the country will see cloudy skies with periods of sunshine, a forecaster said Thursday.
During the three-day National Day holiday weekend starting Friday, the greater Taipei area and eastern Taiwan will see more moisture, with heavier rain expected on Sunday, Central Weather Administration (CWA) forecaster Chang Cheng-chuan (張承傳) told CNA.
Areas south of Taoyuan are expected to see partly cloudy to sunny skies, with isolated afternoon showers possible in southern mountainous areas, Chang said.
Photo: CNA
The weather pattern is expected to persist through next Thursday due to seasonal northeasterly winds, he added.
The lowest temperature is forecast to stay between 22-25 degrees Celsius over the coming week nationwide, with some areas potentially 1-2 degrees cooler, he said.
Daytime highs are expected to reach 28-30 degrees in northern Taiwan and 33-34 degrees in central and southern areas, while some places could see wider day-night temperature differences, he added.
The CWA said Tropical Storm Nolo, the year’s 27th, was about 3,250 kilometers east of Taipei as of 2 p.m. and moving northwest, while Tropical Storm Koguma, the 28th, was about 4,080 kilometers east of Taipei and moving west- northwest.
Neither system is expected to impact Taiwan, and no other tropical systems are forecast to develop over the next week, Chang said.

Hong Kong introduced a candidate vetting system in 2021 under Beijing’s "patriots governing Hong Kong" principle, under which only those deemed loyal to Beijing are allowed to run for office.

It also warned that those who profited from the Chinese market while "flirting with Taiwan independence" would eventually "pay a price too heavy to bear."

On Monday, Chiang defended Tsai’s right to attend political events and invited him to the opening of his own campaign headquarters. Tsai said he would be happy to attend once he received an invitation with the details.
Shen has been on Beijing’s list of "diehard Taiwan independence separatists" since October 2024. Chinese authorities have been conducting a criminal investigation into him since October 2025 for allegedly supporting Taiwanese secession.
China views Taiwan as part of its territory and has not ruled out the use of force to bring about unification.

Hospital touts doctors’ rankings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:45:50 UTC
01:45:50 KST

Three Chang Gung Memorial Hospital doctors have been named among Taiwan’s top 20 researchers in clinical medicine in this year’s World’s Top 2% Scientists rankings.
The list is compiled by Stanford University based on data from Elsevier’s Scopus citation database, ranking top researchers using standardized bibliometric indicators.
The three doctors are Liaw Yun-fan (廖運範), Tain You-lin (田祐霖) and Kuo Ho-chang (郭和昌).
Photo: Wu Liang-yi, Taipei Times
Chang Gung steering committee chairman Cherng Wen-jin (程文俊) yesterday said the hospital has long invested in research and fostered an environment that encourages doctors to conduct clinical and basic research.
Tain has emerged as a prominent researcher at Chang Gung, Cherng said, adding that he published 167 academic papers between 2020 and last year.
His research has included developing tests for nitric oxide, short-chain fatty acids and oxidative acids.
Kuo, a pediatric rheumatologist, has focused on Kawasaki disease research for many years and is regarded as a leading expert in the field.
Kuo’s research has combined microRNA with machine-learning algorithms to develop a highly accurate diagnostic model for Kawasaki disease, which has been published in leading international immunology journals and contributes to doctors being able to tell Kawasaki disease from normal fevers.
The work has helped advance molecular testing for Kawasaki disease and has been published in leading international immunology journals, Cherng said.
Kuo has published about 284 academic papers, received 115 academic awards in Taiwan and abroad, holds 15 invention patents, and has authored five Chinese and English-language textbooks, Cherng said.
At Academia Sinica, Liaw spent decades researching viral hepatitis and liver cancer, Cherng said.
Liaw’s research has focused on the natural history of hepatitis B, immune mechanisms, and clinical research on hepatitis B and C. He has also participated in developing clinical guidelines on hepatitis and liver cancer in the Asia-Pacific region.
Liaw is an internationally recognized authority on viral hepatitis research, Cherng said.
So far, only the rankings of Taiwan’s top 20 clinical medicine researchers have been released, and Chang Gung would continue to monitor this year’s list, Cherng said.
According to last year’s World’s Top 2% Scientists rankings, 75 researchers from the Chang Gung medical system appeared on the annual scientific impact list, while 52 appeared on the career-long scientific impact list.
The two lists accounted for 127 entries. After removing duplicates, 88 people were included: 76 physicians, three medical professionals and nine researchers, Cherng said.
According to Chang Gung’s internal statistics, the number of researchers from its medical system included in last year’s World’s Top 2% Scientists rankings was the highest among medical institutions in Taiwan, Cherng said.

Call for more defense hackathons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:45:50 UTC
01:45:50 KST

I served as a mentor and judge for last weekend’s inaugural Taiwan Defense Tech Hackathon, which was cohosted by the European Defense Tech Hub, National Taiwan University’s Unmanned Vehicles Research and Development Center, and the Institute for National Defense and Security Research, providing feedback to students, researchers, entrepreneurs and engineers who developed concepts for dual-use technology solutions to certain challenges and problems.
The value of this experience was being in the same room as the people who ordinarily sit outside Taiwan’s national security establishment, and observing them produce unconventional solutions using commercially available off-the-shelf technologies with civilian and military applications in a crisis.
Several teams proposed concepts focused on Taiwan’s coastal security gaps to help the National Police Agency (NPA), coast guard and navy address problems ranging from protecting undersea cables to alerting users to suspicious coastal activity. Before deployment, prospective end users would need to test and evaluate these concepts in realistic conditions.
To ensure that Taiwan continues to build its defense innovation and dual-use technology ecosystems while strengthening whole-of-society defense resilience, hackathons should become a regular part of the ecosystem. Taiwan’s existing competitions, research programs and accelerators could expand scenario-based experimentation to develop dual-use technologies that help sustain communications, logistics and other essential services during disasters or conflict.
Taiwan’s whole-of-society defense resilience can draw on an immense reservoir of technical expertise and ingenuity. Ukraine’s experience shows how civilian skills and networks can support national defense. Regular defense technology hackathons around Taiwan could help build those connections before a crisis, provided they lead to sustained collaboration and usable capabilities.
Hackathons could complement existing competitions, including the upcoming National Chungshan Institute of Science and Technology’s AEGIS CTF International Invitational Tournament & National Defense AI Competition and the Presidential Cup Drone Competitions, which are scheduled later this year.
Such events can expose more of the nation’s technology sectors to security problems through rapid team formation, intensive prototyping and interaction with end users. Taiwan’s civilian technology sector offers a reservoir of expertise that could bolster whole-of-society defense resilience through closer connections with end users, as Ukraine’s experience illustrates.
Following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, civilian expertise was rapidly turned toward national defense, with programmers, engineers, drone enthusiasts and volunteers from various fields contributing to its whole-of-society effort to resist Russian armed coercion.
Some of Ukraine’s civilian technical networks were established before the full-scale invasion, including Aerorozvidka, a non-governmental organization founded in 2014 that pioneered drone warfare. By February 2022, Aerorozvidka had modified commercial drones, built a team of experienced operators and contributed to the military’s response. Hackathons can help technically capable people engage with civil defense and national security problems before a crisis hits.
During this year’s Han Kuang live-fire exercise, the Ministry of National Defense’s Cyber Command mobilized more than 100 civilian cybersecurity specialists to test and assess the defenses of energy, transport and telecommunications infrastructure. Similarly, the ministry’s All-Out Defense Mobilization Agency (ADMA) mobilized civilians to help military units set up barriers and provide civilian transport capacity to move ammunition and other supplies.
Hackathons themselves would not deter “gray zone” activities, coercive behavior, compellent actions or a full-scale invasion by China. However, a robust ecosystem of these events and similar competitions could help build resilience and deterrence, and shape an adversary’s judgement of Taiwan’s ability not only to absorb a attack, but also to improvise, repair and mobilize civilian expertise. If these connections produce credible, tested capabilities that can function under an attack, they could undermine Beijing’s expectations of rapid success.
Policymakers, industry and other stakeholders should work toward creating a repeatable pathway for similar events so the hackathon’s impetus does not end on Sunday last week. Taiwan needs a pathway that lets more problem solvers address operational problems, build prototypes, test with end users, secure funding and ultimately field capabilities for civilian and, if needed, military end users.
Hackathon organizers should publish six-month results documenting continued collaboration with end users, realistic prototype testing, follow-on funding and any adoption. Holding such events alongside military exercises could connect civilian technologists with end users to explore problems exposed by unscripted scenarios.
Taiwan already has a starting point in this integration through the ministry’s Defense Innovation Office. The office offers prototype calls, research cooperation and small-quantity procurement for evaluation. A solicitation in February last year included intelligent warehouse management. Promising teams need operational sponsors and follow-up resources to navigate these mechanisms; funding and military adoption would depend on further evaluation.
It is key to do this all around Taiwan, not just in Taipei, given the unique insights that might come from Taichung’s advanced manufacturing sector, Kaohsiung’s maritime focus or rural areas, such as Taitung. Entities such as ADMA, the Industrial Technology Research Institute, the NPA and others could host hackathons.
Bryce C. Barros is a visiting fellow at the Institute for National Defense & Security Research. He previously served as a US Senate national security adviser from 2023 to 2024. The views expressed do not reflect those of the US government or other affiliations.
China prefers to win without firing a shot in its bid to strangle Taiwan’s strategic autonomy. Chinese military strategist Sun Tzu (孫子) would have approved. Its central tool at sea is the “cabbage strategy”: the Chinese People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) layers fishing boats, maritime militia, coast guard cutters and warships around Taiwan’s contested waters in overlapping rings. Each layer normalizes daily coercion, narrows Taiwan’s freedom of movement and chips away at its maritime sovereignty — all while staying below the threshold of armed conflict. This is “gray zone” warfare at its most cost-effective — one of Beijing’s most promising

It would create what Chiang called Taipei’s version of Omotesando — an upscale, tree-lined boulevard and shopping district in Tokyo — to attract young people and international tourists. The idea is not new. More than NT$200 million (US$6.28
