2026-10-08
16:27:58 UTC
01:27:58 KST

Pakistani Air Force fighter jets have already been used in attacks against the Houthis, a senior Pakistani military official Thursday morning anonymously told the New York Times on Thursday. Pakistan’s Information Ministry issued a denial of that claim later in the day.
The report came hours before several loud explosions were heard Thursday afternoon in Riyadh, the capital of Saudi Arabia, and reports said the kingdom’s main international airport, King Khalid International Airport, was struck again in an attack launched by Yemen’s Houthi rebels.
Pakistan confirmed Wednesday night that it had sent military forces to Saudi Arabia. According to the Times report, experts tracking Pakistani assistance estimate that around 8,000 Pakistani troops are already deployed in the kingdom.
Another Pakistani official told the newspaper that Islamabad’s assistance would focus on air defense against the Houthi missile and drone threat, rather than offensive operations inside Yemen.
Reuters also reported that Pakistan had sent military equipment to pro-Saudi forces in the southern Yemeni city of Aden, where the government fighting the Houthis is currently based.
Reuters, citing eyewitnesses and several sources familiar with the details, reported that one aircraft was hit and caught fire Thursday afternoon at the international airport in Riyadh. The sources said the plane was apparently empty and was struck while parked at the airport.
Saudi Arabia has not yet confirmed that report, but said it intercepted two ballistic missiles fired by the Houthis at Riyadh and another missile launched toward Khamis Mushait in the south of the kingdom. It said debris from the interception of one of the missiles over Riyadh damaged a kindergarten and a medical center.
The Houthi attacks on Saudi cities, which have intensified in recent days, have largely focused on airports as part of an effort to disrupt the kingdom’s aviation sector and “close its skies” in retaliation for extensive Saudi airstrikes against the rebels. Riyadh has been carrying out the attacks in an effort to support Yemeni government forces fighting the Houthis on the ground.
Saudi Arabia acknowledged Wednesday that three people had been killed in earlier attacks this week on airports in Riyadh and the city of Abha.
Severe disruptions were reported at Riyadh airport Thursday afternoon following the strike, and according to flight-tracking site Flightradar24, the airport was effectively closed. An eyewitness told The Associated Press that fire crews and ambulances were dispatched to the scene and smoke was rising from the area. Passengers were told to leave behind luggage they had already checked in and evacuate the airport, he said.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree confirmed that the group had again attacked Riyadh airport Thursday and claimed that the missile “hit its target, caused damage and disrupted air traffic at the airport.”
He also renewed a warning issued by the rebels in recent days to international airlines against operating in Saudi airspace, claiming it had now become an “arena” for Houthi attacks and saying the group would not be responsible for the consequences if airlines ignored the warning.
In his remarks Thursday, Saree called it a “final warning” to airlines. He also threatened that the Houthis would continue attacking oil facilities in the kingdom and urged workers in the sector to stay away from those sites “so as not to endanger their lives.”
At the same time, the Houthis reported additional Saudi strikes that they claimed had killed civilians. The Houthi-affiliated Saba news agency reported that several civilians were killed and wounded in the al-Shamayatayn area in southern Taiz province after two Saudi airstrikes allegedly hit a passenger bus.
Earlier, Houthi leader Abdul-Malik Badr al-Din al-Houthi sought to portray Saudi Arabia as acting in partnership with Israel.
“The Saudi enemy, in partnership with the United States and Israel, is deliberately committing crimes against the Yemeni people,” he said. “All Islamic peoples should view it as a criminal regime. It does not represent Islam, but rather the Zionist approach.”
The escalation between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia began in July, ending four years of relative calm in Yemen’s civil war, which erupted in 2014 and in which Riyadh supports forces loyal to the internationally recognized Yemeni government.
The renewed escalation began after a Houthi attempt to break the Saudi-imposed air blockade on the rebels, alongside an escalation at the time in the war with Iran, a Houthi ally.
Last month, the Houthis launched a rapid offensive in which they seized strategic coastal areas in southwestern Yemen overlooking the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
Even before taking that territory, the Houthis were able to attack ships from a distance using drones and missiles, but capturing the area gave them tighter control over traffic through the strategic waterway, which connects Europe and Asia via the Red Sea and Suez Canal and carries about 12% of global trade.
The importance of the strait, particularly for Saudi Arabia, rose sharply after the Strait of Hormuz on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula was blocked during the war with Iran.
At the beginning of this week, Yemeni forces loyal to Riyadh launched a major ground offensive, which they call “Dawn of Yemen,” in an attempt to drive the Houthis out of the newly captured areas and seize control of Bab al-Mandab.
Saudi Arabia is providing extensive air support for the operation with heavy bombardment. Reports say pro-Saudi forces have indeed advanced in the area around the strait, although the extent of those gains remains unclear.
The Houthis, for their part, denied claims by the Yemeni government that it had already retaken Bab al-Mandab.
Houthi Foreign Minister Abdul-Wahid Abu Ras warned Thursday that fighting in the strait area “could negatively affect maritime traffic,” which the Houthis have so far largely avoided deliberately targeting during the escalation, aside from attacks on Saudi oil tankers.
“We have many cards that will be revealed in the coming period if the Saudi regime continues with these steps,” he threatened.
The Houthis also scored an important gain this week by imposing a siege on the city of Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city and a major strategic stronghold of government forces.
The renewed fighting has revived the severe humanitarian crisis that engulfed Yemen at the height of the civil war. According to reports, at least 200,000 residents have so far been displaced.
As the fighting intensifies, questions are also growing internationally over possible Pakistani and Turkish involvement on Riyadh’s side as part of the “Mecca Alliance” they signed with Saudi Arabia just two months ago.
The agreement states that an attack on one member constitutes an attack on all. So far, Islamabad and Ankara have officially limited themselves to condemning Houthi attacks.
Turkey, meanwhile, said Thursday afternoon that it would not join active combat against the Houthis.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said the “Mecca Alliance” was “primarily a defensive alliance, not an offensive one.”
He said Turkey and Pakistan were still examining how to support Saudi Arabia in the face of Houthi attacks, but stressed: “We will not send military forces into the territory of another country to carry out an attack there. We are studying how to provide Saudi Arabia with military assistance, air defense and electronic warfare capabilities within the framework of the alliance.”
His remarks came two days after senior Houthi official Mohammed al-Bukhaiti threatened that the rebels would respond to any foreign involvement in the Yemen war.
“We do not expect Turkey and Pakistan to become directly involved in the fighting inside Yemen,” he said. “The involvement of Turkey and Pakistan in the war, even indirectly, means partnership in the oppression of the Yemeni people. We will not stand idly by in the face of any country’s involvement in the war in Yemen.”

Italy probes gaming giant Activision Blizzard over in-game spending by children
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:24:55 UTC
01:24:55 KST

Italy’s antitrust authority is investigating whether monetisation practices in Call of Duty Mobile and Diablo Immortal amount to a “widespread infringement” of EU consumer protection rules, particularly in relation to children.
Italy’s antitrust authorities have launched an investigation into Microsoft-owned gaming company Activision Blizzard amid claims it has used predatory game monetisation such as “loot boxes” and pay-to-progress designs in its popular mobile games Diablo Immortal and Call of Duty Mobile to target and exploit children and other players.
Italy, supported by consumer protection authorities in Norway and Denmark, is first seeking to find if the games company’s practices constituted a “widespread infringement” of EU consumer protection rules following player and public backlash in recent years.
Activision Blizzard is one of Microsoft's most well-known game publishers, known worldwide for genre-defining game series Call of Duty, Warcraft, StarCraft and Diablo, among others, and was bought by the big tech company in 2023 for $75.4 billion (€67.29bn)
Should the company be found in breach of the Italian Consumer Code it could face fines of up to 4% of its annual turnover in each of the affected countries, according to the European consumer law framework.
Italy’s investigation is part of a wider EU coordination launched at the end of September by the European Commission’s Consumer Protection Cooperation (CPC) Network, with actions set to launch across the EU with the aim of strengthening the protection of gamers’ rights targeting nine video games companies.
The CPC Network is coordinating action against Activision Blizzard UK Limited, Crytek GmbH, InnoGames GmbH, King.com Limited, Mojang AB, Plarium Europe S.à.r.l., PLR Worldwide Sales Limited, Riot Games Limited, Supercell Oy and Ubisoft EMEA SAS.
Italy’s investigation is the first step of this EU-wide approach.
Chief among the Italian authorities’ concerns is how the company’s practices have targeted children who are more at risk of gaming addiction and unable to understand or keep track of how much they are spending, especially as the company relies on virtual currencies paid for with real money to make purchases of in-game items, benefits and features.
Authorities highlighted the “lack of transparency and fairness in the use of virtual currencies” within the games, said the Authority in a statement.
The move is part of a wider drive at European and global level against tech companies over concerns their platforms’ and games’ designs negatively harm young people’s mental health, following a spate of suicides.
Just last month, the European Commission unveiled a proposal to protect children online known as the EU Kids Act, which aims to introduce a requirement for digital service providers to first prove that their platforms are “safe by design” and age-appropriate before children can use them.
The proposal specifically targets video games, including a ban on loot boxes — virtual mystery packages containing random items such as equipment and cosmetic gear — for children, as well as a requirement to clearly display real currency costs for in-game purchases and purchase alerts.
The proposal also aims to curb addictive behavior in children including banning “streak” mechanics that require players to login regularly or even daily as well as notifications encouraging children to resume or keep playing longer than they want.
The EU-wide action follows an open dialogue launched by the CPC Network with the video games industry last year, which the organisation diplomatically saying that it “did not bring satisfactory results,” especially in addressing monetisation and virtual currencies practices.
Parallel to these actions, the Commission is expected to present an EU Digital Fairness Act later this year, with measures including banning “dark patterns” (manipulative designs and false urgency), unfair personalization practices and subscription traps.
The CPC Network is also investigating Activision Blizzard UK Limited to see if they are complying with EU consumer law in their games.
“Roughly half of Europeans play video games… With that reach comes responsibility. The industry must ensure that its games do not expose players — especially children — to harmful or unfair practices,” said Michael McGrath the EU’s consumer protection commissioner.
“The game must be fair, and the rules must be respected. National authorities, with the support of the Commission, will make sure they are enforced,” he added.
Many gamers have also complained over the years over what they see as pay-to-win mechanics being employed more frequently by video game publishers.
These mechanics reward players who have spent more money in game, giving them an unfair advantage over players who have not despite them being more skilled.
This reduces the game to a battle of bank accounts rather than skill or merit. Games companies have often defended this decision by saying their games are free to play, and that paying is optional.
In a July 2022 interview with the Los Angeles Times, the former head of Blizzard Entertainment Mike Ybarra defended their gaming business model saying the company “gives a free Diablo experience to hundreds of millions of people, where they can literally do 99.5% of everything in the game".
He also claimed the vast majority of players had not spent any money and that players could complete the game without paying.

U.S. President Donald Trump said Thursday that the United States will not attack Iran before the November 3 midterm elections, drawing a clear public line on military action just hours after reports that the Pentagon had been preparing options for renewed strikes against the Islamic Republic before Americans go to the polls.
“We are having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. He said Iran was in “very bad condition” economically and militarily, but stressed that the U.S. blockade would remain in force. Trump claimed that 22 million barrels of oil had passed through the Strait of Hormuz the previous night, with none entering or leaving Iran. “We will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections,” he wrote, adding: “Iran will not have a nuclear weapon!”
The statement came after a series of U.S. media reports suggested the possibility of renewed military action was being actively prepared. NBC News reported that Trump and his national security team had discussed large-scale operations that could begin within weeks, while The Atlantic reported that the Pentagon had been asked to develop options that could be carried out before the November 3 elections. Axios reported that U.S. Central Command had been instructed several days earlier to complete preparations for a possible resumption of major combat operations, although no date had been set and Trump had made no final decision.
According to Axios, a renewed campaign could involve extensive strikes on Iranian energy infrastructure, other strategic facilities and nuclear targets. The Atlantic, citing administration officials, reported that the pre-election planning was linked in part to Trump’s desire to demonstrate progress in the conflict before the vote, although officials stressed that the scope, timing and even whether strikes would take place remained undecided.
The possibility of military action before the election represented a shift from the administration’s earlier messaging. In August, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told U.S. allies that Washington was not planning a return to major combat operations “for the time being,” with an American official saying that policy was expected to remain in place at least until after the midterms. The administration instead focused on sanctions, a naval blockade and increasing the flow of non-Iranian oil through the Strait of Hormuz.
At the same time, Washington has continued strengthening its military presence in the region. Ynetnews reported last week that the aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt and an additional Marine unit were being sent toward the Middle East amid the confrontation with Iran, the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz and escalating fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen. U.S. officials have also said stalled diplomacy has increased concern that major fighting could resume.
Trump’s latest statement now appears to remove one of the most immediate possibilities raised in those reports: a U.S.-initiated attack before November 3. It does not, however, rule out military action after the elections, while leaving Washington’s economic pressure campaign and military preparations in place.

Veteran actor Nana Patekar dies of cardiac arrest: Why every minute counts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:22:40 UTC
01:22:40 KST

Doctors say, for a sudden collapse in an adult, a bystander can start hands-only CPR with chest compressions rather than wait for formal training or mouth-to-mouth rescue breathing, provided the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally.
NEW DELHI: The death of veteran actor Nana Patekar at 75 has put the spotlight on sudden cardiac arrest, a medical emergency in which the heart abruptly stops pumping blood effectively and requires immediate resuscitation.According to details shared about his final hours, Patekar reportedly felt unwell in the early hours and was later found sweating and losing consciousness at his residence in Dona Paula, Goa. He was taken to Manipal Hospital, where doctors attempted to revive him with CPR for around 45 minutes to an hour but could not save him, said Dr Shekhar Salkar.Dr Ambuj Roy, Professor of Cardiology at AIIMS Delhi, said cardiac arrest can ultimately be the final common pathway of several serious medical emergencies. “If somebody is feeling unwell, particularly at night, you should immediately call for help and take the person to a hospital,” he said.Once cardiac arrest occurs, the priority is immediate CPR and defibrillation. “Once cardiac arrest occurs, CPR should be started immediately, within two minutes of the onset of cardiac arrest, and a defibrillator used as soon as possible,” he said.The urgency of starting CPR quickly is underscored by its steep impact on survival.
Dr Rakesh Garg, professor at AIIMS and an expert involved in developing Indian CPR guidelines, said the chances of survival can decrease by 7% to 10% with every minute without intervention.“If possible, a layperson should start CPR as soon as possible,” Garg said. Chest compressions act as a manual pump, helping circulate blood to the brain and other vital organs until professional medical help arrives. The circulation generated by CPR is not the same as that produced by a normally functioning heart, but it can help keep vital organs supplied with blood while emergency treatment is arranged.For a sudden collapse in an adult, a bystander can start hands-only CPR with chest compressions rather than wait for formal training or mouth-to-mouth rescue breathing, provided the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally.Garg said prolonged interruption of blood flow can deprive the brain of oxygen and cause brain injury. Medical intervention after eight to 10 minutes without effective resuscitation may be too late, he said, adding that brain injury can occur within 10 to 15 minutes.
He urged families to learn basic CPR so they can begin chest compressions while waiting for an ambulance or medical team, particularly when someone suddenly becomes unresponsive at home.Garg also said unexplained symptoms should not be ignored, particularly by people with cardiac risk factors. For those living alone, recognising warning symptoms early and seeking medical attention promptly becomes even more important, he said.

Strong US free speech safeguards in the First Amendment to its Constitution mean the US has maintained a comparatively hands-off approach to combating disinformation — both in the political and legal spheres. This has arguably intensified, however, under President Donald Trump's leadership, with critics alleging it's partly because of his own often uneasy relationship with the truth.

German authorities then alerted their Japanese counterparts. Germany and Japan do not have an extradition treaty, but extradition can still take place after judicial review.
In Germany alone, 152 organizations have been targeted by Qilin, with the group demanding more than $70 million in total. About one-tenth of that amount was paid. Over the course of four years, the group sought $2.9 billion in ransom payments worldwide, and victims transferred more than $140 million. North Rhine-Westphalia Interior Minister Herbert Reul said:
“This is the biggest blow German investigators have managed to strike in the fight against cybercrime.”
Authorities have identified three other leading Qilin members, but they are believed to be in Russia.

Three recently fired OpenAI researchers urged the company to preserve its ability to monitor how AI models reason and to cooperate with independent safety auditors, The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday.
In a letter to OpenAI's board and safety committees reviewed by the Journal, the former employees warned that AI developers risk losing visibility into the reasoning processes of increasingly advanced models.
“As an industry, we do not yet know how to safely develop and deploy models that we cannot monitor,” the letter said.
“OpenAI and other frontier companies should not move forward with developments that further decrease” the ability to monitor AI, it added.
The researchers urged OpenAI to preserve chain-of-thought monitoring, a technique that examines written traces of an AI model's reasoning to help detect potentially harmful or deceptive behavior.
Although the technique does not provide a complete picture of how AI systems operate, researchers consider it a potentially valuable tool for identifying risks as models become more capable.
The letter was signed by Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak and Mikita Balesni, who previously worked on OpenAI's safety and alignment research teams.
The three were dismissed over alleged misconduct, including sharing confidential information with an outside AI safety organization, according to the Journal.
OpenAI said an internal investigation found that the employees had mishandled sensitive information, “violating our policies and breaking the trust essential to our work.”
The researchers disputed the allegations, saying they did not believe they had “engaged with external parties outside the mandates of our jobs.”
The former employees called for greater cooperation with independent safety organizations, warning of the “risk that something truly catastrophic will happen.”
The warning comes amid growing scrutiny of autonomous AI agents after OpenAI disclosed that its models had bypassed internal safeguards during testing in July, gaining unauthorized access to company infrastructure and systems belonging to AI platform Hugging Face.
OpenAI subsequently acknowledged weaknesses in its monitoring and incident response procedures, saying it would strengthen safeguards and invest more resources in chain-of-thought monitoring to detect potentially dangerous AI behavior.

FSSAI cracks down on misleading 'healthy food' claims, tightens noose on brands
NEW DELHI: A nutrition product promoted for people undergoing GLP-1/GIP therapy, loose raisins carrying unsafe pesticide residues and expired or rotten food sold through Flipkart have all landed on the radar of the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), which has initiated separate enforcement action in the three cases.FSSAI has issued a notice to Dr Reddy’s and Nestle Health Science Ltd, Tirupati Wellness Pvt Ltd, Flipkart India Pvt Ltd, Amazon Seller Services Pvt Ltd and Netmeds Healthcare Ltd over non-compliant advertising and claims for Celevida GLP+ on e-commerce platforms.Among the claims flagged by the regulator was that the product provided “high protein support for lean muscle preservation during GLP-1/GIP therapies”. FSSAI also flagged claims such as “helps maintain lean muscle”, “supports muscle strength” and “preserve lean mass” and questioned the use of the brand name “Celevida GLP+” along with therapy-related claims, saying this could create a misleading association between the product and such therapies.The regulator further objected to descriptions including “complete daily nourishment” and “dependable nutrition in every serving”, saying these could portray the product as a complete nutrition product or meal replacement.
A representation that it was “imported from Europe for purity” was also found misleading, as European origin by itself does not establish enhanced or superior protein quality.FSSAI also flagged the claim “Contains 100% RDA BCAA” as misleading and directed food businesses to discontinue use of “100%” on food labels, packaging and promotional material. It also said the disclaimer that “Celevida GLP+” was merely a brand name did not offset the misleading impression created by the overall presentation, while claims on muscle strength, immunity support and energy metabolism were also found potentially misleading.In the raisins case, FSSAI has sanctioned prosecution against Nex International after a regulatory sample of loose raisins was found unsafe. The company appealed against the Food Analyst’s report, following which the counterpart sample was sent to a referral laboratory. The referral laboratory confirmed the sample was unsafe, with pesticide residues including carbendazim and lambda-cyhalothrin.
FSSAI has meanwhile suspended with immediate effect the licence of Shreyash Retail Pvt Ltd, a Flipkart seller, after receiving over 130 complaints, including more than 70 about expired or rotten food. Inspections of Flipkart facilities in Delhi and Noida also found expired and near-expiry products and hygiene deficiencies. In some cases, consumers reported vomiting after consuming expired food.According to Amazon spokesperson, Amazon.in operates as an online marketplace where independent third-party sellers list and sell their products. We confirm that the said product is no longer available on our marketplace.

FlyDubai co-pilot bashed women in thousands of "manosphere" X posts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:14:02 UTC
01:14:02 KST

FlyDubai co-pilot Hamam al Hamami spent a year bashing women with "manosphere" rhetoric on X, posts show
The FlyDubai co-pilot whose alleged violent attempt to crash a flight to Israel last week and kill everyone onboard has a history of writing and sharing misogynistic remarks on social media using the rhetoric of the so-called manosphere, CBS News has found.
Many posts written and shared by Hamam al Hamami on an X account that has since been deleted used derogatory language about women espoused by misogynistic online influencers. Some of his posts included violent rhetoric. In one, he threatened to "stamp on your head, wipe the floor with you, make you an example to others, and then release you." It is not clear if he was speaking about one person in particular, or referring to women in general.
Multiple sources familiar with the investigation into the alleged hijacking attempt told CBS News last week that al Hamami is an Omani national and was the co-pilot who attacked the plane's captain with a cockpit emergency ax as it approached Israel on Sept. 27. Passengers and crew managed to subdue him, according to their own accounts, and an off-duty flight crew on the jet made a safe emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
An Israeli security official told CBS News authorities were investigating the possibility the incident could have been an attempted Sept. 11-style terror attack. President Trump suggested a couple of days after the incident that the co-pilot could have links to Iran, "based on what I'm hearing."
The co-pilot's posts on X, which were made between November 2021 and late October 2022, paint a picture of a man who, at least during that period, had a very skewed view of women and a low opinion of men who, in his words, "grovel" to them.
"No matter how much you grovel or 'lick their feet,' you can forget about ever being with them; you chose the cheap, easy route to approach the opposite sex instead of elevating your own value as a man," he said in one post, which CBS News found an archived version of online. The posts were written in Arabic.
The Financial Times reported Wednesday that it discovered some 3,000 misogynistic messages posted or shared by al Hamami as part of an investigation, including him calling women "rotten meat."
According to the FT, he also lauded flying as "the safest means of public transport."
CBS News has not independently reviewed all of the posts cited by the FT.
Al Hamami's posts mingled the rhetoric of extremist interpretations of Islam with that of the manosphere movement. The only woman he spoke of positively was his mother, whom he credited with raising him and his siblings "on religion, morals, and virtue."
In one archived post seen by CBS News, al Hamami uses the manosphere term "simp" to describe a man "who hangs around feminist circles, licking women's feet in hopes of gaining their approval and getting closer to them. Typically, only a low-value male resorts to this behavior, turning to foot-licking as the easiest way to ingratiate himself with women. Does this mean I have to lick women's feet? The only woman whose feet I would kiss is my mother. As for the 'simp,' he has no dignity; he licks the feet of any woman — worthy or unworthy — just in hopes of getting close to one of them."
Al Hamami said in January 2022, that he was hoping to get married and move out of his parents' home as he neared the age of 25, but that he would only consider a woman who met very specific criteria.
He turned to a Muslim dating website in the hope of finding a woman between 18 and 23, according to the FT, and said he was seeking a "religious Saudi from a tribal background" who was willing to wear a face cover, not seek work outside the home, and to live abroad.
His failed search led him to conclude, according to the X posts viewed by FT, that most women "care primarily about money" and are "skilled at pretense."
The posts seen by the British newspaper included more aggressive language, including the assertion that a woman's "only obligation is to lift her legs," and that women who seek a divorce deserve "a good thrashing."
Israeli investigators believe the co-pilot acted as a lone wolf in the alleged hijacking attempt at the end of last month, people familiar with the matter told CBS News. He is in the United Arab Emirates, where he is undergoing interrogation by Israeli and UAE authorities.
Speaking to Fox News last week, Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu said Israel knew the co-pilot "underwent Islamist radical indoctrination," based on "personal information" gathered during questioning. He did not offer any further information on the alleged indoctrination, but added to Fox that the attacker was "suicidal," and that after he was subdued by other crew members and passengers, he shouted: "Kill me, kill me!"
Al Hamami worked for a short time for Oman Air, where he entered new pilot training. Surveillance by the Omani government discovered that he was visiting radical websites, the sources said. Oman Air then transferred him to an office job.
One source told CBS News that he resigned from his job at Oman Air after being placed on desk duty, and then left the airline around 2024.
At one point, sources said, al Hamami posted a video of planes belonging to Israeli flag carrier El Al airlines in Dubai with a photo at the end of the clip showing Ayman al-Zawahiri, the al Qaeda leader believed to have helped plan the Sept. 11 terror attacks on the U.S., who was killed in a U.S. drone strike in 2022.
Al Hamami moved to Dubai, and FlyDubai hired him without vetting him with the Omani government, the sources told CBS News.
It remains unclear how, despite his history of espousing both Islamic radicalism and misogyny — and questions over whether he should have been cleared to fly to Israel at all as an Omani national — he managed to become a pilot flying dozens of people to and from Tel Aviv.

FSB-linked charges appear in 67% of Russia’s political cases in 2026, Memorial report finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:12:29 UTC
01:12:29 KST

At least one charge falling under the investigative jurisdiction of Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) appears in 67% of politically motivated criminal cases recorded in Russia during the first nine months of 2026. While the overall number of prosecutions connected with defendants’ speech has declined, cases under other statutes handled by the FSB have increased. While the overall level of political repression in Russia remains roughly unchanged, the charges brought against defendants are becoming more severe, according to the new Barometer of Repression report by Memorial’s Support for Political Prisoners project covering the third quarter of 2026.
A catalyst for repression
Russia’s FSB has the authority to conduct investigations connected to extremism, terrorism, and state security. In the first nine months of 2026, the number of new defendants facing charges of “calls for extremism” rose by 26%, and charges involving calls for activity against state security rose 13%. Meanwhile, cases involving calls for terrorism or its justification fell by 1%. The report’s authors hypothesize that the FSB is becoming more active in politically motivated prosecutions.
Not more cases, but harsher ones
Overall, the scale of politically motivated criminal prosecutions inside Russia has not changed significantly. Memorial recorded 1,393 new defendants in the first nine months of 2026, compared with 1,339 during the same period last year, an increase of 4%. But the structure of repression is markedly new: the number of people prosecuted under statutes related to freedom of expression fell from 487 to 380, or 22%, while cases that rights advocates classify as restrictions on freedom of association rose from 219 to 328. Meanwhile, a previous rise in treason, terrorism, and sabotage cases effectively leveled off.
Much of the growth in the “freedom of association” category came from separate repression campaigns. Prosecutions against individual supporters of Alexei Navalny rose from 69 to 143 over the year, cases against Jehovah’s Witnesses increased from 45 to 91, and defendants from the so-called “Citizens of the USSR” movement jumped from 13 to 29. Nearly all cases Memorial classifies as prosecutions of Navalny supporters involve allegations of financing extremist activity through donations to his Anti-Corruption Foundation. In every quarter of 2026, at least 40 new such prosecutions became known.
Authorities also continued to prosecute people accused of involvement with Vyacheslav Maltsev’s Artpodgotovka movement. Memorial recorded 44 such cases in the first nine months of 2026, compared with 20 over the same period last year. Human rights advocates say the reasons for the simultaneous intensification of several unrelated campaigns remain unclear: it may reflect a shift in law enforcement attention toward alleged “organized” structures, though the authors do not rule out the possibility that several separate trends simply coincided.
At the same time, political prosecutions are becoming more severe. The share of cases involving at least one charge classified as especially serious rose from 29% in the first nine months of 2025 to 34% in 2026. Although the overall number of speech-related cases declined, their severity increased: the offense of “justifying or promoting terrorism” now accounts for more than 60% of prosecutions in the speech category, and in more than 80% of such cases, defendants are deprived of their liberty.
Russian-occupied territories and prosecutions of Ukrainian service members
In the Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine, Memorial recorded 307 new politically motivated criminal prosecutions in the first nine months of 2026, compared with 338 over the same period in 2025, a decline of about 10%. Human rights advocates, however, attribute that mainly to the end of a sharp surge in repression that had been seen in the second and third quarters of last year, rather than to a sustained easing of Russian legal pressure. Notably, the intensity of prosecutions in the occupied territories remains far higher than inside Russia itself: in Crimea and Sevastopol, the rate is 4.6 cases per 100,000 residents a year, while in occupied parts of the Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions, it is 9.1 — compared with 1.2 inside the country’s internationally recognized borders. Unlike other major categories, speech-related prosecutions in occupied territories rose by 17%.
The number of new criminal prosecutions of Ukrainian service members also fell — from 484 in the first nine months of 2025 to 330 in 2026. The main reason was the winding down of a mass campaign against Ukrainian Armed Forces personnel captured during fighting in Russia’s Kursk region, with the number of newly recorded prosecutions in that group falling from 258 to 72. Russia has not engaged in the systematic prosecution of Ukrainian prisoners of war captured elsewhere; however, captives taken during Ukraine’s Kursk operation were widely charged with “terrorism” simply for participating in combat on Russian territory.
Memorial believes the peak of that campaign has passed, as most prisoners whom Russian authorities intended to prosecute have already become defendants in criminal cases. New cases are still being discovered with a delay, however: in the third quarter of 2026, the number of newly recorded prosecutions of Ukrainian troops rose from 101 to 129, while among captives from the Kursk region the figure increased from 17 to 40. Russian authorities have said more than 500 Ukrainian service members were captured there, and Memorial is currently aware of prosecutions against 400 of them.
Prosecutions of Ukrainian service members remain the harshest category of political cases, rights advocates say: in 86% of such cases, the charges include at least one especially serious offense. By comparison, the figure is 59% for civilian defendants in the occupied territories and 34% inside Russia.
The number of people formally recognized as political prisoners by the Memorial project rose from 1,680 to 1,825 in the third quarter. A broader list of people deprived of their liberty in criminal cases where Memorial sees signs of political motivation grew from 5,567 to 5,740. The authors caution that some prosecutions become known only after a delay, meaning figures for individual periods may later be revised.

Researchers find 180,000 giant tortoises living on island in Seychelles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:11:53 UTC
01:11:53 KST

A survey of the world’s largest free-roaming giant tortoise population has discovered that the once endangered species is thriving.
A population of Aldabra giant tortoises lives on an island in Seychelles called Aldabra Atoll.
The most recent survey, led by Seychelles Islands Foundation (SIF) and the University of Exeter, revealed there were approximately 180,000 tortoises living on the island. This is the highest figure ever recorded for the species and far exceeds the human population of Seychelles.
The new figure was obtained by a team who analysed five years of tortoise counts between 2018 and 2022. It is the first update since a widely cited figure of 100,000 tortoises from the late 1990s.
Aldabra Atoll is one of only two places in the world where giant tortoises are found in the wild, with a much smaller population living in the Galápagos.
Dr Frauke Fleischer-Dogley, the CEO of SIF, said: “More than 180,000 giant tortoises roaming freely on our atoll is proof of what long-term commitment to conservation can achieve. This is wonderful news for Seychelles, for the world, and for everyone who has worked to protect Aldabra.”
The study, published in the scientific journal Ecology and Evolution, found that the population was relatively stable for this period, with a best estimate of almost 183,000 adult and sub-adult tortoises.
In the 19th century, exploitation of the animals meant there were fewer than 1,000 Aldabra tortoises left on the island, but a recovery programme led to it becoming a strict nature reserve in 1981 and a Unesco site in 1982.
Researchers are now saying it is one of the greatest conservation success stories of the Indian Ocean, with the new study confirming it. “Aldabra’s giant tortoise monitoring programme is one of the longest running in the region, but the atoll’s dense vegetation makes counting tortoises genuinely difficult in places,” said Dr Nancy Bunbury, one of the study’s co-authors.
“By modelling what we didn’t see, as well as what we did, we’ve produced the most reliable baseline yet for this iconic Seychelles species, establishing a benchmark we can use to track the population for decades to come.”
Despite the good news, the study’s authors say that vigilance is essential. Aldabra’s climate is changing, with longer and more frequent droughts predicted to reduce the shade and food available to tortoises, while rising sea levels threaten low-lying parts of the atoll.
The study authors say invasive mammals remain a threat including feral cats and black rats that prey on tortoise eggs and hatchlings. The planned eradication of these remaining invasive mammals, the authors say, could lift the last barriers to further growth of the population and help it withstand future climate pressures.
“These results are great news for the tortoises and testament to the fantastic work done in the field,” said Dr Dave Hudson, a postdoctoral research associate at the University of Exeter’s Cornwall campus.
“But it’s important to remember that the numbers provide a baseline – not an endpoint.
“Hopefully we have provided the conservation managers the evidence they need to track future change and act early as the tortoises face increasing pressures from climate change, drought and invasive species.”

Ethiopia launches drone attack against Eritrean troops who crossed into Tigray
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:11:32 UTC
01:11:32 KST

Eritrean troops who crossed into Ethiopia’s Tigray region have come under drone attack from government forces, raising the risk that renewed internal conflict in Ethiopia could trigger an all-out regional war between the neighbouring countries.
Military vehicles carrying soldiers drove across Eritrea’s southern border into Tigray on Wednesday, reaching the town of Adigrat 25 miles (40km) south, according to civilian witnesses, a militia commander and the conflict monitoring group Acled.
Eritrean troops were then targeted by Ethiopian government drones on Wednesday evening and Thursday morning, Acled said.
Eritrea has a historical enmity with the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which launched an offensive against the Ethiopian government on 23 September, but that previous hostility has been superseded by Eritrea’s desire to head off a perceived risk of Ethiopia invading it, in order to access the Red Sea.
In the last two weeks, the TPLF and six other armed groups in Ethiopia have fought the government in Tigray and the neighbouring regions Amhara and Afar. Ethiopia’s military pushed back and an allied militia, the Tigray Peace Force, took over Tigray’s regional capital, Mekelle, on 4 October after the TPLF withdrew from the city.
Eritrea’s information minister, Yemane Ghebremeskel, said in a statement: “We are not in the business of refuting wild allegations or narratives.” He did not explicitly confirm or deny the presence of Eritrean troops in Ethiopia.
Ethiopia’s foreign ministry said in a statement on Monday: “Ethiopia stands ready to defend its sovereignty, territorial integrity, and core national interests, while urging all regional actors to address shared challenges through constructive dialogue, partnership, and adherence to the principles of good neighbourliness rather than confrontation and zero-sum approaches.”
The TPLF and Ethiopia’s government fought a brutal civil war from 2020 to 2022. Between 300,000 and 800,000 civilians died, according to British government estimates. Both sides and their allies were accused of war crimes.
Eritrea intervened on the side of Ethiopia in that conflict, after a rapprochement between the two countries in 2018, which earned Ethiopia’s prime minister, Abiy Ahmed, the 2019 Nobel peace prize.
Eritrea, which gained independence from Ethiopia in 1993, has a long enmity with the TPLF, which ruled Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018. The two countries fought a war from 1998 to 2000.
Relations between the countries have deteriorated again in recent years. Abiy has said Ethiopia needs access to the Red Sea, and state media has claimed the country has historical rights to the Eritrean port of Assab. The US-Israeli war on Iran – leading Iran to limit shipping through the strait of Hormuz – has further raised the stakes of Red Sea access.
In its statement on Monday, Ethiopia’s foreign ministry said: “Any serious discussion of regional maritime affairs and security architecture must account for Ethiopia’s legitimate interests and its enduring connection to the Red Sea.”
Yemane said in a post on X on Wednesday that Ethiopia was “incessantly beating the drums of war and openly stating … that it will launch a war of aggression against Eritrea to acquire what it calls ‘sovereign access to the sea’ … In recent weeks, it has tried to repackage this war agenda in terms of ‘self-defence’ by fabricating various allegations against Eritrea.”
Magnus Taylor, Horn of Africa deputy director at the Crisis Group thinktank, said: “The big worry is that [Abiy] might try to solve all his problems at the same time, by invading Eritrea, possibly a regime change move and also a land grab for the Red Sea port, and also solving his problem with Tigray at the same time. It’s a very ambitious military agenda, though.”
While the full impact of the fighting on Tigrayan civilians is not clear, reports have emerged of the TPLF forcibly recruiting boys as young as 15 to fight.
“The civilians in these three regions [Tigray, Amhara and Afar] didn’t get healed from the first round of violence that was halted by the peace agreement [in 2022],” said Acled Ethiopia analyst Jalale Getachew Birru. “They just started healing recently.”

How the Houthi conflict is affecting countries along Africa's Red Sea coast — and beyond
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:11:00 UTC
01:11:00 KST

How the Houthi-Saudi conflict is affecting African countries
October 8, 2026
In September, one of the major conflicts in the Middle East came within sight of Africa, as Iran-backed Houthi rebels captured Yemen's Perim Island.
The island forms the narrowest point of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the southern entrance of the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. It is roughly 20 kilometers (12 miles) from Djibouti and 20-minutes by air to Ethiopia.
In early October, Yemen's armed forces and their Saudi allies launched a counteroffensive. TheIran-backed Houthis have been firing on merchant ships since the start of the Gaza war in 2023.
The economic consequences for Africa is coupled with a refugee inflow
African economies are already suffering from crisis in the Strait of Hormuz, which is making particularly fuel and fertilizer scarce and more expensive.
If the Bab el-Mandeb Strait also becomes impassable, the situation could deteriorate further. Shipping companies would have to make detours via the Suez Canal, which is controlled by Egypt or the southern tip of Africa, as some already do. The additional costs would be passed on to consumers.
The human cost of the escalation in Yemen hit Djibouti almost immediately. According to the UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR), at least 3,700 refugees have crossed from Yemen into Djibouti since September 10. Most of those who made it to the country's northern Obock region are women and children.
The UNHCR is preparing to assist another 10,000 people who have not yet crossed into Djibouti. But Obock, which is on the border with Eritrea, is extremely dry and this is causing other issues.
"We don't have much water here; there's no groundwater at all," Alessandra Roccasalvo, the UN Development Program (UNDP) representative for Djibouti, told DW. "Everything has to be desalinated."
Djibouti is a strategic military hub
Despite its small size, Djibouti — a Muslim-majority Horn of Africa country with a population of just over a million — is a major player in the region. Its position at at the entrance to the Red Sea makes it an attractive commercial and military shipping hub.
The United States, China, France, Italy, and Japan all operate military bases in Djibouti. The German Bundeswehr was also present until 2021, as part of a naval mission to combat maritime piracy.
The country's civilian ports serve as transshipment, or intermediate, hubs for global shipping cargo, goods and containers. So far, the Houthi advance has not led to empty docks in Djibouti.
But there are still potential consequences, said Roccasalvo: "Basically, there's an economic upswing here — which means, as in any country experiencing an upswing, building materials are needed: cement, raw materials, and other things."
Less of that money is now coming in because ships have to pay nearly twice as much for insurance and reinsurance as they used to. "Many ships no longer want to pass through the Suez Canal; many no longer want to pass through the Red Sea."
Knock-on effects for landlocked neighboring Ethiopia
Ethiopia — the world's most populous landlocked country — handles about 95% of its imports and exports through Djibouti's ports. Price hikes resulting from higher war-risk shipping insurance premiums are affecting the country greatly.
Shortly after the Houthis seized Perim, Ethiopia's economy faced another, even more immediate threat: On September 23, fighting broke out in the country's northern Tigray region.
Since then, the Ethiopian National Defense Forces (ENDF) have reportedly made gains against the Tigray-led rebel coalition that aims to overthrow the national government. The rebels briefly advanced toward the main corridor used for transporting goods between Djibouti's ports and the Ethiopian hinterland.
According to certain experts, the ENDF's advances have since reduced the threat of yet another trade blockade — but as long as the conflict remains unresolved, the situation could potentially deteriorate again.
For months now, Ethiopia has suffered more than almost any other African country from the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz and has already had to ration fuel at times. In the long term, the country aims to reduce its dependence on imports, for example by powering vehicles with domestically generated electricity instead of imported gasoline.
Can the conflict in Ethiopia affect Bab el-Mandeb access?
Ethiopia and its northern neighbor, Eritrea, have severed diplomatic ties; other regional powers such as Sudan, Egypt, and Somalia may find themselves siding with Eritrea rather than with Ethiopia.
Eritrea sees itself as facing a threat that Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has reiterated on several occasions: With Ethiopia deprived of access to the sea since Eritrea's independence, Abiy has often alluded to rectifying this perceived injustice — either through a political agreement, as was once sought with Somalia's breakaway region of Somaliland, or by force.
The port of Assab is located on the edge of Eritrea's panhandle — and is often described as the most likely target should Abiy choose the path of aggression. If the fighting within Ethiopia further escalates into a full-blown regional war, this could also lead to additional restrictions on safe passage through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the surrounding waters.
Experts have also raised concerns about the Shiite Houthis increasingly collaborating with the Sunni terrorist group Al-Shabab, which is based in Somalia. Although their ideologies are fundamentally different, they are particularly united by their hostility toward Israel and the US.
What tools are at the disposal of African countries to help remedy the situation?
The three African non-permanent members of the UN Security Council — the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Liberia, and Somalia — held an emergency meeting in mid-September, jointly calling for free shipping lanes and endorsing the demand that the crisis in Yemen be resolved under the auspices of the UN.
The situation at Bab el-Mandeb and in northern Ethiopia once again demands flexibility from Africa. In fact, some African economies could also benefit from relocation activities: Ports inKenya and Tanzania, for example, are becoming increasingly attractive for transshipment.
And while many countries are suffering from high oil prices, Nigeria's Dangote Group has announced an initial public offering and a new refinery in Kenya.

UAE blocks Israeli flights after flydubai cockpit attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:10:47 UTC
01:10:47 KST

Breadcrumb
UAE blocks Israeli flights amid reports of dispute over flydubai cockpit attack
The UAE has withdrawn landing permission for Israeli airlines attempting to repatriate passengers stranded in Dubai, forcing the cancellation of flights amid tensions over the handling of an suspected hijacking attack aboard a flydubai aircraft last week.
Israeli carriers Arkia, El Al and Israir cancelled flights scheduled for Wednesday and Thursday after Emirati authorities revoked the necessary authorisations, leaving passengers scrambling for alternative routes home.
Arkia said it had been working with the relevant authorities to restore permission but had been unsuccessful.
"Arkia has engaged with all relevant parties to regain authorization and operate the flights," the airline said in a statement cited by the Times of Israel.
"Unfortunately, these efforts have so far been unsuccessful, and we are therefore forced to cancel the flights."
The airline said affected passengers would receive full refunds, while those able to reach another destination served by Arkia would be offered a discount on flights to Israel.
The cancellations follow the suspension of flydubai's services to Tel Aviv after a violent incident aboard flight FZ1073 on 30 September, when an Omani co-pilot allegedly attacked the aircraft's Indian captain with an emergency axe.
The Dubai-Tel Aviv flight, carrying more than 170 passengers and crew, plunged more than 16,000 feet in approximately 30 seconds as the confrontation unfolded in the cockpit.
The wounded captain managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers to intervene and overpower the co-pilot. Two off-duty pilots subsequently took control and landed the aircraft safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.
Emirati prosecutors have described the incident as an attempted terrorist attack, although investigators have yet to establish the suspect's motive.
Flydubai subsequently suspended its Tel Aviv services until at least 14 October, disrupting a major air link between the UAE and Israel.
The suspension initially left an estimated 10,000 Israelis stranded in Dubai and other destinations, prompting Israeli authorities to arrange special repatriation flights.
According to Israel's Transportation Ministry, at least 7,415 passengers had returned by Tuesday aboard special flights operated by Israeli carriers or commercial services through Abu Dhabi.
However, the latest withdrawal of landing permissions has disrupted the final stage of the operation, which Israeli authorities had expected to conclude on Thursday.
The precise reason for the Emirati decision remains unclear, although the dispute has exposed disagreements over how the aviation crisis has been handled.
A source close to the UAE, speaking to The Jerusalem Post, criticised Israeli officials for describing the flights as a rescue operation, arguing that the terminology wrongly suggested that Israelis were in danger in the Emirates.
"'Rescue flights' is a term used for a country where it is dangerous to be. That is simply not the case," the source said.
The source also claimed that flydubai had been prepared to resume flights to Israel under revised security arrangements, similar to those used by Abu Dhabi-based Etihad Airways, but that Israeli authorities had rejected the proposal.
The claims have not been independently confirmed.
Etihad has continued operating between Abu Dhabi and Tel Aviv, increasing services to help accommodate stranded passengers.
The dispute comes as authorities in several countries investigate the flydubai incident and the apparent security failures that allowed the suspect to operate flights to Israel.
Saudi Arabia has launched an aviation safety investigation into the incident, while the UAE is conducting a separate criminal investigation.
According to Reuters, Saudi authorities have notified international aviation agencies that they will examine the incident under established international safety procedures.
The UAE, where the aircraft is registered, is participating in the Saudi-led investigation, while Israel has expressed willingness to assist but has not been formally included.
The episode presents an unusual challenge for relations between Israel and the UAE, which established diplomatic ties under the US-brokered Abraham Accords in 2020.
Direct commercial flights became one of the most visible symbols of normalisation, facilitating tourism, business and investment between the countries.
However, there has been no indication that the aviation dispute represents a wider suspension of diplomatic relations, with commercial flights through Abu Dhabi continuing despite the disruption in Dubai.

Rubio Warns Russia's War Could Spill Beyond Ukraine's Borders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:06:52 UTC
01:06:52 KST

LISBON -- US Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned that Russia's war against Ukraine is at a stalemate but could escalate into a broader regional conflict if the deadlock pushes either side toward increasingly dangerous actions.
Speaking in Lisbon on the final stop of a three-country swing through NATO allies Iceland, Greece, and Portugal, Rubio said Washington believes the war ultimately requires a negotiated settlement and remains ready to facilitate diplomacy.
His remarks came as a Russian strike on two buses in the Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk killed at least 33 people on October 8, according to local authorities.
Asked by RFE/RL about Russia's attacks on Ukraine and the security of NATO's eastern flank, Rubio called the conflict “a very dangerous war” that has reached reached a stalemate, which generally ends either through negotiations or escalation.
The first option requires both sides to make difficult compromises. The second could involve Russia or Ukraine intensifying the conflict in an attempt to change the military balance.
“That’s very dangerous,” Rubio said.
He warned that escalation could include sabotage in neighboring NATO countries, a strike, or other actions that could rapidly widen the conflict.
That could “quickly turn what is a war between two countries to a much broader, far more dangerous regional conflict,” he said.
“In the end, we do not believe that there will be military solutions...We think this war needs to end, and the negotiated settlement is sooner and better.”
Portugal's foreign minister backed diplomatic efforts to end the war, saying Russia's invasion violates international law and that any settlement should respect Ukraine's sovereignty.
Rubio also recast the debate over NATO defense spending, describing increased military outlays as an investment in defense rather than simply “spending more.” He said stronger individual NATO members would strengthen the alliance and its deterrence.
Rubio said NATO is fundamentally a defensive alliance and that its credibility depends on the capabilities of its members.
“NATO is important. For NATO to matter, NATO has to be strong,” he said. “For NATO to be strong, NATO's member states need to be strong.”
He said NATO members have different circumstances and cannot all contribute in the same way, but each should develop the strongest capabilities it can. “
He also called for greater cooperation on advanced military technology and the next generation of weapons, saying allies need to work together to meet future threats.
Asked whether European allies could continue to rely on the US amid possible changes to the American military presence in Europe, Rubio stressed the importance of maintaining strong NATO capabilities and deterrence.
He did not provide details on future US troop deployments but said the alliance's members share responsibility for maintaining its strength.
Rubio also sharply criticized Iran when asked about concerns surrounding the use of Portugal's Lajes air base and allegations raised by Amnesty International over potential violations of international law.
He declined to comment on a Portuguese investigation, saying it was a matter for Portuguese authorities.
Rubio instead accused Amnesty International of failing to focus on alleged abuses by Iran's government against protesters, including the "murders in cold blood of tens of thousands of people in the streets.”
“Those are war crimes. Those are crimes against humanity. Those are crimes committed against their own people,” Rubio said.

Bear kills man, seriously injures woman in their home in Mongolia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:05:55 UTC
01:05:55 KST

Bear kills man, seriously injures woman in their home in Mongolia as encounters rise across Asia
A bear killed a man and seriously maimed a woman in their home in the outskirts of Mongolia's capital, authorities said Thursday, warning that sightings of the animals have skyrocketed across the country this year.
The man in his 40s and the woman in her 50s were attacked on Wednesday night in the Bayanzurkh district on the outskirts of Ulaanbaatar, the city's environment department chief Munkhbayar M told a news briefing.
The woman fled after sustaining injuries and sought help from neighbors, and she is being treated in a hospital, he said.
A team of 35 rangers is trying to locate and kill the bear.
Bear sightings have risen in Mongolia, with 24 confirmed sightings in Ulaanbaatar so far this year, compared with just two in 2018 and one in 2019, Munkhbayar said. Across Mongolia, 754 bear sightings have been reported in 11 provinces and the capital in 2026. Of those, 80% involved cubs or female bears accompanied by cubs.
Investigations are underway to determine what has caused the rise in sightings. Authorities have issued bear-hunting permits across eight provinces and are seeking to procure tranquilizer dart guns to support rangers in rural areas.
A bear that was hunted and examined in the eastern province of Khentii was found to have no food in its stomach, Baljinnyam N, an official at the Environment and Climate Change Ministry, told reporters.
As a result, authorities banned in September the harvesting of nuts and berries from mountainous areas for this year, he said.
Bear attacks increasing in parts of Asia
A spike in human-bear encounters has been reported in other parts of Asia recently.
In September, prosecutors said at least six people had been killed in bear attacks in Russia's vast Siberian region of Krasnoyarsk over a one-month period, and an official in a neighboring region reported bears had put one town "under siege."
Prosecutors said they opened a probe into criminal negligence, accusing local officials of failing to control bear numbers.
Russia's brown bear population has more than doubled since 1990, from around 130,000 to almost 308,000 in 2026, according to Russia's natural resources ministry.
Meanwhile, Japan has also recorded a sharp rise in bear sightings and attacks on humans in recent years, including in the outskirts of towns and cities. A record 13 people were killed by bears in Japan last year, and there has been a jump in encounters as the animals emerge hungry from hibernation.
The animals have been seen on airport runways, walking on golf courses, roaming near schools and causing panic in supermarkets and hot spring resorts almost on a daily basis.
The problem was so bad that last year, the U.S. State Department warned Americans in Japan to be alert for bears.
 The causes are complex and include variations in food available — something potentially linked to climate change — as well as rural depopulation, experts say.

The law provides for 50% of Inspector General posts, at least 67% of Additional Director General posts and all Director General and Special Director General posts in CAPFs to be filled by IPS officers on deputation.
NEW DELHI: The Central Armed Police Forces (General Administration) Act, 2026 — which stipulates that 50% of the posts in CAPFs at the level of Inspector General, a minimum 67% posts at the level of Additional Director General and 100% posts at level of Director General and Special Director General-level, be filled by IPS officers on deputation — came into force on Thursday.The home ministry, in a notification, specified October 8, 2026 as the “appointed day” on which the provisions of the Act shall come into force.The operationalisation of the IPS quota in senior CAPF posts comes days after Union home secretary Govind Mohan told the Supreme Court that deputation of 46 IPS officers across five paramilitary forces — CRPF, BSF, CISF, ITBP and SSB — since the court’s May 26, 2025 direction for a gradual reduction in the number of IPS officers on deputation within two years, was as per the law since the SC had not held that such deputation should be discontinued altogether.
While CAPF cadre officers are opposed to senior posts in CAPFs being “cornered” by IPS officers, on the grounds that it blocks their career progression, the govt has backed deputation of IPS officers, describing them as crucial to coordination between the Centre and the states in view of national and inter-state roles of the CAPFs.

U.K., Israel both claim a moral win with apparent truce in diplomatic feud
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:02:43 UTC
01:02:43 KST

U.K. and Israel appear to reach tense truce, but diplomatic feud highlights Israel's strained ties with Europe
London and Tel Aviv — The U.K. and Israel appeared Thursday to have narrowly avoided a major diplomatic confrontation, reaching a compromise to allow Britain's nearly 200-year-old consulate in east Jerusalem to remain open, but under a new name and with a significantly reduced staff.
Israel had threatened to shut the facility down completely in a dispute over British sanctions barring the import of goods from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
The agreement — which has been framed very differently by London and Tel Aviv — may prevent the tension between the two longstanding allies from escalating, but it has highlighted how strained ties have become between Israel and several European governments over Israel's ongoing actions in the Palestinian territories.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said talks with the U.K. had taken place "with the aim of preventing further deterioration in relations," following weeks of escalating tension.
The dispute began in September when London announced sanctions — along with 11 other Western nations — targeting Israeli settlements in the West Bank. The measures include a ban on goods produced in the settlements and sanctions against companies and individuals involved in facilitating settlement expansion.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband described the measures as the "beginning of a new approach" to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.
Israel retaliated by giving Britain 30 days to close its east Jerusalem consulate. The facility has been operating since 1839, when Jerusalem was still part of the Ottoman Empire, predating the founding of Israel by more than a century. The consulate has historically operated independently of the U.K. Embassy in Tel Aviv, as Britain's principal diplomatic link with Palestinian officials in east Jerusalem, the West Bank and the Gaza Strip.
On Thursday, both governments sought to claim the diplomatic high ground.
Saar, in his statement, presented the agreement as a demonstration of Israel's willingness to respond to measures taken against it.
"It is not possible to act against Israel without Israel taking appropriate measures in response," he wrote. "We did not want to reach this point, but the actions of the UK Labour Government brought us here."
Saar insisted Israel had followed through on its September vow to retaliate for the sanctions, including by lifting the U.K. consulate's previous diplomatic status.
Under the new arrangement, Britain's consul general and 19 diplomats will leave Israel, while no more than seven diplomats will remain at the renamed mission, according to Saar.
Israeli officials have not said explicitly whether the remaining diplomats at the mission would retain their accreditation and diplomatic immunity, but Britain's top diplomat Miliband said in his statement that, "without an understanding, we would not have the necessary assurances for the security and protections of our staff and premises," indicating that those protections were likely part of the negotiations.
Miliband also said in his statement that the U.K. did "not accept that the Government of Israel has the legal right to close the British Consulate General in Jerusalem," reaffirming Britain's longstanding position that "East Jerusalem is occupied territory."
Miliband said the newly renamed U.K. Mission would remain independent and operational, continuing to work with Palestinians. He also pledged to rebuild Britain's diplomatic presence in the coming months and ruled out any retaliatory measures — as long as "credible" discussions with Israel continue.
Both sides appeared to have moderated their responses because their bilateral security and business ties are too important to risk, Israeli political scientist Jonathan Rynhold told CBS News on Thursday.
The U.K. is an important economic market, and it punches above its weight diplomatically on the global stage, said Rynhold, a senior researcher with the Begin-Sadat Center at Israel's Bar Ilan University.
"They found something to do without blowing the whole relationship up," Rynhold said of the compromise.
Israel regards Jerusalem as its capital, while Britain and much of the international community do not recognize Israeli sovereignty over east Jerusalem, which Israel captured from Jordan in the 1967 Six-Day War and subsequently annexed.
The dispute comes amid a broader deterioration in Israel's relations with several European governments.
Spain has withdrawn its ambassador from Israel and imposed an embargo on arms sales to the Jewish state, while France formally recognized Palestinian statehood last year, drawing rebukes from the U.S. and Israel. Israel has also clashed with Ireland and Norway over their recognition of a state of Palestine.
The other nations that joined the U.K. in September in announcing sanctions or plans to impose sanctions targeting West Bank settlements were Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain, Sweden.

French, US and Russian astronauts return to Earth after eight months in space
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:02:26 UTC
01:02:26 KST

French, US and Russian astronauts return to Earth after eight months in space
SpaceX brought France's Sophie Adenot and fellow astronauts Jessica Meir, Jack Hathaway and Andrey Fedyaev back to Earth on Thursday after an eight-month mission on board the International Space Station that saw Adenot become the first French woman to walk in space.
Four astronauts returned to Earth from the International Space Station on Thursday after hurrying there eight months ago to replace an ailing colleague and his crew.
SpaceX brought the US, French and Russian flyers back with a splashdown in the Pacific off the coast of Los Angeles.
NASA’s Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway, France’s Sophie Adenot and Russia’s Andrey Fedyaev departed the orbiting lab on Wednesday, eager to reunite with their families after a lengthy separation. Their replacements arrived three weeks late because of capsule repairs, stalling this crew’s homecoming.
They couldn’t wait to feel the breeze on their faces, hit the shower and, for Adenot at least, plunge back into water sports.
“We are so excited to be back on Planet Earth after an incredible mission on the International Space Station,” Meir radioed moments after splashing down. While still in orbit, she said the crew had “a lot of mixed, swirling emotions” and would miss the “extraordinary views of our home planet”.
Read moreExclusive: French astronaut Sophie Adenot recounts her ‘miracle’ mission from orbiting ISS
Meir and her crew left the planet in February to replace four station occupants who were sent home early after one of them – NASA's Mike Fincke, now retired – fell ill. It was NASA's first medical evacuation in 65 years of human spaceflight.
The new foursome watched with pride two months later as the Artemis II astronauts flew around the moon. They also celebrated the United States’ 250th birthday up there, with Meir joining the Boston Pops with her piccolo for a Fourth of July concert.
Meir took part in four spacewalks, while Adenot ventured outside three times for maintenance and upgrades to the 28-year-old outpost.
In the middle of all the work, the astronauts found time for fun, throwing a dance party last month and holding regular cooking demonstrations complete with aprons and a chef's toque.
Meir presented a how-to video for curly-haired spacewomen like herself, while Hathaway kept his bushy moustache – a space rarity – groomed to perfection. He grew the naval aviator-style moustache before rocketing into orbit as a way to honour his Navy ties, and found it no harder to maintain in weightlessness than on Earth. Some ground controllers grew moustaches in solidarity.
Will his moustache disappear now that his mission is over?
“It’s kind of become a little bit of my brand up here,” Hathaway said in August, “so I don’t know if it’ll go away right away or I’ll end up keeping it for a while.”
Seven astronauts remain aboard the space station, representing the US, Russia and Canada. The outpost has welcomed 298 visitors from 26 countries since the doors swung open in 2000, by NASA's count.
