Bengal, Tamil Nadu, Assam and Puducherry brace for closely watched bypoll verdicts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
15:51:46 UTC
00:51:46 KST

Polling officials check Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs) and other polling materials at a distribution centre (ANI photo)
NEW DELHI: Votes cast in five assembly constituencies and one Lok Sabha seat will be counted on Friday, with the results of the bypoll elections likely to be closely watched for broader political signals.The elections were held on October 6 in five assembly seats — Nandigram and Rejinagar in West Bengal, Madurantakam and Dharapuram in Tamil Nadu and Thattanchavady in Puducherry. The Lok Sabha seat of Nagaon in Assam also went to polls. Counting of votes will begin at 8am.The contests are not necessarily referendums on the governments in power, but they have acquired significance because they come at different points in the political transitions taking place in these states, particulary Tamil Nadu and West Bengal.
BJP's first poll after the mega Bengal victory
The spotlight will be firmly on West Bengal, where the BJP replaced the TMC after 15 years in power. The Nandigram and Rejinagar results would perhaps offer an early indication of how the BJP is performing after moving from the opposition to government.Turnout was high in both seats, with nearly 80 per cent of the 5.24 lakh electors voting. Nandigram recorded 80.89 per cent polling and Rejinagar 80.08 per cent.The polling, however, was not without controversy as there were allegations of voter intimidation, booth-level irregularities and sporadic clashes.
The arrest of Aam Janata Unnayan Party chief Humayun Kabir after a confrontation with police in Rejinagar and Congress' demand for repolling in both seats added to the political tension.Nandigram carries particular weight because of its history as the constituency was central to the anti-land acquisition movement that helped bring the TMC to power in 2011. Suvendu Adhikari defeated Mamata Banerjee there in the 2021 Assembly election and won the seat again in 2026, while retaining Bhabanipur, leading to the bypoll.The BJP has fielded Hasirani Rath, whose son Chandranath Rath, a former aide of Adhikari, was shot dead two days after the BJP won the Assembly election. Her candidature therefore added an emotional element to the contest.The Opposition vote is also divided as the TMC faction led by Mamata Banerjee withdrew its candidate and backed Congress nominee Milan Pradhan. A rival TMC faction led by Ritabrata Banerjee is contesting separately. The result could therefore indicate whether opposition coordination can translate into votes or whether the division benefits the BJP.Rejinagar presents a different contest where Humayun Kabir, who had won both Rejinagar and Nowda in the Assembly election, retained Nowda, leaving Rejinagar vacant. His AJUP has fielded his son Golam Nabi Azad. The contest includes candidates from the BJP, Mamata-led TMC, rival TMC faction, Congress and CPI(M).With a sizeable minority electorate, Rejinagar is particularly important for parties trying to consolidate or expand their respective support bases. For the Mamata-led TMC faction, it is also a test of whether it can retain support without relying on the familiar party name and symbol.
Tamil Nadu tests TVK's early popularity
Tamil Nadu's Madurantakam and Dharapuram bypolls will also be closely watched, particularly because they are the first electoral test for the TVK government after it came to power in May.The AIADMK is seeking to win back the two seats it lost to the TVK in the April Assembly election, making the results an early measure of whether the new ruling party has retained its electoral momentum.Madurantakam recorded 86.26 per cent turnout, while Dharapuram saw 80.30 per cent polling. Both figures were lower than in the Assembly election five months ago. Turnout fell by nearly seven percentage points in Madurantakam and about 9.5 percentage points in Dharapuram.Counting centres in both constituencies have been placed under three-tier security. The EVMs and VVPAT units were moved to sealed strongrooms after polling, with round-the-clock surveillance and central and state security personnel deployed at the sites.
Assam and Puducherry complete the day's picture
In Assam, the Nagaon Lok Sabha bypoll is being seen as a three-way contest between BJP candidate and former bureaucrat Devasish Sharma, Congress nominee and former MLA Sibamoni Bora, and AIUDF chief Mohammed Badruddin Ajmal.The seat fell vacant after Congress MP Pradyut Bordoloi, who had won Nagaon for a second consecutive term in 2024, left the party, contested the Dispur Assembly seat on a BJP ticket and won it.Around 76 per cent of Nagaon's 19.05 lakh electors voted. Fifteen candidates are in the fray, although the contest is expected to be primarily between the BJP, Congress and AIUDF candidates.
In Puducherry, the Thattanchavady Assembly bypoll recorded 80.8 per cent turnout. The seat fell vacant after AINRC chief and Chief Minister N Rangasamy resigned from it while retaining Mangalam.By the end of Friday, the results across these six contests would provide more than individual winners and losers. In West Bengal, they will offer an early look at the BJP's ability to consolidate power and at the opposition's ability to regroup. Tamil Nadu will provide an initial test of the TVK's popularity after its assembly victory, while Nagaon will show how the BJP, Congress and AIUDF fare in a three-way contest.

Sudan war: Burhan rejects talks and vows to defeat RSF
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
15:50:42 UTC
00:50:42 KST

Breadcrumb
Sudan war: Burhan rejects talks and vows to defeat RSF
Sudan’s army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan has rejected negotiations, vowing to retake all territory held by the rebel paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), as fighting widens in Kordofan and thousands are displaced in Blue Nile.
During an address at a gathering in Village 5, in the northern Sudanese locality of Merowe, al-Burhan vowed to seize “every inch” of RSF-held territory, adding that the “military option” would continue until the RSF was removed from Sudan.
Burhan declared that "there will be no negotiations with the rebels or with any other party,” without specifying whom else he was referring to.
The RSF rebels, who are led by Burhan's erstwhile ally Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo (commonly known as Hemedti) are widely believed to be backed by the UAE.
According to a statement from the office of the Transitional Sovereignty Council (TSC), which is headed by Burhan, he reiterated his determination to continue efforts to defeat and eliminate the RSF.
Lauren Fortgang, Director of PAEMA (Preventing and Ending Mass Atrocities), told The New Arab that Al-Burhan’s push to continue the offensive in Sudan was further evidence of the international community’s “continued failure to hold either party responsible for attacks against civilians and gross human rights violations”.
“Burhan will continue to reject negotiations, including the US-led diplomatic efforts, unless there are incentives to stop fighting,” she said.
“The international community's continued failure to hold either party responsible for attacks against civilians and gross human rights violations only signals to both Burhan and Hemedti that they can continue to act with impunity.”
Al-Burhan’s comments came after Massad Boulos, the US senior adviser for Arab and African affairs, met the army chief in Egypt earlier this week as Washington stepped up efforts to broker an end to Sudan’s devastating three-year war.
Boulos said the meeting took place during a lunch hosted by Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi in the north-western Egyptian city of New Alamein at the weekend, on the sidelines of the African Union’s eighth mid-year co-ordination meeting.
Boulos did not describe the encounter as a formal bilateral meeting.
Following the encounter, Boulos reiterated US support for Sudan’s unity, sovereignty and territorial integrity, writing on X that peace could be achieved “through an inclusive Sudanese-owned and Sudanese-led national dialogue [and] transition toward a civilian-led government”.
“The United States stands ready to support all efforts leading to a comprehensive dialogue among the Sudanese political forces, leading to a preliminary road map of the future of the Sudan,” Boulos wrote.
“We encourage the Sudanese to be inclusive and to engage actively with regional and international stakeholders to co-ordinate views.”
The diplomatic engagement was followed by a dispute between Washington and al-Burhan after the US reportedly withheld a visa from the Sudanese army chief ahead of the UN General Assembly in New York.
Saudi Arabia subsequently allegedly threatened to withdraw from the Quad mechanism for Sudan, a diplomatic grouping seeking to mediate an end to the war and comprising the US, UAE, Egypt and Saudi Arabia.
The US decision not to issue the visa was reportedly linked to Sudan’s army-led administration resisting a US proposal for a 90-day humanitarian ceasefire, followed by political negotiations aimed at ending the war and reviving a transition towards civilian rule.
PAEMA director Lauren Fortgang stated that any US-led efforts to secure a ceasefire or advance a political settlement must require both the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and RSF to be held accountable for violations of international law.
“For the U.S. efforts to achieve a ceasefire, or any work towards a political settlement to be successful, all parties to the conflict must be held accountable for the violations of international law that they continue to commit,” she told The New Arab.
She also argued that accountability must extend beyond Sudan’s rival forces to countries accused of supporting the conflict.
The UAE, Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Russia have all faced allegations from experts, human rights organisations and several Western governments of seeking to shape the war via arms supplies, financial and logistical assistance and diplomatic support.
“It’s not just the warring parties that need to be held accountable. The external backers of the war must also be held responsible. Tools that can be utilized, such as the UN arms embargo, remain in jeopardy while a political impasse festers amongst the Security Council.”
As al-Burhan has pledged to continue fighting, clashes are intensifying in Kordofan, a strategically important region where the SAF and RSF are battling for control of territory.
Fortgang said this showed the “blatant disregard for civilian lives by both SAF and RSF is evident”.
The PAEMA director added that civilians and life-sustaining infrastructure are being targeted in both Kordofan and Blue Nile, while thousands have been displaced from their homes.
The RSF has been massing in West Kordofan as the Sudanese army advances towards the cities of En Nahud and Al Khuway following gains in neighbouring North Kordofan, according to multiple reports.
In one of the latest attacks by the RSF, ten civilians were killed and several others wounded in Sudan’s West Kordofan state, according to reports by The Dar Hamar Emergency Committee- a local, community-led relief and monitoring group.
The committee also accused the RSF of multiple violations against civilians in Abu Ajal village, in the south-eastern countryside of En Nahud.
In Blue Nile state, more than 5,500 people were displaced from villages over three days amid deteriorating security, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said on Tuesday.
Following the outbreak of the war between the army and the RSF in April 2023, Sudan has faced one of the world’s largest humanitarian crises.
"The humanitarian situation continues to deteriorate, compounded by mass displacement and extreme weather conditions," Fortgang told TNA.
"Food insecurity and famine conditions that communities are experiencing could be prevented if humanitarian access was granted, local responders had the resources they needed to operate, and the targeting of humanitarian workers ceased."
More than 14 million people have been displaced and nearly 20 million face hunger, according to the UN World Food Programme.
Repeated diplomatic initiatives have failed to secure a lasting ceasefire.

India to come out with a national plan to boost small-scale fisheries sector
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
15:50:01 UTC
00:50:01 KST

India already has policies and schemes covering several aspects of small-scale fisheries. The NPOA-SSF is intended to bring these strands together into a single, measurable and participatory national framework, with clearly identified priorities, responsibilities, resources and monitoring mechanisms.
NEW DELHI: The government is preparing to come out with a National Plan of Action on small-scale fisheries to promote the sector in a coordinated manner, keeping an eye on the country’s target to scale up its seafood exports to Rs 1 lakh crore by 2030. The livelihood of about 30 million fisherfolk is linked to fisheries and allied activities in India.As part of the exercise, the department of fisheries has sought fishers’ views before framing the plan, whose draft is expected to be released around World Fisheries Day on Nov 21, and has written to coastal states and UTs to designate a nodal officer or team, organise stakeholder consultations this month and share the feedback with a dedicated national task force which will prepare the draft.India already has policies and schemes covering several aspects of small-scale fisheries. The NPOA-SSF is intended to bring these strands together into a single, measurable and participatory national framework, with clearly identified priorities, responsibilities, resources and monitoring mechanisms.The National Plan of Action on small-scale fisheries (NPOA-SSF) is being developed in line with the voluntary guidelines for securing sustainable small-scale fisheries of the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) and India’s national policy on marine fisheries, 2017.
“The plan will address a broad range of issues affecting small-scale fishing communities, including access to fisheries resources, sustainable fisheries management, gender equality, climate change and disaster risk,” said P Krishnan, director, Bay of Bengal Programme Inter-Governmental Organisation (BOBP-IGO).The BOBP-IGO is facilitating and coordinating the exercise as the Centre requested coastal states and UTs to conduct their own state-level consultations and consolidate fishers’ views for framing the plan.As part of strengthening the sector, the govt last year released a national framework to establish a centralised digital traceability system for fisheries and aquaculture to ensure compliance with international regulations, promote food safety and improve market access.
The move is expected to help India expand its export markets for fisheries in the wake of the imposition of high tariffs by the US on Indian shrimp and other marine products. India’s seafood exports amounted to Rs 62,408 crore in 2024-25, with a substantial amount of it coming from shrimp exports.Since the framework for the centralised digital traceability system will facilitate enhanced transparency and robust quality assurance, the marine commodity can easily be accepted in other markets, as it will enable real-time, end-to-end tracking of seafood products from ‘farm to plate’ and ‘catch to consumer’ — an essential requirement in many countries.

Iraq rejects Syrian request to repatriate suspected IS detainees
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
15:47:14 UTC
00:47:14 KST

Breadcrumb
Iraq rejects Syrian request to repatriate 4,000 suspected IS detainees
Iraq has rejected Syria's request to repatriate thousands of suspected Islamic State members transferred from Syrian detention centers to Iraqi custody earlier this year, a senior Iraqi security official said on Wednesday.
Iraqi National Security Advisor Qasim al-Aboudi said that a meeting had been held recently between Syria, Iraq and the United States to discuss the fate of the prisoners.
Al-Aboudi said Syria had requested that the 4,000 Syrian prisoners be handed over to be tried in Syria, but Iraq refused. Iraq has repatriated about 50 Syrian detainees who were determined not to be IS members, he told The Associated Press, while the Syrian prisoners remaining in Iraq include about 400 who are believed to be high-level members of the extremist group.
“Iraq is conducting investigations, and anyone proved to have committed crimes in Iraq will be tried under Iraqi law,” he said.
Some prisoners could later be transferred to their home countries to complete their sentences, he said.
Syria did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
More than 5,700 prisoners with alleged IS ties - including some 4,000 Syrians - were transferred from northeast Syria to Iraq after fighting broke out in January between Syrian government forces and the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces, which had long guarded the detention centers where they were held.
Some IS-linked prisoners managed to flee during the chaos of the clashes, and there were fears that a larger-scale escape would take place. While the extremist group lost control of the territory it once seized in Iraq and Syria years ago, its cells still periodically carry out attacks in both countries.
The discussions about the prisoners' fate come as the United States has ended a 12-year mission to fight IS in Iraq, with the last US troops withdrawing from the country last month.
Al-Aboudi said Iraq has asked for financial support from the US and other countries taking part in the global coalition against IS to help with the costs of housing the prisoners.
“Iraq asked for an allocation of $500 million. The coalition promised support, but Iraq is still waiting,” he said.
A US defense official and the office of Tom Barrack, the US envoy to Syria and Iraq, referred questions about the prisoners to Iraqi and Syrian authorities.
Many of the prisoners transferred to Iraq had been held in Syria for years without charges. Rights groups have raised concerns about detention conditions in both countries.
Human Rights Watch said in a report this week that “the Iraqi justice system has a documented history of torture and unlawful executions.” It urged Iraqi authorities to “adhere to international fair trial and detention standards” and abolish the death penalty.
Al-Aboudi said prisoners from countries that do not enforce capital punishment would not face the death penalty.
Those from countries with prisoner exchange agreements with Iraq could be transferred home to complete their sentences after conviction, he said.
Many Western countries, however, have been reluctant to repatriate citizens accused or convicted of IS ties, as well as women and children believed to be militants’ family members.
(The Associated Press)

====================================================================================================

NASA releases Artemis II’s massive trove of moon science
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
15:45:32 UTC
00:45:32 KST

NASA’s Artemis II mission—a slingshot around the moon earlier this year that sent four astronauts to lunar space for the first time in more than half a century—was an unequivocal success. The voyage was chiefly a technological stepping stone for future crewed forays to the lunar surface, which should culminate with the founding of a small base near the moon’s south pole. But it was also a chance to carry out novel observations of the lunar farside, a largely mysterious realm that has been rarely glimpsed by human eyes.
Although Artemis II’s Orion spacecraft carried minimal science payloads, its astronauts were equipped with digital cameras (and iPhones)—and between April 1 and 10, they captured 814 gigabytes of lunar science data. At a press conference yesterday NASA presented its preliminary findings, which touch on everything from the moon’s surprisingly colorful craters to a series of curious flashes that the astronauts spied in lunar shadows. The release also includes more than eight hours of audio from the crew, videos of their nail-biting return to Earth, hand-annotated images, and much more—all available in a vast online repository.
Besides being breathtaking, the mission’s high-resolution imagery helps address more pragmatic queries: Which landing sites might be best for upcoming missions, and how safe would an outpost somewhere on the lunar farside be? “These findings are going to help shape future Artemis mission architectures,” said Marie Henderson, Artemis II’s deputy lunar science lead, during the press conference.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The crew’s sojourn around the moon may have been brief—just under seven hours—but they still surveyed a large swath of the farside, some of which was cloaked in total darkness. Arguably, the mission’s most important discovery emerged from those shadowy regions: five flashes of light, each in a different location on the lunar farside.
These were meteorite impacts. That isn’t inherently surprising: the airless moon gets bombarded by cosmic debris all the time. Sometimes these impactors—either asteroids or cometary fragments—are relatively big: in the spring of 2024, for example, a 15-meter object slammed into the moon with the force of an atomic bomb, cutting out a 222-meter-long pit.
Mostly, though, the moon is pelted by meteoroids the size of bullets or footballs. Each could, with a direct strike, kill an astronaut or trash a fancy new moon rover, so it’s good to know how often these small-but-lethal space rocks rain down on the lunar surface.
That’s why understanding what the Artemis II crew saw on the farside “matters for the future of human exploration,” said Jen Heldmann, a member of Artemis II’s lunar science team and deputy project scientist for Artemis IV, at the press event. Based on the brightness and brevity of the five flashes, scientists think each meteoroid was around 8.5 grams in mass—about as much as two dice. That may seem harmless, but they were moving at tens of kilometers per second, so these impactors are akin to space bullets.
The Artemis II crew flew outside any major annual meteoroid streams, meaning the five impacts they saw in just under an hour likely represent the typical background rate of small meteorite impacts on the lunar surface. With that in mind, NASA gauged the likelihood for a similar space bullet striking a future moon base: about a one-in-10,000 chance per decade. “We’re probably safe going forward,” Heldmann said.
The astronauts were also on the lookout for swarms of lunar dust. This jagged microscopic debris, easily dispersed by meteorite impacts and rocket exhaust, is corrosive, abrasive and adhesive. It makes quick work of wires, space suits and other hardware, chewing through them like space piranhas. Everyone hates it; it’s a major long-term hazard.
During the Apollo moon missions of the 1960s and 1970s, astronauts occasionally reported seeing hazes of sunlight-lofted dust drifting over parts of the lunar surface. But the Artemis II crew didn’t see any, suggesting that this strange phenomenon may be a transient problem rather than a persistent one.
The Artemis II images also revealed the subtle colors of lunar geology, showing that the moon’s seemingly monochrome surface is actually dappled with greens, yellows, grays and browns. Each of these hues, NASA’s analysis confirms, correspond to different types of ancient volcanism, from glasslike oozes to rubbly pyroclastic flow deposits. NASA also hoped that the crew could spy tectonic landforms during their flyby—things like faults, including those that could rupture and create prolonged, and potentially structure-toppling, moonquakes.
At one point, the crew caught a surreal series of arching crevasses in Oceanus Procellarum (the “Ocean of Storms,” a huge basin filled with primeval lava). These were wrinkle ridges, thought to form when the weight of the erupted lava squashes down on the moon’s crust, causing it to snap and contract. “The fact that they were able to see that from orbit was pretty phenomenal,” says Debra Needham, a member of the Artemis II science operations team.
Despite the fanfare of an official press conference, in truth, nothing in NASA’s report is especially revelatory. If anything, it serves as a reminder that unlocking the moon’s secrets—its alien geology, its hazardous landscapes and any scientific or economic treasures it may hold—relies getting a closer, surface-level look via more crewed and robotic investigations. In late September NASA also announced three new science payloads for near-future landings, all building on Artemis II’s success and adding to the case for an eventual moon base. One will monitor micrometeor impacts and other environmental threats at the lunar south pole, a second will search for hollow “lava tubes” that could be sites for underground habitats and a third will study how water ice might accumulate in and change the stability of lunar soil.
The report’s emphasis on future exploration was also tempered by an intentional callback to the past. NASA officials noted that their report’s release date, October 7, has significance in spaceflight history: on this day, back in 1959, the Soviet Union’s Luna 3 space probe beamed back the first-ever images of the moon’s farside, showing it to be a heavily scarred, crater-filled wasteland.
Luna 3’s images were eye-opening but still blandly colorless and fuzzy—especially compared with the kaleidoscopic, panchromatic views from Artemis II’s lunar pirouette. The alluring vistas the astronauts captured on digital cameras and iPhones helped ensure that “the entire world was united around our mission, and our crew,” says Kelsey Young, Artemis II’s lunar science lead. If NASA sticks to its plan and voyages to the moon become commonplace, then extraordinary images like these will quickly become glorious in their ordinariness.

How Mike Flanagan's Take on Carrie Upends the Tragedy of Stephen King's Horror Classic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
15:45:11 UTC
00:45:11 KST

Warning: This post contains spoilers for the finale of Carrie, now streaming.
If you ever wished Stephen King's Carrie was actually a story about a telekinetic teenager getting whisked away from the violence and isolation of her sheltered small-town life to join a secret society of fellow psychic outcasts, then the ending of Prime Video's new eight-episode Carrie series may appeal to you. But if you were hoping for an adaptation that more meaningfully captures the tragic finality of King's 1974 novel, showrunner Mike Flanagan's open-ended take on the horror classic may leave you feeling a bit frustrated.
Over the course of the past decade, Flanagan has made a name for himself as one of the genre's leading auteurs with a steady output of Halloween season Netflix horror series, which ranged in quality from the superb Haunting of Hill House (a modern reimagining of Shirley Jackson's acclaimed 1959 novel) and Midnight Mass (an original work in the vein of King's Salem's Lot) to the disappointing Midnight Club (a remix of the the YA horror novels of Christopher Pike). Prior to taking on Carrie, Flanagan also received high praise from King for his film adaptations of Gerald's Game (a book that was long considered unadaptable) and The Shining sequel Doctor Sleep (which bridged the divide between Stanley Kubrick's 1980 film and the author's literary universe).
However, Flanagan apparently had reservations about putting his own spin on a property as well-trodden as Carrie, especially considering how beloved Brian de Palma's 1976 Sissy Spacek-led film remains to this day. "It initially started as a conversation that Amazon initiated, and they said, 'Hey, would you have any interest in Carrie?,'" he told MovieWeb in 2024. "And I had to think about it, because my first instinct is always—why? It's been done perfectly by De Palma. It's then been done three other times after the fact. Why do it again?"
But he ultimately came to the conclusion there was an opportunity to reframe the story through a modern lens in a way that would bring new relevance to King's themes. "Carrie is a story about high school violence and bullying, and that feels immediate and important today. Unfortunately, even more kind of sharply relevant than I think it was when he wrote it," Flanagan said. "So there felt like a chance for some true modernization beyond just changing the time period, and to use it to talk about the issues that affect high school kids in America today. You know, Carrie White walking through a metal detector is interesting to me. Carrie White with social media. The iconic scene in the locker room is very different when people have phones in their hands. So that was the first germ of an idea, like, there is room for this to actually have a lot to say that's very relevant."
To that extent, the series achieves what it set out to do. Following an open sequence in which we learn Carrie's conspiracy-theorist father Ralph White (Tahmoh Penikett) was killed in a bizarre accident while at work on a construction site, Carrie (Summer H. Howell) is introduced as a naive yet overly good-natured bookworm who has lived out the first 16 years of her life sequestered at home under the care and tutelage of her overbearing religious mother Margaret (Samantha Sloyan). Carrie is ignorant to the realities of teenage life, including the workings of social media, the threat of school shootings, and, as a young woman coming of age, the concept of getting a period. Once she begins her court-ordered attendance at local public high school Ewen High, Carrie gets acquainted with resident popular girls Sue Snell (Siena Agudong) and Chris Hargensen (Alison Thornton). Chris soon launches a targeted cyberbullying campaign against Carrie to take out her frustration and rage over her own family woes and fracturing home life.
From there, the show hits the signature beats of King's story, including the infamous locker room incident, prayer closet punishments, and, of course, the pig's blood prom prank and ensuing fiery massacre, while also reinterpreting and expanding on the motivations of a number of characters. However, the addition of a totally new storyline in which Carrie is being recruited by a shadowy collective of psychically powered women led by the mysterious Adelaide (Flanagan’s wife and frequent collaborator Kate Siegel) ultimately leaves the show feeling somewhat bloated and unsatisfying.
After Carrie is finally pushed to her breaking point by her prom humiliation, she uses her telekinetic powers to yank down the scaffolding where Chris and her partner-in-crime Billy Nolan (Arthur Conti) were hiding with their buckets of blood, accidentally bludgeoning and killing her date, Tommy (Joel Oulette), in the process. Horrified by what she's done, Carrie then allows astral projector Emaline (Thalia Dudek) to take over from inside her mind and use her abilities to wreak havoc and destruction on Ewen High and the surrounding town of Chamberlain. In King's book, Carrie executes her vengeance all on her own, never encountering another psychic.
When Carrie returns home after killing Billy and Chris (the only two murders she is fully in control of her powers for), Margaret attempts to put a stop to her daughter's reign of terror by stabbing her through the ear. But Carrie psychically rebuffs the attack and brings their home crashing down around them, trapping Margaret in the rubble. In the book, Carrie kills her mother by telekinetically stopping her heart, but later bleeds out and dies from her stab wound, bringing the tragedy of King's indictment of societal cruelty and institutional failure full circle. In the show, both Margaret and Carrie survive, with the former demonstrating she possesses some latent powers of her own by calling on them to keep the house from crushing her and the latter being spirited out of town by Emaline to join the network of other psychics. Adelaide, who has been posing as a documentary filmmaker interviewing the survivors of that fateful night, ends up being the one to kill Margaret using the same method Carrie does in the book.
This ending leaves Carrie's future entirely up in the air, opening the door for Flanagan to take her story in a variety of new directions. And considering he made sure to have Adelaide mention the existence of "the shine," a reference to the psychic ability young Danny Torrance possesses in The Shining that allows him to see ghosts, communicate telepathically, and demonstrate clairvoyance, it seems as though the show might be setting up some future King universe crossovers. While Prime has yet to officially renew Carrie, Flanagan has said his "dream scenario" is for the story to play out over three seasons. "I think Carrie has a wonderful three-step arc," he told Collider. "It’s a trilogy, really."

Georgia Scraps Offshore Intermediary in Azerbaijani Power Imports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
15:45:00 UTC
00:45:00 KST

Reported by
Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze announced that Georgia will eliminate intermediary companies from its electricity imports from neighboring Azerbaijan, a move he said would save the state millions of dollars annually.
The trade has long been plagued by a lack of transparency, with power purchases between the two South Caucasus nations funneled almost entirely through opaque offshore companies, as previously reported by OCCRP and its regional partners. For years, the dominant player in the trade was Sulkhan Papashvili, an influential Georgian businessman.
“Having an intermediary meant additional costs for the state,” Kobakhidze said during a recorded cabinet meeting. “Specifically in the case of Azerbaijan, as a result of removing the intermediary, the state will receive several million annually.”
In 2020, Studio Monitori, OCCRP’s Georgian member center, reported that ordinary Georgians were paying inflated rates for Azerbaijani power due to the middleman arrangement — at the time handled by a Belize-registered firm, Elgreen Holdings.
A 2024 joint investigation by OCCRP, Studio Monitori, iFact, and Mikroskop Media traced the trade through multiple offshore companies in which Papashvili was the sole beneficiary and shareholder. The investigation also revealed that Papashvili maintained separate business ties with relatives of the Azerbaijani officials responsible for approving the energy deals. His legal team denied that these relationships yielded preferential treatment.
In response to a request for comment regarding the government’s announcement, Papashvili’s lawyer, Kakha Sharabidze, said the businessman “has reviewed the prime minister's statement and understands the reasons behind the decision taken.”
Georgian authorities have long kept the details of the import deal secret. The Ministry of Economy and the energy regulator, GNERC, repeatedly redirected investigative inquiries to the state electricity system operator, ESCO, which refused to disclose its contract with Elgreen, citing confidentiality clauses.

EU supportive of extending UNIFIL Lebanon mandate, says Kallas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
15:42:13 UTC
00:42:13 KST

Breadcrumb
EU supportive of extending UNIFIL Lebanon mandate, says Kallas
Visiting EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas told AFP on Thursday that the bloc favoured avoiding a security vacuum and extending a UN peacekeeping mandate in south Lebanon, where Israel invaded while fighting Hezbollah.
The EU's top diplomat also said that the bloc would soon be launching a training mission for the Lebanese army, calling it "a major upgrade in the security relationship" with the Mediterranean country.
Lebanon's cash-strapped, under-resourced military faces enormous challenges, including in completing its deployment to south Lebanon under a US-sponsored framework agreement reached between Israel and Lebanon in June.
"Our member states have been saying that there can't be any security vacuum in southern Lebanon, so everybody is worried about the UNIFIL mandate ending," she said in an interview during a visit to Lebanon where she met senior officials.
"It would be most welcomed if this mandate is extended, so that is the position of the member states," she added.
The United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon, which now counts some 7,500 personnel from nearly 50 countries, has been in place since 1978, although its presence has not prevented repeated outbreaks of conflict.
Under US pressure, the UN Security Council voted last year to end UNIFIL's mandate on 31 December 2026.
'Dangerous'
But in March, Lebanese militant group Hezbollah drew the country into the broader Middle East war by attacking Israel, which responded with massive airstrikes and a ground invasion that Lebanon says have killed more than 4,300 people.
Israel now maintains troops in a self-declared "security zone" running around 10 kilometres (six miles) inside Lebanon along the border.
Violence has decreased since a ceasefire following a US-Iran understanding in June, and the US-sponsored Lebanon-Israel framework agreed later that month.
The framework deal involves the disarmament of Hezbollah, a gradual withdrawal of Israeli forces from Lebanon's south and the deployment of the Lebanese army to the region, starting in test areas known as "pilot zones", but the process has largely stalled.
Kallas said that under the deal, "there should be somebody who is verifying whether the parties are keeping to their agreements".
"So, as long as you don't have any kind of international force yet ready to do that... it's dangerous when one mission like UNIFIL ends and the other one has not started yet," she said.
Lebanese officials have repeatedly called for the mandate to be extended.
President Joseph Aoun's office said that he told Kallas that Lebanon is "counting on the support of the European Union to find an alternative formula" for after the UNIFIL mandate ends.
France and Italy, major contributors to UNIFIL, have previously said they are willing to set up a multinational coalition to succeed the force.
EU training mission
Kallas also said a planned EU training and advisory mission would soon be established, emphasising that it would not replace the peacekeepers.
On Monday, "we sit down with the EU foreign ministers to give this final push... to launch this mission", she said.
She expressed hope that the civilian-military mission, which will not only focus on south Lebanon, "would be ready already by the end of this year".
"The focus is on supporting the Lebanese Armed Forces, and supporting the Lebanese Internal Security Forces, in order to keep control of the country and security," she said.
"That means training, that means also working on the capabilities," she added.
"Lebanese sovereignty and territorial integrity is very important. So, it has to be the Lebanese government that is providing services and keeping control of the country," she added.
At a joint press conference with Lebanese Foreign Minister Youssef Raggi, Kallas emphasised that "Lebanon must have full control of its whole territory. That also means moving towards disarmament of Hezbollah".
The EU is a major source of assistance to Lebanon with Kallas noting that in September, the bloc announced 505 million euros ($615 million) in financial assistance until 2027, completing a one billion euro package announced in 2024.
Lebanon is also the third-largest beneficiary of its European Peace Facility fund, she added.
(AFP)

Jewish security group launches survivor testimony project to combat rising antisemitic threats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
15:42:01 UTC
00:42:01 KST

The Secure Community Network (SCN), the safety and security organization for the Jewish community in North America, announced the launch of “Standing with Strength: Stories of Survival” last Thursday. A new oral history initiative developed alongside Emmy- and Golden Globe-nominated producer Craig Turk, it will preserve firsthand accounts from individuals who survived targeted antisemitic terror attacks.
The project compiles testimonies from survivors of major terror attacks targeting Jewish institutions across the US, specifically focusing on the atrocities in Pittsburgh, Poway, Colleyville, Overland Park, and Surfside. Featuring 10 participants who recount the events, their immediate responses, and the critical survival lessons learned, the initiative directly integrates these oral histories into SCN’s security training programs throughout North America.
The project highlights how security preparedness and training save lives during targeted attacks. Many featured in the project credit the security training they received directly from SCN and local Jewish Federations with helping them develop the situational awareness and survival skills needed to endure anti-Jewish terror attacks. SCN is now incorporating these hard-won lessons into its security training infrastructure, which has instructed more than 91,000 community members since 2024, to prepare individuals to recognize, prepare for, and respond to threats.
Michael Masters, national director and CEO of SCN explained to The Jerusalem Post that the project originated directly from the survivors, who wanted to share everything from foundational resilience against violence to practical, granular survival details.
Masters told the Post that SCN is weaving these testimonies directly into its ongoing educational work by having survivors actively participate in community training. As an example, Masters pointed to one participant who survived being a hostage for 11 hours at Congregation Beth Israel in Colleyville, noting that the survivor volunteered to turn his experience into a dedicated course that he now travels and delivers on his own.
Survivor testimonies highlight how security training and preparedness can save lives
Masters said, “The survivors who came forward gave us something no report or statistic can: the truth of what it takes to live through the unthinkable. The vulnerability we need to guard against the most is the feeling that it could never happen here. These stories are proof that it can, and proof that preparation saves lives.”
While highlighting that SCN has built a robust training infrastructure, instructing over 40,000 community members last year alone, Masters stressed that Jewish communities face a threat environment “unlike anything that’s been witnessed in North America,” noting that SCN referred over 850 threats to life to law enforcement last year.
Urging the need to expand, Masters noted, “We’ve got a population of 7.2 million, and so we really need to elevate the community getting involved, getting engaged, and also expanding the security initiatives around the country that work as part of our federation system to be resourced to be able to do this work at the scale that we know is necessary.”
Turk told the Post that, as soon as he heard about it, he felt an immediate desire to participate. Turk said, “As soon as the idea just began to take the faintest of shapes, I thought what an incredible honor to be able to participate in something like that.”
Turk noted that the survivors view sharing their stories as a moral and civic duty rather than something to avoid. Turk explained that these individuals choose to speak out despite the heavy emotional toll, telling the Post that it’s really hard “to revisit these absolutely frightening, terrible, [and] devastating” experiences to their lives and the lives of the ones they love, but “all of them stood up to it with such grace. It was extraordinary.”
Survivor testimonies connect remembrance with preparedness for future attacks
Turk also told the Post that capturing the faces and voices of those who lived through these atrocities creates a profound human connection. He stated: “Being able to see these faces and hear these voices will help people connect to these experiences in the most profound way possible.”
Turk added, “These modern-day heroes offer lessons in resilience we can’t afford to forget. SCN is doing essential work by connecting memory to preparedness, ensuring we are ready not if, but when, the next crisis emerges.”
The Post spoke with survivor Audrey Glickman, whose testimony is included in the project. Glickman recounted her experience surviving the October 2018 massacre at the Tree of Life congregation in Pittsburgh’s Squirrel Hill neighborhood, emphasizing the life-saving impact of preparedness.
Glickman, who was leading the service when the gunman attacked, told the Post how she and her partner sought shelter during the attack, hiding in a small room beside the choir loft behind the ark, where they covered themselves with their prayer shawls (tallitot) and crouched on the floor.
Glickman said that having previously undergone security training meant that standard survival protocols kicked in automatically, noting, “You know run, hide, fight, and it kicks in automatically once you’ve had the training. And maybe every couple years, you should probably go over it again, but once you’ve had it, you remember somehow.”
Glickman added, “Think about it ahead of time, and then your brain will just do it.”
SCN security operations help prevent violent attacks on North American Jewish communities
The launch coincides with a sustained and elevated threat environment facing North American Jewish communities, where security training and real-time intelligence operations serve as vital safeguards against violent extremism. Through its 24/7 Jewish Security Operations Command Center (JSOCC) and national monitoring networks, SCN’s active threat management has successfully intercepted and thwarted multiple violent plots before they materialized.
Case studies illustrating this impact include the arrest of an offender in Ogden, Utah, possessing six operational homemade bombs and an assault rifle; the federal indictment of a suspect following an armed standoff in Atlanta; and the interception of a heavily armed individual targeting a rabbi and imam in Needham, Alabama.

He is also envoy to Iraq, which means he coordinates US policy in a broad part of the region. “The meeting also addressed prospects for cooperation and coordination on issues of mutual interest, as well as efforts to support security and stability in the region,” Syrian state media reported.
Relations between the United States and Syria have undergone a dramatic transformation since the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s regime in December 2024. After decades of hostility, sanctions, and diplomatic isolation, Washington has moved toward working with Sharaa, Syria’s new president.
During the Assad era, relations were strained by Syria’s support for Hezbollah and other terrorist organizations, its close ties with Iran and Russia, and its involvement in Lebanon. The US imposed sanctions on Damascus and withdrew its ambassador in 2005, although diplomatic talks later resumed. Then-US secretary of state John Kerry and House speaker Nancy Pelosi appeared open to better ties.
Relations deteriorated following the Syrian protests in 2011 as part of the Arab Spring. The regime’s violent crackdown led to the US essentially closing its embassy in 2012. It helped provide limited support for the Syrian rebels.
US pursues closer ties with post-Assad Syria despite concerns over Sharaa's past
The fall of Assad opened a new chapter. US diplomats visited Damascus in December 2024, establishing contact with the new authorities.
However, some in Washington urged caution because Syria’s new leader had previously led Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), an organization with roots in al-Qaeda. Israel also urged caution. However, US President Donald Trump has actively pursued ties with Damascus.
The major breakthrough came on May 14, 2025, when Trump met Sharaa in Riyadh. The meeting, arranged with MBS, was the first between American and Syrian presidents in 25 years. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan participated by telephone. Trump encouraged Sharaa to cooperate against ISIS, address foreign terrorist activity, and pursue improved relations with Israel.
US envoy Tom Barrack plays key role in Syria rapprochement and regional security talks
Barrack, the US ambassador to Turkey and special envoy for Syria, became the central figure in the rapprochement. He visited Damascus in May 2025, raised the American flag at the US diplomatic residence, and held discussions with Sharaa. His role expanded to mediating regional security issues, including Syria’s relations with Israel and the integration of armed groups into state institutions.
Syria has strongly condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. Riyadh is now working with Pakistan, Turkey and US Central Command (CENTCOM) regarding the Houthi threats.
The Houthis targeted Saudi Arabia on October 7. Riyadh has backed a Yemeni government offensive against the Houthis this week.
Syria, UAE discuss stronger economic ties and regional security cooperation
As Barrack met with Syria’s Foreign Minister, the Syrian President Shara’a held a call with UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan.
“During the call, the two leaders discussed bilateral relations between the two countries and ways to develop them in a manner that serves their shared interests, as well as the latest regional developments,” Syrian state media SANA said.
“The two sides also explored ways to boost economic and investment cooperation and expand partnerships between the two countries, stressing the importance of continuing coordination and communication on issues of common interest.”
Syria has sought to keep out of a conflict in Lebanon. It is unlikely it will want to send more than a limited force to Saudi Arabia. Nevertheless, it remains to be seen what happens next.
Barrack posted on X/Twitter on October 3 that “President Trump opened the door to Syria’s recovery. Restoring financial connectivity is how we help turn that opportunity into lasting prosperity.” He was “pleased to join the Treasury banking roundtable with Syrian financial leaders and US banks and payment providers,’ he added.
“Combating illicit finance, advancing credible reforms, and rebuilding confidence are essential to responsibly reconnecting Syria to the global financial system,” Barrack wrote.

Houthis abduct, indoctrinate kids to believe they are fighting Jews, Yemeni journalist tells 'Post'

The Houthis have forcibly recruited children to fight in their war against Saudi Arabia and the Saudi-backed government, threatening families in territories they control and indoctrinating young people to believe they will be fighting against Jews and Zionists, a journalist who formerly worked in Houthi-controlled territory for a decade told The Jerusalem Post on Wednesday.
“A,” who spoke on condition of anonymity, explained that he feared the Houthis would punish his friends and colleagues still working in Yemen if they became aware of his communication with the Post. He noted that the Houthis are already holding several international humanitarian workers hostage, in addition to local aid employees.
Human Rights Watch (HRW) announced earlier this week that the Houthis have already sent at least eight people involved in human rights and humanitarian work for criminal prosecution on espionage-related charges punishable by death, since August 18.
Though the Houthis’ use of child soldiers has long been documented, A said, “The problem is escalating and increasing with the recent developments.”
Houthis threaten citizens with death in order to recruit more soldiers
“Whenever they control new areas, the first thing they do is force people to be recruited. Otherwise, they will be punished, they will be imprisoned, or they will be killed,” he explained.
“So this is one of the most significant issues and one of the least reported issues when it comes to the war in Yemen, and Houthis also want to compensate for what they lost over the past days because they lost a lot of fighters in Mokha and in their recent fighting and battles.”
On the day that A spoke to the Post, he received a call from humanitarian contacts on the ground in Houthi-controlled territory warning him that the Houthis had begun indiscriminately shelling homes and schools and that bodies of women and children were being piled high.
Given that A spent years working in Houthi-controlled territory, the Post asked him how the Houthis could justify killing Yemeni civilians, particularly given that the vast majority of their victims are Muslim.
Explaining that the reason the Houthis are comfortable killing their own people is the same reason that makes a peace agreement with them impossible, A said that it was “firmly” embedded in their ideology that they have the “divine right to govern... not only controlling all of Yemen, but also they want to control Mecca and Medina and Saudi Arabia.”
“They believe that they have the divine right to govern the world, not only the Arabian Peninsula, and so they consider people who fight them or who try to resist them as traitors, and recently as Zionists,” he continued, adding that the issue has only worsened since October 7, 2023.
Houthis use Israel-Hamas War to recruit child soldiers
A said the Israel-Hamas War had been a “good excuse to recruit,” with videos of the war in Gaza regularly played to children to incite them against Israel. He added that, before October 7, there had been growing discontent with the Houthis, particularly over unpaid wages; still, many were more willing to tolerate the missed payments either because they wanted to support the Palestinian cause or because they did not want to be labeled as Zionists.
Estimating that tens of thousands of children had been enlisted into the Houthis’ ranks since Hamas’s invasion, A noted that children aged between 12 and 15 had been captured attempting to fight government forces, proclaiming that they had traveled to the front to fight the Jews.
The anti-Israel popular opinion in Yemen among the entire population, A said, had also made the indoctrination of children easier, as many didn’t need to shift their thinking on the issue dramatically to align with the Houthis.
“They exploited what they called the Islamic background and people’s support for the Palestinian cause,” he said, adding that it has now begun to backfire and there is a growing number of Yemenis who feel resentful toward the Palestinians.
“People are fed up even with the Palestinian cause because it has caused a lot of damage to the country. The sentiment of people toward the Gaza issue and the Palestinian cause has gone down sharply because they saw how the Houthis decided to kill Yemenis in the name of Gaza.
“They saw how the Houthis isolated Yemen by attacking vessels in the Red Sea in the name of Gaza. They saw how the Houthis even cut the income of thousands of fishermen who went jobless because of the Houthis’ ventures in the Red Sea,” A added.
“So people saw the economic consequences of the Houthis’ actions over the past three years and started complaining and also started realizing that the Palestinian cause is not our cause. Yemen is our cause. So this sentiment has shifted dramatically, but they continued to recruit and mobilize support inside Yemen in the name of fighting the US and Israel.”
Adding to the bitterness, A said it was hard watching pro-Palestinian activists in the West celebrate the Houthis and ignore comments from Yemenis trying to tell them that the group was a terrorist organization even if it partially aligned with their viewpoint.
“Gaza became a trend and profitable thing for many people, including Palestinians, and the shocking fact is how many Palestinian activists, journalists, and thinkers turn and support the Houthis at the expense of Yemenis and at the expense of Yemeni suffering,” A said.

Securing Your Family's Future: Multi-Generational Coverage Through Strategic Foreign Investment  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
15:41:14 UTC
00:41:14 KST

The Problem
Many rich families keep most of their money, things they own, how they live, and what they want to do in the future in just one country. This means they use only one type of money, live in one area, and follow one set of rules.
Family planning is part of this. Kids can get too old to be counted as dependents for immigration. A parent might need other healthcare or a new place to live. These are real reasons to keep your choices open, and to think about how greece residency by investment can fit the future that your family may have.
Why It Happens
Relying on one country gives you fewer choices. It can also limit where your family can live. This can decide where your things are kept, where your kids go to learn, and how easy it is for you to move around Europe.
That is why more families today use residency-by-investment programs. They do this to help with wealth and planning for the next generation.
The Golden Visa program gives you a five-year permit to live in the country if you make a qualifying investment. You can renew this permit later. According to Law 5275/2026, the five years start on the day you get the residence card. With one investment, you can cover:
- your spouse or registered partner
- unmarried children under 21 (this can go up to 24 with a separate permit, if there are certain conditions; unmarried children under 21 years old can be extended up to age 24 under specific dependency/student conditions)
- the parents of both you and your spouse (with no age or dependency restrictions required)
Solution 1: Qualifying Real Estate in Greece
In accordance with Law 5100/2024, together with further specifications in Law 5275/2026 and Circular 1/2026, the property route includes three tiered real estate thresholds:
- €800,000: Applies to high-demand areas, including all of Attica (including Athens and Piraeus), Thessaloniki, Mykonos, Santorini, and other Greek islands which exceed the population of 3,100 inhabitants. Must be a single property of at least 120 sq. meters.
- €400,000: Applies to all remaining municipalities across Greece (single property, min. 120 sq. meters).
- €250,000 Exception: Restricted strictly to specific property types: conversion of commercial/industrial property into residential use or the restoration of historically listed buildings.
For the €800,000 and €400,000 thresholds, you need to acquire one property that has a minimum of 120 square meters of livable area. You cannot put smaller units together anymore. The €250,000 route does not need a minimum floor area. But, it does have rules of its own. The change of use has to be fully checked and done before you send in your file. A property changed through this route can support a permit only one time. So, if another non-EU buyer comes, they must meet the usual rule for that area.
Solution 2: Schengen Mobility and Rights & Scope of Residency
Having a Greek residence permit provides visa-free travel within the Schengen Area for up to 90 days in any 180-day period. It can take several months to have your residence permit.
Holding a Greek residence permit does not grant the legal right to live, work, or access public healthcare/benefits in other EU/Schengen countries; it grants full residency rights only within Greece. Furthermore, regarding work restrictions, while the Golden Visa permits business ownership/shareholding in Greece, it does not allow direct local employment (unless the holder converts to a work permit or acquires long-term EU status/citizenship).
Solution 3: Multi-Generational Coverage
This is where the Greek program works best for families. One qualifying investment can cover the main applicant, their spouse or registered partner, unmarried children under 21 years old (which can be extended up to age 24 under specific dependency/student conditions), and parents of both the main applicant and spouse (with no age or dependency restrictions required). There is no extra qualifying amount for family members. This lets three generations be in one plan without anyone needing to move right away.
There is no rule about how long you must stay to keep or renew the permit. You can keep the permit as long as you keep your investment and meet the other rules. You do not have to move because of the permit. It is your choice if you want to live there or not.
Tax Residency Criteria
The Golden Visa alone will not make you a tax resident in Greece. Note that physical presence of 183+ days per year is not the only test for Greek tax residency. An individual can be deemed a Greek tax resident—regardless of physical day-counts—if their center of vital interests (main family, financial, or personal ties) is in Greece, or if Greece is established as their habitual abode or principal domicile.
Citizenship & Selling the Property
The visa does not give you citizenship; for that, you must live in Greece for many years and pass a language test.
Continuous ownership of the qualifying investment is required to retain and renew the 5-year residence permit. If you sell the property that got you the visa, your residence permit—and all associated family permits—will be revoked immediately, unless you simultaneously substitute the asset with another qualifying property of equal or greater required value. The property can be sold freely without affecting immigration status only after the investor transitions to EU Long-Term Resident status or acquires Greek citizenship (typically after 7 years of actual physical residence).
Short-Term Rental Restrictions & Fines
Properties acquired under the Golden Visa cannot be used for short-term vacation rentals (e.g., Airbnb, Vrbo). In case of violation of this regulation, the owner risks immediate revocation of the Golden Visa residence permit as well as having to pay an administrative fine of €50,000. Properties may only be leased on long-term residential contracts, where the owner might obtain rental income and maintain a permit to stay.
Conclusion
Relying only on one country can make it hard for a family to have many choices. International diversification is not about guessing what will happen next. It is about getting ready and having more options before you really need them.
If you and your family are thinking about moving to Greece, the Golden Visa can help. It gives you a permit to live there if you invest in a property that meets the rules. This permit can include your husband or wife, your kids, and your parents. mercan group has Greek Golden Visa options starting from €250,000. One option is Keranis Residences in Piraeus. This big development changes an old factory site into new homes by using the commercial-to-residential plan. The rules to get the permit depend on the paperwork for the property and how the use of the building has changed. You should let a lawyer check all of this before you pay or sign anything.
This article is for general information. It is not legal or tax advice. Rules about immigration can change, so check the latest requirements with a qualified adviser.

Volta SKAI, Tallinn’s new landmark, tops out  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
15:41:11 UTC
00:41:11 KST

On Wednesday, 7 October, real estate developer Endover held a topping-out ceremony to celebrate the Volta SKAI high-rise duo reaching its full height. The area’s only high-rise development now stands out clearly on the city skyline, and the first apartments will be completed as early as this autumn. Alongside the traditional topping-out celebration, the event featured discussions on how artificial intelligence is changing real estate development and what makes a good home today.
The Volta SKAI high-rise duo, rising in the historic Volta residential and business quarter, has reached a milestone in its development, with the first homes and businesses set to be completed this year. The traditional topping-out wreath was duly in place, and for the first time guests were able to visit the building under construction, which offers a 360-degree view of the sea, the Old Town, the city-centre towers and the greenery of the Kopli peninsula.
“Volta SKAI reaching its full height is an important milestone not just for one building but for the entire Volta Quarter, which we have been developing for ten years now. Tallinn’s skyline now shows what only a few years ago existed solely on drawings: a former industrial area is turning into a revitalised district right next to the city centre,” said Endover CEO Roul Tutt.
“Today, people are not looking for mere square metres but for a complete living environment that is quiet and green, yet has everything they need close at hand. In Volta, this is not a promise for the future but an environment that already exists. A family doctors’ centre has also recently opened in the quarter, so one of the most essential everyday services – alongside the sports, childcare and dining options already in place – is now quite literally on residents’ doorstep. We will also soon open the fully modernised Kalaranna–Tööstuse–Krulli signalised junction, an important step in improving mobility in the area,” Tutt said.
Buyers judge a home by its surroundings too
The topping-out event hosted several discussions on what kind of urban space buyers are looking for, where the Estonian real estate market is heading and what shapes development processes. Speakers stressed that quality today means more than good build quality, which every buyer expects anyway. Increasingly, people value the home and its living environment as a whole: light, views, a logical layout, proximity to services, mobility options and the surrounding urban space – and also how the home meets residents’ changing needs over the years.
“A good home does not come from solving a single room, but from getting the whole right. Architecture and layout must serve a purpose, with every decision, from the siting of the building to the interior layout of the apartment, supporting the way people actually live there. We create lifetime homes that suit a young family as well as an older person or someone with special needs. This means, for example, wider doorways and easy movement both within the building and around the quarter,” Tutt explained.
In the view of Endover’s CEO, Tallinn offers worthy alternatives to a private house, as a large city home provides just as much space and privacy, with everything needed close by. That is why large apartments are increasingly preferred by those moving back to the city from a private house, too. Volta SKAI sales bear this out: most of the large apartments and upper-floor SKAI Villas have already found owners, and their interior layouts are being designed together with each buyer to suit their wishes.
Artificial intelligence in real estate development
The second main topic of discussion was the use of artificial intelligence in real estate development, something Endover has been working on for quite some time. Endover’s Head of Innovation Dmitri Garbuzenko explained how the company uses AI in practice and what opportunities it creates in real estate development. Taking a developer’s practical perspective, the panel discussed the benefits as well as the challenges and risks of AI, and shared examples of how AI has been applied in developing Volta SKAI.
“Technology is developing so fast today that the real estate and construction sector has to keep pace with it too. At the same time, AI is only useful if the team knows what a good result looks like. It does not replace experience, professionalism or good taste – it amplifies them. When routine work gets done faster, architects and engineers have more time for what truly creates value for residents,” said Garbuzenko.
In the development of Volta SKAI, AI creates value above all as an auditor. It checks project documents such as construction schedules, budgets and procurement tables, looks for inconsistencies and prepares risk analyses that used to be done by hand. AI also helps analyse design briefs that bring together input from specialists in different fields, such as ventilation and interior architecture. This makes it possible to pinpoint where different parts of the design might conflict with one another.
“This way, we catch potential errors or inconsistencies at the desk, before they ever reach the construction site. AI runs the checks and raises the flag, but the decision is always made – and the responsibility always borne – by a person. For us, this is above all a matter of quality control and quality assurance,” Garbuzenko added.
About Volta SKAI
Volta SKAI is located in the Volta Quarter, which has a 125-year history, and consists of two 12-storey towers with a total area of 18,600 m². The duo will house a total of 111 apartments, ranging from 35 to 340 square metres, featuring ceilings up to 3.8 metres high, floor-to-ceiling windows and architecture built around curved corner balconies and terraces, with commercial premises to complement them. The first apartments in the high-rise duo will be completed in autumn 2026. The project’s architecture was designed by ARS Projekt, the main contractor is Metropoli Ehitus and the developer is Endover.
About the Volta Quarter
The Volta Quarter is part of the Volta, Krulli and Noblessner area, where former factory blocks have given way to modern urban space. Its historic industrial heritage has turned it into a new “golden mile” of the real estate market, and for the third year running it has been Tallinn’s most sought-after new residential and business district. For just as long, according to Citify, the Volta Quarter has been Tallinn’s most popular new development by both sales turnover and the number of apartments sold, and the trend is continuing this year.
The area’s popularity is also reflected in the market figures. In the first eight months of 2026, Tallinn’s new-build market picked up moderately, and the average price per square metre sold rose by 6% to nearly €5,000. In Põhja-Tallinn, new-build sales turnover grew by as much as 20% year on year, and the average price per square metre stands at €5,546. Endover ranks first in Tallinn’s new-build market by sales turnover for the first eight months of the year. The company’s sales turnover from new transactions accounts for almost a tenth of the entire market, and its average price per square metre sold is €6,085. Tallinn’s largest known new-build transactions in 2025 and 2026 were also concluded at Volta SKAI, worth €2.5 million and nearly €4 million respectively.
The private and secure quarter operates on the principle of the “15-minute city”, meaning that everything needed for everyday life is within walking distance. Volta HUB, completed at the end of last year, is home to the largest MyFitness sports club in Põhja-Tallinn, and the quarter also has a padel club. The area also offers cafés, shops, a bakery, childcare and a recently opened family doctors’ centre, with a kindergarten on the way. At the heart of the quarter lies a 15,000-square-metre park planted with trees.
Facts about the Volta Quarter:
- Detailed plan area 11.25 ha
- Total development volume 142,000 m²
- Residential space to be built 90,000 m² and commercial space 52,000 m²
- A total of 29 buildings
- Number of apartments 755
- Approx. 1,400 parking spaces, plus bicycle parking
- A kindergarten and a 15,000 m² park
- New infrastructure and two new streets completed: Mootori and Uus-Volta
- The entire quarter will be completed by 2029
- By 2030, nearly 25,000 people will live and work in the Volta area
Endover is an Estonian real estate developer with more than 25 years of experience, creating value for the urban space and building comprehensive residential and business environments. The company’s portfolio includes 70 buildings and 2,840 apartments with a total area of 368,000 m².
