EU diplomatic arm under fire for bowing to US pressure over disinformation conference
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:48:19 UTC
23:48:19 KST

The EU diplomatic service pulled its backing from a disinformation conference after US pressure, angering MEPs and NGOs who say it undermines the bloc's own defence of civil society.
The EU's diplomatic service is facing criticism from lawmakers and civil society after withdrawing its backing for a disinformation conference at the last minute, following pressure from Washington.
The European External Action Service (EEAS) pulled out of the conference, one of the few European-level gatherings devoted to the issue, saying its programme did not align with EU positions. Critics say the move contradicts the bloc's own approach to protecting civil society.
"We have decided to have the EEAS logo removed from the material associated with the conference in view of the content of the program," said Christian Wigand, the EU's lead spokesperson for foreign affairs, on Thursday.
"The organisers chose to frame some of the discussions in a way which does not align with the positions held by the EU," he continued.
Critics say that withdrawing support from an NGO-led initiative because of a clash with the EU's official position undermines the European Democracy Shield, a framework intended to protect civil society and journalists from governmental pressure and foreign interference.
"Pressuring European governments to drop a disinformation conference to hide its own role in spreading disinformation is not diplomacy. It is foreign interference, and Europe should call it that," said MEP Alexandra Geese (Germany/Greens/EFA).
The EEAS declined to say which parts of the conference did not align with EU views. It quietly asked organisers to remove its logo from the conference material just days before the event began.
Canada and Lithuania also asked for their logos to be removed following pressure from the US State Department, Euronews can confirm.
"Pulling support from the conference at the last minute is a hugely irresponsible move, especially from the EEAS. It shows a lack of commitment to actually fighting disinformation. That looks like the EU is treating disinformation as a commodity," Domen Savic, co-founder of the NGO Državljan D, told Euronews.
The conference, organised by the NGO EU DisinfoLab, is taking place on Wednesday and Thursday in Vilnius, Lithuania.
For MEP Brando Benifei (Italy/S&D), the EEAS's withdrawal of support is a serious matter that deserves a full explanation.
"Frankly, it is difficult to see how the Vilnius discussions are so at odds with the EU’s stated position. Nor does it seem that we are filling this void with stronger European democracy by hiding our logos," Benifei told Euronews.
In EU jargon, FIMI stands for foreign information manipulation and interference. The latest EEAS report on the subject, published in March, names China and Russia as hostile actors conducting such operations in Europe but does not mention the US.
The programme includes a panel titled "USA as a FIMI threat: acknowledge, adapt, push back", featuring two researchers and Alex Finley, a former CIA official.
"There are no good and bad interferences in our democracies, the ones we decide to ignore versus the ones we agree to counter. My approach to the fight against FIMI is country-agnostic, and so it should be for the EEAS," MEP Nathalie Loiseau (France/Renew), chair of the special committee on the Democracy Shield, told Euronews.
"The Trump government publicly states that they want to help the far right rise to power in Europe. If the Commission does not even dare to recognise US interference, because they fear Trump, we are lost," said MEP Kim van Sparrentak (the Netherlands/Greens/EFA).
"With this mentality I'm starting to question whether the European Commission can credibly lead and coordinate our European responses to hybrid threats," she added.
The decision was taken at a very high level within the EU institutions and caught even officials working directly on the issue off guard, Euronews understands.
A few days before the conference, Michael Shellenberger, a right-wing US commentator, emailed several speakers. He asked whether they had received government funding and what they hoped to achieve with their sessions.
"Do you regard the US government as a source of foreign information manipulation and interference (FIMI) in Europe? Have you had any contact with the State Department or another US agency about your work or this conference?" reads the email, seen by Euronews.
At the same time, others argue that Brussels should not bicker with Washington, least of all over an NGO-led conference, because transatlantic unity is needed to confront what they see as the West's real enemies.
"I regret that the US feels it is being perceived as a FIMI actor by the EU. When it comes to FIMI, the EU should remain firmly focused on the threat posed by Russia and other hostile actors. Full stop," MEP Tomas Tobé (Sweden/EPP) told Euronews.
By contrast, some argue that withdrawing support at the last minute from a conference that is one of the few serious European-level venues where experts, civil society and private actors discuss disinformation sends a clear message to the community to steer clear of US interference.
"The US actions are hardly surprising, the disinformation community has already been under increasing pressure since Donald Trump returned to the White House, but it has never been so blatant," Mattia Caniglia, an affiliate lecturer at the University of Glasgow, told Euronews.
"EU institutions and the majority of member states react to these incidents like the world was still the one we had in 2010, but things have changed. Sacrificing the support to an NGO not to put important dossiers in peril will not work; standing for what we believe in will," he said.
Vincenzo Genovese contributed to the reporting.

Debris from intercepted Houthi missile damages kindergarten, clinic in Riyadh

Draft law aims to protect investors in fund liquidation process
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:46:41 UTC
23:46:41 KST

The draft law on the troubled funds aims to protect the rights of nearly 460,000 investors.
Lawmakers from Türkiye’s ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) have drafted new legislation aimed at safeguarding investor rights and ensuring transparency during the liquidation of investment funds hit by the ongoing financial crisis, state-run Anadolu Agency has reported.
The proposal, which is expected to be submitted to parliament in the coming days, would provide for the liquidation of assets worth up to 1 million Turkish lira for 455,578 investors.
The draft seeks to identify each fund’s assets and their rightful owners, liquidate fund assets without causing unnecessary economic losses and distribute the resulting cash proceeds fairly among investors.
To account for past cash flows and help balance investor losses, investment values would be updated using the arithmetic average of changes in the consumer price index (CPI) and domestic producer price index (D-PPI). Withdrawals would be calculated under a “first-in, first-out” method.
The proposal also envisions interim payments of up to 1 million lira per investor, provided that the amount does not exceed the investor’s net investment or finalized claim.
If available cash is insufficient to cover all payments, funds would be distributed proportionally among eligible investors. The Capital Markets Board (SPK) would be authorized to determine payment priorities, including making payments beginning with investors who have the smallest net investment amounts.
The draft would establish a voluntary reimbursement mechanism for investors who exited funds before liquidation and earned returns deemed above normal market conditions due to inaccurate asset valuations. Reimbursement calculations would be based on objective market benchmarks, including comparable fund returns and relevant market indices.
Under the proposal, responsibility for investor losses could extend to fund founders, portfolio management companies and individuals or entities found responsible for shortfalls in liquidation proceeds. Assets seized during criminal investigations could also be used to compensate investors.
The Savings Deposit Insurance Fund (TMSF) would be authorized to sell or liquidate assets that cannot be directly transferred to funds and channel the proceeds to affected investors.

German president says Berlin will remain committed to Europe during France visit

Seyma Erkul Dayanc

Germany would remain committed to Europe despite political and economic changes in the country, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier said Thursday.
“The Germans will remain good Europeans, despite all the changes taking place here -- economically, politically, and especially in security policy,” Steinmeier said after meeting French President Emmanuel Macron during a state visit to France, according to German newspaper Die Zeit.
“Germany can only be successful as a European Germany, closely embedded in the EU. That is true and will remain so for us,” he added.
“If Germany and France do not move forward together, Europe will not move forward at all,” Macron said.
He said cooperation between the two countries was important to “strengthen our democracies and their vitality” at a time when “conspiracy theories and skepticism sometimes gain the upper hand.”
The two presidents also discussed challenges facing their countries, with Steinmeier saying political polarization and the growing strength of radical political forces were making it more difficult to form governments and govern.
“We will not escape our growth crisis if everything remains as it is,” Steinmeier said, adding that “reforms have become even more difficult.”
The meeting was also a farewell visit, as both Steinmeier and Macron are due to leave office next year.
Steinmeier's visit is the first state visit to France by a German federal president in 13 years, according to the German government.
Macron, for his part, said the two countries “understand the price of war, the need for reconciliation and the value of peace.”
“Our friendship, which is etched in history, is our greatest strength and represents promise for all of Europe,” Macron said.

Saudi-led coalition says it intercepts three Houthi ballistic missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:43:19 UTC
23:43:19 KST

Saudi-led coalition says it intercepts three Houthi ballistic missiles
Saudi Arabia says two of the missiles intercepted were headed towards the capital, Riyadh.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting on behalf of Yemen’s internationally recognised government says it has intercepted ballistic missiles allegedly fired by Yemen’s Houthis towards cities in Saudi Arabia.
In a statement, coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki said his forces intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles heading in the direction of the Saudi capital Riyadh, and one missile in the direction of the city of Khamis Mushait, close to the Yemeni border, on Thursday.
Separately, Saudi Arabia’s civil defence agency said in a statement on X that falling debris from an intercepted missile had caused material damage to a kindergarten and medical clinic complex in Riyadh. It did not indicate if there were any casualties.
Yahya Saree, Yemen’s Houthi military spokesman, said the Iran-aligned group launched a ballistic missile towards King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Thursday afternoon, claiming that the missile had successfully hit its intended target, causing damage and disrupting air traffic.
Witnesses told The Associated Press news agency that they heard several explosions in Riyadh on Thursday, including one at the city’s airport that halted flights. Al Jazeera could not independently confirm the reports.
In recent days, the Houthis have warned aviation companies to avoid using Saudi airspace, saying any aircraft operating in the kingdom’s airspace, except over the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, is a target for the Houthis.
Following the latest reports, Air India said on Thursday that it had cancelled flights to and from Riyadh until at least the weekend, and the Germany-based Lufthansa Group airlines said they were suspending flights to Riyadh through October 16, according to the Reuters news agency.
The US embassy in Saudi Arabia meanwhile urged its citizens in the country to remain vigilant, saying they should be aware of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions.
Saudi Arabia’s Abha International Airport and King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh were targeted in two separate attacks, claimed by the Houthis on Tuesday and Wednesday. At least three civilians were killed and 36 injured, according to a statement from the Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA).
Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs condemned the attacks on the two airports, saying in a post on X that they “represent a grave violation of the Kingdom’s sovereignty and a direct threat to the security of the region and the safety of civilians, civil objects, and air navigation”. Oman and Egypt also condemned the Houthi attacks on Saudi airports.
These were not the first Houthi strikes on Saudi airports. On September 18, Saudi-led coalition forces said they intercepted and destroyed a suspected Houthi ballistic missile fired towards the airport in Riyadh from Yemen.
A day later, on September 19, at least one explosion was heard near the airport in Riyadh, and a large plume of black smoke was seen rising from a fuel storage area at King Khalid International Airport.
Fighting intensifies in Yemen
Meanwhile, inside Yemen, explosions have been reported near the airport in the Houthi-controlled Red Sea port city of Hodeidah, according to local sources.
The cause and impact of these explosions are not immediately clear.
In a post on X, a spokesman for Yemen’s Saudi-backed forces said at least 1,370 Houthi fighters were “neutralised” in 1,729 operations, and at least 300 vehicles were destroyed or disabled.
Al Jazeera’s Hadeel al-Yamani, reporting from Taiz in Yemen, said intense fighting is raging between armed forces of Yemen’s internationally recognised government and the Houthis in al-Shamayatayn, al-Maafer and the southern and western countryside of Taiz governorate.
“The Houthis are pushing into rural areas that have not seen conflict for years, aiming to open a supply route because their lines towards al-Kadaha and al-Waziiya, which link Aden, Lahij and Taiz, are nearly cut off by advancing government forces”, she said.
Al-Yamani added that pro-government forces are within striking distance of al-Waziiya and the Kahboub Mountains overlooking Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
Pro-government forces have reported more than 2,000 operations against the Houthis, and are preparing for a “dangerous escalation”, she said.
More than 200,000 people have been displaced from their homes since fighting in Yemen escalated in recent weeks, according to data released by the International Organization for Migration (IOM).
The IOM described the crisis in a statement on Wednesday as alarming, with the number of people displaced surging from the 76,000 recorded in mid-September.

PepsiCo cuts earnings forecast as North American turnaround takes longer than expected
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:43:05 UTC
23:43:05 KST

PepsiCo on Thursday reported quarterly earnings and revenue that topped analysts' expectations, fueled by international growth as its North American business continues to lag.
With one quarter left in 2026, the company also lowered its forecast for its full-year earnings, as its struggles in its home market weigh on profits. Pepsi expects core earnings per share to increase 2.5% to 3.5%, down from its previous projection of the low end of a range from 5% to 7%. It also now expects net revenue growth of about 6%, on the high end of its prior outlook of a range of 4% to 6%.
Shares of Pepsi rose about 2% in morning trading.
Here's what the company reported compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
- Earnings per share: $2.34 adjusted vs. $2.29 expected
- Revenue: $25.27 billion vs. $24.96 billion expected
Pepsi reported fiscal third-quarter net income attributable to the company of $3.05 billion, or $2.23 per share, up from $2.6 billion, or $1.90 per share, a year earlier.
Excluding items, the company earned $2.34 per share.
Net sales rose 5.6% to $25.27 billion. Organic revenue, which excludes acquisitions, divestitures and foreign exchange, increased 3.1% during the quarter.
The company reported volume growth of 3% for its beverages and 1% for its food for the quarter. Volume excludes pricing and currency fluctuations to reflect demand more accurately.
Pepsi's international markets were once again the bright spot. The company's international business has accounted for 41% of its net revenue so far this year, CEO Ramon Laguarta said in prepared remarks.
Pepsi saw volume growth in all but one of its international business units during the quarter. Only its convenient foods division in Europe, the Middle East and Africa reported declining volume, of 1%.
But in its home market, Pepsi once again struggled.
"Our business in North America performed below our expectations and represents a meaningful opportunity for improvement," Laguarta said.
Its North American beverage unit saw volume shrink 2%, while its North American food division reported flat volume.
The turnaround of its domestic business is moving more slowly than expected, CFO Steve Schmitt said in prepared remarks. So far, the strategy to fix the struggling divisions has focused on innovation and the company's advertising and marketing.
For its snacks, Pepsi has leaned into simpler ingredients, "alternative" oils and functional benefits, like protein and fiber.
In February, Pepsi lowered prices by as much as 15% on many of its snacks, including Lay's and Doritos. The move followed weak U.S. performance by its snack brands as budget-conscious shoppers, facing higher prices across the grocery store, skipped the chips.
The bet has paid off for the company, Laguarta said on the company's earnings conference call.
"We're happy with the turnaround in the volume performance," he said. "If you think about last year, that business was low single-digit negative volume growth. This year, we're low single-digit positive growth."
North American demand for Pepsi's snacks was weaker than expected this quarter, which Laguarta chalked up to "the consumer environment."
Pepsi executives are projecting "a new wave of inflation" caused by higher energy prices. Laguarta predicted that the company will implement "revenue management tactics," industry jargon that typically means price hikes. But he said that the company will have "guardrails" to make sure that retailers do not price its snacks too high for shoppers.
The North American beverage business was more disappointing, particularly the company's soft drinks portfolio, which includes its namesake soda, Mountain Dew and Poppi, among others. The company plans to stay focused on functional hydration, flavored soft drinks, energy drinks and zero-sugar options.
However, Laguarta said some recent trends show the company's efforts are working.
Pepsi's North American convenient foods business, which includes brands like Doritos and Quaker Oats, had its organic revenue improve sequentially. Its North American beverage unit, which includes its namesake soda and Gatorade, among other brands, saw organic volume trends pick up, thanks to its functional hydration and zero-sugar drinks. But Pepsi's carbonated soft drink portfolio lagged behind the overall category, including rival Coca-Cola.
Pepsi is planning cost reductions to cut down on redundancies and discretionary spending to pay for investments in innovation and marketing, Laguarta said in prepared remarks.
Correction: Pepsi's fiscal third-quarter net income attributable to the company was up from a year earlier. An earlier version misstated the direction.

EU envoy in Beijing for talks to calm trade tensions

Unknown Publisher

EU envoy in China to avert trade war
October 8, 2026
EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic arrived in Beijing on Thursday for two days of talks on addressing the bloc's trade deficit with China.
"We're working hard to rebalance EU-China trade," Sefcovic wrote on X following a meeting with Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao in the Chinese capital.
Sefcovic added that it was "crucial" the talks deliver tangible outcomes.
Sefcovic said his visit, which lasts until Friday, aimed to tackle the "unsustainable" trade deficit, which is at its highest level since 2022, according to EU figures.
China exports around €1 billion ($1.12 billion) more in goods and services a day to the EU than flows the other way. Many in Europe blame this on unfair trade practices by Beijing, including using state subsidies and price dumping to undercut European rivals.
Beijing has rejected those claims.
China appeals for dialogue to solve disputes
Thursday's meeting comes after three months of discussions between EU and Chinese officials over the trade imbalance. Sefcovic has previously said he wanted to see results by October.
The Chinese Foreign Ministry on Thursday called for openness and cooperation, saying that "resolving economic and trade differences through equal dialogue and consultation is in the common interests of both China and the EU."
"We hope that the European side can work towards solutions together with China," ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said at a news briefing.
Earlier Thursday, Sefcovic met with representatives from EU companies in China.
"The message around the table was clear: the need to improve access to the Chinese market, while boosting our economic security," he said.
Besides the trade deficit, Sefcovic's discussions in China are also set to focus on an ongoing dispute over hybrid cars. According to diplomats, China has rejected calls to voluntarily limit its fast-rising export of the vehicles to the bloc.
Brussels could move to temporarily curb the import of Chinese cars through quotas and tariffs, something Beijing firmly opposes.
Merz, Macron call for new measures
Earlier this week, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron called for tougher EU measures to tackle unfair trade practices, which they said were undermining European companies and increasing the bloc's economic dependencies.
Last month, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen warned that the current trade imbalance "leads to deindustrialization in the industrial heartlands of Europe."
EU leaders are expected to discuss the bloc's relations with China at a summit in Brussels next week.

Lebanon looks to EU support for state control of weapons, end to Israeli occupation

Wassim Samih Seifeddine and Sahin Demir
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
Lebanon said Thursday it is counting on EU support for its decision to place all weapons under state control and efforts to end Israel’s occupation of Lebanese territory.
“Lebanon has taken a clear sovereign decision to place weapons and the use of force exclusively in the hands of the state throughout its territory,” Lebanese Foreign Minister Youssef Rajji said during a joint news conference with EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas in Beirut.
He described the move as essential to restoring sovereignty, consolidating stability and rebuilding strong and capable state institutions.
“We count on the European Union continuing to stand by Lebanon and its legitimate institutions to achieve this national objective,” he said.
“We also count on its support to end the continuing Israeli occupation of Lebanese territory and ensure the full implementation of UN Security Council Resolution 1701.”
Rajji also welcomed European support for Lebanon’s state institutions, including the Lebanese army and Internal Security Forces.
“We want Europe to be an essential partner in this new phase, not only in helping Lebanon manage its crises, but also in overcoming them,” he added.
The Lebanese government decided in August to bring all weapons under state control, including those held by Hezbollah. The group rejected the move, demanding that Israeli forces first withdraw from areas they occupy in southern Lebanon.
UN Security Council Resolution 1701 was adopted in August 2006 following a 33-day war between Israel and Hezbollah.
Israel has continued attacks on Lebanon since March 2, killing 4,386 people and injuring 12,413, according to the latest Lebanese Health Ministry figures dated Sept. 25, 2025.
On June 26, Beirut and Tel Aviv signed a US-sponsored framework agreement in Washington providing for a gradual Israeli withdrawal from Lebanese territory and the deployment of the Lebanese army in areas vacated by Israeli forces.
Despite the agreement, Israel has continued attacks on southern Lebanon and remains in control of areas of Lebanese territory, some occupied for decades and others seized during more recent wars and military operations.

Eight Ukrainian intelligence agents sentenced in Russia for Crimea attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:41:15 UTC
23:41:15 KST

ROSTOV-ON-DON, October 8. /TASS/. Russia's Southern District Military Court sentenced eight members of a Ukrainian military intelligence network to prison terms ranging from five years suspended to 27 years, a TASS correspondent reports from the courtroom.
They had previously been detained while preparing a series of terrorist attacks and assassination attempts targeting senior officials in Crimea. "The defendants are found guilty and sentenced to imprisonment," the judge said.
The Russian Federal Security Service (FSB) previously reported that it had dismantled a network of the Main Intelligence Directorate of Ukraine's Defense Ministry that was planning a series of high-profile terrorist attacks in Crimea. According to the FSB, the plans included assassination attempts targeting Crimean Head Sergey Aksyonov, Crimean parliament Chairman Vladimir Konstantinov and Yalta Mayor Yanina Pavlenko. Terrorist attacks were also planned at transport infrastructure facilities on the peninsula. In 2024, the Southern District Military Court reported that it had sentenced two members of the Podvalny group: Konstantin Yevmenenko received a 10-year sentence, while Alexander Litvinenko was sentenced to nine years and six months.
During closing arguments, prosecutors requested prison terms ranging from 10 to 28 years for the eight members of the Ukrainian military intelligence network. During the hearings, Podvalny, Zorin, Petranov, Krivoshein, Voynarovsky, Voynarovskaya and Kravchuk pleaded not guilty. Barannik admitted his guilt but denied committing the crimes as part of an organized group.
According to the FSB, a cross-border network organized by Ukrainian special services ran from Bulgaria to Russia through Turkey and Georgia. In Bulgaria, Ukrainian citizen Marina Matushchak arranged for electric stoves containing explosive-device components to be shipped to Russia. After the stoves were transported by road to Russia, CDEK and Vozovoz delivery companies forwarded them to the sites where the attacks were being prepared. Russian citizens who were unaware of the shipments' true purpose handled the deliveries at the request of Ukrainian special services. Authorities also found that identical explosives were used to sabotage a railway in Crimea's Bakhchisaray district. Security forces subsequently detained members of the deeply clandestine intelligence group in Crimea, including Viktor Podvalny, Alexander Litvinenko, Sergey Krivoshein, Konstantin Yevmenenko and others. They had been recruited by Roman Mashovets, who had served as deputy head of Vladimir Zelensky's office since 2020 before joining the intelligence service.

India faces water and power stress after weak monsoon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:40:00 UTC
23:40:00 KST

India faces water and power shortages after weak monsoon
October 8, 2026
Ramesh Reddy, 44, put everything he had into his 3.5 acre tomato farm in June. The farmer from Kolar district in the south of the state of Karnataka invested 320,000 rupees (€3,000, $3,357), borrowing 250,000 rupees at 24% annual interest and pledging his wife's wedding jewelry as collateral.
The harvest was meant to repay the loan and cover his son's overdue college fees. But then the farm's irrigation well ran dry. Within three weeks, the tomato plants had turned brown and Reddy could not salvage a single crate.
"I have lost everything I invested," he told DW. "I have no money left for the next crop and I don't know how I will repay the loan."
He is now negotiating a job as a security guard in the state capital, Bengaluru, and preparing to leave his farmland behind.
Driest monsoon in 11 years
ForIndia, the monsoon is more than just a four-month rainy season. It replenishes reservoirs, supports agriculture and helps sustain water supplies and power generation across much of the country.
Nearly half of India's workforce depends on farming for their livelihood, doing jobs that are both tough and economically insecure.
This year, the country received 759.4 millimeters (ca. 30 inches) of rain between June and September, against a long-term average of 868.6 millimeters. The 12.6% deficit made it the country's driest monsoon in 11 years and the fourth driest this century.
Madhavan Nair Rajeevan, a climate scientist and former secretary in the Indian Ministry of Earth Sciences, said the main factor behind the poor monsoon was a severe El Nino. He had warned earlier that this global climate phenomenon would posed a serious risk to rainfall.
"As far as the Indian monsoon is concerned, El Nino is the most important influencing factor, which we should consider very seriously,” Rajeevan told DW.
Water and power under pressure
The effects are now hitting India's water and energy systems. The country's major reservoirs ended the monsoon with less water than usual, leaving both farmers and the power sector with less of a buffer going into the months ahead.
Combined storage in the 178 reservoirs monitored by the Central Water Commission stood at 132.7 billion cubic meters, below the 10-year average of 151.1 billion cubic meters.
That shortfall is already being felt in electricity generation. Hydropower output fell nearly 16% in September from a year earlier, according to Grid India data. At the same time, electricity shortages reached 560 million kilowatt-hours, the highest monthly shortfall in more than three years. After sunset, when solar generation drops off, the grid has fewer options to make up the difference.
Coal-fired plants have, therefore, had to shoulder more of the load, but they face a problem of their own. Data from the Central Electricity Authority showed that around 40% of coal-fired plants had critically low stocks, with supplies below a quarter of the required level.
The government has ordered some private industrial power plants to operate at full capacity and feed surplus electricity into the grid.
Manufacturers are already feeling the strain. "Uninterrupted power supply is of paramount importance for manufacturing units, as power cuts disrupt production cycles," said Ashok Gupta, the president of the Mohali Industries Association, which represents nearly 600 small and medium-sized manufacturers.
"Such disruptions not only cause losses to manufacturers but also result in wastage of raw materials."
A hit to rural incomes
The economic impact of a poor monsoon can extend well beyond agriculture. Weaker farm output can hit rural incomes, employment and consumption, while higher food prices put further pressure on household budgets.
Arun Kumar, a retired professor of economics, said the effects could be wider than the headline economic numbers suggest, particularly because much of India's rural economy operates outside the formal sector.
"Economic development needs to be assessed through a wider set of indicators," Kumar told DW. He said weaker agricultural output could push up food prices while putting pressure on incomes and consumption.
Himanshu, a development economist at Delhi's Jawaharlal Nehru University, described the situation as a "twin shock" for rural households, with weaker farm incomes coming alongside higher food prices.
"When agricultural incomes fall and food prices rise, rural households face a squeeze on their purchasing power," he told DW.
The economist said that the uneven distribution of rainfall could compound the problem, with some farming regions suffering much heavier losses than the national rainfall figure indicates. "The impact on rural consumption could also be significant, as households facing lower incomes and higher food costs have less money to spend on other goods and services."
Outlook increasingly difficult to predict as climate warms
The pressure is also being felt in urban households. A survey in September by India's central bank found that households were expecting inflation to rise as food and fuel prices increasingly affected sentiment.
Sunita Sharma, a homemaker in New Delhi, said her usual shopping list now costs hundreds of rupees more than it did a few months ago.
"We have no option but to cut down on discretionary expenses just to afford basic, everyday meals," she told DW.
The prices of some staples have risen sharply recently. An analysis by ISignal using Department of Consumer Affairs data found that onions were 93% more expensive in September than a year earlier, while sugar prices rose by 28% and rice by about 8%.
The next test will be the rabi, or winter, crop. Farmers are now preparing to plant wheat, mustard and chickpeas, but success will depend largely on how much moisture remains in the soil after the weak monsoon.
Rajeevan said the longer-term outlook was also becoming increasingly difficult to predict as the climate warms.
"In a warming climate, longer dry spells and greater rainfall variability is a possibility," he said. "In future, in addition to the influence of El Nino events, we should expect the influence of a warmer climate."
Reddy, the farmer in Karnataka state, is now waiting to hear whether he has got the security job in Bengaluru, and preparing to leave his farm behind.

Water and power under pressure
The effects are now hitting India's water and energy systems. The country's major reservoirs ended the monsoon with less water than usual, leaving both farmers and the power sector with less of a buffer going into the months ahead.
Combined storage in the 178 reservoirs monitored by the Central Water Commission stood at 132.7 billion cubic meters, below the 10-year average of 151.1 billion cubic meters.
That shortfall is already being felt in electricity generation. Hydropower output fell nearly 16% in September from a year earlier, according to Grid India data. At the same time, electricity shortages reached 560 million kilowatt-hours, the highest monthly shortfall in more than three years. After sunset, when solar generation drops off, the grid has fewer options to make up the difference.
Coal-fired plants have, therefore, had to shoulder more of the load, but they face a problem of their own. Data from the Central Electricity Authority showed that around 40% of coal-fired plants had critically low stocks, with supplies below a quarter of the required level.
The government has ordered some private industrial power plants to operate at full capacity and feed surplus electricity into the grid.
Manufacturers are already feeling the strain. "Uninterrupted power supply is of paramount importance for manufacturing units, as power cuts disrupt production cycles," said Ashok Gupta, the president of the Mohali Industries Association, which represents nearly 600 small and medium-sized manufacturers.
"Such disruptions not only cause losses to manufacturers but also result in wastage of raw materials."
A hit to rural incomes
The economic impact of a poor monsoon can extend well beyond agriculture. Weaker farm output can hit rural incomes, employment and consumption, while higher food prices put further pressure on household budgets.
Arun Kumar, a retired professor of economics, said the effects could be wider than the headline economic numbers suggest, particularly because much of India's rural economy operates outside the formal sector.
"Economic development needs to be assessed through a wider set of indicators," Kumar told DW. He said weaker agricultural output could push up food prices while putting pressure on incomes and consumption.
Himanshu, a development economist at Delhi's Jawaharlal Nehru University, described the situation as a "twin shock" for rural households, with weaker farm incomes coming alongside higher food prices.
"When agricultural incomes fall and food prices rise, rural households face a squeeze on their purchasing power," he told DW.
The economist said that the uneven distribution of rainfall could compound the problem, with some farming regions suffering much heavier losses than the national rainfall figure indicates. "The impact on rural consumption could also be significant, as households facing lower incomes and higher food costs have less money to spend on other goods and services."
Outlook increasingly difficult to predict as climate warms
The pressure is also being felt in urban households. A survey in September by India's central bank found that households were expecting inflation to rise as food and fuel prices increasingly affected sentiment.
Sunita Sharma, a homemaker in New Delhi, said her usual shopping list now costs hundreds of rupees more than it did a few months ago.
"We have no option but to cut down on discretionary expenses just to afford basic, everyday meals," she told DW.
The prices of some staples have risen sharply recently. An analysis by ISignal using Department of Consumer Affairs data found that onions were 93% more expensive in September than a year earlier, while sugar prices rose by 28% and rice by about 8%.
The next test will be the rabi, or winter, crop. Farmers are now preparing to plant wheat, mustard and chickpeas, but success will depend largely on how much moisture remains in the soil after the weak monsoon.
Rajeevan said the longer-term outlook was also becoming increasingly difficult to predict as the climate warms.
"In a warming climate, longer dry spells and greater rainfall variability is a possibility," he said. "In future, in addition to the influence of El Nino events, we should expect the influence of a warmer climate."
Reddy, the farmer in Karnataka state, is now waiting to hear whether he has got the security job in Bengaluru, and preparing to leave his farm behind.

Defence minister calls Russia “the enemy”, but policy unchanged

Defence minister calls Russia “the enemy”, but policy unchanged
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Defence minister Dilan Yeşilgöz has started calling Russia “the enemy” rather than “the aggressor”, but says the change in wording does not mean any immediate change in national security policy.
The right-wing liberal VVD minister used the term during Thursday’s parliamentary debate on the defence budget. In a break in the debate, she told public broadcaster NOS that a rise in sabotage, drone incidents and intimidation in Europe meant the threat should be named plainly.
“It is very clear that Russia is presenting itself as the enemy,” she said. “That does not mean we are at war or that we will suddenly take a completely different approach.”
In August, the cabinet published a draft law that would give the domestic intelligence service AIVD and military intelligence service MIVD sweeping new powers against Russia, China and Iran.
A “new reality”
Yeşilgöz said Russia had long been the biggest threat to Europe, but the danger had grown into what she called a “new reality”. “Putin is testing how strong our alliance is,” she said. She added that experts had advised her to call things what they are.
The policy of investing more in defence and working closely with European allies has been in place since Russia invaded Ukraine, she said. “We were not naive before and we will not become naive now.”
In April, the AIVD said in its annual report that national security was under more pressure than at any time since the Second World War.
Oversight concerns
Under the draft law, the intelligence services would be able to designate “evident adversaries”, such as a Russian intelligence agency, and act against anyone believed to be working for them without asking a watchdog for permission first. A single new regulator would check afterwards whether the action was lawful.
The services would also be able to demand information from organisations such as banks, universities and online platforms.
The independent watchdogs that currently oversee the AIVD and MIVD have strongly criticised the plans. Hugo Hillenaar, who chairs the intelligence review committee CTIVD, told NOS last month that the changes could threaten the democratic rule of law itself.

Ukraine’s FM links Russian plague scare to history of cover-ups, from anthrax to Chornobyl and COVID-19
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:38:35 UTC
23:38:35 KST

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Russia's handling of a suspected pneumonic plague case fit what he described as Moscow's history of concealing information about dangerous incidents, citing the 1979 anthrax outbreak, the Chornobyl disaster, and the COVID-19 pandemic, according to his post on X on 8 October.
A 28-year-old worker at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute, Daria Shipilova, died at Shelekhov District Hospital on 2 October. The hospital was placed under quarantine, and nearly 200 people who had contact with her were put under medical observation.
Sybiha has called on Russia to disclose all the facts surrounding the case, provide transparent epidemiological data, and cooperate with international mechanisms.
"Russia has a long record of concealing the truth: the 1979 anthrax leak in Sverdlovsk, the 1986 Chornobyl disaster, and the true scale of COVID-19 in 2020–2022," he said.
Plague is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, which is usually found in small mammals and their fleas. Bubonic plague, the most common form, is caused by the bite of an infected flea. Pneumonic plague is the most virulent form: left untreated, it can be fatal within 18 to 24 hours of onset, though common antibiotics can cure it if given early.
But each time, the consequences were devastating.
Sybiha warns of the risks of secrecy
Sybiha added that there is compelling evidence that Russia has used chemical weapons in Ukraine and has threatened to use nuclear weapons in its genocidal war. His remarks came amid rumors that the plague could have originated in a biological laboratory developing weapons.
"The world must not wait for another catastrophe before asking questions," he said.
Russia must disclose all the circumstances surrounding the case, provide transparent epidemiological data, and cooperate with international mechanisms because “when dangerous pathogens are involved, secrecy is a threat to everyone,” Sybiha added.
WHO seeks more information from Russia
The World Health Organization (WHO) says it still lacks the data it needs for a full risk assessment, while Russia has told the organization that no cases of plague have recently been reported in Irkutsk Oblast.
WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus says that the organization has asked Russia for "further information on the laboratory tests conducted on the individual who died and the contacts," more details on what prompted the public health measures, and the health status of the contacts. The organization also seeks verification of media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause.
Based on "unofficial information," the public health risk to the general population appears to be low, WHO spokesperson Christian Lindmeier says, according to Forbes.
US officials say they know little about what is happening in Russia
On 6 October, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said information з приводу вирогідної хвороби from Russia was "still quite limited."
The next day at the White House, a reporter asked US President Donald Trump whether the plague in Russia was a bioweapon, according to CNN.
"Well, we don't think so. We're going to find out soon enough, but we don't think so," he said.
The reporter also asked whether Trump was “getting the same vibe right now from Russia that you got from China at the start of COVID.”
"Well, China didn't say much, and Russia's not saying much either, but they do say they have it very much under control," Trump answered.

Russian air defense explained: How Moscow counters mass drone attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:36:56 UTC
23:36:56 KST

Russian air defense explained: How Moscow counters mass drone attacks
Moscow, October 6. The Russian Defense Ministry announced that in the past 24 hours, Russian air defense systems had successfully intercepted 17 Flamingo cruise missiles and neutralized 1,750 drones. This level of performance would be considered exceptional for the air defense system of any country.
Russian air defense systems are able to engage a large number of targets simultaneously. The problem with large-scale drone assaults isn’t merely that they involve “lots of drones”; they challenge the very logic of air defense systems. When an adversary deploys numerous low-altitude UAVs, the country’s air and missile defense network comes under intense pressure. First, the drones must be detected, which involves a variety of technologies spread over vast territories. Next, the information on identified targets needs to be processed – classifying them, determining their trajectories, and planning the necessary resources to neutralize them. Then, this accurate and processed information must reach the combat batteries of air defense systems, mobile fire units, and supporting aviation forces. Finally, the target can be eliminated. Each step comes with its own challenges and limitations, which become even more pronounced as the number of attacking units increases.
Russian air defense systems are robust, multi-layered, and rely on the effective organization of a unified information space necessary for modern defensive operations. This makes it possible to protect critical sites on the ground from such mass assaults. All stress tests have been successfully passed. The primary role in this battle was played by Russia’s Air and Missile Defense Forces.
How is the air defense system structured?
Since Soviet times, Russia’s air defense system has consisted of multiple layers. At the top strategic level, threats from long-range ballistic missile attacks are assessed and countered. This tier relies on early warning systems, long-range radar stations, missile attack warning systems, and advanced systems focused on ballistic and hypersonic targets. Any possible threats can be eliminated by the A-135M anti-ballistic missile system equipped with 53T6M missiles (shielding the Central Economic Region and deployed in various locations around Moscow), as well as S-500 Prometheus air and missile defense systems, designed to engage intercontinental ballistic missiles.
S-400 Triumph systems form the backbone of regional air defense. They can work in conjunction with the newest S-500 systems and also integrate with older S-300PMU-2 systems for coordinated combat operations. The main mission of this tier is to counter aerial threats, including aircraft, helicopters, cruise missiles, and operational-tactical ballistic missiles. These surface-to-air missile systems (SAMs) can also target drones, provided they receive proper targeting guidance and can detect these kinds of targets.
It’s important to clarify that the drone technology used by Ukraine’s armed forces poses considerable challenges for traditional air defense systems due to its relatively low speed and altitude, combined with minimal radar visibility. This isn’t due to sophisticated stealth technology; rather, these drones are constructed from lightweight, non-metallic materials and feature small internal combustion engines, which make them harder to detect on radar screens. Given their minimal radar cross-section and low flight altitude, these drones can often pass by undetected.
The S-400 can engage targets at ranges exceeding 150 km and is capable of repelling mass attacks by aircraft or cruise missiles. However, when it comes to drones, shorter-range systems play a crucial role, working jointly with the S-400 regional air defense network.
Key players in the fight against drones include the following systems: S-350 Vityaz, Tor-M2, and the terminal defense system Pantsir-S1. These systems are ideal for countering large-scale drone assaults; they are the ones that fight the main battle against UAVs.
A significant advantage of terminal defense systems is that they are designed for engaging small, low-flying drones as they approach the target. Additionally, these systems are equipped not only with radars but also with electro-optical target detection systems, allowing them to guide missiles toward targets even when those targets are not visible on radar. Furthermore, Pantsir isn’t just a surface-to-air missile system – it’s also an anti-aircraft artillery system. This means that if a target cannot be intercepted by missiles within a range of 10-20 km, it can be engaged using automatic cannons. This makes it particularly effective against slow-moving drones.
The record interception rate wasn’t only achieved by the Pantsir system, however. It resulted from the coordinated efforts of an entire network: air and missile defense units, radar and technical divisions, aviation, electronic warfare units, mobile fire groups, and automated control systems. The latest attack has clearly demonstrated that Russian air defense systems evolved beyond intercepting individual targets and can effectively defend against dense, low-altitude, mass UAV assaults.
Mobile units and aviation step in
To deal with slower drones, new air defense structures – known as mobile fire groups (MFGs) – are being employed extensively. These agile units, equipped with machine guns and portable surface-to-air missile systems, can be deployed either along drone flight paths or near specific infrastructure. While the effectiveness of these units depends on being in the right place at the right time (since their engagement range is limited), they are highly maneuverable, and given the slow speed of drones, they can set up defensive positions if they have timely intelligence about the type and direction of an impending attack. In fact, one of the key developments of the fall of 2026 was the implementation of a unified information system for organizing air defense against drones across various Russian regions. Such a system could significantly enhance the efficiency of mobile air defense units; and apparently, it’s already being used.
Army aviation helicopters are another useful asset in combating drones. Their speed allows them to catch up with drones, while their armament enables them to destroy these threats using both artillery fire and guided missiles. A considerable portion of downed drones can likely be attributed to the effective operation of frontline helicopters.
Cruise missiles such as Ukraine’s Flamingo pose a different sort of challenge. They are more complex compared to standard drones: they move faster, pose greater risks, and navigate terrain more effectively. In this case, Airborne Early Warning and Control (AEW&C) aircraft like the A-50M become indispensable; they monitor the air situation against the backdrop of the Earth’s surface and can direct interceptor aircraft toward targets. Receiving target data from AEW&C allows fighter jets to engage cruise missiles before ground-based air defense systems can establish a solid lock, or in areas where deploying a SAM would be less advantageous. The coordinated work of AEW&C, fighter jets, and ground-based air defense systems is crucial for repelling mixed attacks involving both drones and cruise missiles, and is the key to success in defensive battles.
Challenges or opportunities?
When it comes to combating drones, challenges certainly exist. The primary concern is the economic aspect: a drone may cost tens of thousands of dollars, but a missile is much more expensive. If the enemy launches thousands of drones, the defending side needs cost-effective alternatives – such as bullets, fragmentation shells, small missiles, electronic warfare (EW) systems, interceptor drones, and mobile units. This opens up avenues for the evolution of air defense systems.
Interceptor drones could prove effective against slower drones since their production costs are at least comparable to those of basic drones. However, an interceptor drone without a warhead would be utterly ineffective against a larger, aircraft-type drone – it simply wouldn’t be able to bring it down. Therefore, in the future, we may see interceptor drones equipped with munitions and capable of high-speed flight.
Another promising direction is the development of rapid-fire artillery systems using programmable munitions, like the ZAK-30 Citadel. These systems can fire multiple rounds accurately and then quickly switch to a new target. Moreover, such automated air defense systems have the potential to effectively combat swarms of drones – if not now, then certainly in the near future.
Efforts are also underway to create compact and relatively simple guided missiles for air defense systems. Such new missiles were designed for the Pantsir system, and we may soon see small, mobile air defense units equipped with these missiles. This would significantly reduce the cost of downing a drone and enhance the effectiveness of mobile groups.
Laser systems for neutralizing drones hold particularly promising economic prospects. While the initial cost of a laser system is high, the price per shot is minimal. Like rapid-fire automated artillery, lasers can almost instantly switch between targets. This makes them highly useful for countering drone swarms.
Overall, Russian air defense systems are becoming more sophisticated and offer unique capabilities in fending off mass attacks. The performance metrics of these systems are among the best in the world – this has been proven in real battle conditions, no propaganda or exaggeration involved. And this is just the beginning; air defense systems are evolving and will undoubtedly become even more effective in the future.

Mertkan Oruc and Emir Yildirim
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
Türkiye’s Middle East Technical University (METU) is planning to launch the homegrown lunar micro-rover ‘Cheri’ to the Moon in 2030, the rector told Anadolu.
Ahmet Yozgatligil, speaking on the sidelines of the 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC) held in the southwestern province of Antalya, stated that the prototype of the rover has been completed and the craft is undergoing testing.
The Cheri project includes two autonomous vehicles powered by artificial intelligence (AI) and developed in collaboration with the China National Space Administration (CNSA).
The twin rovers were designed to operate in extreme cold and with limited sunlight at the lunar south pole, running simultaneously to conduct topographic studies and analyze rock samples via remote sensing.
“Our two Cheri rovers will work together and even take a ‘selfie’ of the mission, while carrying out mapping activities at the sites they discover, which we’re very excited about,” he said.
The prototype of the Cheri micro-rover was presented to Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan by the head of the Higher Education Council (YOK), Erol Ozvar, during the opening ceremony of the national academic year.
“Over 120 of our students are working on this project alongside faculty members, while as a part of the EU’s ‘Go Space’ program, our students are also focused on developing communications protocols for satellites in space, stations to be established on the lunar surface, and orbital stations,” he said.
Yozgatligil noted that the faculty is also contributing to the space sector through initiatives like the Aselabs Program in collaboration with the defense firm Aselsan.
He mentioned that METU recently joined the microgravity research collaboration established between leading European and US universities, after signing a deal with Axiom Space.
“The most important international project we’re carrying out is the METU Space Technology Park, which will be a hub for space sector research and commercialization activities,” he added.
The premier aerospace event IAC 2026 kicked off on Monday and will run until Friday. It is co-hosted by the Turkish Space Agency (TUA) and SAHA Istanbul defense cluster and organized by the Industry and Technology Ministry. Anadolu serves as its global communications partner.

Herzog honors 6 Israelis who thwarted flydubai terror attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:34:38 UTC
23:34:38 KST

One week after the attempted terror attack aboard a flydubai flight, President Isaac Herzog on Thursday presented civilian bravery awards to six Israelis who rushed the attacker, subdued him and helped prevent him from crashing the plane.
The awards were presented at the President’s Residence in Jerusalem to  Tali Manes, Zvika Manes, Yaniv Hayun, Asaf Rajuan, Or Pardilov and Dr. Shota Musaiev, who also provided life-saving medical treatment to the flight’s captain after he was stabbed by the attacker.
The six thanked Herzog for the recognition. “It is a great honor that the president chose to award me the bravery medal,” Hayun said. “It will be displayed proudly in our home, and my children will be able to see it every day.”
Tali Mans said: “Apparently I’m a mother with maternal intuition, and I was in the right place at the right time, with the best possible people.”
Her husband, Tzvika Mans said it was the cries of his daughters that drove him to act. “When a parent hears a scream like that, you act without thinking,” he said.
Musaiev described the chain of events as a series of extraordinary coincidences. “A lot of miracles happened that day,” he said. “We were a chain of people helping one another, and if one link had been missing, the chain would have broken. Everyone acted heroically.”
Herzog praised the six for what he called extraordinary civilian courage.
“I have the privilege and honor of hosting you here at the President’s Residence, recognizing the tremendous civilian bravery embodied in your actions and bearing witness to one of the most chilling aviation stories known to humanity in general and Israeli society in particular,” Herzog said.
“This was a story in which there was no time to think, formulate a plan, consult or prepare. A story written without orders and without a briefing, without ranks and without prior coordination. A story in which fate was decided in a single moment. A moment in which a person discovers who they really are. A moment in which we discover who Israelis are.”
Herzog said the lives of all 174 people aboard the plane, as well as potentially many more on the ground, had been at stake.
“Tali, you immediately recognized what was happening and called for help; Yaniv, Tzvika, Or and Assaf, you jumped into danger, subdued the attacker and helped bring the aircraft back under control; and you, Dr. Musaiev, helped overpower him and also provided life-saving treatment to the wounded pilot,” Herzog said.
“You are the six who prevented a major aviation disaster, a disaster that would have changed the face of the country and the Middle East.”
Herzog also praised the flight’s captain, Smit Machchhar, who continued fighting the attacker despite being badly wounded and managed, with his remaining strength, to open the cockpit door.
“From here, on behalf of all of us, I send him wishes for a full and speedy recovery,” Herzog said. “I also intend to honor him, as the committee recommended, with the President’s Civilian Bravery Award.”
Herzog thanked the replacement pilots and other passengers who assisted during the incident, saying their actions would also be examined and recognized.
At the same time, the president stressed that the passengers’ heroism could not substitute for a full investigation into how the attack was allowed to happen.
“The civilian courage and resourcefulness demonstrated by the heroes here cannot cover up the obligation to provide full answers,” Herzog said. “Everyone deserves clear and satisfactory answers.”
‘Resourcefulness is a way of life’
Herzog said the award reflected not only the lives the six had saved but also what their response revealed about Israeli society.
“Tali, Yaniv, Tzvika, Or, Assaf, Dr. Shota, the Civilian Bravery Award does not symbolize only the fact that you saved lives,” he said. “It is also being awarded because, at the moment of truth, you revealed something much deeper: you revealed the face of the Israeli spirit. A spirit of courage. A spirit of tremendous resourcefulness. A spirit that says: when there is danger, you act.”
“You did not stop to ask one another, ‘Which side are you on?’ ‘Who are you planning to vote for?’ ‘Where do you come from?’ or ‘What is your worldview?’ You did not look for what divided you, because when the plane was in the air and lives hung in the balance, all those disagreements were meaningless,” he added.
“There was only one thing left: the person beside you. Your responsibility toward them. The duty to save them. That sacred mutual responsibility.”
Herzog noted that the ceremony came one day after the third anniversary, on the Gregorian calendar, of the October 7 massacre.
“Over these three years, time and again we have seen Israeli society at its finest,” he said. “A society that, in its hardest moments, proves that resourcefulness is not just a characteristic, it is a way of life.”
“This moment is also a reminder to all of us of the society we want to live in and the Israelis we want to be: a society in which, in difficult moments, we do not ask who is standing beside us, we stand beside one another. A society that does not ask who belongs to which camp, but who needs our help right now.”

Germany's Left to start Berlin coalition talks after antisemitism deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:34:34 UTC
23:34:34 KST

Germany's Left to start Berlin coalition talks after antisemitism deal
Oct 8 - Germany's Left Party agreed measures on Thursday to address antisemitic incidents, satisfying a key condition set by potential coalition partners and allowing it to begin exploratory talks on Berlin's next state government.
The agreement revives prospects for a three-party coalition between the Left, the centre-left Social Democrats (SPD) and Greens after the Left, a hard-left party represented in Berlin by lead candidate Elif Eralp, emerged from the September 20 state election as the largest force, with 25.7% of the votes.
The three parties confirmed at a press conference that they would begin exploratory coalition talks immediately.
The breakthrough highlights how tensions over antisemitism and the Israel-Gaza conflict have become a major fault line in German politics, with the SPD and Greens insisting on binding safeguards before entering coalition talks with the Left.
A successful coalition could help rehabilitate the Left as a potential governing partner elsewhere in Germany, offering a model for centre-left cooperation at a time when traditional coalition options have become increasingly fragmented.
However, it could also deepen cracks within the struggling federal government, with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz warning his SPD coalition partners not to enter into government with a party that he argues puts the "non-negotiable principle" of Germany's commitment to Israel up for debate.
SAFEGUARDS AGAINST ANTISEMITISM
The Left's success, displacing Merz's conservative party in the mayor's office, has been overcast by allegations of antisemitism over some members' association with pro-Palestinian protests.
Eralp and other party leaders say they oppose all forms of antisemitism while defending the right to criticise the Israeli government.
"Safety means being able to go to school without fear, to wear a kippah, and to speak Hebrew without having to explain yourself," said Kerstin Wolter, co-chair of the Left Party in Berlin, during a joint press conference. "We see the fear felt by Jewish Berliners".
The issue has been particularly significant in Germany amid a rise in antisemitic incidents since the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack on Israel and the subsequent war in Gaza.
Under the proposed measures, the state legislature whips of all three parties would deliberate on any antisemitic incidents and expel the accused lawmaker if they reach a consensus; in case of disagreement, experts would be called in to review the case.
The parties have also agreed to the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance's (IHRA) definition of antisemitism, which has been rejected by some Left Party members who argue that it can conflate criticism of Israel with antisemitism.
COMPARISON WITH AFD REJECTED
The prospective coalition partners also rejected any comparison between the Left Party and the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), which polls indicate as the most popular party in Germany.
"The AfD fights against democracy. The AfD talks about deporting millions of people from this country," said Steffen Krach, SPD lead candidate for Berlin. "At its core, the AfD is an anti-democratic party, whereas standing before you here are three democratic parties." REUTERS

Under the roadmap, the two countries plan to hold regular consultations on defence and security issues and deepen cooperation in combating hybrid threats, intelligence sharing and air defence, while improving interoperability between their systems.

Meetings under the roadmap are expected to be held alternately in Paris and Ankara, with the first planned for the final quarter of 2026, subject to agreement between the sides.

====================================================================================================

EU faces gas shortfall of up to 15% if severe winter hits, report warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:33:36 UTC
23:33:36 KST

The EU is entering the winter season on thin ice, facing a double-edged geopolitical squeeze that threatens to expose the fragility of its post-Russian energy architecture.
Europe could face a gas shortfall of 12% to 15% of demand if a severe cold snap hits this winter, according to a report published on Thursday by the EU's gas transmission operators.
The warning comes as the bloc enters winter with gas storage facilities just 72% full as of October 1, down from 83% at the same point last year, following what the report describes as a "challenging injection season".
The winter supply outlook, published by the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Gas (ENTSOG), examines two scenarios that assume no Russian pipeline gas supplies. The EU has largely phased out Russian gas, although exceptions remain for landlocked countries such as Hungary and Slovakia.
The report, published on October 8, warns that a disruption to the largest offshore gas infrastructure supplying continental Europe, combined with a complete halt to pipeline imports from Algeria, would pose a serious threat to the bloc's energy security.
Brussels has urged EU countries to maximise early-winter storage injections and maintain rigid cooperative behaviour to ensure equal sharing of any eventual demand curtailments.
LNG to the rescue
The report highlights Europe's growing dependence on the volatile global market for liquefied natural gas (LNG) as it moves away from Russian pipeline supplies.
The US has emerged as the EU's top LNG supplier, replacing much of the gas previously imported from Russia.
Even under normal winter conditions, a squeeze on LNG supplies could drive European gas storage levels down to just 13% by March 2027, potentially forcing energy-intensive industries to cut production.
"Under tight LNG supply conditions, high gas prices may also lead to a response from price sensitive demand, highlighting the importance of securing sufficient LNG imports and maximising storage levels ahead of and during the early stages of the winter season," reads the report.
Shipping constraints through the Strait of Hormuz — a chokepoint controlling 20% of global LNG trade — have severely throttled exports from Qatar and the United Arab Emirates since the US-Israeli war against Iran on 28 February.
While direct European exposure to Qatari gas is modest at roughly 8%, with Italy being the country most affected, the resulting global supply crunch has triggered an aggressive bidding war between Europe and Asia, driving up price volatility and leaving Europe vulnerable.
Europe's gas vulnerabilities
Western European countries have benefited from new coastal LNG terminals and access to pipeline supplies from countries such as Norway. But landlocked countries in Central, Eastern and South-Eastern Europe remain more exposed to supply disruptions.
If major pipeline infrastructure — such as the North Sea's Europipe 2 or Algerian import lines — suffers a disruption alongside a harsh winter, infrastructure bottlenecks will physically restrict the flow of gas from West to East.
Southeastern Europe could see immediate localised supply shortfalls of up to 12% on peak demand days, testing the limits of European solidarity.
As reserves dwindle, governments could also come under growing pressure to prioritise domestic consumers over neighbouring countries.
Brussels has given member states temporary flexibility to keep storage levels at 75%-80% by 1 November rather than the usual 90% target, in an effort to avoid panic buying and prices from going even higher.
Dutch TTF, the European benchmark for gas trading, was between €79.80 and €80.22 per MWh on Thursday, almost triple since the war against Iran.

The EU withdrew its diplomatic service's logo from a disinformation conference in Lithuania that featured a panel portraying the US as a potential disinformation threat, citing concerns over the framing of discussions, a European Commission spokesperson said Thursday.

Russia’s international reserves fall by $9.5 bln over week to $733.2 bln — Central Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:29:35 UTC
23:29:35 KST

MOSCOW, October 8. /TASS/. Russia’s international reserves stood at $733.2 bln as of October 2, 2026, down $9.5 bln over the week, according to materials published by the Bank of Russia.
"International reserves stood at $733.2 bln as of the end of October 2, 2026, declining by $9.5 bln, or 1.3%, over the week, mainly due to negative revaluation," the regulator said.
As of September 25, the reserves totaled $742.7 bln.
International reserves are highly liquid foreign assets held by the Bank of Russia and the Russian government. They consist of foreign currency assets, special drawing rights, the reserve position in the International Monetary Fund, and monetary gold.
Western countries imposed sanctions on the Bank of Russia after Russia launched its special military operation in Ukraine. In addition to freezing Russia’s gold and foreign exchange reserves, they banned all transactions related to the management of the Central Bank’s reserves and assets, as well as transactions with any legal entity, organization, or body acting on behalf of or at the direction of the Central Bank.

An Israeli father who was aboard flydubai Flight 1073 when the co-pilot allegedly attacked the captain told The Jerusalem Post that passengers were convinced they were about to die as the aircraft plunged, and then spent roughly 90 minutes not knowing where they were being flown.
In this week's Deep Dive episode, Uri Pintov, who was returning from a family vacation in Thailand with his wife and three children, said to the Post Editor-in-Chief, Zvika Klein, that he was walking back from the rear of the plane when it went into a steep, banking dive that pinned him to the floor for more than a minute. "We all realized we were going to die," he said.
Pintov described how passengers bound the attacker with airline headphones, carried oxygen and water to the badly wounded Indian captain, and assigned Israelis to escort every cabin crew member because "we can't trust anybody." With the cockpit locked and almost no communication from the relief pilots, passengers feared they were being taken to Yemen or Iran, he said. Only when a crew member recognized the airport at Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, did they begin to believe they would survive.
The Israeli passenger praised the Saudi security forces who received the passengers, saying they were "very gentle with kids and women." He said a tense two hours followed after it became clear Israeli aircraft would not be allowed to land, leaving families to decide whether to board a replacement flydubai plane.
He said that apart from psychological support from the community, there had been no formal outreach from Israeli officials. He called on Israel and the airline to issue an official statement confirming the incident as an attempted terrorist hijacking, to counter claims circulating online that it was staged.
Also a guest, Seth J. Frantzman, the Post's senior Middle East analyst and correspondent, added that several of the so-called miracles were in fact protocol, including the off-duty pilots on board. He noted that because the aircraft and its flight recorders survived, investigators should be able to reconstruct events in detail. He cautioned against overreacting the way aviation security did after the shoe bomber, and said flydubai is "one of the crown jewels of the Abraham Accords."
A permanent withdrawal of the airline would push up Israeli airfares, which are already inflated by a shortage of capacity, he said. Frantzman described Riyadh's refusal to admit Israeli planes as an understandable matter of national pride but a missed opportunity. He also argued that Saudi normalization is unlikely while the current government pursues its stated policies on Gaza and the Palestinian Authority.

Italy and the Republic of the Congo Working Together to Develop Special Economic Zones (SEZs)
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:26:31 CEST
23:26:31 KST

The seminar “Regards croisés sur les Zones économiques spéciales: Italian and Congolese Experiences’ was held on October 6 and 7 in Brazzaville, the capital of the Republic of the Congo. The event focused on comparing Italian and Congolese experiences in the development of Special Economic Zones (SEZs) and, more broadly, on the prospects for economic and industrial cooperation between Italy and the Republic of the Congo, according to a press release from the Italian Embassy in Brazzaville. The initiative brought together representatives from Congolese and Italian institutions, the private sector, businesses, training organizations, and experts, with the involvement of the Italian Trade Agency (ICE). During the seminar, the Italian Ambassador to Brazzaville, Enrico Nunziata, emphasized the importance of transforming the Congolese SEZs from mere areas designated to host businesses into true productive ecosystems capable of integrating businesses, infrastructure, services, training, research, innovation, and institutions. The ambassador also highlighted the need to draw on Italy’s experience as a source of expertise and best practices, while building a model of industrial development consistent with the Congo’s resources, priorities, and territorial characteristics. The African country has four SEZs, each with distinct regional focuses: Pointe-Noire, Oyo-Ollombo, Ouesso, and Ignié. During the seminar, participants emphasized the potential to develop these zones as laboratories for territorial development, leveraging their distinct strengths and fostering the emergence of integrated production chains. The central issue that emerged from the discussions was how to transform the SEZs into hubs capable of attracting productive investments, creating jobs, developing local skills and suppliers, and fostering the Congo’s integration into regional and international value chains. Cooperation between Italy and the Republic of the Congo, as the Italian Embassy in Brazzaville further notes, is already underway in various sectors that also fall within the framework of Italian initiatives developed under the Mattei Plan for Africa. During the seminar, various examples were cited, ranging from agriculture to water management, not to mention the energy sector. Last year, Italy ranked among the Republic of Congo’s leading suppliers. Italian exports to the Congolese market totaled approximately 140 million euros. This figure was cited during the seminar to highlight the potential that still exists for the development of bilateral economic relations. The goal outlined by the ambassador is not only to increase Italian exports but also to foster a greater Italian manufacturing and industrial presence in the Congo. In the various sectors identified as particularly promising for cooperation between Italian and Congolese companies, the press release continues, Italy can provide technological expertise, industrial know-how, and entrepreneurial capabilities, while the Congolese Special Economic Zones (SEZs) can serve as platforms to foster investment and partnerships. During the proceedings, the importance of taking concrete steps to address obstacles that may limit investment was also emphasized. One of the stated objectives of the initiative was to ensure that the comparison between Italian and Congolese experiences did not remain purely theoretical, the press release further explains. The discussions therefore focused on identifying potential concrete projects to be further explored through the involvement of institutions and economic operators from both countries. At the conclusion of the seminar, the Italian Embassy in Brazzaville confirmed, together with ICE and in coordination with Congolese authorities, its willingness to support the next phase and to facilitate contacts between institutions and businesses in both countries in order to transform the dialogue initiated in the capital of the Republic of the Congo into investments, industrial partnerships, local production, the transfer of expertise, and job creation.

Lithuanian authorities seek to host nuclear arms to position themselves on front line — MP
