Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:25:41 UTC
23:25:41 KST

KALININGRAD, October 8. /TASS/. Lithuania’s leadership is obsessed with positioning the country on the front line of a confrontation with NATO’s "enemies." Against this backdrop, Vilnius’s plans to allow the deployment of nuclear weapons send an alarming signal that it intends to move from rhetoric to action, Yevgeny Mishin, Deputy Chairman of the Committee on International and Interregional Relations, Security, and Law and Order, told TASS.
On October 6, it was reported that Lithuania’s Seimas had voted to lift the country’s constitutional ban on the deployment of nuclear weapons. The parliamentary resolution calls for the repeal of Article 137 of the Constitution, which prohibits the deployment of weapons of mass destruction, including nuclear weapons, on Lithuanian territory. The article also bans the presence of foreign military bases. Vilnius is currently seeking to have the United States station a military base in the country.
During the parliamentary plenary session, 106 lawmakers voted to repeal the constitutional provision, 18 voted against and six abstained.
"We can be absolutely certain that Lithuania will go to any lengths to position itself at the forefront - on the very first line of defense - of efforts to contain the North Atlantic Alliance’s alleged ‘enemies.’ That is why they are moving from rhetoric to action. Naturally, this is an alarming signal for us, including because of the potential environmental impact," Mishin told TASS.
"We fully understand that the Lithuanians will be used without their consent; however, they are obsessed with the idea of fighting ‘invisible enemies’ and are adopting restrictive measures and various sanctions packages against Russia, specifically targeting the Kaliningrad Region," he added.
Mishin said he found it difficult to imagine a civilized state voluntarily seeking to host nuclear weapons or foreign military units and bases on its territory. Yet Lithuania has chosen precisely such a historical role for itself.
The Kaliningrad Region is a Russian semi-exclave separated from the rest of the country by the territory of European Union member states. EU sanctions restrict the overland transit of certain goods to the region, while rail shipments of sanctioned cargo are permitted only within quotas established by the EU.
To prevent shortages in the Kaliningrad Region, Russian authorities have shifted some cargo shipments to maritime routes through neutral waters in the Baltic Sea, increasing the number of freight ferries operating on the Ust-Luga-Kaliningrad route.
Rhetoric concerning potential measures against the Russian region has intensified in recent months, with some foreign media reports discussing the possibility of an economic or territorial blockade of the Kaliningrad Region.

Iran reviews US response to seven-day plan to reopen Hormuz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:24:37 UTC
23:24:37 KST

Iran is reviewing US feedback on Tehran’s proposed seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and expects to respond within the next few days, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has said.
“The negotiation process is still ongoing, and messages are being exchanged through mediators,” Araghchi said, according to Iran’s official IRNA news agency on Thursday.
“We presented our proposal, which was called the ‘seven-day plan,’ and we heard the Americans’ views in response,” he said. “We are currently reviewing them. I believe we will respond within a few days.”
Tehran links Hormuz reopening to new talks
The seven-day initiative centres on restoring normal navigation through the strategic waterway while restarting negotiations between Tehran and Washington.
Araghchi said in late September that Iran could reopen the strait within seven days if the United States accepted the proposal conveyed through Qatari mediation.
Under the plan, Washington would be expected to take agreed steps during the first four or five days. Normal navigation through the strait would then resume on the sixth day, with negotiations on a final agreement beginning on the seventh.
Iran’s stated demands include an end to hostilities, the release of frozen Iranian assets, the lifting of restrictions on Iranian oil exports and an end to the US naval blockade of Iranian ports.
The proposal was discussed through Qatari mediation during indirect Iran-US contacts on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York in September.
On September 30, Iranian government spokeswoman Fatemeh Mohajerani said Araghchi had received Washington’s response to the Qatari-mediated proposal but did not disclose its contents.
Hormuz remains at center of Iran-US tensions
Iran has kept restrictions on the Strait of Hormuz while demanding that Washington fulfill commitments under a June memorandum of understanding, saying the waterway will not fully reopen until its conditions are met and US commitments are implemented.
The United States and Israel launched a war against Iran on February 28, after which Tehran responded with missile and drone attacks across the region and effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz.
Washington later imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports.
The two sides later signed a memorandum of understanding in June on freedom of navigation through the strait, but implementation stalled over disagreements on security arrangements in the strategic waterway.
The latest exchange of proposals suggests that indirect diplomatic channels remain open as both sides consider steps to ease tensions along one of the world's most important energy and shipping routes.

Experts in Baku urge action as missing persons surge worldwide and in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:21:34 UTC
23:21:34 KST

Around 280,000 people are registered as missing in Ukraine alone, with 10,000 new cases added each month, part of a 70% global rise since 2019. Forensic experts meeting in Baku said the obstacle was not forensic capacity but governmental reluctance.
Hundreds of thousands of people worldwide remain missing in wars, as experts who met in Baku warned that political will, not technology, is the obstacle to identifying them.
The figures have continued to grow, rising 70% between 2019 and 2024, according to the ICRC.
In Ukraine alone, around 280,000 people are registered as missing as of September 2026, with an estimated 10,000 new cases added every month, according to the same data.
Government officials, forensic experts, and diplomats met at the fourth International Conference on Missing Persons in Baku, under the Baku Dialogue on Missing Persons, to discuss how countries can cooperate to identify the dead and locate those who disappeared in both historical and ongoing conflicts.
Argentinian forensic anthropologist Luis Bernardo Fondebrider, who has worked across 66 countries over 42 years, said the pattern he encounters is consistent.
"In every country, I see the same pattern. The families want justice, want reparation, want memory, and want to know what happened," he said, attributing failure to act to a "lack of political will from the states."
He was unambiguous about governmental pledges. "The speeches about the commitment of the states" were "just words," he said.
"Today, there are almost no governments with the willingness to really investigate how it's happened with the missing and to ask for justice for the perpetrators."
Lord Brady, a member of the UK House of Lords who last visited host country Azerbaijan 16 years ago during the Karabakh conflict, said much had changed since then.
"We've had so much progress in the last few years," he said, adding that technological advances had opened up possibilities that "simply couldn't have been done in the past."
Christian Rivier, head of the ICRC's Central Tracing Agency, told Euronews that technology was only part of the answer.
"We don't need to be blindsided by the fact that technology helps us," he said. Processing the information it generates remained the central challenge, he added.
According to Rivier, it required "the human capacity to understand the information, to make sense of it, to ensure that there is an investigative medical-legal process that follows processes that are efficient and that avoid misidentification."
Azerbaijan's search continues
As of 31 August, 4,010 Azerbaijani citizens remain registered as missing linked to the first and second Karabakh conflicts.
Azerbaijan's State Commission says it has collected DNA samples from more than 11,000 donors to help identify more than 3,700 missing persons.
Rizvan Nabiyev, a member of the State Commission, said cross-border information-sharing was essential for "confidence-building measures" and "trust between societies".
Iranian-French photojournalist Reza Deghati, who presented a collection at the conference documenting the human cost of the Karabakh war, said he had set out to understand who those 4,010 people were.
The state, he said, had begun systematically collecting DNA from the relatives of the missing, "a list of all the families that are missing people."
Finding Ukraine's missing 'a colossal job'
The scale of the challenge is most acute in Ukraine, where the ICRC described in September 2026 "a staggering 280,000 people registered as missing amid the Russia-Ukraine war".
An average of 10,000 new cases have been registered every month since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Former Ukrainian President Viktor Yushchenko told Euronews that recovering the bodies of Ukrainian soldiers remained an enormous undertaking, describing it as "a colossal job."
Yushchenko said he did not expect Russia to provide information on those who remain unaccounted for. "In short, I am not sure that we will get such information from Russia, because it is Russia," he said.
"Russia is a permanent member of the Security Council of the United Nations, the most peaceful organisation in the world. Russia is a criminal," Yushchenko added.

Canada’s Anne Carson wins Nobel literature prize
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:20:53 UTC
23:20:53 KST

Copies of books by Canadian author Anne Carson are on display at the Swedish Academy in Stockholm after the press conference on Oct 8. (AFP Photo)
The Nobel Prize in Literature was awarded on Oct. 8 to Canadian poet Anne Carson, an essayist and classicist who brings a modern twist to mysticism and antiquity in her writings about love, desire and despair.
The 76-year-old was honored “for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature,” the Swedish Academy said.
The permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy, Ingrid Carlberg, said she had briefly spoken to Carson.
“We didn’t have so much time to speak. All she had time to tell me was that she is for the moment in Iceland, where she’s listening to the wind.”
“She was taken by surprise, but very happy. I could hear that in her voice.”
The Academy said almost all her literary production “has centred upon the intersection between the philologist’s obsession with words and the poet’s desire for new meaning.”
It singled out her poem “Nox,” printed on one continuous sheet of paper in homage to her dead brother, as “an unforgettable work.”
Carson has been mentioned as a possible Nobel laureate for years.
Many literary critics had predicted the award would go to a woman this year, given the frequent criticism directed at the Academy over the overrepresentation of Western white men among its picks.
There have been just 19 women laureates out of 122 since the Nobel literature prize was first awarded in 1901.
A 2018 sex assault scandal left the Academy in tatters and more than half of its 18 members were replaced.
Since then, every other literature laureate has been a woman.
Last year, the award went to Hungary’s Laszlo Krasznahorkai, whose works explore themes of postmodern dystopia.
The Nobel Prize comes with a diploma, a gold medal and a $1.2 million prize sum.
Carson will receive the award from King Carl XVI Gustaf in Stockholm on Dec. 10, the anniversary of the 1896 death of scientist and prize creator Alfred Nobel.

ATHENS, October 8. /TASS/. A military conflict between Turkey and Greece stemming from their disagreements over the Aegean Sea is unfathomable, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in an interview with the Greek newspaper Kathimerini.
Rubio was asked whether the United States would intervene if relations between Greece and Turkey in the Aegean Sea or in Cyprus deteriorated sharply, and whether it would prevent such a deterioration.
"It seems unthinkable to me that something like this could happen. These are two allies and two NATO partners - so it simply can’t happen. It won’t benefit anyone," Rubio replied.
"It won’t benefit Turkey or Greece, but it also won’t benefit the United States. So instead of even thinking about it, I would just say that for me it is unthinkable, something that we will never allow, and I do not believe that this will happen."
Turkey has not signed a UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, under which countries can expand their territorial waters up to 12 nautical miles. In 1995, during the ratification of this convention by the Greek parliament, Ankara said that if Greece expanded its territorial waters from six to 12 nautical miles in the Aegean Sea, it would be considered a violation of Turkey's national sovereignty and a casus belli. In recent years, Turkish politicians have continued to threaten Greece with war if it expands its territorial waters to 12 nautical miles in the Aegean Sea.
Turkey does not recognize Greece's 10-mile air zone around the islands, considering that Greek airspace, like territorial waters, is limited to six nautical miles. This is why Turkish fighters with weapons on board invade the Greek airspace and flight information area without providing a flight plan, and Athens raises its planes to intercept them. After a reduction in such violations in 2023 and a complete cessation in 2024, there was an upward trend in the last two years.

Drugs gangs adapting as customs faces cuts, chief tells MPs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:18:18 UTC
23:18:18 KST

Drugs gangs adapting as customs faces cuts, chief tells MPs
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The Dutch customs service will have to endure substantial budget cuts because it is not formally counted as part of the country’s security system, its director general has told MPs, warning of the impact cutbacks could have as criminal gangs step up pressure on the country’s ports.
Customs chief Nanette van Schelven told parliament in a position paper on Wednesday that the agency will be hit by cuts planned for government departments. It will also miss out on the extra money the cabinet has made available to strengthen the national security sector.
The agency’s role in tackling organised crime “requires continuation and intensification”, Van Schelven wrote. Customs is looking for smarter ways of working, she said, “but efficiency alone will not resolve this tension.”
Customs, which comes under the finance ministry, has a budget of almost €982 million for 2027.
New smuggling methods
Customs officers seized 19,332 kilos of cocaine in the first half of this year, up 20% on the 16,104 kilos seized in the same period of 2025, according to the paper and figures provided by customs. That is already close to last year’s total of almost 24,500 kilos.
The paper also cited more than 106 million illegal cigarettes seized in the first half of the year.
Gangs adapt quickly, Van Schelven wrote, and customs has to anticipate trends rather than rely on seizures alone. She named dropping drugs at sea for collection, soaking cocaine into other materials, chemically disguising it, and smuggling via private aircraft.
The risk of drop-offs means smaller Dutch ports need to stay alert, the paper said.
Pressure on staff
Van Schelven’s “first concern” was criminal networks’ growing willingness to use violence and the pressure they put on the organisation and individual officers.
Arrests of customs staff for corruption show how concrete that threat is, she wrote.
Measures like periodic screening take a long time to introduce, and customs needs proper resources to protect its people, the paper said.
The hearing was held by parliament’s justice committee to discuss the government’s first national threat assessment of how organised crime undermines Dutch society. MPs will debate organised crime with justice minister David van Weel later this month.

Earlier on Thursday Union of Islamic Communities of Italy

It comes as Prime Minister Andy Burnham met with the German chancellor on his first official visit to the country this week.
Advertisement
Burnham and Merz were due to talk about possibilities for Britain’s future relationship with the EU — after the British prime minister put rejoining the bloc back on the table of U.K. politics for the first time in a decade.
Berlin’s position on EV tariffs is significant as Germany has broadly backed a tolerant policy towards the U.K. on trade matters since Brexit — in contrast to more hard-line positions taken by countries like France.
The EU is in the process of drawing up new Made in Europe rules that would favor European producers over those outside the bloc — in response to trade practices by competitors like China and the United States.
The U.K. is worried that the measures will hit British business — especially automakers — and wants assurances from Brussels that it will get an opt out. If Berlin gets its way, those assurances could be dependent on emulating EU trade policy with regard to Chinese EVs.
Predatory strategy
Germany’s vaunted car industry, arguably the jewel in the country’s economic crown, has faced stiff competition from Chinese imports in recent years.
EU countries have accused China of dumping low-cost, state-subsidized electric vehicles into the European market and in December 2024 imposed countervailing duties as high as 35.3. percent on some manufacturers.
Advertisement
Industry Commissioner Stephane Séjourné accused China of pursuing a deliberate “predatory strategy” with state subsidies to the tune of €10,000 per vehicle.
The U.K.’s Trade Secretary Jonathan Reynolds told POLITICO last month that the government was keeping tariffs “under review, to be frank, more closely than lots of other issues” and that “different parts of our own sector want different things from” the government’s policy.
Hamish Falconer, the U.K.’s minister for European relations, told POLITICO's Brussels Playbook Podcast this week that he was “surprised” at reports tariffs might be a condition of Made in Europe opt-outs, adding: “That’s not the kind of conversation that I’m having with my European counterparts.”
Going ahead with higher tariffs risks alienating Beijing, which has expressed serious concerns about the policy. It would also raise the price of electric vehicles on the market, potentially making it harder for the government to meet its decarbonization targets.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

Russian Oil Gets Too Expensive for India as Imports Sink to Lowest Level Since 2022
Indian refiners are cutting purchases of Russia’s flagship Urals crude for November delivery as higher prices erase much of the discount that helped Russian oil capture a dominant share of the Indian market after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Bloomberg reported on October 8, citing people familiar with the matter.
The pullback is being driven primarily by economics rather than political pressure. Urals crude loaded at Russia’s Baltic ports is now being offered at a premium of more than $10 per barrel to Dated Brent, according to Bloomberg’s sources, making it far less attractive to Indian buyers than it was when Russian barrels were sold at steep discounts.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Cargoes that once undercut competing grades by a wide margin are now priced close to crude from the Middle East, prompting Indian refiners to reconsider suppliers in the Persian Gulf. Some Russian barrels originally aimed at India are also being offered to independent Chinese refiners as traders look for alternative buyers.
India, the world’s third-largest crude importer, had already begun reducing its exposure to Russian oil after the adoption of new US sanctions legislation raised the threat of punitive tariffs. However, Bloomberg’s sources said pricing has now become the more immediate factor shaping purchasing decisions.
Russia’s share of Indian crude imports fell to about 35% in September, according to analytics firm Kpler, down sharply from a peak of 56% in July. The drop reflects both growing sanctions risk and the narrowing price gap between Russian and competing crude grades.
The decline is also visible in tanker-tracking data. During the four weeks through October 4, Russian crude shipments averaged only about 310,000 barrels per day, according to Bloomberg data—the lowest level recorded since March 2022, shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
China and India remain the two largest buyers of Russian crude, although the final destination of many cargoes is not always fixed when tankers leave port. Traders often decide where to send individual shipments while the vessels are already underway, depending on prices, sanctions exposure, and demand.
Earlier, the US House of Representatives passed bipartisan legislation granting US President Donald Trump expanded authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top importers of Russian oil and gas in an effort to squeeze Moscow’s war revenue.

08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
Italy’s Chamber of Deputies gave final approval on Thursday to a contested electoral reform backed by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government, in a 227 - 164 vote, public broadcaster Rai reported.
The lower house approved the legislation in a secret ballot on its third reading, following amendments adopted by the Senate.
Meloni welcomed the result as evidence of unity within her ruling center-right coalition.
“And to those who hoped to see the center-right divided, today we respond with action: we are united, united, and determined to fulfill the commitments we made to the citizens. Let’s keep going,” she wrote on US social media company X.
The reform provides for a proportional electoral system with a seat bonus for the leading political force or coalition reaching at least 42% of the vote. It also requires coalitions to identify their candidate for prime minister before the election.
Other changes include the return of preferential voting alongside party-selected candidates heading electoral lists, and provisions allowing voters away from their registered place of residence, including family caregivers, to cast ballots.
Foreign Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Antonio Tajani said the vote demonstrated that the majority remained solid and intended to seek another five years in government.
Opposition parties, however, criticized the provisions on candidate selection and women’s representation.
Democratic Party leader Elly Schlein said fewer than one in five lawmakers would be elected through preferential votes, arguing that party-selected list leaders would limit voters’ choices.
Five Star Movement leader Giuseppe Conte similarly alleged that party leaderships would determine more than 80% of the next parliament’s membership. He also warned that list leaders could all be men.
A network opposing the reform has announced plans to file legal challenges once the legislation takes effect, seeking a referral to the Constitutional Court.

How to tell if you have been blocked on Telegram: the main signs
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
17:13:07 EEST
23:13:07 KST

How to tell if you have been blocked on Telegram: the main signs
Kyiv • UNN
The status "last seen a long time ago," a missing photo, and calls without ringing may indicate that you have been blocked. We explain how to check.
The status "last seen a long time ago," the absence of a profile picture, and calls without ringing are the main signs that you have been blocked on Telegram. UNN explains how to check whether you have been banned, how this differs from a deleted profile, and how to block or unblock a contact yourself.
Main signs of being blocked on Telegram
One of the signs that you have been blocked is the activity status of the user who may have blocked you. Telegram has two activity status options — "recently," which hides when the user was last online, or a visit time, such as "just now," "active 20 minutes ago," and so on.
If you have been blocked, this status will be displayed as "last seen a long time ago."
Another sign of being blocked is the profile picture. If the user had their own photo rather than Telegram’s default image, it will no longer be displayed when you are blocked, and you will not be able to tap it to view it.
Another way to check whether you have been blocked is to make a call. If, after many attempts to call the user, the call ends even without ringing, you have most likely been blocked.
How to distinguish a block from a deleted account
As already noted, one sign of being blocked is the profile picture. If you have been blocked, the profile picture will be Telegram’s default image with the first letter of the user’s name. For example, if the user’s name is "Andrii," the photo will simply display the letter "A."
A deleted account, by contrast, will be labeled "Deleted Account," its activity status will be displayed as "last seen a long time ago," and the profile picture will show a "ghost."
How to block or unblock a contact yourself
To block a contact, you need to open the chat with the user. If you plan to do this on a desktop computer or laptop, scroll down to the section containing the user’s information and select "Block."
On a phone: open the chat with the user and tap either their profile picture or their name. Then tap the three dots and select "Block."
To unblock a user, open the chat with them; at the bottom of the screen, you will see the "Unblock" option.

BBC pays white staff less than ethnic minorities – report
Unknown

BBC pays white staff less than ethnic minorities – report
White employees at the BBC earn less than their ethnic minority colleagues in six of seven salary grades, according to the British broadcaster’s 2025/26 annual report. The figures have raised new questions about the corporation’s drive to promote ethnic minority staff and its possible impact on pay.
According to the BBC’s 2025/26 pay gap report, highlighted by The Telegraph on Wednesday, black, Asian, mixed-race and other ethnic minority employees earn 13.2% more in median hourly pay than white colleagues in the lowest salary band. Even among the broadcaster’s most senior executives, the gap stands at 5.3%.
White employees came out ahead in just one category, where their median hourly pay was 0.6% higher. Across the BBC as a whole, however, white staff still earned 0.7% more, largely because they held a greater share of the highest-paid jobs.
The pay figures have drawn attention to the BBC’s push to advance ethnic minority employees. The broadcaster runs special mentoring and career development programs designed to help Black, Asian and other minority staff climb the career ladder, raising questions about whether the drive could be contributing to the pay gaps.
The corporation has set a target for ethnic minorities to make up 20% of both its workforce and senior leadership. The BBC insists these are goals rather than quotas and says they have no bearing on pay decisions.
Former UK Culture Secretary John Whittingdale questioned the BBC’s pay practices, telling The Telegraph that the broadcaster “ought to be paying staff entirely on the basis of the value and merit they contribute for the job they are doing.”
He said the BBC had previously moved to correct gender pay disparities and should apply the same principle of “fair pay” regardless of race, sexuality, or gender.
The broadcaster has faced repeated scandals over unequal pay. In 2020, journalist Samira Ahmed won a landmark employment tribunal case after judges found that she had been paid less than male presenter Jeremy Vine for equivalent work.
In 2024, four female BBC presenters accused the corporation of sex and age discrimination following a shake-up of its news division. In November 2025, the BBC disclosed six internal equal pay cases, including two appeals.
The BBC has rejected suggestions that the latest figures demonstrate unequal treatment, saying it is “committed to fair and equal pay for all.”

Economic Watch: Holiday travel, spending boom mirror vitality of China's vast market
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
22:12:04 CST
23:12:04 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- From bustling transport hubs and crowded scenic areas to fully booked restaurants and busy shopping districts, strong travel flows and vibrant consumption during the National Day holiday highlighted the resilience and momentum of China's holiday economy.
Data from the Ministry of Transport showed that during this National Day holiday from Oct. 1 to 7, known as "Golden Week," cross-regional passenger trips reached 2.14 billion, averaging 306 million a day, slightly above the daily average recorded a year earlier.
Longer breaks, richer local experiences, rising inbound travel and policy-supported consumption... What stood out this year was not just the sheer number of travelers, but how the holiday economy was changing shape.
LONGER JOURNEYS, DEEPER EXPERIENCES
With the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day holidays separated by only three working days this year, some travelers took three days of leave to link the two breaks into a 13-day extended holiday. Data from Trip.com Group showed that one in every 10 travelers combined the two holidays into such a break.
That extra stretch has helped reshape travel preferences, driving demand for longer-distance trips, a more relaxed pace and more immersive experiences.
Online travel platform Qunar said bookings for flights covering more than 2,000 kilometers rose by more than 40 percent year on year during the National Day holiday, while hotel bookings involving stays across four or more cities jumped 53 percent year on year.
Improved transport links are making long-distance trips more accessible than ever. Before the holiday, new high-speed rail sections, including the Xiong'an-Shangqiu, Xi'an-Ankang, and Harbin-Yichun lines, began operation, connecting more destinations across the country.
For families like Wang Lei's from Harbin, who traveled to Yichun to enjoy the autumn scenery, a journey that once took seven hours now takes just over one hour. "The time we used to spend on the road can now be spent enjoying the destination," Wang said.
Experts said longer breaks extend the consumption chain and expand spending opportunities, giving transport, hospitality, catering and scenic spots a longer operating window and deeper spending potential.
Official data showed that during the National Day holiday, average daily sales in service sectors rose 19.5 percent year on year, with tourism, sightseeing and entertainment services up 23.6 percent, catering services up 9 percent, cultural and arts services up 20.9 percent, and sports services up 29.4 percent year on year.
A noticeable shift unfolded during this year's National Day holiday: more travelers are looking beyond big-name cities and turning to smaller counties for their getaways.
In Mile City, southwest China's Yunnan Province, tourist Chen Jinhui from Shanghai in east China ordered a cup of local coffee and joined a community concert. "Coming to a small city, basking in the sun and relaxing -- that's the Yunnan way of life," he said.
Data from Qunar showed that hotel bookings in popular counties rose 32 percent year on year, with Jiuzhaigou County in southwest China's Sichuan and Burqin County in northwest China's Xinjiang among the most sought-after destinations.
In August, nine government departments, including the Ministry of Commerce, jointly issued guidelines to energize lower-tier markets and boost county-level consumption. The measures aim to streamline consumption channels, broaden the range of available brands, improve service quality, and create diverse and locally tailored consumption experiences in smaller cities and towns.
Small counties are no longer marginal players in the consumption landscape; they are becoming an important source of new domestic demand. McKinsey has projected that by 2030, more than 60 percent of China's personal consumption growth will come from third-tier cities and below, as well as county and rural markets.
Inbound tourism also remained robust during the holiday. Data from the National Immigration Administration showed that during the holiday, 682,000 foreign nationals entered China, of whom 505,000 arrived under visa-free policies, up 5.4 percent and 9.2 percent, respectively, from a year earlier.
As October arrives, autumn colors are spreading across Zhangjiajie National Forest Park in central China's Hunan Province. Tourists of different nationalities can be seen pausing for photos, listening to guides explain the area's unusual landscape, or watching local Tujia ethnic performances.
"Zhangjiajie is beautiful. We walked through the forest, felt close to nature, and it was very relaxing," said Noah, a tourist from Germany. He said he was especially impressed by the Tujia intangible cultural heritage performances and that the warmth of the local people made the visit truly memorable.
POLICY TAILWINDS, SMARTER SPENDING
Strong storefront demand and supportive policies are boosting consumption momentum. In the first six days of the National Day holiday, foot traffic and revenue at 78 major shopping streets and commercial districts monitored by the Ministry of Commerce rose 2.5 percent and 4.7 percent year on year, respectively.
Notably, the government's consumer goods trade-in program drove 33.48 billion yuan (about 4.97 billion U.S. dollars) in sales over the same period, benefiting 6.39 million consumers.
"During the holiday, we bought a new refrigerator. The subsidy saved us more than 1,000 yuan," said a Tianjin resident surnamed Wang.
The National Development and Reform Commission said before the holiday that it, together with the Ministry of Finance, had allocated the fourth and final batch of 62.5 billion yuan in ultra-long special treasury bonds for consumer goods trade-in programs, bringing this year's total to 250 billion yuan.
Data from the Ministry of Commerce showed that from Oct. 1 to 6, sales of embodied AI robots on key platforms surged 130 percent year on year, while sales of smart glasses doubled.
In Huaqiangbei, a sprawling electronics marketplace in south China's tech hub Shenzhen, new robots, AI translators and other tech gadgets have become popular purchases among foreign tourists.
"The number of overseas visitors has clearly increased. Most of them are buying tech products. Many come empty-handed and leave with full suitcases," said a local shop owner.
More international travelers are flocking to China to experience the country firsthand, riding a rising wave of global fascination with everything from the scenery and culture to its lifestyles and, more recently, Chinese brands and design.
From "China Travel" to "China Haul," the trend not only shows how Chinese manufacturing and innovation are winning over global visitors, but also confirms the potential and resilience of China's vast domestic market, supported by visa-free entry, expanded duty-free shopping and improved tax refund services for international visitors, said Zou Yunhan, a researcher with the State Information Center. ■

European Commission backs Italy's bid for defense, energy spending flexibility
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
22:11:55 CST
23:11:55 KST

BRUSSELS, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- The European Commission backed Italy's request for greater flexibility under European Union (EU) fiscal rules to increase spending on defense and energy security, a Commission spokesperson said Thursday.
Italy submitted its request on Sept. 11, becoming the 19th EU member to seek activation of the national escape clause, which allows countries to temporarily deviate from EU fiscal spending requirements under certain conditions.
"Our assessment has concluded that indeed the activation of the clause does not endanger fiscal sustainability over the medium term in the case of Italy," the spokesperson told reporters. "In other words, our assessment is positive."
The request will now be submitted to the Council of the EU, which has one month to give its final approval. The clause can only be formally activated for Italy following the Council's decision, the spokesperson said.
The national escape clause is part of the EU's Stability and Growth Pact, which sets fiscal rules for members. It allows countries facing exceptional circumstances to temporarily exceed their agreed government spending limits, provided that doing so does not undermine medium-term fiscal sustainability.
The mechanism was activated for a number of EU countries in 2025 to accommodate higher defense spending, allowing additional expenditure of up to 1.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) annually over the 2025-2028 period.
Earlier this year, the EU expanded the scope of the mechanism to include certain energy security measures aimed at reducing Europe's dependence on imported fossil fuels.
Under guidelines issued by the Commission in August, eligible energy security spending can benefit from fiscal flexibility of up to 0.3 percent of GDP annually and 0.6 percent cumulatively over 2026-2028, within the existing overall ceiling of 1.5 percent of GDP. ■

China Focus: Crime drama leads China's National Day box office as market dips from last year
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
22:11:54 CST
23:11:54 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- Crime drama "Traces of Justice" topped China's National Day holiday box office, in a market that fell from a year earlier, with some analysts citing the absence of a blockbuster-scale title.
The seven-day holiday frame ending on Wednesday generated 1.165 billion yuan (about 173 million U.S. dollars) from nearly 32 million admissions, according to the China Film Administration. Daily takings exceeded 100 million yuan throughout, but the total was well below last year's eight-day holiday, which grossed 1.835 billion yuan, according to ticketing platform Maoyan.
"Traces of Justice" grossed 423 million yuan. It was followed on the charts by comedy "Mr. & Mrs. Pardon," imported horror title "Resident Evil," war drama "Once Upon a Time in the Middle East" and animated feature "Peppa Pig: Perfect Holiday." The top three earners accounted for more than 70 percent of total revenue.
Directed and co-written by Chen Sicheng, "Traces of Justice" is based on the life and work of renowned trace-evidence expert Cui Daozhi. The film, starring Zhang Yi, follows investigators as they solve challenging cases using forensic evidence like fingerprints and bite marks, while also tracing the development of forensic techniques in China over several decades.
A report released Thursday by the Maoyan Research Institute found that the share of multi-person movie outings during the National Day holiday fell to its lowest level in six years, while solo moviegoers made up 25.7 percent of admissions, also a six-year high.
The report said family demand was not fully met, and that the continued strength of some summer holdovers reflected a lack of new family-oriented releases.
"This year's top three films each found their own path to success, but audience interest remained relatively subdued overall because there was no blockbuster-scale title capable of generating broader excitement," said Lai Li, a Maoyan analyst.
Lai added that as audiences become more selective, there will be a greater need for innovation in both content and form.
Among the standouts was "Resident Evil," which opened on Oct. 5. Lai said the globally recognized franchise and better-than-expected word of mouth converted core fans into ticket buyers and helped boost its box office and buzz.
Other indicators were more resilient. Maoyan counted 12,800 cinemas and 79,400 screens in operation, both the highest for a National Day holiday in six years.
After a soft opening day, the market held up well, with new releases lifting daily takings on the third and fifth days. Fifth-day revenue rose 22.9 percent from the previous day to become the holiday's strongest single day, which Maoyan said underscored the role of new film supply in stimulating the market.
Chen Jin, an analyst at film data platform Beacon, expects leading titles to continue supporting the box office through mid-to-late October.
Maoyan forecasts Chinese mainland box office totals of 670 million yuan for "Traces of Justice," 550 million yuan for "Resident Evil" and 390 million yuan for "Mr. & Mrs. Pardon."
The Chinese mainland's annual box office has surpassed 30.7 billion yuan so far this year. ■

BUDAPEST, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- Testing of the European Train Control System (ETCS) on the Hungarian section of the Budapest-Belgrade railway has been completed, marking an important step toward launching passenger services, a senior official said Thursday.
Construction of the Hungarian section is nearing technical completion, Hungarian Minister of Transport and Investment David Vitezy said in a Facebook post. The ETCS testing followed a full-load test conducted over the weekend.
The proper functioning of the ETCS is a prerequisite for launching passenger services, he said. Based on the test results, the necessary official documentation is expected by mid-October.
Meanwhile, contractors still need to complete track adjustment work to ensure that the railway can maintain operating speeds of up to 160 km per hour over the long term.
According to the construction schedule, track adjustments on the section between Hungary's Ferencvaros and Kunszentmiklos-Tass stations are expected to be completed by the end of October, paving the way for the launch of domestic passenger services and subsequent operations.
Vitezy said that if domestic passenger services run smoothly during the first few weeks, the next phase is planned for December, when trains would operate at speeds of up to 160 km per hour and international passenger services between Budapest and Belgrade would begin.
Although extensive testing, corrective work and verification have been completed, there is further work to do, he said.
The 350-km long Budapest-Belgrade railway, linking the Hungarian and Serbian capitals, is a flagship project under the Belt and Road Initiative, jointly developed by China and countries in Central and Eastern Europe. It is also the first project to align Chinese railway technology and equipment with the European Union's railway interoperability standards.
The Hungarian section, spanning about 158.6 km, is an electrified railway designed for both passenger and freight transport, with a maximum design speed of 160 km per hour. Freight services on the section officially began on Feb. 27 this year. ■

The fourth Forbes Ukraine CEO Summit took place in Kyiv on Oct. 1. The event brought together Ukrainian business leaders to discuss the key question of the day: how to build companies amid a draining war while preserving the energy of leaders, teams and organizations.
“Among all the entrepreneurs I know closely, I haven’t seen a single one who gave up,” said Nova Poshta co-founder Viacheslav Klymov. Some of them have suffered millions in losses and keep working despite them.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Restructuring the operating model is not necessarily degradation or a loss of efficiency,” Klymov said. By decentralizing Nova Poshta’s system in response to Russian attacks, the team is finding ways to make its processes more efficient.
Block 1. The Leader’s Energy
In the block on the leader’s energy, Roman Yanovych, CEO of Nestlé in Ukraine and Moldova, and Khrystyna Kovtun, CEO of EKO market, shared their experience. Both are new to the CEO role: each took over their company in 2026. Yanovych spent his first 100 days rebuilding relationships with colleagues. His main tasks are to preserve the business’s efficiency and the global office’s confidence that investing in Ukraine makes sense. Kovtun’s priorities are aligning the team, setting a strategic direction and securing small wins that help people see results.
Shadow Tanker Hit by Ukrainian Drones Threatens Spill Off Russia's Black Sea Coast
Kyivstar President Oleksandr Komarov spoke about the balance between short and long horizons, day-to-day work and change, speed and precision, results and care. Every four months, the company updates its forecasts through the end of the year, for the next 12 months and for the next three years.
IDS Ukraine CEO Marko Tkachuk and MacPaw founder Oleksandr Kosovan discussed how a manager can avoid turning into a function. A leader’s condition affects how they manage people, and taking care of oneself becomes as much a responsibility as running the business, moderator Nataliia Kadia concluded.
Block 2. The Team’s Energy
The second block focused on the team’s energy. “An employer’s task is to create conditions and give people opportunities,” said Taras Chmut, head of the Come Back Alive foundation. The foundation covers employees’ visits to a psychologist, but its support does not end with payment: if a person has a session during working hours, the team’s job is to keep that slot free of meetings.
In a conversation with Olena Zhyltsova, founder of the School of Managerial Thought, robota.ua CEO Valerii Reshetniak said the team is motivated by being needed in tackling the labor shortage. Citrus CEO Artem Shevchenko stressed the link between employees’ personal aspirations and the company’s goals.
Nataliia Savchuk, deputy chair of PrivatBank’s management board, spoke about the resilience of operations. After a strike on the card personalization and logistics center, the bank resumed shipping cards a day later but reviewed its operating model: centralization had concentrated risks. The priority became the ability to restore operations through backup scenarios and locations.
Block 3. The Organization’s Energy
The third block focused on the energy of organizations. Jeff Smart, founder of ghSMART, shared advice from his bestseller “Who: The A Method for Hiring.” Among other things, he recommended systematically sourcing candidates through current employees, who know people they can recommend.
RIEL developer CEO Oleksii Zozulia and Askania group of companies CEO Serhii Zhyla talked about the CEO’s role with Renata Delporte. Zozulia dreamed of becoming an architect and a tour guide; at the start of his career, he would advise himself not to hesitate and to study more theory. Zhyla wanted to be a writer and found in the CEO job a combination of systematic thinking and creativity. His advice: “Hire hungry people,” meaning those who want to prove something to themselves and the world.
Khartiia founder Vsevolod Kozhemiako closed the summit, thanking the entrepreneurs who keep working and investing and stressing the mutual support between business and the military. “I am confident that the future will belong to us,” he said.

====================================================================================================

Three years of genocide: How Gaza war has changed Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:10:15 UTC
23:10:15 KST

Three years after Israel launched its war on Gaza, the consequences extend beyond the devastated territory, reshaping Israeli society, its political debate and its relationship with the world.
Former Israeli diplomat Alon Liel told Anadolu the war has hardened attitudes toward Palestinians and pushed peace further from mainstream politics, with implications that could outlast Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government.
“The Israeli public, especially the Jewish public, moved towards nationalistic attitude. More hatred, more fear, more feelings of revenge,” he said.
For Liel, a former director general of Israel’s Foreign Ministry and ambassador to South Africa, the transformation is reflected in both public attitudes and what politicians are prepared to discuss.
Beyond the immediate consequences, Liel sees a deeper change in the prospects for peace with Palestinians.
“The word peace disappeared ... Nobody is speaking about the peace today among the Israeli politicians,” he said.
A Pew Research Center report published Sept. 15 found that only 17% of Israelis believed Israel and an independent Palestinian state could coexist peacefully. For the first time in Pew’s polling, a majority, 56%, considered it impossible.
Liel believes that pessimism limits the prospects for a negotiated settlement, even under a different government.
“I don't see the future coalition working for peace because this is the public attitude and politicians do not speak about peace because they feel that the public doesn't want and doesn't believe in peace.”
“So politicians who speak in the election campaign about peace are in danger of losing votes.”
Israel’s rightward shift predates the war. An Israel Democracy Institute survey in 2022 found that 62% of Israelis identified with the right.
Before October 2023, the government’s proposed judicial overhaul had also exposed deep political divisions, bringing huge crowds onto the streets.
However, Liel believes the war has reinforced the rightward shift.
“In terms of left and right, the Israeli public moved in the last 3 years more to the right.”
The fallout from Oct. 2023 remains central to electoral politics.
An Israel Democracy Institute survey published in September found that 68% of Israelis considered the attacks a central factor in deciding how to vote, with foreign affairs and security narrowly outranking the economy and living costs among their priorities.
Yet this does not necessarily mean stronger support for Netanyahu.
Polls ahead of the Oct. 27 election have pointed to losses for his coalition, with former military chief Gadi Eisenkot emerging as a leading rival.
The conflict has spread beyond Gaza, drawing Israel into renewed fighting with Hezbollah in Lebanon and direct war with Iran.
Israeli forces have also occupied areas of southern Lebanon, while fighting has continued despite ceasefire efforts.
An Israel Democracy Institute poll in early March found that 82% of Israelis supported the military operation against Iran.
Liel fears the rightward shift will sustain confrontation across the region.
“If this trend to the right will continue, we will go on with wars ... not only with the Palestinians, also with Lebanon and Syria and Iran and the Yemenites.”
The election campaign has exposed tensions over Palestinian political participation in Israel.
Balad leader Sami Abu Shehadeh withdrew his candidacy after the Supreme Court indicated it would likely uphold his disqualification.
Adalah, the legal rights organization representing him, said he withdrew to avoid a ruling that could set a damaging precedent for Palestinian political participation.
Four Arab parties also faced exclusion from the election until Israel’s Supreme Court last week overturned the Central Elections Committee’s September decision to bar them.
The war has also sharpened divisions between Israel’s Jewish and Arab citizens.
Human Rights Watch reported in January 2024 that Israeli authorities held thousands of workers from Gaza incommunicado for weeks after the Oct. 2023, subjecting some to inhumane and degrading conditions.
Christian communities in Israel and surrounding communities have also reported a spike in violence and hate incidents.
The Rossing Center, an Israeli nonprofit, documented 155 incidents against Christians in Israel and occupied East Jerusalem in 2025, including 61 physical attacks. Recorded incidents included spitting, verbal harassment and attacks on church property.
Artists critical of the Gaza war have also faced pressure.
In September, Culture Minister Miki Zohar threatened to seek the revocation of Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s citizenship, accusing them of betraying their country through their documentary ‘NAZA.’
The film, which won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival, draws on testimony from 24 Israeli military and intelligence personnel about the Gaza campaign.
Speaking to Spanish daily El Pais, Abraham described hostility toward their work and the difficulty of confronting public attitudes.
“It’s painful to see so many people losing the most basic moral and human principles,” he said.
The consequences of the Gaza war have also extended into the occupied West Bank, where rising occupier violence and Israeli military operations have intensified pressure on Palestinian communities.
The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs recorded more than 1,600 attacks by Israeli occupiers causing Palestinian casualties or property damage between January and August 2026.
The attacks affected 275 Palestinian communities, averaging 6.7 a day, up from five in 2025. Damage included water supplies, farmland, homes and other infrastructure.
Military operations have displaced tens of thousands more.
A UN human rights report released in September said more than 33,000 Palestinians had been displaced from the Jenin, Nur Shams and Tulkarem refugee camps during an Israeli operation launched in early 2025 and remained barred from returning.
The war has also raised questions about Israel’s ability to retain its younger and highly educated population.
Figures presented at a Knesset hearing in June showed that about 40,500 Israelis emigrated annually on average between 2009 and 2021.
The number rose sharply to 59,400 in 2022, 82,800 in 2023 and 69,500 in 2024.
About 18,800 Israelis returned in 2024, the lowest figure in recent years.
The report found emigrants were more highly educated than the population overall, with an average age of about 32.5 in 2023.
The hearing reflected growing concern about the long-term demographic and economic consequences of increased emigration.
The changes inside Israel have also coincided with a deterioration in the country's international standing.
Pew polling this year found unfavorable views among 78% of respondents in Spain, 73% in Germany and 65% in Canada. In the US, 60% viewed Israel unfavorably, up from 53% in 2025 and 42% in 2022.
An Israel Democracy Institute survey marking two years since October 2023 also found that 73% of Israelis believed their country’s international standing had worsened.
Liel believes the damage extends particularly to Israel’s image as a democracy and its association with the pursuit of peace.
“Israel is much weaker now internationally,” he said.

There has been mounting concern about the increase in civilian deaths and injuries in the nearly five-year conflict, as both sides step up long-range attacks beyond their borders.
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, Ukraine has accused its forces of deliberately attacking and killing civilians.
The United Nations has verified more than 17,000 civilian deaths throughout the war but says the real number is considerably higher.
Last week, Zelensky said his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin had sanctioned massive attacks on civilian areas, a claim the Kremlin denies.
During a tour of the site of the Pryluky attack on Oct 8, visiting UK foreign minister Ed Miliband said there was “no clearer sign of Putin’s evil, evil intent and strategy in this conflict”.
“Putin once said that he was going to win on the battlefield,” he told reporters, as London announced more sanctions on Moscow. “He is trying to win by terrorising civilians.”
Zelensky urged the US to “raise the pressure” on Russia, including through providing better air defence systems, to force Putin to the negotiating table.
Security worsened
Ukraine’s capital, Kyiv, has come under increasing attack, including on Oct 7 from a barrage of Russian ballistic and cruise missiles, and jet-powered drones.
Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko said three people were killed and 14 wounded on Oct 8.
Key transport bridges in the city, as well as the rail network and energy grid have been hit.
For the first few years of the conflict, Kyiv had been relatively spared from the devastation wrought on the frontline but should now be on a war footing, he argued.
Kramatorsk, which was home to some 150,000 people before the war, is one of the key cities that Russia has not yet captured in the eastern Donetsk region, which Moscow claims as its own.
It has been a logistics and supply hub for the Ukrainian military for much of the war and is part of the so-called “fortress belt” which troops are fighting to keep hold of.
Russian forces have edged close to the city’s eastern fringes, which has prompted calls for the civilians who remain to relocate to safer regions of Ukraine.
Filashkin said the Oct 8 strike represented a “sharp deterioration” in security and ordered the suspension of public transport in Kramatorsk and neighbouring Sloviansk.
Ukraine in September launched a counter-offensive against Russian troops around Lyman – to the north of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk – claiming some success in regaining pockets of territory. AFP

Former Labour MP cleared over role in fraudulent Covid-19 testing company
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:06:34 UTC
23:06:34 KST

A former Labour MP and justice minister has been found not guilty of charges around his role in a fraudulent Covid-19 testing company.
Shahid Malik, 58, was MP for Dewsbury between 2005 and 2010 and served as a minister in three departments in Gordon Brown’s government.
Malik was one of five people charged with offences relating to RT Diagnostics, a company that prosecutors said was a “cash cow” set up to take advantage of the UK government’s expanding test-and-trace system in March 2021.
On Thursday, Malik was found not guilty of fraudulent trading, causing a public nuisance and money laundering in a trial at Bradford crown court, which was, unusually, conducted without a jury.
The trial began in October last year and jurors were sent out to start their deliberations in March. In April, they were discharged by Judge Smith after an allegation of jury tampering.
Smith took the decision to continue the trial without the jury, and that he would decide on the verdicts.
The court heard that Malik started the business with the pharmacist and former Labour councillor Faisal Shoukat, 39, when the third national lockdown was ending in March 2021.
Shoukat was found guilty of all three offences.
Paul Moore, 57, who had a senior role in RT Diagnostics and was Malik’s office manager when he was an MP, was cleared of causing a public nuisance and of fraudulent trading.
Lynn Connell, 64, a manager at the company, and Alexander Zarneh, 70, who was its clinical director, were also cleared of the same two offences.
Prosecutors said RT Diagnostics, which made £6.67m in three weeks, was set up in “shoddy and inadequate premises” in Halifax and gave out false negative results to customers.
The defence barrister, Jonathan Laidlaw KC, said Malik’s role in the business had been “very limited indeed” and he had acted as “a facilitator – putting the money up and making introductions”.
Giving his closing speech to jurors in March, Laidlaw said Malik never went to the premises when it was in operation.
He told the court that for most of the time the business was operating, Malik was out of the country and there was no evidence he was told about any of its issues while he was abroad.
Laidlaw said the fact that the former MP had made money from RT Diagnostics “can’t possibly be the basis for a guilty verdict”.
The court heard that as the third national lockdown was ending in March 2021, the government was looking to expand its test-and-trace system by increasing the number of laboratories offering PCR testing.
The defendants were accused of “taking advantage” of that process with an “inadequate and non-compliant” testing company which, prosecutor Jonathan Sandiford KC said, “generated a suspiciously low number of positive results”.
Sandiford said the Halifax laboratory was set up in inadequate premises with holes in the walls and ceilings, and rubbish strewn around.
Jurors heard that the company employed “numerous young people who had little or no training in the handling of Covid-19 samples” and set them to work with no social distancing and no personal protective equipment.
Malik and Sadiq Khan, now London mayor, were the first British-born Muslims to become MPs, and Malik was the first to become a government minister.
He was appointed as an international development minister in 2007 and he later had ministerial jobs at the Department of Justice and the Department for Communities and Local Government.

China trade talks test EU’s appetite for tougher action
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:05:36 UTC
23:05:36 KST

Maroš Šefčovič speaks with reporters during the second day of the G20 Trade Ministerial in Milwaukee, U.S. on Oct. 1, 2026. | Kamil Krzaczynski/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS — European Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič opened two days of talks in Beijing on Thursday aimed at rebalancing a gaping trade deficit, with failure to reach a deal likely to test Brussels’ resolve to impose tougher trade restrictions.
The meeting marks the final round of an effort launched in June to reset the lopsided trading relationship, and will hinge on whether China’s Commerce Minister Wang Wentao is prepared to make substantial concessions.
If no agreement can be reached to narrow the EU’s €1 billion-a-day goods trade deficit, Brussels and Beijing could find themselves on a collision course. EU leaders will review the outcome of the talks at a summit in Brussels next Thursday, where they will consider next steps.
The discussions have zeroed in on cars, with Chinese exports increasingly eating into the market share of European automakers. In August, one in eight cars bought in the bloc was Chinese, thanks largely to a boom in sales of plug-in hybrid electric vehicles.
European negotiators have been pushing China to commit to some form of export restraint — in particular for hybrids. Unlike Chinese-made battery-electric vehicles, which were hit with extra countervailing duties in 2024, plug-in hybrids are not subject to such measures.
Without meaningful commitments from Beijing, the Commission has warned it will resort to unilateral trade restrictions. For cars, it is considering safeguard measures that would mix import quotas and tariffs to protect European automakers.
Chemicals are next. Industry Commissioner Stéphane Séjourné said Thursday that the Commission plans to introduce targeted safeguards on plastics and composite materials, subject to a request from EU governments that Brussels do so.
Wind in his sails
Šefčovič flew to Beijing with the backing of the leaders of Europe’s two biggest economies — France and Germany — to take a tougher approach to trade.
Advertisement
In a joint appeal on Monday, President Emmanuel Macron and Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the Commission should be given a freer hand to shut off access to the EU for goods from countries that distort the bloc’s single market.
While the two leaders did not mention China in their letter to Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, there was no mistaking the target of their proposed trade “kill switch,” which could be blocked only by a qualified majority of EU countries.
The EU already has a powerful trade weapon in its Anti-Coercion Instrument, designed to counter economic bullying by foreign powers.
But Brussels has yet to muster broad support from member countries to deploy it, most recently in January when U.S. President Donald Trump threatened to seize Greenland, a Danish territory.
The EU’s difficulty in responding swiftly to trade threats has heightened concerns about a surge in Chinese exports that European officials say benefit from unfair government subsidies. With Trump hiking U.S. tariffs, ever more Chinese exports are heading to Europe — increasing pressure on industries that are already being forced to retrench.
Europe’s heavy dependence on China for processed rare earths and other critical raw materials also leaves it vulnerable to retaliation should relations deteriorate.
Advertisement
“If we aren’t willing to fix the way our model works, then we’ll be destroyed,” said one EU diplomat, summing up the concerns flooding Brussels.
“What’s the point of having [more tools] if the Chinese can shut down our strategic production in a matter of days?”
Low expectations
Although Šefčovič entered the talks strengthened by the Franco-German letter, a second diplomat said they didn’t foresee a deal with Beijing this week.
“He knows that a lot of member states are behind the Franco-German push,” the diplomat said, adding that this “has been seen in China.”
But Beijing has little room to compromise, given its reliance on exports to sustain growth amid weak domestic demand and a prolonged property slump.
“The Chinese side is starting to recognize that there is a problem. But I don’t think they are ready to enter into a substantial deal,” said Gunnar Wiegand, a former head of the EU diplomatic service’s Asia-Pacific department.
Advertisement
Wiegand, now a visiting fellow at the German Marshall Fund, said Šefčovič had earned a reputation as a dealmaker in talks on Britain’s exit from the EU and in last year’s trade deal with Trump. This time, however, “both sides are bound by their own circumstances,” he said.
Europe is desperate to halt the erosion of its industrial base, while China remains heavily dependent on exports to sustain economic growth.
“The Chinese are going to object to being singled out. Even if a deal with the EU would be the most rational solution, other important markets for Chinese exports, such as ASEAN countries, will start asking the same. It will undercut their global market,” he said.

The disease that once ravaged Europe still exists: could plague return to Spain?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:05:28 UTC
23:05:28 KST

The death of a scientist in Russia has reignited fears of plague. Spain has seen no local cases for decades, yet the disease persists elsewhere. How real is the risk in Europe?
Plague, one of the deadliest diseases in history, has once again made headlines in recent days following the death of a scientist in Irkutsk, in Siberia. The woman died from pneumonia of unknown origin, which raised suspicions of a possible pneumonic plague infection.
However, the Russian authorities have stated that no cases of plague have been confirmed in the region and that tests carried out on the deceased woman’s contacts have come back negative. The World Health Organization (WHO) has requested additional information to clarify what happened and has offered its support to the Russian authorities.
Although no cases of routine transmission of this disease have been recorded in Europe for decades, the bacterium that causes it remains present in different parts of the world and continues to cause human infections every year.
Does plague currently exist in Spain and Europe?
Plague is not currently circulating routinely in Spain or in the rest of Europe. According to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC), the disease has been absent from the continent for more than 50 years.
This does not mean, however, that the bacterium has been eradicated from the planet. Plague is caused by Yersinia pestis, a microorganism that lives naturally in certain populations of small mammals, especially rodents, and in the fleas that infest them.
The bacterium can be transmitted to humans through the bites of infected fleas, contact with tissues or body fluids from infected animals and, in the case of pneumonic plague, via respiratory particles from sick people.
Therefore, although the current risk for the Spanish and European population is very low, the disease can still appear wherever there are animal reservoirs of the bacterium.
Is there a risk of plague in Spain? What the Health Ministry says
Spain has gone decades without registering locally acquired cases of plague, but it maintains active epidemiological surveillance of the disease. In April 2026 the Public Health Commission updated the national protocol, revising case definitions, the epidemiological characteristics of the infection and the information that must be collected in the event of possible infections.
This update, which predates the incident in Siberia, adds to the early-warning mechanisms already in place in Spain. For its part, the European Union examined the Russian case on 7 October, although international health authorities are still awaiting information that could clarify the cause of the researcher’s death.
Where does plague still occur in the world?
According to the WHO, plague remains endemic in several countries in Africa, Asia and the Americas. Between 2019 and 2025, most of the human cases reported to the organisation were concentrated in Madagascar and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. In Madagascar, for example, cases of bubonic plague are recorded virtually every year during the epidemic season, which usually runs from September to April.
The disease also appears sporadically in regions of Asia and the Americas. In the United States, an average of around seven human cases are reported each year, mainly in rural areas in the west of the country.
The persistence of the bacterium in wild animals explains why it is so difficult to eliminate the disease completely, even when human cases are rare.
What is the difference between bubonic and pneumonic plague?
Plague can present in three main forms: bubonic, pneumonic and septicaemic. Bubonic plague is the most common and usually occurs after the bite of an infected flea. It causes fever, general malaise and painful swelling of the lymph nodes, known as buboes.
Pneumonic plague affects the lungs and is particularly dangerous because it can be transmitted from person to person via respiratory particles. Without treatment, it can progress rapidly and prove fatal. Septicaemic plague, meanwhile, occurs when the bacterium multiplies in the bloodstream and can lead to a severe, generalised infection.
Unlike what happened during the great epidemics of the past, plague can now be treated with antibiotics. However, early diagnosis is essential to avoid serious complications and reduce the risk of death.
What risk does the Siberia case pose for Europe?
The suspected case of pneumonic plague in Siberia has prompted European health authorities to monitor the situation closely. The European Commission included the Russian incident on the agenda of its Health Security Committee meeting on 7 October, while the ECDC pointed out that there was no evidence of secondary cases or sustained person-to-person transmission.
The WHO has also concluded that the risk to the European region is very low. Although the disease has not been eradicated worldwide, its presence on other continents does not mean that Europe is facing a new epidemic.
Epidemiological surveillance, early detection of cases and treatment with antibiotics are crucial tools to prevent its spread. Plague still exists, but today’s health situation is very different from the one that allowed the Black Death to devastate Europe in the 14th century.

Kremlin says Russia confident that comprehensive settlement in Ukraine necessary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:04:01 UTC
23:04:01 KST

Burc Eruygur
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
The Kremlin said Thursday that Russia believes a comprehensive settlement in Ukraine is necessary.
Speaking to journalists at a press briefing, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Moscow has repeatedly stated that “piecemeal solutions and agreements” to the ongoing war would prevent a comprehensive settlement from being reached.
“It is a highly complex matter, and the settlement must be comprehensive,” Peskov said, noting that a “freeze” of the conflict would not help either.
“We need a solution for future generations — one that is guaranteed and safeguarded against setbacks,” the spokesman said, adding that Russian President Vladimir Putin had spoken about this, including at the Valdai Discussion Club.
He went on to express Russia’s gratitude to India for showing interest in efforts toward a settlement in Ukraine.
“We welcome any attempts or efforts by states that might in any way contribute to a settlement regarding Ukraine — or help nudge the Kyiv regime and, above all, the Europeans — toward a peaceful phase,” he added.
The Kremlin spokesman also commented on Putin’s birthday Wednesday, saying the Russian president did not receive a congratulatory telegram from US President Donald Trump.
Noting that the exact time of a telephone conversation between Putin and Trump has yet to be agreed upon, Peskov said there was no delay in coordinating such a call.
Commenting on Iran’s potential withdrawal from the Non-Proliferation Treaty, Peskov said the issue could be raised at a meeting between Putin and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on the sidelines of the upcoming Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) leaders’ summit in Turkmenistan on Friday.
Putin is due to embark on a two-day visit to the Central Asian nation later Thursday to attend the CIS summit and participate in an environmental summit involving all five Caspian littoral states — Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Iran, Russia and Turkmenistan.

Prison unit at Kærshovedgård could take five years to complete
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:03:41 UTC
23:03:41 KST

The government’s planned prison unit at Departure Centre Kærshovedgård may take four to five years to become operational, the Ministry of Justice told Danish public broadcaster DR.
The ministry is also working to establish temporary prison spaces at the centre. These are expected to be ready within a few years.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats announced the plan Tuesday during her speech at the opening of the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
The proposed unit would hold Kærshovedgård residents sentenced to prison for offences such as repeatedly violating their reporting obligations.
“For far too many years, you have seen your local area marred by theft. Drug dealing. And reckless driving,” Frederiksen said.
Kærshovedgård operated as a prison from 1951 until it became a departure centre in 2016.
It now houses foreign nationals who have been deported or whose asylum applications have been rejected but who have not left Denmark.
Some fear persecution or torture in their countries of origin, while others cannot return because their home countries will not cooperate with Danish authorities.
Several parties, including the Danish People’s Party, have called for residents to be prevented from leaving the centre. The government has rejected that proposal because residents who are not serving sentences cannot legally be detained.
The planned prison unit would apply only to residents convicted of criminal offences.
