Stolen CPR data could make phishing attacks more convincing, cybersecurity expert warns
Personal information obtained through unauthorized access to Denmark’s CPR register could help criminals create more convincing phishing attacks, a cybersecurity expert said.
Names, addresses, identification numbers and birth dates can be used to make fraudulent emails and text messages appear to come from authorities, Aarhus University professor Jens Myrup Pedersen said.
“The more data you have about people, the more realistic attacks you can also create,” he said.
Phishing is digital fraud in which criminals pretend to represent a company, public authority or police force to obtain sensitive information.
Denmark’s Digitalization Ministry said Monday that unauthorized people had accessed names, addresses and CPR numbers belonging to about 8.8 million people.
CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers. The register includes living and deceased people, as well as former residents.
Pedersen said the information should not be sufficient by itself to obtain loans in another person’s name. Service providers cannot assume that someone knows a person’s identity simply because they possess a CPR number, he said.
However, the information could support other forms of identity misuse and might be sold or combined with publicly available data and photographs.
Pedersen described the breach as unusually extensive.
Unlike a 2015 incident in which records on more than five million Danes were mistakenly delivered to a visa company, the new unauthorized access appears deliberate, he said.
Danish minister says security was inadequate after access to 8.8 million personal records
Security surrounding a private company’s access to Denmark’s national personal information register was inadequate, Digitalization Minister Christina Egelund said Monday.
Unauthorized parties used the small Danish company’s legal access to obtain records on 8.8 million people over about 10 days in September.
“It is clear to me that the security measures surrounding this company’s access to CPR have not been good enough,” Egelund of the Moderates told the Danish news agency Ritzau.
The accessed information includes names, addresses and CPR numbers, Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The total exceeds Denmark’s population of about six million because the records also cover deceased people, emigrants and others registered in the system.
An employee in the CPR administration detected unusual activity Friday, October 2. Authorities had established by Saturday that a security incident had occurred.
The company had permission to search the CPR register, but unauthorized people abused its access. That access has since been closed.
Egelund acknowledged that warnings should have been triggered sooner because the activity continued for several days.
“It is a serious incident. It should not be able to happen,” she said.
The minister declined to identify the company or say whether authorities believe those responsible had criminal intentions, citing the ongoing investigation.
Authorities have not disclosed who accessed the records or how the company’s credentials were compromised.

Voxmeter conducted the poll among 1,034 representative Danish adults for Digitalt Ansvar, an organization promoting responsible use of digital technology.
A total of 62.3 percent agreed or strongly agreed with an overnight block. Another 15.9 percent were neutral, while 17.4 percent disagreed or strongly disagreed.
The European Union’s proposed Kids Act includes an overnight block for users ages 13 and 14.
Digitalt Ansvar wants the measure expanded to include teenagers through age 17.
Director Ask Hesby Holm said nighttime social media use harms sleep and can leave students unprepared for school.
Aarhus University research found that more children arrive at school tired and that tiredness is linked to poorer academic results.
Previous studies reviewed by the researchers associated screen use, particularly before bedtime, with later, shorter and lower-quality sleep.
Digital Affairs Minister Christina Egelund of the Moderates said action was needed but questioned whether a complete ban was the right solution.
“Social media should not be allowed to take our night’s sleep,” she told Danish broadcaster TV 2.
The EU estimates that young Europeans spend four to six hours daily using screens.

Professor: Old IT makes universities hacking targets
Danish universities hold vast amounts of personal data while some continue to rely on ageing IT systems that may not meet modern security standards, a cybersecurity professor warns following the major attack on DTU.
Old IT systems combined with large amounts of sensitive personal data make Danish universities particularly vulnerable to cyberattacks, according to Jens Myrup Pedersen, professor of cybersecurity at Aarhus University.
His warning comes after the Technical University of Denmark (DTU) revealed Friday that hackers had gained access to its user database and extracted a large amount of data.
“Universities possess a very large amount of personal data,” Pedersen told Ritzau.
“And then it is my impression that several universities have quite a few older systems that probably do not have the security level one can expect in 2026.”
Pedersen stressed that he cannot comment specifically on the quality of DTU’s IT security.
But he said the attack raises important questions about how universities protect access to sensitive information.
“The question is which accounts have had access to all this personal data, and how well they are protected,” he said.
Another key question, according to Pedersen, is whether university IT systems can detect when unusually large amounts of data are being extracted and trigger an alarm before the damage becomes more extensive.
Universities face a ‘very high’ cyber threat
The problem extends beyond DTU.
Danish universities have been targeted by hackers several times in recent years, while a 2025 assessment from the Danish Agency for Societal Security (Styrelsen for Samfundssikkerhed) rated the cybercrime threat against Danish universities as “very high”.
Universities can be attractive targets because they combine extensive personal databases with large and complex IT environments used by thousands of students, researchers and employees.
The latest attack has brought renewed attention to whether security measures have kept pace with that complexity.
More than 200,000 potentially affected at DTU
As previously reported by The Copenhagen Post, more than 200,000 people could be affected by the DTU attack.
Unauthorised parties compromised several DTU user profiles and used them to access the university’s user database. DTU says a large amount of data was extracted and that the information involved could include CPR numbers, home addresses and telephone numbers.
The university has not yet determined exactly what information was taken or how many people are affected.
The incident has been reported to the Danish Data Protection Agency (Datatilsynet), while the National Special Crime Unit (NSK) is in contact with DTU about the case.
It has not been disclosed who is suspected of carrying out the attack.

King David Hotel bombing to consulate row: A timeline of UK-Israel tension
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:01:54 UTC
23:01:54 KST

King David Hotel bombing to consulate row: A timeline of UK-Israel tension
Israel’s order to shut UK’s Jerusalem consulate is the latest downturn in a relationship strained since before 1948.
The British Consulate General in occupied East Jerusalem has ceased operating under that name after Israel ordered it to close in retaliation for the United Kingdom’s sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
However, UK officials insisted on Thursday that it remains open, albeit under its new title of “UK Mission”.
This isn’t the first time tensions have arisen between Israel and the UK, however. Here’s more about the times relations have faltered.
Why did Israel order the British consulate to close?
Last month, Israel gave the UK 30 days to close the consulate, after which it said British diplomats working there would lose their diplomatic status.
The order came a day after Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced the UK would ban imports of all goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank and would bar companies from providing them with services, including financing, construction and real estate.
As the deadline expired, the two governments reached a last-minute compromise, however.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said Israel would allow a team of seven British diplomats to work from the building, while 20 diplomats, including the consul general, would leave Israel. The name of the building has also been changed.
Miliband said the building would not close and would now be called the “UK Mission, Jerusalem”, and insisted that the UK does not accept that Israel has the legal right to close a consulate, which the UK owns and which has stood for nearly 200 years.
Besides assisting UK nationals in Palestine, the mission provides support to Palestinians and generally represents the UK in East Jerusalem, the occupied West Bank and Gaza.
Britain and Israel have mostly enjoyed strong and warm relations. But Israel’s move against the consulate is not the first time there has been tension between them.
Here is a timeline of some of those moments of strain:
The King David Hotel bombing
Britain’s role in the founding of Israel dates back to a single letter. On November 2, 1917, Foreign Secretary Arthur Balfour wrote to Lord Rothschild that the British government viewed the establishment of a national home for the Jewish people in Palestine “with favour”, provided nothing was done to prejudice the civil and religious rights of existing non-Jewish communities.
Britain went on to rule Palestine under a League of Nations mandate. By the 1940s, Zionist armed groups had turned their guns on the British administration itself.
The deadliest attack came on July 22, 1946. Members of the Irgun, a Zionist underground group, disguised themselves as hotel staff and carried about 350kg of explosives into the basement of the King David Hotel in Jerusalem. The hotel housed the Secretariat of the Government of Palestine and the headquarters of British forces in Palestine and Transjordan.
Menachem Begin, then head of the Irgun, ordered the bombing. The blast killed 91 people: 41 Arabs, 28 Britons, 17 Jews and five others. Begin later became Israel’s prime minister.
The Irgun claimed it had called in three warnings ahead of the explosion by telephone to the hotel switchboard, the French Consulate and the Palestine Post, giving occupants time to evacuate.
The British authorities did not deny that warnings were sent, but maintained that none reached anyone “in an official position with any power to take action”. The exact sequence of events remains contested: some accounts claim the hotel warning was ignored entirely, while others suggest hotel management did not take the threat seriously. What is not disputed is that the building was not evacuated in time.
The Irgun also claimed that a senior British official, Sir John Shaw, refused to act on its warning, which he strenuously denied.
Close to war during Israel’s formation
Britain withdrew from Palestine in May 1948, and Israel declared itself an independent state. Amid the war that followed with neighbouring Arab states, British and Israeli forces came close to direct confrontation.
In late December 1948, Israeli forces pushed into Egyptian territory in Sinai. A United States Department of State message to its ambassador in Tel Aviv warned that unless Israeli forces withdrew, Britain would be bound to fulfil its obligations under its 1936 treaty with Egypt, so Israel pulled back.
Days later, however, the two sides clashed in the air. On January 7, 1949, Israeli forces shot down four Royal Air Force Spitfires, and a Hawker Tempest later that day. The precise location is unclear, but some sources place it near the Deir el-Balah area of what is now the Gaza Strip, but was then about 25km (15 miles) inside Egyptian territory. Two British pilots were killed, including the Tempest’s pilot, David Tattersfield. Israel said its pilots had mistaken the British aircraft for Egyptian ones.
On January 8, the UK announced it was sending forces to Aqaba, on modern-day Jordan’s Red Sea coast, at Transjordan’s request. In his diary, David Ben-Gurion wrote that he had consulted his top commanders on how to deal with the threat of British intervention. Washington helped calm things down: President Harry Truman criticised the British handling of the crisis.
Historians still debate how close the two sides came to war. Some argue the UK worked to avoid confrontation and never issued a formal ultimatum. Either way, Britain withheld de jure recognition of Israel until April 1950.
UK weapons embargo over invasion of Lebanon
When Israel invaded Lebanon in June 1982, the UK took action. Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher later wrote that Britain restricted defence sales to Israel in June 1982 in direct response to the invasion. The embargo lasted until 1994.
Foreign Secretary Francis Pym publicly condemned the invasion, and government papers declassified years later show London was furious in private as well. The UK even refused to send Israel gas masks during the 1991 Gulf War, when Iraqi missiles struck Tel Aviv.
Falklands tensions
The same year – 1982 – the UK went to war with Argentina over the Falkland Islands, and Israel sent arms to the other side.
According to declassified British files, Israel sold Argentina weapons including Skyhawk jets, which killed dozens of British troops. Foreign Secretary Geoffrey Howe personally asked Israel to stop, but his request was ignored. Israeli arms were also routed through Peru so that the UK would not find out.
Israel denied involvement at first but, by 1984, admitted to supplying Argentina in order to sustain its arms industry. British officials suspected another motive, however. They believed Begin, by then prime minister, still bore a grudge against the UK from the Mandate era.
Gaza genocide: The current crisis
Relations between the UK and Israel have also dipped since the start of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023. More than 74,000 people in Gaza have been killed in Israeli strikes and its siege of the strip, including about 1,400 of those since a supposed US-led “ceasefire” was declared one year ago. Most of the dead are women and children. Thousands more are lost under the rubble and presumed dead.
In September 2024, the UK suspended 30 arms export licences to Israel. In May 2025, it suspended trade talks and sanctioned individuals and companies linked to settler violence. In September 2025, it formally recognised the State of Palestine.
Last September, London went further. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who is himself Jewish, said the UK now regards Israel’s occupation of the West Bank, not just the illegal settlements there, as illegal. He told parliament that Palestinians are being ethnically cleansed by settlers in parts of the West Bank.
Israel’s response was swift. National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir said he had urged Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to close the consulate, accusing it of working on behalf of the Palestinian Authority. Israeli Foreign Minister Saar blamed London: “We did not want it to come to this, but the Labour Government’s actions have led us here.”
The compromise has eased the immediate standoff without resolving it. Saar said the UK had agreed not to retaliate, while Miliband said it would hold off on reciprocal action as long as talks remain credible.
“What’s happening here is that Israel and the UK seem to have found some kind of compromise at the 11th hour, at least for now,” Al Jazeera’s Camille Nedelec said, reporting from London.
“Strictly speaking, the consulate has shut its doors,” she said. “That’s in official language, but practically speaking, there is still a diplomatic presence that is going to be maintained in occupied East Jerusalem by the UK.”
That, she said, “allows both sides to essentially say that they’ve won the argument”.
“We absolutely are at a low point with UK-Israeli relations,” Nedelec said, adding that in a post on X, Saar listed measures including “shuttering that consulate, and he also cited banning some 12 MPs from entering Israel”.
“Gideon Saar also did say, though, that they are allies and that the intelligence sharing continues,” she added.
Israeli anger has been heightened by a resolution passed by the UK’s Green Party at its recent party conference, equating Zionism with “racism”. The party’s leader, Zack Polanski – who is also Jewish – was not present for the vote. However, he liked a post by Green Party member Gill Tavner after the vote, calling on opponents of the motion to “get over yourselves and move on”. “The decision is made. Sometimes they don’t go your way. If you’d prefer to be with genocidal Labour, maybe just go,” she wrote.
Nihad Abu Ghosh, a Palestinian journalist, told Al Jazeera from Ramallah that Israel’s reaction to rising opposition in the UK to its war on Gaza is “driven by the election context, and by its heightened stance towards those it sees as infringing on or undermining Israel’s sovereignty”.
“Britain recognises the Palestinian state, and Israel is trying to resist that by all possible means,” he said, noting that Israel has also punished Spain, Norway and Ireland over the issue.
He compared the move with Washington’s decision to close its own Jerusalem consulate and handle Palestinian affairs through its embassy. “This is what Israel wants: it wants every country in the world to deal with Palestinians as an Israeli matter,” he said.
“Israel’s problem here is that it is punishing itself,” Abu Ghosh said. “If this involved only one country and a limited, partial tension with a country here or there, it could indeed take tough measures. But this is a widening trend.”
He also linked the standoff to history. “Britain in particular bears primary historical responsibility for the creation of the State of Israel, for supporting it, for suppressing the Palestinian people,” he said, citing the Balfour Declaration. “Unless Israel reverses its policies, the situation is likely to escalate further.”

‘This is a crisis of hope’: Echoes of 1968 as France’s students rise up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:01:13 UTC
23:01:13 KST

‘This is a crisis of hope’: Echoes of 1968 as France’s students rise up
Like in 1968, when student protests triggered nationwide strikes, today’s crisis is about generational discontent, experts say.
The scale of protests raging across France over the education system, attracting hundreds of thousands of pupils, teachers and parents, has been described as exceptional by unions and student movement organisers.
“I think this is very historic and unprecedented by how big it is,” Alice Cohen-Morzadec, international spokesperson for France’s Student Union, said on Tuesday, when government sources put the number of protesters at 266,000.
“Some are saying this is the biggest movement since May 1968,” she added.
The student protests at Paris universities nearly five decades ago were initially driven by opposition to an outdated and overcrowded system, limited opportunities and broader political concerns.
The unrest soon spread beyond campuses, expanding into nationwide strikes involving millions of workers that virtually paralysed the country.
Back then, President Charles de Gaulle was in power. Today’s protests come as France heads into next year’s presidential elections, which are being eyed by the far right.
As in 1968, the protests that started on September 21 at an underdeveloped Paris suburban high school are about funding for education, teacher shortages, overcrowded classes, and school facilities.
But those are triggers and not the deeper causes, according to historians and student movement organisers.
“For the young people, this is a crisis of hope. You can see they are bombarded daily with economic problems, political extremes, dangers of warfare in Europe, the threat to their careers from AI, high youth unemployment rates, the climate crisis,” Andrew Smith, historian of modern France and lecturer in Liberal Arts at Queen Mary University of London, told Al Jazeera.
He said students are dissatisfied because of a lack of substantive interaction between the government and student representatives and unions in recent years.
“It has been difficult for the government to meet with interlocutors and try to have dialogue with social partners,” he said.
Robi Morder, a researcher on social movements in France, said the lack of communication reflects the current government’s approach.
“In 1990 and 1998, governments were led by socialists and leftists. Some of the ministers had been in the youth movement. So when there was an issue, the government knew how to negotiate. In 1990, the president himself received a delegation of students,” said Morder.
“We are not in the same situation because the government is not only from the other side politically, but they also don’t have the experience of the old political class,” he added. “They don’t know how to negotiate a social conflict. The government’s first answer is, ‘It is nothing; we will call the police, and everything will be OK.’”
Student organisers say they are frustrated because they feel the government is not taking them seriously.
“This is too much. Enough is enough. We have been making these demands for years. We need more money for education, we need more teachers, we need better facilities,” said Chloe Grunenwald, vice president of the Federation of the General Association of Students (FAGE), the largest organisation of its kind in France, representing some 300,000 students.
When interviewed by Al Jazeera, several students said they had joined recent protests in solidarity with those who first took to the streets. The broadening of the coalition is illustrated by the fact that both Grunenwald and Cohen-Morzadec represent university unions rallying in support of high school pupils.
Smith and Morder spoke of the differences between now and 1968.
“This school year started very differently. The never-ending heatwaves is one thing that really provoked it and made it catch fire. We had classrooms with over 40 people in temperatures exceeding 40 degrees [Celsius;104 Fahrenheit]. That is untenable,” Smith said.
Alleged police brutality
Protest organisers and unions have also complained about what they see as police brutality.
“Unfortunately, the media are talking about how bins are being burnt, schools are being blocked, and how it is a form of violence. The real violence is actually coming from the government side,” said Cohen-Morzadec.
In a sign of conciliation, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu on Wednesday said, “Students must be heard,” while Interior Minister Laurent Nunez ordered police to suspend the use of stun grenades against protesting high school pupils.
But those moves might not be enough to calm the anger.
“We are going to mobilise until we get our demands, especially because we have October 17 and November 20 – as an international date for the youth in all Europe to mobilise for our future, so we want to continue at least until those dates, if not further,” said Cohen-Morzadec.
Nationwide strikes and antigovernment demonstrations are scheduled for October 17, expected to bring together a large number of unions to air their grievances against soaring energy and food prices, proposed budget cuts, and freezes on public sector salaries.
The strikes are backed by the left-wing France Unbowed (LFI) party, led by Jean-Luc Melenchon, and the country’s main labour union, known by its French acronym, CGT.
Critics have accused the LFI and Melenchon of inciting violence to score points against the government, an accusation they and protest organisers deny.
“Our message has been the same. We are fighting for our rights and our demonstrations are passive. We are not working on behalf of anyone else,” said Grunenwald.
Student unions have published a list of 10 demands they say will cost the government 1 billion euros ($1.1bn), and have promised to keep up the pressure until all those requirements are met.
Among the demands are calls for greater investment in schools and universities and more staff and space in higher education. Students are calling for stronger financial and housing support, affordable university meals, and an end to higher fees for international students. They also want an end to what they call “all forms of repression linked to the high school and student movement”.

Investigation Finds That Former High-Ranking Uzbek Security Official Acquired UAE Citizenship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:01:00 UTC
23:01:00 KST

In April 2023, when he was serving as deputy head of the Presidential Security Service, Otabek Umarov – Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev’s son-in-law – reportedly acquired citizenship in the United Arab Emirates. He’s also alleged to be the owner of around $7 million worth of Dubai real estate.
Those are the central allegations of a new investigation published by the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP) and RFE/RL’s Uzbek Service, Ozodlik.
Under Uzbek military law, which governs the position Umarov held at the time, holding a second citizenship is prohibited. Since acquiring citizenship typically includes swearing an oath of allegiance, many countries bar security (and other) officials from doing so – a second passport represents possible divided loyalties and a counterintelligence risk.
As OCCRP and Ozodlik reported, “Under UAE law, foreigners can only obtain citizenship through a nomination by a royal court or senior official, and [the process] requires swearing an oath of allegiance to the Emirates.”
Umarov was shifted out of his security service role in November 2024, in the extended wake of the assassination attempt on Komil Allamjanov.
Allamjanov, at the time of the October 2024 attempt, had recently stepped down from his role as deputy head of the presidential administration. He has since returned to government service, as an adviser to the powerful head of the presidential administration, Saida Mirziyoyeva (the president’s eldest daughter). As of January 2026 he was also appointed to a seemingly bespoke role: advisor-ambassador and representative of the presidential administration in the United States.
Umarov, meanwhile, was named first deputy chairman of Uzbekistan’s National Olympic Committee – his father-in-law, the president, is the chairman.
According to OCCRP and Ozodlik, at some point in 2025, Umarov became the owner of 13 properties in Dubai, worth around $7 million. The properties previously belonged to his younger brother, Oybek Umarov, who purchased them in 2021 and 2022, according to leaked Dubai real estate data obtained by OCCRP.
It is not clear precisely how or when they came to be listed with Umarov’s name on the deeds, whether the properties were gifted or purchased.
While Umarov has notably expensive tastes – for example, he’s been pictured wearing a limited edition Richard Mille watch valued at up to $1.9 million – his government position doesn’t quite explain his apparent wealth. Uzbek officials do not have to disclose their income declarations publicly.
OCCRP and Ozodlik reported, “Public commercial registries show no record of [Otabek Umarov] owning private companies during his time as deputy presidential security chief.” His brother, however, does have extensive business holdings, including in banking, cement, and metalwork.
A high-ranking government source told The Diplomat in late 2024 that Umarov’s assets and businesses were held in the names of others, including Ulugbek Shadmanov who was implicated in an apparent attempt to manipulate the U.S. sanctions system to target Allamjonov and another Uzbek official in the months before the assassination attempt. Shadmanov was earlier named in the Pandora Papers as connected to an offshore company, though there are few details available. In December 2024 he was detained in Dubai and extradited rapidly – apparently without the proper legal process – to Uzbekistan, regardless of the fact that he held what’s known as a “Golden Visa” in the UAE. Despite high-powered legal representation and a campaign on his behalf, very little has been reported since about his case.
Ultimately, the OCCRP and Ozodlik investigation raises far more questions than it answers; that’s the nature of investigations into the opaque underbelly of Uzbek politics (and those of the UAE, to boot). As I told Ozodlik, we don’t know exactly how Umarov acquired UAE citizenship, who was involved, and who knew about it. As noted above, the process to acquired UAE citizenship necessitates a nomination by a royal court or senior official. It’s nearly impossible to believe that Umarov’s role and connections were unknown at the time to the UAE’s authorities.
Then there are questions of what comes next. Uzbekistan does not officially recognize dual citizenship. Holding a second citizenship isn’t illegal per se – though it does violate laws related to Umarov’s specific position at the time. Nevertheless, “voluntarily acquiring a passport of a foreign state” is listed as possible grounds for revocation of Uzbek citizenship.

====================================================================================================

Eye contact may act as a learning “switch” for babies’ brains
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:00:44 UTC
23:00:44 KST

Direct eye contact from an adult speaker appears to guide how infants choose which words to learn by aligning the baby’s brain activity with the adult’s. A new study suggests that this one-way neural coordination may help link an adult’s communicative gaze to an infant’s selective word learning. The findings were published in Nature Communications.
Infants grow up in busy environments where many sights and sounds compete for their attention, requiring them to figure out which information is worth learning. To navigate this challenge, babies rely on social signals known as ostensive cues, which are communicative acts like direct gaze or infant-directed speech that indicate an adult intends to share information. The central focus of the new study is interpersonal neural coupling, a measure of how much activity in one person’s brain predicts later activity in another person’s brain.
Past developmental research has shown that social cues play an active role in how young minds acquire language. For example, a 2003 study indicated that nine-month-old infants learned unfamiliar foreign speech sounds when interacting with a live person, but did not learn when watching identical recorded video lessons. Expanding on how social cues operate in the brain, a 2017 study found that when an adult made direct eye contact with a baby, their brainwaves synchronized more strongly than when the adult looked away.
Even so, scientists still faced an unresolved question about what this shared brain activity accomplishes. As the authors of a 2020 review noted, it remained uncertain whether brain-to-brain synchrony helps infants learn or represents an incidental byproduct of two individuals watching the same event. In a related vein, a study covered by PsyPost in 2024 showed that communicative infant-directed speech heightened attention-related brain activity in toddlers and was linked to better word learning.
The research team, which included first author Wei Zhang of Nanyang Technological University and Victoria Leong, a professor in the School of Social Sciences at Nanyang Technological University and the Department of Pediatrics at the University of Cambridge, set out to address this question. “We had previously published a seminal demonstration that eye contact modulates adult-infant neural synchrony,” Leong told PsyPost. “The current study replicates (across two countries) and extends these findings to show that neural synchrony underpins infants’ selective learning in social contexts.”
The researchers tested 47 infants who were roughly nine months old, with an average age of 286 days. The sample consisted of 29 infants from the United Kingdom and 18 infants from Singapore. All infants were developing typically, with the British infants coming from English-speaking households and the Singaporean infants coming from bilingual English-Chinese families.
During the experiment, infants sat facing a monitor that displayed pre-recorded video clips of a female speaker reciting three different artificial languages. Each artificial language was constructed from four three-syllable words, like “pe-tu-do” or “di-lo-ga,” spoken continuously at a steady pace without pauses or emotional inflections. In these sequences, syllables within a word always occurred together, while syllables crossing between words occurred together only a third of the time, mimicking how real speech contains statistical patterns that help infants identify word boundaries.
To isolate the impact of eye contact, the speaker wore glasses with polarizing lenses, paired with an adjustable polarizing filter on the camera, while looking straight ahead. In the full gaze condition, the glasses appeared transparent, leaving her eyes entirely visible. In the partial gaze condition, the lenses were darkened like sunglasses, and in the no gaze condition, the lenses were made completely opaque. Adjusting only the filter on the camera allowed the researchers to manipulate how visible her eyes were while her own view remained unobstructed, so her delivery would not differ between conditions.
Each experimental block included a familiarization phase and a testing phase for each gaze condition. During familiarization, babies watched the speaker recite an artificial language for 60 seconds while their visual attention and brain activity were recorded using electroencephalography, a non-invasive technique that detects electrical signals through sensors on the scalp. During the testing phase, the infants heard either valid words from the language or artificial nonwords made by joining syllables that crossed word boundaries. The researchers measured how long babies looked at the screen, relying on the tendency of infants to look longer at less familiar sounds when they have recognized the underlying patterns.
The behavioral results showed that infants learned selectively depending on the speaker’s gaze. Infants showed evidence of learning only for the language paired with the full gaze condition, looking an average of 1.22 seconds longer at nonwords than at words, a small to moderate effect. In contrast, learning was not statistically significant for the languages accompanied by partial gaze, where the difference was 0.76 seconds, or no gaze, where the difference was 0.34 seconds.
“We let the infants listen to all three languages and it turned out they were selective in what they learned,” Leong said in a news release from the University of Cambridge. “They’re not just passive sponges. They heard all three languages, but only learned the one, which was when they could see the speaker’s eyes.”
This learning preference did not stem from differences in general visual attention. Infants spent roughly equal amounts of time watching the speaker across all conditions, averaging about 23 seconds in the full gaze condition, 21 seconds in the partial gaze condition, and 23 seconds in the no gaze condition. In addition, statistical analysis showed that the link between total looking time and learning was not statistically significant.
Kaili Clackson, a study co-author from the University of Cambridge, described the gap between looking and learning this way. “Even when the infants seemed to be staring at a screen attentively, unless there was eye contact, nothing was going in – the information washed over them,” Clackson said in the release. “The brain synchrony shows that it’s a selection process.” She added, “These cues are really powerful because when you preface new information with them, they tell the baby: this is important, you need to listen.”
When comparing the two geographic groups, Singaporean infants watched the speaker on screen longer than British infants did, which the authors suggested might reflect an interest in a speaker with unfamiliar Western facial features. However, learning performance itself did not differ significantly between the Singaporean and British infants. Both groups responded similarly to the presence or absence of the speaker’s gaze.
Leong noted that this pattern sheds light on early cognitive development across backgrounds. “This suggests that although there are already cultural differences in what we pay attention to or find novel from 9 months of age, the brain’s learning mechanisms set infants up to learn in a fundamentally similar way across cultures,” she told PsyPost.
To examine brain connections, the authors focused on alpha rhythms, a type of brainwave that in infants cycles about 6 to 9 times per second, using data from the 42 infants whose recordings were usable. Because the speaker’s brain activity had been recorded while she filmed the videos, the researchers could test whether patterns in her brain activity predicted later patterns in the infants’ brains as they watched.
This adult-to-infant coupling predicted learning better than chance, explaining about 25 percent of the variation in learning compared with about 20 percent for models built on shuffled data. The infants’ own internal brain connectivity did not predict learning, but it was linked to their scores on a parent-reported checklist of early communicative gestures, explaining about 34 percent of the variation compared with about 22 percent for shuffled data.
The team also evaluated neural entrainment, which is the tendency of a listener’s brainwaves to track the rising and falling loudness of speech. Full gaze strengthened this tracking at a few recording sites, but entrainment did not predict learning. A statistical mediation analysis suggested that adult-to-infant coupling may link the speaker’s eye contact to infant learning: coupling was stronger with full gaze than with no gaze, though not reliably different from partial gaze, and stronger coupling went along with greater learning. The authors call this result preliminary, partly because the coupling measure was selected for how well it predicted learning.
“Eye contact helps the baby decide what is important to learn in a social context, acting as a ‘switch’ to synchronize their brainwaves with those of the speaker and facilitating learning,” Leong told PsyPost.
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2023, which found that eye contact promotes aligned brain activity between interacting individuals. However, that earlier study examined spontaneous synchrony between familiar adult pairs rather than adult-to-infant coupling during learning.
Beyond theoretical insights into early development, the authors noted practical takeaways for parents and caregivers. “As parents, we need to be conscious of the need to use social cues like eye contact and calling your child’s name, as these cues don’t just focus your child’s attention, they activate the learning process,” Leong said in the release.
“If you’re on your phone and distracted when you’re trying to give them instructions or teach them something, there’s less of a likelihood that they’ll take it seriously or learn compared to if you put your phone down and look them in the eye,” Leong added in the release. “This is an important way of signaling your intentionality, your seriousness, that you want them to pay attention and learn something.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The study involved a modest sample size of 47 infants for behavioral testing and 42 for brain recordings, meaning subtle effects in the partial gaze condition might be detected more reliably in larger groups. Additionally, the infants watched pre-recorded videos rather than interacting with a live adult, and the study did not test everyday interactions or phone use directly. Notably, infants in this study succeeded in learning statistical word patterns from video, in contrast to the 2003 findings where infants required live interaction to distinguish non-native speech sounds.
There are a few other things to keep in mind regarding the findings and measurements. The authors noted that eye contact may play a different role in communities where adult-infant interaction relies more heavily on touch and physical closeness, as observed in some Arab cultures. Methodologically, the researchers analyzed brainwaves within a single shared frequency band of 6 to 9 Hertz to meet computational requirements, even though adult alpha waves typically peak higher. Finally, while the statistical models highlight an association, experimental manipulations would be needed to establish whether neural coupling directly causes learning gains.
The study, “Adult-to-infant unidirectional neural coupling mediates selective social learning in infants from the United Kingdom and Singapore,” was authored by Wei Zhang, Kaili Clackson, Stanimira Georgieva, Lorena Santamaria, Vanessa Reindl, Valdas Noreika, Nicholas Darby, Vaka Valsdóttir, Priyadharshini Santhanakrishnan, and Victoria Leong.

Italy approves Meloni's electoral reform in confidence vote ahead of 2027 election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:00:36 UTC
23:00:36 KST

The Chamber of Deputies has passed electoral law reform by 227 votes to 164, despite possible Constitutional Court objections. Italy now formally enters the election campaign, with an early vote increasingly likely.
Italy's Chamber of Deputies approved a new electoral law on Thursday, clearing the way for its use in the next general election, due in 2027.
The legislation, backed by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's government and formally known as the Stabilicum, - dubbed the Melonellum by opposition parties, - passed by 227 votes to 164 in a secret ballot.
The vote effectively marks the unofficial start of the election campaign. While the current legislature runs until September 2027, speculation about an early election is already circulating in the corridors of parliament, though as we explain below, a vote before 14 April remains unlikely.
The immediate political battle now shifts to alliances. Meloni has so far ruled out joining forces with National Future, the party of MEP Roberto Vannacci, while the opposition has yet to agree on a common leader. Significant divisions remain within the centre-left, particularly over the war in Ukraine, where Democratic Party secretary Elly Schlein and Five Star Movement leader Giuseppe Conte remain at odds.
Meloni moved quickly to claim the vote as a show of unity.
"To those who hoped to see the centre-right split, today we answer with facts: we are united, solid and determined to carry forward the commitments made to citizens," she wrote on social media.
During the sitting, opposition MPs protested, brandishing placards reading: "Rigged law", "No to the fix" and "With Meloni diesel at 3 euros".
"Seats first. That is your slogan. We will vote firmly against this electoral law, which has been designed not for voters but to protect those already elected. With our progressive alliance we will be able to win under any electoral law and change Italians’ lives," said Elly Schlein in her explanation of vote.
Five Star Movement leader Conte also used exceptionally harsh words, arguing that the law has been written to ensure victory for the current ruling coalition.
He concluded: "There is only one further detail missing to guarantee your future control of Parliament: specifying that the majority bonus goes to a prime minister with light-coloured eyes".
How the new Italian electoral law was approved
The governing majority held firm in the secret ballot. This was the third parliamentary reading, after the amendments passed by the Senate, which introduced preference voting with blocked list leaders and increased the number of signatures required from parties not represented in Parliament in order to stand in elections.
On Wednesday the Chamber had approved the third confidence motion tabled by the government on the first three articles of the law. Thursday saw the final, most delicate, vote. If this last vote had gone against the government, the text would have been rejected, but the cabinet would not formally have been obliged to resign.
The most significant changes are contained in the first two articles, which were approved through a confidence vote. They introduce preference voting alongside blocked list leaders and set out the rules for electing both the Chamber and the Senate under the new system.
The signature threshold for parties without parliamentary representation has also been raised, from 1,500 to 6,000, and the rules on gender representation have been amended.
A third article addresses single-member constituencies in the province of Bolzano, while article 8 introduces one of the most anticipated changes: the right to vote for people living away from their registered place of residence.
The confidence vote is a mechanism that allows governments to fast-track legislation and limit debate and filibustering by the opposition. Under this procedure, MPs vote on the government's text as presented, without the ability to propose amendments.
The government stakes its survival on the outcome, if the Chamber votes it down, the administration automatically falls.
The issue of first-term MPs’ pensions
Faced with the threat of a government crisis, it was widely expected that most MPs would back the reform.
There is one date that Italian political scientists are all trying to pinpoint precisely: the moment when the current legislature reaches 4 years, 6 months and one day of its total five-year term.
On that date, first-term MPs become entitled to a parliamentary pension (around 1,500 euros, payable only from the age of 65).
For the current government, that threshold falls on 14 April 2027, and Italian political history shows that it is very unlikely that an election will be called before then.
There is nonetheless concern that the Constitutional Court could overturn the reform, which would complicate the government's plans and expose the right to fierce criticism during the campaign.
The opposition has identified three potentially unconstitutional elements: the majority bonus in the Senate, the requirement for parties without an established ballot logo to gather 300,000 signatures, and the absence of any requirement that at least 40 percent of lead candidates be women.
According to critics, the law potentially leaves Italy in political deadlock.

An AI boom is sending San Francisco rents through the roof: ‘nowhere left for people to go’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:00:22 UTC
23:00:22 KST

To say that Maria Zamudio and her team have been busy lately would be a gross understatement.
Every Monday at 9am, the phone lines at the downtown clinic of San Francisco’s Housing Rights Committee start ringing, and they keep ringing until closing at 5 pm. In-person counseling appointments for renters facing eviction or landlord misconduct fill days in advance. After every weekend, the staff of seven sits in their office and sifts through more than 150 voicemails. The rental assistance hotline averages 200 calls a week.
“Our clinic is completely at capacity,” said Zamudio, the non-profit’s executive director.
San Franciscans have long been squeezed by high rents. The pressure spikes during the city’s legendary boom periods and is worsened by its struggle to build enough affordable housing. Now, the AI industry – with its high salaries and the astronomical paydays it promises shareholders when firms go public – is pushing rents higher still.
Today, the average one-bedroom in the city by the Bay costs $4,400, a figure that is up more than 25% from last year and that is nearly three times the national average. Want a two-bedroom? Expect to pay $6,000. A centrally located four-bedroom for a family? Easily over $10,000, if not more.
The exuberant prices have meant that even people with six-figure salaries can have a hard time finding housing. And for the city’s most vulnerable groups, it has meant it’s simply increasingly hard just to survive.
Roughly two-thirds of residents in San Francisco rent, and the city has stronger tenant protections than most US cities, including rent control on more than 160,000 of its more than 250,000 units. But landlords looking to cash in on the boom are exploiting loopholes that leave tenants exposed to surprise rent hikes, condo conversions and mass evictions. Calculations by the San Francisco rent board show eviction notices are up 44% citywide compared to last year.
In September, the city’s mayor Daniel Lurie declared a “rent emergency”. Pointing to soaring costs driven by the AI boom, he proposed funding for eviction legal aid, larger payments to displaced renters and caps on rent increases for newly vacant rent-controlled units.
Critics say the measures address symptoms, not causes.
“This is San Francisco on repeat,” said Quintin Mecke, executive director of the San Francisco Council of Community Housing Organizations, “We treat housing like a commodity rather than a home that people have a right to, and we don’t learn any lessons.”
Across the city, there are landlords trying to capitalize on the boom. The dynamic is especially pronounced in neighborhoods such as SoMa and Mission Bay, the industrial and waterfront neighborhoods which are home to the offices of AI giants such as Anthropic and OpenAI.
Anand Singh, of the hospitality and tourism union Unite Here, said he’s heard stories of tenants facing 40% rent hikes in recent months.
“When margins are as slim as they are, an extra $100 per month is easily enough to stress test a person’s ability to live in the city,” Singh said. State law caps annual increases on some units, but newer buildings are exempt from limitations entirely.
Rent control, which applies to many buildings in the city built before 1979, is also meant to shield tenants from big shocks, but in boom times, it can perversely incentivize landlords to oust long-term tenants who pay below-market rent so they can relet the unit at market rate. A growing number of landlords are relying on legal pathways to do so, advocates say.
Under the Ellis Act, a property owner can evict every tenant in a building if they go out of the rental business, and thereafter sell the vacant property. And with properties selling for as much as $1m over asking price to buyers working in AI, these evictions are popping up more and more.
Some are predicated on turning long-term rental units into luxury condos to sell at a massive profit. On Powell Street in San Francisco’s North Beach neighborhood – just a mile and change from the Anthropic headquarters – the new owners of a seven-unit building occupied by the same tenants for decades are trying to combine the units into four larger, upscale condos.
San Francisco also allows eviction for “just causes”, including nonpayment and lease violations. Increasingly, landlords are designing circumstances that trap renters into missteps, such as by changing the way rent is collected from in-person to online platforms, organizers say.
When a rent-controlled building in the Tenderloin changed hands after the original owners defaulted on their loan, for example, many residents were not told that they needed to re-route their monthly payments. When those tenants paid the old landlord instead, they were issued nonpayment eviction notices en masse.
Speculating on a big AI-fuelled payday, some landlords are growing increasingly brazen in their efforts to provoke this type of “self-eviction” by refusing to address infestations, repair broken appliances or collect trash, housing advocates said. Others do what are colloquially known as “renovictions”: remodels that are loud, inconvenient, unnecessary and designed to annoy a resident so much that they leave.
Zamudio said her organization has seen a 23% increase in landlord disputes related to repairs over the past year. Danny Sauter, a city supervisor whose district covers much of downtown, said that renters now feel uneasy when their landlords move to make improvements. “All of a sudden their landlord is paying attention and wanting to fix something that has been broken for years,” he said. “Folks are getting nervous.”
Predatory landlords are counting on certain tenants, especially those who are older or who speak limited English, to quietly move on. Since tenant protections are largely self-enforced, “most predatory landlords are going to first aim at who they think doesn’t know their rights and who they think would be scared to assert them”, explained Molly Goldberg, director of the San Francisco anti-displacement coalition.
In Chinatown – which spans some 30 blocks adjacent to the financial district and is the oldest Chinatown in the nation – an investor purchased a rent-controlled building of mostly older Cantonese-speaking residents and almost immediately started issuing eviction notices, claiming renters who had lived there for decades were hoarders “simply because their belongings demonstrated four decades of living”, Goldberg said.
The residents of 1120 Jackson St. have since formed a union and are fighting back, but under the shadows of the federal anti-immigration crackdown, many immigrants are unlikely to risk going to court. “These sorts of dynamics make it much more difficult for immigrant families to avail themselves of their rights,” said Shamus Rolller, CEO of the National Housing Law Project.
Some landlords are even using deportation fears as leverage. Goldberg’s neighbor abandoned their rent-controlled unit voluntarily after their landlord threatened to report their marriage as fraudulent for the purposes of acquiring a green card, she said. “They left in fear.”
Displaced renters who want to stay in San Francisco have few options.
Since he first moved to San Francisco 20 years ago, Frederick Jones, 47, has lived with roommates. After he lost his last apartment to a condo conversion, he moved into the smallest room of a three-bedroom house in the Sunset neighborhood. Every month, he spends half of his earnings from his job at the flagship factory of famed chocolate maker Ghirardelli on rent. “I would love to have a place of my own, but in San Francisco, with its high rents, you can’t,” he said.
As AI wealth further inflates rental prices, people who are evicted from or priced out of their homes are moving into units that are smaller or in poor – even substandard – condition. “People are being shown places without a bathroom, with no working lights, with no kitchen,” said Roller.
Many “double up”, cramming into a shared space meant for one. Advocates describe multiple families sharing a single family home, with four or five people to a bedroom, and as many as 10 immigrant workers bunking together in a studio.
Overcrowding takes a toll on residents’ mental health, explained Margot Kushel, director of the UCSF Benioff Homelessness and Housing Initiative. “Can you imagine trying to do homework in a studio apartment with eight people, or trying to get some sleep when people are coming and going to their night shifts?” she asked. “It creates stress for everybody.”
Kushel and her colleagues are increasingly seeing patients put their physical health on the line to remain housed. Some delay important preventive care because they can’t afford to take time off work. People start to drink more because of the stress, she said, or they turn to stimulants such as meth so that they can stay alert at their multiple jobs and stave off hunger. Patients with life-threatening conditions stop taking their medications because they can’t afford the $10 co-pay.
Some even starve themselves. “I had one elder patient who had not eaten in three days, who kept missing appointments because he didn’t have money to pay for the bus and couldn’t risk falling behind in rent,” Kushel said. “It’s heartbreaking and it’s real.”
Meanwhile, the services that once helped people through displacement are thinning. Interfaith agencies offering support services and charity have closed as landlords have refused to renew leases or have raised rents to unattainable levels. Many struggle to recruit staff while demand for their services is “through the roof”, said Michael Pappas, executive director of the San Francisco Interfaith Council. Proposed cuts at the local and federal levels could add more fuel to the fire.
Still open is the council’s winter shelter, which gives meals and beds to up to 100 people experiencing homelessness during the coldest months. Last year, the shelter was nearly always full, Pappas said – with many residents only having recently become unhoused. “I’m afraid of what we’re going to see this year,” he said, noting that the AI companies behind the wealth surge have yet to go public.
For the many who move out of the city, those whose jobs are tied to the city commute into San Francisco from increasingly vast distances. “Super-commuting” – traveling more than 50 miles to get to work – has surged in recent decades, explained Sarah Karlinsky, director of research & policy at the UC Berkeley Terner Center for Housing Innovation.
The AI boom will likely intensify the trend. “For communities at the center, at the eye of the storm, it’s a lot of pressure,” Karlinsky said.
Unite Here’s Singh has seen the shift firsthand. When he first started working for the union 24 years ago, more than half of the members he represented lived in San Francisco or very close to it. Now, most live outside it.
A decade ago, members commuting from Tracy (60+ miles), Modesto (90 miles), and other towns in the agricultural Central Valley were outliers. Now they are common – but whereas previously people were moving far away to purchase a home, they’re now doing it just to find affordable rent. “It’s astounding,” he said. “That is hours and hours spent in cars and trains.”
Entire industries are feeling the strain. Hospitality, still recovering from the pandemic, is short on workers, restaurants are struggling to hire line cooks and dishwashers and grocery stores are finding themselves chronically understaffed.
The dynamic is fundamentally reshaping the city, as many of the workers who keep it running live beyond its limits. According to Kim Tavaglione, executive director of the San Francisco Labor Council, only 7% of union members – comprising nurses, teachers, orchestra workers, fire fighters and others – were able to afford living in the city before the most recent rent spike.
“Folks are living on the edge,” she said. “Even workers who on paper seem to be doing OK are struggling. There is nowhere left for people to go except outside the city.”
In recent months, Tavaglione has heard of janitors who live in homeless shelters and healthcare workers commuting from as far away as Lake county. Between back-to-back shifts, they live in their cars and take showers at the local YMCA. “It’s frightening,” she said.
The AI-fuelled surge is also making the city less diverse – a trend that has been underway for decades. While San Francisco’s Black population peaked in 1970 at 13%, today it hovers at around 5%. “The loss of the Black population in the city is a major dynamic that I’ve seen over the time since I’ve been here,” said Roller.
This is what happens when a city doesn’t support residents at various points on the income scale, explained Michael Lens, director of the Lewis Center for Regional Policy Studies at UCLA. “We need a diverse workforce to support all the things we do,” he said. “We can’t just have an economy of lawyers and tech bros. We need people who work at restaurants and who teach at schools to be able to afford to live somewhere nearby.”
Housing advocates are at odds about the best way to increase the supply of affordable rental units. Some, such as Matthew Lewis of pro-housing non-profit California Yimby, are adamant that the solution is simply to build “as much housing” as possible so that competition softens and market rates drop. Others want the city to commit to building more affordable housing that shelters renters from market whims and unscrupulous landlords.
But both sides agree the system is broken. “For tenants who aren’t looking at stock options, this is a lottery that most people lose,” said Lewis.
That’s the sense housing advocate Shanti Singh conveyed from her rent-controlled apartment in Nob Hill. Despite living in the same unit for 10 years, never missing a payment, and working in tenants’ rights, she “always” worries about being evicted. If that were to happen, she said, she couldn’t afford a similar place at today’s market prices and would likely have to leave.
“Unless you’re really rich, everybody is on edge.”

Rally Estonia put on WRC calendar also for next season

Rally Estonia put on WRC calendar also for next season
FIA and the WRC promoter unveiled the calendar for next season's World Rally Championship on Thursday, with Rally Estonia also included. The event will take place on the roads of southern Estonia from July 22-25.
In August this year, the FIA World Rally Championship's promoter changed hands, with French automotive technology company Cosmobilis and private equity investor Park Square Capital acquiring WRC Promoter GmbH. The new owners aim to make the championship and its individual rounds even more attractive, turning each rally into a major event offering a wide range of entertainment alongside exciting racing.
The championship's new CEO, Eric Boullier, also visited Delfi Rally Estonia this summer and was highly impressed by what he saw. He praised the high standard of organization and the organizers' ambition and ability to combine world-class rallying with a comprehensive sports and entertainment experience.
Following this year's rally, the Rally Estonia team held several further meetings with representatives of the promoter. These discussions resulted in an agreement for Rally Estonia to remain a round of the World Rally Championship in 2027.
"Rally Estonia's continued inclusion in the WRC calendar is a major recognition of everyone who has contributed to the event's success. A big thank you to the Estonian state, local governments, private sector sponsors and the entire organizing team and of course to local residents, rally fans, drivers and teams," rally director Urmo Aava said.
"WRC Delfi Rally Estonia is much more than four days of top-level racing. It is a major international event that boosts Estonia's economy, supports regional development, generates tax revenue for the state and provides memorable experiences for tens of thousands of spectators along the stages and hundreds of millions of viewers across various platforms. The desire of foreign visitors to return to Estonia and recommend us to their friends creates value long after the rally weekend has ended," Minister of Culture Heidy Purga added.
WRC Rally Estonia will be the ninth round of the 2027 FIA World Rally Championship, taking place from July 22–25. The 2027 WRC calendar will feature a total of 15 rounds.
The WRC is set to become even more global in the coming years, with the United States also hosting a championship round in 2027. The series will also enter a new era with the introduction of new Rally1 cars and technical regulations. Several new private teams are expected to join the championship, while Ford recently announced that it would return as a factory team after a decades-long absence. These developments promise to make the championship even more exciting and competitive.
Of the 43,894 unique spectators who attended this year's WRC Delfi Rally Estonia, foreign visitors accounted for 31.9 percent or 14,002 people. According to a study, the event generated an estimated €44.9 million in additional revenue for Estonian businesses, up 36 percent from 2025. Direct tax revenue associated with this turnover was estimated at €8.3 million.

Greece agrees up to $4 billion US arms deal, sources say
ATHENS, Oct 8 - Greece has agreed to spend up to $4 billion upgrading more of its F-16 fighter jets and buying advanced missiles from the US, two senior sources told Reuters on Thursday, a day after a visit by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Greece had already planned to spend about €28 billion by 2036 to buy US made F-35 fighter jets and helicopters, and to build the "Achilles Shield" a multi-layer anti-ballistic and anti-aircraft system with Israeli-made weapons.
"The agreement includes new advanced missiles and bombs for the F-16 Viper the F-35 fighter jets, and the Black Hawk helicopters. Also the upgrade of old F-16 fighter jets to Viper version," a senior defence Ministry official told Reuters.
The official added that most of the procurements have been included in the government's multi year defence plan and will not put additional pressure to the country's financials.
A senior foreign ministry official confirmed the above, adding that the cost will be spread over several years.
Rubio said on Wednesday in Athens that the two NATO allies had agreed on a joint security plan for counterterrorism information sharing between their law enforcement agencies.
Greece agreed to buy 20 Lockheed Martin F-35 fighter jets and 35 Sikorsky UH-60M Black Hawk helicopters in 2024. Is upgrading about 82 F-16s to Viper version and wants to upgrade 37 more Block 50s to Vipers at a cost of about $1 billion.
The move is part of Greece's bid to modernise its armed forces as it emerges from the 2009-18 debt crisis that led to years of austerity.
Greece spends nearly 3.5% of its gross domestic product on defence, a higher proportion than many other NATO countries, due to its long-standing dispute with Turkey. REUTERS

Xbox launches a new film and television division
Kyiv • UNN
The new XP division will bring together Xbox’s film projects, merchandise, live events, and partnerships. It will be headed by Mojang’s Cailin Walters.
Xbox is launching a new division called XP, which will focus on Xbox projects unrelated to video games, including films and television adaptations, consumer products, live events, and partnerships with creators and brands. UNN writes about this, citing The Verge.
Details
Various Xbox teams are already doing this work, but it will now be consolidated into the centralized XP division.
According to a blog post by Xbox Chief Strategy Officer Matthew Ball, XP formalizes four "areas of investment":
-  “XBOX PICTURES: bringing our worlds and characters to new audiences through film, television, and other forms of linear storytelling”; 
-  “XBOX PRODUCTS: creating products that are authentic to the fan community and allow fans to celebrate and express their feelings for their favorite franchises”; 
-  “XBOX PLACES: bringing communities together through live events, immersive experiences, attractions, broadcasts, and leisure destinations”; 
-  “XBOX PARTNERSHIPS: working with content creators, brands, and communities to develop new projects, sponsorships, and brand partnerships.” 
XP will be led by Kailyn Walters, who is moving from her position as head of Mojang, the company that created Minecraft, to become president of the new division. Mojang’s next leader will be Maria Angelidou-Smith, who will leave her position as Reddit’s Chief Product Officer to become CEO of Mojang and Minecraft; she will begin work on October 19.
Xbox is already developing several film and television adaptations, including a sequel to the successful film A Minecraft Movie, the third season of the Fallout series on Prime Video, a Call of Duty film, and an animated Diablo series for Netflix.
"Great games remain at the center of these franchises and at the heart of XBOX," Ball said. "XP will work with the best creative minds across all our studios, as well as trusted partners, to build on this foundation and create more opportunities for people to discover the worlds they love."

Senior advisor to Mike Huckabee blocked and altered reports critical of Israel, investigation finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:57:48 UTC
22:57:48 KST

David Milstein, a senior adviser to U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, repeatedly blocked or substantially altered reports critical of Israel in an effort to present Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government in a more favorable light to the administration in Washington, a New York Times investigation published Thursday alleges.
For the investigation, Times reporters interviewed 15 current U.S. officials who had worked with Milstein in some capacity, as well as nine former diplomats who helped provide background. The newspaper also obtained or reviewed dozens of documents, cables, memos and other internal communications that it said showed Milstein’s involvement in changing embassy reporting.
Most of those who spoke to the Times said they did so out of concern that Milstein’s actions were undermining standard diplomatic work. Some also expressed concern that, in certain cases, his actions contradicted President Donald Trump’s stated policies.
One example cited in the investigation took place in late March, at the height of the war with Iran, when Israel quietly approved more West Bank settlements at once than ever before. A sharply worded, urgent report on the move never reached the U.S. administration. According to three U.S. officials, Milstein blocked it.
A similar case occurred in April, when senior IDF officials warned that settler violence in the West Bank could ignite a new Palestinian uprising. Embassy personnel tried to relay those warnings to Washington, but Milstein prevented the reports from being sent in their original form, according to three officials.
Instead, Milstein praised Netanyahu’s “new and unprecedented initiatives” to combat violence in the West Bank. The report was titled: “Government Acts Forcefully Against Escalating Violence in the West Bank.”
Another case involved members of Congress who requested information about the deaths of nine Palestinian Americans in the West Bank over the past four years. According to multiple officials, Milstein blocked a detailed report prepared by embassy staff, effectively thwarting lawmakers’ efforts to obtain the information.
The main findings in the blocked report showed that in most cases the investigations had made very little progress, that some files had been closed and that no one had been prosecuted over the deaths, according to those officials. Instead of sending the report, Milstein argued that the embassy should send a letter stating that Israel was handling the investigations properly.
Officials who spoke with the Times said that, shortly after returning to the embassy in Jerusalem at the start of Trump’s second term in the White House, Milstein began insisting on approving outgoing correspondence from the embassy section dealing with Palestinian affairs.
The volume of reporting fell from several reports a week to only a handful a month, because some staff members stopped writing reports out of fear that Milstein would block or rewrite them, those officials said.
According to several officials, Milstein’s interventions went far beyond those of any of his predecessors. They and others said they were speaking out because they feared officials in Washington were receiving a distorted picture of Israeli actions through key diplomatic channels.
Milstein’s efforts, they said, helped shield the Netanyahu government from potentially harsher responses by the Trump administration.
The Times noted that it is unclear to what extent Huckabee was aware of Milstein’s actions. Both Huckabee and Milstein declined the newspaper’s requests for interviews. Huckabee is required to approve most major reports and decisions made by Milstein, but officials said the adviser sometimes acted on his own.
According to those officials, Huckabee at times worked with Milstein to withhold information or present it differently to the administration. In other instances, however, he believed Milstein had gone too far and stopped him.
Milstein’s efforts to influence embassy reporting were first exposed about a year ago by the online magazine of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, a Washington think tank that advocates reduced tensions and greater restraint in U.S. military policy.
The Times investigation, however, presented documented evidence and previously unreported cases in which Milstein allegedly sought to tilt information in favor of the Netanyahu government. The documented activity, the report said, continued throughout the past year.
Those who spoke with the Times included career government officials and political appointees, including strong supporters of the U.S.-Israel relationship.
Concern over Milstein’s conduct also spread to senior administration officials in Washington, including in the White House, who expressed frustration to colleagues over some of his actions, according to four people.
It remains unclear whether or how Milstein’s interventions affected White House policy toward Israel. Since Trump declared a year ago that he would not allow Israel to annex the West Bank, he has rarely spoken publicly on the issue.
In response to questions sent to the embassy about Milstein’s actions, Huckabee did not address the specific cases described in the investigation.
“The events in the investigation are so incomplete, in fact, that they are consistent with other ridiculous efforts by the Times. I personally and categorically reject the allegations presented in the investigation,” he said.
The U.S. State Department said: “The entire State Department team remains focused on advancing President Trump’s America First agenda.”
Who is David Milstein?
Milstein is a familiar figure in right-wing circles in the United States and Israel, and has repeatedly arranged meetings between Huckabee and senior Israeli officials. Still, he is not especially well known in either country, and his role as a gatekeeper for information flowing to Washington had received relatively little attention until now.
His stepfather is right-wing radio host Mark Levin, a close ally of Trump. Netanyahu has also appeared on Levin’s program several times in recent years. The connection among the three is well known in Washington and at the embassy, officials in Jerusalem and Washington told the Times.
Milstein identifies as a conservative and longtime Republican. He previously served as an aide to pro-Israel Texas Sen. Ted Cruz from 2013 to 2018, before moving to Israel to study at a Jerusalem yeshiva. In 2020, he took a job as an aide to then-U.S. Ambassador David Friedman.
As an adviser to Huckabee, Milstein is now one of the most senior officials at the U.S. Embassy in Jerusalem. According to the Times, he functions as a kind of chief of staff for the ambassador.
Huckabee has authorized him to oversee much of the mission’s portfolio, particularly developments in the West Bank and Gaza. His responsibilities include reviewing and editing information sent to Washington, including the reports he allegedly softened in Israel’s favor.
Officials with professional familiarity with Milstein said he goes to unusual lengths to portray Israel positively. They said he has blocked critical reporting, rewritten reports to convey a different — sometimes opposite — message from the original, and delayed approving drafts until the issue was no longer relevant.
One prominent case cited in the investigation occurred in the summer of 2025, when dozens of Palestinians arrived at a food distribution point in Gaza run by the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation, or GHF, which was backed by Jerusalem and Washington.
U.S. diplomats drafted a report for the Trump administration warning that the foundation’s distribution process was chaotic and deadly, and cautioning about additional “mass casualty incidents.”
According to officials who saw the original report, Milstein rewrote it to declare the GHF operation a success, while omitting the mass casualties.
The discrepancy did not go unnoticed at the White House, which saw a striking gap between news reports and embassy reporting. As a result, White House and State Department officials sought a clearer picture of events and, on at least two occasions, contacted embassy staff directly to obtain a more reliable account.
Former U.S. diplomats who spoke with the New York Times said distorting information sent to Washington should raise serious concerns.
“The embassy should tell Washington everything — the good, the bad and the ugly,” said Dan Kurtzer, who served as U.S. ambassador to Israel under President George W. Bush.
