Russian strike kills 33 in Ukraine as drones hit Yandex data centre
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:57:36 EEST
22:57:36 KST

A Russian air strike on two passenger buses in the eastern Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk killed at least 33 people and injured 18 on Thursday, 8 October, Ukrainian authorities said. On the same day, a drone attack disrupted operations at Russia's largest Yandex data centre in the Ryazan region.
The attack in Kramatorsk struck a street near a public transport stop at around 10am, setting buses on fire and leaving bodies and debris scattered across the road, according to Ukrainian police and emergency services.
Ukraine's State Emergency Service confirmed 33 deaths and 18 injuries, while Donetsk regional governor Vadym Filashkin later reported that the number of injured had risen to 19. Authorities suspended public transport in Kramatorsk and neighbouring Sloviansk following the bombing.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Russia of deliberately attacking civilians and said doctors were treating victims whose conditions remained critical.
"This strike will not go without our response. Russia is trying to destroy all life in Donbas, and the world needs to react to this," Zelenskyy said in a statement on telegram.
Filashkin also accused Russian forces of deliberately targeting buses carrying passengers, saying the attack demonstrated Moscow's disregard for civilian lives.
The bombing struck Kramatorsk, one of the last two major cities in northern Donetsk under Ukrainian control. Together with Sloviansk, the city forms part of Ukraine's defensive positions against Russian forces seeking control of the remaining Ukrainian-held territory in the region.
The attack followed a Russian strike on an apartment building in Pryluky, northern Ukraine, on Wednesday, which killed at least 22 people, including five children.
Separately, Russian drone strikes on Kyiv killed three people and injured 14 on Thursday, according to the city's mayor, Vitali Klitschko.
Ukraine's air force said Russia had launched 142 Shahed-type drones overnight, including 82 jet-powered variants. Ukrainian air defences reported intercepting or suppressing 126 of them.
Meanwhile, a drone attack struck a data centre belonging to Russian technology company Yandex in Sasovo, southeast of Moscow.
According to reports, the attack caused a fire and forced Yandex to suspend operations at the facility.
Yandex confirmed disruptions to its cloud infrastructure and reported power supply problems affecting one of its availability zones.
Open-source intelligence groups Exilenova+ and ASTRA identified the affected facility as Yandex's Sasovo data centre.
The facility houses tens of thousands of servers supporting Yandex's internet services and cloud computing operations.
Yandex initially acknowledged an infrastructure incident without identifying its cause. Russian regional authorities and Ukraine's military had not publicly commented on responsibility for the strike.
The Sasovo facility stands within the industrial complex of machine-tool manufacturer Sasta, which produces equipment used in Russian manufacturing, including the defence, aerospace and energy industries.
Britain placed Sasta under sanctions in 2024 over its involvement in Russia's defence sector. Western restrictions on exports of advanced electronics to Russia would complicate the replacement of equipment damaged in the attack.
Open-source monitoring groups reported disruptions to some Yandex services, although public outage trackers showed no evidence of widespread failures across the company's main consumer platforms.

The US Democratic candidate in Michigan's Senate race said President Donald Trump is using his name and faith to "distract" voters from the rising cost of living.
"He knows my name is Abdul. He says it everyday," Abdul El-Sayed said in a post on US social media platform X, adding, "but he's not just attacking me. He's attacking all of us. He thinks so low of us."
He said Trump "thinks he can use my name and my faith to distract us from the suffering his policies are inflicting on us at the pump, at the grocery store, and at the doctor's office."
"He thinks we don't know any better," he said, noting, “It's time for change."

El-Sayed, a physician and former Wayne County health director, won the Democratic nomination in August, defeating Rep. Haley Stevens in a close primary.
He ran unsuccessfully for governor in 2018 and is backed by Sen. Bernie Sanders. If elected, he would be the first Muslim to serve in the Senate.
He will face Republican candidate Mike Rogers, a former congressman, in the Nov. 3 midterm elections for the seat of retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters.

South Africa pushes for local medicine production
South Africa is stepping up efforts to manufacture medicines and pharmaceutical ingredients locally to reduce reliance on imports and strengthen its ability to secure critical medical supplies during future health emergencies, the government has said.
President Cyril Ramaphosa, accompanied by Science, Technology and Innovation Minister Professor Blade Nzimande and Health Minister Dr Aaron Motsoaledi, toured the FuturePharma facility at the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) in Pretoria. The facility is expected to strengthen South Africa’s pharmaceutical manufacturing capabilities by helping researchers move technologies from laboratories towards large-scale production and commercialisation.
”The facility will also support local API and medicine production, helping to reduce dependence on imports and strengthen security of supply,” the Government Communication and Information System (GCIS) said.
The move towards greater domestic production is aimed at giving South Africa stronger control over the availability of essential medicines while building local pharmaceutical capacity.
According to GCIS, one of the major objectives of the facility is to close the gap between scientific discoveries and medicines or pharmaceutical technologies that can be produced commercially. ”It will provide researchers, innovators and industry partners with access to specialised infrastructure and expertise to advance technologies towards manufacturing, while supporting technology transfer and skills development,” GCIS added.
This means pharmaceutical innovations developed by researchers could receive the technical support and infrastructure required to move beyond experimental laboratory stages and towards manufacturing.
The facility is also expected to form part of South Africa’s preparations for future pandemics and other major public health emergencies. The Covid-19 pandemic highlighted the risks countries face when they are heavily dependent on international supply chains for medicines, vaccines and other critical health products.

Chinese parcel service Speedaf challenges Swiss Post
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:55:20 UTC
22:55:20 KST

Chinese parcel service Speedaf challenges Swiss Post
Chinese online retailers Temu and Shein are creating a flood of parcels into Switzerland. A Chinese logistics firm is looking to capitalise on this phenomenon.
Massive advertising and aggressive low prices: the Chinese online retailers Temu and Shein are already firmly established in Switzerland, and are rapidly taking market share away from local online shops.
Now a Chinese logistics firm is also making inroads into the Swiss market. Speedaf is currently setting up a parcel network here which, according to Swiss federal technology institute ETH expert Stephan Wagner, could quickly reach a significant scale.
More
Chinese retail platform Temu challenges consumers and retailers
This is because the planned sorting capacity of up to 50,000 parcels a day is substantial for a new entrant, says the professor of logistics. At full capacity, this would amount to around 15 million parcels a year.
Speedaf could also put pressure on the dominant logistics providers – Swiss Post and DPD – in terms of pricing. Wagner points out that little can be said about the pricing structures at present. However: “It may well be that parcel delivery becomes cheaper in the medium term.”
Furthermore, there is certainly room for another strong player in the growing parcel market. This is particularly true given the sharp rise in parcel imports from China. “And this is precisely the area Speedaf intends to focus on initially,” said Wagner.
Speedaf is currently building its own Swiss parcel network. Plans include a sorting centre covering around 4,000 square metres, capable of handling up to 50,000 parcels a day, plus regional distribution centres in Zurich, Bern and Lausanne.
Founded in 2019, the logistics company has been operating in Switzerland for a few months.
The company is already active in more than 30 countries and handles parcels from Shein, Temu and Aliexpress, amongst others.
The Chinese parcel giant ZTO Express is one of its founding shareholders.
According to Wagner, Chinese logistics firms are increasingly seeking to organise international transport themselves, right through to the last mile in Europe.
Should Speedaf establish itself firmly in Switzerland via international parcel delivery, the Chinese logistics firm could become a serious competitor for Swiss Post.
More
Swiss lawmakers demand curbs on Chinese online retailers
“If the network is stable and deliveries are reliable, Swiss mail-order companies and smaller firms could also switch to Speedaf,” Wagner said. “That would certainly pose a threat to Swiss Post.”
Switzerland’s small size an advantage
Furthermore, Switzerland’s compact geography is fundamentally an advantage when it comes to building a nationwide network, Wagner added. “With one distribution centre and a few depots, you can cover a lot of ground here quickly. In larger countries such as France, that’s not so easy.”
However, the costs are high. Wagner considers it sensible that Speedaf intends to rely on local delivery partners for the last mile. This enables market entry without first having to build up its own fleet of vehicles and a large number of delivery staff.

A traffic accident can be handled without the police or paperwork — how to use the European Accident Statement in Diia and whether your “driver’s license” will be taken away

16:55:11 EEST
22:55:11 KST

A traffic accident can be handled without the police or paperwork — how to use the European Accident Statement in Diia and whether your “driver’s license” will be taken away
Kyiv • UNN
The European Accident Statement in Diia is available when there are no injured parties and both drivers agree. After it is completed, licenses are not confiscated and no report is drawn up.
From now on, the full process of completing a European Accident Statement can be done directly in the Diia app — without traffic jams or paperwork. This was reported by Oleksii Biloshytskyi, Head of the Patrol Police Department, according to UNN.
According to Biloshytskyi, Diia will automatically fill in the required data from official registers, which will help complete the accident report faster and avoid errors during completion.
When you can complete a European Accident Statement in Diia:
- only two cars are involved in the accident, with no trailers, and both are at the scene of the collision;
- there are no injured or dead persons;
- no property other than the cars has been damaged;
- both participants have valid compulsory third-party motor liability insurance policies;
- the drivers are sober and are not under the influence of medications that may reduce attention or reaction speed;
- the participants have reached an agreement regarding the circumstances of the accident.
Important: if the other driver does not have the Diia app with verified documents, complete a paper European Accident Statement.
If you have not reached an agreement regarding the circumstances of the accident, call the police at 112 or 102.
Will your driver's licence be taken away after completing it?
No. You settle the situation with the insurance company without involving the police, so the driver's licence is not confiscated and no administrative report is drawn up.
How do you complete a European Accident Statement?
Diia → Services → For Drivers → European Accident Statement.
After both drivers sign via Diia.Signature, the data is sent to the Motor (Transport) Insurance Bureau of Ukraine and the insurance companies.

In attacks on Ukraine from the territory of Belarus, Russia likely used Belarusian Long-Term Evolution (LTE) networks, as well as a network of repeater stations on Belarusian territory, to help provide stable signals to Russian Shahed-type drones used in mass attacks on Ukraine, two Ukrainian officials said on Sept. 14, 2026.
The revelation came two days after Russia sent hundreds of drones, hugging Ukraine's northern border, in a rare a mass attack targeting regions in western Ukraine on Sept. 12.

Poland will change procedures for military aircraft and helicopters that engage objects entering from the direction of Russia, Deputy Defense Minister Cezary Tomczyk said on Sept. 28, 2026.
Under the current peacetime procedure, Polish pilots must fly close enough to visually confirm a target in Polish airspace before firing at it.

====================================================================================================

FDA-approved epilepsy drug may help reverse osteoarthritis damage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:52:56 UTC
22:52:56 KST

FDA-approved epilepsy drug may help reverse osteoarthritis damage
- Date:
- October 8, 2026
- Source:
- Yale School of Medicine
- Summary:
- Researchers at Yale have identified a promising new approach to osteoarthritis that could do more than simply ease pain. The epilepsy drug lacosamide appears to block a protein involved in both pain signaling and cartilage destruction, helping damaged joints shift back toward repair in preclinical studies.
- Share:
For millions of people with osteoarthritis, pain and stiffness can make everyday activities increasingly difficult. Common treatments, including over-the-counter medications and steroid injections, may reduce symptoms for a time, but they do not prevent the underlying joint damage from progressing.
New research from Yale suggests a different approach. In a study published in Bioactive Materials, scientists found that the medication lacosamide can serve two purposes in osteoarthritis, reducing joint pain while also reversing cartilage damage. The effects were particularly strong when the drug was delivered directly into the joint using a specialized hydrogel.
Why osteoarthritis damages cartilage
Osteoarthritis is often called a condition caused by wear and tear, but that description leaves out much of the biology involved.
Within a healthy joint, cells known as chondrocytes help maintain cartilage by continuously balancing the creation of new tissue with the removal of old material. Osteoarthritis disrupts that balance. Cartilage begins to break down faster than it can be replaced, eventually allowing bones to rub against one another. As the disease advances, some patients may ultimately require joint reconstruction procedures such as a total knee replacement.
"There is a major unmet need in osteoarthritis," says the study's principal investigator and Charles W. Ohse Professor of Orthopaedics & Rehabilitation, Chuan-Ju Liu, PhD. "We need therapies that don't just mask pain but actually change how the disease progresses."
At present, no medicine approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration can both stop osteoarthritis pain and prevent the structural breakdown of cartilage. The work led by Liu suggests that it may be possible to address both problems with a single therapeutic strategy.
The researchers repurposed an existing medication and paired it with an advanced gel designed to keep the drug inside the joint. The approach could potentially preserve joint tissue while delivering sustained pain relief without relying on addictive opioids.
A protein linked to pain and cartilage loss
The research focuses on Nav1.7, a protein that functions as a sodium channel. These channels act as microscopic gates in cell membranes and play an important role in electrical signaling.
Nav1.7 was long thought to operate primarily in specialized nerve cells that transmit pain signals to the brain. More recent work from Liu and his team, however, revealed that the protein is also highly active in chondrocytes, the cells responsible for maintaining cartilage.
Nav1.7 is relatively quiet in healthy joints. In osteoarthritis, however, its activity increases substantially. The researchers found that this heightened activity can intensify pain signaling while also pushing chondrocytes toward breaking down the cartilage they would normally help preserve.
That makes Nav1.7 an unusual therapeutic target because it appears to influence both the sensation of pain and the physical deterioration of joint tissue.
"When Nav1.7 becomes dysregulated, it contributes to both joint degeneration and pain," Liu says. "Our findings suggest that Nav1.7 is a dual-acting target. By blocking this single protein, we can potentially quiet the pain nerves and tell the cartilage cells to not only stop breaking down but start repairing as well."
Epilepsy drug shows potential for cartilage repair
Instead of creating an entirely new medication, Liu's team tested drugs that already inhibit sodium channels. Among them, lacosamide produced strong biological effects at considerably lower concentrations and offered a better safety profile than older drugs in the same class.
Lacosamide is already used as a treatment for epilepsy, but the researchers found that its effects on cartilage depended heavily on the dose.
More was not necessarily better. At an ideal low concentration, lacosamide encouraged cells to produce proteins involved in building cartilage while also suppressing processes that break tissue down. When the concentration was either too high or too low, those benefits began to fade.
"This tells us the system is finely tuned," Liu notes. "There is an optimal range where the drug helps restore balance without overcorrecting. What stood out was not just its effectiveness, but how little of a dose was needed."
Further investigation revealed that lacosamide also changes the way cells communicate. The drug stimulated the release of two beneficial signaling proteins, HSP70 and midkine.
HSP70 helps cells respond to stress and supports tissue repair, while midkine helps regulate inflammation and protect joint tissue from degeneration. Together, the proteins appear to create conditions that are more favorable for maintaining cartilage.
"These proteins create a supportive environment for cartilage maintenance," Liu explains. "They allow the effects of the drug to extend beyond individual cells and influence the entire tissue."
Smart hydrogel keeps the drug inside the joint
Oral treatment with lacosamide was effective in preclinical testing, but drugs taken by mouth circulate throughout the body, increasing the potential for unwanted effects elsewhere.
The researchers therefore investigated intra-articular injection, which allows the medication to be placed directly inside the affected joint.
There was still a significant problem to overcome. "The knee joint, which is also the most common location for osteoarthritis, naturally acts like a leaky bucket," Liu says. "The body's drainage system can clear out liquids injected into the knee within hours."
To keep the medication in place longer, the team created a specialized hydrogel made from Collagen II. The material responds to temperature. It remains liquid while inside a cool syringe, then becomes a firm, jelly-like material after reaching body temperature.
Once inside the joint, the gel acts as a storage site for lacosamide, keeping the medication concentrated in the affected area while gradually releasing it over several weeks.
"The hydrogel acts as a local reservoir," Liu says. "It holds the drug in place in the location it is needed most and releases it slowly over time. It transforms a daily pill into a long-lasting, local treatment that stays active for a month or longer."
In the same preclinical studies, one injection of the lacosamide-containing gel every four weeks prevented cartilage loss more effectively than taking an oral dose every day.
Existing drug could speed clinical testing
One important advantage of lacosamide is that the medication is already approved for use in people. That could make it possible to move toward clinical studies in osteoarthritis patients more quickly than would be possible with a completely new drug.
Lacosamide has also been tested in humans with certain nerve-related pain conditions caused by Nav1.7 mutations. Those results give the researchers greater confidence that the effects seen in laboratory studies could eventually translate into meaningful pain relief for patients.
The work also reflects a broader direction in medicine that combines drugs with advanced biomaterials to control exactly where and how treatments are delivered. If the approach proves successful in people, it could eventually reduce the number of procedures patients need, limit unwanted side effects, and provide longer-lasting protection against structural joint damage.
"We are not just developing a treatment," Liu concludes. "We are developing a system that allows the medicine to work more effectively where it matters most. Our goal is to move beyond symptom control and towards true disease modification. This effort brings us closer to that reality."

Collagen II hydrogel-mediated sustained delivery of lacosamide attenuates cartilage degeneration and pain in osteoarthritis. Bioactive Materials, 2026; 61: 640 DOI: 10.1016/j.bioactmat.2026.02.045

Canadian Anne Carson wins 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature

Canadian Anne Carson wins 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature
The Swedish Academy praised the 76-year-old poet and essayist’s work for being ‘bold and inventive’.
Canadian poet and writer Anne Carson has won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature, the award-giving body has announced.
Carson was selected “for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature,” the Swedish Academy said in a statement on Thursday.
The 76-year-old, whose work is praised for blurring the lines of poetry and fiction, and for giving ancient works new translation, is also a professor of classics.
She has written more than 20 books, some of which have been adapted into plays, and has received numerous literary awards.
“Almost all her literary production has centred upon the intersection between the philologist’s obsession with words and the poet’s desire for new meaning,” the academy said.
“She has herself identified the etymology of words as the starting point for all her work. Her translations from Classical Greek may be regarded as independent works in their own right.”
Ingrid Carlberg, permanent secretary of the academy, which awards the prize worth 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2m), said Carson “was very taken by surprise”.
“We didn’t have so much time to speak, and all she had time to tell me was that she is for the moment in Iceland, where she’s listening to the wind.”
Shortly after the announcement, Carson reacted to her win to Icelandic broadcaster RUV. “Crazy. I think they’re all crazy … Well, you know, it’s crazy,” she said.
Carson, who was born in Toronto, also spends time in Iceland, where she also has citizenship.
One of her most notable works includes the Beauty of the Husband, a poignant and moving book-length narrative poem depicting a doomed marriage.
The Trojan Women, published in 2021, is a graphic retelling of Euripides’s ancient story, infused with modern vernacular.
In August 2024, she revealed in the London Review of Books that she was living with Parkinson’s disease.
The Nobel Prize, awarded by the Swedish Academy, is widely considered the most prestigious international award in literature.
Last year’s prize was won by Hungarian writer Laszlo Krasznahorkai.
Established in the will of Swedish dynamite inventor and businessman Alfred Nobel, the prizes for achievements in literature, science and peace have been awarded since 1901.
Literature was the fourth of this year’s Nobels to be announced this week, following medicine, physics and chemistry. The peace winner will be announced in Oslo on Friday.

A top adviser to the US ambassador to Israel has systematically suppressed, delayed, and rewritten internal diplomatic cables to shield the government of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu from scrutiny by Washington, The New York Times reported Thursday.
David Milstein, an influential gatekeeper at the US Embassy in Jerusalem since April 2025 and principal aide to US Ambassador Mike Huckabee, repeatedly stymied assessments intended for senior policymakers, according to an investigation based on interviews with more than a dozen US officials and reviews of internal State Department records.
In late March, Israel approved record-breaking occupation expansions across the occupied West Bank. Embassy personnel drafted an alert warning that the move risked violating US President Donald Trump's explicit red line against annexation. Milstein quashed the memorandum, framing the land acquisitions as a domestic matter before sending a revised text claiming the move addressed unspecified humanitarian needs of occupiers.
Milstein similarly altered reporting on surging violence in the occupied West Bank. When Israeli military commanders warned that attacks by occupiers could trigger a widespread Palestinian uprising, he blocked the dispatches suggesting that Israel failed to take action. Instead, an embassy cable authored under his name praised Netanyahu's initiatives and claimed authorities were actively combating the unrest.
The aide also suppressed a detailed embassy inquiry into the killings of nine Palestinian Americans by Israeli forces and occupiers, effectively thwarting accountability requests from members of the US Congress. Despite findings showing investigations stalled without criminal charges, the mission forwarded an alternative letter claiming active cooperation with Israeli authorities.
Milstein also edited dispatches regarding aid distribution by the US-backed Gaza Humanitarian Foundation to describe the operations as successful, removing diplomatic warnings that the process was "chaotic, deadly," and risked "mass casualty events."
Staff members noted that the interventions caused reporting from the embassy's Palestinian affairs section to drop from several weekly cables to a few per month and prompted some officials to bypass official embassy channels to obtain unfiltered ground intelligence.
"The elements of the story The New York Times is trying to assemble are so lacking in fact that it ranks up with other Times farcical endeavors," said Huckabee. The US State Department said its personnel remain focused on advancing the administration's foreign policy priorities.

Two commercial vessels were hit within 24 hours — one off Qatar, the first attack in that area in six months, and one off Fujairah in the Gulf of Oman — as IRGC-affiliated outlets suggested Tehran had extended operations beyond the crucial strait.
Iran's armed forces struck two commercial tankers outside the Strait of Hormuz within 24 hours this week, in what appeared to be a deliberate expansion of attacks beyond the strait, as Iranian officials issued a fresh wave of warnings against the United States.
The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said several projectiles hit the oil and chemical tanker Acers, flagged in Antigua and Barbuda, 51 nautical miles north of Madinat ash Shamal in Qatar on Wednesday. Casualties were reported.
Maritime intelligence firm Vanguard identified the vessel and said it was heading toward the Strait of Hormuz.
It was the first attack in that area in more than six months.
In a separate incident on Thursday, Vanguard reported a fire on a tanker some 40 kilometres off Fujairah in the Gulf of Oman, which it identified as likely the Marshall Islands-flagged Dhalgout.
The UKMTO had not recorded the incident, and the cause of the fire was not immediately clear. NASA's FIRMS fire-detection system confirmed the blaze, and US military aircraft — including two KC-46 tankers, a KC-135, a P-8A maritime patrol aircraft and several helicopters — were over the area at the time.
Iran and media affiliated with the IRGC did not officially claim responsibility for either attack. IRGC-affiliated outlets implicitly suggested that Tehran had "extended the scope of its operations against commercial vessels that violate Iranian laws and regulations in the Strait of Hormuz to waters beyond the strait."
Both incidents fall outside the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly one-fifth of global oil and gas shipments normally pass. The strait has been effectively closed since the war began in late February, after Iran and the US imposed concurrent naval blockades.
"The distance between you and us is determined by our missiles," Acting Defence Minister Majid Ebn ol-Reza posted on X on Thursday.
"Yesterday the Gulf of Oman, today the Indian Ocean and tomorrow the Bay of Pigs. If you make a mistake, you will see a new set of dividing lines.," ol-Reza added in an apparent reference to a failed, US-backed military landing on the southwestern coast of Cuba from April 1961 aimed at overthrowing the communist government of Fidel Castro.
Yahya Rahim Safavi, a senior military adviser to Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, had earlier warned that if the US or Israel attacked Iran again, Tehran could extend the war "as far as the Indian Ocean or other places," adding that Iranian forces had prepared contingency plans for worst-case scenarios.
Ebn ol-Reza was appointed acting minister after Aziz Nasirzadeh, Iran's then defence minister, was killed on 28 February — the first day of the war — alongside several other military commanders. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has nominated Mehrdad Akhlaqi as a permanent replacement, and parliament is due to hold a confidence vote on 18 October.
Iran's army spokesman said separately that its forces were ready to carry out pre-emptive operations, if necessary, to prevent what he described as "any aggression or attack by the enemy."
At a midterm election campaign rally in Nebraska, US President Donald Trump defended the decision to go to war with Iran. "This is a small price to pay for keeping the world and our country safe. They can destroy a city. Let them destroy it. Let them destroy Los Angeles, let them destroy San Diego," he said.
At a separate rally in Texas on Wednesday night, Trump walked back those remarks after criticism. "We protect our own cities. We will not allow such a thing to happen," he said.

Estonian Spa Association: There may not be enough customers for all new spas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:49:00 UTC
22:49:00 KST

Estonian Spa Association: There may not be enough customers for all new spas
Several new spas are set to enter Estonia's market in the coming years, but Aire Toffer, CEO of the Estonian Spa Association, warns that there may not be enough solvent customers to fill both the new and existing facilities.
Toffer said that the completion of several new spas is planned for the end of next year and the beginning of 2028. In her view, an incorrect impression may have formed about the spa market, as if large amounts of money were circulating there.
"These perceptions have arisen from the fact that during school holidays and on Saturday evenings the prices in spas are very high," she explained. Toffer said these are isolated days when visitors have time to go to the spa, which makes it possible to charge higher prices.
She said that starting spa entrepreneurs may lack an understanding of what the cost side of spas looks like, such as electricity and water consumption. "It's worth looking at companies' financial reports — the accommodation sector is not a very profitable business," Toffer noted.
Still, she is optimistic that every product has a consumer if it is created in the right place and is distinctive and innovative. But at present, according to Toffer, Estonia does not have enough solvent customers to fill all spas.
Gross: if you do it well, there should be enough customers
Next year, a spa hotel will rise by Lake Viljandi, owned by Lääne‑Virumaa entrepreneur Oleg Gross. He said that if you do something, you must do it very well. "And if you do it very well, there should be enough customers," he added.
Gross noted that a spa must offer a premium‑class product. "Besides, life has shown that Estonians have started going to spas more," he said. Gross explained that although foreign tourism has decreased, Estonia's climate encourages Estonians to visit spas more. He stated that a spa hotel is not a profit project but rather an emotion project. "But that it would start running losses — I don't believe that," he said.
According to Gross, there is room on the spa market for one more spa. At the same time, he noted that many developers have built a hotel with a spa only with bank loans and have no other business. "But we have a parent company in food retail," he said.
Gross said that if the spa should run a slight loss in its early years, he does not plan to sell or close it, and the spa will be kept alive by force if necessary. "It will get going in any case, there is no doubt about that," he noted.
According to Toffer, whether every spa will have enough guests does not depend solely on Estonian visitors. "Many other things also play a role here — for example, how accessible Estonia is, whether we have flight connections, what will happen with airBaltic," she explained. Toffer stated that when designing a tourism service, foreign visitors are always considered as well.
Foreign visitors are also needed
"Certainly, we also need to do something at the national level to find visitors from other target markets outside Estonia who would come to Estonia because of the spas," she said. Toffer explained that this requires better marketing messages and promoting Estonia even more as a health‑oriented country.
While it is often visible how various companies close their doors because customers do not have the money to visit them, this is not seen much with spas. "Perhaps spa entrepreneurs have been more patient and have become accustomed to the fact that this is not a very profitable business," Toffer suggested.
She explained that in the current economy most entrepreneurs are trying to make ends meet, and if many more spas are added, it is not excluded that someone may have to close their doors.
"Entrepreneurs have a very high tax burden, and our VAT is unreasonably high compared to neighboring competitor countries," Toffer said. She added that if someone decides to end their activity in the current economic environment, they cannot be blamed for it.

French economists urge $140B deficit reduction, sweeping policy reforms

Necva Tastan Sevinc
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
France’s Council of Economic Analysis urged policymakers to reduce the public deficit by €125 billion ($140 billion) by 2032 and overhaul public policies, Le Monde reported Thursday.
All 23 members of the council, which advises the prime minister, signed its first collective note since 2014, warning that policies pursued over the past three decades had become unsustainable.
The economists identified population aging, deteriorating public finances, weak productivity growth and declining educational performance as major challenges, alongside rising poverty and wealth inequality.
They warned that higher interest rates could trigger an uncontrolled increase in public debt, forcing France to repair its finances urgently on terms it could no longer determine.
The council recommended achieving roughly half the proposed deficit reduction during the first two years to restore market confidence and stabilize debt within five years.
Drawing on previous reports, it outlined 150 possible measures, including freezes on central and local government spending, changes to pension indexation, higher taxes and reductions in business subsidies.
The options include restoring housing or wealth taxes and raising value-added and corporate taxes.
The economists also proposed scaling back research tax credits to limit windfall benefits for large companies.
They argued that the adjustment could not fall mainly on a small section of the population or depend on uncertain future growth.
Alongside fiscal consolidation, the council called for €4 billion in additional annual investment in schools, wider adoption of digital technologies and artificial intelligence, and a “France 2040” innovation program.
It also urged stronger climate adaptation measures and higher taxation of large inheritances to address inequalities linked to inherited wealth.
The appeal comes seven months before France’s 2027 presidential election.

US retaliates after being labeled disinformation threat in EU – media
Washington has reportedly pressured several governments to withdraw their support for a conference organized by an EU-funded “anti-disinfo” NGO that designated the US a potential source of foreign disinformation.
The event host is EU DisinfoLab, one of Brussels’ info-gatekeepers deployed to scapegoat and smear dissidents opposing the bloc’s political course. The NGO notoriously launched its career by labeling online critics of French President Emmanuel Macron as “Russophiles.”
Organizers of the #Disinfo2026 conference in Vilnius, Lithuania, reportedly classified the US as a “foreign information manipulation and interference” (FIMI) actor, according to two news outlets with insider sources in Brussels. The EU normally uses the term to describe alleged malicious online activities by geopolitical rivals such as Russia and China.
By the time the conference opened, the logos of the EU’s diplomatic service, the European External Action Service (EEAS), and the foreign ministries of Canada and Lithuania had disappeared from all material, leaving only the French Foreign Ministry and the Vilnius city administration.
Rapporteur, formerly known as Euractiv, attributed the changes to a pressure campaign initiated by American writer Michael Shellenberger, who withdrew as a speaker after learning that the US had been designated a FIMI actor.
Politico cited the US State Department and cables instructing American embassies to convey Washington’s objections.
“Labeling the United States a ‘FIMI threat’ – a term normally reserved for describing influence operations of adversaries – undermines shared goals and should alarm those involved,” officials told the outlet.
Experts in (spreading) disinformation
The Russiagate hoax, involving a concerted campaign by former US President Barack Obama and his secretary of state, Hillary Clinton, to falsely claim US President Donald Trump was somehow compromised by links to Russia, helped fuel the emergence of an industry of self-described experts in combating online disinformation and misinformation. Critics have accused such organizations of serving as proxies for government-backed censorship that authorities cannot impose directly.
Belgium-based EU DisinfoLab first attracted widespread attention in 2018, when it alleged Russian efforts to amplify a political scandal involving Macron’s security aide, Alexandre Benalla, who had been filmed assaulting protesters while wearing police equipment.
The NGO’s research identified alleged “Russian bots” and “French Russophile” Twitter accounts supposedly fueling public outrage over the affair. Critics questioned its methodology, prompting the organization to publish detailed information about the accounts it had studied, including those of opposition politicians Jean-Luc Melenchon and Marine Le Pen.
In 2022, the Belgian Data Protection Authority (APD) fined EU DisinfoLab €2,700 ($3,000) and its lead researcher, Nicolas Vanderbiest, €1,200 ($1,300), while formally reprimanding both. The regulator, which investigated the case in cooperation with France’s data protection authority, the CNIL, found that the researchers had unlawfully processed personal data revealing political opinions and exposed users to potential discrimination through political profiling.
The decision prompted French National Rally MEP Virginie Joron to question whether EU DisinfoLab should continue receiving funding from Brussels. Grants allocated by the European Commission to the NGO over the years have added up to at least €1.4 million ($1.6 million), according to financial disclosures.
It’s a small disinfo world
EU DisinfoLab’s leadership reflects the close ties between the Western “counter-disinformation” industry and government-backed infowarfare operations.
Board member Emma Le Mesurier is the widow and former colleague of James Le Mesurier, a former British Army officer who helped establish the White Helmets in Syria. The Western-funded group aided jihadist forces in overthrowing President Bashar Assad.
Fellow board member Andy Pryce is a veteran British diplomat who launched and led the Foreign Office’s program intended to thwart Russian strategic communications. His name also appeared in the “UK Cluster” of the Integrity Initiative, a British-funded media manipulation project exposed by the leak of its internal documents in 2018.
Former board member and researcher Camille Francois worked on an investigation into the 2016 “Russian interference” in the US on behalf of the Senate Intelligence Committee.
Laser-focused away from Western disinformation
The EU DisinfoLab annual conference program includes a yoga session and discussions of “identity-based disinformation” and “Russia’s global information war.” Cases of debunked Western disinformation, plentiful as they are, received little attention.
One example was the alleged Russian attempt to jam the navigation system of a plane carrying European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen over Bulgaria last year. The story unravelled when Bulgarian authorities said their monitoring systems had detected no GPS interference, contrary to statements by EU officials.
A similar case last month involved a claim that a Russian drone had nearly struck a plane carrying Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky, which Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store stated during a joint press conference. However, Moldovan authorities later clarified that Zelensky’s flight from Chisinau to Oslo had merely been briefly delayed by a drone alert. The drone in question crashed some 160 km from the airport.

UN mission in Libya affirms commitment to working with new parliament leadership

2026-10-08

Mutaz Wanees and Ikram Kouachi
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
The UN Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL) on Thursday affirmed its commitment to engaging with the new leadership of Libya’s House of Representatives and all its members to advance the political roadmap toward holding elections.
The statement came in response to the election earlier this week of Al-Salihin Abdul Nabi Al-Obaidi as speaker of Libya’s House of Representatives, succeeding Aguila Saleh.
The mission said it followed an earlier session attended by 102 members, with 98 voting in favor of amending the House’s internal regulations and establishing a rotating presidency for the chamber for a maximum term of 12 months.
It added that a second session held the following day, with the participation of 111 members, saw the election of a new leadership for the House of Representatives.
It said it would “continue working with the legislative institution to advance the political roadmap facilitated by the United Nations.”
The mission said the aim was to unify state institutions, implement urgent reforms and hold elections within the timeframe stipulated in the agreement reached by the mini-dialogue committee in August.
Last week, the 4+4 mini-dialogue committee signed an agreement at the UN mission’s headquarters in Tripoli to hold elections within 24 months.
The committee comprises four members representing the Government of National Unity and four representing the eastern Libya-based military leadership.
The 4+4 committee has been holding UN-sponsored talks since April 2026 to break the political deadlock and advance implementation of the UN roadmap, particularly on elections and the unification of executive authority.
Libyans hope long-awaited elections will end political and armed conflicts and bring an end to successive transitional periods that have continued since the ouster of Muammar Gaddafi’s regime in 2011.

'Leaves in the Wind': a song from a world where only sound remained  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:45:11 UTC
22:45:11 KST

On Monday 12 October, Justinas Stanislovaitis releases a song and music video from his mu‐ sic-theatre performance “Where the Sound Remained” – on what a person is worth once the applause has stopped
Vilnius – On Monday 12 October 2026, the Lithuanian singer-songwriter Justinas Stanislovaitis offi‐ cially releases the song and music video “Leaves in the Wind” (in Lithuanian, “Vėjo Blaškomi”). The song comes from his music-theatre performance “Where the Sound Remained” (“Kur liko garsas”), a post-apocalyptic story about a man who, at the end of the world, must finally face the question he has spent his whole life avoiding.
The performance is set in an imagined apocalyptic landscape. The cities are empty, the power has failed, and people fight to survive – for warmth, for food, for somewhere safe to pass the night. In such a world everything must justify its weight: what to carry, what to leave behind. And yet one musician sets out with the bare essentials – and a guitar.
That small gesture becomes the question at the heart of the piece. What is a song for when the only task left is to stay alive? What remains of a musician with no stage and no audience? “Am I worth any‐ thing if no one is listening? Am I valuable without approval?” The questions echo through an aban‐ doned concert hall where people once rose from their seats to applaud – and where now there are only empty chairs, darkness and the low flicker of a fire.
“Where the Sound Remained” explores the origin, essence and meaning of the human need for recog‐ nition: where the longing to be seen comes from, what recognition truly is, and what it means. Is our worth measured in applause, ratings and the gaze of others – or was it given to us before the first per‐ formance ever began? It is not a question reserved for those on stage. In one form or another, almost everyone asks it today, whatever their work – teacher or doctor, programmer or builder: am I of any value when no one notices what I do?
“Leaves in the Wind” is one of six original songs in the performance, each arriving at the point where words are no longer enough. Its chorus sounds almost like an answer the singer offers himself:
Maybe we’re just leaves in the wind,
Dreaming where the blue skies begin.
Still we rise while we can,
Leaving our light where we land.
The music video opens onto a cinematic world of muted, earthy colours: a journey across open country, fire and wind, and translucent memories drifting through the frame – the things that stay with a per‐ son even when everything around them has fallen apart.
The song is released in both English and Lithuanian. It is also the way into Stanislovaitis’s chamber concert programme “Between Silence and Light”, in which his original songs stand alongside his own interpretations of songs by Leonard Cohen, Sting, Nick Cave and Peter Gabriel. On stage: Justinas Stanislovaitis (voice, acoustic guitar) and Martynas Vaičekauskas (accordion, keys and lumzdelis, the traditional Lithuanian wooden flute). Concerts are planned in Riga, Gdańsk, Toruń and Vilnius – dates and venues are to be announced shortly at justinasstanislovaitis.lt.
CREDITS
Camera – Martinas Kaminskas
Editing – Justinas Stanislovaitis
Music – Justinas Stanislovaitis, Marius Matulevičius
Lyrics – Justinas Stanislovaitis
ABOUT THE ARTIST
Justinas Stanislovaitis is a Vilnius-based singer-songwriter, performer and composer. In 2014 he founded the band Justin 3; he has appeared on The Voice of Lithuania and, in 2022, took part in Lithuania’s national selection for the Eurovision Song Contest. He is the creator of the music-theatre performance “Where the Sound Remained” and the chamber concert programme “Between Silence and Light”.

Latvijas Banka is issuing a symbolic collector coin 'Chestnut'  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:44:44 UTC
22:44:44 KST

On Thursday, 8 October, Latvijas Banka will issue "Chestnut", a silver collector coin with gilded details, symbolically depicting one of the heralds of autumn. The coin gives a new expression to a work by the artist who won Latvijas Banka's open design competition on the theme of nature last year.
Chestnut trees were first introduced to Latvia around the turn of the 17th–18th centuries and were found mainly in the parks of manors. One of the great chestnut trees served as the inspiration for the prose masterpiece Straumēni by Edvarts Virza. Beneath the branches of the chestnut tree, the household and their guests are depicted celebrating or resting after a day's work. In the early 20th century, the renowned Latvian landscape painter Vilhelms Purvītis immortalised a grove of these trees in his painting Blooming Chestnut Trees. A small number of sweet chestnut trees (Castanea sativa) also grow in Latvia, mainly in Kurzeme.
Figurines fashioned from chestnut fruits have become favourite playthings for children, and chestnuts are also believed to have healing properties. Carrying a chestnut in one's pocket is believed to protect against misfortune. For women, good fortune has traditionally been associated with a chestnut in the left pocket; for men, in the right.
The chestnut coin is like a talisman, embodying all the positive qualities of the tree and its fruit. In Latvian, the word for chestnut tree is used in both the masculine (kastanis) and feminine (kastaņa) grammatical gender. This means that the tree, and now the coin, belongs to everyone. Yet the reasons for carrying it in one's pocket remain individual.
The collector coin "Chestnut" was designed by artist Kaspars Līdums, who entered and won the 2025 design competition on the theme of nature with his design proposal.
The collector coin will be available for purchase only on the website e-monetas.lv/en from 12:00 (noon) on 8 October. The price of the coin is EUR 147.00; the purchase limit for one buyer will be 3 coins. The mintage of the coin is 3000. The coin has been struck by UAB Lietuvos monetų kalykla in Lithuania.
CHESTNUT
Face value: 5 euro
Weight: 23.00 g
Shape: irregular; the longest distance between the edges of the coin, measured through its centre – 35.00 mm

Reverse
A relief depiction of a cracked chestnut husk with part of the gilded fruit shown from the back. The inscription "LATVIJA" is arranged diagonally at the top.

Plain, gilded
The horse chestnut (Aesculus hippocastanum) was introduced to Latvia around the turn of the 17th–18th centuries, first appearing in the parks of manors. It soon became a favourite tree for lining roads and avenues and for planting beside homes, valued for its rapid growth, shelter from the wind, and magnificent blossoms. Many chestnuts have grown into venerable trees, reaching at least 23 m in height and 3 m in circumference. One such tree stands at Billītes, home of writer Edvarts Virza in Jelgava Municipality. It served as the inspiration for the great chestnut in his prose masterpiece Straumēni. Beneath the branches of the chestnut tree, the household and their guests are depicted celebrating or resting after a day's work. The renowned Latvian landscape painter Vilhelms Purvītis, while living in Tallinn in the early 20th century, immortalised a grove of these trees in his painting Blooming Chestnut Trees. A small number of sweet chestnut trees (Castanea sativa) also grow in Latvia, mainly in Kurzeme.
From its spiny husk emerges a brown, smooth, and round chestnut fruit, cherished in Latvia both as a favourite childhood plaything and a folk remedy. Carrying a chestnut in one's pocket is also believed to protect against misfortune. For women, good fortune has traditionally been associated with a chestnut in the left pocket; for men, in the right. The chestnut coin is like a talisman, embodying all the positive qualities of the tree and its fruit. In Latvian, the word for chestnut tree is used in both the masculine (kastanis) and feminine (kastaņa) grammatical gender. This means that the tree, and now the coin, belongs to everyone. May you always have a chestnut in your pocket!
Activity of Latvijas Banka regarding the issuance of collector coins and 2 euro commemorative coins
Since 1993, Latvijas Banka has issued 98 lats collector coins and 66 euro collector coins. Overall, more than 50 artists from Latvia and 1 artist from Ukraine have participated in designing Latvian coins.
The design of Latvian coins has earned high international recognition. They are regularly honoured with prestigious awards in various competitions. In the 2010 international competition "Coin of the Year", the "Coin of Latvia" received the main prize in the "Coin of the Year" category, while in 2020, the collection coin "Honey Coin" of Latvijas Banka became the "Coin of the Year" – the absolute global winner, as well as took the first prize in the "Most Artistic Coin" category.
The Coin Design Committee of Latvijas Banka, which has been active since 12 November 1993, plays an important role in the coin issuing process. The Committee consists of employees of Latvijas Banka, outstanding experts in Latvian art and culture, as well as artists and scientists.
After the euro changeover, Latvijas Banka has carried on the tradition of issuing collector coin series with motifs characteristic of Latvia and executed in high artistic quality. These coins are legal tender only in the issuing country. They are unlikely to come into general circulation, for, by nature, they are works of art enjoying high demand from the numismatic community and other interested parties.
The face value of collector coins must differ from that of coins in general circulation (it must be, e.g. 5 euro or 10 euro). Their specifications, including colour, diameter, weight, material, etc. have to be cardinally distinctive from those of the coins in general circulation.
For information on the collector coins on sale at e-monetas.lv/en and the Cashier's Office of Latvijas Banka, see https://www.e-monetas.lv/en.
The issuance of 2 euro commemorative coins (2 euro circulation coins of special design) is another area of coin art. Each year, every euro area country is entitled to issue two 2 euro commemorative coins (similar to 1 lats special circulation coins previously issued in Latvia), featuring events of national, European, or global significance. The euro area countries can additionally produce a third 2 euro commemorative coin, provided that it is issued jointly and that it commemorates events of European Union-wide importance.
Commemorative coins bear the same features and the same common or European side as the normal 2 euro circulation coins, while their national sides differ and feature a national commemorating motif.
Euro commemorative coins are legal tender throughout the euro area. This means they can be used – and must be accepted – just like any other euro coin.

Oleksandr Stepura's Skyeton: An Estonian-Based Holding Building Drones for Europe  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:44:34 UTC
22:44:34 KST

The Baltic states have built a reputation as a home for technology companies that think internationally from day one. One of the less familiar examples is Skyeton, a developer of long-endurance unmanned aircraft whose holding company is registered in Tallinn. Founded by Ukrainian engineer Oleksandr Stepura, the company has spent the last few years reorganising itself into a European group, combining engineering roots in Ukraine with corporate and manufacturing presence across the European Union.
Why Estonia
Skyeton's parent company, Skyeton Holding AS, is based in Estonia. For technology founders from the region, Estonia has become a natural choice for a holding structure. The country offers a transparent corporate environment, fully digital administration, e-residency for foreign entrepreneurs and a strong reputation among international investors.
For a company working in aerospace and dual-use technology, that reputation matters. Partners, customers and investors in Europe want to work with companies that operate within EU law and governance standards, and an Estonian holding provides exactly that framework.
A group spread across Europe
The holding is only one part of the picture. In 2024, the company launched aircraft production in eastern Slovakia, near Prešov, bringing manufacturing inside the European Union. The broader group structure also includes entities in other European countries, reflecting a model that is becoming common among technology companies from Ukraine: engineering talent at home, corporate structure in a business-friendly EU jurisdiction, and production close to European customers.
This distributed setup allows Skyeton to work with European suppliers and partners, take part in EU programmes and offer customers the reassurance of buying from a company based in the Union.
The product: endurance as a feature
Skyeton's flagship product is Raybird, a fixed-wing unmanned aircraft designed to stay in the air far longer than typical drones. According to published specifications, it can fly for up to 28 hours, cover up to 2,500 kilometres and operate at altitudes of up to 4,500 metres. The aircraft is launched from a portable catapult and recovered by parachute, so it does not require a runway.
Long endurance changes what a drone can be used for. Instead of short flights that provide snapshots, a single aircraft can maintain continuous observation of a large area for an entire day.
Why it matters for the Baltic region
Several of the use cases for long-endurance drones are especially relevant to the Baltic states. Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania share long land borders on the EU's eastern frontier, and monitoring them continuously is a significant operational challenge. Persistent aerial observation can support border services by covering remote sections where ground patrols are limited.
The region also has an extensive coastline along the Baltic Sea. Maritime monitoring, from detecting oil spills to supporting search and rescue, is another area where an aircraft that stays airborne for a full day offers clear advantages over helicopters. Large forested areas add environmental tasks such as early wildfire detection, while monitoring of energy infrastructure, including pipelines, power lines and undersea cable landing points, has become a growing priority across the region.
A regional voice on dual-use technology
Oleksandr Stepura has taken part in regional discussions on the future of technology and security. At the Lublin Triangle Economic Forum, which brings together Lithuania, Poland and Ukraine, he joined a panel on high technology and dual-use goods. The discussion focused on rising demand for unmanned systems, the challenges facing the security sector and the role of EU funding in developing high-tech industry across the participating countries.
The message from that panel resonates in the Baltics: investment in European technology capacity today is closely connected to the region's long-term security and economic resilience.
From engineering startup to European group
Skyeton's development has been studied beyond the industry itself. IMD, the Swiss business school, published a case study on the company, examining how a startup from Eastern Europe reached technical parity with much larger global manufacturers and the strategic choices it faced as it grew, from moving beyond government customers to deciding whether to sell products or services.
Under Oleksandr Stepura's leadership, the company has followed a path that many technology firms in the region are now taking: build deep engineering expertise, then scale through European structures and partnerships. With its holding in Estonia and production in Slovakia, Skyeton is an example of how Ukrainian technology and the wider European ecosystem, including the Baltic states, are becoming increasingly connected.

Russia’s Defense Ministry proposes establishing rapid response units in military police
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:44:26 UTC
22:44:26 KST

MOSCOW, October 8. /TASS/. The Russian Defense Ministry has proposed creating rapid response units within the Russian army’s military police - the relevant draft presidential decree drawn up by the ministry is published on the federal portal of draft normative legal acts.
According to the document, it is proposed to add the term "rapid response unit" to the Charter of the Military Police of the Russian Armed Forces. It specifies that such a unit will consist of two or more military police personnel with an assigned vehicle, "designated in accordance with established procedures to perform, when necessary, duties related to the prompt suppression of crimes, administrative offenses, and/or disciplinary infractions, to detain the perpetrators, to repel attacks on military personnel and civilian staff, on Armed Forces facilities guarded by the military police, as well as to carry out other tasks aimed at ensuring law and order, military discipline, and combating crime among military personnel."
The draft decree also introduces the position of the "patrol duty detail." The patrol duty detail’s duties are planned to include ensuring public order and military discipline within the garrison area and its adjacent territory "within sight and earshot, where military personnel on patrol duty perform their assigned duties around the clock or during a specified period of time."

Laith Al-Junaidi and Ikram Kouachi
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
The Syrian Network for Human Rights documented at least 453 ground incursions by Israeli forces into Syria and the killing of at least 69 people between Dec. 8, 2024, and Oct. 6, 2026, according to the Syrian Al-Ekhbariya channel on Thursday.
The figures were included in a report by the group examining the practices and violations of Israeli forces on Syrian territory since the fall of the former regime.
The incursions were concentrated in the southern provinces of Quneitra and Daraa, and to a lesser extent in the Damascus countryside, according to the report.
The network recorded at least 162 cases of arbitrary Israeli detentions. Of those detained, 127 were released, while the fate of 35 others is unknown to the network and their families.
It also documented the demolition of at least 15 civilian homes by Israeli forces following the incursion into Hamidiya village in the Quneitra countryside.
The report documented extensive land-leveling operations in the Jabata al-Khashab Nature Reserve in the northern Quneitra countryside on Oct. 17 and 18, 2025.
In late January, the network recorded Israeli troops spraying grazing lands in Quneitra with a substance whose nature it was unable to determine.
It said Israeli forces resumed land-leveling operations Oct. 4 west of Al-Asha village and Al-Rafid town.
Regarding air attacks, the network documented hundreds of Israeli airstrikes on the provinces of Damascus, Damascus countryside, Hama, Latakia, Homs, Tartus, Sweida and Idlib, without providing an exact toll in the published data.
The figures come amid the continued Israeli military presence inside the buffer zone and at sites around it in southern Syria since December 2024.
On Dec. 13 of that year, the United Nations Disengagement Observer Force (UNDOF) said Israeli forces had entered the buffer zone and remained at several positions inside, stressing that the movements constituted a “violation of the 1974 disengagement agreement.”
A UN report issued in September 2025 also documented the continued Israeli military presence in the buffer zone and neighboring positions, pointing to Israeli steps to consolidate its presence in the occupied Syrian Golan Heights and territories it entered after December 2024.
The disengagement agreement signed between Syria and Israel in 1974 provides for the establishment of a separation zone monitored by the United Nations, while Damascus continues to demand the withdrawal of Israeli forces and respect for the agreement.

A controversial overhaul to electoral law that critics say is aimed at boosting Giorgia Meloni’s chances of clinging on to power in elections next year has been given final approval by the Italian parliament.
Meloni, the Italian prime minister, says the new system, which introduces a fully proportional model, including bonus seats for any coalition that wins the most votes, will bring about greater political stability, while opposition parties argue that it mainly serves the interests of those in power.
The change was passed in a secret ballot in the lower house with 227 MPs voting in favour and 164 against.
There were protests from opposition politicians who held up signs decrying the law as a “scam” and a “con” when the result was announced.
Opposition parties have vowed to challenge the changes in the constitutional court, arguing that the bonus seat element, which would be granted to any coalition that reaches a vote threshold of 42% of the vote, distorts voter representation.
Another contentious requirement of the changes is that parties and alliances would be required lay out their government programme and name their candidate for prime minister well before a general election.
Meloni, who leads the far-right Brothers of Italy, had made the vote a test for her ruling rightwing coalition, warning MPs from her allies, including Forza Italia and the League, that, if defeated, the government would face a crisis.
While there are tensions within the coalition, which has suffered setbacks in recent months and is under threat from the rise of new far-right rival Roberto Vannacci, leader of Futuro Nazionale, it has put on a show of unity and has stability on its side after becoming Italy’s longest serving government since the second world war in early September. Whereas the broad leftwing alliance, led by the Democratic party, is highly fractious with no clear leader or programme.
Meloni said the victory was a response to those who wanted to see her coalition divided. “Today we respond with action: we are united, cohesive and determined to fulfil the commitments made to citizens,” she wrote on social media.
Elly Schlein, the leader of the Democratic party, said Meloni’s alliance sought to change the electoral system because it feared losing the next general election, which is officially due to be held before October 2027 but could be brought forward to April or May.
According to a recent survey by Ipsos Doxa, the opposition coalition could reach the 42% threshold if it overcame internal divisions and managed to convince two small radical parties to join forces.

US efforts to persuade India to stop purchasing Russian oil and to secure market access for American agricultural products remain the main obstacle to signing a trade agreement between the two nations, according to a report by BMI, a unit of the Fitch international rating agency.
"We expect India and the US eventually to conclude a narrow interim trade deal, although the remaining differences make a near-term breakthrough unlikely," the agency said.
The conflict in the Middle East and difficulties in transporting oil from Persian Gulf nations have reinforced India's incentive to maintain alternative sources of energy supplies, the agency noted.
Despite a narrowing of differences between India and the US, purchasing oil from Russia and importing US agricultural products remain the most politically and commercially sensitive matters for New Delhi. India might potentially allow limited imports of US agricultural goods, but importing American dairy products and genetically modified crops would entail significantly higher political costs.

This implies that the direct benefits of the agreement could be limited unless a deal with the US secures preferential access for Indian goods to commercially significant sectors of the American market.
"India will resist costly concessions unless the US offers it a clear advantage over competing exporters," BMI said.
Trade negotiations between India and the US have also become more complicated due to Washington's efforts to reduce the bilateral goods trade deficit, which stood at $58.42 billion in 2025. India could narrow this gap by increasing purchases of US aircraft, energy products, technology, and weaponry. However, such purchases would not resolve US concerns regarding access to the Indian market.

Türkiye, China strike satellite technology deal for joint space development
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:40:16 UTC
22:40:16 KST

Türkiye and China will carry out joint work on space technologies under a joint R&D, product development and commercialisation agreement signed between TURKSAT and China Satcom.
The 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC 2026) continues at the Antalya NEST Congress Centre with Anadolu as the Global Communications Partner.
The congress is organised by the International Astronautical Federation (IAF) and hosted by the Turkish Space Agency (TUA) and SAHA Istanbul under the coordination of the Ministry of Industry and Technology.
Turkish companies are showcasing their products at the congress while also signing agreements with international partners.
According to information obtained by Anadolu, TURKSAT and China-based satellite operator China Satcom have signed a comprehensive protocol aimed at developing new technologies.
The protocol was signed at a ceremony held at the TURKSAT stand by TURKSAT Deputy General Manager for Satellite Services Selman Demirel and China Satcom CEO Ma Haiquan.
The agreement aims to bring together the engineering expertise of the two countries through joint R&D, product development and commercialisation.
Innovative products and solutions to be developed
The partnership between the two institutions, which began last year with capacity sharing, was expanded through decisions reached at World Space Business Week in Paris.
With the cooperation now moving into hardware and software development, the agreement marks a new phase of joint R&D and production in space technologies between Türkiye and China.
Under the agreement, TURKSAT and China Satcom plan to develop UAV communication systems, satellite-based Internet of Things technologies and smart border security technologies.
TURKSAT will also expand its solution portfolio by applying its existing capabilities in developing end-to-end satellite and communications solutions to new technologies and application areas.
The cooperation will cover the full process, from analysing market needs and developing initial prototypes to testing, validation and commercialisation. Turkish and Chinese engineers will work together to develop new products and solutions.
TURKSAT aims to become a leading technology supplier
Smart border security and Internet of Things technologies are among the other key areas covered by the agreement.
The partnership aims to develop specialised devices for areas without terrestrial communications networks.
The agreement also covers the development of hardware that will allow devices used in sectors such as energy, agriculture and logistics to be managed via satellite in remote areas without mobile networks.
Limited terrestrial communications infrastructure in many parts of the world creates gaps in border security and industrial data transmission.
The TURKSAT-China Satcom partnership aims to develop smart satellite monitoring and IoT systems capable of providing real-time data transmission in remote and challenging areas beyond the reach of cellular base stations or fibre networks.
Through these integrated satellite-based hardware and software solutions, TURKSAT aims to become one of the leading technology suppliers in the global ecosystem.
A joint steering committee with equal representation from the two institutions will also be established to oversee R&D and product development activities, with the work to be reviewed every three months.

Bestselling Hungarian newspaper shut down under Orban relaunches online
BUDAPEST, Oct 8 - Nepszabadsag (People's Freedom), a leading left-wing Hungarian newspaper shut down a decade ago in a blow to media diversity under former prime minister Viktor Orban, relaunched on Thursday as an online news site and weekly magazine.
The newspaper - founded during Hungary's abortive popular uprising against Soviet domination in 1956 - was abruptly closed in 2016 by former owner Mediaworks.
Staff said at the time they believed the move was driven by their coverage of Orban, noting that their publication was Hungary's best-selling daily paper. Mediaworks cited financial losses.
Nepszabadsag's new Editor-in-Chief Akos Toth told Reuters independent journalism in Hungary "needs to return to a very classic, news-based journalism, to ask questions again and not state an opinion."
The relaunch of Nepszabadsag is funded by four Hungarian businessmen mainly involved in real estate investments abroad during Orban's tenure, Toth said.
"They are transparent, not hiding behind complicated company structures," Toth said, adding that, with Orban out of power since his April election defeat, the investors saw a business opportunity in reviving the widely recognised brand.
HUNGARY IS A TOUGH MARKET FOR A NEW OUTLET, EXPERT SAYS
Orban's Fidesz, which had a firm grip on Hungary's institutions for 16 years, is now backed by just one-fifth of voters. Hungary's parliament has set a two-term limit for prime ministers, effectively barring Orban from returning to power.
During his years in power, critics said media pluralism eroded as state media came under tighter government control and several private outlets - including Nepszabadsag - were shut down or acquired by pro-government owners.
Critics then accused the government of silencing dissent, but Orban's government denied exerting pressure on the media and said Hungary met European Union standards on media freedom.
The new outlet will employ about 90 staff members, mostly former employees of Nepszabadsag or left-wing daily Nepszava, which ceased its print edition in May.
The investors acquired Nepszava and rights to the Nepszabadsag brand last month, Toth said, committing to finance operations for two years with plans to break even through advertising revenue and subscriptions.
Market challenges persist, however, with Hungary's media heavily affected by distortions from state advertising channelled to political allies under successive Orban administrations.
Agnes Urban of the think tank Mertek Media Monitor said that market-based advertising money has not replaced state advertising, and companies are more interested in advertising near entertainment content than politics and news.
"It is a tough scene for a startup, and Nepszabadsag will be exactly that after a hiatus of 10 years." REUTERS
