Search warrants used in Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor raids were unlawful, court rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:38:20 UTC
22:38:20 KST

Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has won his legal challenge against Thames Valley police over search warrants used to raid his home after they arrested him.
The former prince brought a judicial review of the legality of the force’s actions and those of the central criminal court, which granted the warrants.
On Thursday, Mr Justice Hilliard, sitting at the high court in central London, said Thames Valley police (TVP) had conceded that it obtained the search powers under the wrong statutory provision and ruled that the warrants were unlawful.
The episode is embarrassing for TVP but police believe it will not affect the success of the investigation.
The warrants were issued by an Old Bailey judge on 18 February and Mountbatten-Windsor was subsequently arrested the following day, on his 66th birthday, on suspicion of misconduct in public office.
The arrest followed information that emerged from the Jeffrey Epstein files. It was alleged that when Mountbatten-Windsor was the UK’s trade envoy he shared sensitive information with Epstein, a convicted child sex offender.
Police began searching the former Duke of York’s residence on the Sandringham estate and his former Windsor home, Royal Lodge, on the same day as his arrest. Documentary material and electronic devices were seized.
Hilliard said the search warrants were quashed but police had made an application, which would be heard next year, to retain the seized property on the basis that it would have been lawful to take it under a different statutory provision. Mountbatten-Windsor opposes that application.
The judge said: “The fact that the search warrants were quashed does not bring the investigation to an end or mean that the whole of the investigation is unlawful.”
A senior police source said: “It’s not going to bring the investigation to a halt or affect the chances of success.”
They added: “The news media might say the police messed up. But it was the judicial decision [to grant the warrant] that was incorrect.”
TVP have been in discussions with lawyers from the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) about the strength of their case and what evidence they would need for a prosecution.
A TVP spokesperson said: “The agreement that led to the quashing of the warrants relates specifically to a decision made by the court regarding the legal basis for these and is not a judgment on our ongoing investigation.
“We ensured the court was presented with all the necessary information and paperwork to inform their decision, following the correct legal processes throughout.
“We accept the position that the initial court’s decision to issue warrants under the specific piece of legislation used was incorrect and therefore these must be legally quashed.”
Hilliard told the court that the grant of a search warrant under section eight of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act (Pace) 1984 was conditional on the issuing judge being satisfied there were reasonable grounds to suspect that the material sought did not include items subject to legal privilege or special procedure material.
Special procedure material includes documents in possession of a person who acquired them in the course of any trade, business, profession or other occupation – for the purpose of any paid or unpaid office – who holds it subject to an express or implied undertaking to hold it in confidence.
The judge said the presence of legally privileged material was expressly envisaged in the application for the search warrants and that material was likely to be in the possession of Mountbatten-Windsor “who had acquired or created it in circumstances which would make it special procedure material”. He concluded that a lawful warrant could only have been issued under section nine of Pace.
Nick Vamos, the former head of special crime at the CPS, said: “Given the technical nature of the errors revealed today, I expect the crown court to rule in due course that the police can keep the material, or at least as much of it as they would have been entitled to seize in the first place, so they may not ultimately pay much of a price beyond today’s red faces.”
Late last year, King Charles stripped his brother of his right to be a prince and of his dukedom over his association with Epstein.
Mountbatten-Windsor receives an annual stipend, the amount of which has not been disclosed, from King Charles’s private funds, but a palace source told reporters it had been made clear this should not be used to fund the judicial review.

Türkiye warned that the Black Sea must not become new front in Russia-Ukraine war
Kyiv • UNN
The Turkish Foreign Minister said that attacks on civilian vessels and risks to shipping and food security were increasing. At the same time, Ankara is preparing the Mecca Pact for ratification.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan warned on Thursday, October 8, that the Russian-Ukrainian war must not turn the Black Sea into a new front, citing the growing number of attacks on civilian vessels and risks to shipping and food security. UNN reports this with reference to Türkiye Today.
Details
"We must never allow the Black Sea to turn into a new front in the conflict," Fidan said at a joint press conference in Ankara with Hungary's Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs Anita Orbán.
Fidan said that Europe's security cannot be considered separately from Turkey's security, capabilities and potential.
"Before permanent approaches to security policy are adopted, qualified discussions must be held. Otherwise, it may be too late," he said.
He said that the Russian-Ukrainian war remains one of the main threats to regional and global stability, the publication writes.
"Since the beginning of the war, we have worked persistently to prevent it from spreading to the Black Sea," Fidan said, citing Turkey's "meticulous" implementation of the Montreux Convention regarding the regime of the straits and the Black Sea Grain Initiative as examples of this approach.
Fidan said that the war is now spreading to the Black Sea, where attacks on civilian vessels have become more frequent, posing a serious threat to life, property, shipping and environmental security.
"As countries of the region and the international community, we must never allow the Black Sea to turn into a new front in the conflict," Fidan said.
He said that Ankara is conveying its assessments and warnings on this issue to both sides.
"The efforts of the two countries to gain a military advantage over each other have a serious impact on the safety of shipping in the Black Sea," Fidan said.
He added that Turkish-flagged vessels, vessels owned by Turkey and vessels with Turkish crews had also been affected.
"We are doing everything possible to put an end to this situation," he said.
Fidan said that the attacks not only harm personnel and vessels, but also create risks to food security, especially when grain shipments fail to reach international markets.
"We need to prevent this situation," he said.
Mecca Pact
Fidan also said that Turkey had completed preparations to submit the Mecca Defense Agreement for approval by the country's parliament, emphasizing that the pact is defensive in nature.
"The work required to submit the agreement to parliament has been completed," he said.
Fidan said that the agreement provides for mutual defense if one of its signatories is attacked.
"As soon as a country that is a party to the agreement is attacked, you support its defense. This is not an offensive agreement," he said.
He also clarified that the pact does not allow Turkey to deploy troops to another country's territory to carry out an attack.

Beavers destroy sign warning about beavers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:38:01 UTC
22:38:01 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
A sign installed to warn the public about damage caused by beavers has been destroyed by the beavers themselves, according to the Polish foresters who erected it.
The incident was reported in a post on social media by the forestry district of Lubliniec in southern Poland, which shared photos of the sign, which read “Warning! Damage caused by beavers”. The wooden post it was displayed on had been destroyed in an apparent beaver attack.
“We wanted to warn you about the potential consequences of beaver activity at the pond and the surrounding area – since beavers dig burrows under the road and fell trees near the pond – but the beavers didn’t want you to be warned, so…they cut down the oak post displaying the hazard notice,” wrote the foresters.
“So, if you are around the pond, please exercise caution; and if you spot a piece of wood sticking out of the ground that has been gnawed by beavers, just imagine there was a sign there reading ‘Warning! Damage caused by beavers’.”
Beavers were once almost hunted to extinction in Poland. By 1928, it was estimated that only 235 remained in the country. However, thanks to postwar efforts to reintroduce the animals into the Polish wilderness, the beaver population has grown and is currently estimated at around 150,000.
Ecologists note that beavers play an important role in tackling drought by retaining water through the dams they build. Those dams also create “oases of biodiversity”, notes the state water agency PGW WP.
However, the rodents can cause damage to roads, houses and farmland, which has led some to call for culls to keep beaver numbers down.

EU presses Russia for more details on suspected plague case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:36:31 UTC
22:36:31 KST

Pressure mounts on Moscow to explain the suspected plague case in Siberia, which has put health authorities on edge. Brussels is calling on Moscow to come clean with precise details "as soon as possible".
The European Commission has stepped up pressure on Russia to provide full details of a suspected plague case in Siberia, echoing calls for transparency from the United States and the World Health Organisation (WHO).
Moscow has pushed back,insisting there is no risk of an epidemic.
"Let me say, for the third time this week in the press room: Russia should make information about the plague available as soon as possible," Eva Hrncirova, the Commission's health spokesperson, said on Thursday.
"We don't have enough information to assess the epidemiological situation, to assess the risks for other countries and to take appropriate measures, if necessary."
The comments came a day after the Commission convened the EU's Health Security Committee, bringing together representatives of the 27 member states, along with the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) and the WHO.
The committee coordinates the EU's response to serious cross-border health threats, allowing national authorities to share information, assess risks and discuss possible measures.
However, Wednesday's meeting ended without any specific decisions because of the lack of reliable information from Russia.
The Commission said it was ready to reconvene the committee at short notice if new information emerged or the situation deteriorated.
"We need information from Russia," Hrncirova said. "It's linked to the Russian membership in the WHO Europe: sharing timely, precise, exact information so that the experts can assess the situation because the situation can have cross-border implications."
The EU delegation in Moscow reached out to the WHO's office in Russia to convey its concerns, the spokesperson said, citing the lack of direct diplomatic contact between Brussels and Moscow since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
"Basically the whole world is waiting for the information from Russia," she added.
The case revolves around a female lab worker at the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute, in south-eastern Siberia, who died on 2 October in uncertain circumstances.
Her death was initially attributed to a "pneumonia of unknown aetiology", sparking global alarm and intense scrutiny.
Rospotrebnadzor, Russia's public health watchdog, says the lab worker was "vaccinated and had immunity to the dangerous infections she was working with", and that nearly 5,000 laboratory tests had detected no dangerous pathogens.
More than 90% of those who had contact with her have completed medical monitoring after being placed under strict observation, it said.
WHO has requested details to clarify the lab worker's death, the pathogen that triggered the quarantine measures, and a reported second case, which Moscow called "false".
The US has also urged Russia to provide accurate and timely information. President Donald Trump said he had scheduled a call with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, to discuss the suspected outbreak.
"We have officially requested additional information from the Russian government. We are also in official communication with other countries around the world to share information," a US State Department spokesperson said.
Pneumonic plague occurs when the bacteria responsible for plague infect the lungs. It is the most serious form of the disease and can spread from person to person. Without treatment, its case-fatality ratio ranges from 30% to 100%.

The Afghan Taliban’s Growing Drone War Against Pakistan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:35:00 UTC
22:35:00 KST

Pakistan’s air defense system shot down eight drones after they entered the country’s airspace from Afghanistan on September 23. Four drones were shot down near the border at Torkham and four were shot down near Kohat in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. In response, Pakistan struck 10 locations in Afghanistan that were being used to launch and store drones by the Afghan Taliban.
This growing use of drones has added a dangerous new dimension to an already fragile Afghanistan-Pakistan relationship. On its western border, Pakistan now faces a two-pronged security challenge: first, the direct use of drones by the Afghan Taliban against Pakistani security positions and other targets, and second, the transfer or facilitation of drone technology to affiliated militant groups such as the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), enabling them to conduct attacks against military check posts and other targets inside Pakistan. What was once primarily a tool of surveillance, propaganda, and battlefield observation has evolved into an instrument capable of extending the reach, precision, and lethality of militant violence.
The Afghan Taliban began using unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in 2016, initially for propaganda purposes. Over time, however, their use expanded into operational roles, including reconnaissance, surveillance, and the delivery of explosives. Between February 27 to March 15, 2026 the Afghan Taliban claimed responsibility for 15 drone attacks in Pakistan’s Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province and Islamabad.
The Afghan Taliban procures its drones from a mix of sources, including commercially available platforms, systems obtained through regional networks, and locally modified or assembled equipment. This has made drone technology more accessible and harder to control.
The Afghan Taliban’s 313th Battalion, associated with the Haqqani network, is using one-way attack drones, referred to as kamikaze drones. The Afghan Taliban drones are launched from Kandahar, Nangarhar, Paktia, and Paktika, reducing the distance to targets in Quetta, Peshawar, Islamabad, and Waziristan in Pakistan. Recently, the Afghan Taliban have reportedly acquired anti-drone systems and are preparing to deploy them at the 205th Corps in Kandahar and near Spin Boldak to counter Pakistani drones along the border.
The concern becomes more acute when this capability is viewed alongside the TTP and other militant groups operating from Afghanistan into Pakistan. These groups have shown considerable adaptability in adopting new technologies, especially drones. This low-cost technology gives militant groups capabilities once associated primarily with conventional military forces. For Pakistan, the challenge is therefore not simply the presence of drones, but the growing ease with which this technology can be acquired, adapted and deployed by multiple actors across the border.
Pakistan has so far effectively intercepted cross-border drone incursions from Afghanistan. However, it needs to take further concrete steps, as drone use is becoming a persistent feature of the Afghan Taliban’s military strategy against Pakistan.
The most worrying possibility is not necessarily that Afghanistan will develop a large drone fleet. It is the multiplication of small, relatively cheap systems. A conventional military platform represents a significant investment and is therefore used selectively. Small unmanned systems can be acquired in larger numbers and employed repeatedly. They can observe a security position, identify a target, test air defense responses, and also carry an explosive payload. Even when they cause limited physical damage, they can create disruption, fear, and uncertainty. Pakistan therefore needs to treat counter-drone capability as a central component of national security rather than as a specialized military requirement.
There has already been movement toward domestic drone production. Pakistan’s defense industry and armed forces have experience with UAVs for surveillance, reconnaissance, and combat roles. Indigenous production is important because reliance on foreign suppliers can become a vulnerability during a prolonged crisis. A country facing an evolving drone threat needs the ability not only to build systems but also to modify, repair, and upgrade them according to its own requirements.
Pakistan also requires a layered counter-UAV architecture. The first layer should be detection. Conventional radar does not always provide an adequate answer against small, low-flying drones, particularly in cluttered urban or mountainous regions like Pakistan’s western tribal borderlands. Pakistan therefore needs a combination of short-range radar, electro-optical and infrared sensors, radio-frequency detection, and other technologies capable of identifying unusual aerial activity.
The second layer is neutralization. Depending on the threat, this could involve electronic warfare, communications jamming, spoofing, and conventional interceptors. No single technology is likely to be effective against every type of drone. A layered approach is therefore essential for Pakistan to counter the layered threat.
Pakistan should also invest in artificial intelligence and data analysis. A modern counter-drone system should learn from repeated attacks: launch patterns, flight routes, frequencies, operating times, and target selection. The objective should be to move from reacting to drones after detection toward predicting likely attacks before they occur. Therefore, working in this direction should be a priority of Islamabad.
Airports, power stations, military facilities, government buildings, oil installations, and major communication centers all require appropriate protection. Border management must consequently become more technologically sophisticated. Pakistan’s long and difficult western border cannot be secured through conventional fencing and physical posts alone. Sensors, surveillance aircraft, drones, ground-based monitoring systems, and rapid-response units need to operate as one network. Intelligence sharing between civilian and military agencies is equally important.
At the same time, Islamabad must avoid allowing the drone issue to become part of a permanent cycle of escalation with Kabul. Retaliatory action may be presented as necessary when attacks occur, but military responses alone cannot produce a stable border. Each strike carries the possibility of further retaliation, civilian casualties, and a broader deterioration in relations.
The Afghan Taliban therefore needs to come to the negotiating table. Dialogue does not require Pakistan to abandon its security concerns or accept attacks against its territory. On the contrary, negotiations should be used to establish verifiable commitments by the Afghan Taliban: Afghan territory must not be used for attacks against Pakistan; militants should not receive access to military technology in Afghanistan; mechanisms for investigating cross-border incidents should be created; and both sides should maintain direct communication during crises.

Turkey says Russia, Ukraine increasing attacks in Black Sea ahead of winter
ANKARA, Oct 8 - Intensifying attacks by Russia and Ukraine ahead of the winter are further endangering navigational safety in the Black Sea, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on Thursday, adding that world powers must not allow the region to be turned into a new front in the war.

Turkey and the United Nations helped to mediate the so-called Black Sea Grain Initiative in July 2022 to allow for the safe export of Ukrainian grain amid the war, but Russia withdrew from the agreement the following year, complaining that its own food and fertiliser exports faced serious obstacles.

Estonia's military conscription no-show rate falls to 2%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:34:00 UTC
22:34:00 KST

Estonia's military conscription no-show rate falls to 2%
The number of young adults failing to report for conscript service in the Estonian Defense Forces (EDF) has fallen steadily in recent years, reaching 2 percent in 2025.
A total of 63 call-up selectees failed to report for conscription last year, down from 4 percent in 2024 and 6.6 percent in 2023, the Defense Resources Agency (KRA) said.
KRA Conscripts Office director Krista Juhanson told ERR that those who repeatedly skip required medical assessments without good reason can be subject to official orders and an enforcement fine.
She said fines for failing to attend a medical assessment, which are intended to encourage compliance, are currently capped at €640, with the exact amount depending on the circumstances. Next year, however, the cap will double to €1,280.
"It's important to note that paying the fine does not exempt you from having to attend the medical assessment," Juhanson said.
KRA can impose fines repeatedly, but if that proves ineffective, the agency can seek to suspend a selectee's driver's license or fishing, hunting and firearms permits.
So far this year, the KRA has sought the suspension of 57 driver's licenses. Juhanson said that in practice, these extra measures generally work.
"Once call-up selectees grasp that failing to fulfill their obligations can result in additional consequences, they usually come in for the medical assessment," she said, adding that the goal is to encourage compliance, not punitive.
More flexible medicals
The KRA official also attributed the decline in no-shows in part to a more flexible approach, including a digital pre-assessment review of health records and allowing call-up selectees to choose when and where to have their assessment done.
"That means no more having to spend all day waiting your turn outside a doctor's office," Juhanson said.
Being summoned to a medical assessment doesn't automatically result in a conscription order either, she added, as when and where a selectee will be sent for conscript service are decided only after the assessment.

Has Israel shut the UK consulate in East Jerusalem – or downgraded it?

Has Israel shut the UK consulate in East Jerusalem – or downgraded it?
British Foreign Secretary Miliband said the consulate building would remain but would called ‘UK Mission, Jerusalem’.
The British government has said it will retain its presence in occupied East Jerusalem after Israel removed the signage of its consulate amid deteriorating diplomatic relations.
The removal of the signage comes as Israel announced that 20 British diplomats, including the consul general, would have to leave the country and return home.
Britain’s Foreign Secretary, Ed Miliband, said on Thursday that the consulate building would remain but would be downgraded to the “UK Mission, Jerusalem”.
The Israeli government’s decision to close the consulate followed Miliband’s announcement last month that Britain would ban trade with illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
Here’s what we know:
What did Israel say about shutting the consulate?
In a post on X, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar reiterated on Thursday morning that “no action can be taken against Israel without Israel taking appropriate retaliatory measures”.
In retaliation for the sanctions on the occupied West Bank settlements, Saar outlined the four steps that Israel was taking against the UK, including:
- Removal of British representatives from the International Assistance Centre for Gaza
- Ending British activity to train Palestinian Authority forces in the occupied West Bank
- Closing the British Consulate in Jerusalem
- Prevention of entry into Israel of 12 elected officials and other British citizens involved in “anti-Semitic and anti-Israeli activity”
“We did not want to come to this, but the actions of the Labour government led us here,” Saar wrote, adding that the sanctions and the “hostile rhetoric” of ethnic cleansing of Palestinians had forced their hand against the British government.
“The British Consulate in Jerusalem ended its duties today. The Consul General and 20 diplomats are ending their duties and will leave Israel,” he said, adding that while the building is the property of the British government, Israel has allowed them to operate a task force of seven diplomats in the building with a “very limited scope of activity”.
The minister explained that the decision was also based on an understanding reached with the British government last night.
But isn’t the UK saying its mission will still function?
Yes.
In a statement, Miliband said that the British government had been “clear” that it did not accept Israel’s decision to close its consulate, which has been around for nearly 200 years, reiterating its “longstanding view that East Jerusalem is occupied territory.”
“The UK Mission, Jerusalem is independent, operational, and will continue to deliver vital services and our work with the Palestinian people.
“This will ensure that we maintain our longstanding British presence and the UK’s role in support of a two-state solution.
“Without an understanding, we would not have the necessary assurances for the security and protections of our staff and premises. Accordingly, the UK has temporarily withdrawn a number of staff and families to ensure their safety and security,” he said.
“We will work in the coming months to build back up our presence and we will not take reciprocal action while such discussions are underway and credible.”
“The UK stands steadfast by the measures we took on September 8 , in concert with the international community, in support of a two-state solution to deliver peace and security for the people of Israel and Palestine,” Miliband added.
Reports of reciprocal action against the consulate closure, including expelling one Israeli diplomat for every British diplomat who had to leave the country, first came from the Israeli newspaper Ynet, citing a message sent to Israeli officials.
On the consulate’s closure, Stephen Doughty, Minister of State in the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office, told BBC Radio on Thursday morning that the British government was continuing conversations with Israel about the issue.
“You can see what’s changed in terms of a name, but crucially a presence remains,” he said.
Asked about reports of a British threat to expel Israeli diplomats, the minister did not comment on it, but said they engaged with Israel in a “mature, responsible and practical debate”.
Reporting from London, Al Jazeera’s Camille Nedelec said the downgrading of the consulate marked “a low point in UK-Israeli relations”.
So is that a downgraded consulate?
Yes.
While a consulate mainly helps citizens, in this case British-Palestinian nationals, a mission usually refers to a diplomatic representative.
However, according to Vincent Fean, former British Consul General in Jerusalem, it did not “matter” what the consulate was now called.
“The Israeli electorate faces elections on October 27 and I think the plan of the British government is to wait and see what comes from those elections and to deal with whatever government the Israeli electorate chooses,” Fean told Al Jazeera.
“I think that the key point is that Ed Miliband acted correctly on September 8, specifically on the issue of E1 – the red line – settlement the Israelis are planning and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich says is designed to bury the two-state solution,” he added. The E1 settlement aims to link Ma’ale Adumim and other illegal Israeli settlements to occupied East Jerusalem, effectively severing the West Bank in two.
The British consulate first opened in 1839 but closed in 1914 at the start of the First World War. It was later re-established as a consulate-general in 1948 after the British Mandate in Palestine ended.
What led to this?
Relations soured following the new Labour government’s decision to impose sanctions on settlers and illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
Miliband announced the measures and said last month that imports of all goods produced by illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank would be banned.
In his speech, he said there was “ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank – perpetrated by settler terrorists.”
“The sanctions regime will target illegal settlements and settlement expansion, not Israel,” he said.
“We will continue to support important and valued trade with Green Line Israel precisely because we support the two-state solution, including security and prosperity for Israel,” he added.
However, Israel condemned the announcement last month and called it a “series of anti-Israel decisions by the Labour Government”.
Saar said the “accusations made today by the Foreign Secretary of the Labour Government in the British Parliament were outrageous lies,” and set out the four reciprocal actions.
Is the Israeli action legal?
No.
As the British consulate is in a part of Jerusalem that Israel captured in the 1967 war and has occupied ever since, it does not have the legal right to close the mission.
However, due to Israel’s ongoing occupation of the Palestinian territories, it practically decides what can function in East Jerusalem.

Scientists accidentally discover a genetic code that breaks the rules of life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:31:39 UTC
22:31:39 KST

Scientists accidentally discover a genetic code that breaks the rules of life
- Date:
- October 8, 2026
- Source:
- Earlham Institute
- Summary:
- Scientists accidentally discovered a microscopic organism with a genetic code that breaks a rule researchers thought was nearly universal. While testing a new DNA sequencing technique, they examined a previously unknown protist collected from a freshwater pond at Oxford University. To their surprise, the organism uses two genetic signals that normally mark the end of a gene to encode two entirely different amino acids instead. These signals were previously thought to evolve together, making the discovery particularly remarkable.
- Share:
A routine experiment involving a microscopic organism from a freshwater pond led scientists to an extraordinary genetic discovery. The tiny creature was found to interpret DNA instructions in a way researchers had never documented before, challenging a long held assumption about how the genetic code works.
The surprise came when scientists examined a previously unknown protist called Oligohymenophorea sp. PL0344. Two genetic signals that ordinarily tell cells to stop making proteins had taken on completely different functions. Even more remarkably, the signals had been reassigned to two different amino acids, breaking a pattern scientists believed was closely linked by evolution.
The discovery, published in PLOS Genetics in October 2023, revealed an unexpected level of flexibility in one of life's most fundamental biological systems. Subsequent research has uncovered additional genetic code variations in related microorganisms, suggesting that many more surprises could be waiting in the microscopic world.
An Accidental Genetic Discovery in a Freshwater Pond
Dr. Jamie McGowan, who was a postdoctoral scientist at the Earlham Institute, made the discovery while studying a protist collected from a pond at Oxford University Parks in England.
The project had originally been designed to test a DNA sequencing method capable of analyzing extremely small quantities of genetic material, potentially from just one cell. McGowan worked alongside scientists at the Earlham Institute and a research group led by Professor Thomas Richards at the University of Oxford.
Rather than investigating genetic code evolution, the researchers were trying to improve the tools available for studying organisms that are difficult to grow and analyze in laboratories.
But when they assembled and examined the organism's genome, they noticed something unexpected. The protist belonged to a previously unidentified species, and its genetic instructions appeared to operate according to an unusual set of rules.
Dr. McGowan said: "It's sheer luck we chose this protist to test our sequencing pipeline, and it just shows what's out there, highlighting just how little we know about the genetics of protists."
What Are Protists, and Why Are They So Unusual?
Protists are among the most diverse and least understood groups of organisms on Earth. Many consist of just one cell and are too small to see without a microscope. Familiar examples include amoebas, various algae, and diatoms, which are microscopic organisms often found in aquatic environments.
However, not all protists are tiny. The broad category also includes organisms such as kelp, slime molds, and red algae, some of which grow into large, complex structures.
The group is so varied that scientists generally define its members by excluding other major branches of life.
"The definition of a protist is loose -- essentially it is any eukaryotic organism which is not an animal, plant, or fungus," said Dr. McGowan. "This is obviously very general, and that's because protists are an extremely variable group.
"Some are more closely related to animals, some more closely related to plants. There are hunters and prey, parasites and hosts, swimmers and sitters, and there are those with varied diets while others photosynthesize. Basically, we can make very few generalizations."
Eukaryotes are organisms whose cells contain a nucleus, a specialized compartment that houses most of their genetic material. Humans, other animals, plants, fungi, and protists all belong to this broad category.
The organism at the center of the discovery belongs to a group of protists called ciliates. These creatures typically swim using tiny hair-like structures known as cilia, which move in coordinated patterns to propel them through water.
Ciliates are widespread in freshwater and marine environments. They are also particularly interesting to geneticists because some have evolved unusual ways of interpreting DNA instructions.
How the Genetic Code Tells Cells When to Stop
To understand why this discovery was so unexpected, it helps to know how cells turn genetic information into proteins.
DNA acts like an instruction manual, storing the information that cells need to build and maintain their structures. However, those instructions must be translated into physical molecules before they can carry out biological functions.
The process begins when a section of DNA is copied into messenger RNA, a molecule that carries genetic instructions to the cell's protein-producing machinery.
A structure called the ribosome then reads the RNA sequence three letters at a time. Each group of three letters is known as a codon, and most codons specify one of the amino acids that serve as the building blocks of proteins.
As amino acids are connected, they form a chain that can fold into a three-dimensional structure. The resulting protein may function as an enzyme, provide structural support, transport molecules, or perform countless other cellular tasks.
In DNA notation, a protein-coding sequence commonly begins with a start codon (ATG) and ends with a stop codon (normally TAA, TAG, or TGA).
These stop codons work like punctuation marks. They tell the ribosome that it has reached the end of the instructions for a particular protein and should release the completed chain.
When the instructions are copied into RNA, the letter T is replaced by U. Consequently, the corresponding stop codons in RNA are written as UAA, UAG, and UGA.
Across most forms of life, these signals have maintained the same basic functions for an extraordinarily long period of evolutionary history.
But nature has occasionally found ways around the usual rules.
Scientists Find Two Genetic Stop Signals With Different Meanings
Researchers have known for decades that some organisms use modified versions of the genetic code. These variations are uncommon across life as a whole, but ciliates are particularly rich in examples.
In certain ciliates, stop codons have evolved to specify amino acids instead of terminating protein production.
Until relatively recently, one pattern appeared especially consistent. Two of the conventional stop codons, TAA and TAG, almost always retained the same meaning. When their functions changed, both generally came to specify the same amino acid.
This suggested that the two signals were constrained to evolve together.
"In almost every other case we know of, TAA and TAG change in tandem," explained Dr. McGowan. "When they aren't stop codons, they each specify the same amino acid."
The genome of Oligohymenophorea sp. PL0344 told a different story.
Instead of functioning as stop signals, TAA and TAG appeared to encode entirely different amino acids. TAA specified lysine, while TAG specified glutamic acid.
Both amino acids are common components of proteins, but they have different chemical properties and biological roles.
Meanwhile, TGA remained the organism's only conventional stop codon.
The findings represented the first reported example of a genetic code in which both TAA and TAG had been reassigned to encode two different amino acids.
That distinction matters because it shows that the evolutionary relationship between the two codons is not as restrictive as scientists had assumed.
"This is extremely unusual," Dr. McGowan said. "We're not aware of any other case where these stop codons are linked to two different amino acids. It breaks some of the rules we thought we knew about gene translation -- these two codons were thought to be coupled.
How This Microscopic Organism Makes the Unusual Code Work
Further investigation revealed clues about how the protist manages to function with its unconventional genetic instructions.
The researchers identified specialized transfer RNA genes associated with the reassigned codons. Transfer RNA molecules act as interpreters during protein production, helping match the instructions in messenger RNA with the correct amino acids.
Their presence supported the conclusion that the unusual genetic code was a genuine feature of the organism rather than a sequencing error.
The team also found an unexpectedly high number of TGA stop codons in DNA regions immediately following protein-coding sequences.
These additional stop signals could act as a backup system. If the ribosome accidentally continues reading beyond the intended end of a protein, a second stop codon may prevent it from extending the protein too far.
That protection could be particularly valuable in an organism that relies on only one of the three conventional stop codons.
Although the researchers could not establish exactly how the unusual code evolved, the findings demonstrated that the machinery responsible for translating genetic information can be far more adaptable than previously appreciated.
Follow-Up Research Reveals More Genetic Code Surprises
The original discovery also opened the door to a broader question: How many other microorganisms are using genetic codes that scientists have not yet recognized?
In December 2024, McGowan and colleagues published additional findings in PLOS Genetics showing that unusual genetic code changes had occurred independently in several other ciliate lineages.
The team investigated genetic information from a group of ciliates known as Phyllopharyngea, including genomic data gathered through the TARA Oceans project, an international effort to study marine life and its genetic diversity.
Their analysis identified three previously uncultivated ciliate species in which UAG, normally a stop codon, appeared to specify leucine instead.
These organisms came from samples associated with the Arctic and Southern Oceans.
The researchers also examined existing genomic datasets and identified two additional ciliates, Hartmannula sinica and Trochilia petrani, in which UAG appeared to encode glutamine.
Evolutionary comparisons suggested that these changes arose independently on at least three occasions.
Importantly, the genetic codes were not identical to the unusual system found in Oligohymenophorea sp. PL0344. In the five ciliates examined in the 2024 research, UAA remained a stop signal while UAG had acquired a different meaning.
Even so, the findings provided further evidence that these two genetic signals do not always have to evolve together.
Rather than being an isolated curiosity, the original discovery had helped illuminate a much wider pattern of genetic code flexibility among ciliates.
Scientists Are Still Uncovering Hidden Protist Diversity
The search for unexpected biology in microscopic organisms has continued beyond the genetic code itself.
In March 2026, researchers from the Earlham Institute and the University of Oxford reported another discovery made possible by techniques designed to sequence individual cells.
Their study, published in Microbial Genomics, investigated Bodo, a group of common protists found in freshwater, brackish water, and soil.
By analyzing just seven uncultured cells, the scientists identified three previously unrecognized evolutionary lineages, each associated with its own distinct bacterial partner living inside the organism.
The work did not demonstrate the same genetic code changes found in PL0344. Instead, it showed how much biological diversity can remain hidden when researchers rely primarily on organisms that are easy to cultivate in laboratories.
Together with the genetic code discoveries, these findings demonstrate the value of examining microorganisms that have received relatively little scientific attention.
Better sequencing technologies could reveal additional unconventional genetic codes, unexpected relationships between organisms, and previously unknown ways that cells function.
Nature May Have More Genetic Rules to Break
For scientists, unusual genetic codes offer more than biological curiosities. They provide opportunities to investigate why the genetic code is so consistent across most forms of life and how evolutionary changes can sometimes alter its fundamental instructions.
Understanding these natural variations could also inform efforts in synthetic biology, where researchers attempt to modify genetic codes to give cells new capabilities or enable them to produce proteins with unusual properties.
However, the evolutionary forces responsible for the extraordinary diversity of genetic codes among ciliates remain incompletely understood.
What began as a routine sequencing experiment ultimately revealed that even some of biology's most familiar rules have remarkable exceptions.
As McGowan observed:
"Scientists attempt to engineer new genetic codes -- but they are also out there in nature. There are fascinating things we can find, if we look for them.
"Or, in this case, when we are not looking for them."

'European Jews want a connection to Israel – but certainly not most of them'

From Athens to Jerusalem: Why Israel should heed the warnings of ancient Greek history - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:30:20 UTC
22:30:20 KST

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s speech in Athens on October 7 presented the world with a clear statement of America’s current outlook on the world under the Trump administration. It also went beyond a statement of policy; it was about the history of the West and the importance of ancient Greece. Rubio discussed the values that underpinned ancient Greek civilization and the heritage that has come down to us through Western history.
This is important for modern Israel. Zionism has always been rooted in several sources. One of the sources is the Jewish people and their connection to the land of Israel. This is a heritage that goes back to the Bible. Zionism was also a modern form of Jewish nationalism, rooted in the era when European nation-states were being formed.
For instance, the First Zionist Congress was held in 1897, and Theodor Herzl had published Der Judenstaat in 1896. By this time, there was already a movement of Jews to Ottoman Palestine in the form of the First Aliyah in the 1880s and the role played by Baron Edmond de Rothschild.
Zionism came of age during an era of change in Europe. Modern Italy was founded in the 1860s, and Germany was unified. Serbia became an independent country, and the Greeks achieved independence from the Ottomans.
The Ottomans themselves were changing with the formation of the Committee of Union and Progress and the rise of the Young Turks. Early Zionists such as David Ben-Gurion and Yitzhak Ben-Zvi, studying in Istanbul, were influenced by this.
Fast forward to 2026 and Rubio’s speech.
Rubio spoke about the importance of nationalism and states that are strong. He praised Greece today as a model ally of the United States. He also spoke about how strong countries don’t allow open borders, and they invest in defense and manufacturing. These are values of modern Israel.
What might we learn from Rubio’s discussion of the ancient Greeks and today’s Israel?
Netanyahu: Israel becoming a "Super Sparta"
Israeli politicians are already in the habit of referencing the Greeks, particularly Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. He has spoken about Israel becoming a kind of “super Sparta.” What he appears to mean is that Israel will be a strong country in the region. Will it live by the sword as Sparta is reputed to have done?
In many cases, the concept of the Spartans being obsessed with war is a stereotype. In the Peloponnesian War (431-404 BCE), it was the Athenians who were seeking a kind of hegemony among the Greek city-states. Sparta was resisting this. As head of the Peloponnesian League, Sparta rallied states to resist Athenian aggression and the aggression of Athens’ Delian League allies. Sparta’s kind warned of the destructive war which engulfed the city-states.
What is Israel’s connection to all this?
Sparta did not have a large industrial base. The city eventually declined and has largely vanished from history. A visit to Sparta today reveals a small town. Athens, by contrast, is still glorious against the backdrop of the Acropolis and Parthenon. Nevertheless, the concept of being a “Sparta” in the Middle East is one that appeals to Israel. Some people want an Israel that is warlike and suspicious of its neighbors. This policy has defined the post-October 7 period, with Israel advancing into buffer zones in Gaza, Lebanon, and Syria.
Israel's allies, long-range operations
Israel today is engaged in an unprecedented number of conflicts. One of those wars is with Iran. This is not a war solely of Israel’s doing. Iran attacked Israel. Iran funded proxies to attack Israel. Iran sought to ring Israel with enemies such as Hezbollah. In 2024, Iran launched massive waves of ballistic missiles at Israel, claiming to be retaliating for Israeli operations in Syria and Tehran.
Ancient Greece also was in the grips of the necessity of city-states to engage in long-range wars. For instance, the siege of Troy, which lasted a decade according to Homer, was waged by sending hundreds of ships to the shore of what is now modern day Turkey. Greek city states had colonies all over the Mediterranean. Anatolia and the Black Sea were areas of Greek colonies. The battle of Troy apparently resulted from this.
What we know of that long war is that the city-states sent forces to the shoreline near Troy, who set siege, camping out for years. When the siege was over, and Troy was destroyed, the soldiers came home. The story told in the recent film Odyssey, based on the book by Homer, relates the disaster that befell those who tried to return home.
Is there a lesson here for Israel?
Israel’s decision to engage in long-range conflict with Iran has risks. This kind of risk was felt by the Athenians during their ill-fated Syracuse campaign. Prodded by the Athenian Alcibiades, the Athenians sent forces all the way to what is modern-day Sicily to wage a complex war. The war sapped the strength of Athens and turned into a disaster, leading to its decline.
Israel must be wary of its overextended lines, fighting on numerous fronts, lest it also find itself a victor but see its strength sapped.
Israel, like ancient Greece, faces powerful enemies
Like modern-day Israel, the Greeks faced powerful enemies. Foremost among them was the Persian Empire. The Persians invaded Greece several times, often with large armies and navies. At key moments, the Persians were defeated, such as at the Battle of Marathon and later at Salamis in 480 BCE. Is there a lesson for Israel’s current challenges with the Islamic Republic of Iran?
In both cases, a small state is facing a much larger one. Iran is around 75 times larger than Israel. Iran’s population is around nine times that of Israel. However, size isn’t everything. This is a lesson from the Bible in the story of David and Goliath. Iran, today, has a relatively weak economy and faces many challenges fighting the US.
The issue for Israel, as it was for the Greeks in the 4-5th centuries BCE, is that fighting a large country can draw one in and force one to engage in many other conflicts. Israel has this problem. Some Israeli officials have already said that they believe Turkey could become the next Iran. What they mean is that a weak Iran will leave a vacuum in the region and Turkey may fill that vacuum. Turkey is a member of NATO. It is more powerful and advanced than Iran.
How might we see a parallel here with ancient Greece?
Alexander of Macedon invaded Persia in 336 BCE. He conquered Persia and even invaded northern India in 326 BCE. As such, he had conquered much of what the Greeks believed was the known world at the time. However, this new Greek empire fell into infighting. The Greek cultural hegemony was felt in areas that are now Israel and Jordan. Greek-influenced towns arose in the areas of Beit Shean and across the Jordan valley, what Rome would call the Decapolis cities.
What matters for our purposes is that the defeat of Persia only led to brief success. In the end, it also led to infighting.
What Israel must learn from the rise of Rome
Israel could do well to consider the fate of the Greeks in the period of the rise of Rome. Israel today is a strong state. However, global changes are taking place. China is potentially rising, and the US is navigating a new world order that is as complex as the world order of the 1990s.
The Greek city-states also had to navigate these changes. After the victories of Alexander and the decline of his brief empire into infighting, the Greek city-states faced challenges from the Romans in Italy. The Greek King Pyrrhus of Epirus fought the Romans in the period 280-275 BCE. The term “Pyrrhic victory” comes from his wars. Even when he won, the attrition for his army added up to losses in the end.
What might that tell us about Israel? Will it suffer attrition from being overstretched in conflicts in Gaza, Lebanon, and the West Bank? Israel’s inability to have a strategy in Gaza, and its unwillingness to decide what the future holds for the West Bank could be a long-term challenge. Jerusalem feels today that it has the upper hand. It feels confident, for instance, to get into diplomatic spats with countries such as the United Kingdom. It assumes that, over time, the rise of the Right in Europe will mean less interest in the Palestinian issue.
Perhaps. However, what ancient Greece teaches us is that overconfidence and hubris can lead to ruin.
This was the case with Athens choosing war with the Spartan allies, as well as its Sicilian expedition. It also ended badly for the Greeks in conflict with Rome. At the Battle of Cynoscephalae, Philip V of Macedon was decisively defeated. Rome essentially annexed Athens in 146 BCE and sacked it in 86 BCE. In 63 BCE the Romans also came to Jerusalem, ending the era of Hasmonean rule.

The imagination that began it all: The Persian-Jewish poet bringing Genesis back to life - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:30:17 UTC
22:30:17 KST

As the annual cycle of Torah reading begins anew, Israeli readers once again find themselves facing the story of Creation. We have known it since childhood: from Bible classes and ceremonies to debates on faith versus science and countless commentaries. Yet, precisely because of this deep familiarity, it can seem as though no surprises remain. The world was created, humanity was placed at its center, Eden was sealed – and we move on.
Yet centuries ago, at the far end of the Jewish world, a poet named Shahin Shirazi dared to do what we often struggle to do today: inject risk, color, and imagination back into a familiar narrative. This was not imagination as mere decoration, but as a driving force allowing us to re-examine the foundational roots of human culture.
Shahin, who lived in 14th-century Persia, was one of Persian Jewry’s greatest and most daring creators. He was not simply a poet writing on Jewish themes; he was an artist who constructed an entire cultural worldview – deeply Jewish in its roots, Persian in its aesthetic language, and Middle Eastern in the scope of its imagery. His monumental oeuvre included expansive epics, among them poetic cycles dedicated to Moses, Ezra, Esther, and the Creation. His final masterpiece, Genesis-Nama, marked his most mature work – a tapestry where memory, faith, Midrash, and fantasy converge within a single vision.
The work of Shahin Shirazi
Shahin’s adoption of the Persian epic form was by no means accidental. He understood that stories do not survive on content alone; they live through rhythm, music, metaphor, and the heroic figures that stir a culture’s soul. He harnessed the artistic tools of his environment in service of Jewish memory. He did so neither apologetically nor to assimilate, but out of a profound conviction that Judaism could engage with Iran’s great cultural landscape and speak there in its own distinct voice.
This is not merely a literary question; it is a profoundly Israeli one: Does an identity gain strength by filtering out every external influence, or by encountering another culture without losing its own essence?
In Shahin’s work, Adam is not merely a naive creature who falls. He is a figure of cosmic, almost majestic stature. The Patriarchs and leaders do not appear as static figures from a textbook, but as heroes endowed with radiance, responsibility, and a sense of destiny. Shahin reminds us of a truth that Israeli discourse often forgets: tradition is not a museum exhibit. It is a living canvas, and every generation possesses the right – perhaps even the duty – to clothe it in the imagery through which it thinks and feels.
One of the most compelling concepts in his work concerns the tension between fire and earth. Azazel, created from fire and light, looks upon the human being formed from earth and concludes that a creature’s material origins dictate its worth. To him, fire appears superior: bright, intense, impressive, and immediate. Earth, by contrast, seems humble, heavy, and devoid of glory. Shahin subverts this perspective. Earth is that which sustains, receives, nurtures, and carries life. Fire consumes itself; earth enables others to be born.
This message resonates far beyond theology. We live in an era that worships the immediate and the flashy: power, speed, virality, victory, and visibility. Whatever makes an instant impression is valued over that which is built patiently over time. Shahin proposes a different hierarchy of values: a thing’s worth is not defined by its brilliance, but by its capacity to contain and nurture. The loudest voice in the room is not necessarily the strongest; true strength often belongs to those capable of sustaining life even when it is complex, slow, and unphotogenic.
This is also a vital lesson in humility. The tragic flaw is not merely a rebellion against a command, but a failure of vision. Anyone who sees only the physical material from which a human being was formed misses the divine breath placed within them. Anyone who judges people solely by their origins, status, or appearance fails to recognize their inner potential. In this sense, Shahin’s Azazel is strikingly contemporary: he falls because he knows how to categorize, but lacks the ability to imagine.
Even the Garden of Eden in Shahin’s work is not a product of simple nostalgia for a bygone paradise. Wheat becomes a symbol of knowledge hard-won through labor, persistence, craftsmanship, and the transformation of nature into culture. This offers an almost Zionist imagery of knowledge: not an instantaneous revelation from the heavens, but wisdom acquired through dedicated effort. Human partnership, too, is presented not as an abstract ideal, but as the capacity to build a life together within physical bounds, time, and human limitations. Perfection is not found in a pure spirit hovering above the world, but in a bond that manages to endure within it.
Here lies Shahin’s unique relevance for Israel today. For decades, we have relied on a narrow narrative of Jewish culture: East versus West, tradition versus modernity, Israeliness versus Diaspora. Shahin dismantles these dichotomies. He reminds us that Judaism can be profound without being closed, faithful to itself without being defensive, and Middle Eastern without apology.
Moreover, he brings to center stage a chapter long relegated to the margins: the Jews of Iran. This is not merely a community that survived, nor simply a diaspora to be recalled on memorial days. It is a vibrant spiritual world that created, renewed, and imagined, bestowing an epic language upon our foundational stories. It is an integral part of the Jewish home, not an afterthought.
In this context, it is essential to acknowledge the dedicated individuals and patrons of culture who work faithfully to preserve and transmit Persian-Jewish heritage through the “Bama Tova” organization (www.bamatova.org). Thanks to key supporters and families, such as the Ganji family and the Mahfar family, this rich heritage does not remain locked in an archive. It continues to breathe, reach the next generation, and claim its rightful place within Israeli culture. Heritage does not preserve itself; it relies on those who believe in it, invest in it, and carry it forward.
As we open the Book of Genesis once again, perhaps we should not rush toward familiar debates over literal interpretation versus Midrash, faith versus science, or past versus present. Instead, we might ask a simpler question: What do we choose to see when we look at a human being? Do we see only earth – weakness, origins, and physical matter – or do we see the capacity to turn matter into a vessel for life?
Shahin does not call on us to return to medieval Persia. He invites us to return to the creative imagination from which all creation begins – the fundamental power that enables us to see possibility where others see only raw material, history, or limitation. In an Israel where everything seems to have already been said about Genesis, imagination may be the newest way to begin the year.
The writer is a scholar of cultures and religions, liturgical poet, filmmaker, and director of the “Bama Tova” organization.

Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis have stepped up their deadly campaign of strikes on Saudi Arabia's capital, Riyadh, where booms were heard on Thursday, flights were disrupted, and some office staff were told to work from home.
The Houthis said they had fired a ballistic missile at Riyadh airport and repeated a threat to force Saudi airspace to close after the kingdom gave support to the forces of Yemen's internationally recognized government in a reignited civil war.
The conflict, now an overspill of the US-Iran war, has added new chaos to a region already aflame, and threatens to draw other states into grueling mountain fighting - with Syria now considering deploying troops to assist Saudi Arabia.
The kingdom has pushed for support from allied nations, including Turkey and Pakistan, even if only in a logistical or defensive capacity, as it tries to reverse Houthi gains in southwest Yemen, by the southern entrance to the Red Sea.
Those requests have taken on more urgency since Saudi authorities said on Wednesday that three people had been killed this week in strikes on Riyadh airport and Abha airport in the southwest.
Civil war reignited by conflict with Iran
The flight tracker FlightRadar24 indicated numerous delayed arrivals and departures at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on Thursday.
Several multinational firms based in Riyadh's King Abdullah Financial District (KAFD) told staff to work from home after Thursday morning's loud booms, five people familiar with the matter said, including some affected staff.
The Saudi government did not respond to a request for comment, and KAFD was not immediately available for comment.
Some diplomats said they had received warnings, and some schools in Riyadh told parents there were orders to shelter in place, though authorities did not issue a public alert. Reuters could not identify the source of the booms.
According to the Saudi Civil Defense Directorate, shrapnel fallout from a missile interception caused damage to a children's nursery and a medical clinic in Riyadh.
Yemen's long-running civil war, which paused with a ceasefire in 2022, has erupted again in recent weeks with the Houthis seizing stretches of the Red Sea coast last month, including along the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The Houthis, who control many of Yemen's most populous areas, including the capital Sanaa, have said they were responding to attacks from the Saudi-backed government, which the government denies.
Their threats to shipping along a waterway that has become ever more critical for Gulf oil exports since Iran's attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, and their attacks on Saudi cities and infrastructure, have drawn the kingdom back in.
This week, Saudi-backed forces launched a counterattack, taking back areas around the strait.
However, in a war with several frontlines, the Houthis have made gains of their own, surrounding Yemen's third-largest city, Taiz, by taking territory along its main mountain road to Aden.
The fighting, which pits the Houthis against a coalition of Saudi-backed forces under the internationally recognized government, has led to a humanitarian crisis in the poorest Arab state, displacing 200,000 people since the conflict resumed.
Syrian aid might be purely defensive, officials say
One US and one Syrian defense official said Syria was carefully considering options for military support, including defensive aid to protect Saudi Arabia from attacks, or an offensive deployment to help take the fight to the Houthis.
In response to a request for comment to the Syrian foreign ministry, a diplomat said Syria stood firmly with Saudi Arabia but that its focus was on domestic priorities such as recovery from its own civil war.
Saudi Arabia this summer agreed to the Mecca Pact with Turkey and Pakistan, committing all three to come to each other's defense, though Ankara has yet to ratify the treaty.
NATO-member Turkey said on Wednesday it was sending mainly defensive and technical support to the kingdom to help in the fight against the Houthis. A Turkish official said this was expected to take the form of military equipment, intelligence sharing and weapons systems.
Turkey, a close ally of Syria's government and a supporter of its forces while they were still rebels fighting the government of Bashar al-Assad, previously brought some Syrians to fight in Libya's civil war in 2020.
Pakistan has flown military equipment to Aden in southern Yemen to help in the battle against the Houthis, sources in Pakistan have said, and has deployed troops within Saudi Arabia to help defend its borders.
The Saudi and Yemeni authorities did not respond to requests for comment.

Middle East economy to shrink 2.1% in 2026, Gulf economies by 4.3%, World Bank forecasts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:29:38 UTC
22:29:38 KST

The economies of the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan, and Pakistan region are projected to contract by 2.1% in 2026, with Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) states expected to be hit harder, contracting by an average of 4.3%, according to a new World Bank report released on Tuesday.
Qatar and Kuwait are expected to be the hardest-hit GCC economies, with GDP forecast to contract by 20.9% and 14.6%, respectively, in 2026. The United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia are projected to be the least affected among GCC members, with their economies forecast to contract by 1.6% and 2.0%, respectively.
Qatar’s economy, facing its weakest growth forecast in decades, has been heavily affected by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Average monthly natural gas production in Qatar fell by approximately 67% between March and July 2026, compared to the same period in 2025.
Gulf oil production collectively has fallen from around 26 million barrels per day before to around 16 million bpd in March, according to the World Bank.
The disruption has also driven inflation higher across the Gulf. Qatar’s food inflation exceeded 12% year-on-year as of June, while average overall inflation remained at around 2%. In Bahrain and Oman, food inflation surpassed 7%, while headline inflation [overall increase] stood at around 3%.
Iraq, Iran face sharp GDP declines as oil production falls and inflation surges
In Iraq and Iran, GDP is forecast to decline by 12.4% and 7.7%, respectively, with both countries operating at just 55% to 70% of their estimated oil production capacity. In Iran, inflation has also surged, rising from around 32% in mid-2024 to 89% in August 2026, according to World Bank figures.
Lebanon has also felt the economic impact of the conflict, although its inflation rate has eased from the sharp rise seen during the early months of the war and currently stands above 15%.
Gasoline prices have risen by at least 40% in Lebanon, while diesel prices have increased by over 80%. Fuel prices in the West Bank and Gaza have also risen by more than 40%.
Oil-importing economies have proved more resilient, with regional growth expected to reach 4.3% in 2026, compared with 3.9% in 2025.
However, importing countries, like Egypt, Jordan, Morocco, Pakistan, and Tunisia, remain vulnerable to the economic fallout of the conflict. They face higher inflation as oil and other commodity prices rise, reduced fiscal room, potentially lower remittances from Gulf economies, and higher borrowing costs, driven in part by increased insurance risk premiums as the conflict continues.
World Bank forecasts 7.8% regional economic rebound in 2027 if conflict ends
Excluding Iran, the World Bank Group macroeconomic models projected that, if the conflict were to end this year, regional economies would rebound sharply, to 7.8% in 2027, driven by a recovery in hydrocarbon production, the normalization of trade routes, and base effects.
The global economy was able to absorb much of the shock from the blockade, the World Bank noted, as pipelines in Saudi Arabia and the UAE bypassed the disruption and brought an additional 2.8 million bpd to global markets. Brazil, Kazakhstan, Venezuela, and the United States also continued exporting, while inventories helped make up shortfalls, and global demand fell by an estimated 5.8 million bpd compared with pre-conflict levels.
World Bank warns extreme weather could worsen food shortages across the region
While the impact of the blockade has so far remained manageable for most countries, the World Bank warned that El Niño could pose an additional threat to food security across the region, where families are already facing risks from declining humanitarian aid funding.
Alongside Pakistan and Afghanistan, which are directly exposed through changing monsoon conditions and heat stress, the World Bank warned that Egypt, Iraq, and Tunisia needed close monitoring given existing water stress.

WTO raises 2026 goods trade growth forecast to 3.9%, cuts services outlook
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:26:34 UTC
22:26:34 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
The World Trade Organization on Thursday raised its forecast for global goods trade growth this year to 3.9% from 1.9%, as strong demand linked to artificial intelligence investment helped offset disruptions caused by the Middle East war.
The organization lowered its services trade growth projection to 3.3% from the 4.8% forecast in March, according to its Global Trade Outlook and Statistics report.
Global merchandise trade volumes expanded 3.5% in the first half of 2026, exceeding expectations despite shocks to energy, fertilizer and transport markets.
Trade in AI-enabling goods, including semiconductors and servers, surged 67% year-on-year, accounting for 47% of global merchandise trade growth during the period.
The WTO said the performance reflected the ability of supply chains to adapt, with alternative suppliers and transport routes helping maintain trade flows.
Alternative supplies cushion disruptions
Middle Eastern crude oil exports fell about 24% year-on-year in the first half, while liquefied natural gas exports dropped 47%.
Increased shipments from other suppliers helped limit the decline in global exports to 6% for crude oil and 1% for LNG.
Fertilizer markets also adjusted as alternative suppliers stepped in, while trade flows were redirected through other ports and corridors.
Global container throughput rose 3.9% year-on-year between the start of 2026 and mid-July.
The WTO expects merchandise trade to grow 4.1% in 2027, with services trade expanding 6.4%.
Gains remain uneven
The organization warned that the benefits of resilient goods trade and AI investment were not evenly distributed, with services trade and some regions more exposed to the conflict.
WTO Director-General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala said an integrated global economy and a rules-based trading system gave economies the flexibility to maintain supplies of essential goods during disruptions.
However, some economies had felt the shock more severely, while access to emerging opportunities such as AI remained unequal, she said.
She stressed the importance of ensuring the trading system continued to absorb shocks and narrow gaps so that opportunities remained open to all.

Early-onset cancer rising worldwide: Causes, risk, prevention
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:26:00 UTC
22:26:00 KST

Early-onset cancer: Why cases are rising in under-50s
October 8, 2026
The numbers are striking. Some cancer rates have doubled in the past 20 years. It's just not yet clear whether we're seeing a rise in actual cases or whether we're seeing more early-stage cases because of better awareness, diagnosis and treatment in hospitals.
Take, for example, colorectal (or bowel) cancer: In 2001, about one in every 26,000 people under 50 in England were diagnosed with it each year. By 2023, the rate of diagnoses was about one in 12,000. Twice what it was at the turn of the century.
That's according to the World Cancer Research Fund (WCRF), an international network of charities, which analyzed registry data from England, the US and the Netherlands. It found the number of new cancer cases had risen for seven cancers in England alone.
So, rates have doubled, but the numbers overall are still small, said Amy Berrington de Gonzalez, a professor of clinical epidemiology at the Institute of Cancer Research in the UK capital London.
"Cancer is still very uncommon among young people," Berrington de Gonzalez told DW. "Three times a small number is still a small number."
But she and other scientists still want to know why this is happening, because it is a worldwide trend. Latin America is a case in point.
Early-onset cancer rates rising in Latin America
A 2025 study analyzed registry data from 50 countries and territories up to 2017. It found early-onset colorectal cancer rising in 27 of those regions.
In Latin America, rates rose in Chile, Argentina, Ecuador, Costa Rica and Puerto Rico. Chile's rise — at almost 4% per year — was among the highest.
In Brazil, the evidence comes directly from hospitals. At the A.C. Camargo Cancer Center in Sao Paulo, the number of colorectal cancer patients under 50 grew by 7.6% per year between 2000 and 2023. That's a five-fold increase.
The number of patients over 50 grew even faster — at 8.1% — or about six-fold.
But since these figures came from a single hospital, they do not show whether cases are rising across Brazil. They may only reflect that this one hospital is treating more patients.
"We need better cancer registration systems," said Berrington de Gonzalez, "especially in countries like Brazil and Mexico, where obesity rates have also been increasing."
Marc Gunter, professor of cancer epidemiology at Imperial College London, said he expected Latin America to follow richer countries as diets there become more Westernized and lifestyles more sedentary. "I think it's already happening," he said.
These six cancers affect young adults most
In another study in 2025, involving 42 countries, Berrington de Gonzalez compared data from two age groups — 20 to 49 years and 50 years and older — between 2003 and 2017.
Six cancers — thyroid, breast, colorectal, kidney, uterine and leukemia — had risen among the younger groups in most countries. All but colorectal cancer were seen to rise in older adults, too.
In fact, colorectal cancer stood out. In about a third of the countries, it rose faster in younger adults than in older ones. "It is the one cancer that seems to be increasing in younger people whilst decreasing in older people," said Berrington de Gonzalez.
This has consequences for research. If cancers are rising in all age groups, the causes are likely to be widespread, so studies looking only at young people risk chasing complicated explanations with too little data to test them, she said.
Better awareness could explain the rise in diagnoses
A US study of pancreatic cancer in adults aged 15 to 39 years found the rise was almost entirely made up of early-stage tumors.
Death rates remained unchanged.
The authors said this suggested that instead of the number of cancer cases going up, it was the number of early diagnoses that had gone up. And that can be explained by better awareness in the community, with people getting checked more often.
But the data for colorectal cancer looks different: Some US studies show it rising in advanced stages of the disease as well, which suggests an increase in the number of cases, not just the number of diagnoses.
The link between cancer and obesity
Obesity is an established cause of at least 13 cancers, according to the WHO's International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC).
According to a 2021 review of existing studies, young adults with obesity were almost twice as likely to develop colorectal cancer before the age of 50.
Obesity has also spread fastest among the young. The WHO reports that obesity rates have doubled among adults since the 1990s and quadrupled among adolescents.
What you consume matters:
- Processed meat is classed as carcinogenic
- Alcohol is also considered a risk factor
- Fiber (vegetables, whole grains and pulses) lowers cancer risk
Some also say ultra-processed foods and microplastics cause cancer. But Gunter said the evidence was inconclusive.
"There's a lot of hype," Gunter said, adding that more research was needed. Berrington de Gonzalez agreed: "Diets have changed, but we don't yet know the role they might play."
How young people can lower their cancer risk
Gunter said individuals should not be blamed for living in societies built around convenience foods and desk jobs, and that lasting change needed public health policy.
But he also said that young people could lower their cancer risk by maintaining a healthy weight, moving more, eating more fiber and cutting back on processed meat.
"Going for a walk, being more physically active, eating more fruits and vegetables," he said. "Those things are maybe not so trendy, but they are really important."
For a 30-year-old reading this, Berrington de Gonzalez's message was one of reassurance: Cancer at a young age remains relatively rare.
Edited by: Zulfikar Abbany

The newly elected advisory body comprises nine representatives of civic organizations: Yevhen Linnyk (D7 Foundation NGO), Oksana Ihnatenko, Serhiy Verenчuk and Mykola Malukha (all three from the Center for Public Control NGO), Tetiana Yatsyk, Alona Shokarieva and Olena Reznikova (all three from the Ukrainian Legal Society NGO), Andriy Tkachuk (Transparency International Ukraine NGO), and Tetiana Nesterenko (Revival of Ukraine Democracy Development Fund NGO).
