MOSCOW, October 8. /TASS/. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and the "gang" in Kiev are part of the same corruption schemes, Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said.
She noted that the EU has firmly embarked on a path of confrontation with Russia, which will only worsen its problems.
TASS has compiled the Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman's key statements.
Merz and Kiev "gang" tied to corruption schemes
Ukraine is so deeply mired in corruption that there's little Zelensky can now do to conceal the true scale of the problem: "Ukraine is so deeply mired in corruption that the full extent of the problem can no longer be concealed. Zelensky's efforts to control the flow of information have done little to hide it, leaving only one mainstream television broadcaster while blocking other television news sources."
"Merz and this entire gang, of course, are part of all these corruption schemes. And he is coming [to Kiev] in part to discuss how the money will be distributed after being funneled through the Kiev regime."
Merz made German taxpayers cover the cost by promising Zelensky a new military aid package worth about €1 billion during his visit to Kiev: "These political bankrupts in Berlin have made German taxpayers cover the cost. They had just received concrete results of their policies. They realized that their own citizens not only do not support their policies in their own country, but are demonstrating their absolute rejection of them."
"It seems that Merz is once again emptying his own citizens' pockets, almost as if in retaliation. He is doing so despite their clear understanding of how futile Zelensky's efforts are."
The current German authorities need war, and Merz's actions prove it.
Nord Stream investigation
Russia will continue working through international forums to identify and hold accountable those responsible for the Nord Stream explosions: "We will continue our efforts, including through international forums, to identify and hold accountable not only the perpetrators but also the true masterminds behind this unprecedented terrorist attack."
NATO actions
Moscow views the possible deployment of additional NATO forces in the Baltic states as an escalation: "We unequivocally view the potential deployment of additional NATO forces, including US troops, and the creation of corresponding military infrastructure in the Baltic states as an escalation."
Worsening problems for EU
"The more problems the EU faces because of its own mistakes and miscalculations in its hybrid war against Russia, the more incredible and large-scale plans it attributes to Russia. It accuses Russia of having plans that do not, in fact, exist."
The EU has firmly embarked on a path of confrontation with Russia, which will only worsen its problems: "The European Union embarked on a path of confrontation with our country, initially under pressure from the United States and then simply out of inertia. And this path will not allow it to resolve its pressing issues, indeed, it will never allow it to do so."
The EU leadership "deliberately and consciously chooses to ignore this simple truth."
Merz is coming to Kiev "both to improve his ratings and to escape his own citizens," as well as to avoid criticism and public discontent within Germany.
Moscow has no plans for an armed conflict with Western Europe, and Russia is not threatening anyone: "If Germany's top intelligence official is publicly voicing his own fantasies, that means Europe really is in great danger. Let me repeat just in case: Russia is not threatening anyone. The Russian president and foreign minister have repeatedly stated that Moscow has no plans for an armed conflict with Western Europe."
Statements on Italy
Russia does not interfere in elections abroad, unlike Western countries: "There can be no question of Russian interference in electoral processes abroad. This is not our style. Western political elites openly interfere in election campaigns in full view of the world. At times, they even abduct presidents, put direct pressure on political groups in countries they are interested in, and, as I said, consider themselves free to do whatever they want."
Italian authorities' allegations of Russian interference in elections are disrespectful to Italians: "It is simply disrespectful to Italians to make such statements at the level of the foreign minister or any other minister, playing the so-called Russian card."
Middle East

Germany lifts 2026 growth forecast to 1.3% as exports, public spending drive recovery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:08:57 UTC
22:08:57 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
Germany on Thursday raised its 2026 economic growth forecast to 1.3% from 0.5%, as stronger exports and public spending underpin a recovery despite the Middle East conflict and rising energy prices.
Presenting the autumn forecast, Economy and Energy Minister Katherina Reiche also announced projected growth of 1.1% for 2027 and 0.6% for 2028.
The economy expanded strongly in the first half of 2026, driven primarily by exports and public consumption, the ministry said.
Foreign trade is expected to provide the main growth stimulus this year.
Exports received a boost in the second quarter as buyers built inventories of energy-intensive goods produced in Germany amid global shortages.
Fiscal stimulus through special funds and defense spending is also expected to support public investment and government consumption throughout the forecast period.
Private demand, however, is expected to recover more slowly.
Energy-driven price increases are projected to keep household spending subdued initially, despite continued growth in real wages.
Private investment is expected to recover only gradually next year, held back by geopolitical uncertainty, low capacity utilization, higher material and financing costs, and structural challenges.
The ministry said the outlook remains heavily dependent on developments in the Middle East and Ukraine.
A lasting resolution to the conflicts could strengthen the recovery by lowering energy prices, while persistently elevated commodity and energy costs could put further pressure on businesses and households.

Slovakia’s Fico calls nude Trump statue a sign of EU decline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:08:45 UTC
22:08:45 KST

Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico on Thursday called for the removal of a satirical statue of U.S. President Donald Trump from the European Parliament, describing it as a “sign of the decline of the entire European Union.”
Writing on X, Fico said that while he does not agree with all of Trump’s policies, “insulting our partners on official premises demonstrates a profound failure to understand the times we live in.”
The sculpture, titled The Orange Plague, was unveiled Tuesday by Danish artist Jens Galschiøt in the Parliament building in Strasbourg. The 2.6-meter work depicts a nude, gold-leaf-covered Trump perched on a frail man’s shoulders, holding a golf club and scales of justice. A plaque reads: “I am sitting on the back of a man. He is sinking under my burden.”
Advertisement
“It is sad that the leadership of the European Parliament, in its blindness, can no longer distinguish between the legitimate right to hold a different opinion and the actions of spiritually bankrupt individuals, adventurers and lunatics,” Fico added, before asking whether the Parliament would tolerate similar depictions of the French president or German chancellor.
The statue was removed on Wednesday, a spokesperson for the European Parliament said after publication. It was part of a two-day exhibition at the initiative of Danish left-wing MEP Per Clausen.
POLITICO was present at the unveiling, where visitors clamored for miniature replicas of the sculpture, which were distributed in several colors. The statue stands in a prominent spot at the entrance to Parliament’s Winston Churchill building, before the corridor linking MEPs’ and Commission officials’ offices with the plenary chamber.
Galschiøt said the work was intended to confront Trump’s policies and start a debate about how the U.S. president was “destroying the world’s only chance to counter the climate catastrophe.”
Clausen defended the installation in a statement. “If someone is so thin-skinned that they cannot tolerate this sculpture … then they have no place on the world stage,” he said.
“MEPs have the possibility to hold cultural events/ exhibitions in the European Parliament … These cultural events and exhibitions by Members shall be authorised in advance by the Quaestors who assess the compliance with the rules in place,” the European Parliament press service said in a statement to POLITICO.
Advertisement
“The rules in place outline that cultural events and exhibitions shall under no circumstances be offensive or of an inflammatory nature or contradictory to the values on which the Union is founded or likely to give rise to disturbances in the designated exhibition areas,” the statement says.
Fico has cultivated ties with Trump, meeting him at Mar-a-Lago in January to discuss closer cooperation, including civilian nuclear energy. He has praised the MAGA movement as “a vision that urgently resonates not only in the United States but across the world.”
The sculpture was previously displayed at protests in Copenhagen and the COP30 summit in Brazil. It is due to appear at next month’s COP31 conference in Antalya, Türkiye.
Trump has not commented on the installation.
Gerardo Fortuna contributed to this report. This article was updated.

Report says German ex-spy chief suspected of passing secrets to China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:07:57 UTC
22:07:57 KST

Ayhan Simsek
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
German investigators are examining whether former intelligence chief August Hanning shared sensitive information with a man from China's intelligence apparatus, news magazine Spiegel reported on Thursday, citing several sources familiar with the case.
Hanning's lawyer rejected the allegations. "My client is being wrongly pursued," Leon Kruse told Spiegel. He said Hanning had been in possession of confidential documents, but added: "What is incorrect, however, is the allegation that he passed on information contained in them to the detriment of the Federal Republic of Germany — let alone in exchange for payment." Further investigations will show that, Kruse said.
The federal prosecutor's office in Karlsruhe, which is investigating the 80-year-old on suspicion of treason, espionage and other offenses, declined to comment on the alleged China link.
Prosecutors say nearly 2,000 files were handed over
Hanning led Germany's foreign intelligence service, the BND, from 1998 until 2005. He was arrested on Tuesday together with his former office director, Manfred D.
Investigators say that after Hanning left the agency, D. supplied him for years with confidential documents from the BND. By June 2022, he had delivered "nearly 2,000 documents" to Hanning, the federal prosecutor's office said.
Prosecutors say Hanning used these documents in at least one case while preparing a security report, as part of his private consulting work, for a member of a foreign intelligence service. They also say he was in intensive contact with another foreign intelligence official. Prosecutors have not named any country.
German public broadcasters WDR and NDR reported earlier that the service in contact with Hanning was not Russian.
Alleged links to a retired Chinese general
Spiegel claimed that the suspected foreign contact is Wang Jianzheng, a retired Chinese major general and diplomat with ties to Hanning.
Wang served at China's mission in East Berlin from 1987 to 1990 and later returned to Germany, most recently as military attache until 2013. He is regarded as one of Beijing's leading experts on Germany.
Hanning made several visits to China after his retirement, Spiegel reported. In 2017, he and Wang apparently met at an official reception in the eastern Chinese city of Huaibei. A city record says the talks covered cooperation and economic development, and that the two jointly visited local companies.
The federal prosecutor's office declined to say whether Hanning's connection to Wang is part of the investigation.

U.K. Expands Sanctions to Cover 90% of Russian Oil Output, Shadow Fleet and Finance Networks

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:07:40 UTC
22:07:40 KST

Britain on Thursday announced sanctions targeting 38 Russian energy companies, shadow fleet oil tankers and financial networks that allegedly fuel Russia’s war effort.
“The message is simple: if you help Russia fund or equip this war, you will face the consequences,” the Foreign Office said in a statement.
London added 17 entities and individuals supplying high-priority goods to Russia, including importers of machine tools and electronics key to the country’s ballistic missile and drone capabilities.
One of the sanctioned individuals is Dutch national Alexander Jan Hendrik Tattersall, who is allegedly associated with the sanctioned Turkish trader Redwing Metal.
Britain sanctioned two Russian energy producers, saying the restrictions now cover more than 90% of Russia’s total oil production capacity.
An additional 12 tankers were also sanctioned, expanding the total number of targeted shadow fleet vessels to more than 600.
Targeting Russia’s alternative payment systems and crypto exchanges used to bypass Western sanctions, Britain designated five financial entities, including one registered in Canada and three in Kyrgyzstan.
The financial measures follow the U.S. Treasury’s recent crackdown on Russia’s A7 shadow banking network, which the U.S. claimed to have processed through sub-agents more than $17 billion in global transactions between January 2025 and June 2026.
The Foreign Office claimed two of the newly sanctioned payment platforms directly facilitated transactions for the A7 platform.

Russian truckmaker signs major deal with Mali

Russian truckmaker signs major deal with Mali
Russian truckmaker KAMAZ has signed a contract reportedly worth about $51.5 million to supply vehicles to Mali, as the landlocked West African country seeks to strengthen its transport network and secure essential supplies.
The deal with the Malian Transport and Logistics Company (SMTL-SA) was signed in Bamako on Wednesday at a ceremony attended by Finance Minister Alousseni Sanou and Transport Minister Dembele Madina Sissoko. Malian broadcaster Kati24 put its value at above 30 billion CFA francs.
In a press release on Thursday, KAMAZ said the contract falls under an intergovernmental agreement between Russia and Mali and aims to expand the country’s capacity to transport food and industrial goods. “In addition to the equipment supply, vehicle repair and maintenance workshops will be established in Mali’s capital, and the possibility of assembling trucks in the country is under discussion,” the company stated.
According to the statement, the parties also discussed spare parts, technology transfer, and training Malian technicians in Kazan, the capital of Russia’s Republic of Tatarstan. KAMAZ did not specify vehicle numbers, models or delivery dates.
The deal comes less than two weeks after Mali’s government approved the creation of SMTL-SA on September 25. The public company is intended to improve transport and storage of strategic goods, including fuel and agricultural products, amid supply disruptions and dependence on regional trade corridors.
KAMAZ already has a supply history in Mali, which Russian state-owned industrial conglomerate Rostec listed among the truckmaker’s African markets in 2023.
The company has also supplied vehicles to other African countries, including Senegal, which KAMAZ described as one of its important export markets. It supplied 167 vehicles to the country, mainly KAMAZ-5460 tractor units for transporting containers from the port of Dakar, and trained Senegalese drivers and mechanics in 2021.
The engagement comes despite Washington’s decision to sanction KAMAZ in June 2022 amid the Ukraine conflict, citing its supply of armored vehicles to Russia’s military.
The latest agreement adds to Mali’s growing economic ties with Russia in recent years as part of efforts by the transitional authorities of the Sahel nation to assert control over strategic industries. In June 2025, Mali launched construction of a gold refinery with Russia’s Yadran to boost national revenues through domestic gold processing, with the state holding a 62% stake. The refinery project followed disputes with Western mining companies, including Canada’s Barrick and Australia’s Resolute Mining, over alleged unpaid taxes and the implementation of a new mining code aimed at increasing state revenues and ownership.

Meetings under the roadmap are expected to be held alternately in Paris and Ankara, with the first planned for the final quarter of 2026, subject to agreement between the sides.

Türkiye has completed preparations to submit the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement to parliament for approval, Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on Thursday, emphasising that the pact is designed for mutual defence and does not authorise offensive military operations.

Ankara weighs defensive support for Saudi Arabia

He said Türkiye and Pakistan had discussed what support could be provided to Saudi Arabia against attacks from Yemen’s Houthi group, while stressing that efforts to resolve the Yemen conflict through peace and dialogue would continue.
Current reporting says Ankara is particularly assessing defensive capabilities, including air-defence support
Fidan warns against Black Sea escalation
Turning to the Russia-Ukraine war, Fidan warned that the conflict must not turn the Black Sea into another front.
“We must never allow the Black Sea to turn into a new front of conflict,” he said, describing the war as a major threat to regional and global stability.
Fidan said Türkiye had worked since the start of the conflict to prevent fighting from spilling into the Black Sea, citing its implementation of the Montreux Convention and its role in the Black Sea Grain Initiative.
He said intensified Russian and Ukrainian attacks ahead of winter were increasingly affecting maritime safety, including Turkish-flagged and Turkish-owned vessels and ships carrying Turkish personnel.
Fidan also warned that attacks on civilian vessels threatened lives, property, navigation and the environment, while disruptions to grain shipments could worsen food-security pressures, particularly in Africa.
Türkiye pushes for Gaza aid and political settlement

====================================================================================================

Student Protesters in France are Holding Signs Referencing May 1968. Here’s Why It’s Significant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:04:57 UTC
22:04:57 KST

French students took to the streets again Thursday and blockaded some high schools as they demanded action from the government they say is underfunding the country’s education system. Now in its third week, the wave of protests has seen hundreds of thousands march after rows over staffing shortages, overcrowded classrooms, and dilapidated buildings reached a crisis point.
The protest movement went nationwide on Tuesday, after student unions called for a wider support of their mobilization, with parents, teachers, and activists heeding the call. Some protests have turned violent, with attendees lighting fires and hurling projectiles, and police using tear gas and water cannons. Since the protests began, at least 6,547 people have been arrested or stopped by police, said France’s Interior Ministry. Hundreds of students and police officers have been injured. The French Education Ministry told TIME that as of midday Thursday, local time, 157 schools remain closed.
Throughout the protests, students and other attendees have held up various signs calling for change. A common theme has emerged, as many of the homemade banners mention the year 1968—and more specifically, May 1968. That’s in reference to the nationwide protests initiated by a student movement in 1968 that led to millions of workers striking and nearly toppled the government.
During the blockade of the University of Perpignan Via Domitia on Tuesday, a banner raised on the gates contained a warning, which roughly translated to “You’re trying to pull a fast one on us, we'll give you May '68.” Elsewhere, as students gathered in Reforme Square in Marseille, a protester held a sign that read “Generation 67 is doing May 68,” thought to be in reference to the Gen Alpha 6-7 trend. In Paris, someone held a black and white sign of a larger figure with their hand over the mouth of a youngster, emblazoned with the phrase “sois jeune et tais-toi,” which means “be young and shut up.” That same slogan was used during the 1968 protests.
“1968 was a seminal moment in the protest history of France,” says Chris Reynolds, professor of contemporary European history at Nottingham Trent University. “Not only because of the sheer enormity of what happened, but that it started out as a smallish student protest that within a very short space of time mushroomed to become arguably the greatest strike in French history.”
What happened in 1968 is anything but a distant memory, experts tell TIME. Not only do the youth of France draw inspiration from the rallying of a generation, lawmakers are also mindful of how powerful such protests can be.
“Ever since 1968, there has been a fear within the state that it could happen again,” says Reynolds. “This idea that somehow the students could be the starting point of a movement that would then elicit support from other sectors of society, leading to a much greater crisis.”
What happened in May 1968?
Students at the Nanterre campus of the University of Paris held protests across 1967 and 1968 in opposition of rules they viewed to be too restrictive and conservative.
“It was a crisis of education. At that point, universities were expanding very quickly in the 1960s,” says Robert Gildea, a professor of European and French history at the University of Oxford.
“Universities then were also very conservative and hierarchical,” he adds, noting that a lack of communication between the faculty and students led to growing frustrations.
One argument centered on restrictions on dormitory visits that stopped male and female students staying in each other’s rooms.
In May 1968, when the Nanterre campus was shut down in an effort to dampen escalating protests, the movement moved to the Sorbonne campus in Paris’ Latin Quarter. Students barricaded themselves within the university grounds and called for a reform of the university system, while accusing French President Charles de Gaulle of running a "police state.” Clashes ensued between riot police and student protesters, hundreds of which were arrested. A particularly violent clash in the early hours of May 11 garnered nationwide attention.
The protest movement expanded when trade unions came on board and organized a series of strikes across the country, demanding better pay and conditions for workers in factories and other industries. At the height of the protests, around 10 million workers went on strike, bringing France to the brink and raising concerns in government about the impact on the economy.
President De Gaulle dissolved parliament and cited a state of emergency. He called a snap election in June, which his conservative party ultimately won as French voters gravitated toward the promise of restored stability. The protest movement lost momentum and withered, but it left a lasting impact.
Gildea says many students now reference 1968 from a place of pride, while also warning a revolution could happen if the youth bands together.
“1968 was the last huge explosion of students and workers, which nearly brought the state down,” he says. “The French are very proud of their revolutionary tradition and all subsequent revolutions want to reference it as an appeal for legitimacy.”
In the years since 1968, French students have often taken to the streets to air their grievances, with notable demonstrations happening in 2006 and 2018—all of which have drawn comparisons to 1968.
“It remains this recurring reference point in French history, which seems to be passed down from generation to generation, without fail,” Reynolds says.

Iran is reviewing US feedback on Tehran’s proposed seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and expects to respond within the next few days, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Thursday.
“The negotiation process is still ongoing, and messages are being exchanged through mediators,” Araghchi said, according to the official IRNA news agency.
“We presented our proposal, which was called the ‘seven-day plan,’ and we heard the Americans’ views in response,” he added.
“We are currently reviewing them. I believe we will respond within a few days,” he said.
The seven-day initiative centers on reopening the Strait of Hormuz and resuming negotiations between Tehran and Washington.
What is the 7-day plan?
Araghchi said in late September that Iran could reopen the strategic waterway within seven days if Washington accepted the proposal conveyed through Qatari mediation.
Under the plan, the US would be expected to take agreed steps during the first four or five days, allowing normal navigation through the strait to resume on the sixth day and negotiations on a final agreement to begin on the seventh.
Tehran’s demands include an end to hostilities, the release of frozen Iranian assets, the lifting of restrictions on Iranian oil exports and an end to the US naval blockade on Iranian ports.
The proposal was discussed through Qatari mediation during indirect contacts between Iran and the US on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York in September.

Tension in Hormuz
Iran has kept the Strait of Hormuz restricted while demanding that Washington fulfill commitments under a June memorandum of understanding. Iran says the waterway will not fully reopen until Iran’s conditions are met and US commitments are implemented.
The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on Feb. 28. Tehran responded with missile and drone attacks across the region and effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, while the US later imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports.
Washington and Tehran later signed a memorandum of understanding in June concerning freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, but implementation stalled over disagreements related to security in the strategic waterway.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher

By Kārlis Mārtiņš Gulbis, Investment Analyst, Signet Bank.
In September the war found its second chokepoint, and markets followed. After Hormuz came the Bab el-Mandeb: the Houthis seized the Yemeni port of Mokha and then Perim Island, which sits in the strait itself. At the same time, drones launched from Iraq forced Saudi Arabia to shut its East-West pipeline, the kingdom’s main route around Hormuz. Brent jumped to around USD 110/bbl, its highest since May. Refined products felt the squeeze most as US diesel hit a record USD 6.53/gal on 22 September, and with midterms on 3 November Trump backed a ban on diesel exports, which had reached a record 1.6m bbl/d in August.
As expected, central banks stopped looking through the energy shock, and three of the majors raised rates within eight days. Then came the flash PMI – US business activity grew at its fastest pace since July 2021, and the selloff that followed carried the 30-year Treasury yield above 5.61% on 29 September, a level last seen in 2002.
The S&P 500 slipped 0.5% and the Dow fell 4.3%, ending a five-month winning streak, while the Nasdaq Composite gained 1.9% as technology was the only S&P 500 sector to finish higher. The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq still closed a second straight quarterly gain. Financials, down around 7%, had their worst month since March 2023, while the STOXX 600 lost 2.5%, ending its own five month run. Gold fell about 6.5%, and Brent eased back to around USD 100/bbl at the end of the month
Back in the hiking business
Strong data left the Fed little choice. August payrolls rose 162k, about three times expectations, and CPI held at 3.4% YoY with energy up 16.3%. On 16 September the FOMC voted 12-0 to raise its target range by 25bp to 3.75%-4.00%, its first hike since July 2023, and 16 of 18 officials projected another hike before year end. Trump replied within hours that US rates “should be 1%, or less”.
The ECB had lifted its deposit rate to 2.50% on 10 September, and the Bank of Japan raised its policy rate to 1.25%, the highest since 1995, on 18 September.
Five percent and counting
In August the pressure on long-dated debt came from supply worries; in September it came from central banks. Almost all of the 49bp rise in the 10-year Treasury yield, to 5.29%, ran through real yields, with the 10-year TIPS yield up about 44bp, its fastest climb in four years. However, this time a central bank blinked: the Bank of England slowed QT, will no longer sell its longest-dated gilts and paused active sales pending a review before April 2027.
France moved from strained to stressed, as the OAT-Bund spread broke 100bp for the first time since the euro area debt crisis and reached 140bp in early October, when the government presented a 2027 budget built on EUR 54b of savings.
A red carpet and a short extension
Xi Jinping’s 23-25 September state visit, his first to Washington since 2015, came with full ceremony but modest results. The trade truce was extended only to 10 January 2027, two months beyond its November expiry. The two sides agreed lower tariffs on USD 30b of non-sensitive goods each way, Chinese purchases of at least 10m tonnes of US coal in both 2027 and 2028 and a new dialogue on advanced AI, but rare earths stayed unresolved after China’s magnet shipments to the US fell 21%.
Pacing the frontier
On 12 September Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei urged AI labs to slow frontier development so safety work can keep up, Sam Altman and Elon Musk agreed. Two days later the Philadelphia
Semiconductor Index fell 5.9% and the KOSPI 3.3%. On 25 September OpenAI paused training of its most capable models after an agent slipped past internet restrictions in testing.
Meanwhile, local opposition blocked or delayed 45 US data centers worth USD 68b in Q2. Spending did not slow however as Nvidia rose almost 3% after a record USD 150b buyback increase.
Micron’s fiscal Q4 revenue reached USD 54.2b, nearly five times a year earlier, and it guided USD 61.5b for this quarter
Firmer dollar and tarnished metals
Currencies remain confined to their familiar range, though shifts in market behavior hint at rising volatility. The dollar has edged toward the stronger side of its neutral zone, and although its next move remains unsettled, we still favor buying it on dips. A EUR/USD climb to 1.1600 would signal renewed dollar weakness, while support at 1.1150-1.1200 should ideally hold, allowing a rebound toward 1.1400-1.1500; failing that, a far steeper decline could follow. Precious metals remain unattractive, with gold especially vulnerable to a deeper fall.

Brain replays motor skills during sleep without help from the memory center
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:00:37 UTC
22:00:37 KST

When we sleep, our brains replay the events of the day to solidify new skills, a process scientists previously thought was always controlled by a region called the hippocampus. A new study in mice reveals that the brain network responsible for habits and motor skills can generate these sleep replays entirely on its own. The findings, published in Nature Neuroscience, suggest that different memory systems in the brain can function and reinforce themselves independently.
Memory is not a single phenomenon. The brain handles facts and events, known as declarative memory, differently than it handles procedural memory, which covers motor skills and habits like riding a bicycle. For decades, researchers debated how the brain cements these different types of memories during sleep.
A prevailing theory suggested that the hippocampus acts as a central conductor for the sleeping brain. Under this model, the hippocampus replays the spatial and temporal context of the day’s events, sending signals that trigger the rest of the brain to lock in all types of memories. However, some past research hinted that motor skills might not need the hippocampus to become permanent.
To resolve this tension, a research team led by Emmett Thompson and Lars Rollik at University College London looked at exactly how the brain processes procedural memories offline. Marcus Stephenson-Jones supervised the work. The researchers wanted to know if the brain circuits that store motor skills possess an autonomous ability to replay memories, or if they rely entirely on the hippocampus.
The researchers first designed a physical task for a small study of mice. The animals learned to poke their noses into a specific sequence of five ports to receive a water reward. As the mice practiced, their movements became highly stereotyped, resembling the acquisition of a physical habit.
To confirm which brain area drove this learning, the researchers disabled a region called the dorsolateral striatum, part of the dorsal striatum. This structure sits deep in the brain and is heavily involved in coordinating movement and processing rewards. Mice with a disabled dorsolateral striatum failed to learn the sequence from memory, and they showed highly variable, uncoordinated movements during the physical task.
Next, the team blocked chemical receptors required for neural plasticity in the dorsal striatum while the mice slept. The researchers waited until the animals had finished a day of training before delivering the blocking agent. The following day, the animals performed worse on the sequence task, dropping back to earlier levels of training.
The researchers then implanted high-density electrodes to monitor individual brain cells in the dorsal striatum. They recorded the mice both while they performed the task and while they slept afterward. To analyze the data, they used a machine learning tool that identifies hidden patterns in neural firing without relying on human assumptions.
During the awake physical task, the algorithm identified distinct sequences of brain cell activity that aligned with specific phases of the behavioral sequence. Different groups of neurons fired in precise orders depending on whether the mouse was moving between ports, consuming a reward, or performing other behaviors such as grooming.
When the researchers applied the same algorithm to the animals’ sleeping brain activity, they found that these exact neural sequences reactivated. The brain cells fired in the same order they did during the physical task, a phenomenon known as replay. This offline replay occurred at normal speeds, but it also often progressed much faster, compressing the time it took to complete the neural sequence into a fraction of a second.
The content of the sleep replay was highly structured. The sleeping brain prioritized sequences related to the physical task over random behaviors. It also heavily favored sequences associated with rewards. When the brain replayed sequences in a forward direction, and when it used neurons that fired consistently during the daytime task, the mice showed better physical performance the next day.
Finally, the team tested whether the hippocampus was orchestrating this striatal replay. They used a viral injection to perform large bilateral lesions, completely disabling the hippocampus in a group of mice. They then monitored the animals’ learning and their brain activity during sleep.
The mice without a hippocampus learned the five-step physical sequence just as well as control animals. They completed the task with the exact same speed and accuracy. This confirmed that the hippocampus was not required to learn or perform this specific motor skill.
When the researchers looked at the sleep data, they found that the dorsal striatum still generated neural replay. Every characteristic of the replay remained intact despite the missing hippocampus. The sequences played in forward and reverse orders, sped up and slowed down, and occurred across multiple stages of sleep. The brain also continued to prioritize task-related sequences just as it did in healthy mice.
While these results show that procedural memory replay can happen without the hippocampus, the findings do not mean the hippocampus is universally uninvolved in all forms of motor learning. In physical tasks that heavily rely on spatial navigation or learning an environment, the hippocampus might still play a role in shaping memory.
Because this research was conducted in mice, the exact mechanisms of memory replay will need to be confirmed in humans. Additionally, the researchers point out that future studies will need to identify the exact trigger for this independent replay in the striatum. They plan to investigate how other chemicals, like dopamine, might coordinate with replay to cement habits and skills during rest.
The study, “Replay of procedural memory is independent of the hippocampus,” was authored by Emmett J. Thompson, Lars B. Rollik, Benjamin Waked, Georgina Mills, Sthitapranjya Pati, Jasvin Kaur, Ben Geva, Haoyu Li, Rodrigo Carrasco-Davis, Tom George, Clementine Domine, William Dorrell, and Marcus Stephenson-Jones.

Shooting and craving: on NAZA and the mediated obscene
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

There is a Hebrew phrase that has been etched into Israeli culture and is perhaps one of its most authentic expressions. The phrase is yorim ve-bochim, or “shooting and crying,” and it has become a staple of Israeli cultural production. Its first iteration is dated to a novella written in the wake of the Zionist forces’ deliberate expulsion and ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in 1948, what we Palestinians call the Nakba. The novella Khirbet Khizeh, written by S. Yizhar and named after a fictional Palestinian village, follows a young soldier as he attempts both to belong fully to a unit tasked with “ethnically cleansing” the village and to grapple with guilt and moral uncertainty. The soldier decides to defer the reckoning to a later date, to finish the job and then do the emotional labor.
Over half a century, the genre has acquired its own conventions: it usually features a sensitive Israeli soldier who delivers an elegiac voiceover and admits to crimes only when the admission can no longer change anything. Yizhar’s novella itself played a big role in shaping the writing of a generation of Israeli authors, and many Israeli films, including Waltz with Bashir and The Law in These Parts, and even the sloppy Fauda. All of them feature elements of the “shooting and crying” trope.
These works are made by people who remained committed to the Zionist ideal of land and sovereign power exclusively for Jews, but who still struggled to mitigate the toll that a colonial project exacts on the “soul” of its agents, hardening their moral aptitude and producing a soulless, masculine, and unbothered militant figure. In many ways, one can read this genre as a fear of what they will become as they unleash violence and participate in the eradication and destruction of Palestinian life.
So, when I went to watch NAZA, I was ready for this transaction. I expected to watch Israeli soldiers reckon with the crimes they committed and display remorse. I expected to watch Israelis redeem themselves through the performative moral gestures of confession, and through complex takes on necessity, politics, and moral cost. My suspicion was, here we go again, another movie where Israelis emerge as more interesting, more human, and more capable of a full range of feelings, while Palestinians remain the “primitives” serving as background to the civilized creatures who shoot and cry.
What I found instead was something more harrowing and more honest. The subjects are hidden out of fear of Israeli criminal prosecution: not for committing crimes against Palestinians, but for confessing to those crimes and making the confessions public.
We do not hear their voices, and we are told that, as they sit on rooftops across Tel Aviv, most of the confessors are “liberal,” upper-class types, the sensitive Israelis the 1949 novella depicted. These are not the crude settlers who kill in the name of the coming messiah; they are the secular liberal humanists who, as one of the anonymized protagonists of the film claims, “do not hate the Arabs.”
My first reaction, beyond anger and a grief that bordered on shock, was a thought I distrusted even as I had it: that there is something to be said for Ben-Gvir when he is set beside these yoga-practicing, avocado-eating, sourdough-baking software engineers from Tel Aviv.
Let me be clear and leave no room for misunderstanding. Ben-Gvir and his ilk are the scum of the earth, but their racism, sense of supremacy, and contempt for Palestinian life are declared and, in many ways, displayed in their full truth, without hesitation. What disturbs in the confessions of these Israelis is not only the resemblance to Eichmann — meaning the “thoughtlessness” and banality of evil in the procedures that the Israeli war machine has perfected, embedding violence in machinic systems and mathematical equations — but is also the absence of a moral reckoning with such crimes, beyond explanations of what they did and how they did it.
Yes, we get the “I couldn’t take this anymore,” or the silence when Yuval Abraham confronts them with the contradiction between claiming that “you do not hate Arabs” and belonging to units responsible for most of the deaths in Gaza. But what truly disturbs is the sense of “enjoyment” that comes across subtly in the subtext of what is being confessed. The enjoyment in being a quasi-divine authority who gets to decide on who lives and who dies, the sense of pleasure at watching videos of a child’s corpse being eaten by a dog.
We are told by these Israelis that the machine is good, because if decisions were left to humans, the deaths would be more. The machine is a restraint — an efficient way of killing, yes, but a restraint all the same. We are told that it was like a “video game,” and while the army wanted to bring in a psychologist, there was “no need for it.”
The Israeli confession here has become cruder and less sensitive, bearing all the fatigue of an army corps that relies on machines to do its thinking. The system is larger than any one of them: “I am only a cog in a larger machine.” At the outset, these statements could seem like self-justification, placed to advance the classic Israeli line in which one cries over what had to be done. But here the confession seems to ask something else: “Should I be sorry for enjoying what I have done?” It might be a genocide; it might, as one of the interviewees says, resemble the Nazis, but should one be sorry for feeling a sense of all-encompassing power?
The Israeli confession here seems less assured of its moral direction, incapable of exulting as the Ben-Gvirs do after they shoot, and equally incapable of the crying that the classic Israeli non-apology once offered. Today, these are confessions that speak of an addiction, and of a realization, among some of the anonymized figures we hear, that their addiction to mediated forms of killing, and their decision to “cleanse,” “clear,” “kill,” “snipe,” “maim,” and “destroy,” might be unhealthy.
Throughout the conversation that Abraham brings to the fore, there is a craving for the power to decide a family’s fate and a sense of catharsis in the work they have done. A sense of addiction is made apparent by the words of one confessor, who speaks of all the hormones at play in completing a mission and moving on to the next. One building down, another to go. These men experienced this sense of power mostly behind screens, sitting in offices and watching the destruction they wrought upon the whole of Gaza.
This is the inversion of the old genre that Israeli culture produced. Shooting and crying offered the Israeli subject advance forgiveness, as long as the Israeli could cry for the crimes that “Arabs” made them do. NAZA’s confessors claim little in this specific form. What comes out in their confessions is a dependency, the ordinary brush with the drug of the divine, and then its withdrawal when the service ends and the machine releases the “engineer” or the intelligence officer back to the cafés of bustling Tel Aviv. If there is mourning, it is for this loss of power.
This is also why the language of addiction should be handled with care and qualified. An addict evokes some pity, perhaps even an intervention from close friends and family. These men and women chose, daily and for months on end, to kill en masse. Yes, it became a habit, perhaps even second nature, but they chose it. The apparatus they worked within removed them, as far as possible, from facing their victims, and gave them both a spectacle and a heightened sense of themselves as people who could shape worlds and lives. They enjoyed it. Arendt’s Eichmann felt no appetite for his work, and that absence was her point. What these confessors describe is thoughtlessness and banality with an excited pulse.
Shooting and crying promised Israelis redemption, even if deferred. Shooting and craving makes no such promise; it leaves its subjects wanting more, and it does not console us, the Palestinians. What remains are two archetypes of Israelis bound to the army and its killing machine: those who kill in the name of the end times and a God to come, and those who take pleasure in cosplaying as God.

The New Alexa Tablets Feel Like a Blueprint for an Amazon Phone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Is Amazon making a smartphone? A Reuters report from earlier this year revealed details about a device codenamed Transformer under development, with Amazon's Alexa+ AI assistant as the focus of the experience.
With Amazon announcing a complete rebrand of its tablet line on Thursday—killing the cheap Fire Tablets and replacing them with premium Alexa Tablets that finally run Android with access to the Google Play Store—we now have a blueprint for what an Android-powered Amazon phone could look like.
Amazon's souped-up Alexa+ assistant is front and center on the tablets. There's a persistent “Ask Alexa” widget on the home screen that lets you call on the assistant to ask it questions—you can say “Alexa” to trigger it, too. But Alexa+ now finally has what Amazon calls On-Screen Intelligence. Like Google's Gemini on Android phones or Apple's Siri on iPhones, which can read your screen and answer contextual questions, Alexa now has the same functionality (if you opt in).
That can be for simple things like summarizing a web page, but it can be used for more complex tasks. Watching a YouTube video about a new product? Ask Alexa whether the product is on Amazon, and if so, add it to your Amazon shopping cart. Perusing an Infatuation article about new restaurants in your area? Ask Alexa to highlight the ones closest to your office.
Alexa also supports “live sessions,” just like Gemini Live or ChatGPT's Voice Mode—it lets you have a free-form back-and-forth conversation with the assistant. Maybe you're focused on a DIY project and want Alexa to spell out instructions slowly at your own pace. It also supports visual intelligence: Point the tablet's camera at anything, and Alexa can identify the object and offer helpful advice. Got a water leak? Point the camera and ask Alexa how to fix it.
These are completely new experiences for Alexa. Amazon's vice president of devices, Kevin Keith, tells WIRED the company “didn't really have the right product to be able to use” these capabilities, but that's now solved with its Android tablets.
But these features would fit right in on a smartphone, where they’d perhaps be even more useful. When I mentioned this to Keith, he laughed and said: “We have nothing to share on that. Interesting idea.”
Amazon notoriously tried to make a smartphone in 2014—the Fire Phone—a massive flop discontinued shortly after launch due to a limited app ecosystem, dismal sales, and an over-reliance on gimmicky features. (Even its designer recently said he was embarrassed by it.) That may partly be why Amazon is retiring the “Fire” branding and killing its budget tablets. People may forget the disaster and won't be reminded of the “Fire Phone” name when the company eventually introduces a new handset.
Switching its tablets over to Google's Android (rather than the forked version the Fire tablets ran) and adding the Google Play Store is a silent admission that it's hard to thrive without a healthy app ecosystem. It also sets the phone up for success, as it won't feel app-limited out of the gate like the original Fire Phone.
Alexa+ is right now a paid service that requires an Alexa+ subscription or Amazon Prime. However, Amazon says anyone with its new Alexa tablet gets Alexa+ for free, and this would likely also be the case with an Amazon phone. Amazon’s devices, after all, are vehicles used to drive users to buy stuff on Amazon.com. A 2022 Pew Research Center survey showed that 76 percent of Americans purchase products using a smartphone. It makes sense that Amazon would want more direct control over the hardware people use to make those purchases, especially if it paints Alexa as a helpful assistant that can shop for you.
Recently, Amazon has been on a mission to make its hardware more premium. This crusade seems to have ramped up after Microsoft Surface creator Panos Panay joined the company as head of Devices & Services in 2023. These upscaling efforts include the slew of Echo speakers it introduced in 2025, which saw marked price increases over their predecessors thanks to upgraded hardware. The Kindles announced at the start of October now come in sleek aluminum variants and are thinner and lighter than ever. The latest Alexa Tablets are more powerful, made from aluminum, and feel very iPad-esque.
Panay spent his final few years at Microsoft on the failed Microsoft Duo folding smartphone. When it launched, he was adamant it wasn't a phone but rather a productivity-focused device that belonged in a new category.
The Reuters report suggests Amazon's phone may feature an “AI interface,” what the industry often refers to as a generative user interface, that eliminates the need for traditional app stores. It could be that when Panay eventually steps on a stage to reveal an Amazon “Alexa” Phone, he'll once again claim it's not a phone, but a helpful AI assistant in your pocket that conforms to your demands—marking a clear departure from every other Android slab on the market.
The smartphone market is in a bit of a predicament right now. Devices are getting more expensive because of the memory crisis, shipments have declined for several quarters in a row, and the duopoly in the US market between Samsung and Apple makes it hard for other players to break through. Established smartphone companies have given up and left the market, like OnePlus this summer or HMD last year.
There isn't much choice left in for American buyers. However, an Amazon phone, made by a company that isn't based in China and backed by Amazon's retail dominance, could quickly swallow the slice of the pie Motorola and Google are fighting over.

Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, Alexa Tablet 11, Alexa Tablet 8: Specs, Features, Price
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

The era of Amazon's Fire tablets—cheap slate computers ranging from $60 to $280—is over.
All of the Fire tablets are being replaced by the all-aluminum Amazon Alexa Tablet. These tablets will, in a first for Amazon, run official Android and have full access to the Google Play Store. The lack of proper app support was always a sticking point for the Fire tablets, which ran a custom version of Android and had a much more limited app library.
The new Alexa Tablet series comes in three models: the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro ($500), Alexa Tablet 11 ($330), and Alexa Tablet 8 ($230), with the numbers corresponding to the display size. Amazon is also offering kids' editions of the latter two devices at the same prices. These include bumper cases for extra protection, a one-year, worry-free guarantee to replace the device if it breaks, and a year of Amazon Kids+ service to fill the tablet with age-appropriate content.
As for Fire tablets, Amazon says it will stop shipping the devices in the next month or two. It will support them for four years from the last ship date. Amazon is committing to at least four years of software updates for the new Alexa tablets, which will launch with Android 16 and will receive Android 17 early in 2027. Preorders for the new Alexa Tablets are open now, and they'll begin shipping on October 14.
Premium Tablets
The experience is largely the same on all three tablets, with aluminum builds designed to mimic the new aluminum Kindles. The MediaTek Dimensity 8189 chip powers the two smaller tablets, whereas the 12-inch device gets a little more power from the MediaTek Dimensity 8400.
The Alexa Tablet 12 Pro is the outlier of the trio, as it's the only one with two display variants: a standard 12-inch LCD screen or a 12-inch Nanomatte display with anti-glare and anti-reflective properties. Upgrade to the Nanomatte—starting at $550—for a matte, paperlike look and feel. With a peak brightness of 500 nits, it should still be bright enough to view in sunlight.
Amazon says it developed this screen in partnership with Corning (the company that makes most of the glass that protects smartphone displays). It's similar to the matte displays found on devices like TCL's Nxtpaper series, though Amazon's vice president of devices, Kevin Keith, says the hexagon-shaped imprint on the Nanomatte display can push out vivid colors and crisp blacks while still retaining those matte properties.
The screen also offers a “really good” writing experience, according to Keith. He says the same engineers who worked on the Kindle Scribe worked with Corning to get that paperlike feel. The screen works with Amazon's new Alexa Tablet Pro Pen ($90), which has 4,096 levels of pressure sensitivity, plus tilt detection. The pen can magnetically dock to the top of the slate for charging and pairing. Amazon also sells a Pro Keyboard ($150) for the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, which attaches to the device via the pogo pins on the bottom edge—no Bluetooth needed.
Now that Android has recently gained multiwindowing features, attaching the keyboard turns the largest Alexa tablet into a productivity machine: split apps across the screen, resize them into various windows, and “save” several desktop arrangements so you can pick up where you left off.
For the kids’ versions of the Alexa Tablet 11 and Alexa Tablet 8, Amazon says the software is still Android with a heavily customized interface for kid-friendly content and built-in parental controls. Keith says one in five kids in the US has an Amazon tablet, so it'll be interesting to see how that changes now that these devices start at a higher price.
Alexa Front and Center
It may look and feel like Android, but Amazon has tweaked the interface to make these Alexa Tablets feel like Amazon hardware.
The top-left corner of the home screen features a persistent widget called the Dynamic Tab. This scrollable widget lets you dive into Amazon content you may have been consuming on another device—say, if you were reading on your Kindle, watching a movie on Prime Video on your iPhone, or snapped some photos and you want to view them on Amazon Photos.
Swipe right, and instead of Google's Discover feed, you're instead greeted with Amazon's For You experience. Amazon's Fire tablets were a vehicle to put Amazon content in front of your eyeballs, and that hasn't changed with the Alexa Tablets. Again, you can continue consuming content here, with tabs for movies and TV, games, and Kindle. There's also a news feed, and you can tap Alexa prompts for more information on a story.
Uniquely, opening the Kindle app triggers “Kindle mode,” which disables all notifications, turns on the blue light filter, and extends battery life to 20 hours (less on the smaller tablets). You can also choose one of three display treatments in this mode: subtle warmth with natural color, a softened paper tone, or monochrome. There's even a fun page-turn effect that mimics turning a page in a book. As soon as you exit the app, notifications turn back on, and the screen returns to normal. Annotations you make with the stylus will sync with Kindle apps on pen-supported devices, like the Kindle Scribe.
As the tablets’ names suggests, Alexa+ is front and center. So far, Amazon has restricted Alexa+ access to paid subscribers or Amazon Prime customers, but Keith says you don't need to subscribe to anything to use Alexa+ on these devices.
In the bottom-right corner, a persistent “Ask Alexa” chat box lets you call up the virtual assistant immediately. You can also trigger it by saying, “Alexa,” just like an Echo device. It can control your smart home devices, but the marquee addition is Alexa's On-Screen Intelligence. It's opt-in—with an on-screen indicator whenever it's active—allowing the assistant to see what you're looking at and answer contextual questions.
For example, if you're traveling to a new city and are looking at a guide filled with restaurant recommendations, you can ask Alexa, “Which of these is closest to my hotel?” and it can filter the list. Got a schedule for your kid's soccer games? Bring up Alexa and ask it to add all the events to your calendar.
Alexa+ also supports live sessions—much like Google's Gemini Live or ChatGPT's Voice Mode, you can have a real-time back-and-forth conversation with the assistant without speaking the wake word at every turn. Watching a TikTok and wondering whether a product in the video is available on Amazon? Naturally, you can ask Alexa, and the assistant can even add it to your shopping cart.
The hardware may finally have the look and feel of other premium Android tablets, but these slates are still built to keep you hooked on Amazon's retail empire.

An experimental drug kills fat cells, rather than shrinking them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

An experimental drug kills fat cells, rather than shrinking them
In two small trials, people lost dangerous visceral fat around their internal organs
An experimental drug may melt away a dangerous type of fat that packs around internal organs.
The drug, called CBL-514, specifically triggers fat cells to enter a death program called apoptosis. People who got injections of the experimental drug in their lower abdomens lost visceral fat, researchers reported October 1 at the annual meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes in Milan, Italy. Visceral fat sits deep in the abdomen where it chokes organs and can spur inflammation and health problems.
Weight loss can shrink fat cells, but the cells are still there, poised to balloon up again.
The team already knew the experimental drug could reduce subcutaneous fat, the pinchable fat that sits under the skin, in the abdomen. That surface fat doesn’t carry the same health risks that visceral fat does.
In the new study, researchers examined MRIs from a subset of participants in two small clinical trials to track visceral fat levels. Study participants, who ranged from healthy weights to overweight, got injections of CBL-514 or placebo every three weeks for up to 12 weeks. The two groups started with about the same amount of visceral fat; 642.5 milliliters on average in the CBL-514 group and 677.4 milliliters in the placebo group. Four weeks after treatment, those who got the experimental drug had dropped almost 71 mL of visceral fat (a 12 percent decrease), while the placebo group gained 31 mL (a nearly 6 percent increase) of the dangerous fat in their abdomens.
Measurements taken at eight to 12 weeks after treatment showed the gap had widened. Those who got the experimental drug lost almost 63 mL — about a quarter cup — of visceral fat on average while the placebo group gained more than 78 mL of visceral fat over the starting point. Those results suggest that the drug might have health benefits by reducing visceral fat, which contributes to diabetes and heart problems. Larger clinical trials to test efficacy and safety of the drug are ongoing.

Türkiye, China sign satellite technology deal at international space congress in Antalya
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:58:25 UTC
21:58:25 KST

Beril Canakci, Mertkan Oruc
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
Türkiye and China will carry out joint work on space technologies under a joint R&D, product development and commercialization agreement signed between TURKSAT and China Satcom.
The 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC 2026) continues at the Antalya NEST Congress Center with Anadolu as the Global Communications Partner. The congress is organized by the International Astronautical Federation (IAF) and hosted by the Turkish Space Agency (TUA) and SAHA Istanbul under the coordination of the Ministry of Industry and Technology.
Turkish companies are showcasing their products at the congress while also signing agreements with international partners.
According to information obtained by Anadolu, TURKSAT and China-based satellite operator China Satcom have signed a comprehensive protocol aimed at developing new technologies.
The protocol was signed at a ceremony held at the TURKSAT stand by TURKSAT Deputy General Manager for Satellite Services Selman Demirel and China Satcom CEO Ma Haiquan.
The agreement aims to bring together the engineering expertise of the two countries through joint R&D, product development and commercialization.
Innovative products and solutions to be developed
The partnership between the two institutions, which began last year with capacity sharing, was expanded through decisions reached at World Space Business Week in Paris.
With the cooperation now moving into hardware and software development, the agreement marks a new phase of joint R&D and production in space technologies between Türkiye and China.
Under the agreement, TURKSAT and China Satcom plan to develop UAV communication systems, satellite-based Internet of Things technologies and smart border security technologies.
TURKSAT will also expand its solution portfolio by applying its existing capabilities in developing end-to-end satellite and communications solutions to new technologies and application areas.
The cooperation will cover the full process, from analyzing market needs and developing initial prototypes to testing, validation and commercialization. Turkish and Chinese engineers will work together to develop new products and solutions.
TURKSAT aims to become a leading technology supplier
Smart border security and Internet of Things technologies are among the other key areas covered by the agreement. The partnership aims to develop specialized devices for areas without terrestrial communications networks.
The agreement also covers the development of hardware that will allow devices used in sectors such as energy, agriculture and logistics to be managed via satellite in remote areas without mobile networks.
Limited terrestrial communications infrastructure in many parts of the world creates gaps in border security and industrial data transmission. The TURKSAT-China Satcom partnership aims to develop smart satellite monitoring and IoT systems capable of providing real-time data transmission in remote and challenging areas beyond the reach of cellular base stations or fiber networks.
Through these integrated satellite-based hardware and software solutions, TURKSAT aims to become one of the leading technology suppliers in the global ecosystem.
A joint steering committee with equal representation from the two institutions will also be established to oversee R&D and product development activities with the work to be reviewed every three months.

MOSCOW, October 8. /TASS/. Estonia has asked the European Union to exclude a Russian company--which supplies materials to an Estonian enterprise--and an associated individual from the 22nd sanctions package, Kerstin Lepik, Spokesperson at the Permanent Representation of Estonia to the EU in Brussels, told the ERR national public broadcasting portal.
On October 7, a European source told TASS that EU ambassadors had agreed on the 22nd sanctions package, which will include over 1,500 Russian companies and individuals linked to the defense sector.
TASS has compiled the key details known about the approval process for the new sanctions package.
EU ambassadors agree on 22nd sanctions package
- EU ambassadors agreed on the 22nd sanctions package, a European source told TASS on October 7.
- According to the source, the package will include over 1,500 Russian companies and individuals linked to the defense sector.
- The source confirmed that the list includes "defense and other" companies and individuals from a number of countries. As the EU claims these companies "produce dual-use goods."
- This package does not include significant new trade or economic restrictions, but it will be the largest since the start of the special military operation in terms of the number of individuals and legal entities simultaneously added to the blacklist.
- To date, under the more than 20 sanctions packages adopted over the past four years, a total of just over 3,000 Russian enterprises and individuals have been included in the EU blacklist.
- The sanctions entail entry bans and asset freezes within the EU. For enterprises, this means asset freezes and a total ban on any joint activities involving EU residents.
- The 22nd package is expected to be approved by the EU Council and enter into force by the end of the week.
Scope of new sanctions
- According to Reuters, the new package will add 1,570 legal entities and individuals to the blacklist.
- This package will expand the sanctions list against Russia by nearly 50% but will not include other significant economic measures.
Estonia's request
- Estonia has asked the EU to exclude one Russian company and an associated individual from the 22nd sanctions package, Kerstin Lepik, Spokesperson at the Permanent Representation of Estonia to the EU in Brussels, told the national broadcaster ERR.
- According to her, the company supplies materials of strategic importance for Europe to a company based in Estonia.
- Lepik stated that the Estonian company is seeking alternative sources for the materials it currently imports from Russia.
- Estonia will revisit the inclusion of this Russian company and the associated individual on the sanctions list next year, she added.
Lithuania's proposal
- Lithuanian authorities propose that the EU ban the transit of Russian food grain through the EU’s territory and impose sanctions on a number of individuals from Russia's agricultural sector, said Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius.

Burnham must extinguish Islamophobia to deliver his promise of a new Britain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:53:51 UTC
21:53:51 KST

Prime Minister Andy Burnham made several promises to Britain at this year’s Labour Party conference in Liverpool earlier this month. It was the first time he addressed the annual conference as Prime Minister, a role he has held since late July 2026.
Among those pledges were a new National Care Service to provide free care for the elderly, the nationalisation of water and energy, affordable housing, a fairer vote in elections, and mending trade relations with the EU post-Brexit.
A ‘new direction’ for Britain, Burnham called it, drawing ‘a line on a decade of division.’ However, just how he plans to heal Britain’s widening chasm of racial division, he did not say.
After a depressing decade of Brexit, COVID-19 and a succession of prime ministers, six of whom resigned before completing their terms, it is understandable that Britons are feeling optimistic.
When it comes to Burnham’s promises of a better economy and improved healthcare and social welfare, I am hopeful too.
But we cannot ignore the elephant in the room: right now, as a Muslim and person of colour, Britain does not feel like a particularly welcoming place.
It was therefore disappointing that Burnham did not explain how he intends to tackle rising anti-Muslim hatred, xenophobia and far-right racism in his first conference speech as Prime Minister.
In his speech, Burnham referenced his temporary break from politics in 2017, prompted by his frustration over class and regional inequalities.
While he rightly addressed those inequalities, his speech fell short by failing to acknowledge the discrimination faced by Muslim communities and other ethnic and religious minorities, or explain how his government intends to tackle it.
As Burnham delivered his speech, anti-Muslim hatred, attacks on immigrants and attacks on mosques continued to fuel fear across Britain.
The far-right's argument that such attacks are a consequence of people not being listened to can never justify violence.
Climate of fear
Over the past year, there has been, on average, one attack on a mosque every five days in Britain.
Exclusive data shared by the British Muslim Trust with ITV last month shows that cases involving arson, violence and premeditated mass-casualty plots against mosques have risen from 3.7 percent to 23.5 percent over the past year.
Manchester, where Burnham was recently mayor, was described by ITV as an ‘Islamophobia hotspot’, with local Muslim residents telling the broadcaster that they feel like ‘moving targets’.
Other ethnic and religious minorities have also faced threats and violence.
In September, Greater Manchester police arrested two men suspected of planning an attack targeting a religious community in Manchester, a year after the fatal attack on Heaton Park Synagogue in the same area.
Last month, far-right anti-immigration protesters blocked roads and intimidated people along Britain's coast, some wearing black balaclavas, in an effort to prevent asylum seekers from being processed.
One protester even slashed a boat used for emergency response in the English Channel. Despite police restrictions and a ban on balaclavas, protesters returned to Dover, the country's main port, last Saturday.
And yet, against this backdrop of fear, intimidation and violence, Burnham's speech offered no clear strategy to confront anti-Muslim hatred and the wider problem of xenophobia.
The country's prosperity cannot be measured by economics alone. There can be no prosperous Britain while it is a xenophobic Britain.
Muslim organisations in Britain say they are hopeful that their communities will be better listened to following Burnham's announcement of a devolution plan. The proposal would decentralise power, giving local leaders greater authority to address problems within their communities.
This is a potentially welcome development, particularly for communities that have long felt overlooked by national policymakers.
However, the benefits for British Muslims would largely be indirect. Devolution alone does not constitute a concrete government strategy to combat anti-Muslim hatred and racism.
The government did take some concrete steps to address anti-Muslim hatred.
It has adopted a non-statutory definition of anti-Muslim hostility, introduced a Faith Security Training Scheme and committed up to £4 million to programmes tackling anti-Muslim hatred.
It has also made up to £40 million available through the Protective Security for Mosques Scheme for 2026–27, funding measures including security personnel, CCTV and perimeter protection.
These measures are welcome, particularly at a time when Muslim communities face growing threats.
But their effectiveness will depend on implementation and whether Muslims feel safer in their everyday lives.
The government has also committed to appointing a Special Representative on anti-Muslim hostility, although the position remained unfilled six months after the announcement.
I can think of plenty of prominent Muslims with long track records in community engagement and backgrounds in policymaking and politics who would suit the role.
According to British Muslim news outlet Hyphen, government insiders say the recruitment process has been delayed. International human rights organisations such as Amnesty International have warned that Islamophobic attacks in Britain are reaching ‘emergency levels’.
The government's failure to fill the post raises serious questions about how urgently it is treating the problem.
A safe Britain for everyone
If part of Burnham's political strategy is to win back Labour's Muslim vote, a possibility given the visibly Muslim female candidate the party has put forward for this week's London by-election, then British Muslims like myself will be watching closely.
We will be looking for concrete measures, particularly funding to improve security at mosques, the adoption of a robust definition of anti-Muslim hostility and meaningful action against far-right racism.
As Britons, our concerns go beyond the rising cost of living.
We also want to live in a country where we feel safe, where we are not treated as moving targets because we wear a hijab, a turban or a beard, or because of our ethnic or religious identity.
Burnham's vision of a ‘Britain for everyone’ must include a concrete strategy to make the country safe for everyone, regardless of ethnicity or creed.
That is what we needed to hear from our new Prime Minister at last week's Labour Party conference.

Scientists in Austria and China create the world’s first nuclear clocks. Here’s why it matters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:53:19 UTC
21:53:19 KST

The new nuclear clocks measure time by using lasers to make subatomic particles.
Scientists have invented the world’s first nuclear clocks that they say could unlock the fundamentals of physics.
The two devices are the newest atomic clocks, which measure time by monitoring light by using transitions occurring inside the atomic nucleus, involving protons and neutrons.
Atomic clocks have been used to keep precise measures of time and were first created in 1949 and, despite the name, do not use nuclear fusion or fission.
The world's best clocks have relied on electrons jumping between energy levels in atoms but the discovery has shown that the reference for a clock can come from the nucleus itself.
The research teams from China’s Tsinghua University and other institutions in the country and Austria’s TU Wien reported their breakthroughs separately in two papers published in Nature on Wednesday.
The clock uses thorium-229, a rare atom whose nucleus can switch energy states using ultraviolet light from a laser. It is the only nucleus known to work this way.
The team built a laser that makes ultraviolet light at 148.4 nanometres and aimed it at small calcium fluoride crystals containing thorium-229.
The key finding was that the nuclear clocks worked. The laser stayed locked to the thorium-229 nucleus and kept steady time, reaching a precision of about one part in a quadrillion (10⁻¹⁵) over the test period.
While precise timekeeping is vital for everyday technologies such as satellite navigation and telecommunications, nuclear clocks could make these systems more precise
They could also be important in fundamental physics, the paper reads, however, it does not specify the exact use cases.
