Fed’s Waller signals further rate hikes as inflation stalls, AI spending drives up costs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:31:36 UTC
21:31:36 KST

Emir Yildirim
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
US Federal Reserve (Fed) board member Christopher Waller forecast that the bank may need to impose additional interest rate hikes to return inflation to the 2% target if incoming economic data continue to meet expectations, speaking at the Istanbul Economic Forum on Thursday.
Waller provided a comprehensive assessment of the American economic outlook at the summit held by the Turkish Central Bank, noting that further tightening may be needed to accelerate progress toward price stability.
The two-day forum was organized by the Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye to address global economic policy challenges by gathering central bank governors and high-level policymakers from around the world, including the US and the UK.
The Fed decided to hike rates by 2 basis points to 3.75-4% at September’s Federal Open Market Committee meeting after maintaining rates for nine months, following 75 basis points of cumulative rate reductions across the final three meetings of last year to combat labor market softening.
Waller stated that the fight to cool inflation had stalled while employment stabilized in the first half of this year, partly due to energy price spikes amid the Middle East conflict.
Waller had initially supported maintaining rates on the assumption that regional wars would be short-lived, but hopes for a swift resolution have since waned. Analysts say high oil prices could persist through next year due to damaged production infrastructure and low inventories.
Recent acceleration drives up future inflation estimates
He noted that while artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure investments surged and drove up the prices of high-tech products, ongoing trade disputes threaten to exert further inflationary pressure through new tariffs.
He mentioned that he backed the September rate hike not only because of August consumer prices but also because of months of evidence showing resilient hiring and stubborn inflation.
He is not overly concerned that tighter conditions will lead to a significant domestic slowdown, as economic activity accelerated in the second half of the year.
Waller was concerned that the recent acceleration in inflation was driving up future inflation estimates among consumers, investors and price-setting businesses.
He noted that interest rate projections among Fed officials show the likely direction of monetary policy, but future rate decisions will hinge on economic data.
“If the economic data continue to come in as expected, I anticipate additional hikes to support a timelier return of inflation to our 2% goal,” he said. “But there is some flexibility about when those hikes will occur. The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings, but they should be in place in an acceptable period of time.”
American consumers show resilience
Regarding Treasury bond yields, Waller stated that the rise in borrowing costs stems from strong economic growth, higher productivity forecasts and expectations of further policy tightening.
He warned that the trillions of dollars that artificial intelligence firms could borrow in the coming years to fund their massive investments could boost the US government’s borrowing costs.
Waller noted that American consumers have shown resilience amid banking, geopolitical and pandemic shocks, in response to a question about whether household finances might suffer under high food and energy prices.
As for AI, Waller called it a “revolutionary technology,” expecting its advent to boost productivity in the coming years as it transforms how quickly work is conducted. However, the impact of expected productivity gains has yet to be clearly reflected in overall economic data.
“(AI) is going to have an impact on jobs, but we’ve known that about every technological change that's ever happened — some jobs disappear, new jobs are created,” he said, noting that the elimination of existing jobs is immediately visible while newly created jobs remain difficult to foresee.
He added that he expects AI to cultivate a broad and shared ecosystem of competitive firms rather than collapse into a zero-sum monopoly that could lead to an economic crash.
He mentioned that the expansion of private credit funds and their potential risks to commercial banks fuel financial stability concerns. He added that well-governed private credit funds pose limited systemic liquidity risks because they lock in capital over multiyear periods and are not obligated to meet on-demand redemptions.

Spain snap election puts ties with Israel on the line, Prime Minister Sanchez at risk - interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:31:27 UTC
21:31:27 KST

Spain will vote on November 29 in a snap general election called by Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez after a parliamentary defeat over housing exposed the fragility of his governing coalition, opening a campaign in which current polling gives the center-right Popular Party and Vox a combined parliamentary majority.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
For Juan Carlos Girauta, a Vox member of the European Parliament, the stakes extend well beyond domestic politics.
“There is a very clear awareness that Spain’s foreign policy under Sánchez needs a 180-degree turn,” Girauta said, looking beyond the election to the changes he would like to see from a new government.
Polling averages currently favor the right, but the campaign has only begun. An October 5 average compiled by Spain’s public broadcaster RTVE projected 137 seats for the Popular Party (PP) and 65 for Vox, giving the two parties a combined 202 seats in the 350-member Congress of Deputies. The Socialists were projected at 104 seats. An absolute majority requires 176.
Vox is a relatively recent chapter in Girauta’s political career. Born in Barcelona in 1961, the lawyer and journalist entered elected politics with Ciudadanos, winning a seat in the European Parliament in 2014 before moving to the Spanish Congress, where he became one of the party’s most visible figures. He left Ciudadanos in 2020 and returned to the European Parliament on the Vox ticket in 2024.
Sánchez called the election on October 5, three days after Congress rejected two government housing decrees. The election had previously been expected in 2027.
Housing decrees' defeat did not create housing crisis
Girauta told The Media Line that the housing defeat mattered, but not because it created the crisis.
“The final trigger, not the fundamental cause, but the last straw, was Sánchez’s attempt to recover the initiative and some popularity,” he said in an interview conducted in Spanish.
That effort followed the eviction of María del Carmen “Maricarmen” Abascal, an 87-year-old Madrid woman whose case became a symbol of Spain’s housing crisis. Protesters rallied in her support and established an encampment in Puerta del Sol. Five days after her eviction, the property-management company reached an agreement allowing her to return under a new lease.
Sánchez responded to the protests with housing measures aimed at protecting vulnerable tenants, regulating temporary and room rentals, restricting certain rent increases, and helping first-time buyers. The package included plans for interest-free loans of up to €50,000 toward a home purchase.
Congress rejected both decrees on October 2 after Junts, the Catalan separatist party led by Carles Puigdemont, joined the PP and Vox in voting against them. Junts’ seven deputies had helped Sánchez secure another term in 2023. This time, their votes helped derail a central government initiative.
Girauta calls the government’s approach “Operation Maricarmen.” He sees it as an effort to take a genuine grievance and turn it into a political rescue operation.
“He takes that banner and says, ‘Now I am going to fix this,’” Girauta said. “Not by building more housing or anything like that, but by creating the kind of legal uncertainty that makes supply contract even further.”
He spoke at greater length about what the housing shortage looks like away from parliament. Young Spaniards, he said, are delaying independence, sharing crowded apartments, and abandoning hopes of buying homes.
“They not only cannot buy. They have to rent with other people,” he said. “There are things happening that were not seen in Spain, at least not in my generation. People from different families have to share a flat and the expenses just to pay the rent.”
Sánchez has acknowledged that his government has not solved Spain’s housing problems. In calling the election, he argued that a larger progressive majority was needed to advance housing, public services, and other reforms blocked in the current parliament.
His government has not abandoned the housing measures. On October 6, the Cabinet approved revised versions of the two decrees, retaining much of the original program and adding a €10 billion financing package for first-home loans. The measures must now go before the Permanent Deputation, the parliamentary body that continues operating after the chambers are dissolved.
The PP and Vox will also try to make the election a referendum on Sánchez himself.
The opposition has spent months pointing to criminal cases involving former Socialist officials and members of the prime minister’s family. Former Transport Minister José Luis Ábalos was sentenced in June to 24 years and three months in prison for crimes including bribery, embezzlement, influence peddling, and participation in a criminal organization.
Sánchez’s brother, David Sánchez, was convicted in July of administrative misconduct connected to his hiring by a provincial government and sentenced to nine years of disqualification from public office. The ruling is being appealed.
The prime minister’s wife, Begoña Gómez, has been ordered to face trial on influence-peddling and embezzlement charges involving alleged misuse of public funds. Gómez denies wrongdoing, and Sánchez himself has not been charged in either family case. He has accused political opponents of using the courts against his family and has argued that wrongdoing by individual officials does not establish broader corruption within his government.
Girauta rejects claim political opponents using courts against Sánchez
Girauta rejects that defense. He said the court cases had become inseparable from the government’s loss of authority. He also described pressure from Socialist regional leaders who feared paying the price for Sánchez’s problems in their own elections.
“They do not want the kick aimed at Sánchez to land on them,” Girauta said. “They want it to land on him first, and then, when their regional elections arrive, to be judged on their own management.”
Girauta’s interest extends beyond who controls parliament. He expects the election to reopen questions about Spain’s relationship with its traditional allies, including Israel and the United States.
Spain formally recognized a Palestinian state in May 2024. Sánchez’s government later codified an arms embargo on Israel, barred imports from Israeli settlements in the West Bank and from certain Israeli neighborhoods in east Jerusalem under its settlement-related trade restrictions, and increased support for the Palestinian Authority and UNRWA, the UN agency responsible for aiding Palestinian refugees. Sánchez has repeatedly described Israel’s conduct in Gaza as genocide. Vox rejects that characterization and opposed the arms embargo.
Girauta said a new government should “stop inciting antisemitism in international forums, stop practicing anti-Westernism, stop doing everything possible to irritate the United States, and stop yielding to Morocco.”
His criticism of Morocco follows the extraordinary migration crisis in Ceuta in late July, when tens of thousands of people crossed from Morocco into the Spanish enclave over two days. Spanish authorities later put the total at about 80,000, with most subsequently returning to Morocco.
Girauta described the episode as “hybrid warfare” by Morocco. A later Spanish police report said Moroccan security personnel appeared to have helped guide migrants toward the crossing, although it did not identify who ordered the operation or assign responsibility to the Moroccan government. Rabat has denied orchestrating the influx and says it cooperated with Spain in returning migrants.
Spanish court lifts arrest warrant for Puigdemont
Catalonia will provide another unpredictable element in the campaign.
The Constitutional Court ruled this week that Spain’s amnesty law applies to misuse-of-public-funds offenses connected to the 2017 Catalan independence drive. The Supreme Court then lifted the arrest warrant for Puigdemont, clearing the way for his possible return to Spain after years in Belgium.
The development is politically awkward for Sánchez. His 2023 agreement with Junts helped secure his return to office and led to passage of the amnesty law, but Puigdemont’s party later withdrew its support on key legislation and helped defeat the housing measures that preceded the snap election.
Girauta also pointed to the political climate surrounding an October 7 pro-Palestinian demonstration scheduled for Barcelona’s Plaça Universitat and associated with Samidoun, the Palestinian Prisoner Solidarity Network. The public call for the event referred to the third anniversary of “Tufan al-Aqsa,” the Arabic name used by Hamas for its October 7, 2023, attack, and urged support for Palestinian resistance.
Samidoun was sanctioned by the US Treasury in 2024, which described it as an international fundraising front for the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine. Canada has listed the organization as a terrorist entity, while Germany banned it in 2023.
Girauta criticized both the amnesty and the government’s housing strategy. His sharpest warning, though, concerned the tone of the campaign and the possibility that political confrontation could spill beyond argument.
“We are in a democracy,” Girauta said. “What counts here is the free exchange of arguments and messages, and then measuring ourselves at the ballot box. Everything else must be rejected and denounced.”
With less than two months until voting day, the polls give Spain’s right a substantial numerical advantage, but they are a snapshot rather than a result. Sánchez has built much of his political career on surviving situations in which his opponents believed his time was up. The Nov. 29 election will determine whether he does so again - and whether Spain’s domestic upheaval produces a sharp change in its policies toward Israel, the United States, Morocco, and the rest of Europe.

It’s time for China to offer more than statements on Hormuz
Beijing does not need to replace Washington as a security guarantor, but it can use its unique access to resolve the crisis

 Listen
Dr Asad Ullah is a postdoctoral researcher in international politics at Shandong University, specialising in Middle East conflict, diplomacy and geopolitical strategy. 
Two summits in five months between US President Donald Trump and President Xi Jinping have produced shared language but not an open Strait of Hormuz. After the May meeting in Beijing, there was little sign the two sides agreed on how to end the war. Xi’s visit to Washington yielded no breakthrough on Iran, though Xi backed a return to the interim US-Iran agreement.
Last week, Trump rejected a truce proposal from Iran and said he was considering resuming US bombing of Iran after the midterm elections next month. The one line the US and Chinese summit readouts shared – that “no country or institution can be allowed to impose tolls on international waterways” – is a principle, not a procedure.
That is the problem in a nutshell. Seven months into the war that began on February 28, China’s diplomacy has been rich in principles and thin on procedures. Foreign Minister Wang Yi told his Iranian counterpart Seyyed Abbas Araghchi on September 16 that the region’s security architecture was imperfect and needed reform and strengthening.
That is the right diagnosis. Beijing does not need to replace Washington as the Gulf’s security guarantor. However, it does need to show that its access can produce something more durable than another call for restraint.

Families with children and a police veteran: what we know about those killed in the Russian strike on Pryluky

On the morning of 7 October, Russian forces attacked Pryluky in Chernihiv Oblast with six missiles. One of them hit a five-storey apartment building, destroying two sections. So far, 22 people are known to have been killed and 54 injured. Rescue workers are still clearing the rubble.
Source: Ukrainska Pravda.Zhyttia (Life)
Details: Ukrainian public broadcaster Suspilne reported that the Russian strike killed Viktoriia Bondarenko, 58, her daughter Kateryna Antypenko, 37, and her one-year-old grandson Oleksandr.
Viktoriia's granddaughter, Olha, survived because she was in another room at the time of the strike. She is currently being looked after by relatives.
The family lived on the fourth floor of the destroyed building. Kateryna worked at a local kiosk to support the family, while Viktoriia looked after her younger grandchild at home. Kateryna's husband works abroad and is already on his way home.
The Russian missile strike also killed 47-year-old police veteran Oleh Malysh. In 2024 he joined the Chernihiv Oblast Police rifle battalion and fought on the front line, but he retired for health reasons.
The oblast police said: "Oleh dedicated his life to serving in the internal affairs agencies, joining the law enforcement service in 2001. He began his career as a criminal investigations officer in Pryluky, where he would go on to serve."
Oleh's wife, who also serves in the police, was seriously injured and is currently in hospital in a critical condition. Her three-year-old niece was injured as well.
Oleh's mother-in-law was also killed in the Russian strike.
A railway worker's family was also among those killed, Ukrzaliznytsia (Ukrainian Railways) CEO Oleksandr Pertsovskyi reported. He said the missile killed a train driver, his wife and their two children – an eight-year-old son and a 13-year-old daughter.
"We have other railway colleagues whose homes were destroyed. But they happened to be on duty at the station and survived. That's the main thing," Pertsovskyi wrote.
Employees of Ukrnafta and Naftogaz – Liudmyla Tsyba and 45-year-old Ihor Chub – were also killed in the attack. Liudmyla worked as a painter with an anti-corrosion protection team and was visiting relatives when the attack occurred.
Ihor was an assistant driller in the department for major and underground well repairs.
The young Maksiut family was also killed in the attack – 23-year-old Daria and her 32-year-old husband Oleksandr – Pryluky school No. 9 reported. The Russian strike also killed their one-and-a-half-year-old son Kyrylo.
Their relative Yuliia told Suspilne Chernihiv that the family lived on the third floor of the building that came under attack.
"In an instant, the family lost the people dearest to them. It is impossible to find words to describe the pain of such a terrible and unjust loss," the school wrote.
The Ivanchenko family was also among those killed. The attack claimed the lives of 38-year-old Yuliia and 39-year-old Oleksandr. They had two children – 13-year-old Iryna and six-year-old Maksym.
In Pryluky, 7, 8 and 9 October have been declared days of mourning for those killed in the missile attack.

Afghanistan and the BLA’s Evolving Capabilities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:30:00 UTC
21:30:00 KST

On October 1, Pakistan’s military said that representatives of several militant groups had met in Kandahar in August to discuss coordinating manpower and operations against Pakistani security forces. Military spokesperson Lt. Gen. Ahmad Sharif Chaudhry said the meeting was chaired by Mullah Shirleen, the Taliban-appointed governor of Kandahar, and involved representatives of the Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA) seeking additional fighters from networks associated with Hafiz Gul Bahadur, a Pakistani militant leader based in North Waziristan. A separate intelligence report identified figures linked to al-Qaida in the Indian Subcontinent (AQIS) among those present.
For the BLA, the significance of the meeting lies less in the presence of other militant groups than in what access to Afghanistan could provide the organization: additional manpower, relationships with established militant networks, and a deeper operating environment beyond Balochistan. The reported discussions therefore point to a possible expansion of the BLA’s external support networks at a time when the group has been developing more sophisticated operational capabilities.
Afghan officials denied that the meeting took place, and the allegations have not been independently established. Pakistan has long accused the Taliban government of sheltering militants, and relations between the two countries are openly hostile. Fighting in October 2025 killed dozens and nearly closed the border; cross-border strikes resumed in February 2026 and continued intermittently through September. Each side’s claims therefore deserve caution. But we can still consider the basic question: what role is Afghanistan playing in the BLA’s evolving military capabilities?
A United Nations Security Council monitoring report published in August found that BLA members had access to U.S.- and NATO-origin equipment left behind in Afghanistan, including M4 and M16 rifles, reconnaissance drones, night-vision devices, and thermal equipment. The report also cited information from a member state that BLA members had trained alongside Tehreek-e-Taliban (TTP) personnel at facilities in Afghanistan, including in drone and urban warfare.
The BLA’s January 2026 offensive illustrated these capabilities being put to use in its operations. On January 31, the group claimed simultaneous attacks across Balochistan, including Quetta, Gwadar, Noshki and Panjgur. Pakistan’s military said 18 civilians and 15 security personnel died and that its forces killed 92 militants, while the BLA said it killed 84 security personnel. Neither tally has been independently confirmed.
A February assessment reported that the group had used drones, satellite communications, and U.S.-made weapons, linking some of the weaponry to equipment left behind in Afghanistan. That does not mean every drone or rifle came from there, however, since commercial drones, communications equipment, and weapons can be obtained through multiple channels.
One such channel is Balochistan’s western border with Iran. BLA and Balochistan Liberation Front (BLF) members have reportedly maintained a presence in Iran’s Sistan-Baluchestan province, and in January 2024 Pakistan struck locations there that it identified as belonging to the two groups. The BLF denied having hideouts there, and there is no established evidence that Iran supplies the BLA with weapons. Afghanistan is different, because the U.N. report documents both equipment access and training.
The BLA’s outreach to Kandahar may also reflect pressure rather than strength. The Associated Press, which saw the intelligence report, paraphrased the document as saying that “BLA representatives told participants that Pakistani military operations had left the group short of fighters and resources.” According to the report, Afghan intelligence officials responded by assuring the BLA that militants with the TTP and AQIS could provide manpower, weapons, and logistical support for operations in Balochistan.
The same report alleged that Afghan and Indian intelligence officials helped arrange the meeting. India has consistently denied backing the BLA, so that claim also warrants scrutiny. Taken together, however, the reported discussions suggest that the BLA may be looking to Afghanistan not simply as a sanctuary, but as a source of personnel, equipment, and connections that could help offset pressure from Pakistani military operations.
Meanwhile, Pakistan has escalated its response to the Taliban’s support for militant groups. Hours before the army’s briefing, Pakistan said it had carried out airstrikes in Helmand and Kunar provinces, while on September 24 it reported strikes on 10 locations in Kandahar, Paktia, and Khost. Such airstrikes may disrupt specific sites, but they do not by themselves cut the flow of weapons, training and recruits.
Three indicators will help clarify the extent of Afghanistan’s support for the BLA: independent verification of the Kandahar meeting, further U.N. monitoring of equipment and training links, and whether the group’s use of drones and coordinated assaults expands beyond the scale documented in earlier operations. The evidence of BLA access to equipment and networks in Afghanistan is significant. What remains unproven is how much of the group’s growing operational sophistication can be attributed to that access.
For Pakistan, the way forward is to address the BLA threat without reducing the wider Balochistan issue to a security response alone. Preventing militant groups from using Afghanistan as a source of recruits, training, and equipment will require continued engagement with Afghan authorities, particularly over the TTP and other groups operating from Afghan territory.
At the same time, greater attention to the security, economic and political concerns of Baloch communities can help separate the grievances of local populations from the armed groups seeking to exploit them. A combination of diplomacy with Kabul, stronger border coordination, and targeted counterterrorism measures, alongside greater engagement with communities in Balochistan, would give Pakistan a more sustainable way to contain cross-border militant networks while reducing the risk of further regional escalation.

Naval Group steps up Europe push as defence spending rises

Naval Group steps up Europe push as defence spending rises
LORIENT, France, Oct 8 - French warship builder Naval Group is stepping up efforts to capitalise on Europe's higher defence spending, betting its ability to deliver frigates quickly will give it an edge over European rivals, executives said.
The state-controlled company, which competes with Britain's BAE Systems and Germany's TKMS, said European clients outside France now account for 20% to 25% of its €4.7 billion ($5.3 billion) annual turnover, up from zero in 2019, thanks to contracts in the Netherlands, Belgium, Greece and Sweden.
It is now preparing a bid to build frigates for Denmark, one of Europe's most closely watched defence tenders, as war in the Middle East and Russian manoeuvring at sea prompt Western governments to strengthen their navies.
"One of the European market's characteristics now is the need for rapid delivery with systems that work," said Guillaume Weisrock, senior vice president for sales and business development in Europe and North America.
DELIVERING ON TIME
Facing growing threats from Russia and waning confidence in US security guarantees, European governments have sharply increased defence spending since Moscow's invasion of Ukraine, including on naval capabilities.
Naval Group, which is 35% owned by French defence technology company Thales, is winning a share of that spending as competitors struggle to deliver ships on time.
Germany scrapped a landmark frigate programme in June, six years after launch, after Dutch group Damen failed to meet deadlines and budget targets. Belgium is also facing delays to a frigate programme involving Damen.
At Naval Group's shipyard in Lorient, western France, last week, three ships for Greece were at various stages of construction or testing following contracts signed in 2022 and 2025. A first frigate was delivered to the Greek navy last year.
Steel was also being cut for the first of four frigates ordered by Sweden under a contract signed in August, while two vessels for the French navy were being built and tested.
"The main advantage our ship has is that it already exists, that there's a production line up and running, and that we are delivering them on time," said Jean-Marie Dorbon, director of Naval's frigate programme.
Naval Group says it can build two Defence and Intervention Frigates per year in Lorient, cutting delivery times to less than four years and ultimately aiming for around three.
Competition remains intense. The company lost a contract to build Norway's frigates to BAE Systems last year and is competing with Britain's Babcock for the Danish deal.
In Germany, TKMS has been tasked with building small Meko frigates to replace vessels initially ordered from Damen.
To win contracts, Naval Group works with local suppliers, including Salamis Shipyards in Greece. In Sweden, where the contract requires Swedish equipment to be integrated on board, it is working with Saab, Dorbon said.
"That also includes incorporating their solutions to our catalogue of options," he said. REUTERS

MOSCOW, October 8. /TASS/. The new data center set up in Armenia could be used in the interests of Western intelligence agencies against Russia, Iran and other countries, Russian Security Council Deputy Secretary Alexey Shevtsov warned.

Shevtsov mentioned Firebird’s plans to increase the Hrazdan facility’s capacity to 300 MW by the end of 2027, which "is almost a quarter of Armenia’s winter peak energy load (1.3 GW)." "That said, given these plans, additional energy capacities will be required to keep the center operational," the Russian Security Council deputy secretary stressed. In his view, "Armenia risks facing a major power shortage that will inevitably affect the country’s people."

08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
The Africa Credit Rating Agency (AfCRA) was officially launched in Mauritius on Wednesday, aiming to strengthen the continent’s financial independence and improve assessments of its economies, the African Union said.
AU Commission Chairperson Mahmoud Ali Youssouf described the launch as a milestone in Africa’s economic history.
Credit ratings directly influence access to financing and borrowing costs, he said, warning that assessments that overlook African economic conditions can leave countries paying more to borrow.
AfCRA will complement existing international rating agencies by providing independent, credible assessments based on African data and expertise.
Credibility and independence
Mauritius’ Financial Services and Economic Planning Minister Jyoti Jeetun said the agency could strengthen Africa’s financial system and attract investment.
She highlighted opportunities in infrastructure, renewable energy, telecommunications, healthcare and agriculture.
African Peer Review Mechanism chief Marie-Antoinette Rose Quatre said the AU endorsed AfCRA’s establishment in 2017.
She urged African governments to provide accurate and timely economic data, stressing that credibility would be the agency’s most important asset.
The initiative aligns with the AU’s Agenda 2063 development goals.

Argo Ideon: Our everyday doomscrolling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:29:00 UTC
21:29:00 KST

Argo Ideon: Our everyday doomscrolling
The vigilant citizen begins their day by examining drone warnings and war maps. Estonia is living in a recurring cycle of war anxiety that social media abundantly feeds, writes Argo Ideon.
A security‑aware citizen wakes briskly, ahead of the alarm clock, as a jittery feeling is already there. They search for the smartphone under the blanket to check whether the Defense Forces have sent a drone warning. Today, there is no air threat, but if there is, then one must examine which area is being talked about. More precise instructions can be found at kriis.ee.
Since no dread‑inducing events occurred overnight, they may briefly wipe the sleepy eyes, but the vigilance cannot be lost. The information‑hungry citizen opens channel X. Yesterday, a map appeared there, where the Baltic states were depicted together with red arrows arriving from the east. Especially thick arrows were painted toward Narva and the Lithuania‑Poland border.
Now they would like to see whether the arrows moved somewhere further during sleep or stayed behind the eastern border. There, where according to retired General Martin Herem preparations may be underway "to do something militarily against us." But the new reports keep coming, the map has disappeared and whoever posted it at night is already forgotten about.
The citizen is confused, but realizes that instead of searching for the map they should visit the bathroom. On the way to get the toothbrush they glance out the kitchen window; against the background of drizzle everything seems even too calm, someone is walking their floppy‑eared dog on the sidewalk. An enemy agent, a saboteur recruited via social media? More likely the downstairs neighbor...
Turning on the shower, the citizen recalls that Estonia's defense expenditure budget next year is €2.2 billion. They set their fingers in pistol position and imitate a K9 Thunder self‑propelled howitzer shot: "Pow!" The wet environment does not hinder the Defense Forces' fire‑support capability.
And then there is HIMARS. The citizen does not know exactly what sound it makes, but they think that flying toward the target the much talked about weapon should sound something like a "Woosh!" As of today there have not been any new messages yet that the long‑ago ordered HIMARS ammunition from the U.S. is to definitely arrive in Estonia, already, soon.
A fresh interview with a national‑defense expert has appeared on the news portal. The situation is tense, the scenarios detailed and the threats hybrid. But it still is not a real war, and after reading the gut feeling remains that nothing new was learned. Therefore all the material must be worked through.
Let's begin with security expert Rainer Saks' every‑morning post. The citizen opens Facebook to see the original text, although several other websites also reprint Rainer's work. Rainer doesn't deal in nonsense — he says what he knows and how things are in Ukraine. Amazing how he has the stamina for this fifth year. Then the citizen opens the latest war diary in Eesti Ekspress. ERR's Ukraine blog constantly adds reports from early morning onward. Armed with up‑to‑date security information, the citizen dares to switch off war topics in their head for a while and focus on today's workday.
In the evening everything begins again from the start. On X there is a new set of maps with arrows. Putin is said to have said something about Estonia, but what exactly and in what context? And what does it actually mean? Are they fortifying the Narva River bank again? All of it seems extremely suspicious.
The worst anxiety takes hold again. Where's the box of pills?
Finally, the vigilant citizen remembers Robert Sheckley's classic sci‑fi horror story "Ghost V": "You can't beat blankets over the head for protection."
It should help against the Grumbler, the Purple-Striped Grabber, and the fear stories that pour daily like a torrent from social media.
In their restless sleep the security‑interested citizen sees how they build together with Pooh and Piglet the Hundred Acre Defense Line. Pooh carries three empty honey jars in front of the bedroom door, but Piglet takes a large wooden spoon and stands guard beside the door.

A drone attack overnight on 8 October caused a fire that hit part of Yandex's data center in Sasovo, Ryazan Oblast, about 580 km from Ukraine, and the site is fully stopped, the Russian tech company told Russian media. The data center sits on the grounds of Sasta, a sanctioned machine-tool plant, Russian outlet Astra said, citing Wikimapia data. Astra's OSINT analyst found from eyewitness footage that the fire hit the plant.
Since late September, Russia has been striking data centers in Kyiv that keep Ukraine's internet and online services running. Now a drone attack has stopped one of the data centers that Russia's largest tech company relies on.
Yandex counts the damage
Yandex warned that some services may be unavailable, while its core services kept running and no one was hurt. Ryazan Oblast Governor Pavel Malkov claimed two drones were downed, a roof caught fire at an enterprise in the Sasovo district, and windows were blown out in several homes.
The power failure took down a wide range of Yandex Cloud infrastructure, including computing capacity, networks, data storage, databases, Kubernetes, cloud services, AI, and security and monitoring systems, Ukrainian outlet ZN.ua reported, citing Exilenova+.
Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ reported that the plant was hit, without naming an attacker. The channel said Sasta, which claims a place on Russia's register of defense-industry companies, makes computer-controlled machine tools, including five-axis machining centers, and previously supplied the Tactical Missiles Corporation (KTRV) and Roscosmos. The plant's value to the arms industry lies in machines that cut precision parts, not in finished weapons, the channel said.
Citing Exilenova+, Militarnyi reported that Ukraine's Defense Forces hit the plant. It also linked Sasta to Iskander missile supply chains. No source has said whether the plant or the data center was the target, and no Ukrainian official has claimed the Sasovo strike. Sasta has been under US sanctions since November 2023, UK sanctions since February 2024, and Ukrainian sanctions since April 2025, a sanctions database shows.
Salavat: Kyiv reports a hit
Ukrainian forces hit the Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat complex in Bashkortostan, about 1,380 km from the front line, causing a fire, Ukraine's General Staff said. It said the complex processes up to 10 million metric tons of hydrocarbons a year and serves Russia's armed forces. Its key unit, the ELOU-AVT-6 primary oil refining unit launched in 2012, can process 6 million metric tons a year, Militarnyi reported. Astra's analyst placed the fire a few kilometers outside Salavat, possibly near the refinery.
Salavat Mayor Marat Zagidullin claimed that debris from several drones fell in the industrial zone that morning and started a fire.
"The enterprise continues to work," he said.
Astra noted earlier hits on the complex on 24 September 2025, on 14 July 2026, when refining fully stopped, and on 13 August 2026.
Russia's strikes on Ukraine's data centers
Russia has repeatedly hit data centers in Kyiv since 23 September. Strikes hit the COSMONOVA data center twice, the second time knocking it out, and the Parkovyi data center stopped working completely on 1 October after a series of strikes. In early October, Russia destroyed the dline.ua data center in Kyiv.

AI for Philosophy: Progress through Capital-Intensive Philosophy (guest post)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:27:59 UTC
21:27:59 KST

“AI systems… will transform the discipline: they will make philosophy more capital-intensive. “
* * *
The following is a guest post by David Strohmaier, a philosopher and computer scientist in the Natural Language and Information Processing group at the University of Cambridge. In it, he explains why he thinks it’s reasonable to believe that AI systems will eventually have the capacities to “drive” philosophy, and how this will change the economics of philosophy.
AI for Philosophy: Progress through Capital-Intensive Philosophy
by David Strohmaier
Introduction
Generative AI has arrived in philosophy. Not only do journals receive significant numbers of AI-generated papers of dubious quality, there has also been increasing talk of AI work dedicated to philosophy.1 I have observed these developments as a researcher working in both AI and philosophy and, from that perspective, want to lay out a shift I see coming for philosophy and why I endorse it: philosophy will become a capital-intensive discipline in which a significant portion of research will be driven by AI systems.
My position depends on the capacities of AI systems. Since I am aware that many philosophers are skeptical about AI technology in general, let me first lay out the skeptical and the optimistic positions on whether AI systems will be able to drive philosophy, i.e. lead to whole new ways of doing philosophy.
The Skeptical and the Optimistic Positions on AI Capacities
The skeptical position about the capacities of AI systems is frequently motivated by the fact that prompting an LLM to write a philosophy paper either produces underwhelming results or requires so much hand-holding that one might question the value of using an LLM. Without massive revisions, AI writing is often atrocious. I recently had the joy of reviewing a computer science paper that was clearly AI-written. The prose was painful. The sentences were endless chains of semicolons and em-dashes. The model had no sense of proportion, blowing up negligible details while relegating important information to one of the numerous appendices.
Beyond stylistic problems, AI models struggle to produce truly innovative insights. Instead, they tend to dwell on rather technical, minor points. From the sceptic’s vantage point, this suggests that AI-driven philosophy would just produce forgettable pieces no one wants to engage with. Sometimes this sceptical assessment rests on a dated understanding of AI systems as mere LLMs that derive their capacities solely from the texts on which they were pre-trained. This picture no longer holds because training regimes have been diversified, but it remains true that the systems have not been specialised for philosophical innovativeness.
The optimistic position regarding the capacities of AI systems is often justified by projecting the current rate of progress into the future. The technology is progressing rapidly, so while AI systems may not yet be able to compose papers that hold up to the rigorous standards of top philosophy journals, we should give the AI labs a few more years. I think that there is much to be said for this projection, but we don’t require bold predictions about superintelligence or anything of that sort to foresee the growth of AI-driven philosophy.
To justify my optimism, I will assume only the application of AI technology as it exists, that is, foundation models and harnesses as they are currently available to frontier labs. Such models have been able to disprove a long-standing conjecture in discrete geometry and to develop a new algorithm for multiplying 4×4 complex-valued matrices. So far, the exploration of such uses is the exception in philosophy, but the technology is available.
While so far there are no well-documented instances of AI systems solving philosophical problems, I am optimistic because philosophy has a crucial feature making it promising for applying AI at scale: widespread inferential dependence across areas. To answer a question in metaphysics, one may have to consider issues in semantics and epistemology or even move beyond the limits of the discipline and take physics into account. Due to these pervasive cross-area dependencies in philosophy, the ability of AI systems to scale is extremely valuable. AI agents can not only identify relevant statements from other debates, but can formalise published theories at scale and then use tools to construct counter-examples.
For such use cases, it doesn’t matter that the prose style of LLMs is grating. Nor do AI systems lack the ingenuity to be employed in this way. The limited innovativeness that AI has been proven to possess, for example in developing novel algorithms for matrix multiplication, is sufficient for exploring various formalisations and testing them against counter-examples. As long as the AI systems can perform these functions at scale, they can lead us to the solution of philosophical problems.
One might respond that the use cases I gestured at require the availability of verification, and it is true that I see areas such as decision theory, axiomatic metaphysics, and formal epistemology as among the most promising candidates for AI-driven philosophy. However, even for the parts of philosophy which do not allow for determinate conclusions, AI systems will help establish which positions can reach a rational equilibrium. After all, these systems have the ability to consider thousands of discursive options and to systematically explore different aggregation schemes for judgements as they are recorded in the philosophical literature or human text in general. They can map the discursive space at a level of granularity that would be too labour-intensive for us.
In the previous paragraphs, I emphasized the ability of AI systems to scale on philosophically relevant tasks. It is due to these scaling abilities that I expect that AI systems will drive a new form of doing philosophy. Importantly, the more capital is spent on scaling AI inference, the better the results. There are always more counter-examples to consider, more aggregation schemes to explore, another angle to try, but you need the compute to do so.
The Transformation to a Capital-Intensive Discipline
Having sketched why I believe that AI systems will have the capacity to drive philosophy, I turn to how they will transform the discipline: they will make philosophy more capital-intensive. Simplifying slightly, over the thousands of years of philosophy’s history, capital, in the sense of external means of production, has played two roles:2
- Capital allows those who own it either to engage in philosophy themselves or to enable others to do so. This form of capital enters philosophy only insofar as it provides the means of living while attention is directed towards philosophical problems. For example, the income from Plato’s estate allowed him to dedicate his time to philosophy.
- Writing and reading materials are a form of capital that more directly supports the philosophical process. They are the means of producing philosophical arguments and insights. In the history of philosophy, getting access to such capital was often challenging, but these days a well-equipped public library may supply these means of philosophy.
If we broaden the use of the term “capital”, the most important form of capital for philosophy may be human capital, the skills and dispositions exhibited by philosophers.3 Being an academic philosopher may not be just a life of the mind, but it comes as close as any profession does. Up to now, free time, a library computer, and a mind honed on philosophical arguments used to be almost all you strictly needed for philosophy. Before the personal computer, all that was required was a typewriter, before that a fountain pen. Changes were rare, progressed at glacial pace, and were small compared to transformations in most industries. The two most impactful inventions may have been writing and the printing press, the means to record and spread our ideas. The arguments and their evaluation still had to spring from our minds. In this regard, the rise of AI-driven philosophy will be transformative.
To glimpse how philosophy will be transformed, it is worth considering how other disciplines function. When I entered computer science after my philosophy PhD, I underwent a culture shock. The role of capital contributed to the shock, not least because access to capital circumscribes what you can do in computer science. The number of GPUs available to you matters. You just cannot address certain questions if you don’t have the required equipment. You need access to the means of producing AI research. During my philosophy PhD, I once jokingly asked a faculty member what philosophy grants were spent on. Armchairs? His response was that the funding freed the philosopher from other obligations, freed them for philosophy. Once the funding suffices to pay your salary (and those of your postdocs/PhD students) and to cover your expenses for conferences/research visits, that’s about it.4
In computer science, and especially in AI research, there is never enough funding. If, instead of $5,000 worth of GPU credits you gave us $2 million, we would have no difficulty spending it. Our research scales with the capital, and while the marginal return on capital diminishes with size, most academic AI research doesn’t reach the point where this becomes relevant. Consequently, not just human capital matters, but access to computational capital. This might also be the future of philosophy as a capital-intensive discipline.
Objections to the Transformation and Why I Endorse It Nevertheless
While a number of principled objections have been raised against the use of AI for philosophy, the prospect of this transformation might very well be behind the distaste some philosophers show for AI. Academic philosophers like doing philosophy and many of them like doing it just the way they are doing it, thank you very much. Most philosophers enjoy engaging with each other in argument. They want to read what another philosopher has written, consider it, and respond carefully after much deliberation. Money matters for this process only insofar as it frees your time for doing philosophy, but it barely affects how you spend this free time.
A common position along these lines is that the process matters more than the result. According to this position, even if capital-intensive AI systems could uncover valid philosophical arguments or true philosophical statements, these would be of little value. What matters is individual reflection and engagement with other philosophers. Process, not product, is the source of value for philosophy.
The type of AI-driven philosophy at which I have gestured would certainly employ a different process, but it doesn’t have to dispense with human understanding of philosophical arguments and results. Even with scaled AI systems engaging in a variety of tasks, I expect us to be able to comprehend the core philosophical moves. However, this understanding will be arrived at by engagement with the output of AI systems. That is a fundamentally different process for arriving at understanding than the one academic philosophers are used to. If one values the current process of private deliberation, the sharing of preliminary drafts, and the exchange of arguments in colloquia or conferences, then one might reject the AI-driven process.
While I feel deep attachment to the traditional way of doing philosophy, an exclusive commitment to it is easy to preserve as long as the process in question is the only one that can produce philosophical insights. So far, there is no price to pay for it. That will change when AI-driven philosophy comes into its own. It will be hard to justify an exclusive commitment to the process when further insights could be achieved if one combined labor with capital. The results will be better once new AI systems transform philosophy.
Personally, I am excited by this development. Although I very much enjoy engaging in philosophy the old-fashioned way, one reason I turned to computer science was that I wanted to solve problems. How often, if ever, philosophers are able to solve the problems their discipline raises is a matter of dispute. In this dispute, I have been (privately) on the side of those who believe that progress is possible but extremely difficult. If AI fulfils its promise, its introduction could be a decisive moment in the history of philosophy. The rate at which we solve philosophical problems might increase!
If my vision came true and if we nevertheless insisted not merely on understanding the results of AI-driven philosophy, but on not having AI drive the process at all, it would suggest that we don’t care all that much about the answers to our questions after all. I don’t think that is the case. We care about the semantics of normative language, whether wholes exist over and above their parts, and whether any of these questions can really be answered. If AI can help us find answers to these questions or show that they are unanswerable, it will be an enormous success. That is why I endorse the transformation.
The vision that excites me might be a source of fear for others. What if AI-driven philosophy proved successful at solving philosophical problems? If the approach failed, if it produced nothing of value, then it would eventually die off, not least because it requires capital that could be employed elsewhere. However, if AI-driven philosophy proved successful, it might crowd out other modes of doing philosophy that current practitioners value. Those willing (and able) to deploy capital on philosophical problems will respond more quickly and with more impressive results. It will become increasingly difficult to sideline their output. Some philosophical problems matter to us because we want to know the answer and, therefore, we will also care about the solution, regardless of how it was arrived at.
I wish I could assuage the worry that AI-driven philosophy will crowd out human-capital-centered philosophy. However, I cannot do so in good conscience, because I have observed how, in NLP, multiple approaches that I genuinely care about have been crowded out by the immense progress of deep learning. Of course, we will continue to exchange arguments and debate, if only for our own entertainment and mostly outside academic obligations. Nevertheless, I expect the discipline to be transformed. If my vision comes to pass, much of the old-fashioned process will be displaced by capital-intensive AI-driven philosophy. The dynamics in a department will shift when a colleague, instead of spending hours carefully considering a draft shared with them, lets an AI system poke holes in it. Something will be lost. Such is the nature of transformative change. If we are able to uncover and understand one more philosophical truth due to this change, I am willing to pay the price.
AI Use for This Post
The original idea was all mine. I used Claude to search the literature, copy-edit, and get feedback. Prompted to take the perspective of an analytic philosopher, Claude proved much more skeptical about the potential of AI for philosophy than I am. To ensure that no slop slipped in, changes were made by me rather than directly inserted by AI tools.
Footnotes
- An earlier proposal on AI contributing to philosophy was made in 2023 by Clay and Ontiveros, but went largely ignored by the discipline. ↩︎
- I focus here on the writing of philosophy and on arguing with other practitioners, not the teaching of philosophy. The latter has been more capital-intensive for a while, especially when attempts are made to scale courses. ↩︎
- If we insist on dragging Bourdieu into this, we can also discuss social capital and issues of prestige, but I will leave those aside for this post. ↩︎
- I am simplifying here by assuming the case of pure armchair philosophy. Many philosophical projects have other uses for funding. For example, experimental philosophers would surely love to scale up some of their experiments. ↩︎

UK’s Burnham ‘open’ to Germany joining GCAP fighter jet programme

UK’s Burnham ‘open’ to Germany joining GCAP fighter jet programme
GCAP pact between the UK, Italy and Japan to build a new fighter jet welcomed Canada as an ‘observer’ in July
Prime Minister Andy Burnham says the United Kingdom is open to Germany joining the GCAP programme, a partnership with Italy and Japan to build a new fighter jet, after meeting Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Berlin.
“I’ve indicated to the Chancellor … our openness to Germany joining GCAP,” Burnham told a news conference on Thursday.
“That is something that we seek to progress in the coming period, working with our other partners, Italy and Japan.”
There has been growing speculation that the founding countries of the Global Combat Air Programme (GCAP) could open the door to Germany after a rival Franco-German fighter programme collapsed in June.
The GCAP pact to build a sixth generation fighter jet welcomed Canada as an “observer nation” in July.
As western nations seek to maintain air superiority over rival powers, the new warplanes will be equipped with AI, next-generation sensors and other technology.
Burnham is on his first official visit to Germany since becoming Britain’s prime minister in July. The leaders are also expected to confirm a new UK-Germany joint security partnership to counter sabotage, cyberattacks and other hybrid threats from adversaries.
“Attacks on our infrastructure, our businesses and our democracies are not a distant threat. They reach into people’s homes and workplaces and they are designed to make us weaker and more divided,” Burnham said in a statement ahead of the visit.
Burnham’s office singled out the threat posed by Russia in a statement on Thursday, but stressed that the partnership would confront security threats regardless of their origin.
As part of the agreement, the UK and Germany will share security information and work together to monitor, deter and disrupt threats.
British MPs have raised concerns in recent months about the potential threats posed by Russia, with Defence Secretary Wes Streeting warning last month that Russia and its President, Vladimir Putin, were the biggest threat to the country’s security.
Germany has also raised concerns about what it sees as a growing security threat posed by Moscow. Last month, Berlin accused Russia of being behind a failed drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport. Moscow denies any wrongdoing.
Reporting from Berlin, Al Jazeera’s Dominic Kane said the security partnership is “supposed to send a message to several countries” about the intention to increase European security.
“It’s a way of demonstrating German and British intent in so far as Ukraine is concerned, but also more broadly about where Europe goes next, remembering of course that the United States plays a role in so far as NATO is concerned,” Kane said.
“We know that Merz and Starmer [Burnham’s predecessor] and we can assume Burnham want to show to the Americans, as much as to the Russians, how much European security means to them.”
Burnham and Merz are also expected to discuss other key issues for Europe, including ongoing support for Ukraine in its war against Russia and disruption to global trade routes, including through the Strait of Hormuz.
The leaders are also expected to formally ratify the 2025 Kensington Treaty. The accord commits both countries to deepening cooperation on science, technology, defence, security and economic growth.

The Russian authorities have downplayed the incident, saying she died from “pneumonia of an unknown aetiology”, and that post-mortem analysis showed no trace of an infection connected with her “professional work” at the Irkutsk anti-plague institute.
Local media reports suggested she could have contracted the disease after breaking a test tube at the laboratory.
The incident has triggered global concern about a possible outbreak and calls for Russia to provide more information.
It has also drawn criticism and comparisons with Moscow’s long history of downplaying or covering up the scale of health disasters, ranging from the Soviet response to the 1986 Chernobyl disaster to the coronavirus pandemic.
In Shelekhov, rumours have filled the information abyss.
“I’ve read about it being some kind of unclear pneumonia or Covid, something like that. To be honest, I don’t believe in anything anymore,” Oksana, who declined to give her surname, said. “There’s so much information that I no longer know what to believe or who to listen to.”

“I’d read somewhere that it was something like Hong Kong syphilis, and that it was actually caused by bears,” she said, referring to a fictional disease from a popular Russian TV show.
“People were absolutely panicking because there were no official statements,” she added.
‘We don’t know’
On the streets, the town appears outwardly calm – no panic and few masks.
Yet many said they are concerned.
“It’s frightening,” said Alina, 22. “My brother’s at primary school. They’ve already made masks compulsory, so they have to wear them everywhere. They’re even allowed to stay off school if they’re really worried.”
She said her aunt works at the anti-plague institute and was also quarantined.
Tatyana, 66, is also frustrated by the lack of official guidance from the authorities.
“Of course, we’re worried. How on earth are we supposed to protect ourselves?” she said. “We don’t know how the infection spreads, or how it’s detected.”
“There are a lot of rumours going around, all kinds of information, and it’s unclear what’s true. In reality, nobody is telling us what actually happened,” she added.
On Oct 7, World Health Organization chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus urged Moscow to clarify “media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause” from the Irkutsk institute.
When asked about a possible second case, the Kremlin appeared to reject it.
“The vast majority of what the media is reporting regarding this situation is false information,” spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
Rospotrebnadzor said on Oct 7 that the situation in the Irkutsk region remained “stable”, and that nearly 5,000 tests had been conducted, none of which revealed dangerous pathogens.
US President Donald Trump has offered to “help” Russia, and said he would call his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin to discuss the reports.
That offer was widely laughed off on the streets of Shelekhov.
“It’s just funny,” said Olga, a 68-year-old former accountant.

The US plans to establish a permanent and economically viable lunar presence rather than repeating the short-lived expeditions of the Apollo era, Amazon CEO Jeffrey Bezos said.
"Today we're going to do it at a lower cost and going to the Moon to stay," Bezos, founder of US space company Blue Origin, told Fox News on Wednesday. "It won't just be a mission and leave. It will be a real sustainable lunar base. That's how we'll explore the Moon and find interesting things."
Bezos contrasted modern commercial spaceflight with the 1969 lunar program, explaining that the initial effort required "almost 3% of GDP" to execute. He noted that establishing routine cargo delivery systems remains a vital precursor to crewed landings and said: "There's every reason to believe that we can put humans on the Moon in 2028."
Highlighting strategic competition, Bezos emphasized that Washington must outpace Beijing and said: "We have to beat China to the Moon. I believe we will beat China to the Moon."
He characterized the Moon as an indispensable logistical stepping stone before attempting crewed missions to Mars, noting that personnel can reach the destination in three days without waiting for complex launch windows. Operating from the lunar surface also requires "28 times less energy to lift something" due to lower gravity while offering abundant local resources, he said.
Blue Origin serves as a central commercial partner in NASA's Artemis campaign, developing the Human Landing System designed to transport astronauts to the lunar surface for the Artemis V mission.
Addressing artificial intelligence oversight, Bezos advocated for targeted restrictions rather than heavy regulations on core foundation models. "You want to regulate murder...you don't want to regulate knives," he said, arguing that governments should focus on harmful applications and malicious actors rather than the tool.

Thousands of Spaniards march to mark death of octogenarian at heart of housing protests
MADRID, Oct 8 - Thousands of Spaniards marched through central Madrid on Thursday to mark the death of the 87-year-old woman whose eviction from her home ignited protests across the country and led to a snap election next month.
Maricarmen Abascal, who died on Wednesday, had been hospitalised for severe anxiety and exhaustion since her eviction on September 23. No cause of death has been announced.
Protests over home shortages and surging rents following her eviction prompted Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez to call a snap general election for November 29 after parliament rejected his government's proposals to address a mounting housing crisis.
As the sun set in Madrid, thousands followed a line of Tenants Union members, dressed in orange vests and walking arm-in-arm, as they carried a wreath of flowers from a protest camp in central Puerta del Sol square to Abascal's former home near Retiro Park.
"They're not deaths; they're murders," the protesters chanted.
Several people who received eviction orders have died by suicide in Spain in recent months.
Political leaders on Thursday traded blame and invoked Abascal's case in attacks on opponents.
Left-leaning parties criticised conservatives who rejected legislation in parliament aimed at curbing soaring rental prices. Right-wingers said the leftist central government had been unable to tackle the crisis after eight years in power.
Alberto Nuñez Feijoo, leader of the conservative opposition People's Party (PP), accused Sanchez and the Socialists of trying to exploit the housing crisis for political gain before the election.
"We will not allow this attempt to manipulate the emotions of the Spanish people; all of this has happened during their eight years in government. It won’t fly," Feijoo said.
In the Madrid regional assembly, opposition leader Manuela Bergerot of the leftist Mas Madrid party said Maricarmen — as she has become known across Spain — had died because of "miserable people who put gain above a person's life."
She said the last thing Madrid regional leader Isabel Diaz Ayuso had done while Maricarmen was alive was "laugh at her" — a reference to Ayuso's quip on September 28: "At what age do I get to stop paying my landlords? Let me know."
Ayuso blamed Sanchez, saying Maricarmen had been evicted under his government.
PROTESTERS BLAME 'GREEDY' LANDLORDS
News of the octogenarian's death enraged protesters camped on squares in Spain's main cities who chanted that she had been "murdered" because of the greed of her landlords.
After an investment fund purchased the building where she had lived for more than 70 years, Abascal lost a lengthy legal battle against rent increases far beyond her pension income, leading to her eviction. While in hospital, she reached a deal to regain her home but she died before she could return.
"When everything is private, we will be deprived of everything," said a placard on Puerta del Sol square, where mourners lit candles and left flowers honouring Maricarmen.
Outside Abascal's building, mourners left flowers, candles, handwritten notes and children's drawings.
"Maricarmen was the straw that broke the camel's back... (she was) a symbol of resistance and unity," said Alex Marinero, a 21-year-old protester.
Tributes to Abascal in the Madrid region's legislature also caused arguments as lawmakers accused each other of cynically exploiting the case.
The PP, which has absolute majorities in the Madrid regional and local assemblies, refused to hold a minute of silence honouring her.
Instead, hard-left deputies staged one outside City Hall and gave Abascal a 60-second standing ovation during a tense debate in the regional assembly, while PP lawmakers remained seated with folded arms.
A survey carried out in June and published by state pollster CIS on Thursday found 76.3% of Spaniards supported intervention in the market to guarantee access to housing, while 79% believe the right to housing should take precedence over treating homes as a market commodity.
Ombudsman Angel Gabilondo said addressing the housing crisis would require greater commitment from all levels of government.
He said his office was preparing a housing report and reiterated proposals including expanding public housing, restricting tourist rentals, increasing rent assistance and strengthening protections against evictions for vulnerable households. REUTERS

Protests and school students’ marches continue in France — what the education minister’s “emergency action plan” is supposed to resolve

Protests and school students’ marches continue in France — what the education minister’s “emergency action plan” is supposed to resolve
Kyiv • UNN
French high school students have been protesting for the third week over a shortage of teachers and the condition of schools. The government has promised funded measures by the end of October.
On Thursday, French high school students blocked the operation of some schools and held marches through cities. The government promised to address the problems students had complained about — including a shortage of teachers and the dilapidated condition of school buildings — but provided few specifics, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
The protest movement, now in its third week, has exposed deep tensions in France: on the one hand, public demands to invest in deteriorating public services, and on the other, a cash-strapped government under pressure from bond markets demanding cuts to public debt and the budget deficit.
Upper-secondary school teacher Diana Di Sciullo joined students during a large march in Marseille; she said that all they want is quality education in proper conditions. She criticized the problem of overcrowded classrooms, saying that 37 students are enrolled in her class this year.
What does France’s Education Ministry say?
According to the Education Ministry, the number of blocked schools was gradually declining. The ministry reported that 224 schools were closed in the morning, but by midday that number had fallen to 157, meaning that 96% of educational institutions were operating normally.
In some places in Paris, blockades led to clashes between police and protesters.
Large-scale protests took place across the country: from Lille in the north to Rennes and Nantes in the west, in the capital Paris, as well as in Toulon and Marseille in the south.
Education Minister Édouard Geffray met with students and teachers at a school in the city of Reims in the east of the country.
"I am now implementing an emergency measures plan to ensure the long-term replacement of absent teachers," he said after the meeting, adding that the issue of the overloaded school timetable was also being reviewed.
In France, it is not uncommon for students to have lessons from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m., as well as to receive large amounts of homework.
Geffray also said he was working on possible improvements to Parcoursup — the national online university admissions portal, which has faced significant criticism because of its complexity and its ability to cause stress among applicants.
Late on Wednesday evening, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu promised that by the end of October the government would present "concrete, swift and fully funded measures" in response to the protests, but gave no details.
One of the main complaints displayed on posters and banners was dissatisfaction with the excessively harsh actions of police during the wave of protests. A typical example of this discontent was the slogan: "Too young for you to listen to us, but old enough for you to fire tear gas at us".
Hundreds of arrests and dozens of injuries have been recorded since the movement began. On Wednesday, the government suspended the use of stun grenades for crowd control at protests after one teenager's hand was blown off in an explosion.
How are French politicians responding to the protests?
Six months before the election that will choose a successor to President Emmanuel Macron after the end of his second consecutive term in office, politicians’ reactions to the wave of student protests have proved sharply polarized.
Far-right leader Marine Le Pen emphasized the damage caused to educational institutions by a small group of protesters and called on them or their parents to pay the repair bills. On Tuesday, she outlined plans to cut public spending if she wins.
Her opponent from the far-left camp, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who also has a chance of reaching the second round of the election, called the protesters "incredible" and condemned police brutality.
According to a poll conducted by Elabe for BFM TV, 72% of French people consider the students’ demands justified, but 55% of them believe that the protests should end.
The government is trying to strike a balance: condemning cases of violence — including arson attacks on schools and injuries to staff — while at the same time expressing understanding of some of the students’ complaints.

Feature: Afghan Post upgrades services, connects Afghans with world
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
20:23:35 CST
21:23:35 KST

KABUL, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- Waiting for his turn to deliver several newly issued passports to their owners in Sara-e-Shamali and Khair Khana neighborhoods in northern Kabul, postman Zakihullah said he was happy to serve people through his work.
"I deliver passports to the recipients at the gates of their homes. It takes a maximum of one hour to make a delivery. Otherwise, it takes only 10 to 15 minutes to hand over a passport to an addressee in Karta-e-Parwan or Sara-e-Shamali," the 20-year-old postman told Xinhua.
Zakihullah made the remarks as Afghanistan is set to mark World Post Day on Friday, commemorating the founding of the Universal Postal Union (UPU) on Oct. 9, 1874.
Postal services, like other national infrastructure, were severely affected by more than four decades of war and foreign intervention in Afghanistan. In recent years, efforts have been made to rebuild and modernize the country's postal system and bring its services closer to international standards.
Afghan Post, the country's state-owned postal service provider, handles both domestic and international mail and cargo. It provides services not only to people inside Afghanistan but also to Afghans living abroad and foreigners seeking to send or receive letters, documents, parcels and other items, including educational certificates and marriage documents.
"The delivery of passports and other documents began about two years ago. I deliver passports to the doors of the recipients, or submit them to the post office in their area, where the recipients can collect them," said Zakihullah, who joined Afghan Post two and a half years ago.
Zabihullah Omar, director of business development at Afghan Post, said the company expanded its services to Kabul and all 34 provinces as part of efforts to upgrade and modernize its operations.
"Afghan Post currently delivers government correspondence, letters, written documents, passports and educational certificates," Omar told Xinhua at his office.
He said the company planned to further modernize and computerize its facilities and services to bring them in line with postal systems in other countries.
"We also provide transportation services for postal items and cargo inside the country and to 192 countries overseas," Omar said.
Afghanistan is a member of the UPU, and a delegation from Afghan Post attended the Asia-Pacific Postal Union (APPU) Congress held in Bangkok recently, where it exchanged experiences with postal authorities from other countries, Omar said.
To facilitate correspondence and mail delivery, Afghan Post has also introduced postal codes for cities across Afghanistan, an initiative approved by the UPU.
Afghans have expressed satisfaction with the post services. "Expanding facilities and modernizing Afghan Post are beneficial to the people. It is like a one-stop service, as we have the post office here and can also pay bank fees here," said Sakhi Murad, who came from the northern city of Mazar-i-Sharif to obtain a stamp from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs for his educational documents through Afghan Post.
Murad called for expanding postal facilities in rural areas to make services more accessible and reduce difficulties for people living in the countryside. ■

Italian parliament's lower house approves new election law
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
20:23:23 CST
21:23:23 KST

ROME, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- The lower house of Italy's parliament on Thursday gave final approval to a new election law proposed by parties in Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's ruling coalition, with 227 lawmakers voting in favor and 164 against.
The new law replaces the current mixed electoral system, which combines first-past-the-post and proportional representation, with a proportional representation system that grants bonus seats to the coalition winning the most votes, provided it secures at least 42 percent of the vote. The mechanism is intended to ensure a working majority in parliament.
If no coalition reaches the 42-percent threshold, or if the results of elections for the lower house and Senate differ, seats will instead be allocated under a purely proportional system.
Under the new system, electoral coalitions will be required to name their candidate for prime minister before an election. The law also allows voters to express preferences for up to three candidates from a party list of six, with male and female candidates required to alternate on the list. ■

MP Serhiy Hryvko (Servant of the People faction) has proposed that the Verkhovna Rada introduce the status of Army Volunteer of the Security and Defense Forces of Ukraine.
A corresponding bill (No. 16129) on amending certain legislative acts regarding the introduction of the status of volunteers of the Security and Defense Forces of Ukraine has been registered in the Verkhovna Rada, according to the parliament's website.
As noted in the document's explanatory note, the bill does not introduce an alternative "combatant" status or alter the procedure for granting it; rather, it establishes an additional special status for individuals whose voluntary participation in the defense of Ukraine meets specific criteria. The status of Army Volunteer of the Security and Defense Forces of Ukraine is proposed for individuals who already hold combatant status and meet one of the criteria for voluntary participation in Ukraine's defense set out in the bill. These criteria include voluntarily applying to an authorized recruitment body or military unit and entering military service during the Anti-Terrorist Operation (ATO), the effort to repel and deter Russian Federation aggression in Luhansk and Donetsk regions, or the period of martial law.
The bill provides for granting volunteers of the Security and Defence Forces of Ukraine the right to a special award, as well as specific additional social and other guarantees, specifically: seven calendar days of additional paid leave, free access to certain sports, wellness, and cultural-educational services, and priority in being selected for civil service positions in the event of tied competition results.
