====================================================================================================

Buried answers: Gaza families' unbearable wait for missing continues amid three years of Israel's genocide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:06:06 UTC
20:06:06 KST

As the Gaza war enters its fourth year, thousands of Palestinian families remain without answers about loved ones who disappeared amid three years of Israeli attacks and destruction.
The scale of the task is immense.
The UN estimates the war has generated millions of tonnes of debris across Gaza, while Palestinian Civil Defense estimates that more than 8,000 people remain missing beneath the rubble.
For many families, even knowing where to search is impossible. Missing relatives could be buried beneath destroyed buildings, detained or otherwise unaccounted for, leaving families unable to hold a burial or know whether to keep hoping for their return.
Pat Griffiths, spokesperson for the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) in Jerusalem, described seeing families gather at hospitals when buses carrying released Palestinian detainees arrive in Gaza.
Some hold photographs of missing relatives, not knowing whether the person they are searching for has been detained or killed.
ICRC psychologists describe what those families experience as "ambiguous loss.”
"You don't know if your loved one you haven't heard from ... is alive or if they've been killed. You don't know if they're detained or not," he told Anadolu.
"Thousands of people live with this limbo. This pain of not knowing what to do or how to feel exactly. They're stuck."
Amani Al Naouq, ICRC spokesperson in Gaza, said families repeatedly bring the organization the same question.
"We just want to know what happened to them," she recalled them saying. "'If they are dead, we can be relieved. But the fact that we don't know if they are dead or alive' – that's one of the most difficult things for them."
Al Naouq told Anadolu that some families keep contacting the ICRC even when they know there may be no immediate answer, simply because they need somewhere to share what is weighing on them.
Others, she said, eventually begin to accept that a missing relative is dead despite having no confirmation.
The uncertainty is unfolding amid an enormous recovery challenge, with much of Gaza's built environment destroyed or damaged and human remains believed to lie within the ruins alongside unexploded ordnance, hazardous materials and potential evidence relevant to investigations into international crimes.
The cost of removing and managing more than 68 million metric tons of debris in Gaza exceeds $1.7 billion, according to the April 2026 Gaza Strip Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment by the European Union, UN and World Bank.
The effort also requires access to heavy machinery and specialized equipment, along with consistent fuel supplies – conditions that are currently far from being met.
Al Naouq said recovery teams have extremely limited heavy machinery, sometimes relying on one or two excavators contracted from private suppliers, while much of the work is carried out with small equipment and by hand.
With limited capacity, teams depend heavily on families to pinpoint where relatives were last seen – the building, the room and who was with them. That forces families to relive moments when they were unable to reach or save their loved ones, Al Naouq said.
"It's actually back again an open wound for these families," she said.
Griffiths, who recently spent a week in Gaza, described seeing "kilometers and kilometers just mountains of rubble," much of it posing dangers from unexploded remnants of war.
The ICRC supports the rental of two excavators for recovery teams, he said, but that is "a drop in the ocean."
"The scale of the task ahead of them – it's daunting. It's huge."
Griffiths said the problem is compounded by access restrictions, with search-and-recovery teams unable to reach much of the Gaza Strip to carry out their work safely.
DNA testing is also currently unavailable in Gaza, according to the ICRC.
Forensic teams instead rely on information including age, sex, height, previous injuries, dental information, clothing, personal belongings and where remains were recovered.
But time can erase those clues through decomposition and skeletonization, while moving rubble can separate remains from their original location.
"The more time passes, the harder identifying the deceased gets," Griffiths said.
Drawing on ICRC experience in conflicts including Syria, Iraq, Afghanistan and the Balkans, he said searches for missing people can continue for years or even decades.
"It's one of the tragedies of armed conflict," he said.
Mayy El Sheikh, of the UN Human Rights Office in the occupied Palestinian territory, recalled interviewing a 37-year-old woman with a disability whose husband remained missing after an attack on his family home in northern Gaza in 2023. The couple have a 5-year-old son.
Almost every member of her husband's family was killed, El Sheikh said. Some were recovered, but her husband was not.
The woman believes she knows the mound of rubble containing him but cannot reach it because it lies beyond the deployment line for Israeli forces – the so-called "yellow line."
Recalling all of this was "excruciatingly painful" for her, El Sheikh said. "She felt that she couldn't support her son recovering as well because he has no grave to visit, and that she failed her husband, that she was not able to honor him."
"For her, the war is not over until her husband is found," she added.
Other families have believed missing relatives were dead only to later recognize them alive in images or videos from Israeli prisons, El Sheikh said.
"It's that level of uncertainty, not knowing even if your loved one is alive or dead," she said.
Concerns over the fate of potential evidence within Gaza's rubble have recently been raised by UN Special Rapporteur on the Occupied Palestinian Territory Francesca Albanese, who warned that the removal, crushing and relocation of debris in areas under Israeli military control could destroy human remains and potential evidence of alleged international crimes.
El Sheikh also warned about what may be disappearing as Gaza's ruins are disturbed.
"It is almost inevitable that evidence is being lost, damaged, or disturbed as we speak," she said, citing the scale of destruction, access restrictions, reported rubble removal and crushing, and shortages of heavy machinery and forensic identification capacity.
She said large parts of Gaza remain inaccessible to independent observers and investigators, particularly areas under Israeli military control, making it difficult to establish what is happening to human remains and potential evidence there.
El Sheikh said there have also been repeated reports since the announcement of the ceasefire of remains being returned to Palestinian authorities without information that could be critical to identification and establishing what happened.
"They have returned remains to the Palestinian authorities, sometimes even partial remains with no identification and no clarity on where they were recovered or how they were killed," she said.
Griffiths said that if remains are moved with rubble, their original location – an important piece of identification evidence – can be lost, while remains may also become fragmented,
Srinivasan Muralidhar, chair of the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel, said the commission has received reports of rubble removal and the possibility of evidence being destroyed.
"We are concerned that the removal of rubble could result in evidence getting lost forever," he said.
Muralidhar compared evidence gathering to assembling a jigsaw puzzle, saying material recovered from the rubble could complement witness testimony and medical and forensic evidence.
Its loss would not prevent investigators from establishing alleged crimes, he said, but could leave important gaps.
Its importance goes beyond potential prosecutions, Muralidhar added.
"In international law, there is a known concept of the right to the truth. Every family wants to know what exactly happened."
For relatives who have waited years without recovering their loved ones, information about what happened can be "very, very valuable as a piece of memory and most importantly for closure," he said.
Griffiths said that resolving the fate of Gaza's missing will require greater humanitarian access and significantly more resources for search-and-recovery teams.
He called for more heavy machinery, including excavators, to be allowed into Gaza so teams can scale up recovery operations, while also stressing the need for safe access to areas they currently cannot reach.
"Humanitarian access for the purpose of search and recovery work – it's also really important," he said.
Muralidhar also called for international cooperation to accelerate the process.
"We have to have cooperation across countries to help clear the rubble quicker," he said, stressing the importance of not creating more rubble.
“This is a huge task right in front of us, and if the attacks do not stop now, things might get further worse and go beyond a point when we'll all be just shrugging our shoulders and watching helplessly,” he warned.
For one family encountered by Griffiths and Al Naouq, that answer eventually came.
The ICRC has supported the establishment of a cemetery for unidentified dead in Deir al-Balah, part of efforts to preserve information about remains that cannot immediately be identified.
Griffiths said that after remains are recovered, forensic teams seek to collect as much identifying information as possible and create a corresponding file. When identification is not possible, the remains can be laid to rest in an individual grave marked with a unique serial number linked to that information.
The ICRC is also supporting efforts to establish an information-sharing system between recovery teams, forensic authorities and those managing cemeteries so that information collected about remains is preserved for possible future identification.
The aim is to preserve both the dignity of the dead and the possibility of identifying them in the future, including if DNA testing eventually becomes available in Gaza.
During a visit to a cemetery for unidentified dead in Deir al-Balah, they met a young woman whose husband's remains had eventually been identified through forensic methods available in Gaza.
Griffiths recalled what finally having a grave meant to her.
"She could visit his grave, she could stand at his grave, to be near him," he said.
It gave her "a sense of closure, a way to mourn."
For thousands of families still searching for someone who disappeared during the war, even that remains out of reach.

🔴Nobel Prize in Literature awarded to Canada’s Anne Carson

Nobel Prize in Literature awarded to Canada’s Anne Carson
The Nobel Prize in Literature was awarded to Canadian poet and essayist Anne Carson on Thursday by the Swedish Academy in Stockholm. Toronto-born Carson, 76, draws from ancient Greek and Roman literature for her works blending elements of poetry, essay and fiction. She will receive 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million) alongside the prestigious award.
Canadian poet and essayist Anne Carson won the Nobel Prize in Literature Thursday “for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature”.
Ingrid Carlberg, permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy, said the author was in Iceland “listening to the wind” when the academy reached her to notify her of the win.
Toronto-born Carson draws on themes and stories from ancient Greek and Roman literature for works that often blend elements of poetry, essay and fiction.
“She was very taken by surprise,” Carlberg said.
Her books include “Eros the Bittersweet”, a look at the pleasure and pain of desire in ancient Greek literature, verse novel “Autobiography of Red”, “Men in the Off Hours”, a collection of poetry and prose that won Canada’s Griffin Prize for poetry in 2001 and “Norma Jeane Baker of Troy”, which compares Marilyn Monroe and Helen of Troy.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Carson also has translated works of classical Greek literature that, the Swedish Academy said, “may be regarded as independent works in their own right.” They include “If Not, Winter,” based on poem fragments by Sappho, Sophocles’ tragic plays “Electra” and "Antigone” and Euripides’s “Bakkhai.”
“Almost all her literary production has centered upon the intersection between the philologist’s obsession with words and the poet’s desire for new meaning,” said Anders Olsson, chair of the literature committee.
Carson has taught classics at several North American universities and has lived in Iceland, where she and her husband, Robert Currie, were granted citizenship in 2022.
The prize was announced by the Swedish Academy in Stockholm.
Last year, Hungarian writer Laszlo Krasznahorkai, whose surreal and anarchic novels combine a bleak world view with mordant humour, won the Nobel Prize in Literature for work the judges said upholds the power of art in the midst of “apocalyptic terror”.
Read moreLaszlo Krasznahorkai: Hungary's 'master of apocalypse'
Three science awards were announced earlier this week. The Nobel for medicine went to three scientists whose work led to a tool that uses light to help unravel how the brain works. The physics award recognised a scientist’s efforts to demystify a rare group of neutrinos. The chemistry prize recognised two scientists for untangling mysterious mirror images in molecules, a discovery that has been used to develop countless drugs.
This week ends with Friday's peace prize. The Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced Monday.
The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), whether for an individual, small group of laureates or organisation.

Dozens Killed In Russian Strike On Passenger Buses In Kramatorsk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:04:33 UTC
20:04:33 KST

KRAMATORSK, Ukraine -- Dozens of people were killed in a Russian strike on the Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk on October 8, according to local authorities, a day after another deadly barrage killed at least 25 people across Ukraine.
The death toll from the Kramatorsk attack has risen to 33, with 18 others wounded, according to the latest reports from regional authorities and the prosecutor's office.
Footage taken by RFE/RL correspondent Serhiy Horbatenko, who visited the site shortly after the attack, showed two buses burned out by the strike, with bodies strewn around the scene.
"The bodies are lying right in the middle of the road," the RFE/RL correspondent said while describing the aftermath of the deadly attack.
The Donetsk Regional Prosecutor's Office said the Russian strike hit two buses that were carrying passengers at the time of the attack. It added that Russian forces likely used guided bombs to strike the vehicles.
The strike came a day after at least 25 people nationwide, including two in the capital, Kyiv, were reported killed in the October 7 barrage.
In Pryluky, about 150 kilometers east of Kyiv, rescuers searched through the rubble of a destroyed apartment building in northern Ukraine for survivors following a Russian missile attack that killed 22 people, including five children.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called it one of the "most vile" attacks in recent memory, and he noted they occurred on the birthday of Russian President Vladimir Putin. Russian forces "destroyed" a residential building "as a birthday 'gift' to Putin," Zelenskyy said in a post to X.
At least 10 other such buildings were damaged elsewhere, along with Ukrainian energy infrastructure, one of Moscow's other "key targets," he said.
"The fire was right in front of my eyes. There were explosions. I was screaming in my apartment. Extremely scary. I can't describe it," one woman, who gave her name as Lidia, told Current Time at the scene in Pryluky.
"So many people have died. I knew everyone here," she added, holding back tears.
With a fifth wartime winter approaching, the bombardment was part of near-daily attacks that have steadily increased in frequency and ferocity as the Kremlin struggles on the battlefield front line.
Moscow has previously sought to pressure Kyiv into accepting its hard-line demands by attacking the country's energy infrastructure and leaving thousands without heat or electricity amid freezing temperatures.
Recently, it has also stepped up attacks on Ukrainian data centers and telecommunications infrastructure, causing Internet outages in some of the country's regions.
Since this year, however, Kyiv has increasingly responded to Russian attacks with a campaign of long-range strikes targeting military and energy sites inside Russia and middle-range strikes targeting its key logistics in Ukraine's occupied eastern and southern regions.
On October 8, Russia's leading AI and technology company, Yandex, said one of its five largest data centers in the Ryazan region had been attacked, adding that the company was trying to restore affected services. The Yandex site hosts tens of thousands of servers.
Zelenskyy confirmed Kyiv had struck the facility, saying it was "mirroring" previous Russian attacks on similar sites in Ukraine.
Separately, Ukrainian forces also struck the Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat oil refinery and petrochemical complex in Bashkortostan, sparking a fire, according to Ukraine's military.
Russia's Defense Ministry reported on October 8 that the country's air defenses had intercepted and destroyed 399 Ukrainian drones overnight.
The developments came amid renewed US interest in negotiating a diplomatic settlement to the long-running war.
While US President Donald Trump has long said resolving the conflict is one of the key goals of his presidency, Kyiv and Moscow remain far apart in their negotiating positions.
Since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, the Kremlin has shown no willingness to compromise on its key demands, including full control over Ukraine's key eastern Donetsk region, which Russian forces have not yet been able to capture.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine expected fresh talks with the United States in the coming days, adding that Kyiv hoped its European partners would join the discussions.

Cuban actors insist the show must go on despite blackouts

Cuban actors insist the show must go on despite blackouts
HAVANA, Oct 8 - When blackouts in an upscale neighborhood of Havana began approaching 24 hours a day, morale plummeted at one of the Cuban capital's many niche but celebrated theater groups.
"It became impossible for the actors to arrive on time; they were exhausted and struggling to cope," said Linda Soriano, director of theater group Impulso Teatro. "I told them they were free to leave."
But the group's members decided the show must go on — and they kept turning up.
Cuban theater, alongside music and ballet, has long been hailed as a cultural hallmark of an island with a tradition of promoting the arts that spans centuries.
However, many of the island's youth — actors, artists and musicians — have left the country in a record-breaking exodus since the COVID-19 pandemic.
Since January, when the US imposed a fuel blockade on Cuba in a bid to upend the communist-run government, those who remain have had to contend with blackouts spanning days, food, fuel and water shortages, and a lack of public transportation.
On a recent Friday evening, actors dripping with sweat pranced about the stage, voices echoing across a large room in a converted mansion in Havana's Vedado business district. Candles flickered outside the theater hall, while the inside was lit by an array of rechargeable lights in all shapes and sizes — similar to those found in many Cuban homes.
There was no electricity, no air conditioning, and no sound system. All the drama was dependent on the acting.
"What keeps us making theater is the determination to ensure ... that it does not die out," said 88-year-old Carlos Perez, a winner of Cuba's national theater prize and by far the oldest of this small company of 14 actors. "But it comes at a cost."
Many actors and stagehands work multiple jobs to make ends meet in a country where prices have soared alongside the plummeting local peso currency, Perez said.
"I don't know if I could have managed if I had been in their shoes at 25," he said.
Amanda Feijo, attending a recent performance at the makeshift theater, said the show had provided its own snippet of light amid all the darkness.
"To see that there is an audience seeking to nourish their souls, despite the truly lamentable situation unfolding right now," she said. "It is heartening." REUTERS

School protests, blockades resume in France despite PM’s promise to act

French police clash with protesters at students’ demonstration in Paris
Interior Ministry says more than 70,000 people took to the streets across France on Thursday.
Police have clashed with protesters in the French capital as thousands of students continue demonstrating to air their grievances against the conditions of schools in the country.
Footage broadcast on Al Jazeera on Thursday showed riot police charging with batons at a group of protesters in a square in Paris as they moved in to try and clear out the area.
Police said they used tear gas in Bastille to disperse some “high-risk profiles”.
Reporting from the scene, Al Jazeera’s Natacha Butler described riot police with shields lining up in front of the protesters, while a water cannon truck moved in alongside them.
Protests resumed at schools across France on Thursday, a day after the country’s prime minister ordered officials to provide an action plan.
The Ministry of the Interior said 71,500 people took to the streets across France on Thursday, with police detaining more than 500 people.
High school students are continuing their demands for more education funding and better school conditions, Butler said, while university students and more trade unions have joined the nationwide protests.
“They are out, they say, in solidarity with high school students because they say it’s important that as many young people join in the protests as possible,” she said.
“There is no doubt they are out here in force,” she added later.
3,000 substitute teachers
The wave of protests began in a high school in a working-class suburb of Paris on September 21.
Tens of thousands of students across the country have since marched with a range of demands, from renovated school buildings to fewer classroom hours.
Education Minister Edouard Geffray told the evening news on the TF1 television channel on Thursday that France is to deploy 3,000 substitute teachers “within the next hours” to struggling high schools.
The protest movement has exposed deep tensions in France between popular demands for investments in deteriorating public services and a cash-strapped government under pressure from bond markets to reduce its debt and deficit.
High-school teacher Diane Di Sciullo joined students at a large march in Marseille, saying all they were asking for was a decent education in decent conditions. She denounced overcrowding, saying this year she had 37 students in her class.
“At the start of every lesson, I have to ask them to check the neighbouring classrooms for spare chairs and desks so they can actually study,” she told Reuters.
The country’s recent PISA score – an annual survey which assesses the performance of education systems by measuring the skills of 15-year-old students – was France’s worst since the rankings began in 2000.
Police response under scrutiny
As protests continue, rights groups have accused security officials of using disproportionate force against demonstrators.
Several protesters have been injured, including one teenager who lost a hand and another whose jaw was shattered by an exploding stun grenade. Their use has since been banned at marches.
Police officers and teachers have also been injured, authorities say, accusing students of committing violent acts. At least 6,600 arrests – mostly of minors – have been made so far, according to the Interior Ministry.
Authorities said 375 schools were either fully or partially closed on Thursday, and that two dozen had been burned or destroyed.
The demonstrations are increasing pressure on the cash-strapped outgoing government of Emmanuel Macron before April elections.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu condemned the violence in a TV address on Wednesday. He faulted “political leaders who use this anger to conduct their electoral battles”, after opposition leader Jean-Luc Melenchon called for protesters to keep marching.
Lecornu has ordered ministers to provide an action plan responding to students’ demands by the end of the month, but protesters remain unconvinced.
“As far as they are concerned, the government only talks about solutions but never actually comes up with concrete actions, so they say they are going to keep coming out onto the streets until their demands are met,” Butler said.

French firm Sesterce plans €10 billion AI data centre in Finland
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:03:05 EEST
20:03:05 KST

French artificial intelligence infrastructure company Sesterce has announced plans to invest more than €10 billion in a data centre campus at the former Kaipola paper mill in Jämsä, central Finland, with construction scheduled to begin before the end of 2026.
The project, announced on Thursday, 8 October, would create around 2,000 jobs during construction and approximately 300 permanent positions once the facility becomes operational, according to the company.
The development will begin with a 200-megawatt facility before expanding to 600 megawatts in a second phase. Sesterce also aims to develop more than one gigawatt of AI computing capacity across Finland over the longer term.
The company plans to use existing electricity connections, water systems, buildings and transport infrastructure at the former industrial site.
Sesterce chief executive Youssef El Manssouri told Finnish public broadcaster Yle that the investment decision had already been made and an agreement signed with the project's future customer.
He described the customer as one of the world's two leading AI laboratories but declined to identify the company or disclose the project's financial backers.
The site previously housed a paper mill operated by Finnish forestry group UPM, which ceased production in early 2021, affecting more than 400 workers.
Jämsä town manager Jori Reijula welcomed the proposed investment but stressed that several regulatory procedures must be completed before construction proceeds.
Speaking to Helsingin Sanomat, Reijula said several internationally recognised companies were involved in the project, although he declined to name them.
Sesterce has pledged to support the development of one megawatt of new renewable electricity generation in Finland for every megawatt consumed by the campus, within ten years of operations beginning.
The company also plans to use closed-loop liquid cooling systems, rainwater and recycled water instead of drinking water.
A €10 million community fund would finance local projects selected with the municipality and residents. Sesterce has promised annual independent audits of its environmental and community commitments.
Electricity network operator Elenia confirmed that the Kaipola site already connects to its high-voltage network, providing infrastructure for the proposed first phase.
The announcement follows other data centre investment plans in Finland. Google announced €13 billion in planned investments in September, while Icelandic-origin operator atNorth recently outlined a €2 billion data centre project in Salo.
Sesterce says it intends to prioritise Finnish contractors and subcontractors during construction and is examining other former industrial sites for future developments.

Spain’s army gets its first Aracne anti-drone vehicles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:02:19 UTC
20:02:19 KST

- The Spanish Army’s 71st Anti-Aircraft Artillery Regiment received its first Aracne counter-drone systems, developed by Indra and EM&E Group.
- The soft-kill evaluation is complete, and hard-kill testing is planned during the army’s next Atlas exercise.
The Spanish Army has received its first Aracne counter-drone systems, delivered to the 71st Anti-Aircraft Artillery Regiment, which serves as the army’s lead unit for defending against drones.
The army announced the delivery on Oct. 8. The system is built to detect drones, identify them and choose a response, and the regiment has already completed its operational evaluation of Aracne’s soft-kill mode, which jams or disrupts a drone without destroying it. Testing of the hard-kill mode, which physically shoots drones down, is planned during the army’s next Atlas exercise. The army did not say how many systems arrived or when that exercise will take place.
Aracne was developed by a joint venture of Spanish companies Indra and EM&E Group, also known as Escribano, with TRC as a partner. Indra supplies the command-and-control system, radar and radio-frequency sensors, while EM&E provides the Oteos electro-optical sensor and Guardian 2.0 remote weapon stations. The command system fuses data from the different sensors to classify a target and help operators decide whether to jam it, take control of its signals or fire on it. Kinetic options include cannons and automatic grenade launchers.
The program covers 14 systems for the Spanish armed forces in two configurations. Fixed versions use a shelter as a command post to protect bases and critical infrastructure, while mobile versions are mounted on two Vamtac ST5 tactical vehicles, one carrying electronic warfare equipment and the other the hard-kill weapons. The army is set to receive 10 systems, five fixed and five mobile, plus a simulator, with two more going to the Spanish Air and Space Force and two to the Spanish Navy. The contract was valued at just over €30 million (about $35 million) when it was signed in February 2025, and it was Spain’s first major defense procurement focused solely on counter-drone systems.
Aracne grew out of the earlier Cervus prototypes, which the companies developed with the army’s electronic warfare regiment and which have protected Spanish troops on NATO missions in Latvia and Slovakia. Spain’s Ministry of Defense also deployed an Indra counter-drone system to protect its contingent in Lithuania last December after repeated incursions by drones and balloons from Russia and Belarus. Indra says it continues to develop that system within the Aracne project.
The 71st Anti-Aircraft Artillery Regiment led the Atlas 2025 exercise at the Médano del Loro range in Huelva in October last year, one of the largest counter-drone drills Spain has held, involving units from all three services as well as the Civil Guard and National Police. Indra demonstrated Aracne there before deliveries began.
The army said the regiment will use the new systems to train personnel and build up its readiness against drones, which it described as one of the fastest-growing challenges in current operations. Spain’s defense ministry is also preparing a new Aracne contract with Indra and EM&E as part of this year’s Special Modernization Programs, though its value and scope have not been announced.

The Hormuz bonus: Sailor salaries soar for transits amid Iran war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:02:09 UTC
20:02:09 KST

The Hormuz bonus: Sailor salaries soar for transits amid Iran war
Reports have emerged that tanker captains are earning $100,000 plus a $50,000 per-trip bonus to transit the strait.
As shipping traffic through the besieged Strait of Hormuz fell to its lowest level since July this week, reports have emerged that sailors are being paid large bonuses for making the dangerous trip through the Gulf waterway.
Some captains are earning base salaries of as much as $100,000 – the high end of usual salaries which vary greatly between shipping companies – plus a $50,000 bonus per voyage through the strait, the UK’s Financial Times has reported.
Oil exports from the Middle East rose above pre-war levels at the end of last month despite ongoing attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz. But shipping data from Kpler shows that about 40 percent of those are leaving the region due to a combination of pipeline exports and small shuttle boats carrying out risky ship-to-ship transfers.
Here’s what we know.
Are oil exports getting through the strait?
Yes. According to shipping data from Kpler, at least 16.5 million barrels left the region last month, matching the pre-war average, excluding Iran, which is under a naval blockade by the United States.
However, about 40 percent of this is being exported via Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline or via ship-to-ship transfers by smaller boats travelling undetected through the strait.
Kpler reported on Tuesday that the number of detectable vessels passing through the strait had fallen to its lowest level in more than two months, with only seven vessels passing through the crucial waterway in the previous week, the lowest figure since July 23.
Data is hard to determine, as many smaller shuttle boats are turning off their transponders to avoid detection when travelling through the strait before offloading oil to larger tankers waiting beyond it.
How dangerous is it for sailors in the strait?
Very. Attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz have continued in the past week.
On Wednesday night, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported several casualties after multiple projectiles struck a vessel sailing off Qatar’s northern coast.
Following the start of the US-Israel war on Iran in late February, Tehran all but closed the strait, with limited vessels receiving clearance. Iran has launched strikes at ships making the crossing without its express permission.
The US, for its part, imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports due to Tehran’s closure and has escorted some vessels through the waterway.
Last week, attacks on tankers in the strait hit their highest level since the war began as regional oil producers tried to increase exports at heightened risk for crew and cargo.
Saul Kavonic, energy head at MST Marquee, told the Reuters news agency: “The frequency of Iranian attacks on ships is now at the highest point since the war began, and likely to intensify further.”
He added that “constrained product flows, extreme logistics costs and high likelihood of Iranian escalation are keeping [oil] prices elevated”.
Mohamed El Hawawy, head of Middle East shipping and insurance at international law firm Stephenson Harwood, said: “I guess more attacks will make more [shipping companies] reluctant to pass the strait, which will perhaps affect trade.”
“It could be more costly on the insurance and other associated costs with transiting the Strait of Hormuz,” he added.
What are oil prices doing?
Oil prices rose on Thursday morning, with Brent crude futures increasing by $2.28, or 2.28 percent, to $102.28 a barrel by 04:27 GMT.
US West Texas Intermediate crude futures gained $1.66, or 1.88 percent, to $89.94.
This is despite oil exports recovering to some extent due to Saudi Arabia using alternative export infrastructure and due to the complex system of ship-to-ship transfers.
The East-West pipeline, which carries oil from fields in Saudi Arabia’s east to the Yanbu port on the Red Sea in the west, has been crucial to this process. However, it has also come under threat and been forced to close at times due to strikes from Iran-backed groups.
What incentives are sailors receiving for crossing the strait?
The Financial Times reported this week that tanker captains can now command a base salary of $100,000, plus a $50,000 per-trip bonus, to make the dangerous transit.
Overall, the crew on board each ship can earn four to six times their normal salaries.
On Monday, The Wall Street Journal reported that shipping companies were spending between $30m and $40m for a single round trip to move oil in and out of Hormuz through ship-to-ship transfers.
It added that oil producers now have to swallow high costs to get oil out of the waterway, with shipowners and individual sailors making some of the best returns the industry has seen in decades. Many sailors willing to risk the trip are coming from India, the Philippines and China to do so.
“One Shandong-based ship-staffing company is even offering as much as $25,000 for a round trip as reward, according to seafarers and recruitment advertisements seen by The Wall Street Journal. For oilers and cadets [low-level crewmembers of a commercial ship] the $25,000 could represent more than a year of wages,” the outlet reported.
El Hawawy explained that the higher captain salaries are part of a “new economics” in crossing the waterway, adding that shipping cannot just stop.
“So far I don’t see a reason for it not to be sustainable, and actually that’s something will happen beyond the cost,” he said.
How are ships navigating Hormuz?
As with the smaller shuttle boats that move in and out of the strait under threat of attack, captains on board larger ships and tankers must turn off their lights and transponders to make the journey.
According to Bloomberg, which spoke to a captain on a vessel that was part of the shuttle runs, his vessel, which frequently carries barrels at night, is given strict instructions: no lights, no phones, and only one radar on as they cross.
Speaking from the Philippines, where he has arrived following a three-month stint taking vessels through the strait, he explained that he and his crew got their bearings by using the coast and lighthouses as a reference, adding that it is “quite challenging”.
After seeing a fire ahead on one trip, the captain said he called the US Navy, which has been assisting ships on routes through the waterway to avoid mines, to warn them of an attack.
He added that his most recent contract through the strait was shorter than usual since he knew the voyage was “not easy”, but he still received several times his usual salary for the trip.
Another captain of a Liquefied Natural Gas tanker told Bloomberg that his journey began by turning off the breaker that connects the ship’s location transponder to hide their whereabouts while they were travelling along the Omani coast.
Crew members also barricade the main decks with sandbags in case drones or missiles attack them.
The report added that shipping executives estimate a one-in-20 chance of being hit while crossing the strait at present.

Nobel Prize in literature goes to Canada's Anne Carson

Nobel Prize in Literature goes to Canada's Anne Carson
October 8, 2026
The Swedish Academy awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature to Anne Carson on Thursday, praising her "bold and inventive oeuvre."
Her work has "in playful dialogue with the classical tradition...created new forms for contemporary literature," said Ingrid Carlberg, permanent secretary of the academy.
The 76-year-old writer is a longtime professor of classics, creative writing, and comparative literature at prestigious institutions like McGill and Princeton universities. She is only the 19th woman of 123 laureates to win the award.
What is Anne Carson known for?
Born in Toronto in 1950, Carson moved with her family among several small towns in Canada during her youth. She has credited a beloved Latin teacher for sparking her interest in language and classics.
Her first book of criticism, 1986’s Eros the Bittersweet, was published to great acclaim and has had significant influence on other classicists, poets, and even film and television. Carson has also published her own poetry such as the 2001 collection The Beauty of the Husband as well as highly regard translation of ancient Greek poets such as Sappho and Sophocles.
Carson is also heavily influenced by the King James Bible and more modern writers including Emily Dickinson and Virginia Woolf. She has received numerous awards such as the T.S. Eliot Prize for Poetry, a MacArthur fellowship, and the PEN/Nabokov Award.
Deeply private, Carson often declines to speak about her personal life in interviews and discourages autobiographical interpretations of her work. However, she did revealed in 2024 that she has Parkinson's disease.
Who else has received a Nobel Prize so far?
- The Nobel Prize in Medicine was awarded Monday to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for their pioneering work on optogenetics, a method of controlling nerve cells with light, that makes it possible to study how the brain works.
- The Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded Tuesday to Francis Halzen, a Belgian-born astrophysicist whose efforts helped demystify a rare group of neutrinos that launched a new era of astronomy.
- The Nobel Prize in Chemistry went to Henri B. Kagan of France and Kenso Soai of Japan on Wednesday, for solving the longstanding mystery of homochirality in living organisms.
What happens next?
The winner of the Nobel Prize in Literature receives prize money of 12 million Swedish kronor, equivalent to about $1.2 million. The winner also receives a medal and a diploma at an official ceremony in December, and is expected to deliver a speech known as a Nobel lecture.
On Friday, the winner of the Nobel Peace Prize will be announced, followed by the Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel on Monday.

In Belgium, protests were taking place outside some schools in Brussels and outside Liege University, broadcaster RTBF reported.

Belgium's Foreign Minister Bernard Quintin said hard-left activists had infiltrated the Liege school protests and were causing damage to property.
Julien Doeche, a member of the Liege Antifascist Front, told RTBF Quintin's claims were "fantasies."

Medication helps adults with ADHD weigh the negative consequences of their decisions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:00:29 UTC
20:00:29 KST

Adults with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder often struggle with choices that require weighing potential rewards against negative consequences. A new experiment reveals that a common stimulant medication improves these choices specifically by helping individuals pay more attention to the potential costs of their actions. The research was published in Psychological Medicine.
Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsive behavior. People with this diagnosis frequently experience difficulties with real-life decisions, which can manifest as reckless driving, substance abuse, and risky sexual behavior. Every day, humans navigate choices that require balancing the positive aspects of an action against its negative aspects. Buying a new phone brings the benefit of better technology but carries the cost of having less money for groceries.
Neurobiological theories suggest that the disorder involves atypical functioning of dopamine and norepinephrine, which are chemical messengers in the brain that help regulate attention, reward processing, and cognitive effort. Stimulant medications like methylphenidate, often sold under the brand name Ritalin, increase the availability of these chemicals in the brain. While researchers know that stimulants generally improve decision-making, the exact psychological mechanisms driving this improvement have remained elusive.
Mads Lund Pedersen, a psychologist at the University of Oslo, and a team of colleagues conducted a study to break down the specific components of decision-making. They wanted to know if medication helps people by increasing their sensitivity to rewards, heightening their awareness of costs, or simply altering the amount of time they spend thinking before they act.
To answer these questions, the research team recruited 61 adults diagnosed with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and 63 healthy control participants. The study utilized a double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover design. The participants with the diagnosis completed the testing twice, once after taking their standard dose of methylphenidate and once after taking an inactive placebo pill. Neither the participants nor the researchers knew which pill was administered on which day. The healthy control participants also completed the testing twice but did not receive any medication.
During the experiment, participants engaged in a computer-based task designed to test how they integrate costs and benefits. First, they completed a training phase where they learned to associate six different shapes with specific numerical rewards and six different colors with specific numerical costs. After learning these associations, they moved on to the main testing phase.
In the testing phase, the computer presented participants with a colored shape for a few seconds. The participants had to mentally combine the benefit value of the shape and the cost value of the color to determine the net value. If the net value was positive, the correct choice was to accept the offer. If the net value was negative, the correct choice was to reject it.
The researchers analyzed the behavioral data using a mathematical framework called the drift diffusion model. This model separates the fast, split-second process of making a choice into distinct cognitive components. One component is the drift rate, which measures how quickly and efficiently the brain accumulates evidence about the choice. Another component is the decision threshold, which represents the amount of information a person requires before they commit to an action, often referred to as the speed-accuracy tradeoff. A third component is non-decision time, which accounts for the physical time it takes to see the image on the screen and press the button.
The results showed that when participants with the diagnosis were given the placebo, they were less accurate than the healthy control group. The mathematical model revealed that the unmedicated participants had a lower drift rate, meaning they processed information about both the costs and the benefits less efficiently. They also exhibited a narrower decision threshold, meaning they acted on less information and responded prematurely.
The researchers also compared how the different groups weighed the positive and negative information. The healthy control participants naturally allowed the cost of the stimuli to influence their decisions more heavily than the benefits. The unmedicated participants with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder showed the reverse pattern, demonstrating a stronger sensitivity to the benefits than to the costs.
Administration of methylphenidate changed how the participants processed the information. The medication caused an increase in the drift rate, but this improvement was highly selective. The drug improved how efficiently the participants accumulated evidence about the costs, while leaving their sensitivity to the benefits entirely unchanged. By boosting cost sensitivity, the medication shifted the overall balance of their decision-making closer to the pattern seen in the healthy control group.
The medication also produced some unexpected effects. Instead of increasing the decision threshold to make participants wait for more information, the drug narrowed the threshold slightly further. However, the medication also increased the participants’ non-decision time. The researchers suggest that the participants might have spent this extra fraction of a second visually encoding the images, which could have improved the accuracy of their stimulus representations and contributed to the higher drift rate observed under medication.
The researchers analyzed individual differences among the participants who had the diagnosis. They found that individuals who reported more severe symptoms in their daily lives had the lowest sensitivity to costs when they were unmedicated. Among those taking medication, higher prescribed doses of methylphenidate were associated with both a stronger sensitivity to costs and a wider decision threshold.
The study includes several limitations regarding how the medication might be acting on the brain. The drug could be improving basic learning and memory rather than the actual moment of decision-making. Because participants had to memorize the values of the shapes and colors during the training phase, the stimulant might simply help them remember those specific values more reliably during the test.
Alternatively, participants might have used simple mental arithmetic to subtract the cost from the benefit. Stimulant medication could enhance this working memory skill independently of how the brain naturally weighs risks and rewards. The study also excluded individuals with severe comorbid psychiatric conditions, meaning the results might not apply to people who have additional severe mental health disorders. Finally, because the medication can cause noticeable physical sensations, some participants might have guessed when they received the active drug, which can influence behavioral performance through expectations.
Future research could separate these potential mechanisms by providing the values directly on the screen, removing the need for participants to memorize the shapes and colors beforehand.
The study, “Selective enhancement of cost sensitivity by methylphenidate in adult ADHD: a randomized placebo-controlled trial,” was authored by Mads Lund Pedersen, Athanasia M. Mowinckel, Sigurd Ziegler, Mats Fredriksen, Atle Bjørnerud, Tor Endestad, and Guido Biele.

I’m the attorney general of Washington state. Here’s how we’re protecting the midterm elections | Nick Brown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:00:18 UTC
20:00:18 KST

Elections have consequences. So do the Trump administration’s exhaustive efforts to undermine them.
Voters will be confident in their choices, but less certain whose voice will count in the face of myriad intrusions by the executive branch. A coalition of Democratic attorneys general are working to make sure voters across the political spectrum have their say.
Led by the attorneys general of Washington, California, Massachusetts and Nevada, 24 states sued to block President Donald Trump’s US Postal Service plot to interfere with voting by mail. Last month, the supreme court upheld our lower court victories and blocked the administration’s unconstitutional power grab, at least for this election.
The law says states decide who receives a mail ballot. The USPS has never had the final say and, according to the American Postal Workers Union, until this year had never in its 250-year history tried to put such arbitrary restrictions on what mail it will deliver.
The case we brought was an important victory in every state, and particularly Washington, where more than 99% of voters cast their ballot by mail. States such as Colorado, Hawaii and Oregon have similarly high mail voting rates. But mail voting is not confined to blue states; it is widely used in red states as well, particularly those like Nebraska and the Dakotas, with large rural populations. It’s also the president’s preferred way to cast his own ballot.
The case of the postal service is just part of the multi-pronged federal attack states are pushing back against. The administration has abandoned the federal government’s traditional role of supporting election security and defending voting rights, work I participated in first-hand as a US attorney.
Recall, in 2020, Trump’s own administration – and particularly the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency – worked to protect the vote and defend the election. Then, efforts to misuse the Department of Justice were thwarted, and Trump relied on insurrectionists to do his bidding. In return for serving honorably, many public servants were sent packing upon Trump’s return to office, and the convicted insurrectionists were pardoned.
Now we have a US solicitor general who described the postal service’s attempt to deprive the rights of millions of eligible voters as only a “modest” use of federal authority.
The Trump administration is not known for its discretion or consistency. While the administration was in court purportedly concerned about election integrity, the president publicly demanded his supporters “cheat like hell” in midterm voting. I don’t think Republican voters want that any more than Democrats do.
We don’t doubt the administration will continue its lawless blitz against voters. Democratic state attorneys general are prepared, and have undertaken the largest multi-state effort to protect the vote in modern American history.
Recent rulings keep state elections on track and show the law is on our side. If Trump attempts to intimidate or discourage eligible voters, or to obstruct the counting of votes or certification of the election, Democratic state attorneys general will take swift action. States have decades of experience countering these threats when lodged by private actors, and they are just as illegal when attempted by the federal government.
Voters can do their part by exercising the right to elect their representatives. The president’s scheming benefits from public doubt and uncertainty. Democracy depends on the participation of its citizens, and every eligible voter should have the opportunity to render a verdict on their elected representatives.
That verdict is unlikely to favor President Trump, who ran on lowering costs, preserving peace, and economic stability, but instead delivered higher prices, hollowed out critical public services, engaged in unprecedented self-dealing, and began a globally destabilizing war with no end in sight.
Presidents don’t decide elections. State attorneys general and the millions of eligible voters we represent will exercise our constitutional powers to help keep it that way.
- Nick Brown is the attorney general of the state of Washington

Houthi Attacks on Saudi Airports Kill 3 Amid Escalating War in Yemen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

The Iran-aligned Houthi rebels said they launched another strike on Riyadh’s main airport, after earlier attacks on Saudi Arabia killed three and injured 36.
The Houthis said they targeted King Khalid International Airport on Thursday, soon after an attack on the airport killed one person and wounded eight. Saudi Arabia has not confirmed Thursday’s attack. Another two people were killed and 28 wounded in an attack on Abha International Airport, the country’s civil aviation authorities said on Wednesday. The earlier attacks happened on Tuesday and Wednesday, although the authorities did not specify the date of each. The Houthis claimed responsibility for those strikes.
On Thursday, Houthi spokesperson Yahya Saree warned airlines “for the last time” not to continue their flights in Saudi airspace, calling it a “theater” for Houthi military operations.
A Saudi-led coalition said late on Wednesday that the attacks “will not go unpunished.” It said it had destroyed 82 Houthi military sites across Saada, Hodeidah, Jawf, and Marib in Yemen.
The rebel group has carried out a series of attacks on infrastructure in Saudi Arabia since Yemen’s government forces launched a major offensive aimed at recapturing key territory around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait that had been seized by the Houthis. Yemeni forces, supported by Saudi airstrikes, said they had reached Mokha on Monday and driven the Houthis back from the strait, although the Houthis dispute those claims.
The fighting has revived the yearslong civil war in Yemen that created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. More than 200,000 people have been displaced since the latest exchange of fire began in June, the International Organization for Migration said on Wednesday. The Saudi-led coalition accuses Iran of arming and funding the Houthis, which both Iran and the rebel group deny.
It has also opened up a new front in the U.S. and Israel’s war against Iran, which began on Feb. 28 with a wave of U.S.-Israeli strikes. The Houthis reportedly received direction from Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps to capture Mokha last month to threaten global shipping and energy flows through another shipping route. The battle over Bab el-Mandeb has become more important amid new attacks on vessels through the Strait of Hormuz in recent weeks, as Iran seeks to re-assert its leverage over Hormuz.
Attacks on airports
Attacks on airports are a recurrent tactic by the Houthis.
The attack on the Riyadh airport killed a Sudanese national, and injured five Saudi citizens, two Egyptian residents, and a Pakistani resident, Saudi authorities said. The attack on Abha airport killed a Moroccan woman and an Algerian woman, and injured Saudi citizens, a Bangladeshi resident, and a Filipino resident.
Earlier on Wednesday, Yemeni authorities said ballistic missile and drone strikes targeted Aden international airport in Yemen. One missile landed near the runway shortly before a flight from Cairo was scheduled to land, Yemen’s Transport Ministry said. The Houthis acknowledged a missile strike nearby but said their target was a military camp.
The Saudi civilian aviation authorities also said two airports in the kingdom’s south were attacked on Monday evening, injuring three people. The airports, King Abdullah bin Abdulaziz International Airport in Jazan and Najran International Airport, suffered material damage, the authorities announced on Tuesday.
Last month, Saudi Arabia accused the Houthis of attempting an attack on Mecca, calling it a “red line.” The Houthis denied the allegations, as did Iran.
War widens
Saudi Arabia has sought help from a number of its allies to fight the Houthis. Turkey has sent defensive and technical support, Reuters reported on Wednesday, citing officials. Saudi Arabia signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement with Turkey and Pakistan in August, and the three parties agreed to implement its collective defence commitments earlier this week.
Syria, another Saudi ally, is also weighing providing military aid, Reuters reported, which could include defensive aid or deploying forces on the ground to support the Yemeni offensive against the Houthis. The Syrian foreign ministry did not confirm any potential plan to Reuters and said, “Should Saudi Arabia request any military cooperation or exchange of expertise, this would take place exclusively through official channels and within the framework of the bilateral agreements governing relations between our two brotherly countries.”
Saudi Arabia also reportedly requested assistance from the U.S., although President Donald Trump has thus far declined requests for direct U.S. strikes against the Houthis. The U.S. has instead provided the kingdom with intelligence support.
Tanker attacks in Hormuz
Although Middle East oil exports have ticked up in recent weeks, renewed attacks on vessels near the Strait of Hormuz have raised the stakes at Bab El-Mandeb, which became a critical alternative route for Saudi oil exports earlier in the Iran War.
Last week, attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz hit their highest weekly level since the Iran War began. There were at least 12 attacks on oil, LNG, and LPG tankers near the Strait of Hormuz between Sept. 28 and Oct. 5, Reuters reported, citing data from three maritime security sources.
Attacks have continued this week.
India’s foreign ministry reported on Tuesday that 12 crew members were injured after an unknown projectile struck a Panama-flagged oil tanker sailing through Hormuz off the coast of Oman.
An unidentified tanker was also struck by multiple projectiles off the northern coast of Qatar on Wednesday, marking a rare attack deep inside the Persian Gulf. The attack resulted in an unknown number of casualties, the U.K. Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said. Authorities launched an investigation into the incident. No one has claimed responsibility for the attack.
Iran said on Wednesday that it would close “illegal” routes that have been used to bypass Tehran’s blockade in the Strait of Hormuz, including a southern route close to Oman’s coast.
“The Strait of Hormuz is closed, and the armed forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran have full control over it,” Mohammadreza Naqdi, an adviser to the Revolutionary Guards’ Commander, told the IRGC-linked Fars news agency.
Naqdi said the “few routes” circumventing Tehran’s blockade were created by blowing up rocky passages in the Strait. He said the routes were used by “small boats smuggling oil and transferring it to tankers.”
Despite Naqdi’s claims, Middle Eastern crude exports exceeded pre-war levels on 14 days in September, according to maritime analytics firm Kpler, which included shipments via Hormuz, the Red Sea, and other routes. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday that Iran had “lost complete control of the Strait” as the U.S. Navy continues escorting some vessels through the Strait.
“There’s almost as much oil flowing out now as there was before this conflict began,” he told reporters while on a visit in Athens.
Nevertheless, analysts previously told TIME that increased attacks in the Strait, coupled with the threat to Bab el-Mandeb, could quickly raise shipping costs and disrupt flows. Brent crude again topped $100 a barrel on Wednesday after retreating from nearly $110 a barrel last month.
The White House has also reportedly asked the Pentagon to develop options for strikes on Iran before November’s midterm elections, although no decision has been made. Trump has sought to ease concerns about the war’s economic toll, claiming Iran is holding out in hopes of hurting Republicans in the midterms and predicting that the war will end soon afterward. Strikes before the vote would end a weekslong lull in U.S. attacks on Iran, and could prompt further retaliation from Iran against energy assets and shipping in the Gulf.

How Massive Is Elon Musk’s Trillion-Dollar Fortune? Spend It Yourself
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

On any given day, Elon Musk is worth about a trillion dollars. This does not mean that he has a trillion dollar bills sitting in an old-timey vault in a dusty basement somewhere; his wealth is mostly tied up in shares of SpaceX and Tesla. But if he were to cash those out, sell Neuralink and the Boring Company, and scrounge together some extra change, his checking account would hit 13 digits.
“Trillionaire” is an easy enough word to say. It’s fun, even! Rolls off the tongue. But research has shown that the human brain has a very hard time comprehending the actual size and scope of large numbers. “Trillion” sounds like a short hop from “billion,” after all, even though it is in fact 1,000 times bigger. And even if you are somehow able to wrap your mind around that immense scale, it still feels abstract, no matter how many times you compare it to the area of Central Park or the weight of a fleet of trucks. Maybe a better way to visualize a trillion dollars, then, is through what you can actually buy with it.
WIRED has partnered with Neal Agarwal, the proprietor of the consistently delightful website Neal.fun, to do just that. Spend Elon Musk’s Money is a new visualization that lets you, well, spend Elon Musk’s money, on anything from Big Macs to aircraft carriers to the Las Vegas Sphere. It keeps a tally as you go, so you can actually see how far a trillion dollars gets you these days, and it shows the items you’ve bought in a physical space.
WIRED spoke with Agarwal about this new project, why it feels so relevant now, and the state of building things on the web. You can read that interview below, and waste a few hours on Spend Elon Musk’s money right here.
This interview has been lightly edited for clarity and length.
WIRED: I’ve known about Neal.fun for a long time, I’m a big fan. But describe it for someone who’s never been there.
Neal Agarwal: I never wanted to constrain the site to one thing, so it ended up being almost like a journal at this point. I’ve been running it since I was 19, and it’s kind of a catalog of everything I’m interested in: visualizations, science, weird game mechanics. For me, it’s mostly an exploration of what you can do with a website.
Why is that important to you, the idea of exploring what a website is and means? If there’s one thing I know about you it’s that you love the web.
Very much so. I grew up on the web; I was 8 years old on forums. I probably spent more time in Club Penguin than any real-world walls. I’m definitely a child of the web, and it’s interesting that I’m around the same age as it. It’s a privilege. Painters are working in a medium that’s a thousand years older, a million years older, so a lot of things have already been found out, been fleshed out. But on the web there’s so much that we haven’t figured out yet. I think there’s still a lot of new stuff to discover, and that’s really interesting to me.
I think every medium has distinct things you can do with it. You can turn a book into a movie but it’s not quite the same. There are some things a book is always going to be better at, and vice versa. I think that’s true of the web too. This visualization we’re working on, you can’t print it in a newspaper.
I suspect people might be familiar with some of your individual projects, if not your site itself. To list some off that are huge in my household: The Password Game, Space Elevator, The Deep Sea, Infinite Craft. When something goes viral, as so many of these have, what’s it like on your end? Is it almost boring now to see things blow up?
I think each project has been very different. The ones that excite me the most now are where a lot of people play it and start doing things with it that I did not expect or intend. Within a few days of Infinite Craft launching, people started crafting Japanese words within the game. And they crafted enough Japanese words that they could play the whole game in Japanese. I’ve never released a game before where they unlocked a language.
I had another one called Internet Road Trip; it’s like a simulated road trip but through Google Street View. A Discord formed around that, and people started backseat driving and arguing over which city to go to next, should they make a pit stop here so they can see this monument. People started birdwatching within that game. All these emergent things started happening, and I think the web is really good at that, too. It’s really good at forming communities out of the silliest things, which I find really exciting.
There’s also this contrast with a more closed-off app environment; you don’t really work in apps as a medium.
When I was a teenager I did make some apps, but I always really disliked that Apple and Google had to approve what I could put in them, and you have to wait a week for approval, and if they don’t like your app you have no recourse. So just the idea of having a homepage where it’s like, this is my homepage. Nobody can tell me what to do with it. I can put whatever I want.
We should talk about this visualization, Spend Elon Musk’s Money. It’s sort of a sequel to Spend Bill Gates’ Money, which was one of your first projects, right?
That actually launched with the website itself. I just wanted to showcase how much $100 billion was, which I guess now seems like a little amount of money compared to the trillion we’re working with.
It’s almost quaint, right? The premise is you’ve got a $100 billion counter and a bunch of things you can buy with prices attached to them: a Big Mac, flip-flops, a lobster dinner, a year of Netflix, all the way up to things like a diamond ring, a Ferrari, a McDonald’s franchise, and then up again to the Mona Lisa. And you just keep trying to add it up. What was the response to that game when it first launched?
It was one of the biggest things I’ve launched, and it was really nice to see that the point got across. People understood that this is a way to visualize wealth that isn’t just graphs and bar charts. The game kept finding a new audience over and over again; it was an idea that kept being interesting to people.
And then we come to 2026, and we have a trillionaire in the world, and it felt like maybe the right time to revisit.
Yeah, I think so. There’s a lot more you can do to visualize that, too. That’s why this one is 3D. I think one thing with Spend Bill Gates’ money is, yeah, you can buy 10,000 cars, but it’s still a number on a screen. With Spend Elon Musk’s Money, I want you to see the cars you’re buying on a screen. The amount of physical stuff you can buy—it is an empire.
One thing that I certainly have a hard time with, and I think most people do, is really wrapping your head around what a trillion is. There’s been research that humans are really bad at processing how big the jumps are even from 1 billion to 2 billion, much less getting up to a trillion. Our brains just break.
I think that’s one thing the web is actually really good at, is that you have infinite space. You can visualize these numbers in ways that you can’t do in the physical world. Even for my project The Deep Sea, it’s a 1:1 of the ocean. If you wanted to print that out on paper, it would be a mile long, but on the web you can just keep scrolling and scrolling. So it’s kind of fun to have this infinite scroll mechanic to visualize these huge numbers.
Some of the items carry over from Spend Bill Gates Money, some are different. How did you think about the best mix of options to give people?
This time I was going for more tangible things, so you can visualize it. It’s honestly hard to think of items; once you get to $100 million, there are only so many things out on the market that you can buy. So we have the Las Vegas Sphere in there, and aircraft carriers.
After a point it’s kind of interesting that you’re like, OK, I could buy 1,000 more tanks, what would that really get me? Part of the fun of this one is just the futility of it. At a certain point, what more could a person need?
For sure. I just bought 1,000 monster trucks, and I still have $999,650,000 left.
There were a few different ideas. One is if you had a trillion dollars and just had a stack of money, and as you spend it you see the trillion dollars go down, but it’s actually pretty hard to render a trillion dollars in bills on the page.
I had thoughts of more abstract things. Once you get to a trillion dollars you’re really buying power, so how many companies you could buy or how much influence you have. But for most people, that’s a harder way to visualize things than, like, oh, that is a million racehorses I just bought.
Did you run into any technical challenges building this?
Initially I wanted everything to be 3D models on the site. But if you try to get your laptop to render a million monster trucks, it’s just going to freeze. So I had to do a lot of trickery to get this 3D effect without actually using 3D models.
It doesn’t just tell us about Elon Musk, it tells us about the things we’re buying. I looked back at the original Spend Bill Gates’ Money, and the Big Mac was $2. It’s $6 now. For anything where there’s a direct parallel, you’ve captured a real price jump.
It’s very inflation-adjusted. Which is crazy, because it’s only been six or seven years. If anyone has any recommendations about other items we should add to this, just let me know.

Key points in Italy's new electoral law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:59:29 UTC
19:59:29 KST

Key points in Italy's new electoral law
ROME, Oct 8 - Italy's lower house of parliament on Thursday gave final approval to new voting rules ahead of a general election due next year, completing a reform championed by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni.
Meloni, whose government last month became the longest-serving since World War Two, says the new rules are intended to increase the prospect of stable government. The opposition says the goal is to favour her ruling coalition at the election.
Below are the main features of the new system.
PROPORTIONAL SYSTEM
The reform introduces a purely proportional system (PR), replacing the previous hybrid one by which around two thirds of seats were elected by PR and one third in first-past-the-post races.
To boost stability, a working majority will be guaranteed to any coalition that wins more than 42% of the vote. Italy's two main camps are Meloni's conservative alliance and the centre-left bloc, which includes the Democratic Party and the 5-Star Movement.
SEAT BONUS
A coalition surpassing the 42% threshold will receive a "majority bonus" of 70 seats in the 400-member Chamber of Deputies and 35 seats in the 200-member Senate.
However, to avoid excessively large majorities, the bonus is capped to prevent the winner getting more than 220 seats in the Chamber and 113 in the Senate.
If more than one coalition passes the 42% threshold, the one with most votes will get the bonus.
PRIME MINISTER CANDIDATE
Each coalition or party running outside a coalition must indicate their candidate for prime minister. However, under Italy's constitution the president formally chooses the prime minister, meaning the party designation will not be legally binding.
MINIMUM THRESHOLDS AND SIGNATURES
Coalitions must secure at least 10% of the vote to enter parliament, while individual parties, both inside and outside coalitions, must obtain at least 3%.
The reform raises to 6,000 from 1,500 the number of signatures parties currently outside parliament must gather in each constituency to field candidates.
Critics say this makes it harder for small or new parties to compete in the elections. REUTERS
