Life Is Asymmetric. The Scientists Who Figured Out Why Won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

The 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded to Henri Kagan and Kensō Soai for discovering a solution to the enigma of nature’s chemical asymmetry, a finding that opened up new avenues for manipulating the reactions used in manufacturing pharmaceuticals and other materials.
Some molecules are chiral, meaning a molecule has two forms that are mirror images of each other but not identical, like your left and right hand. One of the most mysterious chemical phenomena in biology is that living organisms contain almost exclusively one of the two forms. This is known as homochirality.
Both versions of the molecules—each called an enantiomer—have similar physical properties but can behave differently. The Nobel Committee used a simple analogy to explain this: A locksmith can create two mirror-image keys, but “only one of them fits the lock—and the lock can be damaged if your customers try to unlock it with the other key.”
In the development of new drugs that use, for example, amino acids or sugar molecules as a basis, homochirality poses a problem: While one of the enantiomers of these chiral molecules produces the desired therapeutic effect, the other can cause unnecessary and, at times, harmful side effects. Scientists can’t always easily control which version of the molecule they get out of their synthesis.
The discovery of chiral molecules dates back to the time of Pasteur, who found two enantiomers that reacted very differently when exposed to bacteria. Since then, various researchers have attempted to replicate homochirality in the laboratory with the goal of understanding its spontaneous origin and applying this knowledge to the design of controlled reactions for various purposes. However, early experiments yielded equal amounts of the two variants, failing to reproduce the selectivity observed in nature.
At the beginning of the last century, the German chemist Willy Marckwald designed an asymmetric reaction capable of producing a slightly greater amount of one of the two versions. He achieved this using a chiral catalyst—a substance that facilitates a chemical reaction without being consumed and favors the formation of one of the enantiomers. The ratio between the two variants, however, only changed a little.
Later, in 1953, theoretical physicist Charles Frank proposed a mathematical model that outlined three conditions for reproducing homochirality. First, there must be an asymmetric reaction capable of favoring one of the two versions; that imbalance has to be amplified; and the reaction itself has to produce the catalyst that drives it. This last characteristic is called autocatalysis and generates a kind of positive feedback loop, in which a small initial advantage can cause one of the variants to assemble at an ever-faster rate until it dominates the reaction.
This framework formed the basis of Henri Kagan’s research. Beginning in the early 1980s, he focused on refining asymmetric reactions through a detailed study of the catalyst. At that time, scientists typically used catalysts consisting of a metal atom that acted as the reaction’s driving force and a chiral substance that ensured the process was asymmetric. They assumed that if they used a mixture containing equal amounts of the two versions of that chiral molecule, the result would also be a balanced mixture.
Kagan began to question that idea. He realized that the metal atom likely did not interact with just one enantiomer but with both at the same time. This meant that, by mixing versions A and B, three different combinations could form: A-A, B-B, and B-A. The first two would produce molecules that were mirror images of each other. But the A-B combination could behave differently during the reaction.
The A-B combination, the scientist discovered, could slow down the reaction, indirectly favoring the formation of one of the two versions of the final molecule. The phenomenon was called the “nonlinear effect” and represented a new way to manipulate chemical reactions.
“In addition to their practical interest, nonlinear effects are a very valuable tool for studying reaction mechanisms and the nature of catalytically active species,” explained José María Andrés García, a professor in the Department of Organic Chemistry at the University of Valladolid, in a statement reported by SMC Spain.
Inspired by Kagan’s findings, Kensō Soai sought to create a reaction in which the product itself would act as a catalyst and help produce more molecules identical to itself—one of those theoretical conditions for the homochirality. He conducted a test with a substance known as 5-pyrimidylalkanol. At the beginning of the experiment, one version was just 2 percent more abundant than the other version of the molecule. By the end of the reaction, that advantage had jumped to 87 percent.
In the years that followed, Soai worked toward achieving reactions that resulted in the near-absolute purity of one enantiomer, replicating the molecular state inside living organisms. Finally, in 2003, he engineered a reaction in which the starting substances had no defined orientation, but as they reacted, a slightly greater amount of one enantiomer appeared by chance. That tiny difference then produced many more molecules of the same variant. Gradually, that form came to dominate the reaction, accounting for up to 99.99 percent of the final product.
In other words, the reaction formed only one of the two possible enantiomers. As the Nobel Committee stated, “Other than life itself, no one had previously achieved this feat.”
This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

Israeli prisons since 2023: sites of torture and 'extermination'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:29:29 UTC
19:29:29 KST

Breadcrumb
Israeli prisons since 2023: Palestinians face abuse, torture and 'extermination'
Three years into Israel's genocidal war on Gaza, organisations representing Palestinian prisoners say a "parallel extermination" is taking place inside Israeli prisons, where abuse, torture, starvation and medical neglect have intensified.
More than 100 Palestinian prisoners have died in Israeli custody over the past three years, while around 9,300 remain imprisoned in increasingly harsh conditions, according to Palestinian prisoners' rights groups.
For Nisreen Abu Ghraibeh, those three years have been marked by constant fear for her son Fadi, who is being held by Israel.
Her anxiety grows with every court hearing, the only opportunity she has to see her son, who appears via video link.
Israel has increasingly used video hearings since October 2023, further isolating Palestinian prisoners from their families, who often struggle to obtain even basic information about their detained relatives.
Speaking during a weekly protest at the Al-Bireh Cultural Centre, near Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, Abu Ghraibeh told The New Arab that her son, like other prisoners, had faced systematic repression while his family received only limited information about his condition.
One of her greatest fears is the spread of disease in Israeli prisons, particularly skin conditions such as scabies. Families have also recently received reports of other illnesses, including mpox.
Whenever Abu Ghraibeh hears that another Palestinian has died in custody, she fears her son or other prisoners could be next.
'Parallel extermination'
At a press conference marking three years since the start of Israel's war on Gaza, Palestinian prisoners' organisations warned of a growing gulf between international legal protections and the reality faced by detainees.
Abdullah al-Zaghari, head of the Palestinian Prisoners' Club, said Israeli prisons could not be viewed separately from the wider context of the war.
"The prison cannot be viewed as a place separate from the context of extermination, but rather as one of the tools through which violence and control over Palestinians are reproduced and perpetuated within a closed system," he said.
Zaghari said testimonies gathered by prisoners' groups and human rights organisations over the past three years provided an important record not only of abuses inside Israeli prisons, but also of the failure of the international system to protect victims and uphold international law.
He warned that allowing violations to continue without accountability risked normalising such practices far beyond the Palestinian context.
Zaghari called for implementation of the International Court of Justice's advisory opinion declaring Israel's occupation unlawful, including the dismantling of what he described as a discriminatory military judicial system used to legitimise repression and collective punishment against Palestinian prisoners.
He also called for greater international pressure on Israel over the death penalty for Palestinians.
Lawyer and prisoners' rights activist Sahar Francis said the past three years had also seen a dangerous shift at the legislative level, including the introduction of the death penalty and the establishment of a new military court to try Gaza detainees accused of involvement in the 7 October 2023 attack.
Francis questioned what Palestinian institutions, political parties and prisoners' families could do in the face of what she described as the failure of international legal mechanisms and states to uphold their obligations.
Helmi al-Araj, director of the Hurriyat Centre for Defence of Liberties and Civil Rights, accused Israel of pursuing a policy of "slow death" against prisoners through systematic torture, starvation and medical neglect.
He said the treatment of prisoners over the past three years was unprecedented and called for greater public mobilisation around their plight.
Al-Araj also held the UN Secretary-General largely responsible for providing legal protection for prisoners and ensuring international protection for Palestinians from violations by Israeli forces and settlers.
More than 100 deaths in custody
In a report examining the abuses suffered by Palestinian prisoners since October 2023, prisoners' organisations said detainees had faced attacks unprecedented in their severity and scale.
They highlighted the introduction of legislation imposing the death penalty on Palestinian prisoners in March 2026 as among the most serious developments.
More than 100 Palestinian prisoners have died over the past three years, according to the report. The identities of 92 have been announced, while Israel continues to conceal information about the fate of dozens of detainees from Gaza and retains the bodies of dozens of Palestinians who died in custody.
Deaths over the past three years account for around 28% of all recorded Palestinian prisoner deaths since 1967, the organisations said.
Around 26,000 arrests have been recorded in the occupied West Bank since October 2023, alongside thousands more in Gaza.
Some 9,300 Palestinians are currently held by Israel, including 118 serving life sentences, 91 women and 350 children.
Another 3,101 Palestinians are being held under administrative detention without charge or trial.
Israel also classifies 1,419 detainees as "unlawful combatants", a category that includes prisoners from Gaza as well as detainees from Syria and Lebanon.
For families such as Abu Ghraibeh's, the figures compound three years of uncertainty over what their relatives are enduring behind prison walls.

Leaked Russian Blueprint Counts 1,000 Weapons to Freeze Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:28:34 UTC
19:28:34 KST

An alleged Russian document calculates that three Kinzhal missiles could be used against each combined heat and power plant and 20 attack drones against each single boiler facility as part of a wider campaign to deprive Ukrainian cities of electricity, heating and water.
The Ukrainian investigative project Schemes, run by RFE/RL, said on Thursday, Oct. 8, that it obtained a copy of the document from sources in Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The file outlines approximately 60 critical targets and calculates that Russia would need roughly 1,000 weapons to disable them: up to 770 drones and drone-missiles, 170 guided aerial bombs and 75 Kinzhal and Iskander-M ballistic missiles.
The document does not constitute a confirmed order for attacks. Experts consulted by Schemes described it as an analytical estimate that could be used to justify weapons production and establish how many munitions would be required for a future operation.
Russia calculates weapons for each target
The document is titled “Analytical Brief: Analysis of Ukraine’s Energy Generation and Utilities” and is dated August 2026.
Its authors are not identified, its metadata has been altered and some pages are missing. It also does not specify which Russian officials received the presentation before Ukrainian intelligence allegedly intercepted it.
Schemes said the file relies partly on publicly available information from OpenStreetMap, Worldometers and the websites of Ukrenergo, Ukrhydroenergo, Kyivteploenergo, the Energy Ministry and DTEK. Other assessments are attributed only to unnamed Russian military experts or a “working group.”
Poland Ends Russian Drone Probe After Failing to Identify Perpetrator
The document names four priority sectors: electricity generation and distribution, water supplies, sewage systems and heating.
Its list of 60 targets includes hydroelectric and thermal power plants, combined heat and power facilities, electricity substations, cross-border interconnectors, boiler houses, water-treatment facilities and pumping stations.
According to the calculations:
- Equipment connecting each of Ukraine’s three operating nuclear power plants to the grid would require two Iskander missiles to disable.
- Each major hydroelectric power plant could require up to 25 Molniya, Geran or Dan-T/Banderol drones, or three Kinzhal missiles.
- Each combined heat and power facility could require 25 drones or three Kinzhals. The document also considers approximately 25 FAB-500 guided bombs and five Iskander-M missiles for each facility.
- A substation or electricity interconnector could require 15 drones or three Kinzhals.
- A boiler house could require 20 Geran or Dan-T/Banderol weapons.
The authors acknowledge that boiler houses are close to residential areas and state that using other weapons against them could cause civilian casualties.
Kyiv, Kharkiv and Odesa are principal targets
The document identifies Kyiv, Kharkiv and Odesa as the main target cities. It also lists Dnipro, Zaporizhzhia, Mykolaiv, Kherson, Poltava, Chernihiv, Kryvyi Rih, Cherkasy, Kropyvnytskyi, Lviv, Vinnytsia and Ivano-Frankivsk as priorities.
Kyiv’s energy system receives particular attention. Although the capital has an extensive network, the authors identify five substations forming part of the “Kyiv ring” as potential weak points.
According to the calculation, disabling 12 key substations serving Kyiv, Kharkiv and Odesa could halt as much as 90 percent of their electricity supply. The document estimates that this would require 40-50 Molniya drones and 130-140 Geran-4 or Dan-T/Banderol weapons.
The same material was previously examined by The New York Times, which reported that Moscow’s apparent objective was to cause a humanitarian emergency by cutting large cities off from electricity, heating and water.
The proposed campaign reportedly begins with attacks on interconnectors through which Ukraine imports electricity from Europe, followed by attacks against 10 major hydroelectric plants and equipment connecting the South Ukraine, Rivne and Khmelnytskyi nuclear power plants to the national grid.
Not a final attack order
Energy Research Center Director Oleksandr Kharchenko cautioned that the document should not be interpreted as a direct combat order.
“This is not a combat directive,” he told Schemes, describing it as a presentation intended to demonstrate the concept to senior Russian officials.
A Ukrainian defense-industry representative who had seen the material before being contacted by journalists offered a similar assessment. The source said the calculations could support requests for manufacturers to produce certain quantities of weapons.
An actual operational plan would be a separate document specifying how weapons would be distributed and when attacks would take place, the source said.
Schemes could not independently establish who prepared the file. The defense-industry representative assessed that it probably originated in the Russian Defense Ministry or one of its subordinate bodies.
Ukraine’s military intelligence, Foreign Intelligence Service and Security Service had not formally authenticated the document by the time the investigation was published.
“Cold terrorist calculation”
Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal presented Russia’s alleged preparations to European partners during a G7+ energy meeting in Paris on Sept. 17.
Shmyhal described the material as a “cold terrorist calculation,” saying it contained tables specifying the weapons considered necessary to destroy individual facilities.
Since the full-scale invasion began, Ukrainian prosecutors have opened investigations into 3,374 Russian attacks affecting 1,177 energy facilities, according to figures provided to Schemes.
At least three facilities attacked during Russia’s large-scale barrage on Sept. 30 – two combined heat and power plants in Kyiv and a thermal power plant in the Kyiv region – also appeared in the document.
On Oct. 7, Russia launched 70 missiles and dozens of attack drones across Ukraine, hitting energy infrastructure and residential buildings. The nationwide death toll later rose to at least 32, including five children.

19:28:32 KST

MOSCOW, October 8. /TASS/. Russian strikes on Ukrainian military facilities have significantly weakened Kiev’s ability to produce and use Flamingo missiles against Russian territory, military analyst Igor Korotchenko, editor-in-chief of the National Defense magazine, told TASS.
"The damage inflicted on Ukraine’s military-industrial complex as a result of strikes by the Russian Armed Forces on factories and workshops producing Flamingo cruise missiles has significantly weakened the Kiev regime’s ability to launch long-range missile strikes against Russian territory. However, some potential still remains in terms of production sites that have not yet been identified, as well as stockpiles held by the Ukrainian armed forces. In any case, the risk has not been completely eliminated, although - and I emphasize this once again - Zelensky’s capabilities in this area have been significantly weakened," he noted.
The analyst also noted that missile production has been set up in more than 10 European countries. According to him, potential deliveries of such weapons to Ukraine must be taken into account when organizing air defense in Russian regions.
"We must take this factor into account when developing the necessary air defense countermeasures, both for the regions themselves and for those potential targets against which Zelensky might authorize such strikes," the analyst added.
Therefore, Korotchenko believes that one of the tasks of the Russian Armed Forces at the current stage is to destroy transport logistics along the border with Poland and Romania on Ukrainian territory, "in order to make the delivery of finished products or components as difficult as possible."
The Russian Defense Ministry reported earlier that the Russian Armed Forces launched a massive strike overnight to Wednesday, targeting facilities involved in the assembly and storage of FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles, as well as their components, in Kiev and five other regions of Ukraine--Kiev, Chernigov, Dnepropetrovsk, Poltava, and Kharkov.

Pakistan joins Saudi airstrikes on Yemen’s Houthis: report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:27:41 UTC
19:27:41 KST

- A senior Pakistani military official told The New York Times that Pakistani fighter jets have carried out strikes against Yemen’s Houthis.
- A second official called it air support against Houthi drone and missile threats and ruled out a Pakistani ground offensive inside Yemen.
Pakistan Air Force fighter jets are being used in strikes against Yemen’s Houthi rebels, a senior Pakistani military official told The New York Times, the first indication from inside Pakistan’s military that its air force has joined Saudi Arabia’s renewed war against the Iran-backed group.
A second Pakistani official told the newspaper that Pakistan’s role is expected to focus on degrading Houthi drone and missile threats through air support, and not on a ground offensive in Yemen. Neither official said how many aircraft are involved, which targets have been hit, when the strikes began or whether the jets are striking inside Yemeni territory, and Pakistan’s military declined to comment.
Col. David O. Smith, a former U.S. Army attaché in Pakistan and former Defense Intelligence Agency analyst, told the Times that analysts broadly estimate about 8,000 Pakistani troops have deployed to Saudi Arabia, including Pakistan Air Force and Army air defense units. He said they would likely help protect oil infrastructure and were unlikely to fight the Houthis directly, given Islamabad’s effort to preserve its relationship with neighboring Iran.
The report follows Monday’s decision by Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey to activate the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, a mutual defense pact the three countries signed on Aug. 7. At an emergency meeting in Riyadh, they agreed to put collective deterrence measures into effect and rapidly deploy Pakistani and Turkish forces to the kingdom, the first time the pact had been invoked. Hours later, Pakistani Defense Minister Khawaja Asif said Pakistani forces were already playing a part, although when reporters asked him on Sept. 30 whether Pakistani forces had joined strikes in Yemen, he did not answer directly.
Pakistan’s military spokesman, Lt. Gen. Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry, confirmed this week that Pakistani troops are stationed in Saudi Arabia but declined to say whether they would operate across the border in Yemen, telling CNN that any involvement would be defensive in nature.
Over the past several days, Saudi Arabia said Houthi missile and drone strikes on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and Abha International Airport in the south killed three people, two women at Abha and a Sudanese man at King Khalid, and injured 36. The Saudi-led coalition said it retaliated by hitting dozens of Houthi military sites in Yemen, including missile storage sites and command centers, and on Thursday residents of Riyadh reported hearing several explosions whose cause was not immediately clear.
The Houthis declared a blockade of the Red Sea in July and attacked shipping there, then seized Yemen’s Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive last month, routing Saudi-backed government forces. The Saudi-led coalition says 100 fighter jets are now supporting a counteroffensive by Yemen’s internationally recognized government to retake that territory, and a United Nations agency said nearly 200,000 people have been displaced in Yemen since early September.
Islamabad has long kept its distance from the Yemen war: in 2015, when Saudi Arabia launched its original campaign against the Houthis and asked Pakistan for jets, ships and troops, Pakistan’s parliament voted to stay neutral. Iran’s Foreign Ministry said on Sunday it hoped reports of a Pakistani deployment for the war in Yemen were untrue.
Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed a separate bilateral mutual defense agreement in September 2025, declaring an attack on either country an attack on both, and the Mecca pact extended that commitment to Turkey, whose parliament has not yet ratified it.

Gaza 3 years on: The unfinished fight for Palestinian workers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:26:46 UTC
19:26:46 KST

Breadcrumb
Gaza 3 years on: The unfinished fight for Palestinian workers
Three years after Israel began its genocide in Gaza, the fate of Palestinian workers detained after 7 October remains unclear, though their odyssey of humiliation, torture, and, on occasion, murder is beyond doubt and is mostly documented by their Israeli tormentors on social media and aired live by the far-right Minister of National Security Itamar Ben-Gvir.
Gazans who had crossed the Green Line desperate to earn a living, mostly in blue-collar jobs, were stripped of their permits, rounded up, and held without contact with lawyers or families. Their treatment should push one to wonder what international trade unions did when fellow workers in this part of the world were imprisoned and abused.
Israel closed the crossings and revoked Gazan workers’ permits, turning people previously authorised to work into supposed illegal residents. Thousands were detained in Israel and the occupied West Bank. On 3 November 2023, more than 3,000 were released into Gaza, where bombardment continued. Release offered no guarantee of safety.
Workers described, in testimonies published by Human Rights Watch in January 2024, beatings, electric shocks, humiliation, and deprivation of food and water. The rights watchdog also independently documented mass detention without contact with the outside world.
International allies
Warnings of the ongoing abuse were already coming out earlier. On 11 October 2023, the Palestinian Democracy and Workers’ Rights Centre denounced violence against Gazan workers. On 25 October, it demanded their immediate release and appealed to the international labour movement. The workers’ predicament was already being placed before their supposed international allies.
Their case cuts through the claim that Palestine is somehow outside a union’s remit. These Gazan workers had employers, wages, and families dependent on their earnings. Stripped of work permits, thrown in torture dungeons for weeks, should have triggered a global public outcry among trade unionists and industrial organisers everywhere.
Calling the subsequent response universal silence would be inaccurate. The International Trade Union Confederation’s 2024 Global Rights Index described thousands of workers held in illegal detention, denied basic rights and legal representation. It recorded reports of abuse and degrading conditions, alongside two deaths in custody. The world’s principal union confederation had publicly acknowledged the violations.
Australia’s Union Aid Abroad–APHEDA published Palestinian union allegations of torture deaths in January 2024. In March 2025, the International Labour Network of Solidarity and Struggle endorsed reports from the Arab Workers Union in Nazareth concerning disappeared Gazan workers, torture and deaths in detention. These were clear acts of solidarity, but circulating allegations is only the beginning.
On 27 September 2024, nine global unions filed a complaint with the International Labour Organisation detailing the draconian working conditions of more than 200,000 Palestinian workers in Israel. The nine organisations condemned “widespread wage theft due to the suspension of work permits and the unilateral termination of their contracts.”
Signatories included the ITUC, IndustriALL, Education International, Public Services International, UNI, and the international federations representing transport, construction, food workers and journalists. The OECD’s Trade Union Advisory Committee also joined. Its stated legal focus was wage protection; however, not accountability for torture.
The demands of Palestinian unions
While such a solidarity move is worth applauding, it still exposes a long-running problem of “economism” that has long marred the trade union movement.
What resources went toward locating missing workers, supporting survivors, securing independent investigations and pursuing those responsible? A complaint about stolen wages surely matters enormously to impoverished families. It cannot substitute for a “political” campaign against imprisonment, torture, military occupation and genocide.
Palestinian unions had also identified what their counterparts could do. Their 16 October 2023 appeal asked workers to refuse to manufacture or transport weapons for Israel, challenge complicit companies and pressure governments to stop military trade. This was an action plan for international unions. Were the latter ready to organise around those demands and protect members prepared to act?
The wider response to Gaza shows that stronger positions were possible. The World Federation of Trade Unions was calling for an end to genocide by October 2023. IndustriALL’s executive committee explicitly condemned the continuing genocide in May 2024 and urged affiliates to support boycott, divestment, and sanctions.
Education International’s 2024 congress demanded an end to arms transfers to Israel. These were formal positions of international organisations, not merely statements by dissident branches.
Other unions organised material support. In November 2023, the International Transport Workers’ Federation created a Palestine Solidarity Fund. Public Services International established its Gaza fund in March 2024. By August 2025, European Union federations were demanding sanctions, suspension of the EU–Israel Association Agreement, and an end to economic relations with Israeli settlements.
Influential national unions in several countries also took a firm position in solidarity with the Palestinians, sometimes aligning with their governments’ stated positions and sometimes opposing them.
South Africa’s teachers’ union SADTU explicitly condemned genocide in 2023. Ireland’s ICTU demanded economic sanctions, while Britain’s TUC called for ending arms licenses and suspending the trade agreement. Canada’s CUPE described the assault as genocide and supported Palestinian workers’ rights organising.
In July 2024, seven US unions demanded an immediate halt to military aid: UAW, UE, SEIU, the postal workers’ APWU, flight attendants’ AFA, painters’ IUPAT and National Education Association. Their demand confronted the material support sustaining Israel’s assault, even if a letter alone could not stop it.
Disrupting the deadly occupation machine
Workplace action offered another, certainly more effective, route. A trade union representing workers in 11 major Indian ports refused to handle weapons shipments for Israel. France’s CGT endorsed workers at Fos and Roissy who refused to facilitate arms deliveries. Such examples show where unions’ distinctive power lies: in their capacity to interrupt production and transport.
Italian unions took action to another level by organising a general strike explicitly in solidarity with Gaza. On 22 September 2025, USB and other grassroots unions organised a nationwide stoppage against the genocide, disrupting transport, schools and ports.
Following Israel’s interception of the Global Sumud Flotilla, CGIL and USB called another general strike on 3 October. According to CGIL, the stoppage disrupted major services, and more than two million people rallied across over 100 cities.
Such organising efforts developed across borders. Italy’s USB, Greece’s ENEDEP, the Basque union LAB, Turkey’s Liman-İş and Morocco’s ODT called a joint ports action for 6 February 2026, demanding an end to arms shipments feeding the genocide and a trade embargo on Israel. Their initiative connected solidarity with opposition to militarisation and the erosion of dockworkers’ conditions.
But other union leaders shamefully obstructed solidarity. In October 2023, the AFL-CIO intervened against a ceasefire resolution adopted by Washington state’s Thurston-Lewis-Mason labour council. The federation eventually, under pressure, called for a negotiated ceasefire on 8 February 2024.
Germany’s DGB declared solidarity with Israel after the Hamas attacks. Its position cannot fairly be reduced to unconditional approval of everything Israel subsequently did: a July 2025 resolution demanded an end to attacks on civilians and supported a ceasefire. Yet the same resolution sharply defended Histadrut against criticism within international union bodies.
The Histadrut, for its part, is hardly an ordinary “trade union.” It has been the backbone of the settler colonisation of Palestine from the start, and a major instrument of segregation and discrimination against Arab workers. The international labour movement should isolate, boycott, and deplatform it.
Union members everywhere need to hold their own leaders accountable for these decisions. Those who blocked solidarity or defended Israel’s actions should face a challenge from below, with their record on Gaza brought into branch meetings, congress debates, and leadership elections. Members can demand disclosure of their unions’ ties to Histadrut and organise to sever them.
The fight is far from over. Missing workers must be accounted for, survivors supported, stolen wages recovered, and those responsible for torture and deaths held accountable. These demands belong alongside the struggle to end the occupation and dismantle the structures that leave Palestinian workers dependent on those who dispossess and exploit them.
The strikes and port actions point toward what comes next: sustained organising to stop arms shipments, challenge complicit employers, and defend workers who face retaliation for taking action. Every solidarity resolution needs an organising plan behind it. Palestinian workers deserve a labour movement prepared to use its power, and a rank and file ready to act when its leaders refuse.
Hossam el-Hamalawy is an Egyptian scholar-activist in Germany, focusing on the military, policing, and labour.

UK airport e-gates to become passport-free and contactless by early 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:24:53 UTC
19:24:53 KST

UK airports have begun rolling out contactless e-gates. The technology allows eligible travellers to pass through without having to show their passports.
The UK has begun rolling out a new contactless border system across its airports. The move means eligible passengers arriving in the country will soon be able to pass through airport e-gates without presenting their passports.
Initially only available for British citizens, the initiative was launched at East Midlands Airport in England this week. In a statement, the government said it plans to upgrade all the country’s e-gates by early 2027 and expand its accessibility to other eligible nationalities.
“We’re delighted to be the first UK airport to have contactless e-gates introduced by Border Force,” Steve Griffiths, Managing Director of East Midlands Airport, said. He added that any technological innovation that can make customers’ journeys “smoother, swifter and simpler” is welcomed.
According to tests, the new contactless system is up to 25% faster compared to presenting a physical passport. Phil Douglas, Director General of the UK's Border Force, said the digital push builds on work from the summer period to extend e-gates to children aged eight and older. This will make life “a little easier” for families, he added.
How does it work?
The contactless system uses facial comparison technology to verify a traveller’s identity. Upon arrival, passengers will approach an e-gate where their photo is taken. The system then checks the live image against verified immigration, travel and passport information. And, if all clear, the barrier will automatically open, meaning the checks are complete.
If further checks are needed, however, travellers will be required to place their passport on the reader or be directed to a Border Force officer.
Officials advise that travellers keep their passport with them at all times, nonetheless. Further, the UK government added that Border Force officers will remain at hand monitoring all e-gates and offering assistance.
For dual British nationals, the advice is to return to the UK with a valid British passport or hold a Certificate of Entitlement to avoid any potential delays at the border.
Which UK airports have the new contactless e-gates?
Currently, a handful of contactless e-gates are available to use at East Midlands Airport.
As part of the phased rollout, however, the technology will also be available across Birmingham, Bristol, Cardiff, Edinburgh, Gatwick, Glasgow, Heathrow, London City, Luton, Manchester, Newcastle and Stansted airports.
The UK has more than 290 standard e-gates in place at 15 air and rail ports. This technology is available to UK or Irish citizens, as well as travellers eligible to obtain an Electronic Travel Authorisation (ETA) to travel to the UK.
Introduced in February, the ETA allows officials to identify potential security risks before someone travels to the country.

Putin just turned 74. Russia’s State Duma isn’t getting any younger either. Here’s how the country’s parliament has aged over the past three decades.
In late September 2026, after reviewing the results of elections to the State Duma, the lower house of Russia’s parliament, Russia’s Central Election Commission chief Ella Pamfilova said:
The Duma has gotten a little younger. It wasn’t old to begin with, but it’s gotten younger.
To support her claim, Pamfilova cited the lawmakers’ average age at the end of the previous session and the start of the new Duma: 57 and 53, respectively.
That comparison is incorrect, however. The newly elected lawmakers are indeed younger on average than those who served during the spring sitting of the eighth, outgoing session.
Comparing lawmakers’ ages at the start of each session shows the State Duma has been steadily aging, according to Meduza’s calculations. BBC Russia reached the same conclusion.
The State Duma’s first session was elected in December 1993, and lawmakers convened for their first meeting in January 1994, when their average age was 45.8. By the second session, the average age had risen to 47.2.
In the fifth session, which began work in 2007, the average age exceeded 50 for the first time.
Since then, the average age has continued to rise, reaching 54.3 in the ninth session. The difference from the first session is 8.5 years.
How we calculated this
Meduza compared lawmakers’ ages as of the date of each session’s first meeting. Vacant seats were not counted, which is why some previous Dumas had fewer than 450 members. The fourth session, for example, began work with 447 lawmakers after the “against all” option won in three electoral districts, leaving those seats vacant until repeat votes were held several months later.
Meduza calculated lawmakers’ average and median ages using their dates of birth, rounding the results to the nearest tenth of a year. The lists of lawmakers and their dates of birth were compiled from Central Election Commission documents, State Duma records, and other published biographies.
Age is calculated as of the day of each session’s first meeting, and party affiliation is based on faction membership on that same date.
Each successive session is older than the last
Nearly one in three lawmakers in the new Duma has already turned 60. United Russia has the most lawmakers in that group: 109, out of 349 seats the party won overall.
United Russia’s lawmakers age 60 and older alone outnumber all lawmakers from every other party combined: only 101 lawmakers in total were elected to the rest of the Duma, including members of Russia’s Communist Party (KPRF), New People, the LDPR, A Just Russia, and Rodina, along with four independent candidates.
Almost a quarter of the Duma’s lawmakers — 106 of 450 — have already reached retirement age (currently 64 for men and 59 for women); 81 of them were elected from United Russia.
How we calculated retirement age
Russia carried out a pension reform in 2019, so Meduza used the retirement age in effect for each given year when calculating the number of retirees in the Duma. Women born between 1964 and 1968 and men born between 1959 and 1963 follow a transitional retirement schedule. The thresholds are listed on the Social Fund’s website.
Northern work experience and other benefits were not factored in.
Lawmakers’ average age depends directly on the Duma’s oldest members: the older they are, the higher the overall figure. To rule out the possibility that a few outliers are driving the increase, Meduza also calculated the median age.
In the first session, the median age was 45.3: half the lawmakers were younger, half older. In the current session, it is 54.2, a difference of almost nine years.
This means aging has affected every age segment of the Duma, though the trend has not been uniform: in 2011, for example, the median age dipped slightly.
The change is visible even without averages. In 1994, 127 lawmakers under 40 were elected to the Duma’s first session, almost a third of the original lineup that convened for its first meeting. In the new Duma, only 51 lawmakers are under 40, or one in nine.
There are now almost as many lawmakers age 70 and older: 49. Just 10 years ago, at the start of the seventh session, there were only 19, and in the Duma’s first session there were none at all.
The record for age at the start of a session had previously belonged to KPRF member Vladimir Dolgikh, who was 87 when the sixth Duma began work in December 2011. In the ninth session, United Russia’s Vladimir Resin broke that record; he turned 90 in February.
Before being elected to the State Duma, Resin spent many years heading Moscow’s construction sector and served as first deputy mayor of Moscow under Yuri Luzhkov. LDPR leader Leonid Slutsky likely owes his career to Resin: in private conversations, he calls Resin “Dad.”
The Duma’s oldest lawmaker has a special duty: under the Constitution, he is the one who opens the first meeting of a new Duma. In January 1994, LDPR lawmaker Georgy Lukava opened the first session at age 68. This year, 90-year-old Resin ceded the right to open the meeting to his United Russia colleague, 79-year-old Yuri Petrov.
Petrov is actually only fourth by age: older than the United Russia member are his party colleague Valentina Tereshkova, 89, and KPRF member Gennady Zyuganov, 82. During his remarks, Petrov asked each of his older colleagues in turn, “Shall we open the meeting?” All three agreed, after which Petrov thanked them “for the trust placed in him,” the Russian business daily Kommersant wrote.
The youngest lawmaker in the new Duma is Georgy Arapov, the former head of New People’s regional branch in Irkutsk region, who turned 27 in September.
Arapov has set the lower end of the age range for elected lawmakers over the past five years: he was also the youngest lawmaker in the previous Duma, when the New People member was only 22.
The record for this metric, however, belongs to 21-year-old Vasily Vlasov, elected to the seventh session of parliament from the LDPR in 2016. Before his election, he worked as an aide to Vladimir Zhirinovsky and headed his secretariat. In March 2021, when Vlasov was 25, he became first deputy head of the LDPR faction. In November 2023, a year and a half after Zhirinovsky’s death, Vlasov lost his parliamentary mandate over absences from meetings.
More about Vasily Vlasov
In August 2017, Yuri Dud asked Zhirinovsky about Vlasov’s path to the Duma on the party’s ticket: “What did he do to become a lawmaker at 21?” The LDPR leader pointed to the legally permitted age for election, 21, and explained: “He knows better what young people his age want.”
Vlasov’s rise within the party caused discontent among its members. According to the Russian business outlet RBC, Zhirinovsky’s son, State Duma Deputy Speaker Igor Lebedev, opposed the appointment. On the independent Russian broadcaster TV Rain, Zhirinovsky denied any conflict with his son and explained his choice of Vlasov simply: “It benefits us [that] he’s good at his job.”
Vlasov now works at the Russian University of Sport in Moscow, where he oversees youth policy.
More than three-quarters of pension-age lawmakers were elected from United Russia
Almost a quarter of the new Duma’s lawmakers — 106 of 450 — are already old enough to retire. A large share of them belong to United Russia.
The KPRF has 16 pension-age lawmakers out of 37 in the faction, A Just Russia has five out of 17, the LDPR has two out of 24, and Rodina has one. New People has none.
A total of 109 United Russia lawmakers are starting their work at 60 or older, compared with 35 in the other parties combined.
Despite the increase in the retirement age, United Russia now has more pension-age lawmakers in the new Duma than before: 81, up from 75. The other factions now have fewer: 25, down from 36 in the previous session.
Over the past three sessions, the share of seats held by lawmakers age 60 and older has grown from 26.9% to 32%. The number of lawmakers in that age group was 121 in 2016, 126 in 2021, and is 144 now.
The number of pension-age lawmakers in the Duma as a whole has fallen. Ten years ago, almost one in three lawmakers fell into this group. Now, about one in four do. The decline, however, is directly tied to the increase in the retirement age — under the pre-reform rules, more than a third of the Duma would now fall into this group.
This last change is particularly telling. Compared with the start of the previous session, the number of lawmakers age 60 and older across the whole Duma has grown by 18. All of that increase came from United Russia, which gained 23 lawmakers over 60. In the other parties, the number is actually five lower.
In 2016, only 19 lawmakers had already turned 70. By 2021, there were 33, and in the current session there are 49, or one in 10. Of these, 34 are United Russia members, 11 were elected from the KPRF, two from A Just Russia, one from the LDPR, and one ran as an independent candidate.
Despite their age, many remain politically active, supporting Putin and the war in Ukraine.
For example, 82-year-old KPRF leader Gennady Zyuganov and his party colleague, 78-year-old Vladimir Kashin, are involved in organizing supplies for the Russian military. In August 2026, the KPRF announced that the two had helped send another convoy to the combat zone. According to the party, along with food and medicine for soldiers, the communists sent drones, thermal imaging devices, camouflage netting, SUVs, and motorcycles.
A Just Russia leader Sergei Mironov is now 73. In January 2023, he received a sledgehammer bearing the insignia of the Russian mercenary group Wagner as a gift from Yevgeny Prigozhin. Wagner mercenaries used a sledgehammer to kill their own comrade at the front, former convict Yevgeny Nuzhin. Even after Prigozhin’s march on Moscow and his death in a plane crash, Mironov said he would keep the gift “in a place of honor” as “a sign of fellowship.”
However, since late August 2026, Mironov has stopped attending party events in person. He said he is being treated for an injury sustained during a trip to Altai. His fellow party members stood in for him during the pre-election debates. Nevertheless, on September 28, Mironov was unanimously reelected as faction leader. He joined the meeting via video link and said he would continue working remotely for now.
The Kremlin openly uses the standing of other experienced lawmakers for its own purposes. For example, in March 2020, Valentina Tereshkova proposed a constitutional amendment allowing Putin to run for president again. She was 83 at the time and is starting the new Duma at 89.
A source in the State Duma told Meduza that Tereshkova’s remarks had been written in the Kremlin. Kommersant wrote that the amendment had been drafted in advance, with Tereshkova’s name added by hand. A source who spoke to Kommersant, close to Russia’s Presidential Administration, said Tereshkova was close to State Duma speaker Vyacheslav Volodin.
After Tereshkova’s remarks, Volodin called on all factions to defend her from criticism: “The attacks being made on Tereshkova today are attacks on our country.”
Hi, I’m Yulia.
I’m an editor at Meduza, and for almost five years now, I haven’t been sleeping well for one reason: I’m worried about my colleagues in Russia.
I’m often woken up by messages from our freelance reporters inside the country. They sometimes work late at night or early in the morning, and they message me at all hours. I never silence my phone at night in case of an emergency. Every notification jolts me awake. Half-asleep, my first thought is always the same: they’re texting me because the police have come to search their home. In Russia, you can go to prison for working with Meduza. Sometimes I have nightmares about my reporters being interrogated by the FSB. Some of those nightmares have come true.
Meduza’s reporters risk their freedom to tell the world what’s happening inside Russia. They believe their work can help make a better future possible, and they refuse to leave. Please donate so they can keep reporting.
New People remains the youngest party. But it’s aging too
The youngest faction, as in the previous session, is New People. Founded in 2020, this was the party’s second electoral cycle, but it, too, has aged in the meantime: the average age of a faction lawmaker was 39.9 in 2021 and is 42 in the current session.
At the same time, the party’s makeup in parliament has changed. The nine lawmakers elected to the Duma for the first time are noticeably younger than their more experienced colleagues: the newcomers average 39.7, compared with 43.8 for the others.
The oldest faction in the new Duma is the KPRF, whose lawmakers average 61.5 years old. The faction has aged by 11.3 years since the first session, though there have been periods in the KPRF’s history when it got younger — after the 2021 election, for example, the average age of the communists fell, though it remained higher than in 1994, when it was 50.2.
Right now, 37 communists have been elected to the Duma. Eleven of them have already turned 70, and another eight have turned 60.
There is only one communist lawmaker under 40: 38-year-old Alexander Ivachev of the Sverdlovsk region. He heads the region’s party branch and previously served as deputy speaker of the regional legislative assembly. Ivachev is known, among other things, for his statements against the Yeltsin Center and his fight to preserve a bas-relief of Stalin on the Officers’ House building in Yekaterinburg, calling the arguments of those who wanted it removed “the sick fantasies of ‘victims of repression.’”
The LDPR faction has aged by 8.2 years over the past 10 years, the largest increase among the four parties represented in the last three sessions. This trend only emerged in recent years — the LDPR used to be one of the youngest parties. In 2000, lawmakers elected from the Zhirinovsky Bloc began their work with an average age of about 40.
A Just Russia lawmakers have gotten an average of 10 years older over five sessions: the figure was 49 in 2007 and is now 59.1.
United Russia’s average age, 54.1, is lower than that of the KPRF and A Just Russia. Within the party, the share of members age 60 and older rose from 26% at the start of the previous session to 31% in the current one.
Some lawmakers have aged along with the Duma. Three of them have voted on bills for almost 33 years in a row.
More than half the lawmakers in the current Duma — 269 of 450 — also served in the previous session, and 143 took part in all three of the last sessions.
A total of 172 people received a Duma mandate for the first time in 2026. About one in eight of them, 21 lawmakers, have already reached retirement age, roughly the same share as five years ago. The average age of newcomers has not changed since the start of the previous session, either: it is about 48.
Overall, lawmakers entering the Duma for the first time are younger than their experienced colleagues, but the incoming generation that has already made it into parliament is not getting any younger from one election to the next.
Not all newcomers, though, help make the Duma younger. For example, former minister and current adviser to the head of Bashkortostan Gennady Bukayev ran for the State Duma for the first time this year. He had turned 79 by the start of the new Duma’s work.
And some of those who received their first mandate already at retirement age have since spent five or 10 years in parliament. United Russia lawmaker Galina Danchikova came to the Duma in 2016, at 62, and is now starting her third session at 72. Her fellow party member Nikolai Doluda became a lawmaker for the first time in 2021, at 69, and had turned 74 by the start of his second session.
Three lawmakers in the current Duma were part of the starting lineup in all nine sessions, including the very first: KPRF member Gennady Zyuganov, his party colleague Nikolai Kharitonov, and A Just Russia member Anatoly Greshnevikov. In 1994, they were 49, 45, and 37, respectively. Now they are 82, 77, and 70.
The Duma’s age makeup does not closely reflect Russia’s population. The most noticeable gap is the shortage of lawmakers under 40: more than a third of Russia’s adult population is under 40, but in the new Duma, only one in nine seats went to a lawmaker that age. Nationwide, there are three times as many people ages 18 to 40 as there are lawmakers in that age group: 35.1% versus 11.3%.
Lawmakers ages 40 to 64 hold more than two-thirds of the seats, even though they make up less than half of the country’s adult population. The share of people 65 and older is nearly the same in parliament and among the population overall, about one in five.
In the new State Duma, 11% of lawmakers are under 40. In Germany’s Bundestag, after the 2025 election, the figure was 28%, and in France’s National Assembly, after the 2024 election, it was 25%. The U.S. House of Representatives, however, had even fewer young lawmakers than Russia at the start of 2025 — only about 8%.
By the end of the ninth session, the average age of State Duma lawmakers is projected to reach 59.3.

U.S. Air Force shows Morocco the F-35A it reportedly wants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:18:46 UTC
19:18:46 KST

- U.S. Air Force F-35As flew with Moroccan F-16s on the opening day of the Marrakech Airshow, which runs Oct. 7-10.
- Morocco’s first new F-16 Block 72 flew on Oct. 6, and reports say Rabat has discussed buying F-35s, though no sale has been approved.
U.S. Air Force F-35A Lightning II stealth fighters flew alongside Moroccan F-16s on the opening day of the Marrakech Airshow, putting the jet in front of a country that has been reported to be interested in buying it and that already fields a growing list of American weapons.
The airshow runs Oct. 7-10 at a Royal Moroccan Air Force base in Marrakech. Lockheed Martin, which builds both aircraft, posted that Morocco’s F-16s and the U.S. Air Force F-35As took to the skies to open the four-day event. According to the U.S. Department of War, the F-35A flyby is the centerpiece of about 45 U.S. military personnel taking part. The fighters come from the 48th Fighter Wing at RAF Lakenheath in England, the largest U.S. fighter wing in Europe, which flies both F-35As and F-15E Strike Eagles.
The U.S. contingent also includes two aircraft on static display: an HC-130J Combat King II search-and-rescue plane from the Alaska Air National Guard’s 176th Wing at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson, and a KC-135 Stratotanker aerial refueling aircraft from the Utah National Guard’s 151st Wing. The Utah National Guard has been paired with Morocco since 2003 under the State Partnership Program, which links U.S. National Guard units with foreign militaries for regular training and exchanges.
“It is an honor to be at Marrakech ahead of the 250th anniversary of the U.S.-Moroccan Alliance,” said U.S. Air Force Brig. Gen. Matthew J. French, Air National Guard assistant to the commander of U.S. Air Forces in Europe and Air Forces Africa. “Hosted by the United States’ oldest Ally, this forum best illustrates our goal of establishing strong and enduring Allied and partner forces for an evolving security environment. It makes us stronger in both our individual and combined capacities.”
Morocco was the first country to recognize U.S. independence, in 1777, and Washington designated it a major non-NATO ally in 2004.
Morocco’s air force is about to receive a major upgrade of its own. On Oct. 6, Lockheed Martin said the first of 25 new F-16 Block 72 fighters built for Morocco had made its maiden flight in Greenville, South Carolina. The U.S. approved that sale, worth an estimated $3.8 billion, in 2019, along with a separate package of about $985 million to upgrade Morocco’s 23 existing F-16s to a similar standard.
Rabat has also been one of the steadier buyers of American ground equipment in Africa, including M1 Abrams tanks, AH-64E Apache attack helicopters and HIMARS rocket launchers. In 2024, the U.S. State Department approved the sale of 612 Javelin anti-tank missiles to Morocco for an estimated $260 million.
Morocco’s interest in the F-35 has surfaced repeatedly. Reports since 2025 have said Rabat was in talks for up to 32 of the stealth fighters. The U.S. government has not announced any approval of an F-35 sale to Morocco, and neither government has confirmed negotiations.
“The Marrakech Air Show is a world-class exhibition of aviation innovation and a powerful testament to the enduring, nearly 250-year friendship between the United States and the Kingdom of Morocco. For decades, our nations have flown side-by-side, from our vital pilot training pipelines to our complex joint operations. The United States remains deeply committed to standing with our Moroccan partners, delivering cutting-edge aerospace capabilities and working hand-in-hand to promote regional peace, stability, and shared prosperity across the African continent,” said Duke Buchan III, the U.S. ambassador to Morocco.

Russian strike on buses kills at least 30, say officials, as deadly attacks on Ukraine surge
- Published
At least 30 people have been killed in a Russian glide bomb attack on two civilian buses in the eastern front line city of Kramatorsk, rescue officials say.
Authorities said three people were also killed in the village of Bilenke, part of the Kramatorsk community.
Another 18 people were wounded, said Donetsk regional head Vadym Filashkin, accusing Russia of targeting buses carrying passengers to kill as many civilians as possible.
Kramatorsk and neighbouring Slovyansk are part of a so-called fortress belt that Moscow is trying to seize as part of Russian President Vladimir Putin's claim to the entire Ukrainian industrial region of Donbas.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said: "This strike will not go without our response."
In a post on Telegram, he said: "Russia is trying to destroy all life in Donbas, and the world needs to react to this. React harshly - exactly as the Russians deserve for all the deaths they have caused."
Images posted by local prosecutors showed the burning metal shell of the bus along with debris and some of the victims on the road.
Moscow is yet to comment on the latest attack. It follows a dramatic surge in Russian attacks across Ukraine and a heavy increase in civilian casualties.
According to the UN, Ukraine saw more civilians killed by August this year than were killed in all of 2025.
In one single attack that destroyed a five-storey block of flats in Pryluky east of Kyiv early on Wednesday, 22 people were killed, including five children. Three of the children were only one year old.
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who together with Zelensky visited the site of the Russian strike in Pryluky, said the attack showed Putin's "evil intent and evil strategy".
He announced "more sanctions on Russia, on the war machine of Putin, on the shadow fleet, on the oil companies, on the crypto, on the financing of the war" and told Zelensky the UK would stand with Ukraine "as long as it takes for you to prevail in this conflict".
After the deadly attack on Kramatorsk, Filashkin appealed to anyone who was still in the eastern front line region to move to safer parts of Ukraine.
Given the sharp deterioration of security in the two neighbouring cities, he said all public transport had been ordered to stop. The safety of civilians was paramount, and "we have no right to risk the lives of passengers and drivers", he said.
Moscow has often cited the "liberation" and "protection" of the predominantly Russian-speaking Donbas as justification for the full-scale invasion of Ukraine launched by Putin in 2022 - a claim rejected by Ukraine and its allies as baseless.
Donbas is made up of two regions - Luhansk and Donetsk - and with most of Luhansk under Russian control, the Kremlin is also aiming to capture remaining 20% of Donetsk territory still held by Ukraine.
For much of the war Kramatorsk acted as a logistics and supply hub for the Ukrainian military, however it has now come under almost daily Russian attack as its military moves closer to the east of the city.
Glide bombs in particular have been launched at Slovyansk and Kramatorsk. The bombs are fitted with winglets so they glide towards their target rather than simply fall. In late August as many as nine glide bombs were fired at Kramatorsk in one day.
Kramatorsk city council described the strike as a "horrific crime committed by the Russian army against the civilian population".
"Once again, the Russians have struck a location where there are absolutely no military targets," it said.

Russia has in recent weeks been launching constant air raids on the capital Kyiv, with sirens ringing virtually non-stop.
On Thursday, Kyiv police said four people were killed and two injured in the latest Russian attack on the city.
The attacks are forcing schoolchildren out of classes into underground shelters, shuttering businesses, and disrupting public transport.
Moscow's strikes on Ukraine's key infrastructure, particularly on its energy grid, are causing power outages already and are even affecting the water supply. Local water authorities in the capital warned on Thursday that pressure was dropping across the city's right bank due to power cuts.
Kyiv's metro network - which millions of residents rely on - on Thursday briefly halted all its train traffic due to a voltage drop from "external power centres". Trains later started moving again - but at greater intervals, local officials said.
Zelensky offered his condolences to families and loved ones affected by the latest attack and said Ukraine's partners needed to provide "concrete action through new defence packages for the protection of Ukraine".
Ahead of the Pryluky attack, the Ukrainian leader had warned this week of intelligence suggesting plans for a major Russian onslaught, and in Kyiv families responded by heading to metro stations for shelter.
Such warnings are for now one of the only defences Ukrainians have.
Interceptor missiles are in short supply around the world, so Ukraine has little chance to stop incoming Russian ballistics.
Both Russia and Ukraine have intensified long-range strikes on each other in recent months, with Russian attacks targeting Ukrainian data centres and logistics warehouses.
On Thursday, Russian state-run media reported that a number of websites in the country were inaccessible following a Ukrainian drone attack on a data centre of Yandex - Russia's largest search engine.

DEHRADUN: As many as 39,815 rural families in Uttarakhand have been provided pucca houses under the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana-Gramin (PMAY-G) since 2022, with Udham Singh Nagar recording the highest number of houses constructed, according to state government figures.Udham Singh Nagar accounted for 4,882 houses, followed by Haridwar with 4,493 and Rudraprayag with 4,032. Chamoli recorded 3,900 houses, while Pithoragarh and Pauri accounted for 3,386 and 3,195 houses respectively. Under the scheme, eligible beneficiaries receive financial assistance of Rs 1.30 lakh per house through direct benefit transfer into their bank accounts.The state has also increased assistance for purchasing kitchen utensils and other kitchen-related items from Rs 5,000 to Rs 6,000 from 2022-23 onwards.
Beneficiaries are provided an additional Rs 12,000 for toilet construction under the Swachh Bharat Mission through MGNREGA/SWajal.Under the BB Ramji Yojana, beneficiaries are also provided 95 days of wage employment for construction of their houses. The housing support is supplemented with access to basic services such as drinking water, LPG connections under the Ujjwala scheme and electricity connections.

A Russian missile strike on a bus in the eastern city of Kramatorsk has killed at least 30 people, officials have said, in one of the worst attacks by Moscow on Ukrainian civilians this year.
The regional prosecutor’s office in the Donetsk region said on Thursday the vehicle had been hit at 10am by an aerial bomb. “As of now, the death toll from this morning’s attack has risen to 30. Eighteen people were wounded,” it said, adding that all local public transport had been suspended.
Images posted by police showed bodies strewn across a street littered with debris, as well as a charred shell of what appeared to be a bus. A second bus had also caught fire, officials said. The strike targeted an area next to a dental clinic on the city’s Yuvileina Street.
Three people had also been killed by shelling in the village of Bilenke, outside Kramatorsk, they added. Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the Kremlin had deliberately targeted an “ordinary public transport stop”.
Some of those killed could not be identified because of the severity of their injuries, Ukraine’s president added. He said the number of victims could “sadly rise”, as doctors fought to save the lives of those wounded.
He said: “This strike will not go unanswered. Russia is trying to destroy all life in Donbas, and a response from the world is a must. A forceful response – exactly as the Russians deserve for all the deaths they have brought. May all those killed rest in peace.”
The bombing follows a gruesome Russian strike on Wednesday on a five-storey block of flats in Pryluky in the northern Chernihiv region. The building collapsed, entombing those inside. At least 22 people were killed, including five children, aged between one and eight.
Visiting the scene with Ed Miliband, the British foreign secretary, Zelenskyy urged the US to expand Starlink satellite internet coverage so that Ukraine could hit targets inside Russia such as launch sites. So far, Donald Trump and Elon Musk have refused Kyiv’s request.
Miliband said there was “no clearer sign of Putin’s evil, evil intent and strategy in this conflict” than this week’s murderous attacks. He said: “Putin once said that he was going to win on the battlefield. He is trying to win by terrorising civilians.”
Writing earlier on social media, Zelenskyy called on western allies to take “concrete steps” to boost Ukraine’s depleted air defences, amid a round-the-clock Russian onslaught in recent weeks featuring ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones.
“Supplies of anti-ballistic capabilities, ammunition for our combat aircraft, and investments in interceptors – all of this is directly helping save lives every day. Important talks with our partners will take place today and tomorrow,” Zelenskyy said.
Kramatorsk and neighbouring Sloviansk form part of a “fortress belt”. They are the last two big cities in northern Donetsk under full Ukrainian military control. Russia has been trying to capture them for more than a decade, after a brief period in which Russian forces occupied Sloviansk in 2014.
The cities are home to thousands of civilians, as well as Ukrainian soldiers. In recent months, roads have been festooned with nets to protect traffic from marauding enemy drones. These defences offer little protection, however, against aerial bombs.
“These are not ‘the consequences of war’, nor dry statistics. These are people killed by the Russian army,” the Donetsk regional governor, Vadym Filashkin, said on Telegram after Thursday’s strike. “Russia comes to Ukrainian land with death.”
He added: “The Russians are deliberately targeting civilians. For them, a bus full of passengers is an attractive target precisely because a single strike can kill as many people as possible.
“Russia deliberately flouts every conceivable rule of warfare and the norms of international humanitarian law. It selects targets where it can inflict the greatest suffering on civilians.”
There was criticism of the White House’s policy of engaging with Vladimir Putin, whom Donald Trump has invited to December’s G20 summit in Miami, Florida. The Kremlin has yet to say if Russia’s leader will take part.
The former US ambassador to Moscow Michael McFaul said on social media that Russia was guilty of terrorism. “There is no other word for it. Putin is running a terrorist state. That officials from my country call this terrorist a nice guy is deeply embarrassing for me.”
Putin has demanded Ukraine cede the rest of the eastern Donbas region still under its control. Kyiv refuses to hand over its territory, believing Russia will take any concessions and carry on fighting.

So that no hospital has to stop operating: the Kyiv City State Administration explained how preparations for winter at medical facilities are progressing
Kyiv • UNN
The capital's hospitals are receiving backup generators, supplies of fuel, water, medicines, and food. The work is expected to be completed by the end of November.
Preparation of the capital’s healthcare facilities within the capable network is ongoing. At the same time, as Tetiana Mostepan, director of the Kyiv City State Administration’s Department of Health, said on air at KyivFM , work is currently underway to improve what has already been done, reports UNN.
Of course, we are strengthening the entire healthcare system, and accordingly, we are not expecting anything good from this winter. Therefore, all facilities are not only equipped with generators, but also with backup generators. We have planned for no facility to stop operating, regardless of any scenarios that may unfold in the city of Kyiv. This concerns engineering networks, generators, fuel supplies, medication supplies, and food supplies. In other words, all areas have been fully taken into account, and each healthcare facility in the city of Kyiv within the capable network, in accordance with its schedules, response plan, and everything else, is not merely preparing… We have already been improving all these things because we have been ready for this for a long time, but now, understanding the vulnerabilities that may arise, we are strengthening every possible area
As UNN wrote, full autonomy includes not only provision with backup power sources, but also autonomous heating (its own boiler rooms or the ability to quickly connect to mobile boiler rooms in the event of interruptions in centralized heating), as well as its own water source.
At the same time, Mostepan acknowledged that there had been certain delays in strengthening the autonomy of some healthcare facilities. These are hospitals located in the historic part of the city, where preparing project documentation, for example, for drilling a water well, requires bureaucratic issues to be resolved. However, she said that 17 wells have now been launched at 13 healthcare service locations.
"We clearly understand that a well is not simply water for people to drink; it is the operation of surgical units, the functioning of departments and sterilization units, and the operation of emergency departments," Mostepan explained.
Work is also continuing to strengthen hospitals’ autonomy in terms of heat supply.
"Last winter, we used the mobile boiler rooms of the city of Kyiv, but given the scale of the needs and the risks of outages resulting from this, of course, each such boiler room is extremely important for the city of Kyiv. Therefore, we are trying to make every healthcare facility completely independent of everything," Mostepan said.
According to the director of the Kyiv City State Administration’s Department of Health, the city allocated substantial funds to strengthen the resilience of healthcare facilities, while the Ministry of Health and the World Health Organization also provided assistance.
According to Mostepan, work to strengthen autonomy at all facilities within the capital’s capable network is expected to be completed by the end of November.
We remind you

"Even before the full-scale invasion, we were offered the installation of a pellet boiler room independent of the centralized heating supply. It is also cheaper.
Today, we are probably the only maternity hospital that can operate completely autonomously. Our own boiler room. Our own well—the water is always available, even when there is nothing else. Water reserves. A food unit that operates without an external power supply. Generators at every branch," he said .
The facility also has fully equipped shelters operating at two of its branches, where doctors can deliver babies and perform operations.

Confessional confidentiality and journalistic sources to be given greater protection
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:13:00 UTC
19:13:00 KST

Confessional confidentiality and journalistic sources to be given greater protection
The Ministry of Justice wants to explicitly enshrine in law the right of lawyers, journalists, notaries and clergy to refuse to provide information or testify in criminal proceedings.
Estonia already recognizes the concept of professional confidentiality and members of certain professions have the right to refuse to testify. However, Justice Minister Liisa Pakosta (Eesti 200) says the relevant provisions in existing legislation are too narrow and unclear.
"Our idea is to establish clear professional privileges. This is different from professional confidentiality. Professional privilege specifically means that people working in certain professions who may come into possession of information that could, for example, be relevant to a criminal investigation are not required, and in some cases are not permitted, to disclose that information to investigative authorities," Pakosta explained.
Such clearly defined professional privileges could apply to lawyers, notaries, victim support workers, bankruptcy trustees, clergy, journalists and patent attorneys.
Estonian Bar Association President Imbi Jürgen said such violations of privacy in criminal proceedings are not merely a theoretical threat.
"The biggest concern at present is the interception of calls between lawyers and their clients during surveillance operations. This is a very serious problem and disputes concerning the issue have also reached the Supreme Court," Jürgen said.
Justice Minister Pakosta acknowledged that protecting members of these professions would also make certain crimes more difficult to investigate.
"If the state wants to convict someone, it must gather all the evidence itself. It cannot assume that just because someone has told their story to a journalist, that means they can be convicted on that basis the following day," Pakosta said.
Chief State Prosecutor Taavi Pern said the Prosecutor's Office welcomes the proposal, as the law governing these professions has so far been relatively unclear.
"Both the Bar Association and the Prosecutor's Office have been telling the Ministry of Justice for years that this bill and more precise regulations are needed," Pern said.
According to Pern, the bill will increase the Prosecutor's Office's workload.
"If we have to carry out various investigative procedures involving people covered by professional privilege, such as conducting searches or arguing in court over whether the contents of certain emails are protected by professional confidentiality, this will add to our workload," Pern said.
Despite the additional workload, the state does not plan to allocate any extra funding to the Prosecutor's Office. This could mean that prosecutors will have to reorganize their work.
"Given how complex criminal proceedings have become, it would be welcome if discussions about any legislative amendments also included consideration of how many resources, for example, the Prosecutor's Office or the courts would need to implement them," Pern said.

U.S. Army updates logistics tool with Iran war lessons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:10:58 UTC
19:10:58 KST

- The U.S. Army upgraded its LOADOUT transportation software with changes based on lessons from Operation Epic Fury.
- New features include customizable dashboards, real-time capacity visibility and a Priority 1 banner, with monthly reviews planned with theater sustainment commands.
The U.S. Army has updated LOADOUT, its software for requesting and tracking military cargo and troop movements, with changes drawn from lessons of Operation Epic Fury, the U.S. campaign against Iran that began in February.
The Army’s Combined Arms Support Command at Fort Lee, Virginia, which develops the system, said the latest upgrades respond to a common complaint from soldiers: too much time spent hunting down where a shipment stands and too little spent moving it. The command developed the changes with the 1st Theater Sustainment Command, which oversees Army logistics in the Middle East, the 8th Theater Sustainment Command in the Pacific, U.S. Army Japan and other units.
LOADOUT handles Transportation Movement Requests, the formal requests units submit when they need equipment, supplies or people moved. The system walks a request through each stage, from submission and coordination to execution and closeout, so units and sustainment staff can see its status without chasing it down through phone calls and email.
The new version adds dashboards that users can customize to show their own movement requests, cargo manifests that can be exported line by line, and improved tools for uploading and assigning a unit’s equipment and deployment lists. A Movement Board now shows available transportation capacity in real time, and a banner flags Priority 1 mission-critical requests so they stand out.
According to the command, LOADOUT also replaces separate workarounds that individual theaters had built for themselves with a single Army-wide system, giving leaders a common picture of transportation requirements across the geographic combatant commands. The Army said the data helps commanders judge how much transportation capacity they need to support Army and joint operations.
Operation Epic Fury put heavy demands on U.S. military logistics. The campaign involved more than 50,000 U.S. troops, and U.S. Transportation Command has said it used AI tools to replan routes after Spain closed its airspace to U.S. military aircraft at the start of the operation.
CASCOM held its first Functional Review Working Group for LOADOUT on Sept. 24 with leaders from the 1st and 8th Theater Sustainment Commands to review the completed upgrades and set priorities for the next round. Theater partners will now meet monthly to refine the system.
Next steps under discussion include interim tracking of diplomatic and customs clearances, which units often need before cargo can cross borders. Over the longer term, the Army plans to link LOADOUT to its ARTEMIS capability suite so movement information can be handed off automatically between systems.
