RCEP fuels Cambodia's trade surge despite global headwinds
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
17:49:18 CST
18:49:18 KST

PHNOM PENH, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- Cambodia's trade with Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) member states rose 21.3 percent year-on-year in the first nine months of 2026, driven by tariff preferences and trade facilitation, official data showed on Thursday.
According to a report from the Ministry of Commerce, the Southeast Asian country recorded 35.79 billion U.S. dollars in trade with RCEP countries during the January-September period, up from 29.5 billion dollars during the same period last year.
Exports to RCEP members increased by 8.1 percent to 8.03 billion dollars, while imports climbed 25.7 percent to reach 27.76 billion dollars.
The RCEP free trade pact remains Cambodia's largest market, accounting for 61.2 percent of the country's 58.48-billion-dollar total global trade volume over the nine-month period.
China, Vietnam, Singapore, Japan, and Thailand rank as Cambodia's top five trading partners within the bloc.
Coming into effect in 2022, the RCEP unites 15 Asia-Pacific nations, combining 10 ASEAN member states with China, Japan, South Korea, Australia, and New Zealand.
Penn Sovicheat, a secretary of state and spokesperson for the Ministry of Commerce, said that the pact has played a vital role in accelerating trade growth locally, regionally, and globally.
"The RCEP is a driving force for our long-term trade growth and a major catalyst for drawing foreign direct investment to Cambodia," he told Xinhua.
Sovicheat said this mega-trade deal, together with other bilateral free trade agreements, will lift Cambodia out of its least developed country status by 2029.
"It provides the economic foundation needed to achieve our goals of becoming an upper-middle-income nation by 2030 and a high-income country by 2050," he said.
Kin Phea, director general of the International Relations Institute of Cambodia, a think tank under the Royal Academy of Cambodia, said that the pact serves as a stabilizing anchor for regional economic integration.
He noted that the deal helps counter global trade headwinds driven by geopolitical conflict, rising transportation costs, and policy uncertainty, even as surging demand for artificial intelligence hardware and technology provides a powerful economic offset.
"Amid rising protectionism and geopolitical rivalries, RCEP proves the enduring value of cooperation," Phea told Xinhua. "Its inclusive framework offers a vital blueprint for stability against global trade headwinds."
Thong Mengdavid, deputy director of the China-ASEAN Studies Center at the Cambodia University of Technology and Science, said that RCEP has proven indispensable for safeguarding Cambodia's trade diversification against global protectionism.
"The substantial growth in Cambodia's trade with RCEP partners proves its real-world value," he told Xinhua. "However, Cambodia should focus on narrowing the import-export gap by boosting domestic production and high-value exports."
Mengdavid added that the mega-pact remains a core economic anchor for the kingdom and the wider world.
"Globally, RCEP has unlocked an immense transformative potential. By gradually eliminating tariffs on over 90 percent of goods, it has catalyzed a more robust, integrated, and cost-effective ecosystem for international trade," he said. "Moving forward, the agreement remains central to anchoring the region's economic stability in an increasingly unpredictable global market." ■

China unveils plan to expand, improve rehabilitation, nursing care services

Unknown Publisher

BEIJING, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- China on Thursday unveiled a plan to expand and improve medical rehabilitation and nursing care services, with measures to increase service resources, strengthen professional training and promote the use of artificial intelligence (AI).
Under an implementation plan issued by the National Health Commission and the National Development and Reform Commission, cities with large populations, a rapidly aging population and growing demand for rehabilitation and nursing care services are expected to have at least one public rehabilitation hospital and one public nursing care facility by 2030.
The plan also aims to provide about 0.48 rehabilitation and nursing care beds per 1,000 people, as well as 0.7 rehabilitation physicians and 1.6 rehabilitation therapists per 10,000 people, by 2030.
To improve the service system, the plan calls for strengthening the rehabilitation and nursing care service network and enhancing the rehabilitation and nursing care functions of medical and healthcare institutions.
The plan prioritizes support for cities at the prefecture level and above with more than 1 million urban residents in expanding and improving medical rehabilitation and nursing care services.
It urges improvements to rehabilitation and nursing care disciplines and programs at universities and vocational colleges, including appropriately expanding enrollment and better aligning training with employment.
Efforts will also focus on ensuring key departments, including intensive care, orthopedics and neurology, have medical professionals with specialized rehabilitation and nursing care skills.
The plan highlights the use of AI in rehabilitation and nursing care services, encouraging the adoption of rehabilitation robots, smart wearable devices and other technologies to support the monitoring of multiple health indicators and provide intelligent rehabilitation training and health management services.
In July, China's State Council unveiled a national health plan for the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), aiming to raise the country's average life expectancy to 80 years by 2030.
It identifies expanding and improving rehabilitation and nursing care services as an important part of broader efforts to develop a high-quality, efficient and integrated healthcare service system. ■

‘We fought global denial’: Cochav Elkayam-Levy says Oct. 7 sexual crimes are now on record
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:47:23 UTC
18:47:23 KST

Three years after the October 7 massacre, Israeli legal scholar and Israel Prize laureate Dr. Cochav Elkayam-Levy said the effort to document Hamas' sexual and gender-based crimes had succeeded in establishing a historical and legal record despite years of denial and attempts to discredit the evidence.
"We fought for three years and achieved something many believed would be impossible," Elkayam-Levy said at a special event at New York University School of Law. "We confronted the most difficult materials imaginable, trauma and enormous forces of denial, distortion and silencing. Today, the truth is here. It is documented, substantiated and anchored in a legal record that the world can no longer ignore."
The event, titled "Standing With Truth," brought together Elkayam-Levy, founder and chair of the Civil Commission investigating Hamas' October 7 crimes against women, children and families, and Professor Carol Gilligan, one of the most influential figures in contemporary feminist scholarship.
Gilligan, whose work has shaped decades of thinking about women's voices, ethics, listening and responsibility, praised the commission's efforts to document sexual violence committed during the October 7 attacks and against hostages held in Gaza.
"Denial was one of the most painful manifestations of the rampant antisemitism we have witnessed in recent years," Gilligan said. "You exposed the truth. You broke the silence surrounding one of the deepest sources of pain for Jewish women around the world."
Gilligan said the commission had accomplished the difficult task of transforming accounts of atrocities into an evidentiary record capable of supporting legal accountability. "We stood behind you, and you succeeded in the hardest task of all: turning testimony that others tried to silence into legal truth and laying an evidentiary foundation that can endure for generations," she said.
The discussion came nearly five months after the commission published Silenced No More: Sexual Terror Unveiled, a report of nearly 300 pages examining sexual and gender-based violence committed during the Hamas-led October 7 attacks and against hostages in captivity.
The report draws on years of documentation, investigation and analysis involving thousands of pieces of evidence and witness accounts. It presents the commission's extensive factual findings and legal analysis of the crimes, intended to support accountability efforts and preserve the historical record.
Elkayam-Levy said the report marked a turning point in an effort that began as an urgent attempt to document atrocities before evidence could be lost or dismissed. "What began as an urgent effort to document atrocities became a struggle for truth itself," she said.
She emphasized that the commission's work was not limited to publishing its findings. Its archive was designed to preserve evidence over the long term, ensuring that survivor testimony and documentation remain accessible to future generations.
"Our responsibility now is to ensure that this truth remains strong decades from now," Elkayam-Levy said. "The archive we established will carry this truth forward for generations. The report and evidence are already being used in legal proceedings and will continue to serve the pursuit of justice."
She added that establishing the facts was only the beginning of a broader process of accountability. "The question is what we do once we know," she said. "How do we translate that knowledge into justice and reparations for survivors and families, and how do we turn remembrance into a responsibility to change reality?"
Rabbi Yehuda Sarna, NYU's university chaplain and former chief rabbi of the Jewish community in the United Arab Emirates, also addressed the gathering, emphasizing the responsibility of academic institutions to engage seriously with difficult testimony.
"Universities are places where young people learn not only what to think, but how to hold difficult truths with seriousness, humility and care," Sarna said.
He described the commission's work as an essential resource for students and the wider university community, praising its careful and humane documentation of the October 7 atrocities. "At NYU, where people from many different backgrounds come together, this conversation challenges us to ask: How do we listen when testimony is painful? How do we resist denial? And how do we allow truth to shape our responsibilities?" he said.
The event was attended by NYU faculty members and students, as well as researchers, public figures and other guests.
Three years after the massacre, the Civil Commission continues its efforts to preserve testimony, safeguard evidence and support legal accountability for the crimes committed on October 7 and during captivity.
For Elkayam-Levy, the challenge now is to ensure that the documentation becomes more than a record of the past, serving instead as a foundation for justice, prevention and remembrance. "The archive we established will carry this truth forward for generations," she said.

Women in this Sardinian village live exceptionally long. Researchers are asking why
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:46:35 UTC
18:46:35 KST

Researchers say Bolotana, a town of just a bit more than 2,000 inhabitants in Sardinia, may join Japan’s Okinawa and Greece’s Ikaria among the world's longevity hotspots.
Women in Bolotana, a small town on the Italian island of Sardinia, can expect to live to 91 years — more than two years longer than the Italian national average, according to a new study.
Women in this village are also three times more likely to reach 100 years old than women living elsewhere in Italy.
Researchers estimated that 13.8% of women in Bolotana who reach age 70 will live to 100, compared with approximately 3.5% of women in Italy and 3.6% of women in the United States.
“We think this is the longest-lived female population in the world, or close to it,” said S. Jay Olshansky, from the University of Illinois Chicago School of Public Health. Among international benchmarks, Bolotana women ranked second only to Hong Kong for both remaining life expectancy at age 70 and survival to age 100.
Bolotana first attracted attention because of its unusual concentration of centenarians. In 2024, six people aged 100 or older were living in the village, a prevalence roughly 11 times higher than that of the United States, according to the researchers’ estimates.
The study, published in the journal Frontiers in Aging, analysed demographic records from the village, which has about 2,300 residents and found a favourable pattern of survival among older adults between 2021 and 2025, particularly women.
The study documented 38 centenarians among 3,060 people born in Bolotana between 1900 and 1925.
The findings suggest the community could represent a new “blue zone” — regions where people have unusually long lives, and where there is a disproportionately high concentration of nonagenarians and centenarians.
While the study confirms that something unusual is happening in Bolotana, it doesn’t determine the exact causes behind this phenomenon.
However, the authors highlight several factors that may play a role, including dietary patterns, genetics, physical activity, family support and social cohesion.
Most food is grown locally, including olive oil rich in healthy fats. Families often live close together, and social isolation is rare.
“You’ve got this close-knit community where people take care of each other,” Olshansky added. “Movement is largely done by walking, not by driving.”
Other blue zones
Establishing blue zones has been contentious and challenging, as it requires extensive record-keeping.
“What makes Bolotana extraordinary is that it has an incredible historical record that allows us to definitively evaluate ages at birth and death,” Olshansky said. “The municipal and baptismal records date back centuries and allowed us to independently verify ages.”
Other blue zones that have been singled out and confirmed by researchers include Okinawa, Japan, the Nicoya Peninsula in Costa Rica and Ikaria in Greece.
A fourth blue zone has also been identified in Sardinia, located across six villages in the east-central part of the island, in a region called Ogliastra.

EU Lifts Belarus-Related Sanctions on Russian Billionaire Gutseriev – RFE/RL

The European Union has removed Russian billionaire Mikhail Gutseriev and Belarusian businessman Viktor Shevtsov from its Belarus sanctions list following successful court challenges, Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty’s Belarusian service reported Wednesday.
Both men had been sanctioned over alleged support for President Alexander Lukashenko’s government. Their removal follows rulings that the EU Council had failed to provide sufficient evidence to justify keeping the restrictions in place.
Gutseriev remains subject to separate EU sanctions linked to Russia’s war in Ukraine. He was added to that list on July 23, with the EU Council citing his involvement in industries that generate substantial revenue for the Russian government and investment projects that support it.
Shevtsov is not subject to any other EU sanctions, RFE/RL reported.
Gutseriev initially failed to overturn the Belarus sanctions. The EU’s General Court rejected his challenge in September 2023, and the Court of Justice dismissed his appeal in May 2025.
But the General Court annulled his 2024 sanctions renewals in October 2025, followed by the February 2025 renewal on May 13 this year.
The court found that the EU Council had not provided sufficient evidence that Gutseriev continued to support Lukashenko’s government or benefit from his ties to it.
The EU first sanctioned Gutseriev on June 21, 2021, describing him as a longtime friend of Lukashenko. It cited his investments in Belarus, including the Nezhinsky mining and processing complex, and his attendance at Lukashenko’s September 2020 inauguration.
Gutseriev founded the Safmar group, whose interests span oil production, coal, real estate, retail and media. Forbes estimates his net worth at $7.7 billion.
The decision follows the EU’s removal of Russian billionaires Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from its sanctions list in September after pressure from France and Luxembourg.
Bloomberg reported that Luxembourg pushed for Fridman’s removal after he filed a $16 billion arbitration claim over frozen assets. France sought to lift sanctions on Usmanov as part of negotiations with Azerbaijan to secure the release of French nationals held there.

Ukraine built ballistic missile in just over two years
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:45:54 BST
18:45:54 KST

A Ukrainian manufacturer took a ballistic missile from nothing to its first combat launch in a little over two years, which its chief executive said is the fastest development of such a weapon on record, the Apex Europe conference in London heard on Wednesday.
Iryna Terekh of Fire Point was asked from the floor how a company that did not exist before 2023 had managed it, and she began with what she had measured it against.
She said: “It is the fastest ever track record for developing a ballistic missile. I made my analysis. The average timeline for such a development is 15 years, the maximum was 30 years, and the minimum before that was seven years.”
“The first flight that we conducted was the last day of February, and three days ago it was the first combat flight. In between there were almost 20 different launches where we tested different things,” she said, adding that the whole programme had taken a little more than two years.
She was candid that the weapon is nowhere near finished, and set out her own measure for when it will be. “I have the rule that the first 100 launches of whatever you are launching, you can still be considered as polishing the product, establishing it to a more mature zone,” she said, describing Ukrainian manufacturing as living permanently at technology readiness level seven because insisting on level nine would cost too much money and too much time.
The method she credited is a document the company wrote at the outset and persuaded the government to sign. “We made a critical decision at the very beginning. We made a book. This book is called the Album of Acceptable Deviations, and we wrote it to present it to our military acceptance unit, who does the quality assurance before it is transported to the unit,” she said.
Inside it, everything that affects the quality of flight goes in one half and everything that does not goes in the other. The acceptance authority signed it, and quality assurance inspections are now carried out against it, which allows the company to use cheap parts wherever the engineering case for an expensive one is absent.
Not everybody who saw the result approved of how it had been built. “Once I saw some critics on the internet, oh my God, you’re using off-the-shelf solutions to fix some of the parts of your missile, your missile should be embarrassed to fly with this detail,” she said. “But this is exactly what cost-effective innovation is. If you are looking for a fancy, high-tech, ideal solution, it will be extremely expensive. You have to be able to be embarrassed as an engineer, but be proud as a Ukrainian providing a good product for a fair price.”
Her description of how the missile was built owes nothing to conventional aerospace practice. “We did it as it’s called in Ukraine from shit and sticks from the beginning, made it fly first and then polished,” she said.
A change in Ukrainian law is what made a company like hers possible in the first place. A bill signed in 2023 set out how new defence products, initially drones, are certified, tested, accepted into the army and procured, with the process published openly. “They took the industry from the shadows and made this a very clear, visible opportunity for any startup that want to try themselves,” she said, and the result is that a drone or a missile can now be certified within about six weeks without dropping safety requirements.
The effect on who builds weapons in Ukraine has been considerable, and she put it in a single sentence. “My generation, for example, who used to build startups, are now building arsenals,” she said.

We now know when El Niño is expected to peak

18:45:34 KST

in brief
- The UN warns El Niño will intensify before peaking in December.
- Record ocean heat threatens to trigger severe global weather disruptions.
El Niño will intensify even more before peaking in December, the United Nations said Thursday, warning it could be among the strongest witnessed since at least 1950.
The naturally occurring weather phenomenon is set to bring higher temperatures to much of the planet, the UN's weather and climate agency said, with its impact compounding the effects of man-made climate change.
"El Niño will continue to intensify ahead of its forecast peak in December," the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) said in its monthly Global Seasonal Climate Update.
"It is likely to bring above-average temperatures to much of the globe and shift rainfall patterns, increasing the risk of drought and floods in different regions."
El Niño warms surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, bringing worldwide changes in winds, pressure and rainfall patterns.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
It typically takes place every two to seven years and lasts around nine to 12 months.
Conditions oscillate between El Niño and its opposite La Niña, with neutral conditions in between.
El Niño 'strengthening rapidly'
"Sea-surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific are forecast to increase to record levels during October-November-December 2026, reflecting the strengthening of the El Niño event which will drive weather patterns and impact economies, ecosystems and communities across the globe," the WMO said.
The forecast is based on consensus across 13 leading national and international meteorological centres.
"El Niño is firmly established and strengthening rapidly," said WMO chief Celeste Saulo.
"WMO forecasts indicate a near-100 percent likelihood that it will persist through February 2027, potentially being one of the strongest since at least 1950."
Saulo explained that El Niño does not add new heat to the planet, but releases heat being stored in the ocean.
"The ocean it's drawing from is the warmest we've ever measured it. There is simply more heat available to release," she said.
Sea temperatures record
The index which measures sea surface temperature anomalies across the central-eastern equatorial Pacific — the region at the heart of El Niño — increased from 1.6C above normal in June to 2.5C above normal in August.
For October-November-December, the anomaly is forecast to reach approximately 3.7C above normal.
This would be the highest since observations began, eclipsing the previous record of 2.6C set in 2015-2016.
The last El Niño contributed to making 2023 the second-hottest year on record and 2024 the all-time high at around 1.55C above the 1850-1900 pre-industrial average.
While El Niño usually peaks between November and February, the resulting spike in temperatures typically comes later.
This El Niño is already hitting some regions hard, including in Central America, where animals and crops are dying from drought.

Eritrean troops have crossed the Ethiopian border and advanced deeper into the Tigray region, where fighting is ongoing between government forces and rebel groups.
The British broadcaster BBC reported this on October 7, citing local residents.
According to eyewitnesses, Eritrean troops were moving from the border town of Zalambessa through Adigrat toward Edaga Hamus, located between Adigrat and Tigray’s administrative capital, Mekelle.
One resident of Adigrat said he saw a convoy of approximately 40 trucks carrying soldiers traveling south. Another eyewitness reported seeing 20–30 large trucks with Eritrean license plates heading toward Edaga Hamus.
According to other accounts, the convoys also included vehicles equipped with heavy weapons, including anti-aircraft guns. Some Eritrean troops were traveling on foot. One BBC source estimated that the convoy seen by his relatives consisted of around 60 trucks.
Local residents also report the deployment of Eritrean units in mountainous areas near Edaga Hamus. According to them, drone strikes targeting military positions have taken place near the town.
Meanwhile, the BBC emphasizes that it has been unable to independently verify reports of Eritrean troop movements. Journalists were also unable to verify the authenticity of videos of military convoys circulating on social media.
A new phase of fighting in Tigray began on September 23 following several months of growing tensions between Ethiopia’s federal government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF).
On October 4, government forces and allied formations regained control of Mekelle after TPLF units withdrew. The rebels said they were temporarily relocating their regional administration.
The day before, on October 1, Eritrea severed diplomatic relations with Ethiopia following the closure of the Ethiopian embassy in Asmara and the expulsion of Eritrean diplomats. Addis Ababa accuses its neighbor of supporting the rebels, although Eritrean authorities have previously denied the allegations.
Ethiopian government representative Abraham Belay accused Eritrea of directly participating in the fighting in an interview with Fana Television. According to him, the Eritrean army suffered casualties and captured personnel, and Ethiopia is preparing a response to its intervention.
From 2020 to 2022, Eritrea, by contrast, fought alongside the Ethiopian federal government against the Tigray People’s Liberation Front. The two-year conflict claimed hundreds of thousands of lives and ended with the signing of the Pretoria Peace Agreement in November 2022.
Since then, relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea have deteriorated sharply. One of the main reasons has been the Ethiopian leadership’s demand for access to the Red Sea, particularly through Eritrea’s Port of Assab. Eritrea views such statements as a threat to its sovereignty.
Militarnyi previously reported that on September 21, seven Ethiopian armed groups announced the formation of a unified alliance against the government of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed. The alliance includes the Tigray People’s Liberation Front, the Oromo Liberation Army, and the Fano militia operating in the Amhara region. The alliance said its goal was to overthrow the current government and establish a transitional administration.
Militarnyi also reported that in August 2026, Tigray People’s Liberation Front rebels used NWF10 FPV drones, manufactured by the Turkish company North Weapon, against the Ethiopian army.

Strait of Hormuz crisis fuels Cairo's plastic recycling business
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on:
In the heart of the Egyptian capital Cairo, within the labyrinthine streets of the Manshiyet Nasser district, nearly 120,000 residents process a third of the megacity's waste every day. Long marginalised, these informal recycling specialists are now undergoing a dramatic transformation due to geopolitical tensions in the Strait of Hormuz, through which polyethylene from the Gulf usually passes.
Faced with a shortage of imported raw materials and a doubling in the price of new plastic, Egyptian factories are now increasingly turning to the backstreets of this Coptic neighbourhood, whose residents sort through and recycle up to 8,000 tonnes of rubbish every day. Up to 90 percent of the plastic waste that arrives in Manshiyet Nasser is given a new lease of life.
FRANCE 24's Mathilde Delvigne and Grégory Holyoke report.

The State Attorney’s Office filed an indictment on Thursday against a 22-year-old pharmacy student from east Jerusalem for allegedly planning a series of terrorist attacks using poisons and explosives against Jewish civilians and security forces.
The plans, according to prosecutors, were intended to cause mass casualties and followed a process of ideological radicalization that was fueled in part by the October 7 massacre and the ensuing Israel-Hamas War.
The indictment, filed with the Jerusalem District Court against Mohammed Shalbi, charges him with preparation for an act of terrorism constituting murder and receiving training for terrorist purposes.
Prosecutors allege that Shalbi regularly consumed material associated with Hamas and ISIS, and decided to use his knowledge and access to chemicals to carry out terrorist attacks.
Shalbi was a third-year pharmacy student at Al-Quds University in Abu Dis, and also worked as a pharmacy assistant.
Suspect began formulating plan to plant explosive device near where enforcement personnel frequently stood
He is from the east Jerusalem neighborhood of Beit Hanina. According to the indictment, at the start of 2025, he began formulating a plan to plant an explosive device where enforcement personnel regularly stood, angered by parking tickets issued to worshipers who parked near a mosque in the neighborhood. The plan was never carried out because the enforcement personnel stopped coming to the area.
Later, prosecutors allege, he began planning what they described as a large-scale attack in which he wanted to kill “a lot of Jews.”
Shalbi joined Telegram groups associated with terrorist organizations, including a group affiliated with ISIS, and downloaded dozens of files. Some contained instructions for making explosive devices, explosives, and lethal poisons. The indictment also alleges that he copied into a notebook two formulas for poisons capable of causing death through contact, inhalation, or ingestion.
Soon afterward, according to the indictment, he erased the downloaded files and his search history from his phone in an effort to conceal his actions.
On two occasions, he traveled to Ramallah and bought chemicals and equipment, splitting the purchases to avoid suspicion, and stored them in his bedroom. Later, he conducted a chemical experiment in the bathtub of his home, igniting a mixture he had prepared to test the materials.
The indictment alleges that, through these actions, Shalbi trained and instructed himself for the purpose of advancing a terrorist offense. The prosecution asked the court to order that he remain in custody until the end of the proceedings against him.

Implementation of the agreement has since stalled amid disagreements, including on security and navigation in the Strait of Hormuz.
U.S. President Donald Trump said last month in an address to the U.N. General Assembly in New York that he expects to reach a deal with Iran after the U.S. midterm elections, warning he faces a "big decision" on whether to pursue an agreement or "annihilate" the country.

U.S. Army fields new cranes for Typhon, Dark Eagle units
Unknown

2026-10-08
09:38:00 UTC
18:38:00 KST

- The U.S. Army delivered two 40-ton all-terrain cranes to long-range fires units at Joint Base Lewis-McChord, with six more due by the end of October.
- The cranes let units operating MLRS-family launchers and the Long-Range Hypersonic Weapon reload missile canisters and do maintenance without outside equipment.
The U.S. Army has started giving its long-range missile battalions their own heavy cranes, delivering two 40-ton all-terrain cranes to Joint Base Lewis-McChord, Washington, in late August so the units can reload missile canisters and maintain launchers in the field without hiring outside equipment.
The Army’s Product Manager Engineer, Maintenance, Support Equipment said on Oct. 7 that six more cranes are due shortly. Once all eight arrive, 1st Battalion, 17th Field Artillery Regiment, and 5th Battalion, 3rd Field Artillery Regiment, will have their full authorized number of cranes by the end of October 2026. Both are long-range fires battalions within the U.S. Army’s Multi-Domain Task Forces, which are built around long-range missiles and are focused largely on the Pacific.
The cranes are the Type 1 model of the Family of All Terrain Cranes, which soldiers also call the All-Terrain Engineer Crane. According to the Army, they give units operating the Multiple Launch Rocket System family and the Long-Range Hypersonic Weapon, known as Dark Eagle, the ability to lift and swap heavy missile canisters, carry out field maintenance and support operations away from fixed bases or commercial lifting gear.
The commander of the battalion’s forward support company said the cranes have also been used to train for reloading the Army’s Mid-Range Capability, the Typhon launcher that fires Tomahawk and SM-6 missiles, and that they save the unit money.
“Operating forward in Japan, the ATEC (All-Terrain Engineer Crane) leverages the multi-role utility of the ATEC crane to streamline organic maintenance and logistical operations,” said Capt. Jacob A. Milton, commander of the 509th Forward Support Company, 1st Battalion, 17th Field Artillery (Long-Range Precision Fires), 3rd Multi-Domain Task Force.
“Beyond its primary role in mid-range capability reload training, the crane’s capability to internally move heavy tactical containers and equipment eliminates the operational requirement to contract external Material Handling Equipment. This self-reliance accelerates forward repair timelines, enhances battery agility, and secures substantial cost savings for the battalion,” Milton said.
The 3rd Multi-Domain Task Force, based in Hawaii, has repeatedly brought its Typhon battery to Japan for exercises, first to Marine Corps Air Station Iwakuni for Resolute Dragon in September 2025 and this year to Kanoya Air Base on Kyushu for Valiant Shield 2026. A Typhon launcher carries its missiles in large canisters, and without a crane of its own a battery has to rely on base facilities or contracted lifting equipment to reload them.
The deliveries fall under a U.S. Army headquarters execution order, EXORD 245-26, intended to close support-equipment gaps in priority strategic fires units. The Army said finishing the eight-crane delivery at Joint Base Lewis-McChord will give its long-range fires units in the Pacific a heavy-lift capability of their own in support of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command.
Program Manager Force Projection is preparing to field cranes to the Army’s other Multi-Domain Task Forces and plans to deliver an average of four units a month, along with operator training.

Wrexham and Rochdale train services rejected over west coast line pressure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:38:00 UTC
18:38:00 KST

Plans to run direct train services to Wrexham and Rochdale from London have been rejected by the rail regulator because of “significant pressure” on the line.
The Office of Rail and Road said that there was insufficient space on the crowded west coast mainline to introduce the two new separate train services.
It also vetoed plans for additional London-Blackpool train services wanted by Avanti.
The ORR had last year knocked back plans for a new independent open access service linking Wrexham and the capital put forward by the Wrexham, Shropshire & Midlands Railway Company (WSMR). WSMR had submitted plans for a slightly less frequent service but the ORR said the new routes would still put the reliability of the wider railway at risk.
The new service could have allowed Wrexham to capitalise further on the town’s Hollywood-meets-football mini-boom, fuelled by the Wrexham AFC co-owners Ryan Reynolds and Rob McElhenney.
Proposals for a new Lumo service between London and Rochdale, again slimmed down after being rejected in 2025, were once more rebuffed.
The ORR also said Avanti could not add more Blackpool services from London. However, it did approve one extra London-Chester evening service from Avanti, which would otherwise have run as a “ghost train”, with crew and the rolling stock returning north to the depot overnight. The decision follows the outcry over the ORR’s initial ruling on a Manchester-London service which was barred from taking passengers last year.
The regulator said its assessment, backed by external reviews, was that the “capacity and performance of the southern section of the west coast mainline has not materially changed since similar applications were rejected in 2025”.
It said gaps in the current timetable were needed to provide important space for trains to recover when things went wrong, rather than escalating chaos.
Stephanie Tobyn, ORR’s director of strategy, policy and reform, said: “New services, destinations and greater choice can bring real benefits for passengers and communities. But the west coast mainline is already under significant pressure, with performance reflecting limited resilience on a heavily used part of the rail network.
“Our detailed analysis has shown that adding more trains to the current timetable would reduce the ability to recover when disruption occurs, increasing the risk of delays spreading and making reliability of the network worse for all passengers.”
Private operators such as First Group, owners of Lumo, have been looking to increase open-access routes as Labour has renationalised major rail contracts in the transition to Great British Railways.
London-Wrexham direct trains briefly ran from London Marylebone from 2008 to 2011 as an open-access service but stopped owing to financial losses.

Estonia wants drone elective added to all high schools' programs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:38:00 UTC
18:38:00 KST

Estonia wants drone elective added to all high schools' programs
Drone technology has been introduced as an elective course in many upper secondary schools this year. The broader goal is to make drone education available in all high schools in the coming years.
This academic year, 53 upper secondary schools are offering an elective course on unmanned aircraft. One of them is Tallinn's Arte High School, which has nearly 1,100 students and also participated in last year's pilot program. Around 50 students completed the course at Arte in its first year. This year, the elective will begin in the second semester, but around 100 students have already expressed interest, said Karl Läll, the school's drone technology teacher.
"Interest in taking part has grown exponentially, making it difficult to keep up with demand, but that's a good problem to have. Drones have a wide range of applications, from filming wedding videos to the Environmental Board using them to map forests and illegal buildings. They're not just the domain of little green men," Läll said.
The course, developed in cooperation with the Ministry of Education and Research, the Estonian Aviation Academy and the Estonian Defense League (Kaitseliit), provides students with both theoretical and practical knowledge of unmanned aircraft over 35 academic hours, said Aare Jamnes, head of the national defense education bureau at the Defense Resources Agency.
"First comes the theory, followed by an exam administered by the Transport Administration and then a training day where students get hands-on experience," Jamnes added.
An online course has been developed for the theoretical component, which students complete at school, for example, under the guidance of a drone technology teacher. The practical training day, which includes flying in a simulator, operating a drone and conducting a reconnaissance flight, is led by Defense League instructors. Although more instructors are being trained, there are still not enough to offer drone education at every upper secondary school, Jamnes said.
"With 53 schools and one training day per school, that means 53 training days over two and a half months. Depending on the spring weather, that's two or three training days a week and you need about 10 instructors for every 20 students. That's quite a large number. Since school days are also workdays, getting instructors time off from their regular jobs is another challenge," Jamnes said.
However, some schools, such as Arte High School, have also purchased their own drones, allowing students to practice flying them while still studying the theoretical material.
"Schools can offer the elective course without having any drones of their own. We want to give our students a little more than the required minimum. This year, we also plan to introduce drone simulators so that, in addition to physically operating drones, students can gain some initial experience using simulators," Läll said.
Jamnes also emphasized that schools do not need to purchase drones to offer the course. The instructors bring all the necessary equipment with them for the practical training day.
"At the national level, we currently have enough drones to run the course. We've recommended that schools and local governments looking to invest in something should consider equipping computer labs with drone simulators. The more minutes or hours students can spend practicing on simulators, the more likely the actual drones are to remain intact when they take them outdoors," Jamnes said.

Bosnia’s political future looks increasingly like its past
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:37:07 UTC
18:37:07 KST

Bosnia’s political future looks increasingly like its past
Three nationalist parties are poised to dominate again, deepening fears of division and paralysis.
The latest general elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina, held on October 4, repeated a pattern familiar from most electoral contests over the past three decades. The decisive victory of parties organised largely along ethnic lines – which many would rightly describe as nationalist – came as no surprise. It is therefore difficult to disagree with analysts and experts who say the country has been set back 30 years and faces an even grimmer future.
The last two years have seen arguably the greatest crisis of the post-war period, and the results of Sunday’s elections offer little hope for improvement in the coming years. The spectre of nationalism, division and overt assaults on the country’s sovereignty and territorial integrity reinforces the increasingly common notion that a “continuation of the war by peaceful means” is under way – meaning that while armed conflict ceased three decades ago, hostilities, objectives and the struggle for power persist through political, economic, diplomatic and information channels.
House of Peoples still in the hands of anti-Bosnian forces
The extremely complicated Bosnian electoral system – one state, two entities, Brcko District, three constituent peoples, 10 cantons and 144 cities and municipalities – should perhaps be studied in law schools as an excellent example of how to create a dysfunctional state. The only thing more difficult – pessimists would say impossible – is explaining to future lawyers, sociologists and political scientists how governments are formed after an election – from cantonal assemblies, through entity institutions to state institutions, including the omnipotent House of Peoples of the Parliamentary Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina – itself almost impossible to explain.
This House of Peoples has been the main tool for blocking the country’s path towards the European Union and NATO over the past two years. Delegates from the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina (HDZ BiH) and the Alliance of Independent Social Democrats (SNSD) – the dominant party in Republika Srpska for the past two decades – have repeatedly worked in tandem to block the work of the chamber, leaving sessions and breaking quorum when the agenda did not suit them – often when some of the most important issues were being decided.
In Sunday’s elections, these two parties once again secured a significant share of the Croat and Serb vote at both the entity and state levels; they will once again be the ones whose input is sought when the new government is formed, and they will again hold at least three delegates each in the state-level House of Peoples. And – logically and predictably – they will dictate the options, rules and laws that suit their own interests. This can readily be interpreted as a “continuation of war by peaceful means”, or, more simply put: the EU will have a long wait before the small, impoverished, increasingly depopulated and beleaguered state known as Bosnia and Herzegovina knocks on its “open door” – an offer and promise made more in words than in deeds for the past 20 years – and steps inside.
Pro-Bosnian parties – at odds and self-absorbed
And what is the third constituent segment – pro-Bosnian or Bosniak, depending on one’s interpretation – to do in such circumstances? How can its parties translate what is largely verbal patriotism and concern for the people and the state into actual practice? The answer could well be quite simple from the outset: they cannot, much as has been the case for the past 20 years or so. Yet this country has endured far worse situations in the not-too-distant past – aggression, ethnic cleansing, war crimes, genocide, and the indifference and lack of empathy of a significant part of the so-called international community – and Bosnians and Herzegovinians are not about to simply give up and renounce their 1,000-year-old homeland.
The pro-Bosnian/Bosniak parties – and there are dozens of them – are deeply divided, at odds with one another and power-hungry; many have – to put it mildly – questionable leadership and are associated with dishonourable deeds and ideas. They now stand at a critical juncture. If they persist with a policy of “as long as we are doing well”, then neither internal nor external enemies – and such enemies do exist; they have neither been defeated nor diminished in number compared with the bloody 1990s – will be needed to bring about our ruin. The “state-building” Party of Democratic Action appears set to return to power once again – owing more to the incompetence of three parties from across the ideological spectrum, which appear set to head back into opposition, than to its own expertise, wisdom or quality – and it has the opportunity, if nothing else, to at least try to fix the very mess it is primarily responsible for creating. For those who know the party and have lived through (or rather, survived) what it has delivered so far – promising much but delivering little – there is little room for optimism; yet, it won the largest share of the vote in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina (FBiH), and that electoral will must be respected.
US pragmatism and European confusion
In the shadow of the traditional dirty pre-election campaign, polling stations equipped for the first time with modern technologies (for us, electronic ballot scanning and election results announced just hours after the polls close represent the height of progress), and the months of negotiations, coalition-building and intraparty agreements – read: trading – that now lie ahead, there remain the poor, the sick and the hopeless, a ruined society and a devastated economy.
While neighbours Serbia and Croatia are rapidly arming themselves, spending billions of dollars on fighter jets, drones, missiles and other weapons systems, Bosnia has a small army of about 10,000 professional personnel, nominally unified but divided in practice. The police, especially at the state level, are hardly more unified or cohesive. On the contrary, the border police and the prosecutor’s office remain politically captured by forces whose loyalties appear to lie more with neighbouring Serbia and Croatia than with Bosnia itself.
Meanwhile, the United States is gradually stepping back from its unwritten role as Bosnia’s protector – although it still stands by the Dayton Peace Agreement and emphasises the country’s sovereignty and territorial integrity – and increasingly favours pragmatic, particularly financial, interests. The EU, meanwhile, does not seem to know what to do with itself, let alone with little Bosnia. It expects reforms and European laws from the domestic authorities, both old and new, while knowing they are unlikely to arrive any time soon. Yet there is a recipe for that too: to begin with, the EU could ask member state Croatia to tell its sister party, HDZ BiH, to stop supporting those seeking to dismantle the very state whose citizenship and passports they hold.
The poorest and leading in organised crime and corruption
Bosnia is one of the poorest European countries and among those worst affected by organised crime and corruption. No one knows how many people live there, because the last census, carried out in 2013, remains disputed. Official turnout in Sunday’s elections was just more than 40 percent, calculated against an electoral roll of 3.4 million voters, even though estimates suggest fewer than 2.5 million people actually live in the country, suggesting turnout among residents was considerably higher.
Hundreds of thousands of people, many of them young and educated, have left for prosperous countries around the world in recent years. They just want a normal life and no longer bother with the painful question that has preoccupied the country for decades: Can Bosnia “survive” the return to power of three nationalist parties at a time when they have fewer and fewer friends in a fundamentally changing world?
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Gaza still has no hospital operating at full capacity: Israeli rights group
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:35:39 UTC
18:35:39 KST

Abderaouf Arnaout and Ikram Kouachi
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
Gaza still has no hospital operating at full capacity a year after a ceasefire took effect, Physicians for Human Rights-Israel said on Thursday.
The Israeli rights organization released a report assessing the state of Gaza’s health system nearly a year after the ceasefire began in October 2025.
It said the period has not brought about a genuine recovery of the health system despite a limited increase in the number of hospitals that have partially resumed operations.
“The number of intensive care beds has practically not changed, the shortage of medicines and essential medical supplies has worsened, while thousands of patients remain deprived of life-saving treatments that are unavailable in the Strip,” the organization said.
“In October 2025, 14 of the 36 hospitals were operating partially. Nearly a year later, the number has risen to 20, but none is still capable of operating fully,” it said.
The report added that Gaza had 103 intensive care beds in October 2025, compared with only 104 in July 2026, noting that kidney dialysis services had failed to recover.
“Dialysis services were available at 17% of health facilities in October 2025, falling to 12% in July 2026, while MRI services remain unavailable in the Strip,” it said.
The World Health Organization documented at least 143 additional attacks on health care during the first seven months of the ceasefire, it said.
The shortage of medicines and medical supplies also persisted. According to data from Israel’s Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories (COGAT), 69% of medical supplies approved for entry into Gaza between January and May 2026 did not actually enter the enclave, the organization said.
The report also highlighted the consequences of the closure of crossings and restrictions preventing Palestinians from leaving Gaza for medical treatment, saying “patients are dying while waiting for evacuation.”
“While the need for treatment is increasing, the number of people leaving for medical care is far below pre-war levels,” the report said.
Before October 2023, between 50 and 100 patients left Gaza each day to receive medical treatment, it said.
Between Oct. 10, 2025 and mid-September 2026, about 3,423 patients were evacuated abroad, a rate three to six times lower than pre-war levels despite the sharp increase in demand for treatment outside the Strip, according to the report.
The Israeli organization said that “killings, injuries and acts of genocide continue in Gaza even under the ceasefire.”
According to figures from the WHO’s Health Cluster, Israeli forces killed at least 1,422 Palestinians and injured 5,150 others between the announcement of the ceasefire and the end of September 2026, the non-profit said.
The figures, the organization said, “do not merely reflect a slow recovery of a destroyed health system.”
Milena Ansari, director of the Occupied Territories Department at Physicians for Human Rights-Israel and author of the report, said a year of ceasefire was supposed to provide Palestinians with genuine relief and recovery. “But the system remains devastated, essential medicines and supplies are not reaching Gaza in the quantities needed, and patients continue to die while being denied treatment available just a few kilometers away in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem.”
“The data show that the ceasefire has not stopped the genocide, but has only changed the way it is carried out,” Ansari added.

Left Alliance to participate in Estonia's 2027 general elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:35:00 UTC
18:35:00 KST

Left Alliance to participate in Estonia's 2027 general elections
The Estonian Left Alliance, which emerged from the Estonian United Left Party, plans to run in next spring's Riigikogu elections. According to the party, it is essentially a new political force whose main goal is to fight for workers' rights.
The Estonian United Left Party, the successor to the Communist Party of Estonia, received enough votes in the 2023 Riigikogu elections, largely thanks to Aivo Peterson who was convicted of treason, to secure €30,000 in annual state funding.
Following the last Riigikogu elections, politically active young people with left-wing views joined the party and began working to change its policies and historical image.
Last year, the party elected a new board and changed its name to the Estonian Left Alliance.
Nikita Leo, 27, who plans to run for the party's board in late October and also stand in the Riigikogu elections, told ERR that it is essentially a new party.
"We are only just getting started, so there is still a lot of work ahead. I definitely want to emphasize that although the legal entity is formally the same as before, in practice this is an entirely new party because all the people and ideas are new," Leo said.
According to Leo, members would have preferred to establish a new party and start with a clean slate. However, because establishing a new political party in Estonia is difficult, they decided it made more sense to build on an existing structure.
The party has just over 500 members, of whom around 60 to 70 are active.
"All the active members are people who joined the party after the rebranding a few years ago. Most of the overall membership consists of longstanding members who are not currently actively involved in the party's activities," Leo added.
"At the moment, we are primarily a party of young people," Leo said. "The age profile of our active members is more like that of a political party's youth wing than a party itself. There are a lot of young people, but of course there are some slightly older people as well. I would say the average age is somewhere in the 20s."
The party plans to run in next spring's Riigikogu elections.
"I can't give an exact number right now, but we probably won't have very many candidates," Leo acknowledged. "We are still trying to find candidates and would also like to involve people from outside the party. We are actively looking for people who are not party members but would be interested in running on our list. We also don't have enough money to field a full slate of candidates."
The electoral deposit for a full slate of candidates is €118,250, while the deposit for an individual candidate is less than €1,000. However, because the party does not have many candidates, it will be able to cover the deposits.
Nevertheless, the party believes the system needs to change.
"Running in elections is effectively behind a paywall, so to speak, and fielding a full slate of candidates is very expensive. This is problematic and people's opportunities to run in elections should not be restricted in this way," Leo said.
The party's election platform is being drafted and is nearly complete.
"I have been involved in putting it together myself and I think it will be quite strong. It includes proposals that no other party dares to make," Leo said.
The party's main focus is protecting workers' interests.
"In politics, you can't always promise everything to everyone and that's not what we're trying to do. Society consists of different groups whose interests may conflict, creating tensions. One of the main conflicts is between workers and owners. We are on the side of workers in this struggle and defend their interests. In fact, this means defending the interests of the majority because most of us are employees who would benefit from having more rights," Leo said.
He noted that the party's election platform may contain many proposals that other parties also promise to some extent. What sets the Left Alliance apart, however, is its ambition to secure worker representation on company boards.
"The current wording, although it may change, is that if a company has more than 50 employees, at least half of its board members must be employees of that same company," Leo said.
The Left Alliance's overarching goal is to ensure that democracy exists not only at the level of government but also in the workplace.
"This is very important because most of us are employees and spend most of our time at work," Leo said. "Unfortunately, we often have virtually no rights there: the owner is like a king and employees have very little say. We believe this needs to change. Just as the Constitution states that supreme power is vested in the people, the economy should operate on the principle that ultimate power within a company belongs to its employees."
The party is not yet certain what its voter base will look like.
"If you look at our new members, most of them are indeed very young, but our voter profile may turn out to be different. We would like to appeal to all age groups to some extent and we certainly don't want to remain exclusively a party for young people," Leo said.
The election platform also includes proposals aimed at pensioners.
"These are not merely promises to raise pensions, but substantive proposals," Leo emphasized. "For example, we want to establish a national program that would create hobby and interest groups specifically for older people. This would give them activities to participate in and opportunities to socialize, which is very important for many of them because they often feel lonely."
The party sees preserving the welfare state as a major domestic policy challenge.
"Free higher education, free healthcare and many other public services are under threat. A great many people would prefer to preserve these services and do not want to see cuts. So one of our goals is not only to maintain existing public services but also to expand them," Leo said.
In foreign policy, the party is particularly committed to standing up for Palestine.
"As you can see from our social media, we have repeatedly spoken out on this issue and participated in demonstrations. This is one particular issue we have been very actively involved in."
Leo emphasized that the party has zero tolerance for pro-Kremlin sentiment when it comes to relations with Russia.
"If you look at the party as a legal entity and what it may have been like historically, attitudes may have been somewhat different in the past. But as I said, all the active members are new. So in practice, this is an entirely new political force and we genuinely have zero tolerance for pro-Kremlin sentiment."
While the party received nearly 15,000 votes in the last Riigikogu elections with Aivo Peterson's support, it is not using that result to forecast its performance in the upcoming elections.
"The Riigikogu elections four years ago took place before the party's rebranding had begun. The rebranding started in late 2023 and all the new members have joined since then," Leo said.
"The party has changed so much in the meantime that it is now an entirely new political force and the people we appeal to have changed as well. I think there will be very little overlap with the people we appealed to in the previous elections. That is why it is so difficult to make any predictions at this point — essentially, these will be our first elections," he added.

German Bundeswehr: A new naval port in Emden
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:34:00 UTC
18:34:00 KST

German Bundeswehr: A new naval port to boost defense
October 8, 2026
After months of evaluating different locations, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius has announced that the Bundeswehr's new naval port will be built in Emden, on the North Sea coast of Lower Saxony.
"Emden offers ideal conditions, such as quick access to the Atlantic Ocean and the far north," Pistorius said. He added that a second port is needed to accommodate the growing German Navy: New ships and boats require berths, and additional service members need housing. Furthermore, he said, "this will enhance the deterrence capabilities of both Germany and NATO."
The commercial port of Emden is the economic heart of East Frisia. Not only does it dominate the cityscape, but it also provides thousands of jobs. Directly adjacent to the port is the large Volkswagen plant, from which cars are exported by ship to destinations around the world. The port also serves as a shipment hub for large components for wind farms in the North Sea. Now, a naval base with up to 2,000 military posts will be built by the early 2030s. Emden hosted a Bundeswehr base until 1997, but it was no longer needed after the end of the Cold War and was consequently decommissioned.
Emden's 'great advantage'
Coastal land is tough to come by in Germany, but that's not the case in Emden. The port city has "the great advantage of having a lot of available space where a new port can be developed," says Johannes Peters, an expert on maritime security at the Institute for Security Policy at the University of Kiel.
"Emden offers the opportunity to build a dedicated naval port that complies with the latest requirements, including those for security and port protection," Peters emphasizes in an interview with DW. Pistorius estimates that up to 450 hectares of land will be needed — equivalent to about 630 soccer fields.
The only naval port currently on the German North Sea coast is located in Wilhelmshaven. From a strategic perspective, it doesn't make sense to have just one port and nothing to fall back on, security expert Peters emphasized. "If some kind of scenario where conflict breaks out were to actually occur and this infrastructure were to fail, then you'd have a real problem. That's why they want to diversify their options here now."
Pistorius said there was a strategic advantage to a second naval port on the North Sea: "This makes us harder to predict in an emergency and expands our operational capabilities."
Relief for Wilhelmshaven
The planned port in Emden is intended to complement and provide relief for the Wilhelmshaven naval base. This is where Operational Flotilla 2 is stationed, a large formation consisting of frigates and supply ships. The Wilhelmshaven naval base is also being expanded as the fleet grows and personnel levels increase.
In reference to Wilhelmshaven, Pistorius said the "smallest navy in the history of the Bundeswehr" now had more responsibilities than ever before. "So the navy must grow, and it will," P{istorius said. "We have laid the groundwork for this in all areas."
Bremerhaven was also on the shortlist. Although it will not be getting a naval base, the German government is investing a great deal of money there as well. The port will be expanded into a logistical hub that could be used to deploy large troop contingents and heavy equipment from NATO allies in the event of an emergency.
That is the plan outlined in "Operation Plan Germany," Germany's defense plan in the event of a crisis or threat to alliance security. The federal government is allocating up to €1.35 billion ($1.51 billion) for the expansion.
Jobs for Emden?
Although Emden has been officially chosen as the site, so far this is only a memorandum of understanding between the Defense Ministry, the state of Lower Saxony and the city of Emden. Construction of the naval port is likely to take years. "There are still major hurdles to overcome," says Defense Minister Pistorius.
"You can't just walk into a home improvement store and buy a new naval base," Pistorius said. "Marine engineering, transportation links, the barracks — we need to get started on these right away."
The city, with its approximately 50,000 residents, is expected to benefit from the construction of the port, especially since the future of the local Volkswagen plant is uncertain because of ongoing economic trouble for the automaker.
Mayor Tim Kruithoff was all the more delighted. "This is a great day for Emden," he said. He called the planned naval base "an extraordinary opportunity" for jobs and for the economic development of the entire region.

German Bundeswehr: A new naval port in Emden aims to enhance Germany's defense capabilities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:34:00 UTC
18:34:00 KST

German Bundeswehr: A new naval port to boost defense
October 8, 2026
After months of evaluating different locations, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius has announced that the Bundeswehr's new naval port will be built in Emden, on the North Sea coast of Lower Saxony.
"Emden offers ideal conditions, such as quick access to the Atlantic Ocean and the far north," Pistorius said. He added that a second port is needed to accommodate the growing German Navy: New ships and boats require berths, and additional service members need housing. Furthermore, he said, "this will enhance the deterrence capabilities of both Germany and NATO."
The commercial port of Emden is the economic heart of East Frisia. Not only does it dominate the cityscape, but it also provides thousands of jobs. Directly adjacent to the port is the large Volkswagen plant, from which cars are exported by ship to destinations around the world. The port also serves as a shipment hub for large components for wind farms in the North Sea. Now, a naval base with up to 2,000 military posts will be built by the early 2030s. Emden hosted a Bundeswehr base until 1997, but it was no longer needed after the end of the Cold War and was consequently decommissioned.
Emden's 'great advantage'
Coastal land is tough to come by in Germany, but that's not the case in Emden. The port city has "the great advantage of having a lot of available space where a new port can be developed," says Johannes Peters, an expert on maritime security at the Institute for Security Policy at the University of Kiel.
"Emden offers the opportunity to build a dedicated naval port that complies with the latest requirements, including those for security and port protection," Peters emphasizes in an interview with DW. Pistorius estimates that up to 450 hectares of land will be needed — equivalent to about 630 soccer fields.
The only naval port currently on the German North Sea coast is located in Wilhelmshaven. From a strategic perspective, it doesn't make sense to have just one port and nothing to fall back on, security expert Peters emphasized. "If some kind of scenario where conflict breaks out were to actually occur and this infrastructure were to fail, then you'd have a real problem. That's why they want to diversify their options here now."
Pistorius said there was a strategic advantage to a second naval port on the North Sea: "This makes us harder to predict in an emergency and expands our operational capabilities."
Relief for Wilhelmshaven
The planned port in Emden is intended to complement and provide relief for the Wilhelmshaven naval base. This is where Operational Flotilla 2 is stationed, a large formation consisting of frigates and supply ships. The Wilhelmshaven naval base is also being expanded as the fleet grows and personnel levels increase.
In reference to Wilhelmshaven, Pistorius said the "smallest navy in the history of the Bundeswehr" now had more responsibilities than ever before. "So the navy must grow, and it will," P{istorius said. "We have laid the groundwork for this in all areas."
Bremerhaven was also on the shortlist. Although it will not be getting a naval base, the German government is investing a great deal of money there as well. The port will be expanded into a logistical hub that could be used to deploy large troop contingents and heavy equipment from NATO allies in the event of an emergency.
That is the plan outlined in "Operation Plan Germany," Germany's defense plan in the event of a crisis or threat to alliance security. The federal government is allocating up to €1.35 billion ($1.51 billion) for the expansion.
Jobs for Emden?
Although Emden has been officially chosen as the site, so far this is only a memorandum of understanding between the Defense Ministry, the state of Lower Saxony and the city of Emden. Construction of the naval port is likely to take years. "There are still major hurdles to overcome," says Defense Minister Pistorius.
"You can't just walk into a home improvement store and buy a new naval base," Pistorius said. "Marine engineering, transportation links, the barracks — we need to get started on these right away."
The city, with its approximately 50,000 residents, is expected to benefit from the construction of the port, especially since the future of the local Volkswagen plant is uncertain because of ongoing economic trouble for the automaker.
Mayor Tim Kruithoff was all the more delighted. "This is a great day for Emden," he said. He called the planned naval base "an extraordinary opportunity" for jobs and for the economic development of the entire region.

At least five arrested over Renoir museum theft
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:31:13 BST
18:31:13 KST

At least five arrested over Renoir museum theft
- Published
At least five people have been arrested in France in connection with the theft of two paintings by Pierre-Auguste Renoir last month, local media report.
The two suspected burglars are said to be among them.
Two of the masterpieces stolen from the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer, a suburb of Nice, have yet to be recovered. Two other works were abandoned by the thieves as they rushed to leave the museum.
The heist was the latest in a series of high-profile art thefts in Europe which thrust the security of galleries and museums into the spotlight.
The suspects cut through a fence to enter the museum's tree-lined grounds at dawn on 8 September, smashed a window to get inside, and used an electric saw to cut through the frame mountings.
The two missing paintings are the Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano (1910) and Jeune fille au puits (1886).
According to the Nice-Matin newspaper, which first broke the news of the arrests, the suspects could be part of an organised criminal gang. Some French news outlets, including Nice-Matin, say the number of those arrested is six.
Local prosecutors have declined to confirm the arrests when contacted by the BBC.
The Renoir Museum is home to 12 of the famous painter's artworks.
Opened in 1960, it was Renoir's last home before his death in 1919, and also features many things that once belonged to him, including his easel and wheelchair, as well as photographs and personal letters.
Several European museums and galleries have seen major thefts in recent months.
In August, paintings by Renoir, Paul Cézanne and Henri Matisse were stolen from a museum in Italy, in a heist that lasted just three minutes. They were later recovered.
One of the most high-profile such incidents was in October last year, when France's crown jewels were stolen in broad daylight from the Louvre in Paris.
The thieves, disguised as construction workers, broke into the Louvre's first-floor Apollo Gallery during the museum's opening hours. Using a angle-grinder to open display cases, they made off with €88m (£78m) of jewels that once belonged to 19th-Century queens and empresses.
The Louvre was subsequently criticised for under-investing in security.

Russia’s top tank maker takes on T-90 repairs as new builds strain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:30:55 UTC
18:30:55 KST

- Russia’s main tank maker Uralvagonzavod is taking on repairs of war-damaged T-90Ms, work analysts say once went to military repair plants.
- A train of heavily damaged T-90Ms was photographed heading to the plant, and analysts say such repairs may be counted as new production.
Uralvagonzavod, Russia’s main tank manufacturer and the only plant building new T-90M tanks, is now taking on major repairs of T-90Ms wrecked in Ukraine, work that analysts say was traditionally handled by military repair plants and now competes with the factory’s production of new tanks.
A train carrying heavily damaged T-90Ms was photographed on its way to the plant in Nizhny Tagil, according to analysts tracking Russian armor. The photos, which circulated on social media this week, show tanks with extensive damage loaded on rail cars.
Andrei Tarasenko, an armored vehicle analyst, said Uralvagonzavod has ended up doing the repairs because Russia’s network of military armored repair plants, known by the Russian abbreviation BTRZ, has broken down, and that rebuilding a tank at a production plant costs about as much as building a new one.
“Damaged T-90Ms on the way to UVZ. Having ruined the BTRZ system, the monopoly corporation is also engaged in capital repairs that are completely outside its core business, since under factory conditions (not at a BTRZ) a repair costs as much as a new tank,” Tarasenko wrote in Russian.
Jakub Janovsky, a lead analyst with the open-source project Oryx, which documents equipment losses in the war from photo and video evidence, said the repaired tanks could also blur the picture of how many new tanks Russia actually builds.
“On the other hand, some organizations might end up counting factory repairs (and/or any additional upgrades) of these tanks as ‘new production,’” Janovsky wrote on X.
Janovsky added that whether a damaged tank can be recovered at all depends heavily on where it is hit. Vehicles disabled in the contested gray zone between the two armies are usually destroyed before they can be dragged out, he said, while tanks damaged farther back can be recovered for repair with much less effort.
Analysts have tied the shift to the pressure on Russia’s tank industry from Western sanctions and labor shortages. Some T-90Ms leaving Uralvagonzavod have been found to use refurbished hulls from older T-90A tanks rather than newly built ones, and the company has openly promoted its repair work, saying in 2024 that it had restored a T-90M in four weeks after the tank was hit by 26 drones.
The plant still ships new and upgraded vehicles. Earlier this week, Uralvagonzavod said it had delivered another batch of T-90M and upgraded T-72B3M tanks with extra protection against drones, without saying how many. Some T-90Ms now carry the Arena-M active protection system, which Russian forces demonstrated shooting down attacking drones during the Tsentr-2026 exercise.

Tytan scales up low cost drone interceptor production
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:30:51 BST
18:30:51 KST

The Munich air defence company Tytan Technologies is building manufacturing capacity to turn out as many as three thousand low cost drone interceptors a month, a company representative told the Apex Europe conference in London on Wednesday.
Kerry Hoppe, who handles business development and government affairs at Tytan, was speaking on the European Industrial Leadership Panel and described the economics that led to the company being founded in 2023.
She said: “Our founders came up with the idea of drone interceptors in 2023, attending a hackathon in Kyiv against Shaheds. Because if you remember, that was a time where we were still combating Shaheds and Cannons with missiles, with IRIS-T, with Patriot, spending about a million per shot to defend from a system that costs maybe 30, 40, 50 grand, so a massive economic imbalance in a time where we’re seeing a massive proliferation of the subsonic layer.”
That imbalance has driven a good deal of European procurement thinking since, and it remains the central argument for cheap interceptors over exquisite ones. Tytan now has three interceptor types aimed at different threats in the NATO Class I and Class II categories, with locations in Munich, Berlin and Kyiv.
Ms Hoppe said the hardware is sophisticated but is not what distinguishes the company. “Really, what sets us apart is the high degree of autonomy that enables operators to operate multiple systems at the same time and doesn’t require manual steering,” she said.
Close contact with Ukrainian units shapes the development cycle, and she named the third army corps, the National Guard of Ukraine and the Ukrainian air force as sources of constant feedback that is taken back into prototyping in Munich.
Getting from prototypes to volume is the part she described as most exciting and most difficult. “It’s one thing producing very innovative prototypes and keeping that iteration speed when you’re making prototypes, but really keeping that speed on your scaling, because really no system is a real solution if it’s not available en masse,” she said. “So we’re building up our manufacturing to produce up to 3,000 per month, and keeping that speed using smart manufacturing technologies while always iterating on software.”
She was careful to place the company inside a wider architecture, and warned against anybody claiming to have solved the problem alone. “We always think of air defence as a multi-layer approach,” she said. “Any company saying we have all the solutions, we’re able to combat all the levels of threats that we’re seeing at the moment, it’s just not possible. It takes all kinds of different industry players, all kinds of systems, and we want to be part of that multi-layered approach.”
Ms Hoppe also noted the collaborative tone of the session itself, observing that the companies on the stage compete in the same market but are working towards the same European resilience, which she described as uplifting.
