Robot boat found its way in the Solent without satellites
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:30:03 BST
18:30:03 KST

An uncrewed surface vessel has been navigated through the Solent using radar matched against stored maps of the coastline rather than satellite positioning, in a demonstration staged for the Ministry of Defence, according to Voyant Innovations.
The Liverpool University spin-out ran its software aboard a Kraken K3 Scout autonomous vessel, using particle filter algorithms to compare live radar imagery against pre-existing reference maps of the terrain and work out the vessel’s position without any help from the Global Navigation Satellite System. The demonstration took place on 5 October and forms part of a wider departmental effort to find resilient technologies for operating where satellite navigation is contested or congested.
James Norwood, chief executive of Voyant, said: “Reliable navigation is fundamental to maritime operations, yet we are entering an era where access to GNSS can no longer be assumed. Working alongside Kraken and the Ministry of Defence, we have demonstrated a practical capability that supports the safe and effective deployment of autonomous maritime systems in challenging operational conditions.
“The demonstration represents another milestone in the UK’s continued investment in sovereign technologies that strengthen resilience, enhance operational freedom and support the next generation of autonomous defence capabilities.”
The littoral is the hardest place to do this, which is why the Solent was chosen. Coastlines, changing terrain and dense infrastructure degrade satellite reception on their own, before any adversary sets out to deny it deliberately, and an autonomous vessel that loses its position close inshore is a hazard to everything around it as well as a loss to its owner.
Voyant’s approach fuses radar returns with probabilistic algorithms to estimate where the vessel is relative to its surroundings, and crucially also to estimate how confident it is in that answer. Rather than listening for a satellite, the system continually matches what it can see against geographic features it already knows about.
The company was founded on more than twenty years of research at Liverpool and sells software intended to extract more from sensors a customer already owns, working with radar, sonar, electronic warfare, electro-optical and infrared systems without requiring new hardware.
Voyant is exhibiting at Apex Europe in London on Wednesday and Thursday, and has a second release out covering a software-defined approach to anti-submarine warfare.

Tristan Harris’ Tech Nonprofit Is Laying Off Most Staff and Going ‘Founder-Led’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

The Center for Humane Technology, the online safety group cofounded by former Google product manager Tristan Harris and featured in the hit documentary The Social Dilemma, is laying off about half of its 16 non-founder employees, ex-staffers tell WIRED. The organization is ending its policy research and litigation work to focus instead on what it calls “founder-led” projects.
The nine departures, which include executive director Julie Guirado and senior director of strategy Camille Carlton, arrive shortly after the center scored a series of major courtroom victories against social media companies. The lawsuits drew on its research alleging that the platforms were deliberately designed to keep kids glued to their screens.
But amid that success, internal debates had been brewing for years over the organization’s direction, according to 16 former workers, most of whom spoke with WIRED earlier this year on the condition of anonymity because they feared professional repercussions.
CHT’s board ultimately determined that trying to operate both as an advocacy group fronted by Harris and a think tank producing policy papers had stretched it too thin. Moving forward, the organization will focus on initiatives with its founders at the forefront, including “public education, targeted briefings, and private coordination,” building upon their success “reaching broad audiences and engaging influential decisionmakers,” the board announced last week.
Functions such as assisting in litigation and evaluating AI tools would be eliminated, the board added, without specifying an exact number of layoffs.
“This moment of accelerated AI risk demands we focus on one strategy, and we have chosen to focus on what we have always done best so that we can meet the moment,” board chair Premal Shah said in a statement to WIRED.
In recent years, Harris has joined a growing chorus of voices sounding the alarm about the risks posed by advanced artificial intelligence, warning of a potential “AI takeover” if the software evades control. “We have to act right now before it’s too late,” he told NBC News last month.
The center encouraged people to sign a major petition to pause AI development and helped organize a hearing in Congress about the dangers of chatbots. It also advised on lawsuits and investigations probing AI labs for their design choices, including an ongoing case filed against OpenAI by parents of a teenager who died by suicide after interacting with ChatGPT. Harris also starred in a documentary released on Netflix last month, The AI Doc, which urges viewers to demand that Congress intervene to protect the public from the technology’s risks.
Founded in 2017, the Center for Humane Technology competes with well-established nonprofits and numerous newer entrants for funding and attention to shape AI policy. Cyberattacks by AI agents from OpenAI and other labs have renewed calls to hold tech developers liable for design and engineering failures.
With an annual budget of roughly $6 million and a similar amount in reserves, the center has been funded by wealthy families and foundations. But as it doubles down on Harris, former employees fear resources might be diverted away from addressing what they believe are more pressing concerns about AI’s impact on democracy and civil liberties.
Gail Barnes, who advised the center on social media strategy in its early days, says the board is dropping work that was supposed to convert Harris’ fame “into durable pressure” that could help facilitate real change inside companies.
“Whether that is wisdom or a retreat depends on whether you think the binding constraint on AI right now is still ‘people haven’t heard the argument’ or ‘the argument has no institutional teeth.’ CHT is picking the first,” Barnes says.
Big Star
Harris excels at producing compelling sound bites, and he has long been a fixture in the media, at conferences, and on Capitol Hill. “He’s brilliant. He’s articulate,” a former CHT colleague says. “He could have easily spent his entire career on the dark side. For whatever reason, he came to appreciate that this was messed up.”
Harris cofounded the center with Aza Raskin, the self-proclaimed inventor of the infinite scroll, and Randy Fernando, who once worked in developer education at Nvidia. The goal was to push tech companies to take more responsibility for the social consequences of their products, which in the early days meant examining issues like whether they were fomenting political radicalization or harming the mental health of teenagers. The language Harris used to describe these problems was quickly adopted across Silicon Valley.
Internal documents from Meta released in court this year show company researchers discussed reaching out to Harris as early as 2018, when his warnings that apps were intentionally designed to be addictive entered the mainstream. His national profile grew further with the release of The Social Dilemma on Netflix in 2020.
“It’s hard to understate how helpful The Social Dilemma was for launching tech accountability” as an advocacy field, says a leader at another nonprofit, who also sought anonymity to protect their relationship with CHT.
But inside the organization, Harris sometimes clashed with his team about whether to focus their efforts on consumers, tech companies, or lawmakers, former staffers say. Some colleagues grew frustrated with Harris’ frequently shifting whims, describing the organization’s culture as needlessly “frenetic” and “insanity-inducing.” Shah disputed the characterization, but acknowledged the center’s culture is fast-paced given the urgency of its mission.
The center developed an online course at one point for tech workers who wanted to learn how to build humane systems, and while it drew thousands of participants, CHT decided to retire it as Harris’ focus shifted to concerns about AI, according to people familiar with the project. Another initiative to create resources for educators to make sense of issues around screen time fell by the wayside, the people say. Harris kept coming back to the center being “a vehicle for him to speak to the world,” according to one ex-employee.
The center’s podcasts and videos featuring Harris and Raskin have attracted large audiences, former workers say. Harris also landed private meetings with US lawmakers and executives at top tech companies. Former employees describe the group’s strategy as putting more emphasis on “grasstops” activism over the more familiar “grassroots,” which some viewed as misguided.
Shah says CHT believes “mass communications creates grassroots pressure, which unlocks action from the grasstops” and that Harris “is one of the very few people in the world who is invited and can communicate effectively to mass media audiences across the political spectrum.”
Some former employees allege that CHT’s founders were eager to remain Silicon Valley insiders, and thus were more reluctant to criticize companies where they previously worked or where close personal contacts have worked. (Shah disputes the characterizations and says CHT “has always been tough on companies.”)
Some ex-employees described Harris’ management style as taxing, which they allege led to high turnover. In 2023, employees returned from a staff retreat feeling upset after being asked to participate in trust-building exercises they felt were overly personal, according to several former workers. CHT’s independent board members got involved, and Harris later stepped down as executive director to become the organization’s president, according to the former employees.
Shah says that employee turnover "stemmed from differences in problem analysis and approaches to achieving the organization’s core mission.” He also denied that Harris’ role change was related to what happened at the retreat.
Whatever turmoil may have been happening inside CHT, the broader strategy Harris used to go after tech companies was paying off. In 2021, state attorneys general across the US opened investigations into Meta and later sued the company for allegedly misleading teens and parents. This year, Meta agreed to settle some of the lawsuits for billions of dollars. Juries, including one that heard testimony from Raskin, put the company on the hook for additional penalties in separate cases. Other social media platforms agreed to settle similar litigation this year.
In an interview with WIRED earlier this year, the leader of the other tech nonprofit praised CHT’s less flashy work in statehouses and courtrooms. The shift away from it is “disappointing,” the person says now. “Change comes from movements and democracy, not celebrities and backrooms.”
Some former employees say they expect that CHT will increasingly resemble what they jokingly refer to as the “Center of Helping Tristan.” Shah says the organization’s sole goal is ensuring “today’s most consequential technologies serve humanity.”

Lithuania will deploy up to 100 troops to help guard its border with Russia’s Kaliningrad region over the next several weeks. Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas said the move was a precautionary measure anticipating Russian men seeking asylum from potential military mobilisation.
Katelynas said he requested military assistance after assessing information from security and border agencies and concluding that the State Border Guard Service does not have enough personnel to handle all existing threats.
“We can face people trying to evade mobilization and seeking to enter Lithuanian territory to request asylum,” Katelynas told reporters in parliament on Thursday.
He also cited a recent incident on Latvia’s border with Belarus, where a group of migrants was reportedly accompanied by masked people who threatened Latvian soldiers and pushed migrants toward the border.
“Seeing that instrumentalised migration is posing growing threats, additional forces were requested at the Lithuanian border with the Kaliningrad region,” Katelynas said.
Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas announced Wednesday that troops would be deployed at the border for several weeks at Katelynas’ request. Up to 100 soldiers are expected to assist border guards through October 16, according to Kaunas.
Katelynas said the decision was based not only on political considerations but also on information and indications provided by security agencies.
The Border Guard Service has long faced pressure along both Lithuania's borders with Belarus and Russia, Katelynas said, citing irregular migration across the border and other incidents.
“Our resources are not unlimited. In fact, our border service is overloaded with work, shifts are getting longer and the number of officers is not increasing,” he said. “Assistance is needed.”
Katelynas said the government was not currently considering deploying troops to the border with Belarus.
He also said Lithuania’s overall threat level had not changed, and that two weeks was considered a reasonable initial deployment period that could be extended if necessary.
“Of course, the threat assessment is carried out by the competent institutions,” Katelynas said.
Despite the decision to deploy troops, the Border Guard Service said Thursday that the situation along the Kaliningrad border was calm. Moreover, no irregular migrants had been detected for five consecutive days on the Belarus border, according to the service.
“The situation is calm. There have been no migrants for several days,” Border Guard Service adviser Giedrius Mišutis told ELTA.
The troops were expected to begin assisting border guards Thursday.
The Latvian incident cited by Katelynas involved at least 20 migrants who attempted to cross the Latvia-Belarus border while accompanied by masked individuals. According to Latvia’s armed forces, the escorts were armed, threatened soldiers and actively urged and pushed the migrants toward Latvia.
Hours later, the masked individuals entered Latvian territory, damaged an electricity distribution box and stole CCTV cameras before returning to Belarus.

The attacks came as Israeli forces detained and subjected about 95 Palestinians to field interrogations across the West Bank overnight and on Thursday morning, according to the Palestinian Prisoners Society.
The non-governmental group said the arrests and interrogations took place in several areas, including Aqaba in Tubas province, Madama in Nablus province, Yatta in Hebron province, as well as areas in Jenin, Bethlehem and Al-Bireh.
It said Israeli forces also carried out a widespread arrest campaign in Qalqilya, targeting former prisoners and family members of current and former prisoners.
Israeli forces raided dozens of homes, including the home of Muayyad Shaaban, head of the Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission, causing damage inside homes and assaulting residents, according to the group.
The West Bank has seen increasing attacks by Israeli occupiers and Israeli forces against Palestinians, their land and property, coinciding with the start of the olive harvest season in October, amid restrictions on farmers’ access to their agricultural land.
According to the Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission, Israeli occupiers have carried out at least 14,742 attacks across the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, since October 2023, killing 66 Palestinians.
The attacks damaged, uprooted, burned, or poisoned at least 147,111 trees, including 100,485 olive trees, the commission said.

U.S. and Russia Explore Nord Stream Restart, Sources Say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:27:22 UTC
18:27:22 KST

Top Russian and U.S. officials, including U.S. Special Envoy Jared Kushner, have held talks about bringing a U.S. investor into the Nord Stream pipelines that delivered gas to Germany before Russia invaded Ukraine, five people with knowledge of the situation said.
The discussions included Kirill Dmitriev, a close adviser to Russian President Vladimir Putin, and Kushner, the son-in-law of U.S. President Donald Trump, the people said.
Kushner, who has been trying to broker a truce between Russia and Ukraine, views doing business as central to restoring peace. Such a deal would enable U.S. investors to profit from energy flows to Europe once the war ends.
Dmitriev and Kushner have met in Moscow and New York in recent weeks. While it was unclear to what degree they discussed Nord Stream on those occasions, the topic remains on the agenda, two of the people told Reuters.
“Any deals will have to be negotiated by Russia with DFC (U.S. International Development Finance Corporation) and Treasury and must benefit United States taxpayers and companies,” a White House official said when asked about the pipeline discussions.
There had been “no Nord Stream discussions recently,” the official told Reuters.
Dmitriev, who has campaigned for a resumption of Russian gas sales to Germany, met last month with U.S. Energy and Treasury Department representatives to discuss potential U.S.-Russia energy initiatives. A representative for Dmitriev declined to comment.
It remains unclear how interested Washington is in pursuing the restart of Russian gas flows to Germany, which is Europe's biggest energy consumer.
A U.S. official said that given the obstacles, a deal is unlikely in the medium term. The Nord Stream gas pipelines are sanctioned by the U.S. and the EU, making any restart illegal.
Trump could waive or soften U.S. sanctions, but if Democrats win control of Congress in next month's midterm elections, this would become harder.
Germany and other European countries, which are spending billions of euros rebuilding their military to defend themselves from Russia, would strongly resist reopening Nord Stream.
A spokeswoman for Germany's economy and energy ministry said Nord Stream and Russian gas were sanctioned in Europe and that Germany had found alternatives. She said any reopening of the pipelines required government approval and this was not desired.
Before Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Germany bought more than half of its gas from Russia through the two Nord Stream pipelines. They were mothballed after Moscow throttled supply to Europe and blown up in a series of underwater explosions in September 2022.
Nord Stream ownership hurdles
Talks between Moscow and Washington are taking place against a backdrop of deep European mistrust of Russia's motives.
Earlier this year, the heads of five European spy agencies told Reuters that Russia did not want to end the war quickly and was using U.S. talks to push for business deals instead.
Relations between Russia and Germany, which is among the biggest providers of military support to Ukraine, have hit a low ebb, as officials in Berlin have accused Russia of mounting a systematic campaign of hybrid attacks.
Some German lawmakers say that business deals would bolster Moscow as it pursues war with Ukraine.
“This threatens to be a dirty deal that will cost Europe dearly,” said Michael Kellner, a lawmaker who was in charge of German energy policy in the aftermath of the Ukraine invasion.
“Americans and Russians will share the profits,” he said.
While Germany's coalition government is opposed to restarting the pipeline, Alternative for Germany (AfD), the country's most popular political party, wants to do so.
Dmitriev will meet the AfD leadership early next year to discuss selling Russian gas again.
But selling ownership of the company that controls the Nord Stream gas pipelines to a U.S. investor or restarting Russian gas faces hurdles.
The company is 51% owned by Russian state energy giant Gazprom, with a further 31% split between two German entities and the rest in the hands of a French and a Dutch firm.
The two German shareholders are seeking to keep their shares to maintain German influence, should Gazprom sell its stake, said another person.
Days after the Moscow meetings, Kushner said in Kyiv he had spoken to European counterparts about how the war pushed up energy prices, advocating “prosperity agreements” to encourage peace and give “leaders ... something to look forward to.”
While a gas deal would please the Kremlin, it would split German public opinion, which is divided over buying Russian energy, and Europe, where Poland and the Baltic states are particularly vulnerable to Russia and reject energy ties.
Poland's political leadership is watching the discussions to reopen the pipeline but remains firmly opposed, said one person with knowledge of the government's thinking.
Kushner and Dmitriev have also been discussing the sale of a collection of businesses, from oil refineries to petrol stations in Europe and elsewhere, which are owned by Russian energy company Lukoil, said two other people familiar with the matter.
Under that plan, a consortium of the DFC federal investment agency and investors from Qatar and the United Arab Emirates would buy the assets, while U.S. authorities would lift sanctions, those people said.
“On Lukoil, Steve (Witkoff) and Jared (Kushner) worked with DFC to negotiate a substantial upfront payment and profits interest for the United States,” said a White House official.
Lukoil and Gazprom did not respond to requests for comment.

Ukrainian agriculture urges EU to talk details, not panic, in future membership negotiations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:26:20 UTC
18:26:20 KST

Ukrainian agriculture urges EU to talk details, not panic, in future membership negotiations
Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi and the sector's main lobby organization in Brussels doubled down on their commitment to integrating Kyiv's geopolitically powerful farming sector into the EU system on Oct. 7.
Their respective interventions came one day after the European Commission published a view on how the future of enlargement could work.
Ukraine's agricultural might could mean that the EU needs "targeted arrangements to significantly limit financial support and market access for sensitive agricultural products," the document argues.
However, Vysotskyi said permanent restrictions on access to the EU's single market are a non-starter, in written comments first shared with Politico and seen by the Kyiv Independent.
"Ukraine cannot agree to such an approach," the Ukrainian minister said.
Likewise, the Ukrainian Agribusiness Club (UCAB) put out a press statement saying, "Ukrainian agricultural producers cannot be expected to bear the full economic cost of alignment with EU standards while being denied the corresponding perspective of full participation in the EU Single Market."
For both Vysotskyi and UCAB, part of the solution relies on baking transition periods into the enlargement process, just as was the case in previous rounds of EU expansion, which would give the bloc and Ukraine time to adapt to one another and stretch out disruption over a longer period of time.
"Transitional periods are a normal part of EU enlargement, and Ukraine is ready for them," Vysotskyi said.
But "transition should facilitate integration, not become a mechanism for permanently excluding Ukrainian agriculture from the internal market," UCAB notes.
Ukraine's farming sector has already begun complying with EU rules, a process that is expensive, essentially irreversible, and undertaken only because it comes with the promise of a level playing field in the EU market.
It is market access rather than financial support that matters most for Ukraine, Vysotskyi said, as the sector already operates with little state support.
But that has not stopped French far-right leader Marine Le Pen already playing to the fears of French farmers that Ukrainian counterparts would take away their share of EU subsidies.
EU farms are typically small-scale, uncompetitive, and dependent on the bloc's Common Agricultural Policy for generous subsidies that keep them operational.
Ukraine's farming sector, by contrast, is a giant capable of competing on the world stage, and with that size comes geopolitical leverage.
Because of that, the European Commission is clear that while Ukraine should gain market access as part of EU membership, Ukrainian agriculture needs to remain competitive on the world stage.
"Our budget can never compensate for gains that Ukraine's very competitive — the only real competitive agriculture sector in Europe — can gain in the world," a senior EU official told the Kyiv Independent, ahead of the publication of the Commission's new plans.
To overcome that obstacle, highly technical negotiations need to take place.
Vysotskyi seems to mirror the European Commission's thinking that for each specific product, there should be "a substantive discussion about adaptation periods, the volumes of market access, and safeguard mechanisms."
That could mean one rule for Ukrainian chicken, another for wheat, another for plant proteins, and so on.
Decisions "must take into account the situation in each specific sector and must not turn into permanent restrictions for the entire Ukrainian agricultural sector," Vysotskyi said.
And UCAB says that "the Ukrainian agricultural sector is ready to contribute constructively to this work."
UCAB calls for agricultural businesses, associations representing the sector, and EU agricultural organizations to all be included in a dialogue on Ukraine's agricultural integration.
"Ukraine is preparing to become part of the European Union. Its agricultural sector should not merely be accommodated within the future European agricultural model. It should be involved in designing it," reads the UCAB press statement.

inflatable sculpture in ghent asks visitors to ‘pump for democracy’ to keep it standing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:25:51 UTC
18:25:51 KST

inflatable sculpture in ghent asks visitors to ‘pump for democracy’ to keep it standing
zweintopf’s seven-meter-high work turns a familiar monument into a physical exercise, requiring visitors to continuously pump air into the sculpture or watch it gradually collapse into an empty shell.
zweintopf’s sculpture ONLY STANDS WITH CONTINUOUS EFFORT
A white inflatable sculpture by Austrian artist duo zweintopf floats on the moat beside Ghent’s Gravensteen, asking passersby to physically sustain a symbol of democracy. Titled Perseverance (Goddess of Democracy), the seven-meter-high work reinterprets the Goddess of Democracy erected by Chinese art students on Beijing’s Tiananmen Square in May 1989, shortly before the military suppression of the pro-democracy protests. At the Belgian castle, the sculpture remains upright only through the continuous work of a pumping station.
Visitors are invited to keep pumping air into the sculpture, with the accompanying exercise described as ‘Train your perseverance!’ Stop, and the figure gradually collapses into an empty shell. The work therefore shifts democracy away from an image of permanence and toward something dependent on participation, maintenance and collective effort.
The work has appeared in several contexts since its first presentation in 2019, including UNIKUM’s Europapark in Klagenfurt, steirischer herbst’s Sculptures in Exile, the Bundeskunsthalle in Bonn, Kunstverein Graz and other exhibitions. For its current presentation in Ghent, the recently reopened Design Museum Gent commissioned a replica of the work.
A NEW LIFE FOR THE GODDESS OF DEMOCRACY
The original Goddess of Democracy was a 10-meter-high statue created by Chinese art students and installed on Tiananmen Square in 1989. It was destroyed during the violent suppression of the student protests. The project by the artist duo zweintopf makes its fragility part of the meaning. The sculpture is made from textile and plastic with wood and metal components, connected to a pumping installation that keeps the figure inflated. Its monumental scale recalls the authority of a public statue, while its dependence on air makes that authority visibly unstable.
The smooth white surface and simplified body of the figure stand in direct contrast to the castle’s masonry, crenellations and defensive architecture. One represents permanence and fortification; the other can disappear as soon as its support is withdrawn. The pumping mechanism asks passersby to contribute physical effort to prevent it from disappearing, creating a small system in which the condition of the object depends on the behavior of the people around it. The symbolism is direct, but the physical experience makes the proposition difficult to ignore.
from gravensteen to design museum gent
The sculpture is currently installed beside Gravensteen and is scheduled to remain there through October 14th, 2026, before moving to the inner courtyard of Design Museum Gent from October 15th. The installation is part of Public Matter(s): Democracy Workout, a program that invites visitors to practice skills such as listening, finding their voice, negotiating compromises, and dealing constructively with conflict, proposing that democracy depends on people actively taking part in it.
project info:
 name: Perseverance (Goddess of Democracy)
artist: zweintopf | @zweintopf
location: Gravensteen, Ghent, Belgium; Design Museum Gent from October 15th, 2026

China militia boat spotted for first time off Taiwan's east coast, patrol finds

A Chinese militia boat was spotted along with two other vessels off Taiwan's Pacific coast in August, according to a surveillance report reviewed by Reuters, the first known sighting of such a craft in the sensitive area.
The report by Taiwan's Apex Aviation identifies the Minfudingyu 07902 as a fishing boat that doubles as a Chinese militia vessel, which was seen operating with a Chinese coast guard cutter and a research vessel one day in mid-August.
China, which views Taiwan as its own territory, has stepped up activity off the island's east coast since June with regular coast guard patrols. Officials in Taiwan, which rejects Beijing's sovereignty claims, say they believe China is practicing for a potential maritime blockade using overlapping military, paramilitary and civilian assets.
Taipei regards the area off its east coast as critical to wartime supply routes from allies in the event of a blockade or conflict.
Fishing boat part of 'harassment drills,' official says
China was "using law enforcement and scientific research as cover for harassment, seeking to expand their scope of operations during a non-conflict scenario to create an illusion of de facto jurisdiction," Taiwan's defense ministry told Reuters in a statement when asked about the Apex report.
Such actions undermine international order and challenge Taiwan's maritime rights, the ministry said, adding that the island's military was using reconnaissance tools to track Chinese activity in coordination with other agencies, including Taiwan's coast guard.
China's Taiwan Affairs Office and defense ministry did not respond to requests for comment.
In a practice dating to the 1950s, China's maritime militia, more commonly observed around South China Sea flashpoints, consists of fishing vessels whose crews receive training and support to operate in disputed waters, often alongside coast guard ships.
Analysts say the fleet helps Beijing assert maritime claims while maintaining a civilian appearance.
Taiwan has confirmed that the Minfudingyu, the coast guard cutter 2502 and the research vessel Xiang Yang Hong 03 were operating near Taiwan in mid-August, said two senior Taiwan officials briefed on the matter.
Authorities identified the fishing boat as part of the People's Liberation Army's maritime militia fleet, which Taiwan was tracking and which was operating "in coordination with Chinese coast guard maritime harassment drills," one official said.
"The purpose of militia boats is to conduct substantive harassment," the official said.
The other official said the three craft were operating "in an area not commonly used by Chinese vessels" and had been "designated for heightened monitoring."
The officials spoke on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the issue.
Private patrol part of Taiwan's 'whole of society' push
The Apex report says a reconnaissance aircraft the company operates detected a Chinese maritime group more than 30 nautical miles off the coast of Taiwan's eastern county of Hualien. The company asked that the date of the spotting be withheld, citing safety concerns related to counter-reconnaissance against its operations.
The report uses radar screenshots, infrared imagery and automatic-identification system data to document the cluster of vessels.
The patrol by Apex, better known for pilot training and charter flights, reflects Taiwan's efforts to involve civilian firms in technologies relevant to the government's "whole of society resilience" initiative, though the company says its patrols are independently run and not carried out for the government.
Chinese warships, coast guard vessels, research ships and some civilian vessels continue to operate in overlapping ways, "creating pressure in the waters surrounding Taiwan," said Honor Hung, Apex's defense and security director.
The three Chinese vessels were spread over a roughly 10-nautical-mile radius, Honor said, adding that one surveillance tracking could not determine their missions or any coordination among them.
Apex uses a civilian light aircraft equipped with a powerful US-made radar that allows its patrols to detect objects on the surface as small as 900 square centimeters (140 square inches).

Belgian parliament to legislate to allow police to enter homes to facilitate undocumented migrant removals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:21:50 UTC
18:21:50 KST

Belgian police will soon be able, in conjunction with the Immigration Office (DVZ), to enter the homes of undocumented migrants who pose a threat to public order or national security. This is set out in a bill drafted by the Belgian Asylum and Migration Minister, Anneleen Van Bossuyt (Flemish nationalist N-VA), and Justice Minister Annelies Verlinden (Flemish Christian democrat CD&V), which has now been approved by the House Home Affairs Committee. The proposal still needs to be OKed during a plenary session of the lower house of the Belgian parliament.
Belgian parliament to legislate to allow police to enter homes to facilitate undocumented migrant removals
Home searches like these are controversial. The aim is to make it easier to deport people residing here illegally and who persistently refuse to cooperate with efforts to facilitate their return.
The new law will make this possible. Following entry into the home, the police may place the person in question – that is, the individual who poses a threat to public order or national security – under administrative detention. However, prior authorisation from an investigating judge is required to enter the home.
Speaking to press agency Belga, Minister Van Bossuyt referred to this as “an historic breakthrough” and had previously said that this “is the final piece in a firm but humane return policy”.
“This is not a witch-hunt against people who have international protection or are simply in the country illegally (..) The law sets out clear conditions, and a search of a home can only take place with the authorisation of an investigating judge.”
(Overly) broad definitions
The bill did, however, attract a great deal of comment and was extensively discussed in parliament.
The opposition, the federal police, investigating judges and lawyers alike were highly critical. They believe that the exact meaning of ‘a threat to public order or national security’ has not been defined clearly enough.
“It will be up to the investigating judge to determine whether someone poses a threat to public order or national security,” says Van Bossuyt. “The judge will independently assess whether that person poses such a threat. That is a crucial test.”
Minister Van Bossuyt finds the debate strange: “The concepts of public order and national security feature in many parts of our legislation. Nowhere is a specific list provided of what they entail.” What is more, according to Van Bossuyt, the Council of State, which vets Belgian draft legislation, has explicitly stated that it is not desirable to define these concepts, as they may evolve over time.
“When the Justice Minister drafts new legislation, she isn’t asked how judges should apply that law, is she?” Van Bossuyt notes.
Van Bossuyt has also tabled an amendment to her own bill: “We have given investigating judges more time to reach a decision, from 5 days to 7.”
She emphasises that their role is not merely reduced to that of a ‘rubber-stamp judge’: “The investigating judge will absolutely not be a rubber-stamp judge, precisely because they play such a crucial role in assessing whether someone poses a threat or not. They will have access to the full case file.”
What about minors?
Another point of criticism concerns the rights of minors. According to critics, these are not sufficiently safeguarded. Government party Les Engagés (Francophone centrist) was only prepared to vote for the bill if greater protection for minors was provided.
“When authorising a search of a home, the investigating judge must determine all the conditions under which that search may take place,” explains Van Bossuyt. “If, for example, children are present, the investigating judge can stipulate that the search must take place during school hours. In that case, the likelihood of children being present is very low.”
The investigating judge may also, for example, require a psychologist to be present during the search, says Van Bossuyt. “So, the possible presence of minors has certainly been taken into account.”
The minister also points to the responsibility of the person who poses a threat to public order or national security: “It is that person who is making life difficult for those children,” says the minister.
Desperately needed, according to Van Bossuyt
Government party, Les Engagés, did not secure all the amendments it had requested, so MP Xavier Dubois boycotted the second reading. However, his group leader, Aurore Tourneur, did defend the amendments in the House Home Affairs Committee.
This enabled the majority to approve the bill after all, with the support of the Flemish liberal opposition party Anders. Although they, too, called for further amendments.
The left-wing opposition parties voted against. The far-right Vlaams Belang abstained. According to MP Francesca Van Belleghem, the law has been “so watered down by coalition negotiations that it will have virtually no effect in practice”.
‘This was a sensitive bill for several government parties: that’s no secret. In practice, there was an absolute need for this,’ concludes Van Bossuyt.
The bill must now be put to a vote during a plenary session, where the law can be definitively approved.
Speaking to Belga, the minister warned local authorities that have already announced they will not permit home visits, such as Leuven. “Be fully aware of what that choice means. If you refuse to implement this law and things go wrong, do not point the finger at the federal government afterwards. Because then you will be jeopardising the safety of your own residents” she said.

Russia’s war against Ukraine sends the bill to its own companies: bond defaults head for a 17-year high. The squeeze is spreading from small firms to Moscow's own budget, which is running a record deficit to keep the war going.

French AI infrastructure firm Sesterce plans €10bn data centre project in Central Finland
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:21:03 EEST
18:21:03 KST

French AI infrastructure firm Sesterce has announced plans to invest more than 10 billion euros in the building of artificial intelligence (AI) data centres at the site of a former paper mill in Jämsä, Central Finland.
If realised, the project would be significant in scale — and only around three billion euros smaller than Google's 13-billion-euro investment across multiple locations, which was announced in September.
Investment confirmed, client undisclosed
Yle has received confirmation from Sesterce's CEO Youssef El Manssouri that the investment decision has already been made and a contract has been signed with the future client.
However, El Manssouri has not identified the company that will become the data centre's client, but said it's one of two leading AI laboratories. He also declined to reveal the project's financial backers.
According to French commercial register data, Sesterce Group is registered in Marseille and was entered into the commercial register in 2021. According to the register, the firm's turnover was 11.95 million euros in 2024.
The former paper mill site is currently owned by real estate company Kaipola Green Port. Its board chair, Martti Inkovaara, told Yle that the firm has been negotiating with Sesterce about selling the entire site.
According to Inkovaara, negotiations about the deal are in an advanced stage — he also declined to discuss the price.
"I'd be surprised if the deal didn't go through," Inkovaara said.
Several companies currently rent industrial space at the Kaipola site. Inkovaara noted that it will be up to Sesterce to decide whether their operations can continue at the site if ownership changes.
Jobs expected
El Manssouri told Yle that the construction phase of the project could bring around 2,000 jobs to Jämsä. Once completed, the AI facility would employ approximately 300 people.
When paper giant UPM shut down the Kaipola mill, it had employed over 400 workers.
The first construction phase is set to begin before the end of this year. It involves building a 200-megawatt liquid-cooled AI data centre at the mill site.
El Manssouri noted that the site clearance and initial interior work are already underway. In the long term, the company aims to build over one gigawatt of AI capacity in Finland.
The former paper mill site already has infrastructure, including an electricity grid, water systems, buildings and logistics arrangements. According to Sesterce's CEO, building the data centre therefore shouldn't cause biodiversity loss.
El Manssouri said the Kaipola site was chosen specifically for its minimal environmental impact in setting up the facility.
"Many supercomputer projects destroy a lot of nature. Finland has excellent industrial sites that we can convert into supercomputer centres. That guided our choice," he said.
The company added that it is committing to contributing the same amount of new renewable electricity production into Finland's grid for every megawatt the "AI campus" uses.
Sesterce has also vowed to establish a 10-million-euro local community fund to finance local projects together with the town of Jämsä and its residents.
An independent third party will monitor and audit the firm's commitments, with the company promising that the results will be publicly reported every year.
Town cautiously optimistic
Locals in the town responded to the major investment news with cautious enthusiasm, at least for now.
Town manager Jori Reijula said he only learned of Sesterce's plans a few weeks ago.
Reijula said he thinks the project is significant for a place whose population and vitality have declined in recent years. But it's not time to celebrate yet.
"There are still many permit processes, and many things need to fall into place. I want to see things progress before we start declaring that a data centre is here," he said.

Diplomats take shelter in Saudi capital as Yemen's Houthis target Riyadh airport
Foreign diplomats and international schools in the Saudi capital took safety measures on Thursday as loud blasts rattled the city and Yemen's Houthi rebels claimed missile attacks against its airport. In a further blow to Riyadh, Turkey ruled out sending troops to confront the Iran-backed militia, despite a defence pact with Saudi Arabia.

Diplomats stationed in the Saudi capital were sheltering in place and international schools took safety measures on Thursday, diplomats and residents told AFP, after explosions echoed across the city.
The explosions heard in Riyadh came as the Houthis in Yemen, which borders Saudi Arabia, claimed their latest attacks on the kingdom, including the capital's international airport.
The Iran-backed militia said they launched two missiles at Riyadh's airport, as well as one at an airport in Najran and another at an airbase in Khamis Mushait. Saudi forces earlier said they intercepted two missiles fired at the capital.
Read moreExplosions heard in Saudi capital Riyadh after Houthis' deadly attacks on airports
The Houthis also called on staff at oil facilities in Saudi Arabia to leave their jobs "so as not to endanger their lives".
The rebel militia have launched a wave of attacks on Saudi Arabia since they began a major offensive in Yemen against the internationally-recognised, Saudi-backed government there.
Saudi Arabia and Yemeni government forces have struggled to contain the Houthis' advance, despite a counter-offensive aimed at recapturing territory including the area around a waterway that is crucial to global energy flows.
In a further blow to Riyadh, Turkey's foreign minister on Thursday ruled out sending troops to confront the Houthis, stressing that a defence pact with Saudi Arabia was "not an offensive agreement".
Evacuating staff
In Riyadh, home to a large number of non-Saudis, diplomats were instructed to shelter in place in their respective embassies, diplomats told AFP.
There was no official statement addressing the morning's incident or text alerts warning residents, which were sent out during earlier periods of the conflict.
A campaign by the interior ministry has repeatedly warned residents against sharing unauthorised information, images or footage of missiles, drones and their impacts, warning that violators could face legal consequences.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Several residents told AFP, meanwhile, that international schools were taking precautions, with at least one facility sending children into a basement for safety.
"My daughter called me," one parent told AFP on condition of anonymity, saying she was "completely distraught".
The measures came after repeated blasts were heard in the city, one of the loudest disturbances there since the start of the Middle East war that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February.
Numerous flights at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport were delayed or cancelled, according to information posted on signage at the facility.
Two people working in Riyadh's business hub, the King Abdullah Financial District, told AFP that some companies were evacuating staff from the area.
200,000 people displaced
The Yemen war predates the Iran war, but it had come to a near-standstill until last month the Houthis launched a lightning offensive against government forces.
They seized large swathes of territory including the area around the Bab al-Mandab strait, a key waterway for global shipping and, crucially, Saudi oil exports.
The fighting in Yemen has in recent weeks become the most active front of the wider regional conflict, which for months has seen violence repeatedly shift focus across the Middle East.
In Yemen, one of the world's poorest countries, it is ordinary civilians paying the price, with more than 200,000 people displaced since July, according to UN data.
Read moreYemen's government declares counter-offensive as Houthis cut vital route to besieged city
After declaring a counter-offensive against the Houthis, Yemen's government claimed to have pushed the fighters out of strategic areas on the Red Sea and the port city of Mocha.
But the Houthis insist they are holding their territory, and military sources from both sides contacted by AFP have not reported any major changes on the ground.
Claims by the warring parties have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast and access for journalists difficult.
In Saudi Arabia, the latest blasts came a day after the Houthis claimed attacks on two international airports, while repeating a warning to airlines to avoid Saudi airspace.
Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said the airports in Riyadh and Abha were "subjected to attacks" on Tuesday and Wednesday.
An Egyptian and an Algerian national were killed at Abha airport, while a Sudanese national was killed at Riyadh airport, the agency said.
The attacks wounded 36 people, it added.
In a subsequent statement, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis blamed them for the strikes and vowed that they "will not go unpunished".
Humanitarian crisis
On Wednesday in Yemen, clashes left at least 62 combatants dead, including 37 Houthis, military sources from both camps told AFP.
Saba also reported that a Houthi missile wounded five civilians in Taiz, a city held by government forces.
"We went out into the street to check on the wounded and saw young civilians who had been hit," resident Al-Fateh al-Eisaei told AFP.
"The Houthi shell landed in the middle of the street, right in an area crowded with civilians."
The humanitarian crisis caused by the war has left most of the nation's population dependent on aid.

Berlin's Left Party, SPD and Greens agree exploratory coalition talks, reports say
Oct 8 - Germany's Left Party, the centre-left SPD and the Greens have agreed on measures to address antisemitic incidents, clearing a key hurdle to the start of exploratory coalition talks in the state of Berlin, local media reported on Thursday.
The agreement comes two-and-a-half weeks after a Berlin state election, in which the Left Party, represented by lead candidate Elif Eralp, emerged as the largest force with 25.7% of votes and began pushing for a coalition with the SPD and Greens.
None of the three parties were immediately available for comment on the reports, which were carried by several local media.
The SPD and Greens made binding commitments on combating antisemitism a precondition for negotiations, amid a debate over pro-Palestinian positions and incidents during events organised by Berlin's Left Party.
According to the tabloid Bild, the parties agreed on procedures for handling future antisemitic incidents, including the involvement of an expert panel if disputes arise.
The parties also agreed to adopt the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance's definition of antisemitism, Bild reported. REUTERS

Permits for wolf culling  rise sharply in Switzerland

Permits for wolf culling rise sharply in Switzerland
At the start of autumn 2026, the Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN) had issued more permits for the preventive culling of wolves than in the same period last year. A legally binding permit decision has been issued for 39 packs. In 2025, the figure stood at 22 packs.
This sharp rise in the number of permits granted can be partly explained by an amendment to the Swiss Hunting Ordinance. The Kora Foundation, commissioned by the federal government, told the Keystone-SDA news agency that “the FOEN can now grant authorisation to cull wolf pups even before their presence has been confirmed”.
+ Swiss canton shot 17 wolves in September
However, young wolves may only be shot once their presence has been confirmed, according to a FOEN spokesperson.
According to the FOEN, the reason for the increase in applications for partial culls is that there are more wolf packs in Switzerland overall.

INTERVIEW - Complicity, censorship and impunity: 'Headline fixer' Assal Rad on how Western media covered Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:18:12 UTC
18:18:12 KST

- Nothing has changed for Palestinians under ceasefire 'except for they're being killed on a slower scale,' says Rad
- Case for war on Iran 'very similar to the sort of playbook' used to justify 2003 Iraq invasion, she says
In her new book, Assal Rad places two New York Times headlines side by side.
One reads: "Russia Pounds Ukrainian Cities in One of the Largest Air Attacks of the War." The other: "Explosion Gazans Say Was Airstrike Leaves Many Casualties in Dense Neighborhood."
Above the first, a note reads: "Attacker named." Above the second: "By who?"
For Rad, a scholar of Middle East history and political advocate known online as the "headline fixer" for striking through and rewriting Western headlines on Gaza, the difference is no accident.
"It's complicity, in my view, because they're very knowingly doing it. It's not an accident," she told Anadolu.
“You see a difference in the way they treat the Russian invasion of Ukraine versus Israel's actions in Gaza,” she added.
Her book, Don't Say Palestine: How the Media Manufactured Consent for Genocide, borrows its subtitle from the 1988 work by Edward Herman and Noam Chomsky, who, she said, argued that the press in Western liberal democracies functions as "a propaganda arm of the state."
Rad said outlets still frame the Gaza genocide “as sort of conventional war" and treat it as "a tragedy or a consequence of urban warfare rather than a deliberate policy being carried out by Israel."
She pointed to a leaked New York Times memo that instructed reporters to avoid words such as “genocide” and ethnic cleansing, according to the US-based news outlet The Intercept.
A Times spokesperson said at the time that "issuing guidance like this to ensure accuracy, consistency and nuance in how we cover the news is standard practice."
"Every major institution and human rights organization in the world, including Israeli human rights organizations, including multiple UN reports, have concluded that Israel has committed genocide. And yet, they want to avoid that language, claiming neutrality," Rad said.
Rad said there is "a very real legal implication" behind that choice.
"If the Western media admits that Israel is committing genocide, then they're also admitting that their own governments are complicit in that genocide and continue to illegally aid it," she said.
But she also sees a "subconscious element" at work.
There is an "internalized Orientalism and racism that informs the way that many people in the Western world think about the region as a whole," she said, describing a “dehumanization process that becomes so ingrained that I think there are genuinely people who are unaware of their own racism.”
'Killed on a slower scale'
For Rad, the decline in Gaza coverage in the Western media over the past year has come "under the banner” of a ceasefire agreement.
"Nothing has changed for Palestinians on the ground except for their being killed on a slower scale," she said.
Her comments come as Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza enters its fourth year, with more than 74,000 Palestinians killed and over 175,000 injured since October 2023, according to Palestinian figures.
Israeli attacks have continued despite a ceasefire that took effect on Oct. 10, 2025. Palestinian figures put the toll since then at 1,454 killed and 5,090 injured.
Rad also pointed to the killing of Palestinian journalists.
"When you slaughter all of the journalists who are telling the world what is happening, it really helps to decrease and decline the amount of footage that people are seeing."
Speaking on the third anniversary of the Oct. 7, 2023 attack on Israel and the launch of its devastating war on Gaza, Rad said the date is "presented as if it exists in this vacuum," erasing the decades of Israeli occupation and blockade that came before it.
'Complete nonsense'
Rad's book also examines State Department briefings under former US President Joe Biden, but she stressed that her criticism is aimed at "institutional bias," not at reporters in the room.
Once their reports are edited, she said, "it turns into, 'Well, this is what they said,' even though the journalists themselves know they're not getting real answers."
Asked about former Biden administration officials who have since distanced themselves from that policy, Rad did not hold back.
"It's complete nonsense. They knowingly did everything that they did," she said.
"The fact that these officials feel comfortable to be in these spaces and feel comfortable to pretend like they were trying to do anything else is all about spinning the narrative and trying to absolve themselves for their own criminality."
Former Biden administration officials have defended their record, saying they pressed Israel to allow more aid into Gaza.
From Iraq to Iran
Rad traces that impunity to the US’ 2003 invasion of Iraq, after which she said neither officials nor media faced consequences.
She sees the same pattern in the war on Iran, calling the case for it "very similar to the sort of playbook that was used in order to justify the invasion of Iraq."
What has changed, she said, is the public, with a majority of Americans opposing the Iran war from the outset "because the trust in government and media has completely declined over watching the Gaza genocide."
"Accountability has to start with the war criminals," she said.
"At the very least, if you're a journalist that is not writing the truth, I don't think you should have a job at the outlet in which you are not writing the truth for."
"There is this idea in the Western world that they toast the notion of a free press, that they celebrate the idea of a free press, and yet for Palestinians, the press vest is a target."

Pakistan reaches $1.2B IMF staff-level deal amid energy shock
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:16:30 UTC
18:16:30 KST

Pakistan has reached a staff-level agreement with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) that could unlock about $1.2 billion in financing as the country faces higher energy costs and supply disruptions linked to the Middle East conflict.
The agreement remains subject to approval by the IMF’s Executive Board.
Once approved, Pakistan would receive about $1 billion under the Extended Fund Facility and another $210 million under the Resilience and Sustainability Facility, which supports climate-related reforms.
The disbursements would bring total financing released under the two programmes to about $5.7 billion.
The IMF said Pakistan had preserved economic stability despite the conflict’s impact, estimating economic growth at 3.6 percent in fiscal year 2026.
Higher energy prices and supply disruptions weighed on economic momentum, while foreign exchange reserves rose to about $21.5 billion by the end of September.
Headline inflation eased to about 10.3 percent in September after peaking in May, while core inflation remained contained, according to the fund.
The IMF said the State Bank of Pakistan should maintain an appropriately tight monetary policy stance to ensure inflation returns durably to its target range.
The additional financing would support Pakistan’s efforts to strengthen its foreign exchange buffers and sustain its economic recovery.
Pakistan remains exposed to disruptions in Gulf energy supplies, with much of its energy imports passing through the Strait of Hormuz.

Hanwha, TOTE lock in deal for Golden Dome tracking ship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:16:01 UTC
18:16:01 KST

- TOTE Services signed a Maritime Administration contract to manage construction of the first Missile Range Instrumentation Vessel and subcontracted Hanwha Philly Shipyard to build it.
- The ship will support the Missile Defense Agency and Golden Dome, replace two vessels built in 1965 and 1970, and is due in 2030.
TOTE Services has signed a contract with the U.S. Maritime Administration to manage construction of a new missile-tracking ship for the Missile Defense Agency, and has subcontracted Hanwha Philly Shipyard in Philadelphia to build it. The first ship is scheduled for delivery in 2030.
The vessel is the first of the Missile Range Instrumentation Vessel class, a planned series of ships that will track missile flights and intercept tests at sea. The first MRIV, which White House budget director Russ Vought named Golden Defender when the program was announced in July, will support the Golden Dome for America missile defense initiative. The shipyard subcontract covers one firm ship with options for two more. Neither company disclosed the value of the new agreements.
The MRIVs will replace Pacific Tracker and Pacific Collector, two Maritime Administration ships built in 1965 and 1970 that now carry out missile range instrumentation work for the Missile Defense Agency. The companies have said the new ships will observe missile intercept tests over the Pacific Ocean, collect test data and support range safety. TOTE Services already manages and operates both of the older ships.
The design draws heavily on the National Security Multi-Mission Vessel, a training ship class that Hanwha Philly Shipyard has been building for the Maritime Administration’s state maritime academies, also under TOTE’s management. According to TOTE, the MRIV uses the same hull and shares about 70 percent of its overall design with that class. The yard will build the new ship using the production line, supply chain and workforce already in place for the training ships.
“Signing the Missile Range Instrumentation Vessel contract and executing the shipyard subcontract brings us closer to delivering the next generation of U.S. defense capability,” said Jeff Dixon, president of TOTE Services. “Our proven Vessel Construction Management model means we’re hitting the milestones sooner and making meaningful progress faster.”
Under the vessel construction manager model, a commercial firm coordinates the shipyard, suppliers and government customers instead of the government running the program itself. TOTE said the approach let it finalize the design, contract terms and firm fixed pricing in under three months, a process it said can take a year or more in traditional government shipbuilding. The company says the model cuts acquisition costs by at least 50 percent by setting requirements early and approving changes quickly.
TOTE is also the construction manager for the U.S. Navy and U.S. Marine Corps Landing Ship Medium program, a fleet of small amphibious ships, under a contract the U.S. Navy announced in July worth up to $2.2 billion.
The MRIV program is a joint effort of the Department of Transportation, the U.S. Department of War and the Missile Defense Agency, run under TOTE’s existing construction management contract with the Maritime Administration.
“The Missile Defense Agency depends on a strong domestic industrial base to keep our nation safe,” said Sen. Dave McCormick of Pennsylvania. “Announced at my 2026 Pennsylvania Defense & Innovation Summit, the partnership between Hanwha Philly Shipyard and TOTE Services will strengthen our military readiness, expand American shipbuilding capacity, and reinforce Pennsylvania’s critical role in our national security. Pennsylvania has long served as an arsenal of democracy, and this project is another example of our Commonwealth delivering for America.”
Hanwha Philly Shipyard, owned by South Korea’s Hanwha Group since 2024, now employs more than 2,000 production workers, according to TOTE, after the training ship program revived a yard that had shrunk to a few dozen workers. When the program was announced in July, Defense News reported that the effort to build two MRIVs was worth about $2 billion.

The Japanese clothing brand saw its China sales recover over the past year despite ongoing political tensions and China’s consumer slowdown
Fast Retailing, the parent company of Japanese clothing retailer Uniqlo, has defied the ongoing political tensions between Beijing and Tokyo and soft consumer sentiment in China to log a rebound in sales and profits on the Chinese mainland.
The company’s full-year revenue on the Chinese mainland climbed 3 per cent year on year in local currency terms, while business profits rose by roughly 18 per cent. Hong Kong and Taiwan also saw increases in full-year revenue and profit over the period, the group said.

Russia wants Europe used to not reacting, Helsing warns
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:15:13 BST
18:15:13 KST

Russia is not just testing Europe’s reaction, it is training Europe not to react at all, Helsing’s UK boss told #ApexEurope.
Russian testing of European defences is meant to wear down the continent’s willingness to respond at all, the UK managing director of the military artificial intelligence company Helsing told the Apex Europe conference in London on Wednesday.
Ned Baker was speaking on the European Industrial Leadership Panel, chaired by Lieutenant General (Retired) Stuart Skeates, the chairman of Apex Europe, and he took up an argument made in the session immediately before his.
He said: “They’re not just testing us to see our reaction, they’re actually testing us to get us used to not reacting, and that’s the worst possible thing that we can do, is settle into a kind of slightly European malaise. The time for delivery, the time for action, is now.”
Helsing describes itself as an Anglo-German company, and Mr Baker set out the thinking behind its founding. “We were founded in 2021, based on the belief that Europe needed new technologies, new capabilities to defend itself, but also that amongst those technologies, military AI was going to become the defining characteristic of defence in the future, and I think we have seen that play out to a certain extent in Ukraine,” he said. “I think there is a lot more for NATO to do to adopt those technologies.”
“We’ve been very fortunate to raise a little bit over 2.5 billion pounds in capital over Helsing’s life, and it’s our responsibility, obviously, to deploy that capital wisely to build these technologies,” he said. “But the fact that we’ve managed to raise that capital is also a kind of a once-in-a-generation opportunity. If the threat is a once-in-a-generation risk, then the capital that is available to us now is a once-in-a-generation opportunity, and it is here in Europe, and we should take advantage of it.”
What the company does with it includes strike drones supplied into Ukraine over several years, work he described himself as very proud of, and what he called Europe’s first fully autonomous fighter jet.
Asked how companies operationalise the rapid iteration seen in Ukraine, he began with a form of information older than any of the technology. “The first one is such an important one, but it’s a piece of data that’s existed for centuries, millennia, is just user feedback, just basic user feedback, getting hands-on with operators, and as much as we can blurring the lines between technologists and tacticians, so that we can learn what works, what they need, and getting close to the end-user problems,” he said.
Helsing can do that, he said, because it uses its own money to develop products to a level of maturity where they can go out on exercise with the British Army or the German Army and be tried in front of soldiers, with the results fed back into development. On Ukraine he was blunt about what the shortened cycle means for everybody else. “If you do not have that kind of 24-7 service of tell me what’s working, oh, you found something, let’s go and fix it, then that is not peculiar to Ukraine,” he said. “That is just the new normal, and it will become the new way of functioning for the new style of warfare we will have to fight.”
Collecting real-world data to train models is expensive, slow and hard to do at the volume modern systems need, which is the problem behind the company’s most striking claim of the session. Helsing has built internal tooling, not sold as a product, to generate synthetic training data.
He said: “We pump lots of money and lots of brains into it to build synthetic AI data, so we can basically simulate environments. These environments can be changed at the touch of a parameter. Make it night. Make it day. Make it snowy. Make it rainy. Show me a T-72. Show me this. And you get then a synthetic AI data pack that you can train your models on.”
He went on: “That has been revolutionary for us. That has changed those model training cycles from months and potentially years down to hours, and that’s not just training strike drones. That is how we are going to do reinforcement learning for fully autonomous fighter jets, for fully autonomous unmanned surface vessels.”

A Scientist Working on the ‘IceCube’ Neutrino Detector Explains the Nobel Prize–Winning Technology
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:15:00 UTC
18:15:00 KST

“for some reason, I woke up at 5:30, and the first thing I did was go to the New York Times website to check the headlines,” Juan Carlos Díaz Vélez recalls of the previous morning. “To my great surprise, there was a breaking news story: Francis Halzen had just been awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics. I immediately started sending messages, only to discover that my colleagues in Europe had found out long before I did.”
Juan Carlos Díaz Vélez works at the Wisconsin IceCube Particle Astrophysics Center at the University of Wisconsin–Madison. The new Nobel laureate is his boss.
“When I arrived at the WIPAC offices, everyone was smiling and congratulating one another,” Díaz Vélez says. “We gathered in the conference room to watch the press conference with Francis Halzen, who was in Italy at the time attending a conference. We’ll wait for his return to celebrate, and in the meantime, we’ll keep working on the neutrino study, because this work never ends.”
That work is detecting an elusive particle using detectors inside a big block of ice.
“Neutrinos are subatomic particles that participate in reactions within the nuclei of atoms,” Díaz Vélez explains. “They are produced by radioactivity on Earth—and even in watermelons and bananas, due to their potassium-40 content—as well as in our own bodies.”
Not that any of us notice. These particles do not interact easily with matter. As their name suggests, neutrinos have no electric charge, so they can travel through space in a straight line without being affected by magnetic fields, and they constantly pass through the entire Earth without interacting with a single atom. “Neutrinos from the sun are so abundant that 1 billion of them pass through the nail of a thumb every second,” Díaz Vélez says.
The neutrinos studied by Halzen’s team are not the run-of-the-mill particles we’re encountering constantly—if unknowingly. They are interested in very high-energy neutrinos that come from deep space. These cosmic particles may originate from supernova remnants or even black holes. The intense magnetic fields of such phenomena can accelerate particles like protons to very high energies.
“When these particles collide with the interstellar medium—which consists of gas and plasma—they produce gamma rays and neutrinos,” Díaz Vélez says. “That is why neutrinos are perfect messengers from high-energy cosmic-ray sources. The highest-energy neutrino sources we have detected come from active galactic nuclei, which contain supermassive black holes.”
And the team Díaz Vélez is part of has detected such neutrinos at a facility located at the geographic South Pole known as the IceCube Neutrino Observatory—no relation to the famous rapper. The observatory contains an array of 5,160 optical sensors buried deep underground, covering 1 cubic kilometer of ice.
“The South Pole ice sheet is very transparent at a depth of 1.5 kilometers, so the sensors can detect the light produced by subatomic particles called muons, which are generated as a result of rare interactions between neutrinos and ice atoms,” says Díaz Vélez, who also participated in the construction of IceCube in 2010. The observatory began operations the following year.
The project’s first major discovery was the detection of neutrinos from astrophysical sources outside our solar system. One of the most notable sources was TXS 0506+056, located in collaboration with other observatories that collected various gamma-ray, optical, and radio signals. TXS 0506+056 is a high-energy blazar, a galaxy that appears extremely bright and revolves around a supermassive black hole. The researchers looked for other objects with similar characteristics and confirmed that this class of sources is capable of producing high-energy neutrinos. More recently, they have been able to observe the Milky Way as a diffuse source of neutrinos.
In addition to astronomy, IceCube has made significant contributions to our understanding of the nature and behavior of these particles. For example, there are three known types of neutrinos, and last year’s Nobel laureates in physics discovered that these particles can transform from one type to another as they travel. IceCube has enabled increasingly precise measurements of this phenomenon.
“Another area of research is cosmic rays, which is what I focus on,” says Díaz Vélez. “We have discovered that they do not come uniformly from all directions but rather from preferred directions, and this tells us about the distribution of their sources in the galaxy.”
Cosmic rays consist of protons and nuclei of heavier atoms, and they constitute a very high portion of the project’s data. “Detecting a neutrino is like looking for a needle in a haystack,” the researcher says. “For every neutrino IceCube detects, more than a million muons produced by cosmic rays are detected.”
Díaz Vélez serves as the product coordinator for the IceCube collaboration, overseeing the processing of experimental data and the production of simulations. “This involves calculating the direction of arrival, the energy, and the type of particle detected every two milliseconds,” he says. “We also need to simulate cosmic rays and neutrinos at comparable rates. Both tasks require high-performance computing networks distributed around the world, totaling approximately 10,000 CPU cores and 1,000 GPUs.”
The researcher notes that while the IceCube project is based in Antarctica and headquartered in Wisconsin, it’s an international collaboration of 450 people at 58 institutions across 14 countries. Many of those involved in the work are masters and doctoral students, and although the award bears only one scientist’s name, behind that name lies the work of dozens of colleagues.
“It’s worth mentioning that Francis is a great figure and a leader but also a very friendly and generous person,” says Díaz Vélez. “In general, we see him more as a colleague than as a boss. In fact, if it weren’t for his passion and dedication, this experiment would never have been successful.”
This story originally appeared in WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.
