LONDON — The U.K. and Israel have stepped back from the diplomatic brink by securing a compromise to prevent the full closure of the British consulate in East Jerusalem.
Most diplomats will leave what will now be operating as a “U.K. Mission” in the occupied territory — but Israel has stopped short of closing it entirely ahead of Thursday’s deadline.
Both sides were presenting this as a good outcome Thursday, in a diplomatic tussle over the U.K.’s plans to impose sanctions on illegal settlements in the West Bank.
Advertisement
U.K. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the diplomats and their families were being “temporarily withdrawn” to secure their safety, but he said the mission will remain independent, operational and continue to work with the Palestinian people.
“We will work in the coming months to build back up our presence, and we will not take reciprocal action while such discussions are underway and credible,” he continued, in a statement released as he was visiting Ukraine.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar set out a list of diplomatic actions taken against Britain, adding: “We established a clear principle: It is not possible to act against Israel without Israel taking appropriate measures in response.”
Sa’ar said the consulate would be “closing its operations today” and that the “sign of the British Consulate in Jerusalem has been removed.” Twenty British diplomats, including the consul general, will be leaving East Jerusalem.
The dispute over the consulate has been the latest marker of declining relations between Israel and the U.K. under its Labour government. Israel threatened to close the consulate within 30 days of Sept. 8, in retaliation against Andy Burnham’s government announcing a ban on trade with illegal settlements in the West Bank.
Advertisement
A person familiar with Israeli government thinking, granted anonymity to discuss a sensitive matter, told POLITICO the mission is “basically an empty shell” that cannot issue visas, renew passports or liaise with the Palestinian Authority. Britain does not tend to issue visas or passports in consulates.
“The seven diplomats there, their work is basically to maintain the building and hold the Union Jack in place,” they said.
A British official presented the deal as a “good outcome” nonetheless. After three weeks of hard-fought negotiations, a feared spiral of tit-for-tat expulsions has been avoided.
The U.K. has told Israel it is keeping the possibility of retaliation open, however, after Israel threatened to expel British diplomats from Israel. The Israeli government had been demanding that the U.K. rolls back its pending package of sanctions on West Bank settlements, but British ministers are holding firm.
Miliband maintained Thursday that Britain does not accept Israel has a “legal right” to shutter the site that has been there for nearly 200 years, because East Jerusalem is deemed “occupied territory.”
The hope in the U.K. Foreign Office is that maintaining a presence will make it easier to build back up after elections in Israel on Oct. 27.
U.K. National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell traveled to Jerusalem last week as part of efforts to persuade the Israeli government not to shut the consulate, but a breakthrough wasn’t reached until Wednesday night.
“The foreign secretary was very clear on our red lines. We’re not reopening the sanctions package and we have to keep our presence in East Jerusalem,” said the U.K. official cited above. “We were very clear about that with the Israelis. We had lots of back and forth with them through officials. It took time but we had been confident we could get to a decent place.”

"Attempts by Western countries and Ukraine to somehow prevent citizens from exercising their electoral rights led, on the contrary, to citizens of our country viewing their electoral rights as an opportunity to show and convey to the outside world: we do not respond to this, it only unites us, we are ready to defend our social and political life and preserve stability here. And look at the voter turnout. Therefore, the effect that our opponents expected turned out to be exactly the opposite," he said.
The elections of deputies to the ninth State Duma were held during the single voting day from September 18 to 20. For the first time, residents of the Donbass and Novorossiya regions participated in them.

Warsaw records EU’s highest employment rate

The Warsaw region, which includes Poland’s capital and its suburbs, had the highest employment rate in the European Union last year, according to new Eurostat data.
The employment rate among people aged 20-64 in the region stood at 86.9%, more than 10 percentage points above the figure for the EU as a whole. It was also the highest recorded for Warsaw since data began to be collected in 2013.
Last year, only four EU regions had employment rates of at least 85%. Warsaw was followed by Prague in the Czech Republic at 86%, Finland’s Åland Islands at 85.5%, and Utrecht in the Netherlands at 85.4%.
The EU average stood at 76.1%, slightly below the target of 78% the bloc set for itself for 2030.
At the other end of the scale, 64 of the EU’s 244 regions had employment rates below 74% last year. The lowest was recorded in France’s overseas departments of Mayotte (36.9%) and French Guiana (50%), followed by Italy’s Calabria (50.3%), Campania (50.8%) and Sicily (51.4%).
After Warsaw, the second-highest employment rate in Poland was recorded in the central Łódź province (80.8%) while the lowest was in the southeastern Subcarpathian province (73.2%). The figure for the country as a whole was 78.8%, which was only the 13th highest in the EU.
In addition to topping the overall employment rate ranking, Warsaw also had the third lowest rate of youth employment (for people aged 15-29) at 3.9%, higher only than Yugozapaden in Bulgaria (3.8%) and Zeeland in the Netherlands (3.6%).
And it had the third-highest rate of employment among people with tertiary education (93.5%), behind only Portugal’s Região Autónoma dos Açores (94.6%) and Yugozapaden (93.6%).

The most recent Eurostat figures, from August, show that Poland’s unemployment rate (3.3%) was the second-lowest among all member states and well below the EU-wide figure of 6.2%.
The strong labour market reflects years of economic growth, rising wages and increased employment. However, Poland’s ageing and shrinking population is creating labour shortages and encouraging companies to invest more heavily in automation.
At the same time, job creation is slowing, while some industries – including manufacturing, automotive, furniture and construction materials – are coming under pressure, according to experts.

US drone firm urges Taiwan to buy autonomous surface vessels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
08:19:29 UTC
17:19:29 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Former US official and Saronic executive Mira Resnick said Wednesday that Taiwan should expand its fleet of autonomous surface vessels to deter Chinese incursions, CNA reported.
The Taiwan External Trade Development Council hosted the 2026 Aerospace and Defense Strategic Forum, a one-day event featuring speakers from defense contractors including Anduril, AeroVironment, and Saronic. Resnick, a former US deputy assistant secretary of state and now Saronic’s senior director for global policy and defense cooperation, spoke about the importance of multipurpose autonomous surface vessels.
Resnick said most of the unmanned boats Taiwan plans to procure are intended for one-way attack missions. She said China has consistently used gray-zone attrition tactics to exhaust Taiwan’s maritime forces and suggested that Taiwan instead purchase multipurpose autonomous surface vessels as more effective deterrents.
Resnick said Taiwan should prioritize lethal, mobile, reliable, and cost-effective weapons systems. She added that Taiwan plans to purchase more than 200,000 unmanned systems, but only about 1,300 are boats intended for one-way missions that would be deployed only during wartime.
Resnick cited an Oct. 1 defense ministry report that recorded 23 PLA aircraft, seven PLA Navy ships, and seven Chinese government vessels around Taiwan during the preceding 24 hours. She added that China uses dredgers and maritime militia vessels to probe Taiwan’s waters, including those around Kinmen and Matsu.
Resnick said China prefers attrition to a full-scale invasion, wearing down Taiwan’s Navy and Coast Guard fleets. She suggested investing in autonomous surface vessels rather than continuing to chase Chinese ships.
Multipurpose autonomous surface vessels can perform round-trip missions such as monitoring, escorting, and relaying signals, Resnick said. Their modular designs allow them to perform different tasks and free personnel for more critical duties, she added.
Resnick highlighted two important aspects of autonomy. First, China is investing heavily in electronic warfare and anti-satellite technology that could render drones useless by disrupting their communications. Second, remotely controlled vessels still require skilled operators, whereas one person should be able to oversee a fleet of autonomous vessels.
Resnick said the government should field-test all vendors to verify performance amid unusual radar returns, fishing nets, and rough seas. She added that US vendors should integrate Taiwanese sensors and command-and-control systems and establish local maintenance capacity rather than simply selling complete vessels.
This would support joint production and help Taiwan develop an autonomous operational system while balancing speed and sovereignty, she said.

For the fourth quarter, Goldman Sachs forecasts continued revenue growth for LandMark, supported by the rollout of next-generation AI server racks, the shift to faster 1.6T optical modules, and the company’s ongoing capacity expansion. The investment bank also expects higher demand for optical communications components such as continuous-wave lasers as AI servers require faster data transmission, supporting growth in the sector, according to TechNews.

Researchers: International plague outbreak highly unlikely
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
08:18:41 UTC
17:18:41 KST

In the Russian city of Irkutsk, a laboratory worker at a plague research institute has died of pneumonia of unknown origin; Russian authorities have stated that the death is unrelated to her professional duties, the BBC reports.
Darya Shipilova, 28, died on the 2nd of October following possible exposure to pathogens, and nearly 200 of her contacts were subsequently placed in quarantine. While officials have sought to allay concerns, various speculations regarding the incident are circulating online.
Shipilova worked at the Irkutsk Plague Research Institute. Unconfirmed reports suggest she fell ill and developed symptoms characteristic of pneumonia either after dropping a test tube containing the plague bacterium Yersinia pestis or following a research trip to the Buryatia region near the Mongolian border, where the plague is endemic among animals.
As of the 7th of October, the cause of Shipilova's death had not been officially confirmed, and laboratory investigations were ongoing. One thing is clear, however: experts believe that even if the death was caused by pneumonic plague, it is unlikely to lead to an international outbreak of the disease. Plague is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. Clinically, it manifests in three forms: bubonic plague, pneumonic plague, and septicemic plague (which represents the fatal outcome of all clinical forms of the disease). 
Bubonic plague is the most common form and is transmitted by infected fleas; the incubation period ranges from two to eight days.
The bacteria enter the lymph nodes, and a painful bubo develops within six to eight hours. Human-to-human transmission of bubonic plague is rare, but the bacteria can enter the bloodstream, causing septicemic plague, or the lungs, causing pneumonic plague.
Unlike the other two forms, pneumonic plague can be transmitted to other people via respiratory droplets. If not detected early and treated with antibiotics, pneumonic plague is also fatal; furthermore, it has a much shorter incubation period—as little as 24 hours.
The so-called Black Death—caused by bubonic and pneumonic plague—killed more than 25 million people in 14th-century Europe, wiping out between one-third and two-thirds of the population. The spread of the plague was facilitated by new trade routes and the transport of grain and flour by ship, which also attracted rodents.
However, modern conditions are far less favorable for the spread of the plague.
 First, although Yersinia pestis is almost always fatal if left untreated, it can now be easily eliminated with simple, widely available antibiotics. Piero Olliaro, Professor of Poverty-Related Infectious Diseases at the University of Oxford, noted that there are two drugs that are highly effective against bubonic plague.
Another reason why a widespread pandemic is virtually impossible is that—unlike COVID-19—pneumonic plague is infectious only after symptoms have appeared; these symptoms usually manifest within 24 hours and are severe and obvious. This means that an outbreak can be quickly detected, and individuals can be isolated and treated before transmission occurs. Zania Stamataki, a professor of immunology at the University of Birmingham, stated that pneumonic plague is not something easily overlooked—the sort of illness where an infected person might board a plane and manage to spread the disease across half the globe.
According to information from the World Health Organization, all of Shipilova’s contacts have been identified and are being monitored, and none are showing symptoms of the disease. In a risk assessment published on the 6th of October, WHO representative Christian Lindmeier rated the risk of an outbreak in Irkutsk as moderate to low, in Russia as low, and for the WHO European region as very low.
In general, contracting the disease in a laboratory setting is a very rare occurrence, as strict operating protocols are usually in place.
 Stamataki noted that these are highly specialized laboratories with a range of protective measures in effect. The professor explained that researchers wear full protective gear and handle samples inside special safety cabinets that maintain negative air pressure; this means air is drawn inward and away from the researcher, so that even if a sample breaks, the contents remain inside the cabinet rather than escaping into the air around the researcher. Even when the test tube is being moved, it is placed inside another container to prevent the contents from escaping into the external environment.
One of the main reasons the plague had such devastating consequences in the 14th century was the living conditions of the time. Streets accumulated waste and food scraps, creating ideal conditions for black rat nests—and, consequently, for fleas. People lived in close proximity to one another, and merchants on ships spent months in extremely cramped quarters. Today, living conditions in most parts of the world are far better.
However, it is important to understand that the plague is not a disease of the past. It remains endemic in rodent populations across Africa, Asia, South America, and even parts of the United States. Human cases are still detected annually; for instance, an average of seven cases of plague are reported in the US each year. Localized outbreaks occur sporadically in some parts of the world, with instances of human-to-human transmission of pneumonic plague also being recorded.

SMEs drive AI job market boom in Switzerland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
08:17:54 UTC
17:17:54 KST

SMEs drive AI job market boom in Switzerland
Artificial intelligence is creating new opportunities in the Swiss labour market. However, not everyone is benefiting equally from the growing demand for AI specialists.
The job market for artificial intelligence (AI) is booming in Switzerland. Between July 2025 and June 2026, just under 5,000 AI vacancies were advertised. This was 32% more than in the previous year, as shown by a study published on Thursday by the Lucerne University of Applied Sciences and Arts (HSLU).
Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) were the main drivers of this boom. They accounted for 76% of the growth in job vacancies. “AI is no longer just the preserve of large technology companies, but is increasingly being integrated into the processes and services of established SMEs,” said the study’s author, Curdin Derungs, according to the press release.
The IT sector offered the most jobs, with 1,211 vacancies (+49 per cent). However, AI specialists were also sought after by banks and insurance companies such as Axa, Julius Bär and the Swiss National Bank, as well as by pharmaceutical firms such as Roche, Novartis and Lonza. In the engineering sector, Siemens, Hitachi Energy and ABB are among the leading employers.
+ As big pharma meets AI, new career paths open in Switzerland
The public sector recorded the strongest growth at 67%. The largest employers in this sector include the Canton and City of Zurich, as well as the Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH). “The growth in AI roles within the public sector in particular suggests that policymakers and public authorities are strengthening their confidence in AI as a technology of the future,” said Derungs.
Regionally, Zurich was clearly in the lead with 2,181 vacancies, accounting for 45% of all AI roles. It was followed by the cantons of Geneva with around 620 and Bern with around 590 roles.
A challenging situation for those starting their careers
There was particular demand for experienced professionals capable of developing and implementing AI systems. The number of vacancies for experienced specialists rose by 42%. For those starting their careers, however, the market remained challenging. Only 5% of the vacancies were for permanent junior roles.
Even for entry-level positions, two to three years’ professional experience was often required, according to the study. University graduates told the authors of months-long job searches and dozens of unsuccessful applications.
“New entrants to the labour market describe the job market as extremely competitive,” study author Derungs added. He was surprised to find that even experienced professionals were increasingly facing difficulties in their job searches.

What’s Happening in Irkutsk? Plague Checklists, Quarantines, and a Researcher’s Death
Restrictions remained in place at several medical facilities in Russia’s Irkutsk region on October 7, while patients at a perinatal center were asked to complete questionnaires for suspected plague infections.
People of Baikal reported the measures in a Telegram post on October 7, rejecting claims by pro-government channels that earlier reports about hospital restrictions had been disproved.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The outlet stated that restrictions continued at Irkutsk Regional Clinical Hospital, where visitors were barred, and patients were not allowed to leave the building. The hospital continued to accept new patients despite internal restrictions.
Measures also remained in place at the Irkutsk Regional Psychoneurological Dispensary. A patient told People of Baikal that the facility had limited time outdoors and later posted a notice restricting visits and requiring masks.
At the Irkutsk City Perinatal Center, patients were asked to complete a “checklist for suspected particularly dangerous infection ‘Plague,’” according to photographs published by the outlet. People of Baikal released fuller images after pro-government channels claimed an earlier photograph of the form had been fabricated.
“I couldn’t have made something like this up,” said blogger Ulyana Gavryunina, who provided the photographs.
The October 7 update reinforced details previously described by People of Baikal co-founder Olga Mutovina in an interview with Meduza about the response to the death of 28-year-old Daria Shpilova. Mutovina explained that journalists determined where restrictions were in effect by contacting hospitals and patients, as authorities had not published a comprehensive list.
Shpilova, an employee of the Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East, died overnight on October 2 in Shelekhov. Authorities described her illness as pneumonia of unknown cause, while reports circulated that she may have contracted pneumonic plague.
Mutovina reported that around 200 people who had contact with Shpilova were isolated, while employees of the anti-plague institute underwent repeated testing during a three-day quarantine. The people of Baikal had no confirmed information about any additional patients with the same illness.
Residents of Shpilova’s apartment building also reported seeing workers wearing gas masks and protective suits disinfecting entrances on October 2. Residents described a strong chemical odor and said workers offered little explanation about the operation.
The response extended beyond individual hospitals. Mutovina reported that Russia’s chief sanitary official traveled to the region, while people who had contact with Shpilova were isolated and, in some cases, accompanied by security personnel to medical examinations.
The uncertainty surrounding Shpilova’s death has fueled speculation about a possible laboratory accident, although People of Baikal emphasized that the cause of her illness remains unconfirmed. The ongoing hospital restrictions and plague-related questionnaires have left those questions open, as authorities provide limited public information about the measures.
The official handling of the case has been marked by shifting messages from regional leaders and the quiet disappearance of public warnings.
The Irkutsk region's governor, Igor Kobzev, referred only to a suspected particularly dangerous infection, while Buryatia's head, Alexey Tsydenov, initially linked the death to plague before softening his wording.
Authorities in Baikalsk removed an advisory urging residents to avoid travel to Shelekhov, and antibiotics reportedly vanished from some pharmacy shelves amid panic buying as public events were canceled.

Russia Shifts Strategy to Direct Sabotage Against Danish Suppliers Fueling Ukraine’s Defense
The Danish Security and Intelligence Service (PET) has announced that Russia has launched sabotage operations aimed at Danish companies supplying goods to Ukraine, as reported by Reuters.
Speaking at an internal security conference in Copenhagen, lead analyst Josefine Christensen stated that this shift reflects a major escalation in Moscow’s ongoing hybrid warfare strategy.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The intelligence service noted that while significant planning was observed in the spring, actual execution was minimal until early summer, when operational activity increased substantially.
According to Christensen, Russian officials concluded that their earlier large-scale attacks had failed to deter Western NATO member states from supporting Ukraine during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Reuters reported.
Moscow maintains political oversight over these missions, though operational boldness continues to grow. PET noted that Russian operations are now focused on hitting targets that directly affect the front line, specifically targeting weapons manufacturing.
To carry out these actions, Russia is increasingly hiring untrained local operatives, including individuals experiencing homelessness or substance abuse issues, through Telegram and other online platforms.
Recruitment often starts with minor assignments such as surveillance or photography before expanding into active sabotage. Christensen noted that recruiters seek anyone looking for quick money, adding that if one individual fails, another is quickly assigned until the objective is completed.
Earlier, in June 2026, a Russian corvette intercepted a Danish unmanned sea drone during trials southeast of Bornholm, approaching within about 200 meters before launching a reconnaissance drone to inspect the vessel at close range.

Three-year-old girl rescued from under rubble in Pryluky lost grandmother and uncle in Russian attack
On the morning of 7 October, following the deadly Russian attack on Pryluky, an emergency worker carried three-year-old Zlata, who had been pulled out of the rubble, away from one of the buildings. A photo of the firefighter holding the child in his arms quickly spread across social media.
The little girl and her mother are currently in hospital.
Source: Vladyslav Stoianov, chief of the Pryluky District Department of the National Police, in a comment to Suspilne Chernihiv
Details: Stoianov said Zlata's family lives in the village of Lynovytsia, 15 km from Pryluky. The day before the tragedy, Zlata and her mum had come to Pryluky to see her aunt, while her dad stayed at home.
Liudmyla, Zlata's grandma, had also come to see the family.
Zlata's aunt, police officer Yuliia Malysh, was injured and remains in hospital in a serious condition. Yuliia's husband, 47-year-old police veteran Oleh Malysh, and her mother, Liudmyla, were killed in the attack.
Background:
- Russian forces attacked Pryluky with missiles on 7 October. The attack hit an apartment building, a creative arts centre for children and young people, and a business.
- As of the morning of 8 October, 22 people are known to have been killed, including five children. Another 54 people were injured.
- Among those killed were 58-year-old Viktoriia Bondarenko, her daughter Kateryna Antypenko and her one-year-old grandson Sashko. Viktoriia's older granddaughter Olha survived the attack because she was in another room when the strike occurred.

- The local authorities have declared 7, 8 and 9 October days of mourning in Pryluky.

Why Israel loves skunk water
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
08:15:52 UTC
17:15:52 KST

Why Israel loves skunk water
Israel’s foul-smelling weapon turns Palestinian repression into a sales pitch.
In the eyes of Israeli authorities, Palestinians in Gaza have it “too good”. Three years into Israel’s genocide, the survivors have been pushed into ever smaller areas of land amid rubble, rubbish and disease, without adequate shelter or sanitation. Apparently, even that is too much.
In late September, a foul smell spread across Gaza City overnight. At first, residents searched for its source around them, wondering whether it was coming from a toilet or even one of their sleeping children. Then reports of the same stench began coming in from across the city. Israeli aircraft had reportedly dropped hundreds of packets containing a foul-smelling substance over populated areas.
“Today, all of us in Gaza City woke up to a foul, rotten smell in the truest sense of the word … Israeli occupation drones were spraying this foul stench to pollute the air. Even the air?” said one witness to AJ+.
Israel has, in fact, spent nearly two decades weaponising foul smells against Palestinians.
Skunk water, the leading Israeli olfactory ordnance now believed to be in use in Gaza, was developed in 2004 by the Israeli company Odortec in partnership with Israel Police’s Technological Development Department, and first deployed against Palestinian protesters in Nilin in 2008. It is classified as a “scent-based non-lethal weapon” for crowd control and can be fired from water cannon or dropped from drones.
From Nilin, its use spread across the occupied West Bank. It became a regular feature of demonstrations in Bilin, Kafr Qaddum and Nabi Saleh, where Israeli forces repeatedly used it against Palestinians protesting settlements, land seizures and restrictions on movement. In 2011, Israeli forces fired tear gas and skunk water on unarmed demonstrators who had attended the burial of a 28-year-old killed by the Israeli army in Nabi Saleh and were then making their way to the village spring that had been “appropriated by the neighbouring settlement, Halamish”. Similar incidents were reported there in 2012 and 2013.
The practice soon spread beyond those West Bank villages. In 2013, activists demonstrating against the closure of Shuhada Street in Hebron and journalists covering the protest were sprayed with the putrid liquid. The following year, Israeli police drove skunk trucks through Palestinian neighbourhoods in East Jerusalem, spraying homes, streets and schools. In at-Tur, four schools were hit, forcing some 4,500 pupils to stay home because of the smell.
By 2018, Israel was also deploying it from the air. During the Great March of Return, the Israeli military used the Shoko drone to douse Palestinian protesters in Gaza with the foul-smelling liquid from a payload of plastic bags.
For Israeli authorities, its usefulness goes well beyond crowd control. Sure, spray it on a protest and people scatter. But spray it over streets, homes and neighbourhoods, and it becomes a tool for making Palestinian space itself unliveable.
That goes some way towards explaining Israel’s enduring enthusiasm for skunk water. There is another reason, too: Israel sells to the world the methods it has developed to control Palestinians.
When skunk water was first deployed in 2008, it was reported that Israeli police had “high hopes of turning it into a commercial venture and selling it to law-enforcement agencies overseas”. Superintendent David Ben Harosh even went on air hugging a “litre bottle of dirty, green liquid” and boasting: “It’s totally harmless, you can even drink it.”
Its use against Palestinians – whom Israel has long characterised as a symbol of pathological evil – also feeds the country’s global reputation as a pioneer of counterinsurgency and policing technologies. Every deployment offers another demonstration of Israeli expertise in controlling the population it presents as uniquely dangerous.
By then, Israel had already begun exporting it. In 2007, Beit Alfa Technologies supplied skunk water to the South African Police Service along with “water cannons and riot-control gear”. These were later used against demonstrators during the Fees Must Fall protests in 2015.
In 2017, India’s Central Reserve Police Force tested skunk water for crowd control in places including Jammu and Kashmir. The Who Profits Research Center has also said it was approached by a company seeking help contacting Odortec to buy the liquid for sale to Colombian police.
In the United States, Mistral Security supplies skunk water, claiming that “the stench of Skunk immediately causes individuals and crowds to cease their activities while allowing Law Enforcement to gain control with minimum injuries and casualties”.
The company’s marketing makes the connection to Palestine unusually explicit: its website uses a photograph of Israeli forces deploying skunk water against Palestinians in the West Bank. The Palestinians subjected to the weapon become part of the proof that it works.
Following the 2014 Ferguson protests, Mistral supplied skunk water to several US police departments. This included the St Louis Metropolitan Police Department in Missouri, which acquired the liquid in 2015 following the protests in Ferguson.
A Quartz report on the shipment to Missouri captured what makes the weapon attractive. “The poisoning of a place”, it observed, can destroy people’s willingness to “reside, congregate, protest, or even document a location” until it is cleaned away. It described skunk water as potentially “a system for maintaining new apartheids”.
What Israel sells, then, is more than a foul-smelling liquid. Skunk water comes wrapped in the reputation Israel has built through decades of controlling Palestinians: a state presented as uniquely experienced in suppressing unrest, countering insurgency and dealing with populations cast as dangerous. Palestinians are central to that brand. Their repression demonstrates the technology; their demonisation helps justify the expertise built around controlling them.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

India defends satellite internet approval process after Elon Musk jab
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
08:15:45 UTC
17:15:45 KST

India defends satellite internet approval process after Elon Musk jab
Musk has claimed unnamed entities are blocking Starlink’s launch to maintain their monopoly.
India has refuted billionaire Elon Musk’s claim that “certain oligarchs” are blocking the launch of his Starlink satellite communication services in the country.
Musk said in an X post on Wednesday that Starlink was being blocked so that unnamed individuals can “maintain their monopolistic chokehold on the Indian people”, adding that it was a “crime against the people of India”.
But India’s Ministry of Communications defended its satellite internet approval process as being fair and non-discriminatory in a statement on Thursday.
“The suggestion that the framework or its application is unfair or discriminatory is baseless and misconceived,” the ministry said without naming Starlink or Musk.
It added that three different entities were at broadly the same regulatory stage and that all were undergoing security assessments.
India’s telecommunications sector is dominated by Reliance Jio, owned by billionaire Mukesh Ambani, and Bharti Airtel, owned by Sunil Mittal.
Both have also ventured into satellite internet. While they have secured early approvals to launch, they are still awaiting final clearances.
Musk has previously had run-ins with Ambani and Mittal over how India should grant them spectrum access. Last year, the two agreed to distribute Starlink systems alongside theirs, but the cooperation appears to have soured.
Starlink has waited since 2022 for licences to operate commercially in India. Last year, it received a key licence from the Communications Ministry to launch, as well as a go-ahead from India’s space agency.
Concerns over security have mounted since 2024 after authorities said they found Starlink devices in a drug seizure operation in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, as well as in another army operation in Manipur state.
At the time, Musk alleged Starlink’s satellite beams were thereafter “turned off over India” and that they were “never on in the first place”.

The Constitutional Court ruled to keep Gibran as VP, but doubts over his education spark impeachment calls and threaten his political future
4-MIN READ4-MIN
 Listen
A legal challenge to the vice-presidency of Indonesia’s Gibran Rakabuming Raka could haunt his political future even though he has survived damning court findings on his educational qualifications.
The Constitutional Court on Tuesday dismissed a petition to unseat the son of former president Joko Widodo, ruling that the plaintiffs lacked legal standing. But it also found no convincing evidence that Gibran’s overseas education met the minimum high-school qualification required for presidential candidates.
Legal experts say the ruling has shifted the battleground to parliament and law enforcement agencies, potentially opening a Pandora’s box for Gibran.
Political observers, however, doubt President Prabowo Subianto would risk a confrontation that could destabilise his government. Gibran, who ran on the 2024 ticket alongside Prabowo – capturing 58.59 per cent of the vote – is likely to retain his office for now, but analysts say he will be dogged by questions over his future political career.

Lower House set for final vote on new election law
Italy

The Lower House is holding the final
vote on Thursday on a bill presented by the parties of Premier
Giorgia Meloni's ruling coalition to bring in a new election law
passed.
                                    
The ruling alliance say the new system will make it more likely
that elections produce a clear winner.
                                    
The opposition, however, has cried foul, saying the ruling
alliance is changing the system because it fears losing the
general election set to take place next year and wants to
minimize the chances of this happening.
                                    
Thursday's final vote is a secret ballot and the ruling
coalition suffered an embarrassing defeat in a previous secret
vote on the bill during its first reading in the Lower House.
                                    
But surprises of this nature are not expected on Thursday, after
the bill got the got the green light with ease in three crucial
confidence votes earlier this week thanks to a show of unity
from the ruling alliance.
                                    
The bill will see the current system, a mix of
first-past-the-post and proportional representation, replaced
with a proportional-representation system with bonus seats for
the coalition that obtains the most votes, as long as it reaches
a threshold of 42%, to ensure it has a working majority in
parliament.
                                    
If no coalition reaches the threshold, or the votes for the
Lower House and the Senate produce different results, a purely
proportional system is used.
                                    
The opposition have said that, among other things, the
envisioned system of bonus seats is unconstitutional and are
ready to appeal to the Constitutional Court.
                                    
Coalitions will have to say who their candidate to be premier is
before the election.
                                    
The bill will also give voters the option to express preferences
for up to three candidates out of six on a party list in which
candidates names must alternate according to gender.
                                    
The opposition says that in reality this gives "fake
preferences" as the head of the ticket would always be
"blocked", arguing this was also be a step back for equality,
as, in theory, it would be possible for all the ticket heads to
be men.
                                    
The current system does not give voters any option to express
preferences about which of the candidates on a party list they
want to represent them.

Lauri Hussar: Continuity of statehood cannot be changed with a vote in parliament
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
08:12:00 UTC
17:12:00 KST

Lauri Hussar: Continuity of statehood cannot be changed with a vote in parliament
The continuity of the Estonian state cannot depend on a simple majority vote by a single composition of parliament, Lauri Hussar writes.
Over the weekend, I attended the reburial in his native soil on Saaremaa of Otto Pukk, speaker of the last Chamber of Deputies of the Republic of Estonia. This solemn occasion also provided an opportunity to reflect on the foundations of the Republic of Estonia.
Otto Pukk was one of the people who upheld the continuity of the Estonian state. In January 1945, in Stockholm, he joined other representatives of Estonia's constitutional institutions in signing a document addressing Estonia's constitutional continuity and the exercise of the duties of the president. In this way, Estonia's parliamentary continuity was carried across the Baltic Sea.
Pukk remained speaker of the Chamber of Deputies until his death in Stockholm in 1951. The Republic of Estonia was occupied, but its legal continuity had not been broken.
That continuity was upheld by people who did not accept the occupation as marking the end of the Estonian state. Otto Pukk was one of them. Another was Otto Tief who in September 1944, on the instructions of Jüri Uluots, formed Estonia's lawful government. Its time in office was brief, but its significance for the continuity of the Estonian state was far greater than the few days during which the government was actually able to operate.
The Tief government declared Estonia's national independence restored and sought to reestablish Estonia's constitutional order at a time when the country was emerging from one occupation only to fall under another. This is one of the crucial links connecting the Republic of Estonia established in 1918 with the Republic of Estonia restored in 1991.
If the Republic of Estonia had ceased to exist in 1940 and a new state had been established in 1991, our understanding of the Estonian state would be entirely different. The principle of state continuity, however, says something else: The occupation interrupted the Estonian state's actual exercise of power, but it did not bring the Republic of Estonia to an end. That is why every step taken to preserve that continuity was worth its weight in gold.
It was precisely from this perspective that last week's vote in the Riigikogu on a statement condemning the events of 1934 and the authoritarian rule that followed raised a serious question for me. Twenty-eight members of the Riigikogu voted for the statement and nine against.
The events of 1934 can, of course, be critically studied, discussed and assessed. But should parliament deliver a definitive political judgment on our country's history and a historical event in a way that could make one interpretation of history effectively mandatory?
The Riigikogu's role is to pass laws and make decisions on behalf of present-day Estonia. The role of historians is to study the past. We can debate history and indeed we should, but we should not try to settle historical knowledge once and for all through a parliamentary majority vote. This is especially true because the causes of the events of 1934, their consequences and their links to subsequent events still require historical research.
It makes little sense to reduce the loss of Estonia's independence to a single domestic political event, as the explanatory memorandum accompanying the statement did because doing so unfortunately also provides Russian propagandists with blanks they can use to sow confusion.
The decisive step in the destruction of Estonia's independence was the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact and its secret protocols, followed by the occupation that the Soviet Union imposed on Estonia on the basis of those agreements. In this light, I agree with my colleague Eerik-Niiles Kross who said from the parliamentary rostrum: "I am not calling for us to justify suspending the activities of political parties, censoring the press or consigning the Riigikogu to the Era of Silence. But 92 years later, the Riigikogu should not take one historical interpretation, stamp it with the seal of the state and then bask in its own righteousness."
To understand the continuity of the Estonian state, we must look at our history as a whole. The occupying power's aim was not merely to destroy the institutions of the Estonian state. It also destroyed the people who carried within them the Republic of Estonia's institutional memory and continuity. State and parliamentary figures who remained in Estonia were arrested, imprisoned, deported and killed. By destroying them, the occupying authorities sought to sever the link between the independent Republic of Estonia and future generations.
That is why historical memory and state continuity still concern us today: History must be studied and debated and, when new sources emerge, reassessed where necessary. The continuity of the Estonian state cannot depend on a simple majority vote by a single composition of parliament. Our task is to pass this country on to the next generation together with its memory, history and continuity.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski

Hong Kong IPO boom at risk as cornerstone backers get cold feet, sources say
At least one listing postponed, while bankers scramble for investors to keep other offerings on track, according to sources
3-MIN READ3-MIN
3
 Listen
Exuberance among cornerstone investors in Hong Kong’s booming initial public offering (IPO) market seems to be fading, forcing some issuers that had hoped to list this month to postpone their offerings.
With more than 60 per cent of new listings in the third quarter now trading below their issue prices, cornerstone investors – who typically receive guaranteed allocations in exchange for holding shares for six months – are reconsidering whether to subscribe to coming deals, according to people familiar with the matter.
At least one IPO originally planned for October had to be delayed until next month at the earliest after some institutional investors pulled out of verbal agreements to be cornerstone backers, they said.

Urogynecologist convicted of raping nine women sentenced to 14 years imprisonment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
08:10:10 UTC
17:10:10 KST

Content warning: This article discusses sensitive topics such as sexual assault.
Menahem Alkalai, a senior urogynecologist, was sentenced by the Tel Aviv District Court on Thursday morning to 14 years in prison after being unanimously convicted of 10 counts of rape by deception against nine patients over more than eight years.
The offenses were committed by the 71-year-old man between 2013 and 2021 against women who were between 23 and 66 at the time. The court found that Alkalai had presented the sexual acts as part of legitimate medical examinations or treatment.
The court also imposed a two-year suspended sentence, effective for three years after his release, and ordered Alkalai to pay a total of NIS 920,000 in compensation.
It recommended that the Health Ministry regulate the presence of chaperones during gynecological examinations, beyond the current voluntary arrangement, to help prevent similar assaults.
Senior Judge Yaron Levy, writing for the unanimous panel with Judges Ilan Zur and Tamar Snunit-Forer, wrote that Alkalai “exploited his position as an expert physician, and the setting of the medical examination, for sexual contact. Specifically, he deliberately massaged the clitoris of each of the nine complainants with prolonged, continuous and focused movements while inserting his fingers into their vaginas, without their informed consent and while falsely presenting the acts as a legitimate medical procedure.”
Levy added that before beginning his actions, Alkalai had told some of the complainants that he intended to massage their clitorises, while making other remarks of a sexual nature to others. As a result of his actions, some of the complainants experienced sexual arousal, and some experienced orgasm.
Victims suffered profound harm to their sense of safety and security, court finds
Victim-impact reports concerning seven of the nine women painted a “harsh and complex” picture of harm extending to “almost every aspect and level” of their lives. Above all, the court noted, their sense of security and safety had been harmed at a “fundamental and deep level.”
Most avoid treatment providers, particularly gynecologists and male doctors, and some avoid medical care in ways that could endanger their health, the reports showed. When they do seek treatment, they are more suspicious and on guard.
They also struggle with feelings of guilt, fear, anxiety, and shame. Many experienced reduced daily functioning that harmed their professional or educational progress.
Assaults affected victims' parenting, relationships, and sense of safety
The reports added that the assaults had damaged some of the women’s sense of competence as parents. As mothers of daughters, they felt a heightened sense of danger and took steps they believed would protect their children, such as ensuring that they saw only female gynecologists. Some also experienced harm to their intimate relationships with their partners.
Some had still not entered treatment, fearing that confronting the trauma and reopening the wound would disrupt their lives. Even for those who had begun treatment, the reports noted, “the road to rehabilitation remains long.”
Alkalai’s defense submitted recommendation letters he had received for positions for which he had applied, letters from senior figures in the medical field and former military commanders attesting to his “positive character,” and thank-you letters from former patients.
The prosecution sought a 17-year prison sentence. Prosecutor Meital Mor noted that police questioned Alkalai in 2019 about conduct that later formed the fourth count, but he went on to commit offenses against three more patients in 2020 and 2021.
Judge highlights patients' vulnerability and breach of trust during gynecological examinations
Levy cited retired Supreme Court justice Mishael Cheshin, who wrote about rape in a 2000 ruling: “The self is trampled, the soul is wounded, freedom is violated, the autonomy of the will is diminished, and dignity is crushed.”
Levy further noted that during a gynecological examination, a patient is at her most vulnerable and places complete trust in the doctor. Her trust in the integrity of the examination, he wrote, is essential and “the only shield against harm to her.”
Attorneys Tami Kalenberg-Levy, Likol Tamsut and Lihi Gutman, who represented three of the victims through the Justice Ministry’s Legal Aid Department, said: “We had the privilege of representing three of the nine victims, impressive and strong women who insisted on their right to have their voices heard.
“Despite the years that have passed, an indictment was filed, and a difficult proceeding was conducted, during which they were required to testify at length. Today, it concluded with a resounding sentence.
“The court reinforced the important message it sent in its verdict: Women must be protected in the sensitive and exposed setting of a medical examination, and anyone who exploits such a sensitive and vulnerable situation will face the full severity of the law.”

MK Ofer Cassif indicted for assaulting police officer during Mount Hebron protest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
08:09:31 UTC
17:09:31 KST

The Jerusalem Magistrate’s Court convicted MK Ofer Cassif of assaulting a police officer during a protest in the South Hebron Hills more than four years ago.
The conviction, handed down on Thursday by Judge Bialin Elazar, was for assaulting a police officer under aggravated circumstances, an offense punishable by between three months and five years in prison. The offense applies when an assault is connected to an officer’s lawful duties and is intended to obstruct, prevent or interfere with their work.
Sentencing arguments are scheduled for January 13 next year.
Responding to the conviction in a post on X/Twitter, Cassif wrote: “I will continue my struggle, together with my friends, against all the crimes of the occupation: genocide, ethnic cleansing, and fascism within Israel. I promise you that we will emerge stronger from the election and send the Kahanists and all the criminals where they belong.”
The incident took place on May 13, 2022, in Masafer Yatta, a cluster of Palestinian communities in the South Hebron Hills at the center of a decades-long dispute over evictions from an area designated as an IDF firing zone. The communities’ struggle against demolition and displacement was documented in No Other Land, the Israeli-Palestinian film that won the 2025 Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature.
According to the indictment, protests were held in the South Hebron Hills on that day in 2022, following a Supreme Court ruling concerning villages in Masafer Yatta. Orders were issued declaring the area around the Route 317 junction and dirt roads leading to the villages a closed military zone.
Cassif arrived by car to join the protesters, after about 80 had arrived at around 11 a.m. and eventually set up camp on one of the dirt roads leading to Masafer Yatta. Because Cassif had parliamentary immunity, security officers allowed him to move freely between the designated and approved protest area and the area outside it.
However, security personnel stopped his vehicle on a dirt road and prevented him from driving into the protest area, citing safety concerns and the prohibition on Israelis entering Area A. He was permitted to continue on foot.
According to the indictment, Cassif later returned to the car to drive it, leading to a heated argument with Border Police Ch.-Insp. Dor Amitai and police officer Yitzhak Azulay.
Cassif called Border Police officers 'scum of the human race,' court says
According to a court summary, Cassif called the officers “dirty liar,” “fraud,” “criminal,” and “scum of the human race.”
Cassif then got into his car. With Azulay standing in front of the vehicle to block it, Cassif reversed several meters and then drove slowly forward until the front of the car struck Azulay’s left leg. The court found that Cassif acted knowingly and intended to obstruct Azulay in the performance of his duties.
Azulay struck the hood of the vehicle with his hand. When Cassif got out, the argument continued. At one point, Azulay raised his finger and lightly touched Cassif’s face. In response, Cassif raised his right hand and forcefully struck the left side of Azulay’s head, causing him pain in his head and leg.
Cassif denied the charge and argued that his parliamentary immunity entitled him to drive through the area. He claimed that striking the officer with his vehicle had been accidental and that hitting him with his hand was an instinctive act of self-defense. He also raised a preliminary claim of selective enforcement.
The court rejected the defense arguments, ruling that the security forces acted lawfully and within their authority to prevent danger to life and unauthorized entry into Area A.
It found that Cassif’s parliamentary immunity allowed him to move freely on foot within the protest area but did not give him the right to endanger people or obstruct police officers by driving.
The court also found beyond a reasonable doubt that Cassif knowingly struck Azulay with his vehicle and intended to obstruct him. It ruled that striking the officer’s head went well beyond self-defense and was grossly disproportionate to what the court described as accidental contact caused by Cassif’s own movement. The court also rejected the selective-enforcement claim, finding a clear evidentiary distinction and no defect in the prosecution’s conduct.

‘Not a single minute to lose’: COP31 chief slams nations for dodging climate responsibility

‘Not a single minute to lose’: COP31 chief slams nations for dodging climate responsibility
- - COP31 chief Murat Kurum says climate action is urgent, and that nations are “running away" from their responsibility”.
- - At a pre-COP event in Fiji and Tuvalu, Pacific states pushed for more resilience funding, ocean protection and keeping warming below 1.5 deg C.
- - Kurum said US$1.5 billion (S$1.9 billion) could help save the Pacific, and he promised Turkey would take Pacific goals seriously at COP31, where 30 countries have backed deep emissions cuts.
AI generated
NADI, Fiji – Restricting global warming is a matter of survival, and too many countries are shirking their responsibility to cut emissions, the official presiding over the UN’s flagship upcoming climate conference said on the final day of the meeting’s precursor event on Oct 8.
“Today is a time where everyone is running away from responsibility,” Murat Kurum, Turkey’s climate minister and president of the 2026 United Nations COP conference (COP31) said at a news conference. “We do not have a single minute, a single day to lose.”
He was speaking on the final day of pre-COP, which brought thousands of delegates to Fiji this week and took a group from 30 countries to Tuvalu ahead of the main event to be held in Antalya, Turkey, in November.
Reflecting on his visit to the tiny low-lying atoll nation of Tuvalu on Oct 6, Kurum said mothers and children were under increasing threat from every high tide.
Pacific Island nations sought to use the pre-COP in their region to embed their priorities into the COP31 agenda.
These include better access to funding for resilience projects, protection of oceans and holding warming beneath 1.5 deg C above pre-industrial levels, something the UN Environment Programme says is impossible in the near term but could be achieved over time with emissions reduction.
But Kurum said holding to that limit is crucial.
“This 1.5 degree goal is a matter of survival,” he said. “The survival of cultures, history, memories, your homeland, your homes.”
Tuvalu consists of thin strips of land on average around 2m above sea level. It is suffering from increasing flooding, saltwater encroachment and volatile weather.
Kurum contrasted the threat that Tuvalu will disappear with commitments by NATO nations to increase defence spending to 5% of gross domestic product.
“What does it mean to spend 5% for defence if you don’t have a country to live on? What does it mean to defend it?“ he said.
“Financing of US$1.5 billion (S$1.9 billion) for 1.5 degrees will save the Pacific. It’s that easy. Life will continue in Tuvalu. Children will be smiling again,” he said.
Kurum pledged that Pacific goals will be taken seriously at COP31 in Turkey. Representatives of around 30 countries signed a declaration on Oct 6 endorsing those goals and calling for “deep, rapid and sustained emissions reductions”.
Turkey is a significant user of coal and oil whose carbon dioxide emissions have risen sharply in recent decades, but it has pledged to cut them to net-zero by 2053 and is expanding renewable energy. REUTERS

Syria weighs military aid for Saudi Arabia amid war with Houthis, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
08:09:27 UTC
17:09:27 KST

Syria is carefully considering providing military assistance to key ally Saudi Arabia amid an escalating war against the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen, a US official and a Syrian military official briefed on the matter said.
Options being considered include defensive aid to protect the kingdom from attacks, or deployment of forces in an offensive capacity to help Saudi-backed Yemeni troops fight the Houthis, the sources said.
The US official said Saudi Arabia had requested that Syria deploy forces to fight the Houthis - an assertion denied by the Syrian president's media adviser, Ahmad Zaidan, in a post on X/Twitter following the publication of this story.
In response to a request for comment to the Syrian foreign ministry, a Syrian diplomat said Syria stood firmly with Saudi Arabia in the face of Houthi attacks but that the government's primary focus was on domestic priorities such as recovery from the country's civil war.
"Should Saudi Arabia request any military cooperation or exchange of expertise, this would take place exclusively through official channels and within the framework of the bilateral agreements governing relations between our two brotherly countries," the diplomat said in a statement.
The Saudi government media office and Yemen's information minister did not respond to requests for comment.
Saudi Arabia seeking support in anti-Houthi efforts
Saudi Arabia has been requesting assistance far and wide, from the US to Europe and the Middle East, for both defensive and offensive support in a renewed war against the group that follows weeks of Houthi missile and drone attacks on the kingdom.
The war is being led on the ground by a patchwork of Yemeni government forces with Saudi air support. They have made limited advances since the campaign was launched on Monday.
Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa made a public visit to Riyadh on Tuesday and met Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, also known as MbS. He discussed potential Syrian military assistance for the kingdom, among other matters, the US official said.
Footage broadcast by Syrian state media showed that he was escorted back to his plane by Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman, a brother of the crown prince who has overseen the Yemen file.
Deployment could deepen tensions with neighbors
Syrian fighters from opposition groups that battled former leader Bashar al-Assad in the country's civil war have in past years been recruited as mercenaries for other conflicts, notably Libya's internal conflict and the Russia-Ukraine war.
But for Damascus, any potential deployment carries risks.
The militias that made up the armed opposition are now under the nascent Syrian state, which has adopted a policy of avoiding engagement in conflict, including the Iran war, to focus on recovery from the 14-year Syrian civil war.
The state is still piecing together its army from the various militia groups from the former rebel coalition that toppled Assad, which included many hardline Sunni Islamist and foreign fighters, and is trying to contain tensions with minorities, including the Alawites, a Shi'ite offshoot to which Assad belonged.
A conflict between that army and the Houthis, who are also adherents of an offshoot of Shi'ite Islam, could have divisive religious undertones that the Syrian leadership and its Western partners want to avoid, the US official said.
It is for this reason that it previously rejected a US request to help fight Hezbollah in Lebanon.
Involvement in a battle against the Iran-backed Houthis could also be viewed as a hostile act by Iran and its allies Hezbollah in Lebanon and militias in Iraq, with which the Syrian rebels-turned-rulers have a history of conflict.
Sharaa keen to show support for Saudis
At the same time, Sharaa is keen to show the country's support for Saudi Arabia and MbS, who played a decisive role helping the former jihadist gain international legitimacy, including by brokering a May 2025 meeting between Sharaa and US President Donald Trump.
Saudi Arabia has also provided financial assistance to Syria, and a Syrian show of support could result in that increasing, the US official said.
"A new Syria sending defensive personnel of a very small number to the most holy places in the Islamic world, alongside technical support to neutralize incoming drones, would be tremendously and positively symbolic," said H.A. Hellyer, senior associate fellow at the Royal United Services Institute in London.
"But anything beyond, particularly in terms of Syrian boots on the ground, I think would be a wholly different proposition, and one I think Damascus would avoid, given the priorities they need to focus on in Syria," he said.

Tokyo considers allowing nuclear weapons to be brought into Japan — newspaper
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08

17:05:40 KST

TOKYO, October 8. /TASS/. Japan’s government currently has no intention of revising the country’s non-nuclear principles but is considering a proposal to permit nuclear weapons to be brought into the country under an exception, the Sankei newspaper reported, citing government sources.
The initiative is viewed as a measure to strengthen the deterrence of potential adversaries based on the idea of the United States’ "nuclear umbrella," the paper noted.
A provision allowing nuclear weapons to be brought into the country as an exception may be included in new fundamental documents on security, which the Japanese government plans to adopt at the end of the year. This would allow ships carrying nuclear weapons to enter Japanese ports, the newspaper said.
According to Sankei, such a move would require addressing numerous issues, including defining the circumstances in which nuclear weapons could be brought to Japan and developing a mechanism to coordinate visits by such vessels with local authorities.
The paper noted that some members of the country’s ruling Liberal Democratic Party were calling for a cautious approach to such decisions, so discussions on the issue were expected to continue. Another proposal circulating in the government is to include a provision in the fundamental security documents on discussing the possibility of providing the country’s Navy with nuclear-powered submarines.
Japan maintains three non-nuclear principles: not possessing, not producing and not permitting the introduction of nuclear weapons into its territory. The principles, which have no force of law, were formalized through a government decision and a regular parliamentary resolution. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has repeatedly said that her cabinet adheres to the three non-nuclear principles. However, she has been consistently moving away from the obligation to pursue the same policy in the future.

‘Where am I?’: Christa Pike wakes six days after surviving botched execution in Tennessee
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
08:04:44 UTC
17:04:44 KST

American convicted murderer Christa Pike, whose execution in Tennessee last week failed in an unprecedented incident, leaving her sedated and on a ventilator in a hospital until she woke up Tuesday, was "angry and confused" in the hours after regaining consciousness. Her first questions were, "Where am I? Who are you?" her attorney, Randy Spivey, said Wednesday night.
Spivey said Pike, believed to be the first person to survive the administration of lethal drugs during an execution carried out by U.S. prison authorities, woke up six days after the execution attempt. Remarkably, she regained consciousness just as preparations were underway to remove her from life support amid fears she was brain-dead. "On Tuesday, to the shock of everyone … Christa woke up and began talking," he said.
Pike, whose case has received extensive international media coverage in recent days, was just 18 when she murdered her classmate, Colleen Slemmer, on January 12, 1995. Slemmer was enrolled alongside Pike and Pike's boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, in a vocational training program in Knoxville. According to prosecutors, Pike feared Slemmer was romantically interested in Shipp and, in a fit of jealousy and rage, lured her to a secluded area of the University of Tennessee campus, where she and Shipp brutally tortured and murdered her.
Among other acts of violence, Pike slashed Slemmer more than 100 times with a utility knife and struck her with a large piece of asphalt. Shipp carved a pentagram, a star-shaped symbol associated with Satan, into her body. The findings at the crime scene caused widespread alarm at the time against the backdrop of the "Satanic panic" of the 1980s and 1990s in the United States, when rumors circulated about satanic cults abducting people, including children, and subjecting them to ritual abuse.
Pike's 1996 death sentence made her one of the youngest women ever sent to death row in the United States. In subsequent years, however, her attorneys and supporters argued that the death penalty was excessive given her young age at the time of the crime and her untreated mental illness. They also pointed to a childhood marked by neglect and severe sexual abuse, including rapes at ages 11 and 17. She was later diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder.
One of Pike's current attorneys, Stephen Ferrell, emphasized that her defense team failed to present the jury with crucial information about her background during the sentencing phase of her trial and did not argue that her young age should be taken into account.
Ferrell noted that far more is now known about adolescent brain development and argued that Pike's death sentence was unusual and exceptional. He also pointed out that Pike's boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, who was 17 at the time of the murder, was sentenced to life in prison with the possibility of parole because of his young age.
Last week, Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee rejected Pike's request for clemency, and the Supreme Court denied a petition to stay her execution. Just an hour before the execution was originally scheduled to begin at 6 p.m. Israel time Wednesday, another court unexpectedly issued a stay to consider several of Pike's arguments. A few hours later, however, the court allowed the execution to proceed.
Pike was therefore set to become the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years and only the 19th woman ever executed in the United States.
Cognitive confusion and a blood clot in her arm
Pike's execution began overnight Wednesday into Thursday, Israel time. The execution team initially administered a dose of pentobarbital, the drug intended to kill her. When the drug failed to render her unconscious, the team administered a second dose, as required by protocol. But Pike survived that injection as well.
Witnesses who attended the execution, along with her attorneys, said that during the procedure she declared, "My arm feels like it's about to burst open," and at another point asked, "Does this happen like that?"
According to witnesses, Pike could be heard crying, whimpering and breathing heavily throughout the procedure. Even as they were escorted out of the viewing room more than two hours after entering, they could still hear her snoring loudly behind the closed curtains.
Pike was taken to a hospital unconscious, with her arms swollen and covered in blisters caused by the injected drug, but still alive. She was intubated and placed on a ventilator.
Pike's attorneys said they believe problems with the intravenous lines caused the pentobarbital to enter her body tissue rather than her bloodstream.
"Apparently, at no point did any member of the execution team realise that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown and that the pentobarbital was, in whole or in part, entering Ms Pike's body," the attorneys wrote in a court filing.
The filing emphasized that Pike had previously appealed on the grounds that executing her would constitute cruel and unusual punishment because of her particular physical and medical conditions, including thrombocytosis, a condition involving an elevated platelet count, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and small veins.
Although Pike, now 50, has regained consciousness, many questions remain about her prospects for recovery. It is also unclear whether Tennessee will attempt to execute her again.
Her attorneys said Wednesday that she had suffered more than enough and called on the governor to commute her sentence in light of the circumstances.
They also reported Wednesday night that she remained unable to move her arms or swallow and was experiencing some degree of cognitive confusion. She also has pneumonia and a blood clot in her arm and faces a long road to recovery.
On Wednesday night, Pike's attorneys asked the court to order the removal of the restraints securing her to her hospital bed and to allow her access to a telephone. The judge has yet to rule on the request.
Dr. Joel Zivot, a professor of anesthesiology and surgery in Atlanta who served as an expert consultant to Pike's legal team, said it could take weeks or months before anyone knows for certain what her recovery will look like and whether she could recover sufficiently for the state to attempt another execution.
In Texas, the injection worked: Death declared after 19 minutes
Following the botched execution, Tennessee Gov. Lee announced a suspension of executions in the state through the end of the year and ordered an independent investigation into Tennessee's death penalty system, to be led by former federal prosecutor Edward Stanton.
Tennessee Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada announced his resignation Saturday in the wake of the failure.
The botched execution became a major scandal, even prompting a response from President Donald Trump, who said the following day, "How does that happen? Should be easy to do. It shouldn't be very difficult."
Meanwhile, Texas carried out the first execution in the United States since Pike's failed execution in Tennessee.
Jamaal Howard, 46, a Texas man who fatally shot a convenience store clerk during a robbery in 2000, when he was 20, was executed by injection of pentobarbital, the same method used in Pike's attempted execution. He became the 30th person executed in the United States this year.
When the prison warden asked whether he wanted to make a final statement, Howard repeatedly apologized to several members of the victim's family, who watched through a window just a few feet from the execution chamber.
"“I wish that you accept my apology and I wish for your forgiveness," Howard said shortly before the injection began. "I’m sorry for what happened. I wish you can learn to forgive me one of these days."
He also thanked his friends and family, told them he loved them and said he was in "a good state of mind to find peace and the Lord, so I thank y’all."
He concluded with the words, "Hey, enjoy life, and peace to y’all.."
As the pentobarbital began to take effect, Howard took two breaths and gasped. He then began making gurgling and snoring sounds, coughed and resumed snoring, with the sounds growing progressively quieter.
Within about 30 seconds, he had stopped moving entirely. He was pronounced dead 19 minutes later.
Texas has executed six people so far in 2026 and plans to carry out two more executions before the end of the year.
Earlier Wednesday, Howard's attorneys tried to block his execution, arguing that he had an intellectual disability and faced risks similar to those that materialized in Pike's case because Texas, like Tennessee, uses pentobarbital in its lethal injections. Their efforts were unsuccessful.

Operator credits speed and suspension
The operator, callsign Tango, named speed and the ability to perform complex maneuvers as the robot's main advantages, according to Militarnyi. What Frodo can carry, and how far
The robot has a 6×6 wheel layout with independent suspension, adjustable ground clearance of 170–330 mm, and a top speed of 40 km/h. Its recommended payload is 200 kg, and its maximum is 400 kg, according to Frontline Robotics. The company lists its range as 150 km on asphalt and up to 90 km over rough terrain with the recommended load. Frodo supports several communication channels, and one person can swap its batteries in about two minutes.
Frodo had passed the Defense Ministry's codification and could carry remote-controlled modules such as the Burya turret, Militarnyi reported on 30 September.
The 92nd Brigade had used ground robots to evacuate wounded soldiers before. In September 2025, the brigade evacuated three wounded soldiers using a ground robot, according to Militarnyi.
