Aviation industry representatives are preparing a draft tax consultation on aircraft leasing for the Ministry of Finance — UATA
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:36:11 EEST
16:36:11 KST

Aviation industry representatives are preparing a draft tax consultation on aircraft leasing for the Ministry of Finance — UATA
Kyiv • UNN
UATA has established a working group in response to the Economic Security Bureau’s cases against at least five airlines. Proposals on the taxation of leasing will be submitted to the Ministry of Finance by October 14.
The Ukrainian Air Transport Association (UATA) has established a working group to prepare a package of documents on the taxation of leasing payments made by Ukrainian airlines to non-residents for consideration by the Ministry of Finance of Ukraine. This became necessary because the Bureau of Economic Security attempted to classify aircraft leasing as royalties, affecting at least five carriers. Mykola Shcherbyna, Executive Director of the Public Union "Ukrainian Air Transport Association," told UNN in an exclusive comment.
Why airlines insist on a unified approach to aircraft leasing
As UNN previously reported, since 2024 the Bureau of Economic Security has begun treating transactions involving the leasing of air transport from non-residents of Ukraine as the use of equipment. According to the investigators’ version, Ukrainian air carriers were required to pay royalties for the rental of aircraft and helicopters. Based on this approach, the BES opened criminal proceedings against at least five air carriers, including UIA, "Constanta Airlines," "Windrose," N3Operations, and "Skyline Express." According to UNN, another airline — "Urga" — may also be involved in a similar case.
The criminal cases were opened despite the fact that the airlines regularly undergo tax audits; as of today, only one company has faced objections concerning leasing.
Representatives of the aviation industry insist that the problem arose because of an ambiguous interpretation of legislative provisions and that it requires the establishment of a unified state approach.
Earlier, in response to an inquiry from UNN , the Ministry of Finance reported that the taxation of aircraft leasing transactions is carried out in accordance with the Tax Code and international treaties of Ukraine. At the same time, the Tax Code of Ukraine does not provide for the possibility of taxing aircraft leasing as royalties.
Therefore, representatives of the aviation industry describe the Bureau’s approach to interpreting aircraft leasing, without changes to tax legislation, as pressure that could destroy the entire passenger and freight transportation sector. According to data from the State Register of Civil Aircraft of Ukraine, 86% of the aircraft fleet of Ukrainian companies is leased.
To resolve the situation, the issue of aircraft leasing was submitted for consideration by the Committee on Tax Policy, Accounting and Auditing of the Public Council under the Ministry of Finance. Following the first meeting, it was decided to initiate the creation of a working group under the Ministry of Finance that would develop a draft general tax consultation on the taxation of leasing payments made to non-residents.
The Ministry of Finance is awaiting documents from the aviation industry
The creation of the working group continued the dialogue between the aviation business and the Ministry of Finance on resolving the issue of taxation of aircraft leasing.
"The Ministry of Finance is working on an issue concerning not the regulation of the leasing market in general, but the application of the provisions of the Tax Code of Ukraine and international treaties of Ukraine on the avoidance of double taxation to income received by non-residents in the form of leasing or rental payments for the provision of aircraft for use," the Ministry of Finance reported in response to an inquiry from UNN.
The ministry added that it is awaiting specific examples of leasing transactions being interpreted as royalties, as well as proposals from the aviation industry on how to resolve this issue. After receiving them, the Ministry of Finance plans to develop a general tax consultation that will serve as a mechanism for establishing a unified approach to applying the relevant provisions.
UATA is preparing a draft general tax consultation on aircraft leasing
According to Mykola Shcherbyna, representatives of the aviation industry decided to establish a working group under the Ukrainian Air Transport Association to quickly develop proposals for the Ministry of Finance.
The Ukrainian Association of Aviation and Aerospace (UATA) decided to establish a working group comprising representatives of the aviation industry. It will be headed by Ruslan Melnychenko, chairman of the Legal Committee of the Aerospace Association of Ukraine, an attorney and business protection expert, and chairman of the Legal Committee of the Aerospace Association of Ukraine. Our task is to prepare specific examples for the Ministry of Finance of the incorrect interpretation of leasing transactions as royalties and to develop a draft general tax consultation
He added that Ukrainian airlines had encountered the problem of the Bureau of Economic Security incorrectly interpreting leasing transactions as royalties, and that it was important for this issue to be resolved as soon as possible so that carriers could continue operating under clear rules.
"Leasing aircraft and helicopters is a global practice. Neither Ukrainian legislation nor international law provides for the payment of royalties on the leasing of aircraft. The unilateral change by government agencies in the interpretation, without amendments to legislation, and the criminal prosecution of airlines constitute pressure on responsible businesses that are forced to survive under conditions of closed airspace and pay taxes in Ukraine. This approach poses a threat to the entire civil aviation industry, and this problem must be resolved," Mykola Shcherbyna emphasized.
According to him, the UATA working group plans to collect specific examples of attempts to tax the rental of air transport from nonresidents as royalties, as well as prepare proposals for a unified approach to their taxation. The cases, along with the draft general tax consultation, are planned to be submitted to the Ministry of Finance for consideration by October 14.
A unified position of government agencies on the taxation of aircraft leasing is necessary, one that complies with the provisions of the Tax Code of Ukraine and international conventions on the avoidance of double taxation
He is convinced that this format will enable industry representatives, together with the Ministry of Finance, to develop a specific solution to the problem within a short period. If adopted, the general tax consultation should establish the Ministry of Finance's official position on the application of tax rules to leasing payments for the use of aircraft and reduce the scope for government agencies to interpret identical transactions differently.

Slovakia sends military attaché back to Russia for first time in 4 years
Slovakia and Russia are resuming the exchange of military attachés for the first time since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine – a decision that has drawn criticism from the Slovak opposition.
Source: European Pravda with reference to Slovak news outlet Aktuality
Details: During his visit to Moscow in May, Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico promised Russian leader Vladimir Putin during their talks that military and diplomatic relations between the two countries would be restored. As part of these arrangements, the countries are resuming the exchange of military attachés after a four-year hiatus.
Fico's government has sent two military officers to Moscow and Bratislava is awaiting the arrival of a Russian attaché.
The last Russian military attaché to serve in Slovakia left the country four years ago. Sergei Solomasov, who held the post, was expelled by the government of Eduard Heger along with other Russian diplomats after Russia invaded Ukraine. Solomasov was also implicated in an espionage case: he bribed Bohuš Garbár, a contributor to the Hlavné správy website, to disseminate disinformation on his instructions.
According to the latest information, Russia's new military attaché in Bratislava could be 46-year-old Maksim Verezhan. The naval officer previously served at the Russian embassy in Rome and has spent the past few years in Moscow.
Slovakia has appointed its military representatives in Moscow. Brigadier General Slavomír Staviarsky will serve as military attaché and Colonel Ivo Gahír will be his deputy.
Tomáš Valášek, an MP from the Progressive Slovakia party, criticised the government's decision to resume military and diplomatic engagement with Russia. He argued that exchanging military attachés would primarily benefit Russia, as the Slovak representative is unlikely to gain access to important information in Moscow.
Valášek also said the Russian military attaché could have an opportunity to take part in disinformation and influence operations in Slovakia, fuel social tensions and sway public opinion towards Russia.
The opposition politician also suggested that the move to restore military relations may have come from Moscow, with the Slovak government simply accepting the proposal.
Background:
- Slovakia's Foreign Ministry, meanwhile, justified the return of military attachés by saying that the government is seeking to establish pragmatic relations with Russia.
- Slovak Defence Minister Robert Kaliňák recently said that Bratislava does not regard Russia as a threat.
- Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico has said he does not want Slovakia to become involved in a military conflict "because of some Article 5".
- It was also reported that Slovakia's opposition is demanding explanations from the government and Fico over reports in the German media linking an attempted attack on a Ukrainian drone manufacturer in Prešov to Russian military intelligence.

Christian union ACV and the ABVV, its socialist counterpart, are staging yet another National Day of Action on Friday to mark their opposition to the policies of the De Wever I government. On Monday strike action is being held across the public sector. Expect disruption: Brussels local transport company MIVB, Flemish local transport company De Lijn and Brussels Airport will be hit on Friday and schools and rail services will be affected on Monday.
National Day of Action and public sector strike to cause disruption on Friday 9 October and Monday 12 October
For the various trade unions, this is at least the 10th major protest against the federal government’s policies. The government’s drafting of the budget is the trigger for the protest this time. The unions fear that ordinary people will once again bear the brunt of the cuts.
ABVV is organising a national demonstration through the streets of Brussels. It will set off from Central Station and head towards Brussels-South Station (Zuid/Midi). “Hands off our pockets” is the slogan calling for the demonstration. “We want to draw a clear line in the sand and warn the government to keep its hands off purchasing power, the cost-of-living index and sales tax VAT,” explains spokesperson Daan Nelen.
ACV has opted for a protest outside the party headquarters of government parties, the Flemish nationalist N-VA, Christian democrat CD&V and socialist Vooruit as well as the Francophone liberals of MR and centrists of Les Engagés. Several hundred activists will take part at each location. The trade union is requesting a meeting with the leaders of each party. At 8.30 am, the procession will halt outside N-VA HQ and the MR, followed by the CD&V, Vooruit and Les Engagés.
The Christian trade union says it wants to convey workers’ concerns to government ministers. The ACV also fears that the government will once again pass the bill on to ordinary people. “Whilst workers have already contributed more than enough. And on top of that, they are paying the price for the rising cost of living, higher energy bills and increasing workloads,” says the trade union.
Both unions also wish again to draw attention to their alternative budget plan: measures that could raise up to 21 billion euros without resorting to harsh austerity measures.
Synova, the independent, formerly liberal, trade union, shares the concerns of the other unions but will not be taking to the streets on Friday. The union intends to roll out its own action plan and engage in dialogue with workers.
The unions day of action will result in disruption
Transit company MIVB in Brussels
Brussels local transport company MIVB expects “significant disruption” to public transport in the conurbation. It does not plan to provide a minimum service.
It will only be able to forecast the exact scope of the expected disruption on Thursday evening. It will provide updates via its social media channels but warns that it will not know the full extent of the impact of the day of action until Friday morning.
De Lijn hit in Flanders
Four in ten buses and trams operated by Flemish local transport company De Lijn will not be running on Friday 9 October due to the national day of industrial action organised by the Christian and socialist trade unions.
The Flemish public transport company announced the expected impact of the action yesterday. De Lijn will operate an alternative service schedule with staff who have indicated they will come to work. 60 per cent of De Lijn’s buses and trams will still be running. Across the provinces, the following percentages of vehicles will be operating:
Antwerp: 58 per cent (Antwerp city: 46 per cent)
Limburg: 61 per cent
East Flanders: 71 per cent
Flemish Brabant: 54 per cent
West Flanders: 65 per cent (Coastal tram: 62 per cent)
NMBS rail services affected on Monday
Anyone wishing to travel by train on Friday will not experience any disruption.
Staff at Belgium's state-owned rail operator NMBS are only taking part in the public sector strike on Monday. It is still unclear what impact this will have on services.
Flights cancelled at Brussels Airport
At Brussels Airport, around 140 flights are expected to be cancelled because ground handling operator Alyzia is affected by the strike. The operator will be operating with a reduced workforce.
According to Brussels Airport, the airlines affected are adjusting their flight schedules and passengers will be provided with information about the status of their flight and any alternatives.
No impact is currently expected on flights handled by a second operator, Aviapartner. This applies to flights operated by Ryanair and TUI fly among others.
Passengers can check which ground handling operator is handling their flight on the Brussels Airport website.
Charleroi Brussels South Airport escapes
All flights at Charleroi Airport are running as normal. However, passengers are urged to leave for the airport in good time. Passengers are advised to check the status of their flight via the airport’s own website or through their airline.
Education also hit
On Friday and also on Monday, there may be disruption in some schools following a strike notice issued by ACOD Onderwijs, the socialist education union.
ACOD Onderwijs will be taking part in the National Day of Action on Friday, as well as in the strike in the public services organised by the socialist trade union on Monday 12 October.
As a result, disruption may be experienced in some schools on both days. Traditionally, ACOD has a stronger presence in the GO! education sector, the official state network.

Russia has shown a drone interceptor built on the Alazan, a civilian anti-hail rocket, Militarnyi reported. The sample went on display at a weapons exhibition that Russian dictator Vladimir Putin toured at the Chebarkul training range in the Urals on 2 October.
Ukraine now sends drones at Russia by the hundreds, by Moscow's own count. Russia's Defense Ministry claimed its air defenses intercepted nearly 900 overnight into 6 October. The converted Alazan, which Militarnyi calls an anti-drone system, is one more piece of that search. From hail reagent to shrapnel
Based on the size of the sample on display, the interceptor builds on the Alazan-2M or Alazan-6 series, Militarnyi assessed. The outlet put the stated cost at up to $12,000 per unit but did not say who named the figure. In civilian service, the rocket flies about 10 km, climbs up to 8 km, and carries about 0.5 kg of reagent. For air defense, the developers plan to replace that reagent with a fragmentation warhead.
Militarnyi's analysis of the published photos describes the front end as a steering assembly: four cruciform deflector fins, probably paired with a seeker or a fuze. At the rear sit folding stabilizers and the open nozzle of a solid-fuel motor, held in a metal cradle.
One sample among 300 exhibits
The Kremlin's account of the visit lists more than 300 weapons on display, including interceptor drones, but does not mention the rocket. Propaganda channel Russia 1 aired the interceptor in its report from the visit, and the Kremlin pool of state news agency RIA posted photos.

France's Le Pen opposes Ukraine EU membership over farming fears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

French far-right politician Marine Le Pen spoke against EU membership for Ukraine on Oct. 7 by whipping up fears that Kyiv's agricultural sector would destroy France's.
Le Pen is leading the polls for France's April 2027 presidential election, and her stance on Ukraine and Russia has already become a key campaign issue for her and her competitors.
"If Ukraine were to enter the European Union, we would be the first to suffer," Le Pen claimed in a video posted to social media.
"We would be the losers, not only in terms of competition with a large agricultural country like Ukraine, but also in the sharing out of Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) (subsidies), because the CAP is a shrinking cake," Le Pen said.
The CAP is an EU program established in 1962 that subsidizes the EU's farming sector, allowing small and uncompetitive farms to continue to exist.
It is also at risk of being reduced already, as Brussels haggles over the bloc's 2028-2034 budget. The fear is that adding a large agricultural country such as Ukraine would exacerbate that situation further.
Le Pen's comments came one day after the European Commission published a communication on the future of enlargement, which noted that the bloc needs to seriously address how to integrate Ukraine's farming sector into the EU smoothly.
Ukraine "will and can become a member of the CAP. Under which conditions, this will be discussed," said the EU's Enlargement Commissioner, Marta Kos, at a press conference on Oct. 6.
"We also have to protect the farmers in the EU, and we are already discussing this subject with Ukraine," Kos added.
Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi said, "We understand the sensitivity of certain segments for European farmers," in written comments shared with the Kyiv Independent.
However, he thinks there are also many opportunities for the EU that come with bringing in Ukraine's farming sector, even for European farmers.
"We do not share the approach under which Ukraine's integration is viewed exclusively as a threat to European farmers," Vysotskyi said.
And Kyiv's lobby for agriculture in Brussels, the Ukrainian Agribusiness Club (UCAB), said that while it understands the concerns of European farmers, it is "increasingly concerned by an excessively protectionist approach towards the integration of Ukrainian agriculture," in an Oct. 7 press statement.
For UCAB, part of the answer lies in communication.
"UCAB has consistently advocated an open and structured dialogue with European farmers, EU institutions, and member states to jointly develop a model for the future enlarged European agricultural market."

From Relic to Infrastructure: Can India's Historic Water Systems Work Again?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
07:30:00 UTC
16:30:00 KST

India's stepwells are usually encountered after their useful lives have ended. They are photographed, restored and interpreted as evidence of a water culture that once existed. Beneath the carved stone and descending stairs is a practical question: what happens when a structure built to manage water is put back to work? As Indian cities face water stress, seasonal rainfall and pressure on municipal systems, researchers and restoration efforts are examining whether traditional water structures can function again.
Traditional water architecture was rarely an isolated object. In Ahmedabad, water management was embedded in the organization of the city. Within the historic pols, wells, courtyards and underground Tankas formed part of a distributed system of domestic and communal water storage. A 2026 study in Built Heritage estimates that nearly 10,000 Tankas may still exist across Ahmedabad, many located beneath domestic courtyards.
The Tanka was simple in construction, but its operation depended on several parts of the house working together. Rainwater was collected from roofs and courtyards, directed underground and stored within lime-lined chambers. The structures were typically constructed several meters below ground, using stone, brick and lime mortar, while sloping bases allowed sediment to be removed during cleaning. Water storage was part of the house itself. The building became part of the catchment and storage system.
Related Article
India's Forgotten Stepwells
More than 200 community wells were constructed within Ahmedabad's Pols by the late nineteenth century, while only 14 of the 94 documented stepwells in greater Ahmedabad lie within the historic Walled City. The monumental stepwell is the most recognizable image of India's water heritage. In dense urban neighbourhoods, however, smaller wells and Tankas could be more practical.
In Ahmedabad, the expansion of piped municipal infrastructure and stormwater drainage gradually made household rainwater systems less necessary. The establishment of the Dudheshwar Water Works in 1892 marked part of this wider shift towards centralised supply. Over time, the Tanka remained physically present while its original role disappeared. A Tanka could remain beneath a house for generations, even as the water entering the building arrived through a municipal pipe rather than a monsoon roof.
Ahmedabad's geology offers one explanation for the emergence of the Tanka. The historic Walled City sits over dense clay strata, with groundwater often deeper than 40 meters. In such conditions, digging and maintaining wells could be difficult. Collecting rainwater close to where it fell provided another option, particularly within a dense urban fabric where larger water structures were difficult to accommodate. The courtyard became a catchment. The floor became a threshold to an underground reservoir. The house became part of a water system.
The 2026 Built Heritage study's survey found that 90 percent of the residents questioned expressed willingness to reintegrate Tanka water into the urban system, although the study also identifies significant barriers around governance, ownership, incentives and water quality.
Bansilalpet Stepwell in Hyderabad provides a different case. For decades, the seventeenth-century stepwell had effectively disappeared beneath a dump. Its restoration involved removing approximately 2,000 tonnes of debris, after which a freshwater source was identified around seven meters below ground. The restored well was reported to have a water-carrying capacity of approximately 2.2 million litres.
The restoration also addressed the surrounding precinct, including rainwater-harvesting measures and changes to surrounding infrastructure. Reports on the restoration record the well's association with the water supply of Gandhi Hospital. Bansilalpet does not yet show that restored stepwells can supply cities at scale. The available evidence demonstrates water recovery, storage capacity and a deliberate attempt to reconnect the site with water management. It has not yet established its long-term contribution to Hyderabad's overall water balance.
The harder problem begins once the water starts flowing. A Tanka depended on more than its masonry chamber. Its operation depended on seasonal cleaning, preparation of roofs and pipes, decisions about when to begin collecting rainwater and knowledge of how the system should be maintained. The 2026 research found that some surviving Tankas remain in use, while others have deteriorated or been repurposed. Water quality also varies, with some existing systems requiring treatment before water can safely be consumed.
Who maintains a privately owned Tanka if it contributes to a neighbourhood water system? Who tests the water? Who pays for repairs? How does a municipal authority regulate infrastructure located beneath private homes?
The researchers argue that the existing governance framework lacks mechanisms to incentivise citizen participation and heritage-based water reuse. They propose a model combining municipal capacity with community involvement. The system depends on routines of cleaning, testing, maintenance and shared responsibility. Without those routines and responsibilities, restoring the masonry does not restore the water system.
Amritvarshini Vav in Ahmedabad is another distinct case. Built around 1723 within the Walled City, the stepwell has an unusual L-shaped plan and extends more than 15 metres below ground. The Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation records that the structure was recharged in 2004. Recharging the well brings one of its original functions back into use.
Reusing a historic water structure also introduces change. Contemporary safety requirements, water-quality standards, public access and urban infrastructure rarely correspond exactly to historic conditions. A restored water structure may therefore need to accommodate systems that did not exist when it was built. Continued use can also be part of its survival. New interventions can change how a historic water structure is experienced. A stepwell restored for public use may become a civic space, a heritage attraction, or both, depending on how the surrounding program is designed.
The restoration extended beyond the well itself into the surrounding public realm, introducing new infrastructure and uses around the historic structure. The restored site now functions both as a water structure and as a civic and heritage destination. At the scale of the house, the Tanka transformed a roof and courtyard into a water catchment. At the scale of the Pol, wells became shared resources within a dense neighbourhood. At the scale of the city, stepwells connected water and public life. Their effectiveness depended on how they worked with surrounding buildings, people and environmental conditions.
Today, these systems could supplement existing municipal infrastructure. Heritage buildings could contribute to rainwater management. Courtyards could become storage systems. Existing structures could be adapted for continued use. Such a shift would also require coordination between architecture, water policy, municipal authorities and the communities that maintain these systems. The Tanka worked because the roof, courtyard, reservoir and routines of maintenance formed one system. Bringing it back into use therefore depends on whether the buildings, institutions and communities around it can support that system again.

NATO-member Türkiye said Wednesday it was sending mainly defensive and technical support to the kingdom to help in the fight against the Houthis, and a Turkish official said this was expected to take the form of military equipment, intelligence sharing and weapons systems.
Pakistan, meanwhile, has flown cargo planes of military equipment to Aden in southern Yemen to help in the battle against the Houthis, sources in Pakistan have said and has deployed troops inside Saudi Arabia to help defend the kingdom's borders.

Beyond condoms: WHO blueprint for new male contraceptives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
07:26:20 UTC
16:26:20 KST

NEW DELHI: Men could have more contraceptive choices beyond condoms and vasectomy, with the World Health Organization (WHO) releasing its first global blueprint for developing novel male contraceptives, including daily pills or gels, longer-acting injections and implants, sperm-function blockers and reversible methods that block sperm transport.The WHO's Target Product Profiles (TPPs) do not approve or launch any new contraceptive. Instead, they set minimum and optimal standards for the effectiveness, safety, reversibility, acceptability and affordability of future male contraceptives. The framework covers three approaches: suppressing sperm production, inhibiting sperm function and blocking sperm transmission or transport.The move comes as research into male contraception gathers pace, with several candidates already in clinical trials. RISUG (reversible inhibition of sperm under guidance), developed in India, has completed Phase 1 and Phase 2 studies, while another hydrogel-based method, ADAM, is in Phase 1 trials.Hormonal candidates including nestorone/testosterone gel, dimethandrolone undecanoate (DMAU) and 11β-methyl-19-nortestosterone dodecylcarbonate (11β-MNTDC) are also being investigated.For methods that suppress sperm production, WHO's minimum target is for 90% of men to achieve sperm concentrations of 1 million or fewer sperm per millilitre within 12 weeks, with a 12-month cumulative pregnancy rate of no more than 7%.
The optimal target is 95% achieving this level within eight weeks, with the pregnancy rate at 3% or less.The proposed methods include daily tablets or gels, injections every three, six or 12 months and implants lasting at least a year. WHO's optimal profile also calls for sperm concentrations to return to the normal reference range within six months of stopping treatment.
Another strategy is to leave sperm present but disable functions needed for fertilisation, such as motility and capacitation. A third is to block sperm transport through the vas deferens, potentially using reversible hydrogels, or temporarily block ejaculation with medication.WHO said the field is rapidly progressing, with several candidates in advanced clinical trials. The new profiles are intended to provide developers and regulators with a common framework for bringing future male contraceptives through research and development.

She specializes in health and heritage reporting, expertly simplifying complex health information to make it engaging and understandable for readers. Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. Over the years, she has worked in Chandigarh, Chhattisgarh and West UP, gaining diverse on-ground experience that shapes her storytelling.

Type 1 diabetes 'should not set the limits on a child's sports dreams'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
07:23:58 UTC
16:23:58 KST

'Exercise, know your body, monitor your glucose and learn to adjust your insulin and your diet correctly,' a Greek professor tells those who have type 1 diabetes.
Around 66 million people live with diabetes on the European continent – that is one in ten adults, with one in three still undiagnosed. Around 2,7 million people in the region have type 1 diabetes – the highest prevalence among all the regions.
Type 1 diabetes can develop as early as childhood or adolescence and requires daily management of glucose levels, but that does not mean a child has to limit play, exercise or even elite sport.
As Thanasis Tziamourtas, professor at the University of Thessaly in Greece, explains, type 1 diabetes is a chronic autoimmune disease in which the immune system destroys the pancreatic beta cells that produce insulin, the hormone that regulates blood glucose.
"Unlike type 2 diabetes, type 1 diabetes is not caused by obesity, poor diet or lack of exercise. Insulin therapy is essential for life, whether via multiple daily injections or through an insulin pump," he said.
But that should not become a barrier to participating in sports for children, Tziamourtas added.
The professor cites German tennis player Alexander Zverev as a striking example. He was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes at the age of four. Tennis is a sport with particular demands, as a match can last several hours and involve repeated bursts of high-intensity effort.
There are also other elite athletes with type 1 diabetes, including American swimmer Gary Hall Jr., winner of 10 Olympic medals, five of them gold, and Dutch volleyball Olympic champion Bas van de Goor.
Can a child with type 1 diabetes take part in sport?
The answer is clear: yes. Physical activity is not only permitted, but it is also a key element of a healthy lifestyle for children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes.
The professor points out that international guidelines recommend around 60 minutes of moderate to vigorous physical activity every day, just as for the general child and adolescent population.
"Exercise is not simply a permitted activity but an important part of a healthy lifestyle for children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes. International guidelines recommend around 60 minutes of moderate to vigorous physical activity every day, as for their peers without diabetes. Regular exercise improves cardiorespiratory fitness, muscle strength, insulin sensitivity, body composition and cardiovascular risk factors. At the same time, it offers significant psychological and social benefits and helps a child feel able to take part in the same activities as their peers."
"Exercise, however, creates a particular challenge: glucose does not respond in the same way to all types of activity," he added.
Why exercise can change glucose levels
The relationship between exercise and glucose is more complex in people with type 1 diabetes. As muscles need more energy during physical activity, they increase their uptake of glucose from the blood.
In someone without diabetes, the pancreas can reduce insulin secretion according to the body's needs. In type 1 diabetes, by contrast, insulin is administered from outside the body and cannot be reduced automatically in the same way.
The result may be hypoglycaemia, particularly in prolonged aerobic exercise such as running, cycling and swimming.
The picture can be different in very high-intensity activities. Sprints, high-intensity drills or a hard-fought match can temporarily raise glucose, as hormones such as adrenaline are released.
"So there is no single 'glucose response to exercise'. It depends," he explains, "on the intensity and duration of the effort, the type of exercise, physical fitness, the previous meal, the amount of active insulin and glucose levels before starting the activity."
The role of monitoring before and after training
For parents and children, the key aim is not to avoid exercise but to prepare properly.
Glucose needs to be checked before activity, during it, particularly when exercise is prolonged, and again afterwards. Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) systems now offer valuable support, providing not only a reading but also information on how glucose is trending.
At the same time, a child who is active should have fast-acting carbohydrates available, such as glucose tablets or an appropriate sugary drink, to deal immediately with possible hypoglycaemia.
Care does not end once training is over. Glucose can fall several hours later, which is particularly important when exercise takes place in the late afternoon or evening, as there is a risk of nocturnal hypoglycaemia.
Similarly, when glucose is very high and ketone levels are raised, vigorous exercise should be avoided.
Insulin adjustment must be individualised
There is no single plan that works for all children with type 1 diabetes. Insulin and carbohydrate needs vary depending on the type, duration and intensity of the activity, the time of day and other factors.
"Adjustments to insulin and carbohydrate intake are not the same for everyone. They must, he stresses, be tailored in collaboration with the care team, taking into account the type of exercise, the time of day, its duration and intensity, and the person's previous experience."
From diagnosis to top-level sport
The message that needs to reach children and their families, according to Thanasis Tziamourtas, is that the disease should not be a reason to exclude them from physical activity.
"A diagnosis of type 1 diabetes undoubtedly changes the daily life of a child and their family. It should not, however, become a reason to be excluded from play, physical activity or sport. Today, continuous glucose monitors, insulin pumps and automated insulin delivery systems offer opportunities that did not exist a few decades ago. Together with the right education, they enable children and adults with type 1 diabetes to be active more safely.
The message to the child and their family should therefore not be 'Be careful, because you have diabetes, don't exercise'. It should be exactly the opposite: 'Exercise, know your body, monitor your glucose and learn to adjust your insulin and your diet correctly.' Type 1 diabetes requires management, but it should not set the limits on a child's dreams."

Russia Disguises Oil Refinery Repair Equipment in Grain Trains Amid Export Bottlenecks

Russia Disguises Oil Refinery Repair Equipment in Grain Trains Amid Export Bottlenecks
The Russian government is reorienting grain logistics to rail transport and granting these shipments the highest third-priority status, according to the partisan network associated with the Freedom of Russia Legion.
Covert intelligence obtained from sources inside Russian Railways and the Ministry of Transport reveals that standard covered railcars and containers are being secretly added to grain trains.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
This measure, reportedly enacted following a decision by Russian leader Vladimir Putin, elevates agricultural freight to the third-highest status level across the national railway network.
While officially presented as a measure to protect agricultural exports affected by port infrastructure issues in Novorossiysk, the resistance movement reports that the initiative is being used to conceal the transport of critical military-related cargo and industrial components.
A significant portion of the grain involved is stolen from Ukrainian territories occupied since Russia’s full-scale invasion.
To avoid labeling the cargo as dangerous goods, the entire train is registered in the ETRAN system under the category of grain and leguminous crops.
These covered freight cars are designated to transport repair equipment for ELOU-AVT units at damaged oil refineries, including distribution trays for atmospheric-vacuum columns, furnace coils made of special steel, technological centrifugal pumps for fuel oil fractions, and automated control system regulators.
The components are being loaded in several regions with specialized manufacturing capacity, including Volgograd at JSC Volgogradneftemash, Penza at JSC Penzkhimmash and JSC Penzcompressormash, Podolsk at PJSC ZiO-Podolsk, and Tambov at JSC Tambov Plant Komsomolets.
Part of the rolling stock is scheduled to head toward the ports of Ust-Luga and St. Petersburg, unloading refinery repair parts along the route in the Moscow, Tver, and Leningrad regions. Trains carrying grain for export to eastern destinations will supply refineries in other heavily damaged regions, including the Samara and Saratov regions, Perm Krai, and Bashkortostan.
The resistance movement notes that drone components could also be loaded into these cars in the future. By using civilian shipments as cover, the Russian authorities aim to secure dual-use components to restore refinery operations and maintain war financing.
In November 2025, fighters from the Freedom of Russia Legion destroyed a key Russian railway line in the occupied Zaporizhzhia region, causing the derailment of a diesel locomotive and 25 freight cars.
The operation completely halted military rail traffic along the route, allowing Ukrainian Defense Forces to subsequently launch an airstrike on the accumulated military cargo.

Lithuania to propose EU ban on Russian grain transit, sanctions on agricultural oligarchs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
07:21:00 UTC
16:21:00 KST

Lithuania will propose that the European Union ban the transit of Russian grain through the bloc and impose sanctions on Russian agricultural oligarchs who support the war in Ukraine, Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said.
“Russia is using European ports and infrastructure, including those of the Baltic states, to export its grain,” Sinkevičius wrote on Facebook. He said the situation was unacceptable and that Lithuania would seek both a transit ban and sanctions against individual Russian agricultural oligarchs.
The EU currently does not prohibit international trade in Russian agricultural and food products, including grain, with third countries. In 2024, the bloc imposed tariffs on Russian and Belarusian grain products, but those measures did not completely prevent their transit through the EU to third countries.
Sinkevičius said Russia was using EU infrastructure while intensifying attacks on Ukraine, including on its ports and grain ships, and exporting grain allegedly taken from occupied Ukrainian territories.
“We will not allow the Russian war machine to profit by using our infrastructure as a gateway to world markets,” he said.
Lithuania has stepped up checks on grain transiting the country from Russia and Belarus. Since the beginning of September, the State Food and Veterinary Service has taken five samples from two shipments whose origins were unclear, with the samples being tested at foreign laboratories.
Sinkevičius said the transit of Russian grain was a common concern for the Baltic states and that Lithuania and Latvia had similar positions.
Estonia banned the transit of Russian- and Belarusian-origin grain through its territory on October 1. Latvia has also called for closer cooperation among the Baltic states on border controls and inspections of Russian grain shipments.
The issue has gained prominence after Russian grain began appearing in Baltic transport flows. Lithuanian officials have said the country’s infrastructure should not be used to facilitate Russian grain exports.
According to the State Food and Veterinary Service, no shipments of feed grain from Russia, Belarus or other countries considered unreliable have arrived at the Port of Klaipėda since 2024.

Senegal and Morocco set for AFCON title rematch – in Swiss sports court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
07:17:51 UTC
16:17:51 KST

Senegal and Morocco set for AFCON title rematch – in Swiss sports court
Senegal and Morocco on Thursday are again set to fight for the African Cup of Nations title – this time, in the Court of Arbitration for Sport in Switzerland. The closed-door hearing comes nine months after the Confederation of African Football stripped Senegal of their trophy after the team's players walked off the pitch to protest a penalty during the chaotic final roughly nine months ago.
Senegal and Morocco played a chaotic Africa Cup of Nations final in January and they contest the title again Thursday – this time at the Court of Arbitration for Sport.
A turbulent match, provoking violent clashes between Senegal fans and Moroccan police, and a hugely controversial fallout will be re-litigated at sport’s highest court in Switzerland nearly nine months after the referee’s final whistle blew in Rabat.
The authority of that referee, Jean-Jacques Ndala of Congo, could be decisive in Senegal’s appeal to regain the trophy that was stripped from players who earned it on the field of play with a 1-0 win over Morocco after extra time.
Read moreSenegal coach receives five-match ban for ‘unsporting conduct’ at AFCON final
The result was overturned in March to a 3-0 win for Morocco by a Confederation of African Football (CAF) appeals panel because Senegal’s team walked off to protest a penalty being awarded, causing a 15-minute delay in play.
A one-day appeal hearing was scheduled with three judges behind closed doors Thursday at CAS headquarters in Lausanne.
No target date has been set by the court for a verdict that should finally crown the champion of African men’s soccer. The next AFCON tournament kicks off in June, co-hosted by Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda.
Leaders of the Senegalese and Moroccan football federations were expected to skip the hearing that clashes with a three-day CAF football summit in Cape Verde being attended by FIFA President Gianni Infantino.
Football's rule book, The Laws of the Game, is clear about the referee’s decision-making power.
“The decisions of the referee regarding facts connected with play, including whether or not a goal is scored and the result of the match, are final,” Law 5.2 states.
Senegal beat host nation Morocco in a game eventually completed to referee Ndala’s satisfaction, despite the chaos.
The referee restarted play once Senegal’s players had returned to the field after protesting a penalty kick awarded to Morocco deep in stoppage time.
Before the referee could decide to abandon the game, which would have gifted the title to Morocco, Senegal’s star forward Sadio Mané helped persuade his team to finish the game as tensions rose in the stadium.
The game restarted with the spot kick that could have won Morocco a first AFCON title since 1976.
What Brahim Diaz did next entered soccer history. The Real Madrid forward placed a delicate slow chip shot, designed to deceive the goalkeeper who typically dives to one side and watches the ball slowly arc into the middle of the goal.
Senegal goalkeeper Édouard Mendy stood up straight and easily caught the ball. In the stadium VIP section, footage showed a visibly shocked Moroccan Prince Moulay Rachid sitting with FIFA's Infantino.
The game went into extra time, and four minutes later Senegal midfielder Pape Gueye surged forward to fire a rising shot into the Morocco net. It was the only goal.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
More than $1 million in total fines for the two federations, plus players and Senegal coach Pape Thiaw, were imposed 11 days after the game by Cairo-based CAF disciplinary judges.
The judges dismissed a request by Morocco to have the result annulled and be declared the winner because of the Senegalese walk-off.
There were appeals to CAF and, two months after the final, Senegal was ruled to have forfeited the game.
CAF appeal judges cited AFCON tournament rules that if a team “refuses to play or leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorisation of the referee, it shall be considered loser and shall be eliminated for good from the current competition”.
Senegal's government promised to help “pursue all appropriate legal avenues” to regain the title and called for an investigation “into suspected corruption” within African football.
The case fueled the sense that 2030 World Cup co-host Morocco has extensive influence within CAF and FIFA.
In May, Morocco's King Mohammed VI pardoned 18 Senegalese football fans who were jailed over the disorder in the Rabat stadium.

‘Vibrant, design-led and surprisingly green’: why the Dutch city of Eindhoven is perfect for a relaxed arty break
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
07:17:33 UTC
16:17:33 KST

A baggily clad skateboarder’s wheels clatter across concrete floors, the noise bouncing off exposed pipes and iron girders. Vaulted skylights set in high ceilings illuminate the industrial space and its central kitchen, from which my main course – a silky lemon risotto, spiked with samphire, rhubarb, garlic, baby onions and basil – has just been transported.
I’m in the Dutch city of Eindhoven, in North Brabant, famous for its historic connection to Philips, the one-time electronics giant. The restaurant, Radio Royaal, is housed in what was once their engine room, in the Strijp-S neighbourhood. Today, Strijp-S buzzes with concept stores, an indoor food market, MU Hybrid Art House and the Area 51 skatepark. The broader area, Strijp, was where the company was largely headquartered: its zones are named S, T and R. In the late 90s, Philips withdrew from the city where it had started in 1891, and the letters I, J and P were never assigned.
Philips had employed about half of the region’s working population, so its departure for Amsterdam inevitably left a huge hole. Fortunately for Eindhoven, this was short-lived, and within a decade the city had reinvented itself as a multicultural hub for design and innovation – so much so that Dutch Design Week, the largest event of its kind in northern Europe, has been held here since 2005.
This year’s iteration, from 17 to 25 October, has a jam-packed programme of exhibitions, workshops and seminars at more than 100 locations around the city, with thousands of local and international designers involved. About 350,000 visitors are expected, with displays spanning everything from a bar made from mushrooms to the manipulation of Dutch wool (which is coarser than other wools, such as merino) for wearable garments. 
Well beyond Design Week, however, Eindhoven packs a punch in terms of creativity. On my visit, I discovered a city that is not only vibrant and design-led, but also surprisingly green.
Completely off-limits during Philips’ heyday, Strijp-S is perhaps the liveliest example of Eindhoven’s reinvention, with innovative businesses making the most of the industrial spaces. It’s distinguished, too, by the Trudo Tower, a 19-storey building where facade planters froth with more than 70 species of greenery. Purpose-built in 2020, these eye-catching apartments were designed to provide affordable housing for low-income residents.
Despite the city’s industrial past, about 40% of Eindhoven’s landscape comprises greenery. Walkways – complete with bat boxes – run alongside the Dommel river, while larger spaces, such as Karpendonkse Plas and Philips de Jongh park, provide walking and biking opportunities. This, plus an average commute time of 15 minutes, helps to explain why Eindhoven was named the world’s least stressed city last year.
As you walk from the UFO-shaped Evoluon (now functioning as an exhibition space and conference centre, and given by the company to the city on its 75th anniversary) on the edge of the Het Ven neighbourhood towards Strijp-R, the area becomes both green and residential. Ahead of the times, Philips saw the correlation between nature and healthy, happy employees. As early as 1910, the company started building workers’ accommodation with large gardens, which today are a mix of social and private housing.
Strijp-R’s primary allure, however, is the RK Complex. Formerly a Philips ceramics factory, it was bought by renowned Dutch designer Piet Hein Eek and opened in 2010. Other designers have workshops here, too: the idea, said Hein Eek, was to give young creatives an affordable space to work. The concept obviously works: in more than 15 years, only five of the 25 studios have changed hands.
Visitors flock here year-round to check out Hein Eek’s eco-forward scrap wood furniture and for glimpses into the studios, the cavernous exhibition space and the shop, packed with smaller design objects – ceramics, books, jewellery. The onsite Green Restaurant favours local, seasonal ingredients in hearty portions; it’s attached to the boutique Piet Hein Eek hotel, also one of the designer’s innovations. It has 14 rooms, each featuring a distinctive design style, with doubles from €135.
What makes a stay in Eindhoven even more interesting, however, are the myriad ways this impulse towards repurposing spaces, reusing materials and thinking sustainably shapes the visitor experience. I stayed at Hotel Mariënhge (doubles from €83) in the centre, a former monastery characterised by clean lines and cheeky art, its interiors effortlessly blending old and new.
From here, it’s a short walk to the retail district, where vintage stores range from the highly curated Yatva Vintage to a Salvation Army ReShare store. Near Strijp-R, I happen upon Luna & Lore, owned and run by Luna Hartogs. “Lore is about wisdom passed on from previous generations, and I learned to sew from my grandmother,” she explains, as I rifle delightedly through rails of upcycled vintage clothing. “For me, it’s also about passing things on for people to enjoy.”
“Eindhoven gets called ‘Vintage Valhalla’ – a paradise,” Erik van Gerwen of Eindhoven 365 tells me over dinner at Fifth NRE, itself housed in a former gas factory. “There’s the Philips legacy, but the presence of the Design Academy also ensures a lively community, passionate about innovatively making use of what already exists.”
Creating opportunities is a recurring theme in Eindhoven. I see it again at New Order of Fashion, a nonprofit organisation providing makers with resources to experiment with, as well as a sellers’ platform. It’s also a lab, researching the future of fashion from a regenerative perspective, and a public space aiming to inspire visitors to think about their consumer choices.
I loiter outside the Muziekgebouw concert hall: since 2024, its facade has featured a massive mural of a street musician and classical concert violinist embracing. Named Echoes of Harmony, it was commissioned by Eindhoven city council to represent music’s ability to bridge barriers, and since named best mural worldwide by Street Art Cities.
On the city’s north-eastern edge, graffers can legally unleash spray cans in Berenkuil, a two-level roundabout and now the country’s largest open-air graffiti zone. Ramps and rails make it a beeline for skateboarders, too; again, I hear wheels grinding on concrete. There are no dibs here: the art lasts mere days before it’s sprayed over by someone else, but that, I’m told, is the point. In Eindhoven, perhaps more than anywhere else, the idea that everything is ephemeral, yet also renewable, seems entirely at home.
The trip was provided by the Netherlands Board of Tourism and Conventions

NEW DELHI: Weeks after the alleged suicide of a postgraduate medical student in Surat triggered fresh concerns over harassment and ragging in medical colleges, the National Medical Commission (NMC) has sought a para-wise report within 24 hours from MGM Medical College and MY Hospital, Indore, on allegations of mental harassment, public humiliation and academic intimidation of a first-year postgraduate resident.The complaint concerns Dr Simmi Yadav, a first-year postgraduate resident in the Department of Obstetrics & Gynaecology. Filed by her brother, it alleges that she attempted suicide by insulin overdose and is currently in the intensive care unit.The case comes amid continuing concerns over the treatment of junior doctors and medical students. In a December 2024 advisory, the NMC said it continued to receive numerous complaints involving undergraduate and postgraduate students, including cases of mental harassment and instances leading to suicide.The complaint alleges that Dr Simmi was repeatedly humiliated over minor mistakes, threatened with adverse academic consequences and made to undertake non-academic work. The NMC has directed the college to examine the allegations against the concerned residents and faculty and furnish their responses.The commission has sought her duty rosters, attendance and biometric records, handover registers and leave records to verify allegations that she was working 14-15 hours despite an official roster showing around 12-hour duties.
It has also ordered confidential interactions with other PG residents to ascertain whether similar instances of harassment, intimidation or coercion have been reported. The college has been asked to preserve WhatsApp messages, emails, complaints, duty and academic records and other evidence.
The NMC has further sought details of the functioning of the college's Anti-Ragging Committee and Squad, counselling and mental-health support available to PG residents, and compliance with anti-ragging regulations.The regulator's own National Task Force on the mental health of medical students found that 26.7% of respondents reported harassment by senior postgraduate students in clinical settings, highlighting concerns about the working environment faced by junior doctors.The commission has directed the college to ensure that Dr Simmi does not face retaliation, victimisation or adverse academic treatment for raising the complaint or participating in the inquiry. The Action Taken Report, supported by documents, has to be submitted within 24 hours.

Royal Navy serviceman arrested under National Security Act
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
07:14:20 UTC
16:14:20 KST

A junior Royal Navy intelligence specialist from Bedfordshire accused of trying to pass military secrets to Russia appeared in court on Thursday.
Teddy Young, 24, was accused of abusing his high-level security clearance to access secret defence and intelligence data after being deployed on a warship.
The navy rating was also said to have made efforts to contact Russian authorities directly, drafting a message in Russian containing classified information that he hoped to pass on.
Young was arrested at his home in Bedfordshire on Tuesday after an investigation by Counter Terrorism Policing London (CTPL). He was charged with offences under the National Security Act, the Metropolitan police said.
The intelligence specialist was first arrested in May last year. At that point he was suspended and relieved of his duties, and was on gardening leave until his latest arrest. He is the first member of the British armed forces to be charged under the National Security Act 2023.
Young appeared at Westminster magistrates court wearing a grey navy tracksuit and spoke only to confirm his name, ate of birth and address in the village of Clapham, near Bedford. No application was made for bail, though the district judge made clear it would be denied.
Annabel Pilling, presiding, told Young: “On the basis of the information I have already read, there are substantial grounds to believe that if granted bail you would not come back to court and that you would make efforts to avoid further court appearances and would commit further offences.”
Young was remanded in custody to appear before a specialist judge at the Old Bailey on 16 October.
The Crown Prosecution Service said between 26 November 2024 and 21 May 2025 Young had engaged in conduct in preparation for committing an offence of disclosing protected information.
It is also alleged that in the same period he obtained, copied, recorded or retained protected information, intending the conduct to benefit a foreign power.
Commander Helen Flanagan, the head of CTPL, said in a statement issued before the court appearance: “These are very serious charges against a serving member of the armed forces.
“We have worked extremely closely with relevant operational colleagues within the Ministry of Defence as our investigation has progressed to ensure appropriate measures could be taken to mitigate any potential risks linked to this matter.”
A Royal Navy spokesperson said: “A member of the Royal Navy has been charged with National Security Act offences following an investigation by Counter Terrorism Policing London. As legal proceedings are ongoing, it would be inappropriate to comment further at this stage.”
The arrest and charges are not connected to the recent investigation into an incident at RAF Fairford.

8 pct of New Zealanders experience sextortion: Netsafe
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
15:12:04 CST
16:12:04 KST

WELLINGTON, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- Eight percent of New Zealanders have personally experienced sextortion, while another 13 percent know someone who has, according to research by online safety organization Netsafe.
The research found 35 percent of victims reported a moderate to severe impact on their mental wellbeing, as Netsafe and digital wellbeing platform Ignite Aotearoa launched a new pilot providing free counseling and wellbeing support to victims of online harm, Netsafe said in a statement on Wednesday.
An increasing number of New Zealanders have been left distressed by online sextortion, image-based abuse and tech-facilitated harm, the statement said.
The Digital Harm Support Pathway pilot will provide victims reporting serious online harm with up to three funded counseling sessions through Ignite's network of professional counselors nationwide, Netsafe said.
Netsafe CEO Brent Carey said the organization's frontline teams were increasingly seeing the human consequences of online abuse, including fear, shame and anxiety.
"People come to us frightened that an intimate image will be sent to their family, their friends, their school or their workplace. Some are being blackmailed for money. Others are being stalked or have intimate images shared without their consent," Carey was quoted as saying.
Netsafe's previous case analysis has found sextortion can result in severe emotional distress, including depression and suicidal thoughts, the statement said.
Netsafe received 53,691 reports of online harm in the two years to March 2026, more than 2,000 every month, the organization said. ■

Explainer-What's happening with Britain's Jerusalem consulate?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
07:09:54 UTC
16:09:54 KST

Explainer-What's happening with Britain's Jerusalem consulate?
Oct 8 - Britain said on Thursday its nearly 200-year-old consulate in Jerusalem would continue operating on a smaller scale and be renamed as the "UK Mission" in the city, after Israel ordered it shut in a dispute over sanctions on settlements.
Here's what to know about the dispute and diplomatic missions in the Holy City.
WHY IS THIS HAPPENING AND WHY NOW?
The dispute is over sanctions. Israel's order for the consulate to shut was retaliation for Britain saying it would impose a ban on the trade of goods made in Israeli settlements.
On September 8, Israel ordered Britain to close the East Jerusalem consulate within 30 days and remove its diplomats from the city. The deadline expired on Thursday, with Britain and Israel announcing a compromise that would keep the facility open.
WHY IS THE CONSULATE IN JERUSALEM, AND WHERE IS THE EMBASSY?
The consulate is located in the Sheikh Jarrah neighbourhood of East Jerusalem and handles Britain's relations with Palestinians in the city as well as in the occupied West Bank and in the Gaza Strip. It also provides consular services to Palestinians.
The consulate has been in Jerusalem since around 1839, according to the National Library of Israel, when the area was part of the Ottoman Empire and long before Israel's establishment in 1948.
East Jerusalem is considered occupied territory under international law.
Britain's embassy in Israel, like most countries', is in Tel Aviv, which is also home to some government departments. The Israeli prime minister's office, presidency and parliament are in Jerusalem.
WHY IS JERUSALEM'S STATUS SO COMPLICATED?
Jerusalem has long had a bitterly contested status.
It was under British control under the Mandate for Palestine. That ended around the time of Israel's creation in 1948.
Under a United Nations resolution, Jerusalem was meant to come under international governance due to its special status in Judaism, Christianity and Islam.
In the event, Arab countries attacked Israel after its establishment, and the 1948 Arab-Israeli war resulted in Israeli control of West Jerusalem and Jordanian control of East Jerusalem, including most of the city's holy sites.
Israel captured East Jerusalem in the 1967 Six-Day War and annexed it in 1980, coming to control the entire city.
Israel considers the whole of Jerusalem as its capital, but most countries do not recognise that claim and consider East Jerusalem occupied by Israel.
Palestinians want East Jerusalem as the capital of a future state. Decades of negotiations have failed to determine a final status.
WHICH OTHER COUNTRIES HAVE THE BRITISH CONSULAR ARRANGEMENT?
Turkey and several Western countries including France, Belgium, Greece, Italy, Spain and Sweden.
HAS ISRAEL CLOSED ANY OF THEIR CONSULATES?
No. France joined Britain in announcing sanctions, along with Canada, which does not have a consulate in Jerusalem. Israel has not taken action against Paris.
WHAT ABOUT THE UNITED STATES, ISRAEL'S CLOSEST ALLY?
The United States moved its embassy from Tel Aviv and merged it with its consulate in Jerusalem during President Donald Trump's first term in 2018, the first US administration to make the move.
The US was meant to have moved it by 1999 under a Congressional law, but successive presidents postponed the move on national security grounds, in efforts to avoid scuttling chances for peace between Israel and the Palestinians. REUTERS

First U.S.-built Iron Dome interceptor delivered to Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
07:08:07 UTC
16:08:07 KST

- A Raytheon-Rafael plant in East Camden, Arkansas, delivered the first Iron Dome Tamir interceptor built entirely in the United States to Israel’s missile defense agency.
- The plant, which opened in November 2025, also holds a $1.25 billion contract for Tamir missiles and will build the SkyHunter variant for the U.S. Marine Corps.
A Raytheon-Rafael joint venture in East Camden, Arkansas, has delivered the first Tamir interceptor for Israel’s Iron Dome air defense system built and assembled entirely in the United States, the Israeli Ministry of Defense said.
The missile was handed over at a ceremony at the plant run by R2S, the joint venture between Raytheon and Israel’s Rafael Advanced Defense Systems, to the Israel Missile Defense Organization, which oversees Israel’s air and missile defense programs within the ministry’s research and development directorate. Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders, U.S. Missile Defense Agency Deputy Director Maj. Gen. Jason D. Cothern and Israel Missile Defense Organization Director Moshe Patel attended, along with Rafael and R2S executives. The ministry did not say how many Tamirs the plant will produce or when the next deliveries are due.
The Camden plant is the first site outside Israel to manufacture complete Tamir interceptors, the ministry said. Raytheon and Rafael have produced parts of the missile together for more than a decade under U.S. workshare requirements tied to American funding for Iron Dome, and the Arkansas line now builds the whole round on U.S. soil.
R2S broke ground on the facility in February 2024 and opened it in November 2025, raising its planned investment from $33 million to about $63 million and expanding its expected workforce from 30 to as many as 60 jobs. When the plant opened, R2S received a $1.25 billion direct commercial sales contract to supply Israel with Tamir missiles, missile kits and test equipment, the joint venture’s first production contract.
The same plant is set to build SkyHunter, the U.S. version of the Tamir chosen for the U.S. Marine Corps’ Medium-Range Intercept Capability program, which uses Iron Dome components to defend against cruise missiles, aircraft, rockets, artillery and mortars.
Iron Dome entered service in 2011 to intercept short-range rockets, artillery shells and mortars fired at Israeli towns and cities, and its Tamir interceptor was developed under the Israel Missile Defense Organization’s leadership with Rafael as prime contractor. The ministry said the system has carried out more than 10,000 operational interceptions over 15 years of service, including during recent regional conflicts.
Iron Dome is one of three Israeli air defense programs run jointly with the U.S. Missile Defense Agency, alongside David’s Sling and the Arrow system. The Israel Missile Defense Organization leads development and co-production of David’s Sling and Arrow, and co-production of Iron Dome, together with the Missile Defense Agency and defense companies in both countries.

High school students to turn out for new protests across France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
07:07:17 UTC
16:07:17 KST

Many protesters have been injured and thousands of children arrested. (AFP Photo)
The police tear gas grenade shattered the 14-year-old’s jaw and many of his teeth. The officer who fired it was taken into custody a week later and charged with violent mutilation, punishable by up to 15 years in prison. Following surgery, the boy cannot speak and can only eat with a straw, his mother says.
Other adolescents have also suffered life-changing injuries blamed on police weaponry during nationwide protests by high school students demanding more funding for run-down schools. In the former mining town of Lens, a 15-year-old lost a hand in an incident involving a police stun grenade. In Tours, in the wine-making Loire region, the prosecutor there says a police riot-control round is suspected in the partial blinding of a 16-year-old.
Beyond physical wounds, the massive use of police arrests and tactics that government critics and human rights campaigners allege have been unnecessarily violent is giving a generation of French schoolchildren, and soon-to-be voters, a real-life education about state power and their rights as citizens, and how the two sometimes clash.
“It politicizes you at an incredible speed,” said Alexis Baudelin, a Paris attorney for more than a dozen youngsters taken into custody.
“For many of them, for all of them, this was one of the first times that they’d taken part in a demonstration, coming together in a public space to voice demands they considered legitimate.”
According to the Interior Ministry, police have made more than 6,500 arrests, mostly of young people, since protests began snowballing last week, including 488 people detained during nationwide demonstrations on Oct. 6. The movement demanding increased funds and more replacement teachers for schools started in a Paris-region high school in mid-September.
Lawyers and researchers who study French policing caution that the muscular response could spawn disillusioned young adults soured on the Republic and its promises of "Liberty, Equality, Fraternity." Police have been less forgiving with teenage protesters than they previously were when farmers, a powerful lobby in France, doused government buildings with manure, blocked roads and set fires.
Baudelin, the lawyer, said his young clients have had a crash course in “unrestrained violence from the police.”
“Being locked up for hours and hours with nothing, in cells that are for the most part extremely unsanitary, in police stations that smell terrible, where you can’t sleep, with police officers telling you that if you don’t talk, if you don’t tell the truth, threatening you, telling you that your life is going to be ruined,” he said.
“It’s an experience that can be deeply traumatic and is completely out of proportion.”
Amid a growing outcry, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez announced on Oct. 7 that the model of stun grenade suspected of mutilating the teenager in Lens will no longer be used against high schoolers, in light, he said, of a “strong possibility” that such a weapon was involved in ripping off the pupil’s hand.
“We need to understand exactly what happened,” Nunez said.
Still, he has also defended police actions as proportionate in “almost all cases.”

Türkiye prioritizes macro-financial stability amid global headwinds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
07:06:54 UTC
16:06:54 KST

Türkiye prioritizes macro-financial stability and a tight fiscal policy to cushion the impact of shocks while addressing global structural headwinds, Turkish Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Simsek said.
Simsek said Thursday during the Istanbul Economic Forum's opening ceremony that the government maintained a tight fiscal policy to cushion the impact of shocks and prioritize macro-financial stability.
The two-day forum was organized by the Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye to address global economic policy challenges by gathering central bank governors and high-level policymakers from around the world, including the US and the UK.
Simsek noted that global structural headwinds included conflicts, trade protectionism, high indebtedness, unfavorable demographics, impending climate disasters and artificial intelligence (AI).
The country plans to increase defense spending by 229% in the 2027 budget against the Central Bank's 21% inflation target for next year to build deterrence.
Simsek added that the value of research and development in defense projects exceeded $100 billion, with around 1,400 defense products and projects, moving the country toward becoming a top 10 exporter.
He said Türkiye ranked among the top three globally for official development assistance and diplomatic footprint.
Turkish Airlines flew to the most destinations compared with other carriers, he recalled.
He also said the government invested in an $8 billion railway project crossing the Bosphorus in Istanbul to connect Beijing to London.
The country also encouraged its neighbors to invest in additional corridors, such as the new development road, to improve connectivity and resilience.
Simsek pointed out that the nation invested in natural gas and oil pipelines to ensure the availability of energy supplies.
The nation boosted the share of renewables in electricity generation to almost 60% and set an ambitious 35% electrification target, up from 23%, as the COP31 host.
The government responded to global trade protectionism by expanding free trade agreements, holding 54 pacts, with three pending and ongoing negotiations with Japan, Indonesia, the Gulf Cooperation Council and Canada.
He pointed out that tourism revenue jumped ninefold over the past quarter-century, placing Türkiye among the top five global tourist destinations.
Simsek mentioned that the country had over 50 internationally accredited healthcare facilities and attracted medical tourists for cosmetic treatments.
He said the nation became the world's third-largest exporter of soap operas and ranked second to London in the gaming ecosystem for startups and unicorns.
The country ranked second to China in the global league of contractors and hoped to aid in regional reconstruction, which required at least $1 trillion over the next decade.
Simsek noted that the nation hosted the sixth-largest number of international students at its universities.
He underscored that total indebtedness remained at 91%, compared with a 230% average for emerging market peers, while public debt to GDP stood at 22%.
The government targeted a 3.1% deficit this year, keeping it well below the 5.8% average for global emerging markets, and reduced current expenditures from 4.6% of the budget to 2.9%.
The administration sought to strengthen its fiscal position by investing in public procurement, state-owned enterprise governance and tax reforms.
Simsek said the working-age population would continue to grow over the next decade and the administration planned reforms to boost women's low labor force participation rate.
He said the country invested in 5G+ technology, expanded fiber capacity and planned nuclear power plants, including small modular reactors (SMRs), to power AI.
The government also helped small and medium-sized enterprises boost productivity to capitalize on the positive potential of AI.
The administration invested in irrigation and climate-resilient agriculture to combat global warming.
Simsek remarked that the country frequently tested its ability to recover quickly from difficulties and adapted its policies despite challenges in a tough neighborhood.
He underscored that delivering price stability remained the primary goal of the medium-term economic program while maintaining fiscal discipline.
The minister added that external imbalances remained manageable even though they deteriorated this year because of the war.
He highlighted that real convergence continued as the economy grew slightly more than 3%, outpacing the 1.5% growth of trading partners, while historical growth over the last 25 years stood closer to 5.5%.
Simsek noted that the Central Bank governor utilized quantitative and selective credit-tightening tools while the government was adjusting its fiscal policy to make support more selective and targeted.
He concluded that recent stress in the asset management sector remained contained and the country maintained plenty of policy space to respond in a shock-prone world.
Touching on the country's disinflation process, the minister said the process had largely stalled this year because of the war, "but we're not giving up."
"This year deficit would have been actually closer to two and a half percent, had we not deployed fiscal space to cushion or to, to slow the pass through from crudes to final products," he added.
