Tesco lifts profit forecast and says consumer confidence is resilient
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
06:52:40 UTC
15:52:40 KST

Tesco has raised its profit outlook as it expects households to splash out this Christmas – despite buying less alcohol – as they shrug off “uncertainty” over the Iran war.
The UK’s biggest grocer said sales rose just 2% to £33.8bn in the 26 weeks to 29 August, but underlying profit was up 6.5% to £1.8bn.
Ken Murphy, the chief executive of Tesco, said growth had been helped by strong online sales, which were up 8%, and a 9% jump in revenue from its premium own-label Finest range.
He said: “Consumers in the UK have been pretty resilient in an uncertain environment and there is a sense that customers want to enjoy Christmas, given everything that is going on in the world.”
The retailer had bought more stock of “key Christmas lines”, understood to be foods such as turkey and mince pies, and added 10% more delivery slots for its online grocery business. It is also ramping up its in-house rapid delivery service, Whoosh, and has signed new partnerships, including with Deliveroo.
Murphy said he expected Britons to seek out a “marginally healthier Christmas” with higher sales of low-alcohol and no-alcohol drinks, including ready-mixed mocktails, but that families would still treat themselves as “customers do love to indulge”.
He said he was not expecting food supplies to be hit by this summer’s drought. Tesco had also hedged its energy costs into next year and was making savings across the business to help keep prices down for shoppers.
He said the business still had room for growth despite being almost twice the size of its nearest rival, Sainsbury’s, with a 28% market share, and that he did not “dwell too much” on the possibility of its closest rival acquiring another leading supermarket.
Sainsbury’s is understood to have walked away from merger talks in January with the UK’s sixth-biggest supermarket, Morrisons, prompting consolidation chatter across the industry.
“Whatever happens in the market we will respond to it,” Murphy said. While Tesco is expanding its reach with financial services and more fashion, he said its strategy “begins and ends in winning in food”.
The company added: “While consumer confidence has remained relatively resilient in the first half of the year, ongoing geopolitical tensions continue to create uncertainty and we remain focused on helping customers get the best possible value.”
Earlier this year, Tesco warned that profits could fall in the year ahead, citing increased uncertainty caused by the conflict in Iran, which began in late February. However, some economic indicators have suggested that the war has not yet had a significant impact. Last week, official estimates for UK growth in the second quarter were upgraded.
The company said it now expected to make underlying annual profits of between £3.15bn and £3.3bn. That represents an upgrade from its previous expectation of at least £3bn in profits but the bottom end of the range would still mark a fall from a year earlier.
Sales at established UK Tesco stores were up 1.5% as food sales motored, but the group’s Booker wholesale arm continued to struggle, with sales falling 2.6%.
The supermarket said it was increasingly using artificial intelligence across the business, including in a meal-planning assistant that was tested from April with 280,000 staff before being launched for customers in September.
It said AI was also helping to cut costs by making in-store stock replenishment more efficient and improving energy efficiency in its supermarkets.
Tesco shares rose 4% on Thursday morning.

British consulate in East Jerusalem will stay open as UK mission, says Ed Miliband
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
06:51:05 UTC
15:51:05 KST

Israel and the UK have backed away from a full-scale diplomatic confrontation, with Britain announcing it is rebranding its consulate general building in East Jerusalem as a UK mission, a move that will result in UK diplomats leaving Israel, with only seven to remain in the building. Among those leaving is the consul general, Helen Winterton.
The change was forced on the UK by the Israeli government as punishment for the decision by the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, last month to ban trade with illegal settlements and introduce a tougher sanctions regime against those who aided the building of settlements. The UK is seeking to protect the two-state solution as the best means of ending the Israel-Palestine conflict.
Miliband has also backed away from a threat to expel a parallel number of Israeli diplomats from London, as was once planned, arguing it would be unwise to do so during the Israeli election campaign.
There has been a dispute within the UK government over whether taking tough measures against Israel at such a sensitive political moment could help the re-election chances of the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, before polls on 27 October if they appear to boost his standing as a leader prepared to confront the nation’s critics.
Israel had ordered the British consulate in East Jerusalem to shut on Thursday, and the foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, said that it had acted on its threat, describing the consulate as closed.
The consulate is separate from the UK embassy, based in Tel Aviv, and has a distinct diplomatic role, covering East Jerusalem, the rest of the West Bank and Gaza, where it provides consular services to Palestinians. Miliband said in a statement: “The UK government reiterates its longstanding view that East Jerusalem is occupied territory.”
Miliband said the mission remained independent, by which he meant it will continue to report directly to the UK Foreign Office in London rather than through the UK embassy in Tel Aviv.
One former Foreign Office diplomat said: “Israel has always wanted to shut the consulates in Jerusalem […] Israel will come for the French next.”
Sa’ar listed four actions to curtail UK activity in Israel, including the removal of British representatives from the International Gaza Support Center in Kiryat Gat and entry bans to Israel for 12 named individuals, including the former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn. “We established a clear principle: It is not possible to act against Israel without Israel taking appropriate measures in response,” he said. “We did not want to reach this point, but the actions of the UK Labour government brought us here.”
He also accused the UK government of “hostile rhetoric, including false accusations against Israel, such as accusations of ‘ethnic cleansing’”.
Miliband, who is currently visiting Kyiv, said in a statement that, having withdrawn a number of staff and families in recent weeks partly for security reasons, it would be possible to work to build up the staffing at the mission in future months.
He said Britain would not take any reciprocal action against Israel while the two sides engaged in talks, in effect suspending discussions until a new Israeli government is formed.
UK sources said Sa’ar had threatened to close the whole consulate, and that it was better for Britain to retain its reduced presence in the hope it could be restored and rebuilt, regardless of the imminent election outcome.
The sources emphasised that the right to take reciprocal action remained, and the UK did not accept that Israel had the legal right to close the consulate, which has stood for 200 years and is in East Jerusalem on territory that Britain and international courts recognise as occupied territory. It was thought not feasible to defy Israel since the UK diplomats would have no security protection.
Miliband said the UK mission would be independent, operational and still able to provide vital services to the Palestinian people. The value of that assertion will be tested by the small number of diplomats remaining and their reduced diplomatic status. The UK national security adviser, Jonathan Powell, travelled to Israel last week to negotiate a version of the deal.
Vincent Fean, the UK consul general to Palestine between 2010 and 2014, said: “The term mission is a generic diplomatic term and does not of itself have any meaning … In terms of numbers, losing 20 staff is a big drop but it’s a better outcome than nothing. It leaves a space, a place and team to build up whatever the outcome of the Israeli election.”
Diplomats from other western countries had been worried about any closure setting a precedent, and suggested Britain had to respond strongly to the Israeli move because it had implications beyond the immediate dispute.
The incident has highlighted growing frustration among Israel’s longtime allies over its settlements in the occupied West Bank, viewed by much of the world as illegal under international law. In his statement last month to the UK parliament, Miliband said settler terrorists, supported by Netanyahu’s government, were committing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank. Israel disputes this.
The UK Foreign Office was advised informally by the former attorney general Dominic Grieve that Israel would be acting unlawfully if it closed the consulate on the basis it was sited in East Jerusalem, which is recognised by the UN and most of its members as being occupied Palestinian territory.
Israel has also said it will revoke the credentials of Dutch diplomats from the country’s mission to Palestine in response to the Netherlands’ ban on imports from illegal Israeli settlements. France and Canada, which joined the UK in the settlement trade ban, have not had action taken against them.
UK-Israeli relations have deteriorated steadily during the war in Gaza, prompted by Hamas’s 7 October 2023 attack on Israel, as Britain has become increasingly critical of the way in which Netanyahu seems prepared to tolerate the deaths of thousands of Palestinians in an effort to render Hamas inoperative, a task successive Westminster governments have thought is unachievable through his methods.
The UK has rescinded a large number of arms export licences to Israel, and Miliband has spoken of evidence of war crimes in Gaza. He has declined to accuse Israel of genocide on the grounds he believed this a matter for international courts to determine.

Yemen’s government needs tribes to defeat the Houthis. Will they join?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
06:50:08 UTC
15:50:08 KST

Yemen’s government needs tribes to defeat the Houthis. Will they join?
Yemen’s tribes could prove crucial to government’s fight against the Houthis, but many may wait for evidence of sustained military gains before choosing sides.
Sanaa, Yemen – The Yemeni government’s new military offensive against the Houthis is testing more than the balance of forces in the country – it is also testing whether the government can persuade powerful tribes in Houthi-controlled areas that the balance of power is beginning to shift.
For years, many of the tribes hostile or wary of the Iran-backed Houthis have stopped short of openly confronting the movement, deterred by their military strength and by previous failed uprisings. Those same tribes are now looking to the internationally recognised government’s newly-activated frontlines – on the Red Sea coast, Marib and al-Jawf primarily – to see if the limited advances made since the Dawn of Yemen military operation launch this week can turn into sustained gains.
The offensive by the Saudi Arabia-backed government forces follows major Houthi gains in September, when the armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God) swept across the country’s Red Sea coast. The Houthis captured vital trade corridors, including the port city of Mocha and territory around the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, one of the world’s most important shipping routes.
While airstrikes have inflicted losses on Houthi forces over the past few days, pushing towards Houthi strongholds where the group has been entrenched since the war started in 2014, including Sanaa, Saada, and Amran, remains a formidable challenge.
With the government declaring an all-out war on the Houthis, pledging to recapture Sanaa, tribal distrust of the government may diminish, prompting tribes to shift positions at the right time, experts say. The role of the tribes could therefore prove critical to the government’s ability to advance deeper into Houthi-controlled territories.
On Monday, Marib governorate – the government’s stronghold in the north – saw a large tribal rally attended by tribal sheikhs and local anti-Houthi fighters from tribes such as the Jadan from Marib, Nihm from Sanaa and other allied tribes.
The rally announced a general mobilisation to support the armed forces in the battle to “restore the state and topple the Houthi coup”.
“If this tribal support translates into actual mobilisation and sustained participation in the battle, tribes will help government troops advance toward Houthi-controlled areas and the Houthi heartland, including Sanaa,” said Adel Dashela, a researcher at the Sana’a Center for Strategic Studies.
Over the past decade of war in Yemen, tribes have repeatedly mobilised against the Houthis at a local level, but deep divisions and a lack of sustained outside backing have prevented the emergence of a unified tribal front. Nevertheless, tribes can potentially be a key source of manpower and influence for the government.
“Tribal fighters remain indispensable to any future campaign against the Houthis. But to be effective, their military engagement must occur through formalised state and coalition command structures, rather than as an independent vanguard,” Dashela said.
‘Wait for the right time’
Tribes in Yemen do not want to risk confronting Houthi forces without support, and they “wait for the right time” to act, Abdulsalam Mohammed, chairman of the Yemeni Abaad Studies and Research Center, said.
“The tribes seek a powerful state, and once they find the state reliable, they can side with it,” Mohammed said.
He added that tribes do not want to repeat mistakes made by tribes that had rebelled against the Houthis, and then not received enough support from the government.
“Those tribes revolted against the Houthis, and they were crushed amid the absence of the government’s effective role,” Mohammed said.
In January 2019, fighting broke out between the Houthis and the Hajoor tribe in northwest Yemen’s Hajjah, lasting several weeks. The Houthis eventually captured the Hajoor areas in March of the same year.
At the time, Saudi Arabia dropped food, medical supplies and weapons to besieged Hajoor fighters, but this did not prevent the tribe’s defeat by the Houthis.
Mohammed said that even in areas where the Houthis have local support, some tribes could gradually shift their allegiance towards the government, if they saw it as serving their interest.
“Not all tribes fighting for the Houthis are staunch supporters. Their motivations range from pragmatism to ideological loyalty and material necessity,” Mohammed said.
‘A friend of the tribe’
Over the past decade, the Houthis have weakened traditional tribal power structures in areas under their control, co-opting some leaders and replacing others with loyalists. They have defeated tribal challenges, and have withstood not only conflict with the Yemeni government and Saudi Arabia, but also bombing by the United States, the United Kingdom and Israel. All of that has reinforced a perception among tribes that the Houthi military capability had become “invincible”.
A tribal sheikh in northern Yemen, who asked not to be named for security reasons, told Al Jazeera that the Houthi military “supremacy” in the country over a decade-long war has “dwarfed the political and military role of the tribe”.
“Before the Houthi takeover of power, the government was like a friend of the tribe,” he said. “Today, the tribe is subordinate to the Houthis.”
The Houthis, according to him, used three tactics to tighten their grip on territories under their control: military force, financial incentives and their public identification with the Palestinian cause.
“The Houthis used military force if negotiations or financial incentives failed to win the tribes’ backing. Moreover, the Houthi military support for Palestine has earned the group additional popular and tribal support,” said the tribal figure.
As the Houthis built up enormous military and financial power over the past few years, the tribal sheikh said tribes acting alone could not match the group’s power. He also said that the government’s reported gains on some frontlines could not by themselves be taken as a sign that the Houthis were collapsing.
“A concrete government advance on the battlefields would reassure some Yemeni tribes that the Houthis have lost ground,” the tribal sheikh said. “Once this materialises, anti-Houthi and neutral tribes can feel confident and begin confronting the group.”

Lithuania, EU and Canada withdraw support for Vilnius disinfo conference under US pressure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
06:49:00 UTC
15:49:00 KST

Lithuania’s foreign ministry, as well as Canada and the EU external action service, withdrew support from a disinformation conference in Vilnius after being pressured by the US administration, Politico reported Thursday.
The reported pressure came after organisers announced sessions discussing US role in spreading disinformation.
The #Disinfo2026 conference is being held Wednesday and Thursday in Vilnius. Its program initially included sessions examining the United States as an actor in foreign information manipulation and interference, or FIMI, which reportedly angered the Trump administration.
According to Politico, the US State Department asked American embassies in several European countries and the EU to express Washington’s concerns and determine whether governments participating in the conference agreed with characterising the United States as a FIMI actor.
One session, titled “USA as a FIMI threat: acknowledge, adapt, push back”, featured two American researchers and a former CIA official and examined how the United States had become a disinformation threat to Europe.
Another, titled “Under attack: How the counter-disinformation community is dealing with US government pressure”, asked lawyers to assess the threat posed by US government entry bans targeting European figures.
Canada and Lithuania asked organisers Monday to remove their ministries’ logos from conference materials, according to a conference participant cited by Politico. The European External Action Service, the EU’s diplomatic service, followed suit Tuesday.
Asked to comment on the report, the State Department said it could not discuss diplomatic conversations but that it should not be surprising that countries distanced themselves from the conference after learning that it characterised the United States as a “FIMI threat”.
“While we are unable to comment on the details of diplomatic conversations, it should not be a surprise that countries would disaffiliate from this conference upon learning that it labeled the U.S. a ‘FIMI threat’,” the State Department said in a statement, according to Politico.
Following discussions with US officials, Canada and Lithuania withdrew their support for the conference, meaning they are no longer participating in discussions or featured in conference materials. The European External Action Service was also removed from the official program.
Photographs reviewed by Politico showed conference displays with the logos of the Canadian, Lithuanian and EU diplomatic services covered up. France remained the only major sponsor listed.
Representatives of the European External Action Service and Lithuania’s Foreign Ministry said they withdrew because parts of the conference program did not correspond with their official positions, but they did not specify which parts.
Lithuania’s ministry won’t comment on US pressure
Approached by BNS for comment, Lithuania’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has not confirmed whether it withdrew from the conference because of pressure from the US, saying instead the program did not align with Lithuania’s national interests.
“The Foreign Ministry withdrew from participating in the Disinfo 2026 conference, formally distanced itself from the conference’s content, and asked the organisers not to include any references to the ministry in the conference materials once it became clear that certain parts of the program did not align with the government’s positions and Lithuania’s national interests,” the ministry told BNS.
Speaking to LRT RADO, Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said that the conference organisers “went way overboard and made a huge blunder”.
He said he was “surprised and shocked” that the US was being put in the same category as Russia or China.
“This does not align with our views and principles, so we decided to withdraw from the event and, in the future, ensure that the topic of combating disinformation is not twisted into an anti-American narrative that weakens our ties with our allies,” Budrys told LRT RADIO.

Higher prices, simpler menus, and fewer customers: In year five of the war, Russia&#039;s restaurants and bars are finally struggling to survive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
06:48:34 UTC
15:48:34 KST

By the end of 2025, 16 restaurants had closed around Moscow’s Patriarch Ponds – five times as many as in previous years. It is just one of many signs that the boom of the war’s early years is over. Revenue at restaurants and cafés across Russia is steadily declining. The number of bars has fallen by 6% nationwide and by 14% in Moscow. Customers are cutting back on spending, while costs and taxes are rising. As expected, the sharpest decline has hit the mid-priced restaurant segment, while the outlook for fast food and high-end eateries remains more favorable — at least for now.
Fewer customers, higher prices
This summer, on the main street in central Moscow, many establishments were unusually empty. The Saperavi café was one-third full, CoffeeMania had few customers, and Chaykhana No. 1 was all but completely devoid of customers. The same was true of Tyrolskie Pirogi, the Kremlin cafeteria, and Art Life. The only places that were consistently full were bars – Harat’s, the Krombacher beer restaurant, and the Czech pub Pilsner, among others.
Alexey (name changed), the owner of several Moscow restaurants and gastro-bars, confirms the downturn: “The past few years can broadly be divided into two stages. After the downturn in 2022, the situation stabilized in 2023 and through the first half of 2025, with even some signs of growth. But starting in the second half of 2025, revenues began to decline, and that trend continues to this day.”
The statistics also confirm the downturn. According to mapping app 2GIS, by spring 2026 the number of restaurants in Russia’s cities (population greater than one million) had fallen by 5%, while the number of smaller cafés had declined by 6%, to 12,500. The drop was partly driven by falling tourist numbers amid increasingly frequent drone attacks. According to the newspaper Kommersant, alcohol sales at restaurants fell by more than 40% on average in the first half of 2026, and wine sales were down by 45%, to 361,000 decaliters.
The number of bars is also declining. As of August, Russia’s million-plus cities had 6% fewer bars, while in Moscow the number was down 14% from August 2025, Vedomosti reports. Russian media conclude that people are trying to save money by cutting back on alcohol. The Insider’s sources confirm the trend: Alexey also reports an average 20% decline in foot traffic and a 20% drop in the average check at his Moscow establishments.
The rising cost of restaurant services, and the resulting increase in the average check, is a trend that began long before the full-scale war. Sergei, a wine restaurateur, says the industry’s problems date back to 2014, when “they seized Crimea and imposed sanctions on themselves.” The problems were less about wine than food. “Our government banned imports of dairy products and all kinds of steaks. What happened? We lost U.S. marbled beef. We had nothing comparable,” Sergei explains.
The industry’s problems date back to 2014, when “they seized Crimea and imposed sanctions on themselves.”
According to him, adaptation has not solved the problem. Although the quality of Miratorg’s Russian beef has improved, it still cannot match the level of Argentine marbled beef. Russian cheeses have also improved considerably, but now they cost as much as European varieties — and sometimes more, even though imports must be routed through Kazakhstan and Belarus, driving up their prices.
“If you want to make good pasta, you need to add Parmigiano Reggiano and Grana Padano, and their prices have soared by 30–40%. On top of that, the dollar has jumped, so the price of the dish in the restaurant has gone up too,” Sergei says.
The Russian government also regularly raises excise duties on alcohol imported from “unfriendly countries.” In 2025, import duties on wine and beer exceeded their cost, as The Insider noted. The proceeds go toward Putin’s “wine Disneyland” and enrich his friends.
Sergei has been working with major wine shops since 2022:
“When I started, a bottle of excellent Trapiche Malbec cost 690 rubles on the store shelf. It was often discounted by 30%, so you could get it for 400 rubles. A glass of the same wine in a restaurant cost about the same. Now the bottle costs 1,490 rubles. The price has more than doubled. Some wines have tripled. Before the war, a bottle of French Petrus cost around 400,000 rubles; now it costs 1.8 million rubles in Russia. And you won’t find it in restaurants anymore. All wine has gone up insanely.”
Excise duties on spirits are rising too. For restaurateurs, Sergei says, that means lower margins. He recalls that before the annexation of Crimea, a bottle of 16-year-old Lagavulin cost 2,600 rubles when purchased for a restaurant, with suppliers bringing it in from Scotland at cost. In stores, a bottle cost 3,000–3,500 rubles, but could be bought for 2,500 rubles on sale.
Now, Sergei says, Scottish whisky enters Russia only through parallel imports. A bottle of Lagavulin costs around 20,000 rubles in stores and about 16,000 wholesale: “In a pub now, 50 grams of whisky costs as much as an entire bottle did 12 years ago.”
Rising prices are already driving away middle-class customers who, Sergei says, come into restaurants and complain: “Your glass used to cost 500 rubles, and now it’s 3,000! How can that be?!” Many simply turn around and leave. To save money, they order food for delivery and buy wine at stores.
To save money, they order food for delivery and buy wine at stores.
Sergei admits that even as a senior manager, he himself goes to restaurants less and less often: “My wife and I used to go out once a week – just to relax, have a meal and drink a glass of wine. Now we hardly do it at all. Maybe once a month, because our incomes have fallen while prices have risen.”
Sommelier Tatyana says consumers have become sharply segmented in recent years: “The first group consists of people who are used to drinking wine of a certain quality. They keep drinking it despite the sanctions, higher transportation costs, duties, excise taxes, and so on. The second group switches to cheaper Russian alternatives.”
Still, it is not only imported wine that is becoming more expensive – Russian wine is too.
Menu: “It was one thing, and now it’s slightly different”
Despite rising costs, restaurateurs are trying to avoid raising prices or switching to cheaper ingredients. Restaurateur Platon, for example, says the prices of products bought by his restaurants have risen 15–20% over the past year: “We raise menu prices on average once every four to six months, but never by 20%.” He says prices at his establishments change only when the menu is updated, “because we keep food costs at an acceptable level.”
Moscow sommelier Tatyana says the industry is gradually adapting, replacing suppliers and, to some extent, recipes. But the changes to menus are not radical. She calls it an “incomplete replacement” — “it was one thing, and now it’s slightly different.”
Unlike Sergei, the sommelier believes Russian food products are no worse than Western ones: “Restaurants are working more with farms. Their products are usually high-quality. Many restaurants emphasize this. We don’t import from France or Germany – we have our own! And our cheese is just as good,” she says.
Still, as Tatyana explains, the new circumstances have taken some getting used to: “If you need to bring in food products or wine from France now, it has to go through a third country. It used to be fairly easy to do this through the Baltic states. Now the process is much more complicated. As a result, many establishments have had to rethink their recipes, and wine imports from countries such as Azerbaijan, Armenia, Belarus, Georgia, Iran, Serbia, Turkey, and Uzbekistan are on the rise."
Even shot bars face similar problems, says Konstantin, a bartender: “For example, Kahlúa, the Mexican coffee liqueur, has tripled in price. At one point, it was a problem because we had to figure out what to use in the hugely popular White Russian cocktail. It’s the same with most Western products – they have gradually been replaced with Russian alternatives. There’s more Russian alcohol now… The bar used to be pretty good, with good whisky, bourbon, liqueurs, absinthe. Now it’s getting worse and worse – we keep hitting new lows in quality.”
Wages: high and off the books
Record-low unemployment has exacerbated Russia’s overall labor shortage, but that is mainly a problem for employers looking for highly skilled workers. Waiting tables is hard work, but generally accessible to anyone. However, the same cannot be said of chefs and cooks.
There are plenty of restaurant-sector vacancies, says sommelier Tatyana: “every establishment is short-staffed, and they are filling the gaps themselves. The shortages are among cooks, bartenders, baristas, couriers. There has never been a shortage of managers and administrators. Everyone wants to manage,” she says.
In the race to attract workers, employers have been forced to raise wages. To keep this from eating into profits – or adding to losses – they resort to tax-avoidance schemes. Svetlana says many Moscow restaurants do not officially employ their workers, paying them under the table instead.
As part of their efforts to cut costs, many establishments are also eliminating ancillary positions. “There were three people: two cooks and a sous-chef. They fired one cook and divided his duties between the other two. That’s optimization for the employer , because now they don’t have to pay a third person. The two who remain won’t get that third salary added to their own – they’ll just get a little extra, and only if they’re lucky,” Svetlana says, describing her own workplace.
A separate problem, unrelated to either the war or sanctions, is Generation Z workers, says Sergei, the wine restaurateur:
“Gen Z doesn’t want to work – they just make demands. When I was 20 and worked as a bartender, I could do ten shifts in a row, pour beer, chat with customers, have fun, and have a few drinks myself. Now a modern 20-year-old Gen Zer will tell you, ‘Fuck off, I’ll work two on, two off. And I want a 200,000-ruble salary!’ You tell him, ‘Well, sorry, we can only pay you 80,000.’
“People like that usually work for two or three days and then quit, citing exhaustion and burnout. And if they leave on a busy day, the establishment loses money. Say it’s Friday or the Champions League final, and half the Gen Z staff say they’re not coming in – the bartender, waiter, and cook. That’s a problem. Young people see no point in working; they want the end result.”
Konstantin, who works for a chain of Moscow shot bars, is a vivid example of what Sergei describes. “It’s easy to start, easy to quit, hard to work,” the bartender says. Many students take these jobs only for a season. Sometimes one team stays at a particular shot bar for a long time, “and then they all suddenly scatter again – it’s like the skin renews itself.”
Shot bars, an island of stability
The low-price segment has also felt the downturn. Near Moscow's Tverskaya metro station, at two of the Vkusno i Tochka locations that moved into McDonald's vacated premises in 2022, there were few customers at the end of the workday. Even at the site of Russia’s first American fast food restaurant, half the cash registers were closed and many tables were empty. Most customers were 35–50, with hardly any young people in sight. A sign outside read, “We pay more than you think,” promising a monthly salary of 142,000 rubles for full shifts.
There are, however, establishments with a steady stream of customers. Bartender Konstantin is confident that even an economic crisis will not force shot bars to close: “A collapse isn’t even close, because prices are low, the PR is good, they’re highly recognizable, and they’re conveniently located near student hangouts. They’re only expanding.”
Shot bars also had to raise prices after the war began, but they have done so in stages, Konstantin says, adding that the bars have introduced deliberately cheap items, such as lavash chips, to boost margins. The chain is also unaffected by problems with imported products, surviving on cheap vodka, infused spirits, and beer – all made in Russia.
Shot bars survive on cheap vodka, infused spirits, and beer – all made in Russia
Restaurateur Alexey confirms that low-priced establishments are holding up better than the rest: “Overall, I’d say establishments at the low and high ends of the market are doing well, while the mid-range restaurant market is shrinking.”
Sommelier Tatyana says the same: “Top-end establishments are growing, and so are fast food, coffee shops, street food, pan-Asian restaurants, shawarma joints, and cheap eateries.”
Outlook: “a wholesale collapse”
All of The Insider’s sources agree that the market is in poor shape. According to Sergei, many restaurants are closing: “With all these sanctions, we’re shooting ourselves in the foot. But this also gives the Russian restaurant industry a bit of a boost, because in a crisis people start improvising – growing their own vegetables. And new chefs emerge. But if you take the average temperature across the food-service industry, there’s a wholesale collapse.”
Alexey is equally pessimistic about the outlook for the restaurant business: “I expect suppliers to keep raising prices and the market to shrink further. And if the promised VAT is finally introduced in December, we’ll consider every option, including closing down.”
Sommelier Tatyana agrees: “I’m very afraid of losing my job because establishments keep opening and closing. It happens constantly. There’s no stability, and the life cycle of individual places is getting shorter. These days, the average restaurant lasts three to five years. Street food, food halls, and food courts will survive, where rents are relatively low and you can at least scrape by.”
The sources also note that Gen Z customers are not exactly the best clientele. According to Tatyana, “they are more selective, drink very little, or don’t drink at all.” At the same time, their numbers are growing, as is their influence on the market.

Kim Jong-un's sister demands 'utmost respect' from Seoul as North Korea rejects dialogue

Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, said on Thursday that Seoul must show “utmost respect” if it wants to improve ties, as Pyongyang continued to reject responsibility for a landmine blast that wounded three South Korean soldiers.
A joint Seoul-United Nations Command investigation found that the explosion last month in the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) was caused by North Korean mines laid on the South Korean side of the border.
Pyongyang has denied responsibility, while South Korea has demanded an apology, calling the incident a violation of the armistice agreement.
“If they (Seoul) really want to reverse the relations between the DPRK and the ROK, they should be conscious of their rival’s feelings in every word and action and show their utmost respect, solicitude and sincerity before anything,” Kim said, using the two countries official acronyms.
Aid dismissed as political manoeuvre
Kim also criticised Seoul’s plan to send medical equipment to North Korea next month under a UN sanctions exemption. The aid, reportedly worth 9.3 billion won ($6.95 million), could include ambulances and medical sterilisation equipment.
Kim dismissed the initiative as an attempt to recover from what she called a “self-orchestrated farce”, adding that Pyongyang had “nothing to exchange or go with the ROK” and no need to meet face to face.
North Korea has strengthened its border fortifications, including laying mines and building anti-tank barriers, after Kim Jong-un designated South Korea his country’s “principal enemy” in 2024.
Seoul warned against interference
South Korean officials have called for dialogue to address border issues, but Kim Yo-Jong said any action by Seoul, whether driven by “evil intention or good faith”, would be viewed as a provocation and violation of North Korea’s sovereignty.
Her remarks come as US President Donald Trump has renewed overtures to Pyongyang, raising concerns in Seoul that it could be sidelined in potential nuclear talks.
Analyst Ahn Chan-il told AFP that North Korea’s priority appeared to be a possible deal with Washington and closer ties with Russia, with South Korean engagement viewed as a potential obstacle.
He added that Kim’s remarks did not necessarily rule out future dialogue, but warned Seoul against intervening without offering something substantial.

Flu season begins in Latvia, but vaccine production delays affect deliveries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
06:47:59 UTC
15:47:59 KST

The 2026–2027 monitoring season for influenza and other acute respiratory infections has begun in Latvia. Data compiled by the Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (SPKC) show that the spread of influenza and other acute respiratory infections remains relatively low at the beginning of the season and is slightly below the level recorded during the corresponding period last year.
The first laboratory-confirmed influenza cases in Latvia this season were registered before the official start of the flu monitoring season and were linked to travel outside Latvia.
During the 40th week of 2026, when monitoring began, influenza was clinically diagnosed in three patients, equivalent to 3.9 cases per 100,000 inhabitants. This is lower than during the corresponding period of the previous season, when the incidence was 9.9 cases per 100,000 inhabitants.
A total of 918 patients sought medical assistance from family doctors for symptoms of other acute respiratory infections, representing an average of 1,179.3 cases per 100,000 inhabitants. The spread of other acute respiratory infections was also slightly lower than during the same period last season.
Laboratory surveillance data show that influenza was not confirmed in any of the 166 samples tested last week,
 while respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection was detected in one sample (0.6%).
The proportion of samples testing positive for Covid-19 was 1.2%, remaining approximately at the previous week’s level. Unlike in previous years, no increase in Covid-19 cases was observed in late summer or early autumn this year.
According to the World Health Organization (WHO), influenza activity in other European countries has remained stable and low.
At the same time, SARS-CoV-2 activity continues to increase in both primary healthcare and hospitals, with most hospitalised patients aged 65 and older.
During the 2026–2027 season, 48 family doctor practices in ten administrative territories are participating in the monitoring programme.
Every week, these practices provide information about patients seeking medical assistance for symptoms of influenza, other acute respiratory infections and pneumonia.
Information is also collected on hospitalisations, severe acute respiratory infections (SARI) and the circulation of respiratory pathogens.
Laboratory testing helps determine the spread of influenza, Covid-19, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and other respiratory viruses in Latvia.
The collected information makes it possible to assess the epidemiological situation and inform the public promptly about trends in the spread of infections.
Monitoring of influenza and other acute respiratory infections is carried out annually in all European Union and European Economic Area countries.
 This ensures timely assessment of the epidemiological situation, surveillance of influenza virus circulation, and the planning and implementation of public health measures.
During the 2026–2027 season, state-funded influenza vaccination in Latvia will be provided using three vaccines intended for different population groups.
Latvia has already received the Fluenz intranasal vaccine, intended for children aged 2 to 17, inclusive, who belong to certain medical risk groups.
Deliveries of the Efluelda influenza vaccine to family doctor practices will begin this week. This vaccine is intended for people aged 60 and older, as well as individuals with moderate or severe immunosuppression.
Meanwhile, the Vaxigrip vaccine, intended for other groups eligible for state-funded vaccination, including adults and children with chronic illnesses, is expected to arrive in Latvia by 13 November.
Influenza vaccine production has been delayed across Europe this season, meaning deliveries to Latvia are taking place gradually and slightly later than usual.
The SPKC advises patients belonging to risk groups to contact their family doctor practices for information about vaccination.

FSB detains two residents of Trans-Baikal over election provocation plot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
06:47:19 UTC

MOSCOW, October 8. /TASS/. Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) has detained two residents of the Trans-Baikal Region who prepared provocations during the recent parliamentary elections, the FSB said in a statement.

U.S. Navy moves bunker-busting Tomahawk toward production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
06:46:16 UTC
15:46:16 KST

- The U.S. Navy plans a sole-source contract with Raytheon for low-rate initial production of the JMEWS warhead for the Tomahawk Block Vb.
- The notice moves the warhead from development into production but does not disclose contract value, quantity or delivery schedule.
The U.S. Navy plans to award Raytheon a sole-source contract for low-rate initial production of the Joint Multiple Effects Warhead System, a new warhead that lets the Tomahawk cruise missile strike bunkers and other hardened targets, according to a notice Naval Air Systems Command posted on October 7.
The contract would move the warhead program out of its engineering and manufacturing development phase and into production for the Tomahawk Block Vb variant. The notice did not give a contract value, the number of warheads to be built or a delivery schedule.
The Navy’s Tomahawk program office at Patuxent River, Maryland, said it intends to negotiate only with Raytheon in Tucson, Arizona, the RTX business that has been the sole developer, designer and manufacturer of the Tomahawk since 1994. The Navy said RTX alone holds the current configuration and manufacturing data for the missile and is the only known source able to do the work on schedule without duplicating costs.
The notice is not a request for competing bids. Other companies may submit capability statements by 4 p.m. EDT on October 22, which the Navy said it will consider. The Navy also noted that Tomahawk data is export controlled and not available to foreign sources.
The warhead, known as JMEWS, combines blast-fragmentation and penetration effects in a single two-stage design. It is meant to give the Tomahawk more options against hardened and heavily defended targets such as bunkers, underground facilities and missile sites, as well as against targets spread over a wide area. The Block IV Tomahawk it builds on carries a 1,000-pound-class unitary warhead.
Raytheon won a $90.4 million contract for the warhead’s engineering and manufacturing development phase, the final stage of development before production.
The Block Vb missile is one of two new variants in the Navy’s Block V modernization, which recertifies existing Block IV Tomahawks with upgraded navigation and communications and extends their service life. The Navy received its first Block V missile in March 2021. The other variant, the Block Va Maritime Strike Tomahawk, adds a seeker so the missile can hit moving ships at sea.
The Pentagon’s weapons testing office reported in its fiscal 2023 annual report that the Navy had conducted JMEWS arena tests and planned to complete the warhead’s live-fire test campaign in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, which ended in September. The office has not yet published an assessment of the warhead’s lethality.
In 2022, the Navy’s Tomahawk program manager, Capt. John Red, said the JMEWS variant was expected to reach initial operational capability in 2027.

Housing crisis set to dominate Spain's snap election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
06:45:12 UTC
15:45:12 KST

Demonstrators gather after learning that Maricarmen Abascal, the 87-year-old pensioner whose eviction triggered nationwide protests over Spain's chronic housing crisis and a political debate that culminated in early elections, had died in hospital in Madrid on October 7, 2026. (AFP Photo)
After simmering below the surface for years, anger at unaffordable housing in Spain has bubbled over and precipitated a general election that will be dominated by the crisis.
The spark was ignited on September 23 when 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from her lifelong Madrid home on a stretcher after the real estate firm that owned the apartment drastically hiked the rent.
Abascal, who died on Oct. 7, became the symbol of a crisis that cuts across Spanish society: young and old, renters and buyers, workers and pensioners.
The uproar at her eviction triggered national demonstrations, with hundreds of people camping in central Madrid's Puerta del Sol square in the most symbolic protest.
As in other European countries, housing has long been a top public concern, particularly for young adults who are priced out of the market and stay with their parents into their 30s and beyond.
Growth in housing prices has far outstripped wages in recent years, eating up far more than the upper limit of 30 percent of income recommended by public bodies and housing professionals.
According to the latest figures by the National Statistics Institute (INE), the average gross monthly salary in Spain is around 2,460 euros ($2,750).
Renting a 50-square-meter apartment in Madrid cost on average 1,170 euros per month in September, according to real estate portal Idealista — around half of a normal income.
Many residents in popular destinations like Barcelona complain that short-term tourist accommodation is limiting supply and driving up prices.
Investment funds with large housing portfolios are another much-maligned group, accused of being "vulture funds" that acquire properties and hike rents for maximum profits.
A tiny public housing supply is another major factor, with Madrid representing an extreme example of the phenomenon.
A paradise for luxury real estate, the capital only has around 10,000 social housing units for its 3.5 million inhabitants.
Such is the demand for them that some public apartments are allocated by lottery.
A history of home ownership partly explains the small public housing stock. Under the dictatorship of General Francisco Franco (1939-1975), a housing minister said he wanted "a country of owners and not proletarians".
But the model is breaking down, especially for the young. While almost three in four households own their main residence, more than half of under-30s rented in 2025, according to the INE.
Jorge Galindo, director of the Center for Economic Policy at Esade business school, said the 2008 global financial crash was a turning point for the Spanish housing market.
The bursting of a real estate bubble sparked the "collapse" of construction and "the destruction of a million jobs" in the sector, Galindo told AFP.
Since then, "supply has not kept up", falling from around 260,000 new builds per year in the 1990s to 92,000 in 2025, he said.
The expert warned that the country of around 50 million people risked becoming "a society of inheritors" in which home ownership depends on parents passing property to their children.
How to solve a puzzle that has bedevilled successive governments will be a central debate of the snap election that Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez called for November 29.
Last week, Sanchez's leftist coalition proposed a series of measures including more restrictions on evictions, a ban on the "speculative" purchase of homes and the automatic renewal of tenant contracts.
But the minority government failed to pass them in parliament, leading Sanchez to call an early vote originally scheduled for 2027.
Spain's main unions have called a general strike for November 11 in large part due to the political paralysis over housing.
In 2023, Sanchez's government passed a law that provided for more social housing, the regulation of rents in areas under the greatest stress, and punishments for owners who left their properties empty.
But the law has not stopped the spiralling prices and popular discontent.
The main opposition right-wing Popular Party advocates a building boom to make up the deficit between supply and demand.
For Galindo, the debate contains a "paradox."
"Those who suffer most from the housing crisis are those with the least weight at the ballot box: young people, who vote less, and immigrants."

When More Material Does Not Mean Better Performance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
06:45:00 UTC
15:45:00 KST

In the story of the Three Little Pigs, the choice of material determines the fate of each house. The wolf's breath brings down the structures made of straw and wood, while the brick house remains standing. The moral is that the more solid the construction, the greater its ability to resist. A building, however, has to respond to much less straightforward questions. Remaining standing is still essential, but heat, light, air, and sound are not forces that necessarily need to be blocked. Sometimes sunlight needs to be kept out; at other times, daylight needs to be let in. Retaining heat may be desirable in winter and counterproductive in summer. Air needs to circulate, sound may need to be absorbed, and the conditions that determine these responses change throughout the day, across seasons, and over the life of the building itself. More material does not necessarily mean better performance. In some cases, it can simply add complexity without improving how the building responds.
This relationship between mass and performance was at the center of Serge Ferrari Architecture's recent reveal of the 7TH MATERIAL, a category currently centered on technical membrane. The category is framed around what materials can do: filtering light, modulating solar gain, guiding airflow, treating sound, or combining several of these functions within a single surface. Membranes do not replace concrete, metal, stone, or glass; they complement them by performing different functions.
For Nic Goldsmith, Founding Director of the Lightweight Structures Group at TYLin and author of Mass to Membrane, this discussion forms part of a much longer architectural trajectory. During the reveal, he described the history of architecture as "one long attempt to do more with less," tracing a shift from massive structures toward increasingly lighter ways of enclosing space. Along that trajectory, new material systems have expanded what architects can ask an envelope to do, a process that, in his view, is still unfolding. As he puts it: "We may not know the precise form future membranes will take. The direction is clear."
Structural stability is only one measure of how well a building performs. Heat, light, air, and sound place different demands on a space, and the goal is not always to block them, but to control how they move through the building. A roof, for example, can be evaluated by the shade it provides, the daylight it allows through, the air that circulates beneath it, and the resources required to perform those functions over time. Its thickness or weight describes only part of the solution. Its properties, geometry, and relationship with the building's other elements also matter.
At The Camp in Aix-en-Provence, this logic can be seen in the organization of the complex itself. Designed by Corinne Vezzoni & Associés, the 11,000-square-meter campus is covered by approximately 7,000 square meters of membrane, beneath which some circulation areas remain open to the air. The surface filters daylight, while its double curvature contributes to the roof's stability, air circulation, and rainwater collection. Under the project's specific conditions and fire safety approval, this configuration also removes the need for mechanical ventilation and smoke extraction within that volume. Its properties and geometry work together to provide shade, daylight, airflow, structural stability, and rainwater collection.
The Material Helps Define the Form
Another example can be found at Hazza Bin Zayed Stadium in Al Ain, where BDP Pattern began with the conditions of a hot, dry climate to develop the enclosure. In this case, the path of the sun, rather than protection from rain, shaped its geometry: a 40-meter cantilever on the west side shades the field and stands at 4:00 p.m. on game days, while the porous façade encourages air to circulate through the envelope. Before settling on the final solution, the team built a full-scale prototype on site using three geometries and, over the course of development, reduced the number of panel types from 320 to 86, making it possible for a local manufacturer to produce them at an acceptable cost. Climate, material behavior, geometry, and fabrication all contributed to defining the form.
Architect and computational designer Nick Tyrer describes this relationship more directly: "Do not specify the material to fit a form you have already decided on. Let the material and the geometry find the form together, in response to the actual conditions of that place." Across projects responding to a headwind, a desert sun, and a coastline, Tyrer returns to the same point: "You don't specify it. You design with it."
At Al Ain, solar exposure, ventilation, geometry, material, and fabrication were therefore treated as parts of the same problem, changing when materials enter the design conversation. A technical data sheet can describe how a product performs under specific test conditions, but a design team still needs to understand how those properties behave within a particular configuration while the geometry can still be adjusted.
What Enters the Comparison
Serge Ferrari uses the idea of performance density to describe a comparison that begins with equivalent functions rather than equivalent quantities of material. Shading, daylighting, acoustic treatment, structural requirements, carbon emissions, and the additional systems needed over time can all become part of the equation. The comparison also considers what a solution makes unnecessary, from additional layers to heavier structures or greater mechanical capacity. There is not yet a single standardized metric that combines all of these variables.
A simulation for an office in Lyon helps illustrate the complexity of this calculation. With Type D glazing and automated external solar shading, cooling demand fell from 60.2 to 29.8 kWh/m²/year, while heating demand rose from 11.4 to 13.4 kWh/m²/year because of reduced solar gains in winter. Overall, combined heating and cooling demand decreased by 39.59%. The result applies to this specific configuration, reinforcing the need to read performance figures alongside the conditions that produced them.
Performance Over Time
Comparing only the amount of material installed on day one also leaves out maintenance, replacement, and end-of-life considerations. In the methodology being developed around the 7TH MATERIAL, the assessment accounts for the materials and carbon mobilized over the entire period analyzed, including replacements, as well as the additional layers and systems each solution requires to deliver equivalent functions. The calculation therefore extends beyond the material itself to everything needed to install, operate, maintain, and eventually replace it.
For anyone specifying materials or systems, this means reading properties such as weight, light transmission, and resistance in context. Their significance depends on supports, adjacent layers, climate, conditions of use, and maintenance over time. Performance is ultimately shaped by how a material works with the rest of the architectural system.
The practical consequence is that material decisions need to happen earlier in the design process, while form, geometry, and system relationships can still be adjusted. Solidity becomes only one part of the equation. A solution also needs to be understood in terms of the functions it can combine, what it requires from the building, and what it may make unnecessary. Resisting the wolf's breath remains a perfectly effective measure for a fairy tale, but in architecture, performance involves a much larger set of variables.

U.S. State Department approves $832M Javelin sale to Egypt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
06:41:25 UTC
15:41:25 KST

- The U.S. State Department approved a possible $832 million sale of up to 2,020 Javelin missiles and 200 launch units to Egypt.
- Lockheed Martin and RTX are the principal contractors, and the approval does not guarantee a final contract will be signed.
The U.S. State Department has approved a possible sale of up to 2,020 Javelin anti-tank missiles and 200 launch units to Egypt, a package estimated at $832 million that would give the Egyptian military the shoulder-fired weapon for the first time.
The approval, dated October 2 and sent to Congress as a formal notification, covers FGM-148F Javelin missiles, including 20 “fly-to-buy” rounds fired during lot acceptance testing, and up to 200 Lightweight Command Launch Units, the reusable sight and firing unit that soldiers attach to each missile tube. The notification does not mean a contract has been signed, and terms will still be negotiated.
The package also includes basic skills trainers, missile simulation rounds, battery coolant units, spare parts, system integration, technical documentation, training and U.S. government technical assistance.
Egypt has never bought the Javelin before, making this its first planned purchase of the weapon.
The Javelin is built by the Javelin Joint Venture of Lockheed Martin in Orlando, Florida, and RTX in Arlington, Virginia, the two principal contractors named in the notification. It is a fire-and-forget weapon: once the gunner locks onto a target and fires, the missile guides itself, and it can dive onto a tank from above, where armor is thinnest. The F-model carries a multipurpose warhead designed for use against both armored vehicles and other targets such as fortified positions.
The State Department said the sale would improve Egypt’s ability to defend its sovereignty and territorial integrity and would not alter the basic military balance in the region. It said Egypt would have no difficulty absorbing the weapons, that no additional U.S. government or contractor personnel would need to be assigned to Egypt, and that it was not aware of any offset agreement tied to the sale.
The Javelin would sit alongside the TOW, the vehicle-launched anti-tank missile Egypt already uses. In 2022, the State Department approved a $691 million sale of more than 5,000 TOW 2A radio-frequency missiles to Egypt.
Egypt has received several large U.S. approvals in recent years, including $740 million for Stinger air defense missiles in September 2024, $4.69 billion for Abrams tank refurbishment in December 2024 and $4.67 billion for the NASAMS air defense system in July 2025.
The Javelin approval was announced alongside two other Middle East packages: up to 10,000 APKWS II laser-guided rocket kits for the United Arab Emirates, estimated at $1.041 billion, and $400 million in Patriot missile repair and return services for Kuwait. Together, the three proposed sales total about $2.27 billion.

Russia attacked Ukraine with 142 drones during the night of October 8. A total of 126 of them were shot down or suppressed. UNN reports this, citing data from the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
What Russia launched and from where
According to the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, during the night of October 8 (from 18:00 on October 7), the enemy attacked with 142 Shahed-type attack UAVs (82 of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones, and Parody-type decoy drones launched from the following directions: Oryol, Kursk, Shatalovo — Russia; the temporarily occupied territory of Donetsk; and the temporarily occupied territory of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea — Hvardiiske.
How the air defense performed
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare units and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
According to preliminary data, as of 09:30, air defense forces had shot down/suppressed 126 enemy Shahed-type UAVs, Gerbera drones, and drones of other types
Hits by enemy air-attack weapons were recorded at 7 locations, as well as the سقوط of downed aircraft (debris) at 4 locations.
The attack is ongoing, with several enemy UAVs in the airspace.

Drones hit Yandex site in first major attack on Russian data hub
MOSCOW, Oct 8 - Drones hit a data centre owned by Russia's Yandex, the country's leading AI and technology company said on Thursday, in the first major attack on a Russian data hub since the start of the war with Ukraine.
Mutual drone attacks by Russia and Ukraine this year have gradually spread across the economy, from energy facilities and refineries to ports and vessels carrying oil and grain, e-commerce warehouses and, most recently, data centres.
Russia has conducted a strike campaign on Ukrainian data centres and telecommunications infrastructure over the past month, including targets in central Kyiv.
Yandex said the attack on its Sasovo hub, one of its five large data centres, caused a fire and forced it to suspend operations at the site, which hosts tens of thousands of servers. It said it was restoring affected services.
The company, often dubbed "Russia's Google", said its core consumer services were not affected, but did not describe the extent of the damage.
On the website of its Yandex Cloud service, the company advised customers there were problems with the electricity supply to one data centre "zone" and recommended using others.
Yandex said in 2021 that the Sasovo hub hosted two of its three supercomputers built around Nvidia A100 chips, which it uses to train its YandexGPT large AI model. Yandex declined to say whether the supercomputers were affected by the attack.
Multiple online services in Russia reported technical issues on Thursday, including real estate aggregator Cian, a book portal called Litmarket, and the websites of Russian Railways and professional football club Spartak Moscow.
A state-owned bus company in the Moscow region said online ticket sales were currently unavailable due to the "temporary shutdown of a data centre".
Online monitoring service Detector404 said it had received 58,268 user complaints over the past day. Yandex shares at the Moscow Exchange, where it is a proxy stock for the Russian technology sector, were down 3%.
Previous Ukrainian attacks on Russia have led to fuel shortages and queues at petrol stations, losses for tens of thousands of small businesses involved in e-commerce, and higher inflation as rising fuel costs feed through to consumer prices.
CRITICALLY IMPORTANT INFRASTRUCTURE
Russian President Vladimir Putin in August gave the state the power to take control of critically important infrastructure if it is deemed to be poorly protected from drone attacks.
There were previously no confirmed major Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian data centres.
Russia's RBC news outlet reported on Thursday, quoting sources, that businesses were in talks with the government on developing data centres in countries deemed "friendly"' by Moscow.
Some Ukrainian data centres were forced to suspend operations after sustaining damage, while 100,000 households suffered temporary internet outages after one attack.
Ukraine's digital minister told Reuters last month that the country was moving digital infrastructure underground in response to Russian attacks.
Yandex, which created Russia's first search engine in 1997 and is one of the few major Russian companies not under Western sanctions, runs YandexGPT, one of Russia's leading AI models, as well as a cloud computing service and a range of other consumer products, including Yandex Taxi and Yandex Music.
Sberbank, Yandex's main domestic competitor, which is developing the rival GigaChat model, says Russian AI developers lag their US and Chinese counterparts by six to nine months, with difficulties in importing advanced chips due to sanctions seen as the main bottleneck. REUTERS

Is it raining harder and harder? Yes, it’s not just your imagination
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
06:39:31 UTC
15:39:31 KST

Is it raining harder and harder? Yes, it’s not just your imagination
Rain may be falling less often, but when it does, it is increasingly intense. In Switzerland, that is not just a perception. Observations show that heavy rainfall has become stronger in recent decades, and climate projections suggest the trend will continue, with short-duration downpours becoming up to 30% more intense in the future.
Historical measurements from Switzerland’s rain-gauge network reveal how precipitation patterns in Switzerland have changed.
“Since the 1980s, when instruments capable of recording rainfall at ten-minute intervals came into use, the intensity of heavy rainfall over ten-minute periods has increased by around 20%,” says meteorologist Luca Nisi.
Over a longer timeframe the trend is equally clear. During the past century, intense daily rainfall events have become about 26% more frequent and roughly 12% stronger. The driving force behind this trend, which is increasing our vulnerability to extreme events, is the familiar culprit: global warming.
More
Switzerland braces for more heatwaves, droughts and violent storms
Warmer atmosphere holds more water
To understand why climate change affects rainfall, we need to look at a basic law of atmospheric physics. “If the temperature rises by 1°C, the air can hold around 7% more water vapour,” says Nisi.
The principle is described by the Clausius–Clapeyron equation. As temperatures rise, evaporation from soils, lakes and oceans increases, allowing more water vapour to accumulate in the atmosphere.
When the conditions for condensation and precipitation are met, that additional moisture can translate into heavier rainfall.
More
Why artificial rain is not a solution to drought
Drier summers, heavier downpours in future
Here lies one of climate change’s most striking paradoxes. According to the CH2025 climate scenariosExternal link, total annual precipitation in Switzerland is not expected to change dramatically. But its seasonal distribution will change: summers will be drier on average, while winters are expected to become wetter.
The strongest increase is forecast for short-lived, high intensity rainfall associated with thunderstorms. In a world that is 3°C warmer, hourly rainfall could increase by around 10% to 30%, while daily rainfall could rise by 5% to 25%.
“You can really see how the increase is linked above all to storm-related rainfall,” says Nisi. South of the Alps, where flooding is already a significant risk, this is particularly important. Many people immediately think of the devastating Vallemaggia floods in 2024. But Nisi adds: “This does not mean that every event will reach that level of intensity, but intense episodes will become more frequent than in the past.”
The Alps and southern Switzerland have always been vulnerable to heavy rainfall because of the presence of the mountains and proximity to the Mediterranean. Climate change is now amplifying those natural conditions.
Return periods cut in half
A rainfall event that, over the 1991–2020 reference period, occurred on average once every 50 years could, in a world that is 3°C warmer, occur on average every 25 years.
Those events are also likely to be stronger. “We expect around 11% more rainfall,” says Nisi. This means that an extreme event that today produces 200 millimetres of rain in 24 hours could produce over 220 millimetres under that scenario.
When drought fuels flooding
Another apparent contradiction emerges: how can drier summers lead to greater flood risk?
“As we have seen this summer of 2026, severely parched soil absorbs water less effectively during the early stages of a very intense storm,” says Nisi.
When the ground cannot absorb rainfall fast enough, water runs across the surface instead, rapidly reaching rivers, streams and low-lying areas. This can worsen flooding, debris flows and landslides.
“Surface runoff is what actually causes a great deal of damage,” the meteorologist notes.
More
Switzerland gets ready for increasing risks of severe drought
What about winter?
The changes are not confined to the warm season. As temperatures rise, the snow line continues to move higher, and an increasing proportion of precipitation will fall as rain at lower altitudes.
“It is reasonable to assume that, with increased winter rainfall and a general rise in the frequency of heavy downpours, the flood season will extend further into the year than in the past,” explains Nisi.
For Switzerland this poses a growing adaptation challenge. Roads, bridges, embankments, drainage networks and other infrastructure are typically designed using historical climate data. But Nisi warns: “If these volumes increase, it is important to adapt our infrastructure to avoid problems.”
More
Why Switzerland is among the ten fastest-warming countries in the world

Defense agency scammed out of nearly €60,000 in email fraud, case closed

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08

Defense agency scammed out of nearly €60,000 in email fraud, case closed
The Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK) lost nearly €60,000 to fraudsters two years ago, Delfi reported, while police closed the case without identifying the perpetrators.
The case only became public this week. Current RKIK director Elmar Vaher said he heard about it days ago and has not questioned staff involved.
The RKIK had already been at the center of scrutiny over payments made for a multi-million euro munitions procurement for Ukraine whose delivery failed to fully materialize.
Helena Jürgenson, an analyst in the analysis and prevention department at the Estonian Information System Authority (RIA), noted that falling victim to business email fraud says a great deal about an organization's processes and security.
"This is a type of fraud in which criminals put quite a lot of effort into the scam. An email account at an organization is taken over. The correspondence is monitored for a long time, and at the right moment an invoice is replaced," Jürgenson said.
Magnus-Valdemar Saar, who headed RKIK at the time of the fraud losses, said he could not remember the company's name and was unable to search for it; the department head and chief financial officer involved are still employed there, he said.
"I believe if you ask the relevant category manager who handled the invoice, they will be able to describe in considerable detail exactly what the trick was. RKIK's invoice processing procedure was already fairly technical before this incident — there were certainly around six pairs of eyes checking it," Saar told "Aktuaalne kaamera".
Asked why the fraud only became public two years later, RKIK's current director, Elmar Vaher, said he had heard about it a few days ago. "I don't know exactly what happened in 2024. The police have investigated it thoroughly and they can answer questions," Vaher, himself a former police chief, said.
Vaher said he has not questioned the category manager or chief financial officer about the matter. "These people have been questioned by the Estonian police. If Magnus-Valdemar Saar has provided explanations, then I guess that is how it was. I have no reason to doubt it."
Saar said that, as far as he could remember, he had also informed then-Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur (Reform) about the incident.
"I don't think we discussed it in much greater detail. It was not an incident that required more extensive management. There was communication with the State Shared Service Center, for example, and the ministry. RKIK notified the investigative authorities of the incident and also filed a criminal complaint," Saar added.
Saar noted that RKIK's security chief at the time had notified the police under his own name because he had to authenticate his identity using an ID card when submitting the complaint. He also confirmed that RKIK had introduced additional invoice processing procedures.
In 2024, RKIK signed four contracts with Datasel, an Italian firm owned by Indian-based Neco Defense Munitions, paying roughly €70 million in advance for artillery shells for Ukraine. None arrived, the contracts were terminated, and the state is pursuing the money through Estonian courts and Swiss arbitration. The scandal contributed to Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur's resignation on September 2.
In the first six months of 2026, police in Estonian authorities received 1,816 reports of telephone and online scams, with losses of €13.2 million.

China’s military is preparing for Ukraine-style drone war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
06:37:16 UTC
15:37:16 KST

- A CSIS study of more than 90 Chinese sources found analysts write up new Ukraine war drone tactics within about four months.
- Turning those lessons into PLA hardware, training and force structure usually takes a year or more, with counter-drone defenses moving fastest.
China’s military is training and building hardware to fight the kind of drone war seen in Ukraine, from sea drone attacks to airfield raids, and its analysts typically write up a new battlefield technique within about four months of its first use, according to a study by the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
The commentary, published on October 7 by Lilly Min-Chen Lee of Taiwan’s Research Institute for Democracy, Society and Emerging Technology and Kateryna Bondar of the CSIS Wadhwani AI Center, draws on more than 90 Chinese-language sources from 45 outlets published between July 2022 and August 2026. They include the Central Military Commission’s PLA Daily and peer-reviewed journals run by China’s state missile, shipbuilding and aviation conglomerates.
The authors found that China studies the war mainly from the position of a likely target. Its most detailed work comes from designers of air and harbor defenses, who treat Ukraine’s sea drones and airfield raids as previews of attacks China could face. Nearly half the sources appeared in publications run by defense industrial institutions, which feed lessons directly into their own requirements and procurement.
“The errors we make in trials are detours the troops will not have to take,” a participant at a PLA center that tests drone swarms against counter-drone defenses told Chinese state media, as quoted in the study.
On offense, Chinese writers have focused on cost and speed. The PLA Daily stated in March 2025 that a single reconnaissance-strike drone costs less than 1 percent of a modern fighter while covering more than 90 percent of its battlefield area, figures the authors describe as rough. Analysts at China’s National Defense University cited Russian forces striking a detected target within three to five minutes, using reconnaissance drones such as the Orlan-10 to cue Lancet and Kub loitering munitions.
The PLA Daily flagged Russia’s fiber-optic drones, which are steered through a thin cable that cannot be jammed, in May 2024, within weeks of their battlefield debut. By April 2025, Chinese state television showed a People’s Armed Police unit in Yunnan province training with first-person-view drones and researching fiber-optic models, about a year after Russia first used the technique.
The study’s deepest material concerns defense against attacks like Ukraine’s. A team from China’s Naval University of Engineering counted more than 10 large Russian naval vessels damaged by Ukrainian strikes and concluded that a sea drone offensive must be met by counter-sea drone equipment working as a system. In August 2025, the PLA Daily reported a missile-boat drill against approaching enemy unmanned boats, 35 months after the first Ukrainian sea drone washed ashore near Sevastopol. An Eastern Theater frigate flotilla held a live-fire drill against unmanned boats in April 2026, and Chinese army drones fired missiles at fast boats in exercises in July and August 2026.
Ukraine’s Operation Spider’s Web, the June 1, 2025 drone raid on Russian bomber bases launched from inside Russia, produced an even faster response. Within four and a half months, a PLA brigade defended against a drone attack team of more than 20 operators in an October 2025 exercise, using detection gear that identifies drones by their radio emissions and checks them against a catalog of more than 800 commercial models.
Chinese writers also adopted the war’s economics of defense, the authors said, citing a Global Times analysis of Ukraine’s interceptor drones.
“The cost of procuring one man-portable air-defense missile buys several hundred air-defense FPV drones,” the Global Times wrote.
Counter-drone weapons have moved into Chinese hardware faster than any other category, according to the study, from the Tianqiong system, Hurricane 3000 microwave weapon and LW-60 laser shown at the Zhuhai air show in November 2024 to the lasers and microwave weapons displayed at the September 2025 military parade.
The authors also found institutional changes. In May 2025, the Central Military Commission created three new military universities from existing academies, including an army combat arms university in Hefei, and new degree programs list unmanned systems command and control. A PLA unit’s tender on the military procurement website sought DJI Matrice enterprise drones and automated docks, despite Beijing’s official opposition to military use of civilian drones.
Some concepts remain unproven in Chinese eyes. In October 2024, China National Defense News asked why drone swarm warfare had produced “all thunder and little rain” in Ukraine, listing problems with flight control, communications, onboard intelligence, power and payload. The PLA is running its own swarm experiments to fill that gap.
