American, Russian officials meet on bringing US investor into Nord Stream gas pipeline to Germany
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
06:09:48 UTC
15:09:48 KST

Top Russian and US officials, including US Special Envoy Jared Kushner, have held talks about bringing a US investor into the Nord Stream pipelines that delivered gas to Germany before Russia invaded Ukraine, five people with knowledge of the situation said.
The discussions included Kirill Dmitriev, a close adviser to Russian President Vladimir Putin, and Kushner, the son-in-law of US President Donald Trump, the people said.
Kushner, who has been trying to broker a truce between Russia and Ukraine, views doing business as central to restoring peace. Such a deal would enable US investors to profit from energy flows to Europe once the war ends.
Dmitriev and Kushner have met in Moscow and New York in recent weeks. While it was unclear to what degree they discussed Nord Stream on those occasions, the topic remains on the agenda, two of the people told Reuters.
"Any deals will have to be negotiated by Russia with DFC (US International Development Finance Corporation) and Treasury and must benefit United States taxpayers and companies," a White House official said when asked about the pipeline discussions.
There had been "no Nord Stream discussions recently," the official told Reuters.
Dmitriev, who has campaigned for a resumption of Russian gas sales to Germany, met last month with US Energy and Treasury Department representatives to discuss potential US-Russia energy initiatives. A representative for Dmitriev declined to comment.
It remains unclear how interested Washington is in pursuing the restarting of Russian gas flows to Germany, which is Europe's biggest energy consumer.
A US official said that given the obstacles, a deal is unlikely in the medium term. The US and the EU have sanctioned the Nord Stream gas pipelines, making any restart illegal.
Trump could waive or soften US sanctions, but if Democrats win control of Congress in next month's midterm elections, this would become harder.
Germany and other European countries, which are spending billions of euros to rebuild their militaries to defend themselves from Russia, would strongly resist reopening Nord Stream.
A spokeswoman for Germany's economy and energy ministry said Europe had sanctioned Nord Stream and Russian gas and that Germany had found alternatives. She said any reopening of the pipelines would require government approval, and that was not desired.
Before Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Germany bought more than half of its gas from Russia through the two Nord Stream pipelines. They were mothballed after Moscow throttled supply to Europe and were blown up in a series of underwater explosions in September 2022.
Europe distrusts Russia as Washington-Moscow talks continue
Talks between Moscow and Washington are taking place against a backdrop of deep European mistrust of Russia's motives.
Earlier this year, the heads of five European spy agencies told Reuters that Russia did not want to end the war quickly and was using US talks to push for business deals instead.
Relations between Russia and Germany, which is among the biggest providers of military support to Ukraine, have hit a low ebb, as officials in Berlin have accused Russia of mounting a systematic campaign of hybrid attacks.
Some German lawmakers say that business deals would bolster Moscow as it pursues war with Ukraine.
"This threatens to be a dirty deal that will cost Europe dearly," said Michael Kellner, a lawmaker who led German energy policy in the aftermath of the Ukraine invasion.
"Americans and Russians will share the profits," he said.
While Germany's coalition government opposes restarting the pipeline, Alternative for Germany (AfD), the country's most popular political party, wants to do so.
Dmitriev will meet the AfD leadership early next year to discuss selling Russian gas again.
But selling ownership of the company that controls the Nord Stream gas pipelines to a US investor or restarting Russian gas faces hurdles.
The company is 51% owned by Russian state energy giant Gazprom, with a further 31% split between two German entities and the rest in the hands of a French and a Dutch firm.
The two German shareholders are seeking to keep their shares to maintain German influence if Gazprom sells its stake, another person said.
Days after the Moscow meetings, Kushner said in Kyiv he had spoken to European counterparts about how the war pushed up energy prices, advocating "prosperity agreements" to encourage peace and give "leaders... something to look forward to."
Germany, Europe split over potential Russia gas deal
While a gas deal would please the Kremlin, it would split German public opinion, which is divided over buying Russian energy, and Europe, where Poland and the Baltic states are particularly vulnerable to Russia and reject energy ties.
Poland's political leadership is watching the discussions to reopen the pipeline but remains firmly opposed, one person with knowledge of the government's thinking said.
Kushner and Dmitriev have also been discussing the sale of a collection of businesses, from oil refineries to petrol stations in Europe and elsewhere, owned by Russian energy company Lukoil, two other people familiar with the matter said.
Under that plan, a consortium of the DFC federal investment agency and investors from Qatar and the United Arab Emirates would buy the assets, while US authorities would lift sanctions, those people said.
"On Lukoil, Steve (Witkoff) and Jared (Kushner) worked with DFC to negotiate a substantial upfront payment and profits interest for the United States," said a White House official.
Lukoil and Gazprom did not respond to requests for comment.

US begins direct talks with Myanmar in reversal of isolation attempts following military coup
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
06:09:44 UTC
15:09:44 KST

The Trump administration has begun direct talks with Myanmar’s military-installed government, according to US officials and others familiar with the outreach, in a sharp reversal of Washington’s efforts to isolate the country’s generals after the 2021 coup.
The US Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research, Michael Vance, played a leading role in the outreach, which has focused on shutting down scam centers that target Americans but could lead to broader engagement, including on Myanmar’s rare-earth mineral deposits, according to seven current and former officials and others familiar with the policy shift.
Vance joined talks with coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing in the capital Naypyitaw on September 15-16. The meeting was aimed at securing the release of American businessman Adam Castillo but also provided an opening for further engagement, four of the people said.
Last month’s meeting - the highest‑level contact since the coup - underscores a broader Trump‑administration foreign policy tilt away from democracy promotion toward transactional engagement.
The presence of Vance, who was confirmed as the State Department’s top intelligence official in August, and his ongoing role in US policy toward Myanmar have not been previously reported.
Min Aung Hlaing, the former military chief, remains under US sanctions for human rights abuses, including the 2016-2017 mass killings and expulsions of hundreds of thousands of Rohingya Muslims that Washington declared a genocide. Less than two weeks after Vance’s visit, Myanmar’s military conducted an airstrike on a crowded marketplace in Rakhine state, killing over 50 people and injuring scores more, according to United Nations human rights officials.
The State Department said it engages with all groups in Myanmar on issues affecting US interests and raises the need to cease violence and release political prisoners.
“You don't solve problems by ignoring them. You solve problems by addressing them,” spokesperson Tommy Pigott said in a statement.
A spokesperson for the military-backed government did not respond to a request for comment. Min Aung Hlaing, who has cited electoral fraud to justify the coup and labeled his opponents as terrorists, is seeking international legitimacy for his nominally civilian government.
Current and former officials say Vance has met players from all sides of Myanmar’s complex conflict and helped shape the Trump administration’s policy toward the country.
Intelligence chiefs - such as Vance - do not typically steer policy because of concerns about compromising analytic independence.
“If you let policy dictate to intelligence, you can't be sure you're getting a real honest assessment of the facts,” said Richard Betts, an adjunct senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations who has consulted for US intelligence agencies.
Pigott declined to address Vance’s role but said the administration “operates as a team with the president as the lead.”
Former US official detained in Myanmar, US holds negotiations for release
Castillo, a former head of the American Chamber of Commerce in Myanmar, was detained at Yangon airport on June 11 by Myanmar authorities on what his supporters have described as trumped-up charges. The US government has not commented on whether Castillo was wrongfully detained.
People familiar with the matter said White House, National Security Council, and State Department officials held back-channel negotiations with Myanmar officials to secure his release. One person said Myanmar asked only "to have an official engagement at the right level with the US government" in return.
Castillo declined to comment beyond crediting US President Donald Trump for his release.
The meeting builds on a June meeting between US and Myanmar officials in Tokyo also involving Vance, four people said. One of the people said officials from the Treasury Department, which oversees sanctions, the Department of Homeland Security, and the Pentagon took part.
It was unclear who represented Myanmar at the talks.
Vance, who became involved in Myanmar policy while advising Vice President JD Vance on Asian affairs, has also met in person and virtually with the democratic opposition and ethnic armed groups fighting the military, five of the people said.
US looking to shut down Myanmar fraud operations
A major focus of the US push is getting Myanmar's help in shuttering scam hubs operating on its territory that run romance and other frauds, which have scammed Americans out of billions of dollars. Two people familiar with the matter said the FBI has had direct contact with Myanmar’s authorities on cyber scams.
Researchers say many scams are run from areas under militia control, with some proceeds flowing to the military, raising doubts about whether Myanmar’s leaders are serious about enforcement.
US officials also discussed access to Myanmar’s massive deposits of heavy rare earths that are used in electric vehicles and wind turbines. US officials acknowledge obstacles: the deposits mainly lie in territory held by ethnic armies fighting Myanmar’s military government, and China, currently the main importer, could see any US role as a challenge.
Still, with Washington seeking to diversify supply chains away from China, Myanmar's deposits remain a recurring topic in conversations, the people said.
After the 2021 coup, US president Joe Biden's administration froze Myanmar's assets at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and imposed sanctions on senior officers and military‑linked businesses.
In 2022, Congress authorized non-lethal support for the opposition, funding early-warning systems for airstrikes and incentives for officers to defect.
Most of those programs were cut during Trump’s foreign-aid overhaul last year, according to four current and former officials and State Department correspondence with Congress reviewed by Reuters.
The State Department said its engagement with the military government does not diminish its relationships with other groups. The US continues to provide assistance to areas outside military control, it said, without detailing that aid.
Top Foreign Affairs Committee Democrat decries shift in Myanmar relations
Rep. Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said the shift was “contrary to both our values and our interests.”
“By engaging Min Aung Hlaing while failing to implement congressionally mandated sanctions and deploy appropriated democracy funding, Secretary (Marco) Rubio is ceding US leadership and providing this murderous regime greater international legitimacy,” Meeks said in a statement to Reuters.
Myanmar's government, installed after elections that rights groups criticized as a sham, has hired lobbyists to press its case in Washington.
In April, Roger Stone, a longtime Trump adviser, began consulting for DCI Group on behalf of Myanmar's Ministry of Information, according to Foreign Agents Registration Act filings. Stone was convicted in 2019 of obstructing a congressional investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election. Trump later pardoned him.
A newsletter distributed by DCI warned in June that Washington risked losing access to critical minerals if it did not engage with Myanmar.

Isaias intensifies into first Atlantic hurricane of 2026

US energy companies such as Shell and Chevron said they were curtailing offshore operations at their Gulf platforms.
US Gulf of Mexico oil and gas producers had shut in about 25.08% of current oil production and 16.37% of current natural gas production as of Wednesday, according to the Marine Minerals Administration. REUTERS

El Nino set to intensify before peaking in December, UN warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
06:09:13 UTC
15:09:13 KST

El Nino set to intensify before peaking in December, UN warns
The United Nations warned on Thursday that El Nino will intensify before peaking in December, bringing higher temperatures to much of the planet and compounding the effects of man-made climate change. The World Meteorological Organization added that this naturally occurring weather phenomenon could be the strongest since at least 1950.
El Nino will intensify even more before peaking in December, the United Nations said Thursday, warning it could be among the strongest witnessed since at least 1950.
The naturally occurring weather phenomenon is set to bring higher temperatures to much of the planet, the UN's weather and climate agency said, with its impact compounding the effects of man-made climate change.
Read moreRare train of cyclones fuelled by historic El Nino make their way across Pacific
"El Nino will continue to intensify ahead of its forecast peak in December," the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) said in its monthly Global Seasonal Climate Update.
"It is likely to bring above-average temperatures to much of the globe and shift rainfall patterns, increasing the risk of drought and floods in different regions."
El Nino warms surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, bringing worldwide changes in winds, pressure and rainfall patterns.
It typically takes place every two to seven years and lasts around nine to 12 months.
Conditions oscillate between El Nino and its opposite La Nina, with neutral conditions in between.
El Nino 'strengthening rapidly'
"Sea-surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific are forecast to increase to record levels during October-November-December 2026, reflecting the strengthening of the El Nino event which will drive weather patterns and impact economies, ecosystems and communities across the globe," the WMO said.
The forecast is based on consensus across 13 leading national and international meteorological centres.
"El Nino is firmly established and strengthening rapidly," said WMO chief Celeste Saulo.
"WMO forecasts indicate a near-100 percent likelihood that it will persist through February 2027, potentially being one of the strongest since at least 1950."
Saulo explained that El Nino does not add new heat to the planet, but releases heat being stored in the ocean.
"The ocean it's drawing from is the warmest we've ever measured it. There is simply more heat available to release," she said.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Sea temperatures record
The index which measures sea surface temperature anomalies across the central-eastern equatorial Pacific – the region at the heart of El Nino – increased from 1.6C above normal in June to 2.5C above normal in August.
For October-November-December, the anomaly is forecast to reach approximately 3.7C above normal.
This would be the highest since observations began, eclipsing the previous record of 2.6C set in 2015-2016.
The last El Nino contributed to making 2023 the second-hottest year on record and 2024 the all-time high at around 1.55C above the 1850-1900 pre-industrial average.
While El Nino usually peaks between November and February, the resulting spike in temperatures typically comes later.
This El Nino is already hitting some regions hard, including in Central America, where animals and crops are dying from drought.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Minister to Ed Miliband: British troops in Estonia strengthen NATO security

Minister to Ed Miliband: British troops in Estonia strengthen NATO security
British troops in Estonia are an important part of NATO's deterrence posture, Minister of Foreign Affairs Margus Tsahkna (Eesti 200) said.
Tsahkna praised the U.K.'s readiness to stand alongside Estonian soldiers after a meeting Wednesday with British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband in London on Wednesday.
Defense cooperation, Ukraine support and pressure on Russia were on the table. The U.K. has been the lead nation in the NATO allied land deployment in Estonia for nearly a decade now.
Wednesday's meeting focused extensively on Russia's aggression against Ukraine. According to Tsahkna, continued support for Ukraine and pressure on Russia to end the war are crucial for the security of Europe as a whole.
"We highly value the United Kingdom's contribution to our security and its readiness to stand alongside Estonian soldiers from the very first moment, jointly defending not only Estonia but the security of the entire NATO Alliance. Estonian and British soldiers work together and train side by side every day. As Brigadier Jamie Murray, the commander of the British troops stationed in Estonia, said recently, he would go into battle immediately if necessary. This is a very clear message both to our people and to our adversary," Tsahkna said.
Today in London, I met Foreign Secretary @Ed_Miliband to discuss support for Ukraine and wider European security, including countering Russia's sabotage and increasing pressure on Russia to end its aggression and secure a lasting peace. We also discussed strengthening our close defence cooperation. British and Estonian soldiers stand together to defend NATO's eastern flank and preserve peace, and we highly value the UK's commitment to our shared security.
— Margus Tsahkna (@Tsahkna) October 7, 2026
"The presence of British troops in Estonia is an important part of a strong deterrence and defense posture. Our task is to continue strengthening defense cooperation between Estonia and the United Kingdom. The growing defense investments of NATO's European Allies and Canada are also important, as they enable NATO to meet the capability targets it has set," the minister carried on, via a press release.
"We are working closely with the United Kingdom to achieve a lasting peace in Ukraine. Russia must understand that the cost of continuing its aggression must be higher than the cost of ending it, and this requires continued pressure on Russia. The United Kingdom's sanctions policy has been very important in this regard, and the European Union must also continue to increase sanctions pressure. We must also continue our cooperation to counter Russia's hybrid activities," Tsahkna went on.
"The outcome of Russia's aggression will affect the security of Europe as a whole. Ukraine must now be provided with everything it needs to defend itself, while Ukraine's supporters must already be preparing for the post-war period and developing security guarantees that will make a recurrence of the aggression impossible".
Tsahkna and Miliband also discussed potential cooperation in light of the Ukraine Recovery Conference taking place in Estonia in January.
"Even while the war is still ongoing, we need to take active steps to support Ukraine's recovery. The Ukraine Recovery Conference taking place in Estonia next January will be crucial for advancing Ukraine's recovery and providing the assistance Ukraine urgently needs during the difficult winter of the war," Tsahkna said on this.
The foreign ministers also discussed further defense cooperation between the two countries.
During his visit, Tsahkna also met with U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham's National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell, to discuss the same issues. Today, Thursday, he is to take part in discussions on European security at the GZERO Summit and the RUSI think tank in London.
The U.K. is the lead nation of the NATO battlegroup based at Tapa, and its deployment to Estonia has been Britain's largest land force deployment for a number of years. The U.K. is also the lead nation in the 10-member Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF), a maritime initiative focused on Baltic Sea security.

What did Palestinians take when they fled after October 7?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
06:08:05 UTC
15:08:05 KST

Gaza Strip - When Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began after October 7, 2023, hundreds of thousands of Palestinians were forced to leave their homes, many under forced displacement orders to move south.
By September 27, 2026, at least 74,018 Palestinians had been killed and 175,079 injured in Gaza since the start of the war, according to Gaza’s Ministry of Health.
Some fled with nothing, leaving behind homes, belongings and memories. Others managed to grab just what they could not bear to leave behind: A book, a musical instrument, a toy, a pet or a keepsake.
We asked people in Gaza what they took with them when they fled their homes after October 7 - and what stays with them after repeated displacements during the war.
When Omar Abdel Hakim Hamad, 30, received a displacement order in Beit Hanoon, north of Gaza, at about midnight, he decided to stay a little longer despite the heavy bombardment. He wanted to collect what he could from his home, fearing he might never return.
The first thing he thought of saving was his personal library of about 500 books.
He managed to take about 200, prioritising old and rare books that he felt could not be replaced.
Since leaving Beit Hanoon on October 30, 2023, Omar has been displaced 13 times, moving first to Gaza City and later south to the Maghazi refugee camp, where he remains displaced.
For Omar, the books were more than possessions. “They are part of who I am,” he says, describing how his love of reading began at 15.
Among the books he carried with him is a 1933 edition of Kalila wa Dimna.
During the famine-like conditions that plagued Gaza for large parts of the war, he even considered exchanging his entire library for one or two kilogrammes of flour, but says he is grateful that he managed to keep most of it.
Today, his Phoenix Library (at the centre of Gaza city) contains about 7,000 books, including about 3,000 rescued from libraries destroyed during the war and another 4,000 that were bought.
When Shahd Abu Khosa, 30, left her home in Gaza’s al-Jalaa neighbourhood on October 16, 2023, she took her two dogs, Lily and Bobby, with her.
Her displacement took her from al-Shifa Hospital to Tal al-Hawa south of Gaza City, then to a house and finally to a school shelter.
The journey was difficult for both dogs, especially Lily, who was frightened by the sound of bombardment and would hide whenever shelling began. Bobby died of starvation after food became unavailable.
“I never thought of leaving Lily behind,” Shahd says, describing her as part of the family.
During the famine, Lily survived by eating what the family ate, including lentils and bread, while Shahd continued to share what little food they had with her.
Shahd says she had once been afraid of dogs, but that changed after her sister brought Lily and Bobby from Egypt.
Lily became especially close to her, spending much of her time with Shahd and sharing her food. She describes Lily as loyal and gentle, saying the dog would sense when Shahd was in danger and try to protect her.
Shahd hopes all pets in Gaza can find a safe place where they have food, water and somewhere to sleep, “away from fear and harm, and without being thrown out”.
As Yaseen al-Qubt, 16, left his home in Beit Lahiya on October 12, 2023, he took his oud with him.
His family moved to az-Zawaida in central Gaza, while their home was later bombed and the instrument was left beneath the rubble.
Yaseen had owned the oud since January 2023 and had learned to play with the help of a neighbour who was an oud player.
He later managed to recover his oud from under the ruins. He picked it up again and continued playing.
For Yaseen, playing is also a way to comfort children in the displacement camp. When the sound of Israeli drones frightens them, he plays the oud to give them a few moments of calm.
He dreams of leaving Gaza to continue studying music, playing on large stages and eventually owning a professional oud that will help him develop his skills.
For now, he says, he remains attached to the instrument because “we still have something beautiful to offer.”
When Huda Helassa, 20, left her home in Tal al-Hawa, southern Gaza city, in the first hours of the war, she took a signed T-shirt from the Access Microscholarship Program, a United States-funded programme that provides English-language and cultural education to young people.
Her classmates had signed the shirt on September 15, 2023, during their final class, two years before she graduated on September 27.
“When we left our home on the first day of the war, the T-shirt was one of the first things that came to my mind,” Huda says.
She put it in her bag almost instinctively, wanting to hold on to something from a part of her life that had ended just days earlier.
Huda and her family first moved to her grandmother’s house in Gaza City, then were displaced south, walking part of the way, and eventually reached Rafah in the south of the Palestinian territory.
In May 2024, they were displaced again, this time to Khan Younis. When they returned to Gaza in January 2025, they found their home completely burned.
“There was nothing left of the life we had there,” she says. “No belongings, no photographs, no memories we could hold onto, just the blackened walls.”
They were displaced again in April 2025, moving to Remal and then Tal al-Hawa, before moving to az-Zawayda in September and returning to Gaza in October. They are currently in Tal al-Hawa.
For Huda, the T-shirt remains a link to the life she had before the war, a period of learning, friendships and experiences that shaped her.
When Mahmoud Hussein, 8 years old, and his family were forced to flee their home from Gaza City to Nuseirat in central Gaza, he insisted on taking his bag of toys with him.
His mother says the family was displaced about seven times, and each time Mahmoud refused to leave without his toys, even when she tried to persuade him to leave them behind.
During a period of truce, the family returned home and found it partially destroyed.
Mahmoud’s room had been destroyed, including his bed, wardrobe and most of his toys.
“He was deeply affected by what happened to his room,” his mother says. He still remembers the toys he lost and the room he once had.
Mahmoud has a neurological condition that causes abnormal electrical activity in the brain and had been taking daily medication for two years. He stopped his treatment two days before the war and was supposed to begin a new one, but the war disrupted his care.
He also needs monthly neurological tests that are currently unavailable in Gaza.
His mother says Mahmoud’s toys became his “safe place” during the war. Because fear, stress and sadness can trigger his seizures, playing and creating stories around his toys helped him escape the atmosphere of war and remain calm.

Texas execution first in US since Christa Pike survived botched lethal injection
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
06:08:00 UTC
15:08:00 KST

Texas has executed seven people so far this year, up from five in both 2025 and 2024. A further two executions are scheduled to take place in the state in November.
Texas has carried out the first execution in the US since Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike survived a failed lethal injection last week.
Jamaal Howard, 46, received a fatal dose of pentobarbital at the state prison in Huntsville and was pronounced dead at 8:03 pm. Howard had been convicted of shooting and killing 42-year-old clerk Vickie Swartout in a convenience store robbery in Silsbee, Texas, in 2000.
Howard is said to have gasped and taken a few breaths as the drug took effect, before making snoring sounds and coughing. All movement stopped within around 30 seconds, and he was pronounced dead 19 minutes later.
Before the execution took place, Howard addressed some members of Swartout's family, apologising and asking for forgiveness.
"I wish that you accept my apology and I wish for your forgiveness," he said. "I'm sorry for what happened. I wish you can learn to forgive me one of these days."
He added that he was "in a good state of mind to find peace and the Lord, so I thank y’all."
"Hey, enjoy life, and peace to y’all."
Howard's attorneys had unsuccessfully attempted to halt the execution, filing a motion before the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals questioning the quality of Texas' execution drugs. They also argued to the Supreme Court that the execution should not go ahead because Howard was intellectually disabled.
The Texas court denied the request relating to the drugs and a second filing without comment.
The Supreme Court has barred the execution of intellectually disabled people, but it has given states some discretion in determining such disabilities. The state told the court that Howard's attorneys did not provide evidence that would show he met the requirements to claim intellectual disability.
The high court also declined to intervene without comment late on Wednesday, clearing the way for the execution to go ahead.
The Texas Coalition to Abolish the Death Penalty, an advocacy organisation campaigning to end the death penalty in Texas, had called on people to urge Texas Governor Greg Abbott to insist on a reprieve for Howard, so that his lawyers could "obtain critical records from the Texas Department of Criminal Justice about when the drug was bought, how it was stored, and what testing was done and when."
Including Howard, Texas has executed seven people so far this year, up from five in both 2025 and 2024. A further two executions are scheduled to take place in November - death row inmates John Rubio and Reinaldo Dennes.

People in Russian-occupied Ukrainian town risk 'road of death' to get food
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
06:04:21 UTC
15:04:21 KST

People in Russian-occupied Ukrainian town risk 'road of death' to get food
KYIV/LONDON, Oct 8 - Trapped and facing starvation, residents of the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine risk their lives to travel for hours by foot and bicycle along mine-strewn roads to get food and water.
The main route out of the town, lying near the front line east of the Dnipro River, heads deeper into Russian-controlled areas. It is littered with burned-out cars and charred by blasts, according to witnesses, relatives, humanitarian groups and video footage verified by Reuters. Attack drones prowl overhead.
Residents say the last food deliveries to a local store took place in May.
"What on earth could possibly be left in your house when you haven't been to the shop for half a year?" a woman living in the town told Reuters, asking not to be identified for fear of reprisals from Russian occupying forces.
She had recently attempted the trip to Radensk, some 20 km (12.5 miles) to the southeast. On her way back, she was injured by a landmine.
"There is no safe way out," she said afterwards, adding that a few days earlier three people had been killed on the same route, which some locals call "the road of death".
Reuters was not able to verify the woman's account independently, although it chimes with those from other witnesses, officials and aid workers familiar with the humanitarian crisis in Oleshky.
That people are even attempting these journeys points to growing desperation.
"The choice Russia forces on civilians every day: to stay — and starve to death; or to leave - and risk being blown up by a landmine," Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said.
He also said Kyiv had offered a local ceasefire and evacuation routes to residents who wanted to leave but that Russia had rejected the proposal.
Russia has acknowledged critical problems with food and medical supplies in Oleshky and said its military was working to resolve them. It blamed Ukraine for the crisis, saying it was obstructing those supplies getting to the town.
'THEY KNOW THEY ARE DOOMED'
Oleshky in Ukraine's Kherson region, with a pre-war population of some 24,000, is still home to around 1,700 residents, including 47 children, according to Danielle Bell, head of the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine.
Drone footage from the town shared by Ukraine's 34th Separate Marine Brigade "Borysfen" and verified by Reuters shows residential and administrative buildings ruined and abandoned after more than four years of war and Russian occupation.
There is no stable power, water or heating. Movement in and out is more dangerous than ever.
Tetiana Hasanenko, head of the local military administration sitting in the Ukraine-controlled part of the region, keeps in regular contact with Oleshky locals.
"They know they are doomed. These are terrible words to say, but they know they will die either from hunger or from strikes," she told Reuters in late September.
Ukrainian troops do not have direct access to the town. In recent days, the Ukrainian military said it had dropped food to residents using drones. Reuters could not independently confirm those claims and some residents expressed scepticism, saying they had seen nothing.
Andrii Sybiha, Ukraine's foreign minister, said Russia, as the aggressor state, bore "full responsibility for this humanitarian disaster."
Russia's defence ministry and the Russian-installed authorities in occupied Kherson did not respond to requests for comment.
FEAR OF HUNGER
Oleshky residents said food supplies became unreliable late last year, but the situation deteriorated significantly after May.
Before then, Ukrainian volunteers were able to take in food and evacuate people. Since then, people have largely lived off the land, and that is becoming untenable as winter approaches.
Larysa, a Ukrainian woman who fled Oleshky shortly after Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, told Reuters in London that her husband was still there and surviving on dwindling rations.
The 72-year-old, who declined to give her full name or that of her husband out of concern for his safety, said he was living on vegetables and homemade flatbread cooked on an open fire. He was using pre-invasion flour stocks that had gone bad long ago.
"He's been living on this for the whole summer, ever since May. There are no eggs, no dairy, no meat – there's nothing," his wife said. He feeds their four cats and a dog with grass mixed with whatever grain is left.
Larysa said she had "forbidden" her husband from taking the road out of Oleshky to Radensk in search of food, describing the journey as a life-and-death gamble, or "Russian roulette".
The Ukrainian brigade footage shows dozens of burnt-out and abandoned vehicles along the route. The buildings on either side have been badly damaged.
Larysa is sure her husband hides the full extent of his difficulties when they speak briefly by phone twice a week.
As winter sets in, homegrown staples like cucumbers, courgettes and tomatoes are running out and fear of starvation grows.
"There really isn't anything left to swap. We've used it all up," the woman injured by the mine said.
The only way to boil water is over an open fire because gas cylinders are impossible to get. Medicines are out of date and she eats just once a day - a thin piece of flatbread with tomato and salt or honey. REUTERS

The iconic train will follow the French Riviera from Paris before reaching Monaco, with the new overnight journey becoming a permanent fixture and fares starting at a cool €4,870 per person.
The Venice Simplon-Orient-Express is adding a glamorous new stop to its European routes in 2027, with Monte Carlo joining the itinerary for the first time.
From May, the legendary train operated by Belmond will travel from Paris along the Côte d’Azur before arriving in Monaco on its onward journey to Venice.
It’s set to become an annual addition to the iconic rail company’s schedule and will allow guests to explore the famously glitzy city, world-renowned for landmarks including the Casino de Monte-Carlo and the star-studded Formula One Grand Prix.
Travellers will start their journey in the French capital, boarding the train’s midnight-blue carriages, all decked out in Art Deco style.
On offer are historic cabins, grand suites, as well as the L'Observatoire carriage, designed by French artist JR. The suite comes complete with a bedroom and en suite bathroom with a freestanding bathtub as well as a spacious living area, library and secret tearoom.
No matter which level of accommodation guests stay in, they can opt to eat dinner in one of the train's two restaurant cars, Étoile du Nord or L'Oriental, before moving onto the Bar Car '3674', where cocktails are accompanied by live music at the piano.
The next morning, guests will enjoy a breakfast of fresh pastries and pressed fruit juices, while taking in views of the beautiful Côte d'Azur.
The route takes passengers along the dramatic red cliffs of the Massif de l'Estérel and winds through Saint-Raphaël towards Cannes and Nice, offering sweeping views across the French Riviera.
Closer to Monaco, the railway cuts into the mountainside before arriving at Monte Carlo station, deep beneath the rock.
According to the company, the decision to add Monte Carlo to the route was an easy one.
“Monaco has long held a special place in the story of European travel, with generations drawn to the Côte d'Azur by its distinctive sense of style, culture, and occasion,” said Pascal Deyrolle, Area Managing Director for Trains – Continental Europe.
“Introducing the destination feels like a natural continuation for the Venice Simplon-Orient-Express, bringing the romance of luxury rail travel to a locale that has always understood the art of arrival.”
With a slated price starting at €4,870 per person based on two guests sharing a historic cabin, with 24-hour steward service, all meals with the sommelier's choice of wine and unlimited soft drinks, and transfers, many of us might need to start saving ahead of May’s launch.

Hundreds of inertial navigation units built to keep working when satellite signals are jammed or spoofed are to be fitted to counter-drone weapon stations bound for Poland, under an agreement worth $18.5 million, according to Advanced Navigation.
The company will supply its Boreas fibre-optic gyroscope inertial navigation systems to Kongsberg for integration into PROTECTOR counter-uncrewed air system platforms. The Norwegian-built turrets are going to the Polish Armaments Agency as part of a deal worth 16 billion Norwegian kroner, or around $1.74 billion.
Inertial navigation works by measuring a platform’s own motion rather than listening for a signal from space, which is why it keeps giving a position when GPS does not. The systems provide positioning, orientation and heading, letting a counter-drone station detect, track and engage an air threat when satellite navigation cannot be trusted.
David Leniewski, managing director of Advanced Navigation for Europe, the Middle East and Africa, said: “As electromagnetic warfare becomes a defining feature of modern conflict, precision is no longer determined by arsenals or sensors alone. It depends on knowing exactly where the platform is, how it is moving and maintaining that accuracy even when GPS is denied. That’s where Boreas becomes mission-critical.
“By providing a resilient source of positioning, orientation and stabilisation independent of satellite navigation, Boreas enables PROTECTOR to maintain accurate sensor alignment and target engagement under conditions that would degrade conventional navigation systems. It ensures operators retain confidence in every engagement, even in the most heavily contested electromagnetic environments.
“Together, PROTECTOR and Boreas deliver a layered C-UAS capability that is both economically sustainable and operationally resilient. One provides the proven kinetic effect; the other ensures that effect can still be delivered when the battlespace is actively trying to deny it.”
The company sets the agreement against two problems it says modern conflict has exposed. The first is economic, since defending against thousands of cheap attack drones cannot be sustained when each interceptor costs millions. The second is electromagnetic, with jamming and spoofing now commonplace and degrading any system that relies on satellites to initialise, stabilise and engage.
Jørgen Andreas Bull, senior vice president for land systems at Kongsberg, said: “Modern threats do not observe fixed boundaries, and countering them requires a fundamental evolution in platform survivability.
“By integrating Advanced Navigation’s inertial navigation technology into our PROTECTOR C-UAS platforms, we are providing forces with a resilient capability that continues when GPS is denied. Whether protecting tactical land convoys from asymmetric attack, safeguarding critical airfields, or defending coastal naval assets against uncrewed swarms, this partnership delivers the reliable, multi-spectrum resilience modern forces demand.”
The two firms have worked together before, with an earlier multi-million dollar deal putting the Boreas D90 onto the PROTECTOR RS4 remote weapon station. Kongsberg PROTECTOR systems carrying Advanced Navigation equipment are already deployed on infantry fighting vehicles, armoured personnel carriers, naval vessels and uncrewed ground vehicles.
Mr Leniewski also made a claim about delivery that speaks to the state of the European market. “Unlike legacy PNT suppliers burdened by years-long lead times, Advanced Navigation’s vertically integrated production facilities enable full internal component sourcing, environmental stress-testing, and simulated EW validation prior to delivery,” he said. “This streamlined capability ensures rapid, high-volume production and delivery timelines as European defense ministries work to fulfil urgent procurement schedules.”
The agreement is supported by the Australian Department of Defence’s Global Supply Chain programme, which exists to get Australian firms into the supply chains of international primes.

Polanski, who leads the Greens in England and Wales, is standing for his party in the north London constituency, previously held by Keir Starmer before he stood down as an MP shortly after resigning as prime minister.

Starmer won it with a majority of 11,500 at the 2024 general election despite strong challenges from the Greens and a leftwing independent candidate, who is not standing again and has endorsed Polanski. In 2019, Starmer won by nearly 28,000 votes.
Polanski has run a highly energetic campaign. He has mobilised a large numbers of supporters to knock on doors, mimicking February’s Gorton and Denton byelection where the Greens overcame an even bigger Labour majority to take the seat.
However, the political landscape has changed. Shortly after Gorton and Denton, YouGov polling put the Greens briefly above Labour, on a peak of 21%. The most recent equivalent had Polanksi’s party on 11%, 16 points behind Labour.
Burnham, who succeeded Starmer as prime minister in July, is seen as having revitalised Labour, and used his speech at the party’s annual conference last month to set out a more ambitious and left-leaning collection of policies.
Polanski’s fortunes in contrast appear to have declined, especially since last weekend’s Green party conference where a vote by members to adopt a policy equating Zionism with racism and calling for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state prompted condemnation and splits in the party.
Four out of the five Green MPs have condemned the policy, while councillors and others have distanced themselves from it or in some cases left the party.
While policy is decided by Green members in direct votes, Polanski has been criticised for not saying whether or not he backed the motion and leaving the conference before the vote took place to resume campaigning.
The stakes are also high for Burnham. Failure to win the seat by a reasonable margin could end his honeymoon period and bring renewed doubts about Labour’s ability to protect inner-city seats from the Greens, who won several London councils in May’s local elections.
Holborn and St Pancras could be promising ground for the Greens, with a young and diverse population that includes many students. About 45% of constituents were born overseas and 48% are aged between 18 and 34.
Labour has campaigned hard, fielding as its candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali, the 42-year-old leader of Camden council who arrived in London in the early 90s, speaking no English, after fleeing war in Somalia with her four brothers and her mother, who trained as a lawyer in Somalia.
In a pre-poll message to voters, Burnham said: “This area gave Sagal a home when she arrived here as a refugee in the 1990s. Camden gave Sagal and her family hope. Now she wants to give that back to the communities that have always been there for her. It’s hard to think of someone more committed to their local area and the care of people than Sagal.”
In his own statement, Polanski said the result was “looking close”, and that voters should choose him to pressure Labour.
He said: “We already have a Labour government, a Labour council and a Labour [London] mayor. Isn’t it time for a Green voice for Camden to push Labour to do better on issues like rent controls and to put Thames Water into public ownership – issues where they’ve been backtracking?”

University students say procrastination is biggest threat to their academic performance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
06:00:12 UTC
15:00:12 KST

Procrastination is the biggest problem that can harm students’ academic performance at university, according to a study of more than 65,000 young people who placed it above issues such as ADHD, anxiety or financial worries.
The study found that nearly half of the students surveyed named procrastination as the thing damaging their ability to do academic work, more than twice the number who named depression, while the same proportion said procrastination caused them significant distress above any other problems including family pressures or bullying.
Itamar Shatz, the author of the study and an affiliated lecturer at the University of Cambridge, said that while he expected the survey of US students would show that they experienced harm from procrastination, he was surprised by how strongly it affected them.
Shatz said: “Pretty much all of us procrastinate but it’s not a huge impediment for all of us. For the people that it is, it can be huge. It’s not just something we occasionally run into but, as we can see in these findings, it can be a major obstacle.
“It’s an obstacle that can interfere with academic success, with success in the workplace, it can cause issues in relationships, it can cause stress, it can cause health issues and stop us reaching out for help.”
The study, published in the journal Plos One, also suggests that procrastination could be a factor in a “vicious cycle” that can cause or exaggerate other issues such as stress.
“An example of such a feedback loop is a student procrastinating on a task, which causes them to feel stressed, which interferes with their sleep, which causes them to procrastinate on the task further,” the study said.
Fuschia Sirois, a psychology professor at Durham University and a co-editor-in-chief of the British Journal of Health Psychology, who was not involved in the study, said: “The salience of procrastination in students’ lives and its harms has been a topic of research for almost 30 years, with the first studies on the impact of procrastination on health and wellbeing conducted in the late 1990s and early 2000s. So this is an issue for which there is an established evidence base that clearly highlights the negative impact of procrastination on students’ lives.
“This descriptive study with a large sample provides some additional insights into the relative impact of procrastination with respect to its range of harms. But it is just a snapshot, so limits the conclusions we can draw.”
Sirois said myths about procrastination “being a character flaw” have persisted despite the existing research.
“People procrastinate to avoid the difficult emotions associated with a task, which affords them short-term mood repair. But in the long run the feelings of guilt, shame and stress from procrastinating catch up to them and take a toll on health and wellbeing,” she said.
Shatz, who has recently published a guide to overcoming procrastination, said that procrastination should not be compared with laziness, because procrastinators can often be highly motivated to tackle a task only to be derailed by other distractions such as perfectionism or burn-out.
Universities should be aware that many of their students are likely to be hampered by procrastination.
“They should understand that procrastination isn’t just a time management flaw that they can fix with a flyer, but it is one of the biggest obstacles that students face and needs to be treated with positive interventions. The good thing is that research shows that interventions can help,” Shatz said.

UK’s military needs to focus spending on domestic defence, not overseas missions – report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
06:00:11 UTC
15:00:11 KST

The UK’s military is too focused on global commitments at the expense of domestic defence, meaning the government’s planned increase in defence spending is likely to result in even greater waste, a thinktank report has warned.
According to an analysis by researchers at the Transition Security Project, Britain has the most overseas-oriented military among European nations, with almost a quarter of the defence budget spent on commitments across five continents.
Calling this a symptom of a “destructive, outdated foreign policy” centred on overseas missions that have often made the world less safe, the report says ministers should prioritise changing their approach rather than immediately increasing spending, with resources shifted from overseas commitments to domestic defence.
The government is committed to spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035 and a defence investment plan (Dip) was unveiled in July at the tail end of Keir Starmer’s premiership.
Starmer’s defence secretary John Healey resigned over a refusal to commit to reaching 3% by 2030, but now that Healey is chancellor that target has been shelved for now.
It would involve a doubling of the defence budget in nominal terms from £70bn in 2026 to £151bn in 2035, according to the Transition Security Project, a research centre that was spun out of Common Wealth, a thinktank with close links to Andy Burnham.
Using figures from 2024-25, the study estimated that about 23% of the military budget for that year was spent on overseas commitments, costing just over £14bn, with the real figure likely to be higher. About £2.8bn was spent on deployments used to project force outside Europe, including bases in places such as Cyprus, Kenya and Oman and elsewhere as “strategic hubs” for projecting UK military power.
The report says this makes the UK the most overseas-committed military among European Nato members, even if France has more personnel posted abroad. The Dip seems unlikely to reverse this, talking about continuing commitments on other continents.
The report questions whether more of the new money should be used for domestic defence, and whether the focus on overseas missions has made the UK safer. Since 2001, the study says, the UK has spent more than £51bn in modern terms on military interventions in Iraq, Afghanistan, Libya and elsewhere.
“Britain’s decision to maintain a global network of military bases and force projection capabilities, combined with high levels of waste in the military procurement system, raise serious questions about how it is allocating public investment,” it says, urging the government to “review its military posture, prioritising defence over the global projection of military force”.
Kevin Cashman, a researcher at the Transition Security Project who co-authored the report, said: “Britain should not pour more money into a bloated military sector geared towards alignment with the United States while Washington starts wars around the world that drive up our bills.”
Khem Rogaly, a co-director of the organisation and also a co-author, said: “The billions of pounds Britain wastes on global military deployments every year symbolise its destructive, outdated foreign policy. Britain should end its support for these attempts at global policing. Instead, it should focus its military resources on defence and its public investment on health, housing and the climate emergency.”
There is an awareness among defence officials of the importance of avoiding waste, including the risk that an arbitrary focus on reaching a certain level of spending could exacerbate this.
The intention is to focus instead on what is necessary – primarily on preparing the UK for a possible war in Europe.

An average of 17 older Australians died each day last year waiting for home care

An average of 17 older Australians died every day waiting for home care last year, new figures reveal
In short:
More than 6,400 older Australians died while waiting to receive home care last year, an increase of more than a third on the previous year.
Advocates have described the figures as an "absolute tragedy".
The federal government has been accused by political opponents of trying to hide the figures.
An average of 17 older Australians died while waiting to receive necessary home care each day last year, according to the latest official figures — an increase of more than a third on the previous year.
New data published by the health department revealed 6,436 older Australians approved for Support at Home, but in the queue for funding, died in 2025-26.
The figure is an almost 34 per cent increase from the 4,812 people who died while waiting under the former National Priority System for home care packages in the previous year.
However, the figures are not directly comparable, because of the transition from the older system to the current one.
"Everybody on the wait list is a person; they're not a statistic or a number,"
Shadow Health Minister Anne Ruston said.
The Opposition said the data emerged after the federal government failed to comply with two Senate orders to produce the figures.
"Rather than fixing the system, Labor has put its energy into avoiding scrutiny. And it is older Australians and their families who are paying the price," she said.
"The extent to which the government tried to hide this information from the public is appalling. The prime minister and his ministers clearly just didn't want older Australians and their families to know the truth."
CEO of the Council on the Ageing Australia, Patricia Sparrow, described the figures as "an absolute tragedy", which demonstrated just how badly the system was keeping up with demand.
"This shouldn't be happening … there aren't enough packages in the system [and] we need to make sure people can get the package they need within about 30 days of being assessed," she said.
Ms Sparrow said when people did not get support at home for basic needs like showering or eating they could end up in hospital or be forced to move into residential aged care sooner.
"We need to make sure older people are respected … they don't put their hand up for assistance until they really need it," she said.
More than 106,000 Australians were on the official waiting list for a Support at Home place as of June 30.
The waitlist, known as the Support At Home priority system, determines how older people are prioritised for funding, and also includes people who are already receiving funding for a lower level of care, and are waiting for a higher level to be allocated.
In August, Four Corners revealed the true number of people waiting for full aged care funding at home was almost 154,000.
In May, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese conceded the state of aged care in Australia was "not good enough", after a report revealed patients were waiting an average of a year for services.
The federal government was also accused of burying that report by its political opponents, quietly dropping it during budget-lock up.
Last year, a Senate inquiry into aged care services heard from the families of people who died while waiting for support, including one Hobart man with Parkinson's and cancer who waited over 12 months for a home care package.
His package was approved three days before his death.
Independent Senator David Pocock said the data was "shocking but sadly not surprising".
"The Senate has been pushing the government hard for years to improve the care we're providing to older Australians. Time and again the aged care minister has dismissed and deflected and ultimately failed these older Australians and their families. It is unacceptable," he said.
"I am also dismayed that this data is released quietly and in a way that is hard to find. Even though it tells a grim story, older Australians and their family still deserve transparency from the government on the state of affairs."
Aged Care Minister Sam Rae said the rate of people who died waiting for Support at Home was "significantly lower than the rate of death for older Australians in the broader population".
"Every single death of someone who is waiting for care is a tragedy. My thoughts and condolences are with every family who has lost a loved one," he said.
Mr Rae said while there was "more work to do" the government had delivered an additional 83,000 home care places in 2025-26, with a further 32,000 rolling out this year.

El Nino could drive Pacific temperatures to record levels, WMO warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
05:58:55 UTC
14:58:55 KST

An ongoing El Nino could push sea-surface temperatures in the Pacific to record levels, increasing the risk of extreme heat, drought and flooding worldwide, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) said on Thursday.
In its latest Global Seasonal Climate Update, the UN weather agency said there was a near-100 percent likelihood that El Nino would persist through February 2027, with the event expected to peak around December.
“El Nino is firmly established and strengthening rapidly,” WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo said, warning it could become “one of the strongest since at least 1950”.
For October to December, sea-surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific are forecast to average about 3.7°C above normal. The WMO said this would be the highest level recorded since observations began.
The previous record was 2.6°C above normal during the November 2015 to January 2016 period.
Shifting rainfall patterns
The WMO said El Nino was likely to bring above-average temperatures across large parts of the world while significantly altering rainfall patterns.
Wetter-than-normal conditions are forecast in the Greater Horn of Africa, parts of Central and East Asia, northern parts of the Arabian Peninsula, parts of North America and southeastern South America.
Drier-than-normal conditions are expected across the Indian subcontinent, southern Central America, parts of the Caribbean and northwestern South America.
Saulo said El Nino does not create additional planetary heat but releases heat already stored in the ocean. She warned that the ocean from which the current event is drawing heat is “the warmest we've ever measured it”.
The WMO said national meteorological services and regional climate forums were providing regular updates to governments and humanitarian partners to support preparedness and risk management.

Gen Z Women Take to the Streets Over Spate of Rapes in India’s Capital
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
05:58:00 UTC
14:58:00 KST

India is globally perceived as an unsafe country for women, with its capital, New Delhi, often described as the “rape capital” of the country. Statistics from the National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) affirm that Delhi is “the most unsafe metropolitan city for women” and children in the country.
The NCRB’s Crime in India 2024 report substantiates this with statistics. In 2024 Delhi recorded 13,396 cases of crimes against women – the highest among all metro cities. The capital also has the dubious distinction of having the highest number (1,058) of reported rape cases among all metro cities.
While these statistics reveal that crimes against women in Delhi continue unabated, the greater irony is that India’s capital is the most policed city in the country with the highest police to people ratio. Delhi has 410 police personnel per million population, three times the national average of 153 personnel per million population.
And yet, Delhi’s streets remain unsafe.
These crime statistics made the headlines once again recently, after a spate of rapes and sexual assaults in the capital in August and September.
On September 21, a 17-year-old girl was gang-raped by three men posing as policemen in Astha Kunj Park, in posh South Delhi, barely 2 kms from the prestigious Lady Sri Ram (LSR) College for Women. Police nabbed the suspects and shot one of them. The incident sparked nationwide outrage, and panic and anger among the student community.
Prior to that, in early September, another 17-year-old was gang-raped and murdered in northwest Delhi’s Swaroop Nagar. The accused allegedly raped and stabbed her to death, and then dumped her body in a field. What makes these rape cases particularly distressing is that the victims were minors. In August, an 11-year-old and a 6-year-old were reportedly raped in separate incidents. The gang-rape of a 16-year-old in a moving bus on the Delhi-Noida border the same month brought back memories of the gruesome gang-rape of “Nirbhaya” 14 years ago in the capital. That victim subsequently died of her injuries. The incident, which led to massive protests in Delhi and other cities, resulted in major changes in sexual assault laws, including the introduction of the death penalty for rape.
These recent shocking incidents occurred amid massive youth and student protests by India’s Gen Z in Delhi and other Indian cities since July this year. The wave of protests started over leaked question papers for medical entrance exams. Protests led by the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) and leftist student organizations at Jantar Mantar in June-July forced Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign.
The success of the Jantar Mantar protests triggered realization among students that if they stand united, peaceful protests could yield unprecedented results. It has given them confidence to raise other pertinent issues like women’s safety.
So when a series of rapes occurred in the capital in August-September, youth anger erupted into widespread protests. On September 23, LSR students, triggered by the Astha Kunj rape and the failure of the authorities to ensure women’s safety, held a women-only solidarity march in Delhi University’s South Campus.
What distinguishes the recent protests against rape from earlier ones is the bold and unfiltered approach of the youth protestors. While some girl students held placards declaring, “Our body is our own,” others demanded freedom to step out at night without fear. Student protestors questioned the methods the authorities used to ensure women’s safety. The LSR college shifted to online classes to ensure the safety of their students, and police authorities mulled closing access to parks in the evening.
Instead of questioning patriarchy, they are restricting the movement of women, imposing late-night curfews for women living in hostels, and shifting classes online, the student protestors pointed out. “Smash the Patriarchy” was the theme of their protest march and they used catchy tunes, memes, and humor, making their anti-patriarchy slogans go viral.
The young women protesting against patriarchy are not intimidated by authority. They are demanding accountability from Home Minister Amit Shah while also lampooning him. Student wings of the opposition Congress and leftist parties organized protests against the failure of the Delhi Police to enforce the law. These protests were held amid ongoing protests in Delhi calling for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over election process irregularities.
Youth anger about women’s safety forced the Supreme Court to address the issue. Describing the recent spate of rapes as a clear “systematic failure” on the part of law enforcement authorities, a two-judge bench said that “accountability needs to be fixed.”
The judges stressed the need for a focused approach to prevent rapes and not on penalty. Merely installing CCTV was not enough, it pointed out, calling for the Delhi Police to monitor it around the clock. Better policing and patrolling would “instill fear in criminals,” it said, adding that public spaces, including parks and buses, should not become “high-risk” zones because of poor lighting and poor surveillance. Having strict laws was not enough, the court said, calling for effective implementation of laws to discourage serious offences like rape. The court will be taking stock of the progress made on its directives again next month.
Young women have been turning up in large numbers at all student protests in Delhi, asserting their place and demanding equal rights. So, when Delhi Police cracked down on women students and journalists protesting at Jantar Mantar, even molesting some of them, they marched to the nearest police station demanding a case be filed against the police officials. On October 4, Neha Bora, president of the All India Students’ Association (AISA), led a Citizens’ March from India Gate to Jantar Mantar, calling attention to the fact that “from streets to protests, women are not safe.”
It is evident that women in India, at least in its cities, are refusing to be cowed down or slut shamed or policed for their attire, or forced to stay indoors in the evenings, to ensure their safety. Rather, they are now vocal in their demands for a safer city and, more importantly, a change in patriarchal mindset within homes and in society at large. As 17-year-old Subhani told The Guardian, “My generation is not afraid to stand up and protest. We know that society has to change.” As she summed it up, “The days of women being silent is over.”

EU needs new money to cover budget shortfall: report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
05:55:03 UTC
14:55:03 KST

(AFP Photo)
Ballooning EU debt could blow a hole in the bloc's next seven-year budget if governments fail to agree on new sources of revenue, auditors warned on Oct. 8.
European Union capitals are locked in the usual battle between so-called "frugal" nations including Germany and higher-spending countries like France.
European leaders will discuss the 2028-2034 budget next week after Ireland, which holds the rotating EU presidency, presents the latest proposal on Oct. 10 that so-called "frugals" say must contain more cuts.
The EU executive proposed a budget worth around 2 trillion euros last year, including plans to raise money from new taxes on large companies, environmental taxation and levies on tobacco.
The European Court of Auditors (ECA) warned the EU economy is facing mounting pressure over the hundreds of billions of euros borrowed to support households and businesses during the COVID pandemic.
The EU's debt has "more than tripled in only a few years," reaching 739 billion euros by the end of 2025, Pierre Moscovici, a member of the European Court of Auditors, told reporters.
The auditors in the report warned: "The EU's rising debt burden could weigh heavily on future budgets. EU borrowing could reach one trillion euros by 2027, largely due to" the COVID recovery funds.
They said the EU would be spending up to 93 billion euros on interest payments alone because of the debt.

ChatGPT for Teens fails to work as intended, poses 'unacceptable risk': watchdog
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
05:51:36 UTC
14:51:36 KST

Some of the guardrails that OpenAI included in its ChatGPT for Teens product don't work as intended and the chatbot poses an “unacceptable risk” to children, according to a report on Wednesday by Common Sense Media.
The watchdog group urged OpenAI to restrict the chatbot to adults “until it can offer a safe, developmentally appropriate experience.”
OpenAI said the group’s testing doesn’t reflect how the chatbot’s safeguards work.
Parents, educators and child development experts have been sounding alarms over children’s use of AI chatbots, which have been blamed for facilitating cheating on schoolwork and even suicide.
While even adults can fall victim to anthropomorphising AI and develop unhealthy relationships with it, teenagers’ brains are not yet fully developed and they can be particularly vulnerable, child development experts say.
“We are concerned that ChatGPT for Teens could give parents false confidence in guardrails that frequently don’t work,” said the report from Common Sense Media, a group that advocates for using digital media sensibly.
Teen-mode features that did not work as intended included alerts meant to notify parents if their child is at risk for suicide, self-harm or eating disorders, along with support for teens in crisis, Common Sense Media said.
“ChatGPT still talks like a friend when teens treat it like a person,” the group said, though OpenAI had promised that the chatbot is prevented from suggesting it has personal feelings towards the user or implying that it is conscious or experiences emotions.
OpenAI said it is “deeply committed to teen safety,” to developing safeguards and giving parents tools to guide their teens’ use of AI.
The San Francisco company said its review of the report’s methodology shows “the bulk of their testing may have begun and concluded before activation of parental controls was complete, making their findings inaccurate.”
Common Sense Media receives funding from OpenAI and other tech companies, including those whose services it evaluates.
