IN DEPTH: New naval port aims to enhance Germany's defense capabilities
Citing the escalating security threat, Germany's Navy has decided to establish a second port on the North Sea coast.
After months of evaluating locations, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said the Bundeswehr's new naval port would be built in Emden.
"Emden offers ideal conditions, such as quick access to the Atlantic Ocean and the far north," Pistorius said.
Read all about why Pistorius said Germany needs another port for its navy and why Emden should host it: A new naval port in Emden aims to enhance Germany's defense capabilities
Steinmeier reassures France over Germany's EU commitment
German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier has pledged that Germany will remain firmly committed to Europe, seeking to reassure France following recent gains by the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) in state elections.
Speaking during a state visit to Paris on Thursday, Steinmeier said Germany could succeed only as a European country firmly embedded in the European Union.
"Germans will remain good Europeans," Steinmeier said at the Elysee Palace, alongside French President Emmanuel Macron.
After bilateral talks, Steinmeier emphasized that Germany "can only be successful as a European Germany, that is, tightly embedded in the European Union.
"That is true, and it will remain so for us," the German president said in Paris.
His remarks followed recent electoral successes by the euroskeptic AfD, including in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt, which have prompted concern in France.
Steinmeier described the current period as "damn difficult," pointing to the war in Ukraine, geopolitical challenges and domestic political tensions in both countries.
"We are experiencing a polarization of society, with the strengthening of the radical fringes," he said.
He warned that this was making it increasingly difficult to form governments and govern effectively, particularly as political debate shifted toward social media.
Macron also spoke of a “time of upheaval."
"We are witnessing how social media is accelerating societal changes and fueling doubts over democracy," he said. "If Germany and France do not move forward together, Europe will not make any progress at all."
Steinmeier was welcomed with military honors by Macron at the Arc de Triomphe, where he laid flowers at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier and rekindled its memorial flame.
At the Elysee Palace, the two presidents attended the signing of an agreement to bring the Franco-German Citizens' Fund under the umbrella of the Franco-German Youth Office. The fund supports cross-border civil society projects and has an annual budget of €5 million ($5.8 million).
On Friday, both presidents will travel to Bordeaux. There, the focus will be on defense and military cooperation.
German spy agency BND approved suspect's side job
Germany's foreign intelligence agency reportedly approved outside work by an employee for a former spy chief who is now suspected of illegally obtaining classified information.
According to German news magazine Der Spiegel, the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) officially authorized Manfred D. to work for former BND head August Hanning, who became a private-sector consultant after leaving government service in 2009.
Prosecutors allege that Manfred D. supplied Hanning with nearly 2,000 internal BND documents, many of them classified, which the former intelligence chief allegedly used for commercial gain.
Investigators believe the arrangement began around 2010, when Hanning and his former chief of staff allegedly agreed that intelligence would be supplied in return for payment.
Manfred D. allegedly passed the documents to Hanning between 2010 and 2022.
Hanning, 80, headed the BND from 1998 to 2005. He is suspected of offenses including intelligence-agent activity, espionage involving state secrets and attempted treason.
Manfred D., 64, served as chief of staff to several BND presidents from March 2012 until March 2026, a position that gave him access to sensitive intelligence.
He is accused of aiding attempted treason and espionage involving state secrets.
Both men have been held in pretrial detention since this week.
According to Der Spiegel, the BND had known about Manfred D.'s work for Hanning for some time and had issued an official authorization for the secondary employment.
The agency declined to answer questions about when the authorization was granted or what activities it covered, the magazine said.
Hanning's lawyer has denied wrongdoing, saying his client was being prosecuted unjustly.
He acknowledged that Hanning had possessed confidential documents but denied he had passed on information detrimental to Germany or had done so for payment.
Merz, Burnham inaugurate new German-British friendship treaty
Chancellor Friedrich Merz received relatively new British Prime Minister Andy Burnham with military honors in Berlin.
During Burnham's visit, the new Treaty on Friendship and Bilateral Cooperation between the UK and Germany — signed last year by previous Prime Minister Keir Starmer — officially comes into force.
Aslo known as the Kensington Treaty, the 27-page document lays out a 17-point action plan for closer cooperation in the post-Brexit era, with the UK no longer a part of the EU.
Merz called it a historic day and said the deal opened up new opportunities for bilateral cooperation, particularly for students and young people.
"That's what we're doing this for," Merz said. "So that the young generation also notices when it comes to bilateral relations between Germany as part of the EU and the UK, how well we Europeans work together and how much we belong together, too."
Burnham said that the Kensington Treaty would improve security in Europe, help both economies grow and improve people's living standards.
"In challenging times, and these are challenging times, we need the strongest possible cooperation with our closest partners and Germany really is one of our closest partners," the former mayor of Manchester said.
Burnham also said that he was open to Germany joining the GCAP program, a partnership between Britain, Italy and Japan to build a next-generation multirole combat aircraft.
"I've indicated to the chancellor ... our openness to Germany joining GCAP," he said at a press conference. "That is something that we seek to progress in the coming period, working with our other partners, Italy and Japan."
A rival Franco-German plan to build a next-generation military jet, FCAS, collapsed in June.
The GCAP project has been set up to allow for different levels of involvement. It expanded in July when Canada signed up as an observer, and Saudi Arabia had also been touted as a potential interested party.
Germany already works with the UK and Italy on the joint Eurofighter Typhoon project.
Italy and Japan would need to join Burnham in indicating a willingness for Germany participating in this project.
Left-leaning parties in Berlin to begin talks on forming new government
Germany's Left Party, Greens and Social Democrats (SPD) have agreed to begin exploratory talks on forming a coalition government in Berlin, two and a half weeks after the city's state election.
The breakthrough follows an agreement on combating antisemitism and organized crime, issues that had threatened to derail negotiations before they began.
The parties said they would protect Jewish life in Berlin and reaffirmed that Israel's right to exist was "non-negotiable."
They also agreed to strengthen the police and domestic intelligence services in their efforts to protect Jewish communities.
Party and parliamentary group members who violate the agreed principles could face expulsion, with the relevant parliamentary group responsible for deciding and publicly explaining any disciplinary measures.
The three parties also pledged to maintain a clear distance from individuals and groups associated with organized crime.
The Greens and SPD had made agreements on antisemitism, racism and organized crime conditions to open talks with the Left Party.
Those demands followed controversy over positions on Israel and the Palestinians held by some members of Berlin's Left Party.
Concerns intensified after an election-night gathering organized by the Left's Neukölln branch was attended by a figure associated with a partly criminal clan and a controversial pro-Palestinian activist.
The activist is alleged to have links to the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine, which the European Union designates as a terrorist organization.
The Left Party emerged as the strongest party in Berlin's September 20 election, winning 25.7% of the vote.
It hopes to form a coalition with the Greens and SPD, potentially making its parliamentary co-leader Elif Eralp Berlin's first mayor from the Left Party.
Waxwork döner kebab put on the menu at Berlin Madame Tussauds
The latest exhibit at Madame Tussauds in Berlin would surely taste just as dire as all the others, but the wax replica of a döner kebab is at least supposed to look appetizing.
The kebab — obviously stuffed "with everything" or "mit alles/mit allem," depending on your level of German grammatical exactitude — is complemented by a recreation of the popular snack stop Mustafa's Gemüse Kebap in Berlin's Kreuzberg district.
Tarik Kara, who owns the restaurant, was present in the flesh for Thursday's unveiling.
The Turkish specialty has long been a mainstay of the fast food culture in Berlin and beyond, given Germany's vast and long-established Turkish diaspora, estimated at around 3 million people.

Low-cost carrier Ryanair cuts flights in Germany, with Berlin hardest-hit
Irish airline Ryanair says it will be offering 700,000 fewer seats on flights in Germany this winter season, citing the "astronomical" cost of various charges, including for air traffic control and security.
This represents a reduction of 10%.
Ryanair said Berlin Brandenburg Airport, which it has dubbed "Europe's least successful airport," would be affected the most, losing around half of its current services from the airline.
Among the 12 routes to be axed in Berlin are those to Gran Canaria, Palermo, Marseille and Thessaloniki.
The Ryanair base at the airport is set to close on October 24. Seven aircraft and their crews are to be relocated to more competitive airports in other European countries, the company said.
Passengers in the German capital will now have much less choice and considerably higher fares, according to the airline's chief executive Eddie Wilson.
Hamburg will see a cut of 5%, but Memmingen and Cologne will have their capacity expanded.
Ryanair's winter schedule also adds regional airports in Saarbrücken and Friedrichshafen.
Sick leave for mental illnesses on the rise — health insurer
The number of days of sick leave in Germany on grounds of psychological problems has risen some 42% in the last 10 years, the AOK health insurance company says.
According to AOK, there were 284 days of sick leave per 100 members in 2015, compared with 403 per 100 members in 2025.
Although absences from work are much more frequently due to respiratory illnesses, those prompted by mental illness tend to be much longer, AOK said.
It said that on average, employees took 28.5 days off on grounds of psychological problems last year compared with 5.7 days because of respiratory illnesses.
However, the AOK said there had been a slight reduction in the average number of days of sick leave taken by employees, from 23.9 in 2023 and 2024 to 23.3 in 2025.
The highest level, 24.5 days, was reached in 2022 during the coronavirus pandemic.

My lifelong Pokemon collection is worth around €400,000, Christoph Kramer estimates
Retired midfielder and 2014 World Cup winner Christoph Kramer — now a TV presenter, podcaster and novelist — discusses another of his longstanding passions in an interview with the dpa news agency published on Thursday.
He may not have caught them all in more than a quarter of a century hunting Pokemon cards, but he's corralled a collection of creatures capable of dropping the jaw of a typical 10-year-old.

"I got myself an original iPhone in its original packaging and laminated. Objects like collectors' cards, rare vintage gear or retro jerseys are, for me, the real art of our era," Kramer said. "Of course it has a lot to do with nostalgia, because these are things from my childhood I simply love."
Spanish and Turkish make gains among school language learners
Although English remains by far the most-learned foreign language at German schools, Spanish and Turkish are becoming ever more popular, while French, Latin and Russian are losing ground, new figures show.
Turkish is being learned by almost three times as many pupils as 20 years ago, with 29,230 of altogether 8.9 million school students taking the language in 2025/2026 (0.31%).
That compares with some 13,000 pupils out of 9.5 million in 2005/2006 (0.13%), according to the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis).
There are also twice as many Spanish learners at German schools compared with two decades ago.
Some 549,000 of the current 8.9 million pupils took the language as a subject in 2025/2026 (6.1%), compared with 243,400 of the 9.5 million pupils back in 2005/2006 (2.56%), Destatis said.
Fewer pupils are learning French than 20 years ago, even if the language is second only to English in the statistics.
Some 14% of pupils learned French in the 2025/2026 school year, compared with 17% in 2005/2006.
Latin and Russian are also being learned by ever fewer pupils, with the former falling from 8.1% of schoolchildren to some 6% over the 20-year period, and the latter now learned by 0.746% compared with 1.25% in 2005/2006.
English remains far ahead at the top of the language-learning table, despite a small decline over the past two decades.
It was learned by 81% of pupils back in 2005/2006 compared with 78% in 2025/2026.

Professor who shared a call to stab ‘Zionists’ sues to overturn antisemitism law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
05:49:21 UTC
14:49:21 KST

A former University of Arkansas professor who praised Iran's late supreme leader Ali Khamenei, called for Israel to be dismantled and shared a social media post calling for violence against "Zionists" is now asking a federal court to strike down an Arkansas law designed to combat antisemitism, arguing that it was used to justify her dismissal.
Dr. Shirin Saeidi, an Iranian-born political science professor who previously directed the university's King Fahd Center for Middle East Studies, alleges in a lawsuit filed this week that the law was used to punish her for her views on Israel. She is seeking reinstatement and financial compensation.
In a post on X, Saeidi described Israel as "a terrorist and genocidal state that must be dismantled by international forces."
In another post, she praised Khamenei, who was killed in late February at the beginning of Operation Roaring Lion, describing him as the leader who "kept Iran intact during the Israeli attack." She added: "May God protect you and the Iranian people from the Israeli regime."
The dean of her college wrote to Saeidi that her personal social media posts undermined the credibility of the center she headed and its ability to serve Jewish and Israeli students.
The controversy was not limited to her comments about Israel. Saeidi had previously used official university letterhead in a submission to a Swedish court concerning Hamid Nouri, a former Iranian prison official sentenced to life imprisonment for his involvement in the mass executions of political prisoners in 1988.
According to the Swedish court's ruling, Nouri brought prisoners before a panel that sentenced them to death and escorted them to the execution site. The university reprimanded Saeidi for using its name without authorization.
Nouri was released in 2024 as part of a prisoner exchange in which Iran returned two detained Swedish citizens. Saeidi's academic work at the University of Cambridge, where she earned a doctorate in politics and international studies, is also facing renewed scrutiny.
Several former female political prisoners have alleged that their testimony was misrepresented in her research. One says she never met Saeidi, despite being identified as an interview subject. Saeidi rejects the allegations, maintaining that her research documents human rights abuses committed by the Iranian regime.
In December 2025, Saeidi shared a post urging someone to "thrust the dagger from Doha into the throats of the Zionists, so that all of them howl," accompanied by smiling emojis and the hashtag #FreePalestine. Saeidi maintained that she had not intended to encourage violence. She pointed to other statements in which she condemned attacks on Jews or Muslims because of the actions of their respective states.
The university rejected that explanation, arguing that Saeidi had not made clear in the repost itself that she opposed the call to attack "Zionists." The incident prompted proceedings to dismiss her from her tenured faculty position, in addition to her removal as director of the Middle East studies center.
The controversy also drew reactions beyond the campus. U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, a native of Arkansas, said at the time that although the decision to dismiss Saeidi belonged exclusively to the university, someone who praised Khamenei might be better suited for a "one-way ticket to Tehran."
Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders, the ambassador's daughter, signed the antisemitism law that Saeidi is now seeking to overturn.
One detail complicates the university's position: An internal faculty review concluded that Saeidi had not violated the institution's antisemitism policy. A faculty committee reviewing her dismissal unanimously recommended reinstatement, finding that even offensive statements do not necessarily justify firing a tenured professor. However, University of Arkansas System President Jay Silveria rejected the recommendation in March.
Silveria expressed concern that the institution could lose public funding if its response to antisemitism was considered inadequate. The university system's Board of Trustees subsequently upheld her dismissal in May.  Saeidi described the loss of her tenured position as an "academic death penalty."
The Arkansas law, enacted in 2025, requires educational institutions to adopt the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance's working definition of antisemitism, including examples addressing criticism of Israel, and to respond to complaints of discrimination and harassment. It also encourages state lawmakers to consider reducing funding to institutions that fail to address complaints adequately.
Saeidi argues that the definition is unconstitutionally vague and effectively makes opinions about Israel grounds for disciplinary action. The law, however, explicitly states that criticism of Israel comparable to criticism directed at any other country does not constitute antisemitism. It also specifies that constitutional free speech protections must not be infringed.
In her lawsuit, Saeidi alleges that her dismissal resulted from a coordinated campaign involving university officials, politicians, journalists, social media users and a group of Iranian exiles opposed to the regime in Tehran.
She previously described the campaign against her as having been taken from the "Zionist lobby playbook." The Iranian exile group is headed by Lawdan Bazargan, whose brother was murdered during the 1988 massacre of political prisoners in Iran.
Bazargan denies that there was any secret coordination to secure Saeidi's dismissal. She says members of her organization raised their concerns publicly and that university officials made their own decisions. Among the defendants named in the 88-page lawsuit are Republican Arkansas state Sen. Dan Sullivan and journalist Benjamin Weinthal, who published investigations into Saeidi. Weinthal said he stands by his reporting.

Taiwan population declines for 33rd consecutive month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
05:49:19 UTC
14:49:19 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s population fell for the 33rd consecutive month in September, as births declined 10.45% year on year and people aged 65 and older made up 20.7% of the population.
A total of 7,704 babies were born in September, down 899 from a year earlier but up 212, or 2.83%, from August, the interior ministry said Thursday. The annualized crude birth rate was 4.04 per 1,000 people.
Meanwhile, 16,712 people died, up 1,325, or 8.61%, from a year earlier and 242, or 1.47%, from August. The annualized crude death rate was 8.76 per 1,000 people.
Deaths exceeded births by 9,008, marking the 69th consecutive month in which deaths outnumbered births. Births also fell by more than 10% year on year in July and August, extending the streak to three consecutive months.
Migration figures produced a net decrease of 2,462 people in September, with 73,134 registered as moving out and 70,672 as moving in. The population fell by 11,470 during the month and was down 103,780 from a year earlier.
As of the end of September, Taiwan had 23,213,251 residents. People aged 65 and older numbered about 4.806 million, compared with 2.606 million children aged 14 and younger, while those aged 15 to 64 accounted for 68.07%, or 15.801 million.
The population aged 65 and older was 1.84 times the size of the child population. Taipei had the highest proportion of residents aged 65 and older at 24.86%, while Hsinchu County had the lowest at 15.52%.
Taiwan’s crude birth rate varied significantly by county and city, with Lienchiang County recording the highest rate at 6.24 births per 1,000 people, followed by Taitung County at 5.80 and Yunlin County at 5.44. Keelung had the lowest rate at 2.86, followed by Tainan at 2.99 and Yilan at 3.39.
Chiayi County had the highest crude death rate at 13.35 per 1,000 people, followed by Taitung at 13.19 and Pingtung at 13.11. Lienchiang had the lowest rate at 2.68, followed by Chiayi City at 5.93 and Hsinchu County at 6.49.
Hsinchu City had the highest proportion of children aged 14 and younger at 14.75%, while Kinmen County had the lowest at 7.50%. Despite the population decline, the number of households rose to 9,938,700, up 101,314 from a year earlier, while the average household size fell to 2.34 people.

Before the council’s vote, about a dozen public commenters, including Cornell students and Ithaca residents, expressed support for the moratorium. Many suggested it would push for changes at the university.
“I strongly urge the city of Ithaca pass this moratorium in the name of justice,” said Max Fan, a graduate student and steward for Cornell’s graduate workers union. “By doing so, you also empower the student voices of Cornell that are crying for help.”

Anwar is Bargaining Myanmar Lives For Political Gain – And He Will Lose
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
05:39:00 UTC
14:39:00 KST

This week, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim received Min Aung Hlaing, Myanmar’s junta chief, who led the 2017 genocide against the Rohingya, to arrange the transfer of 200,000 refugees, including Rohingya, back to Myanmar. The first deportations have already begun.
The plan is not just morally bankrupt. It makes no practical sense. It appears driven by months of coordinated online hate speech against Rohingya refugees in Malaysia and the targeting of community leaders by authorities, including the recent arrest of Zafar Ahmad Abdul Ghani.
In case anyone needs reminding, Min Aung Hlaing is the subject of an arrest warrant from the Argentine Federal Court for commissioning the atrocities against Rohingya as commander-in-chief. Prosecutors at the International Criminal Court have also requested an arrest warrant for him on similar grounds. He is yet to face justice, and the military remains as brutal as ever. He led the coup in 2021 and has razed half the country in the years since in his desperate bid for power. He still represents the Myanmar military, an institution whose sole purpose is to exploit the population through force, as it has for more than 50 years, and is the root cause of all Myanmar’s suffering.
Deporting refugees to Myanmar under an agreement with Min Aung Hlaing is a violation of international law and the fundamental principle of non-refoulement. And it will not ease the burden of the Myanmar crisis on Malaysia or the wider region; indeed, it will worsen it.
Time and time again, Min Aung Hlaing has proven that he can’t be trusted, not only by the people of Myanmar, but also by our neighbors. He has treated ASEAN with contempt since the coup, ignoring the basic requirements of the Five-Point Consensus, which called for an immediate cessation of violence, inclusive dialogue, and humanitarian access to the country. This is the precise reason why the refugee numbers continue to grow.
Min Aung Hlaing is also not the sole arbiter of power in Myanmar. He controls less than half of the country. He does not even control northern Rakhine State, the Rohingya homeland. That region, and most of Rakhine, is now largely held by the Arakan Army, which is committing its own grave abuses against Rohingya.
Just last week, the military bombed a market in Kyauktaw township in Rakhine State, killing nearly 50 civilians, including Rohingya. Where then will these refugees be returned to? To the killing field? Or will they be housed in internment camps outside Sittwe alongside 120,000 other Rohingya who have been confined there for 14 years? Or will they be left to face the exploitation of trafficking networks and armed groups, including the military, that will forcibly recruit them and send them to die on the front lines?
The plan will fail, while emboldening Min Aung Hlaing and fueling instability, making a lasting solution harder to reach.
Malaysia has offered safety to Myanmar refugees, and those refugees have in turn contributed to Malaysia’s economy. But this is not a permanent solution. Of course, Anwar has an obligation to address the issue, and he is right to pursue diplomatic efforts in that regard.
But if he genuinely wanted to improve the situation and resolve the crisis, rather than reacting to populist pressure, these are a number of diplomatic steps he would take. The first is to work through ASEAN and the U.N. to secure a nationwide ceasefire in Myanmar and uninhibited humanitarian access to all parts of the country, including by defining concrete benchmarks to measure Min Aung Hlaing’s implementation of the Five-Point Consensus.
Second, he should support efforts to hold Min Aung Hlaing and leaders of the military and other armed actors to account for the genocide and decades of grave violations against Rohingya and other civilians across Myanmar. The same principles that Anwar applies to Palestine apply in Myanmar: without an end to impunity, the devastating cycles of violence will not end.
Third, Anwar should develop a diplomatic strategy that responds to the reality of Myanmar’s multiple centers of authority, engages Myanmar’s legitimate authorities and stakeholders, and works toward inclusive dialogue for a genuine political solution.
Fourth, he should lead a coordinated international effort to dismantle the regional human trafficking networks that are flourishing in the conflict, exploiting the most vulnerable and fueling the refugee crisis.
Finally, he needs to consider how a mission of independent international monitors could be stationed in Rakhine State, with a mandate to monitor and report on the protection of civilians, as a means of building confidence towards the eventual sustainable, voluntary, and dignified return of Rohingya and other refugees from Myanmar.
Rohingya and other Myanmar refugees want nothing more than to return safely to our homes. We are not objecting to Anwar’s plans because we want to live the rest of our lives in insecurity and exile; we are objecting because we know it will only make things worse.
And deep down, I believe Anwar knows this too. These are not the actions of the wise and principled leader whose release many human rights activists and I supported. These actions are a dangerous betrayal that bargains away our lives, in the vain hope of short-term political gain.

Estonian Orthodox Church takes Moscow ties law to European rights court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
05:35:00 UTC
14:35:00 KST

Estonian Orthodox Church takes Moscow ties law to European rights court
The Estonian Christian Orthodox Church and Pühtitsa Convent in Kuremäe, Ida-Viru County, have filed complaints with the European Court of Human Rights over a law requiring them to sever ties with Moscow.
A law, upheld by the Supreme Court on June 8, requires the church to sever administrative links with Moscow and appoint a new metropolitan by December 28. If ties are not severed, the interior minister intends to seek their compulsory dissolution, their lawyer says.
"If ties with the church have not been severed by then, the interior minister intends to go to court to seek their compulsory dissolution. The law refers to statutes and affiliations. However, what the Interior Ministry actually wants is for local Orthodox believers to renounce their religious ties with a church that has existed for more than a thousand years," said Artur Knjazev, sworn attorney representing the church and monastery.
"The church and convent are not simply being asked to amend a document," Knjazev said. "In Orthodox Christianity, you cannot rewrite the rules of the church yourself and remain Orthodox. Anyone who does so has renounced the faith they have chosen and have considered true until now. The Interior Ministry is offering a choice between two impossible options – choose another church or we will put an end to your current activities."
"The European Convention on Human Rights regards the aspect of religious freedom concerning a person's beliefs as an absolute right. The state may regulate how religion is practiced publicly. It may not force a person to change their faith. That is exactly what is happening now," Knjazev added.
On June 8, the Supreme Court sitting en banc upheld the law by interpreting it as prohibiting administrative ties rather than religious ties. However, six of the 17 judges, including the chief justice, dissented, finding that the law failed to meet the requirement of legal certainty.
"The concept under which this law was rescued does not appear anywhere in the law itself," noted sworn attorney Steven-Hristo Evestus, also acting for the church.
"Throughout this process, the Interior Ministry has maintained that both administrative and religious ties must be severed. The court's interpretation is one thing, but the ministry's actual demand is another. According to the ministry's own position, the church and monastery fall under the prohibition established by the law, and this is precisely the basis on which pressure is being exerted. Such pressure must not be applied," Evestus added.
"No Estonian authority has established that the church or convent has done anything unlawful," Evestus noted. "There has been no court ruling, no charge, no proceedings. There is a punishment, but no offense. Our church and convent have not endangered anyone, cannot endanger anyone and have no desire to do so. Yet their religious identity is being interfered with."
"The monastery is home to around 90 nuns whose average age is over 60. Nuns have been praying there for more than 135 years. They always pray for our country, Estonia, too. If the prayers of 90 elderly women can undermine national security, then the problem is not with the nuns. The problem lies somewhere else," Knjazev continued.
According to Knjazev, the church will continue its dialogue with the Interior Ministry. The ministry has not invited the monastery to a separate meeting.
The amendments to the Churches and Congregations Act entered into force on June 27, 2026, giving religious associations six months to comply.
The Estonian Christian Orthodox Church, formerly the MPEÕK, dropped "Moscow Patriarchate" from its name in March 2025 to become the Estonian Christian Orthodox Church (EKÕK). The Interior Ministry nonetheless judged this break symbolic but insufficient, as the church's statutes still required Patriarch Kirill of Moscow's signature on major decisions.
There are two major Orthodox churches in Estonia — the EKÕK, and the Estonian Apostolic Orthodox Church (EAÕK), historically tied to Constantinople and not Moscow.
Interior Ministry: Law must be implemented
Ringo Ringvee, adviser at the Interior Ministry's religious affairs and civil society department, commented later on Thursday that Estonia is a state governed by the rule of law, where the supremacy of law applies.
"Freedom of religion is guaranteed in Estonia and will remain so. The state does not interfere in how anyone practices their faith. The Interior Ministry proceeds from the amendments to the Churches and Congregations Act that entered into force in the summer, which prohibit an Estonian religious association from having ties with a religious organization or spiritual leader based in a foreign country whose activities endanger the Estonian state," Ringvee said.
Ringvee added that the ministry has begun advising those religious associations, including the EKÕK, who feel affected by the legislative changes.
"Last week we met with the EKÕK and agreed to begin reviewing statutory ties. It is therefore surprising that the press release from the EKÕK and Pühtitsa Convent lawyers states that the interior minister has a firm intention to go to court to forcibly dissolve entities linked to the Moscow Patriarchate. We take the position that we are currently in a phase of dialogue. At the same time, the law must be implemented," Ringvee said.
Ringvee noted that everyone in Estonia also enjoys the right to take things to court.
"Nearly 600 religious associations operate in Estonia, and only the EKÕK, which is administratively linked to the Moscow Patriarchate, has challenged a law which the Supreme Court has recognized as constitutional," Ringvee said.
Ringvee added that the Interior Ministry cannot assess the arguments presented in the media, as the ministry has not seen the text of the complaint. "Based on the lawyers' press release, we cannot make a judgment on the text of the complaint. Nor has the Interior Ministry been involved in the proceedings by any court in connection with this complaint, so no steps are planned either," Ringvee added.
Editor's note: This piece was updated to include comment from Ringo Ringvee.

Why single Ebola death in Kenya has prompted fears of wider African spread
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
05:34:34 UTC
14:34:34 KST

Why single Ebola death in Kenya has prompted fears of wider African spread
According to the WHO, the Kenyan patient first got sick in the DRC, where they had been living, and was treated there.
Kenya reported its first death from a deadly strain of Ebola virus which had spread widely, starting in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) earlier this year.
The Bundibugyo (BDBV) strain of Ebola was first detected in Uganda in 2007, according to the WHO. The ongoing outbreak in the DRC has killed at least 4,148 people out of 8,300 reported cases. It also spread across the border to Uganda, which had about 20 cases before being declared Ebola-free in July.
However, the person who died in Kenya from the disease had travelled from the DRC to Uganda over land before taking a flight to Nairobi, raising questions about Uganda’s status as “Ebola-free”, concerns about the rigidity of Kenya’s screening processes for people coming into the country and fears that Ebola may have spread further than previously thought.
On Tuesday, the World Health Organization said the Kenyan government is now enhancing its disease surveillance with more targeted screening at high-risk points of entry.
But Wolfgang Preiser, a professor and head of medical virology at Stellenbosch University in South Africa, explained that while efforts are being made to bring the outbreak under control, it has grown so much that “sheer numbers and the speed of spread are overwhelming for many systems.
“I am not surprised that cases have reached other provinces in DRC and neighbouring countries. I expect that this will continue to happen until such time that the trajectory has been reversed and case numbers are in decline,” he told Al Jazeera.
Here’s what we know:
What is Ebola?
It is a serious, potentially deadly viral infection which can be caught when a person comes into contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person or wild animal, including fluid lingering on surfaces. People have also been known to contract the disease through eating contaminated meat.
There have been many outbreaks in Central, West and East Africa.
A West African outbreak from 2014 to 2016 killed at least 11,300 people of a reported 28,600 cases and accelerated the push to develop a vaccine. That was a different strain of the Ebola virus, known as Zaire, for which there is now a vaccine.
The strain behind the latest outbreak is Bundibugyo virus (BDBV), which is believed to have been caused by a new transmission from animals to humans, before then spreading between humans, rather than by variants linked to earlier outbreaks. There is no vaccine for Bundibugyo.
Symptoms can appear between two and 21 days after infection and can start suddenly with flu-like symptoms, including a high temperature, fatigue, and a headache. It can lead to internal and external bleeding, impaired liver and kidney function and organ failure.
How did this case of Ebola reach Kenya?
Kenyan Health Minister Aden Duale told reporters that the Kenyan patient, who has not been named, first became sick one month ago in the DRC, where they had been living for several years, and was treated there.
On October 2, the patient travelled by road to the Ugandan capital, Kampala, via Beni, then flew to Nairobi, arriving the next day.
After he arrived at the airport in Kenya, a relative and a friend took him to a hospital, where he was quickly isolated, and tests showed he had the virus, Duale said. Despite receiving care, the patient died from the virus on Monday and was buried on Tuesday in line with the country’s Ebola protocol.
So far, health authorities in Kenya have identified 28 potential contacts, including family members and health workers who cared for the infected patient. Authorities are also separately tracking 23 passengers and four crew members from his flight, “with arrangements under way for appropriate follow-up and quarantine of people assessed to be at risk”, the WHO reported.
Jean Bisimwa Nachega, a professor in infectious diseases at Stellenbosch University, emphasised that the virus does not “respect national borders”.
“Population mobility, displacement, cross-border trade, and fragile healthcare systems make containment particularly challenging. In eastern DRC, ongoing insecurity further complicates surveillance, contact tracing, and access to affected communities,” he told Al Jazeera.
“Regional cooperation is therefore essential.”
How did a sick patient get past screening in Uganda and Kenya?
Passengers travelling to, from or through Uganda and Kenya must pass multiple airport temperature checks and complete at least two digital forms intended to flag any potential exposure to the virus in the DRC. Somehow, the infected person in this case was missed by these checks.
Ugandan government spokesperson Alan Kasujja said Kampala was not to blame for the Kenyan man catching the virus and wrote on X, “Leave Uganda out of this conversation. We don’t have Ebola here.”
In a statement issued Tuesday, the Ugandan Ministry of Health said the man had a “normal temperature” when he was screened at Entebbe airport before his departure.
Kenyan authorities say he may have taken medication to mask his symptoms when he was later screened at Nairobi airport. Investigations are continuing, however.
“We are trying to retrieve the digital form he would have filled out at Entebbe airport when he went through the thermal scanning process to see what he declared in that form. The form includes questions about recent health problems but also whether a traveller was recently in DRC,” Richard Mugahi, a senior Ugandan health official, told the Reuters news agency.
“We are also going through airport security camera footage to see if we can identify the driver who dropped him at the airport so we can trace any contacts here.”
Preiser, the medical virology professor, also said the tracking system “seems to work as it did in Uganda”, with a diagnosis made rapidly as soon as the patient sought care in Kenya.
“It will be instructive to try and trace back what happened at the various stops during his travels, and lessons should be heeded by all countries,” he said.
He cited an example from a previous Ebola outbreak in West Africa, when a “British nurse fell sick during her return trip to the UK and reported to the medical check in Heathrow, only to be sent onwards to her destination where she was diagnosed with Ebola”.
The lesson, he said, was that “even cooperative travellers and good systems may fall through the net.”
Where else has Ebola spread?
Since it began in the DRC’s northeastern Ituri province, the latest outbreak has spread this year to seven provinces in the country’s north and east. It was officially declared an outbreak in the DRC in May.
Weak infrastructure, the remoteness of the region in eastern DRC, and ongoing conflict with armed groups near the borders with South Sudan, Uganda, and Rwanda have hindered efforts to respond to cases quickly and effectively.
Several factors have further complicated the response to the outbreak, including strikes by unpaid health workers, misinformation and cultural traditions. These have included open-coffin family burials of several of those killed by the virus earlier during the outbreak, potentially increasing the risk of further transmission.
The United Nations reported on October 2 that an Ebola-hit camp housing a transit centre for infected patients was burned by soldiers earlier this week when they were looking for weapons on the outskirts of Bunia, the capital city of Ituri province, which is at the epicentre of the outbreak.
The incident forced 19,000 people to flee the camp.
The disease also spread to Uganda, where 20 people who had travelled from the DRC were treated before the country declared it was free of Ebola in July.
Recently, it has become increasingly hard to contain within the DRC.
On Monday, Doctors Without Borders, known by its French initials MSF, warned that there had been an “alarming surge” of cases in eastern North Kivu province, which borders Uganda, and where 40 percent of new cases are currently being recorded.
“It is like fighting a megafire,” Stephanie Hoffmann, coordinator at MSF’s Ebola treatment centre in the city of Butembo, said. “Multiple outbreaks are developing at the same time, with varying intensity and in different locations.”
Some two million people live in North Kivu’s city of Butembo and surrounding areas, but it has only four Ebola treatment centres, two of which opened recently, MSF told the media. Patients often have to be transferred elsewhere, increasing the risk of infection to others, Hoffmann said.
What happens now?
The WHO is working with Kenyan authorities to trace contacts and strengthen checks for travellers coming into the country.
Mohamed Janabi, WHO regional director for Africa, said on Tuesday that “health emergency preparedness gives us a head start.
“Kenya has put important outbreak control measures in place. The priority now is to move swiftly to detect any further cases before the virus has an opportunity to spread. We’re supporting the ongoing efforts to strengthen the response, and with rapid and coordinated action, we can prevent the virus from gaining a foothold and stop a potential larger outbreak,” Janabi said.
The agency also said it has delivered about 1,000 Ebola tests and “1,000 personal protective equipment kits to high-risk counties in Kenya”.
In June, the Kenyan government granted the United States permission to set up an Ebola quarantine facility at the Laikipia airbase, 193km (120 miles) from the capital, Nairobi, to treat infected Americans travelling from African nations before they arrived in the US. The scheme generated uproar from locals who feared transmission of the disease, and Kenyan courts halted the plan.
Overall, Nachega said strengthening border screening wasn’t enough. It was also important to “reinforce the entire public health response”.
“This means training front-line healthcare workers, ensuring rapid laboratory diagnosis, promptly isolating suspected cases, and tracing and monitoring contacts. Kenya’s ability to identify this case provides an important opportunity to strengthen preparedness,” he added.

America shut out Chinese EVs. Britain welcomed them — and now faces a difficult choice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
05:30:49 UTC
14:30:49 KST

The U.K. broke with the U.S. by opening its doors to China's electric vehicle juggernaut.
Chinese EVs face only a 10% standard import duty in Britain, one of the largest major overseas markets without additional China-specific tariffs. Japan and Norway also lack them.
It's in contrast to the U.S., where a 100% tariff effectively shut Chinese EVs out. The European Union, the U.K.'s biggest trading partner, has manufacturer-specific duties on Chinese EVs of up to 35.3%, in addition to a standard 10% import duty on all foreign cars.
Now, the U.K. faces a difficult choice, as EU proposals may force it to impose tariffs to match the bloc's.
At the weekend, The Sunday Times reported that U.K. Business Minister Jonathan Reynolds is considering matching the EU's levy on Chinese EVs to avoid the pain of so-called Made in Europe proposals, which could hurt domestic companies selling into the EU.
A U.K. government spokesperson reiterated to CNBC that it had not imposed tariffs on Chinese EVs but added, "We continue to engage closely with industry so that our approach reflects the sector's and UK's national interests."
The Made in Europe legislation, part of the EU's Industrial Accelerator Act, is designed to protect the bloc's industries from unfair international competition by prioritizing European-made goods.
Read more
An EU official told the Financial Times in September that London would need to raise tariffs on Chinese EVs and align more closely with EU trade policy to avoid "Made in Europe" barriers.
The decision is finely balanced, given Prime Minister Andy Burnham's desire to reset relations with the EU, which the U.K. formally left in 2020, and the likelihood of China responding with retaliatory measures.
A spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in London said it had expressed "serious concern" to Britain about the reports about potential tariffs.
"China is firmly opposed to any discriminatory practice involving tariff hikes or restrictive measures on Chinese products," a spokesperson said Tuesday. "We will continue to follow developments and respond accordingly," they said.
Chinese automakers rapidly made inroads in the U.K.
Chinese car brands have swiftly captured market share in the U.K.
Analysis by Jato Dynamics found that registrations of Chinese automakers, or original equipment manufacturers, across both battery-electric and hybrid powertrains, rose to 519,424 between the start of January and the end of August, lifting their total market share to 28.1%. That's up sharply from 12.9% in the same period in 2025.
Hybrids accounted for the larger increase, adding 62,655 registrations versus 32,565 for battery-electric vehicles.
"That matters for policy," Paul Hilton, head of retail at Jato Dynamics, told CNBC by email.
"Tariffs aimed only at Chinese-built battery EVs could slow one part of the expansion, but would not address hybrid growth, vehicles made outside China or the underlying advantages in cost, product cadence and supply chains," Hilton said.
"A durable UK response should pair any evidence-based trade remedy with incentives for local production, competitive energy and battery costs, charging infrastructure, skills and alignment with European market-access rules."
'Temu Range Rover' takeover
The bestselling car in the U.K. last month was not a Tesla or a Ford — but the Jaecoo 7 from China.
The mid-size SUV, nicknamed the “Temu Range Rover,” starts at about £29,000 ($38,350) in the U.K., compared with roughly £45,500 for a Land Rover Discovery Sport.
The Jaecoo 7's nationwide sales climbed to 10,814 in September, according to the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders, outpacing the Tesla Model 3, Ford Puma and Kia Sportage.
Rico Luman, senior sector economist for transport and logistics at ING, said the growing policy gap between Britain and the EU is leaving the U.K. with limited options, besides tariffs, if it wants to maintain a level playing field with the bloc.
Speaking to CNBC by email, Luman said exclusion from the Made in Europe initiative could have “significant consequences” for existing businesses, making closer alignment with EU trade policy increasingly difficult to avoid.
"It's generally quite remarkable that batteries from China are exempted from EU tariffs," Luman said.
"At the same time this is logical as production in Europe isn't up to speed and Europe lacks the rare earth minerals and refinery capacity behind it," he added.

Finland has rejected six applications involving buyers from outside the EU and European Economic Area seeking to acquire properties in four municipalities, with one transaction blocked over concerns about national security and security of supply.
Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen issued the decisions on Wednesday, covering properties in Kotka, Viitasaari, Miehikkälä and Imatra.
The applicants seeking properties in Kotka, Viitasaari and Miehikkälä included citizens of Russia, Montenegro and Israel, according to the Ministry of Defence.
An application concerning property in Imatra came from a company registered in Italy whose owners are from outside the EU and EEA.
The proposed uses included rental and recreational purposes.
The ministry rejected the application concerning the property in Kotka after assessing that the transaction posed a potential threat to Finland’s national security and security of supply. The decision was made under the Act on Permit Requirements for Certain Real Estate Acquisitions.
The ministry did not disclose details about the property or the security considerations linked to its location.
The other five applications involving properties in Viitasaari, Miehikkälä and Imatra were rejected because the applicants failed to provide information and statements requested by the ministry despite receiving reminders.
The ministry based those decisions on the law governing permits for certain property acquisitions and the Administrative Procedure Act.
“A rigorous control of real estate transactions reduces security threats against Finland,” Häkkänen said.
“In one of the cases, we prevented a transaction that could have had implications for Finland’s security because of the location of the real estate.”
Häkkänen said applicants cannot avoid the permit process by failing to submit information required for a security assessment.
The six decisions are not yet legally final.
Finland requires buyers from outside the EU and EEA to obtain permission from the Defence Ministry for property purchases under legislation that took effect in 2020. Authorities have the power to prevent transactions when they identify risks involving national security, defence or security of supply.
Earlier this year in June, Häkkänen blocked 14 property purchases involving non-EU and non-EEA buyers in Asikkala, Hyrynsalmi, Imatra, Laukaa, Pöytyä, Rautjärvi and Rovaniemi.
Those applications involved citizens of China, Ukraine, Turkey and India as well as companies owned by citizens of those countries.

Powell said that smaller-scale investors in the housing market could be forced to sell properties if they cannot raise rents further to offset holding costs. ■

====================================================================================================

High Court's coalmine emissions ruling says 'the quiet part out loud'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
05:26:30 UTC
14:26:30 KST

Why activists, politicians and the resources sector are fired up about a High Court ruling
Resources company MACH Energy probably never expected its High Court appeal over the future of a Hunter Valley coal mine to trigger a legal precedent that has been celebrated by climate activists.
The court's decision has the resources sector nervous, the federal government downplaying the ruling's wider significance, and the opposition apoplectic about its potential to cripple the Australian fossil fuel industry.
Whether the ruling is a narrow interpretation of a planning statute or spells doom for the fossil fuel industry depends on who you talk to.
So, let's step through it all carefully.
What was the case about?
MACH Energy operates the Mount Pleasant open-cut mine near Muswellbrook.
It wants to double the amount of coal it exports from the mine and keep it open until 2048.
NSW's Independent Planning Commission (IPC) approved that expansion in 2022. But the plan came to a dramatic halt when a residents' group convinced the state's Court of Appeal the IPC got it wrong.
The Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group (DAMSHEG), led by two retired schoolteachers, said the planning panel failed to properly consider that climate change caused by the exported coal's "downstream" or scope 3 emissions would cause harm to the Hunter.
What are scope 3 emissions?
Under climate regulations, Scope 1 emissions are those that come from the source, such as methane leaks from a coalmine.
Scope 2 emissions are caused by electricity that has been generated using fossil fuels.
Scope 3 emissions are indirect emissions, and in this case describe the "downstream" or "chain emissions" that occur when a product is sold on and used — in this case, when the exported coal is burned overseas.
Globally, they account for the vast majority of emissions from coalmines and other fossil fuel production.
In July 2025, the NSW Court of Appeal agreed with DAMSHEG's argument, finding that none of the IPC's conditions expressly addressed scope 3 emissions, despite it being a legal requirement to "ensure greenhouse gas emissions are minimised to the greatest extent possible".
The court sent the case to be reviewed again, this time by the Land and Environment Court.
Frustrated with the delays, and in an effort to get some clear guidance on a path forward, the coal company took its case to the High Court, which agreed to review the planning process.
University of Melbourne environmental and climate change law expert Jacqueline Peel said it was a "very unusual case" for the High Court to take up, given the case was "largely an issue of statutory interpretation, what the words of the statute meant".
"On one take it's just a narrow decision interpreting a specific provision or provisions of New South Wales planning law," she said.
What did the High Court find?
In its original approval, the IPC accepted that 860 million tonnes of emissions would be generated overseas from the project, and that this would contribute to climate change.
But the planning panel said that "would be accounted for" by the countries that imported the coal, "through broader national policies and international agreements (such as the Paris Agreement)".
MACH Energy's appeal to the High Court argued the same: that the Paris Agreement was enough, and that essentially once the coal left Australia, it was not the company's problem.
But the High Court dismissed that argument in a majority 3 to 2 ruling.
The court found NSW law required the IPC to "consider imposing conditions to minimise to the greatest extent practicable all greenhouse gas emissions, including Scope 3 emissions".
What does it mean for fossil fuel projects?
Professor Peel said at its most narrow reading, the High Court ruling essentially enforced NSW planning law that already existed.
But she said the potential big change was that the High Court was now "saying the quiet part out loud", which "means taking account or having accountability for those emissions, which is something we really haven't seen in Australia to date".
"If you start requiring mines to actually deal with and be accountable for their scope 3 emissions and have to do something to minimise those, then it makes the coal mine a much different economic prospect than it would be if you can just deal with scope 3 emissions as someone else's problem," she said.
The Australian Conservation Foundation's Adam Bandt said the outcome was something governments and corporations had long been fighting against.
"There came a time when we understood that asbestos was a product that when you used it as intended would cause harm," Mr Bandt said.
"That's now the same with coal and gas. We don't mine and export asbestos anymore."
The Minerals Council's Tanya Constable said she was "very concerned about the decision".
"This will send shudders down everybody's spine," she said.
It is the requirement to consider emissions overseas, not just those happening in Australia, that has the industry and conservative politicians so worked up.
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said it was "absurd" to ask local planning authorities to consider climate impacts in other countries before approving a mine in New South Wales.
"Under the international rules … emissions are counted where coal is used, not where it is mined," he said.
But those rules appear to be changing.
In July 2025, the International Court of Justice issued an advisory opinion putting accountability for climate-related harm onto coal and other fossil fuel producers at the point of extraction.
The UK Supreme Court also ruled that the future impact of fossil fuel projects must be assessed by planning bodies when deciding whether to approve projects.
High Court Judge Gordon appeared to accept this argument in her own findings from the MACH Energy case.
"The impact of greenhouse gas emissions is the same, regardless of how they are categorised," Judge Gordon found.
The fact that scope 3 emissions were accounted for by other countries through the Paris Agreement did "not address the Commission's obligation … which relates to all greenhouse gas emissions (including Scope 3 emissions), and which requires it to consider imposing conditions to minimise to the greatest extent practicable those emissions".
What's next?
Both the NSW and federal governments have downplayed the broader significance of the ruling.
NSW Premier Chris Minns warned climate activists not to "get overexcited" and said the mine's operators were still "looking to continue an application through the IPC" to expand the mine.
Federal Industry Minister Tim Ayres said the High Court decision was "not a big deal" and "confined to the provisions of the NSW Act and the way that the NSW planning authority did their work".
But Professor Peel said that was a "narrow" interpretation of the ruling.
"It's entirely understandable that the minister at the federal level would be trying to say: 'No, this is just a NSW problem,'" she said.
"But I just don't think we've had that argument in the court yet."
She said she expected new litigation to result from the decision.
"Groups will now want to explore what that added set of arguments from the High Court decision might offer in terms of challenging approvals for fossil fuel projects," she said.

El Nino will intensify, then peak in December: UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
05:23:52 UTC
14:23:52 KST

A farmer drinks water during a break while cutting a corn crop ruined by the lack of rainfall in Tecoluca, San Vicente department, El Salvador, on August 26, 2026. (AFP File Photo)
El Nino will intensify even more before peaking in December, the United Nations said on Oct. 8, warning it could be among the strongest witnessed since at least 1950.
The naturally occurring weather phenomenon is set to bring higher temperatures to much of the planet, the U.N.’s weather and climate agency said, with its impact compounding the effects of man-made climate change.
“El Nino will continue to intensify ahead of its forecast peak in December,” the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) said in its monthly Global Seasonal Climate Update.
“It is likely to bring above-average temperatures to much of the globe and shift rainfall patterns, increasing the risk of drought and floods in different regions.”
El Nino warms surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, bringing worldwide changes in winds, pressure and rainfall patterns.
It typically takes place every two to seven years and lasts around nine to 12 months.
Conditions oscillate between El Nino and its opposite La Nina, with neutral conditions in between.
“Sea-surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific are forecast to increase to record levels during October-November-December 2026, reflecting the strengthening of the El Nino event which will drive weather patterns and impact economies, ecosystems and communities across the globe,” the WMO said.
The forecast is based on consensus across 13 leading national and international meteorological centers.
“El Nino is firmly established and strengthening rapidly,” said WMO chief Celeste Saulo.
“WMO forecasts indicate a near-100 percent likelihood that it will persist through February 2027, potentially being one of the strongest since at least 1950.”

Political ad ban on social media sends Estonian politicians writing their own posts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
05:22:00 UTC
14:22:00 KST

Political ad ban on social media sends Estonian politicians writing their own posts
As restrictions on purchasing political advertising on social media will be in place for this year's Riigikogu elections, political parties are putting more effort than before into creating their own posts.
Political advertising has been banned on Meta and Google's social media platforms since last fall.
Isamaa betting on organic spread
Isamaa Secretary General Andres Metsoja said political content itself has not been banned on social media, only its promotion through paid advertising. "This means that content needs to be engaging and resonate with people and then it will spread on its own," Metsoja said.
He noted that outdoor advertising is certain to reach everyone in Estonia.
Metsoja added that organic reach is always better than paid advertising when it comes to how social media works. "Ahead of elections, paid advertising becomes 'wallpaper' because all parties would be using it extensively. In other words, if the content doesn't have a 'hook' that makes readers or viewers stop scrolling, its impact won't be particularly significant anyway," Metsoja said.
"Isamaa has people who are very good at capturing viewers' attention on social media. Sandra Laur and Jüri Ratas are certainly the best-known examples, but Aivar Kokk's gardening and cooking videos are also very popular. As a party, we will certainly invest in producing quality content over the coming months to ensure it spreads and that the positions we are campaigning on reach as many people as possible," he added.
Metsoja said that, according to publicly available data, Isamaa and its affiliated candidates spent a total of €35,000 on paid advertising on Meta platforms during the final month before the 2023 Riigikogu elections. This was €20,000 less than both the Reform Party and the Social Democrats spent and €40,000 less than EKRE.
"The cost of living in Estonia has risen significantly over the past four years, including a substantial increase in value-added tax. This means the overall cost of campaigning ahead of the elections will rise by a much greater amount than the so-called 'extra money' freed up by the ban on social media advertising," Metsoja said.
Metsoja said an election campaign should be viewed as a whole, with everything starting from the party platform. Advertising, whether on the streets, on television, on the radio or on online news portals, serves to reinforce the messages of that platform.
SDE's hopes on active posting
Social Democratic Party Secretary General Piret Hartman acknowledged that the inability to advertise on Facebook and Instagram will certainly affect the party's ability to reach voters. "That's why we're putting even more effort into actively posting content ourselves and sharing and amplifying each other's posts. We've also started producing more video content," Hartman said.
"We also need to make our activities more appealing and find ways to improve the organic reach of our posts. We're also trying to increase the number of party members who actively use social media. To support our members, we're organizing training sessions for this purpose," she added.
"We're also trying to have more direct contact with our voters, both on the streets and at various events. We've also launched a poster campaign in different counties to increase our visibility," Hartman said.
According to Hartman, the loss of social media advertising will not have a major impact on the party's campaign budget, as it did not account for a particularly large share of spending in the previous elections. "We'll redirect those resources toward advertising in other channels," she said.
Eesti 200 prioritizing constant visibility
Eesti 200 Executive Director Anneli Kannus said restrictions on political advertising on social media took effect just before last year's local elections, meaning parties have already had to rethink their campaign strategies.
"Parties also generally know the profiles of their potential voters and the ways they are likely to reach them with their messages. We're also running our campaign a little differently this time than in previous elections. The fact that social media is no longer flooded with different parties' colors and slogans immediately before elections is probably a positive development for most people," Kannus said.
She pointed out that Eesti 200 and its members maintain a constant presence on social media. "For politicians, communicating with people or explaining their plans and decisions isn't something that should be limited to the campaign period. Political activity needs to be approached more comprehensively and deliberately because without an established reputation and a track record, no poster or banner will bring in enough votes at election time," Kannus said.
According to Kannus, it would be an oversimplification to suggest that young voters can only be reached through social media. "People who are interested in politics and social issues get the information they need to make their voting decisions from a variety of sources throughout the year, not just from social media ads during election campaigns. We believe younger voters are well-informed and can find information both on party websites and through party members' social media accounts. It would be truly sad if elections were won through paid advertising," Kannus said.
Center sees no great tragedy in the political ads ban
Center Party Secretary General Anneli Ott also said the ban had been known about in advance and that Center Party members are active on social media.
"The Center Party has invested heavily in social media in recent years and because our posts also spread organically, the advertising ban doesn't affect us very much," Ott said.
According to Ott, the ban poses a problem for parties and politicians who only become active immediately before elections and have so far relied on expensive outdoor advertising to gain support.
Ott said the Center Party's strengths have been its campaign tents and direct communication with people. "We do this year-round, although naturally more intensively during election campaigns," Ott said.
"The last local elections showed that people dislike enormous election posters and parties that spent more than €1 million on their campaigns ended up shooting themselves in the foot. The Center Party, which took a more frugal approach, emerged as the most popular party. People appreciate clear solutions to pressing problems and in Tallinn, we've already delivered on several of our promises," Ott said.
"As for younger people, whose voter turnout has been lower, all parties need to take a hard look at themselves and ask whether they've paid enough attention to young people's proposals and tried to address their concerns. The Center Party's election platform will certainly include measures concerning quality, accessible education and homeownership," Ott added.
Reform Party channeling ad money into direct contact and content creation
Reform Party Secretary General Kristo Enn Vaga said what matters most in elections is the future that parties offer Estonia, not how much they spend on advertising on Facebook or Instagram.
"Direct contact with voters remains the most effective campaign method and that's what we'll focus on in these elections as well. This will be supported by outdoor advertising, radio, print media and television. Good content can reach people on social media even without paid advertising. Young people are no exception. Content matters," Vaga said.
"We'll redirect the money previously spent on Meta platforms toward meetings with voters, content creation and increasing our visibility in public spaces, on radio and on television. It's also still possible to post political content and videos on social media," he noted.
According to Vaga, the party plans to focus on more modern and engaging content on the Reform Party's social media channels to increase its organic reach.
"The Reform Party's strength has always been its substantive platform and strong team. The central question in the upcoming parliamentary elections is how to keep Estonia secure and its economy growing. Electoral success will depend largely on how specifically and credibly parties can answer that question," he added.
EKRE refuses to divulge campaign details
Aarne Mäe, an adviser to EKRE's Riigikogu parliamentary group, said the party does not disclose details of its campaign in this way.

Ukraine Opens Gas Exports for Private Producers for First Time Since 2022
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
05:21:22 UTC
14:21:22 KST

Ukraine’s government on Oct. 7 approved the partial opening of natural gas exports, lifting a ban that had been in force since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022, according to ExPro, citing its own sources.
Private producers will be allowed to sell up to 15% of the gas they extracted in the previous month to foreign buyers. The mechanism excludes the state-controlled majors.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Discussions on whether to open exports intensified in the summer, and the government returned to the issue in September after initially postponing it until spring 2027, ExPro reported. Market participants tied the need to restart exports to a gas surplus in the commercial segment, a wide gap between Ukrainian and European prices, and producers’ need for funds to restore and protect their facilities.
A plan of priority actions for 2026, adopted by Cabinet order No. 999-r on Sept. 30 and published on the government portal, instructs the Ministry of Energy to create the legal and organizational conditions for a controlled export mechanism covering 15% of domestically produced gas.
The plan argues this would help the gas production sector by drawing in investment, and it set September 2026 as the target for opening exports. The order replaces an earlier version of the plan, adopted on March 30 under order No. 306.
Why government is relaunching gas export for the first time since 2022
Gas consumption by industrial users fell by almost half after the full-scale war in Ukraine began, ExPro reported, while output by private companies, the main gas suppliers to industry, has held relatively steady despite Russian attacks. According to ExPro, private companies produced more than 370 million cubic meters of natural gas in August 2026.
New €1.2 Billion EU Defense Package Arrives as Ukraine Faces Funding Uncertainty
European prices jumped after the war in the Middle East began, while Ukrainian prices remained stable. By mid-September, gas in Ukraine was 2.5 times cheaper than in Europe.
Ukraine’s underground storage facilities have been holding more than 15.8 billion cubic meters of gas, according to ExPro’s calculations based on data from Gas Infrastructure Europe (GIE). That is 1.2 billion cubic meters more than the government’s plan required by Nov. 1.
How the gas export policy will work
The resolution takes effect on the day of its publication, and the mechanism will apply each year from March 1 to Nov. 30.
It does not cover gas produced under production sharing agreements, which are governed by separate legislation. It also does not apply to market participants with special obligations under Cabinet Resolution No. 222: Ukrgasvydobuvannia, Ukrnafta and Chornomornaftogaz.
The Ministry of Energy will approve a list of eligible companies and the volume each may sell by the 12th day of every month, based on data from the Gas Transmission System Operator of Ukraine (GTSOU) on actual gas supplied to the system the previous month.
Gas will be sold at specialized sessions of a commodity exchange, likely the Ukrainian Energy Exchange, according to ExPro. Only companies on the ministry’s list can sell, and only non-resident companies can buy. The highest bidder wins. Sellers must state the volume, a starting price in euros per megawatt-hour and a delivery point, defined as an exit point on Ukraine’s border with EU countries or Moldova.
A producer’s unused monthly limit will not carry over. Gas already sold on the exchange can be exported in the month of the auction or during the following two months. GTSOU will report each seller’s actual export volumes to the ministry by the 15th of every month.
Gas exports will have their safeguards
In a crisis, exports can be suspended temporarily by a decision of the Crisis Committee under the Ministry of Energy, taken on the ministry’s initiative or at the request of Naftogaz or GTSOU. The ministry must then approve the decision.
Unless it says otherwise, the decision takes effect on the day it is adopted and halts specialized exchange trading. Gas sold for export before that date can still be shipped, provided the established procedure is followed.
