This is one of Norway’s most pristine fjords. So why is it being used as a dumping site for mine waste?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
04:00:09 UTC
13:00:09 KST

Shortly after the Norwegian stock market closed on 17 June 2026, a few dozen local people from the small west coast town of Vevring crowded around a laptop in a school. Surrounded by children’s drawings and windows looking out over Førde fjord, they listened as news arrived from Oslo. Norway’s supreme court had ruled against its government: a permit to release mining waste directly into the fjord two miles upstream was illegal, the court said.
The moment marked the end of a 17-year fight, one of Norway’s most protracted environmental battles in living memory. In Oslo, Ingvild Fonn Asmervik, the project leader for Naturvernforbundet (Friends of the Earth Norway), compared the joy she felt to giving birth to her child. For Anne-Line Thingnes Førsund, a third-generation fisher living on the banks of the fjord in Vevring and a volunteer for the charity’s local branch, it was more of a relief. Like a mountain lifting off her shoulders, she said.
These feelings of elation were short-lived. While Førsund and others celebrated, a government lawyer appeared on a television debate show to set out plans for a new temporary permit, and to allow the mine to continue to release waste directly into the fjord in the meantime. Four days later, the mine applied for fresh permission, and in late September, it was granted by Norway’s climate and environment ministry.
“When we heard the pollution would continue, it was like they snatched the carpet from under us,” says Førsund. “We have answered every letter, commented on every consultation, complained whenever we could. We have been knocked down so many times and this could have been the opportunity for change.”
While the government insists that it is acting lawfully, critics say the dumping threatens to foul one of Norway’s most pristine fjords. Others worry that the decision heralds a new wave of permits to pollute Norway’s fjords in the race to secure critical minerals.
“This is not only about the fjord and us and our lives,” says Førsund. “This is about principles. When you have a government that doesn’t respect the supreme court you’re changing the system itself.”
The move comes just as a wider spotlight is being shone on the issue of polluted waters in Norway. A recent report showed that Norwegian fish farms are filling fjords and other coastal waters with nutrient pollution equivalent to the raw sewage of tens of millions of people each year.
Meanwhile, populations of Atlantic salmon are at a historic low in the country – 155 of Norway’s 450 or so salmon rivers were closed to fishing at the start of the season this year.
Submarine tailings deposition (STD) – known colloquially by Norwegian critics as “fjord dumping” – is the process of pumping crushed rocks and chemical waste into the sea through pipelines hundreds of metres underwater. Proposed as an alternative to disposing of waste on land, the Norwegian government’s own Institute of Marine Research (IMR) warns that STD releases fine particles of toxic waste that can accumulate in smaller sea life and disrupt ecosystems at large.
STD is outlawed in all of North America, Australia, Russia, Brazil, China and most of Europe. The few countries that still permit the practice include Papua New Guinea, Indonesia and Turkey.
The Engebø titanium mine, on Førde fjord near Vevring, was first proposed by Nordic Mining in 2006 and the government awarded a permit to release waste into the fjord less than 10 years later. In response, Friends of the Earth Norway launched legal challenges that worked their way up the country’s legal system, arriving at a week-long supreme court hearing in spring 2026. Meanwhile, the mine came online and began releasing waste late in 2024.
Nordic Mining is financed by investors including Japan’s Iwatani Corporation and the British offices of the international banks Morgan Stanley, UBS and Goldman Sachs. Other banks, including Standard Chartered and Citigroup, explicitly ban financing projects using STD.
Nordic Mining did not respond to repeated requests for comment from the Guardian, but said in a social media post shortly after the supreme court decision that it would continue with how it disposed of waste, with the encouragement of Norwegian officials.
“It has been said that our operation is illegal, that we have to close, that our work must stop. That is not the situation,” Nordic Mining said, adding that it was continuing “with the ambition to act responsibly, with respect for the fjords and mountains, and for the local community around us”.
Legal wrangling over the permit came to focus on the EU’s water framework directive (WFD), which applies to Norway as a member of the European Economic Area. The WFD allows industrial activities to pollute water bodies only when there is an “overriding public interest”.
The supreme court ruled that the reasons given when the permit was first awarded were not strong enough. However, the government argues they have grown stronger since the EU added titanium to its list of “critical minerals” in 2020.
“The Norwegian government considers the Engebø project to be of significant importance for Norway and Europe,” a ministry spokesperson said, because “the Engebø mountain contains one of the world’s largest known deposits of rutile, a titanium-bearing mineral. Within Europe, Norway and Ukraine are the only countries with significant resources of this kind.”
Legal scholars have questioned this logic. “That’s wrong. A permit exists or it doesn’t, and the supreme court decision is quite clear: the permit is illegal,” says Tarjei Ellingsen Røsvoll, associate professor of administrative and constitutional law at the University of Inland Norway.
“The government is then openly allowing a company to dump a bunch of stuff in a fjord illegally. That is unprecedented; it damages trust and undermines a fundamental structure of constitutional and administrative law. They should take responsibility for having made an invalid and illegal decision, morally and legally.”
While Nordic Mining awaited its new three-year permit, it continued to dispose of waste into Førde fjord. Økokrim, Norway’s central office for white collar and environmental crime, is now considering whether to investigate the dumping for illegality.
While there have been few comprehensive studies of the impact of STD on marine ecosystems, scientists have linked heavy metal pollution now present in some fjords to STD decades earlier.
The impact is particularly damaging when the waste is milled into small pieces, according to Terje van der Meeren, a research professor at the IMR, who co-authored the institute’s response to the Engebø mine application and testified during the supreme court hearings.
“It’s like flour,” says Van der Meeren, adding that waste from Engebø includes a chemical that degrades into carbon disulphide, a neurotoxin. “Our concern is that this fine dust will pass into the rest of the fjord. What will happen with the [fish] spawning in this fjord? We don’t know.”
In 2016, Van der Meeren and other IMR researchers travelled to the Arctic Repparfjord, in Hammerfest in the far north of the country, where a copper mine dumped waste for six years in the 1970s. Decades later, they found haddock with higher levels of lead, arsenic and chromium in their muscles than those in nearby waters, according to research published this year. Other Norwegian studies have found historic STD contamination in plankton, crabs and fish eggs.
Back in Vevring, Førsund and other campaigners are now preparing for a fresh legal battle over the temporary waste permit – though dumping is likely to continue for as long as it takes for a new decision to be reached.
She looks back on the first protests against the mine with nostalgia. In one photograph, taken more than a decade ago, protesters gathered for a meal on the banks of the fjord; Førsund’s daughter, now an architect, was only a child. “So many of these people are dead now,” she says.
“The fjord is bigger than us. It has given us food and income and meaning and music and fish and birds for thousands of years. Now it gives us the energy to keep fighting.”

Maricarmen, the 87-year-old woman whose eviction triggered major protests, has died in hospital, lawyer says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
03:55:56 UTC
12:55:56 KST

The 87-year-old whose eviction sparked a domestic crisis and triggered nationwide anti-government protests has died in hospital late on Wednesday. Protesters say they will continue to demonstrate to uphold her legacy.
María del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old woman whose eviction from her longtime Madrid home sparked nationwide protests across Spain and unleashed a political crisis in the country culminating in the government calling for snap elections, died on Wednesday while hospitalised.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez led the way on social media offering his condolences after housing activists and Abascal's lawyer announced her death. Known widely as “Maricarmen,” she had become a symbol for renters struggling with Spain's housing affordability crisis.
“All my love to Maricarmen’s family and loved ones,” Sánchez wrote in a post on X. “A hug as well to all of us who feel this loss as our own today. Rest in peace.”
The emotions ran into anger on the street among the protesters gathered near Spain's Parliament who chanted “Maricarmen lives, the fight goes on!”
“A great deal of sorrow. And above all, the thought that she is the cause, the head of this whole revolution that has happened, and that she can’t see it,” said Iciar López, a 32-year-old psychologist and protester in the capital Madrid.
“It makes me very sad that she can’t see if anything comes of it. That’s what angers me the most, honestly.”
Spaniards increasingly frustrated by housing costs periodically march in major cities demanding action from lawmakers.
But a fresh wave of indignation has swept the Iberian nation since 23 September, when Maricarmen, who used a wheelchair, was carried on a stretcher from her home of seven decades after police cordoned off the street and removed protesters.
She was taken to a hospital because of her fragile health. Televised images of the eviction prompted thousands of people to protest in Madrid and other cities across the country.
Maricarmen's lawyer, Beatriz Duro, did not disclose the cause of death when she confirmed it to Cadena Ser radio. Duro said that she and the activists were all devastated.
“Maricarmen's case, which captured media attention and travelled around the world, leaves us the image of the shameful violence of these types of evictions and the impact they can have on people’s health,” said Duro.
She had been expected to return home after leaving the hospital. The real estate company that evicted her in order to rent the property at a much higher price eventually caved in under immense public pressure and agreed to let her return to the apartment.
“Although a historic agreement was reached that would have allowed her to return home, this solution came too late,” the Madrid Tenants' Union said in a statement on Wednesday. “It was an entirely avoidable situation following a harrowing ordeal.”
The average rent for Spain has almost doubled in the last 10 years. The government said that 26% of Spaniards who rent housing spend an average of 40% of their income on rent and utilities, compared with the European Union average of 18% of renters who do so.
Protesters camped in Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol square held a minute of silence after learning of her death.
Maricarmen spent almost her entire life in her apartment, where she first lived with her parents and brother. She later worked as a secretary for the board of a pharmaceutical company, according to Spanish media outlets.
After retiring in 1998, she spent her days walking around the neighbourhood, running errands and taking care of the precious items in her home.
Spanish media reported that black-and-white family photographs were among the only things she had brought with her to the hospital.
“Maricarmen only wanted to die in her home. She wasn’t asking for anything else,” Eugenio Melchor, 22, said at the protest in Madrid.
“She was dying in her home and she almost did. They have killed her. I mean, there’s no other word for it, and I hope those responsible for this pay and go to trial.”

An unidentified hacker believed to be a Chinese speaker used artificial intelligence-powered tools to breach several South Korean financial institutions and steal data, according to the US cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike.
The attacks occurred between late September and early October, Yonhap News Agency reported Thursday, citing a CrowdStrike report.
The attacker used ARTEX, a Chinese-developed open-source penetration-testing tool, alongside large language models to compromise banking systems.
Targets included a bank's loan inquiry service and another lender's employee mobile-support platform.
CrowdStrike identified two servers linked to the attacks, including one in Hong Kong.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told a news conference Thursday that Beijing rejected “spreading disinformation out of political agenda.”
China "opposes hacking activities and fights these activities in accordance with the law," she said, adding that AI profoundly affects cybersecurity.
Mao urged the international community “to step up cooperation and dialogue and set up new international rules to jointly safeguard cybersecurity.”
CrowdStrike said the hacker appeared financially motivated, citing searches for marketplaces selling stolen South Korean data.
However, the attacker's identity, the extent of the breaches and the volume of stolen information remain unconfirmed.
The findings follow recently reported data breaches involving Hana Bank, KB Kookmin Bank and Shinhan Bank, which prompted investigations by financial regulators and law enforcement authorities.

Japan beer giants raided over suspicions they colluded to set the price of beverages
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
03:54:38 UTC
12:54:38 KST

Japanese authorities have raided the country’s four biggest breweries over suspicions they colluded to set the price of beer and other beverages – a practice media reports said could have forced drinkers to pay over the odds.
Officials from the Fair Trade Commission this week searched the offices of Asahi Breweries, Kirin Brewery, Suntory Beer and Sapporo Breweries – which together control more than 90% of the domestic market. The quartet are suspected of violating the anti-monopoly law.
The commission’s secretary general, Hiroo Iwanari, confirmed an investigation had begun, but declined to give details. The companies said they would cooperate with authorities.
The commission is understood to have launched the investigation given the potential effect the alleged cartel has had on prices after wholesalers sell their products on to supermarkets, convenience stores, bars and restaurants, the Mainichi Shimbun said.
Japanese media quoted sources as saying that sales managers and other executives from the breweries were suspected of meeting secretly over a prolonged period to coordinate on the timing and scale of retail price increases, which ranged from several yen to several dozen yen a time.
Prices for beer and a low-malt version called happoshu have risen multiple times to reflect the rising cost of raw materials and logistics. The commission suspects the breweries bypassed proper pricing competition and collaborated to ensure they made a profit, the Mainichi said.
Alcohol consumption in Japan has declined in recent decades as a result of depopulation and changes in drinking habits among younger people. But sales still reached ¥3.8tn ($24.3bn) in 2024, with beer accounting for 30% of the total, followed by happoshu and third-category beer, which contains little or no malt, with a combined 11.9%
The four breweries have all raised their prices at the same time, most recently in April last year, citing the rising cost of materials and distribution. Prices also rose in October 2022 and October 2023.
Shares in Asahi, Kirin, Suntory and Sapporo fell after Wednesday’s raids – the first investigation of its kind involving the food and beverage industry.
Japanese media quoted sources as saying the commission had judged the case to be particularly serious given its potential impact on consumers, adding that the probe could result in a criminal complaint.
The probe comes three months after the commission raided six Japanese ice-cream makers over allegations of operating a cartel.

Indonesia accused of ‘gross negligence’ in wildfires lawsuit as haze tests region
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
03:54:09 UTC
12:54:09 KST

The Indonesian government has been accused of “gross negligence” in a class action lawsuit over its handling of wildfires that have cloaked large parts of South-east Asia in a toxic haze, shuttered schools and caused a spike in respiratory illnesses.
The lawsuit, filed by indigenous and civil society groups in the Indonesian part of Borneo, named President Prabowo Subianto and the governor of West Kalimantan among 10 defendants. The case seeks comprehensive recovery and rehabilitation measures that would include covering the healthcare costs of residents.
None of those named in the lawsuit attended the opening day of court in West Kalimantan’s provincial capital Pontianak on Wednesday, leading judges to adjourn the hearing until 21 October.
“We feel sad and regretful about their absence … But on the other hand, we also understand that perhaps this haze condition caused them to be unable to land in Pontianak,” the plaintiffs’ lawyer, Glorio Sanen, told reporters.
Sanen said the case was “a step to address the problem” of wildfires that flare up annually in Indonesia, where they are often lit as a cheap way to clear land for oil palm planting.
Indonesia, the world’s largest producer of palm oil, has been accused of not doing enough to stop the so-called “slash and burn” land clearances, although the government has vowed a crackdown and deployed the military to fight the fires.
The blazes hit a crisis point this year due to an unusually intense El Niño weather phenomenon, which has created drier-than-usual conditions, sending a putrid smog to Malaysia, Brunei and Singapore, and even the Philippines.
The transboundary haze has angered Indonesia’s neighbours. Schools in the Malaysian state of Johor, just north of Singapore, were to be closed on Thursday and Friday due to deteriorating air quality, local authorities said.
The four plaintiffs in the West Kalimantan lawsuit, which was filed last month, include a chapter of Indigenous NGO AMAN and the local branch of Catholic Youth.
Yakobus Kumis, a plaintiff representing a Dayak ethnic group, indigenous to the island of Borneo, expressed disappointment that government representatives did not attend this week’s hearing, saying it was a “way of the central government teaching the people that violating the law is OK.”
He said the government ignored warning signs ahead of the fires breaking out, and called for the smoke crisis to be classified as a national disaster.
A similar lawsuit filed last year at a court in South Sumatra was dismissed.
The presidential office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Agence France-Presse and Reuters contributed to this report

Breaking: NZ Rugby launches court bid to protect 'Chiefs' name from PNG league franchise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
03:43:10 UTC
12:43:10 KST

New Zealand Rugby has launched a court bid to stop the Papua New Guinea National Rugby League team from using its name in New Zealand.
The move is an effort to protect the Waikato-based Chiefs, who have played in the Super Rugby competition for 30 years.
The Australian Rugby League Commission says it will defend the claim.
Rugby union officials have launched New Zealand High Court proceedings to prevent the National Rugby League's (NRL) new Papua New Guinea-based franchise from using the "Chiefs" name in New Zealand.
New Zealand Rugby (NZR) said the move was an effort to protect the brand of the Waikato-based Chiefs, who have played in the Super Rugby competition across Australasia since rugby union turned professional in 1996.
The NRL, which is Australia-based but has one team in the New Zealand city of Auckland, announced the expansion of the league to Papua New Guinea in 2024.
The island nation's Prime Minister James Marape unveiled the name "Chiefs" the following year.
NZR said attempts to engage the Australian Rugby League Commission (ARLC) over the issue had been unsuccessful and it was seeking an interim and final injunction against the use of the name before the Papua New Guinea team was officially launched later this month.
"For 30 years the Chiefs and their players have built an incredibly strong identity that is widely recognised and loved by fans," NZR chief executive Steve Lancaster said in a statement today.
"We have raised our concerns with the ARLC directly and consistently over the last year in attempting to find a resolution. We now have a responsibility to protect the Chiefs brand."
Action branded 'hypocritical'
ARLC executive chairman Peter V'landys said the complaint was hypocritical given the New South Wales rugby league team had used the "Blues" brand for more than half a century before the Auckland Blues Super Rugby franchise was launched 30 years ago.
"We will defend this vigorously," he said.
"The hypocrisy is mind-blowing, considering the Auckland Blues in 1996 used the NSW Blues name without any consultation or approval.
"Rugby union is obviously feeling threatened by rugby league in New Zealand, with sell-outs at most rugby league games."
Super Rugby Chiefs chief executive Simon Graafhuis told Pacific Beat that he was confident of a resolution, adding that he would prefer the NRL team to change its name.
"Peter V'landys is the head honcho [and] is pretty adamant he's not going to do that. IP law is pretty clear. I think we're on pretty solid ground. So it could be an interesting ride," he said.
"We're open to working with them [the NRL]. This is all about protecting our brand that's taken 30 years to generate value and that's what's important to us at this stage.
"This week we had a request from a funeral celebrant to see if our logo could be used on a headstone. It's just a reminder of what it actually means to our community and yeah, absolutely worth fighting for."
Mr Graafhuis said a drastically different colour scheme would not be enough to satisfy the club that the PNG team was not infringing on its name and trademark.
"I suppose it'll come down to the courts, won't it? The longer this goes on, the higher the costs, but also the bigger the damages. So, hopefully we're all keen to avoid that one," he said.
IP Australia, the government agency that administers rights to trademarks, has examined the PNG Chiefs' case and given it an initial acceptance, triggering an "opposition period".
Any party that opposes the application has two months to lodge an appeal.
Rugby league split from rugby union in the late 19th century in a dispute about amateurism.
While union is the more popular game globally, league rules the roost on Australia's eastern seaboard and has been making great strides in New Zealand.
Papua New Guinea is the only country in the world where rugby league is the most popular sport.
The new team has already signed a slew of top NRL players ahead of its first season in 2028, and will be backed by hundreds of millions of dollars in funding from the Australian government, which is looking to shore up its influence in the Pacific Islands.
"We want to be absolutely clear, this is not about rugby league's growth in the Pacific," Mr Lancaster said.
"We welcome the development of the Pacific region through sport and the passion that the people of Papua New Guinea have for both rugby and rugby league."
The ABC has contacted IP Australia and Mr Lancaster for comment.

France's school protests: What lies behind the anger
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
04:38:46 BST
12:38:46 KST

France's school protests: What lies behind the anger
- Published
Since late September students across France have been holding protests against underfunding in education, and have been blocking access to many high schools.
The movement has turned violent in places – hundreds of students, teachers and police officers have been injured. Thousands of people – including an unknown number of outside troublemakers – have been arrested.
The protesters are complaining about staff shortages and dilapidated facilities in the country's lycées, schools which are attended by 15-18-year-olds.
"Sometimes our teachers are absent for several weeks without being replaced," Madalena, a Paris student, told the BBC on Tuesday as demonstrations brought out hundreds of thousands across France. Her school buildings, she added, were "boiling hot" during the recent heat waves.
There is a variety of other complaints. Some resent the banning of mobile phones or school days that last until 18:00. "You get home at 19:00, and have no time to sleep or do your homework," one lycéen told France 2.
France's online platform that allocates places in higher education, Parcoursup, is another sore point.
The frustration has deep roots. About 80% of each cohort now passes the baccalauréat, which entitles students to a university place - though not necessarily their preferred choice. This leads to a scramble for desirable courses, and an anxiety focused on Parcoursup, which many regard as opaque.
Those grievances are real. But do they by themselves explain the form the protest movement has taken? How does France compare with other countries?
According to a recent report by the OECD, a club of developed nations, the French government spends more per lycée student than the EU average for upper-secondary schools.
Teacher shortages are indeed acute, but no worse than elsewhere. By OECD measures they are actually milder – fewer posts go unfilled – although French teachers receive relatively low pay.
Schooldays that stretch into the late afternoon are indeed a problem for French pupils. This is the result mostly of long lunch breaks and complex schedules rather than making up for holidays, which are not especially long compared with other EU countries.
The extended day has always been a sad fact of French school life and can hardly account for the present eruption. Neither can pressure created by a dysfunctional higher-education system.
In most European countries, 80-90% of young people complete secondary education, and competition for good university places creates stress elsewhere too.
And while underfunding, dilapidated buildings and fears about the future are behind the students' discontent, those complaints do not by themselves explain why the movement has become "unprecedented" in terms of the number of schools, pupils and the degree of violence involved, in the words of Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez.
The scale of protests is all the more remarkable as those involved are taking considerable risks.
Blockading a school or university by threats or force is illegal, and draws in police, as well as casseurs (vandals), and pupils have become caught up in police crowd-control operations that are often heavy handed.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, in his latest message, has insisted security forces are not under orders to "confront high-school students", only to enforce the law.
To understand the pupils' tactics, one must look beyond the barricaded school gates to a political tradition. In France, the power has often resided on the street as much as in elected bodies. Students know this as well as anyone else.
In October 1990, a rape at a school in Seine-Saint-Denis – an area north of Paris that has been a focus for the present unrest – was the trigger for mass rallies against underfunding and staff shortages. It resulted in the government releasing the equivalent of €1.2bn (£1bn) in today's money for lycées.
In October 1998, 500,000 pupils marched across France over similar demands, resulting in almost €1bn to renovate schools and 14,000 extra staff.
On several occasions student protests defeated government reforms – such as a university overhaul in 1986 and a lower youth minimum wage in 1994.
Probably the most striking display of student power came in 2006, with the withdrawal of a law designed to loosen hire-and-fire rules for those under 26 to try to tackle youth unemployment.
The measure, passed by parliament and signed by then-President Jacques Chirac, was scrapped after weeks of blockades in universities and lycées often marred by violence.
French adults have shown how blockading roads can prevail over elected officials.
The gilets jaunes (yellow vests) uprising of 2018-2019 – which saw shops ransacked and government buildings attacked across the country – led the government to drop a rise in fuel taxes and approve €10bn in spending.
The street does not always win.
In 1968 – a heroic precedent cited by every French protest movement – a student uprising was actually brought to an end by election. But the lycéens are heirs to a political culture in which demonstrators compete with elected officials to be seen as the legitimate voice of the people.
On the face of it, the current balance of power favour the pupils. A poll for BFMTV suggests that that 72% of French people regard their demands as legitimate and 55% support the movement.
Backed by many teachers, labour unions and left-wing politicians, the protesters are on the front foot. Another rally is planned for Thursday afternoon.
The government, by contrast, has never been weaker. After nine years in power, Emmanuel Macron is a deeply unpopular lame duck, barred from standing in the presidential election due in six months' time.
His decision to call a snap election in June 2024 has resulted in a hopelessly gridlocked assembly. Lecornu has described himself as the "weakest prime minister" in living memory and seems unlikely to get a budget through parliament.
But that very weakness could prove an asset in his showdown with students. Faced with rising borrowing costs, a deficit of 5.4% of GDP and a public debt at its highest level since the 1940s, Lecornu is financially as well as politically hamstrung.
Unlike his predecessors under intense pressure from the street, he has nothing to give.

Faisal Mahmud
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
Two earthquakes struck eastern Japan within three hours early Thursday, shaking Chiba and Ibaraki prefectures, but neither triggered a tsunami, according to the country's weather agency.
The first earthquake, with a preliminary magnitude of 4.8, struck northeastern Chiba Prefecture at 4.13 am local time (1913GMT Wednesday), Kyodo News reported, citing the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA).
The quake originated at a depth of approximately 50 kilometers (31 miles) and registered 4 on Japan's seven-point seismic intensity scale in the city of Asahi.
Tremors were also felt in neighboring areas, including Ibaraki Prefecture.
Around three hours later, a second earthquake measuring 4.0 in magnitude jolted Ibaraki, registering an intensity of 3 in Hitachiomiya, according to the agency.
Neither earthquake generated a tsunami, the agency said.
The second tremor occurred at 7.14 am (2214 GMT Wednesday), at a depth of approximately 60 kilometers (37 miles).
Japan has experienced several recent earthquakes. A magnitude 5.1 quake struck northeastern Chiba on Oct. 1, following a magnitude 4.9 tremor in eastern Japan on Sept. 29. Earlier, a magnitude 5.9 earthquake struck the region on Aug. 23, injuring more than 40 people in Tokyo.

Pakistan's terror monsters now wreak havoc in its own backyard: India at UN

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08

‘You cannot run with the hares’: India tears into Pakistan’s terror record at UN
NEW DELHI: India used the UN stage to turn Pakistan’s own words against it, arguing that the terror networks Islamabad once nurtured have now come back to haunt their own backyard, a reality, New Delhi said, that even Pakistan’s leaders have begun to acknowledge. India also urged the international community to take stronger action against states accused of sponsoring terrorism.Speaking at the UN General Assembly’s Sixth Committee, which deals with legal affairs, India’s first secretary Raghoo Puri said Pakistan had long portrayed itself as both a victim and a frontline state in the fight against terrorism."Pakistan has presented itself as a frontline state in combating terrorism and as a victim, while masking the fact that the Frankenstein’s (monster) the Pakistani state has created and lost control over have moved from wreaking havoc in neighbouring countries to doing the same in Pakistan," Puri said on Wednesday."This was exposed recently by a provincial chief minister of Pakistan, and may I jog the memory of colleagues to an interview in 2018 by her father and former prime minister of Pakistan, exposing this dark secret," he said."You cannot run with the hares and hunt with the hounds," Puri warned. "Reality never works like that".Puri was responding to remarks by Pakistan’s deputy Permanent Representative Usman Jadoon, who had launched an attack on India during the committee proceedings.
Pakistan’s own leaders expose terror threat
Puri pointed to recent remarks by Punjab chief minister Maryam Nawaz, who said her province faced a bigger threat from neighbouring Pakistani provinces than from neighbouring countries.Maryam Nawaz, who leads Pakistan’s Punjab province, said last month in Lahore: "Unfortunately, the threat Punjab, a province of 130 million, faces comes less from my neighbouring countries and more from my neighbouring provinces."Earlier this month, she also questioned the idea of distinguishing between different forms of extremist violence, saying anyone involved in terrorism should be treated as a terrorist regardless of their political motives.Puri also referred to an interview given by Maryam Nawaz’s father, former Pakistan prime minister Nawaz Sharif, to Dawn in 2018. Sharif had spoken about militant groups operating from Pakistan and questioned whether they should be allowed to cross the border and carry out attacks in India."Militant organisations are active. Call them non-state actors; should we allow them to cross the border and kill 150 people in Mumbai?" he had said.Puri did not name either Maryam Nawaz or Nawaz Sharif while making his remarks.
‘Bombed-out airfields’ are not victory
Puri also hit back at Pakistan’s claims about the outcome of Operation Sindoor, India’s counterterror military action to the Pahalgam attack."If bombed-out airfields and cratered runways look like victory to Pakistan, they are, of course, welcome to enjoy it," he said.He accused Pakistan of continuing to spread false claims about the operation and said its approach was part of a wider campaign of disinformation.Puri said the "Pakistani representative’s desperation to falsely tout the Pakistani military’s narrative on the outcome of Operation Sindoor" was consistent with Pakistan’s long-running use of state-backed misinformation and psychological warfare.
'Circular economy of words'
Puri also took a swipe at Pakistan after its delegation made a second intervention, repeating what he described as old arguments."Pakistan believes in the circular economy of words and narratives," Puri said."If this much effort had actually been made in countering terrorism rather than narrative building, misinformation, and disinformation, the world would have been a better place," he said."But nothing more can be expected from a Form 47 government," he added, referring to Pakistan’s political system and alleged manipulation of the electoral process.Puri also challenged Pakistan’s claims on minority rights and accused Islamabad of allowing religious extremism to flourish.
‘The victims in Pahalgam were not asked about their political orientation’
"The victims in Pahalgam were not asked about their political orientation; they were asked about their religion," Puri said."It is therefore deeply ironic that Pakistan speaks of combating religious hatred while allowing the conditions that enable it to persist and thrive, especially by fomenting cross-border terrorism," he added.Puri referred to the Pahalgam terror attack, in which terrorists targeted tourists after asking about their religion.He said the attack showed the consequences of allowing extremist groups and crossborder terrorism to continue.
India raises Masood Azhar issue
Puri also questioned Pakistan’s claims that it was taking action against Jaish-e-Mohammed chief Masood Azhar, who is listed by the UN as a terrorist.Pakistan had increased the reward for information leading to Azhar’s arrest from Pakistani rupees 50 lakh to 70 lakh."Pakistan glosses over its state support for terrorism by announcing enhanced rewards for apprehending UN-listed head of Jaish-e-Mohammed, terrorist and mastermind of several attacks against my country," Puri said."When the media can reach Masood Azhar and get confirmation from him about the success of Operation Sindoor, surely the Pakistani state knows his whereabouts," he said.Azhar had earlier appeared in a video in which he claimed that his family infrastructure had been destroyed during India’s strikes on Bahawalpur as part of Operation Sindoor.Puri also recalled Pakistan’s earlier claims that Jaish-e-Mohammed was no longer active."Just a few months ago, Pakistani representatives used this forum to call the Jaish-e-Mohammed a defunct organisation," Puri said. "The world has seen the script play earlier, and we are clear-eyed that this time also it is going to be no different."
India invokes 9/11, 26/11 and Pahalgam
Puri warned that allowing terrorist groups to operate with political protection could undermine international efforts against terrorism."When terrorist groups are allowed to operate under state political power, international commitments become meaningless, and when perpetrators are provided safe havens, the victims of terrorism are denied justice," he said.He also cited the example of al-Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden, who was found in Abbottabad, Pakistan, years after the 9/11 attacks."The world has not forgotten 9/11, and where its perpetrators, including Osama bin Laden, were caught," Puri said.
He then pointed to the 2008 Mumbai attacks."The world has not forgotten 26/11," when Pakistani terrorists killed 166 people in Mumbai, he said. "The world has not forgotten Pahalgam."Puri also referred to Pakistan’s record on terror financing and the upcoming meeting of the Financial Action Task Force (FATF)."The world is aware of Pakistan’s financial support to terrorism, as also, the FATF plenary meeting coming up soon," he said.The FATF, the global body that monitors terror financing and money laundering, is scheduled to hold its next plenary meeting in Paris from October 26 to 30.

French Education Minister Édouard Geffray pledged Thursday to deploy 3,000 replacement teachers "in the coming days" to address the crisis in French high schools as student protests that have rocked the country for more than a week showed no sign of ending. Earlier, riot police used tear gas and water cannons to disperse thousands of protesters gathered on Place de la Bastille in Paris. Follow our liveblog for the latest updates.
French PM vows concrete action to address teacher shortages
French PM Sébastien Lecornu has detailed the measures put forward earlier by the education minister.
These include deploying the 3,024 supply teachers currently not assigned to any classes, with priority given to the 114 secondary schools facing the greatest difficulties.
“Every hour of lesson lost due to a lack of supply teachers penalises the pupils. This is a major concern,” he said.
Lecornu added that his government would table amendments to the 2027 budget to "translate some of the proposals voiced by pupils into concrete measures".
Support for protesters on the left, for police on the right: how French parties have reacted
Prime Minister Lecornu has accused LFI, the largest single left-wing party in parliament, of stoking the protests and having a "political agenda" to "throw the country into chaos" ahead of the 2027 presidential election.
LFI, meanwhile, has accused police of a disproportionate response against protesters, many of whom are minors.
Here's a look at where other parties stand.
Marseille teacher files criminal complaint over alleged student attack
The Paris protest was mostly peaceful, although there were occasional clashes between small groups of demonstrators and the police during the evening.
Elsewhere, arsonists attacked a Bordeaux police station, a school in Saint-Etienne was ransacked and a teacher in Toulouse was hit by a demonstrator, said the Interior Ministry.
In Marseille, police said a teacher at Victor Hugo High School was attacked during the latest protests and has filed a criminal complaint over the incident.
Education minister vows to boost teacher numbers in bid to ease school crisis
Education Minister Edouard Geffray has pledged to deploy an additional 3,000 supply teachers "in the coming days" to address the crisis in French high schools.
Geffray said the teachers were currently waiting to be assigned to a school.
"Within the next hours, 3,000 teachers will be joining these institutions," Geffray told the evening news on the TF1 television channel, adding they would be affected to schools between Friday to Tuesday.
Teacher shortages rank among the main concerns voiced by protesters at rallies across the country.
School protests see 71,500 march nationwide, hundreds arrested (interior ministry)
Officials say 71,500 people demonstrated in France today, including 24,500 in Paris.
The interior ministry says 504 people were arrested and 48 officers were injured.
Police clash with protesters on Place de la Bastille in Paris. Credit: Pedro Nunes, Reuters
The ministry also reported an increase in violent acts, adding that 55,000 people took part “in actions outside schools, only some of whom joined the demonstrations”.
Police use a water canon to disperse protesters in Paris. Credit: Abdul Saboor, Reuters
UNICEF calls for 'de-escalation', urges France to protect minors
The UN agency for children has called for “a de-escalation of violence” and “the protection of minors”, urging the French authorities to respect young people’s right to “demonstrate peacefully”.
“Young people have the right to be heard, to participate in decisions that affect them and to demonstrate peacefully,” the French branch of the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) said in a statement.
“The right to demonstrate freely and safely is a fundamental right for children and teenagers,” added the UN agency, emphasising that this right is enshrined in the Convention on the Rights of the Child.
Teen protesters urge equal education opportunities for all
Protests in Paris and elsewhere have featured many pupils from top schools in affluent areas calling for equal opportunities for all.
Jeanne, a 15-year-old student from a top Paris high school, told AFP reporters at the Bastille rally that she wanted to show solidarity with pupils in less privileged areas outside the capital.
"Everyone has the right to be educated at the same level. There shouldn't be people who are more educated than others when we're all in the public education system," she said.
Marianne, a 20-year-old university student who also did not want to give her second name, said she was also there to protest excessive police force in recent days of protest.
"For me, that's just unacceptable," she said.
Student protesters 'showing no signs of backing down'
Students who have been protesting classroom conditions in France for days are "not looking like they are willing to back down", reports France 24 reporter Claire Paccalin from Paris, despite promises by the French prime minister to bring in measures to address their grievances.
Education minister to announce 'concrete measures' later today
Education Minister Edouard Geffray will announce "first concrete measures" for high-school students this evening, the prime minister's office has said.
Geffray is set to make the announcements during the 8pm news programme on French television TF1.
French youth must be priority for 2027 election, says ex-president Hollande
Youth must be the priority of candidates in next year's presidential election, says former president François Hollande, who is widely believed to be mulling a run of his own.

The left-wing mayor of the northern suburb of Paris has been a prominent supporter of the protest movement, and was greeted with chants of "Bally! Bally!" at the earlier march on Tuesday.
Bally Bagayoko (centre) attends the protests on Bastille square in Paris. Credit: Simon Wohlfhart, AFP
"The Republican promise (of equality) — in particular for the working-class neighbourhoods, and also rural areas — is not respected," Bagayoko told Reuters in an interview earlier today.
He said the government should prioritise investing in education and levy heavier taxes on billionaires.
The government has suggested that Bagayoko's LFI party was behind the protests, an accusation that Bagayoko dismissed as insulting to the young protesters.
PM's change of tone leaves students unconvinced
In a televised address on Wednesday evening, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu promised a plan to respond to the crisis by the end of October.
Although he denied security forces had been given "orders to confront" pupils, and said the country could not be "indifferent" to their demands, many were unconvinced.

"We expected more from him," agreed fellow student Salyna, 17.
For French students, protesting is a rite of passage
Demonstrating is something of a rite of passage for young people in France, a moment when teenagers discover politics and their collective voice.
How has this “protest culture” manifested itself in recent history? And why are some student protests effective at bringing about change and others not?
FRANCE 24’s Florence Villeminot and Genie Godula take a closer look.
Student and teacher unions call for new day of strikes and protests
Unions representing teachers, students and high-school pupils have called for a new nationwide strike next Tuesday, October 13.
"Until we have 10 billion euros on the table, we will continue to take action," said Sabrine Kharbach, spokesperson for a student's union.

'My students help me catch cockroaches in class'
High-school teacher Diane Di Sciullo joined students at the march in Marseille, saying all they were asking for was a decent education in decent conditions.
She denounced overcrowding, saying this year she had 37 students in her class.
"At the start of every lesson, I have to ask them to check the neighbouring classrooms for spare chairs and desks so they can actually study," she said.
A woman stands at her window with a sign taped reading "Support for High School Students". Credit: Manon Cruz, Reuters

Education Minister Geffray to announce 'contingency plan' to replace absent teachers
French Education Minister Édouard Geffray said on Thursday that he would soon present a “contingency plan” to replace absent teachers.

The French government said Wednesday it would suspend the use of stun grenades in its attempts to manage the student protests roiling the country after a 15-year-old boy had his hand blown off during a clash with riot police.
An investigation was opened after a 17-year-old boy suffered a head injury on Wednesday outside a secondary school in Marseille, the local public prosecutor’s office told AFP.

Margaret Hamilton, scientist who led NASA’s Apollo software development, dead at 90
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
03:25:00 UTC
12:25:00 KST

Margaret Hamilton, scientist who led NASA’s Apollo software development, dies at 90
- Margaret Hamilton, who led NASA Apollo software development, died at 90. MIT called her a “computing pioneer” and NASA praised her role in Moon landings.
- She was the first programmer on the Apollo project at MIT and later led the Command and Service Module software team with more than 400 workers.
- Hamilton won the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016 and later founded two software companies after publishing more than 130 papers.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – American scientist Margaret Hamilton, who led the development of the computer system used by NASA’s Apollo lunar programme, has died at the age of 90, her former employer said on Oct 7.
In a statement, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) called Hamilton, who taught at the prestigious university from 1959 to the mid-1970s, a “computing pioneer” and said she died on Sept 30.
“To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer – to say she was ahead of her time – would be a dramatic understatement,” said Olivier de Weck, the Apollo programme professor and interim head of the MIT Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics.
“She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy, and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved,” Weck added.
The famed Apollo programme allowed the United States to beat the Soviet Union in the race to become the first humans to land on the Moon.
NASA chief Jared Isaacmen paid tribute on X, calling Hamilton “a pioneer whose work helped make Apollo and humanity’s first journeys to the moon possible”.
Born in Indiana in 1936, Hamilton studied mathematics before moving to Boston, Massachussetts, with her husband in 1959.
She found employment at MIT, working in meteorology before she joined a lab in 1965 that was seeking people to develop software to “send a man to the Moon”.
Hamilton “was hired as the first programmer for the Apollo project at MIT, as well as the first female programmer in the project”, the university said.
“By 1968, she was assistant director in charge of (Apollo’s) Command and Service Module team, and more than 400 people were working on Apollo’s software,” MIT said.
Hamilton was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom by former president Barack Obama in 2016 for her achievements.
In 2009, Hamilton told MIT News: “There was no second chance. We knew that. We took our work seriously, many of us beginning this journey while still in our 20s.”
“Coming up with solutions and new ideas was an adventure. Dedication and commitment were a given. Mutual respect was across the board. Because software was a mystery, a black box, upper management gave us total freedom and trust,” Hamilton added.
“Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers,” she said.
Hamilton went on to publish more than 130 papers, and started her own software companies Higher Order Software and Hamilton Technologies. AFP

US: Award-winning Kashmiri filmmaker detained

US: Award-winning Kashmiri filmmaker detained
October 8, 2026
A filmmaker whose award-winning work has explored conflict in his native Kashmir has been detained by United States immigration officials on suspicion of residing and working in the country illegally.
Arfat Sheikh was detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) after disembarking a flight from California at Washington Dulles International Airport on September 24, according to a statement from friends and relatives who labeled his detention "unlawful" and are calling for his release.
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, confirmed to the Reuters news agency on Wednesday that Sheikh had "legally entered the US on a temporary basis and illegally overstayed his lawful admittance."
Sheikh, 42, entered the US in 2019 on a student visa and enrolled on a graduate course in film studies at Georgia State University, according to the statement from friends and family.
Having applied for asylum in 2020, the statement said he had a pending immigration application and was authorized to work and live in the US. It did not mention the ground for asylum.
The DHS said Sheikh would receive due process but that a pending application does not confer legal residency status.
ICE arrests up amid Trump immigration crackdown
US President Donald Trump has been pursuing an immigration crackdown and deportation drive that he claims is aimed at improving domestic security.
His administration said in August it was to "identify and revoke the non-immigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the US claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently."
The number of ICE arrests hit record levels this summer, with about 51,000 recorded across August.
Critics say the crackdown has violated due process and free speech rights and has created an unsafe environment, particularly for ethnic minorities, who have raised concerns about racial profiling.
Sheikh, who hails from India-administered Kashmir, won the Emerging Filmmaker Activist Award at the Teaneck International Film Festival in 2025.
His first feature film, 2024's "Saffron Kingdom," won Best Feature Film at the Chicago Filmmakers Awards, the LA Film and Documentary Awards, the Melbourne Independent Film Festival and the Wake Forest Film Festival.
The film explored conflict in Kashmir, a disputed Muslim-majority region claimed by both Hindu-majority India and Islamic Pakistan, which each control only part of it and have fought wars over it.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of National Defense tracked three Chinese military aircraft, six naval vessels, and one official ship around Taiwan between 6 a.m. on Wednesday and 6 a.m. on Thursday.

A tanker sailing off the north coast of Qatar has been attacked, causing an unknown number of casualties, a British maritime security agency said. The attack came as Iran declared it would close a route in the strait of Hormuz being used to circumvent Tehran’s blockade of traffic.
The vessel was in the Gulf, about 500km (300 miles) west of the strait of Hormuz, when it reported being struck “by multiple projectiles”, the UK Maritime Trade Operations said on Wednesday. The UK authority did not specify the origin of the ship.
Wednesday’s attack comes as strikes on tankers sailing through the strait of Hormuz hit their highest weekly level since the Iran war began, according to maritime security firms, as oil prices climbed above $100 per barrel.
In the week to 5 October, there were at least 12 attacks on oil, liquefied natural gas and liquefied petroleum gas tankers around the strait, according to data from three security sources.
On Tuesday, India’s foreign ministry said 12 crew members were injured after an attack on a Panama-flagged oil tanker passing through the strait of Hormuz.
Attacks, attempted attacks and harassment activity including drone overflights and surveillanceby Iran’s Revolutionary Guards have persisted in the strait, a US Navy-led agency said on Sunday.
“These actions continue to demonstrate Iran’s intent to assert presence along key transit lanes and maintain pressure on transiting vessels,” the Joint Maritime Information Center said.
Ships in the Gulf and those attempting to transit the strait, the only way in or out of the oil-rich region for vessels, have come under repeated attack since the US and Israel attacked Iran on 28 February.
On Wednesday, Tehran said it would further choke Hormuz, declaring transit routes in the strait deemed illegal by Iran would soon be closed, in reference to a southern pathway hugging Oman’s coast.
Mohammadreza Naqdi, an adviser to the Revolutionary Guards’ Commander, said these “few routes” had been created by blasting and damaging some of the rocky passages and were used by “small boats smuggling oil and transferring it to tankers”, despite evidence Gulf oil exports are regaining prewar levels.
“The strait of Hormuz is closed, and the armed forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran have full control over it,” he told the Fars news agency.
The IRGC has consistently denied that seaborne crude flows in the strait are rebounding thanks to US Navy help. IRGC adviser Majid Mirahmadi said on Thursday that a daily average of 10 ships were transiting the waterway against an average of 125 before the war.
The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, disputed that account on Wednesday, saying Iran had “lost complete control” of the strait. “There’s almost as much oil flowing out now as there was before this conflict began.”
Amid mixed messaging and supply concerns, the price of oil rose on Wednesday, with Brent crude topping $100 per barrel.
The continuing stalemate in the war is heaping pressure on Donald Trump.
On Thursday, the US president announced he would not attack Iran before the midterm elections, contrary to recent reports in US media that he was considering resuming military operations against Iran in the coming weeks. On social media he wrote that “while Iran is in very bad condition, both Economically and Militarily, and while the Blockade will remain in full force and effect, with Oil flowing in Record Numbers of Barrels through the Hormuz Strait (22 Million Barrels, last night alone, with not one barrel coming from, or going to, Iran!), we will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections”.
Last week, a third US aircraft carrier set sail for the region. It could mean that three carriers are in the region as early as the end of October.
As a result of Trump’s war with Iran, Americans have been grappling with high gas prices and soaring diesel costs.
The US has set up its own counter blockade of Iranian ports and occasionally fires on vessels linked to Tehran. It has also bombed Iranian targets in retaliation for Tehran’s attacks on ships, although there have been no such reported strikes since 1 September.
Hormuz is vital to the world economy, with around a fifth of the planet’s oil and liquefied natural gas passing through the strait before the war began.

Massive internet outage in Russia after Ukraine reportedly hits largest Yandex data center in drone attack
Outages occured in many segments of the Russian internet at about 16:00 p.m. local time on Oct. 8, especially in Moscow and St. Petersburg, after Ukraine struck a Yandex data center, the Moscow Times said.
Several banking services, as well as Google, RuTube, the website of the Russian Railways, as well as many retail websites were not reachable, according to the Moscow Times.
A major Yandex data center in Russia's Ryazan Oblast was reportedly damaged in an overnight drone attack, with a large fire reported at the industrial site.
OSINT groups Exilenova+ and ASTRA identified the site as Yandex DC Sasovo, located in the city of Sasovo. Yandex describes the facility as its largest data center, supporting the company's services and cloud infrastructure.
Yandex Cloud later acknowledged an "incident" and power-supply problems in its “ru-central1-b availability zone”. According to company updates, disruptions began at around 1:31 a.m., and roughly 40 minutes later the situation had not yet stabilized.
Yandex warned that the outage could affect other parts of its cloud network and advised customers to move some services elsewhere while engineers worked to restore operations.
The company did not publicly link the incident to the reported drone attack.
Exilenova+ also reported disruptions affecting some Yandex services following the strike. Public outage monitors, however, did not show evidence of a widespread outage across Yandex's main consumer services.
The Sasovo data center is located on the grounds of the Sasta machine-tool plant, a manufacturer of metal-cutting and high-precision CNC metalworking machines used across Russian industry, including the defense-industrial, aerospace, oil and gas, and heavy machinery sectors.
Sasta says its production complex includes machining and assembly workshops, a foundry, and research and development facilities, and that its equipment is used by enterprises in Russia's defense industry.
The plant has been under U.K. sanctions since 2024 over its role in Russia's defense sector.
It remains unclear whether the Yandex data center, the Sasta plant, or both were the intended targets of the reported attack.
In 2022, Ryazan Governor Pavel Malkov described the Sasovo complex as a high-tech facility housing tens of thousands of servers used to rapidly process requests across Yandex services.
Neither regional authorities nor Ukraine's military had publicly confirmed the reported strike at the time of publication. Yandex acknowledged the infrastructure incident and power problems but did not say what caused them.

'A new normal': American Jews are more connected to Jewish life than ever, survey finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
03:10:39 UTC
12:10:39 KST

The Jewish Federations of North America (JFNA) on Thursday released its third comprehensive survey tracking Jewish life since the October 7, 2023, attacks. The survey reveals that heightened community engagement has evolved into a sustained behavioral shift rather than a temporary reaction.
Conducted between May 4 and May 27, the poll surveyed 2,836 Jewish Americans using an SMS-to-web methodology managed by research firm Burson.
The study defines the ongoing phenomenon known as the “Surge” by tracking individuals who changed their behavior regarding Jewish life following October 7 across three main categories: communal engagement, educational exploration, and social connection. According to the report, 38% of the American Jewish community is part of the Surge, showing a slight rebound or holding steady compared to previous years.
Mimi Kravetz, chief impact and growth officer at Jewish Federations of North America, noted the persistence of the trend: “Many people expected the increased interest in Jewish life to fade as time went on, but our data shows the Surge sustaining and even building momentum since last year.”
“Jewish Americans are actively creating and seeking Jewish life in many different ways, and Jewish institutions, including Federations, are continuing to respond to this need,” she added.
Ties to Israel, concerns over antisemitism drive surge in American Jewish engagement
The data indicates that the Surge is driven primarily by two core factors: deep emotional attachment to Israel and heightened concern regarding antisemitism. Among those actively surging, 93% report feeling emotionally attached to Israel, compared to 51% of those who never surged, while 75% state that Israel makes them proud to be Jewish. Additionally, 75% of those in the Surge report being targeted online, and 53% state there is a significant amount of antisemitism in the United States today.
When examining how engagement manifested, the report highlights that 29% of American Jews surged socially, 14% educationally, and 13% communally, with significant overlap between categories. Among those engaging communally, 65% connected through a local synagogue or temple, 32% through Chabad, 28% via Jewish or Israel advocacy groups, and 24% through a Jewish federation or foundation. The analysis suggests that informal, social settings such as private Shabbat dinner tables and workplace affinity groups served as primary catalysts, allowing individuals to experience community in a grounding rather than reactive manner.
Despite the positive momentum, the study identified significant barriers to sustained participation, noting that political tension surrounding Israel and antisemitism was cited 140 times as the single largest deterrent. Respondents described feeling alienated from multiple perspectives, with some feeling their criticism of Israel was unwelcome while others felt their communities were insufficiently supportive of the Jewish state. However, the report points out that rather than abandoning Jewish life entirely, most individuals experiencing political friction navigated it by finding alternative congregations or affinity groups that better aligned with their personal values.
Confidence in community safety and institutional preparedness showed notable improvements over the past year.
Fifty-eight percent of respondents stated that they know where to turn if personally targeted by antisemitism, up from 46% in 2025, while awareness of specific community security programs rose from 39% to 57%. Furthermore, 60% of Jewish Americans believe local organizations are effectively providing safety and security, compared to 47% the previous year.
JFNA provided actionable insights based on the survey’s findings for community leaders, advising organizations to leverage informal social structures, foster welcoming environments driven by ordinary peers rather than staff alone, and provide clear entry points for the sizable population of previously disengaged individuals who are still seeking a comfortable fit within the Jewish community.

Israel must follow through on British consulate closure after Miliband sanctions - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
03:10:20 UTC
12:10:20 KST

On September 8, just hours after British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced sweeping sanctions against trade with Jewish communities beyond the Green Line – the West Bank, Golan Heights, and east Jerusalem – Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar angrily shot back.
“Whoever acts against Israel – Israel will act against them, and they will lose their influence and relevance in the region. Measures against Israel will not go unanswered.”
Sa’ar announced several retaliatory steps, including closing the nearly 200-year-old British consulate in the Sheikh Jarrah neighborhood, which serves east Jerusalem and the West Bank, removing British representatives from the international aid center for Gaza in Kiryat Gat, and ending British activities to train Palestinian Authority forces through the British Support Team in Ramallah.
He also announced entry bans on 12 British elected officials and other citizens involved in antisemitic and anti-Israel activities. At the top of that list was ex-Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn.
Since then, the rhetoric of Miliband and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham against Israel has gotten even more strident.
Outlandish lie of ethnic cleansing by pro-Palestine validator Miliband
At the Labour Party convention last week, Miliband validated the pro-Palestinian protest movement that has swept Britain since October 7 – demonstrations that have, at times, left Jews feeling that parts of their own country were out of bounds. “We hear you, you were right,” he said, while repeating the outlandish lie of ethnic cleansing in the West Bank.
He stopped short of accusing Israel of genocide, saying this will be decided by international courts, even though he knows full well there is no genocide in Gaza.
Miliband and Burnham have dramatically reset Britain’s relations with Israel, to the detriment of both countries. Israel is entitled to respond.
Sa’ar was therefore right to order the closure of the British consulate. It is, indeed, high time for Israel to demonstrate that actions against it will be repaid in kind.
Britain and several other European countries seem to assume that they can punish Israel, try to dictate the contours of a future diplomatic agreement, and continue to enjoy the same access, cooperation and influence.
That assumption needs to be forcefully challenged.
At the Labour convention, Miliband said, “We will ban the import of goods from illegal settlements. We will disrupt the supply lines of British finance, British construction, and British services for illegal settlements. And when it comes to the attempt to destroy the two-state solution, this party, this movement, this government, says ‘we will not let you succeed.’”
But who are you, Mr. Miliband, to tell Israelis what arrangement they must accept for their future security?
Many Israelis regard a Palestinian state as an existential threat. Gaza is central to that fear.
Britain is entitled to its policies, Israel is entitled to levy consequences
Israel withdrew its soldiers and settlements, and Hamas turned the territory – essentially a mini Palestinian state – into a launching pad for attacks against Israel, culminating in the horror of October 7. British declarations do not answer the security questions that experience raises.
Britain is entitled to its policies. Israel is entitled to attach consequences to them.
Sa’ar should therefore ensure that the measures he announced are carried out, despite British threats to expel an Israeli diplomat from London for every diplomat expelled from the consulate.
To that we say: so be it.
Israeli diplomats in London serve Israel’s interests, but this relationship also serves Britain through intelligence sharing and security cooperation. A diplomatic rupture would cost Israel, but Britain would pay a price as well.
Those costs deserve consideration. But they do not justify allowing Britain to assume that its confrontational policies come free of charge, particularly when its approach – as its leaders have admitted – is designed to encourage others to follow their lead.
In the summer of 2025, when France recognized a virtual Palestinian state, and several other countries, including Britain, followed suit, Israel threatened to close the French consulate in the city. For various reasons, it didn’t follow through.
It should have. Threats not implemented weaken the credibility of the next warning.
Closing the British consulate would demonstrate that Britain cannot take its diplomatic access and influence in the region for granted while pursuing policies Israel considers harmful to its security.
Israel need not respond to every hostile statement with a diplomatic crisis. But when a government translates hostility into concrete punitive measures, a concrete response is warranted.
Sa’ar has announced that response. He should now carry it out.

- The proposal could boost Trump’s legacy and Palm Beach’s global profile, but it also adds to local disruption and anger over flights, road closures and other changes.
AI generated
WEST PALM BEACH, Florida – US President Donald Trump is seeking approval from local officials in the state of Florida to designate his West Palm Beach golf course into a permanently-designated presidential retreat that would host summits, world leaders and current and former occupants of the White House.
“Just like Camp David, Windsor Castle or the Elysee Palace are known worldwide, so too will the Presidential Golf Course in Palm Beach County,” according to a September letter from a lawyer representing Trump, Harvey Oyer, to the Palm Beach County commission.
The letter, which outlines the proposal, was viewed by Bloomberg.
Trump said on Oct 7 that the US military and Secret Service asked him to make the golf course into a retreat.
A White House official familiar with the plans confirmed the request to turn the facility into a space for high-level meetings and presidential golf sessions.
“They could spend the weekend there, like a retreat, like sort of a Camp David retreat, and they asked if I’d be willing to do it, and I said I would be,” Trump said at a press conference at the White House.
He also highlighted the course’s security features and proximity to the airport.
The potential presidential golf course adds to a slew of Trump efforts to use his name to memorialise his legacy.
In Florida, a road to his residence at Mar-a-Lago bears his name, as does the airport, which now goes by Donald J. Trump International instead of Palm Beach International.
In Washington, Trump has threatened to scrap efforts to renovate the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts unless his name is added to the building. The US Institute of Peace headquarters already bears his name.
At the golf site, the Trump family operates a club that would potentially benefit if the course becomes a major presidential hub. The retreat would have a separate entrance from the club, the Washington Post reported.
Oyer said Trump’s company would pay for construction of a presidential lodging facility at the course and that the President would be out of office before the project is completed.
Access to the club’s facilities would be provided at “no cost to the federal government”, Oyer said. The plans were first reported by the Palm Beach Post.
Trump’s presidency has had a profound impact on Palm Beach County, a relatively small community 110km north of Miami that’s historically known as a haven for retirees and winter retreat for the wealthy.
Besides the renamings, residents are constantly reminded of Trump’s presence with frequent road closures, blocked waterways and his now-permanent helipad.
Residents on the island of Palm Beach and on the mainland of West Palm Beach were incensed when the Federal Aviation Administration rerouted the flight path to avoid flying over Mar-a-Lago, a change the agency is seeking to make permanent even after Trump leaves office.
Palm Beach County owns the land where the golf course is located and leases it to Trump.
Under the proposal, Trump would give the county rights to the portion needed for the presidential retreat facilities, and the county would then lease that property to the federal government.
Oyer said that the presidential golf course would “further cement Palm Beach County on the global stage and do so in perpetuity”.
In December, Trump will host G-20 leaders at another of his golf courses, the Trump National Doral just west of Miami. BLOOMBERG

NTPC is also exploring technology collaborations with global players such as Holtec International and Westinghouse of the US, Rosatom of Russia and EDF of France for pressurised water reactor projects to be deployed at these locations, said an official aware of the development.With an installed power generation capacity of 89GW, including thermal, hydro and renewable capacity, the company is targeting 149GW by 2032 and 244GW by 2037, besides adding significant battery and pumped storage capacity. Its first nuclear project in Rajasthan’s Mahi Banswara, comprising four 700-MW units, however, is being developed through Anushakti Vidhyut Nigam Ltd, a joint venture with Nuclear Power Corporation of India.
The three identified locations, if approved, will have 2-4GW of nuclear capacity each, the official said.
NTPC entered into non-disclosure agreements with Rosatom and EDF earlier this year to explore technology collaboration for deploying large pressurised water reactor projects in India.“Technology transfer and localisation will be key factors in finalising the technology. There will be a separate joint venture with a global player for technology and design engineering,” said the official.Fuel availability will also be an important consideration in finalising the technology, the official said, adding that fuel sourcing falls within the domain of the Centre.
Atul Mathur is a Senior Assistant Editor at The Times of India with over 27 years of experience in journalism. He currently tracks the energy sector, writing on power, renewable energy, coal and mines.

Interview: GDI advances global development, South-South cooperation, says Pakistani envoy
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:52:49 CST
11:52:49 KST

by Wang Lu, Ma Ruxuan
GENEVA, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- The Global Development Initiative (GDI) has played a key role over the past five years in revitalizing the global development agenda and promoting South-South cooperation, a Pakistani envoy has said.
The initiative was proposed at an important time, bringing development back to the mainstream global agenda, which is an important contribution, Tahir Andrabi, Pakistan's Permanent Representative to the United Nations Office at Geneva, said in an interview with Xinhua.
Over the past five years, the GDI has implemented more than 1,800 "small and beautiful" projects in more than 120 countries, mobilizing over 23 billion U.S. dollars, he said.
Andrabi stressed that the GDI complements the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) while responding to the reality that the world still needs greater focus on development.
The latest UN data show that only 36 percent of the Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) targets with available trend data are on track or making moderate progress, and 15 percent have even regressed below their 2015 baselines.
"The world, particularly developing countries, is falling behind in meeting the needs of its people and the SDG targets. The GDI is an important initiative to fill these gaps," he said.
On China-Pakistan cooperation, Andrabi perceived the GDI as an important platform for charting the future trajectory of development and economic cooperation between the two countries.
"We believe that the GDI, together with the BRI and its flagship project CPEC (the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor) 2.0, will continue to further diversify avenues of development cooperation between Pakistan and China in the context of CPEC, and between China and the larger developing world in the context of the BRI," he said.
Andrabi expressed hope for deepening cooperation in high-tech fields such as AI, quantum computing and robotics, citing the immense opportunities in these areas.
"The GDI provides an opportunity to make these technologies available to developing countries, thereby harnessing the potential of these technologies to deliver direct benefits and generate employment," he said.
Andrabi also mentioned the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO) established in Shanghai this year with Pakistan among its founding members.
"We hope that WAICO, together with the GDI and the efforts of the Chinese government, will promote complementarities and work together to bring modern technology benefits to developing countries," he said. ■

Japan logs 4.06 trln yen current account surplus in August
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:52:27 CST
11:52:27 KST

TOKYO, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- Japan posted a current account surplus of 4.06 trillion yen (about 25.7 billion U.S. dollars) in August, up 12.0 percent from a year earlier, government data showed Thursday.
In August, the goods trade balance swung to a deficit of 687.7 billion yen, due to higher imports of crude oil and other commodities, compared with a surplus of 113.8 billion yen a year earlier, the Finance Ministry said in a preliminary report.
Exports rose 16.9 percent to 9.86 trillion yen and imports increased 26.7 percent to 10.55 trillion yen.
Meanwhile, primary income, which reflects how much Japan earned from overseas investments, expanded 21.6 percent from the previous year to 5.13 trillion yen, the ministry said.
The current account balance is one of the widest gauges of international trade. ■
