Feature: Learning Chinese in vogue among Kyrgyzstan's youth
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:52:09 CST
11:52:09 KST

BISHKEK, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- Initially a fan of Chinese TV series, 19-year-old Zuura Zakirova is now a student of the Chinese language.
Recently, the third-year Confucius Institute student at Kyrgyzstan's Osh State University performed a modern Chinese song and played the guzheng, a traditional Chinese zither, winning thunderous applause at an institute event -- one of her accomplishments after two years of Chinese learning.
She loves watching Chinese fantasy TV series. "I am particularly fascinated by the actors' period costumes," a tiny part of her obsession with Chinese culture, according to her.
Respecting the elders and valuing family ties, as highlighted by Chinese culture, particularly resonates with the Kyrgyz girl.
"Our culture has similar concepts. I love it when my family gathers around the festive table and everyone chats happily. I feel happy in that warm atmosphere," she said.
The experience of learning Chinese at the Confucius Institute has a profound impact on her, she said. "I've become more self-confident ... I was shy. Here, I've met many teachers and made a lot of friends."
"Now, I can communicate freely with Chinese people in their own language," she said.
Zakirova said she wants to be a teacher, just like her parents, and "I hope to teach the Chinese language to people in Kyrgyzstan and help with their personal growth through this language."
As Kyrgyzstan's ties with China have deepened, learning Chinese has become increasingly popular among young people in the Central Asian country.
The Confucius Institute where Zakirova studies has provided Chinese language courses for about 17,000 people since its establishment in 2013. Nearly 600 in total have won scholarships to study in China.
Some graduates have returned to join the institute. Among them is Gulperi Kadyrbekova.
One of the institute's first students, she became a teacher there in 2019.
In her early days of teaching Chinese, what frustrated her most was the failure to immediately answer the students' questions about such broader topics as Chinese society or economy, she said.
Hence, her extensive preparations for each class -- invaluable training and experience -- have brought her to career success today.
Kadyrbekova takes pride in her students' successes, such as passing language examinations and earning overseas study opportunities. "This year, the first group of students I taught graduated from Chinese universities. Some have already found good jobs. I am so happy for them," she said.
For Baikazak Sultanbekov, who studies at the foreign languages college of Jalal-Abad State University, the dream now is to get a chance as soon as possible to study in China.
It was prompted by his cousin's account of living in China.
"My older cousin studied at a university in Shanghai. He told me that Chinese is a difficult but interesting language, and that China is a rapidly developing country with skyscrapers and wide roads everywhere. Life there is very convenient," he said.
"I felt envious, so I decided to start learning Chinese."
The enthusiasm persists. "I think the most interesting thing about Chinese is its characters ... every Chinese character is like a work of art. That is precisely where their charm lies," he said.
Vowing to improve his linguistic proficiency as quickly as possible, Sultanbekov dedicates nearly six hours of a day to studying Chinese.
"In addition to my college studies and courses at the university's Confucius Institute, I review what I learned in class at home, read textbooks to prepare for Chinese language exams, and practice writing Chinese characters," the young man said, who also makes a point of speaking Chinese whenever possible.
Sultanbekov plans to follow in the footsteps of his cousin to pursue further study in Shanghai, and to work in the future as an interpreter.
"An increasing number of Chinese companies are operating in Kyrgyzstan ... This means I'll have a wide range of career options." ■

US bars Fiji-based man over corruption tied to China
The State Department has accused the official of paying bribes to Fijian citizens to advance Chinese interests.
The US Department of State has publicly designated a Fiji-based man for his involvement in corruption on behalf of Chinese actors.
Zhao Fugang, the director of the Overseas Chinese Service Center, “abused his public position by paying bribes to Fijian citizens to advance China-based government, business, and criminal interests”, the State Department said in a press release on Wednesday.
“His actions constituted significant corruption and adversely affected U.S. interests in Fiji.”
The designation renders Zhao and his immediate family members “generally ineligible for entry into the United States”.
The US embassy in Suva, Fiji’s capital, said Zhao’s actions left the Pacific nation open to “malign foreign influence facilitated by Chinese government, business, and criminal actors”.
The embassy also said, “Public reporting shows an established trend of criminals operating across the Pacific with ties to China.”
Beijing says Overseas Chinese Service Centers help its nationals with administrative issues abroad, such as renewing driving licences. However, rights groups have alleged they are fronts for Beijing to push interests abroad, including the targeting of dissidents.
In February, the Trump administration sanctioned two leaders of Pacific island nations for alleged corruption tied to China. The US Department of State issued a notice alleging that Hokkons Baules, the president of Palau’s Senate, and Anderson Jibas, a former mayor in the Marshall Islands, had created openings for China to increase its influence in the region.

Tanker hit by multiple projectiles off north coast of Qatar, UKMTO says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
02:48:25 UTC
11:48:25 KST

Tanker hit by multiple projectiles off north coast of Qatar, UKMTO says
British maritime agency has recently reported a rise in attacks on vessels in the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz.
A number of casualties have been reported after a tanker sailing off the north coast of Qatar was struck by multiple projectiles, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency has announced.
The vessel was hit by several projectiles 94 kilometres (58 miles) north of Madinat ash Shamal, UKMTO said on Wednesday. The incident comes as the British maritime agency reported a recent rise in attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz.
UKMTO did not say how many people were killed or injured in this latest attack, adding that authorities were investigating. It did not specify the origin of the ship.
An attack on a vessel in the middle of the Gulf is unusual. The Maritime Executive, a publication specialising in commercial shipping, said it was the first reported attack on a tanker in the western half of the Gulf in weeks.
Qatar has not commented on the reported attack, which falls within its exclusive economic zone.
Vessels have more commonly been targeted in the strategically important Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway linking the Gulf with the Gulf of Oman.
Before the United States-Israel war on Iran began on February 28, the strait typically handled about 125 large commercial vessels a day, and shipments through it accounted for about 20 percent of global crude and liquefied natural gas supplies.
In retaliation for US-Israeli attacks, Iran effectively closed the strait, while Washington has maintained a blockade on Iranian ports.
UKMTO said on Tuesday that there had been nine attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz this month, representing half of the September total in the waterway and the Gulf combined.
Despite the attacks, oil exports from the Middle East have risen to, and according to provisional data even surpassed, pre-war levels in recent weeks.
The seven-day moving average of Middle East crude exports reached 18.3 million barrels per day (bpd) on September 30, compared with about 18 million bpd on average in the 12 months before the war, according to Kpler, a data firm.

02:44:00 UTC
11:44:00 KST

MOSCOW, October 8. /TASS/. Ukraine has lost more than five billion dollars in foreign exchange revenue due to downtime at the Odessa ports, according to TASS calculations.
Commercial merchant ships continue to avoid the ports of Odessa, Chernomorsk, and Yuzhny. Only vessels affiliated with the Ukrainian armed forces are calling at those ports. Consequently, maritime trade is being routed through Danube ports - that is, Izmail in Ukraine and Constanta in Romania - which together can potentially handle no more than one-third of the exports that previously passed through the ports of Odessa. As a result, Ukraine exported only 44% of its planned agricultural exports in September. Exports of metallurgical products ceased completely by the end of September. These two commodities together accounted for about 65% of Ukraine’s total exports and about $26 billion in foreign exchange earnings per year.
The Odessa port shutdown has been ongoing since July 22.

Rubio blasts globalism and open borders at birthplace of Western civilization (VIDEO)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
02:39:34 UTC
11:39:34 KST

Rubio blasts globalism and open borders at birthplace of Western civilization (VIDEO)
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has delivered a blistering attack on open borders, globalism and the erosion of national sovereignty in Europe, warning from the ancient heart of Athens that the West risks sliding into “atrophy, servitude and decline.”
Speaking on Wednesday from the Pnyx, the ancient assembly site beneath the Acropolis, Rubio argued that Western governments had spent decades dismantling the very principles that had made their civilization successful.
“‘Nationalism’ became a dirty word,” Rubio said. “So we tore down our monuments, we condemned our own history, and in too many places we taught our children to be ashamed of the countries they would inherit.”
“In the process we opened our borders, and outsourced our industry, and allowed our militaries to wither and to decay,” he added.
Rubio contrasted the globalist approach embraced by much of the European political establishment with the Trump administration’s “America First” doctrine, arguing that governments have an obligation to put their own citizens above international institutions.
“It has become fashionable today to believe that enlightened foreign policy means prioritizing the global community over one’s own people,” he said, insisting the ancient Greeks understood that there was “nothing selfish or wrong about loyalty to your nation” or defending its interests “above all else.”
The remarks amount to the latest broadside from Washington in an increasingly bitter ideological dispute with the EU over migration, censorship and national sovereignty. The Trump administration has repeatedly portrayed Brussels and Western European governments as having betrayed their own populations.
US Vice President JD Vance has previously warned that Europe risks committing “civilizational suicide” through uncontrolled migration and curbs on free expression. At the Munich Security Conference last year, he argued that the continent’s greatest danger came not from Russia or China, but from an internal retreat from democratic values. The administration formalized much of that critique in its 2025 National Security Strategy, which warned that Europe faces potential “civilizational erasure.”
The trans-Atlantic clash has become particularly visible over immigration. Just this week, US President Donald Trump blamed violent unrest in France on “out of control mass migration,” rejecting claims that the nationwide student protests were primarily about underfunded schools. US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz similarly blamed Europe’s “open borders” and “unchecked immigration” for growing public anger.
Rubio nevertheless stopped short of calling for a rupture with Europe. Instead, he urged the continent to follow Washington’s nationalist turn, praising Greece as a “model ally” and saying there were already signs of a broader shift.
“We believe that Europe can awaken from its long slumber and rekindle the fire that was lit here millennia ago,” he said.
Rubio declared that the US, under Trump, had already chosen the “unapologetic pursuit of national power,” including reindustrialization, securing critical supply chains, rebuilding the military and seeking dominance in artificial intelligence, advanced manufacturing, weapons, space and other strategic industries.
The West, he warned, is now at an “inflection point,” with decisions made over the next decade potentially determining whether it remains at the center of global power or accepts a future of decline.

The Republican campaign to maintain control of the Senate has become increasingly focused on Texas, where Democrat James Talarico has emerged as a serious threat. A New York Times/Siena College poll released last weekend showed Talarico leading Paxton 51% to 45% among likely voters. Texas has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988.
Trump won the state by almost 14 percentage points in 2024, but his approval rating has fallen sharply. A Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on Monday put his approval rating at 32%, while registered voters preferred Democrats to Republicans 44%-37%.
Trump’s relationship with Paxton has sometimes appeared uneasy. Trump called Paxton “a pain in the ass sometimes” last week, but on Wednesday did not discuss a leaked recording of Paxton in which the Senate candidate reportedly complained about the war in Iran, rising fuel prices and the way his campaign was being run.
Instead he spent much of the rally attacking Talarico, whom he repeatedly referred to as “Tala-freako”. He claimed without evidence that Talarico is vegan and recently disappeared: “He’s sick because he’s been forced to eat meat for political reasons and he’s throwing up all over the place.”
Trump insisted: “The people of Texas are not going to let weak, gutless, self-hating, transgender-promoting freak shows destroy everything that we’ve built.”
The president’s political difficulties in Texas were underlined by the absence of the Republican governor, Greg Abbott, a close Trump ally who is himself facing a competitive re-election race against the Democratic state representative Gina Hinojosa.
Abbott was instead due to attend the dedication of a hospital about 330 miles away. Democrats seized on his decision not to appear with Trump.
Republicans have now devoted more than $300m to elections in Texas, according to the Associated Press, while Trump’s broader 32-day campaign blitz has taken him through several Republican-leaning states, including Oklahoma, Alabama, Ohio and Nebraska.

Major share market float of Firmus in trouble as interest wanes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
02:35:03 UTC
11:35:03 KST

Data centre company Firmus tries to save its mega share market float as interest underwhelms
In short:
The $44 billion Australian float of data centre operator Firmus appears to be in trouble.
But Firmus is not currently listed on the ASX's "upcoming floats and listings" webpage, and analysts who spoke to the ABC have raised concerns over the firm’s debts and the wild increase in its valuation over a short period of time.
What's next?
The company is scheduled to float on the ASX on October 23.
It was touted as the biggest float since Telstra in the 1990s, but the share market debut of data centre operator Firmus is in trouble before it has even hit the share market.
Investment banks stopped taking bids for the initial public offering (IPO) today and will now determine at what price the company lists on the Australian Securities Exchange (ASX).
But Firmus is not currently listed on the ASX's "upcoming floats and listings" webpage, and analysts who spoke to the ABC have raised concerns over the firm's debts and the wild increase in its valuation over a short period of time.
Adding to concerns, Goldman Sachs was reportedly tapped to rescue the float from collapse at midday today.
The ABC has contacted several industry players directly connected with Firmus's fundraising, including Wilson Asset Management, Bank of America and Goldman Sachs.
The investment bank told the ABC it had no comment.
Fund manager Roger Montgomery said there had been inconsistencies in the messages given to market participants about the capital raising.
"Investors were previously told that indicative orders were already above the size of the offer at $11 a share," he said.
Indicative orders are what investors suggest to brokers they are willing to pay for a stock before orders are formally taking for a public listing.
"If that were true, why has the price been cut to get the deal away?" Mr Montgomery said.
"Warren Buffett said you want to invest with people who are energetic, intelligent and honest."
No signs of life on ASX
The ASX told the ABC it does not comment on individual companies.
The floats and listings webpage, however, makes it clear that "it only records new listings for which ASX has received a formal listing application".
"A formal application would typically only be made late in the listing process when the entity has made all necessary preparations to list in the near term (i.e. within four to six weeks)," it says.
This would suggest a formal application has not been made by Firmus to the ASX within 15 days of its expected listing.
The caveat to this is that the ASX webpage also states that is "usually updated within three business days of receiving a formal application", meaning the official application may have been lodged.
Firmus was set to hit the boards of the ASX at $11 per share, but reports suggest that price may have been set too high.
Market participants have been underwhelmed by the float's roadshow, with some criticising it for having an "unprecedented lack of detail" and others concerned about its debt and energy needs.
The float, or total number of shares on issue, is reportedly having to be revalued down because of the lacklustre interest, with reports it could drop to about $8 per share.
Late on Wednesday, the company's representatives also pulled out of an appearance before a parliamentary inquiry into artificial intelligence today, with reports the troubled IPO was the reason for the no-show.
Mounting concerns from investors
Firmus is a so-called neocloud technology company.
It builds, owns and operates upscale data centres or so-called "AI factories", used to run and train artificial intelligence models.
The firm is raising cash from investors to build an AI factory in Launceston and plans for two more in Tasmania.
But its ambitions extend across Australia and into South-East Asian markets as well.
Reports suggest Firmus intends to raise up to $7 billion from institutional and retail investors in its IPO, which could value the company at more than $50 billion.
But the conclusion of a $73 billion partnership with data centre firm CDC and community backlash for proposed suburban data centres has caused concern for investors.
Firmus co-founder Oliver Curtis was also jailed for 12 months in 2016 for a 2007 insider trading scheme.
Portfolio manager 'steering clear'
Ten Cap portfolio manager Jun Bei Liu said she was steering clear of the Firmus IPO, concerned about what she said was an "unprecedented lack of detail" being disclosed and enormous structural risks.
"Firmus is probably one of the most polarising IPOs I have ever seen," she observed.
"I think Firmus is a very high-risk proposition — very high profile, but with enormous risk involved."
She said 97 per cent of the data centre capacity Firmus had promised had not been built.
"They might deliver cheaper earnings in two years if they build what they promise, but that's speculative," she said.
"We much prefer to be in the companies that actually build those data centres — the engineers, the electrical contractors.
"There are a lot of those smaller businesses now benefiting from the huge build-out that Australia is about to see."
Caution over Firmus 'euphoria'
Morningstar senior market strategist Lochlan Halloway said he saw "the hallmarks of the boom phase … if not outright euphoria" because of Firmus's wild increase in valuation in such a short period of time.
The company's valuation surged from about $6.9 billion in April and is now at $15.5 billion.
"Not bad for a start-up,"
he said.
Mr Halloway was particularly concerned with the company's debt.
"The neoclouds are heavily geared. The model is to borrow against customer contracts to buy chips, then use the rent to repay the loans," he said in an economic note.
Once its data centres are built, Firmus expects to be carrying about US$30 billion of debt, around six times the US$5 billion of operating earnings it forecasts for 2028.
"Borrowed money alone does not make a bubble, and plenty of infrastructure is sensibly funded with debt. But credit is the common thread running through essentially every boom and bust cycle," he wrote.
But he did not write the company off completely.
"For investors, what matters is how that fair value compares to the float price,"
Mr Halloway said.
'Ambitious' data centres plans need major local power upgrades
Accela Research published one of the first comprehensive reports on data centres in January this year.
Its lead data centre analyst Naomi Wagura described the company has having "ambitious growth plans" that could "significantly reshape electricity infrastructure" in areas where its data centres would locate.
In Tasmania, Firmus's three planned data centres would make it the state's largest energy consumer, needing some 444 megawatts if they went ahead, and would crucially require the island state to add extra generation.
"This infrastructure investment needs binding customer commitments and realistic demand forecasts, with clear arrangements for who pays if demand arrives late or falls short,"
Ms Wagura said.
And while there were clear potential benefits to locals, she cautioned there also needed to be "clear disclosure and enforceable obligations".
The company is scheduled to float on the ASX on October 23.

Footage sheds light on Iranian attacks that drove US troops from Kuwait base - report

2026-10-08
02:34:02 UTC
11:34:02 KST

A group of US soldiers who remained at Kuwait’s Camp Buehring after a prewar evacuation eventually left the installation amid repeated Iranian attacks and ammunition shortages, CBS News reported Wednesday.
The network’s investigation combines newly obtained footage of strikes and damage with accounts from personnel who served at the base during the opening stages of the war.
Most of the approximately 7,000 troops stationed there had been moved before fighting began, sources told CBS.
More than 100 stayed behind, with service members describing fears that they lacked the resources to manage an attack causing large numbers of casualties.
“We had to abandon the base,” one source told CBS anonymously, citing military restrictions on speaking to the media.
Soldiers moved to remote desert positions
According to CBS, the remaining troops took equipment with them in vehicles and departed at night for the Kuwaiti desert, where they established forward operating bases.
Their departure followed attacks involving ballistic missiles and drones, as well as what three service members identified as Iranian F-5 aircraft. NBC News had reported the accounts of fighter jets in April.
CBS also reported a critical shortage of .50-caliber ammunition at Camp Buehring. An Army logistics official working elsewhere in Kuwait corroborated concerns about ammunition supplies and other defensive resources.
The footage provides a visual record of the attacks and their consequences for the installation. CBS said it checked the recordings’ metadata and compared them with photographs of damage to establish their authenticity.
CENTCOM declines comment on soldiers’ accounts
CENTCOM declined to comment to CBS. The Pentagon referred the network to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s March 4 explanation of the military’s efforts to move personnel away from vulnerable locations.
Hegseth said more than 90% of Americans previously stationed at US bases had been moved beyond the range of Iranian fire while the military built up its offensive forces.
The soldiers interviewed by CBS nevertheless described continued risks after leaving Camp Buehring. Two were struck by lightning during desert sandstorms in late April, suffering burns and a ruptured eardrum, respectively, officials told the network.
CBS reported that commanders had sought to relocate the troops before those incidents but had not completed the move in time. The personnel transferred to Camp Arifjan in May before receiving further assignments inside and outside the Middle East.
No soldiers were killed by enemy fire at Camp Buehring or the desert positions, according to CBS, although several were injured.
Damage and supply shortages across US bases
Camp Buehring has supported US military deployments across the Middle East for more than two decades. The CBS investigation adds detail to earlier reporting about the vulnerability of American installations during the war.
The Jerusalem Post reported in September that a Pentagon inspector general assessment documented damage to hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases across the region, including Kuwait.
The assessment covered February 28 through June 30, estimated equipment losses at $3.7 billion and identified ammunition shortfalls and supply-chain bottlenecks.
The Pentagon disputed those findings in a response to the Post, saying the inspector general lacked access to all relevant information and rejecting claims that US munitions were depleted.

Russia has begun sabotage operations against Danish companies supplying Ukraine after concluding that broader disruption efforts failed to curb Western military support for the country, a Danish intelligence official said on Wednesday.
The shift reflects a significant escalation in Moscow's hybrid warfare campaign, the official, from the Danish national security and intelligence service (PET), told a homeland security conference in Copenhagen.
"What we saw in the spring was a lot of planning, but very little carried out; what we saw in early summer is that they started to carry out a lot more," the official said.
Russia concluded that its previous broad-spectrum targeting "did not have the effect of deterring the Western (military alliance) NATO from supporting Ukraine," the official added, and while Moscow maintains political control over operations, its operational boldness is growing and Russia is now "trying to hit targets that have a direct impact on the front line. That means weapons production."
Russia denies involvement in warfare operations
Moscow has repeatedly denied involvement in sabotage or hybrid warfare operations. The Russian embassy in Copenhagen rejected the allegations on Wednesday, accusing Danish authorities of making unfounded accusations against Russia.
The official cited a Russian defense ministry list of alleged European drone and drone component manufacturers that Moscow said in April amounted to potential military targets, without elaborating further.
Russia is increasingly using untrained proxies — including homeless people and people addicted to drugs — recruited via Telegram and other social media platforms. Recruitment typically starts with low-threshold tasks such as reconnaissance or photography, then escalates toward actual sabotage operations, PET has said.
"It could be anyone just looking for quick money," the official said. "If the first person isn't successful, they'll throw another one at the problem until they succeed."
Denmark's defense intelligence service last month said Russia is likely to intensify hybrid attacks against the West in coming months, after Germany blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport in August.
In September 2025, before Denmark hosted an EU summit, drones disrupted air traffic at six Danish airports, including Copenhagen, the Nordic region's busiest, in what Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen called a hybrid attack on her nation.

The quartz crystal component sector rebounded after losses in the previous session. Siward Crystal Technology gained 8.33%, Acer Cyber Security rose 6.79%, and Tai-Saw Technology added 3.82%, according to Sinotrade.

Interest in low-jitter, miniaturized, high-frequency control components has also increased with the development of high-speed computing interfaces for AI servers and automotive electronics.

In optical communications, Ezconn and Apac Opto Electronics hit daily limits, while Truelight and LandMark Optoelectronics gained more than 7%. Among silicon wafers, Avid Electronics and Formosa Sumco Technology hit limit-ups.
In chip packaging and testing, Winstek Semiconductor hit limit-up on expectations of strong demand for customized AI chips and growing expectations for higher memory prices. Chipboard Technology and Formosa Advanced Technologies gained more than 6%, while Lingsen Precision Industries rose 4.14%.
The market’s short-term focus has shifted from major AI-related stocks to second-wave opportunities in sectors benefiting from higher prices and favorable supply-demand conditions. Concord Securities investment director Liao Chi-hung (廖繼弘) said the TAIEX is approaching a key psychological level, while recent gains have made the market more prone to short-term fluctuations, according to CTEE.
Looking ahead to the fourth quarter, Liao expects the broader trend to remain upward but volatile. A pickup in trading volume could provide stronger support for further gains.
Liao expects the TAIEX to trade around 50,000 points this month, with the year’s high more likely to come in December. If the market stabilizes and attention shifts to next year’s outlook, Liao said the TAIEX could rise toward 53,000 points.
Liao said investment remains concentrated in technology stocks, with AI-related capital spending and continued infrastructure needs supporting the sector. Corporate earnings are also expected to remain an important source of support for the market.
Liao recommended focusing on individual stocks after market pullbacks rather than chasing gains. He said technology and traditional industries have continued to rotate, with advanced substrates, copper-clad laminates, and cooling-related stocks remaining among the stronger-performing sectors.

At San Antonio Rally, Trump Warns He’ll ‘Never Forgive’ Texas if Talarico Wins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
02:30:00 UTC
11:30:00 KST

Digging in to defend both his pride and his political fortunes, President Donald Trump on Wednesday returned to deep-red Texas to rally for Ken Paxton’s Senate bid, while revealing at times his own trepidation that one of the Republican Party’s longest winning streaks may be about to end on his watch.
As multiple polls show state Rep. James Talarico with a shot at becoming the first Democrat to win statewide in Texas in more than three decades, Trump warned the crowd in San Antonio, “We’ll never forgive you for what you have done if you let that happen."
“The people of Texas are not going to let a weak, gutless, self-hating, transgender-promoting freak show destroy everything that we built," Trump said at another point during his third trip to Texas in less than a month. "So you need to go and vote for Ken Paxton for U.S. Senate.”
Trump centered much of his remarks on Talarico, deploying nicknames and repeating incorrect claims that he is vegan. “Now he says he loves meat. But he’s a vegan. … He wants to eat a little piece of lettuce,” Trump said. “He’s sick because he’s been forced to eat meat for political reasons. And he’s throwing up all over the place. He’s sick.”
During a rally that was repeatedly interrupted by protesters, Trump largely made his remarks an emotional appeal to Texas machismo, reminding voters that he plans a firing-squad execution—the first since World War II—of a man convicted of attacking troops in Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009. He also mocked climate change and falsely claimed Democrats want to kill thousands of oil and gas jobs in Texas. He said gun rights and his own legacy are on the ballot this fall.
“I’ve basically been off-script for the entire night,” Trump said, stating the obvious.
The sprawling speech of discursives and legacy polishing came as Republicans try to weather the drag Trump has become for their candidates up and down the ballot. A Reuters-Ipsos poll of U.S. voters released Monday shows Democrats with a seven-point lead when it comes to which party should control Congress after this election. Others, such as The Economist-YouGov and Quinnipiac polls, have that figure in the double digits.
In the state with the longest border with Mexico, Trump repeatedly turned to amping up fears over an increase in illegal immigration, connecting it to the prospects of Democrats gaining power in Washington.
“If they get in, they will open your borders and let the entire world pour in like they did before. We can’t let that happen,” Trump said. “A vote for Talafreako is a vote to turn Texas into a dirty, failing, crime-ridden third-world dumping ground.”
The San Antonio rally was the latest sign of Trump’s effort to maximize his base’s turnout amid his slumping poll numbers. Multiple surveys now show almost two-thirds of Americans disapprove of how Trump is doing his job.
To counter that, Trump repeated his promise of $5,000 to every American if Republicans hold the majorities in the House and Senate. And in a more recent play, he promised new money for seniors. “Starting tomorrow, over 20 million seniors on Medicare will receive checks or deposits for over $100 each,” Trump said from the stage. He left out the part that less than a third of Medicare participants will get the one-time payments, checks, which will actually be $90.
Notably absent from Wednesday’s rally: GOP Gov. Greg Abbott, who is in an expectedly tight re-election bid on the same ballot as Paxton. But Trump appeared far more concerned about helping Republicans keep their narrow majorities in the House and the Senate. And central to the GOP holding on to the Senate is holding on to Texas.
“For decades, Texas has been the state where people flee to escape the economic oppression and social collapse of Democrat-run California, New York, Illinois, and other failing blue states. But if Talafreako and the Democrats get their way, all of that squalor, misery, poverty, homelessness,” Trump said, adding that he doesn’t even know Talarico’s real name. “I have no idea what the hell his name is,” the President said. “I just know him as Talafreako.”

Wallabies keep Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii on wing for Bledisloe Cup Test against All Blacks
In short:
The Wallabies will keep Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii on the wing for Saturday night's Bledisloe Cup Test at Eden Park.
Isaac Henry is the only change to the Wallabies' starting XV after being included at outside centre.
What's next?
ABC Sport will live blog the Bledisloe Cup Test on Saturday night.
The Wallabies have kept Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii on the wing for Saturday night's Bledisloe Cup Test at Auckland's Eden Park, with Isaac Henry named in the centres.
Henry has been included at outside centre to partner Len Ikitau in the Wallabies' midfield against the All Blacks.
Ikitau, who has recovered from an ankle injury, moves from outside to inside centre in the wake of Hunter Paisami's suspension.
Wallabies coach Les Kiss resisted the temptation to shift Suaalii from the wing back to the centres.
He has shown faith in 27-year-old Henry, who he coached at the Queensland Reds.
Kiss also handed Henry his Test debut two months ago, against Japan in Osaka.
Henry, who will be playing his fifth Test, is the only change to the Wallabies' starting XV following their stunning 42-38 win over world champions South Africa in Perth late last month.
The Wallabies made four changes on the reserves bench, opting for a 5-3 (forwards-back split).
Hooker Josh Nasser, prop Massimo De Lutiis, back-rower Nick Champion de Crespigny and fly half Declan Meredith earned call-ups.
De Lutiis and Champion de Crespigny are the respective replacements for Taniela Tupou and Tom Hooper, who have returned to their European clubs.
"Keeping consistency in the starting side gives us a solid foundation, while adding some freshness on the bench will provide energy late in the game," Kiss said in a statement.
The Wallabies have enjoyed a six-match unbeaten streak after beginning the Test season with defeats to Ireland and France in the Nations Championship.
Since Kiss took over from Joe Schmidt as coach, the Wallabies have recorded four wins and a draw.
But the All Blacks pose an almighty challenge, especially at Eden Park.
The Wallabies have lost 24 consecutive Tests against the All Blacks at the venue, with their most recent victory coming in 1986.
They did, however, beat Wales at Eden Park in the third-place play-off at the 2011 Rugby World Cup.
"There aren't many tougher challenges than playing New Zealand at Eden Park, but it's one we're excited by and know that we will need to be at our best in all aspects of our game," Kiss said.
Meanwhile, injury has forced the All Blacks to name Damian McKenzie at fly half as they look to maintain their stranglehold on the Bledisloe Cup.
McKenzie will start at 10 after Ruben Love (ankle) and Richie Mo'unga (calf) were ruled out.
Beauden Barrett will play fullback, with McKenzie having held down the role for all four Tests in the All Blacks' recent 3-1 series loss to the Springboks.
All three Barrett brothers will start against the Wallabies, with ex-captain Scott named at lock and Jordie slotting in the backline at inside centre.
The All Blacks have held the Bledisloe Cup since 2003.

IMF reaches tentative $1.21 billion bailout deal with Pakistan

IMF, Pakistan reach tentative $1.21 billion bailout deal
October 8, 2026
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has reached a staff-level agreement with Pakistan that could unlock about $1.21 billion (roughly €1 billion) in financing, the lender said on Wednesday, as the South Asian country grapples with spiking food and fuel prices, and high unemployment.
The bailout deal still needs to be approved by the IMF Executive Board.
IMF negotiator Iva Petrova said Pakistan had successfully navigated the impact of the Middle East conflict, with strong policies helping preserve macroeconomic stability.
How does the Middle East conflict impact Pakistan?
Pakistan's economy grew 4% in the first three quarters of fiscal 2026 with full-year growth estimated at 3.6%, the IMF said.
Petrova attributed the weakened momentum to "higher energy prices and supply disruptions."
Inflation eased to about 10.3% in September after peaking in May, while core inflation remained contained, Petrova said.
Pakistan remains dependent on external financing to shore up foreign exchange reserves and meet debt repayments.
A prolonged Middle East conflict makes it particularly vulnerable due to its dependence on Gulf energy imports, remittances and financing from the region, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence economist Ahmad Mobeen earlier this year.
In the recent past, Pakistan has had to turn to the IMF to tackle Islamabad's acute balance-of-payments crisis.

Labor split on ATO credit card ban as businesses call for leadership
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
02:19:12 UTC
11:19:12 KST

Business groups call for 'political leadership' as ATO digs in on credit card ban
In short:
The federal government is under pressure to intervene after the Australian Tax Office announced it would stop accepting credit card payments.
It is unclear if the government supports the change after conflicting comments from Labor frontbenchers.
What's next?
Business groups are calling for "political leadership" and say credit card use is critical for cash flow.
The federal government is facing growing pressure over the Australian Taxation Office's (ATO) decision to stop accepting credit card payments for tax bills, with small business groups and crossbench MPs warning the move could make it harder for businesses to manage cash flow.
Labor frontbenchers have presented a confusing picture of the government's position, with some urging the tax office to resume discussions with the business sector, while Assistant Technology Minister Andrew Charlton has said the government backs the ATO.
Housing Minister Clare O'Neil defended the Reserve Bank's decision to scrap the credit card fees, but indicated the government was worried about the ATO's response and the impact on small businesses.
"The government does have some real concerns about what the ATO is proposing to do here," Ms O'Neil said on Thursday.
"We really want the ATO to go back and talk to business about what they have decided to do here and think about how they can find a solution that works for everyone."
Small Business Minister Anne Aly yesterday urged the ATO to "keep talking with small businesses" and "find a way forward".
"I've spoken to small businesses, and they were rightly shocked by this decision, and I do think they should have been consulted," she said.
But Mr Charlton said small businesses that had previously relied on credit cards to pay tax bills would be able to find a workaround, pointing to flexible repayment schedules already available through the taxation office.
"The government supports the ATO's decision," he said.
"If we're saying that surcharges can't exist in the private sector, then surcharges shouldn't exist in the public sector."
In a statement this afternoon, Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the ATO was an independent authority and "made this decision on their own".
"The government insisted that if the ATO took this decision, they must provide a transition period to support businesses, which they have done," he said.
"We are continuing to engage with the ATO on this matter."
Business groups call for government intervention
The ATO met with small business groups on September 30 to foreshadow the public announcement the following day.
Business groups were then invited to a meeting yesterday "to answer follow-up questions and work through implementation and transitional arrangements for affected taxpayers".
The tax office ban on credit card use will start on December 1.
"The ATO will continue to engage with stakeholders, supporting taxpayers and tax practitioners, and seek opportunities to promote awareness through consistent communication and key messages," an ATO spokesperson said.
Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry chief executive Andrew McKellar said there should be a "clear message from government" in support of small business.
"It's now time, I think, for the political leadership in government to stand up and really say to the tax office, 'This is not how it works,'"
Mr McKellar said.
"Hopefully by the end of today or certainly by the end of the week … the tax office will be listening."
Members of the crossbench have also raised concerns about the change, with independent Kate Chaney calling on the ATO to reconsider the ban or grant businesses a longer grace period to adjust.
"Times are tough for small business owners," she said.
"Credit cards are one way businesses manage cashflow when a tax bill lands. Removing that option with around eight weeks' notice makes things harder."
Community Strong Australia MP Allegra Spender said the government must work with the ATO to find a "workable solution".
"Managing cash flow is difficult at the best of times, and businesses need to have the flexibility offered by credit," she said.
Government tries to tap into public frustration
The change was announced after the Reserve Bank of Australia, which is independent, banned credit card surcharges across the board, a move hailed by Labor as a cost-of-living win for taxpayers.
Last week, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Attorney-General Michelle Rowland posted videos to social media celebrating the change, which Mr Albanese said would save Australians money "every time you tap".
But public sentiment has swiftly turned since cafes and other small businesses simply increased prices for consumers in a bid to recoup fees still owed to the banks.
Mr Charlton rejected concerns that ending surcharges would force businesses to lift prices, saying payment processing costs had fallen.
"That reduction means that card payments are cheaper for businesses to process, so there's no reason as a result of this reform that consumers should be paying more when they tap their card for a coffee," he said.
The Coalition had slammed the credit card surcharge ban as a farce, with Nationals senator Bridget McKenzie saying ending the surcharge would not make everyday items cheaper.
"The prime minister promised that removing the surcharge would make coffees go down," she said.
"Guess what? It doesn't disappear. Businesses are being expected to absorb it."
Independent member for Fowler Dai Le said the government had failed to "read the room" and said small businesses were already under strain due to rising fuel and energy costs, but did not want to raise prices for consumers.
"This is one more blow to the ever-increasing costs of running their own business, and they don't know if they can keep their doors open into the future," she said.

Australia wants to regulate AI like banks and airlines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
02:19:08 UTC
11:19:08 KST

Australia outlines plans to make AI companies prove their safety systems work
In short:
The federal government wants AI developers to demonstrate their safety systems are effective under proposed laws drawing on banking and aviation regulation.
It argues voluntary safeguards are inadequate when companies face intense pressure to develop increasingly powerful technology.
What's next?
Labor is finalising national AI standards due by the end of the year with plans to legislate the new rules in 2027.
Australia would require AI companies to prove they are properly testing models and preventing harm under proposed new laws modelled on banking and aviation safety rules.
The federal government is finalising plans to regulate frontier artificial intelligence through national standards due by the end of the year, with recent incidents involving rogue agents underscoring the risks of the rapidly advancing technology.
Assistant Minister for Science, Technology and the Digital Economy Andrew Charlton has signalled the government wants to make AI companies demonstrate their safety systems are effective, rather than dictate how they should manage every risk.
He outlined the case for tougher frontier AI oversight in a speech in Sydney today, arguing Australia should put the "burden" where the risk was created.
"AI needs regulating because its harms are severe, hard to undo, borne by people who never chose them and sometimes invisible until they arrive,"
he said.
"The market will not fix this alone, because the incentives reward speed and capability, and even the people at the top of the industry cannot slow down by themselves."
Safety rules for banks, aviation show path for AI
Rather than trying to keep pace with the technology by banning specific dangerous behaviours, Australia's approach would require AI companies continually test for risks and show they can prevent harm.
Mr Charlton said there was not enough incentive for companies to comply with "voluntary" regulations or codes when it came to frontier AI risks.
"You cannot ask firms to volunteer against their own competitive interest amid a manic race involving trillions of dollars and then be surprised when they do not," he said.
He also warned detailed prescriptive rules could end up "out of date before the ink is dry" due to the pace of the technology's development.
"For these reasons, there is much that Australia can learn from systems-based regulatory approaches, that puts the onus and accountability on companies for managing how they develop products and services safely," he said.
Mr Charlton said this model was already used in workplace health and safety, supervision of banks and aspects of aviation safety.
"The goal is to ensure companies are meeting the expectations of safety, without trying to specify every hazard," he said.
"The question isn't only 'did something go wrong' but is there a serious system in place to detect risks and prevent incidents occurring."
Shadow Defence Minister James Paterson said Australia should be "very pragmatic and sensible" about regulating AI, adding he believed the position outlined by Mr Charlton was heading "in the right direction".
"The details will matter. We look forward to understanding what the government is proposing exactly," he told Afternoon Briefing.
Senator Paterson said the Coalition would not give Labor a "blank cheque" on AI but would support policies that landed in a "sensible place".
"The AI opportunity before Australia is a once-in-a-generation opportunity, but it does come with a very real risk, and it is important parties of government act in the national interest and with goodwill to try and get this right on behalf of our country," he said.
AI race not one Australia can 'win' or 'sit out'
The push for tougher regulation has been sharpened by revelations OpenAI agents gained unauthorised access to Australian government websites, including a Medicare statistics portal, during testing.
OpenAI has now backed mandatory safety requirements, independent assessments and incident reporting, while also calling for international standards.
The company's chief executive, Sam Altman, told the United Nations last month the "most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone".
"We need accurate and speedy incident reporting, classification and reporting protocols, so the world can learn from failures before they become catastrophes," he said.
Mr Charlton said frontier AI labs were currently putting "capability ahead of safety" as they raced each other, with a broader competition also playing out between the US and China.
He said Australia's task was not to "win" that race or "sit it out" but to "change it so that this technology is built to serve people".
Australia must 'host and build' AI
Mr Charlton said safety standards alone would not be enough due to "hostile states or criminals who were never going to comply".
"Relying on regulation alone is like building a fence around a horse, only to realise that horse has wings," he said.
Mr Charlton said if Australia wanted a say in how AI technologies were built and governed, it needed to be a country that could "host and build them".
"This is our chance to shape this technology, for our standards to set the rules of the road globally over decades," he said.
Shadow Foreign Minister Ted O'Brien has called for Australia to strike a deal with the United States to secure preferential access to the most advanced AI models and strengthen defences against cyber attacks.
"We can use AI as a shield to counter AI being used as a sword,"
he said.
In a speech at the University of Technology on Wednesday, Mr O'Brien said Australia should pursue a government-to-government agreement guaranteeing continued access to American technology, while developing its own sovereign AI capabilities.

wood, ratchet straps, and metal joints shape mobile installations for design festival in denver

wood, ratchet straps, and metal joints shape mobile installations for design festival in denver
common ground festival brings together designers, students, and community organizations to create five reusable installations that can move beyond the festival site and continue supporting community activity across denver.
Five installations bring community stories into Denver Festival
The inaugural Denver Community Design Festival, co-developed by Leyuan Li and the Denver Mayor’s Office of Community Outreach, takes place at the Denver Performing Arts Complex from September 24th to October 7th, 2026. Titled Common Ground, the festival brings together CU Denver students, practicing designers, city leaders, and community organizations to explore community-led approaches to architecture and public space.
The festival features five temporary installations developed in collaboration with five community-based organizations, including the Colorado Immigrant Rights Coalition and Empower Media Exchange. Each installation responds to the needs and stories of its partner organization, taking forms such as a performance stage, storytelling kiosk, or mobile bookstand.
Dismantlable structures extend festival into community spaces
The structures are organized within a linear display framework and use a flexible assembly system of wood, ratchet straps, and metal joints. Designed for easy dismantling and reassembly, the installations can be transported and adapted to different locations.
During the festival, the structures host community-led performances, discussions, and workshops. After the event, they will be relocated to the neighborhoods of their partner organizations, allowing the temporary installations to continue functioning as spaces for public interaction and community activity.
Through its combination of design-build installations, community partnerships, and reusable construction systems, the festival, co-developed by Leyuan Li and Office for Roundtable, positions architecture as a tool for public exchange while bringing community-authored perspectives into Denver’s built environment.

AU-mandated Africa Credit Rating Agency officially launched in Mauritius
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:04:34 CST
11:04:34 KST

This photo taken on Oct. 7, 2026 shows the logo of the Africa Credit Rating Agency (AfCRA), an African Union (AU)-mandated institution, in Balaclava, Mauritius. Headquartered in Port Louis, the capital of Mauritius, AfCRA aims to strengthen how international financial markets assess and understand African sovereigns, sub-sovereigns, and businesses by improving data, expertise and context on African credit risk, helping enhance Africa's voice in global financial governance. (Photo by Ally Soobye/Xinhua)
PORT LOUIS, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- The launch ceremony of the Africa Credit Rating Agency (AfCRA), an African Union (AU)-mandated institution, was held on Wednesday in Balaclava, northern Mauritius.
Headquartered in Port Louis, the capital of Mauritius, AfCRA aims to strengthen how international financial markets assess and understand African sovereigns, sub-sovereigns, and businesses by improving data, expertise and context on African credit risk, helping enhance Africa's voice in global financial governance.
The agency is a private sector-driven, self-funded independent entity founded under the oversight of the AU's African Peer Review Mechanism. Governments cannot own shares in the agency, which is intended to ensure its independence from political influence, according to the AU.
AfCRA's ratings will cover African sovereigns, sub-sovereigns, corporates, public and private institutions, and may also rate non-African entities, subject to management decisions.
At the ceremony, AU Commission Chairperson Mahmoud Ali Youssouf said that AfCRA aimed to provide African and international investors, as well as economic partners, with reliable studies and analysis of African economies.
He said that when risk assessments were driven by "political considerations," the resulting high cost of capital could hinder investors and African countries from investing in infrastructure, health, education, energy and industrialization, further compounding the "significant debt service pressures" facing member countries.
According to the AU, Africa's external debt service rose from 61 billion U.S. dollars in 2010 to 163 billion dollars in 2024, with interest payments exceeding public spending on health or education in most countries. Against this backdrop, the agency will seek to reduce such burdens by improving investor confidence and market transparency.
The AU figures also show that currently only 32 African states carry ratings from the three major international credit rating agencies, while the rest remain unrated. AfCRA will therefore expand coverage to open capital markets to more African issuers.
However, Youssouf said that AfCRA was not intended to replace existing international credit rating agencies, but to complement them by providing an "additional Africa-focused perspective." ■
Guests attend the launch ceremony of the Africa Credit Rating Agency (AfCRA), an African Union (AU)-mandated institution, in Balaclava, Mauritius, Oct. 7, 2026. Headquartered in Port Louis, the capital of Mauritius, AfCRA aims to strengthen how international financial markets assess and understand African sovereigns, sub-sovereigns, and businesses by improving data, expertise and context on African credit risk, helping enhance Africa's voice in global financial governance. Polanski’s final pitch in Holborn by-election: I’ll keep Burnham honest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

LONDON — Zack Polanski promised to smash Britain’s two-party political system — but his campaign for a U.K. parliamentary seat has leaned heavily on the idea that he can keep the existing prime minister honest.
POLITICO analysis of the online battleground in the Holborn and St. Pancras by-election – which takes place Thursday — shows the Green leader has been pitching himself as a protest vote for Labour-backing constituents in the London seat, which has been held by Labour since its creation in 1983.
The party has spent nearly £5,000 pushing ads on Meta’s platforms, which include Facebook and Instagram, promising that a Green win would help “keep the government in check.”
In one campaign video, Polanski takes credit for a series of Labour U-turns on their “most unpopular policies” over the last 12 months. A victory in the seat, he claims, would add further pressure on Prime Minister Andy Burnham to listen to the Greens, rather than “Nigel Farage, Donald Trump, or their corporate donors.”
An additional £7,000 has been spent by the party promoting graphics of recent newspaper headlines it thinks demonstrate the influence it holds over Burnham’s Labour government — including a Guardian story flagging a possible delay on North Sea gas field decisions until after the by-election.
“When Zack Polanski speaks, Labour listens. That is the power of the leader of the Green Party,” the accompanying ad copy states.
Building Brand Zack
The by-election marks Polanski’s first attempt to win a seat in the House of Commons.
The left-wing leader oversaw a rapid polling increase for the Greens after taking charge in September 2025, snatching a Labour safe seat in Gorton and Denton under former Labour Prime Minister Keir Starmer the following February.
But its polling momentum appears to have stalled since Labour switched to Burnham, and the party has also faced internal rows over anti-semitism.
The party has spent around £8,000 on targeted ads highlighting endorsements for Polanski from local residents, including former independent candidates and NHS workers.
And at least £500 of that has been spent promoting effusive praise of the Green leader from his own local hairdresser.
Alongside a picture of the pair hugging, barber Rami is quoted saying: “I’ve been cutting Zack’s hair for years. When you chat to him you can tell how much he really cares.”
A significant number of the showcased endorsements come from former Labour backers and members as Polanski seeks to convince voters that Burnham’s majority — and the mid-term timing of the contest — means they can register a protest vote in the symbolic seat previously held by Starmer.
One standalone advert features former Labour member Gopa, who says: “We all know there will still be a Labour government whoever wins, so I’m excited for a Green candidate who will listen to us and help push Labour to do better.”
Other endorsements include a Labour member of three decades who says she is now backing Polanski after her former party “lost its way and let me down.” Ex-Labour councillor Naser says he’s switched his allegiance to “keep the pressure on, and keep Labour in check.”
The Labour pitch
By contrast, Labour candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali has kept her campaign local.
She has spent more than £21,000 with Meta promoting dozens of slick cinematic clips and polished graphics pitching herself as a “local champion.”
Supported by Labour’s well-oiled digital team, Abdi-Wali’s online campaign focuses heavily on her experience of arriving in the area as a child refugee, and her subsequent career as a local councillor.
Labour has also pumped more than £20,000 into Google’s ad program. The majority of that sum was spent on bitesize YouTube ads, with the remainder spent on buying up sponsored Google search results in an attempt to grab the attention of voters hunting for information about the contest.
Also running
Britain’s hard-right Restore Britain has also been making a pitch to voters in Holborn and St Pancras — while openly admitting it has no chance of winning in “one of the most left-wing seats in Britain.”
Rupert Lowe’s party has spent around £30,000 on Meta ads positioning itself as a “genuine patriotic alternative” to Nigel Farage’s Reform UK — which has not spent significant cash in the contest.
Restore’s spending included £1,500 promoting a “quiz” comparing comments from Reform politicians with Restore’s more hard-line agenda. A further £2,000 went on promoting a graphic of the “ten reasons” why voters should support it.
That list includes removing “millions of foreign nationals who hate who we are,” a promise to “reverse the Islamification” of London, deport “foreign tramps who ruin our city” and force “healthy” benefit claimants to clean graffiti and pick litter.
In a further attempt to present his insurgent party as a credible alternative to Reform or the Conservatives, Lowe’s paid online content repeatedly describes the by-election as a “free hit” for right-wing voters to “vote with your heart.”
“They don’t want the capital reformed, or conserved,” one paid ad states. “They want London restored.”

====================================================================================================

Far-right Vox sees election as its big chance to reshape Spain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

MADRID — Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has finally done something the far right approves of — calling a snap election on Nov. 29 that the anti-immigrant Vox party is hailing as “Spain’s last chance to be Spain again.”
Polling third in the race, Vox is Spain’s leading nationalist, euroskeptic force and it sees next month’s contest as its prime opportunity to remold the country after eight years of Sánchez’s socialist premiership by getting its people into top ministerial jobs.
Party leader Santiago Abascal greeted Monday’s election announcement as “excellent news.” His delight is hardly surprising given that polls suggest Vox is on track to make the biggest gains of any major party.
Advertisement
While the center-right People’s Party is expected to come first — with about 33% of the vote, according to POLITICO’s Poll of Polls — it will almost certainly have to team up with Vox, which commands support of about 18%, to build a stable coalition.
Abascal will then be able to demand the inclusion of key elements of Vox’s agenda as its price for that partnership. Its goals include deportations of undocumented migrants, a benefits preference for Spaniards over foreign nationals, slashing EU health and safety rules in the farming sector and rolling back support for gender equality and the LGBTQ+ community.
Vox secured 33 of the 350 seats in Congress in 2023, but is now set to double that. Under the PP’s coalition leadership, it should be able to form part of a comfortable majority.
“This time round, Vox is much stronger,” José Antonio Fúster, spokesperson for the party and a member of the Madrid regional parliament, said. “We are going into a very important election, not so much for us, as for Spaniards … This is the last hope for Spain to be Spain again.”
Fúster would not be drawn on which ministries his party has set its sights on, warning against “selling the bearskin before it has been hunted.”
Pointing to talks with the PP in recent months in four regions where the two parties now govern in coalition, he said the shaping of policy was being prioritized ahead of institutional power. “That is the last thing we negotiate because it is the least important,” he said.
Advertisement
Pet portfolios
In August, Vox MEP Jorge Buxadé told POLITICO that forming part of the government was not the only option open to his party, but that in a hypothetical coalition with the PP, his party would seek a number of ministries “in proportion to our vote share.”
That would amount to a significant percentage. If current polls translate into results in November, Vox would be in a position to claim about a third of ministerial posts.
Analysts expect Vox to press for portfolios that focus on its pet policies, such as agriculture, domestic policy, immigration and industry. The culture and education portfolios could also be of interest to the party, given their relevance in the hard right’s campaign against so-called wokeism.
The regions where the PP and Vox currently govern together — Andalusia, Aragón, Castile and León, and Extremadura — offer clues: The government departments that Vox controls are mainly linked to agriculture, welfare benefits and the family.
The party is heading into the election campaign espousing three main ideas: the concept of “national priority” — ensuring that Spaniards have access to public services and benefits ahead of foreign nationals — a clampdown on immigration and broad deregulation.
Although Vox’s rise to prominence was driven by its fierce stance against Catalan nationalism nearly a decade ago, that debate has faded from the political arena. Now, its focus is, like its European far-right counterparts, more firmly on immigration-related matters.
Advertisement
“Before, Vox talked about immigration, but it wasn’t the nuclear issue it has become,” said Guillermo Fernández Vázquez, a political scientist at Carlos III University and author of a book about the European far right. “Now, when Vox talks about social security payments, it talks about immigration; when it talks about the economy, it talks about immigration. Immigration is the issue that dictates everything.”
Vox also subscribes to the “remigration” policy being touted by many far-right parties, under which undocumented migrants and those who commit crimes would be deported. The PP has appeared to respond to Vox’s hard line by toughening its own stance, calling for the expulsion of foreign criminals and opposing a government migrant legalization program.
In each of the regions where the two parties are in coalition, Vox has ensured that its senior partner agreed to formally include the national priority principle in their governing agreement.
Alberto Núñez Feijóo speaks at the People’s Party congress in Madrid on June 5, 2026. | Thomas Coex/AFP via Getty Images
“But when it comes to national priority, the PP has added the caveat that it has to be implemented in line with the law,” said Miguel González, a journalist at the El País daily newspaper and author of a book about Vox. Legislation prevents discrimination against foreign nationals when it comes to accessing public benefits and services, meaning the policy is currently little more than symbolic in those regions.
“In reality, in order to implement this properly, you’d have to change the immigration law,” González added.
Vox is eyeing an overhaul of that legislation to make it a workable policy.
Advertisement
“It’s very possible to change laws that are bad for Spaniards, so we have to roll them back and introduce new laws, making sure that Spaniards are not last in line,” Fúster said.
Deregulation nation
Deregulation also offers a platform from which to attack EU health-and-safety norms that are reviled by the farming sector, one of Vox’s main voter bases.
Fúster accepted that this could lead to clashes with the European Commission, but insisted that pressure from what he described as a rising tide of European parties sharing Vox’s values would “make sure that Brussels returns to the path of common sense.”
PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo has criticized phytosanitary restrictions on farmers but has shown little appetite for conflict with European institutions.
In social policy, González said Vox might use the broader notion of deregulation to dismantle funding for gender equality and LGBTQ+ departments and projects, as it has done on a local level. Fúster was reluctant to be drawn on this: “We believe in the equality of Spaniards,” he said. “We don’t believe that anyone should have privileges above others.”
Fernández Vázquez of Carlos III University said that the origins of Vox suggest a bumpy ride for the PP. Vox would be the first far-right party to enter government in half a century since the death of Francisco Franco in 1975 — and there would likely be clashes.
Advertisement
The far-right party formed in 2013 as a breakaway from the conservatives in frustration at what its founders saw as the pusillanimity of the PP in the face of Catalan separatism.
“I think the relationship between Vox and PP [in government] will be a bad one,” the researcher said. “Abascal and his colleagues are going to enjoy showing up Feijóo whenever they can, portraying him as lukewarm and weak.”
Fúster accepted “it could be a difficult relationship,” adding that the PP “don’t see things the way we do and we don’t share their vision.”
“We’re not willing to make concessions, we’re willing to have a frank, open and reasonable negotiation.”
But for now, the priority is simply to remove the Socialists. In his traditionally combative style, Abascal insisted the election was a chance to hold on to “the peace, prosperity and freedom that a mafioso government wants to snatch from us forever.”

====================================================================================================

Far-right surge threatens Europe’s drive to rearm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

The growing popularity of far-right parties across Europe is sparking worries in NATO that they could weaken public support for rearmament and military aid to Ukraine as risks grow of a confrontation with Russia.
In France, Italy, Belgium, Germany, Poland and Romania, these parties are looking to turn voters’ cost-of-living concerns into opposition to aid for Kyiv, and rejection of higher national defense budgets and a greater role for the EU in defense — although each party has often sharply diverging views on those issues.
France’s National Rally leader Marine Le Pen last month called for limiting aid to Ukraine, saying: “financially, we can’t do it anymore.”
Advertisement
Roberto Vannacci, a former general and MEP who leads the far-right National Future party, which is increasingly challenging Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, called for a rethink of defense spending. “Let’s evaluate whether this military spending is justified: in my opinion, it isn’t, especially at a time when commodity prices are hitting record highs,” he said last week.
The challenge for Europe’s mainstream parties is how to sustain support for higher defense budgets even if that means competing with welfare and other priorities.
“People are struggling with the rising cost of living across the board … so there’s room for populistic rhetoric about how much should we support Ukraine financially, or how much should we invest in defense,” said Janne Kuusela, permanent secretary at Finland’s defense ministry.
The dilemma is sharpening as several large NATO members, including France, Italy and Poland, face elections in 2027, when far-right parties stand a real chance of coming to power. Many countries are also beginning talks on next year’s budgets.
For NATO, a spending slowdown would complicate efforts to meet the alliance’s target of spending 5% of GDP on defense and security by 2035. Four NATO diplomats, granted anonymity to speak freely, said the risk is a growing concern, though some said its effects may not be clear until next year’s budget cycle.
“We’re already in a situation where we need to catch up” with Russia, said a NATO military official. “So far, we’re on a positive trajectory — if someone closes the faucet, there’s a risk of losing capabilities.”
Advertisement
Turning the tide
European countries and Canada are expected to spend $634 billion on core defense needs this year, an 11% hike relative to 2025. But public support has limits.
In eight European countries, an average of 46.2% of respondents said they would not back higher defense spending if it meant higher taxes, while 35.5% were in favor, according to an August poll assessed by the European Council on Foreign Relations and shared with POLITICO. More people were opposed to increasing taxes to finance military spending in Germany, France, Italy, Spain and Poland. Respondents in the Netherlands, Sweden and the U.K. were more likely to accept higher taxes for military spending.
Protests against higher defense spending have taken place in Rome, Brussels and Madrid this year, with demonstrators criticizing cuts to funding for hospitals, universities and social services.
A damaged residential building is seen in Kyiv after a Russian missile strike on July 6, 2026. | Genya Savilov/AFP via Getty Images
Support for Ukraine is declining as well, according to NATO’s internal polling from this spring, falling from 59% in 2025 to 55% this year, with lethal aid the least popular form of support.
Far-right pushback on defense varies across Europe and falls broadly into three categories: opposition to military aid for Ukraine; rejection of EU-level defense projects; and criticism of defense spending more broadly. Yet all threaten to halt the continent’s effort to rearm rapidly and jointly — and limit Russia’s aggression against Ukraine.
The right’s political foes warn that opposition plays into the Kremlin’s hands. “The pressure from the right doesn’t actually come from the right, but largely from Moscow,” German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said. Parties such as National Rally and the AfD have longstanding ties with Russia, though they have sought to shake off their links in recent years.
Defense spending pressure
The political risk varies by country. Le Pen is a front-runner to become French president, while the AfD has made gains at the regional level but is unlikely to take national office soon.
Far-right gains are putting centrist parties under pressure to defend higher spending or consider cuts to retain public support.
“There is a risk that the formally pro-European mainstream across Europe might be too timid to spend … as would be necessary on defence,” said Paweł Zerka, senior policy fellow at the ECFR.
While Le Pen’s National Rally has indicated that she would respect France’s current trajectory of increasing military spending, Italy’s Meloni last week proposed spending €8 billion less on defense than the government’s initial proposal amid pressure from her far-right coalition partner, the League.
“You can’t spend on weapons what you can’t spend on pensions, excise tax relief, or utility bills,” Claudio Borghi, a League senator, said last week.
Advertisement
In Poland, President Karol Nawrocki, backed by the right-wing Law and Justice party, tried but failed to block access to nearly €44 billion in EU SAFE defense loans, saying the scheme risked making Poland dependent on Brussels and saddling future generations with debt.
Pressure to rethink defense spending could make it harder for NATO members to fund the capabilities officials say are needed to deter Russia, as capitals begin talks this month on determining the alliance’s war plans, which are due by 2029.
A slowdown by larger members such as France and Italy would have broader effects because they account for a greater share of defense investment and aid to Kyiv, one of the NATO diplomats said.
“If bigger countries stop making progress, then NATO will stop making progress,” the diplomat said. “You weaken NATO, you weaken Europe’s ability to defend itself, and you make Ukraine … more vulnerable.”
It could also affect the sum earmarked for defense in the EU’s next long-term budget if talks stretch on into next year, said Guntram Wolff, a senior fellow and defense economics analyst at the Bruegel think tank.
“Nationalists are all only interested in their country, they don’t want to work together with other European countries,” said German lawmaker Marie-Agnes Strack-Zimmermann, who chairs the European Parliament’s defense committee.
