‘In my story I’m the hero, but I’m the failure’: Tank commander haunted by Oct. 7
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
01:58:43 UTC
10:58:43 KST

If Bar Zonshine had been asked on Oct. 6, 2023, what his life would look like, his answer would have been very different from the one he gives today. He wanted to become a mechanical engineer, travel through Alaska and eventually leave the IDF.
Three years later, at 26, when asked where he sees himself in another three years, his answer is simple: “Probably in some trench beyond enemy lines.”
Between those two answers lies Oct. 7.
The interview is part of Ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth’s “Where Are They Now?” project, revisiting several people whose actions during the Oct. 7 massacre became symbols of courage and survival.
‘In the end, I did not accomplish my mission’
Zonshine was 23 on Oct. 7 and commanded a tank company in the 77th Battalion of the IDF’s 7th Armored Brigade in the Kissufim sector near the Gaza border.
For two and a half days, he and his men fought continuously. At one point, his tank was the only one operating along a 19-kilometer stretch of the sector.
Four soldiers from Tank 3 under his command were abducted: Omer Neutra, Oz Daniel, Shaked Dahan and Nimrod Cohen.
His actions became one of the best-known battlefield stories of that day, and some compared him with Avigdor Kahalani, the celebrated Israeli tank commander whose forces held off Syrian armor during the 1973 Yom Kippur War.
But “hero” is almost the last word Zonshine would use to describe himself.
“In my story I’m the hero, but I’m the failure,” he said. “However you turn it around, that’s what it is. Today I can give exact numbers, how many I killed, how many encounters there were, how much fighting there was. But when you’re a commander in the IDF and you have responsibility, there’s an unwritten contract between you and the people and the kibbutzim.”
“I look at the four-year-old riding his bicycle and I commit to protecting him. He looks at me and knows I’ll do everything I can to protect him.”
Asked whether there is room for self-compassion, given that he was a young officer suddenly thrown into an event of almost unimaginable scale, he refuses to give himself that concession.
“In the end, I did not accomplish my mission. They penetrated our defenses. People were abducted in our sector. Residents were murdered. We failed, even with all the actions and all the heroism.”
“The entire Israel Defense Forces failed that day in protecting the residents of the Gaza border communities. That stays with us.”
Nir Oz and the tank that never leave him
There are two images from Oct. 7 that Zonshine knows will remain with him forever.
The first is the tank carrying his four soldiers. The second is Kibbutz Nir Oz.
“Those are two moments that will stay with me forever and accompany me every day,” he said. “One is reaching the crew’s tank. The second is Nir Oz, which we did not enter and whose residents we did not reach in time.”
The question “what if?” still surfaces every day.
Looking back, Zonshine says he can explain to himself why it took hours of fighting before he reached his soldiers’ tank.
Nir Oz is harder.
While fighting in the area that morning, he saw terrorists arriving from the direction of the kibbutz. Amid the chaos, he could not understand what that meant in real time. Only later, when he learned what had happened there, did the picture become clear.
Asked whether, in hindsight, he would have changed his priorities and gone first to his soldiers rather than the communities, his answer is unequivocal.
“My first duty was to go to the kibbutzim. Even looking back, I would do the same thing. I would do everything to save the residents before myself.”
The four abducted soldiers remained with him when his company later entered Gaza.
“Every day, every hour, every mission,” he said. “No matter the level of risk, whenever there was even the slightest indication involving captives or missing people, we did everything, absolutely everything, to try to bring them back.”
Just over two weeks after Oct. 7, his company was back in combat.
“Those soldiers are the real heroes of Israel,” he said. “This was a company that had an entire platoon wiped out and half the company had gone through an enormous event, and yet they entered Gaza and fought there for more than a year.”
‘Oct. 7 is not my calling card’
For Zonshine, the war did not end on Oct. 7.
He continued fighting in Gaza for the following year. He later moved on to command the training of armored corps officers, fought alongside his cadets and in November 2025 began studying law.
Even then, the army called him back to combat. Along the way, he lost more soldiers.
Meetings with bereaved families were among the hardest moments.
“You arrive and lower your eyes because you come with this feeling of colossal failure,” he said. “My job as a company commander is to win the battles my commanders give me and bring my people home.”
“When a soldier is killed under my command, I failed. Going to a mother who raised her son for 21 years and telling her that he didn’t come home is very difficult.”
Counterintuitively, those meetings strengthened his decision to remain in the military.
“The message from the families, both of the hostages and of the fallen, was to keep moving forward and make sure their sons did not die for nothing,” he said. “Something in that continuing last will and testament directed me toward serving the State of Israel through the IDF.”
Zonshine was wounded twice during the war. On one occasion, he said, he woke up in intensive care.
Even then, the company was what occupied his thoughts.
“When you command people, you walk around with a nine-ton weight on your back, always,” he said. “All I could think about was getting back to the company. That was the only thing that mattered.”
“If there is a situation on the battlefield where I have to risk my life to save my soldiers, I will do it without thinking twice.”
Between rounds of fighting, Zonshine suddenly found himself somewhere that felt almost foreign: university.
“I was in shock,” he recalled. “I said, how does the average person wake up in the morning without being responsible for about 100 people running around them? At first it drove me crazy. Being responsible only for myself was almost too much for me.”
The ordinary problems of people his age look different now as well.
“It aged me an entire lifetime,” he said. “Sometimes I look at the problems people have, at the things that keep them awake, and I think it’s worlds apart. The car breaks down, things like that. For me, everything else has become smaller.”
But the change goes beyond perspective.
Over the past year, Zonshine has been in a relationship with Neta, who also serves in the military. They met at an army conference where he had been invited to speak about Oct. 7.
He saw her and approached her the old-fashioned way, face to face.
But he told her the full story of that day only months later.
“Oct. 7 is not my calling card,” he said.
“One of the things that changed is that you become a little more numb, and that shows in your emotions too. To go out and fight for such a long time, you put layer after layer of body armor over yourself, over your feelings and over your soul.”
“Only when I let that vest open did I feel it was right to speak to her openly.”
They are already talking about having a family.
Zonshine knows that if he remains on the path he has chosen, there will be a price: months away from home, field assignments and wars that cannot be planned.
When he describes the periods in which he is studying and seemingly living as a civilian, he uses an unexpected phrase.
“I feel like I’m dressing up as a civilian in my everyday life, because it isn’t real,” he said.
“Neta jokes that she wishes I would smile at her the way I smile when I put on a uniform and get the call to come back to the army. That’s my inner fire.”
Before Oct. 7, he wanted to become a mechanical engineer and travel through Alaska.
Today, the dreams have changed.
“Having a family has become one of the dreams of my life,” he said. “Another dream is that things will be better for us in this country.”
‘We must carry it like a warning sign’
Unlike others whose lives were overtaken by Oct. 7 and who have tried to find their way back to the people they were before it, Zonshine has little desire to return.
The three years since the massacre have bound him more closely to the army, to responsibility and to the day on which everything changed.
“God help us if I disconnect from that day,” he said. “We need to walk around with it like a warning sign above our heads.”
“This wasn’t some battle that went badly and you say, OK, we’ll investigate it, learn the lessons and move on. It has to be a milestone for us. That day cannot become something that belongs to the past.”
“We owe it to those people who were abducted and murdered that this day remains with us and serves as a compass, so we make sure something like this never happens again in the State of Israel.”
Perhaps that is why, when asked to picture himself three years from now, Zonshine does not talk about a degree, a civilian career or the trip he still has not taken.
“Probably in some trench beyond enemy lines,” he said, “making sure things are better here.”
And when the question turns from the officer to the 26-year-old underneath the uniform, another version of his future briefly appears.
“A family man who is probably more afraid of changing a diaper than confronting a terrorist.”

US senators urge Trump administration to enforce new Russia sanctions law ahead of Oct. 18 deadline
Unknown

01:52:29 UTC

US senators urge Trump administration to enforce new Russia sanctions law ahead of Oct. 18 deadline
U.S. Senators Jeanne Shaheen and Roger Wicker are pressing the Trump administration to begin implementing the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act as soon as possible. While most of the law's provisions take effect on Oct. 18, the bipartisan senators urged the administration not to wait until the deadline.
In a letter shared with the Kyiv Independent and later made public, Shaheen and Wicker argued that Russia's intensified missile strikes targeting Ukraine's civilian population and energy infrastructure, along with new North Korean troop deployments, make immediate economic pressure necessary.
The senators called for tougher action against Russia's oil revenues and sanctions-evasion networks, urging the administration to match European and U.K. designations of shadow-fleet vessels. The EU and U.K. have designated more than 600 vessels, compared to 216 by the United States, most of them in early 2025.
Shaheen and Wicker warned that the gap leaves hundreds of tankers able to continue transporting oil and ultimately feeding the Russian war machine while avoiding U.S. restrictions. They urged Washington to match allied shadow-fleet designations one-for-one, arguing that U.S. sanctions have added impact by cutting vessels off from the global dollar system and Western maritime services.
In the letter, Shaheen and Wicker acknowledged the administration's sanctions against Lukoil and Rosneft in 2025, saying they dealt a significant blow to a major source of Moscow's revenues. They noted, however, that Russia has since bypassed those sanctions, routing transactions through intermediaries concentrated in the UAE and Hong Kong, and called on the administration to target those networks.
The senators also urged Washington to impose secondary sanctions on third-country suppliers in China, the UAE and Türkiye that provide advanced machine tools, microelectronics, and other dual-use components used in Russian ammunition production and jet-powered drones.
The letter further called for sanctions against companies supporting Russia's Rassvet low-Earth-orbit satellite network, including Bureau 1440, 5C Group and Eltex. The senators warned that a fully deployed constellation could strengthen Russian battlefield communications and targeting capabilities.
Shaheen and Wicker also pointed to recent reports of a possible multi-billion-dollar deal involving Lukoil's international assets, arguing that the Treasury Department should make clear that financing Russian state-linked businesses would violate the law's investment restrictions.
Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act into law on Sept. 18.
Most provisions take effect Oct. 18, marking the first major deadline for the administration to demonstrate how aggressively it intends to wield the new sanctions authority.

What is celebrated on October 8 in Ukraine and around the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
04:40:25 EEST
10:40:25 KST

What is celebrated on October 8 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
In Ukraine, Lawyers’ Day is celebrated, while around the world, it is Vision, Dyslexia and Octopus Days. The Church calendar commemorates Pelagia and Thais.
On October 8, Ukraine celebrates Lawyer's Day, while the World Sight Day is held worldwide under the auspices of the WHO, as well as World Dyslexia Awareness Day. According to the new-style church calendar, Saint Pelagia of Antioch and Saint Thais of Egypt are commemorated, while according to the old style, Saint Euphrosyne of Alexandria is remembered, UNN writes.
Lawyer's Day in Ukraine
An official professional holiday established by a Decree of the President of Ukraine in 1997. The date has deep historical roots: it is believed that on October 8, 1016, Grand Prince Yaroslav the Wise of Kyiv issued the first codification of the laws of Kyivan Rus—"Ruska Pravda," which formed the basis of the Eastern European legal tradition.
The holiday brings together legal scholars, judges, lawyers, prosecutors, notaries, investigators, and legal consultants, emphasizing their fundamental role in building a state governed by the rule of law, protecting citizens' constitutional rights and freedoms, and ensuring the rule of law.
World Dyslexia Awareness Day
A global observance intended to draw public attention to dyslexia—a specific learning disorder associated with difficulties in acquiring reading and writing skills despite preserved general intelligence and normal visual and auditory perception.
The day emphasizes the importance of early diagnosis of this neurological condition, the introduction of inclusive teaching methods in schools, the provision of speech therapy and psychological support, and overcoming the stigmatization of people with dyslexia.
World Sight Day
An international medical observance held under the auspices of the World Health Organization and the International Agency for the Prevention of Blindness, observed on the second Thursday of October. The event aims to draw the global community's attention to blindness, visual impairment, and ensuring access to quality ophthalmological services.
According to the WHO, more than 2.2 billion people worldwide have a vision impairment, and at least half of these cases could have been prevented or treated in time with early diagnosis and appropriate medical care.
World Octopus Day
An unofficial observance dedicated to one of the most intelligent and unusual invertebrates on the planet. The date was not chosen by chance: the English name for October derives from the Latin word "octo," meaning eight, which echoes the eight limbs of cephalopods.
The purpose of the day is to spread scientific knowledge about the unique biology of octopuses and their ability to learn and camouflage themselves.
Commemoration of Saint Pelagia of Antioch
According to the new calendar, Orthodox and Greek Catholic faithful commemorate Saint Pelagia of Antioch and Saint Thais of Egypt.
Saint Pelagia lived in the 3rd century in Antioch and led a luxurious and sinful life as a dancer. However, influenced by the preaching of Bishop Nonnus, she sincerely repented, was baptized, distributed her property to the poor, and, disguised as a monk, lived as a recluse on the Mount of Olives in Jerusalem.
According to the old calendar, the faithful commemorate Saint Euphrosyne of Alexandria, who secretly left her parents' home, took monastic vows under the male name Smaragdus, and lived in a men's monastery.

An unprecedented artwork can be difficult to place. Encountering it for the first time, we give it a…
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
01:37:40 UTC
10:37:40 KST

An unprecedented artwork can be difficult to place. Encountering it for the first time, we give it a tentative interpretation, which offers some context and structure to what we are seeing. This provides us with some stability, which allows us to look closer and discover details and complexities we hadn’t noticed before. Often these complicate our initial interpretation, challenging us to consider the artwork in a different light.
Our inclination then might be to posit several interpretations, trying them on one by one to see what fits. Sometimes we will land on one that feels more substantial than the others, and feel assured that we have grasped the meaning of the work. But on other occasions, the artwork will resist any interpretation we give it. Here, our desire for a final and perfect interpretation is thwarted.

Bipartisan US Senators Press Trump Administration to Crack Down on Russia’s Shadow Fleet and War Financing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
01:36:23 UTC
10:36:23 KST

Two senior US senators from both parties are pressing the Trump administration to intensify economic pressure on Russia by targeting its shadow oil fleet, financial networks and foreign suppliers of military technology before sweeping new sanctions provisions take effect on Oct. 18.
In an Oct. 7 letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Democratic Senator Jeanne Shaheen and Republican Senator Roger Wicker warned that Moscow continues to exploit gaps in Western sanctions to finance its war against Ukraine.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Every day that passes without maximum economic pressure allows Moscow to sustain this military escalation,” the senators wrote.
Shaheen, the ranking Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and Wicker, chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, urged the administration to fully implement the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, signed into law by President Donald Trump last month.
“The majority of the Act’s provisions go into effect on October 18th, and it is vital that the Departments of State and the Treasury use these new tools to cut off the revenue streams and dual-use technology pipelines keeping Russia’s war machine alive,” they wrote.
The bipartisan appeal comes as Russia intensifies missile and drone attacks on Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure.
The senators specifically cited Russia’s use of additional North Korean troops and its escalating strikes against Ukrainian civilians as reasons for urgent action.
Russia’s Donbas Advance Goes Into Reverse as Ukraine Retakes Ground
The senators identified Russia’s shadow fleet – tankers used to transport Russian oil while evading Western restrictions – as the most urgent target.
According to the letter, the European Union and United Kingdom have sanctioned more than 600 vessels, compared with just 216 designated by the US, most of them in early 2025.
That disparity, they warned, allows hundreds of tankers to continue transporting Russian oil and generating revenue for the Kremlin.
While European restrictions have disrupted shipping operations through asset freezes and port bans, US sanctions could cut vessels off from dollar-based transactions and Western maritime services.
The senators urged Washington to coordinate with European allies and match their existing designations vessel by vessel.
They also called for expanding sanctions against intermediaries in Dubai and Hong Kong that facilitate Russian oil exports despite earlier US restrictions on major Russian energy companies Lukoil and Rosneft.
The lawmakers acknowledged the Trump administration’s October 2025 sanctions against the two companies but argued that Moscow had adapted by routing transactions through new networks of intermediaries.
Banks in China and Kyrgyzstan under scrutiny
The letter also demanded a crackdown on financial networks that help Russia move billions of dollars beyond the reach of Western restrictions.
Shaheen and Wicker urged the Treasury Department to expand enforcement against the A7 financial network and its associated entities, which they described as a channel for Russian sanctions evasion and illicit procurement.
They specifically identified remaining overseas branches of Russia’s VTB Bank, including in Shanghai, and financial institutions in Kyrgyzstan accused of facilitating transactions involving sanctioned capital.
“Foreign banks must be forced to make a choice: They can either do business with the United States or finance Russia’s war. They cannot do both,” the senators wrote.
The proposed measures would extend US financial pressure beyond Russia itself, targeting foreign institutions and companies that help Moscow maintain international commercial and banking operations.
China, Turkey and UAE identified as Russian military supply hubs
The senators urged Washington to crack down on foreign networks supplying Russia’s military-industrial complex, identifying China, Turkey and the United Arab Emirates as major transit hubs for sensitive Western technology.
They singled out advanced machinery used to manufacture ammunition and critical microelectronics powering Russia’s jet-powered attack drones – equipment that helps Moscow sustain its war against Ukraine.
Calling for “mandatory secondary sanctions to penalize entities feeding Russia’s military-industrial complex,” the senators demanded tougher measures against foreign companies helping Moscow evade restrictions and maintain weapons production.
Their warning comes as Russia continues to expand drone and missile production while intensifying attacks on Ukrainian cities.
Russia’s satellite ambitions also targeted
Beyond conventional weapons production, the senators urged the administration to sanction Russian companies involved in developing low-Earth orbit satellite capabilities.
They specifically named Bureau 1440 LLC, 5C Group LLC and Eltex Enterprise LLC, along with procurement networks operating across China and Central Asia.
The lawmakers warned that a functioning Russian low-Earth orbit communications network could provide Moscow’s forces with more resilient command-and-control capabilities and improved targeting.
They argued that disrupting these satellite projects before their large-scale deployment would be crucial to protecting Ukrainian forces and civilians.
The senators also called for strict enforcement of provisions barring new US investment in Russia and prohibiting American persons or institutions from dealing in Russian sovereign debt.
They said the Treasury Department must issue clear guidance before Oct. 18, including in connection with publicly reported negotiations involving Lukoil’s international assets.
Bipartisan pressure ahead of sanctions deadline
The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act was passed by Congress with broad bipartisan support and signed into law in September.
Named after the late Republican senator who championed tougher sanctions against Moscow, the legislation provides additional authorities to target Russian energy revenues, financial institutions, foreign intermediaries and companies supporting Russia’s military production.
“The October 18 implementation deadline is a critical opportunity to show both our allies and adversaries that U.S. sanctions are comprehensive, dynamic, and strictly enforced,” Shaheen and Wicker wrote.
Their letter makes clear that, in the senators’ view, sanctions against major Russian companies alone are insufficient while Moscow can continue selling oil, accessing foreign financial institutions and importing critical weapons components through third countries.
The question now is how aggressively Washington will use its new powers to close those gaps – and cut the financial and technological pipelines sustaining Russia’s war against Ukraine.

Ebola spirals out of control in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo — NGO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
01:34:00 UTC
10:34:00 KST

NAIROBI, October 8. /TASS/. The spread of the Ebola virus in the North Kivu Province in the east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo has spiraled out of control, Africanews reported, citing the Doctors Without Borders (MSF) international non-governmental organization.
According to the news outlet, North Kivu accounts for nearly 40% of the country's new confirmed Ebola cases. Stephanie Hoffmann, coordinator of the Ebola treatment center in Butembo, said most new cases are not linked to previously identified chains of transmission. "Seventy-five percent of all deaths stemming from Ebola are community deaths, meaning people that are never seen in treatment centers or transit centers," she noted.
According to Hoffmann, an additional problem is residents’ reluctance to acknowledge possible infection and seek medical care due to fear of Ebola and specialized treatment centers. As a result, many patients remain at home, where they are cared for by relatives, increasing the risk of further transmission.
Initially, the outbreak was concentrated in the area around the city of Butembo, but cases have now been reported in all neighboring health districts. The organization warns of new outbreaks emerging every week and a lack of capacity to treat patients.
The current Ebola outbreak began in the Ituri Province and spread for several months before being officially identified in May. It is caused by the Bundibugyo strain of the virus and, according to Africanews, has already become the deadliest outbreak in the history of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. According to the latest reports, there have been more than 8,600 cases, with over 4,100 deaths.

EU seeking to target US Big Tech without angering Trump – FT

Unknown Publisher

EU seeking to target US Big Tech without angering Trump – FT
The European Union is exploring ways to raise taxes on US tech giants such as Apple, Meta, and Google without provoking retaliation from Washington, the Financial Times has reported.
The discussions come as Brussels seeks to avoid a new trade confrontation with US President Donald Trump while raising revenue amid contentious negotiations over the bloc’s next long-term budget and spending pressures at home.
The European Commission is considering a broader corporate levy that would apply to all companies operating in the EU rather than explicitly targeting Big Tech, the FT reported on Wednesday, citing six officials familiar with the discussions.
”Some [EU] capitals are opposed to a pure digital tax because they don’t want to upset the Americans,” an EU official told the FT. “The solution is to expand [the tax] to cover pretty much all the big companies.”
Trump has repeatedly threatened trade retaliation over measures he says discriminate against American companies. In June, he warned that countries imposing digital services taxes on US firms could face 100% tariffs on their exports to the US. Washington has also clashed with Brussels over the EU’s Digital Markets Act, under which the Commission has imposed hefty fines on Google, Apple, and Meta.
The levy, known as the Corporate Resource for Europe (CORE), would require companies operating in the EU with annual revenue above €100 million ($112 million) to pay a fixed yearly contribution, raising an estimated €6.8 billion annually from 2028 to 2034. Officials are reportedly considering raising the threshold and contributions to focus the tax on the largest corporations.
CORE is one of five proposed revenue sources expected to collectively raise around €60 billion a year from 2028. The package requires unanimous approval from EU member states.
At the same time, the EU is moving to sharply increase military spending. Under its proposed €2 trillion budget for 2028-2034, the Commission wants to allocate €131 billion to defense, security and space – five times the amount under the current framework. Brussels has urged member states to rearm in response to what it describes as a growing threat from Russia, a claim Moscow has dismissed as “nonsense.”

World’s largest penguin colony loses nearly two-thirds of population amid climate change: Study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
01:27:39 UTC
10:27:39 KST

Halis Sunnetci
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
A remote island near Antarctica that was home to the world's largest penguin colony has lost nearly two-thirds of its chinstrap penguin population since 2011, according to a new study published Wednesday.
Researchers led by the British Antarctic Survey (BAS) found that the number of chinstrap penguins on Zavodovski Island in the South Sandwich Islands fell by 63% between 2011 and 2025.
The population declined from an estimated 1.09 million breeding individuals in 2011 to about 402,000 in 2025, representing a loss of more than 680,000 penguins.
Researchers used drone surveys, aerial photography, satellite data and tracking devices fitted to penguins to assess changes in the colony.
They found that the decline was linked to climate-driven changes in the Southern Ocean affecting the availability of Antarctic krill, the main food source for chinstrap penguins.
"Our tracking data shows they prefer to forage in cooler waters to the northwest of the island, where they would expect to find Antarctic krill – the prey that make up the bulk of their diet," said Norman Ratcliffe, a penguin ecologist at BAS who led the research.
The findings raise concerns about chinstrap penguins across the wider South Sandwich Islands, which are home to a significant share of the global population of the species.
Researchers said the scale and speed of the decline could also support reassessing the chinstrap penguin's conservation status, which is currently listed as "Least Concern" by the International Union for Conservation of Nature.

Tropical Storm Isaias forecast to hit US Gulf coast as hurricane early Oct 10
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
01:27:00 UTC
10:27:00 KST

Tropical Storm Isaias forecast to hit US Gulf Coast as hurricane early Oct 10
Tropical Storm Isaias formed in the Gulf of Mexico on Oct 7 and is forecast to strengthen into a hurricane before slamming into the southern US coast early on Oct 10, bringing heavy rains, storm surges and possible tornadoes across several states, the National Hurricane Center said.
The storm is expected to pass through areas with significant offshore oil and gas production, along with onshore refining facilities, which could pressure inventories and already-high prices at the pump.
Michael Brennan, director of the NHC, said in a video briefing on Oct 7 that Isaias could be a “major” hurricane – Category 3 or higher – when it makes landfall and could have “multiple, life-threatening impacts from storm surge, heavy rainfall flooding and hurricane force winds”.
Isaias would be the first hurricane of the season in the Atlantic, according to the NHC, and could tie the record for the latest first Atlantic hurricane with one that hit on Oct 8, 1905.
The strong El Nino weather pattern in 2026 has suppressed Atlantic hurricane development by increasing vertical wind shear, which disrupts the formation of strengthening tropical storms.
About 11.2 million barrels of oil production could be lost across the Gulf through the duration of the storm, a marked increase from the 7.1 million barrels impacted by Tropical Storm Bertha in July, according to a model forecast from consulting firm Earth Science Associates.
Quick development, tornadoes
The NHC expects Isaias to develop into a hurricane by Oct 8 as it quickly picks up power over the warm Gulf waters before making landfall early on Oct 10, most likely somewhere along the Mississippi, Alabama or Florida Panhandle coast.
The storm was located about 805km south of the Louisiana coast early on Oct 7.
Isaias could produce isolated rainfall amounts of 25.4cm across parts of the Gulf Coast, stretching from Louisiana to the Florida Panhandle, the NHC said in its latest bulletin.
Tornadoes are possible in the rainbands of Isaias across the Florida Panhandle and Alabama from the evening of Oct 9 through Oct 10, with more tornadoes expected further inland as the storm moves north.
The storm could also produce 7.62cm or more of rain further inland, with the NHC warning that “flash and urban flooding, along with isolated river flooding, will be possible” across the south-east.
Isaias is expected to run into strong upper-level winds, known as vertical wind shear, in the final 24 hours before it reaches the northern Gulf Coast, which could weaken the storm.
Still, the NHC says it is “looking more likely that Isaias will be a significant hurricane when it reaches the coast”.
Florida Governor Ron DeSantis on Oct 6 had already declared a state of emergency for portions of the state. Some officials across the region were urging residents to voluntarily evacuate.
Florida Senator Rick Scott wrote on social media that he had spoken with US President Donald Trump about the storm, and that “the federal government is going to show up for Florida and make sure we have everything needed to prepare, respond and recover”.
Impacts on oil and gas
The Marine Minerals Administration, which monitors offshore oil and gas operators in the Gulf of Mexico, said on Oct 7 that personnel have been evacuated from eight production platforms and two non-dynamically positioned ahead of the storm.
About 25% of current oil production in the Gulf, or 511,619 barrels of oil per day, has been shut in, the agency said, citing operator reports.
Just over 350 million cubic feet per day of natural gas production has also been shut in, or about 16.4% of total output from the region.
The companies with the most exposure to the storm include BP, Chevron, ENI, Murphy Oil and Shell. REUTERS

Democrats sue US President Trump over taxpayer-funded ad campaign
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
01:21:26 UTC
10:21:26 KST

Democrats sue US President Trump over taxpayer-funded ad campaign
Trump has faced a bipartisan backlash over ads that critics say violate prohibitions on taxpayer-funded propaganda.
The Democratic National Committee has filed a lawsuit against United States President Donald Trump over television advertisements that were publicly funded and allegedly used to promote his political policies.
Ken Martin, who heads the Democratic Party’s leadership body, suggested in a statement on Wednesday that the ads were designed to bolster Republican odds in the upcoming November 3 midterm elections.
“Donald Trump is misusing millions of taxpayer dollars to fund pure propaganda ads in a last-ditch attempt to save Republicans in November,” Martin said.
Later that day, Common Cause, a democracy watchdog group, filed a second lawsuit over the same set of ads.
It argued that the ads were “overtly political” and therefore ran afoul of laws that bar public funds from being used for political propaganda.
“These ads are not public-service announcements,” Common Cause said in its lawsuit, citing a justification Trump has offered for the television spots. “They are personal publicity and political propaganda through and through.”
Both lawsuits argue that, to create the ad campaign, Trump directed the White House to repurpose $20m in funds that Congress allocated for commemorative activities related to border security, including for those killed in the line of duty.
That manoeuvre, they argue, violates the separation of powers established in the US Constitution.
“The founders made clear more than 200 years ago that the executive can spend money only according to Congress’s direction,” Common Cause’s lawsuit said.
The two lawsuits also point to a provision Congress includes in its appropriations bills barring the use of taxpayer funds for “publicity or propaganda purposes”.
Both complaints seek to have the ads declared illegal, and the expenditures stopped. They also call for steps to be taken to recover any money already spent on the ads.
The Democrats’ lawsuit was filed in Washington, DC, while the Common Cause complaint will be heard in the Southern District of New York.
Trump has faced mounting criticism over the ads, which began airing in September.
So far, the advertising campaign has cost more than $12m to run, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact.
The $20m Trump tapped for the ads comes from a $175m package Congress assigned to the Department of Homeland Security as part of Trump’s immigration enforcement agenda.
Critics have pointed out that one of the ads appears nearly identical to a television spot Trump used in his 2024 re-election campaign.
Three ads have aired so far. In one, a choir sings “love me” over a montage of Trump as he declares the US will “never be a communist country”. Another uses images of Mount Rushmore as Trump heralds a new “golden age of America”.
The third is darker: Trump walks towards the camera in black and white, warning of a “final battle” against the “deep state” and other perceived enemies.
On Wednesday, the news agency Reuters and the research firm Ipsos released a poll showing the ads are highly unpopular. Some 86 percent of the Americans surveyed, including four out of five Republicans, said it was inappropriate for Trump to have used public money for them.
Trump has defended the ads as “promotion for the country”, and he has argued they were similar to public outreach campaigns put out by previous administrations.
But after a bipartisan backlash, Trump said on Monday that taxpayer funds would no longer be used for future ads.
He did not, however, commit to paying back the money already spent on the existing ads.
Members of Trump’s Republican Party have been among those speaking out against the ad campaign.
Senator Thom Tillis, a Republican from North Carolina, said the advertisements resembled something former Hungarian leader Viktor Orban would put out.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune, meanwhile, indicated he agreed with the message in one of the advertisements, but he emphasised that “it shouldn’t be paid for with taxpayer dollars”.

Elitzur Hajbi, the last victim killed in the October 7 massacre in Moshav Yachini, was laid to rest on Wednesday, the third anniversary of the attacks, according to a statement released by ZAKA.

"For three years, that room remained frozen in time for Elitzur’s family," said Moshe Rosenberg, Executive Director of ZAKA US.
"Opening the door was an incredibly difficult moment, but it allowed the family to finally take this painful step. ZAKA was there to ensure that Elitzur was treated with dignity and respect and that his family could bring him to burial."
"Unlike three years ago, today we were not working alone among destroyed homes, but together with Elitzur’s son and brother," said Deri.
"It is difficult to put the feelings into words. We worked with reverence and sensitivity, praying that our work would bring the family some measure of comfort."

File photo: Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Governor Sanjay Malhotra
MUMBAI: Reserve Bank of India governor Sanjay Malhotra said the rupee was undervalued and the central bank would intervene to ensure orderly movement in the currency market even as it closed at 96.78 on Wednesday, down 36 paise from its previous close, after falling to a five-month low of 96.85 during the day."By a number of estimates, including the real effective exchange rate, the rupee is not overvalued. It may be undervalued," Malhotra said at a press conference after the MPC meeting. He was responding to a question on whether the rupee market was irrational."Markets can be quite irrational in the short run. It's only in the long run that they are able to find the right value," he said.
The governor said RBI would support the rupee's orderly movement and help it find its "correct value", while ensuring there was no excessive volatility.Malhotra also said a correction in the valuation of global AI stocks could redirect foreign capital to emerging markets such as India. He said a correction in AI stocks would not have a major negative impact on India and "if at all, there may be" a positive impact.Malhotra said that US tariffs and the absence of a trade deal would be a negative but could be offset by a trade deal with other countries.Despite a robust services trade surplus and strong net remittance receipts, the current account deficit widened in July because of a higher merchandise trade deficit, Malhotra said.
The merchandise trade deficit rose to $58.7 billion in July and Aug from $55.1 billion in the same period a year earlier, mainly because of higher imports of electronic goods and crude oil. On external financing, Malhotra said net FDI had shown sustained improvement, with inflows rising to $13.8 billion in the first four months of the year from $9.6 billion in the corresponding period a year earlier. The increase was driven by higher gross inflows and a slowdown in the growth of outward FDI."Robust gross FDI reflects the strong interest of global investors in India," he said. FPI recorded net outflows of $10.3 billion during the period up to Oct 5. However, capital-flow measures announced in the June policy had supported inflows, he said. The balance of payments is consequently expected to record a healthy surplus this year.
Malhotra also clarified that the new trade rules are aimed at improving ease of business and do not impose a reporting burden on individuals who get paid from overseas for software or other services. Nor does it apply to individuals paying for software or some subscriptions. Small exporters can use a self-declaration for bills up to Rs 10 lakh; and banks, not exporters or importers, handle reporting on the RBI's system. The aim is to simplify trade procedures while improving RBI's data on services exports, he said.

The Ukrainian company ranks second among participants in the first stage of the programme in terms of the size of its additional order.

Yemeni government forces claim 1,860 Houthis ‘neutralised’

Yemeni government forces have said they “neutralised” 1,860 Houthi fighters since launching a large-scale counteroffensive to retake territory under the control of the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah or Supporters of God.
The spokesperson for the internationally recognised government’s military said in a social media post early on Thursday it had carried out 2,103 “precise targeting operations” against Houthi military positions across several fronts as part of the ongoing “Dawn of Yemen” campaign.
The Yemeni government, backed by Saudi Arabia, also says its forces have captured strategic mountain positions in western Taiz overlooking the coast.
Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, announced on Sunday the Dawn of Yemen operation to retake all Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa, which the Iran-backed group has controlled since 2014.
Battles in Yemen have focused in recent days on areas around the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a shipping route that has become more crucial for energy exports since the US-Israel war on Iran restricted trade through the Strait of Hormuz.
Forces aligned with the Yemeni government launched an operation on Tuesday to recapture strategic territory near the strait and around the city of Mocha, which the Houthis had taken last month.
Coalition targeting
The Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen said on Wednesday it destroyed 82 Houthi military targets in the Yemeni governorates of Saada, Hodeidah, al-Jawf and Marib.
The spokesperson for the coalition said in a statement that the targets included missile sites, including “11 mountain-based ballistic missile storages in Saada, command and control centres, communication systems, missile and weapons storages”.
The latest operation followed Houthi attacks on Tuesday and Wednesday targeting King Khalid international airport in Riyadh and Abha international airport, according to the spokesperson.
The Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) said the attacks on the two airports killed three people.
One person was killed and eight were wounded in an attack on King Khalid airport, while two people were killed and 28 were wounded in the attack on facilities at Abha airport, the GACA said in a statement.
The attacks have drawn condemnation from across the region. Kuwait denounced the attacks as a “flagrant violation” of Saudi sovereignty and international law. Egypt said the attacks threaten the security of the entire region.
The Mecca-based nongovernmental organisation Muslim World League also condemned the strikes, describing them as “treacherous terrorist attacks”.
As the fighting rages on, Yemen’s permanent representative to the United Nations, Abdullah al-Saadi, met the UN secretary-general’s special envoy to Yemen, Hans Grundberg, on Wednesday to discuss the situation in the country.
During their talks, al-Saadi accused the Houthis of rejecting peace initiatives and de-escalation efforts proposed by the Yemeni government.
He stressed that the government’s goal is to extend its control across the entirety of the country and end the Houthis’ ability to wage war. He said the government is seeking a permanent end to the war and is not interested in a temporary truce, arguing that such a scenario would only lead to fighting later.

OpenAI says teens use ChatGPT for under 15 minutes a day as worries over risks grow
- OpenAI said teens use ChatGPT for under 15 minutes a day on average, and fewer than 2% chat for over three hours straight.
- The company said its teen version gets more education use and is adding study tools, while break reminders and parental controls aim to reduce risk.
- Common Sense Media said safety alerts were often late or missing in tests on suicide and self-harm, but OpenAI said the testing did not reflect real safeguards.
AI generated
Teens spend under 15 minutes a day on average on ChatGPT, while less than 2% of them interact with the chatbot for over three straight hours, OpenAI said, as technology companies face scrutiny over the risks AI chatbots pose to children.
Sam Altman’s AI company released the figures in its first report on teen use on Oct 7 as rapid adoption of AI platforms raises concerns about their impact on adolescent mental health and developmental safety.
Such worries have been amplified by research on social media’s harms to young users, with Meta in August agreeing to pay up to US$18 billion (S$23 billion) and limit teens’ use of Facebook and Instagram to settle claims that it designed the platforms to addict children.
OpenAI said in nearly half of teen conversations where a break reminder appeared, the user either took a break or ended the chat within five minutes, aiming to show that its steps to regulate teen usage were working.
The company said users with access to its dedicated teen version sent more education-related messages and used tools like learning visualisations and Study Mode.
It is looking to add a college application planning tool that will help students with requirements, deadlines and financial-aid steps, as well as new study features such as flashcards and easier quiz-making tools.
OpenAI began rolling out ChatGPT for Teens in August. The mode switches on automatically, based on age information or when a user is estimated to be under 18, allowing parental controls and limiting conversations on sensitive topics.
But a report by non-profit Common Sense Media on Oct 7 said ChatGPT for Teens often alerted parents late or not at all when teen accounts held conversations about suicide, self-harm or eating disorders.
The study, which is based on more than a dozen accounts created for testing, found the chatbot did not reliably suggest a crisis hotline or professional help.
An OpenAI spokesperson said the testing does not accurately reflect how ChatGPT’s teen safeguards work. Citing security and scale as reasons, the company said it may take hours for parent and teen accounts to link and for safety alerts to be active.
“The bulk of their testing may have begun and concluded before activation of parental controls was complete,” the spokesperson said.
Common Sense Media said some of its test accounts were linked for long enough and some were not, but none of them produced timely alerts. Notifications came through only for accounts with weeks of sensitive-topic history, it said. REUTERS

Stanford scientists turn a cancer driver into a kill switch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
00:52:42 UTC
09:52:42 KST

Stanford scientists turn a cancer driver into a kill switch
Scientists rewired a lymphoma-driving protein to destroy cancer cells, wiping out aggressive tumors in mice within 11 days.
- Date:
- October 7, 2026
- Source:
- Stanford Medicine
- Summary:
- A Stanford-designed molecule turns a major lymphoma-promoting protein against cancer cells, activating their own self-destruct machinery instead of simply blocking tumor growth. In mice, the treatment completely eliminated aggressive human lymphoma tumors within 11 days, although much more testing is needed before it could reach patients.
- Share:
Stanford Medicine researchers have developed a two-part molecule that turns a major driver of B-cell lymphoma against the cancer cells that depend on it. In mice, twice-daily treatment with the experimental compound caused aggressive lymphoma tumors to disappear within 11 days.
The work advances a strategy the research team has been developing for years. Instead of simply shutting down a cancer-promoting protein, the scientists designed a small molecule that connects it to another protein capable of activating the cell's built-in death program. The researchers believe this type of molecular rewiring could eventually have applications beyond lymphoma, including other cancers and some autoimmune diseases.
"We're trying to essentially fight cancer with its cause -- taking the driving force of the cancer and then rewiring it to activate cell death mechanisms," said Gerald Crabtree, MD, the David Korn, MD, Professor in Pathology and a professor of developmental biology.
Crabtree shares senior authorship of the study, which was published in Cell, with Nathanael Gray, PhD, the Krishnan-Shah Family Professor and a professor of chemical and systems biology; Stephen Hinshaw, PhD, assistant professor of molecular and cellular physiology; and Michael Green, PhD, director of translational and laboratory research, lymphoma/myeloma at the MD Anderson Cancer Center. Graduate student Meredith Nix and postdoctoral scholar Sai Gourisankar, PhD, are the lead authors of the research.
How BCL6 Helps Lymphoma Cells Survive
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is the most common form of non-Hodgkin lymphoma, a type of blood cancer. In many cases, the disease is driven by a protein known as BCL6.
In healthy immune cells, BCL6 attaches to DNA and temporarily shuts down genes that would normally stop cell growth or initiate cell death. This temporary suppression gives immune cells time to multiply during an immune response.
Once the immune threat has passed, other proteins modify BCL6 so that it can no longer silence those genes. The excess immune cells can then die through apoptosis, a controlled form of programmed cell death that allows the body to remove unneeded, damaged or cancerous cells without causing inflammation or harming nearby tissue.
Problems arise when BCL6 remains permanently active. In lymphoma cells, the protein can stay stuck in the "on" position, continually suppressing death-related genes and allowing malignant cells to keep multiplying.
Crabtree, Gray and their colleagues wanted to do more than simply remove that suppression. Their goal was to push those same cell-death genes into a highly active state. To accomplish this, they turned to a technique known as chemically induced proximity, which uses chemical connections to bring together molecules that normally interact only rarely, if at all.
A Two-Sided Molecule Rewires the Cancer Protein
The researchers created a molecule called TCIP3 that functions somewhat like a two-sided key.
"One side binds to BCL6," Nix explained. "The other side binds either of two proteins called P300 and CBP that add chemical tags called acetyl marks onto nearby proteins."
When an acetyl tag is added to BCL6, the protein loses its ability to suppress the cell-death genes downstream from it. P300 and CBP also place acetyl tags on nearby histones, the structures that help package DNA inside cells. Those modifications cause the histones to loosen their grip on DNA, opening up access for transcription factors that are needed to turn genes on.
That produces a different effect from existing drugs that target BCL6 by blocking or degrading it.
"We're not just relieving the repression conferred by BCL6; we're also actively driving the expression of these cell death genes, which is why we're able to get really potent compounds," Nix said, comparing the difference to easing off a car's brake versus flooring the accelerator.
Why TCIP3 Acts Like "Molecular Glue"
To investigate why TCIP3 was so effective, the researchers examined the compound at the atomic level. They crystallized the molecular complex and exposed it to X-rays -- allowing them to see precisely how TCIP3 connects the proteins.
The structural analysis uncovered an unexpected feature. Once TCIP3 brought the proteins together, they formed several additional chemical contacts with one another. Those interactions helped stabilize the entire complex, strengthening the effect of the hybrid molecule beyond what the researchers had initially expected.
"We used structural studies and biophysical measurements to determine that TCIP3 acts as a kind of molecular glue, anchoring these proteins together," Gourisankar said.
Using that structural information, the chemists were able to make the connection between the molecule's two halves more rigid. This helped preserve the favorable interactions instead of allowing the molecule to flex and lose energy. The resulting TCIP3 compound killed lymphoma cells grown in the laboratory at very low concentrations.
Lymphoma Tumors Disappeared in Mice
The team then tested TCIP3 in mice implanted with human lymphoma cells. After allowing the cells to develop into tumors, the researchers treated the animals with TCIP3 twice a day.
"By 11 days, the tumors that had been treated with TCIP3 were completely gone, whereas the tumors in the control animals remained," Nix said.
The treated mice showed no obvious signs of toxicity, and blood tests did not reveal an increase in inflammatory signals. At the same time, TCIP3 was also eliminating germinal centers -- clusters of rapidly dividing immune cells that depend heavily on BCL6 and represent the same type of cells that become abnormal in lymphoma.
That effect pointed to another possible application for the technology. Germinal center cells also play an important role in certain autoimmune diseases, including rheumatoid arthritis and myasthenia gravis. Because of that connection, the researchers think molecules similar to TCIP3 could eventually be explored as treatments for those conditions as well.
A Broader Strategy for Reprogramming Cancer
TCIP3 is not yet ready for use in people. The compound still requires further chemical refinement and must be tested in additional animal species before researchers can consider moving toward human clinical trials.
Even so, the broader strategy may have wide potential. The researchers are using bivalent, or two-headed, molecules to redirect the activity of cancer-driving proteins instead of merely blocking them. They are now looking for additional cancer-promoting proteins that could be vulnerable to the same type of molecular matchmaking.
"This could be a powerful approach to tackling other cell death repressors or transcription factors that control genes we want to activate in cancer," Nix said.
Researchers from MD Anderson Cancer Center and the AI-powered drug discovery platform Deep Origin contributed to the study.
The study was funded by the National Institutes of Health (grants CA276167, CA163915, R01CA3044298, MH126720-01, S10OD028697-01, R01CA201380 and 1K99CA296700-01), the Howard Hughes Medical Institute, the Mary Kay Foundation, the Williams Foundation, the Victor Family Fund, Ed and Beatriz Schweitzer, the David L. Sze and Kathleen Donahue Interdisciplinary Fellowship, and a PhRMA Foundation Predoctoral Fellowship in Drug Discovery.
Crabtree is a founder and scientific advisor for Shenandoah Therapeutics, which has a license from Stanford University for the TCIP technology described in the study. Gray is a founder, scientific advisor and board member for Shenandoah Therapeutics.

‘I carried God in my pocket’: Reservist who identified Oct. 7 victims recounts horrors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
00:50:15 UTC
09:50:15 KST

For two years, Shlomo Efrati served as a reservist at Camp Shura, the military facility near Ramla where the bodies of those murdered in the Oct. 7 massacre were brought for identification and, later, where fallen IDF soldiers from the ground campaign in Gaza were prepared for burial.
The exposure came at a severe psychological cost. Yet Efrati, 39, says he does not regret answering the call on Oct. 7.
“I would have been willing to pay this price another thousand times if necessary. I’m talking to you after four nights without sleep,” he told Ynet. “I wish none of it had happened, all the suffering of those who were murdered and their families. But once it did happen, I feel that my service at Shura was the mission of my life.”
During the first two weeks after the Hamas-led attack, Efrati and his fellow reservists took fingerprints from about 700 murdered civilians from the Nova music festival, the Gaza border communities, Zikim Beach, Sderot, Ofakim and elsewhere, helping identify victims so their families could bury and say goodbye to their loved ones.
He later began handling the bodies of fallen IDF soldiers and preparing them for burial.
His experiences at Shura have now been collected in the Hebrew book Bein Chalal Lechalal (“Between the Fallen”), published by Yedioth Books, a harrowing poetic diary edited by Yondav Kaplan and illustrated by Barak Toito.
On Oct. 7, 2023, Efrati was called up under an emergency reserve order to the IDF’s casualty data collection unit, part of the Military Rabbinate command responsible for handling the fallen. His reserve commander contacted him after the Simchat Torah holiday ended that Saturday night.
“I drove to Shura and had no idea what I was going to encounter,” he recalled. “There was a long line of refrigerated trucks at the entrance and lots of stretchers with bags on them.”
“I was trying to understand how this was supposed to work. They gathered us together and I sat next to someone. I asked his name and he said, ‘Oded.’ I told him, ‘I’m Shlomo, and from now on we’re together.’ From that moment until the end of our reserve service, we were inseparable. His name is Oded Kind, and I dedicated the book to him.”
In one poem, written after the birth of his daughter Ori Sheva in July 2025, Efrati juxtaposed the blood of childbirth with the blood he remembered from Shura:
After the birth of my daughter, Ori Sheva, yesterday, as I rolled the metal crib down the corridor, with the baby inside, I noticed: my shoes were stained with blood. from the birth I remember well another metal bed and other blood staining my shoes.
A lack of coordination between IDF and police records meant Efrati and his colleagues were asked to help identify murdered civilians by taking fingerprints from their bodies.
“A very high percentage of those murdered were identified that way,” he said.
Returning to what he saw remains emotionally difficult, but Efrati believes testimony matters, particularly in a world where some deny the Oct. 7 massacre.
He describes victims who arrived with their legs bound and bodies bearing signs of gunfire and severe injury around the groin and genital areas.
“When victims came to me with their legs tied, I could only imagine where they had been taken from, where they had been and exactly what had happened,” he said. “I remember people whose legs were tied with ropes, or who had bruising in the groin area, or bullets in those areas.”
“Sometimes there was a severed hand or a severed leg. Some bodies arrived completely burned. We couldn’t take fingerprints from them, but under the procedures we still had to go in and examine them.”
The terrorist’s body
In his book, Efrati describes how the body of a Palestinian terrorist who participated in the attack was mistakenly brought to his team.
Three grenades and an opened package of condoms were found in the man’s pockets, Efrati said. He also recalled that the man was wearing flip-flops, leading him to believe he may have been a civilian who joined the terrorists entering Israel rather than a trained member of Hamas’ Nukhba force.
In a passage written on Oct. 28, 2023, he described the encounter:
One day in the valley of slaughter, the body of a terrorist arrived by mistake. How much darkness entered the room. The body lay helpless on the table. How vulnerable he is now, I thought. And in his pocket was the essence of evil: three grenades and a pack of condoms. Suddenly, an ancient melody from the Yom Kippur prayer began playing in my head: Have mercy upon Your creations. How much compassion is missing from our world. What a tragedy that there are people imprisoned for an entire lifetime inside this evil. I am uncomfortable admitting it, but I felt pity for him. Not for his death, but for the life he lived, for his ability to choose good and for the choice he made: evil.
“Everyone treated him respectfully, just as they treated every other body, but the conversations among the guys were difficult,” Efrati said.
He found himself separating the terrorist’s choices in life from the body left behind after death.
“He chose to do the worst things a person could possibly do with his life. But once the soul is no longer in the body, only the second part remains, his body. And the body contains what we call tzelem, the image of God.”
“At that point, his body is like my body. I see a human being lying in front of me, and the part that chose to commit the atrocities is no longer there.”
“This is a person who, in my eyes, represents absolute evil, without question, and it is good that he died. It would have been better if he had died before committing the terrible acts he committed. But after he dies, his body still bears the image of God, and it must be treated with sanctity and respect.”
Asked about writing that he even felt pity for the man, Efrati described what was found in his clothing.
“It was terribly difficult. We emptied his pockets and he had grenades, a lighter and an opened packet of condoms. He also had a small Quran, like those pocket-sized editions of Psalms.”
“You see absolute evil there. This man came to murder and rape. That is what he came to do. In my internal dialogue with God, I said: How does a person reach a point where this is his choice in life? How does that happen?”
For Efrati, the question became inseparable from his faith.
“Just as there is an encounter with God through good, there is an encounter with God through what is not good,” he said. “I walked around Shura with God in my pocket.”
“Of course I had grievances. I have a profound grievance with God. At the same time, I have a deep recognition of the value of my life and of the soul inside a human being. I have profound gratitude for the privilege of living this life and accomplishing whatever can be accomplished here.”
The bitter contradiction, he acknowledged, is that the terrorist himself may also have believed he was acting in God’s name.
“That’s absolutely right. Religion is the most wonderful thing in human existence and the most terrible thing in human existence,” Efrati said.
“It is responsible for a great many wars, atrocities and hatred between people, and it is also responsible for a great many good deeds and for people’s desire to do good. It depends on where you take it.”
Efrati distinguishes religion from the spiritual experience he underwent at Shura.
“Religion is clothing. I am a religious person, but that is my clothing. It is the mother tongue I grew up speaking. My way of speaking with God is through religious elements, prayers and commandments, and that is how I am raising my children.”
“But it is one language, and I do not fool myself into believing it is the only language that exists. I have great respect for people who speak other languages.”
Oded Kind, who served alongside Efrati, confirmed to Ynet the details Efrati described, including the objects found on the terrorist’s body and the signs of abuse and severed limbs encountered by the unit.
On the edge of infinity
Efrati lives in Harish with his wife, Maayan, and their five children. Their youngest daughter, Ori Sheva, was born during the war.
He grew up in Givat Shmuel in a religious Zionist household, and his writing is steeped in Jewish texts and imagery.
He previously served as assistant director-general of the Harish municipality, director-general of the West Bank community of Etz Efraim and director-general of the Oranit local council. Today he works independently advising local authorities on large-scale projects.
During his mandatory IDF service, Efrati originally enlisted in the Nahal Brigade. Knee problems during advanced training led to his transfer to the Military Rabbinate, where he served in a religious affairs role. Only during his reserve service was he assigned to casualty identification work.
The pieces in his book were originally written as messages on his phone.
“It was the most readily available outlet I had for unloading what I was going through,” he said. “At first I wrote in a WhatsApp group with my siblings, then with some friends from the reserves.”
Some of the writing later appeared in Haaretz’s culture and literature supplement. Former supplement editor Benny Ziffer compared Efrati’s work to Haim Nahman Bialik’s poem “In the City of Slaughter,” written after the Kishinev pogrom.
The first poem in the book was written on Oct. 8, 2023, after his first night at Shura.
“In the morning I step outside for a moment / and there is light in the sky! / As if, thankfully, at least this / the Holy One remembered today / to do as He should.”
“That was written at the end of the first night,” Efrati said. “We had entered a conveyor belt. We didn’t even have time to sit down and breathe.”
“More and more bodies kept arriving. We saw things I never imagined I would see in my life. At some point I felt as though I had entered a loop and that night would never end. Like I had entered an episode of ‘Black Mirror’ and it was going to continue forever. Then suddenly there was light in the sky.”
Despite all the unanswered questions, Efrati still defines himself as a believer.
“My conversation with God is not one of doubt, but obviously these were days of a tremendous hiding of God’s face,” he said.
“Every fallen person there tells a story through their clothing or their tattoos. You try for a moment to categorize them: She is an elderly woman from Ofakim, he is a cool guy from the party with long hair, she has glitter around her eyes.”
“Every body tells a story. But at the same time, the body has been separated from the soul. It emphasized to me that a living human being is a divine creation, a creation of the soul, because I know what the body looks like without a soul.”
“When you spend so much time on the edge of the abyss, on the edge of infinity, life can no longer be taken for granted. A living person is not something to take for granted.”
‘The triggers are endless’
Like many who served at Camp Shura after Oct. 7, Efrati was diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder and recognized by Israel’s Defense Ministry as a disabled IDF veteran. He was eventually released from reserve duty along with the rest of his unit.
Even mundane moments can bring the images rushing back.
“Lots of everyday situations remind me of Shura,” he said. “I have a thing about gel nail polish because of the fingerprints we took.”
“I can remember Shura when I stretch sheets over my children’s beds. It can remind me of burial shrouds. In the community garden below my home there are long wooden garden beds where I grow tomatoes, and they look exactly like coffins.”
“The triggers are endless. For two years I handled many hundreds of bodies. There was a time when I took a phone out of a soldier’s pocket and saw that his mother was calling.”
‘They abused the Thais too’
Some passages in Efrati’s book concern Thai agricultural workers murdered in the Gaza border communities.
“There was severe abuse of the Thai victims’ bodies,” he said. “You could see that they had been sprayed with gunfire, including long after they were dead.”
“You see it and think about the person who did it: Seriously, what is wrong with you? What do you have against the Thais? Why? What did they do to you?”
“You came to fight over land, fine. Leave the Thais alone. What do you have against them? Say you didn’t like that they received a paycheck from the Zionists, so you killed them. Fine. Why abuse their bodies?”
“There was something there that made clear to me how much of it was simply evil. How much of it was sitra achra,” he said, using the Aramaic Jewish term for the forces of evil. “There is a sitra achra in the world.”
In another poem, written in February 2025, he wrote:
Dear doctor, I need a prescription for breathing. And while we’re at it, if possible, how does one breathe inside a dream?
Much of Efrati’s writing has now been translated into English and was published on Oct. 7 in a digital edition of the journal Liberties. The intention is eventually to publish the full book in English.
“At the deepest level of what we do in this world, we did not come here in order not to suffer,” Efrati said. “We came here to fulfill our souls, to let our souls shine. I felt this was my life’s mission.”
Asked whether that meant all the large municipal projects he had managed now seemed insignificant compared with his work at Shura, Efrati went further.
“I was assistant director-general of Harish when they were building the city. We implemented projects worth billions. We built schools, kindergartens, roads, streets and neighborhoods. I was part of a national project, and in my eyes that is nothing compared with this mission.”
“I felt there was nothing better on earth that I could be doing at that moment than being there and caring for those who had been murdered. I feel I was given a different internal, spiritual language.”
Amid colleagues doing everything they could to respect the dead and allow families to say goodbye, Efrati says he reached another conclusion.
“I understood that good is infinite, and what is not good is infinite too,” he said.
“Humanity is constantly trying to create technology that is more sophisticated and advanced, and the artificial intelligence that erupted during these years is the ultimate technology, the ultimate machine.”
“In that situation, what remains for a person is to make their soul shine. If all knowledge exists and a machine can tell me everything, now is the time to define what I know how to do. What do I know how to say? What can the divine part within me create in this world?”
In other words, AI is pushing you to be more fully human?
“Exactly. You were created, so create. Make art,” he said. “Publishing the book and having the text recognized as possessing artistic value makes me think I need to answer that call and reveal my art to the world.”
Despite everything, Efrati remains optimistic about Israel’s future.
“In the story of the war and the way it developed, you see God speaking with us,” he said. “The pager operation and Hezbollah, Syria, Iran. Just as God blinded our eyes for several hours on Oct. 7, God knew how to open them and show us which room in Iran Haniyeh was in and when to eliminate him.”
“It is clear to me that the story with Iran is not over. Evil wants to destroy itself. What did Sinwar think, that he would manage to destroy us? Evil has some deep death wish.”

Brazil: Thousands of students march against Bolsonaro
October 8, 2026
Thousands of people joined a student march in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, on Wednesday to protest the possibility that Flavio Bolsonaro could become president after the far-right candidate came out on top in the first round of the country's presidential election on Sunday.
Bolsonaro, the son of jailed former President Jair Bolsonaro, won about 2 million more votes than the incumbent president, the left-leaning Lula da Silva.
But since neither reached the 50% hurdle to win the presidency, the pair will face off in a run-off on October 25, in which Bolsonaro is considered the favorite.
"If Bolsonaro wins, Brazil will become a colony of the United States," said 20-year-old literature student Joao Victor Vieira, voicing the fear of many on the left in Brazil that Bolsonaro is too ideologically aligned with US President Donald Trump.
Brazil: 'Never again Bolsonaro'
Other marchers held signs with messages such as "Brazil isn't anyone's backyard," "I don't vote for someone who sells Brazil," and "Never again Bolsonaro" – all against a soundtrack of drums, fireworks and chants.
"We're fighting for Brazil, not for Lula," said Talita Amaral, a 19-year-old environmental sciences student, wearing Brazil's iconic yellow and green football shirt, often worn by nationalist Bolsonaro supporters but which opponents have been aiming to reclaim for themselves.
"We don't have time to be sad, we need to be doing this, occupying the streets, sending messages in WhatsApp groups, trying to convince people," she told the Associated Press.
For Alice Carneiro, a 25-year-old maritime shipping administrator, the prospect of another Bolsonaro conjures fears of far-right policies which will discriminate against Brazil's minorities – such as her transgender wife.
"I'm here because I believe in democracy," she told the AFP news agency. "Because I'm scared."
Witnesses reported that the march was notably more crowded and animated than President Lula's rally on the same street on Friday, the culmination of a lackluster campaign ahead of the election.
After the third, fourth and fifth places all went to right-wing candidates, who polled over eight million votes between them, Lula and the left appear to have a mountain to climb in the run-off.
The incumbent's campaign has shifted its focus to social media, where the far-right dominates but Lula has largely been absent, arguing he "like[s] to say only what is essential." But on Wednesday, the president convened leftist influencers who won legislative seats on Sunday to advise his campaign.
