Moldova to build drone shelters near Ukrainian border amid escalating Russian attacks
Moldova plans to build protective shelters at border crossings with Ukraine where border guards and people in nearby areas can take cover during drone incursions, Moldovan Interior Minister Daniella Misail-Nichitin said on Oct. 7.
The announcement followed an increase in drones violating Moldovan airspace in recent weeks.
The protective structures would provide a place of refuge in the event of incoming drone strikes, and will be placed at checkpoints along the country's border with Ukraine, Misail-Nichitin told Moldovan media outlet NewsMaker.
In addition to the new structures, some Moldovan border guards currently stationed on the Ukrainian side of the border, at "Kryva" and "Palanka" stations, will be moved to the Moldovan side, she said.
Ukrainian officials are also in talks with neighboring countries about restructuring border operations to improve security and make border crossing easier as drone incursions increase, Heorhiiy Tykhyi, a spokesperson for the Foreign Ministry, said on Oct. 7.
Drones have crashed into Moldovan territory throughout Russia's full-scale war, with multiple incidents occurring in the past two weeks.
A projectile fired during a Russian attack on Ukraine on Oct. 5 ricocheted and struck a passenger bus and a border control booth at the Palanca-Maiaky-Udobne crossing, lightly injuring a border guard, Moldova's Border Police said.
"The security environment around Moldova has become more difficult," Moldovan Prime Minister Vasile Tofan said during a press conference in Brussels on Oct. 5. "Russian drones and missiles pose a serious risk to our population and infrastructure."
During another Russian overnight attack against Ukraine on Oct. 3, five Russian air attack weapons, including Banderol missiles and drones, violated Moldova's airspace and exploded on the country's territory, Moldovan President Maia Sandu said.
Sandu condemned the attacks in a post on social media on Oct. 3.
"(Russia's) war is dangerously reaching Moldova," she said, adding that "Moscow is putting lives at risk across Europe and must be stopped."
Drones also invaded Moldova's airspace three separate times on Sept. 30, as Russia launched a day-long attack against Ukraine overnight and into the following afternoon.

EU-China trade talks begin in Beijing amid escalating pressure
Talks will focus on the €1 billion daily deficit and rare earth export restrictions.
European Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic has arrived in Beijing for talks on the European Union’s (EU) growing trade deficit with China.
Sefcovic will meet Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao on Thursday and Friday after months of discussions over the EU’s trade deficit of more than €1bn ($1.12bn) daily, as well as Chinese curbs on exports of rare earths and other critical minerals.
Meanwhile, Chinese companies are increasingly challenging Europe’s top car brands. China rejected the EU request for voluntary curbs on Chinese hybrid car exports as the two sides enter negotiations, the Financial Times reported on Wednesday. The European Commission now hopes to get Beijing to accept a unilateral EU measure to cap hybrid imports instead, the outlet said, citing two diplomats briefed on the plan.
The two days of discussions come just as a majority of EU lawmakers called for a more assertive trade policy towards Beijing in a non-binding resolution on Wednesday. China vowed a “resolute response” to safeguard its industries if the European Union goes ahead with restrictions against Chinese companies or products, according to its commerce ministry.
Germany and France propose rapid EU measure
French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, leaders of the bloc’s two biggest powers, on Tuesday urged the EU to prepare a “credible instrument” that could be quickly activated to strike back against countries that harm the bloc economically.
The new measure would not target any specific country. German officials said the EU needed a tool as powerful as the Section 301 tariffs imposed by the United States or China’s restrictions on critical-mineral exports.
The proposed weapon – to be discussed at an EU leaders’ summit next week – would give the European Commission the power to respond to a trade aggression within days.
China responded to the letter by urging Paris and Berlin to steer clear of “protectionist” measures.
“We hope that France and Germany, as major economies in the world, will uphold openness, cooperation and free trade,” the commerce ministry said in a statement.
“They should avoid going down the wrong path in the wrong way, only to ultimately suffer the consequences themselves.”
G20 finance leaders, except China’s, agreed in September to act against “non-market” distortions that exacerbate imbalances. Beijing says that hyping up issues such as economic imbalances and overcapacity is a form of protectionism designed to exert pressure on and restrict China.
Ongoing trade talks
EU and Chinese officials have been discussing trade imbalances since June. Sefcovic said he wanted “tangible results by October” as well as some form of commitment that can be put to EU leaders meeting in Brussels.
Trade relations with China top the summit’s agenda next week, as ballooning debt has prompted auditors to warn about the next seven-year EU budget and has spurred protests in France.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen told the European Parliament last month that the trade imbalance had reached a tipping point and that Europe would use every tool at its disposal to rebalance the relationship.

Kenya conducts first Ebola burial as number of contacts linked to patient rises to 57
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
23:44:30 UTC
08:44:30 KST

Andrew Wasike
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
Kenya conducted its first Ebola burial under strict health protocols after a Kenyan man became the country’s first confirmed case and death from the disease, as authorities stepped up efforts to prevent further transmission.
The patient was buried Wednesday at Lang'ata Cemetery, about 7 kilometers (4.3 miles) southwest of Nairobi's central business district, under strict health protocols designed to prevent transmission of the virus.
Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale said Kenya does not currently have an Ebola outbreak, stressing that the only confirmed infection was imported from the Democratic Republic of Congo.
Authorities have expanded the number of people identified as having had contact with the patient from 55 to 57, according to Duale.
"Of the initial 55 identified contacts, an additional two have been added, bringing the total (number) of contacts to 57. Ten of them have been accounted for, and they are already under a quarantine facility," he said.
"They're undergoing daily symptom monitoring at the National Police Service Hospital in Nairobi. Efforts today to trace the remaining contacts have been intensified, and by the time I was coming here, close to about 17 have been traced and they are already at the location," he added.
The 10 people in quarantine are being monitored for symptoms, while health teams continue efforts to locate and monitor the remaining contacts.
The deceased was a Kenyan citizen who had been living in Congo, where he became ill before traveling by road through Uganda and flying to Nairobi on Oct. 3. He was taken to Nairobi Hospital and isolated before laboratory tests confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease, a rare and severe viral hemorrhagic fever caused by the Bundibugyo ebolavirus.
The patient died days later, prompting authorities to step up contact tracing and surveillance. Kenya has screened more than 652,000 travelers and tested 267 suspected samples since going on heightened alert over Ebola, while nearly 5,000 health workers have been trained in prevention and case management.
Ebola spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person or through contaminated materials.

New York alleges TikTok gave teens, children placebo safety feature in experiment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
23:40:00 UTC
08:40:00 KST

New York alleges TikTok gave teens, children placebo safety feature in experiment
- New York’s lawsuit says TikTok ran “ghost” tests on thousands of teens and children, giving them fake safety features like Algo Refresh that did not work.
- The suit alleges TikTok misled users about safety, used tests to study time on site and ad revenue, and ignored an employee warning that the placebo group was “misleading”.
- It also says TikTok turned off safety tools in other tests; one teen later died by suicide after seeing self-harm content, raising serious concerns over harm to young users.
AI generated
NEW YORK - TikTok ran an experiment on thousands of users who tried to switch on a safety feature on the platform, giving them non-functional versions of the tool, according to allegations in New York’s lawsuit against the company unsealed on Oct 7.
In the so-called “ghost” or placebo experiments, TikTok selected thousands of users, including teenagers and children, who opted to use safety features like Algo Refresh, a tool designed to reset recommendations for users seeking to escape unwanted or potentially harmful content.
According to the lawsuit, those users believed they had activated the feature, but their feeds did not change, unlike users who got the fully functional version.
The newly unsealed allegations are part of New York attorney general Letitia James’ lawsuit against the company, one of more than two dozen brought by states accusing TikTok of designing its platform to addict children and of misleading users about its safety.
Many documents in state cases across the country have been sealed or heavily redacted as TikTok has sought to keep details about its operations from public view.
The lawsuit claims TikTok assures users that safety is a top priority and that its platform is appropriate for kids and teens, while knowingly preventing some groups of users from accessing certain safety tools, including users who had specifically sought to avoid unwanted or potentially harmful content.
“We continuously make improvements to our platform which means that, like most companies, we regularly test new products and features to validate the experience and understand how they work in the real world,” a TikTok spokesperson said in a statement.
The company has broadly denied New York’s allegations in court filings and has said that keeping young users safe is a priority.
In September, TikTok settled the first state lawsuit set for trial, agreeing to pay Alabama up to $300 million and change how its platform functions for teens in the state.
James, a Democrat, originally sued in 2024. The claims about the tests were included in an updated, sealed version of New York’s complaint filed at the end of August and later ordered unsealed by a judge.
Employee flagged test
Internally, a product manager for digital well-being at TikTok said doing placebo tests on the Algo Refresh feature was problematic and that users might find it misleading, the lawsuit alleges.
“This feature is about algorithm transparency and control,” the person wrote in an internal chat, according to the lawsuit. “A placebo group completely conflicts with that.”
Ultimately, the company did the tests repeatedly on thousands of users in 2023, comparing users who did not get the feature with those who did to study how long users stayed on the site and the impact on ad revenue, the lawsuit alleges.
The lawsuit also alleges that TikTok misled consumers about how Algo Refresh worked, telling them it would reset the algorithm that recommended videos to them when it was only a temporary change.
The TikTok spokesperson said the allegations mischaracterise how Algo Refresh works.
The unsealed portions of the lawsuit also allege that TikTok conducted a separate set of experiments, which were previously revealed in a report by Bloomberg.
In them, TikTok randomly selected users and turned off safety features on their accounts that limited their exposure to harmful content.
A teen boy in New York who was part of the test committed suicide after he was shown content about self-harm and suicide, Bloomberg reported.
Internal reviews showed the boy had been shown an “onslaught” of content about suicide and self-harm, the lawsuit said. REUTERS

Patricia Krenwinkel, former Manson follower, granted parole for third time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
23:37:11 UTC
08:37:11 KST

Patricia Krenwinkel, a former Charles Manson follower, was granted parole on Tuesday after nearly six decades in prison for her role in the infamous Tate-LaBianca murders in Los Angeles.
This is the third time that Krenwinkel, 78, has been approved for release by California’s board of parole hearings. After both of her last two parole grants, Gavin Newsom, California’s governor, reversed the parole board’s decisions and denied her freedom, and Krenwinkel’s attorneys are now urging the Democrat to allow this latest ruling to stand.
Krenwinkel, who was 21 at the time of the 1969 killings, has been imprisoned longer than any other woman in California, and the parole board has repeatedly acknowledged her record of rehabilitation over 57 years in prison, concluding she would not in her elderly age be a danger to society.
She was convicted in 1971 for her role in the violent crime spree over two nights that claimed the lives of actor Sharon Tate, who was eight months pregnant, and her four friends, and grocery owner Leno LaBianca and his wife, Rosemary. The killings were gruesome and became one of the most notorious crime stories in the US.
Krenwinkel was 19 years old when she “fell under Charles Manson’s control” and was exploited and psychologically abused by the cult leader, her attorneys have said.
“Reaching this moment has taken decades of hard, deliberate work to confront who she was, what she did, and the devastating harm she caused,” her longtime lawyer, Keith Wattley, said in a statement after the parole grant. “She fully accepts responsibility for her actions, everything she contributed to, and every life she destroyed in 1969. Pat does not excuse or minimize that harm.”
Over her decades in prison, Krenwinkel has had a clean disciplinary record, and nine consecutive psychological evaluations in the past 40 years have found her to be a low public safety risk, according to Wattley, who has represented Krenwinkel for 16 years. He said she has participated in extensive therapy and group counseling, earned a college degree and trained service dogs for people with disabilities.
“I have seen the depth of her remorse and the extraordinary work she has done to change her life. I firmly believe she is ready to return home,” Wattley added.
Debra Tate, Sharon Tate’s sister, has repeatedly objected to the release of Krenwinkel and other Manson followers.
When Newsom denied Krenwinkel parole in 2022, after the board first found her suitable for release, the governor acknowledged that she had been a “victim of Mr Manson’s abuse” and said she had “matured in prison and engaged in commendable rehabilitative efforts”. But he argued she had “not developed sufficient insight into the causative factors of her crime and her triggers for antisocial thinking” and was still dangerous.
When Newsom again denied her parole in 2025, he also acknowledged her “serious chronic medical conditions” had diminished her strength, but concluded she “must do additional work to deepen her insight before she can be safely released”.
The governor is required to consider her elderly age and that she committed the crime as a youth in his review of her case.
Krenwinkel’s attorneys and advocates have repeatedly argued the governor was caving to political pressures by denying parole to people convicted in high-profile cases. Newsom previously vetoed the release of Leslie Van Houten, another former Manson follower, but an appeals court sided with her and granted her freedom in 2023. Newsom also faced scrutiny for overturning the parole grant of Sirhan Sirhan, convicted of assassinating Robert F Kennedy, even after two of Kennedy’s sons favored his release.
The push for Krenwinkel’s release comes at a time of growing concern about the increasing number of elderly people languishing in US prisons after decades of incarceration. Krenwinkel’s longtime friends from inside California’s women’s prison said last year that she was a mentor and support system to others in the prison.
Wattley, the founder of UnCommon Law, a non-profit organization that represents people at parole hearings, urged Newsom to “uphold the law” and approve Krenwinkel’s freedom: “The parole process exists because people can change, rehabilitation matters, and public safety must be grounded in evidence. Pat’s case raises a fundamental question: if three parole grants don’t lead to release, what is the point of this process?”
Spokespeople for Newsom did not immediately respond to an inquiry on Wednesday.

Trade Agreement With US Close to Completion, Thai Prime Minister Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
23:35:00 UTC
08:35:00 KST

Trade negotiations between Thailand and the United States are in the final stages and an agreement is expected to be signed as soon as next month, Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said yesterday.
Speaking at a forum in Singapore, Anutin said negotiations on the Agreement on Reciprocal Trade (ART) are now on “the last paragraph” and that he expected to sign the final agreement during U.S. President Donald Trump’s next visit to Asia, Reuters reported. This could take place during the ASEAN Summit in the Philippines on November 16–18, which Trump has confirmed he is attending, or the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meetings in Shenzhen on November 18–19. Trump’s attendance at the latter summit has not yet been confirmed.
Anutin said that he received a letter from the U.S. president last week confirming the deal is at its final stage. “He told me that I was to make sure that my people and the United States Trade Representative would write up the final clause,” the Thai leader said.
The U.S. is Thailand’s largest export market, and the country’s imports of Thai goods totaled $91.3 billion in 2025, according to U.S. government figures.
Bangkok and Washington have been negotiating a “reciprocal” trade deal with the U.S. since Trump’s initial “liberation day” tariff day announcement in April 2025, which hit Thailand with a 36 percent tariff.
In October 2025, the U.S. and Thailand announced a “framework” for an agreement on reciprocal trade, which reduced the tariff to 19 percent in exchange for a Thai pledge to “eliminate tariff barriers on approximately 99 percent of goods, covering a full range of U.S. industrial and food and agricultural products.” Under the framework, Thailand also promised to purchase more American energy, agricultural products and aircraft in order to close its $71.7 billion goods trade surplus with the U.S.
However, the negotiation of a final agreement has been complicated and delayed by recent shifts in U.S. tariff policy. In February, the U.S. Supreme Court struck down the “liberation day” tariff regime.
As a workaround, Trump imposed a temporary 10 percent global tariff under Section 122 of the Trade Act, which expired in July. The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) also used Section 301 of the U.S. Trade Act of 1974, which allows Washington to investigate and impose tariffs on foreign countries for unfair trade practices. In March, it initiated two separate investigations, one examining 60 nations’ alleged failures to take action on forced labor, and another examining excess industrial capacity on the part of 16 major trading partners.
Thailand was a target of both investigations, and in June, it was hit with a 12.5 percent tariff in the forced labor probe. The USTR has also accused Thailand of maintaining a “structural overcapacity” in three sectors – automotive and parts, machinery, and rubber products – although this investigation has not yet been concluded.
The Commerce Ministry says Thailand and the U.S. have already agreed on the main substance and principles of the ART, leaving technical teams to settle remaining details and legal wording. Thailand’s aim, according to The Nation, “is to keep the eventual overall tariff burden around the previous 19 percent benchmark, or at least no higher than that faced by regional competitors.”
The finalization of the ART would undoubtedly be a positive development for the U.S.-Thailand relationship, which has not been helped by the drawn-out negotiations. In August, Bloomberg reported that Thailand was going so far as to consider using military cooperation as leverage in the trade talks. According to its report, which quoted an unnamed Thai official, Bangkok was preparing to warn the Trump administration that steep U.S. tariffs might force it to scale back military cooperation, including the Cobra Gold exercises that have been a cornerstone of the U.S.-Thailand alliance since the 1980s.
Thailand’s government denied the reports.

AP: US senators urge Trump to step up pressure on Russia through sanctions
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08

AP: US senators urge Trump to step up pressure on Russia through sanctions
The Associated Press has reported that almost a month after US President Donald Trump signed into law the Graham Act authorising sweeping sanctions against Russia, the bipartisan Senate leadership is calling on the administration to move faster to restrict the flow of financial resources fuelling the war against Ukraine.
Source: Associated Press
Details: In a letter to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, the senators said the most urgent priority for the US should be targeting the shadow fleet of tankers that Moscow uses to transport oil and circumvent US sanctions. They also insisted that the development of Russia's emerging satellite system be halted, which Ukraine has warned could prove devastating because of real-time bombardments this winter.
"Every day that passes without maximum economic pressure allows Moscow to sustain this military escalation," wrote Senator Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the ranking Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and Republican Senator Roger Wicker of Mississippi, chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee.
The senators noted that most of the provisions of the law take effect on 18 October, after the administration's 30-day review period ends. Trump's administration has largely been silent since the bill was passed.
Over the past month, the momentum appears to have stalled, with no public steps by the administration to implement the law.
With bipartisan support, Shaheen and Wicker called on the administration in a letter sent late on 6 October to take a series of specific steps to implement the sanctions regime. Many of these measures align with objectives Ukraine has been pushing for.
The senators, who played a key role in passing the bill, said the US should focus first and foremost on several hundred illicit tankers that can "transport Russian oil with impunity and thereby provide the Kremlin a financial lifeline".
They also stressed that it is crucial that "the administration paralyse the global financial networks that allow Russia to evade our sanctions".
They further said that the Kremlin continues to "move billions of dollars through networks that shield it from scrutiny". They called on the administration to focus, in particular, on overseas branches of banks, including in Shanghai, and "a growing network of Kyrgyz financial institutions", which they said serve as clearing houses for sanctioned capital.
"Foreign banks must be forced to make a choice," the senators wrote. "They can either do business with the United States or finance Russia's war. They cannot do both."
The senators said the Trump administration should act against Russia's "weaponisation of space", citing its development of a new low-Earth-orbit satellite system. Ukraine has warned that the technology could become a major threat this winter as Russia readies further attacks.
They also noted that the sanctions law prohibits any new US investment in Russia and transactions involving sovereign debt. They stressed that the US Department of the Treasury must "issue clear regulatory guidance ahead of the October deadline to ensure American financial institutions completely sever these capital pipelines".
The senators also stated that the US must stop the flow of dual-use technologies and electronics used by Russia to conduct combat operations on the line of contact and use existing sanctions tools to "penalise entities feeding Russia's military-industrial complex".
Background:
- On 18 September, Trump signed the Russia sanctions bill, which was co-authored by the late Senator Lindsey Graham.
- On 16 September, the US House of Representatives passed the Russia sanctions bill on the introduction of tariffs on countries that buy Russian energy. The bill was passed by the US Senate on 7 August.
- On 22 September, Trump said that, if necessary, he was ready to implement the Graham Act on sanctions against Russia.
- A bipartisan group of members of the US House of Representatives, responding to reports of a new strategy towards Russia, urged Trump not to ease sanctions against Russia but instead to use the Graham Act.

UN peacekeeping force in Lebanon says shots fired at Israeli border post
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07

UN peacekeeping force in Lebanon says shots fired at Israeli border post
The United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon said there were no casualties after small arms fire targeted a border post.
The United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) says one of its posts on the Lebanon-Israel border was targeted by small arms fire, with no casualties reported.
The UN force said the incident occurred on Wednesday morning with several rounds of small arms fire targeting a UNIFIL position near Kfar Shouba along the UN-drawn border with Israel, known as the Blue Line.
“Such deliberate attacks gravely endanger the lives of peacekeepers,” UNIFIL said in a statement, adding that it was investigating the incident.
Under pressure from the United States and Israel, the UN Security Council decided earlier this year to set December 31 as the end of the mandate for the UN peacekeeping force in Lebanon.
UNIFIL was initially created to oversee the withdrawal of Israeli troops from southern Lebanon after Israel’s 1978 invasion, and its mandate has been renewed annually since then.
The mission was expanded after the 2006 war between Israel and Hezbollah. Proponents say it remains important to maintaining a demilitarised buffer between the two sides along the volatile Israeli and Lebanese border.
Israel has long accused UNIFIL of failing to prevent threats posed by Hezbollah and has increasingly pushed for the end of its mission since cross-border fighting escalated in the wake of the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks on Israel and the start of Israel’s war on Gaza.
UNIFIL currently has 7,500 peacekeepers from around 50 countries operating in Southern Lebanon.
Last month, Lebanon’s Prime Minister Nawaf Salam pressed the UN on the need to “avert the vacuum” that would be caused by withdrawing the mission from the country’s south without a viable replacement.
Violence has decreased since a ceasefire following a June memorandum of understanding in the US-Iran war. Lebanon and Israel concluded a US-sponsored framework agreement later that month.
The Israel-Lebanon deal involves the disarmament of Hezbollah, a gradual withdrawal of Israeli forces from Lebanon’s south and the deployment of the Lebanese army to the region, starting in test areas known as “pilot zones”.

Christa Pike was nearly taken off life support before waking, lawyers say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
23:20:01 UTC
08:20:01 KST

Christa Pike was nearly taken off life support before waking, lawyers say
Death-row inmate who survived execution by lethal injection is said to be ‘angry and confused’ about what happened.
Lawyers for Christa Pike, the Tennessee woman who survived a botched execution attempt, have said that their client was nearly disconnected from life support before she awoke this week in a United States hospital.
In a news conference on Wednesday, Randy Spivey, who represents Pike, described her as feeling “angry and confused” about what happened.
“Monday night, our understanding was that Christa was brain dead, and life support would be removed the next day,” Spivey told reporters.
But on Tuesday, he said, “Christa woke up and began talking.”
Spivey added that Pike did not seem to recall the execution attempt itself. Upon waking up in her hospital room in Nashville, she reportedly asked those in the room, “Where am I?” and “Who are you?”
Pike had been scheduled to die by lethal injection on September 30. But after receiving two doses of pentobarbital, she remained alive, becoming the first person believed to have survived such an injection in the US.
The incident has renewed questions about the use of the death penalty in the country and its legality.
Critics have long called such procedures a violation of the Eighth Amendment of the US Constitution, which prohibits “cruel and unusual punishments”.
Prior to her execution date, Pike’s lawyers had also sought to have her sentence commuted, citing concerns about her mental health. She had been convicted and sentenced to death in 1996 for participating in the murder of a classmate, 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer.
On Wednesday, her legal team described her as cooperating with Tennessee officials during the scheduled execution.
“She was kind and polite as they worked for an hour, stabbing her arm with needle after needle, and then she felt the burn of the pentobarbital,” Spivey said.
“And then she woke up in a hospital surrounded by people she didn’t know.”
While the lethal injections were meant to go into Pike’s veins, experts have speculated that the pentobarbital instead pooled in the tissue of her arm. Her arms and hands remain heavily swollen and covered in blisters, Spivey added.
It is unclear whether the state of Tennessee will attempt to execute Pike a second time.
But Spivey has indicated he and Pike’s other lawyers will once more seek to have her sentence commuted, based on the suffering she experienced during the botched execution.
On Wednesday, in anticipation of such legal proceedings, Nashville Judge I’Ashea Myles ordered the state to save evidence from the execution attempt, including drugs, syringes and IV lines, as well as recordings and any communication records between officials.
Since the execution attempt, Tennessee’s Republican Governor Bill Lee has also ordered a halt to carrying out other death penalty sentences. Another execution had been scheduled in the state for later this year.
“Carrying out a lawfully imposed sentence is among the State’s most serious responsibilities, and the people of Tennessee expect it to be done in a manner that is not only legal and constitutional, but is effective,” Lee said in a statement.
In the wake of the botched execution, the state’s top prison official, Tennessee Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada, has announced he will resign this month.
Pike’s lethal injection was not the only botched execution in Tennessee this year.
Governor Lee granted a one-year reprieve to Tony Carruthers, whom officials attempted to execute in May 2026. But after an hour of trying, they could not find a vein to connect an IV for the pentobarbital, and the execution was suspended.
Other states, however, have signalled they would proceed with carrying out death penalty cases despite the Tennessee incidents.
A Texas court refused to halt the execution by pentobarbital of 46-year-old Jamaal Howard, scheduled for Wednesday, despite appeals from his lawyers citing Pike’s botched execution.
Those opposed to the death penalty have argued that such executions can cause unnecessary suffering. In Pike’s case, she reportedly kicked a sheet off her body during the execution attempt and said she was feeling pain.
Before her scheduled execution, Pike had warned authorities about the difficulty of finding veins in her arm and had even requested to be executed by firing squad.

China’s succession crisis: a generation of entrepreneurs is retiring, but are their children ready to take over?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
23:19:03 UTC
08:19:03 KST

Growing up, Ayu would watch his parents put together hand made leather shoes on the ground floor of their three storey home in the Chinese city of Wenzhou. Their relatives in Europe would send photographs of designer products from Italy for the workers to base their designs on, and in the decades that followed, the tiny family-run workshop transformed into a 700 person factory.
“The factory and the home were the same place. I watched them make shoes by hand, piece by piece, using small machines,” Ayu recalls of watching his parents work in the 1980’s.
By the mid eighties, Chinese economists had a name for this type of bottom up economic growth story: the Wenzhou model. It was a system that saw small companies secure finances through family connections and operate underground factories to produce cheap goods that would end up on the busy streets of China and beyond.
But now many of the family-run manufacturing businesses that helped to fuel China’s economic success are facing a succession crisis, with the children of factory owners unable or unwilling to take them over.
Ayu – who today runs an online e-commerce platform – says it’s not that his generation doesn’t want to take them over, but that the market is much more competitive than when their parents started, and the crucial institutional knowledge and commercial relationships that powered their success will be impossible to pass on.
Personal relationships, experience and instincts are difficult to hand over to the next generation, says Hanqing Fang, an associate professor at Missouri University of Science and Technology.
“Shares can be passed to a son or daughter overnight,” Fang says. “But the heir is being asked to take over something that looks like a company on paper but, in practice, is closer to the founder’s personal belongings.”
“The network is very difficult to inherit,” Ayu says. “You have to build it yourself. In the end, some people inherit an empty shell. On paper they’re the boss, but the people underneath them have already begun to leave.
“We inherited the wealth, but we couldn’t inherit the industry.”
‘I’m not ready yet, because it’s not easy’
According to HSBC Life research, two-thirds of wealthy Chinese people have no legacy plan. In a study led by the University of Ningbo, just 10 out of 114 private companies surveyed said they were being managed by the families’ second generation.
Many of China’s second generation business owners speak of a profound anxiety about taking over the family firm.
“I really don’t want to take over because there are so many interpersonal relationships and financial connections that I’d have to handle and learn about,” says Wu, a graduate who works in marketing in Hong Kong.
His family own a snack processing factory in the Chinese city of Shanwei, as well as dozens of stores in Shenzhen and Hong Kong. But he is reluctant to join the family business.
“Most young people dream of getting rich overnight, but I know there’s no such thing. When inheriting a fortune, you also have to consider all the complicated paperwork and whether you really have the ability to handle those responsibilities,” Wu says.
According to official estimates, China’s private sector accounts for more than half of the country’s tax revenue and 60% of its GDP. Economists say unsuccessful handovers can lead to firms losing value or even closing.
Because family-run companies represent such a large percentage of China’s private sector, if they fail in their thousands it could threaten the country’s future growth.
“The risk is not that these family firms simply disappear. It is that the capabilities embedded in the founder – including the knowhow, the supplier networks and the relationships – are lost in the handover,” Fang says.
For Wu, the idea of one day taking control of the family business is not completely out of the question, but he concedes he still has a lot to learn.
“I’d say that one day my parents’ company will be mine. But I’m not ready yet, because it’s not easy,” Wu says.
“If I could just have the money without any responsibilities, I’d take it without hesitation. But the thing is, it’s not that simple.”
Additional reporting by Yu-chen Li in Taipei
*Given names only have been used

====================================================================================================

Those OpenAI Math Results
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
23:16:38 UTC
08:16:38 KST

In what is being called “the most important event in the history of mathematics” (by an AI), OpenAI, using an advanced model not yet available to the public, yesterday released 722 mathematics manuscripts containing 337 results it has generated on open mathematics problems.
“OpenAI deluged mathematicians with hundreds of new findings that span a wide swath of topics including algebra, number theory, theoretical computer science, mathematical logic and topology,” the New York Times reports. Adding insult to injury, “the average result took about three hours of computing, the company said.”
One AI engineer on x.com put it this way: “Reasoning models are two years-old. In that time they went from incapable of basic arithmetic to solving problems humans couldn’t solve for decades.”
What were the results like? Computer scientist Scott Aaronson shares some of his thoughts and those of his wife, complexity theorist Dana Moshkovitz, here. Moshkovitz says: “It feels like something written by someone who’s on psychedelics…” and “so horribly written that it’s impossible to read it without AI help…”, but: “of course there’s a lot for us to learn from the aliens”.
After mathematicians raised concerns about an earlier breakthrough on the Navier-Stokes problem by OpenAI, the firm formed an mathematics advisory group to advise it on the “review and communication of emerging results.” Their job is to
help OpenAI assess their significance, advise on how to coordinate their dissemination, and advise on academic and professional standards of mathematical research… The group will operate independently from OpenAI. The group will have the freedom to offer advice we have not requested, comment on OpenAI’s impact on mathematics, and make its advice public.
In the wake of the new results,
the advisory board released a statement that called the public release “the beginning, not the completion, of the process of human understanding and the incorporation of the work into mathematical knowledge.” “We want to create standards and practices so that results released from A.I. labs can be understood by mathematicians and can advance the field,” Melanie Wood, a mathematician at Harvard who is a member of the advisory board, said in an email
The advisory group also called for the release of “all of the prompts to the A.I. agents and the agents’ chains of thought.”
Mathematicians were already wondering about the future of their field in light of AI’s capacities. It seems like the discipline of mathematics must “change or risk extinction,” as Jordana Cepelewicz puts it in a recent piece at Quanta.
Readers of Daily Nous might be wondering about whether philosophy will face a similar reckoning. And indeed much of what Cepelewicz says about mathematics—especially on what seems to be missed when machines provide us with the answers—could be said about philosophy. Here are some examples:
Many people don’t know what mathematics really is, or why mathematicians do it…
I always found that “pure math” — the study of mathematical concepts for their own sake, without a care for real-world applications — existed somewhere between the sciences and the arts. It prizes logic and certainty, but at its core lie fuzzier notions of beauty, intuition, and depth. “Math is either the most science-y humanities or the most humanities-type science, depending who you ask,” said Marcel Goh, a doctoral student at McGill University…
In mathematics, it’s not a cliché that the journey matters more than the destination. Problems are posed not so much because their answers will be practical and important, but because they represent interesting journeys. The hope is that as mathematicians struggle to solve a problem, they’ll come up with intriguing tools and connections, stumble on novel ideas and directions, take fruitful detours, and answer new questions they never would have thought to ask….
Mathematicians have always known that understanding is more valuable than an answer…
The whole piece, worth reading, also discusses some ways that academic mathematics will likely have to change.
Still, it is not obvious that philosophy is susceptible to the same kind of threat that mathematics is currently dealing with. While there are no shortages of open problems in philosophy, one might nonetheless say: philosophy is not in danger of its problems being solved by AI because its problems cannot be solved.
I think such a response is both too pessimistic and too optimistic. It’s too pessimistic because some of philosophy’s problems are at least in principle solvable. Examples: Is principle P compatible with judgment J? Is argument A valid? What are the implications of belief B? Which theory of X is most compatible with this particular theory of Y and current science? And so on. It’s too optimistic because it seems quite likely that some future form of AI will be able to answer these kinds of questions (and similar ones with scopes too wide and variables too numerous for a human mind to keep track of). Generally, most of the philosophical “solutions” that humans offer are the consequents of explicit or tacit conditionals, and I would think that AIs will be quite good at conditional reasoning. (See “Hey Sophi“.)
Tomorrow there will be a guest post about how AI might change philosophy, but I wanted to give people a chance to discuss the mathematics results, and perhaps the relevant similarities and differences between mathematics and philosophy.

23:13:27 UTC
08:13:27 KST

NEW DELHI: Doctors and hospitals cannot use AI to create patient testimonials, clinical outcomes or promotional content, nor can they pay to manipulate rankings like those on search engines and apps, under new ethical advertising guidelines issued by National Medical Commission Tuesday, effective immediately.NMC has barred registered medical practitioners and hospitals from using AI-generated content to advertise their services, solicit patients or disseminate unverifiable information about diagnoses, treatments or outcomes. AI cannot be used to create synthetic patient testimonials, voices, clinical outcomes or fake endorsements, or misrepresent the nature or quality of medical services.Doctors can't pay for manipulate search rankings. They also can't make unverified claims such as "best", "number one", "most trusted", "guaranteed cures" or "100% success".Doctors cannot engage influencers, advertising agencies or online platforms in arrangements involving payment linked to procuring patients. Doctors and hospitals cannot offer limited-period discounts, coupons, gift packages or referral benefits if these are likely to encourage unnecessary consultations. However, NMC allows doctors to use social media for factual, non-promotional health education. Hospitals can similarly share objective details.
The guidelines restrict the use of patient photographs without valid consent and safeguards. Patient testimonials, before-and-after images and treatment-success claims that could create unrealistic expectations or mislead are also prohibited.NMC has prescribed a warning and mandatory ethics training for a first violation, censure and monetary penalty for a second, suspension for three to six months for a third, and six to 12 months for serious violations. Repeated violations can lead to removal from the medical register for one to three years.
Anuja Jaiswal is a Senior Assistant Editor at The Times of India, with an impressive 18-year career in narrative journalism. She specializes in health and heritage reporting, expertly simplifying complex health information to make it engaging and understandable for readers. Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. Over the years, she has worked in Chandigarh, Chhattisgarh and West UP, gaining diverse on-ground experience that shapes her storytelling.

Coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki said the operation targeted Houthi positions in Saada, Hodeidah, Al-Jawf and Marib.
The targets included 11 ballistic missile storage facilities in mountainous areas of Saada along with command and control centers, communications systems, missile and weapons depots and Houthi headquarters, he said.

Fighting intensified in September when the Houthis seized strategic positions in the provinces of Al-Hudaydah and Taiz, including the port city of Mokha, before advancing to Mayyun Island in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and several provinces in September 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.

Iranian strikes forced US troops to ‘abandon’ Kuwait base – CBS (VIDEO)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
23:05:14 UTC
08:05:14 KST

Iranian strikes forced US troops to ‘abandon’ Kuwait base – CBS (VIDEO)
Iranian strikes forced US troops to effectively abandon a major military base in Kuwait during the opening stages of the US-Israeli war on Iran, according to newly released footage and accounts from American servicemen obtained by CBS News.
Videos shared by American soldiers in breach of the Pentagon’s strict media policy show several drones nosediving into Camp Buehring, a major US Army staging facility roughly 40 km from the Iraqi border, as well as damage to buildings and military equipment. CBS said it authenticated the recordings using embedded metadata and imagery of the aftermath.
The installation came under repeated attack by Iranian ballistic missiles and drones after hostilities began on February 28. A US service member also told CBS that Iranian F-5 fighter jets flew missions against the base “so close to us I could see their helmets.”
Most of the roughly 7,000 troops stationed at Camp Buehring had already been dispersed before the war under what the Pentagon called its “get off the X” strategy, aimed at moving personnel away from fixed positions vulnerable to Iranian retaliation.
Some 100 soldiers, however, remained behind to defend the installation, where they were repeatedly forced into bunkers and ran critically low on ammunition, including Patriot interceptors.
“They hit us bad,” one serviceman told the outlet. “It was horrible... We had to abandon the base.”
The remaining troops eventually fled the base and established improvised forward operating outposts in the Kuwaiti desert, where they remained for weeks. No US personnel were killed, although several were injured, including two who were struck by lightning during desert sandstorms.
“CBKU got demolished,” the serviceman said. “They need to do an investigation. How come no one came to reinforce us?”
The Pentagon declined to comment directly on the CBS report, instead referring the outlet to remarks made by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in March, when he acknowledged that more than 90% of American personnel had been moved away from US regional bases.
The revelations come days after an Associated Press investigation raised separate questions about US preparations elsewhere in Kuwait. An Iranian drone struck an American operations center at Port Shuaiba on March 1, killing six soldiers and wounding dozens in what remains the deadliest known single attack on American troops during the conflict. Some of the wounded said troops initially treated each other with basic first-aid supplies and had to use Google to locate the nearest hospital in Kuwait City. The Pentagon has maintained that its medical response was appropriate.
The devastation at Camp Buehring was part of a much broader campaign against the US military footprint across the Middle East, with Iranian missiles and drones striking bases and installations in multiple countries and damaging aircraft, radar systems, hangars, barracks, and other infrastructure.
By September, CENTCOM said the war had already cost Washington $43.6 billion, a figure that did not include extensive damage to US bases across eight countries. The true personnel toll has also remained disputed: the Pentagon publicly listed 18 military deaths as of mid-September, while military sources cited by the Washington Post put the figure at 22 or 23.
As the damage mounted, the Pentagon tightened control over images emerging from the region. After an Iranian missile and drone strike on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan on July 17 killed three US service members, CENTCOM commander Admiral Brad Cooper warned troops against filming strike sites, claiming that publicly posted footage was helping Tehran assess the accuracy and effects of its attacks. US allies hosting American bases have likewise imposed strict bans and penalties on filming military sites and strike aftermaths, making independent footage of Iranian attacks increasingly rare.

Stark 73% decline in the average size of monitored wildlife populations since 1970, India presents ground for hope: WWF Living Planet Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
23:05:00 UTC
08:05:00 KST

NEW DELHI: There was a stark 73% decline in the “average size of monitored wildlife populations” globally over a 52-year period (1970-2022), whereas India became one of the most important countries that were successfully involved in wildlife recovery by turning around the populations of certain animals, including tigers, one-horned rhino and Ganga river dolphins, according to WWF’s biennial Living Planet Report (LPR) released on Thursday.Though the LPR remains silent on country-specific data, experts explaining certain points ahead of the release noted “significant changes” in biodiversity in India where nine species of mammals figured in the “critically endangered” list, 39% of 942 bird species reported “clear decline” and 32% (136 species) of the amphibians have been “threatened” by a combination of factors including agricultural practices and climate change.Nine mammals classified as critically endangered (CR) in India under International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) criteria are Kashmir Stag/Hangul, Malabar Large-spotted Civet, Chinese Pangolin, Andaman Shrew, Jenkin’s Shrew, Nicobar Shrew, Namdapha Flying Squirrel, Large Rock Rat and Leafletted Leaf-nosed Bat.The report is based on Living Planet Index (LPI), which tracks how species populations are faring around the world.
The Index, produced by Zoological Society of London, includes 35,803 population trends of 5,790 vertebrate species (mammals, birds, amphibians, reptiles and fish) from 1970 to 2022.It noted the strongest decline in freshwater ecosystems (-85%), followed by terrestrial (-69%) and then marine (-59%) over the 1970 baseline. Region-wise, Latin America and the Caribbean registered the highest decline of 95%, followed by Africa (80%), Asia-Pacific (49%), North America (28%), and Europe and Central Asia (23%).The report said the “habitat loss and degradation” are the most frequently reported threat affecting monitored wildlife populations, followed by overexploitation, climate change, pollution, invasive species and disease. “These threats are, in turn, driven by broader systemic failures across the food, energy and finance systems,” it said.Although the overall trend is negative due to the magnitude of the declining trends, LPR noted that half of the populations included in the Index are “stable or increasing”. It highlighted recoveries in populations of green turtles, bluefin tuna, tigers and southern African elephants, which demonstrate that targeted conservation interventions can deliver proven results.Asked about the biggest takeaway in the LPR that flagged an upward trend in the numbers of species in India including tigers, Asiatic lion, common leopard and snow leopard, Sejal Worah, programme director, WWF-India, said one big message is that the country can actually turn around wildlife populations and species with the right combination of factors, including political will, required finances, civil society engagement and involvement with local communities. India has shown that wildlife recovery is possible, she added.WWF-India, during its pre-release presentation, however, underlined certain significant changes in biodiversity in India. It noted that the country is home to around 135 bat species that face neglect due to a “lack of research” and are threatened by urbanisation, deforestation, land-use changes and climate change. It also said that freshwater fish are among the most threatened vertebrates.“The LPR 2026 is both a stark reminder of the scale of the biodiversity crisis and a message of hope. While the LPI continues to highlight significant declines in monitored wildlife populations, the report also shows that these declines are not inevitable. Species recoveries, including those of tigers in India and globally, demonstrate what sustained conservation action, collaboration and long-term commitment can achieve,” said Ravi Singh, secretary general & CEO, WWF-India.
Referring to data, the report said, “Although the overall global trend is negative, half (50%) of the populations included in the LPI are stable (7%) or increasing (43%). The magnitude of the declining trends, however, exceeds that of the increasing trends resulting in an average decline of 73% for the global LPI.”It, however, clarified that the percentage change in the index reflects the cumulative average proportional change in monitored animal population sizes at sites around the world since 1970, not the number of individual animals lost, nor the number of populations lost.It also said that the LPI are not directly comparable as they contain different sets of species (967 more populations and 295 more species have been added to the dataset since the LPR 2024) and cover a longer period each time.

He has been covering Parliament since 2003 to see how politics shaped up domestic policy and India’s position at global platform. Before switching over to explore sustainable development issues, Vishwa had covered internal security and investigative agencies for more than a decade.

World must change way it produces food to avoid biodiversity collapse, says WWF
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
23:01:03 UTC
08:01:03 KST

Conservation comebacks for wild tigers, tuna and green sea turtles prove that global nature loss can be reversed, scientists have said. But a report warns food production must be the next “positive tipping point” if the world is to avert biodiversity collapse.
The World Wildlife Fund (WWF) analysed nearly 36,000 animal populations and more than 5,000 species, producing the largest ever database of vertebrate wildlife. Scientists found populations had declined by an average of 73% since 1970, showing that “nature continues to be degraded at an alarming scale”, with “no sign of losses slowing”.
Nature loss is no longer just an environmental challenge but a direct threat to the global economy, the report says, noting that about half of global GDP – roughly $58tn (£44tn) in 2023 – depends on nature and its ecosystem services. The authors write that species collapse now poses an “existential threat to economic stability, geopolitical security and human wellbeing”.
Animal populations were found to be falling most sharply in tropical, biodiversity-rich regions, while trends in northern temperate parts of the world appeared much gentler.
In Latin America and the Caribbean, land and freshwater wildlife populations fell by an average of 95% between 1970 and 2022, while the equivalent declines were 80% in Africa and 23% in Europe and Central Asia.
Freshwater wildlife suffered the sharpest losses across the world’s ecosystems, with monitored populations in rivers and lakes down by an average of 85%, compared with 69% for land species and 59% for marine species.
Tanya Steele, the chief executive of WWF UK, said: “Nature loss is not just a crisis for wildlife. It’s already sending us the bill through growing risks to our food security, water supplies, economy and resilience to climate shocks.
“We stand at a fork in the road: either we continue paying the rising price of nature loss, or we invest in nature’s recovery and a future where people and wildlife can thrive together.”
But despite the pattern of global biodiversity decline, wild tigers, green sea turtles and bluefin tuna are recovering, the report said, showing that “it is still possible to reverse the global loss of nature when action is taken”.
In 2010, about 3,200 wild tigers remained globally and the species was sliding toward extinction. After sustained and targeted conservation interventions, the population has grown to roughly 5,700, an increase of more than 70%.
Becci May, WWF UK’s tiger lead, said the remarkable comeback of wild tigers demonstrated the “science of hope” and proved that when climate and ecological action was taken, change was possible.
The report said Atlantic and Pacific bluefin tuna populations, which were collapsing after decades of overfishing, had now recovered to the point where neither was now considered threatened.
Last year, the green sea turtle became the first marine turtle ever downlisted from endangered to “least concern” on the IUCN red list, reflecting 50 years of coordinated conservation work across about 80 countries.
Dr Mike Barrett, the chief scientific adviser for WWF UK and a co-author of the report, said: “These are examples that show that nature can recover even when pushed right to the brink, and they provide us with inspiration. It’s also very clear that conservation alone cannot tackle the scale of threats facing nature.”
He said nature would have no chance of recovery if “negative tipping points” – self-reinforcing, irreversible ecological changes that accelerate climate crisis – were passed. “The systems which drive nature’s loss have to be transformed. And that’s energy, food and finance,” he said.
“Our report shows that we’ve already passed the tipping point in the energy sector with the take-up of renewable energy. That transition is now unstoppable. It’s not happening fast enough, but it is unstoppable.”
Humanity must likewise adapt the way it produces food, he said. “Agriculture is the single largest cause of habitat loss and degradation and therefore the loss of biodiversity. It’s also a major source of greenhouse gas emissions and so helps drive climate change, so you have that feedback.”
Dr Steve Smith, a research fellow from the University of Exeter and a co-author of the report, said: “The biggest prize for nature recovery would be a sustainable and healthy food system, but it’s currently the farthest away from positively tipping. For example, agricultural expansion drives almost 90% of deforestation worldwide.”
Positive tipping points are thresholds beyond which a sustainable technology or practice becomes increasingly cheap, widespread or politically popular, allowing progress to become self-propelling.

Bendy elm still standing against all odds crowned UK tree of the year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
23:01:03 UTC
08:01:03 KST

The “astonishing and bizarre” Bendy Tree in Northern Ireland has been crowned the winner of this year’s tree of the year competition.
The wych elm tree, located in Newcastle, County Down, owes its name to its near horizontal trunk, which has grown sideways owing to the strong seaside winds coming off the Irish Sea.
The 150-year-old tree has resisted Dutch elm disease, a fungus that has destroyed most of the UK’s 30m elms, making it a worthy winner of the competition’s “against the odds” theme.
The tree was originally planted in the mid-19th century as part of a row of wych elms along the town’s promenade to shelter the main street from sea winds. Many of those trees were felled during redevelopments of the town, with the bendy tree now the last one standing.
“When you look at this astonishing and bizarre tree, there’s no doubt about what it has endured,” said May Chemais, ancient tree inventory lead for the Woodland Trust, the charity that runs the annual competition.
“We’ve all been through changes and hardships that have shaped who we are: I think that’s why the Bendy Tree has struck a chord with people,” she said.
For John Martin, director of the Woodland Trust NI, it is the whimsical nature of the tree that makes it a worthy winner.
Having grown up visiting Newcastle as a child, Martin recalls seeing the tree out of the corner of his eye and being surprised to see a tree growing this way.
“You expect nature to behave in a certain way and we would expect a tree, most of the time, to grow upwards, whereas this one has grown sideways,” he said. “I guess it gives people a bit of a smile on their day.”
The tree’s unusual shape has also provided welcome shade to residents and visitors resting on the bench located beneath its branches.
“Older trees like this one are providing our communities with so much – from shade, wellbeing and health benefits, to stories, culture and pride of place,” said Chemais.
Other trees nominated in this year’s competition included the Crowhurst Yew in Crowhurst, Surrey, England. Villagers hollowed out the trunk in 1820 to create a parish meeting room within the tree. The roof of this room collapsed during a storm in 1845, but the tree lived on, with the wooden door to the secret room remaining to this day.
Also in the top 10 shortlist was the Culmstock Yew in Culmstock, Devon, England. This tree is perched on top a 20-metre high church tower, with its existence pre-dating residents’ living memories.
Last year’s honour went to a 75ft ash tree that shades homes on one of Glasgow’s busiest roads.
The Woodland Trust has this week launched its Igniting Innovation competition for anyone aged 16 to 25 to share their ideas for projects that could benefit nature and make life better for woods, trees and people.
Three winners will receive £5,000 in funding and up to a year of expert mentoring to bring their projects to life.

In Helping Ukraine, We Protect Ourselves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
23:00:00 UTC
08:00:00 KST

In Helping Ukraine, We Protect Ourselves
Supporting Ukraine is self-interest, not charity: Russia threatens democracies well beyond Europe, and Ukraine’s battlefield innovation and civilian resilience hold lessons for the West.
Your authors have just returned from a 10-day visit to Ukraine, with meetings in Lviv, Kyiv, Kharkiv and Dnipro. We met extraordinary innovators at drone factories and visited war-weary but motivated soldiers close to the kill-zone. We heard from NGOs, media outlets and common citizens, all of whom shared a basic message: they will not break us.
As Ukrainians face a fifth winter of war, anticipating severe power and heating shortages due to Russian attacks on energy infrastructure (now including petrol stations), their ongoing resilience is remarkable. This is even more impressive when we are reminded of the numerous and brutal Russian human rights transgressions since the start: the murder of civilians in Bucha and Izyum, the torture and deaths of prisoners of war, the abduction and exfiltration of children into Russia. The indiscriminate attacks against civilians – with ballistic missiles, glide-bombs and drones – all ensure that nowhere feels safe, a deliberate tactic in the Russian government’s ‘cognitive warfare’ campaign.
Casualties are mounting, with as many as 250,000-300,000 killed and wounded on the Ukrainian side and over five times this number on the Russian. Though defiant, Ukrainians are also understandably exhausted. Today, some of Ukraine’s staunchest allies are also experiencing fatigue, with increased pressure back home due to high energy costs, inflation and strained social services. Far-right parties in Europe, many cosy with Russia, are surging in the polls in countries that have been major supporters of Ukraine, including Germany and France. Public backing is already weaker across southern Europe, where governments and citizens have to contend with security threats to their south in addition to the threat posed by Russia.
In today’s transactional, realpolitik world, many governments and their citizens are asking why they should keep sending billions of dollars to Ukraine. What is in it for us? It is a fair question and one that demands greater public debate about the merits of continued support to Ukraine.
This question has two distinct answers.
A Threat to All Our Democracies
The first is that Russia poses a threat not just to its immediate neighbours, but to all our democracies. Indeed, over the last decade, Russia has been conducting grey-area, subthreshold attacks against most NATO Allies. This includes – but is not limited to – cyberattacks on critical infrastructure; drone incursions at airports; interference with undersea cables (which we rely on for financial transactions, energy and internet connectivity); arson attacks on warehouses; the murder/attempted murder of Russians abroad – even with chemical weapons; the weaponisation of migrants; shadowing of NATO vessels; and disinformation campaigns and election interference.
Ukraine’s incredible advances in drone technology and innovations on the battlefield are well known. The country’s military is now the most advanced and practised in Europe, and they are ready to share their accumulated wisdom and experience with us
These hybrid attacks all fall below the threshold that would require a kinetic response, and have only increased in pace and reach over the last year. It is only a matter of time until one of these triggers a response above the threshold. In today’s more mercantilist geopolitical framework, where countries have interests before friends, relying on a willing Ukrainian military to confront the Russians with Western treasure is cheaper than having to invest Western blood.
We should take Putin at his word: the threat to European security is real. He has made clear his objectives. In 2024, in an address to the Federal Assembly of Russia, he stated he was seeking to create 'a new equal and indivisible security framework in Eurasia'.
This new framework would be Eurasian in nature, lean towards the BRICS in which leadership would come, of course, from Russia. Putin added: 'I would like to reiterate (I think this is important for everyone) that no enduring international order is possible without a strong and sovereign Russia.' In other words, the security of Ukraine would ultimately be guaranteed by its aggressor, Russia.
But the same goes for other European countries. Russia would hold a veto power over decisions by countries it considers under its sphere of influence. Those countries would no longer be free to choose their allies, their political model or even the core values of their societies, without first receiving authorisation from Moscow. This is closest to the control imposed on African countries under colonialism.
This makes, for example, Europe’s withholding of old Patriot stocks from Ukraine an act of self-harm. Any attempt to sell (rather than donate) them to Ukraine makes it an act of selfishness and short-sightedness at best, extortion at worst.
Beyond Europe
The impacts of this war do not, however, stop at Europe.
Africa in particular has faced a different type of threat from Russia. While there is evidence of Russian involvement in election malfeasance, not least in South Africa and Zambia, the presence of its mercenaries in propping up regimes across the Sahel can only amplify the underlying problems of governance and exclusion. Presumably Moscow accrues added benefit when migrants become weaponised as a result.
The second reason to support Ukraine, even more apparent on this recent visit, is that we can all learn from Ukraine, on both the military and civilian sides. Ukraine’s incredible advances in drone technology and innovations on the battlefield are well known. The country’s military is now the most advanced and practised in Europe, and they are ready to share their accumulated wisdom and experience with us.
Ukraine’s lesson is less in cutting-edge invention than innovation and most importantly in expediting implementation at much lower costs than their counterparts in Western Europe and North America. The existential nature of its struggle has removed many – but not all – of the frictions in the system of arms procurement, especially as younger generations prefer this newer market and the governance it offers over the Soviet, centralised model.
But it is especially among the soldiers on the frontline that this spirit of resistance coupled with pragmatism abounds: ‘We have no choice but to fight for our freedom and our right to choose,’ says Fedir Sediuk, an expert in drone warfare. ‘Supporting our struggle,’ he adds, ‘is not only to be firmly on the right side of history, but also to be acting in the interests of countries who want to gain from Ukraine’s experience as much as they share the interest of stopping Russia’s imperial ambition.’
‘The key to be a good unit,’ says ‘Django’, the call-sign of the deputy commander of the 413th Unmanned Systems RAID Regiment, ‘is to be flexible in your technology and to be free in its use. Since 2022, we have been using multiple types of systems. Commanders have to be available 24/7 to soldiers on tactical issues.’ He believes that through the DELTA integrated command and control and effectiveness measurement system ‘we can control the battlefield online, and it immediately shows how good or bad we were on which day, how we can improve, and how we can strengthen our flanking units.’
Or as a member of your authors' group, Grahame Wilson, the legendary ‘Phantom Major’ Zimbabwean Special Air Service commander, reminded us when speaking to Ukrainian soldiers in Dnipro: 'The connection between different eras of warfare is the individual – the men and women who run all the machines.'
The determination is clear. As Danyil Vakhovskyi, the executive director of General Cherry, a drone-producing company which has rapidly ramped up production from humble beginnings to over a remarkable 100,000 units per month, stated wryly: ‘We focus on targeting Russian aggression more efficiently every day in ensuring the maths of war is in our favour.’
This sentiment is unlikely to change given the increased tempo of Russian bombings of Ukrainian cities. In July, Russia launched a single-month record of 376 missiles (including 126 ballistic missiles) and 4,956 attack drones nationwide. In September, Kyiv alone logged around 190 air raid alarms, three times the count seen in July. Country-wide drone numbers increased too, with Russia deploying 3,177 jet-powered drones alone by late September alongside expanded ballistic and cruise missile packages. UN figures show 2,222 civilians killed in Ukraine during the first eight months of 2026, more than in all of 2025. Yet as strategic bombing campaigns remind from London’s Blitz through the firestorms of German and Japanese cities to Vietnam, such actions tend to temper rather than weaken civilian resilience.
This is a grim business, one that Europe would be sensible in keeping away from its borders by supplying Ukraine with what it needs, and not only what Europe no longer requires. As Natalia Kurdiukova of the Kharkiv Media Hub puts it: 'Ukrainians fight on because we have paid such an immense price for our freedom that every day we live, every step forward, and every centimetre of our land bears the name of someone who sacrificed for it.'
A Society That Will Not Break
We can also learn from Ukraine’s domestic resilience and ability to uphold collective resolve. On this visit, we joined Ukrainians in respecting the nationwide, daily one minute of silence to honour fallen soldiers and civilian victims. We did this in petrol stations, at drone factories and on the streets of Kharkiv.
Ukraine’s resilience can also be seen in its rapid rebuilding of almost everything that the Russians have destroyed, often within a matter of weeks. All these send the same message: ‘you will not break us’.
Ukraine is fighting for its survival. But the conflict is also exposing the stakes for everyone else. A world in which individual rights and freedom of choice become negotiable is ultimately a world in which our own rights become negotiable too. Continued support not only helps Ukrainians in their time of need, but it will increase our own domestic resilience and defence.
Supporting Ukraine is not an act of charity. It is an act of self-interest.

Tarek Chouiref
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
The Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) called Wednesday for a “firm and deterrent” international response to attacks by Yemen’s Houthi group on Saudi Arabia, saying its members stood united with the kingdom against threats to its security and sovereignty.
GCC Secretary-General Jasem Albudaiwi condemned attacks on Abha International Airport in Abha and King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh that left civilians dead and injured.
Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation said earlier Wednesday that three people were killed and 36 others injured in attacks on the two airports on Tuesday and Wednesday.
Albudaiwi said targeting civilian airports and endangering passengers, workers and other civilians represented a “dangerous escalation” and a flagrant violation of international laws and norms.
He said the attacks required a “firm and deterrent” international stance to prevent further actions threatening regional and international security.
The GCC secretary-general reaffirmed that member states stood “as one” with Saudi Arabia and backed measures taken by Riyadh to protect its territory, security and sovereignty.
Earlier Wednesday, the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said it intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis north of Riyadh.
The attacks come amid intensified fighting in Yemen and Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia, while the Saudi-led coalition has stepped up military operations against Houthi positions.
Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognized government against the Houthis since March 2015.

From Riyadh to New Zealand: flydubai attack probe widens as rescue flights are canceled
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
22:59:01 UTC
07:59:01 KST

Arkia announced Wednesday that its repatriation flights from Dubai to Israel have been canceled, creating a new crisis in efforts to bring home Israelis stranded in the United Arab Emirates following the attempted attack on a flydubai flight.
All flights have been canceled, including those scheduled for Thursday, the final day on which the repatriation flights were due to operate.
Arkia said: “Authorization to operate the flights was valid through Tuesday, but in the evening the authorities decided to revoke the permits allowing Israeli airlines to operate flights from Dubai.
“Since then, Arkia has been working with all relevant parties and has done everything possible to obtain the permits again and operate the flights. Unfortunately, our efforts have so far been unsuccessful, so we have been forced to cancel the flights.”
The airline said passengers would receive a full refund for their tickets. "In addition, passengers who can make their own way to a destination served by Arkia will receive a 10% discount on a flight from there to Israel,” it added.
Following the incident, flydubai suspended its flights to and from Israel pending completion of the investigation, leaving hundreds of Israelis in the United Arab Emirates without their planned flights home. Emirates, flydubai’s sister airline, also immediately suspended until further notice its codeshare agreement with flydubai on routes to and from Israel. The airline also said that, for now, passengers whose final destination is Tel Aviv will not be allowed to board Emirates flights to Dubai to connect to flights to Israel.
Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia is continuing to investigate the security incident aboard the flight, in parallel with the criminal investigation being conducted by the United Arab Emirates, in which the Shin Bet is also participating.
Ofer Vaknin, director of the Israel's Aircraft Safety Investigation Authority, told Reuters that Israel had offered to participate in any safety investigation led by Saudi Arabia but had not yet been invited to take part.
“We are still waiting for a notification from Saudi Arabia to invite us to take a part in the investigation,” he said.
The U.S. news network NewsNation reported that New Zealand is also conducting an investigation. Al-Hammami, the terrorist pilot, spent six months there for flight training between November 2018 and May 2019.
Britain’s Telegraph reported that Al-Hammami, who intended to crash the flight with its Israeli passengers at Ben-Gurion Airport, studied at L3 Airline Academy, one of Britain’s largest flight schools, in a training program that apparently connected him with a flight school in Hamilton, New Zealand.
New Zealand Police told the news network that Al-Hammami spent a total of 175 days in the country, where he completed part of his flight training.
The Telegraph noted that Al-Hammami wrote on social media that he was most devout in his religious practice during his student years, which he described as his “golden years.”
