Democrats sue to stop Trump from using taxpayer funds for self-promoting ads
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
22:58:45 UTC
07:58:45 KST

The Democratic National Committee sued the Trump administration in federal court on Wednesday, asking a judge in Washington DC to stop the president from using taxpayer funds to air a series of ads promoting himself, arguing that the ads are illegal government-sponsored propaganda.
The ads promoting Donald Trump, including one recycled from his 2024 presidential campaign, have cost taxpayers more than $12m so far, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact.
Ken Martin, the DNC chair, said in a statement that Trump was misusing taxpayer dollars in “a last-ditch attempt to save Republicans in November. Americans deserve better than to have their hard-earned tax dollars used for Trump’s illegal schemes.”
After a bipartisan backlash to the use of public money to promote himself during the final month of the midterm campaign season, Trump claimed on Monday that he would direct the Maga Inc Super Pac he controls to pay for the ads instead.
The next day, however, the White House said Trump’s political action committee would not reimburse taxpayers for the money it had already spent on the ads. Then, when the government unveiled a fifth ad in the series, celebrating Trump’s military intervention in Venezuela, it was also paid for by the US government. 
The DNC complaint, filed in the US district court for the District of Columbia, alleges the ads violate federal law, including a ban on congressionally appropriated money being used for “publicity or propaganda”.
“President Trump personally directed this illegal activity. The White House office crafted the partisan campaign. The office of management and budget shifted $20m to pay for it. And US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) has carried it out. These unlawful actions are ultra vires and violate the Administrative Procedure Act (APA),” the complaint states.
The suit also notes the first ad in the series features an image of Fifa’s president, Gianni Infantino, awarding Trump the so-called “Fifa peace prize” to support its case that the ads all violate a prohibition on the use of taxpayer funds for “self-aggrandizement”.
The complaint also references new polling from Reuters/Ipsos released on Tuesday which found that an overwhelming majority of Americans, 86%, called it inappropriate to use taxpayer funds for TV ads featuring the president around an election. The survey reported that about 80% of Republicans called the ads inappropriate, with only 17% of the president’s party approving of them.
According to the suit, the ads have been broadcast on ABC, NBC, MS Now, CBS, CNN, Fox News and Newsmax, and appeared during popular NFL and college football games, and news and entertainment shows in which the president has been criticized, including Meet the Press, Jimmy Kimmel Live! and Saturday Night Live.
The federal lawsuit also includes details of another eight ads that have already been prepared for broadcast and were found “in a Dropbox account controlled by LMD Agency Inc, the government contractor bringing the ads to air”.
The ads ready to be broadcast include: one that celebrates the UFC fights staged at the White House on Trump’s birthday in June; one titled “God Made Trump”, a fan-created hymn of praise to Trump that was shown during the Republican midterm convention; one titled “Resilience”, which includes images of Trump announcing his candidacy for the presidency in 2015, then being charged in Fulton county, Georgia, in 2023 for conspiring to overturn the results of the 2020 election, and video of the assassination attempt on him during the 2024 election campaign; one titled “King of the Jungle”, which shows a lion hunting in the wild and disparages Trump’s political enemies, including former president Barack Obama. In February, Trump shared a racist video on social media that portrayed him as a lion and Barack and Michelle Obama as apes.
According to CNN, which gained access to the Dropbox last week, another ad in the series features attacks on Joe Biden, including the mocking image of the former president as an autopen installed by Trump on an exterior wall of the White House.

Inside IDF’s Oct. 7 raid in Nablus to ‘prevent the next massacre’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
22:56:39 UTC
07:56:39 KST

The short drive through the darkness toward the city passed quickly. The destination was Nablus, long regarded by the IDF as one of the main centers of terrorism in the northern West Bank. The timing was deliberate: The Samaria Brigade chose Oct. 7 for a major operation targeting Hamas terrorists and infrastructure in the city.
At exactly midnight, as the date changed to Oct. 7, the forces moved out. Two reserve battalions were joined by the Nahal Brigade’s 931st Battalion.
“We’ve been in this sector for three weeks,” said Lt. Col. N., commander of the battalion. “Before that we were in the Ephraim sector and then in Lebanon. The soldiers and commanders in my battalion understand exactly what they are doing here.”
“Before we arrived, I told them our job was to prevent the next Oct. 7. At the same time, if there is terrorism, it should encounter the army, not civilians. The soldiers understand what they are protecting here, at the intersections and in the communities. When residents pass by and tell them ‘thank you,’ it reinforces that understanding.”
Weapons, drones and terror funds
Each force participating in the operation was assigned a specific mission. Some distributed IDF leaflets telling residents that Hamas was exploiting them. Others posted warnings on streetlights urging residents to stay away from dangerous locations and not take part in incitement or terrorist activity.
Reports from units operating across the city came in continuously: large sums of money allegedly intended for terrorism were seized, along with tactical vests, ammunition and even drones. A reservist from Battalion 8208 described the large cache of weapons found in one home.
Battalion 8208 is also responsible for the Jalud area, where two homes belonging to the Tubasi family were set on fire a week earlier.
“We focus only on the mission, whether it is a brigade operation or dealing with lawbreakers, and block out all the background noise,” one soldier said.
The Samaria Brigade carries out arrest operations almost every night, with commanders describing nonstop counterterrorism activity as the guiding principle.
“We don’t leave targets sitting on the shelf,” said the brigade commander, Col. D. “If a target comes up for arrest, we act on it that same day. Throughout the week we arrested terrorists who were talking about terrorism connected to Oct. 7. We see that the date carries great significance for them.”
‘We will reach every site’
“This is Martyrs’ Square. It will be demolished in the coming hours,” one soldier said during the operation.
The square displayed the names of terrorists who carried out attacks against Israelis and had become a gathering place for young people in the city. As IDF troops approached, youths began throwing stones before quickly fleeing.
The demolition of memorials was carried out together with Border Police forces in the West Bank and under the direction of Maj. Y., the brigade’s engineering officer.
“Demolishing the memorials is a small but significant part of the overall brigade operation,” he said. “After searching homes and questioning suspects, what remains is to destroy places we know serve as centers of incitement.”
Fourteen memorials and signs honoring terrorists were demolished overnight using engineering equipment.
“Even when an incitement site is in a crowded or remote location, we will reach it,” Maj. Y. said. “We are not afraid to enter these places.”
Several months ago, MK Zvi Sukkot drew widespread attention after requesting an IDF escort, stopping near one such memorial and beginning to smash it himself.
After Palestinian social media accounts reported the demolitions from the latest operation, claims circulated that they had been carried out following mapping conducted by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich and Sukkot. Military officials said that was incorrect, saying the demolitions had been planned earlier and were carried out after the required legal approvals and an operational assessment.
“Dealing with memorials and centers of terrorism and incitement is routine, daily work involving both brigade intelligence and the Shin Bet,” Maj. Y. said. “We are very familiar with these memorials. This is nothing new for us.”
“There are many more memorials and signs in villages throughout the sector, and we will continue reaching them and demolishing them. Wherever we are told to go, we will go and carry out the mission. We are not dependent on any outside party.”
Some 200 detained or questioned
As morning broke over Nablus, the forces began preparing to return to their base. Stone throwers targeted military vehicles as they left the city, and troops responded.
The IDF described the overnight operation as a success. Around 200 people identified with Hamas were detained, questioned or arrested on suspicion of incitement linked to Oct. 7. Weapons and funds allegedly intended for terrorism were seized, while memorials and signs honoring terrorists were dismantled or demolished.
“Our operation made an impact in Nablus, and the messages were delivered directly,” Lt. Col. N. said. “Those who needed to be arrested were arrested, and the weapons were found. That is thanks to the soldiers and commanders who keep pushing forward.”
“To finish such a successful operation on a day like this is a privilege for us.”

Lithuania to deploy troops along border with Russia's Kaliningrad after Latvia incident
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
22:56:37 UTC
07:56:37 KST

Lithuania to deploy troops along border with Russia's Kaliningrad after Latvia incident
Lithuania's Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas called for troops to be deployed to the country's border with Kaliningrad, a Russian exclave, in a statement on Oct. 7.
The request came in response to an incident in neighboring Latvia the day prior, as well as the overall security situation in the region amid escalating tensions between Russia and NATO regarding Kaliningrad.
"I have appealed to the Defense Minister, Robertas Kaunas, to have Lithuanian Armed Forces units deployed to help border guards protect the border with the Kaliningrad region," Katelynas said in a statement on social media.
The move is a preventative measure in response to signals that Russia may announce mobilization, he said.
The requested deployment follows two security breaches at the Latvian border on Oct. 6. First, armed guards escorted groups of illegal migrants across Latvia's border with Belarus. Shortly after, masked individuals once again crossed the Latvia-Belarus border, stealing equipment before returning.
The Lithuanian minister said that there was no reason to panic and that the situation at the border is calm.
"Deploying soldiers is a preventive decision, so that we are prepared and can stop similar incidents," he said.
The move comes a day after Lithuania's parliament took the first step toward lifting the country's ban on deploying nuclear weapons on its territory.
The measure would repeal Article 137 of Lithuania's constitution, which currently prohibits weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases on Lithuanian territory.
NATO has expanded its presence in the Baltics in recent months, with a German military brigade permanently stationed in Lithuania, as security concerns over Russian provocations have grown in the region.
Kaliningrad, officially part of Russia, is an exclave on the Baltic Sea, sandwiched between Poland and Lithuania. The region has become a flashpoint between Russia and NATO.
In a warning to NATO in September, Russia claimed that it was "ready to use the entire arsenal of forces and capabilities at its disposal, including nuclear weapons, in order to defend its territory should NATO countries undertake any attempt aimed at isolating the Kaliningrad Region from the rest of the country."
Russian President Vladimir Putin invoked the threat of nuclear force again in remarks the following day.
"Can we be sure this weapon will never be used? Of course not," Putin said about nuclear weapons in a speech on Oct. 1. "We're all familiar with the saying: If a gun is hanging somewhere on the stage at the beginning of a performance, on the wall, it's bound to go off eventually."

How Vika and Linda made leap from backing singers to hall of famers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
22:50:13 UTC
07:50:13 KST

Vika and Linda Bull on their values, singing career and Paul Kelly
Australian Tongan siblings Vika and Linda Bull are among our nation's most celebrated and dynamic vocal duos.
Beyond their sublime harmonies, however, the singing sisters are very different people whose music tastes were "polar opposites" growing up.
"I'm a little bit country, and Vika's a little bit rock'n'roll," Linda says on Take 5 with Zan Rowe.
"We're 17 months apart, but our attitude to life, at times, has been radically different."
Older sister Vika admits to being the wilder of the two growing up. But she was also a natural leader and trailblazer.
"I have the guts to do that," she says. "But business? It's this one.
"Linda's very careful. Considers everything. Sometimes too much, and it drives me crazy.
"She's seen me just bumble through and make a wreck of things."
Linda adds: "I did watch that and go, 'I don't think mum would survive two of us like that.'"
The pair's differences are their strength, Linda reasons.
"Our voices, personalities [and] tastes are different. But we cover a lot of ground because we work as a team."
Across four decades as successful recording artists, the OAM recipients and recent ARIA Hall of Famers have stuck to the same motto:
"Sisters first, singers second."
Finding their voice
The first person to notice how Vika and Linda's dissimilarities complemented each other was their mother.
"She recognised Vika had a higher voice, and I naturally had a lower one. She would coach us with holding the note, how to sing in tune," Linda says.
"Teach us different parts people were singing on the radio. We'd just go around the house practising."
Raised in the conservative suburb of Doncaster in 1970s Melbourne, "we stood out," says Linda.
Their mixed heritage and cultural practices set them apart at primary school. But they delighted in attending Tongan church each Sunday and the visceral experience of the choir.
"It's frightening and exhilarating; just the best thing you'll ever hear," gushes Vika.
Mama Bull was less than happy when Vika, who had left school early to pursue singing, convinced her little sister, a few years into a university degree, to do the same.
"That was a bad day in the Bull household," Vika smirks.
"Mum goes, 'Not you too!' It's your fault, you taught us!" Linda jokes.
"That was our pact with mum: we'll stick together. 'Don't get the tattoos. Don't take drugs.' And so we didn't."
"Well, you didn't!" Vika counters.
In the late 1980s, Vika and Linda gained wider attention with The Black Sorrows, their intimate harmonies and soulful power the secret sauce on tunes like Chained To The Wheel and Never Let Me Go.
"I didn't know what a gift Joe [Camilerri, band leader] was giving me at that time. It was a great band to be in [and] Joe just said, 'Go for it.'"
During this era, Vika and Linda moonlighted as celebrated singers-for-hire on albums from Hunters and Collectors, John Farnham, Deborah Conway and more.
"You don't want to overshadow the singer," explains Vika. "You're kind of like the icing on the cake. You're there to support and lift."
By 1994, they departed The Black Sorrows to step out on their own.
"I remember the day. It was hard to leave that band. Being in the Sorrows, we would've remained backing singers. We just thought, 'We want to start telling stories as well.'"
Linda adds: "In our own way. We'd been interpreters of [other people's] music, but we felt if we don't try … we're wasting our time."
Going solo together
When the Bull sisters were ready to leap, side by side, some Australian music royalty was ready to help give them a push.
Featuring on Archie Roach's 1990 classic Charcoal Lane introduced Vika and Linda to Paul Kelly.
"He said we should sit down and write songs; 'Give it a crack!'" remembers Linda.
"He was the first person to say that, even though we hadn't written one song."
Kelly devoted a "year of Thursday afternoon writing sessions" to the duo, coaxing them with yarns and musical sketches.
"He'd be so patient, just trying to draw us out of our shells. He realised the key to Vika and I would be conversation. 'That's a good story; that's a good idea to write a song.'"
Vika confesses the Gravy Man made her especially shy.
"I was always incredibly intimidated at those sessions. Too worried about [saying] something stupid. 'He's going to think it's corny!'
"I'd hold back a lot. 'I'll go make a cup of tea.' I wish I was more bold … I could've used the time better."
Regardless, Kelly got results, kicking off a lifelong friendship and collaboration with Vika and Linda, including the early single We've Started A Fire.
"As soon as he busted out that, and it was a reggae feel, I'm like 'Ooh, this is for us!'" recalls Linda.
The track featured on the duo's 1994 self-titled album, a platinum-selling release co-produced by Kelly and featuring breakout hit When Will You Fall For Me, written with Hunters & Collectors frontman Mark Seymour.
"[Kelly] had a lot of faith in Vika and I. Watching him in action really taught us a lot."
No bull
The aging combination of experience and wisdom means those butterflies have long been quelled. And Vika and Linda are more confident than ever.
Their career-spanning memoir, No Bull, inspired Where Do You Come From? the duo's ninth album and among their best, including a title track exploring experiences of childhood racism.
"When you're older females and been doing it for a long time, you have a duty to be honest," says Linda.
"You hear women say it a lot at our age: I don't give a shit anymore.
"Shake off all this stuff that's happened and just be me. For Vika and I, we've done it together and at the same time."
Vika adds: "It certainly gave me confidence. Linda has always had it, but I've been a bit shy to show my words or sing them.
"Most of my life I haven't felt calm. I've [felt] reckless, wild, just want to punch everyone in my way.
"But I'm just not like that anymore. I'm at peace, I'm happy to just let things happen; if they do and if they don't, I don't care."

AI is changing Russia’s drone war on Ukrainian cities, deputy air defense commander says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
22:46:21 UTC
07:46:21 KST

Russian forces appear to use AI to plan air attacks and recognize targets amid raids on Ukrainian cities. This may include recent air attacks on Odesa that have come in waves with short gaps, Deputy Air Force Commander for Air Defense Colonel Yurii Cherevashenko says, Ukrinform reports.
Russia has already equipped its jet-powered Geran-4 drones with machine vision, allowing them to recognize and track targets on their own in the final seconds of flight. Recently, a single jet drone hit a locomotive in Odesa Oblast in late September and killed two railway workers.
The scale of Russia's AI use is hard to measure, Cherevashenko continues, but Ukrainian specialists already see its elements in how attacks are organized. The long, wave-by-wave strikes on Odesa would be far harder to plan and coordinate without it, he believes.
"Russian forces use AI to lay out attack routes and to recognize targets," Cherevashenko says, framing it as his own assessment rather than a confirmed fact.
The sea is harder to defend than land
Odesa Oblast is home to the biggest port in Ukraine, "Southern". Protecting it is a challenging task as guarding the airspace over water is tougher than over land, Cherevashenko says. Some air defense assets do not perform as well at sea, and in some cases, crews can intercept a target only as it approaches.
Weather adds to the problem, with storms and fog, while the open sea gives Russia more freedom to choose drone routes and launch points. To protect ports and the coast, Ukraine uses drone motherships, platforms that carry other drones aloft to extend their flight time and keep watch over set areas.
Ukraine answers AI with AI
Ukraine is also building its own AI for air defense. Automated turrets using machine vision now help counter Russian drones. According to Army Media, the Air Force says such turrets have scored their first shoot-downs, including of Geran-5 jet drones, with one soldier saying 50 rounds were enough to bring down a Geran.
Ukraine's Defense Ministry is going further. In late September, it unveiled an AI system called SPECTR, built by its A1 Artificial Intelligence Center and already in testing with several combat units, to analyze battlefield data, predict Russian moves, and suggest options to commanders.

A 68-year-old Russian man who swam across the Nemunas River from Russia's Kaliningrad exclave into neighbouring Lithuania in an attempt to seek asylum has been sentenced to six years in a strict-regime penal colony in Russia for "publicly justifying terrorism."
A Russian court sentenced a 68-year-old man who swam across the Nemunas River from Kaliningrad to Lithuania in an attempt to seek asylum to six years in prison, according to Lithuanian media Lrytas.
He was sentenced to six years in a maximum-security penal colony and barred from administering websites or online channels for three years following his release.
The man, identified by Russian media as Igor Yuryevich Odintsov, was convicted by the Baltic Fleet Military Court of "publicly justifying terrorism," according to the court. He also holds "a negative attitude towards the state authorities of the Russian Federation" and is opposing Moscow's war in Ukraine — what Moscow calls a “special military operation,” according to the court's press release.
Court proceedings were suspended on September 17 after Odintsov went into hiding, according to Russian media ruwest.ru. That was also the day he crossed the Nemunas River and reached the Lithuanian side.
The head of the Lithuanian community in Kaliningrad, Sigitas Šamborskis, told Lrytas that he knew the man and said Odintsov had been trying to escape persecution.
“He had a case opened against him, which is why he swam across the Nemunas. He wanted to save himself,” Šamborskis said.
The man allegedly told Lithuanian authorities that he was fleeing Russia because of persecution over his activity on social media. But after assessing the circumstances, "inconsistent" information provided by the man and “information concerning the threat posed by this person if he were to enter the EU”, Lithuanian authorities decided to return him, a spokesperson for Lithuania’s State Border Guard Service, Giedrius Mišutis, said last month.
Šamborskis added that the Lithuanian side did not have sufficient grounds to keep him, as the Russian court case had not yet been concluded.
The 68-year-old was detained four days later, on September 21, and the court handed down its verdict at the next hearing, on September 30.

Syria weighs joining Saudi fight against Houthis as attacks escalate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
22:43:20 UTC
07:43:20 KST

Saudi Arabia’s war against the Houthis is intensifying — and now a country that endured more than a decade of civil war is considering providing it with assistance. A U.S. official and a military official briefed on the matter told Reuters that Syria is “carefully considering” providing military assistance to its ally Saudi Arabia.
According to the officials, the options under consideration include defensive assistance intended to protect the kingdom from attacks or the deployment of forces to help Saudi-backed Yemeni forces fight the Houthis. The U.S. official said Saudi Arabia had asked Syria to deploy forces to fight the Houthis.
Syria is not the only country Saudi Arabia has approached for assistance. After weeks of Houthi missile and drone attacks, it has sought help from numerous countries, from the United States to countries in Europe and the Middle East, for both defensive and offensive support.
A Syrian diplomat said in response that Syria stands with Saudi Arabia in the face of Houthi attacks, but that the government’s main focus is on domestic priorities, such as reconstruction following the civil war.
“Should Saudi Arabia request any military cooperation or exchange of expertise, this would take place exclusively through official channels and within the framework of the bilateral agreements governing relations between our two brotherly countries,” the diplomat said.
On Tuesday, Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa visited Riyadh and met with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. According to the U.S. official, their discussions included possible Syrian military assistance to the kingdom.
Footage broadcast by Syrian state media showed Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman, the crown prince’s brother, accompanying al-Sharaa back to his plane. Khalid bin Salman is considered the Saudi official responsible for the “Yemen file.”
It remains unclear, however, whether the Syrians will ultimately agree to provide military assistance. Involvement in fighting against the Iran-backed Houthis could be viewed as a hostile act by Iran and its allies — Hezbollah in Lebanon and militias in Iraq — all of which have a history of conflict with the Syrian rebels who are now the country’s rulers.
Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia continues to suffer casualties, including on the home front. On Wednesday, it acknowledged in an official statement that three people had been killed in Houthi missile attacks on its airports over the past two days.
The Saudi-led coalition, meanwhile, said it had “destroyed a ballistic missile launch platform in Sanaa that was used to attack Riyadh” and released footage of the strike. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree claimed that Saudi Arabia had carried out 156 airstrikes and missile launches over the previous 24 hours. According to the Houthis, Saudi Arabia has carried out 1,798 airstrikes and missile attacks since the current war began.
On Tuesday, the Houthi spokesman denied claims by Yemen’s internationally recognized, Saudi-backed government that its forces had succeeded in pushing back the Houthis and capturing territory overlooking the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait in the country’s southwest.
Government forces, backed by extensive air support from Saudi fighter jets, had earlier announced dramatic advances in the area, which the Houthis captured only a month ago. However, the actual extent of the advances remains unclear, and the Houthis deny they took place.
Yemen’s government announced on Sunday the launch of a large-scale ground operation, code-named “Dawn of Yemen,” aimed at recapturing territory that pro-Saudi forces lost during the Houthis’ rapid offensive in early September. During that campaign, the Houthis seized several strategic locations in southwestern Yemen, particularly the towns of al-Mokha and Dhubab, which lie very close to the Bab al-Mandab Strait, as well as islands located within the strait itself.
Those gains gave the Houthis tight control over traffic through the strategic waterway, which connects Europe and Asia via the Red Sea and the Suez Canal and carries 12% of global trade.
The strait’s importance, particularly for Saudi Arabia, has increased dramatically following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula amid the war with Iran. The Houthi takeover of Bab al-Mandab sent oil prices surging amid fears of further disruption to the flow of oil to global markets.

Hormuz navigation

The agreed maritime arrangement will soon be submitted to international maritime authorities.
The diplomatic movement comes as the US-Israel war against Iran enters its eighth month.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian previously criticised Washington for launching attacks during earlier diplomatic overtures, though Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi stressed that fair talks could still secure peace.
An earlier Iranian proposal submitted during the UN General Assembly offered to reopen the strait and commence nuclear discussions within seven days in exchange for a comprehensive ceasefire across all fronts, the lifting of the US naval blockade and oil sanctions, and the release of frozen assets.

Netanyahu manipulated account of warnings before Hamas attack: Israeli investigation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
22:32:31 UTC
07:32:31 KST

Zein Khalil and Tarek Chouiref
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu manipulated his account of warnings he received before the October 2023 attack by Hamas on Israel, omitting material and altering the context of security discussions, according to an investigation published Wednesday by an Israeli newspaper.
The Yedioth Ahronoth daily and Ynet, a subsidiary news outlet of the Yedioth Ahronoth Media Group, compared a 55-page document released by Netanyahu in February with original records, meeting summaries and testimonies.
The investigation found omissions and changes in wording and context, particularly concerning warnings issued in the months before the attack and proposals for military action against Hamas.
Netanyahu’s document portrayed him as pressing for the assassination of Hamas leaders while senior security officials resisted such moves and favored maintaining calm in Gaza.
The original records, however, showed that Netanyahu repeatedly sought to preserve calm, declined to approve proposed strikes and maintained that Hamas remained deterred despite warnings from security officials, according to the investigation.
In April 2023, then-Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar and then-army chief Herzi Halevi recommended targeted killings in Gaza, the newspaper said.
A month later, Bar warned that a military campaign in Gaza would eventually be unavoidable and urged preparations for an opening strike and targeted killings.
Netanyahu, however, said there was a “strong deterrence balance” with Hamas and did not approve the proposed operations.
The investigation also cited an August warning from Bar that Israel’s deterrence was eroding and that preemptive action in Gaza should be considered.
On Sept. 10, Bar warned that Israel was facing a “serious security situation” with a significant risk of several fronts converging.
Netanyahu subsequently defined the objective as keeping the upcoming holiday period “as quiet as possible,” according to the report.
The newspaper said Netanyahu’s February document also retained an intelligence assessment that Hamas was building up its capabilities at a “moderate pace” but omitted a recommendation to act even at the risk of military escalation.

"I also stressed the importance of a peaceful Afghanistan and concrete action against terrorist groups operating from Afghan soil," he said.
UN chief highlights humanity's shared challenges in address
Guterres also highlighted humanity’s shared challenges, including climate change, conflict, inequality and artificial intelligence, during his address at the Foreign Service Academy in Islamabad.
He warned that the shift toward a multipolar world does not guarantee stability, as conflicts are increasing, human suffering is deepening and international law is being undermined.
On Gaza, he called for the full implementation of the peace plan and said the two-state solution can not be "allowed" to be "bulldozed away."
He also warned of rising debt burdens, insufficient development financing and stalled Sustainable Development Goals, while reaffirming support for reform of the international financial architecture.
On climate change, Guterres said its impacts are intensifying, with developing countries bearing disproportionate costs.
He described climate change as a "threat multiplier" driving displacement, increasing resource pressures, undermining food security and fueling instability.
He also called for AI governance to reflect the interests of all humanity, with its benefits broadly shared and its risks managed collectively.
Pakistan Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar also highlighted four priorities at the event: upholding the UN Charter and international law; placing diplomacy at the center of international relations; addressing the security implications of emerging technologies; and strengthening the UN’s legitimacy and capacity to deliver.
"Sovereign equality, territorial integrity, non-interference, the prohibition of the threat or use of force, and self-determination must be respected," he said, adding that treaty obligations and Security Council resolutions must be implemented.
"Just and peaceful settlement of the Palestinian question and the Jammu and Kashmir dispute remain fundamental tests of this commitment," Dar said.

Democratic party sues Trump administration over taxpayer-funded TV 'propaganda'
The Democratic National Committee sued US President Donald Trump’s administration on Wednesday over taxpayer-funded television ads promoting his political message, alleging illegal government propaganda. The lawsuit seeks to halt federal funding for the ads, which have cost more than $12 million to air ahead of November’s midterm elections, according to AdImpact.
The Democratic National Committee on Wednesday sued President Donald Trump’s administration for recent television advertisements that promoted his political message while costing taxpayers millions of dollars.
The complaint, filed in the US District Court for the District of Columbia, alleges that the ads are illegal government-sponsored propaganda and accuses Trump of personally directing them. It asks the court to declare the ads illegal and stop the use of federal funds to pay for them.
Watch moreWhite House promotes 'Trump TV' with AI-altered photo
Trump has faced bipartisan backlash for the ads, which glorify him and echo his campaign pitch as voters cast early ballots with the midterm elections less than a month away.
The spots, which began airing in September, already have cost more than $12 million to run, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact, and a total of $20 million in Homeland Security Department funding has been tapped to pay for them.
Responding Monday to the criticism, Trump defended the ads as “positive promotion for our Great USA” but said he’d pay for them using his MAGA Inc. super PAC going forward.
Read moreTrump targets tax-free diesel as Republicans approach midterms
But on Tuesday, the fifth ad in the campaign began airing with the notice “paid for by the US Government”, promoting Trump’s military actions in Venezuela earlier this year. The same day, Trump made it clear he hasn’t committed to reimbursing any money that has already been spent, telling reporters “we’ll decide”.
DNC Chair Ken Martin said in a statement that Trump is misusing taxpayer dollars in “a last-ditch attempt to save Republicans in November”.
“Americans deserve better than to have their hard-earned tax dollars used for Trump’s illegal schemes," he added.
Legal experts have suggested the ads run afoul of a federal statute against congressionally appropriated money being used for “publicity or propaganda”, and potentially other federal laws. The Homeland Security money tapped for the ads comes from a $175 million package Congress gave to the department as part of Trump’s immigration enforcement agenda.
The White House has defended the ads as public service announcements akin to what past administrations have done to promote various policies. Legal experts have said the recent ads differ from many past public service announcements because they aren’t aimed at helping members of the public benefit from specific government programs.
The defendants in the lawsuit – Trump, the White House, DHS and the Office of Management and Budget – didn't immediately respond to requests for comment.

Last year, Australia Post delivered over 111 million parcels in November and December — its busiest peak season yet — and this year it is preparing for the same.
"We expect millions of Australians to take advantage of sales and start their Christmas shopping earlier than ever," Australia Post executive general manager parcel, post and e-commerce services Gary Starr said.
"Whether you're sending a gift close to home, across the country or internationally, getting organised early can help take some of the stress out of the festive season.
"Our message is simple: check the dates, shop early, send early and get one more thing ticked off your Christmas to-do list."

If you want to start planning, here are all the deadlines you should know about:
Australia Post Christmas 2026 parcel cut-off dates
For Parcel Post, if you're sending a parcel within your state or territory, you have until 22 December.
For interstate deliveries, you should send your parcel by 21 December for most states. People sending to or from Western Australia, Tasmania, the Northern Territory, and regional and remote areas should allow a few extra days, depending on the parcel's starting point or final destination.
If you are sending an Express Post, you have a bit more time.
Over-the-counter Parcel Post and Express Post items must be lodged by 2.30 pm, according to Australia Post.
Send Christmas letters and cards by 18 December for interstate deliveries and by 21 December for deliveries within the same state.
Australia Post Christmas 2026 international parcel cut-off dates
Depending on where you're sending from, Parcel Post to Norfolk Island should be sent by mid-November. For Christmas Island and the Cocos (Keeling) Islands, send it by the end of October, and for Lord Howe Island you have until the start of December.
Here are the deadlines for other major international destinations:
Items sent from South Australia, Tasmania, and the Northern Territory must first travel to another state or territory before leaving Australia, which means people in these areas should add two business days for Express items, and five business days for Standard and Economy items.
Australia Post also warns that "overseas deliveries may be affected by factors that are beyond our control such as customs delays and overseas postal disruptions — so it's best to send as early as you can".

Ukraine’s drone pilot calls it his proudest strike: cheap FPV drone detonating over two tons of explosives packed inside Russian mine-clearer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
22:25:47 UTC
07:25:47 KST

"Skipper", an FPV company commander in Ukraine's 413th Raid Unmanned Systems Regiment, has described destroying a Russian UR-77 mine-clearing vehicle with drones during the 2023 counteroffensive as the strike he is proudest of, according to Army TV.
The UR-77, nicknamed "Zmiy Horynych" after a fire-breathing serpent of Slavic folklore, carries a rocket-fired line charge to blow paths through minefields, as per Militarnyi. Each charge carries more than two tons of explosives, which is why a cheap FPV hit can trigger a blast far larger than the drone itself.
"It exploded so hard that I thought it was a small nuclear blast. There are more than two tons of plastic explosive inside, and when it went off after the second hit, it was something unbelievable," Skipper says.
Skipper joined the army at the start of the full-scale invasion and moved from infantry and aerial reconnaissance to commanding an FPV unit. His regiment now operates on the Zaporizhzhia front, where FPV drones conduct combat missions.
From sailing yachts to FPV drones
In civilian life, Skipper was a sailing instructor, and he says the sport partly helps in military work, especially his knowledge of navigation and radio communication. He is convinced that a technological edge can be one of the keys to victory.
He counts the UR-77 strike among his unit's early work, from a time when few Ukrainian units were using FPV drones at all, he says. The hit came during hard fighting in the counteroffensive, when his crews were among the first to work the FPV niche.
Russia turns a mine-clearer into a wrecking tool
The UR-77 was built in the 1970s for a different war, one of fast tank thrusts that needed enemy minefields cleared quickly. Its base rides on the chassis of the 2S1 Gvozdika self-propelled howitzer, and its charge can cut a lane six meters wide, with some anti-personnel mines detonated across a band up to 15 meters wide.
Modern combat changed that role. The classic mine-clearing use remains, but Russia now more often turns these machines on Ukrainian fortifications, using the line charge to flatten defenses rather than open a path.

Iran threatens to block ‘illegal’ routes through Strait of Hormuz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
22:22:44 UTC
07:22:44 KST

Iran threatens to block ‘illegal’ routes through Strait of Hormuz
Iran has threatened to block what it calls “illegal” traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, saying it retains full control of the passage despite US claims to the contrary.
The waterway is one of the world’s most important energy routes, normally carrying around a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments. Traffic through the strait has been severely disrupted since the US-Israeli war on Iran began in late February, driving up energy prices. Brent crude was trading at around $101 a barrel on Wednesday, compared with roughly $72 before the conflict.
Mohammad Reza Naqdi, a senior Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) commander and adviser to Iran’s Supreme Leader, said on Wednesday that several transit routes through the strait along Oman’s coast would soon be closed.
Naqdi said the routes had been created by blasting and damaging rocky passages and were being used by small boats to carry oil through the waterway before transferring it to tankers. He described the shipments as “smuggling” and argued that they were too limited to show that traffic through Hormuz was returning to normal.
”The Strait of Hormuz is closed, and the armed forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran have full control over it,” Naqdi said, adding that the restrictions would remain until Tehran’s “legitimate demands” were met.
Iran has previously offered to reopen the strait if Washington eases military pressure and lifts its blockade of Iranian ports.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio offered a sharply different assessment on Wednesday, saying the strait is “open” and that Iran had “lost complete control” of Hormuz.
”There’s almost as much oil flowing out now as there was before this conflict began,” Rubio told reporters.
President Donald Trump has also said the US military is helping oil shipments pass through the strait, claiming that daily flows have risen above 20 million barrels. He has blamed the global diesel shortage primarily on Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries rather than the Middle East conflict and has urged Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky to halt the attacks.
Regional crude exports have rebounded significantly. A seven-day moving average reached 18.3 million barrels per day on September 30, according to provisional Kpler data cited by Reuters. The figure includes oil shipped through routes other than Hormuz.
Security risks in the strait remain high. The Panamanian-flagged tanker On Peace was hit by a projectile near Oman on Tuesday, injuring 12 crew members, according to the Indian authorities. No group has claimed responsibility.

GENEVA, October 8. /TASS/. Thousands of suspected cases of plague are reported each year in various countries around the world, World Health Organization’s (WHO) Epidemic and Pandemic Preparedness and Prevention Department Director Maria Van Kerkhove said.
"There are thousands of cases of suspected plague every year that happen around the world," she told reporters.

08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
Chilean authorities declared a yellow alert for the Santiago Metropolitan Region on Tuesday due to intense rainfall, flooding and the activation of ravines, according to the National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (SENAPRED).
Under a yellow alert, authorities progressively deploy additional resources as needed to prevent an emergency from escalating and reduce risks to people, property and the environment.
The alert was issued after heavy rain affected several municipalities across the region, with authorities reporting flooded streets and underpasses, a landslide in Melipilla, a municipality southwest of Santiago, and activated ravines in San Jose de Maipo, a municipality southeast of the capital, according to Chilean local media outlet BioBioChile. 
Emergency teams have been deployed at several locations to respond to incidents and monitor the development of the weather event, SENAPRED said.
The alert will remain in effect until weather conditions no longer warrant the measure, according to the agency.
Chile's Meteorological Directorate has issued warnings for moderate to heavy rainfall in the coastal mountain range, valley and foothill areas of the Santiago Metropolitan Region.
The agency is also forecasting thunderstorms accompanied by hail and strong local wind gusts across the coastal mountain range, valley, foothills and mountain areas.
The National Geology and Mining Service, known as SERNAGEOMIN, has warned of a high probability of debris flows and landslides in the coastal mountain range, valley and foothill areas.
The risk of such events is considered lower in the higher mountain range, according to the geological assessment.
Based on the meteorological and geological information, SENAPRED canceled an earlier Preventive Early Warning for the region and raised the alert level to Yellow in coordination with the Metropolitan Regional Presidential Delegation.
Under the yellow alert, authorities will progressively deploy the resources needed to respond to the weather event according to its development.
The measure is intended to prevent the situation from increasing in scope or severity and reduce its potential impact on people, property and the environment, SENAPRED said.
Authorities have urged residents to remain attentive to official information and follow instructions from emergency services as rainfall and associated risks continue to be monitored.

‘No to the father, no to the son’: Thousands march in Rio against Bolsonaro
Students and other protesters marched against Flavio Bolsonaro after he advanced to Brazil’s presidential runoff.
Thousands of people have taken to the streets of Rio de Janeiro in a student-led protest against presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro and the growing influence of Brazil’s far right.
The march happened on Wednesday, just days after far-right Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, earned the most votes in the first round of the country’s presidential race.
Bolsonaro won 47 percent, ahead of his closest rival, incumbent left-wing President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who gained 45 percent support.
Since neither candidate surpassed the 50 percent threshold, they will face each other in a run-off on October 25.
The results have triggered fears that Brazil could become the latest Latin American country to see its presidency switch from left to right.
Protesters marched through downtown Rio carrying signs reading “Never again Bolsonaro” and “No to the father, no to the son”. Others held banners reading “Dictatorship never again” and “Get out Bolsonaro”.
“I’m here because I believe in democracy. Because I’m scared,” said Alice Carneiro, 25, an administrator in maritime shipping who participated in the protests. She explained that, under a far-right government, she feared a backlash against her wife, who is transgender.
Jair Bolsonaro, the former president, led the country from 2019 to 2023. But his single-term tenure was marked by a series of controversies related to his far-right policies.
He voiced support for Brazil’s past military dictatorship, which was responsible for the disappearance and murder of hundreds of perceived dissidents. He also spread unfounded claims about the accuracy of Brazil’s election system, leading to a court ruling that barred him from holding office for eight years.
Currently, the former president is serving a 27-year sentence after being convicted of plotting to overturn his 2022 election defeat. After Lula’s inauguration in 2023, Bolsonaro’s supporters stormed government buildings in the capital, reportedly hoping to trigger a military uprising.
Critics have framed Jair Bolsonaro’s actions as a threat to Brazil’s democracy.
But Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has received his father’s endorsement, and he has backed amnesty for his father, a prospect that has raised concerns among protesters.
“I find this rise of the far right and the rise of Bolsonarism in Brazil very, very sad,” said Emmanuel Araujo, 19, who is preparing for university entrance exams.
“Lula might not be my preferred candidate,” Araujo added, “but amid this barbarism, we have to choose between someone we can keep criticising and someone who might take away our right to speak.”

AI generated
WASHINGTON – US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth flew to the flight deck of the aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln on Oct 7 and praised the resilience of sailors who endured an extended, wartime deployment that drew scrutiny over suicide attempts on board.
The Lincoln, which is due to dock on Oct 8 in San Diego, is the flagship of a carrier strike group that had eight suicide attempts among US sailors during its time at sea, according to the Navy. Its deployment included 264 continuous days without a port call, a record, according to the Pentagon.
Hegseth, whose speeches regularly target the media, accused reporters of trying to turn the crew of the Lincoln strike group into symbols of dysfunction instead of heroes of the conflict, and presented a citation from US President Donald Trump for their achievements during the Iran war.
The Lincoln’s accomplishments included sinking 64 Iranian warships, destroying 21 anti-ship cruise missiles, executing 3,693 combat sorties, launching 450 Tomahawk land attack cruise missiles and firing 1.37 million pounds of ordnance against Iran, he said.
Despite the fast pace of combat operations, he added, it suffered no casualties and had no aircraft mishaps.
“What makes the US military and the US Navy and all these sailors different is that you adapt and that you’re resilient and you overcome – you finish the mission nonetheless,” he told the crew. “Yes, it’s hard. That’s why you’re here. You do difficult and hard things.”
Typically, naval deployments are for between six and nine months but can be extended during times of conflict. Mental health issues on long deployments have long challenged the US Navy.
In August, amid reports of low morale and supply shortages on board, Trump was asked whether he thought the Lincoln had been deployed too long. His reply: “No, no, no. Not nearly long enough.”
Hegseth acknowledged some challenges on board, saying: “There wasn’t an easy resupply.”
Ahead of the carrier’s return to port, Hegseth joked that he was “the only thing standing between you and home” and that he was also the one who signed the orders repeatedly extending the deployment. “You deserve to see your families and see them as soon as possible,” he said, adding that he just wanted to see them for “a moment on the route, on the way in, just to say thank you”.
The carrier’s return comes at a crossroads in the US-Iran war, which has jolted global energy markets and become a political liability for Trump and fellow Republicans ahead of November midterm elections.
The war – and its US$3 billion (S$3.8 billion) monthly price tag – has become a key issue on the campaign trail. Higher energy prices have put Trump and the Republicans on the defensive in competitive states that will decide control of Congress.
Trump is weighing next steps against Iran, including whether to escalate strikes before or after the elections, as he presses a naval blockade meant to pile economic pressure on Tehran to reach a deal to end the conflict.
Vice-President J.D. Vance said on Oct 5 that Iran must make a “meaningful” reduction in its uranium enrichment capacity to satisfy US demands and end the seven-month war.
Hegseth said the crew of the Lincoln had helped ensure the US’ objective of preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.

The latest round of India-Canada security dialogue saw both sides welcoming efforts to advance negotiations for a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA), while underlining the growing potential for advancing a “substantive bilateral defence relationship in keeping with the vision of the leadership".The 2 sides are expected to sign the CEPA during PM Narendra Modi’s visit to Canada which, according to official sources, is tentatively scheduled for December 11-13. It will come days before the G20 summit for which Modi and Canadian PM Mark Carney will join President Donald Trump and other leaders in Florida. India and Canada are currently holding the 5th round of negotiations for CEPA. Both leaders have called for an ambitious and mutually beneficial CEPA that can serve as a durable anchor for the economic partnership, while allowing India and Canada to boost bilateral trade to CAD 70 billion (49 billion USD) by 2030.Both sides believe CEPA will be an apt culmination of the process of normalisation of ties, which started with Carney assuming office last year, amid the ongoing stalemate with the US over a trade deal . Efforts to ramp up defence cooperation could also lead to some significant outcomes during what will be Modi’s first bilateral visit to the country since the diplomatic row over the killing of a Khalistan separatist.
Canada’s trade and foreign ministers, Maninder Sidhu and Anita Anand respectively, will also visit India this month.In a joint statement, NSA Ajit Doval and his counterpart David Morrison noted with satisfaction the sustained and constructive bilateral engagements over the past year, guided by mutual trust, respect for each other’s concerns and sensitivities, and a shared commitment to strengthening bilateral relations.“Both sides acknowledged the guidance provided by their respective Prime Ministers during their meetings in New Delhi in March 2026 and on the margins of the G7 Summit in Évian in June 2026,” said the joint statement, adding that Doval and Morrison reviewed progress in bilateral security and law enforcement cooperation, including the implementation of the shared Security Work Plan concluded in February 2026.
They also reaffirmed their commitment to identifying additional areas for practical cooperation, including exploring the establishment of structured dialogues on cyber security and economic security.Both sides agreed to strengthen existing institutional mechanisms and establish new channels, to facilitate “streamlined communication” and timely information-sharing on matters of mutual concern.“They agreed to deepen coordination and cooperation in combating transnational organised crime, terrorism and violent extremism, human and drug trafficking, cybercrime, extortion, and extradition of criminal offenders,” said the statement.

Rubio in Greece digs into past to tout Trump’s ‘America first’ approach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
22:05:51 UTC
07:05:51 KST

The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, delivered a classically inspired apologia for Donald Trump’s “America first” foreign policy on Wednesday, giving a sweeping speech to the backdrop of the Parthenon in Athens that appeared tailor-made for campaign ads if he runs for president in 2028.
In the speech, the top US diplomat drew historical parallels from the founders, philosophers and conquerers of antiquity to the modern American spirit – as well as his family’s own journey to the United States – as he called on Europe to “awaken from its long slumber” and reject a “future of atrophy and servitude and decline”.
The highly produced speech contained a forceful rejection of the kind of globalist politics that Trump has blamed for America’s and Europe’s ills, including growing illegal immigration and the outsourcing of manufacturing. In it, Rubio warned that the western world was at an “inflection point” and defended America’s “unapologetic pursuit of national power”.
“The word ‘nationalism’ became a dirty word, so we tore down our monuments,” Rubio said. “We condemned our own history, and in too many places, we taught our children to be ashamed of the country they would inherit.”
Now, he said, the western world had found itself at a crossroads, where it either must “maintain its place at the head of the world or [resign] itself to a future of atrophy, servitude and decline”.
“Under President Trump, the United States has made its choice,” Rubio continued. “We choose the unapologetic pursuit of national power: to take back control of our critical supply chains, to reindustrialise our economy, to rebuild our defense, to fight for dominance of the technologies and industries of the future.”
The speech comes as relations between the US and Europe are facing numerous strains, including the US war in Iran, Washington’s scattershot support for Ukraine’s defense against Russia, disputes inside Nato including Trump’s recent demands for sovereignty over Greenland, and a growing ideological divide being driven by powerful officials including the US vice-president, JD Vance.
The shift in the Trump administration’s use of national power has unsettled many European allies, who have continued to seek compromises in order to keep the Trump administration onside on major issues including support for Ukraine and economic cooperation through the European Union.
Vance, a likely contender in the 2028 elections, put European allies on notice last year in a speech at the Munich security conference, when he accused leaders of being “terrified of their own people” and warned about the “threat from within” that Europe would reject values it shared with the US.
Rubio has developed a less aggressive – but nonetheless pointed – message of calling for European powers led by the US to fight against “civilisational erasure”.
Rubio addressed the tensions as he invoked Abraham Lincoln’s first inaugural address in 1861 on the eve of the civil war, saying: “Though passions may, at times, have strained the bonds of affection between the United States and Europe, it must not be allowed to break them.”
“Together, we must strengthen an alliance capable of confronting threats of our age,” he said, extolling the recent agreement between the US, Denmark and Greenland that he claimed will “reshape the Arctic and bolster the security of all of Nato.”
But the speech on Wednesday indicates that the shift in US geopolitical power may remain through a following presidency, as two of the most prominent Republican officials in the current administration have delivered forceful declarations to Europe that there will not be a return to the politics of the past.
On Wednesday, speaking to a crowd of 250 invited Greek and European officials, as well as journalists, Rubio sought to rally European allies, saying they should follow the example of the current government of Greece, to embrace a partnership with the US on “everything from energy to migration to defense, where Greece has been a model ally”.
“We believe that Europe can awaken from its long slumber and rekindle the fire that was lit here millennia ago,” Rubio said, pointing to positive tendencies including increases in European defense spending, expanded manufacturing and production, and a “flurry” of new partnerships and programs.
To bolster his case, Rubio delivered a selective reading of history from antiquity to the present, saying that the values of the ancient Greeks imbued those of later scientists and explorers, including some controversial choices including Christopher Columbus and the Spanish conquistador Hernán Cortés, whose legacies are associated with the subjugation of Latin America.
But Rubio said that they, as well as many others, carried a frontier spirit that was born in antiquity.
“The greatest Americans of every generation have carried the unmistakable features of their forefathers – born in Athens, formed by Rome, baptized in Christendom, hardened in the furnace of medieval Europe, endowed with the English genius for liberty, and then carried across the Atlantic to be reborn on the shores of a new world,” he said.
The Acropolis speech was heavily produced, with four cameras including one mounted on a crane, and was unusual for a secretary of state delivering a speech during a three-country swing through Iceland, Portugal and finally Greece.
In an unusual aside for the US’s top diplomat, Rubio also linked his own journey back to Europe, and then back to the Greeks of antiquity as well.
“Two and a half centuries after the founding of the American republic halfway across the world from where I stand now – I stand here today as the secretary of state of that republic, and a great-grandson of settlers who arrived in the new world from Spain – I stand here to testify to a debt that no lapse of time, no distance of space can ever extinguish,” he said.

Thousands protest Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro, fearing far-right return
Thousands of people joined a student march in downtown Rio de Janeiro on Wednesday to protest against presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro ahead of Brazil's October 25 presidential runoff. Bolsonaro led Sunday's first-round vote, prompting demonstrators to rally behind incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and oppose the far right's return to power.
Thousands of people joined a student march Wednesday in downtown Rio de Janeiro to protest against election favorite Flavio Bolsonaro and the prospect of the far right's return to power in Brazil, as the campaign for a runoff election swung into action.
Flavio Bolsonaro, 45, son of far-right former president Jair Bolsonaro, came out in front in Sunday's first-round election, sending shockwaves through Brazil's left which is scrambling to claw back votes ahead of an October 25 runoff.
Read moreFlavio Bolsonaro: In the name of the father, sons, and holy ideology
With drums, fireworks, and spirited chants, thousands of students spilled into downtown Rio de Janeiro declaring "Never Again Bolsonaro" and calling for votes for leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.
"I'm here because I believe in democracy. Because I'm scared," said Alice Carneiro, 25, an administrator in maritime shipping, crying as she expressed fears about a possible backlash against her wife, who is transgender.
Protesters evoked life under Jair Bolsonaro, who was in office from 2019 to 2022 and is remembered for his government's handling of the Covid pandemic, which he dubbed a "little flu" and which claimed more than 700,000 lives in Brazil, the second-highest death toll in the world after the United States.
"I remember my family's lives being at risk during the pandemic... I remember the vaccine denial," said Carneiro.
The march was strikingly more crowded and animated than Lula's rally at the same spot on Friday before the election, after a campaign many had criticised as lackluster.
Watch moreBrazil 'has moved to the right progressively over the last two decades', expert says
Fears of social spending cuts
Flavio Bolsonaro has vowed sweeping budget cuts, using a pair of scissors to echo the chainsaw of libertarian Argentine President Javier Milei, whose economic reforms he has praised.
Brazil is battling soaring public debt exacerbated by high interest rates, and the election result saw the Sao Paulo stock exchange rally to record highs.
Amid uncertainty over what cuts Flavio will make, protesters recalled those made by Jair Bolsonaro to federal universities, research scholarships and the government-subsidised Farmacia Popular program, which provides free or discounted medicines.
Read moreHow Lula’s successes in Brazil may have paved the way for his presidential defeat
"It's pointless for me to pass the entrance exam only to end up at a university that lacks funding," said Emmanuel Araujo, 19, who is preparing to take university entrance exams and described the rise of the far-right as "very sad".
Iara Pinheiro, 16, who voted for the first time, carried a placard reading: "No to the father, no to the son."
"I am a Black woman and I think we'll lose our rights if things continue the way they are and we elect Bolsonaro again. I think we will end up losing our democracy."
Some protesters expressed concern about Flavio Bolsonaro's plans to seek amnesty for his father, currently serving a 27-year sentence for attempting a coup after his 2022 election loss.
"Granting amnesty for coups gives the green light for new coups," read another placard.
Several other pro-democracy rallies are planned in the coming days.
Campaign reset
Both Flavio Bolsonaro and Lula are shaking up their campaigns to prepare for the runoff.
Flavio Bolsonaro has focused on building coalitions and doubled down on his plans to shrink the state and modernise the tax system. He also promised to use the right's new dominance in Congress to make constitutional reforms.
Lula, who at almost 81 years old is seeking a fourth term in office, has hit reset with a major focus on social media – where the right has long held the advantage – posting a video selfie on Wednesday for the first time.
Read moreBrazil’s Lula gears up for ‘last dance’ with run for fourth presidential term
"Come on, folks, let's hit the streets; let's go talk to people," he said in the video posted to Instagram and TikTok.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

The White House has asked the Pentagon to prepare options for strikes on Iran that could take place before the November 3 midterm elections, The Atlantic reported Wednesday, citing two administration officials.
US Central Command is developing the options, a US official told the magazine. The potential targets, scope of an operation, and whether US President Donald Trump will authorize military action remain under discussion.
According to the report, administration officials linked the planning to Trump’s desire to show progress in the conflict and address high gasoline prices ahead of the vote.
Supporters of limited strikes believe an operation could help the president present a military success before the elections, the magazine reported.
However, even advocates acknowledged that such attacks alone would not secure an agreement with Tehran, restore safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz, or reduce gasoline prices before election day.
White House weighs timing of renewed strikes
The Pentagon has also presented options for operations after the elections, ranging from limited attacks to a broader campaign that could include additional strikes on Iran’s energy industry, according to The Atlantic.
Some presidential advisers favor waiting until after the vote, the report said, amid concerns that renewed fighting, particularly if American troops are killed, could hurt Republican candidates.
A White House official told the magazine that Trump “has all options available at any time,” but did not answer questions about the timing of potential strikes.
The deliberations follow earlier reporting on preparations for possible escalation. The Jerusalem Post reported on October 2, citing The Washington Post, that the Pentagon was considering increasing its naval presence in the Middle East as Trump weighed renewed attacks after the elections. That report put the existing US deployment in the region at approximately 50,000 troops.
Negotiations continue amid military planning
Washington and Tehran are continuing to communicate through intermediaries, The Atlantic reported, although disagreements remain over a ceasefire, the US blockade, and reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
The magazine also reported that Iranian attacks on shipping earlier this week had prompted some shipowners to reconsider transiting the waterway.
The military planning comes alongside continuing disputes over Iran’s nuclear program. In a Reuters interview published by The Jerusalem Post on Wednesday, Vice President JD Vance said an agreement would require concrete reductions in Iran’s enrichment capacity.
Vance also said Washington was uncertain how decisions were being made within Iran’s leadership and how much authority its negotiating counterparts held.
A senior Iranian official told Reuters on Wednesday that Washington’s nuclear demands conflicted with Tehran’s position, adding that recognition of Iran’s right to enrichment remained a red line.

Tropical Storm Isaias Set to Be First Atlantic Hurricane of 2026 Season
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
22:00:24 UTC
07:00:24 KST

The 2026 Atlantic hurricane season has been mercifully dull, but that’s set to change this week. Tropical Storm Isaias is forecast to become the season’s first hurricane before making landfall somewhere between Mississippi and Florida by the weekend.
El Niño has turned the Atlantic basin into a graveyard by changing winds high in the atmosphere so that they rip apart storms. That’s helped depress tropical cyclone activity to near-record-low levels and resulted in zero hurricanes. That could change imminently, though.
Isaias is churning in the Gulf of Mexico with winds of 65 mph, according to the latest update from the US National Hurricane Center. That’s just a shade below hurricane strength. The storm is forecast to pass over a patch of abnormally warm water, providing fuel for it to blossom into a hurricane. It could peak as a Category 2 storm with winds of 110 mph as it lumbers to the northeast. The storm is expected to weaken due to those aforementioned gnarly winds shortly before it makes landfall somewhere along the Gulf Coast.
The NHC has issued hurricane watches for all the coastline in Mississippi and Alabama as well as parts of the Florida Panhandle. (Tropical storm watches extend into Louisiana as well.)
Folks in that region can expect rainfall totals of up to 7 inches, though some spots in the Panhandle could see as much as 10 inches and storm surge as high as 7 feet. Tornadoes aren’t out of the question either. In other words, it’s a storm to take seriously.
Isaias could make also (or at least tie) history as the latest first Atlantic hurricane to form on record. The current record was set in 1905, when the season’s first hurricane formed on October 8. There’s still one more update scheduled for Isaias on Wednesday, so it’s possible it could just miss out on tying that mark.
Record or not, Isaias is indicative of the hurricane season that wasn’t. This year’s Atlantic hurricane season was forecast to be below average. But it’s been even quieter than expected owing to an El Niño that’s been dubbed “super,” “Godzilla,” and “supersized.” The superlatives—which meteorologists will be quick to tell you are not official designations—are indicative of the strength of this year’s event. El Niño is measured by ocean temperatures in a part of the tropical Pacific, and this year’s iteration has seen record highs throughout the summer and first part of fall.
The intensity has had a heavy hand in rearranging the atmosphere around the world, including over the Atlantic. Saharan dust has also played a role in quieting things by making the air in one of the major areas where hurricanes develop too damn dry.
For a sense of how that has impacted the Atlantic hurricane season, we can look at some averages. From 1991 to 2020, the basin saw an average of 14 named storms, seven hurricanes, and three major hurricanes—that is, storms of Category 3 or greater—annually, according to NHC data. This year has seen eight tropical storms and one soon-to-be hurricane.
Another metric to measure the season is accumulated cyclone energy (ACE for short), which takes into account not just the number and intensity of storms but how long they stick around. The ACE to date for 2026 is 10.8 units. The average for this time of year? Nearly 102, according to data maintained by Colorado State University. Most of that energy typically accumulates from mid-August through late September.
None of this is to say there might not be another surprise storm in the coming weeks. But with El Niño continuing to intensify and the peak of the season well past, the odds of this season seeing a sudden spurt of activity are minimal at best.

FBI arrests man for plotting mass shooting at Mall of America
WASHINGTON, Oct 7 - The FBI has arrested an 18-year-old man who had been plotting to carry out a mass shooting at the Mall of America near Minneapolis in the name of ISIS, according to court filings.
He was arrested on Tuesday after an FBI undercover agent sold the Minnesota man, Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud, an AK-47, ammunition and magazines for $600, according to the complaint. Mohamud told the informant he planned to use the items to kill 30 to 60 people at an event at the mall in late October.
Mohamud was charged with one count of knowingly receiving a firearm and ammunition in order to commit an act of terrorism. His lawyer did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
According to the complaint, Mohamud told an FBI source on various messaging platforms that he intended to travel overseas to fight on behalf of al-Shabaab, a designated foreign terrorist organization. He said if he couldn't travel, he planned to conduct a mass shooting. He later said he wanted to join ISIS.
He also allegedly expressed support for a man who rammed a truck into a crowd in New Orleans on January 1, 2025, killing 14, before being killed in a shootout with police.
In July, Mohamud allegedly said he wanted to kill 30 to 60 people at the Mall of America because he claimed its owners were Jewish, and he wanted to kill non-Muslims. He told the informant he planned an attack for October 24 because there was a "Hmong Arts Celebration" that day at the mall.
The Mall of America is the largest mall in the United States, with a theme park, an aquarium and more than 500 stores.
On Tuesday, Mohamud allegedly bought the AK-47, four 30-round-capacity magazines and about 200 rounds of ammunition from an FBI undercover agent. Soon after, FBI agents arrested him.
Mohamud made his initial court appearance before US Magistrate Judge Elizabeth Cowan Wright on Wednesday. REUTERS

The family of a student who took his own life after being wrongly told he would not be eligible to graduate have said the University of Glasgow “will be held to account”.
Ethan Scott Brown, 23, was due to graduate in December 2024 after studying geography.
However, his family said that in September that year, the university told him he had not been awarded a grade for one course and would therefore not be eligible to graduate with an honours degree.
His family said as a result, he took his own life on 13 December 2024, the day he should have been graduating.
He was found dead in his bedroom by his mother, Tracy Scott, that morning.
Scott, who collected her son’s degree posthumously, has called for a fatal accident inquiry to be held into his death.
The university has said it is “profoundly sorry” and is implementing a series of recommendations after a review.
The university’s internal inquiry found “systemic” errors in the way Brown’s degree had been graded, and that he had enough marks for a 2:1 honours degree. It also found that although Brown had told staff that he had concerns about his mental health, they had failed to offer him support.
On Tuesday it was reported that the family had settled a civil court action with the university. The sum of the settlement has not been disclosed.
On Wednesday, the family met the Scottish education secretary, Màiri McAllan, at St Andrew’s House in Edinburgh.
Speaking after the meeting, their solicitor Aamer Anwar said they had placed “the University of Glasgow on notice that they will be held to account”.
Anwar claimed that in its drive to become a global institution, the university had “forgotten its soul”.
He added: “Their failures were catastrophic and systemic. They failed not just in their duty of care to Ethan, but to many other students over the years.
“Today’s meeting with the minister was important and was welcomed. The minister offered to ask the QAA [Quality Assurance Agency for Higher Education], who are investigating the university, to meet with the family.
“The family welcomed the apology by Ms McAllan for her predecessor’s statement in September 2025 which implied an acceptance of the university’s position that Ethan’s case was an isolated incident.”
Anwar added that the university’s governance process was “not fit for purpose”.
A spokesperson for the University of Glasgow said: “The university is profoundly sorry that Ethan tragically took his own life and fully understands the deep distress this has caused his family. We repeat our sincere apology as well as our deepest sympathy.
“Following an internal investigation into assessment regulations, the university self-referred to the Scottish Funding Council.
“The Quality Assurance Agency subsequently carried out a targeted peer review, which resulted in a series of recommendations for action.
“The university fully accepted the recommendations and is on track to implement them.”
A spokesperson for the Crown Office said the circumstances of Brown’s death were being investigated by the Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service, adding that the family would be kept updated on any developments.

Israel marked the third anniversary of Hamas's October 7 attack on Wednesday with silent tributes, new strikes on Gaza and intense political debate, weeks before elections in which the country's deadliest day will be front and centre.
At the site of the Nova music festival, where Hamas militants in trucks and paragliders opened fire around dawn on October 7, 2023, family members bowed their heads quietly – although at least one instead put on techno music in tribute to the fallen.
Watch moreNo longer the same Israel? October 7 and the future of the Jewish State
Both at Nova and the Kfar Aza kibbutz, another site of mass killings three years earlier, AFP reporters heard loud bangs from across the border in Gaza during the commemorations as Israel carried out new strikes, despite a ceasefire officially in place for the past year.

The U.S. and Greece announced $4 billion in Foreign Military Sales on Wednesday to support Athens’ long-term defense plans as the NATO allies moved to expand security and economic cooperation.
The announcement came after U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Greek Foreign Minister George Gerapetritis presided over the sixth U.S.-Greece Strategic Dialogue in Athens, according to a joint statement released by the U.S. State Department.
The two sides said the military sales would support Greece's defense plans and deepen interoperability, while they would also explore further cooperation between their defense industries, including in innovative technologies.

They also highlighted cooperation in high-performance computing, cybersecurity and advanced technologies as well as energy ties involving the Vertical Gas Corridor and hydrocarbon exploration.
The two governments additionally extended their Cultural Property Agreement to protect cultural heritage and combat illicit trafficking networks.
