FBI concerned accused Chinese foreign agent is serious flight risk, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
21:34:39 UTC
06:34:39 KST

Alleged Chinese agent to remain in custody, judge rules, amid FBI concerns of flight risk
An alleged Chinese agent arrested at Los Angeles International Airport over the weekend will remain in federal custody, a federal judge ruled Wednesday during a court hearing. The decision comes amid concern from the FBI that she may try to flee the country if released, law enforcement sources previously told CBS News.   
Prosecutors successfully argued that 34-year-old realtor Wanying Zhang posed too great a flight risk. She had offered to post more than $1.2 million in property for her bond.
Prosecutors told Judge Steve Kim at the L.A. hearing that Zhang has a brother with a history of working for the Chinese government, and that her parents and siblings live in China.
The Orange County mother is now facing federal prosecution for allegedly surveilling the Taiwanese president's son in Washington last year at the direction of Chinese government officials.
Investigators have said Zhang owned a business in China, regularly has money deposited in a Chinese bank account and has parents, a brother and sister currently living there, CBS News has learned.
One law enforcement source said Zhang also had a Chinese passport that was not recovered during an FBI search of her home. Assistant U.S. Attorney Amanda Elbogen confirmed this Wednesday in court.
The sources provided information anonymously as they were not authorized to speak on the record. Zhang's husband and sister declined to comment.
Elbogen told the court Wednesday that Zhang had received $190,000 into a Chinese bank account from an "unregistered cryptocurrency exchange" business and had "hundreds of thousands of dollars" at her disposal in China.
Zhang is currently in the custody of U.S. Marshals in Los Angeles. She was arrested Sunday trying to board a flight to Shanghai at LAX, CBS News was first to report.
She previously appeared briefly in court on Monday, represented by a public defender. The judge had told Zhang to get a private defense attorney by the time of her detention hearing Wednesday, which she did.
Prosecutors Wednesday accused Zhang of lying on the forms she filled out declaring her assets after her arrest, saying that she only had one property when in fact she had several.
Zhang's defense attorney, Craig Harbaugh, told the judge it was a "misunderstanding."
However, Kim noted "inconsistencies" about the number of properties and assets Zhang owns and "where the money is coming from."
During the hearing, Elbogen also referred to Zhang as a "secret agent of a hostile foreign power" and accused her of "spying" on behalf of the Chinese government.
"She has been lying to her own family about who she is," Elbogen told the court. Elbogen claimed Zhang has traveled to China 12 times since 2014 and internationally 29 times, including to Paris, France and Japan.
Harbaugh countered that the only allegation the government has made of spying dated back to September 2025, and that his client's last contact with her Chinese government handlers, according to the complaint, was in October 2025.
Zhang appeared in court Wednesday in shackles and a white jumpsuit. Her husband, Eric Ding, a realtor at the same Irvine, California, firm as his wife, watched from the public gallery with his sister, attorney Elaine Lori, beside him. Both Ding and Lori attended Monday's hearing as well.
According to the criminal complaint against Zhang, she attended the University of International Relations in Beijing between 2010 and 2014, which is run by China's Ministry of State Security, the country's intelligence agency and secret police.
FBI counterintelligence special agent Kevin Holt wrote in his affidavit in the complaint that the ministry "recruits heavily" from the university.
Two law enforcement sources told CBS News that Zhang was one of the top students in her class at UIR.
Zhang's Facebook page shows she is friends with eight current or former staff and students at the university.
As an example of Zhang's alleged Chinese government connections, Elbogen said Wednesday that when Zhang lived in China, she was able to fast-track government permission to move her residence from Beijing to another city.
In its criminal complaint, the FBI said it obtained Zhang's text messages with Chinese intelligence officials, plotting and executing a plan last year to secretly film Taiwan's first son, Lai Ting-yu, and his family in the Seattle suburb where they live. Investigators alleged they have footage from a neighbor's security camera catching Zhang in the midst of her alleged surveillance mission.
Zhang's suspected accomplice on her alleged Seattle trip, named only as Individual 1 in the complaint, left on a one-way ticket to China about two weeks ago, prosecutors said during Wednesday's hearing.
On Tuesday, CBS News also revealed Zhang's links to a Chinese American advocacy group with deep ties to the Chinese government.
She traveled to San Francisco with the organization, the All American Chinese Association, to celebrate Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit there in 2023. Pro-China activists then attacked pro-democracy protesters outside Xi's hotel. There is no evidence Zhang was involved in the violence.
A photograph shows her behind an AACA banner, standing next to the group's leader, Edward Cai, who previously served as vice president for an organization so close to the Chinese government, it was forced to register under the Foreign Agents Registration Act.
FARA requires agents of foreign governments to inform the Justice Department of their status and any lobbying, attempted influence or other activities in the U.S.
Cai and the AACA did not respond to a request for comment.
Reached by phone on Sunday, Ding told CBS News, "I don't know anything yet." He declined to comment further on Monday in federal court.

South Sudan steps up Ebola alert after Kenya case
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
05:32:45 CST
06:32:45 KST

JUBA, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- South Sudan has stepped up nationwide preparedness and surveillance against Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus after neighboring Kenya confirmed an imported case, the Ministry of Health said on Wednesday.
No cases have been detected in the country and the health system has been placed on high alert, according to the ministry.
The ministry said this heightened posture is a proactive response to increased regional mobility and vital trade corridors linking South Sudan with affected areas in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), as well as key transit routes through Kenya and Uganda.
"The geographical expansion of the outbreak to Kenya further increases the risk of cross-border spread and underscores the urgent need for heightened vigilance at points of entry," Caretaker Minister for Health Dak Duop Bichiok told a press conference in Juba, the capital.
The ministry said South Sudan has reactivated its Ebola preparedness and response system, with screening being conducted at points of entry, along the border in 15 high-risk counties and at Juba International Airport.
Ader Machar Aciek, acting executive director of the National Public Health Institute, announced that a dedicated national task force has been established and is convening regular sessions to coordinate ongoing preparedness operations.
Aciek noted that South Sudan has established eight specialized infectious disease units dedicated to isolation and clinical case management should any cases be confirmed.
Moses Ongom, World Health Organization (WHO) Officer in Charge in South Sudan, said that national response preparedness has climbed significantly, rising from 29 percent in May and 45 percent in June to 65 percent currently.
Ongom emphasized that infectious disease control units and response capabilities have been reinforced in priority zones, while urging local communities to remain vigilant and immediately report suspected cases.
Tolbert Geewleh Nyenswah, country director for the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) in South Sudan, said the country has active systems for surveillance, detection, rapid response and laboratory testing.
Nyenswah added that the Africa CDC and the WHO are actively coordinating a regional incident management support mechanism based in Kampala.
Nyenswah said the mechanism is designed to strengthen cross-border cooperation among countries affected by or bordering the DRC.
The Ministry of Health has urged the public to remain calm yet vigilant, practice regular hand hygiene, and avoid direct contact with individuals exhibiting symptoms associated with Ebola.
It said anyone with suspected symptoms, including fever, vomiting, diarrhea or unexplained bleeding, should report to the nearest health facility or call the toll-free emergency hotline 6666. ■

Six regions plan to introduce reduced fares on suburban buses from Oct. 12, while the Trnava and Trencin regions implemented the measure as early as Oct. 1. Although detailed data are not yet available, the regions have reported an increase in bus passenger numbers, Fico said. Public transport fares in regional capitals are also scheduled to be reduced from Oct. 12.

UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- The UN Security Council on Wednesday held its fifth straw poll on the candidates for the next UN secretary-general.

====================================================================================================

Explainer: How 2026 Nobel laureates solve chemistry's "one-handed" mystery
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
05:32:09 CST
06:32:09 KST

STOCKHOLM, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- Hold up your two hands. They look almost identical and are mirror images of each other, yet no matter how you turn them, your left hand can never perfectly overlap your right.
Many molecules behave in much the same way. This seemingly simple feature lies at the heart of the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, awarded Wednesday to French chemist Henri Kagan and Japanese chemist Kenso Soai "for the discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis."
Their work helped answer a question that had puzzled chemists for more than a century: How can chemical reactions produce only one molecular "hand," as the chemistry of life does?
WHY DO MOLECULES HAVE "LEFT" AND "RIGHT" HANDS?
Some molecules can exist in two forms that have the same chemical composition but are mirror images of each other. Chemists call this property chirality, and the two forms enantiomers.
"What makes chirality important is that life itself is selective about molecular handedness," Zou Xiaodong, a member of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, told Xinhua.
Amino acids, the building blocks of proteins, can exist in two mirror-image forms, but only one of these forms is found in the proteins in our cells. The sugars in DNA also favor one form.
Chemists call this "homochirality," literally meaning "same-handedness."
The mystery dates back to the 19th century, when French scientist Louis Pasteur discovered that some molecules could exist as mirror images. Yet when chemists later tried to make such molecules in ordinary reactions, they generally obtained roughly equal amounts of both forms.
HOW DID KAGAN AND SOAI HELP SOLVE THE MYSTERY?
The challenge was to find a chemical way to favor one mirror image over the other.
Kagan took a decisive step in 1986. Chemists had generally assumed that if a catalyst contained a certain proportion of one molecular "hand," the product would show roughly the same proportion. He showed that this relationship could be non-linear. A small imbalance in the catalyst could create a much larger imbalance in the product.
In simple terms, chemistry could amplify a slight preference.
Soai then went further. In the 1990s, he developed a reaction in which the product could help make more copies of itself, a process known as autocatalysis.
In one experiment reported in 1995, a starting imbalance of just 2 percent grew to 87 percent. By 2003, Soai had demonstrated a reaction that could begin without a built-in chiral preference and still end up overwhelmingly dominated by one mirror image.
A tiny difference appearing by chance could therefore reinforce itself again and again until one molecular "hand" took over almost completely.
Put simply, Kagan showed how a small chiral preference could be amplified, while Soai showed how that advantage could reinforce itself through autocatalysis.
The Nobel Committee described the Soai reaction as one of the most spectacular chemical experiments ever conducted.
WHY DOES IT MATTER?
The discoveries help explain how homochirality can emerge, but their importance goes far beyond a century-old scientific puzzle.
Chirality is crucial in drug development because the human body itself is chiral. Two mirror-image versions of the same molecule can interact very differently with proteins and other biological targets.
"Drug molecules need to match the chirality of the human body, just as a right hand does not fit properly into a left-hand glove," Zou said, adding that being able to favor one molecular form therefore allows chemists to make medicines more precisely and reduce unwanted effects.
The same principle is important in the production of flavors, fragrances, agricultural chemicals and some advanced materials.
Kagan's discovery of non-linear effects also gave chemists a new way to understand and optimize asymmetric reactions, while Soai demonstrated how an extremely small initial difference can be amplified through a self-reinforcing process.
That, according to the Nobel Committee, is why Kagan and Soai "made chemistry choose a mirror image." ■

UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- Civilians in Yemen continue to flee their homes amid the ongoing conflict, as the humanitarian crisis worsens by the day, UN humanitarians said Wednesday.
Since Aug. 1, more than 184,000 people have been displaced nationwide, including over 21,000 people in the past week alone, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said, citing the International Organization for Migration.

The World Health Organization warned of major funding shortfalls as rising displacement, disease outbreaks and conflict put more pressure on an already fragile health system, OCHA said. Key roads connecting Taiz governorate with major surrounding cities, including Hodeidah, Aden and Sanaa, remain blocked, the office said, adding that the closure severely restricts the movement of civilians and commercial supplies, as well as humanitarian access.
Shortages of essential commodities and medical supplies are being reported, with sharp increases in food and fuel prices, and growing concerns over the availability of flour, cooking gas and medicines, OCHA said.
The office said it was alarmed by reports of civilian casualties, damage to civilian property and heightened risks from explosive hazards, which are further constraining humanitarian access and the safe movement of civilians.
"OCHA continues to assess the humanitarian impact and calls on all parties to protect civilians and facilitate humanitarians' efforts to safely and swiftly reach them with the support they need," it said. ■

====================================================================================================

World Insights: Three years into Gaza conflict -- destruction, deadlock and regional fallout
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
05:32:03 CST
06:32:03 KST

CAIRO, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- Three years after the Gaza conflict broke out on Oct. 7, 2023, the coastal enclave lies in ruins and tens of thousands have been killed. A ceasefire has been reached, but the fundamental deadlock remains unresolved.
Analysts contend that irreconcilable differences between Palestinian and Israeli demands, coupled with the United States' perceived bias, have left a comprehensive end to the conflict and lasting peace out of reach. The war has also had far-reaching repercussions across the region, with instability spilling over into Lebanon, Syria, Iran and the Red Sea.
GAZA IN RUINS, WEST BANK SQUEEZED
On Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas's "Al-Aqsa Flood" assault saw thousands of rockets fired from Gaza and fighters infiltrating southern Israel, killing around 1,200 people and taking about 250 hostages.
Israel then declared war and launched "Operation Iron Swords," pounding Gaza with airstrikes and a ground offensive that evolved into a prolonged and devastating conflict.
Over the past three years, Gaza has suffered catastrophic destruction, leaving a profound humanitarian catastrophe across the territory. More than 74,000 people had been killed in the enclave since Oct. 7, 2023, according to Gaza health authorities.
"Large-scale Israeli military campaign resulted in a significant number of casualties, particularly among women and children, widespread destruction of homes and infrastructure, and the displacement of more than two million Palestinians," Bahraini political analyst Abdullah Al Huwaihi commented.
Amid mounting global outrage over the killings in Gaza, a ceasefire was eventually reached in October 2025. Under phase one of the U.S.-proposed Gaza ceasefire plan, Israeli forces were required to retreat to the "Yellow Line" and swap hostages for prisoners. Phase two, launched in mid-January, focused on the demilitarization of Gaza and the establishment of technocratic governance.
By the end of July, Hamas had agreed to include the handover of heavy weapons in the demilitarization arrangements, conditional on Israel's full withdrawal and a halt to "aggressions."
Yet the phased agreements have failed to translate into lasting peace. Khaled Al Hroub, professor of international conflicts at Northwestern University in Qatar, said the failure of successive frameworks shows that any real settlement requires moving beyond managing recurring violence to tackling the political roots of the conflict.
Alongside the devastation in Gaza, violence and the erosion of Palestinian territory in the West Bank have also intensified.
UN data shows that as of Aug. 10, some 3,800 Palestinians had been displaced by settler violence, house demolitions and evictions this year. The UN has recorded over 1,430 settler-related incidents this year, affecting about 260 Palestinian communities.
"The West Bank is at the breaking point," Ramiz Alakbarov, the UN humanitarian coordinator for the occupied Palestinian territory, has said.
DEADLOCK AND WASHINGTON'S DOUBLE BIND
Analysts attribute the prolonged deadlock in Gaza to irreconcilable differences between Israel and Hamas.
Akram Attaallah, a political analyst from Gaza, explained that Israel insists on Hamas's complete disarmament before any full withdrawal, while Hamas demands an end to Israeli military operations and a total Israeli retreat before discussing weapons.
"Israel and Hamas view the issue as a completely zero-sum equation. Hamas wants to remain, while Israel wants to eliminate any presence of Hamas in the Gaza Strip," he said. "Between these two positions, the crisis continues."
Baghdad University professor Adel al-Ghurairi said the U.S.-proposed framework, including the so-called "Board of Peace," the stabilization force and the transitional committee, remains largely on paper, with disarmament and Israeli withdrawal still pending.
"The big pieces of the roadmap -- disarmament, an Israeli pullout, who governs during the transition -- are all still sitting unfinished," he said.
Behind the scenes, the United States plays a deeply contradictory role, observers told Xinhua.
Ali Al Hail, professor of political science at Qatar University, said Washington's role as chief mediator is undermined by its military aid and diplomatic backing for Israel, raising questions about its impartiality and allowing the conflict to persist.
"The United States has played a dual role: it remains Israel's principal strategic ally while also being an essential actor in diplomatic efforts," he said. "This dual position creates questions about how effectively it can act as an intermediary acceptable to all sides."
Al-Ghurairi added that the United States wants the war over, but it hasn't shown the will to actually force that outcome. "The absence of a genuine multilateral mechanism, and the reliance on unilateral American hegemony, renders any settlement fragile."
SPILLOVER AND THE TWO-STATE SOLUTION
Across the region, analysts see the conflict as having profoundly reshaped the geopolitical landscape.
Sudanese political analyst Mohamed Amin noted that the conflict's regional spillover has been felt in the Red Sea, where Yemen's Houthis have attacked ships in what they describe as support for the Palestinians.
"This has turned part of the repercussions of the Gaza war into an issue involving the security of international shipping and trade," he said.
The balance of power between the U.S.-Israel alliance and the Iran-led resistance front, including Hamas, the Houthis and Lebanon's Hezbollah, has shifted, Al Huwaihi added.
"Israel came to believe that, after what it viewed as its gains in Gaza, the confrontation should move toward Iran as the principal state supporting these groups," he said. "It subsequently succeeded in persuading the U.S. president to launch war against Iran on Feb. 28."
Amid such complexity, the prevailing view is that true and lasting peace remains impossible without fully implementing the two-state solution and restoring legitimate Palestinian rights.
Lebanese political analyst Youssef Diab said the Palestinian cause may remain a central conflict shaping the region.
"There can either be peace for the Palestinians, including the establishment of a sovereign Palestinian state with genuine authority, or there will continue to be instability and chaos," he said.
"Regional stability will also depend on the ability of regional and international powers to contain interconnected tensions in Iran, Yemen, the Red Sea, and the Gulf and establish broader security and political arrangements," Amin added. ■

According to military intelligence, construction of the complex involved interference with the site's historical and archaeological environment. In particular, construction work caused significant damage to and destruction of part of the cultural layer.
The HUR published details of four people involved in the project, including:
- Natalya Solovyova, director of the Center for Rescue Archaeology at the Institute of the History of Material Culture of the Russian Academy of Sciences;
- Ivan Yesin, director of the "My History" Foundation for the Support of Humanities;
- Maksim Zhukalov, the so-called deputy governor of the city of Sevastopol;
- Larisa Shepko, a professor at the Department of World History of the "Donetsk State University."
"Among those whose details have been published is also Nadezhda Milikhina, a junior researcher at the Department of the History of Ancient Culture of the Russian Academy of Sciences' Institute of the History of Material Culture. She was deputy to Russian archaeologist Alexander Butyagin during the illegal Myrmekion archaeological expedition of the State Hermitage Museum in the temporarily occupied territory of Crimea," the intelligence agency added.
The HUR said that in 2024, the Prosecutor's Office of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea and the city of Sevastopol notified Butyagin of suspicion of intentionally and unlawfully partially destroying a cultural heritage site. In 2026, the suspicion was amended to "violations of the laws and customs of war." He was detained in Poland in late 2025, and in April 2026, Poland released him and handed him over to Russia as part of a prisoner exchange.
In addition, the HUR published information on 14 cultural artifacts stolen from the "Ancient City of Myrmekion" during the expedition. They include a coin of King Sauromates II of the Bosporan Kingdom (AD 180–196) and a black-glazed one-handled kantharos (370–350 BC).
The HUR had previously published information on 20 Ukrainian cultural artifacts stolen by Russia, as well as seven people involved in illegal archaeological work, the distortion of history and the justification of the seizure of Ukrainian territories.

How a (Weirdly Chill) Celebrity Thinks About Personal Cybersecurity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
21:31:51 UTC
06:31:51 KST

At a promotional event in Times Square on Wednesday for the security company NordVPN, brand ambassador Shaquille O’Neal said he is eager to raise awareness among regular people about the importance of digital security and personal privacy.
“I have a video of me beating up Charles Barkley, and I wouldn't want the world to see that. That was a joke,” O'Neal says. “But everybody needs to have control of their own information.”
After being targeted by scammers who claimed that he was trying to buy a house and they were working on the transaction, O’Neal says, he realized he needed to learn more about cybersecurity and digital defense.
“I was hacked for the first time, not a bad hack, and I didn't know what to do,” he told reporters. “So I had to look into it. Once that happened, I really had to start paying more attention, because I would think nothing like that could ever happen to me, but it could happen to anybody.”
O'Neal, of course, is not just anybody. Still, the four-time NBA champion and media personality says that he doesn't have particularly sensitive data on his devices and tries to live a normal life as much as possible. When WIRED asked, though, whether he worries that he needs to take extra precautions to protect himself and loved ones as a result of his high profile, O'Neal said, “Yes, I think about it all the time, but I don't let it consume me, because if you let it consume you you can go crazy. But you have to be able to have great reactionary skills if something happens.”
A prolific tech investor who was early to AI, O'Neal emphasizes that the goal of his relationship with NordVPN is to inform the public and help people protect themselves. NordVPN is, well, known for its VPN. But the company has other offerings, including antivirus, threat detection, and scam-defense products that are geared toward accessibility for consumers. Marijus Briedis, the company's chief technology officer, says he was surprised by the findings of a recent NordVPN poll showing that 73 percent of Americans have an overconfidence in traditional antivirus and believe it can protect them against anything from identity theft to online tracking.
“The weakest link is between the computer and the chair, and I've been thinking so much about how to solve that problem,” Briedis told WIRED. “So the thing we are doing right now is focusing on education. It's a really interesting problem, how to do it in the best way. It's still haunting me in my dreams.”

Can the Gulf aviation superhub model survive the war?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
21:30:05 UTC
06:30:05 KST

Can the Gulf aviation superhub model survive the war?
The problem is not that war disrupts flights, but that this time, the hubs of Dubai, Doha and Abu Dhabi have become part of the battlefield
For decades, the Gulf superhubs of Dubai, Doha and Abu Dhabi performed an improbable trick. They redirected millions of people travelling between the West and Asia to connect through their airports. Last year, the three airports handled about 182 million passengers, three times the traffic at Hong Kong airport. Dubai alone handled 95.2 million, the highest ever recorded by an airport.
The Gulf’s hub-and-spoke model – funnelling passengers through a central airport to multiple destinations – created economies of scale that redesigned global commercial aviation flows through a routing system solid enough to become the new standard of travel between West and East.

From Military Base to Pax Silica: Clark and Capas in Philippine History
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
21:30:00 UTC
06:30:00 KST

New Clark City in the Philippines is in the news for being the site of the planned industrial hub of the Luzon Economic Corridor under the United States-led Pax Silica coalition. It is part of the Clark special economic zone and also covers the municipalities of Capas and Bamban in the province of Tarlac. The history of this place can help us better understand the political narratives in favor of and opposed to Pax Silica.
As the colonial ruler of the Philippines in the first half of the 20th century, the U.S. established an air base in Angeles in the province of Pampanga in the central part of Luzon, the country’s biggest island. After the end of World War II, the Philippines became an independent republic but the U.S. maintained the Clark base in Pampanga. It soon became the largest overseas U.S. military camp and a crucial hub during the Cold War era. In 1991, Clark was turned over to the Philippine government after the Senate rejection of the U.S. bases treaty. It was converted into a commercial area and designated a special economic zone to attract investments.
Today, Clark is a strategic business center since it is only less than a two-hour drive from the capital region of Metro Manila. Its international airport is already one of the country’s busiest aviation terminals.
Meanwhile, Capas is outside of Clark but it used to host Camp O’Donnell, an American military reservation. Thousands of prisoners during World War II died in a “death march” from Mariveles in Bataan to Capas. The communist-led New People’s Army was also established in this rural municipality in 1969.
Parts of Capas were incorporated into the New Clark City, which was originally envisioned as a government center and alternative capital to decongest Metro Manila. Sports facilities were built here when the country hosted the Southeast Asian Games in 2019. The stadium cauldron was reported to be overpriced, which implicated key allies of former President Rodrigo Duterte.
The pandemic affected the development of New Clark City and there has been no substantial discussion about the earlier plan to build a new capital in the area.
It generated attention again when it was named as a possible location of the Luzon Economic Corridor, a trilateral initiative unveiled in 2024 between the Philippines, the U.S., and Japan. This was confirmed last April after the Philippines officially joined the Pax Silica coalition.
In several social media posts, U.S. Undersecretary of State Jacob Helberg stated that the hub will be a “forward deployed industrial base” aimed at securing vital supply-chain inputs for American companies and its allies.
“Four thousand acres. Roughly one-third the size of Manhattan – the equivalent of everything from Times Square south to the very tip of the island,” Helberg added, referring to the land “gifted” by the Philippine government for the Pax Silica project.
After this, concerns were raised about the project’s potential grave impact on energy and water resources in the provinces of Pampanga and Tarlac. Farmers and indigenous peoples said their communities have been threatened with eviction to give way for the rise of the industrial hub.
In response, authorities said data centers will not be a component of the Pax Silica site, although these facilities will still rise in other parts of Luzon. They also assured local communities that consultations will be conducted, even if they initially denied that there were residents in the project site.
The Philippine government also assured the public that the country’s laws will prevail and no immunity will be granted to foreign investors in the hub. Nevertheless, concerns persist about the role of Pax Silica in supporting the military operations of the U.S. in the country and in the Asia-Pacific. What is clear is that it is seen as a counterpart to the China-led World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization.
Negotiations are ongoing and expected to continue for the next two years. A framework deal could be signed next month during the summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, and it could be the highlight of U.S. President Donald Trump’s visit to Manila.
Pax Silica is more than just a real estate transaction since it is touted as the next big opportunity for the Philippines to promote industrial development through mineral processing and technology transfer. The history of Clark and Capas is a reminder that local political dynamics can get entangled with regional and global geopolitical issues. The Pax Silica hub will rise on a land that hosted foreign bases, military operations that led to war atrocities, and protests that represented the Filipino people’s assertion of sovereignty.
As the Philippines under the government of Ferdinand Marcos Jr rushes forward with this bold initiative, the challenge is to address the criticism that this is another unfair deal that favors the country’s former colonizers rather than a development blueprint that prioritizes the national interest.

US folded to EU pressure on Ukraine – Lavrov
The US gave in to pressure from the EU, which has openly gloated about undermining the Anchorage understandings and declared them “buried,” Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has said.
The top diplomat made the remarks on Wednesday while speaking at a press conference following a ministerial meeting of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS).
Lavrov reiterated Moscow’s position that the Anchorage initiative had ultimately been derailed by European nations.
”Our conscience is clear, not to mention the fact that we fully accepted the United States’ proposal last August, which was made during the summit… in Alaska,” he stated.
It is not our fault that the Americans could not withstand the unprecedented and brazen pressure from Europe, which later proudly declared that it had buried Anchorage.
US President Donald Trump hosted his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin in Anchorage, Alaska, last year, with the two leaders reaching an understanding on how the Ukraine conflict could be settled.
While Moscow has portrayed the outcome of the summit as an “agreement,” despite some “nuances” remaining, Washington has repeatedly disputed that characterization. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio previously said that there was “a proposal in Alaska, but there was no agreement.”
According to Lavrov, the Anchorage understandings were ultimately undermined over the following months by EU and British leaders. During the G7 summit in Evian in June, French President Emmanuel Macron openly declared that Anchorage had been “buried.”
While the US has displayed a declining commitment to the “understandings,” Trump has never explicitly declared the framework dead. Last month, Washington attempted to revive negotiations between Russia and Ukraine, but the process stalled once again amid continued long-range strikes by Moscow and Kiev.
According to Lavrov, Russia agreed to a Washington-proposed trilateral meeting with Ukraine, which was expected to be held after the recent Russian parliamentary elections. Kiev, however, actively attempted to disrupt the polls and launched a massive attack while voting was underway.
”We made it clear that, under these circumstances, we want to know what proposals exactly [Vladimir] Zelensky’s negotiators would bring. This is very important to us, and the American side has taken our arguments with understanding,” the foreign minister added.

Pakistani military spokesman Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry has confirmed that Pakistani forces are deployed on the ground in Saudi Arabia across multiple operational domains, serving under long-standing bilateral arrangements and the recently established Mecca Joint Defence Agreement.
In an interview with CNN, Chaudhry stated that the presence of Pakistani armed forces in the Kingdom is firmly established rather than novel, pointing out that military personnel have maintained continuous operations alongside Saudi counterparts for decades.
"I can confirm that we, the forces of Pakistan, are already there [in the Kingdom]. That I can share (with) you," Chaudhry said when questioned about deployments under the mutual defence alliance.
"Pakistani troops have been there for decades, and multiple capabilities have been there for decades in Saudi Arabia. As I said, this Mecca Alliance is not something that has come out in a vacuum. There is a sustained diplomatic, political, military relationship, people-to-people relationship between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye. So I can share with you that the Pakistani forces in multiple capabilities and domains are already there."
Trilateral coordination
The spokesman's remarks follow a session of the Strategic-Political and Defence Committee of the Mecca Alliance for Defence held in Riyadh on 5 October, where officials from Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Türkiye convened to address urgent security developments and threats directed at the Kingdom.
The meeting followed a series of drone and missile strikes by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis targeting civilian and economic infrastructure across Saudi territory.
During the Riyadh talks, officials reaffirmed their shared rejection of attacks against the Kingdom’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.
Under an earlier bilateral agreement signed in September last year, Islamabad dispatched 8,000 troops, a fighter squadron, and air defence batteries to reinforce the Kingdom.

Latvian court sentences woman to six years in prison over €43 transfer investigators say was intended for drone-jamming equipment for Russian troops
The Riga City Court has sentenced Polina Kamleva, a resident of Rēzekne, to six years in prison for financing an armed conflict, Delfi reported. The outlet called her a pro-Russian activist.
Kamleva was accused of transferring 43 euros to buy a drone-jamming device that was to be supplied to Russian forces. Latvia’s State Security Service detained her in December 2025. Delfi reported at the time that she was a member of the Latvian Russian Union Party.
During a WhatsApp exchange in December 2024, Kamleva agreed to help raise money for military equipment for the Russian army, according to investigators cited by Delfi. An acquaintance from Russia’s Kaskad military-patriotic center asked her to help raise money for a mobile electronic warfare system.
Investigators said Kamleva contacted another acquaintance, who lives in Belarus, and asked him to transfer the money on her behalf because transfers from Latvian banks to Russian banks were impossible. He transferred 157 Belarusian rubles (about 43 euros) from his personal account.
In her final statement to the court, Kamleva said she had not intended to finance the Russian army and that the messages found on her phone did not clearly establish that the money was intended for Russian forces. She said she was out of work at the time and in serious psychological distress, so she had been unable to turn down the person who asked her for help. “What I did was wrong. I ask you to distinguish between doing something wrong and having criminal intent. I had no such intent,” she said.
Prosecutors had sought an eight-year prison sentence for Kamleva. Under Latvia’s criminal code, financing an armed conflict carries a prison sentence of up to 10 years.

Christa Pike 'angry and confused' after botched execution

Christa Pike 'angry and confused' after botched execution
October 7, 2026
A US judge told the state of Tennessee to preserve all evidence related to the failed attempt to execute Christa Pike, who lawyers say is "angry and confused" after waking up in hospital nearly a week after the ordeal.
Pike, who was sentenced to death for torturing and killing classmate Colleen Slemmer in 1995, survived despite being given two lethal doses of pentobarbital, a lethal injection drug.
What do we know about Christa Pike's current state?
One of her attorneys spoke about the 50-year-old's state after the failed execution.
"She is angry and confused about everything right now," Randy Spivey said during a news conference, adding Pike is "very aware" of what was done to her.
"She cannot move either of her arms, both of her arms and hands are tremendously swollen, and we do not know what, if any, function she will regain in her arms," Spivey said, adding that "there's a long road ahead" for her recovery.
Pike is the only person known to have survived after receiving lethal injection drugs, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.
Luke Ihnen, another lawyer for Pike, said that "medical staff have asked that the shackles be removed and have been denied that request."
Her lawyers continue to demand that Tennessee Governor Bill Lee commute Pike's sentence to life in prison and never reattempt her execution. The Republican governor had denied a clemency appeal two days before the failed execution.
Pike's recovery period unclear
Experts say it is possible that the failed execution was due to a problem with the IV line that caused the injection to pool in her tissue rather than enter her bloodstream.
"Apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown," her attorneys wrote in their court filing.
Pike's arms were burned and blistered due to the injection, according to her legal team, who are demanding that the prison authority holds all information from the attempted execution, including needles and execution logs.
It is not yet clear how Pike's recovery might unfold and whether she will be subjected to another execution attempt.

Maduro expected to face new charges alleging torture of Americans in Venezuelan prisons, sources say
Federal prosecutors are expected to bring new charges against former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, for allegedly torturing Americans who were held in Venezuelan prisons, according to multiple sources familiar with the case.
The sources said that additional people could be charged in their role for the torture of more than a dozen Americans who were wrongfully detained by the Venezuelan government while Maduro was in power.
One source said the new charges could be announced as soon as Thursday.
Barry Pollack, an attorney for Maduro, told CBS News that he has not been provided any notice that additional charges could be coming.
Flores is due in federal court on Thursday in the Southern District of New York for a bond hearing, and a trial date has been tentatively set for June 2027.
CNN was first to report the potential new charges.
A Justice Department spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Maduro and Flores were indicted by a federal grand jury in January on charges stemming from what prosecutors said was his role in a scheme to import "thousands of tons" of cocaine into the United States and enrich themselves, their family and senior members of the Venezuelan government. The U.S. military took the couple into custody in an overnight operation and brought them to the U.S. to face the charges. They have pleaded not guilty.
Prosecutors said Maduro was at the "forefront of the corruption" and that he and his associates worked with drug traffickers and narco-terrorists to flood the U.S. with drugs.
Maduro faces four charges: narco-terrorism conspiracy; cocaine importation conspiracy; possession of machine guns and destructive devices; and conspiracy to possess machine guns and destructive devices.
The case against them was brought in the Southern District of New York, where Maduro and 14 others were first indicted in March 2020, during the first Trump administration.
Maduro and his wife have asked U.S. District Judge Alvin K. Hellerstein to dismiss the drug trafficking indictment against them on the grounds that they have immunity as the leaders of a foreign country. The judge has not heard arguments on those motions yet.
In September, Alex Saab, a former minister of industry in Maduro's government, pleaded guilty to one count of money laundering tied to an alleged bribery conspiracy and agreed to cooperate in ongoing federal investigations into the regime after being deported to the U.S. from Venezuela.
In May, CBS News reported that federal prosecutors in Miami were ordered to open a new criminal investigation into Maduro amid some concerns that the pending prosecution against him is weak.

Christa Pike ‘angry and confused’ about Tennessee’s failed execution effort, lawyers say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07

Christa Pike ‘angry and confused’ about Tennessee’s failed execution effort, lawyers say
- - Christa Pike woke up in hospital “angry and confused” after Tennessee’s failed execution, which left her critically ill, swollen, and unable to swallow or move her arms.
- - A judge ordered Tennessee to preserve syringes, drugs, and internal records after the botched execution, as Pike’s lawyers pushed for more transparency and chemical testing.
- - The case has renewed scrutiny of capital punishment in Tennessee, and Governor Bill Lee has paused all executions while investigators review Pike’s case and another failed execution.
AI generated
NASHVILLE - Christa Pike, sentenced to death for a 1995 murder, awoke “angry and confused” in a hospital this week with a long recuperation ahead after surviving Tennessee’s botched effort to execute her, her lawyers said on Oct 7.
A week ago, Pike, 50, was taken from the execution chamber to a Nashville hospital, unconscious, critically ill and with severe arm injuries after two injections of the caustic barbiturate pentobarbital failed to kill her at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution.
As late as Oct 5, her lawyers believed Pike was brain dead and that life support would be removed the next day following the second botched execution in Tennessee this year, which has renewed scrutiny of capital punishment in the US.
“But on Tuesday, to the shock of everyone, including me, including her team, and including the medical team, Christa woke up and began talking,” Randall Spivey, one of her lawyers, told reporters after a court hearing on Oct 7, where a judge ordered Tennessee officials to preserve syringes and other evidence from the botched execution.
“She is angry and confused about everything right now,” Spivey said.
“She is very aware that the state tried to execute her.”
Governor Bill Lee has suspended all executions for the rest of the year while investigators look into the botched executions of Pike and of Tony Carruthers in May, when prison officials were unable to set up intravenous lines.
Pike remains very sick and shackled to her hospital bed, facing a long road to recovery, her lawyers said.
She cannot swallow or eat, has pneumonia, cannot move her “tremendously swollen” hands or arms, and it is unclear if she will regain her lost mobility, they said.
Although she still has “cognitive confusion,” the lawyers said, she has been speaking with those around her.
“She has wanted to know what’s happened, and she’s asked about several people,” Spivey said. “She’s asked about the victim’s family.”
Pike was sentenced to death for her role as a teenager in the 1995 torture and murder of her 19-year-old schoolmate Colleen Slemmer.
She is the first person known to have survived a “completed execution attempt” in the US, her lawyers say, calling it a violation of the Constitution’s prohibition on cruel and unusual punishments.
A unique case
Pike’s lawyers are unexpectedly continuing their litigation against state officials, seeking to pierce the secrecy that normally surrounds execution procedures in Tennessee and other states.
Earlier on Oct 7, a judge in Davidson County Chancery Court, I’Ashea Myles, agreed to order Tennessee officials to preserve all evidence from the failed execution, including syringes, drug packaging and lot numbers, catheters, intravenous lines and gurney restraints.
The all-female execution team requested by Pike used at least seven needles during a gruelling ordeal that lasted more than two hours, and one needle was bent 90 degrees when it was pulled out, her lawyers said.
Myles largely sided with Pike’s lawyers at the end of the Oct 7 hearing, describing the litigation, which began in January in an effort to prevent the scheduled execution, as unusual because no one had anticipated Pike surviving.
“This case is unique, to say the least,” Myles said.
She also ordered the state to preserve internal communications about the attempted execution, including incident reports, witness accounts and encrypted messages.
She has yet to rule on a request by Pike’s lawyers that the Tennessee Department of Correction let them take any residual traces of the execution drugs for chemical analysis.
The Tennessee Department of Correction has opposed what it says is a “duplicative and unnecessary” preservation order, arguing it is already legally required to preserve all evidence and that it was already willing to share most, if not all, of what Pike’s lawyers sought.
Tennessee and other US states have long struggled to acquire execution drugs. They cannot be obtained from major pharmaceutical companies because of a European trade ban on companies that sell products for use in torture or executions.
Tennessee, like other states, has turned to small, largely unregulated compounding pharmacies to make small batches of the drugs, promising to hide their identity.
“Today’s hearing was about transparency, about why Christa, the courts, the media and the public should not simply take the state’s word about what happened last Wednesday,” Luke Ihnen, another lawyer for Pike, told reporters after the judge’s ruling.
He repeated the demand that Tennessee Governor Bill Lee commute Pike’s sentence to life in prison and never attempt to execute her again. A spokesperson for Lee, who denied a clemency appeal two days before the failed execution, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Pike’s lawyers had sought an alternative to lethal injections, saying her small veins and related medical conditions made her afraid that something would go wrong. REUTERS

56 Ukrainians still missing as Nepal ends flash flood search-and-rescue operation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
21:18:21 UTC

56 Ukrainians still missing as Nepal ends flash flood search-and-rescue operation
Fifty-six Ukrainians remain missing after Nepal ended its search-and-rescue operation following August's deadly floods, Ukraine's Foreign Ministry said on Oct. 6.
Devastating flash floods ravaged Nepal after a glacier collapsed in the Himalayas on Aug. 26, drowning villages in mud and debris. At least 1,455 people were killed in the floods, and over 5,200 people were unaccounted for.
While active rescue operations have been suspended, the search and identification of remains continue, the ministry said.
"Unfortunately, despite weeks of efforts by diplomats, consuls, and rescuers, (the missing Ukrainians) have still not been found among either the dead or the injured," the Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
Out of the missing Ukrainian citizens, 46 were traveling together in a tour group. Contact with the group was lost when the flash flooding began. Rescue efforts have been ongoing for over 40 days, but none of the missing Ukrainians have been identified.
While there have been no official reports of Ukrainians killed, Nepalese officials said they were considering commencing the legal process of declaring missing persons as dead.
"We are initiating due processes to complete required legal formalities," Phanindra Paudel, chief of the National Emergency Operation Centre, told Reuters.
These formalities would allow families of the missing individuals to complete relevant administrative tasks, such as filing life insurance claims, in their home countries.
The Ukrainian embassy in India has contacted relevant authorities concerning procedures for official documentation, the ministry said.
The Ukrainian National Police is also working to finalize a database of DNA profiles of those missing in the floods to share with Nepalese authorities.

Sahin Demir
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
Iran said Wednesday that its response to US proposals concerning efforts to end the conflict will be delivered through mediators while announcing progress with Oman on establishing safe shipping routes through the Strait of Hormuz.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said Tehran had clearly outlined its “considerations and conditions” for ending the war on all fronts and restoring security to the Gulf region and the Strait of Hormuz, according to state-run IRNA news agency.
“The necessary response to the proposals of the other side will also be provided through the mediators,” Baghaei said, adding that messages between Iran and the US are being exchanged through intermediaries.
Baghaei also responded to remarks by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio earlier Wednesday that Iran had failed to take advantage of “multiple opportunities” to reach an agreement with Washington over its nuclear program. Rubio made the remarks during a visit to Athens.
“Distorting historical facts cannot erase from public opinion the reality of the United States’ repeated breaches of its commitments,” Baghaei said.
He cited the US withdrawal from the 2015 nuclear agreement in 2018, what he described as Washington’s disruption of diplomatic processes and military attacks against Iran during negotiations.
Baghaei accused the US of responsibility for the current insecurity in the region and its economic consequences in the US and around the world.
On navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, he said Iran and Oman had made progress in consultations aimed at restoring maritime security.
He said the two countries had agreed on the geographical coordinates of safe inbound and outbound shipping routes through the strategic waterway.
The two sides also reached an understanding on how the arrangement would be communicated to the relevant international body, a step Baghaei said would take place “soon.”
Baghaei also said that Iran would continue its efforts to strengthen trust and engagement among countries in the region.

French mayor caught in viral video clash says student protesters 'could be my children'
SAINT-DENIS, France, Oct 7 - In a video that has gone viral on social media, Bally Bagayoko, the mayor of the French town of Saint-Denis, stands facing police at a march in Paris on Tuesday, shielding young protesters and shouting "stop."
Bagayoko said he has been supporting the students in his working-class Parisian suburb and on Tuesday was asking the police not to charge.
"They had decided to charge and effectively go after the students, many of whom had shown no aggressive behaviour whatsoever toward the police officers," Bagayoko, who is part of the hard-left France Unbowed party (LFI), told Reuters in an interview on Wednesday at his town hall office in Saint-Denis, on the northern outskirts of Paris.
In the end, the police fired tear gas at the group, including the mayor, he said.
The wave of student protests, which began in Paris' marginalised suburbs, has been going on for more than two weeks and has exposed widespread public anger six months ahead of an election to replace French President Emmanuel Macron.
There have been more than 6,000 arrests and dozens of student injuries since the protests began. Rights groups and unions accuse the police of using heavy-handed tactics against minors, including the use of batons, tear gas and non-lethal flashball guns. Authorities say hundreds of police officers have also been injured, schools have been burned or ransacked, and teachers and members of the public have been attacked.
The town of Saint-Denis, where poverty levels are more than double the national average, was one of the first sites of student protests in late September over overcrowded and unsanitary classrooms, teacher shortages and unequal opportunities.
"Protests are not new here, they happen at every start of the academic year," Bagayoko said. "The Republican promise (of equality) — in particular for the working-class neighbourhoods, and also rural areas — is not respected."
He said the government should prioritise investing in education and levy heavier taxes on billionaires.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said on Wednesday that the government would review demands made by students and present proposals at the end of October, but gave no details.
The government has suggested that LFI politicians were behind the protests, an accusation that Bagayoko dismissed as insulting to the young protesters.
A father of four, he said that "the high school children who were in the street could be my children ... it is my responsibility to be at their side." REUTERS

Germany’s far-right AfD and left-wing populist BSW party now hold a majority in an eastern state parliament. Their first joint proposal: End aid to Ukraine and restore ties with Russia.
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party and the left-wing populist Union for Social Justice plan to pass their first joint resolution soon, calling for an end to military aid to Ukraine, Reuters and Deutsche Welle reported. Together, the parties hold a majority in Saxony-Anhalt’s state parliament following the election.
The resolution’s authors call on the state parliament to declare that the policy of imposing sanctions on Russia and providing arms and financial aid to Ukraine has failed. They say further escalation in Ukraine must be prevented and call for “a policy that promotes peace.”
The authors call for “an immediate ceasefire and the start of peace talks with Russia,” as well as restoring normal economic relations between Germany and Russia and lifting sanctions.
A vote on the resolution is scheduled for October 14. DW and Reuters said it will be symbolic because state governments have no influence over Germany’s foreign policy. Reuters reported, however, that the initiative underscores the AfD’s persistent push to end German support for Ukraine and restore ties with Russia.
Representatives of the Union for Social Justice said Germany needs policies that prioritize Köthen, a town in Saxony-Anhalt, over Kyiv.
In early September, Alternative for Germany won the election in Saxony-Anhalt with its best-ever result — 43.8% of the vote. The party took 39 of the state parliament’s 83 seats. Together with the Union for Social Justice, it holds 44 seats.
The AfD said it was already in talks with Russia about resuming gas supplies to Germany. The party’s foreign policy spokesperson, Markus Frohnmaier, discussed the issue with Gazprom chief Alexey Miller.

NEW DELHI: CUET-UG 2027 could see some of its biggest changes yet - fewer subjects, shorter papers and a new grouping system aimed at ensuring that a student can finish the entire entrance test in a single day instead of making repeated trips to examination centres.The ministry of education, University Grants Commission and National Testing Agency are working on a formula to shorten the overall examination cycle and simplify the experience for candidates, sources said.At present, a candidate can take up to five subjects in CUET-UG, with each paper lasting 60 minutes.
Under one proposal being examined, the duration of individual papers could be reduced so that even a student taking five subjects can complete all tests within about 180 to 200 minutes.
CUET-UG also mulls reducing number of subjects from 5 to 4
Another option under discussion is whether the maximum number of subjects should be reduced from five to four. Sources said senior officials of the education ministry, UGC and NTA recently discussed the proposed changes and asked officials to examine how the examination could be compressed without affecting university admission requirements.A key part of the plan is to create subject groups based on commonly chosen combinations.
This would allow NTA to schedule related papers together and complete a candidate’s examination in one sitting or on the same day.For example, physics, chemistry and biology could form one group for those seeking admission to science programmes. General studies could be added as a fourth paper where universities give weightage to its score. The idea is to bu-ild these groups around eligibility rules followed by universities.
For instance, a student seeking admission to physics (Hons) at DU could choose the relevant three-subject combination rather than taking papers not required for the course.Officials believe such grouping could reduce the number of examination days and make scheduling easier. It could also end the problem of students having to travel to examination centres on different days for different papers. The proposals will depend on consultations with universities and the testing agency.

Germany Plans New Naval Port in Emden as Navy Expands
Germany plans to build a new naval port in Emden on the North Sea as it expands naval capacity for operations in the North Atlantic and High North, according to the joint press release posted on the City of Emden website on October 5.
Germany’s Defense Ministry, the state of Lower Saxony, the Federal Institute for Real Estate, and the City of Emden signed a letter of intent supporting the project and further planning.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The decision reflects NATO defense plans, Germany’s national military requirements, and the expected expansion of the Bundeswehr. The navy will need additional berths, support infrastructure, accommodation, and training facilities as new ships and personnel enter service, the press release stated.
Germany currently has only one naval port on the North Sea, in Wilhelmshaven. According to the statement, that base will not be able to meet future requirements for berths, pier capacity, and logistical support linked to operations in the North Sea, Atlantic, and High North.
After examining several possible locations, the navy identified Emden as the strongest option because of its geography, infrastructure links, and access to the Atlantic and High North.
“The navy is growing. New ships and boats need berths. Our soldiers need accommodation and training facilities. That is why we need a new naval port. And we want to build it in Emden,” German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius stated.
“The navy carried out an intensive review, and Emden offers ideal conditions, including rapid access to the Atlantic and the High North,” he added.
The agreement is not legally binding, and a final decision has not yet been made. Further feasibility studies are expected to be completed before construction can formally proceed, according to the joint press release.
Germany has been steadily increasing its naval role within NATO. In September, the German Navy tested a ship-launched LORA ballistic missile in the North Atlantic, while German and Dutch forces had earlier established a joint command center in Estonia as part of NATO’s eastern-flank defense.

Newly obtained footage shows Iran attack on major U.S. post in Kuwait

"They hit us bad": Newly obtained footage, witness accounts detail Iran attack, and U.S. retreat, at major post in Kuwait
Washington — New videos obtained exclusively by CBS News show Iranian attacks on a major U.S. military base in Kuwait as the war with Iran kicked off seven months ago. American forces faced ballistic missiles, drones and what witnesses described as Iranian F-5 fighter jets.
The footage obtained by CBS News was recorded by a person stationed on the ground at Camp Buehring, and captures the moments of impact and their explosive aftermath. Damage to buildings and military equipment can also be seen in the videos.
The attacks on Camp Buehring offer a window into the strain Iranian attacks placed on American forces during the opening days of the war. CBS News has learned that soldiers defending the base ran critically low on .50-caliber ammunition as some soldiers were repositioned into the Udari Desert in Kuwait. Two soldiers were injured by lightning there in late April, according to U.S. officials with knowledge of the matter.
Contacted by CBS News, U.S. Central Command, the primary unit which oversees American military operations across the Middle East, declined to comment.
The Pentagon did not comment, but pointed back to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's comments on March 4 regarding the removal of U.S. troops from bases and the employment of defensive measures.
"As we built up offensive combat power, we moved the vast majority of American troops — over 90% of Americans that were on our bases — what we say off the X, out of the range of Iranian fire," Hegseth told reporters in March.
Camp Buehring, or CBKU, sits about 25 miles from the Iraqi border and has for more than two decades served as a major staging ground for American forces deploying across the Middle East.
CBS News authenticated the videos using metadata embedded in the files and compared the footage to other photographs showing damage to the base.
Ahead of the war, sources said most of the roughly 7,000 troops there were moved elsewhere — as were the majority of U.S. forces in Kuwait — as a part of the Pentagon's "get off the X" plan, military shorthand for moving away from a position vulnerable to attack.
Once the war started, Iranian attacks, some originating from Iraq, repeatedly threatened the installation. Missiles and drones forced soldiers into bunkers. Three U.S. service members told CBS News that Iranian F-5 fighter jets were also used during the attacks, a detail first reported in April by NBC News.
"They ran so close to us I could see their helmets," the eyewitness described. "They came in, they hit us, and then took off."
While most of the U.S. service members were moved off of Camp Buehring, a tranche of more than 100 soldiers stayed behind. The service members feared the isolated base was ill-equipped to handle a mass-casualty event if the attacks continued.
"They hit us bad," the source told CBS News on condition of anonymity because of the military's strict media restrictions. "It was horrible. There were a lot of brave guys who stayed to fight there — and people at home don't know what happened. We had to abandon the base."
A senior Army official working in logistics, managing operations from another post in Kuwait, confirmed to CBS News there were concerns about the availability of .50 caliber ammunition and other "exquisite" munitions like Patriot missile batteries.
The decision ultimately was to leave. Service members packed up, loading their vehicles with whatever equipment they could and drove at night deep into the Kuwaiti desert. Their remote locations would emerge as forward operating bases, or "FOBs," where the soldiers would remain indefinitely.
No one was killed by enemy fire at Camp Buehring or at the FOBs, but several were injured, including two soldiers who were struck by lightning in desert sandstorms. One soldier suffered burns after the direct strike while the other suffered a ruptured eardrum, according to U.S. officials with knowledge of the matter.
Before the lightning strike, Army leaders had been trying to move the troops out of the area, but were not able to do so quickly enough. In May, the soldiers left the FOBs for Camp Arifjan, and then relocated to other positions both in and out of the Middle East.
"CBKU got demolished," the source added. "They need to do an investigation. How come no one came to reinforce us?"
The Defense Department's inspector general last month released a report on the war with Iran that revealed "equipment losses" worth up to $3.7 billion — including nearly 60 aircraft. On Monday, the Congressional Research Service, which provides nonpartisan analysis to members of Congress, reported that 81 fixed or rotary-wing aircraft including drone assets had been lost or damaged by Iran since February, according to news reports and statements from the Defense Department.
In a first-of-its-kind mandatory report to Congress, the inspector general added that U.S. Central Command had reported Iranian strikes at U.S. bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan.
Although strikes were mentioned in the report, pictures and videos of any impact zones have been extremely limited. Beyond Camp Buehring, CBS News earlier obtained exclusive photos of damage at Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia and Camp Arifjan in Kuwait.
CBS News has also reported extensively on the deadliest attack of the war against U.S. troops at the Port of Shuaiba, which killed six American service members.

Gene therapy can partly restore sight in blind people, researchers reveal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
21:00:01 UTC
06:00:01 KST

A type of gene therapy based on Nobel prize-winning science is safe and can partly restore sight in blind people, researchers have revealed.
The approach, known as optogenetic therapy, harnesses the technique for turning nerve cells on and off using light that scooped the 2026 Nobel prize in physiology or medicine.
It was first shown to partly restore vision in a single blind person in 2021. Now researchers have reported the results from a larger trial involving the original patient and a further nine people.
“What we can say for sure is that the concept of optogenetics is valid for vision restoration,” said Prof Botond Roska, director of the Institute of Molecular and Clinical Ophthalmology Basel and a lead author of the study.
Roska added the aim is now to work towards restoring high-resolution vision, with the hope of achieving the goal in five to 10 years.
All 10 of the trial participants had advanced retinitis pigmentosa – a group of genetic disorders thought to affect more than 1.5 million people worldwide.
In these disorders, light-sensitive cells in the retina gradually lose their function. However, ganglion cells in the retina, which send visual information to the brain, deteriorate less quickly.
“These cells are not the primary cells targeted by the disease, so that’s why they are good candidates for the therapy,” said Dr José-Alain Sahel, another lead author of the study from the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center in the US.
The gene therapy involves giving a single injection into the eye. This injection contains a harmless, synthethic virus that delivers the genetic instructions for producing a light-sensitive protein into a ring of surviving ganglion cells. As a result, these cells are made light-sensitive.
Each patient then receives a pair of light-stimulating goggles. These capture images of the world around the patient and convert them into pulses of light of a single wavelength These pulses activate the ganglion cells that have been made light-sensitive, allowing the wearer to perceive a monochrome image.
Crucially, the technique does not depend on the exact genetic cause of the patient’s sight loss.
Writing in the New England Journal of Medicine, the researchers report how for each patient they treated only the eye with the worst vision, adding participants’ outcomes were then followed for up to five years.
Only one severe eye-related side-effect occurred, but this was resolved within minutes, while there were no side effects related to the therapy in the rest of the body.
However, six of the 10 participants had clinically meaningful improvements in light sensitivity after the treatment.
What’s more, some of the participants showed improvements in a range of tasks when wearing the light-stimulating goggles after the gene therapy – such as detecting, locating and touching a notebook, locating a door and walking on a line.
The team added that participants who spent more time training with the goggles tended to do better on the tasks.
However, the study has limitations.
“[Patients] can detect objects, but they cannot yet detect faces,” said Roska. That, the team say, is down to the treated ganglion cells being in a ring-like arrangement around the fovea – the tiny pit in the retina responsible for sharp central vision.
Mark Hankins, professor of Visual Neuroscience at the University of Oxford, who was not involved in the work, welcomed the study, noting it provides reassurance on the safety of the approach and its application to people who still have some residual vision.
“We’ve gone from one patient to 10 patients, we’ve seen improvement in their light sensitivity … and we’ve seen that we can give a stable restoration of some visual function, some light sensitivity, that lasts for four or five years in these patients,” he said. “They’re baby steps, but they’re critical.”

‘Neither war nor peace’: Palestinians in Gaza on existing amid disease, despair and ruins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
21:00:01 UTC
06:00:01 KST

Ahmed Ishtaiwi has six chairs. They are cheap and plastic and battered, but they are among the 43-year-old driver and mechanic’s most valuable possessions.
Ishtaiwi lives in a tent near Deir al-Balah in central Gaza with his two daughters. Their former home is far to the north, in the now ruined town of Beit Lahiya, uninhabitable and impossible to reach.
“When I sit on those chairs, I remember sitting in the garden at home, having breakfast and drinking tea. They remind me of my life there,” he said last week.
Wednesday is the anniversary of the raid on 7 October 2023 by Hamas militants into southern Israel that killed 1,200 people, mostly civilians, and triggered a relentless Israeli military offensive that killed 73,000 Palestinians, mostly civilians, wounded many more and reduced swathes of Gaza to rubble.
When Layan al-Jbour, a 15-year-old from the southern city of Khan Younis, tries to bring some order to the crowded makeshift shelter she shares with her parents, brothers and sisters in al-Mawasi, a strip of coastline at the southernmost end of Gaza, she recalls life before the war.
“When I tidy the tent, I remember our home and how I used to tidy it. I remember my room and how I used to make my bed. When I put a sheet over a table and arrange the bedding, the place looks like our old home,” al-Jbour said.
“We hardly took anything with us from our home. We left everything behind, and the only thing I took was my schoolbag. It is the most precious thing I own now. It reminds me so much of my school days. I loved going to school and meeting my friends there.”
Across Gaza, Palestinians describe daily routines full of challenges that nothing in their former lives prepared them for: shortages of water and of nourishing food, minimal healthcare, disease, unemployment, economic collapse and the continuing threat of death or injury.
Despite a ceasefire a year ago, Israel’s airstrikes continue. Palestinians who have approached the “yellow line” that divides Gaza into zones controlled by the Israeli military and by Hamas have been shot dead. In the last year, the overall death toll has risen by a further 1,400 people.
In recent days, Israeli attacks have intensified, killing at least two Palestinians in Gaza on Tuesday, according to health officials. The Israeli military said the strikes targeted militants.
On Wednesday, Gaza medics said at least two Palestinians were killed and others wounded in airstrikes in Beit Lahiya and Khan Younis.
“It is what we feared … a ceasefire that just isn’t a ceasefire,” said one international aid worker now based in Amman, Jordan, who worked in Gaza throughout much of the conflict. “Daily life is horrible. People aren’t hungry any more but they are still malnourished. Our local staff are telling us that this is just the next stage of the conflict.”
Ramiz Alakbarov, the UN’s humanitarian coordinator for the Occupied Palestinian Territory, told the UN security council last month that despite the increase in supplies entering Gaza, the health situation remained critical, with “infectious diseases … widespread amid overcrowded displacement sites and inadequate water, sanitation and hygiene conditions”.
Inadequate funding for relief efforts exacerbated the “shortages of medical supplies, fuel and the overall humanitarian response”, Alakbarov said, while “restrictions on the entry of critical humanitarian items imposed by Israel” were slowing preparations for cold weather.
Israeli authorities deny shortages and say adequate supplies are reaching Gaza, with more than 600 trucks entering the territory each day.
Saleh Kilani, 70, from Beit Lahiya, used to have a farm and olive trees before the war. “Around this time of year, I used to press about 60 containers of olive oil. But I lost all of that too. If I go to my home I may die, and if I go to my farm, I may die too. This is not a life. We are exhausted and we have lost hope.”
Kilani said life before the conflict seemed very distant. “We never used to think twice about seeing orange and peach trees, green fields, grapes and figs. These things were simply part of our lives. Now when we see them, we are surprised,” he said.
Hamas, which swiftly reimposed its authority over the 2.3 million Palestinians who live in the third of Gaza not under the control of the Israeli military, has rebuilt a rudimentary administration which provides patchy education, some healthcare services and limited policing based on deterrence through often arbitrary punishment.
Donald Trump’s plan to definitively end the war in Gaza has stalled, with little progress towards disarming Hamas, securing the withdrawal of Israeli troops and beginning the vast job of reconstruction.
“My biggest fear is that this situation will continue. We are living through a period that can be described as neither war nor peace,” said Kilani.
The only time Esraa Abu Taiba recalls her life before the war is when she gets to practise her former profession: beautician.
The 26-year-old lived in Bani Suheila, a town to the east of Khan Younis and now within the zone controlled by Israel. Of her five brothers, two were killed in the conflict, two were wounded, and one is among the more than 1,500 Palestinians from Gaza in detention in Israel.
“Before the war my life was quiet and good,” she said. “I could go wherever I wanted without fear or restrictions. We lived in our own home. We had a washing machine, a tap and a garden. The house belonged to us and we lived there comfortably.
“Now we live in a tent. Our lives depend on carrying water and getting food from the community kitchen. A water truck comes to the end of the street and … I go to collect it because my mother cannot carry it.”
Like most Palestinians in Gaza, her family was displaced multiple times during the conflict, and they have lost everything from their former home – except a house key, which her mother keeps close.
“The only thing I still do from my old life is some beauty work. I cut girls’ hair in the tents around us and do their makeup for weddings,” said Abu Taiba.
“It takes me back to a beautiful and happy period of our lives, when we used to celebrate weddings and other happy occasions before the war. It takes me away from the misery we are living through, even if only for a little while.”
