19,551 breaches, $47 million in financial impact: regulator of banking's code tallies industry problems
The annual report of the Banking Code Compliance Committee (BCCC) has been released.
It notes 19,551 breaches of the Code and $47 million in financial impact on customers.
Breaches of the Code must be reported when they affect more than 20 customers or result in more than $20,000 in financial impact
I've written previously about the BCCC, a well-meaning body that does good work but has few powers and rarely uses them.
The committee was set up in the wake of epic failures with the industry exposed at the Hayne royal commission. It holds members to standards set out in a Banking Code of Practice, a set of guidelines that has no weight in law but is written into the contracts when you buy a product from a bank.
I hope you're sitting down: it's most substantial power is to publish the name of the organisation that it has found in breach of the Code.
And it doesn't even do it that often.
It is funded entirely by the banking industry's key lobby group, the Australian Banking Association, and a few years ago asked for the ability to routinely name banks in breach of the rules, and to force them to publicise it (such as a note on the bank's website).
The ABA said... no thanks.
So it's a body that does solid behind the scenes work but is in no way a watchdog.
Here's what the BCCC's report says about the model of self-regulation that it operates under:
"The Code is a fundamental element of successful self-regulation.
"Self-regulation involves the industry setting its own standards of conduct and enforcing these standards through breach identification, reporting, and remediation.
"This model allows the industry to demonstrate a commitment to ethical and responsible behaviour, helping to build trust with customers.
"It also reduces the need for costly and time-consuming regulatory intervention.
"Our work monitoring the Code is crucial to the success of the self-regulation model working to its full potential."
So either a win for the reduction of red tape, a safeguard for customers, a weak system that shows the strength of the banking lobby in avoiding regulation or a little of all three.
Key Event
HIA attacks ATO proposed ban on tax debts being paid by credit card
The residential construction industry is the latest to attack the Australian Taxation Office (ATO) over an announcement that it will withdraw individuals and businesses being able to pay tax debts by credit card from December 1.
The agency convened a meeting with business groups this week to discuss the changes in the wake of widespread backlash from business groups.
The Housing Industry Association (HIA) says while the ATO's decision does not change the amount of tax owed, it removes one of the tools some businesses use to manage the timing of payments and maintain cash flow.
"HIA is calling on the ATO and the federal government to reverse the decision before it takes effect on 30 November and retain access to credit card payments for taxation liabilities," HIA's chief executive industry and policy Simon Croft said.
"Removing payment flexibility does not reduce a business's tax obligations. It simply makes managing cash flow more difficult at a time when many builders are already facing significant cost pressures."
He said given small and medium-sized builders construct the majority of Australia's new homes, "at a time when governments are looking to increase housing supply, every effort should be made to support the businesses responsible for delivering those homes, not impose further costs and complexities on their business".

ASIC issues stop orders following surveillance of private credit market
The corporate watchdog has put stop orders on three private credit funds over concerns that retail investors may have been misled by some of the information on offer.
The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) has placed interim stop orders that prohibit Australian Secure Capital Fund from offering, issuing, selling or transferring interests in three managed investment schemes — the ASCF Premium Capital Fund, ASCF Select Income Fund and the ASCF High Yield Fund.
ASIC says it made the interim order to protect retail investors from acquiring products under a Product Disclosure Statement (PDS) that "may be defective and not worded and presented in a clear, concise, and effective manner".
The interim stop order arose from ASIC's surveillance of private credit funds.
ASIC said as of June 30, the three funds had $251.8 million in assets under management. Each invest in short-term mortgages secured over Australian property.
"Firms must ensure their disclosures to investors are transparent and support informed decision making, including to help investors understand the strategies and risks of their products," ASIC Commissioner Simone Constant said.
"We will act swiftly to protect investors from potential harm and promote higher standards across the sector."
ASIC said ASCF will have an opportunity to make submissions before a decision is made about any final stop orders.

20:29:48 UTC
05:29:48 KST

In the months leading up to the release of The Social Reckoning—a sequel to David Fincher’s 2010 film The Social Network, which covered the rise of Mark Zuckerberg and Facebook—movie people, at least, spent a fair amount of time grumbling about the fact that the film’s writer-director, Aaron Sorkin, is no David Fincher. That, of course, is demonstrably true. Sorkin wrote the script for The Social Network and won an Oscar for it. Fincher was for a time in talks to direct The Social Reckoning, but ultimately that gig landed with Sorkin, and the grousing began. Sorkin specializes in crackling dialogue and heartfelt, if often self-righteous, liberal views, but the movies he has directed (The Trial of the Chicago 7, Being the Ricardos) haven’t been considered particularly dynamic. His excessive earnestness can be both a plus and a minus: While it’s great that he cares, too much caring can be exhausting.
Which is why it’s something of a surprise that The Social Reckoning moves along as briskly as it does. This is an account of how Wall Street Journal writer Jeff Horwitz (played here by Jeremy Allen White) cracked the story of how, ahead of the 2020 election, Facebook founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg essentially encouraged the amplification of extremist views, a factor that fed directly into the violent January 6 attack on the Capitol. Horwitz can’t write that story alone; he enlists the clandestine help of a loyal Facebook engineer—part of the organization’s civic integrity team—who has become skeptical of certain company policies. Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison) at first offers only minimal information; she loves her job and doesn’t want to lose it. But the deeper she digs into Facebook’s sinister practices of promoting rage bait to increase engagement, the more disenchanted she becomes.
The Social Reckoning is at its core an old-school shoe-leather journalism thriller. Sorkin’s point seems to be that even in the digital age, there aren’t really any new ways to be a thorough, ethical journalist—all the old rules still apply. His script is dense with information, and the story—which opens in 2019 with Horwitz’s joining the paper’s San Francisco bureau and more or less wraps up with the publication of his Pulitzer-winning multi-part 2021 expose the Facebook Files—leapfrogs from one year to another and back again. (The time shifts are helpfully indicated by a sliding timeline appearing at the bottom of the screen.) Sorkin’s approach to telling this story is somewhat professorial—there’s a lot of telling without much showing. But cinematographer Jeff Cronenweth—the frequent Fincher collaborator who also shot The Social Network—gives the picture a handsomely polished look. Somehow, the runtime slips by faster than you might have expected.
Maybe that’s thanks, in part, to Sorkin’s casting choices. Zuckerberg is played by shapeshifter du jour Jeremy Strong, who radiates a kind of robotic clamminess. In many of his scenes, he’s ensconced in a mock Congressional hearing, overseen by a “crisis specialist” (played by a take-no-prisoners Wunmi Mosaku) who has been hired to make him more likable, a Sisyphean task if ever there were one. He sits, straight-backed and tense, in a dark suit, working terrifically hard at the task of appearing human. At one point in the film, when he’s grilled about his company’s role in promoting the views of hate groups, he snaps, “We’re a corkboard. We don’t control what people pin to it.” Strong is attracted to playing unlikable people, and he’s good at it, though often—as with his portrayal of fixer extraordinaire Roy Cohn in The Apprentice—he offers a dash of tempered sympathy to remind us that these people are actually human. Not so with Zuckerberg: he focuses almost solely on the tech oligarch’s calculating, evasive nature. It’s the right choice.
As Horwitz, White serves up a classic, muted portrayal of a guy so dedicated to his job that he’s seriously fun-deprived. Oddly enough, it takes a smart, ultra-serious tech engineer to loosen him up, and his scenes with Madison, in which their characters banter and spar, are the movie’s best. At one point he refers to Frances as a Cassandra, citing the story of the cursed Trojan princess who has the gift of predicting the future, though no one believes her. Only he’s mangled and misapplied the myth; Frances sets him straight, and fills him in on the correct metaphorical meaning of Chicken Little and the Boy Who Cried Wolf as well. It’s Madison who anchors the movie. Frances wears studious-schoolgirl glasses, and she suffers from neuropathy: In chilly San Francisco, she needs to bundle up in chunky leg warmers and wristlets to keep numbness at bay—this garb gives her a waifish air. At one point she describes herself as “the girl in class with her hand raised that nobody wants the teacher to call on.” That’s a mouthful of classic Sorkinese if ever there were one, but as she spins the words out, Madison is so plaintive that she makes you see that girl. Frances Haugen is the conscience and the true hero of The Social Reckoning, and Sorkin knows it. He practically hands the movie over to Madison, and even in a movie filled with talking—and often with guys talking—it’s her stalwart yet unassuming presence that makes it sing.

Venezuela's Maduro to face new US charges over alleged torture of Americans, official says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
20:29:18 UTC
05:29:18 KST

Venezuela’s Maduro to face new US charges over alleged torture of Americans, official says
WASHINGTON - Ousted Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores are expected to face new criminal charges in the United States over allegations that Americans detained in Venezuela were tortured, a US official said on Oct 7.
The new charges could come as soon as Oct 8, according to the official, who was briefed on the investigation.
Maduro, who led Venezuela for 13 years, and Flores were captured by the US military from their home in Caracas on Jan 3 and brought to New York to face drug trafficking charges. They have pleaded not guilty and are scheduled to go on trial starting June 1, 2027.
A spokesperson for the Manhattan US Attorney’s office, which brought the charges, declined to comment.
Lawyers for Maduro and Flores did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The possibility of new charges was first reported by CNN on Oct 7.
Details of the new charges, including the identities of the alleged torture victims, were not immediately available.
Maduro’s tenure was marked by tensions with the United States. Washington accused his government of detaining Americans as leverage to extract concessions such as relief from financial sanctions.
Americans whom the US classified as wrongfully detained during Maduro’s tenure included five oil executives arrested on graft charges. They were freed in 2022 in exchange for two of Flores’ nephews, who had been convicted in the US of drug trafficking.
Others detained included two former US Army Special Forces members who were arrested in Venezuela in 2020 in connection with a botched raid aimed at ousting Maduro. They were freed in 2023 as part of another prisoner swop.
Since Maduro’s capture, Venezuela has been led by his former vice-president, Delcy Rodriguez, who has increased cooperation with the Trump administration.
Maduro, 63, and Flores, 69, have been held in a federal jail in Brooklyn.
Flores is due to appear in Manhattan federal court on Oct 8 to urge US District Judge Alvin Hellerstein to release her from jail before trial for health reasons. Prosecutors oppose her release. REUTERS

What three years of the Gaza war reveal about Israel and the world

What three years of the Gaza war reveal about Israel and the world
On October 7, 2023, Hamas and other Palestinian resistance organizations launched an attack out of the Gaza Strip and into Israel under the code name “Al-Aqsa Flood.” Israeli and Western mainstream media and politicians rapidly labelled this a massive act of terrorism and flooded the world with tales of horrific atrocities allegedly perpetrated by the Palestinians, such as sadistically murdering children and women and committing mass rape.
We now know that these atrocious tales were lies calculated to generate domestic and international outrage against the Palestinian resistance and Palestinians in general. They were part of the same poisonous Israeli narrative that labeled these people “Amalek” – a reference to a perversely “exemplary” genocide in the Old Testament – and denied that they were human beings. They were taking steps, in other words, to start a genocide.
These atrocious propaganda lies were made up and spread by, for instance, Israel’s Zaka activists and Western mainstream journalists, such as the New York Times, high public officials such as the UN’s Pramila Patten, and activists. For instance, former Meta executive Sheryl Sandberg acted as a Zionist propagandist, who chose to rely on Israeli disinformation.
In reality, there were no mass rapes, there were no sadistic baby murders by beheadings or in microwave ovens, no pregnant woman was found killed with a headshot, with her baby stabbed and still attached to the umbilical cord. It “simply didn’t happen,” as a detailed investigation by Israeli newspaper Haaretz found.
What did happen on October 7, 2026 was not a savage, sadistic rampage but a daring military resistance operation. It was also a mass break-out from the Gaza Strip, which was under a long Israeli siege so brutal that Israeli sociologist Baruch Kimmerling had already called the Strip the “world’s largest concentration camp ever” almost a quarter-century ago.
The core of this offensive targeted Israel’s Gaza Division, which, according to high-ranking Israeli officers was “overpowered.” In the process, Palestinian resistance fighters killed and captured Israeli military personnel. While Israel’s propaganda has done its best to obfuscate this fact, these actions were neither “terrorism” nor hostage-taking but legitimate acts of armed resistance under international law.
The Palestinian fighters also attacked a music festival as well as several settlements. There, according to an Amnesty International summary in early 2024, they did commit crimes, including the deliberate killing of civilians and the taking of hostages, that is, civilians, not soldiers, whose capture makes them POWs and not hostages. A crime, in any case, is a crime even if it’s only realistic to recognize plenty of mitigating circumstances in the immense injustice, dispossession, and often sadistic and humiliating violence Palestinians have suffered from Israelis over decades.
Honesty also dictates that we take three key facts into account: First, the leader of the pro-Israeli UAE, has revealed that he warned Israel’s leader Benjamin Netanyahu personally of Hamas’s plans. In a similar vein, Qatar’s leader claims that Hamas was ready to free all civilian hostages immediately after the attack (which would have left it with only military prisoners). Yet the Israeli leadership ignored the warning and rejected the offer to free all civilians.
It’s almost as if it wanted the attack to happen, as a pretext to initiate a massive ethnic cleansing-by-genocide campaign, and for the civilian hostages to stay in Gaza, as a pretext for continuing that campaign.
Second, it has long been clear that Israeli authorities activated an expanded “Hannibal Directive”: Usually prepared to kill their own soldiers rather than let them be captured, on October 7, Israeli forces also killed Israeli civilians and, most likely, in large if unknown numbers, deploying tanks as well as helicopter gunships to – in the words of an Israeli officer – “mass Hannibal” their own. Of the roughly 1,200 casualties on 7 October, hundreds are likely to have been due to Israeli-on-Israeli violence; others were soldiers and as such legitimate targets.
And finally, a simple point all too often drowned out by Israeli and pro-Israeli propaganda: A legitimate military force does not lose its overall legitimacy – or that of its goals – even when some of its members commit crimes. If that were the case, most armies in this world would have to be dissolved because none of them have a history entirely free of crimes. Armed Palestinian resistance is fundamentally legitimate under international law – and morally, too, obviously – and remains so. In fact, in the future, the outnumbered, outgunned, and abandoned Palestinian defenders of Gaza will be remembered as heroes, as they should.
Things are different, as a matter of fact, if we look at the actions of the Israeli military since October 7. Unlike with anything that individual Palestinian resistance fighters may have done, in the case of Israel’s euphemistically mis-labeled Defense Forces – a “citizen army [and] representative sample” of Israeli society – we are looking at a clear case of a whole, large organization deliberately and enthusiastically dedicated to committing every war crime and crime against humanity in every book, including ethnic cleansing and genocide.
Because that is a precise description of what Israel has been doing to the Palestinians of Gaza – and not only – since October 7, 2023. It is also by now the consensus among honest observers, including the global community of genocide experts. This, indeed, has been the most public genocide in human history, despite Israeli attempts to seal Gaza off and mass murder its journalists under false pretexts.
Israeli perpetrators – high and low – have proudly advertised their own crimes. Israeli society as a whole, virtually continuous polling has shown consistently, supports the genocide. In a world of real-time media and social media, the reality of Gaza could not be hidden. Only recently, Google has finally adjusted its maps to reflect it.
The nature and extent of Israel’s crimes is obvious and exceedingly well documented, and that is a very important thing. Humanity owes an enormous debt of gratitude to those Palestinians and others who have undertaken the harrowing task of compiling and analyzing the evidence, such as, to name only a few, UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese or the tireless staff of the Electronic Intifada.
What needs at least as much attention is what the Gaza genocide says about our world as a whole: namely that genocide is not only possible – it was before – but can take place over years and in full view of the global public, with the active support of most of the establishments of virtually the entire West and the passive acquiescence of the elites of most other countries.
In a more or less sane world, fulfilling its obligations under the short and clear UN Genocide Convention of 1948 – it bears recalling – the Israeli genocide perpetrators would long have been stopped by a combination of diplomatic, economic, and, of course, military intervention. That would have been the minimum of what both international law and basic ethics obviously demand.
Yet, instead, we live in a world, where – apart from the Palestinian resistance itself – only a handful of states and political organizations have done anything at all to interfere with Israel’s mass murder campaign: Iran, Hezbollah in Lebanon, and Ansarallah – the Houthis – in Yemen.
Think about the above what you want, like or dislike their politics, it is a fact that no one else has even remotely tried to apply the Genocide Convention in practice. If that is irritating, don’t blame Ansarallah, for instance, but blame the many who have failed to act.
But failure to act has been only part of this real-life horror story. In the West, many governments and mainstream establishments, including in the media and academia, have pro-actively supported Israel. This is a shameful history of criminal collaboration and complicity still to be written. Indeed, in the worst cases, such as the elites of the US, the UK, and Germany, complicity seems too weak an expression: they are better described as genocide co-perpetrators.
The obvious inference from this state of the world is that international law does not matter. There is no more devastating attack on the very idea of international law and a law-based order than the impunity of Israel and its accomplices. Benjamin Netanyahu, with an International Criminal Court warrant to his name, has been able to brazenly deny his and his country’s crimes at the recent UN General Assembly and even repeat the Amalek reference, as Craig Mokhiber has pointed out. Outside, meanwhile, his critics were being arrested.
Annalena Baerbock, in her time as one of Germany’s most embarrassing foreign ministers ever, also justified, shielded, and supported Israel; she has just finished her ill-begotten sinecure as the UN General Assembly’s president and made a lateral move to an absurdly undeserved position at Columbia University. The examples could be multiplied endlessly: the elites of the West, including American presidents Joe Biden and Donald Trump, have devastatingly compromised themselves by their complicity with Israel. And yet, they keep thriving.
So, not only has international law been discredited as literally never before, but international establishments also have, and in particular those of that part of the world that still has the arrogance to claim global leadership as if it were some kind of birthright, the West.
Now add the fact that Israel has not “only” been committing the Gaza genocide. It has also escalated ethnic cleansing terror in the West Bank, invaded Syria and Lebanon, attacked Yemen, participated in and triggered brutal assaults against Iran that have also tanked the world energy economy, and, in general, has followed its usual modus operandi of assassination, subversion, torture, rape, and relentless aggression. And yet it faces no discernible consequences beyond ludicrously inappropriate, purely symbolical measures at best and, of course, massive continued support.
Meanwhile, those in the West who dare be human and show their solidarity with the Palestinians and other victims of Israel and its accomplices and co-perpetrators are harassed, beaten up by police, arrested, and blacklisted.
What the Gaza genocide has shown with respect to the world as a whole is simple: Those who rule us will go much farther, much more shamelessly and openly than most of us, even the pessimists, used to be able to imagine. More importantly, they will get away with it, and they will let each other get away with it. Gaza is not an exception. It is a harbinger of a world of horrors. Resistance is not an option; it is the only one.

US Republicans, independents express low trust in election integrity: Poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
20:27:47 UTC
05:27:47 KST

US Republicans, independents express low trust in election integrity: Poll
A Gallup survey highlights a deep – and historic – partisan divide over confidence in the country’s elections.
With less than a month to go before the United States’ pivotal midterms, a new survey found that most independent voters and supporters of President Donald Trump’s Republican Party do not believe the elections will be honest.
Polling from the research firm Gallup, released on Wednesday, found that 37 percent of Republicans and 35 percent of independents have confidence in the country’s electoral system, significantly lower than the rate for Democrats, at 63 percent.
The numbers highlight a deep, historic partisan divide over confidence in US elections.
The survey also suggests a counterintuitive relationship wherein the US voters who approve of Trump’s leadership also distrust the electoral system.
“Since 2025 and Trump’s return to the White House, the relationship between leadership approval and confidence in elections has disappeared,” Gallup wrote in a statement highlighting the results.
The firm added that the US is the only country out of more than 100 polled annually over the past 15 years to show this pattern: Trust in US election integrity is markedly higher among those who disapprove of the country’s leadership under Trump than those who approve.
That marks a shift in voter sentiment. In 2025, at the start of Trump’s second term, confidence in US elections “was nominally higher among approvers (51 percent) than disapprovers (45 percent)”, according to Gallup.
Now, 52 percent of those who disapprove of Trump’s leadership express confidence in US elections, compared with 41 percent of those who approve.
Overall, 49 percent of Americans said they were confident in the honesty of elections, while 51 percent said they were not. Those figures are unchanged from the country’s last midterm election in 2022.
Michael McNulty, the senior policy director at Issue One, a nonprofit that tracks the role of money in politics, has worked on more than 30 elections across the world.
He said the numbers, especially among Republicans, do not point towards problems in the US election system itself.
Rather, he blames Trump for sowing distrust in the election system among his base, particularly ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.
“The fact that Republicans trust elections less really is exactly the result of that false fraud narrative perpetrated over many years,” McNulty said. “I think Americans can trust the people who run their elections.”
Still, the US perspective towards election integrity appears to be a global outlier.
In more than 100 countries where Gallup tracks views of national leadership and confidence in elections, people who approve of their governments have generally been more likely to trust their country’s elections.
In 2025, a median of 70 percent of people across those countries who approved of their national leadership expressed confidence in the honesty of their elections, compared with 30 percent among those who disapproved.
“The current US pattern is highly unusual compared with the rest of the world,” Gallup wrote.
Under former US President Joe Biden, 81 percent of Americans who approved of the government also expressed confidence in elections, compared with just 30 percent of those who disapproved.
Gallup said this year’s unusual divide could have implications for the November elections, raising questions about whether some voters will view the results as legitimate.
Over the course of his second term in office, Trump and members of his administration have taken steps to upend the US voting system, including by launching investigations into the 2020 election, issuing executive orders to change voting procedures and demanding voter data from states.
Speaking to reporters outside the White House on Monday, Trump once again claimed that mail-in voting was prone to fraud, without providing evidence.
“No, vote by mail … I’d rather have a vote in person. But they can vote by mail if they want, because we seem to have no choice,” Trump said.
“What we’re concerned about is … there is a lot of cheating in vote by mail,” he added.
McNulty said Trump’s remarks are part of what he describes as an “election takeover playbook” aimed squarely at the president’s supporters.
“You use these false fraud narratives. You sow chaos. You undermine confidence, particularly among his own base and his own voters, because they’re the ones listening to him,” McNulty explained.
“And then you use that narrative to justify efforts” against the US electoral system, he added.
McNulty said voting organisations like his are preparing for the “very real threat” that Trump or Republican-aligned groups could challenge the midterm results.
But he is “confident” the US electoral system will stand up to any possible attempts to undermine it.
In response to a request for comment from Al Jazeera, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis instead blamed any decline in election-season trust on the Democratic Party’s refusal to implement Trump’s changes.
“Every American should be asking why the radical Left continues to fight against commonsense election integrity measures, like Voter ID and citizenship verification,” Bis wrote.
“President Trump has made clear: Anyone who illegally votes in our elections will be held accountable.”
State and federal law already prohibits non-citizen voting in federal elections. Critics, however, have accused Trump of seeking to implement further restrictions that would discourage or prevent citizens from exercising their legal right to vote.

Historical records cast doubt on Zack Polanski’s family Nazi escape story
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
20:27:40 UTC
05:27:40 KST

Zack Polanski, leader of Britain’s Green Party, is at the center of a public controversy after historical records contradicted his account of his ancestors fleeing the Nazis. The party has made headlines in recent days after passing a motion declaring Zionism to be racism and following revelations that one of its members is a close friend of an al-Qaeda terrorist.
In his keynote speech at the party conference in Bournemouth last year, Polanski, 43, said his Jewish ancestors fled pogroms in Latvia and Ukraine, made their way to Nazi-occupied Poland and ultimately escaped to England, where they encountered antisemitism. However, a review of public birth, marriage and census records from 1891 and 1901 found that his family had settled in Britain in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
Despite the records, Polanski repeated the story of his family fleeing the Nazis on several occasions, including on “The Rest Is Politics” podcast and the BBC’s “Question Time” in December. The Daily Mail reported that the mystery deepened last month when Polanski himself acknowledged, during a podcast interview with Iain Dale, that his great-grandparents had arrived in Britain “way before the Second World War.”
In the same interview, he said they changed their surname from Polanski to Paulden to escape antisemitism in Britain, not the Nazis. Polanski, who was born David Paulden in 1982, changed his name to Zack Polanski to reconnect with his Jewish heritage and distance himself from his stepfather.
The Green Party declined to explain the discrepancy to the Daily Mail. A party spokesperson said that “Jewish family history is often confusing and muddled, as Zack has acknowledged” adding that “it’s astonishing that the only current Jewish leader of a British political party is having his family history raked over by the press in an attempt to discredit him.”
The controversy comes as the Green Party opens its 2026 conference in Brighton and less than a week before Polanski is due to contest a parliamentary election in Holborn and St Pancras in north London, a seat held by Labour since 1983 and previously represented by Keir Starmer, who stepped down as prime minister.
This is not the first time Polanski, who serves as a member of the London Assembly and earns nearly £66,500 ($88,000) a year, has faced scrutiny over contradictory statements. Earlier this year, he apologized for an “unintentional mistake” after failing to pay council tax on a residential property because of “financial hardship.”
In May, he admitted that he had not voted in local elections because he was not registered to vote, despite publicly promising his party’s candidate that he would vote for him. His spokesperson had claimed he had done so by postal ballot. The party attributed the incidents to a “misunderstanding.”
Anti-Zionism and ties to terrorists
The Green Party on Sunday approved a controversial motion declaring Zionism a form of racism. The wording of the motion implies a call for the effective elimination of the State of Israel. In response, Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar decided to bar Polanski from entering Israel.
The approved motion calls for the establishment of “a single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine with Jerusalem as its capital.” It also calls for a sweeping boycott of Israel and broad sanctions similar to those imposed on South Africa’s apartheid regime, arguing that “Zionism has created, and seeks to maintain and, where possible, expand, a system of apartheid between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea.”
On Tuesday, Britain’s Telegraph reported that party member Lubna Speitan, who spearheaded the motion, is a close friend of an al-Qaeda terrorist who plotted a suicide attack at Heathrow Airport that was intended to kill hundreds of people, with a particular focus on passengers arriving from Israel or the United States.
According to the report, Speitan had previously offered to testify in defense of the terrorist, Minh Quang Pham, who was convicted in the United States of membership in al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula, or AQAP, and of plotting the attack. Court documents from 2015 described her as a “close friend” of his.
Speitan has previously said Hamas should not be designated a terrorist organization. She has also called for Zionism to be “dismantled from the world” and said the time would come when Zionists would be “hunted down as the Nazi oppressors were hunted down.”
When initially asked about her relationship with the terrorist, Speitan called the question “insulting” and said it had “no relation to the work that I’m doing.” She accused the “mainstream media” of seeking to “demonise” Palestinians and suggested that Pham had been wrongfully accused.
Asked about his 44-year prison sentence, she said: “People are demonised for all sorts of things and wrongfully accused of all sorts of things.”

He was arrested on Tuesday in a public park after he paid $600 to an undercover FBI employee posing as a member of the Islamic State for an AK-47 and 200 rounds of ammunition, according to the criminal complaint.
His messages with a confidential informant revealed Mohamud expressed intent to join terrorist organizations overseas but those plans soon became a planned attack in Minnesota when those plans failed. The messages date back as far as December 2024.
Mohamud was seen on the mall’s security cameras walking around “nonchalantly” and eventually robbing a Lids store at gunpoint before being apprehended, according to Minnesota police.
“I wanna get martyred inshallah,” he said in the messages with the informant.
“That’s why I wanna save up to go to another country or…get a gun here and just start killing a bunch of white ppl.”
Daniel Rosen, a US attorney, said Mohamud “needed to be watched”.
It’s unclear what initially promoted the FBI’s investigation. According to Rosen, agents “were able to detect a threat, and disrupt it, before the defendant carried out his intention to kill, in his words, maybe 30 to 60 people, as we allege in far greater detail in the complaint”.
The potential shooting at the mall comes after two recent shootings by Somali teens as victims and suspects, including a gang-related shooting in Bloomington where more than 100 rounds of ammunition were fired.
As terrorism and violence are an increasing concern in Minnesota, some in law enforcement are calling for a regional taskforce to address more harm in the state.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

Life in Gaza, three years after October 7: Hamas keep a low profile, but armed men still roam the streets at night
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
20:25:59 UTC
05:25:59 KST

- i24NEWS
- Middle East
- West Bank & Gaza Strip
- Life in Gaza, three years after October 7
Life in Gaza, three years after October 7
Hamas operatives largely keep a low profile, but armed men still appear in the streets at night
In the three years since the October 7 massacre, the state of Israel and the region as a whole have changed beyond recognition. The same applies to the Gaza Strip. According to the most recent available satellite imagery, roughly 80% of all buildings in Gaza have been damaged or destroyed during the war.
Israeli forces currently control 63% of Gaza's territory. In the remaining 37%, some two million Gazans live in the densely populated city centers and tent cities across the Strip. And life there is uncertain, with many fearing a resumption of the fighting as Hamas refuses to concede power and disarm.
The prevailing mood is one of frustration and despair. For three years, residents have waited for the war to end and for the technocratic committee meant to run Gaza to begin operating there. That moment still seems distant. "Three years have passed with people hoping that the war would end, but it hasn't, and we are still stuck," one woman in Gaza told i24NEWS. "As you know, people have been living in tents for three years, and this is extremely difficult."
Tension rose in the days leading up to the anniversary, as many families stockpiled food in case of an emergency. The fear that a major military operation could see the IDF take over what remains of the Strip has not gone away. "We don't feel stable, and honestly, we don't feel that there is any real hope for peace," she said.
Hamas operatives largely keep a low profile, but armed men still appear in the streets at night. Residents often cannot tell whether these men belong to Hamas or to one of the armed groups operating from behind the Yellow Line. "To be honest with you, we don't know who they are," she said.
Residents also say Hamas finances itself in part by imposing various taxes on residents and merchants, which some describe as extortion. "Here, we know very well that Hamas must hand over all its weapons," the Gazan said. "The people of Gaza want to get rid of Hamas and its rule, so that this situation we are living through and suffering from can finally come to an end."
Food and basic goods are available, the woman said. "There is no famine at all. Food and other goods are available, but not everyone has the means to buy them. The poor and those who don't have jobs depend on free aid and on groups that cook free food in the streets and distribute it to them."
Work in Gaza is scarce. Many of the available jobs in the various NGOs operating in the Strip are subject to Hamas's approval, as it decides who can get hired. If you're not affiliated with Hamas, chances are you won't find work.
Despite criticism in Western and Arab capitals, where Israeli plans to encourage emigration from Gaza have been branded "ethnic cleansing," the woman who spoke with i24NEWS said she hopes to leave at the first opportunity. "I intend not to return," she said.

Ukrainian strikes blast Russian frigates at Novorossiysk
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
21:19:50 BST
05:19:50 KST

A single Ukrainian drone attack on Novorossiysk has significantly degraded the land-attack cruise missile capability of Russia’s Black Sea Fleet, accounting for forty per cent of its Kalibr-capable surface ships, according to a Defence Intelligence update published by the UK Ministry of Defence.
In its update on Thursday, Defence Intelligence said: “Ukraine has launched two large scale uncrewed aerial system (UAS) attacks against the Russian Novorossiysk Naval Facility and Commercial Port within the last two months. The 08-09 September 2026 attack led to successful strikes against a GRIGOROVICH class frigate and a SVIYAZHSK light-frigate.”
It went on: “Both vessels have likely sustained sufficient damage to prevent them taking part in KALIBR Land-attack Cruise Missile (LACM) firings into Ukraine, likely for the short-medium term. This single attack has significantly degraded the LACM strike capabilities of the Black Sea Fleet, representing 40% of the KALIBR-capable surface fleet.”
Two ships out of action amounting to two fifths of the capability says as much about the size of the remaining fleet as it does about the damage. Russia has been firing Kalibr missiles at Ukrainian cities and infrastructure from Black Sea platforms since the opening days of the full-scale invasion, and the surface ships able to carry them have never been numerous.
The Admiral Grigorovich class are Project 11356R frigates, the newest conventional surface combatants the Black Sea Fleet has, each able to carry Kalibr in a vertical launch system. Defence Intelligence describes the second vessel as a Sviyazhsk light-frigate, a smaller Kalibr-armed surface combatant.
Ukrainian strikes drove Russian warships out of Sevastopol over the course of 2023 and 2024, and the Krasnodar Krai port became the main operating base for what remained. Pushing the fleet east was supposed to put it beyond easy reach.
Defence Intelligence uses a probability yardstick in which “likely” sits between 55 and 75 per cent, so the assessment that both ships cannot take part in Kalibr firings is a confident judgement without being a certainty. The phrase short to medium term carries no fixed definition, though repairs to a vertical launch system and the surrounding structure on a frigate are not quick work, particularly in a yard under periodic attack.
UK Defence Intelligence publishes its guidance on the use of probabilistic language at this link.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher

The public sector powerhouse, NTPC, has earmarked three strategic locations across India for the establishment of nuclear power plants.
NEW DELHI: Public sector NTPC has identified three locations, one each in Madhya Pradesh, Bihar and Odisha, to set up nuclear power plants as it aims to add 30GW of nuclear capacity across 14 states by 2047.The company has submitted detailed feasibility reports for each site to the Atomic Energy Commission for approval. NTPC is also exploring technology collaborations with global players such as Holtec International and Westinghouse of the US, Rosatom of Russia and EDF of France for pressurised water reactor projects to be deployed at these locations, said an official aware of the development.With an installed power generation capacity of 89GW, including thermal, hydro and renewable capacity, the company is targeting 149GW by 2032 and 244GW by 2037, besides adding significant battery and pumped storage capacity. It has set up NTPC Parmanu Urja Nigam Ltd as its wholly owned nuclear subsidiary to foray into nuclear power. Its first nuclear project in Rajasthan’s Mahi Banswara, comprising four 700-MW units, however, is being developed through Anushakti Vidhyut Nigam Ltd, a joint venture with Nuclear Power Corporation of India.
The three identified locations, if approved, will have 2-4GW of nuclear capacity each, the official said.
NTPC entered into non-disclosure agreements with Rosatom and EDF earlier this year to explore technology collaboration for deploying large pressurised water reactor projects in India.“Technology transfer and localisation will be key factors in finalising the technology. There will be a separate joint venture with a global player for technology and design engineering,” said the official.Fuel availability will also be an important consideration in finalising the technology, the official said, adding that fuel sourcing falls within the domain of the Centre.

Atul is known for investigative depth and strong human-interest narratives as he strives to bring clarity and context to complex issues. BARCELONA, Spain, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- Artificial intelligence (AI), automation and ingredient innovation are among the technological advancements on show at Alimentaria FoodTech, one of Europe's leading food industry trade fairs, being held in Spain from Oct. 6 to 8.
The fair has attracted more than 330 companies from 22 countries and regions in the Spanish city of Barcelona to share the latest breakthroughs in equipment and technologies for food and beverage production, processing and preservation.
One of the central goals is to address major challenges currently facing the food industry, including enhancing production efficiency, advancing automation and digitalization, and improving sustainability.

The FoodTech Innovarena space features 60 presentations, panel discussions, and events involving more than 140 domestic and international experts from companies, technology centers and universities, who are analyzing the trends shaping the food industry in the coming years.
The event's organisers said that the emerging technologies having the greatest impact on the sector include the application of AI to the evolution of the foodtech ecosystem, advances in food safety, new packaging materials, as well as healthier and more sustainable alternative ingredients. ■

Interview: GDI advances global development, South-South cooperation, says Pakistani envoy
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:52:49 CST
11:52:49 KST

by Wang Lu, Ma Ruxuan
GENEVA, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- The Global Development Initiative (GDI) has played a key role over the past five years in revitalizing the global development agenda and promoting South-South cooperation, a Pakistani envoy has said.
The initiative was proposed at an important time, bringing development back to the mainstream global agenda, which is an important contribution, Tahir Andrabi, Pakistan's Permanent Representative to the United Nations Office at Geneva, said in an interview with Xinhua.
Over the past five years, the GDI has implemented more than 1,800 "small and beautiful" projects in more than 120 countries, mobilizing over 23 billion U.S. dollars, he said.
Andrabi stressed that the GDI complements the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) while responding to the reality that the world still needs greater focus on development.
The latest UN data show that only 36 percent of the Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) targets with available trend data are on track or making moderate progress, and 15 percent have even regressed below their 2015 baselines.
"The world, particularly developing countries, is falling behind in meeting the needs of its people and the SDG targets. The GDI is an important initiative to fill these gaps," he said.
On China-Pakistan cooperation, Andrabi perceived the GDI as an important platform for charting the future trajectory of development and economic cooperation between the two countries.
"We believe that the GDI, together with the BRI and its flagship project CPEC (the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor) 2.0, will continue to further diversify avenues of development cooperation between Pakistan and China in the context of CPEC, and between China and the larger developing world in the context of the BRI," he said.
Andrabi expressed hope for deepening cooperation in high-tech fields such as AI, quantum computing and robotics, citing the immense opportunities in these areas.
"The GDI provides an opportunity to make these technologies available to developing countries, thereby harnessing the potential of these technologies to deliver direct benefits and generate employment," he said.
Andrabi also mentioned the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO) established in Shanghai this year with Pakistan among its founding members.
"We hope that WAICO, together with the GDI and the efforts of the Chinese government, will promote complementarities and work together to bring modern technology benefits to developing countries," he said. ■

Japan logs 4.06 trln yen current account surplus in August
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:52:27 CST
11:52:27 KST

TOKYO, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- Japan posted a current account surplus of 4.06 trillion yen (about 25.7 billion U.S. dollars) in August, up 12.0 percent from a year earlier, government data showed Thursday.
In August, the goods trade balance swung to a deficit of 687.7 billion yen, due to higher imports of crude oil and other commodities, compared with a surplus of 113.8 billion yen a year earlier, the Finance Ministry said in a preliminary report.
Exports rose 16.9 percent to 9.86 trillion yen and imports increased 26.7 percent to 10.55 trillion yen.
Meanwhile, primary income, which reflects how much Japan earned from overseas investments, expanded 21.6 percent from the previous year to 5.13 trillion yen, the ministry said.
The current account balance is one of the widest gauges of international trade. ■

US imposes fresh sanctions on Iran's shadow fleet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
20:06:26 UTC
05:06:26 KST

Breadcrumb
US imposes fresh sanctions on Iran's shadow fleet
The US imposed fresh sanctions on Iran on Thursday, targeting individuals, networks and 17 vessels for transporting Iranian crude, oil products and petrochemicals, the Treasury Department said, as Washington stepped up economic pressure on Tehran.
The sanctions are part of the department's "Operation Economic Outcast," which aims to cut Iran's funding for the war with the US, missile construction, cyberattacks and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, or IRGC.
"Today's action represents the most significant blow yet to Iran's remaining illicit maritime infrastructure by neutralizing the vast majority of the shadow fleet," a Treasury official told reporters on a call. "Treasury is cutting off the regime's last major source of illicit revenue and strengthening international pressure to hold Tehran accountable."
The move tightens the squeeze on Iranian oil sales after the US reimposed its blockade of Iranian ports on 14 July following the breakdown of a memorandum of understanding between Tehran and Washington to end the war.
Iran has only about 20 million barrels of crude oil left on vessels outside the blockade, off Singapore, Malaysia and China, the Treasury official said. The world uses about 100 million barrels of oil per day.
A second Treasury official said Iran has stopped loading and offloading crude oil vessels due to the blockade and sanctions.
President Donald Trump said on social media on Thursday that the US is having "productive discussions" with Iran over the war that began on February 28. Trump said the US will not attack Iran before the midterm elections on November 3.
An analyst said the fact that the US is sanctioning vessels after Iran has delivered virtually all of its oil at sea means the impact will be muted.
"This is economic warfare conducted in the rearview mirror, designed to generate headlines rather than results," said Brett Erickson, a managing principal at Obsidian Risk Advisors.
Vessels targeted by the US sanctions include the Comoros-flagged Paritosh, the Panama-flagged Bitu and the Bahamas-flagged Gas Lucky.
(Reuters)

US suspends Microsoft, Adobe from filing for green cards
October 8, 2026
The Trump administration on Thursday said it was suspending major tech firms, including Microsoft, from applying for a program that allowed their foreign workers to work permanently in the US.
US Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling accused those tech firms of abusing the program — the Permanent Labor Certification Program (PERM) — that had so far been a legal pathway for workers to apply for green cards.
"I am hereby suspending from the Permanent Labor Certification Program some of the largest IT outsourcing firms in the world, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini," US Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said.
Sonderling said the suspensions were due to ongoing federal investigations into those firms.
There are good reasons that Indian media firms covered the issue so urgently because many of those firms are either Indian or rely on thousands of Indian professionals who've moved to the country.
Trump administration accuses Microsoft of abusing program for green cards
Vice President JD Vance said the PERM system required companies to advertise work in the US before they applied for green cards for foreign workers due to a lack of qualified American job applicants.
"They'll put an advertisement in a small-town newspaper. They'll go out there and say that 'We have advertised for a position with our company, and nobody is responding to it.' And they will use that lack of response to then go and replace American workers with what is effectively foreign indentured servants," Vance claimed.
"There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has used this system more than Microsoft," Vance said.
The announcement came hours before US President Donald Trump was scheduled to award the National Medal of Technology and Innovation to Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella.
Microsoft says majority of its workers are Americans
Microsoft said in a statement that it looked forward to providing the administration with additional information, saying the majority of its workers are Americans and that a large part of the H-1B filings have to do with the status of people already based in the US.
"We pay our employees some of the highest compensation in the tech sector, and our wages are among the highest of all H-1B filings," the company said.
The H-1B visa program is another part of the Trump administration's crackdown on immigration, as concerns have long persisted that the visa for skilled workers has displaced Americans in favor of lower-cost foreign labor.
Microsoft employs 125,000 US workers and 103,000 international workers, according to the company's 2025 annual report.

Autism and ADHD traits appear to follow different social paths to mental health problems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
20:00:09 UTC
05:00:09 KST

Children who show traits of autism and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder often face elevated risks of emotional and behavioral problems as they grow up, but the social pathways connecting these traits to mental health are complex. A long-term study published in Psychological Medicine suggests that difficulties with classmates, schoolwork, and family members do not simply follow neurodevelopmental traits in a straight line. Instead, day-to-day social struggles and mental health challenges appear to be linked in both directions over time, which may create self-reinforcing cycles as students develop.
Autism spectrum disorder, commonly known as ASD, involves differences in social communication, social interaction, and patterns of behavior or interests. Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, or ADHD, is characterized by ongoing patterns of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity. Both conditions exist on a continuum, meaning that many children display noticeable traits without having an official clinical diagnosis. Even when these traits fall below diagnostic thresholds, children are at elevated risk of emotional distress, including internalizing problems like anxiety and depression, or externalizing problems like anger and disruptive behavior.
Earlier research suggested that everyday hardships may help explain these links. For instance, a 2018 longitudinal study tracking youth from childhood to age 18 found that elevated autistic traits increased the risk of developing depressive symptoms, an association partly explained by social hardships such as bullying. In a similar vein, a 2020 study of adolescents indicated that childhood ADHD symptoms predicted teenage depression in part through academic setbacks and peer problems.
Strained relationships with parents and peers also helped account for the link between attention difficulties and later depression in a 2013 study of two samples of young people, although academic struggles did not independently explain that link in that research.
Because autistic and ADHD traits frequently co-occur in the same individuals, researchers faced a challenge in untangling which specific social hurdles stem uniquely from each set of characteristics. Many previous studies examined either autism or ADHD in isolation, making it difficult to understand how distinct traits relate to social adjustment across different settings.
“In school settings, many children show mild ASD or ADHD traits that do not meet diagnostic criteria, yet they may still experience difficulties with peers, learning, or relationships with adults,” lead author Eriko Hashimoto, a doctoral student in the Graduate School of Humanities and Sciences at Ochanomizu University in Tokyo, told PsyPost. “These children may fall outside formal support systems.”
“However, we still know relatively little about how such traits relate to social adjustment and mental health over time,” Hashimoto explained. “Together with my supervisor and co-author, Professor Hiroyuki Ito, I wanted to address this gap by examining these developmental associations over several years in a large, community-based sample of school-aged children.”
To investigate these questions, Hashimoto, Professor Hiroyuki Ito of the Faculty of Core Research at Ochanomizu University, and their colleagues analyzed data from a large population-based cohort involving all public elementary and junior high schools in a medium-sized municipality in Chubu, Japan. The final analysis included 9,619 students from an initial group of 11,549 enrolled children. Students were surveyed once per school year from fourth through ninth grade, with data from 11 grade cohorts collected between 2012 and 2023. By gathering information from students, their parents, and their homeroom teachers, the authors were able to capture behavioral and emotional patterns across both home and classroom environments.
Parents reported on their children’s autistic tendencies using a shortened version of the Autism Spectrum Screening Questionnaire and assessed ADHD traits using the ADHD Rating Scale-IV. Students completed questionnaires detailing their subjective difficulties in three areas: keeping up with classwork, conflicts with teachers, and arguments with family members. Problems with classmates were evaluated using the peer relationships subscale of the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire, combining ratings from students, teachers, and parents into a single composite score.
Mental health outcomes were grouped into two broad categories. Internalizing problems, reflecting inward emotional distress such as anxiety and depression, combined child self-reports on a depression scale with parent and teacher ratings of emotional symptoms. Externalizing problems, capturing outward behavioral difficulties such as hostility and aggression, brought together student self-reports with adult ratings of conduct problems. The researchers used cross-lagged structural equation modeling, an advanced statistical technique that tests whether one variable predicts changes in another variable over time while controlling for student sex and grade level.
The analysis produced standardized coefficients, which express how strongly one measure predicted later changes in another. By the guidelines the authors used for this kind of analysis, values around 0.03 count as small, 0.07 as medium, and 0.12 as large.
The findings indicated distinct developmental patterns for autistic and ADHD traits. Autistic traits showed consistent links over time with subsequent peer difficulties, showing standardized coefficients between 0.146 and 0.190 across grade transitions, which fall in the large range. Autistic traits were also linked with later internalizing problems, with small-to-medium coefficients ranging from 0.068 to 0.097. In contrast, autistic traits were not consistently associated with later academic struggles or conflict with teachers.
ADHD traits showed a different pattern of associations. Elevated ADHD traits were linked to subsequent externalizing problems, with coefficients between 0.064 and 0.118, with the strongest associations appearing during late elementary school. ADHD traits were also associated with higher levels of academic difficulties over time, particularly in fourth and fifth grade, but showed weak and mostly inconsistent links to later internalizing problems directly. Instead, academic difficulties themselves predicted later internalizing symptoms during elementary school, suggesting that learning struggles may act as an intermediate pathway linking attention difficulties to emotional distress.
Rather than revealing one-way effects, the analyses indicated notable bidirectional processes. For instance, while peer problems predicted increases in subsequent internalizing symptoms, higher levels of internalizing symptoms were also associated with worsening peer problems over time. Similarly, externalizing behaviors predicted more frequent conflicts with teachers and parents in later years, and those strained adult relationships were linked with subsequent increases in behavioral difficulties. Academic problems consistently predicted greater family conflict in the following year, with coefficients ranging from 0.105 to 0.163.
The social environment also appeared to feed back into parent ratings of neurodevelopmental traits. Experiencing peer problems was linked to higher reported autistic traits in later grades, with coefficients up to 0.164. In an analogous manner, elevated externalizing behaviors predicted higher reported ADHD traits in subsequent waves. These patterns suggest that neurodevelopmental traits may not be fixed and could shift with a child’s social experiences, though they could also reflect changes in how parents perceive and rate their children’s traits once problems emerge.
“One important message is that ASD and ADHD traits showed different patterns of association with later difficulties,” Hashimoto said. “These findings highlight the importance of considering not only children’s individual characteristics but also the social environments in which they develop.”
These findings align with prior research into how childhood difficulties unfold over time. The results are consistent with a study covered by PsyPost in 2026, which found that childhood ADHD traits were linked to greater psychological distress in midlife, partly through experiences of social exclusion in adulthood, though that research followed individuals into adulthood while the current study tracked youth through junior high school.
The observed connections also touch upon research covered by PsyPost in 2025 linking ADHD symptoms to emotional problems across development, though that earlier project pointed to shared genetic factors, based on twin data, as an underlying driver rather than school-based social pathways.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. “This study does not demonstrate causality,” Hashimoto noted. “The findings show temporal associations, not proof that one factor directly causes another.”
“It is also important to emphasize that children with elevated ASD or ADHD traits are highly diverse; our results describe group-level patterns and should not be interpreted as predictions for any individual child,” she pointed out. “In addition, we examined ASD and ADHD traits dimensionally in a general school population rather than focusing specifically on children with clinical diagnoses.”
There are a few other things to keep in mind. Many of the associations, including most links between the traits and later mental health problems, were small to medium in size. Also, the questionnaire used to evaluate autism primarily captured a relatively narrow set of characteristics, focusing mainly on Asperger-type social and behavioral traits rather than the full spectrum.
Future research could build on these findings by incorporating direct observational measures alongside questionnaires and testing whether supportive social settings can buffer these links. The authors suggest that early support for academic organization, peer relationship skills, and positive communication between families and schools might help interrupt these cycles, though the study did not test any interventions.
The study, “Longitudinal associations among autism and ADHD traits, social maladjustment, and mental health in school-aged children,” was authored by Eriko Hashimoto, Hiroyuki Ito, Megumi Hamada, Takahiro Nakajima, Nobuya Takayanagi, Mitsunori Myogan, Yasuo Murayama, and Masatsugu Tsujii.

Israeli settlers take Palestinian olives, and their harvest traditions
As Israeli settlers harvest olives on Palestinian land, farmers face growing violence and the loss of a tradition passed down through generations.
Ramallah, occupied West Bank – The video shared in Israeli settler groups shows two men bashing an olive tree with long wooden sticks. Smiling and congratulating one another, they try to knock the olives to the ground. They call the result “Pure Olive Oil”.
But as Palestinian activist Bashar Qaryouti explained, the two men don’t own the land, the trees, or the olives.
They’re Israeli settlers who set up an illegal settlement outpost on private property in the village of Qaryut, in the northern occupied West Bank, and made their way into this olive grove, some 200 metres (656 feet) away from Palestinian homes.
“No one has come near here for about three years, thank God,” one of the two men in the video says in Hebrew.
Local Palestinians know the man by name, and he does little to hide. The man is Avichai Suissa, an Israeli settler sanctioned by the European Union, United Kingdom – and previously by the United States – who runs a farm on the outpost. It was established more than a year and a half ago, and videos like this help Suissa raise donations for it.
On his campaign page, he says the goal is to rebuild and expand the farm, which was once dismantled by the Israeli army, to prevent it from falling “into enemy hands”.
“We’re gradually starting to work our way into the area,” Suissa said in the video.
But the land belongs to Palestinians – residents of Qaryut – who have not been able to reach it since the genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023. “A few months ago, farmers tried to plough their land, but the army stopped them,” Qaryouti said.
Worst year yet
“After we complained, the army declared the area a closed military zone a few days ago, so settlers are going to other lands, to other olives to steal,” Qaryouti explained.
Suissa and others are part of a growing movement of settlers who have intensified their campaign against the olive harvest. The campaign, part of a settler pogrom against Palestinians in the West Bank, has turned the olive harvest season in October into a source of fear and danger.
Many Palestinians in the occupied West Bank describe this year as the worst yet in terms of settler attacks, and the season has barely started.
On Wednesday, armed Israeli settlers on tractors raided lands between the villages of Ramin and Burqa, in the northern occupied West Bank. They opened fire on farmers heading to their trees.
Ali Bazzari, a 44-year-old farmer, was killed. His only “crime”, the family says, was trying to pick his olives.
Witnesses say the Israeli army prevented ambulances from reaching the wounded. Palestinians had to carry the injured through the mountains to hospitals.
The Israeli Rights Group Yesh Din says it documented 109 incidents of violence directly related to the harvest in 75 Palestinian communities between September 27 and October 6, an average of 11 per day.
Longtime tradition
Israeli settlers are increasingly attempting to adopt the rituals of the olive harvest season, while pushing out the Palestinians who have kept those traditions for generations.
Several new farms have been set up in the occupied West Bank. One shares videos of olives being pressed. Others invite Israelis to “join in” the experience.
Palestinians say the videos circulating show a disregard for the actual owners of the land taken by the settlers, and a clear attempt to appropriate the season, imitating its rituals and claiming them as their own.
Those rituals – things like collective picking, singing, and shared meals on the farms – are rooted in a deep connection to the land.
The olive harvest season may be an exhausting time of the year for Palestinians, with its hard work and long hours in the sun, but it’s a rewarding one. Olive farmers traditionally gather for family get-togethers, with neighbours and friends volunteering to help one another harvest the olives, in a cultural tradition known as “ouneh”.
The season has a light-hearted element, with debates about whose land produces the best oil, who should charge the most, and who knows how to pick the most olives and not drop any to the ground.
Older generations pass down lessons from history, such as the best time to harvest and how to nurture the trees – an inherited knowledge of climate, agriculture and the land itself.
“They planted so that we can eat. We plant so they [will] eat,” a well-known Arabic saying goes. It highlights the continuity of this inheritance, and the responsibility towards future generations.
Last harvest?
These trees, which are meant to be protected, nurtured and passed on, are being taken away – not only by settlers, but by soldiers, too.
Hazem Sanaf, 61, stood on a nearby hill in the village of Beit Rima and watched as Israeli bulldozers ploughed through his lands in late September, after he had received an Israeli military order. The bulldozers destroyed and uprooted more than 400 trees belonging to Hazem and his neighbour, some of them decades old, and his only source of income.
“They just want to take our olive trees from us,” he said, his eyes reflecting his pain.
Hazem is not alone. Several Israeli military orders to uproot olive trees have been handed out across the occupied West Bank. Some have been carried out, while others await their turn.
In the past, the Israeli military has cited the need to clear land of trees to prevent security threats or ambushes on troops. But Palestinians say it reflects a pattern of dispossession and impoverishment.
According to the Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission (CRRC), Israeli settlers and soldiers have destroyed approximately 50,000 trees this year alone.
Fuad Daraghmeh, from the village of al-Lubban Asharqiya, near Ramallah, carried the thick, broken stem of a tree.
“I took care of it for 30 years,” he said, and headed home. He did not say what he planned to do with the stem, but others said that their trees had been uprooted before, and that they had managed to nourish them back to life.
Others are resigned to saying goodbye to the trees. They sit by the bulldozed trees with small hand tools, picking the last fruit of what they believe is their last crop.
Palestinians have been watching videos of settlers harvesting their olive trees, including the one shared by Suissa.
Beyond the pain, one remark keeps coming up: the method used by Suissa in vigorously beating the tree is no way to treat it, and no way to harvest olives.
“The people who have tended to their lands for decades know that,” one Palestinian activist, who did not wish to be identified for security reasons, said.

India’s Cockroach movement says members detained as protests continue
India’s opposition and student-led CJP movement demand election chief’s resignation, plan mass demonstration on Saturday.
India’s Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) says that authorities have detained many of its members as thousands of the group’s supporters and members of several student groups continue to protest, demanding the election chief’s resignation.
Thursday’s demonstrations come ahead of CJP-led antigovernment protests planned for Saturday, with thousands expected to march to Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in the capital, New Delhi.
Ashutosh Ranka, a spokesperson for the movement, said in a post on X on Thursday that “at least 10,000” people from CJP demonstrations, student organisations, affiliated grassroots groups and political parties had been detained across the country.
Among those arrested is CJP national spokesman Deepak Baliyan, who was taken into police custody on Thursday, according to the group’s statements.
Al Jazeera could not immediately verify the claims, but videos posted on X showed activists being taken away in vans.
Opposition parties and students affiliated with the CJP movement have been demanding the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, over a controversial revision of voter lists.
They accuse the poll body he heads of benefitting Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
On Thursday, CJP said that among those detained was a group of students from the city of Pune who were headed for New Delhi to participate in planned protests at the iconic Jantar Mantar observatory. CJP said they were taken away in a bus to an unknown location.

‘Every vote matters’
India’s Election Commission has so far removed more than 130 million names from the voter lists, with millions appealing the removals. About 969 million people were eligible to vote in the 2024 election.
Protesters allege the changes disproportionately removed voters who support opposition parties while preserving or adding voters more likely to back Modi’s party.
The commission and government deny the allegations. They say the revision has no political motive but is aimed at removing duplicate and ineligible entries while ensuring eligible voters remain registered.
Earlier on Thursday, thousands of supporters of the CJP youth movement protested in the tech hub of Bengaluru.
Many of the protesters held posters that said, “Every name counts, Every vote matters” and “Stop the Murder of Democracy”.
Khushi Shrivastava, a 22-year-old architecture student at the protest, told the Reuters news agency: “I think voting right is the most basic point of democracy … People who actually want to vote, who actually care about the future of India, they are just being [denied] voting rights.”
On Wednesday, Indian opposition leader Rahul Gandhi was briefly detained for the third time in two days, as his Congress Party accused police of using “brute force”.
Police said the allegations were being used to “defame” them. BJP’s spokesperson Gaurav Bhatia said the allegations were “being levelled by an irresponsible, anarchist opposition”.

At least 81 US aircraft worth up to $3.3bn lost or damaged in Iran war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
19:43:39 UTC
04:43:39 KST

At least 81 US aircraft worth up to $3.3bn lost or damaged in Iran war
The damage, documented in a Congressional Budget Office report, comes as Trump faces criticism over war’s cost.
At least 81 United States military aircraft, including fighter jets and drones, have been lost or damaged during Operation Epic Fury, the code name for Washington’s military campaign against Iran launched earlier this year.
The statistic comes as part of a report released on Monday by the Congressional Budget Office (CBO), a nonpartisan government agency that provides budget-related research to the legislature.
It estimated that, as of August 1, the cost of the American aircraft losses during the US-Israeli war against Iran was between $1.9bn and $3.3bn.
The report this week highlights the growing price tag for the war, which began on February 28. A lasting ceasefire has remained out of reach as the conflict continues into its eighth month.
“The asymmetries of warfare show that even small countries with small militaries can inflict damage on the world’s best militaries,” said Harlan Ullman, a former naval officer and chairman of the Killowen Group, a government advisory firm.
He told Al Jazeera that Iran has managed to achieve a degree of success in damaging US military hardware and bases in the Middle East.
“Iran has plenty of US targets available, and you can imagine what a small drone can do to a major military asset. We have seen examples of that in the Gulf countries during the conflict,” Ullman explained.
Monday’s report listed 12 F-15E Strike Eagle fighter jets, one F-35A Lightning II jet and seven KC-135 Stratotanker aerial refuelling aircraft among those affected. Forty-five of the 81 aircraft identified in the report were MQ-9 Reaper drones.
Evolving nature of warfare
Experts like Ullman trace some of the US vulnerabilities to the changing nature of modern warfare, which is increasingly reliant on low-cost drones that are widely available.
Many have pointed to Russia’s war against Ukraine as an example of how a smaller military like Kyiv’s can keep a larger adversary at bay through drone warfare.
Rumours of a potential drone attack on Royal Air Force (RAF) Fairford — a British base that has hosted US assets during the Iran war — also resulted in the sudden departure of a dozen US aircraft on Sunday.
Ullman pointed to those instances as examples of how the threat of drone attacks has been effective in putting larger militaries on the defensive.
“We have seen the US had to relocate its B-1 bombers from the UK fearing Iranian attacks, and we have seen how the Ukrainian Operation Spiderweb, where small drones were launched from inside Russia, targeted and destroyed Russian military assets,” Ullman said.
Cost of war?
The rising costs associated with the war against Iran have also placed political pressure on the administration of US President Donald Trump.
Earlier this year, his administration requested a record $1.5 trillion in defence spending for fiscal year 2027, citing the demands of the war.
But the soaring price tag has sparked scepticism in Congress, particularly from Democrats.
Last month, 45 Senate Democrats and one independent wrote an open letter to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth demanding transparent accounting of the war’s costs.
They argued that a “detailed breakdown” of the costs was necessary before Congress considers further supplemental funding.
“American taxpayers have already paid an extra $100 billion out of their pockets for higher gas and diesel prices alone and at least another $60 billion in higher costs for things like groceries, mortgages, and plane tickets as a result of the war,” the senators wrote.
“Now you are asking that they pay again to fund a war of choice that Congress never authorized and the President launched with no strategic plan.”
In a separate report issued in September, the Congressional Budget Office estimated that the war with Iran has cost roughly $38bn, as of August 1.
That amount reflects the costs of replacing expended munitions and equipment lost in battle, as well as increased fuel costs and other operations.
“An additional month of conflict would cost $2 billion,” the office said.
However, it added that, “if the intensity of the conflict increased to roughly the level experienced in July, the cost per month would increase to $3 billion”.
The Pentagon said it had “nothing further to provide” in a response to Al Jazeera’s query about whether the losses reported this week were expected and how they would impact the department’s budget.
Polls indicate the war is widely unpopular among US voters, and analysts have speculated about whether reports of rising costs may have an impact on the US midterm elections, which will decide whether Trump’s Republican Party will retain control of Congress.
But Ullman is sceptical that reports like Monday’s will be a determining factor in the outcome of the vote.
“I do not think that report will influence the course of the upcoming midterm elections, as many Americans, even those who oppose the war, would see it as expected damage in a military operation,” Ullman said.
