Russia has spent a decade trying to stop people from bypassing internet censorship. Now it plans to spend nearly 60 billion rubles over three years on traffic filtering.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
19:42:18 UTC
04:42:18 KST

Russia has spent a decade trying to stop people from bypassing internet censorship. Now it plans to spend nearly 60 billion rubles over three years on traffic filtering.
Russia is preparing a new wave of restrictions on tools used to bypass internet blocks. The budget for the next three years includes a record 60 billion rubles for traffic filtering. The Digital Development Ministry wants to make mobile internet much more expensive for VPN users, and there are plans to put companies’ corporate networks under strict oversight by the Federal Security Service (FSB). Dozens of other restrictions have accumulated in recent years. We looked back at the main ones to show how the state has methodically cut Russians off from the free internet — and where we are on that timeline right now.
VPN services were banned from bypassing Russian internet blocks (2017)
On November 1, 2017, a new Article 15⁸ was added to the law “On Information, Information Technologies, and Information Protection” to address VPNs and other ways to bypass internet blocks:
Measures to prevent the use within the Russian Federation of information and telecommunications networks and online resources that provide access to online resources and information and telecommunications networks to which access is restricted within the Russian Federation.
The authorities did not ban VPNs outright. Instead, they required providers to filter their Russian users’ traffic and block access to resources on the banned list. If providers failed to comply, Russian telecommunications operators were required to block their VPN services on instructions from Roskomnadzor, Russia’s internet regulator. The only exemptions were for the authorities themselves and companies that needed unrestricted access “for technical purposes necessary to support their operations.”
Internet providers were banned from explaining how to bypass blocks (2018)
In February 2016, the Association for the Protection of Copyright on the Internet proposed administrative fines for promoting VPN use to access banned websites. Roskomnadzor supported the idea but proposed fining only internet providers. An agency spokesperson said in April that inspections had uncovered “several instances in which telecommunications operators posted information about ways to bypass blocks on their block notification pages.”
In the end, no separate fine was introduced. But starting November 1, 2017, telecommunications operators were required to comply with rules governing “posted information about restrictions on access to online resources.” Roskomnadzor published the corresponding order in March 2018. It prohibited the following on block notification pages:
- News content
- Information about ways to access online resources containing information to which access is restricted under Federal Law No. 149-FZ
A center was created to manage Russia’s internet, along with equipment to filter traffic and block access (2019)
After their failed attempt to block Telegram in 2018, the authorities learned from their mistakes and passed a law on the “sovereign internet.” It took effect on November 1, 2019.
Among other things, the law allowed centralized control over the Russian segment of the internet. To that end, the authorities established a Center for Monitoring and Management of the Public Communications Network within the Main Radio Frequency Center, which reports to Roskomnadzor. The new center was supposed to be able to take control “in the event of threats to the stability, security, and integrity” of internet operations in Russia.
To counter such threats, every telecommunications operator was required to install TSPU, or “technical means of countering threats.” These hardware and software systems allowed Roskomnadzor to filter traffic at its discretion and block sites and services it deemed objectionable. The agency later made extensive use of TSPU to target VPNs and other tools for bypassing blocks. If you want to understand exactly how TSPU works, watch this five-hour video.
In October 2023, Roskomnadzor head Andrey Lipov said that all communications nodes in Russia were “100% covered by TSPU.”
Mass blocking of VPN services began (2021)
In May 2021, Lipov threatened to block VPN services that continued to ignore Russian legal requirements. The agency began targeting individual providers the following month. Roskomnadzor made its plans public in advance so the blocks would not affect companies using those VPN services “to keep technical processes running at businesses and organizations.”
By the end of the year, the agency had said it was restricting VyprVPN, Opera VPN, Hola! VPN, ExpressVPN, KeepSolid VPN Unlimited, Nord VPN, Speedify VPN, IPVanish VPN, Betternet, Lantern, X-VPN, Cloudflare WARP, Tachyon VPN, and PrivateTunnel.
Hi, I’m Yulia.
I’m an editor at Meduza, and for almost five years now, I haven’t been sleeping well for one reason: I’m worried about my colleagues in Russia.
I’m often woken up by messages from our freelance reporters inside the country. They sometimes work late at night or early in the morning, and they message me at all hours. I never silence my phone at night in case of an emergency. Every notification jolts me awake. Half-asleep, my first thought is always the same: they’re texting me because the police have come to search their home. In Russia, you can go to prison for working with Meduza. Sometimes I have nightmares about my reporters being interrogated by the FSB. Some of those nightmares have come true.
Meduza’s reporters risk their freedom to tell the world what’s happening inside Russia. They believe their work can help make a better future possible, and they refuse to leave. Please donate so they can keep reporting.
All instructions for bypassing Russian internet blocks were banned (2023)
On July 31, 2023, a new provision allowed authorities to add online resources to the unified register of banned websites for another reason:
Article 15¹. Unified register of domain names, website page addresses, and network addresses identifying websites containing information whose distribution is prohibited in the Russian Federation
5. The grounds for adding the information specified in Part 2 of this article to the register are:
m) information about ways and methods of providing access to online resources and/or information and telecommunications networks to which access is restricted within the Russian Federation;
Fines were introduced for VPN service operators (2025)
On September 1, 2025, a new Article 13.52 was added to the Code of Administrative Offenses:
Violation of the rules governing the use within the Russian Federation of hardware and software tools for accessing online resources and information and telecommunications networks to which access is restricted
It provides for fines for refusing to cooperate with Roskomnadzor or to block Russian residents’ access to banned resources. The fines can reach 80,000 rubles for individuals and 500,000 rubles for companies. Repeat violations carry steeper penalties: up to 200,000 rubles and 1 million rubles, respectively.
Using a VPN became an aggravating factor in criminal offenses (2025)
On September 1, 2025, a new item was added to the Criminal Code’s list of aggravating factors:
committing a crime using hardware and software tools for accessing online resources and information and telecommunications networks to which access is restricted
Now, if a court finds that an offender used a VPN to commit any crime, it can impose a harsher punishment. It can even deny offenders certain forms of leniency under the Criminal Code, such as sentencing limits for those who voluntarily report their crimes to the authorities or enter into a pretrial cooperation agreement.
VPN advertising was banned, and fines were introduced for it (2025)
On September 1, 2026, a new provision was added to Article 5 of the law “On Advertising,” which sets out general requirements:
10⁸. It is prohibited to distribute advertisements for hardware and software tools that provide access to online resources and information and telecommunications networks to which access is restricted under the laws of the Russian Federation
At the same time, fines for such advertising were added to the Code of Administrative Offenses (Part 18 of Article 14.3). The maximum fine is 80,000 rubles for individuals and 500,000 rubles for companies.
Major Russian companies began detecting users with active VPNs (2026)
In April 2026, the Digital Development Ministry forced major Russian companies with the most heavily visited websites and services to detect active VPNs on users’ devices. The companies were required to block those users’ access and, according to RBC, share data about their VPN connections with Roskomnadzor. In theory, this was meant to help the agency gather information about VPNs that successfully bypass blocks or go entirely undetected, so it could block them more effectively.
Authorities tried to cut VPN services off from Russian hosting providers (2026)
On June 26, 2026, the law “On Information, Information Technologies, and Information Protection” was amended to prohibit Russian hosting providers from serving VPN services that bypass Russian internet blocks:
Article 10²⁻¹. Specific rules governing hosting providers’ activities
5¹. A hosting provider may not supply computing capacity for storing information in an information system permanently connected to the internet to owners of information and telecommunications networks or online resources (a website and/or website page, information system, or computer program) that provide access to online resources or information and telecommunications networks to which access is restricted within the Russian Federation under this Federal Law, if those owners have applied to the hosting provider and have not complied with the requirements set out in Paragraph 1 of Part 7 of Article 15⁸ of this Federal Law.
Okay, folks, this brings us to the present day…
Roskomnadzor would monitor corporate VPNs that bypass blocks
Since 2017, the authorities have officially allowed companies to use VPNs that can bypass Russian censorship “for technical purposes necessary to support their operations.” Companies must also determine in advance which employees will use such a VPN.
A new bill to combat phone and cyber fraud would require companies to notify Roskomnadzor that they use corporate VPNs, though it is unclear how. The government and the FSB would also jointly approve rules for using these services and set requirements for employees who have access to them.
Using Russian hosting providers would become even harder for VPN services
The same bill would create a new Roskomnadzor register of individuals and companies that use servers in Russia to host VPN services. If caught bypassing blocks, they would be barred from entering into contracts with any provider in Russia for a full year. The government would develop procedures for Roskomnadzor and hosting providers to exchange this information.
Charges for international mobile internet traffic would be introduced to combat VPNs
According to Forbes, the Digital Development Ministry’s plans to charge mobile subscribers for international internet traffic first became known in March 2026. At the time, the ministry proposed an additional charge for subscribers who used more than 15 gigabytes of international traffic. This would put VPN users in a bind: When they connect to foreign servers, all their traffic becomes international. Using a good VPN on a mobile phone without additional workarounds would become very expensive.
At the time, telecommunications operators asked for the measure to be postponed. But officials have now returned to the idea. According to Kommersant, the government is proposing to raise the free international internet traffic allowance to 50 gigabytes and, for now, introduce the additional charge only on 5G networks.
The authorities plan to allocate even more money to combat VPNs
The draft federal budget for 2027–2029 provides for a sharp increase in spending on traffic filtering and internet blocks using TSPU. The annual subsidy to the Main Radio Frequency Center had been set at 9,870,441,200 rubles for 2027 and 9,844,821,700 rubles for 2028. The new draft budget simply puts a 1 in front of each figure. The planned subsidy for 2029 is roughly the same: 19,870,474,200 rubles. That amounts to nearly 60 billion rubles over three years. By comparison, in 2024, the authorities planned to spend almost the same amount, 59 billion rubles, on upgrading TSPU — but over six years (through 2030).

Sweden counts its difficult waters as an advantage
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
20:41:19 BST
04:41:19 KST

The Baltic archipelago that makes sonar so unreliable also gives a navy that knows it cover, concealment and freedom of manoeuvre, the commander of the Royal Swedish Navy’s 4th Naval Warfare Flotilla told the Apex Europe conference in London on Wednesday.
Captain Anna Jonsson, whose flotilla operates in the waters around Stockholm, opened a panel on countering undersea threats by describing the conditions her crews work in.
She said: “Sweden and my unit operates in a complex underwater environment. Our archipelago consists of tens of thousands of islands, narrow passages, shallow waters, and highly variable seabed conditions. Below the surface, rocks, wrecks and seabed formations create a challenging environment for our sensors.”
The behaviour of the water itself compounds everything the seabed is already doing. “Add variations of depth, temperature and salinity to that, and the performance of the sonar and underwater systems can change significantly from one area to another,” she said.
Her argument was that none of this amounts to a handicap for the navy that has learned to live in it. “Complexity is not necessarily a disadvantage always. For the force that understands the environment, it can provide cover, concealment and freedom of manoeuvre,” she said. “This has shaped the Swedish naval platforms, sensors, weapons and tactics for generations.”
That inheritance shows in what the Swedish navy buys, since small shallow-water submarines, mine countermeasures vessels, and corvettes built for the archipelago are a different proposition from blue-water designs, and the tactics that go with them have been refined over decades of operating in exactly these conditions.
“Sweden is in some way a small state. I have limited resources within my flotilla, but we still need to achieve combat effectiveness,” she said. “It’s important for us to understand the underwater terrain better than our adversary.”
The chair observed that the Baltic condenses problems that navies meet in diluted form elsewhere, with the Black Sea the closest comparison, and that anti-submarine warfare there is a different business from where NATO navies usually operate.
Commodore David Burton, who leads the alliance work on an allied underwater battlespace network, said understanding the environment is built into how NATO is organising its experimentation, with Allied Command Transformation targeting demonstrations region by region. The Baltic has had its turn, the Mediterranean has had another, and the High North comes next.
Sweden brought all of this into NATO when it joined.

Eye Cells May Have Been Rejuvenated for the First Time in People
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
19:20:04 UTC
04:20:04 KST

Three people have received an innovative treatment designed to rejuvenate vision cells. In a presentation at the annual meeting of the American Academy of Ophthalmology, researchers from Life Biosciences reported that the treatment appears safe, and two of the recipients show early signs of improved vision.
The study is among the first approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration using a novel strategy of reprogramming cells to restore their normal function—essentially rejuvenating them. The scientists used a modified version of a reprogramming strategy that earned a Nobel Prize in 2012 for turning mature, adult cells back to an embryonic-like state from which they could become any of the cells in the body—including healthy new versions of diseased or older cells. In that work, Japanese scientist Shinya Yamanaka used four genes to trigger the cellular time warp.
In the current Phase 1 trial, which is ongoing, scientists used three of the four factors to perform a modified reprogramming of diseased retinal ganglion cells in the eye in people with a form of glaucoma—not returning the cells all the way back to their embryonic-like state, but to a point before they stopped functioning properly. Retinal ganglion cells have long arms that connect them from the retina in the eye to the optic nerve, which transmits visual signals to the brain. In some people, over time, fluid in the eye fails to drain properly, putting pressure on the retinal ganglion cells, which lose their delicate connections to the optic nerve, causing loss of vision. While the cells don’t necessarily die, they become dramatically less able to do their job of transmitting critical visual signals.
To try to restore their function, in the trial, scientists injected specially designed proteins, or transcription factors, coding for three of the genes into the vitreous: the gel-like fluid cavity at the back of the eye near the retina. It’s an advantageous location to test such a therapy, since it’s protected from the body’s immune defenses which could attack the newly made proteins. The proteins then did their work to reprogram the damaged and aging cells so they became functional again.
The experimental therapy is based on work from the lab of David Sinclair, professor of genetics at Harvard Medical School and co-founder of Life Biosciences. It's a test of his theory that aging cells lose their ability to work properly because they accumulate too many confusing instructions for which genes they need to turn on or off—so-called epigenetic noise that disrupts the original marching orders cells follow. Sinclair believes that restoring the proper epigenetic information, and removing the epigenetic “noise” by reprogramming the cells to a younger, more functional state could address diseases associated with aging, such as glaucoma.
“We are scientifically reversing epigenetic age to restore youthful function,” Sinclair says.
“We think of it as restoration,” says Sharon Rosenzweig-Lipson, chief scientific officer at Life Biosciences, who presented the new data at the conference. “We’re restoring the code back to what it was when [the cells] were healthy and functional.”
Full reprogramming with the four Yamanaka factors comes with a risk of cells growing out of control and forming teratomas, a type of tumor that can sprout partially or fully developed tissues like teeth, muscle, and bone. Sinclair’s goal was to exploit this reprogramming process to help cells regain their proper instruction manual, and together with his graduate student Yuancheng Lu, launched studies involving just three of the genes, dropping one that is most associated with cancers. There was no guarantee that using three of the factors would trigger reprogramming, since all of the previous studies employed all four. And for three years, Lu learned why—while working with mice with age-related vision loss like glaucoma, he struggled to reprogram retinal ganglion cells with only three of the factors. Experiment after experiment failed. Frustrated, Lu sought out Sinclair, hoping to move onto another project. “He said reversing aging is probably the hardest biological question in the world, and if it were easy, it would have been done already,” Lu says. But there was at least one element working in Lu’s favor. “Removing the fourth factor allowed the three other factors to be small enough to fit into the viral tool we used to deliver them into [animals],” he says. “If the three genes were a little bigger, then we couldn’t fit them into the viral vector.”
In 2018, Lu finally succeeded and texted Sinclair images of the first mouse with glaucoma that had regenerated the delicate connections between the retinal ganglion cells and the optic nerve that had been lost. When Lu asked Sinclair what he saw, Sinclair replied: “the future.”
Lu and Sinclair published their findings in 2020, and that therapy is very close to the one that Life Biosciences ended up using in its trial in people. Two days before the trial was launched in June, Rosenzweig-Lipson gave Lu the good news that the experiment he had worked on for three years was ready to test in the first people with glaucoma. “I was in the lab, and I couldn’t believe it,” Lu says. “I know these patients are suffering. My own family has the macular degeneration risk allele, and I carry the risk allele. So it means a lot to me. My great aunt died when she crossed the street because she couldn’t see well, so I feel like it’s destiny helping these people.”
While the study’s main goal is to show that the therapy is safe, two of the three participants showed early signs of improved vision as well, Rosenzweig-Lipson says. All three took a test before receiving the therapy to establish their visual field by noting when they could see strategically placed lights that flashed above, below, or to the left or right when they looked straight ahead. Eight weeks after receiving the reprogramming factors, two of the participants had improvements in their visual fields. “In places where they weren’t seeing as well, or weren’t identifying lights, we are now seeing better evidence that they can,” says Rosenzweig-Lipson.
She says the results are encouraging enough to begin testing a higher dose—three times that of the initial one—to determine if the treatment remains safe, and, ultimately, what dose would bring the biggest improvement in vision to patients.
The results could also lay the foundation for including people with another eye disease, NAION, which occurs mostly in people over 50 and is similar to a stroke in the eye. NAION causes sudden vision loss when retinal ganglion cells stop functioning for still unknown reasons. If the reprogramming factors can restore the function of some of these cells, the researchers are hopeful that people could regain some of their vision and avoid the blindness that results if left untreated.
So far, the researchers have not seen any adverse effects from the therapy: only side effects related to the injection, they say, and not the reprogramming itself. To be safe, however, the three factors can only be activated in the presence of the antibiotic doxycycline, which acts as an on-off switch for the treatment. After receiving the injection of the three factors, the participants took doxycycline for eight weeks, which ensured that the factors were active and produced the proteins needed to reprogram the retinal ganglion cells. Once they stopped taking the antibiotic, the proteins were no longer made. If further studies show that additional reprogramming is needed to improve vision, they could begin taking the antibiotic again to reprogram more aging or damaged cells.
These initial results will fuel additional studies on using the same method to rejuvenate other cells. Sinclair’s lab has reported promising findings with brain, knee, back, and liver cells in animals.
If the approach continues to be safe and show benefit, eye diseases could be just the beginning of rejuvenating different cells. “We have a wide array of [animal data] support now to suggest that it’s not just a one-organ phenomenon, but that it’s something that transcends organs and potentially has opportunities across a wide range of age-related diseases,” says Rosenzweig-Lipson.

Northern Irish police contact Sinn Fein members over investigation into parade protest
BELFAST, Oct 8 - Northern Irish police have contacted representatives of Sinn Fein in relation to their investigation into a protest that has blocked a Protestant parade from marching through a Catholic area for almost two weeks, the Irish nationalist party said.
Thousands of protesters, including Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O'Neill of Sinn Fein and party leader Mary Lou McDonald, gathered on the Catholic Garvaghy Road to stop the September 26 march after it was allowed to proceed for the first time since the contentious route was banned in 1998.
Annual attempts by the Orange Order to march through the area triggered unrest across the British-run region before the route was banned the same year the Good Friday Agreement largely ended the three decades of violence known as the "Troubles."
Police opened an investigation into what it called an unlawful protest and said on Thursday that individuals would receive letters regarding interviews after it had identified people reasonably suspected of committing offences.
Sinn Fein, which leads Northern Ireland's power-sharing government alongside its main pro-British rival, said a number of its representatives and party members received correspondence from police, without naming them.
"Sinn Féin will continue to stand with the Garvaghy Road residents who should be allowed to live in peace and free from sectarian intimidation," the party said in a statement.
Gerry Carroll, a lawmaker from the smaller People Before Profit party, said separately that he had received an invitation from police to attend a voluntary interview under caution in connection with the protest.
The dispute has destabilised the British-run region's fragile devolved government - a key plank of the 1998 peace deal - with Sinn Fein's partners the Democratic Unionist Party calling for O'Neill and other lawmakers to be prosecuted.
"A political title is not a shield, and no one is above the law," the party said in a statement on Thursday. REUTERS

The Great Healthcare Cost Hike Is Here
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
18:59:22 UTC
03:59:22 KST

American healthcare, the priciest healthcare system in the world, is set to get even more expensive
In the coming weeks, the roughly 160 million Americans who get health insurance through work will log into their benefits portals and pick a plan for 2027. Even for people used to rising healthcare costs, what they see may come as a shock. Employer health plan costs are projected to rise 8 to 10% next year, the largest increase in more than 20 years and double the average increase of the 2010s.
This spike is just the second in a series of three successive shocks to healthcare costs and coverage. The first came in January 2026, when the 24.3 million ACA Marketplace enrollees saw their after-subsidy premiums rise by an average of 114%. The second is the sharp increase in premiums and out-of-pocket costs for those who get insurance at work, the third year in a row of elevated increases. The third comes next January, when Medicaid work-reporting requirements take effect, which CBO projects will eventually push nearly 6 million people out of coverage.
History suggests that the American political system makes a bold attempt to reform healthcare about once a generation. President Harry Truman fought for national health insurance in 1945. President Lyndon B. Johnson signed Medicare and Medicaid into law in 1965. President Bill Clinton pushed for reform in 1994. And President Barack Obama passed the Affordable Care Act in 2010. With healthcare costs already among voters' top concerns, these shocks may create the next generational window for reform.
In the meantime, here’s how the looming healthcare hike will impact insurance costs, wherever you get your coverage.
If you buy your own insurance
The enhanced premium tax credits were first passed in the 2021 American Rescue Plan Act pandemic relief bill, then extended in the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act. They expired on December 31, 2025, after Congress declined to renew them in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA).
KFF estimates this decision raised after-subsidy premiums by 114%, or about $1,000 a year. In response, some people left the market and enrollment fell 12%, from 21.8 million to 19.2 million. New Mexico, the one state that replaced the federal subsidies with its own money, was the only state where enrollment grew. Others traded down to skimpier plans, but still are paying more. The share of enrollees in the least generous bronze plans went from 30% to 40%, and the average deductible rose by more than $1,000 to $3,786.
Even after all that switching and leaving, the average premium paid by people on the Marketplaces hit $178 a month in 2026, 58% higher than in 2025 and above the $164 people paid in 2021, the last year before the enhanced credits. Those who left were healthier than those who stayed, so insurers have proposed another 15% increase for 2027, stacked on top of this year’s 20%
If you get insurance through work
About 160 million Americans get health insurance through an employer. Most employers hold open enrollment for two or three weeks starting in October or November, for the plan year beginning Jan. 1.
The best data we have on 2027 costs comes from the large benefits consulting firms. They project total costs will rise 8 to 10% next year, the largest increase since 2003 and double the average increase of the 2010s. These firms point to more use of care, expensive new drugs, GLP-1s, hospital consolidation, and AI-assisted billing. For a typical worker, an increase that size works out to roughly $400 to $500 more next year.
And these totals understate the full cost increase, since many employers have made plans less generous to hold costs down. One common change is to raise deductibles, which shifts costs onto workers. Another is to cut back on what's covered. The share of large employers covering GLP-1s for obesity, for example, has fallen from 72% to 60%. Remove those changes, and the consulting firms estimate costs would have climbed another one to three percentage points.
If you’re on Medicaid
The third shock is to the Medicaid program. Starting January 1, 2027, OBBBA requires the 44 states (including Washington, D.C.) that expanded Medicaid to require adults covered by the expansion to document 80 hours a month of work, school, or community service. The CBO estimates that the requirement will push about 5.7 million people off Medicaid by 2034, leaving 5.3 million more people uninsured.
Most of those people should not lose coverage. The evidence suggests they will meet the criteria and lose coverage anyway because of the paperwork burden. When Arkansas imposed a work requirement in 2018, employment did not change. Instead, more than 18,000 people lost coverage within seven months, even though 95% either met the requirement or qualified for an exemption.
The work requirement is not the only Medicaid cut. OBBBA also requires eligibility checks every six months instead of once a year, shortens retroactive coverage, and limits the provider taxes states use to fund their share of the program. Counting those provisions, CBO projects 7.5 million more people will be uninsured by 2034
All of this means we are in the middle of the great healthcare cost hike. In January, after-subsidy premiums on the Marketplaces rose 114%. This fall, we expect the 160 million people who get insurance at work will see the largest increase in a generation. Next January, work-reporting requirements will start pushing millions of people off Medicaid. These shocks will strain family budgets.
They will also create a generational opportunity for reform. The best thing we can do is seize it.

After botched US execution, Christa Pike walking, mentally ‘foggy’, says lawyer
- - Christa Pike, 50, was walking around her hospital room but was still mentally “foggy” after a botched Tennessee execution, her lawyer said.
- - Pike was given two lethal pentobarbital doses on Sept 30 and was later due to have life support removed, but she woke up and started talking on Oct 6.
- - Her lawyers want Governor Bill Lee to commute her sentence, while Tennessee has paused executions and ordered evidence from the failed execution to be preserved.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - The convicted US killer who survived a botched execution was walking around her hospital room though she was mentally “foggy,” her lawyer said in an interview broadcast on Oct 8.
Christa Pike, 50, had been considered braindead following two lethal doses of the drug pentobarbital on Sept 30 that failed to kill her.
Doctors had been planning to remove life support on Oct 6 when she unexpectedly woke up and started talking, her lawyers have said.
“She is up and walking for the first time today, but just around the room, you know, not very far,” lawyer Stephen Ferrell told the BBC.
“She’s also somewhat foggy. She can lose her train of thought really easily, and forgets where she’s going.”
“There could be some permanent damage. We don’t know that yet,” said Ferrell, who has not personally seen Pike or spoken with her, but is getting updates from colleagues who have.
Pike was sentenced to death in the state of Tennessee for murdering a classmate, a crime committed when she was a teenager.
Since the botched execution, her lawyers have repeatedly called on Governor Bill Lee to commute her sentence to life in prison.
Lee has suspended executions in Tennessee pending an independent investigation.
‘Uncharted waters’
Whether the state will eventually attempt to execute Pike again was not known.
“We are very much in uncharted waters,” Ferrell said.
Pike is the only inmate to ever survive after being injected with lethal doses of execution drugs, according to the Death Penalty Information Centre (DPI).
Other cases of botched executions in the United States were because the procedure did not go according to plan though those inmates ultimately died, according to DPI.
There were seven executions that were halted when personnel were unable to set IV lines for the lethal injection.
On Oct 7, a court ordered Tennessee corrections officials to preserve all evidence related to Pike’s botched execution including medical supplies, waste, and audio and video recordings.
Excluding Pike’s case, there have been 30 executions in the United States this year, all by lethal injection.
The most recent was that of Jamaal Howard, who was put to death in Texas on Oct 7 for killing a store clerk during a 2000 robbery.
The death penalty has been abolished in 23 of the 50 US states, while three others – California, Oregon and Pennsylvania – have moratoriums in place.
The Pentagon said this week that President Donald Trump has approved the execution of Nidal Hasan, a US Army psychiatrist who shot dead 13 people and wounded more than two dozen at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009.
Hasan’s execution by firing squad, set for Dec 3, would be the first carried out by the US military since 1961. AFP

Netanyahu’s ex-military secretary says PM’s office falsified Oct. 7 records
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
18:58:11 UTC
03:58:11 KST

Maj. Gen. (res.) Avi Gil, who served as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s military secretary before and during the October 7 attack, said Thursday that a stenographer in the Prime Minister’s Office told him she had been instructed to change the recorded time of a key phone call on the morning of the massacre, an act he described as “falsification.”
Gil told Channel 12 that, in January 2024, the stenographer entered his office and said she had been ordered by the prime minister’s chief of staff to change the time of a four-minute call from 6:40 a.m. to 6:29 a.m. “She told me, ‘I’m not allowed to change it. The computer shows and says 6:40 to 6:44,’” Gil said. “Those are facts, and there is no dispute about them.” He said he immediately documented the account in a handwritten note to the attorney general and recommended that any future commission of inquiry demand the original recordings rather than relying solely on transcripts. Earlier reporting by ynet had detailed suspicions surrounding an effort to change the time of the call.
“The first thing I asked myself was why anyone was dealing with the transcript of a four-minute conversation on the morning of October 7,” Gil said. “Who cared about it, and what was in that conversation that made it important?” He added that, in his view, “someone was dealing with certain narratives” months after the attack. “This is changing a transcript, changing the truth. Factually, there was an instruction to change the time of a call.”
Gil also said that before October 7 security officials had periodically recommended targeted operations in Gaza that the political leadership chose not to approve. “There were recommendations from time to time to carry out targeted operations in Gaza. Those recommendations were not accepted,” he said. “I’m talking about the facts, and the leadership has broader considerations. There were actions that were recommended and not approved, and I stand behind what I’m saying.”
The former military secretary also confirmed an earlier report that then-Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar had delivered a warning to Netanyahu in July 2023 that Israel was facing the danger of war. According to the warning previously reported by Yedioth Ahronoth, Bar told Netanyahu: “I am giving you a warning of war today. I cannot give you an exact day and hour, but this is the warning.” Gil stressed, however, that it was not a specific warning of an impending attack from Gaza. “Was there a specific, focused warning from Gaza? Absolutely not,” he said. Bar has separately said he instructed that Gil be updated at 5:15 a.m. on October 7, although Netanyahu’s first documented conversation with Gil came at 6:29 a.m.
Gil said he received a call from the Shin Bet chief’s office at 6:12 a.m. that morning and was told of suspicious signs in Gaza, including unusual SIM card activity and movement underground, alongside indicators that appeared to reduce the urgency because similar behavior had previously occurred during Hamas exercises. He said the Shin Bet planned further assessments and had ordered an operational team south as a precaution. “While we were talking, the many alerts began at 6:29 a.m.,” he said.
Looking back at the preceding night, Gil rejected the idea that Netanyahu would ordinarily have been awakened based on the intelligence picture then available. He said the intelligence officer who saw the overnight message understood that the word “routine” appeared repeatedly and that there was no indication of immediate urgency. 
“Cases in which a prime minister, in a phone call, decides against all the heads of the security establishment are rare, if they exist at all,” Gil said. “The chief of staff and the head of the Shin Bet do not call the prime minister directly. That is what the military secretary is for. There is one address.”
Gil was also asked about reports that Netanyahu may have received warnings from Egypt or the United Arab Emirates before the massacre. He said he was not in the office on the dates associated with the reported Emirati meeting and therefore could not say what occurred. But he pointed to recent reports of an Egyptian aircraft arriving in Israel and departing shortly afterward. “A plane like that does not come for a training sortie,” he said, while stressing that he did not know who, if anyone, had met its passengers.

Putin calls Middle East situation pressing problem

South Africa vs Australia Test series, everything you need to know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
18:54:40 UTC
03:54:40 KST

Australia is back in South Africa for one of the most eagerly anticipated Test series in recent history.
It has been eight long years since Australia last toured South Africa in red-ball cricket, in a series that will forever be remembered for its ignominy.
Sandpapergate is what that contest will be remembered for, but even before that, it was crossing a red line in despicable behaviour unbecoming of the sport.
Here's everything you need to know ahead of the three-Test series.
When are the Test matches?
The two teams will play three Tests.
The first is at Kingsmead in Durban from October 9 to 13.
The second is at St George's Park in Gqeberha from October 18 to 22.
And Newlands in Cape Town will host the third from October 27 to 31.
What time are the Test matches?
The Durban Test starts at 6:30pm AEDT and will likely run through to 2am AEDT.
That AEDT time relates to New South Wales, the ACT, Victoria and Tasmania.
In Queensland, the action begins at 5:30pm.
In South Australia, at 6pm.
In the Northern Territory, at 5pm.
And the first ball will be bowled at 3:30pm in Western Australia.
How can I watch the Test series?
The entire series is live on Fox Sports and Kayo.
ABC Sport will also have live radio commentary on the ABC Listen App or online.
You can also follow every ball in our live blog on the ABC Sport website.
Who is playing in the series?
Australia's squad: Pat Cummins (c), Scott Boland, Alex Carey (wk), Cooper Connolly, Cameron Green, Sam Harper (wk), Josh Hazlewood, Travis Head, Matthew Kuhnemann, Marnus Labuschagne, Nathan Lyon, Nic Maddinson, Michael Neser, Matt Renshaw, Steven Smith, Mitchell Starc, Beau Webster.
South Africa's squad: Temba Bavuma (c), Marques Ackerman, David Bedingham, Corbin Bosch, Gerald Coetzee, Tony de Zorzi, Simon Harmer, Marco Jansen, Keshav Maharaj, Aiden Markram, Wiaan Mulder, Senuran Muthusamy, Anrich Nortje, Dane Paterson, Kagiso Rabada, Ryan Rickelton (wk), Tristan Stubbs (wk), Kyle Verreynne (wk).
Australia's record against South Africa
Australia has won 54 of the 102 Test matches between the two teams, with 21 draws and 27 defeats since their first meeting in 1902.
On South African soil, Australia also has a winning record, with 29 victories against 16 defeats and nine draws.
Australia has won six of the 11 Tests played at St George's in Durban, including winning each of the last three Tests it has played there, while South Africa has won three with two draws.
The two teams also drew a Test at the city's old Lord's ground in 1921, before the venue's demolition in 1922.
South Africa has a much better record at St George's Park in Gqeberha though, winning four of the seven matches played there, including the last two.
Before 2021, Gqeberha was Port Elizabeth, but is now known by its Xhosa name, and this is the first time Australia will play in the city under its new name.
Australia has a great record at Newlands though, winning 10 of the 14 Tests played in the shadow of Table Mountain. However, it has only won one of its last four Tests at the ground considered one of the most beautiful in the world.
The two teams last played a Test in June 2025, when South Africa shocked Australia at Lord's to win the World Test Championship.
In the 2022/23 summer of cricket, Australia claimed a 2-0 Test series victory over South Africa on home soil.
The last time Australia played a Test series in South Africa was 2018, and it's safe to say things were … complicated.
The fiery 2018 series
It is fair to say the 2018 series was combative, fiery, febrile and chaotic.
Australia won the first Test at Kingsmead in Durban, but not before David Warner and Quinton de Kock almost came to blows in a stairwell at the end of the fourth day.
South Africa won the second Test in Gqeberha, but man of the match Kagiso Rabada, who took 5/96 and 6/54, was subsequently banned for barging into Steve Smith after dismissing him in the first innings.
Rabada was then handed a reprieve after an appeal involving one of South Africa's highest-profile lawyers, freeing him to play the next two matches.
The third Test was in Cape Town where, in the shadows of Table Mountain, Australia's descent into the dark arts was exposed.
On the third day, host broadcaster Supersport captured Cameron Bancroft rubbing the ball with a square of sandpaper to help encourage the prodigious reverse swing that had featured throughout the series thus far.
While South Africa romped to a 322-run win and a series lead, the full extent of Australia's cheating was exposed, leading to a moral reckoning about the team's approach back home, with then-prime minister Malcolm Turnbull leading the criticism of the offending players.
Smith, Bancroft and Warner were all sent home in disgrace, and an under-manned Australian team was thumped by 492 runs at the Wanderers in Johannesburg.
What's happened since?
Australia has toured South Africa twice since the 2018 Test series, in 2020 and 2023 for limited-overs matches, with Smith and Warner both involved.

03:35:58 KST

Power outages have returned to Kyiv after Russian attacks damaged the energy infrastructure supplying the capital, with authorities warning that the situation could worsen as Russia intensifies its campaign against Ukraine’s energy system ahead of winter.
Russia has repeatedly targeted Ukraine’s power, heating, and other critical infrastructure to disrupt the systems civilians depend on and create a humanitarian crisis during winter. Ukrainian officials have repeatedly warned that this winter will be especially severe, as Russia has expanded its strike capabilities since the summer and Ukraine continues to face shortages of air-defense systems needed to protect its energy infrastructure.
Ukrenergo said on 8 October that emergency outages were being imposed in parts of Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast because of falling voltage in the high-voltage network. Previously announced hourly schedules were suspended, with predictable schedules to resume once the system stabilizes.
In the evening, further disruption came after a Russian attack on an energy facility important to Kyiv. Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal said that energy workers were working to restore power.
Kyiv has been under Russian attack throughout the day, with four people killed and 19 injured.
The attack continues into the evening of 8 October, with air raid alerts active across most of the country.
Kyiv loses power, water, and public transport
The damage throughout the day quickly spread beyond electricity.
The Kyiv City Military Administration said power disruptions temporarily halted metro trains and escalators. Part of the capital’s public transport system was also suspended because of the lack of electricity.
Reduced power to water infrastructure caused lower pressure on the right bank of the Dnipro, particularly in the Holosiivskyi, Sviatoshynskyi, Solomianskyi, and Shevchenkivskyi districts. Some buildings could temporarily lose water, the administration warned.
Russia is hitting the energy system as winter approaches
The outages come as Russia has stepped up attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure ahead of the heating season.
Ukrenergo said Russian attacks had caused new power outages in Donetsk, Kharkiv, Sumy, and Zaporizhzhia oblasts. The company said damaged equipment was already limiting the grid’s ability to supply consumers and warned that further Russian strikes could rapidly change the situation.
For 9 October, Ukrenergo announced all-day power restrictions in affected regions, including hourly outages for some consumers. Industrial and business consumers will also face restrictions. The company urged Ukrainians to conserve electricity, particularly during the evening peak from 5 p.m. to 10 p.m.
Ukraine’s energy authorities have been warning about the consequences of repeated Russian attacks for months. In late September, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said attacks on energy facilities had been occurring almost daily since the summer, with the September 29–30 attack marking the first massive combined strike on the energy system since the previous heating season.
The renewed strikes mark the beginning of Russia’s winter campaign against the energy system, with Russian missiles and drones increasingly targeting power-generation and transmission infrastructure in Kyiv and surrounding regions.
Russia has openly threatened another winter of blackouts
The campaign follows years of Russian attacks aimed at disrupting the infrastructure that keeps Ukrainian homes heated and supplied with electricity and water during the winter.
In August, Russia’s Defense Ministry openly taunted Ukrainians over its attacks on energy-related infrastructure, posting images of attack drones with the message that Ukrainians would “get a freeze” in winter.
Russia’s strategy has repeatedly linked attacks on electricity infrastructure to disruptions in heating and water supplies. This makes damage to the power grid particularly consequential as temperatures fall: a strike on an electrical facility can leave not only homes without lights, but also affect water pumps, heating systems, transportation, and other essential services.
The return of blackouts to Kyiv before the heating season is fully underway is an early indication of the pressure Russia’s renewed energy campaign is putting on Ukraine’s civilian infrastructure.

08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
South Korea conducted its first test launch of a hypersonic glide vehicle Thursday, a presidential spokesperson said.
The test was conducted to verify core hypersonic technologies, including flight trajectory and speed, for a strategic asset capable of surprise precision strikes against enemy targets, Kang Yu-jung said, according to the Yonhap news agency.
“The HGV successfully separated from its booster and seamlessly executed its planned flight path under hypersonic conditions,” she said.
“This successful launch marks a major milestone in that preparations are complete to secure a new deterrent capable of striking critical targets across the theater of the Korean Peninsula,” Kang added.
She said the launch aimed to test super-high-temperature thermal protection materials, guidance and control systems, as well as irregular maneuverability at low altitudes.
President Lee Jae Myung, Defense Minister Kang Shin-chul and other officials witnessed the launch, according to Kang.
HGV missile systems use a booster to accelerate and ascend into the upper atmosphere before separating from the booster and gliding at lower altitudes at hypersonic speeds.
While the location was not officially disclosed, Yonhap reported that the launch took place on a barge at a test center operated by the Agency for Defense Development in Taean, about 130 kilometers (81 miles) south of Seoul.
Lee commended the HGV development team, stressing that national security should be protected through the country's own strength.
“The government will fully support the development and operational deployment of advanced weaponry so that our people can live without concern,” Lee said, according to Kang.
Lee later inspected the military's Hyunmoo-5 surface-to-surface missile, known as the “monster missile” for its massive weight and destructive power.
It was the first time the government officially referred to the previously undisclosed weapon by its name, Hyunmoo-5.
Yonhap said the launch was “widely seen as a countermeasure” to last month's land mine explosion on South Korea's side of the Military Demarcation Line that severely injured two South Korean soldiers.
Seoul accused Pyongyang of deliberately planting two mines inside the Demilitarized Zone, while North Korea rejected the accusation, calling it “blame shifting.”
On Saturday, North Korea also launched an intermediate-range strategic missile capable of changing its flight trajectory at low altitude and using artificial intelligence technology during a firing drill off its east coast.

Elective egg freezing costs thousands, but most women never use them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

In short:
Only one in four women from Australia or New Zealand who freeze their eggs for non-medical reasons return to use them, according to a study.
The study's lead author cautions that elective egg freezing doesn't provide a guaranteed path to parenthood.
What's next?
Experts say there's a need for more accurate, evidence-based information about the process.
Anna Parle describes herself as an "early adopter" of egg freezing.
She froze her eggs 12 years ago when she was 37 and still single, aware her fertility was starting to decline.
Knowing she wanted to be a mum, Ms Parle asked herself: "How do I keep this dream of mine alive going into my late-30s?"
"It was a great backup plan because it took a lot of the pressure off," she said.
After meeting her now-husband, Ms Parle retrieved her frozen eggs and used them to conceive her sons, giving birth to one at the age of 40 and the second when she was 42.
Elective egg freezing is becoming an increasingly popular option for women, like Ms Parle, looking to extend their reproductive years.
Also known as planned or social egg-freezing, it preserves the biological age of the egg, which is generally a stronger indicator for successful pregnancy than a woman's age.
A single egg-freezing cycle in Australia costs between $7,000 and $12,000 up front, then an extra $500 to $1,000 a year in storage fees.
But a study published this week in Human Reproduction found just over one in four women from Australia or New Zealand who electively freeze their eggs return to use them within 10 years.
Study lead author Oisin Fitzgerald, research fellow at University of New South Wales Sydney, said it highlighted the need for people to set realistic expectations about the likelihood they would thaw their eggs within a decade, or that the procedure provided a guaranteed pathway to parenthood.
Higher return rate than expected
Dr Fitzgerald said elective egg freezing had become "very very, popular" over the past five years.
In 2009, 55 women underwent planned egg freezing, compared to 4,919 women in 2023.
Dr Fitzgerald analysed data from the 20,209 Australian and New Zealand women who underwent planned egg freezing for non-medical reasons between 2009 and 2023.
As egg freezing grew more popular over the latter part of the study's time period, more people were followed over five years than over 10.
"If we looked at how many returned after five years, it was 22 per cent and then after 10 years it was 28 per cent," Dr Fitzgerald said.
Most people who thawed their eggs returned after 4.9 years.
Of the people who used their frozen eggs, about half used donor sperm and a third went on to have a live birth.
Devini Ameratunga, a Brisbane-based reproductive endocrinologist not involved in the study, said the return rate was higher than she expected.
"In general, we tend to counsel patients that about 10 per cent of people come back and use their eggs," she said.
"This new paper really gives us Australian and New Zealand data, and it's quite a significantly higher number of people that do come back."
Egg freezing decision information
Egg freezing is a complicated decision, said Sherine Sandhu, a research fellow at the University of Melbourne who led the development of a new egg freezing decision aid to help people make informed choices about the procedure.
Dr Sandhu said most women who froze their eggs electively in Australia did so because they did not have a partner to co-parent with.
Other reasons included pressure from their "biological clock" and to avoid potential future regret.
Hannah (not her real name) described her own decision to freeze her eggs at 34 as "empowering", allowing her some time to consider her options following a relationship breakdown.
But four years on, Hannah is unsure about whether she will use them.
"I'm getting older and I'm not sure if I actually even want kids," she said.
"I really don't know what I'm going to do; you can only keep them on ice for so long."
Hannah is not alone. More than three in four of the women Dr Sandhu's team spoke to while researching the egg freezing decision aid felt "high uncertainty" about what to do.
"If you can understand what your decision means and the implications of it, you are less likely to regret it," Dr Sandhu said.
Dr Ameratunga said it was important for patients to have access to accurate, evidence-based information, which they could then discuss with their doctor.
"Medical misinformation is quite high in society at the minute," she said.
Egg freezing offers 'no guarantee'
Planned egg freezing was often portrayed as an insurance plan, Dr Fitzgerald said.
But his study highlighted that the procedure had limitations, with success heavily influenced by the age someone froze their eggs and the number of eggs thawed.
Ms Parle, who spent about $30,000 on egg freezing and four rounds of IVF, knows how lucky she is.
She is well aware not everyone who freezes their eggs has the same unwavering confidence in their decision or the same result as her.
"I had a very positive egg freezing experience, very successful IVF journey, and I'm very mindful of the fact that it's not how it always goes," she said.
"It's not always a guarantee."

====================================================================================================

We have always found a route to yes, says air regulator
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
19:11:52 BST
03:11:52 KST

The Military Aviation Authority has yet to meet an uncrewed system for which it could not find a path to approval, its head of regulation and certification told the Apex Europe conference in London on Wednesday, and he asked industry to keep testing that.
Commodore Neil Mathieson closed a panel on the interoperability of uncrewed systems with a short message to the companies in the room. “From a safety perspective, industry keep challenging us. I do like a challenge. We have not found any case yet where we have not found a route to yes,” he said.
Certification is triggered by a combination of size, speed, complexity and the job an aircraft is doing, by his account, with casualty evacuation and anything carrying a person taking a system firmly into the regulated category. Most of what Britain currently flies sits below that threshold, leaving one of the roughly 180 uncrewed systems in the inventory holding a certification. “Of 180 odd uncrewed systems in the UK inventory, only one is certified,” he said.
The question that prompted the answer came from the floor, from a representative of a company with an American parent and a British arm set up last year, who argued that the heavier end of the market will bring a different set of regulatory demands than the small systems dominating the discussion. He gave the example of an autonomous aircraft carrying four hundred kilograms and asked how the behaviour of the latches holding that load could be guaranteed unless the software had been engineered to a standard such as DO-178C, the civil benchmark for airborne software.
Commodore Mathieson agreed with him and set out where the heavier end of the market takes the regulator. “If we are going to get into those large uncrewed systems flying around in unsegregated airspace, potentially they will have to be certified to the same level as crewed platforms, because none of you in this room want to take off from Heathrow Airport on your way to Orlando and be hit by something that I have not certified properly that’s flying in civil airspace,” he said.
“At the moment, though, defence goes back to the demand signal. There is no demand signal in defence right now. Everyone is concentrating on the smaller stuff,” he said. “When that day comes, and it will come, we are going to have to certify things to the same standards as we’ve certified MQ-9B.” A panellist put that day at the start of next year, and observed that collaborative combat aircraft are now eight or nine tonne jets.
The MQ-9B he referred to flies in British service as Protector RG1, and its certification is the proof that the route exists. It was designed from the outset to operate in unsegregated airspace, and getting it there took sustained work between the manufacturer, the Military Aviation Authority and civil regulators, which is a reasonable guide to what the next generation of large uncrewed aircraft will need.

Morocco is also one of the five countries that have pledged to send troops to Gaza, under the US-backed International Stabilization Force (ISF) as part of US President Donald Trump’s so-called Board of Peace.

New Kyiv Business Centre opens in Ukraine
The inaugural meeting has been held at the centre, which provides a permanent foothold in Ukraine for UK companies.
The UK’s first dedicated business centre for industry in Ukraine has now opened, offering companies a permanent presence in Kyiv to deepen industrial ties with our ally.
The Kyiv Business Centre (KBC) is the first of its kind in the Ukrainian capital and is the result of close collaboration between the National Armaments Director (NAD) Group, industrial partners and finance industry, demonstrating the sustained commitment to Ukraine under the 100-Year Partnership.
The KBC gives UK companies, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), a base from which to build trusted relationships with Ukrainian partners, access battlefield insight and pursue co-development, co-production and investment opportunities.
Until now the cost, security requirements and administrative complexity of operating in Ukraine have made it prohibitively difficult for smaller firms to establish a presence in the country.
Luke Pollard, Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, said:
  Britain has stood firmly with Ukraine since the first days of Russia’s illegal invasion, and with the Kyiv Business Centre now open, we are helping to unlock new opportunities for investment, growth and long-term recovery.
By supporting UK companies in Kyiv, we are deepening the 100-Year Partnership and turning our shared resolve into shared innovation.
The KBC’s operating model is built around three principles: industry, innovation and investment, giving members access to a networking platform to help form partnerships, raise investment and scale-up production and capability.
National Armaments Director Rupert Pearce met with senior industry figures and SMEs to mark the start of the centre’s work connecting UK and Ukrainian industries.
NAD Rupert Pearce said:
  This new facility is not just a centre; it’s a permanent gateway transforming the UK’s ability to collaborate meaningfully with our Ukrainian partners now, and for the long term.
Until now the costs, security considerations and other restrictions created by Russia’s full-scale invasion have made it difficult for firms, especially smaller firms, to work in Ukraine.
Our previous Trade Missions successfully addressed some of those challenges - this centre breaks down those barriers, giving UK firms a permanent centre in Kyiv embedding real opportunities for innovation, investment and export.
It builds on more than 40 major UK-Ukraine industrial partnerships already in place and on the success of the MOD’s trade missions to Ukraine. The KBC also supports Ukrainian firms seeking UK industrial partners or establishing UK-based subsidiaries.
UK companies interested in doing business in Ukraine can find out more by emailing enquiries@kyivbusinesscentre.com, or visiting www.kyivbusinesscentre.com.

Top bosses at Goldman Sachs to share bonus pot worth up to $500m
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
18:09:14 UTC
03:09:14 KST

Top bosses at Goldman Sachs are in line to share a bonus pot worth up to $500m (£378m) this year, marking one of the biggest payouts in the Wall Street bank’s history.
The eye-watering sum will be shared between 20 bankers, with its chief executive, David Solomon, due to take about $100m (£75.6m) of the reward, which is made up of Goldman Sachs stock.
That is more than double the value of the record $47m (£35.5m) annual pay packet he was granted last year.
The $500m bonus pot is the culmination of a long-term investment plan first crafted by the bank in 2021.
The final sum, which is due to be confirmed later this month, is tied to how high Goldman’s share price has climbed over the past five years, as well as how its stock price has performed compared with peers such as JP Morgan and Bank of America over that period.
Goldman Sachs said the bonuses were meant to persuade bosses to stay at the bank “in an increasingly competitive market”.
The bank’s president, John Waldron, who is widely expected to succeed Solomon as chief executive, is also in line for a payout, alongside other top bosses such as the co-heads of global banking and markets, Ashok Varadhan and Dan Dees.
News of the bumper bonus, which was first reported by Bloomberg, comes days before Goldman is due to report third-quarter earnings on 13 October.
The bonuses reflect the value of Goldman Sachs stock, which has surged roughly 146% over the past five years, and climbed about 300% since Solomon took the helm as chief executive.
A spokesperson for the bank said: “The board created these awards to achieve three principal objectives: align compensation with rigorous performance thresholds, ensure leadership continuity and enhance retention of our top talent in an increasingly competitive market. It’s no secret our firm has performed exceptionally well in the years since.”
The payouts are the latest in a string of large payouts for executives in the US, particularly on Wall Street.
The US lender Citigroup announced earlier this year that its chief executive, Jane Fraser, had been paid a record $42m (£31.8m) for 2025. Meanwhile, JP Morgan’s chief executive, Jamie Dimon, took home a total pay package worth $43m (£32.5m) last year, up 10% from a year earlier. Dimon’s own long-term incentive award is worth about $270m (£204.1m), according to Bloomberg.

Colombian embassy to open in Jerusalem, Israeli FM says
Colombian President Abelardo De la Espriella had promised closer ties with Israel on the campaign trail.
Israel has announced that Colombia will open an embassy in Jerusalem, becoming the latest country to establish a diplomatic mission in the disputed city claimed as a capital by Israelis and Palestinians. Most countries have their embassies in Israel in Tel Aviv.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said Thursday the Latin American country’s embassy would open next week as he touted expanding relations with the region.
“Next Wednesday, we are going to inaugurate … the Colombian embassy,” Saar told attendees at a conference in Jerusalem.
An official at the Colombian Foreign Ministry in Bogota told AFP news agency the country’s Foreign Minister Omar Bula Escobar would travel to Jerusalem on Sunday ahead of the opening.
Colombian President Abelardo De la Espriella, who was sworn in as president in August, promised close relations with Israel during his election campaign. When he came into office, he restored diplomatic ties between Colombia and Israel. Colombia had previously severed ties with the country over Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza.
The announcement comes as a small but growing list of countries has opted to route their diplomatic ties with Israel through Jerusalem.
Since 2018, the US, Guatemala, Paraguay, Kosovo, Honduras, Papua New Guinea, Fiji, Nauru and Somaliland, which has been recognised as an independent entity only by Israel, have opened embassies in the city.
Other countries that have diplomatic relations with Israel have located their embassies in Tel Aviv, as Jerusalem is not recognised by the international community as Israel’s capital.
“We will work hard because this is the diplomatic battle over the truth. And the truth is, Jerusalem was always the capital of one nation,” Saar said, dismissing Palestinian claims to the capital.
The Israeli minister said the Democratic Republic of the Congo would open its embassy in Jerusalem “very soon” and hinted at another opening.
“I think that with the possible results in Brazil, they might have the same move,” he said after right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro won the first round in the country’s presidential election.
Protesters in Colombia took to the streets of Bogota on Wednesday to rally against the new far-right government’s policy towards Israel, including the decision to open the Jerusalem embassy.
“When diplomatic relations with Israel were broken off, the message was that we would not be a nation complicit in their atrocities,” Nicolas Isaza, who took part in the protest, told Al Jazeera.
“Today our government is no longer drawing a line against the atrocities being committed in Palestine,” he added.

Trump made ‘clear’ that media ban was due to critical coverage, court told
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
17:56:04 UTC
02:56:04 KST

Donald Trump continues to be the strongest witness for the media companies arguing that they were unfairly barred from the White House at his direction, a lawyer representing CNN, MS Now and Politico told a federal judge on Thursday afternoon.
The media coalition was in court asking the judge to extend the temporary restraining order (TRO) he issued on 24 September requiring the White House to lift the ban for 14 days. That temporary reprieve was scheduled to expire on Thursday, but district court judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, said he would extend it until Tuesday and that he would probably rule on a motion for a preliminary injunction by that day. That means the White House will be forced to allow journalists from CNN, MS Now and Politico to continue accessing the building until at least Tuesday.
Theodore J Boutrous, who has represented numerous media companies that have sued the Trump administration over access issues, said the president made abundantly clear in a recent interview with Time magazine that he chose to bar the three news organizations because of their critical coverage of him. (Under binding court precedent, news organizations cannot be removed from the White House for editorial or viewpoint-based reasons.)
Asked by Time for the “impetus” for the ban, Trump replied: “It’s just bad story after bad story, and when I say bad story, I can handle bad stories. I’ve got a lot of bad stories. Most of them are fake, and it’s not only CNN, and it’s not only MSDNC [sic]. It’s a lot of other people.” He made no mention of national security concerns, one of the primary reasons that has been given by government lawyers as a rationale for the ban.
“The case has gotten stronger for the plaintiffs thanks to President Trump,” Boutrous told the judge, citing what he said was “a confession of viewpoint discrimination and retaliation”. He added: “It’s really just absolutely clear … President Trump, to give him credit – he’s not hiding it.”
While the judge didn’t give a strong indication of which direction he was leaning, he accepted Boutrous’s argument when questioning the lone lawyer representing the White House, Michael Velchik.
“The decision-maker seems to have said I’m taking this action because of X and Y, and the government is saying: ‘No, it’s Z,’” the judge said. “It just seems like that fact pattern is a hard one around.”
Velchik, who began his argument by saying “the White House is a sacred place,” said a failure to adhere to basic standards of journalistic conduct was also one of the precipitating factors in the decision, something he said was in line with Trump’s comments criticizing the way that these three specific news organizations operate.
He also faulted the media companies for not responding to post-hoc letters giving the plaintiffs a chance to rebut the charges against them, something that Boutrous later described as a “sham process”.
In his ruling granting a TRO for the media plaintiffs, Kelly said the White House had violated constitutional requirements for due process by not giving the companies adequate notice for what the standards for acceptable conduct are and not giving them a chance to protest against the potential sanction in advance.
Nothing from Thursday’s hearing seemed to indicate that the judge had changed his thinking on that important standard, suggesting he is likely to adhere to his earlier decision-making and extend the lifting of the ban.
The judge told the government’s lawyer that they “still have a notice problem, it seems to [him], or at least a notice issue”. Kelly said the standards for adequate advance notice laid out in a binding circuit case involving a similar White House access issue “are probably the biggest hurdle you have”.

US, Russia confirm Trump's latest Ukraine peace push is falling apart
Ending Russia's war against Ukraine through negotiations is currently unattainable, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Greek media outlet Kathimerini on Oct. 8, casting further doubt on President Donald Trump's latest push to broker peace.
The comments confirm earlier Kyiv Independent reporting that Washington's latest effort to advance negotiations faces growing uncertainty.
At this point, there appears to be no prospect of a negotiated settlement, Rubio said. He added that the goal remains out of reach because Russia insists on gaining full control over Ukraine's Donetsk Oblast without fighting, a demand Kyiv has rejected.
The latest rounds of peace negotiations have also stalled over Moscow's territorial demands.
The Kremlin has repeatedly rejected a ceasefire and demanded that Kyiv surrender the partially occupied Donbas, a strategically important region in eastern Ukraine. Moscow is effectively seeking territory that Russian forces have failed to capture militarily.
Ukraine has instead called for a ceasefire along the current front line.
The diplomatic effort now faces another obstacle: Moscow has given little indication that it intends to take part in further talks. Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov said on Oct. 7 that there were currently no plans for U.S.-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine.
"There are currently no plans to hold talks in this format," Ryabkov told reporters.
The latest effort began in early September, when Trump's envoys traveled to Kyiv and Moscow seeking progress before the U.S. midterm elections. The trips produced one tangible outcome: an agreement in principle to hold a trilateral meeting between Ukraine, Russia, and the U.S.
A month later, however, even the trilateral meeting remains uncertain.

UK ramps up sanctions against Russian shadow fleet, crypto industry, big oil
The U.K. published 38 new sanctions listings on Oct. 8, targeting ships helping Russia evade existing sanctions and a range of companies in Moscow's military-industrial complex, energy, and cryptocurrency sectors.
"The message is simple: if you help Russia fund or equip this war, you will face the consequences," reads a U.K. government press release.
Among the businesses in the new sanctions listings are three cryptocurrency exchanges and two payment platforms.
Xeltox Enterprises, one of those listed entities has "been involved in obtaining a benefit from or supporting the government of Russia by carrying on business in a sector of strategic significance (...) the financial services sector," reads the U.K. government's sanctions listing.
Russia has increasingly sought to use cryptocurrency, which is hard to track, to circumvent global sanctions, and the new U.K. sanctions target the "A7" network, which is at the heart of Moscow's attempts to evade financial sanctions.
That has prompted the U.K., the U.S., the EU, and Ukraine to target crypto schemes in recent sanctions packages.
Also featuring on the listings are two further oil companies: Zarubezhneft and INK Capital.
"The U.K. was the first country in the G7 to sanction the top four Russian oil companies," reads the press statement.
The U.K. has also added 12 ships to its list of sanctioned vessels accused of being part of Russia's shadow fleet — dilapidated vessels suspected of helping Moscow evade price caps and bans on its trade in oil and gas.
That takes the number of ships sanctioned by the U.K. to 645 and the total number of Russia sanctions to 3,537.
