Wired for War: The German spymaster caught in Mossad’s web
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
17:53:45 UTC
02:53:45 KST

Wired for War: The German spymaster caught in Mossad’s web
It took a bungled kidnapping for Germany’s former spymaster to be charged with espionage and treason, but August Hanning’s ties to Israeli spies and criminals should have set alarm bells ringing in Berlin long ago.
Hanning, who led Germany’s Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND) from 1998 to 2005, was arrested on Tuesday and charged with espionage, the disclosure of state secrets, and treason.
Prosecutors have alleged that Hanning bought state secrets from his former BND aide – identified as ‘Manfred D’, who remained in the agency after Hanning’s departure and served several of his successors. They claim Hanning acquired nearly 2,000 BND documents between 2010 and 2022, which he then leveraged in his work as a private security consultant at-large to the rich and powerful.
Hanning, part of the woodwork on the security conference circuit, used this material to prepare a report for an employee of a foreign intelligence service, and maintained “close contact with a representative of another foreign intelligence service,” to whom he passed information obtained by Manfred D “for several years.”
Prosecutors haven’t identified which foreign services Hanning collaborated with, though media reporting suggests one is believed to be the Foreign Intelligence Service of Azerbaijan, a country Hanning has openly lobbied for since the mid-2010s. As for the other, Hanning’s involvement in a bizarre kidnapping plot suggests one obvious culprit.
The Israeli kidnapping plot
German investigators picked up Hanning’s trail last September, when Hamburg police searched his apartment as part of an investigation involving multi-millionaire Christina Block, whose father built Germany’s most popular steakhouse chain, as well as a burger franchise, boutique hotels and gastro-resorts.
Ms. Block has been in a custody dispute with her ex-husband, Danish banker Stefan Hansel, since 2021. She is currently on trial for ordering the kidnapping of her two youngest children from their father’s care in Denmark. According to prosecutors, Block hired Hanning’s consulting firm, System 360, to carry out the abduction in 2022, but Danish police intervened before the System 360 team could snatch the children.
Hanning apparently gave up on the direct approach and decided to outsource the job to his contacts from the world of intelligence. These contacts were Yaakov Perry, the former chief of Israel’s Shin Bet domestic intelligence agency, and Danny Yatom, the former head of Mossad.
Block’s trial is ongoing and details are murky, but the allegations are as follows: Hanning hired Perry and his private intelligence firm, CGI Group, to assemble an eight-man team to kidnap the children; the German spymaster requested that Yatom be involved; Perry brought in David Barkay, a former member of the IDF’s Unit 504 intelligence wing and alleged Mossad agent; Barkay led the team that carried out the kidnapping on New Year’s Eve, 2023.
Barkay’s team assaulted Hansel and dragged the children – a ten-year-old boy and 13-year-old girl – across the German border on foot, taping their mouths shut and threatening to kill them if they screamed for help.
Hanning denies any role in the kidnapping, as does Yaakov. Barkay has confessed to orchestrating and carrying out the operation, but has not implicated Hanning or Yaakov. Yatom has told Israeli media that he has “no connection to this case,” and furthermore, that his relationship with Hanning was a strictly professional one dating back to the late 1980s.
However, Yatom invited Hanning to join the board of his private cybersecurity company, World Health Energy Holdings (WHEN), in 2021. Speaking to the Jerusalem Post at the time, Hanning said that his “contacts with states, law enforcement and intelligence agencies” would be valuable to WHEN, a company that markets spyware to businesses seeking to monitor their employees.
Hanning added that he maintained “very close working relationships, even friendships” with Yatom and other Mossad officials long after he left the BND. Both men are still listed as board members on WHEN’s website.
The gray man
During his tenure at the BND, Hanning was the consummate ‘gray man’ of intelligence: a gaunt and bespectacled bureaucrat in the mould of John le Carre’s ‘George Smiley’. Le Carre met Hanning several times, and described the German spymaster as “courtesy itself.”
Yet his “career was clouded by speculation about his loyalties, with persistent whispers of too-close-for-comfort ties to Israel and Russia,” according to a recent Irish Times report. Prosecutors have ruled out any suspicion that Hanning colluded with Russian agents, according to German media, leaving only one possibility.
Hanning once remarked that “a good agent is one who doesn’t draw attention to himself.” In the murky world of Israel’s ‘private’ intelligence sector, however, Hanning could hardly have chosen a more conspicuous duo to work with than Yatom and Perry.
The Congo debacle
Perry’s private intelligence firm, CGI Group, is an outfit that will sound familiar to readers of our ‘Wired for War’ series. Founded by former Israeli spies and specializing in illegal or quasi-legal private spycraft, the company boasts that it hires “senior personnel from elite IDF units, the General Security Services and the Mossad.” Among them are:
- Yaakov Perry, president, Shin Bet Director from 1988 to 1995
- Zvika Nave, founder, described by CGI as serving “in many classified positions in the defense system”
- Oren Ziv, Italy manager, described by CGI as a “key figure in Israeli diplomacy and national security”
- Alon Pinkas, consultant, former foreign policy adviser to Israeli Prime Ministers Ehud Barak and Shimon Peres, former Israeli Consul General in New York
Before its alleged involvement in the Block kidnapping, CGI Group became infamous when it attempted to steal $60 million from the Bulgarian government in 2019. Some 30 years earlier, Israeli businessman Gad Zeevi attempted to buy a stake in Bulgaria’s national airline, but the deal fell apart and Zeevi claimed that he was owed $10 million in compensation from Sofia. International arbitrators agreed, but Bulgaria refused to comply with the judgment, and the Israeli government refused to chase the Bulgarians down for the money.
Zeevi reached out to Perry and Nave, who came up with a long-shot scheme to collect the debt. CGI Group would ask the government of the Congo to order $60 million worth of weapons from Bulgaria, with Yatom acting as a go-between. Once the Bulgarians had sent the arms and the Congolese government transferred the money to his account, Yatom would hand it to Zeevi, minus a generous cut for him and his co-conspirators in CGI Group.
It was never clear how CGI would convince the Congolese to order weapons that would never be paid for, and the plan never came to fruition. Zeevi and CGI Group threatened to sue each other for damages, but the case never made it to court.
Yatom and CGI Group refused to comment, giving similar answers as they did when questioned about the Block kidnapping. “I don’t want to talk about my business activities,” Yatom told Israel’s Globes news outlet in 2022. “We don’t talk to the media,” Nave said.
Red flags ignored
Despite the fact that Yatom and the CGI spies colluded to defraud a NATO and EU member state in 2019, German investigators didn’t ask questions when Hanning joined Yatom’s company two years later. No investigation was opened when he spoke to the Israeli media of his “close friendship” with the former Mossad chief behind the swindle. Hanning’s ties to the Israeli intelligence underworld, apparently the subject of “persistent whispers” in the corridors of the BND, were evidently brushed aside or ignored.
None of this is to say that Shin Bet or Mossad is, without a doubt, the “foreign intelligence service” that Hanning passed secrets to. However, his contacts with Perry and Yatom certainly point that way, as does his work to advance Israeli foreign policy goals.
Hanning aided Israeli efforts to push the US into war with Iraq in late 2002, when he told then-CIA Director George Tenet that the BND had “plausible and convincing” evidence that Saddam Hussein was developing chemical and biological weapons. Hanning’s source, an Iraqi defector codenamed ‘Curveball’, later admitted to fabricating the claims.
Hanning now sits on the board of ‘United Against Nuclear Iran’, a Washington-based think tank funded by pro-Israel megadonors Miriam Adelson and Thomas Kaplan, which has explicitly advocated for military strikes on Iran since 2008. Adelson and Kaplan supply around three quarters of the group’s funding, with the remainder coming from smaller Jewish organizations and individual donors.
Europe’s wilful ignorance
Anyone following our ‘Wired for War’ series will recognize the pattern here. Over and over again, the actions of private Israeli spy firms are ignored by European governments, even when the Israeli state itself is involved in the skulduggery. The British government has refused to investigate Israeli meddling in Scottish elections, in order to “avoid giving offense” to the perpetrators. The EU has stayed silent on Israeli interference in elections in Cyprus and Slovenia, and on the proliferation of Israeli spyware throughout the union.
Meanwhile, governments at the EU and national level continue to sound the alarm about Russia’s invisible and unprovable “hybrid war” against the West. Fires, false drone sightings, and even natural disasters are all presented as examples of this shadow war, while the most blatant malfeasance from other foreign powers is ignored.
One day before Hanning’s arrest, his successor at the helm of the BND, Martin Jaeger, warned German MPs that Russia is “waging a shadow war,” and that “no other country currently poses such a direct, comprehensive, and concrete threat to Germany.” Had he looked at the company August Hanning kept, he might have reassessed his position.

Callous Kallas: The bitter diplomat dragging the EU down the warpath with Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
17:53:32 UTC
02:53:32 KST

Callous Kallas: The bitter diplomat dragging the EU down the warpath with Russia
Kaja Kallas, the Estonian diplomat and former prime minister currently serving as the vice-president of the European Commission, has shown a deeply confrontational attitude towards Russia and the Russians.
It is perhaps worth pausing here to note that this is particularly personal, given her family history. Her mother, Kristi Kallas, was only six months old when she, together with her mother and grandmother, was deported to Siberia during the Soviet mass deportations of March 1949. She remained there until she was ten, and later studied medicine and worked as a pediatrician.
Her father, Siim Kallas, had a very different experience with the Soviet system. He was a member of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union from 1972 to 1990 and held senior positions in the financial system of Soviet Estonia, including heading the Estonian branch of the USSR Savings Bank. He later became President of the Bank of Estonia, Prime Minister of Estonia and a Vice-President of the European Commission.
These two sides of her family history – one marked by deportation and the other by a successful career within the Soviet system – form a striking background to Kaja Kallas’s present-day political position.
Last month, Kallas described the German people as being blind to the Russian threat because of their resistance to providing further financial support to Ukraine. Now, I suppose Russian people are also considered blind because of the convincing victory of President Vladimir Putin’s party in September’s legislative election. I am definitely not blind.
Kaja Kallas is not alone in her hostility towards Russia. Other senior EU officials, including European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, have supported substantial financial and military assistance to Ukraine. The EU has committed up to €90 billion in support for Ukraine for 2026 and 2027, including funding for both defense and general budgetary needs.
The question Europeans should be allowed to ask is how these decisions affect their own societies. Public money is limited, and European citizens also need investment in healthcare, education, transport, housing and infrastructure.
Since 2022, Europeans have been paying a heavy price for the transformation of their energy system. The decision to move away from Russian pipeline gas was made in the name of security, and the EU has succeeded in diversifying its supplies. But security has come at a considerable economic cost. The European Commission reports that although wholesale energy prices have fallen substantially from the extraordinary peaks of 2022, industrial gas and electricity prices remain two to four times higher than in the EU’s main trading partners. The Commission warns that this continues to threaten the long-term competitiveness of European industry.
The EU’s energy import bill reached €604 billion in 2022 before falling to €427 billion in 2024. Meanwhile, industrial energy prices remain considerably above their pre-crisis levels. Germany, the industrial heart of Europe, has felt the consequences particularly sharply. German industrial energy consumption fell by 9.1% in 2022 and another 7.8% in 2023, with the German Federal Statistical Office explicitly linking these declines, particularly in energy-intensive industries, to significantly higher energy prices and associated production reductions.
Germany’s broader economic performance tells the same story. Its economy contracted for a second consecutive year in 2024, while manufacturing gross value added fell by 3%. The Federal Statistical Office identified high energy costs, together with stronger international competition and other structural pressures, among the factors weighing on the economy. Manufacturing remained under pressure in 2025, when value added in the sector fell another 1.3%.
Europe faces an uncomfortable question: Is it prepared to accept permanently higher energy costs while production and investment increasingly move towards countries where energy and manufacturing costs are lower? It is one thing to pursue energy security; it is another to allow the foundations of European industry to become the price of achieving it.
The issue of NATO and Ukraine is equally contentious. The argument that NATO expansion towards Ukraine ruined Moscow’s relations with Europe is not just a Kremlin talking point – reputable Western analysts, like Professor Jeffrey Sachs, have repeatedly argued the same point. Even if that analysis remains disputed, it is an argument that deserves to be heard in any serious discussion of the origins and continuation of the war, which continues to have devastating consequences for Ukrainians.
European leaders should be asking what policies can bring the conflict closer to a negotiated settlement rather than simply allowing the confrontation to continue indefinitely.
Perhaps the most revealing part of this story is that the argument is no longer simply between the EU and its critics. It has begun to unfold within Europe itself.
Defense spending in the EU is rising at an extraordinary pace. According to the Council of the EU, member states spent €418 billion on defense in 2025, and expenditure is estimated to reach €454 billion in 2026 – 75.3% higher than in 2021. Defense investment alone is projected to reach almost €163 billion in 2026.
But the question of who decides how this enormous effort should be organized is becoming increasingly contentious. In September, Kaja Kallas withdrew plans for a new high-level advisory group on European defense after several member states objected. Reporting by Defense News and Euractiv identified Germany, France and Italy among the governments pushing back against the initiative. The German position was that NATO remains the primary framework for military capability and defense planning.
The disagreement was not about whether Europe needs defense. It was about who should set priorities, how decisions should be coordinated, and whether another Brussels structure was the right way forward. Even as European governments prepare to spend hundreds of billions more on defense, there is no agreement about the political direction those resources should serve.
The EU, in other words, is having two conversations at once: how much it should spend, and what kind of Europe that spending is meant to create.
Ms. Kallas, Europe needs diplomacy as well as security policy. European citizens need their governments to protect their interests, use public money responsibly and keep open the possibility of a peaceful future.
If the EU continues indefinitely along the present path, the economic and political consequences for European societies will deserve much greater public discussion.
EU citizens have the right to ask difficult questions about how their money is being spent and what kind of Europe they want to build. They may disagree strongly about Russia, Ukraine and NATO, but that does not make their questions illegitimate.
I was born in Ireland and have been affiliated with Russia for thirty years. I have been living here for the last eight years. From that perspective, I believe Europeans should be able to discuss these issues without being dismissed as blind, naïve or sympathetic to one side simply because they question current policies.
Europe has enormous resources and enormous human potential. With wiser choices about priorities, Europeans should be able to expect excellent healthcare, education, transport and infrastructure alongside a responsible security policy.
The statements, views and opinions expressed in this column are solely those of the author and do not necessarily represent those of RT.

Diia explains how to file Europrotocol in event of traffic accident
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
20:52:45 EEST
02:52:45 KST

The Diia app now features a function for filing a Europrotocol report, which allows users to report a traffic accident via their smartphone without calling the patrol police or filling out a paper form.
According to a statement from the Diia press service on Thursday, to use the service, users must update the Diia app and navigate to the "Services," "Driver," and "Europrotocol" sections.
Next, users should verify the details; specifically, information about the drivers, vehicles, and insurance policies will be automatically retrieved from government registries.
The press service added that drivers will need to fill out the details of the accident and upload photos of the damaged vehicles at the scene. Subsequently, drivers will receive the other driver's consent and signature via a QR code or a notification in the Diia app.
It is noted that after completing these preliminary steps, users will need to sign the document using Diia.Sign and submit it. It is expected that after both parties have successfully signed the document, the app will automatically submit the Europrotocol to the Motor Transport Insurance Bureau of Ukraine (MTIBU), and MTIBU will subsequently forward it to the insurance companies.
"Next, contact your insurance company for further instructions," Diia said.
According to the press release, before filing the claim, you should ensure that no one is injured, that only two vehicles were involved in the accident, that neither driver is under the influence of alcohol or drugs, that both have valid MTPL insurance policies, and that they have reached an agreement regarding the circumstances of the accident.
It is expected that drivers who have the following in Diia at the same time can complete the Europrotocol: a verified RNOKPP (IPN), a digital passport (ID card), foreign passport, or residence permit, a driver's license, and a vehicle registration certificate – as the owner or authorized user – as well as a valid MTPL policy for the vehicle involved in the accident.
"In other cases, fill out a paper Europrotocol or call the police," Diia said.

Several explosions were heard in Saudi Arabia's capital on Thursday, including a large blast at Riyadh’s international airport, according to reports, a day after the kingdom said an attack on the civil aviation hub killed one person and wounded others.

Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighboring Yemen claimed responsibility for the new attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, saying the ballistic missile caused damage but giving no evidence. The Saudis had no immediate comment about the claim.

The spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition fighting the rebels, Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki, said they intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis toward Riyadh, along with a ballistic missile fired toward Khamis Mushait, in the southwest near the Yemen border.
Saudi civil defense authorities said debris from an interception damaged a kindergarten and a medical complex, with no mention of any casualties.
The Houthis have repeatedly claimed attacks against Saudi airports, military and oil facilities in recent days.

Also Wednesday, the spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition said forces destroyed a platform in Yemen's rebel-held capital of Sanaa that had been used to launch attacks on the Saudi capital.
Saudi Arabia has sought support from allies, including the United States, in the face of the Houthi attacks. Officials have said U.S. support has included intelligence sharing, target identification and planning for the latest offensive.

Russia’s censorship agency bans two dystopian novels by Olga Ptitseva about an alternate Russia ruled by the ‘Party of Cold’

Russia’s censorship agency bans two dystopian novels by Olga Ptitseva about an alternate Russia ruled by the ‘Party of Cold’
Russia’s communications regulator, Roskomnadzor, has banned Olga Ptitseva’s novels “Dvesti trety den zimy” (“The 203rd Day of Winter”) and “Vesna vody” (“Spring of Water”). A notice appeared on the God Literatury portal on October 7, Vyorstka reported.
“The book in question has been added to Roskomnadzor’s Unified Register of Prohibited Information and the Registry of Book Assessments kept by the Russian Book Union’s expert center and must be withdrawn from public circulation in Russia,” the website said.
On October 2, Roskomnadzor ordered the portal to remove information about “Vesna vody.” On July 16, the portal had removed information about “Dvesti trety den zimy,” the first book of the duology, at the regulator’s request.
The books have also disappeared from the website of their publisher, Polyandria No Age, and from the catalogs of LitRes and Chitai-Gorod. Polyandria confirmed that Roskomnadzor had banned them. The ban may have been prompted by signs of “propaganda of nontraditional sexual relationships” in the books, The Blueprint reported.
The two novels form a dystopian duology set in an alternate Russia, where eternal winter sets in after the Party of Cold comes to power. Residents are required to maintain a prescribed level of snow cover, food is distributed using ration cards, and dissenters are sent to freezers.
Ptitseva confirmed that her books had been withdrawn from sale. “Friends, it’s true that DTDZ [the novel ‘Dvesti trety den zimy’] has been pulled from sale, but I’m OK. Hugs to all of you,” she said on her Telegram channel.
Olga Ptitseva has written several novels and collections of contemporary prose. In 2023, her novel “Tam, gde tsvetet polyn” (“Where Wormwood Blooms”) was adapted into a television series of the same name. A year later, the book was nominated for the Yasnaya Polyana literary prize in the Youth category. Her novel “Vyidi iz shkafa” (“Come Out of the Closet”) was shortlisted for the FICTION35 prize, while “Krai chudes” (“Land of Wonders”) was longlisted for the Lyceum prize.

NATO announced plans to begin its annual nuclear deterrence exercises in Italy on Tuesday, as growing concerns over Russia heighten security tensions across Europe.
Its "Steadfast Noon" drills will run from Oct. 13 to 23 and will involve 17 nations, it said Thursday.
"The exercise is a long-planned, routine training activity that is part of NATO's efforts to maintain readiness and test procedures that contribute to the alliance's deterrence and defence," said a NATO statement.
"No live weapons are used in Steadfast Noon. The exercise is not linked to current world events and is not directed against any country," the alliance added.

Russia, embroiled in an invasion of Ukraine since 2022, has accused NATO of staging "provocative" actions around its exclave of Kaliningrad.
It has warned that it is ready to use "its entire arsenal."
NATO condemned the comments, but its officials say the alliance has not seen major changes in Russia's nuclear posture.

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
17:37:30 UTC
02:37:30 KST

Fabien Mandon is pictured upon arrival at the Elysée Palace in Paris for a defense council meeting on Sept. 16, 2026. | Benjamin Vodant/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images
PARIS — France's top general Fabien Mandon admitted on Thursday that the Franco-German next-generation battle tank project had failed.
It's one of the first times a French official has publicly acknowledged that the plans have faltered, after months of speculation about the fate of the Main Combat Ground System.
"The outcome isn't good. We had hoped to build a future tank in cooperation with the Germans, but unfortunately, we have to acknowledge that the Germans have withdrawn from the project," the French chief of defense staff told lawmakers during a hearing on next year's budget.
Advertisement
MGCS — which involves KNDS France, KNDS Germany, Rheinmetall and Thales — has been bogged down by years of delays, industrial disputes and political tensions. POLITICO reported in June that the next-generation tank project was increasingly doomed.
Mandon's admission comes only a few months after another high-stakes Franco-German defense industrial program — the Future Combat Air System — abruptly ended.
However, answering a question from a far-right National Rally lawmaker, the French general pushed back against the word "failure" to describe the MGCS's fate.
"It's not a complete failure; it's an important decision by Germany, but our land forces have worked together for several years to determine what a future main battle tank should look like," he said. "It wasn't a waste of time. But from an industrial standpoint, this isn't good news."

Russian attacks plunge Kyiv into near-total darkness, disrupt power, metro, water supply

Russian attacks plunge Kyiv into near-total darkness, disrupt power, metro, water supply
Residential buildings are seen without power during widespread outages following Russian attacks on Kyiv, Ukraine on Oct. 8, 2026. (Olga Rudenko / The Kyiv Independent)
Editor's note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
The Russian attack on Ukrainian energy infrastructure on Oct. 8 has caused widespread power outages across the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, home to over 3 million people.
As of 8 p.m. local time, the city was experiencing power outages in most neighborhoods, with the city metro shut down due to lack of electricity. Lack of power has also led to many residents reporting lack of running water.
"There was an attack on one of the energy facilities important for the city of Kyiv," Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal said. "Energy workers are doing everything possible to restore electricity as quickly as possible."
Kyiv Independent reporters across the city observed power cuts in Podil, Pechersk, Solomianskyi districts, and the left bank. Ahead of winter, the sound of generators returned to Kyiv throughout affected neighborhoods, as businesses sought to keep operating.
The drop in voltage temporarily halted Kyiv Metro train services and escalator operations, the Kyiv City State Administration (KMDA) said. Other parts of the capital's public transport network were also affected.
The city administration said that some services had been temporarily suspended because of the drop in voltage, while authorities were working to replace part of the Borshchahivka high-speed tram line with buses.
Kyiv Independent reporters described heavy traffic, people hailing taxis, and streets filling with people, as commuters sought alternative transportation.
The power disruption also affected Kyiv's water network. The city administration warned that residents on the right bank could experience interruptions in water supply because lower voltage had reduced pressure in the system, particularly in the Holosiivskyi, Sviatoshynskyi, Solomianskyi, and Shevchenkivskyi districts.
Earlier on Oct. 8, Ukraine's largest private energy company, DTEK, announced emergency power shutdowns in parts of Kyiv Oblast, including the Brovary, Bucha, Vyshhorod, and Boryspil districts.
The Kyiv Oblast Military Administration said Russia had significantly intensified attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure in recent weeks, targeting power lines and transformers and disrupting electricity transmission to consumers.
Energy workers are operating around the clock to repair damaged equipment and stabilize the grid, the administration said.
The disruptions followed a morning of repeated Russian drone strikes on Kyiv and the surrounding region that killed and injured civilians and damaged buildings and infrastructure.
Russian drone strikes on Oct. 8 have killed four people and injured at least 19 in Kyiv, the city's Mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said.
As of the publication time, the attack on Kyiv was ongoing.

UK plans to announce ban on workers’ non-compete clauses in push for growth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
17:34:20 UTC
02:34:20 KST

Andy Burnham gives a TV interview following his meeting with the German chancellor in Berlin on Oct. 8, 2026. | Pool photo by Sean Gallup/AFP via Getty Images
LONDON — The U.K. government is planning to commit to a full or partial ban on non-compete clauses in workers’ employment contracts, six people with knowledge of the discussions told POLITICO.
All six of the people, who were granted anonymity to discuss government policy, said they believed an announcement is due imminently and could be made as soon as Friday. Three of those people said they believed the announcement was likely to be fronted personally by Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who is expected to give a speech Friday.
The government of Burnham’s predecessor, Keir Starmer, set out options in November 2025 to limit the use of non-compete clauses, which aim to restrict a person’s ability to work for or set up a competing business after they leave their job.
Advertisement
The founders of more than 20 U.K. tech start-ups wrote to the government last month saying the restrictions, along with long notice periods and enforced gardening leave, were and “undermin[ing] the innovation that drives economic growth”.
The options set out 11 months ago ranged from a total ban on non-compete clauses to a partial ban, such as allowing non-compete clauses only for workers earning more than a set salary threshold, or limiting their length.
However, two of the six people quoted above said that the government would stop short of backing a specific option at this stage.
Ministers are expected to set out a broad intention of ensuring that non-compete clauses are no longer a hiring problem for start-ups and innovative firms, but finer details will be worked out further down the line in consultation with industry.
No. 10 declined to comment.
The announcement comes after Chancellor John Healey said he wanted to tackle the costs for businesses in his budget on Oct. 28. One of the six people quoted above said: “They want to sell it as pro growth and freeing up the labour market.”
Advertisement
AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said last week that the government was “working extremely rapidly” on potential changes to the system.
Non-compete clauses are common in the financial services industry. The lobby group TheCityUK opposed a ban earlier this year, arguing that non-compete clauses “promote competition and innovation in high-value industries” as they are often the “only way to pre-emptively protect confidential information and intellectual property.”
The government argued last year that even though non-compete clauses are “unenforceable” as a starting point under current law, ministers were “concerned about the behavioural effect of including a non-compete clause in an employment contract. Even if broadly drafted and unlikely to be enforceable, workers may perceive the clause as binding and comply with it for fear of legal repercussions.”

Switzerland national football team and Sunderland captain Granit Xhaka said Thursday that he received a suspended fine of 150,000 Swiss francs ($180,000) after admitting to obtaining a fake coronavirus vaccination certificate during the pandemic.
The 34-year-old midfielder said the penalty, comprising 50 daily fines of 3,000 francs, would not be enforced if he committed no additional offenses during a two-year probation period.
"I accept the decision and take responsibility," Xhaka wrote on US social media platform Instagram.
Xhaka admitted last month that he obtained the certificate in 2022 because of his mistrust of COVID-19 vaccines, describing his decision as a mistake.
The case was investigated by prosecutors in the Swiss canton of Lucerne, where Xhaka provided a statement.
Xhaka, Switzerland's most-capped male footballer with 152 appearances, missed four recent UEFA Nations League matches after he and the Swiss Football Association agreed that he would sit out the international window.
The Swiss Football Association said it would hold additional discussions with Xhaka following the conclusion of legal proceedings.

Germany withdrawing from joint tank project: French military chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
17:32:47 UTC
02:32:47 KST

Necva Tastan Sevinc
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
Germany has decided to withdraw from a project with France to develop a future battle tank, French Chief of the Defence Staff Gen. Fabien Mandon said Thursday, the French broadcaster BFMTV reported.
“The Germans have decided to leave the project,” he said, referring to the Main Ground Combat System (MGCS).
“This is not a complete failure, it is an important German choice. Our land forces have worked together for several years to consider what a future battle tank should be,” he said at a National Assembly hearing.
Mandon stressed that the work had established the tank’s main principles, while acknowledging that the withdrawal was “not good news from an industrial point of view.”
The MGCS program was launched in 2017 to replace France’s Leclerc and Germany’s Leopard 2 tanks with a ground combat system centered on a new tank.
The project has faced delays and disagreements on industrial work-sharing, financing and technological choices, with deployment pushed toward 2040 or 2045, the broadcaster reported.
Mandon said France still needed a heavy combat capability, emphasizing the continued relevance of tank firepower.
He urged complementary platforms incorporating robots, artificial intelligence and greater data sharing, potentially requiring fewer personnel to operate.
“We will have a gradual withdrawal of the Leclerc starting in 2038. In 2027, we must launch the studies to be ready for this deadline,” he said.
The announcement marks another setback for Franco-German defense cooperation, coming four months after the failure of the Future Combat Air System project.
That program, also launched in 2017 and involving Spain, was intended to develop a next-generation fighter aircraft to replace the Rafale and Eurofighter sometime in the 2040s.

US suspends Microsoft and Adobe from visa programme amid fraud claims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
17:25:02 UTC
02:25:02 KST

US suspends Microsoft and Adobe from visa programme amid fraud claims
Visa probe also targets universities for allegedly exploiting international students to reduce US wage costs.
The United States government is suspending several major tech companies, including Adobe and Microsoft, from a programme that gives skilled foreign workers a path to permanent residency amid allegations of fraud.
The move comes as the White House ramps up pressure on companies to hire more Americans. “Our message to Microsoft is: You’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers,” US Vice President JD Vance said at a news conference on Thursday.
Vance claimed that the Redmond, Washington-based tech giant laid off 6,000 American workers while obtaining 6,300 H-1B foreign work visas and almost 3,000 permanent residencies known as green cards.
“You cannot lay off American workers and replace them with foreign indentured servants,” Vance said.
Across the technology sector, there have been more than 131,000 layoffs in 2026 alone, according to Layoffs.fyi, which tracks job cuts across the tech and startup industries.
“When someone comes in, they are completely subordinate to that company. If they lose that job, they have to leave the country.”
Microsoft pushed back on Vance’s claims in a blog post, saying that “80 percent of the visas were to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees.”
“The remaining filings for new employees were for individuals already legally in the United States who decided to come work for us, and they equal only 1% of our U.S. workforce. They are not new arrivals to our country,” the company said in the post.
Microsoft is No 5 among US employers when it comes to using H-1B visas, according to data from US Citizenship and Immigration Services. Amazon is No 1.
Adobe did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.
Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling also said that several major information technology firms will be suspended from the programme as well. Among them are Indian tech giants Infosys and Tata Consultancy Services.
The H-1B programme has long been a target of supporters of US President Donald Trump who say that the programme undercuts American workers and is rife with abuse.
H-1B visas are meant for high-skilled jobs that are difficult to find US workers to fill. Technology companies are the biggest users, with nearly three-quarters of approvals going to workers from India.
The Department of Labor also said it had uncovered $22bn worth of visa fraud.
“Today we are protecting something far more valuable than any dollar amount. We are protecting the American worker,” Sonderling said.
The news came hours before Trump was to honour Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella with the National Medal of Technology and Innovation. India-born Nadella was one of six business leaders to be awarded on Thursday. Five of the leaders were foreign-born, including Tesla boss Elon Musk and Google co-founder Sergey Brin.
Crackdown on universities
During the news conference, officials also announced a crackdown on alleged J-1 visa fraud involving nine universities, including MIT, Harvard, Yale, Stanford and Cal State, amid allegations that they brought in international students to undercut US wages. A J-1 visa allows foreign nationals to enter the US temporarily for education or cultural programmes. Universities use these visas to bring in international PhD candidates or scholars.
Vance claimed that when schools employ an American as a researcher, that person earns $20,000 more than someone brought in under a J-1 visa.
Al Jazeera asked for data supporting this claim, but the White House did not respond.
Microsoft’s stock slumped 1.5 percent on the heels of the news, while Adobe was up 2.1 percent in late day trading on Thursday.

During his first visit to Ukraine in this capacity, British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced nearly EUR 64 million in additional winter aid for Ukraine and reaffirmed continued support for Kyiv.
According to the British government, Miliband announced a winter resilience funding package totaling GBP 54 million (EUR 63.73 million). He also noted that today's new sanctions mean that more than 90% of Russia's total oil production capacity is now covered by the UK's sanctions regime.
The government said the UK's new humanitarian and energy funding will help strengthen Ukraine's preparedness for the fifth winter of Russia's full-scale invasion. Upon arriving in Ukraine for his first visit as foreign minister, Ed Miliband, together with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, visited the site of a recent strike in the Chernihiv region that claimed the lives of at least 22 people. There, he also announced new sanctions against Russia and GBP 6 million in funding for the investigation of war crimes.
During his meeting with President Zelenskyy, the foreign minister announced a sweeping package of sanctions against individuals and organizations that help sustain Russia's war.
The package, which targets approximately 40 entities in Russia's financial, oil, and technology sectors, is designed to disrupt Russia's supply chains and cut off its sources of funding.
"£54 million in combined energy and humanitarian funding is expected to support ordinary Ukrainians during the winter months – as Putin once again attempts to weaponize winter and plunge communities into darkness. The UK is backing Ukraine through a triangle of support – bolstering Ukraine's resilience; going after those who help to fund Russia's war machine; and shoring up NATO security and meeting threats to our national security with robust action," the statement reads.
Miliband said "Russia could end this war tomorrow. Instead we've seen escalating attacks, including on key infrastructure and Ukrainian cultural landmarks."
"My message to Putin is clear – You cannot wait us out. Until you choose the path of peace, the UK will not relent in its support for Ukraine, our values, or our national security. You will remain a pariah," he said.
Government officials said the United Kingdom has supported more than one million vulnerable civilians by providing much-needed generators and assistance in restoring damaged water and heating systems.
It is noted that the UK's current contribution includes GBP 20 million to support Ukraine's energy security: funding for teams carrying out emergency repairs to the power grid following attacks, investments in backup generators and solar energy sources for periods of outages, as well as investments in new technologies to diversify energy supplies.
The package also includes GBP 34 million to protect and support heating and water supply for Ukrainian families ahead of winter and to provide direct cash assistance in cooperation with the Ukrainian government and local partners, including UNICEF, UNHCR, and the Ukrainian Red Cross.
After his visit to Chernihiv, the Foreign Secretary returned to Kyiv and visited a hospital where Ukrainian veterans were receiving medical care. There, he announced GBP 6.3 million in support from the United Kingdom for Ukraine's domestic efforts to hold those responsible for the horrific war crimes committed during Russia's full-scale invasion accountable.
To date, the United Kingdom has provided over GBP 1 billion pounds in humanitarian and energy support to Ukraine since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion.

US suspends major IT firms from green card programme, including Microsoft, Adobe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
17:22:18 UTC
02:22:18 KST

The US government is suspending Microsoft, Adobe and several large IT firms from a programme that allows skilled foreign workers to gain permanent residency, senior US officials announced, citing alleged fraud and as part of an effort to push companies to hire more Americans.
"Our message to Microsoft is: You're a great American company, but you've got to hire great American workers," US Vice President JD Vance said on Thursday.
Secretary of Labour Keith Sonderling added that some of the largest IT firms in the world would also be suspended from that programme, including Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini.
"We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labour certification applications involving these companies," Sonderling said.
Microsoft did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Under the PERM process, employers seek certification from the Department of Labour that there is no qualified, willing or available US worker for a specific job. It's a step required before filing petitions for most employment-based green cards.
Vance also said nine universities, including Harvard, Yale and Stanford, would be investigated for allegedly bringing in international students to undercut American wages. Labour Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito said subpoenas had already been served.
"We will investigate whether foreign influence, improper financial relationships, or visa abuse are compromising federally funded research," D'Esposito said.
"If an American university is breaking the law to save $1 while exposing American research to a foreign adversary, that is not academic excellence. It's institutional betrayal."

“When partners are literally standing alongside Ukrainians, it truly matters,” he continued, thanking Miliband for standing beside him in Pryluky and alluding to Western partners who continue supplying Kyiv with funding and air defense it needs to protect itself against Russia’s aggression.
A city left without homes and shelters
The damage extends far beyond the destroyed building. According to Zelensky, more than 100 residential buildings across Pryluky were damaged, along with schools, kindergartens, shops, businesses and other critical infrastructure the city depends on.
Residents who spoke with the president described a shortage of both shelters and housing. In response, Zelensky ordered the head of the Chernihiv Regional Military Administration to quickly help those who have nowhere to live, adding that temporary assistance should eventually be followed by permanent solutions.
Trump Envoys in Talks With Putin’s Money Man Over Russian Gas, Reports Say
“It is also important that the victims ultimately receive new housing,” he said.
Those whose homes were in the destroyed building should be allowed back into their apartments once the security situation permits, Zelensky said, placing the head of the State Emergency Service (SES) in charge of the process.
Human cost of Russia’s war
Ukrainian authorities consistently remind their partners that the war is not a distant fact on paper, but a reality measured in human lives and relentless terror.
This became particularly visible in the last few weeks, as Russia increased its strikes on civilians and civilian infrastructure following the departure of senior US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner from Moscow.
The two visited Moscow on Sept. 5 to hold talks with Russian diplomats and Putin himself, aiming to broker an end to the war. For the first time ever during their tenure, the envoys also visited Kyiv just a day after.
Despite all three sides describing the negotiations as positive and productive, Russian barrage amplified.
The latest attack on Pryluky left 17 civilians hospitalized, including a five-year-old girl. It also highlighted gaps in the city’s protection.
After the health minister briefed him on efforts to build shelters in medical facilities, Zelensky ordered officials to speed up the work and secure additional funding. The hospital’s own shelter must be repaired as a priority, he said, while a new, modern one is built in its place.
Together with city authorities, the health minister and the head of the Chernihiv Regional Military Administration will be responsible for the project, Zelensky said.
He also tasked the interior ministers with inspecting every shelter in the city.
Deadliest strike in a wave of attacks
The Pryluky attack was the deadliest in a broader Russian assault launched on Wednesday, Oct. 7.
A Kh-101 cruise missile was used to strike the five-story apartment block as Russia targeted cities across Ukraine with ballistic and cruise missiles, as well as Shahed drones, before continuing with aerial bombs during the day.
As rescuers continued recovering bodies, the toll from Russia’s latest attacks kept rising. By Thursday, Zelensky said strikes on Pryluky, Kramatorsk, Kyiv and other cities had killed 78 people and injured 215 in recent days alone.
He described the attacks as a severe escalation and “terror directed against people and life,” warning that world leaders must not ignore what is happening.
EU and US support to continue
The same concerns were raised during a telephone call with European Council President António Costa later on Thursday.
Zelensky also thanked Costa for the €1.2 billion (l $1.4 billion) tranche that arrived in Ukraine on Wednesday, saying the money would go toward defense, primarily drones.
“This will provide tremendous support,” Zelensky said.
Beyond immediate military needs, the two leaders discussed the timeline for opening the next clusters in Ukraine’s EU accession talks, a winter energy package and further financial assistance. The call came ahead of the EC summit in Brussels, scheduled for Oct. 15-16.
Between Zelensky and Costa, an agreement was reached to meet in a trilateral format with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
Zelensky also briefed the EC President on meetings with US officials planned for the coming days, particularly Oct. 9-10, noting that a Ukrainian delegation is already on its way.
